rationale: Walls require a solid foundation to bear the structural load and provide a level base for construction.
Floor slabs provide the base surface upon which walls are erected, especially in multi-story construction.
Roofs rest on and are supported by the walls, so walls must be completed before roof framing and installation can begin.
Window and door frames are typically installed after the wall structure is erected and openings are formed.
Electrical wiring runs through wall cavities, so walls should be framed before electrical rough-in work begins, though some pre-wiring can occur in open stud walls.
Beams require a stable foundation to transfer loads; without completed foundations, beams cannot be safely placed.
Beams typically rest on or connect to columns, so columns must be in place to support beam ends.
Cast-in-place concrete beams require formwork to shape and support the wet concrete until it cures.
Reinforcing steel must be placed within the beam formwork before concrete is poured to ensure structural integrity.
Floor or roof slabs are typically supported by beams; beams must be in place before the slab can be formed, poured, or installed above them.
The ground must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and uneven terrain before any foundation work can begin, as the foundation requires a stable, level, and prepared subgrade.
Excavation for footings, trenches, or a basement must be completed before concrete or foundation elements can be placed, as the foundation material needs a void to be poured or installed into.
The soil must be tested for bearing capacity and properly compacted to ensure it can support the foundation loads without excessive settlement.

Underground utilities such as drainage pipes, water lines, and conduit must be laid and stubbed up before the foundation slab or footings are poured, otherwise they would have to be routed through or under the foundation later, which is structurally problematic.

The foundation must be fully cured and achieved sufficient strength before vertical structural elements (columns, walls, beams) are erected, as the superstructure depends on the foundation for load transfer and stability.
Waterproofing membranes and coatings are applied directly to the exterior of foundation walls and slabs; the foundation must be in place and cured before these protective layers can be installed.
Backfilling around foundation walls can only occur after the foundation is complete and waterproofed, as the fill material would otherwise obstruct access to the foundation.

While ideally rough-in is done before the pour, some post-pour work is possible with core drilling; however, best practice is to complete all under-slab utilities before the foundation slab is poured.
Columns require a stable load-bearing base. Foundations must be completed to provide the structural support and anchorage for columns.
Steel reinforcement must be placed and tied within the column formwork before concrete is poured to ensure structural integrity.
Formwork (molds) must be erected and secured to contain and shape the concrete pour for the column.
Columns support beams and slabs above; the vertical load path requires columns to be cured and gain sufficient strength before beams/slabs are constructed on top.
Column formwork cannot be removed until the concrete has cured to sufficient strength to be self-supporting.
The slab requires a stable, level base provided by the foundation/footings to support its load and prevent cracking or settlement.
The ground must be properly excavated, graded, and compacted before pouring the slab to ensure uniform support and proper drainage.
A vapor barrier (polyethylene sheeting) must be laid over the prepared subgrade before pouring concrete to prevent moisture migration from the ground into the slab.
Steel reinforcement must be positioned and tied in place within the formwork before concrete is poured to provide tensile strength and crack control.
Edge forms must be set up to define the slab boundaries, thickness, and elevation before concrete can be placed.
After the slab is poured and finished, it must undergo a curing period (typically 7-14 days) to achieve proper strength and durability before any loads are applied.
Walls and vertical structural elements must be built on top of the finished, cured slab as the slab provides the working platform and base support.

Any underfloor plumbing, electrical conduits, or mechanical chases that run within or below the slab must be installed prior to the pour, but above-slab rough-in work begins after the slab is complete.
The door frame requires a structural rough opening (with headers and king/jack studs) to be framed before the door can be installed.
The door must be installed and hung in place before trim and casing can be nailed around it.
Drywall must be installed and finished up to the door frame; however, the door itself must be in place to define the opening edge for drywall mudding and taping.
Door knobs, handles, locks, and hinges are attached to the installed door; the door must be hung before these components can be fitted.
The floor surface must be prepared (or at least the rough subfloor in place) so the door can be installed at the correct height with proper clearance.

The structural frame must be complete to provide the load-bearing support and attachment points for the curtain wall system. Curtain walls are non-structural cladding that attach to the building's structural frame.
Floor slabs provide lateral support and anchorage for curtain wall spans between floors. The curtain wall system typically anchors to slab edges at each floor level.
Waterproofing and sealants are applied to curtain wall joints and interfaces after installation to ensure the building envelope is watertight and air-sealed.

Interior drywall, millwork, and finishes adjacent to the curtain wall must be installed after the curtain wall is in place to create proper seals, transitions, and aesthetic integration with the glazing system.
The curtain wall framing (mullions, transoms) must be erected first to provide the structural grid into which glass panels and infill units are subsequently installed.
The structural frame must be in place to provide the load-bearing support onto which cladding panels or systems are attached.
The roof structure must be completed to provide the top anchoring point and weather seal for wall cladding systems.
A weather-resistant barrier (WRB) or air/moisture barrier must be installed on the substrate before cladding to protect the building envelope from water ingress.
Cladding systems typically incorporate flashings and openings that must be in place before windows and doors are set to ensure proper integration and weather sealing.

While not a hard physical constraint, interior finishes (e.g., drywall, plaster) are typically sequenced after cladding to avoid water damage to interior materials if the cladding is not yet weathertight.
The parapet is an upward extension of the roof edge, so the main roof deck structure must be in place to anchor and support the parapet wall.
Roof sheathing provides the underlying surface and edge support onto which the parapet can be framed and fastened.
The roof edge framing (including rafters or trusses at the perimeter) must be completed to provide a load-bearing connection point for parapet construction.
The parapet structure must be erected before waterproof flashing and coping caps can be installed to seal and protect the top of the parapet.

successor: Roof Membrane / Waterproofing at Parapet Base
rationale: Roof membrane is typically turned up the face of the parapet; the parapet must exist as a vertical surface for the membrane to adhere to and seal against.
The staircase must be supported by a stable foundation; the foundation must be completed before any structural elements like staircases are installed.
The main structural framing (columns, beams, slabs) must be in place to provide support and connection points for the staircase installation.
Staircases connect different floor levels; the floor slabs at each level must be cast and cured to provide landing points for the staircase.

While some MEP work can proceed in parallel, rough-in for services that pass through or adjacent to the stairwell (e.g., electrical conduits, plumbing) is often sequenced after the staircase structure is in place to avoid rework.
Plastering, painting, tiling, and handrail installation on and around the staircase must be done after the staircase structure is complete and stable.
The ground must be properly graded, compacted, and excavated to the correct slope and elevation before a ramp can be installed or poured.
A stable sub-base (e.g., gravel base or concrete footing) must be in place to support the ramp structure and prevent settling or cracking.
Any underground utilities such as drainage pipes, electrical conduits, or water lines that would run under the ramp area must be installed before the ramp is built to avoid future demolition.
The structural ramp (e.g., poured concrete or framed wood/metal) must be fully set and cured before applying the final surface finish, anti-slip coating, or wearing surface.
Safety railings and handrails are typically installed after the ramp structure is complete so they can be anchored securely to the ramp.
Excavation must be completed to create the open space in the ground where the lift shaft foundation and structure will be built.
The building foundations (including lift pit base) must be constructed first to provide a stable load-bearing base for the lift shaft structure.
The slab at the lowest level must be cast to provide the base support and working platform for constructing the lift shaft walls.
The lift shaft is often constructed ahead of or integrally with the main structural frame to serve as a vertical core providing lateral stability to the building.
The lift shaft structure (walls and brackets) must be fully completed and cured before the lift guide rails can be installed inside the shaft.
The shaft must be fully enclosed and structurally complete before any lift car equipment can be installed within it.
The lift shaft pit area must be constructed before waterproofing membranes can be applied to prevent groundwater ingress.

successor: MEP Rough-In (Electrical conduits for lift controls)
rationale: The lift shaft walls and pit must be in place before electrical conduits, lighting, and control wiring can be run within the shaft.
The construction area must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and topsoil before any excavation or wall construction can begin to provide a clean working surface and access.
Rough grading and earthwork must be completed to establish the correct subgrade elevations and slopes before retaining wall construction can proceed.
Soil bearing capacity, groundwater conditions, and other geotechnical parameters must be assessed to properly design the wall foundation and drainage system before construction begins.
Any existing underground or overhead utilities within the wall footprint must be relocated or protected prior to excavation for the retaining wall foundation.
The retaining wall structure (including any required drainage systems) must be fully constructed and cured before granular backfill can be placed behind the wall to avoid damaging the uncured wall.
Waterproofing membrane or coating application must occur after the wall is complete and cured to protect it from moisture ingress.

successor: Final Grading and Landscaping Adjacent to Wall
rationale: Final grading, topsoil placement, and landscaping adjacent to the retaining wall is typically performed after wall construction, though this is a logical sequence preference rather than a physical necessity.

Weep holes, drainage aggregate, and perforated drain pipes are typically installed concurrently with or immediately after the retaining wall structure but before backfill, requiring the wall to be in place first.
The ground must be cleared of debris, vegetation, and existing structures before pile installation can begin to ensure unobstructed access and a safe working area.
Soil bearing capacity, ground composition, and groundwater conditions must be determined to select the appropriate pile type, length, and installation method.
The exact locations of piles must be marked on site based on structural drawings to ensure piles are installed at the correct positions and alignment.
Pile caps are cast over the tops of piles to distribute loads; the piles must be installed and cured first before the cap concrete can be placed.
Ground beams spanning between pile caps rely on the piles for support; therefore piles must be completed before beam formwork and reinforcement can be placed.
Pile caps are structural elements that transfer loads from columns/walls to piles. Piles must be installed first to provide the foundation support that the pile cap sits on and connects together.
The ground must be excavated down to the design level (pile cut-off level) to expose the pile heads and provide a working platform for constructing the pile cap.
Pile heads must be trimmed to the correct level and the reinforcement exposed to ensure proper bonding and load transfer between the piles and the pile cap.
Freshly poured concrete requires sufficient curing time to gain strength before any subsequent loading or construction activities can proceed on top of the pile cap.
Columns and structural walls rise from the pile cap, which serves as their foundation. The pile cap must be completed and cured to provide a solid base for constructing vertical structural elements.

The ground beam is a reinforced concrete element that rests on foundation piles or footings, so the site must be cleared and excavated to the required formation level before any ground beam construction can commence.
Ground beams typically span between pile caps or foundation columns, so the pile caps must be completed and cured to provide bearing support for the ground beam.
A layer of lean concrete (blinding) is required beneath the ground beam to provide a clean, level working surface and prevent contamination of the reinforcement from soil.
Backfilling around and above the ground beam can only occur after the concrete has achieved sufficient strength (typically 7-14 days curing) to withstand the lateral earth pressures and loading.
The ground beam forms part of the substructure foundation system; columns and upper structure must be built on top of the completed and cured ground beam as it transfers loads to the foundation.

predecessor: Column and Wall Construction below Transfer Slab
rationale: Transfer slabs distribute loads from upper structures to vertical supporting elements below. Columns and walls that support the transfer slab must be constructed first to provide the necessary structural support and load-bearing capacity.

predecessor: Formwork and Falsework Installation for Transfer Slab
rationale: Formwork and falsework must be erected to create the mold and temporary support system for casting the transfer slab.

predecessor: Reinforcement Steel Placement for Transfer Slab
rationale: Rebar and reinforcement cages must be placed within the formwork before concrete is poured to provide tensile strength and structural integrity.

successor: Upper Floor Column/Wall Construction Above Transfer Slab
rationale: The transfer slab must be completed and cured to provide a stable base for constructing vertical elements of upper floors, as the transfer slab is designed to carry and redistribute loads from above.

successor: Transfer Slab Curing and Striking of Formwork
rationale: After the transfer slab concrete is poured, adequate curing time is required before formwork and falsework can be safely removed to prevent structural failure.
Shear walls require a solid foundation to transfer lateral loads to the ground; without foundation, the wall has no base support.
Reinforcement steel must be placed and tied before concrete is poured to form the shear wall.
Formwork must be erected to contain and shape the concrete before pouring the shear wall.
Shear walls provide lateral stability and support for floor slabs above; slabs typically bear on or connect to completed shear walls.

Waterproofing is often applied to the exterior face of shear walls below grade; it can be done after the wall is cured but is a preference rather than a physical impossibility to reorder in some cases.
Excavation must be completed before core wall construction begins to expose the foundation area and allow for proper footing installation.
Core walls require a stable foundation or footings to transfer vertical loads to the ground; the footings must be poured and cured before core wall construction.
Core walls provide vertical structural support and lateral stability; floor slabs often bear on or connect to the core walls, so core walls must be in place first.
Core walls enclose elevator shafts; elevator rails and guide systems are mounted directly to the core wall structure, so walls must be complete before installation.
Staircases within the core rely on the core walls for support and enclosure; the walls must be erected before stairs can be installed.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing risers run vertically through the core; core walls and shafts must be complete before running MEP lines through them.
Soffit is attached to the underside of roof eaves; roof framing must be complete to provide the structural support and nailing surface for soffit installation.
Soffit typically abuts exterior walls; wall sheathing must be in place to define the wall plane and provide a backing for soffit trim and attachment.
Fascia is installed along the edge of the roof, often overlapping or abutting the soffit; soffit must be in place to establish the proper alignment and finish transition for fascia boards.
Gutters are mounted on or against the fascia, which sits atop the soffit; soffit completion ensures the eave area is fully enclosed and ready for gutter attachment and water drainage systems.
While soffit is often pre-finished, any final painting or caulking of eave areas and trim should occur after soffit is installed to ensure seamless color matching and sealant application.
The foundation must be completed to provide structural support for the building before any balcony can be installed.
The main structural frame of the building must be erected to provide the load-bearing support onto which the balcony structure will be attached or cantilevered.
The floor slab at the balcony level must be poured/cast to provide the base deck for the balcony structure.
The balcony structure itself must be in place before railings or guardrails can be installed onto it for safety.
The balcony structural slab must be completed before applying waterproofing membranes and surface finishes such as tiles or decking.
The structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) must be in place to provide the supporting structure onto which facade panels are attached.
Waterproofing layers behind the facade must be completed before closing the exterior with facade panels to ensure weather tightness.
Insulation materials placed behind the facade must be installed before the facade panels are fixed, as the panels enclose and protect the insulation layer.
Facade panels define the exterior wall openings; windows and doors are then installed into those prepared openings for proper fit and sealing.

While interior work can partially begin in other areas, completing the facade panel enclosure protects interior spaces from weather, enabling sensitive finishing works like drywall, painting, and flooring without weather damage risk.

The roof drainage system (gutters, downspouts, drains, and scuppers) must be installed after the roof deck and structural framing are in place, as they need a solid substrate for attachment and proper drainage slope.
A waterproof membrane or underlayment is installed before drainage components to ensure the roof deck is sealed; roof drains are then flashed into this membrane to prevent leaks.
Finished roofing materials (shingles, tiles, metal panels) are installed after the drainage components are in place, allowing the roofing to be properly lapped over flashings and drip edges.

Soft preference: exterior wall finishes should ideally be installed after downspouts are in place so that downspout brackets can be integrated cleanly, but cladding can be installed first with brackets added later.

Downspout extensions and drainage outlets must direct water away from the foundation; final grading and landscaping should be completed after the drainage system is fully connected to ensure proper water flow and prevent pooling.
Expansion joints are typically placed where structural elements meet or where slabs are poured; the foundation or slab must be prepared before expansion joint installation can begin.

In building structures, expansion joints are often installed between structural frames or at column lines; the structural frame must be erected first to define the locations requiring expansion joints.
Expansion joints must be in place before final concrete pouring or floor finishing to ensure the joint is properly embedded and functional for accommodating thermal movement.
Exterior wall expansion joints need to be installed before cladding or masonry is completed to allow proper sealing and movement accommodation at joint locations.
Expansion joints, especially in roofs and decks, must be installed and sealed before waterproofing membranes are applied to ensure continuity and leak prevention.
Waterproofing must be applied onto a clean, smooth, and properly cured concrete slab or substrate to ensure proper adhesion and effectiveness of the membrane.
Concrete must be fully cured (typically 7–28 days) before applying waterproofing to prevent entrapped moisture causing delamination or blistering of the membrane.
The substrate must be cleaned of dust, dirt, oils, and debris, and primed if required, to ensure the waterproofing membrane bonds properly.
A protective screed or cover slab is poured over the cured waterproofing membrane to protect it from physical damage during subsequent construction activities and UV exposure.
Floor finishes such as tiles cannot be installed until the waterproofing membrane is fully cured and tested, as the membrane must form a continuous watertight layer beneath the finish.
The foundation must be completed and cured to provide a stable base for formwork installation, as formwork is typically placed on top of the foundation to shape concrete elements.

Rebar installation must be completed before formwork is placed, as the reinforcement cage needs to be positioned and tied in place before the formwork encloses it; formwork cannot be installed around rebar effectively after the fact.
The ground or working surface must be properly graded, leveled, and compacted before formwork can be set up to ensure correct alignment and stability of the forms.
Concrete cannot be poured until the formwork is fully installed, aligned, braced, and secured, as the forms shape and retain the wet concrete until it cures.

After formwork is installed, an inspection of the reinforcement and formwork assembly must be conducted before concrete placement to verify rebar cover, spacing, and form stability, ensuring compliance with structural drawings and safety standards.
Concrete must be poured and allowed to achieve sufficient strength before formwork can be removed, as the formwork supports the wet concrete until it can self-support.

Concrete needs adequate curing time to develop the required structural strength (typically 1-7 days depending on mix and conditions) before formwork can be safely stripped without damaging the concrete.
Formwork must first be installed, aligned, and secured before it can later be removed after concrete has been placed and cured.
After formwork removal, exposed concrete surfaces may require patching of bolt holes, filling of surface defects, or rubbing/finishing work to achieve the specified surface appearance.
For foundation walls and retaining walls, formwork must be removed before waterproofing membranes can be applied and before backfill operations can commence against the finished wall surface.

Steel reinforcement must be positioned and tied within the formwork before concrete is poured to provide structural tensile strength; pouring concrete first would make reinforcement placement impossible.
The ground must be excavated, leveled, and compacted to provide a stable foundation before any concrete can be placed.
Concrete must be poured before the curing process can begin; curing is the time-dependent hydration process that follows immediately after placement.
Formwork cannot be removed until the poured concrete has gained sufficient strength to support itself; removing formwork before concrete is poured is physically impossible.
Concrete must be poured and placed into forms before curing can begin, as curing is the process of maintaining moisture and temperature conditions to allow hydration of cement after placement.
Surface finishing operations like screeding and floating must be completed before curing starts, as curing should begin only after final finishing is done to avoid disturbing the surface.
Formwork should not be removed until concrete has gained sufficient strength through curing to support its own weight and any imposed loads.
Curing must be completed before applying coatings, sealants, or waterproofing membranes, as these would trap moisture or prevent proper hydration if applied prematurely.
Construction loads, equipment, or subsequent structural elements should not be placed on concrete until sufficient curing time has elapsed to achieve the required strength.
All rough-in work for electrical wiring, plumbing pipes, and HVAC ductwork must be completed and inspected before walls are closed up with finishing materials like drywall, plaster, or paneling.
Insulation must be placed within wall and ceiling cavities before they can be covered by final finishing surfaces such as drywall or ceiling tiles.
The structural framing of walls, floors, and ceilings must be complete to provide a substrate for finishing materials to be attached.
After all finishing work (painting, flooring, trim, fixtures) is complete, the final inspection and system commissioning can proceed to verify the building is ready for occupancy.
All finishing work must be fully completed before a building can be legally occupied or furnished for use, as unfinished surfaces and trim pose safety and hygiene risks.
Structural framing must be complete to provide the supporting framework for glazing installation.
Window and door openings must be framed and prepared before glazing units can be installed.
Weather barriers and waterproofing around openings must be in place before glazing to prevent moisture intrusion.
Interior finishes such as drywall, trim, and painting should follow glazing to avoid damage to finishes during glass installation.
Air sealing and building pressurization tests require installed glazing to achieve proper building envelope performance.
Drywall must be installed and finished before painting can begin, as paint adheres to the finished drywall surface.
Taping and mudding (finishing) of drywall joints and screw holes must be completed and sanded smooth before painting to ensure a proper surface.
Primer must be applied to bare drywall, wood, or other surfaces before the final paint coat to ensure adhesion, coverage, and uniformity.
Typically painting is done before flooring installation to avoid drips on finished floors and to allow easier touch-ups, though it is a soft preference rather than a physical necessity.

successor: Trim and Cabinet Installation (if painting walls/ceilings)
rationale: Painting walls and ceilings before installing trim and cabinets is preferred to avoid masking and cutting in around installed elements, but it's a sequencing preference not a hard constraint.
All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) systems must be fully installed before they can be tested and commissioned to ensure they operate correctly.
Fire protection systems such as sprinklers, alarms, and detectors need to be installed before commissioning can verify their functionality and compliance.
All electrical wiring, panels, and connections must be in place before electrical testing and commissioning can proceed.
Plumbing pipes, fixtures, and drainage systems must be installed before pressure testing and commissioning of plumbing systems.
HVAC units, ductwork, and controls must be fully installed before the system can be tested for airflow, temperature control, and efficiency.
While some finishing can proceed in parallel, final finishes such as ceiling tiles and wall coverings are preferably completed after commissioning to allow access for system adjustments and repairs.
The building or facility must be fully tested and commissioned to verify all systems operate correctly before it can be handed over to the client and occupied.
Testing and commissioning results provide the evidence needed for regulatory inspections and certification of building systems.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and existing structures before excavation can begin to ensure unobstructed access and a clean working area.
Boundaries, building footprints, and utility locations must be marked by a surveyor so that excavation proceeds in the correct location and depth.
All underground utilities (gas, water, electric, telecom) must be identified and marked to avoid accidental strikes during excavation.
The excavated trench or pit provides the space needed to pour footings and foundation walls; foundation work cannot begin until earth has been removed.
After excavation reaches depth, shoring systems (e.g., soldier piles, lagging) and dewatering pumps must be installed to keep the excavation safe and dry for subsequent work.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and existing structures to provide unobstructed access for piling equipment and to accurately mark pile positions.
Accurate survey and setting out of pile positions is required before piling begins to ensure piles are installed in the correct locations as per structural drawings.
Soil investigation must be completed to determine ground conditions, bearing capacity, and pile design requirements before piling operations commence.
Pile caps are constructed on top of completed piles to distribute structural loads; piles must be installed and cured first.
Pile integrity testing (e.g., low strain or sonic logging) must be performed after piles are installed to verify their soundness before proceeding with further works.
Ground beams and foundation slabs connect pile caps and transfer loads; they can only be constructed after piles and pile caps are complete.
After pile installation, excavated areas around piles can be backfilled and compacted to restore ground level, though this may be done concurrently in some sequences.
Formwork must be installed and erected first to provide the mold and support structure into which reinforcement bars are placed and tied.
Reinforcement bars must be cut, bent, and shaped to the required specifications before they can be placed, positioned, and tied in the formwork.
Reinforcement must be fully placed, tied, and inspected before concrete is poured, so that the steel is properly embedded within the concrete to achieve structural composite action.
Reinforcement fixing must be completed before inspection can be carried out to verify bar spacing, cover, tying, and compliance with structural drawings.

Cover blocks are typically placed concurrently or after reinforcement fixing to maintain concrete cover, but may also be placed during fixing; this is a soft preference as sequencing can vary by method.
Masonry walls and structures require a stable, level foundation to bear the load. Without completed foundations, masonry construction cannot proceed as there is no base to build upon.
Masonry work often begins from a concrete floor slab or base. The slab must be cured and ready before masonry units can be laid.
The building site must be cleared, excavated, and graded before any structural work including masonry can commence.
Roof structure typically rests on masonry walls. Load-bearing masonry walls must be completed and cured before roof framing can be installed.

While some rough-ins can be done before masonry, much of the in-wall electrical and plumbing work in masonry walls must wait until after the masonry is complete, as chasing or embedding services into masonry is done after wall construction.
Structural steel requires stable foundation supports (footings, piers, or pile caps) to bear the loads of the steel frame. Without completed foundations, steel columns have no base to anchor to.

Anchor bolts must be accurately set and aligned in the foundation to receive the base plates of steel columns. Steel erection cannot proceed until bolts are placed, surveyed for position/tolerance, and concrete has cured sufficiently to hold the bolts.
Foundation concrete must reach adequate compressive strength before steel loads can be applied. Erection forces (cranes, steel weight) would otherwise damage uncured concrete.
While not strictly mandatory, proper site grading and drainage around the building footprint allows crane access, laydown areas, and prevents mud/water issues during the steel erection process.

Roof decking, metal panels, and cladding are attached directly to the steel frame. The structural steel frame must be erected and stabilized before any roof or wall enclosure systems can be installed.

successor: Steel Deck and Concrete Slab Pour
rationale: Composite steel deck spans between steel beams and serves as formwork for the concrete floor slab. The steel frame must be in place before the metal deck can be laid and concrete poured.
Structural steel members must be erected and connected before fireproofing material (e.g., spray-applied fire-resistive material) can be applied to the steel.
Overhead mechanical, electrical, and plumbing runs (conduit, ductwork, piping) are often supported by or hung from the steel frame, so the frame must be erected first to provide support points.

The erection crane(s) may be needed for placing heavy steel members; once steel erection is complete, the crane can be dismantled and removed from site. This is a soft preference if there are no other heavy lifts requiring the crane.
The roof structure requires the building frame (walls, columns, beams) to be erected to provide support and attachment points for roof trusses, decking, and roofing materials.
Roof sheathing or decking (e.g., plywood or OSB) must be installed over the roof trusses/rafters to create a solid substrate before applying underlayment and roofing finishes.
Underlayment (felt, synthetic membrane) must be laid down over the sheathing as a moisture barrier before the final roofing material (shingles, tiles, metal panels) is installed.

Soft preference: While not physically required, roofing is typically completed before siding to allow the roof to protect the building interior and to simplify flashing integration at wall-roof intersections.
The building must be weathertight (roof completed) before interior work such as drywall, insulation, painting, and flooring begins to prevent water damage to finished materials.
The structural frame (steel or concrete) must be fully erected and stable to provide the supporting framework onto which cladding panels or curtain walls are attached.
The roof structure must be in place (or at least the roof steel) to provide top lateral support and weather protection during cladding work; cladding often connects to roof perimeter details.
Floor slabs at each level must be cast and cured to provide working platforms and anchorage points for cladding support brackets and fixing channels.
Windows and glazed units are typically integrated into the cladding system or installed after the main cladding framework is in place to ensure proper sealing and weatherproofing of openings.

While internal finishes can begin after cladding is installed to avoid weather damage, this is a soft preference rather than a hard physical constraint since temporary weather protection could allow some parallel work.
The structural frame must be in place to provide support and enclosure for mechanical systems, including ductwork, piping, and equipment mounting.
Roof must be installed to protect mechanical equipment and ductwork from weather damage during installation, and to allow for rooftop mechanical units to be placed.
Mechanical ductwork, pipes, and conduits must be installed within wall and ceiling cavities before they can be enclosed by linings and finishes.

While mechanical and electrical installations often occur in parallel, mechanical ductwork is typically roughed in before electrical wiring to avoid conflicts in overhead spaces, though this can be sequenced flexibly.
Mechanical ducts, diffusers, and grilles must be installed and tested before ceilings are closed up, as access to overhead mechanical systems is required.

Electrical conduits, cabling, and boxes must be routed through structural elements (walls, slabs, columns). Structural framing must be complete to provide the substrate for electrical rough-in and to avoid rework or damage to installed electrical components.
Weather-tight enclosure is required before installing electrical panels, sensitive equipment, and wiring to prevent water damage, short circuits, and safety hazards.
Electrical wiring, outlet boxes, and switch boxes must be installed, inspected, and approved before interior walls can be closed with drywall sheeting.
All electrical components must be physically installed before energizing the system and performing functional tests, continuity checks, and commissioning procedures.
Electrical cables, conduits, and light fixture mounting must be completed before ceiling grids or panels are installed to allow access for connections and inspection.
Plastering is applied onto brick or block walls to provide a smooth finish. Brickwork must be completed and cured sufficiently to provide a stable substrate for plaster application.

Electrical conduits, cables, and back boxes must be installed within walls before plastering, as plaster covers and embeds these elements. Retrofitting after plastering would require cutting into finished surfaces.
Water supply pipes and drainage pipework embedded in walls must be installed and pressure-tested before plastering covers them.
Plaster must be fully dry and cured before paint or wallpaper can be applied. Painting wet plaster causes adhesion failure and surface defects.
Sockets, switches, and faceplates are mounted onto finished plastered walls. The plaster provides the final flush surface for these fittings.
Screed is typically laid over underfloor heating pipes or cables to encase and protect them; the heating system must be installed first.
The base subfloor must be clean, level, and sound before screed can be applied to ensure proper adhesion and a uniform finish.
A damp proof membrane is often required beneath screed to prevent moisture ingress from the subfloor; it must be laid before screeding.

successor: Floor Covering Installation (e.g., tiles, wood, vinyl)
rationale: Screed provides a smooth, level base for final floor finishes; the screed must be cured and dry before any floor covering is installed.

successor: Floor Grinding / Polishing (if exposed screed finish)
rationale: If screed is to be the finished surface, grinding and polishing can only commence after the screed has fully cured.
The foundation trenches must be excavated and prepared to the correct level so that the damp-proof course (DPC) can be laid at the required height above ground level.
The concrete foundation (strip footing or raft) must be poured and sufficiently cured to provide a stable, level base upon which the DPC can be installed.
Wall construction above the DPC level cannot commence until the DPC membrane or course is fully laid, as the DPC must be continuous within the mortar joint to prevent rising damp.
The DPC must be installed prior to casting the ground floor slab to ensure the damp-proof membrane (DPM) ties into the DPC, creating a continuous moisture barrier.
While backfilling can technically occur after the DPC is installed, it is a soft preference because the DPC should be protected and visible for inspection before earth is placed against the wall.
The site must be cleared of obstacles, vegetation, and existing structures before surveying can accurately establish reference points and boundaries.

predecessor: Site Access and Temporary Facilities Setup
rationale: Surveyors need access to the site and a base area to store instruments and set up temporary control points before commencing survey work.
Surveying and setting out establishes the exact positions, levels, and boundaries that guide excavation; digging cannot begin without these reference markers.
Foundation positions must be precisely set out on the ground before any foundation excavation or concreting can proceed.
Underground utility routes and locations need to be marked out before trenching and pipe-laying can commence.
The substrate must be cleaned, dry, and free of debris/contaminants before jointing and sealing can be applied, otherwise sealant will not adhere properly.
The tiles, pavers, or cladding panels must be fully installed and set before jointing (grouting) and sealing can be performed, as the joints are between these installed units.
Any underlying waterproofing membranes must be in place before sealing joints to ensure the waterproofing system is continuous and effective.
Final surface finishes, coatings, or topcoats are applied after jointing and sealing are complete to avoid contaminating or damaging the sealant and to ensure a uniform finish.
Once jointing and sealing is complete, a final quality check or snagging inspection typically follows to verify sealant application, uniformity, and adhesion before handover.

Backfilling occurs after foundation construction because the foundation walls and footings must be in place and cured before soil can be placed against them; backfill supports and protects the foundation structure.
All underground utilities (drainage, plumbing, electrical conduits) must be installed and inspected before backfilling, as covering them with soil would prevent access for installation or correction.

Waterproofing membranes and damp-proofing coatings must be applied to foundation walls before backfilling to protect the structure from moisture; backfilling without waterproofing would trap moisture against the foundation.

Final grading and landscaping can only begin after backfilling is complete because backfilling establishes the base grade levels and soil contours needed for topsoil placement, seeding, sodding, or paving.

successor: Slab on Grade / Floor Slab Construction
rationale: Interior floor slabs or slabs on grade are poured after backfilling because backfill provides the compacted sub-base and proper drainage plane beneath the slab, and backfilling must be done before slab forms are placed.
The lift shaft and supporting structural elements must be fully constructed to provide the physical enclosure and support for lift installation.
The lift shaft must be waterproofed to prevent water ingress that could damage lift equipment during and after installation.
Lift equipment must be physically installed before electricians can connect permanent power supply to the lift control panels and machinery.
The lift must be fully installed before any testing, load testing, safety checks, and commissioning procedures can be carried out.

It is preferable to complete lift installation before finishing lobby walls, ceilings, and flooring to avoid damage to finished surfaces during heavy equipment movements, though not physically mandatory.
Structural framing (steel beams, joists, or trusses) must be erected before the roof deck can be installed, as the deck is laid on and supported by the structural frame.
The roof deck surface must be fully installed to provide a substrate for the roof membrane and waterproofing layers.
Roof insulation is typically placed on top of the roof deck; therefore the deck must be complete before insulation can be applied.
Roof drains, scuppers, and gutters are installed after the deck is in place to ensure proper integration with the deck surface.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems that serve rooftop units cannot be roughed-in on the roof until the deck provides the structural platform and safe working surface.
Roof rafters are typically installed on top of or between roof trusses, which form the primary structural framework for the roof.
Roof rafters bear on and are fastened to the top plates of the walls, so walls and their top plates must be in place before rafters can be installed.
This order seems reversed - actually roof sheathing is installed AFTER rafters. Let me correct this.
Roof decking (plywood/OSB) is fastened directly to the rafters, so rafters must be in place before sheathing can be installed.
Roof underlayment (felt paper or synthetic) is installed over the roof sheathing, which itself is installed on top of rafters.

The ridge beam is typically installed at the peak of the roof where opposing rafters or trusses meet. Therefore, the roof trusses or rafters must be erected first to provide support and define the position for the ridge beam.

Roof decking (such as plywood or OSB) is laid over the rafters/trusses and ridge beam. The ridge beam forms the structural apex that helps support the roof sheathing, so it must be in place before decking can be installed.

predecessor: Complete Wall Framing and Top Plate
rationale: The ridge beam often bears on the top plates of the end walls or on structural columns. Wall framing must be complete to provide the bearing support for the ridge beam.
Roof insulation is applied after the structural roof elements (including ridge beam and decking) are in place, as the insulation sits between or under the rafters and above the ceiling.

successor: Install Ridge Vent / Ridge Cap Shingles
rationale: Ridge vents and ridge cap shingles are installed along the peak of the roof, directly on top of or adjacent to the ridge beam area, and thus require the ridge beam to be in place first.
Eaves are typically mounted on or supported by the exterior walls; walls must be erected to provide a structural base for the eave assembly.
Eaves extend from the roof edges and are part of the roof system; roof framing (rafters or trusses) must be in place to support the eave overhang and soffit.
Soffits are the underside of the eave overhang; they are installed after the eave structure (fascia, subfascia, and lookout blocks) is in place.
Fascia is the vertical finishing edge along the eave; it is attached directly to the eave structure (rafter tails or lookout blocks) after the eave framework is complete.

Gutters are typically mounted onto the fascia board at the eave line; while physically dependent on the eave being present, scheduling is a soft preference since temporary gutter attachments could theoretically be retrofitted.
Fascia boards are fixed directly to the ends of roof trusses or rafters, so the roof framing must be in place first to provide the structural attachment surface.
Roof decking provides the backing and establishes the roof edge profile that the fascia board covers and seals.
Gutters are mounted directly onto or against the fascia board, so the fascia must be installed first to provide the mounting surface and support.
Soffit panels typically fit up against the underside of the fascia board, requiring the fascia to be in place as a guide and attachment point.

While painting can be done after installation, it is a soft preference to paint or pre-finish fascia boards before installation for better coverage and efficiency, but painting could also be done later.
Flashing is installed over sheathing to provide a weather-resistant barrier; sheathing must be in place first to provide a structural base.
Flashing around windows and doors requires the rough openings to be framed so that flashing can be properly integrated.
Flashing directs water away from vulnerable joints; siding is installed over and around flashing to complete the exterior cladding system.
Flashing must be installed before windows and doors are placed so that the pan flashing and other waterproofing layers sit behind and beneath the units.
Roof flashing (e.g., step flashing, valley flashing) is installed on top of or integrated with roof decking, which must be in place first.
The parapet wall is constructed on top of and along the edge of the roof slab; the roof slab must be in place to provide the structural base for the parapet wall.

The primary structural frame (columns, beams) provides the overall building skeleton; parapet walls are non-structural infill at the roof perimeter and require the main frame to be complete for support and alignment.

Parapet walls define the roof edge and provide a upstand for the waterproofing membrane to be lapped up and sealed; the parapet must be in place before the waterproofing can be properly terminated at the perimeter.
Coping (cap/covers) is placed on top of the parapet wall to protect it from water ingress; the parapet wall must be fully constructed and cured before coping is installed.

successor: Exterior Cladding or Plastering at Roof Level
rationale: Any external finish, cladding or plaster on the parapet wall requires the parapet substrate to be complete; finishing works logically follow the structural/backing wall construction.
The structural framing must be completed to provide the support structure for the skylight
The roof deck must be in place to provide the substrate into which the skylight is installed

Waterproofing membrane is typically integrated with the skylight curbing; skylight installation may occur after or concurrently with membrane work, but in many sequences the membrane is prepared first
Skylight must be installed before interior finishes are applied to avoid damage to finished surfaces and to allow proper daylighting integration
Final roofing and flashing details around the skylight curb can only be completed after the skylight unit is set in place
The roof window requires the load-bearing roof structure (rafters, trusses) to be in place to provide support and an opening into which the window can be installed.
The roof decking forms the continuous surface around the rough opening; the roof window is mounted onto or into this decked surface.
Flashing must be applied after the window is set in place to seal the gap between the window frame and the roof deck, preventing water intrusion.
Roofing materials are laid up to and over the window flashing after the window and its flashing are installed, ensuring a continuous weatherproof membrane.

Interior drywall and trim work around the roof window shaft can be completed after the window is installed, but this is a soft preference as interior work could theoretically proceed in parallel if the opening is protected.
The roof hatch must be installed on a completed structural steel frame that supports the roof deck, providing the necessary structural support.
The roof deck provides the surface and opening into which the roof hatch is mounted; the hatch cannot be installed without the deck in place.
Flashing around the roof hatch must be applied after the hatch is installed to create a watertight seal and prevent leaks.
Insulation around the roof hatch perimeter is typically installed after the hatch is in place to ensure proper fit and thermal continuity.
Final roofing membranes and finishes are applied after the hatch and its flashing are installed to maintain a continuous weatherproof surface.
The dormer is a roof projection that must be built on top of the main roof structure; the main roof framing must be complete to support the dormer.
Roof sheathing provides the base surface onto which the dormer is installed and integrated.
After the dormer structure is erected, its roofing material and waterproof flashing must be applied to seal the junction with the main roof.
The dormer frame must be built before the window can be fitted into the dormer opening.
Interior drywall, insulation, and trim work within the dormer space typically follow the structural installation, though minor overlap may be possible with careful sequencing.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and compacted before the valley component can be installed to ensure a stable foundation.
The concrete foundation must be poured and cured to provide a solid base for the valley structure.
The valley component serves as a load-bearing element; structural framing relies on it for support and alignment.
The valley channels water flow; drainage systems must be installed after the valley to properly connect and route water away.
The valley defines the roof intersection line; roofing materials are laid over and around the valley for waterproofing and aesthetic finish.
The hip component requires a stable foundation to bear its load; foundation preparation provides the necessary structural base.
The hip connects to and is supported by wall framing, so walls must be framed first.
The hip is a structural ridge/rafter element that must be in place before roof sheathing can be attached to it.
The hip serves as a primary structural member that supports connecting roof trusses or rafters.
Weatherproofing is applied over the hip and roof structure, requiring the hip to be installed first.
Gutters are attached to the roof edge/fascia, which requires the roof sheathing to be in place to provide structural support and proper alignment for water drainage.

Roof underlayment (e.g., felt paper or synthetic membrane) must be installed before gutters to ensure proper water shedding and to protect the roof deck from moisture before gutter system directs water away.
Downspouts connect directly to gutters at designated outlet points; gutters must be in place to establish the correct locations and connections for downspout attachment.

While soffits can technically be installed before gutters, it is often preferred to install gutters first to avoid damaging newly installed soffit material during gutter work, though this is a practical preference rather than a physical necessity.
Downpipes must be attached to the roof drainage system, which requires the roof structure to be in place first.
Downpipes connect directly to gutters to channel water from the roof; gutters must be installed before downpipes can be attached.
Downpipes must be in place to connect to underground drainage systems for water runoff.
While downpipes are typically installed before final wall finishes to allow for integration, it is a soft preference as it can sometimes be done afterward with careful fitting.
Downpipes should be installed before final landscaping to ensure proper drainage routing, but this is a soft preference as adjustments can be made later.
Roof requires load-bearing walls to be complete to provide structural support and attachment points.
The structural frame (columns, beams) must be erected to support the roof structure.
Roof must be completed to create a watertight enclosure before interior work begins to protect materials from weather.
While electrical work can technically proceed in parallel, completing the roof first avoids weather damage to exposed wiring and provides a safer, dry working environment.
Roof completion is preferred before plumbing rough-in to protect pipes and fittings from rain and debris, though not a strict structural requirement.
The structural frame, including roof slabs and decks, must be fully completed and cured to provide a stable substrate for waterproofing application.
The roof deck must be cleaned, leveled, and any penetrations or protrusions installed before waterproofing membrane can be applied.
The concrete roof slab must be fully cured to avoid moisture entrapment and ensure proper adhesion of the waterproofing membrane.
Waterproofing membrane must be installed first to create a watertight barrier before placing insulation layers on top.
Roof drains and drainage components are typically installed after waterproofing to ensure proper integration and sealing around drain openings.

The roof structure (trusses, rafters, and decking/sheathing) must be fully erected and secured to provide the underlying support base for roof tiles and cladding. Tiling cannot begin without this structural substrate.

A waterproof underlayment (roofing felt or synthetic membrane) must be laid over the roof deck before tiles are installed to provide a secondary weatherproof barrier and prevent water ingress during and after installation.

While not strictly required for structural integrity, installing fascia, soffits, and gutters before tiling provides finished edges that guide tile overhang and prevents the need for scaffolding rework, improving quality and efficiency.

If roof-mounted solar panels or electrical conduits are planned, they are typically installed after tiling is complete to avoid damaging the finished roof surface and to integrate properly with the tiles.

The roof must be watertight before interior attic insulation and ceiling finishes are installed to protect these materials from weather damage and to ensure a dry working environment inside the building.
Structural framing must be complete to provide the substrate and support for the roof system before it can be inspected.
The roof deck (typically plywood or metal decking) must be installed as the base layer before the overall roof assembly can be inspected.
The waterproof underlayment (e.g., felt paper or synthetic liner) must be in place before the roof inspection can verify proper layering and moisture protection.
The roof inspection must be passed to ensure the substrate and underlayment are acceptable before the final roofing material (shingles, membrane, etc.) is permanently installed.
While gutters are often installed after roofing is complete, this is a soft preference based on workflow efficiency rather than a strict physical requirement.
Walls must be erected to provide vertical support and a bearing surface for the flat roof structure.
The roof deck (substrate) must be installed prior to applying the flat roof membrane and waterproofing layers.
Roof drains, scuppers, and gutters are installed after the roof membrane to ensure proper integration and waterproofing at penetration points.
Insulation and cover boards are placed on top of the completed roof membrane or as part of the built-up system after the structural deck is in place.
While interior ceilings can begin after the roof is closed in to protect from weather, this is a soft preference rather than a strict physical constraint.
The pitched roof must rest on and be supported by load-bearing walls; walls must be constructed to provide structural support for the roof.
The roof trusses or rafters are the primary structural framework of the pitched roof and must be fabricated or assembled before they can be installed as part of the roof structure.
Wall plates are fixed to the top of walls to provide a bearing surface for roof trusses or rafters; they must be installed before the roof structure is erected.
The structural framework of the pitched roof (rafters/trusses and roof decking/sarking) must be complete before roof tiles, shingles, or other weatherproof covering can be applied.

While gutters are typically installed after the roof covering is in place to collect rainwater, this is a soft preference as gutters could theoretically be installed simultaneously with the roof edge; however, standard practice places them after roof completion to ensure proper alignment and water flow.
The structural framing (rafters, trusses, or roof deck) must be in place to provide the load-bearing support for the mansard roof structure.
Load-bearing walls must be completed to support the weight and transfer loads of the mansard roof system.
Roof sheathing or decking is applied directly over the mansard roof frame to create a solid base for roofing materials.
Waterproof membrane and underlayment are installed after the mansard roof structure and sheathing are complete to protect against moisture ingress.
The final roofing material (slate, shingles, or metal panels) is installed only after the mansard roof framing and underlayment are in place.
The foundation must be completed to provide a stable base for the walls and roof structure that support the barrel vault.
Load-bearing walls must be erected before the barrel vault roof can be installed, as the vault rests directly on these walls.
Temporary formwork or centering must be constructed to support the barrel vault during its construction until the arch is self-supporting.
Waterproofing and insulation can only be applied after the barrel vault structure is fully completed and cured.

Interior ceiling finishing work (such as plastering or painting the underside of the vault) typically follows roof completion, though some finishing could theoretically proceed in parallel if access is available.
The structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) must be in place to provide support and define the building's grid before non-load-bearing walls can be safely installed.
The floor slab must be poured and cured to provide a stable base for the non-load-bearing walls to be built upon.
Electrical conduits, plumbing pipes, and HVAC ductwork that will run inside or behind the wall must be roughed in before enclosing them with the wall assembly.
After the wall framing and boarding are complete, finishing layers such as plaster, drywall taping, or cladding can be applied.
Electrical switches, outlets, and plumbing fixtures that mount onto or penetrate the wall must be installed after the wall is erected and finished.

The load-bearing wall must be built on a properly cured foundation or footings that can transfer the wall's vertical loads to the ground. Without a stable foundation, the wall would lack structural support and could settle unevenly or fail.
If the load-bearing wall is a ground-floor wall, the slab or floor must be in place to provide a level working surface and to anchor the wall. The wall bears on this slab/foundation element.
Floor joists or the next-floor structure bear directly on top of load-bearing walls. The wall must be fully installed, aligned, and braced before it can support the floor framing above.
Roof trusses or rafters transfer vertical and lateral loads to load-bearing walls. The walls must be complete and properly anchored to safely carry roof loads.

While electrical, plumbing, and HVAC rough-in can technically occur after wall framing, it is standard practice to run MEP lines after walls are erected but before drywall. This is a soft preference because the wall must be framed first to provide a chase for services.
Party walls must be built on a solid foundation to ensure structural stability and load distribution.
The site must be cleared and excavated to the required depth before any wall construction, including party walls, can begin.
Floor slabs or decks are often supported by or bear onto party walls, requiring the walls to be in place first.
The roof structure typically bears onto load-bearing party walls, so the walls must be completed to support the roof.
Finishing work is preferably done after the party wall is in place, as it protects the wall surface and avoids rework, though not physically mandatory.
Cavity walls must be built on a stable foundation or strip footing to distribute load and prevent settlement.
The ground floor slab provides the base and damp-proof course level from which the cavity wall construction can begin.
A damp-proof course must be laid at the base of the wall to prevent rising damp before the cavity wall masonry is built up.
Floor joists bear onto or into the cavity wall, so the wall must be built to the required height first to support them.
The roof trusses or rafters typically bear on the inner leaf of the cavity wall; the wall must be completed to full height to support the roof.
Insulation is placed within the cavity after the wall leaves are built to the required height but before the cavity is sealed at the top.
Wall ties are installed as the wall is being built (integral to the process), but final tying and checking typically follow the wall construction.
Openings in the cavity wall must be formed first; window and door frames are then fitted into these prepared openings.
Internal plastering and finishes are applied after the wall structure is complete and the masonry has cured.
While the outer leaf is built as part of the wall, final pointing and cleaning of external brickwork typically follow complete wall construction.
Fire walls require a stable load-bearing foundation to support their weight and structural integrity before they can be erected.

predecessor: Slab on Grade / Floor Slab Pouring
rationale: Fire walls typically rest on the foundation or floor slab, which must be poured and cured first to provide a solid base.
Fire walls provide fire-resistive separation and structural lateral support; steel or roof framing often bears on or ties into the fire wall, so the wall must be in place first.

MEP penetrations through fire walls must be properly fire-stopped; it is a soft preference to complete the fire wall first to avoid rework, but penetrations can be coordinated concurrently if sealed correctly.
Fire walls act as fire-rated partition boundaries; interior finishes on both sides cannot be applied until the fire wall is fully constructed and inspected for fire-resistance ratings.
Partition walls must be built on top of a finished slab or structural deck; the slab provides the supporting surface and substrate for the wall.
The primary structural frame (columns, beams) must be in place before non-load-bearing partition walls can be installed, as the partitions fit within the structural grid.
Plaster or finishing applications require the partition wall substrate to be fully installed and stable before surface treatments can be applied.

Electrical wiring, outlets, and switches within partition walls must be installed after the wall framing is in place but before final cladding, however the rough-in typically occurs after framing but before full finishing.
Partition walls provide the rough openings and structural support for doors and windows; these components are installed after the wall framing is complete.
Demountable partitions require a level and finished floor surface to ensure proper alignment, stability, and straightness of the partition base track.
Demountable partitions typically fix into ceiling grid systems; the ceiling structure must be in place to provide top fixing support and to define partition alignment.
Electrical and data cables routed above ceiling or within wall cavities must be installed before enclosing them with demountable partitions to avoid costly retrofitting.
Final wall finishes such as painting or applying wall coverings must be done after partition panels are erected to achieve a seamless, continuous finish.

While furniture placement can proceed after partition installation for spatial definition, it is a soft preference as furniture could be moved into place concurrently in open areas not affected by partitions.
Masonry walls require a stable, level base (foundation or slab) to transfer loads and ensure alignment. Without a cured foundation, masonry cannot be safely or accurately erected.
Reinforcement placed in the foundation or bond beams must be installed prior to masonry work to ensure structural continuity (e.g., dowels projecting from foundation into masonry wall).
Lintels or bond beams are placed directly above doors and windows as masonry is laid up; walls must be built to the height of the opening before the lintel can be set in place.
Roof framing bears on or attaches to the top of masonry walls; walls must be completed and cured to support roof loads.

Electrical conduits, outlet boxes, and switch boxes embedded in or attached to masonry walls must be installed after the wall is built to avoid damaging fresh masonry and to align with finished wall surfaces.
Concrete walls require a stable foundation to bear their load and prevent settlement cracking.
Steel reinforcement must be placed and tied within the formwork before concrete is poured to provide tensile strength to the wall.
Formwork (molds) must be assembled and braced to contain and shape the wet concrete until it cures.
Waterproofing membranes or coatings are applied to the cured concrete wall surface to prevent moisture intrusion.
Backfill against the wall can only proceed after the concrete has achieved sufficient strength to resist lateral earth pressures.
The steel frame wall must be erected on a stable, level foundation or concrete slab to provide structural support and load distribution.
The wall frame must be erected first to support the roof structure; the roof bears on the walls.
Exterior sheathing and cladding are attached directly to the steel frame, so the frame must be in place first.
Electrical rough-in can proceed after the steel frame is erected; while it could theoretically be done simultaneously, practical sequencing typically places rough-in after framing for easier access.
Insulation is placed within the cavities of the steel frame, so the frame must be complete before insulation can be installed.
The timber frame wall requires a level, stable base foundation to bear the load and provide anchorage for the bottom plate. Without a completed foundation, the wall cannot be erected.
The bottom plate (or sill plate) must be anchored to the foundation as the base member before the timber frame wall studs and panels can be erected on top of it.
If the timber frame wall sits on a wood-framed floor (e.g., platform framing), the floor deck must be completed to provide the working surface and support for the wall assembly.
The roof structure bears directly on top of the timber frame walls. The walls must be erected, plumbed, and braced before roof trusses or rafters can be installed.

Exterior wall sheathing (e.g., OSB, plywood) or cladding is applied to the exterior face of the timber frame after the frame is erected to provide lateral bracing and the substrate for the weatherproofing layer.
A level, load-bearing foundation (e.g., concrete slab or stem wall) must be in place to support the weight of straw bale walls and protect them from ground moisture.

A structural frame (post-and-beam or similar) is typically required to support roof loads and provide lateral stability before straw bales are stacked, as bales alone are not structural in most designs.

A capillary break or moisture barrier (e.g., polyethylene sheet or damp-proof course) must be placed between the foundation and the first course of bales to prevent rising damp from wicking into the straw.
Straw bale walls must be in place and fully stacked before plaster (e.g., lime, clay, or cement render) can be applied to both interior and exterior faces to seal and protect the bales.

successor: Electrical and Plumbing Rough-In (within bale walls)
rationale: While not a hard physical constraint, it is strongly preferred to run electrical conduits and plumbing within the straw bale walls after stacking but before plastering, as the plaster would seal access to the wall cavity.

A stable foundation (e.g., concrete strip or reinforced footing) must be completed and cured before rammed earth wall construction begins, as the massive weight of rammed earth requires a load-bearing base to prevent settlement or cracking.
Temporary formwork (shuttering) must be erected and braced to define the wall shape and contain the earth material during compaction; rammed earth cannot be formed without rigid formwork in place.

The soil mix must be tested and adjusted to the correct optimal moisture content before being placed and compacted, as overly dry or wet soil will not achieve the required density and structural strength.
Formwork cannot be removed until the rammed earth layer(s) have been compacted and allowed to initially set/cure; premature stripping would cause wall collapse or deformation.
After compaction, the wall must be protected from rapid drying, rain, and frost during its curing period to develop full strength and prevent surface erosion or cracking.

It is generally preferred to embed conduits or chase routes after the wall is built (by cutting or core-drilling) since embedding them during compaction is difficult; however, this is a soft preference because some designs do embed conduits during construction.

Rammed earth walls must be completed to their full height and sufficiently cured to bear vertical loads before roof beams or upper floor structures are placed on top of them, as the walls serve as load-bearing elements.
The ground must be excavated and leveled before any foundation or wall construction can begin; ICF walls require a prepared footing or foundation to be placed upon.
ICF walls must be erected on top of a properly poured and cured concrete footing or foundation slab to provide structural support and load distribution.
Vertical rebar dowels extending from the footing must be placed prior to stacking ICF blocks so they can be tied into the wall reinforcement.
The ICF blocks must be fully stacked, braced, and aligned before concrete can be pumped into the forms.
The concrete poured inside the ICF forms must be allowed to cure and gain sufficient strength before any loads are placed on the wall or forms are removed.

While chases can be cut into ICF after concrete cure, it is a soft preference to embed conduits/pipe within the ICF before pouring concrete; if not pre-installed, routing can be done after wall completion but with more difficulty.
Interior and exterior finishes cannot be applied until the concrete core has fully cured and the ICF surface is stable for attachment of cladding or drywall.
Structural floor joists or roof trusses bear on the ICF walls; the walls must be complete, poured, and cured to support the vertical loads from upper floors or roof.
Excavation must be completed to expose the soil and provide a clean working surface for placing wall footings.
The ground must be properly compacted and prepared to provide adequate load-bearing capacity before pouring or placing the wall footing.
Survey and layout must be completed to mark the exact location, alignment, and dimensions of the wall footing before construction begins.
The wall footing provides the foundation base; the wall cannot be constructed until the footing has been placed and cured.
Waterproofing applied to the footing must be done before backfilling, but after the footing is complete and cured.
Wall ties are used to connect walls to the structure; a stable foundation is required before any wall-related work can begin.
Wall ties are embedded into or attached to the inner leaf of a cavity wall during construction; the inner wall structure must be erected first.
Wall ties are placed between the inner and outer leaves of a cavity wall; the outer leaf is built up after ties are positioned to connect the two leaves.
Wall ties must be in place before cavity insulation can be installed, as the ties provide structural connection across the cavity and insulation is placed around them.
While generally DPC is installed during wall construction at the same time as ties, in some sequences ties are placed first; this is a soft preference depending on construction methodology.
Walls must be built on a stable foundation to ensure structural integrity and load distribution.
Steel reinforcement must be placed and tied inside the formwork before concrete is poured to create reinforced concrete walls.
Formwork must remain in place until the concrete has cured sufficiently to support its own weight; only then can forms be safely removed.
Waterproofing can only be applied after the concrete wall has fully cured and the formwork is removed to expose the wall surface.
Proper curing (moisture and temperature control) must begin immediately after concrete placement to achieve design strength and durability.

Masonry walls require a stable, level, and cured foundation or footing to bear the compressive load. Laying masonry on unprepared or uncured ground would result in settlement, cracking, and structural failure.
Freshly laid masonry (mortar and units) must be allowed to cure and gain sufficient strength before any load is applied or subsequent trades work on it.
Lintels over openings and vertical reinforcement are placed during or immediately after masonry laying to integrate structurally with the wall system.
Backfilling against a masonry retaining wall can only proceed after the masonry has been laid and the mortar has cured to withstand lateral earth pressure.
Plaster or stucco application requires the masonry substrate to be fully complete, stable, and cured to provide a proper bonding surface.
Wall insulation is installed within the cavities of the wall framing; the framing structure must be fully erected and stable to provide the enclosure into which insulation is placed.
Plumbing pipes running through walls must be installed before insulation, as insulation would block access to run and secure pipes within the wall cavities.
Electrical wiring, boxes, and conduits within walls must be installed and inspected before insulation, as insulation would obstruct access for running wires and installing fixtures.
HVAC ducts and vents routed through walls must be installed prior to insulation, because insulation fills the wall cavity and would prevent duct installation and sealing.
A vapor barrier (if required by design) is typically installed over the insulation on the warm side of the wall to prevent moisture diffusion; this must be done after the insulation is in place.
Drywall (gypsum board) is installed over the wall framing and insulation; the insulation must be fully in place before the walls are closed up with drywall.
Building code typically requires an inspection of the insulation, framing, and rough-ins before drywall is hung; this inspection can only occur after insulation is installed.
Wall framing must be constructed first to provide the structural framework within which openings (windows, doors) are formed.
Window openings must be formed in the wall before windows can be installed into those openings.
Door openings must be formed in the wall before doors can be hung and installed.
Openings must be formed to provide space for placing lintels or headers above the openings to support the wall above.

While typically sheathing comes after framing, openings can be formed before sheathing is applied; however, for structural panel sheathing, openings are often cut after sheathing, making this a soft preference depending on the method.
Wall waterproofing requires a stable structural support; framing provides the substrate to which waterproofing membranes or coatings are applied.
Exterior sheathing (e.g., plywood or cement board) must be in place as a continuous backing layer before waterproofing membranes can be installed.
Drainage boards or mats are placed directly over the waterproofing membrane to protect it and channel water; they cannot be installed before waterproofing is applied.
Backfilling against a foundation or retaining wall must only occur after waterproofing is fully cured and in place to avoid damaging the unprotected wall structure.
