Rigid insulation boards are often placed over the waterproofing layer; while this is typical, some systems integrate insulation differently, making it a common but not absolutely mandatory sequence.

Walls must be built on top of completed foundations; surveying and setting out for walls cannot begin until the foundation is fully constructed and cured to provide a stable and accurate reference base.
The site must be cleared and leveled before any surveying and setting out can take place, as debris or uneven ground would prevent accurate measurement and marking of wall positions.
Formwork for walls must follow the precise layout established during surveying and setting out; the marked lines and reference points define exactly where formwork panels are to be placed.
Masonry walls require the exact positions and alignments marked out by surveying before any blocks or bricks can be laid.
Steel reinforcement must be placed according to the wall layout and dimensions established during setting out; the marking defines the boundary and spacing for reinforcement bars.
A structural assessment must be completed before any wall demolition to identify load-bearing walls and ensure safe removal without compromising building stability.
Legal permits and approvals from local authorities are required before any demolition work can commence to comply with building codes and safety regulations.
All electrical, plumbing, gas, and other utility lines running through or near the wall must be identified, isolated, and disconnected to prevent hazards during demolition.
A survey must be conducted to check for asbestos, lead paint, or other hazardous materials in the wall, and if found, remediation must occur before demolition to ensure worker and occupant safety.
Containment barriers, dust screens, and protective coverings must be installed to protect adjacent areas and equipment from dust, debris, and vibration during the demolition process.
Demolition waste, rubble, and debris must be removed from the site after the wall is taken down to clear the work area for subsequent construction activities.
New wall framing or structural modifications can only begin after the existing wall has been fully demolished and the area has been cleared and prepared.
An inspection must be performed after demolition to verify that adjacent structures remain stable and that no unforeseen structural issues exist before proceeding with further work.
Relocation or installation of new MEP systems in the area of the demolished wall can only proceed after the wall is removed and the space is accessible.
Wall finishing (such as drywall installation, plastering, or paneling) requires the structural framing to be complete so there is a substrate to attach the finishing materials to.
Insulation must be placed within wall cavities before they are enclosed by wall finishing materials.
Electrical wiring and outlet boxes must be installed in the walls before the wall surfaces are closed up with finishing materials.
Plumbing pipes and fixtures within walls must be installed and pressure-tested before walls are finished and enclosed.
Paint and primer require a finished wall surface (drywall, plaster, etc.) to be applied to.
While flooring can technically be done before wall finishing, it is a strong soft preference to finish walls first to avoid dust, debris, and damage from wall work falling onto new flooring.
Baseboards, crown molding, and other trim are typically installed after the wall surface is complete so they can be properly fastened and aligned.
Cabinets are often installed before final wall finishing in some sequences, but it is generally preferred to have walls finished first for a cleaner look and proper fit against finished surfaces.
The ground surface must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and topsoil, and graded to the required elevation before any foundation work can begin to provide a stable, level working platform.

Soil bearing capacity, groundwater conditions, and soil classification must be determined through subsurface exploration to design the shallow foundation and verify that the ground can support the loads.
The soil must be excavated to the planned foundation bearing elevation and the base must be properly leveled and compacted before placing any foundation concrete or masonry.
Waterproofing membranes, damp-proof courses, and perimeter drainage systems are applied directly onto the cured foundation surfaces to protect against moisture ingress.
Vertical structural elements such as columns and load-bearing walls require the completed foundation to transfer loads to the ground; they cannot be built without a finished foundation to rest upon.

The ground must be cleared of vegetation, topsoil, and obstructions, and excavated to the required depth and width before strip foundations can be laid, as the foundation concrete must be placed onto undisturbed or properly prepared bearing soil.

The exact positions, alignments, and levels of the strip foundation trenches must be marked out and surveyed before excavation and concreting begins, otherwise the foundation may be incorrectly positioned.
Freshly poured concrete strip foundations must be allowed to cure and gain sufficient strength before any subsequent loads are applied or further construction proceeds.
A damp proof course is typically laid on top of the finished strip foundation or the masonry built off it; the foundation must be complete and cured before DPC work can commence.
Strip foundations provide the load-bearing base for walls; the foundation must be fully constructed, cured, and inspected before masonry walls can be built upon it.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and topsoil to provide a clean working surface for deep foundation equipment and to accurately locate pile or shaft positions.

Subsurface soil conditions and bearing capacity must be assessed through soil borings and tests to determine the appropriate deep foundation type (e.g., piles, caissons, drilled shafts), depth, and design parameters.
Survey control points and foundation layouts must be established to accurately position each pile or shaft in the correct location and alignment.
Pile caps are structural elements that transfer loads from the superstructure to the pile group; they cannot be constructed until the piles or shafts are installed and their heads are prepared.

While static or dynamic load testing is typically performed after installation to verify capacity, it is a verification step rather than a physical prerequisite for subsequent work; however, results may affect design acceptance.

Grade beams and foundation walls distribute loads from columns and walls to the deep foundation elements; they are constructed directly on or connecting to the piles/caps and therefore must follow deep foundation installation.
Backfilling is preferred after pile caps and grade beams are in place to protect exposed excavations, but some sequencing flexibility exists depending on project phasing.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and obstructions before any excavation or forming of pad footings can begin.
Surveying and setting out of building lines and column positions must be completed to accurately locate where each pad footing is to be excavated and poured.
Bulk earthworks and site grading to achieve the required formation level must be completed before excavating individual pad footings to the correct depth.

Pad footings must be cast and cured before a ground slab can be poured, as the slab bears on the ground and may tie into the footings, and the footings provide support for columns that will be constructed prior to the slab.
Pad footings must be fully cured with holding-down bolts cast in place before steel columns can be erected and bolted down to the footings.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated to the required depth before any foundation work can begin, as the raft slab requires a prepared subgrade.
The subgrade must be compacted and prepared to the specified bearing capacity to provide a stable base for the raft foundation.
A thin layer of lean concrete (blinding) is often poured over the prepared subgrade to provide a clean, level working surface and prevent reinforcement from contacting the soil directly.
Waterproofing membranes or coatings are applied to the cured raft foundation slab to protect the structure from moisture ingress before backfilling or further construction.

successor: Reinforcement and Formwork for Superstructure Columns/Walls
rationale: The raft foundation must be fully cured and achieve sufficient strength before any superstructure elements (columns, walls, shear walls) are constructed on top of it, as the raft acts as the load-bearing base.
After the raft foundation is complete and waterproofed, backfilling around the edges and pouring the ground floor slab can proceed.
Excavation must be completed to expose the subgrade and provide the proper elevation and space for forming and pouring the grade beam.
The subgrade must be compacted and leveled to provide a stable, uniform bearing surface for the grade beam, preventing differential settlement.
Forms must be set and braced to define the shape, dimensions, and alignment of the grade beam before concrete can be placed.
Rebar cage must be assembled and positioned within the forms to provide tensile strength before concrete is poured.
After concrete placement, a specified curing period is required to allow the concrete to achieve sufficient strength before any loads are applied or subsequent work begins.
Backfilling can only occur after the grade beam concrete has cured adequately to prevent damaging the green concrete.
Vertical structural elements bearing on the grade beam require the grade beam to be fully cured and strong enough to support their load.
While waterproofing is typically applied after curing, it is a protective measure rather than a structural dependency, though best practice is to apply it before backfilling.
The ground surface must be cleared, leveled, and graded before drilling or excavating for caissons/drilled shafts to provide a stable working platform and access for drilling equipment.
The exact locations of each caisson/drilled shaft must be surveyed and staked out on site before drilling can commence to ensure proper positioning and alignment per design drawings.
Subsurface soil conditions and bearing capacity must be assessed through geotechnical investigations to determine the required depth, diameter, and design of the drilled shafts.
If caissons are to be installed near existing structures or deep excavations, temporary shoring systems must be in place to prevent ground collapse and protect adjacent facilities during drilling.

Underground utilities (gas, water, electric, telecom) in the vicinity of proposed caisson locations must be located, relocated, or protected to avoid damage during drilling and to ensure worker safety.
After drilling the shaft to the required depth, a steel reinforcement cage must be placed into the excavated hole before concrete is poured to provide structural reinforcement.
Concrete must be placed into the drilled shaft (typically via tremie method) immediately following reinforcement cage installation to form the structural caisson element.
The caisson/drilled shaft must be completed and its concrete cured to sufficient strength before the pile cap or grade beam can be constructed atop the shaft to distribute loads.
Vertical structural elements (columns or walls) that bear on the caisson foundation can only be erected after the caisson is complete, cured, and tested for integrity.

While often performed, load testing is a quality assurance step that typically follows caisson completion; it is a soft preference because in some projects testing may be omitted or performed on sacrificial test shafts beforehand.
The ground must be cleared, graded, and compacted to provide a stable and level surface for excavating and pouring the spread footing.
Excavation must be completed to reach the required bearing soil depth and to create the void where the spread footing will be formed and poured.
The soil at the footing base must be inspected and verified to have adequate bearing capacity before concrete is placed, to ensure structural support.
Spread footings provide the load-bearing base; foundation walls or columns must be built directly on top of the cured footing to transfer loads to the soil.
After the spread footing is poured and cured, waterproofing membranes and drainage systems can be applied to the footing and surrounding foundation to protect against moisture.
Backfilling around the foundation can only commence after the spread footing and any foundation walls are in place and sufficiently cured, to avoid disturbing the fresh concrete.
The ground must be excavated to the required depth and width before the combined footing can be placed, as the footing needs a prepared trench or excavation to sit in.

A layer of lean concrete (blinding) must be laid over the excavated soil to provide a clean, level, and stable working surface for the combined footing reinforcement and concrete placement, preventing soil contamination and ensuring proper cover.
The steel reinforcement cage and bars for the combined footing must be positioned and tied in place before the concrete is poured, as the reinforcement is embedded within the footing concrete.
The concrete of the combined footing must be poured and allowed to cure sufficiently before the formwork can be stripped, as formwork supports the wet concrete until it gains enough strength.

Waterproofing membrane or coating is applied to the cured combined footing surface to protect against moisture ingress; this can only commence after the footing concrete has fully cured and formwork is removed.
Excavation must be completed to provide a clear and prepared trench or area for casting the cantilever/strap footing.
Soil bearing capacity and ground conditions must be verified to design and safely construct the strap footing.
A mudmat or blinding layer is often placed before footing construction to provide a clean, level working surface, though in some sequences the footing is cast directly against earth.
Cantilever/strap footings must cure and gain sufficient strength before columns or walls bearing on them can be formed and reinforced.
Waterproofing is applied after the footing has cured and its surfaces are accessible; it cannot be applied before the footing is placed.
The ground must be cleared and excavated to the required depth and dimensions before any foundation wall can be constructed, as the wall sits within the excavated trench.
Foundation walls are typically built on top of concrete footings, which distribute the load. The footings must be poured, cured, and set before the wall can be formed and poured on them.
Waterproofing membranes and drainage boards are applied directly to the exterior surface of the finished foundation wall; the wall must exist first.
Soil is backfilled against the foundation wall only after the wall is fully constructed, cured, and waterproofed; backfilling before the wall is built would be impossible.
The foundation walls enclose the basement or crawl space and provide support for the ground floor; the floor slab or framing must wait until the walls are in place.
Excavation must be completed to reach the required depth and create a level subgrade for the basement slab to be poured on.
Footings must be poured and cured to support the foundation walls and slab; the slab is often poured between or after footings are in place.
Foundation walls (or stem walls) must be constructed to enclose the basement area before the slab can be poured, as the slab ties into or bears on these walls.
Exterior waterproofing, dampproofing, and perimeter drainage systems must be installed before the slab to prevent moisture issues from below.
Plumbing rough-ins, electrical conduits, and any other underground utilities running beneath the slab must be laid and inspected prior to concrete placement.
The ground must be cleared, excavated, and prepared before underpinning work can begin to expose the existing foundations and provide safe access for underpinning operations.
Existing structures must be temporarily supported and shored before underpinning to ensure structural stability during the excavation and underpinning process.
A thorough survey and structural assessment of the existing foundations and loading conditions must be completed to design the underpinning scheme and determine the required depth and method.
Excavated areas around the underpinned foundations must be backfilled and compacted only after underpinning concrete has cured and the new foundation is fully load-bearing.
New structural walls or vertical superstructure elements can only be built after underpinning is complete and the foundation is stable enough to support additional loads.

Geotechnical data (soil bearing capacity, groundwater level, obstructions) is needed to design micropile depth, diameter and grouting method; piling cannot proceed without confirmed subsurface conditions.
Structural design, load calculations and pile layout drawings must be approved before any installation work begins.
Drilling rigs, grout plants, and material deliveries require cleared access roads and staging areas before pile installation can start.
Proof testing must be performed after grout has cured to verify design capacity before the micropile is put into service.
Micropile heads must be installed and cut to level before the pile cap or foundation beam can be cast to transfer superstructure loads.
The ground must be cleared, graded, and excavated to the required elevation before helical piers can be positioned and driven into the soil.
All existing underground utilities must be identified and marked to avoid striking them during helical pier driving, which could cause service disruptions or safety hazards.
Soil bearing capacity, composition, and depth to competent strata must be assessed to select the correct helical pier size, helix configuration, and installation torque requirements.
After installation, helical piers must be tested (e.g., compression or tension load tests) to verify they meet design capacity before supporting any structure.

successor: Foundation Concrete Placement / Pile Cap Construction
rationale: Helical piers serve as deep foundations; the pile caps, grade beams, or foundation slabs can only be constructed once the piers are fully installed and verified.

The ground must be excavated and graded to the proper depth and elevation before any frost protection or foundation insulation can be installed, as the insulation is placed against or below the exposed foundation walls and footings.
While often done concurrently, under-slab insulation should ideally be placed before perimeter frost protection to ensure a continuous thermal break at the foundation perimeter.
Frost protection insulation around the perimeter footing must be in place before the concrete slab or floor is poured, as the insulation will be embedded or directly adjacent to the pour.

Exterior foundation insulation and rigid foam frost protection boards must be installed on foundation walls before backfilling can occur, as they would be inaccessible or damaged by backfill after the fact.
Rough-in plumbing and electrical should be completed after frost protection is in place to avoid disturbing the insulation, though in some sequences under-slab utilities precede the insulation layer.
The project must be formally initiated and site access granted before any site investigation can begin.
Equipment, crew, and temporary facilities must be mobilized to site before soil investigation activities can commence.
Soil parameters (bearing capacity, soil type, groundwater level) obtained from investigation are essential inputs for foundation design.
The data collected during soil investigation must be analyzed and compiled into a geotechnical report before it can be used for design.
Soil conditions and groundwater levels must be known to plan safe excavation methods, slope stability, and dewatering requirements.
The ground must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and obstructions before any pile driving equipment can access the site and begin installation.
Accurate layout and staking of pile locations is required to guide the pile driving equipment and ensure piles are installed in the correct positions according to design drawings.
Soil conditions and bearing capacity must be evaluated through geotechnical testing to determine required pile type, length, and driving criteria before installation begins.
Pile caps are constructed atop the installed pile groups to distribute loads; piles must first be driven and cut to grade before concrete pile caps can be formed and poured.
Post-installation testing such as PDA or low-strain integrity testing is typically performed after pile installation to verify structural integrity and driving stresses.
Formwork provides the mold that shapes and supports wet concrete until it cures; without formwork in place, concrete cannot be shaped or contained.
Steel reinforcement must be positioned and tied inside the formwork before concrete is poured to ensure structural integrity and proper embedment.
Formwork cannot be removed until the concrete has been poured and has gained sufficient strength to support its own weight.
Curing is the process of maintaining moisture and temperature conditions after pouring to allow proper hydration and strength development.
Surface finishing operations such as troweling or screeding must be performed on freshly placed concrete before it hardens completely.
Formwork provides the mold and support structure into which rebar is placed; without formwork, rebar cannot be properly positioned and supported.
Concrete must be poured after rebar is fully fixed in place so that the reinforcement is encased within the concrete as designed.
Rebar must be cut and bent to the required shapes and sizes before it can be placed and tied in position.
Post-tensioning ducts and tendons are installed after rebar fixing, then tensioned after concrete gains sufficient strength.
Concrete must be fully cured (typically 7-28 days) before waterproofing can be applied, as moisture trapped in uncured concrete will cause waterproofing membrane failure and blistering.
The substrate must be clean, dry, and free of debris, dust, oil, or laitance for proper adhesion of the waterproofing membrane.
Most waterproofing systems require a primer coat to ensure proper bonding between the substrate and the waterproofing membrane.
A protective screed or drainage layer must be installed over the waterproofing membrane to shield it from UV damage, mechanical damage, and foot traffic during subsequent construction activities.
Floor finishes, tiles, or paving must be installed after waterproofing to prevent water ingress beneath the finished surface and ensure the waterproofing layer is continuous and unbroken.
Backfilling and Compaction occurs around the completed foundation or substructure; the structure must be built first so that backfill can be placed against it for support and drainage.

predecessor: Underground Utility Installation (if any beneath slab)
rationale: Any utilities, conduits, or piping that will run under or through the backfill area must be installed before backfilling to avoid digging up compacted material and to ensure proper embedment.
Waterproofing membranes and coatings on foundation walls must be applied and fully cured before backfill is placed to protect the wall from moisture and to prevent damage to the membrane.
The subgrade must be compacted to the required density before a concrete floor slab is poured on top, to prevent settlement and cracking.

While finishing grading and landscape work typically follows backfill for a neat finish, minor grading adjustments can sometimes be done concurrently; thus it is a soft preference rather than a hard physical constraint.
Concrete must reach sufficient strength (usually 28-day curing) before load testing can be applied to avoid structural damage or failure.
Steel frame must be fully erected and connections completed to provide the load-bearing structure before testing its capacity.

predecessor: Installation of Test Equipment and Sensors
rationale: Data acquisition systems, strain gauges, and load application equipment must be installed and calibrated before testing begins.
For foundation or pavement load tests, backfill must be placed and compacted to ensure proper soil support and realistic test conditions.
Load test results are required data inputs for verifying structural performance and issuing final approvals.
The foundation must be poured and cured to provide a stable load-bearing base for steel beam installation.
Steel beams must be fabricated, cut, and prepared to the required specifications before they can be delivered and erected on site.
Steel beams must be transported to the construction site before they can be lifted and positioned into place.
Steel beams must first be erected and positioned before they can be permanently connected via bolting or welding.
Steel beams must be in place to serve as the structural support system before metal decking or flooring can be installed on top.
The excavation must be completed to expose the ground surface and provide access for foundation work before the foundation can be inspected.
The concrete footing or foundation must be poured and cured before it can be inspected for structural integrity, rebar placement, dimensions, and concrete quality.
Formwork must be in place and properly aligned before inspection can verify correct dimensions, level, and positioning of the foundation.
Reinforcement steel must be placed and tied before inspection can verify rebar size, spacing, coverage, and connection details.
Backfilling around the foundation can only commence after the foundation has been inspected and approved to avoid burying uncertified or defective work.
The foundation must be inspected and approved before pouring a slab on grade to ensure the subgrade, vapor barrier, and reinforcing are correct.
Vertical construction of walls and structural framing cannot begin until the foundation has been inspected and certified to carry the imposed loads.
While waterproofing typically follows inspection, it is a soft preference because inspection could be done after waterproofing in some cases if the membrane is transparent or removable.
Formwork must be installed and secured before concrete can be poured into the beam mold to give the beam its shape and support.
Steel reinforcement bars must be placed and tied within the formwork before concrete pouring to provide tensile strength to the beam.
Concrete must be poured and cured to sufficient strength before formwork can be safely removed without damaging the beam.
Once concrete is poured into the beam formwork, the curing process begins immediately to ensure proper hydration and strength development.
Post-tensioning cables can only be tensioned after the concrete beam has been poured and reached the required initial compressive strength.

Timber beams require a stable and level foundation to bear the load. Without proper foundation preparation (e.g., footing excavation, concrete curing), the beam cannot be placed safely or structurally supported.
Timber beams serve as primary horizontal supports; deck joists and floor framing are typically attached to or supported by these beams, so they must be installed first.
In timber-framed structures, roof rafters or trusses often bear onto timber beams. The beams must be in place to transfer roof loads to the columns or walls.
Timber beams need to be treated with preservatives or fire retardants before installation to ensure durability and code compliance; treatment cannot be effectively applied after installation.

In some timber-frame construction, the beam forms a structural tie at the top of a wall or between posts; upper wall sections or additional framing layers can only proceed once the beam is securely in place.
Formwork must be installed to provide the mold and support for the concrete portion of the composite beam before the beam can be cast or placed.
The structural steel beam must be erected and in position before concrete can be placed to form the composite section.
Shear connectors (studs) must be welded to the steel beam prior to concrete placement to ensure composite action between steel and concrete.
After the composite beam is formed by placing concrete, sufficient curing time is required for the concrete to gain strength before loads can be applied.
The composite beam must be completed and in place before the deck slab can be poured, as the beam supports the deck formwork and loading.
Formwork provides the mold that shapes and supports the wet concrete until it cures; without formwork, the concrete beam cannot be formed.
Steel reinforcement bars must be placed and tied within the formwork before concrete is poured to provide tensile strength within the beam.
The concrete must be poured into the prepared formwork to create the beam; this is the actual construction activity that produces the beam component.
After the concrete is poured, sufficient curing time is required for the concrete to gain strength before the formwork can be safely removed.
The reinforced concrete beam must be fully cured and capable of supporting loads before any slab or deck that rests on or is supported by the beam can be constructed on top of it.

Pre-stressed concrete beams require tensioned steel tendons (strands/wires) to be stressed and anchored before the concrete is poured. The prestressing force is applied to the tendons first, then concrete is cast around them, allowing the bond to transfer compression to the concrete after curing.
A mold or formwork must be constructed to shape the wet concrete into the beam geometry before concrete placement can begin.
Non-prestressed reinforcing steel (mild steel reinforcement) must be tied into a cage and placed within the formwork before concrete is poured, to provide ductility and handle secondary stresses.

After concrete is placed for the pre-stressed beam, it must be allowed to cure and gain sufficient compressive strength (often to a specified percentage of design strength) before the prestressing force can be transferred from the tendons to the concrete (in post-tensioning) or before form removal and handling (in pre-tensioning).
Once the concrete has cured to adequate strength, the formwork can be stripped from the hardened pre-stressed concrete beam.

After the pre-stressed concrete beam is cast, cured, and the prestressing force is transferred (if post-tensioned, after grouting), the beam can be lifted, transported to storage, and later erected at its final location.
The pre-stressed concrete beam must be fully fabricated, cured, and prestressed before it can be transported to the construction site and lifted/placed onto its supporting piers or abutments.
Glulam beams are heavy structural elements that require a stable, load-bearing foundation to support their weight and the loads they transfer.
Glulam beams typically bear on or connect to steel columns or vertical supports; the supporting columns must be erected first to provide the bearing points.
Glulam beams serve as primary roof or floor framing members; decking or sheathing is applied directly onto the beams after they are in place.
Permanent bracing, moment connections, and lateral restraint details must be installed after the glulam beam is positioned and aligned to ensure structural stability.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing runs are often routed above or through glulam beam bays; it is efficient to complete beam erection before overhead MEP rough-in, though not a strict physical necessity in all cases.
Steel must be manufactured in a steel mill before it can be formed into an I-beam structural component.
The steel must be hot-rolled or shaped into the I-beam profile (with its characteristic flanges and web) before it can be placed in a structure.
The I-beam must be cut, drilled, and fabricated to the required dimensions before being hoisted into position.
After the I-beam is placed in its structural position, permanent connections (bolting or welding) must be completed to secure it to the frame.
If the I-beam supports a composite concrete deck, the beam must be in place and shored before concrete is poured over it.
T-Beams are precast concrete elements that require cast-in-situ concrete to be placed and cured before they can be installed as part of the structure.
Formwork must be erected to support the T-Beam and cast-in-situ concrete topping before the T-Beam can be positioned.
Reinforcement steel must be fixed in position within the formwork before the T-Beam is placed to ensure structural integrity.
After T-Beams are installed, a concrete topping or screed is poured over them to form the composite deck.
The composite deck curing process can only commence after the T-Beam is installed and the concrete topping has been placed.
Concrete must be fully cured to achieve sufficient strength before supporting the weight of box beams.
Formwork must be assembled and securely braced before concrete can be poured to shape the beam.
Reinforcement steel must be positioned and tied within the formwork before concrete is poured to ensure structural integrity.
Box beams must be fully fabricated (cast and cured) in a precast yard before they can be transported and installed on site.
Box beams must be installed and properly seated on bearings before the deck slab can be poured on top of them.
Formwork provides the necessary mold and temporary support structure to shape and hold the concrete for the cantilever beam before it cures and gains sufficient strength.

predecessor: Steel Reinforcement (Rebar) Placement for Cantilever Beam
rationale: Steel reinforcement bars must be placed and tied within the formwork before concrete is poured to provide tensile strength to the cantilever beam.

predecessor: Column/Support Structure Construction at Beam Location
rationale: The vertical support elements (columns or walls) that will carry the cantilever beam must be constructed first to provide a bearing surface and load transfer path.

successor: Cantilever Beam Curing and Formwork Removal
rationale: After pouring the cantilever beam concrete, sufficient curing time must elapse for the concrete to develop design strength before formwork and shoring can be safely removed.
Waterproofing membrane or coating is applied to the completed and cured cantilever beam surface to protect it from moisture ingress and environmental damage.
Transfer beams require stable foundation support to distribute loads; without proper foundations, the transfer beam cannot be placed.
Transfer beams typically rest on or connect to columns; columns must be installed first to provide vertical support for the transfer beam.
Formwork must be erected to shape and support wet concrete for in-situ cast transfer beams before pouring can commence.
Transfer beams carry loads from upper floors; upper floor construction can only proceed after the transfer beam is in place to transfer column loads to the foundation.
While load testing is recommended to verify the beam's capacity before proceeding with upper structure, it is a quality control preference rather than a physical necessity.
Spandrel beams are structural elements that span between columns; columns must be in place to provide support and connection points for the spandrel beams.
Formwork must be erected, aligned, and secured before concrete can be poured to shape and support the wet concrete of the spandrel beam.

predecessor: Reinforcement Steel Fixing for Spandrel Beam
rationale: Steel reinforcement bars (rebar) must be placed and tied within the formwork before concreting to ensure structural integrity of the spandrel beam.
Spandrel beams often support the edges of floor slabs; the beam must be in place to provide bearing and load transfer for the slab.
Concrete must be poured before the curing process can begin; curing is the time-dependent process that allows the concrete to gain strength.
Formwork provides the mold and support structure for the coupling beam; rebar cannot be placed without the formwork in position.
Steel reinforcement must be in place before concrete is poured to ensure composite structural action.
Freshly poured concrete must gain sufficient strength through curing before any loads are applied or subsequent work proceeds.
Cured concrete must reach adequate strength to be self-supporting before formwork can be safely removed.

predecessor: Shear Wall Construction at Same Level
rationale: Coupling beams connect adjacent shear walls; the supporting wall segments must be in place to anchor and support the beam.

successor: Floor Slab Pouring at Coupling Beam Level
rationale: The coupling beam is typically cast monolithically with or before the floor slab to ensure proper load transfer and diaphragm action.

successor: Vertical Structural Elements Above Coupling Beam
rationale: Upper-level walls and columns rely on the completed coupling beam and supporting structure below for load transfer.

successor: MEP Rough-In Within Coupling Beam Zone
rationale: MEP work after beam construction avoids damaging fresh concrete but minor coordination could allow pre-installed sleeves, so this is a strong preference but not always physically impossible.
Rafters rest on and are supported by the top plates of wall frames, so walls must be framed and in place before rafters can be installed.
The top plates on the wall framing provide the bearing surface for the rafters; rafters cannot be placed without completed top plates.
Roof sheathing (e.g., plywood or OSB) is nailed directly onto the rafters to create the roof deck, so rafters must be installed first.
Ceiling joists often tie into or are supported by the rafter system (or the same top plate), and are typically installed in coordination with or after rafters to complete the roof structure.
Roof underlayment (felt or synthetic membrane) is applied over the roof sheathing, which in turn is installed on the rafters; rafters must be complete before underlayment can be laid.
Lintels are structural elements placed over openings in walls (doors, windows) to support the load above. The wall must be built up to the height of the opening before the lintel can be positioned.
The lintel must be in place to support the masonry or wall structure that continues above the opening. The load from the wall above bears directly on the lintel.
The lintel provides the top structural support for the opening; door or window frames are installed after the lintel is in place to ensure proper fit and load transfer.

successor: Arch or Decorative Finish Above Opening
rationale: If an architectural feature like an arch or decorative course is planned above the opening, it is typically built after the lintel is installed, though this is a design preference rather than a structural necessity.
If the lintel is cast-in-place concrete, it must cure to sufficient strength before bearing any load from the structure above.

Header beams are typically installed within or above wall openings (such as windows or doors). Wall framing must be completed first to create the rough opening and supporting structure for the header beam.
Header beams provide structural support above door and window openings. Doors and windows cannot be installed until the header beam is in place to carry the load above the opening.
The foundation and slab/floor system must be completed to provide a stable base for the wall framing that supports the header beam.
Exterior wall sheathing is applied over the framed walls including header beams. The header beam must be installed as part of the wall frame before sheathing can be attached.
The header beam material must be fabricated, sourced, and delivered to the jobsite before installation can begin.
Purlins are horizontal members that are installed on top of roof trusses or rafters; the primary roof supporting structure must be in place to provide the bearing surface for purlins.
In steel buildings, purlins are attached to the steel frame (columns and rafters); the main structural frame must be erected first to provide the connection points.
Roof sheathing (plywood, OSB, or metal decking) is fastened directly to purlins; purlins form the substrate onto which the roof deck is attached.
Roof insulation is typically placed between or over purlins; the purlins must be in place to support or enclose the insulation material.
Roof cladding (metal roofing, tiles, etc.) is fastened to the purlins; purlins provide the structural attachment points for the final roof covering.
The flange must be mounted on a stable foundation or pedestal to provide structural support.
Pipes connecting to the flange need to be in place or prepared to ensure proper alignment and connection.
The gasket is placed between flange faces; the flanges must be installed first to provide the mating surfaces.
Bolts secure the flanged connection; flanges must be in position before bolts can be tightened.
After flange assembly with gaskets and bolts, the joint must be tested for leaks under pressure.
The web (a structural component of a building) requires a stable foundation to be built upon before it can be erected.
The roof is typically installed after the main structural web or frame of the building is complete.
Exterior cladding is applied onto the structural web/frame of the building.
Interior walls and partitions are built after the main structural web is in place.
The steel frame or primary structural frame must be erected before the web (secondary structure or infill) can be installed.
Shear connectors are typically welded or bolted to steel beams before concrete placement. The steel beam must be in place first to attach the shear connector.
Shear connectors protrude from the steel beam to embed into the concrete deck; formwork must accommodate these connectors, but the connectors must be in place first to define the formwork layout.
Shear connectors are designed to be encased in concrete to transfer shear forces; concrete placement cannot begin until connectors are installed.
After welding shear connectors, weld quality must be verified through inspection before proceeding to subsequent construction steps.
The steel beam surface must be cleaned and prepared (e.g., removal of rust, debris, and primer) before shear connectors can be welded or attached to ensure proper bond and weld quality.

The beam bearing plate supports the steel beam at its bearing point; the beam must be erected and in position first so that the bearing plate can be placed underneath or at the bearing location to transfer loads properly.

The beam bearing plate is typically anchored to or set on top of a concrete pier, abutment, or column; sufficient curing of the concrete is required to achieve the strength needed to support the plate and the beam loads.
Precise survey and layout of the bearing plate location (elevation and alignment) must be completed before installation to ensure the plate is positioned accurately for beam support.
After the bearing plate is installed at the correct location and elevation, the steel beam can be connected (e.g., bolted or welded) to the plate to complete the load-bearing assembly.

If the plate is set on a concrete support, non-shrink grout is typically pumped or placed under the plate after installation to ensure full bearing and uniform load transfer; grouting cannot be done before the plate is positioned.
End plates are typically welded or bolted to the ends of steel beams; the beam must be fabricated first so the end plate can be attached.
The end plate component itself must be manufactured (cut, drilled, welded) before it can be delivered and installed on site.
End plates are often anchored to concrete foundations or support structures; the foundation must be cured and ready to receive the anchored end plate.
Once the end plate is installed (e.g., anchored to foundation or column), the steel beam can be bolted/welded to it as part of the structural frame erection.
After the end plate is positioned and initial bolts are placed, final bolting and torqueing of the connection can proceed to secure the beam-to-end-plate joint.
The steel beams must be erected and in place before splices can be made between beam sections.
Beam sections must be properly aligned and positioned before splice connections can be executed.
After completing the splice, welded connections must be inspected and tested for quality assurance before any load is applied.
The beam splices must be completed and cured/accepted before deck or formwork loads are placed on the spliced beam.

Splice areas are typically painted or coated after completion to protect the connection; however, some touch-up painting may be done earlier, making this a soft preference rather than a hard constraint.
Columns must be erected and in place before beam-to-column connections can be made, as beams are supported by columns.
Beams must be lifted and positioned between columns before the bolting or welding connection can be executed.
While bolts or welds should ideally be inspected after connection, pre-inspection of bolt materials or welder qualification can precede but is not physically mandatory.
After beams are placed, the connection must be made (bolts inserted or tack welded) before final torqueing or full welding completion can be performed.
The entire beam-to-column connection must be completed so that the steel frame is stable and can be inspected for alignment, plumbness, and connection integrity.
Beams are typically supported by columns, so columns must be erected first to provide structural support for the beams.
Foundations must be completed to provide a stable base for columns and the overall structural frame before beam erection can commence.
Concrete must reach sufficient strength before structural loads from beams can be applied.
Beams form the primary horizontal structural support; slabs or decking are placed on top of or between beams.
Temporary or permanent bracing between beams provides lateral stability and is installed after beams are in place.
Columns must be concreted and cured to provide structural support before beam formwork can be installed.

Beam bottom reinforcement (rebar) must be placed prior to formwork installation because the rebar cage sits within the formwork and the bottom bars need to be positioned before the side forms are erected.
Formwork must be fully installed to provide the mold and support for placing side and top reinforcement bars.
Concrete cannot be poured until the formwork is completely installed, aligned, and secured to contain the wet concrete.
Support scaffolding or falsework must be erected first to provide a stable platform and load-bearing support for the beam formwork.

Formwork must be installed first to create the mold or void into which reinforcement bars (rebar) are placed; reinforcement cannot be positioned without the formwork in place to define the shape and support the bars.
Rebar must be cut and bent to the specified shapes and dimensions before they can be placed into the formwork; placement requires ready-to-install reinforcement materials.
Concrete cannot be poured until all reinforcement steel is properly positioned, tied, and inspected; the rebar must be in place to be encased within the concrete for structural integrity.
After reinforcement is placed, an inspection must be completed to verify correct positioning, spacing, cover, and ties before concrete placement can proceed.

Any conduits, sleeves, or embedded services that pass through the reinforcement must be installed after rebar is placed (or concurrently) but before concrete pouring, as they are embedded within the reinforced concrete element.
Concrete must be poured and placed into forms before curing can begin, as curing is the process of maintaining moisture and temperature conditions for freshly placed concrete to develop strength.
Surface finishing operations (troweling, brooming, etc.) must be completed before curing starts, as curing compounds or wet covering methods would interfere with finishing work.
Formwork must be erected and secured before concrete can be placed into the forms.
Curing must achieve sufficient concrete strength before formwork can be safely removed to prevent structural damage or collapse.

Curing must be complete and concrete must reach specified strength/maturity before any surface-applied finishes, coatings, or toppings can be installed to ensure proper adhesion and avoid entrapped moisture.
Tendons must be installed and positioned within the formwork before post-tensioning can be applied, as the stressing operation requires the tendons to already be in place.
Concrete must be poured and reach sufficient initial strength (typically around 3-7 days of curing) before post-tensioning can begin, as the tendons are tensioned against the hardened concrete.
Formwork must be erected before concrete is placed, which must then be cured before post-tensioning can proceed.
After the tendons have been stressed to the required force, the ducts must be grouted to protect the tendons from corrosion and lock in the prestress force.
Post-tensioning must be completed before formwork can be safely removed, as the structure becomes self-supporting only after the prestress force has been applied to the concrete.
Steel beams must be positioned and secured in place before welding can commence, as welding joins pre-placed beams.
Beams must be properly aligned, leveled, and fitted with gaps set before welding to ensure structural accuracy and weld quality.
Tack welding is used to temporarily hold beams in alignment before the final full-strength welding process.
Welds must be completed before they can be inspected (e.g., ultrasonic or visual inspection) to verify quality and structural integrity.
Final welding must be finished before applying protective coatings or paint, as welding would damage or burn off any pre-applied coating.
Steel beams must be fabricated, cut, and welded to their final dimensions before they can be painted and coated.
The beam surface must be cleaned, derusted, and roughened to ensure proper adhesion of paint and coating systems.
A primer coat must be applied as a base layer before topcoats or final coating systems can be applied.
Beams must be fully painted and coated (corrosion protection) before they are hoisted and installed into the structural frame.
After coating application, sufficient curing or drying time must pass before the coating can be inspected for quality, thickness, and defects.
Concrete must be fully cured to achieve design strength before beams can be inspected for structural integrity.
Formwork must be installed and aligned to create the beam geometry before inspection can verify dimensions and placement.
Steel reinforcement must be placed and tied within the beam formwork before inspection can check cover, spacing, and lap lengths.
Beam inspection must confirm structural adequacy and concrete strength before formwork can be safely removed.
Beam must pass inspection before subsequent concrete pours (e.g., for slabs or upper beams) can proceed, ensuring load-bearing capacity is verified.
Beams must be fabricated and cured before they can be subjected to load testing to verify their structural capacity.
Beams must be installed in their final position before load testing can be conducted to verify performance under design loads.
Temporary support systems must be in place before load testing to ensure safety and proper load distribution during the test.
Load testing results must be completed and documented before the structural engineer can verify compliance and provide final sign-off.

successor: Deck or Slab Placement on Beams
rationale: Load testing must confirm beam capacity before subsequent dead loads (deck/slab) are placed, to avoid overloading untested members.
Engineers must first assess the existing beam condition and calculate load requirements to determine the appropriate repair method and material specifications.
Temporary supports must be installed to safely transfer loads away from the damaged beam before any repair work can commence, ensuring worker safety and structural stability.

predecessor: Removal of Damaged Concrete and Exposed Reinforcement
rationale: Spalled or deteriorated concrete must be removed and reinforcing steel exposed and cleaned to prepare the substrate for repair material application.
New repair materials (e.g., epoxy, mortar, or FRP wraps) must cure and gain sufficient strength before any loads can be reapplied or subsequent finishing work is performed.

successor: Stripping of Formwork and Removal of Temporary Shoring
rationale: Scaffolding and formwork cannot be safely removed until the beam repair is complete and the strengthened member has achieved design strength.

The concrete beams must first be cast and fully cured to achieve sufficient strength and maturity before non-destructive testing (such as ultrasonic pulse velocity, rebound hammer, or ground-penetrating radar) can be performed, as testing on uncured or green concrete would yield inaccurate results and could damage the beam surface.
Formwork must be removed to expose the beam surfaces so that testing equipment (e.g., transducers, hammer, scanner) can make direct contact with the concrete for accurate readings.

Non-destructive testing should be completed first to assess internal integrity, identify voids, cracks, or delaminations, and establish baseline conditions before subjecting the beams to potentially damaging load tests, ensuring safety and proper test interpretation.

Non-destructive testing must be performed while beams are still accessible and in a controlled environment (e.g., precast yard or casting bed) to allow comprehensive scanning from all sides; once installed, access is limited and defects cannot be as easily remedied.

The results of non-destructive testing provide the objective evidence of beam quality and integrity required for formal acceptance documentation and quality sign-off before the beams are incorporated into the permanent structure.
Column base plates must be mounted on a solid foundation or footing to provide a stable load-bearing surface; concrete must be cured to sufficient strength.
Anchor bolts must be embedded and aligned in the foundation prior to placing the column base plate over them for proper positioning and structural connection.
Column base plates serve as the mounting interface; steel columns are welded or bolted onto the base plate after it is positioned and leveled.
Grout is applied under the base plate after it is installed and leveled to fill voids and ensure full bearing transfer to the foundation.
After placing the base plate, its levelness and alignment must be checked before proceeding with column erection to ensure structural accuracy.
Column capital sits atop the column shaft and requires the column formwork to be in place to support its construction
Reinforcement bars must extend into the capital region to provide structural continuity; the capital cannot be placed without reinforcing steel in place
The column shaft must be cast and cured before the capital is formed on top of it
The column capital provides bearing support for beams and slabs; slab formwork rests on or is supported by the capital
Reinforcement for the capital itself must be placed after the capital formwork is set up but prior to concrete pouring
Column reinforcement (rebar cage) must be in place before the column splice connection can be made, as the splice connects the reinforcement of the upper column to the lower column.
The lower column segment must be erected and positioned before the splice connection to the upper column can be performed.
The column splice connects the upper column to the lower column; thus the splice must be completed before the upper column segment can be placed and secured.
Formwork cannot be installed around a column until the column segments are spliced and fully connected in their final position.
If the column splice is welded or bolted, concrete can only be poured after splice completion to ensure structural continuity and stability.
The longitudinal reinforcement bars are placed inside the column formwork, so the formwork must be installed first to provide the containment and positioning for the rebars.
Longitudinal bars (vertical main reinforcement) must be positioned and tied before any lateral ties or stirrups can be placed around them.
Lateral ties or stirrups are placed around the longitudinal bars to confine the concrete and resist shear; they cannot be installed until the longitudinal bars are in place.
All reinforcement (longitudinal bars and ties) must be fully placed and inspected before concrete can be poured to encase the steel.
Inspection of the installed longitudinal reinforcement must occur before proceeding to subsequent steps like concreting to ensure compliance with structural drawings and codes.

Column ties (lateral ties) are wrapped around the main vertical column reinforcement bars to hold them in position and prevent buckling. The main rebars must be installed first so the ties can be placed around them.

Typically, ties are installed before formwork is closed, as formwork encloses the reinforcement cage. However, in some cases formwork may be partially erected; generally reinforcement including ties precedes full formwork closure.
Concrete must be poured after the lateral ties are in place because the ties provide confinement to the core concrete and ensure proper reinforcement positioning during the pour.
Once column ties are installed, the column formwork can be fully closed and secured before concrete placement. The ties must be in place before the formwork is finally closed.
Inspection of the completed reinforcement cage including lateral tie spacing, hooks, and cover requirements must occur before concrete pouring, and after all ties are installed.
The reinforcement cage (rebar) must be in place before casing/encasement can be poured or installed, as the rebar provides the structural strength within the concrete encasement.
Formwork must be erected and secured around the rebar to contain and shape the concrete casing before pouring can begin.
After the concrete casing is poured, it must undergo a curing period (time for the concrete to gain strength) before any subsequent loads or finishing work can be applied.
The concrete casing must be poured and gain sufficient initial set strength before the formwork can be safely removed (stripped).

Once the casing is poured and cured, surface treatments such as plastering, painting, or waterproofing can be applied; this is a soft preference because some finishing may be done later in the schedule but typically follows casing completion.

The column reinforcement must be installed before the corbel can be cast, as the corbel is typically cast monolithically with or after the column, and its reinforcement needs to be tied into the column cage.
Column formwork must be in place before the corbel can be formed, as the corbel projects from the column and requires the column formwork to be set to define its position and shape.

If the corbel is cast separately, the column below the corbel must be poured and cured first to provide a stable base; if monolithic, the column and corbel are poured together but the column portion is still essential prior in the same pour sequence.
The corbel must be fully cured and achieve sufficient strength before any beam or structural element is placed on it, as the corbel acts as a load-bearing support ledge.
The corbel concrete must be sufficiently cured before formwork can be stripped to prevent damage to the projecting element and ensure structural integrity.
The column haunch is a reinforced concrete element that requires the column reinforcement to be in place before concrete can be poured for the haunch.
Formwork must be erected around the column at the haunch location to contain and shape the concrete pour for the haunch.
The column haunch provides the bearing surface and support for beams or slabs; thus slab/beam formwork can only be installed after the haunch is complete and cured.
After pouring the column haunch, sufficient curing time must be allowed for the concrete to gain strength before any loads are applied.
If a steel beam bears on the haunch, the haunch must be fully cured and hardened to provide a stable bearing surface before the beam is placed.

Anchor bolts must be embedded in the foundation concrete while it is still wet or set into the cured foundation; typically they are positioned and set before the concrete hardens, meaning the foundation concrete must be placed and cured enough to hold the bolts in position.
Anchor bolts must be installed and secured in the foundation before a steel column can be erected on top of them and bolted down.
The exact locations for anchor bolts must be marked and surveyed according to foundation plans before the bolts can be set in place.
A steel column requires a structural foundation (concrete footing or slab) to support its load and provide a level, stable base for erection.
Anchor bolts embedded in the foundation must be set and cured before the column base plate can be bolted down to secure the column.
The exact column centerline and grid location must be surveyed and marked on the foundation to ensure the column is placed in the correct position.
Steel beams and girders frame into the columns at connections; the column must be erected and plumbed before beams can be attached to its web or flange.
Permanent or temporary bracing between columns can only be installed after columns are in place to provide lateral stability to the frame.
The foundation provides the structural base and anchorage for the HSS column; without a completed foundation, the column has no support or load-bearing surface to stand on.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and prepared to allow access for cranes and equipment needed to erect HSS columns.
Underground utilities (drainage, electrical conduits, water lines) must be placed before columns are installed to avoid conflicts and the need to work around vertical structural elements.
Beams and girders frame into or connect to the HSS column at designated connection points; the column must be erected and fixed in place before any horizontal members can be attached.
Cross-bracing or lateral bracing systems connect to the column to provide stability; these cannot be installed until the column is in place.

successor: Floor Deck / Slab on Steel Frame
rationale: The HSS column supports floor levels above; the floor deck and concrete slab can only be poured or placed after the supporting columns and beams are erected.
Fireproofing spray or encasement is applied to the HSS column after it is fully installed and connected, as the coating requires access to all surfaces and must not be damaged during erection.

Although cladding can technically be sequenced differently, it is standard practice to erect the structural frame including HSS columns before attaching facade panels or curtain walls for dimensional accuracy and alignment.
Formwork provides the mold that shapes the composite column, so it must be installed before the column can be cast or assembled.
Steel reinforcement cage must be placed within the formwork before the composite column (concrete/grout) is poured to ensure structural integrity.
Beams and slabs typically bear on or connect to columns; the column must be erected and cured before transferring loads from beams or slabs.
Formwork around the composite column cannot be removed until the column concrete has gained sufficient strength to be self-supporting.
The composite column requires a load-bearing foundation or footing to support its weight and transfer loads, so foundations must be completed first.
Reinforced concrete columns transfer loads to the foundation; the foundation must be in place and cured to provide a stable base and load-bearing support for the column.
Steel reinforcement cage must be assembled, tied, and placed within the column formwork before concrete is poured to ensure proper structural reinforcement.
Formwork (shuttering) must be erected and braced to contain the wet concrete and shape the column; concrete cannot be poured without forms in place.
After pouring, the concrete column must undergo a curing period to achieve adequate strength before any loads are applied or formwork is removed.
Column forms can only be removed after the concrete has sufficiently cured and gained strength to be self-supporting.
Columns support beams and slabs above; beams and slabs cannot be constructed until the columns below are poured and cured to carry the load.

Surface finishing and plastering are typically done after the column is fully cured but often before major vertical loads from upper floors are applied, though this is a construction sequence preference rather than a strict physical necessity.
Foundations must be prepared and cured to support the load of precast concrete columns before they can be erected.
Column footings or foundation pads must be in place and leveled to provide a stable base for precast column installation.
Precast concrete columns must be manufactured, cured, and delivered to the site before they can be erected.
Beams and joists typically bear on or connect to columns, requiring columns to be in place first.
Splices and connections between stacked or adjacent columns can only be completed after columns are erected and aligned.
The timber column/post requires a stable and level foundation or footing to bear its load and prevent settlement or tilting.
Primary beams/girders typically rest on or connect to columns/posts, so the vertical support must be in place before horizontal structural members are installed.
Temporary or permanent bracing and shear walls provide lateral stability to the column/post frame and must be added after columns are erected but before full loading.
The roof structure bears on columns/posts (via beams/trusses), so columns must be erected to provide vertical support for the roof system.
While not a strict structural necessity, wall cladding typically follows column installation to enclose the building; the column frame provides the support surface for cladding attachment.
A slender column requires a stable foundation to bear its load and resist buckling; the foundation must be in place before column erection can begin.
The reinforcement cage must be assembled and positioned within the column formwork before concrete can be poured to create the slender column element.
Formwork must be erected and aligned to the correct position and plumbness before concrete is placed to contain the wet concrete and shape the slender column.

Concrete must cure and achieve sufficient strength before formwork can be safely removed to avoid damaging the slender column, particularly important for slender elements prone to cracking or instability.
The slender column must be fully erected, aligned, and capable of carrying vertical loads before any beams or slabs that rest on or are supported by the column can be constructed.
Short columns rest on top of the plinth beam or foundation; the foundation must be completed to provide a stable base.
The rebar cage for the short column must be tied and placed before concrete can be poured into the formwork.
Short columns define the top of the plinth level; backfilling and plinth filling are done up to the top of the short column.

successor: Ground Floor Slab / Floor Beam Construction
rationale: The ground floor slab or floor beams are cast on top of or tying into the short columns; the short columns must be completed to support the slab framework.
DPC is often applied at plinth level (top of short column) to prevent moisture rise; this is a standard practice but not always a hard sequential dependency if other methods are used.
The corner column requires a stable foundation to bear its load; foundation must be completed before any vertical structural element is erected.
The base plate anchors the column to the foundation and must be in place before the column itself can be positioned and secured.
Beams that frame into the corner column require the column to be erected first as a support point before they can be connected.
The column must be in place before its vertical alignment can be verified and adjusted.
Temporary or permanent bracing relies on the column being erected to provide a structure to brace against.
Edge columns require a stable foundation or pile cap to transfer loads to the ground; the column cannot be erected without a finished base.

predecessor: Rebar Cage Fabrication & Placement for Edge Column
rationale: Reinforcement steel must be tied and positioned within the column formwork before concrete is poured.
Formwork (shuttering) must be assembled and braced to give the concrete its shape and support until it cures.
Edge beams and slabs bear on edge columns; the column must reach sufficient strength before supporting these horizontal members.
Formwork cannot be removed until the column concrete has cured to the required strength, ensuring structural integrity.
Interior columns require a stable foundation to transfer loads to the ground; columns cannot be erected without an existing foundation system.

predecessor: Slab on Grade / Ground Floor Slab
rationale: The ground floor slab or base must be poured and cured to provide a level working surface and embedment for column reinforcement dowels.
Steel reinforcement cages must be pre-assembled and placed within the column formwork before concrete can be poured for the column.
Interior columns support beams and floor slabs above; these structural elements cannot be placed until the column is erected and cured to bear the load.

While partition walls can technically begin after columns are erected, this is a soft preference because sequencing may allow some non-load-bearing walls to be framed earlier for efficiency, though typically columns precede walls for structural integrity.
Rebar cage must be in place before formwork can be erected around it, as formwork encloses the reinforcement.
Formwork provides the mold that shapes and contains the wet concrete; concrete cannot be poured until the formwork is complete and secured.
Formwork must be in place before it can be removed after the concrete has cured.
The installation process itself must be completed before the formwork is considered 'in place' and ready for concrete.
While column formwork is typically erected before slab formwork to support it, in some sequences they can be done concurrently; this is a soft preference for sequential work to avoid access issues.
General setting out of the building grid and reference lines must be completed before specific column positions can be marked out, as columns are located based on the established grid lines.
The site must be cleared and excavated to the required formation level so that the column positions can be physically marked on the prepared ground surface.
Column positions must be marked out before reinforcement bars can be placed, as the reinforcement must align with the designated column locations.
The column layout must be completed before formwork can be erected, as formwork panels are positioned based on the marked column outlines.
Column positions must be set out before concrete can be poured, ensuring the column is cast in the correct location as per the structural drawings.
The column position and alignment must be marked on the slab before any rebar can be placed, otherwise the rebar would not be positioned correctly.

Typically column rebar is fixed first, then formwork is installed around it. If formwork is installed first, it would obstruct rebar placement. However, some sequences install one side of formwork first; generally rebar precedes formwork.

Column reinforcement must be fully tied and in place before the formwork is closed, because the formwork encases the rebar and cannot be installed after the rebar is in place (unless one side is left open).
Concrete cannot be poured until all rebar is fixed and inspected, as the rebar provides the structural reinforcement that must be embedded within the concrete.
Rebar fixing must be complete before the inspection can take place, as the inspector needs to verify the full rebar cage, lap lengths, cover, and ties before concrete is poured.
Steel reinforcement cage must be installed and tied before concrete can be poured; concrete needs the rebar to provide tensile strength and structural integrity.
Formwork (molds) must be erected around the rebar cage to contain and shape the wet concrete during pouring and curing.
Concrete must be poured and achieve sufficient initial set/strength before formwork can be safely removed without damaging the column.
Curing (keeping concrete moist and at proper temperature) begins immediately after concrete placement to ensure proper hydration and strength development.

While structurally columns can be cast and then slabs built on top, in many sequences slab formwork is supported by column shores; however this is often a soft/logical preference depending on the construction method (e.g., simultaneous vs. sequential).
Reinforcement cage must be assembled and tied in position before formwork can be erected around it, as the rebar is enclosed within the formwork.
Formwork must be fully erected, aligned, and secured to contain the wet concrete during the pour; concrete cannot be poured without the mould in place.
Formwork stripping (removal) can only occur after the concrete has been poured and has reached sufficient strength, but the erection of formwork obviously precedes stripping.
Inspection and approval of the placed reinforcement must be completed before formwork is erected, as the formwork would block access to verify rebar placement and cover.
In typical construction sequences, columns are poured after adjacent slab/beam formwork is prepared to ensure continuity and support; columns support beams so beam formwork is often erected first.
Column steel requires a stable base; foundations must be cured and ready to support the vertical load and anchorage of steel columns.
Anchor bolts embedded in the foundation provide the connection point for steel column base plates; they must be set, aligned, and grouted before columns can be erected.
Column centerlines and grid lines must be accurately surveyed and marked on the foundation to ensure correct positioning of steel columns.
Beams and girders span between columns; columns must be erected and temporarily braced before beams can be placed and connected.
After columns are set in position, the bolted connections (base plates, splice plates) must be tightened and torqued to achieve structural integrity before additional loads are applied.
Columns must be placed and aligned in their final position before welding can begin, as welding permanently joins column sections or connects columns to base plates.
Tack welding or temporary bolting is required to hold column pieces in alignment before the final continuous welding process is performed.
Welding edges must be cleaned of rust, oil, and debris, and bevels/grooves must be prepared to ensure proper weld penetration and quality.
Non-destructive testing (ultrasonic, magnetic particle, or radiographic inspection) can only be performed after welding is complete to verify weld integrity and detect defects.
Excess weld material (reinforcement) must be ground down and surfaces finished only after the welding pass is completed.
The column must be cast and cured with concrete before load testing can be performed, as the test applies stress to the hardened concrete element.
Formwork must be installed to shape and support the column concrete prior to testing.
Steel reinforcement must be placed and tied within the column before concreting and subsequent load testing.
After load testing, any cracks or defects discovered may need finishing or repair, but this is a soft preference as finishing could also be done before testing if no damage is expected.
Load testing must be completed and passed before the column can be formally accepted as meeting structural design requirements.

Column reinforcement (rebar cage) must be installed before plumbing and alignment, as the rebar defines the structural framework that the column must be aligned to, and plumbing activities (setting vertical alignment and positioning) require the reinforcement to be in place to check cover and positioning.

Column formwork (shuttering) must be erected prior to plumbing and alignment, because the plumbing and alignment process involves adjusting the formwork to ensure the column is vertically plumb and correctly positioned on the grid.

Concreting can only commence after the column is plumbed and aligned, because pouring concrete into misaligned or out-of-plumb formwork would result in a defective column that cannot be corrected after the concrete sets.
Proper curing can only begin after concreting, which itself requires plumbing and alignment to be completed first; curing is the subsequent step in the sequence.
Formwork can only be struck (removed) after the concrete has been placed and cured, and both depend on the column being correctly plumbed and aligned first.

A full structural assessment and condition survey must be completed to identify the extent of damage, concrete spalling, reinforcement corrosion, and load-bearing capacity before any repair work can be designed and executed on the column.
Safe working access at height around the column must be erected before repair and strengthening work can commence.
Temporary shoring must be installed to relieve load on the column during repair, ensuring structural safety during the strengthening process.

If the column has spalled or deteriorated concrete, the damaged concrete must be broken out prior to applying repair mortar or strengthening wraps; however, this is part of the repair process itself and may be considered a sub-activity rather than a separate preceding activity.
Flat slabs are supported by columns or shear walls, which must be constructed first to provide vertical support.
Formwork (soffit formwork or table forms) must be erected to provide the mold and temporary support for the flat slab concrete before pouring.
Steel reinforcement bars or mesh must be placed within the formwork before the concrete slab is poured.
After pouring, the flat slab concrete must be cured to achieve design strength before any subsequent loads are applied.
Columns for the next storey are typically constructed on top of the completed flat slab, as the slab provides the working platform and load distribution for the upper columns.

Waffle slab requires a formwork or mould system (typically dome-shaped or waffle pods) to be installed first to create the voided grid pattern. Without the formwork, the concrete cannot be shaped into the waffle configuration.

Steel reinforcement bars and mesh must be placed within the formwork before pouring the concrete. The reinforcement provides tensile strength to the slab and is embedded within the concrete during pouring.
After pouring the waffle slab, the concrete must undergo a curing period to achieve the required strength before any construction loads are applied or subsequent activities commence.
