The formwork/pods can only be removed after the waffle slab concrete has sufficiently cured and gained adequate strength to be self-supporting. Removing formwork too early could cause slab collapse or cracking.

Waterproofing is typically applied after the slab is fully cured. This is a soft preference because waterproofing could be delayed further but should not be done before the slab is complete and cured.
Hollow-core slabs are typically supported by structural steel beams or load-bearing walls; the steel frame must be erected first to provide the supporting structure for the slabs.

predecessor: Foundation and Ground Floor Slab Completion
rationale: The hollow-core slab installation for upper floors requires that the ground floor or substructure is complete to provide a stable base and staging area for crane and material placement.
After hollow-core slabs are placed, a structural concrete topping or grouting between slab joints must be applied to ensure diaphragm action, load distribution, and composite structural behavior.

While MEP services can sometimes run below the slab, it is preferable to complete hollow-core slab installation first so that mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work can be coordinated and installed without interfering with slab placement sequencing.

successor: Floor Finishing and Partition Wall Construction
rationale: The hollow-core slabs form the structural floor deck; partition walls and floor finishes cannot be installed until the structural slab is in place and the topping has cured.
Formwork provides the temporary mold and support structure that shapes and holds the wet concrete for the post-tensioned slab until it cures and gains sufficient strength.
Reinforcing steel (rebar) must be placed within the formwork before concrete is poured, as it provides structural reinforcement and must be embedded within the slab.

Post-tensioning tendons (steel cables within ducts) must be positioned and anchored within the formwork before the concrete is placed, as they are embedded in the slab and tensioned after the concrete reaches sufficient strength.

Post-tensioning (tensioning/stressing of the cables) can only begin after the concrete slab has been poured and has cured to achieve the required compressive strength to withstand the prestressing forces.
Formwork cannot be stripped until the post-tensioned slab has been poured, cured, and post-tensioned (stressed), as the slab must be self-supporting before the temporary supports are removed.
Composite slabs typically require steel beams or metal decking as a supporting substructure before the slab can be placed.
The metal deck acts as both formwork and reinforcement for the composite slab; it must be installed before concrete is poured.
Shear studs must be welded to the steel beams through the deck to ensure composite action between steel and concrete before the slab is cast.
After the composite slab is poured, sufficient curing time is required for the concrete to gain strength before any loads are applied.
Upper floor construction or wall erection cannot begin until the composite slab has been placed and cured, as the slab provides the working platform and structural support for the next level.
Formwork must be installed and leveled to provide the mold and support for the concrete of the ribbed slab before pouring can begin.
Steel reinforcement bars and mesh must be placed within the formwork to provide tensile strength before concrete is poured for the ribbed slab.
After the ribbed slab is poured, a curing period must be observed to allow the concrete to reach sufficient strength before any loads are applied or further construction proceeds.
The ribbed slab concrete must be sufficiently cured and hardened before the supporting formwork can be safely removed to prevent collapse or damage.
The ribbed slab must be completed and cured to provide the working platform and load-bearing surface for constructing vertical elements on the next story or adjacent areas.
The raised access floor slab must be installed on top of a completed structural slab or base floor to provide a stable and level substrate.

Underfloor mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) services must be laid out on the structural slab before the raised access floor is installed, as after installation these services become inaccessible without lifting panels.

successor: Floor Covering / Finishing (e.g., carpet tiles, vinyl)
rationale: The final floor finish is applied on top of the completed raised access floor system and cannot be installed until the raised floor panels are in place and leveled.

While partitions can sometimes be built directly on the structural slab before the raised floor, it is generally preferred to complete the raised floor first to allow consistent level references and easier MEP access coordination.
Furniture and room fit-out typically occurs after the raised floor is complete to avoid damaging the access floor system and to provide a finished walking surface.
The ground must be cleared, excavated, and leveled before a ground-bearing slab can be poured, as the slab rests directly on the prepared subgrade.

The subgrade soil must be compacted to the required density and prepared (including any hardcore fill or blinding layer) to provide a stable, uniform base for the slab; otherwise the slab would crack or settle unevenly.
A damp-proof membrane (or vapor barrier) must be laid over the prepared subgrade before the concrete slab is poured to prevent moisture migration from the ground into the slab.
The ground-bearing slab provides the structural floor and working platform upon which load-bearing walls or the superstructure are erected; walls cannot be safely built without a completed slab.

successor: Underfloor Services / Ductwork (if laid in slab)
rationale: Any underfloor services such as drainage pipes, conduits, or ducts that are embedded within or pass beneath the slab must be installed before the concrete is poured; however, once the slab is cast, any above-slab services or finishes can follow.
Formwork must be erected to provide the temporary mold and support structure for the wet concrete of the suspended slab before pouring can commence.
Steel reinforcement bars must be placed and tied within the formwork before concrete is poured to provide tensile strength to the suspended slab.

Electrical conduits, plumbing sleeves, and other embedded services must be positioned within the formwork and reinforcement before concrete pouring, as they cannot be installed after the slab is cast.
After pouring, the suspended slab concrete must undergo a curing period to achieve design strength before any construction loads or subsequent activities can be applied.
Formwork and shoring can only be removed after the concrete has cured to sufficient strength (as per design specifications) to be self-supporting.
The formwork supporting the slab must be removed to allow erection of columns, walls, or other vertical elements that bear on or rise above the completed suspended slab.
The topping slab is a secondary layer poured on top of the structural slab; the structural slab must be fully cured and load-bearing to provide a stable base for the topping slab.
The structural slab must reach sufficient strength before the topping slab can be placed to avoid cracking or structural failure.
Floor finishes such as tiles, screed, or coating are applied onto the topping slab surface; the topping slab provides the final flat substrate.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing installations that sit on or above the slab surface typically follow after the topping slab is complete; however, some in-slab conduits are placed before.
Interior walls bear on the finished slab; the topping slab must be in place to provide a level bearing surface for wall framing.
Precast slab panels require a stable, level foundation or substructure (e.g., beams, columns, walls) to bear on. Without completed support structure, the panels cannot be placed safely or accurately.
Precast slab panels are heavy and require a crane or lifting equipment to be erected and positioned on site before the panels can be unloaded and installed.

After precast slab panels are placed, the connections between panels and supporting structure (e.g., grouting of pockets, welding of inserts, bolting) must be completed to ensure structural continuity and load transfer.

A topping slab or screed is often poured over precast slab panels to achieve a level finished floor surface and composite action; this cannot occur until the precast panels are fully installed and connections are secured.

While some MEP (mechanical, electrical, plumbing) work can proceed concurrently, final routing and installation of services above the slab (e.g., conduit, piping, ducts) is typically sequenced after the slab panels are in place to avoid conflicts and to use the completed slab as a working platform.
The formwork provides the mold and support structure for the slab; reinforcement bars (rebar) must be placed on top of the formwork before concrete is poured.
Reinforcement steel must be fully placed, tied, and inspected before concrete can be poured to ensure the rebar is properly positioned within the slab.
Vertical structural elements (columns/walls) need their reinforcement extended into the slab area; these must be completed to allow slab rebar to be tied into them.
While conduits are often laid before slab rebar or interleaved with it, the bulk of conduit work should follow the bottom layer of reinforcement to ensure proper cover and positioning.
Edge forms define the slab perimeter and must be in place so that reinforcement can be cut and placed to the correct dimensions within the slab boundaries.

predecessor: Formwork Installation for Slab Edge Beam
successor: Concrete Pouring for Slab Edge Beam
rationale: Formwork must be installed and secured before concrete can be poured to contain and shape the concrete.

predecessor: Rebar/Steel Reinforcement Placement for Slab Edge Beam
successor: Concrete Pouring for Slab Edge Beam
rationale: Reinforcement steel must be placed and tied within the formwork before concrete is poured to ensure structural integrity.

predecessor: Concrete Pouring for Slab Edge Beam
successor: Concrete Curing for Slab Edge Beam
rationale: Freshly poured concrete must undergo a curing period to gain sufficient strength before any subsequent loads or activities are applied.

predecessor: Concrete Curing for Slab Edge Beam
successor: Formwork Stripping for Slab Edge Beam
rationale: Formwork cannot be removed until the concrete has cured to a minimum required strength to support its own weight and avoid damage.

successor: Masonry or Façade Work Above Beam
rationale: The slab edge beam must be fully cured and capable of bearing load before any wall, façade, or vertical construction is built above or attached to it.
Drop panels are typically cast integrally with or supported by columns/walls; vertical structural supports must be in place before drop panel formwork and reinforcement can be installed.
Drop panel formwork is usually part of the slab formwork system or requires the slab formwork to be set first to establish the correct elevation and support.
Drop panel serves as a thickened section around columns; bottom slab reinforcement often passes through or rests on the drop panel, so the drop panel must be cast first.

Drop panels are typically poured monolithically with the slab, or they must be completed first as they are at the slab base; the slab concrete pour follows after drop panel reinforcement and formwork are in place.
Post-tensioning tendons are stressed after the concrete has gained sufficient strength; the drop panel (being part of the slab) must be cast and cured before post-tensioning operations.
Formwork provides the mold/shuttering that shapes and supports the concrete slab soffit until it cures; without formwork in place, the soffit cannot be formed.
Steel rebar must be placed and tied within the formwork before concrete is poured for the slab soffit; the reinforcement gives the soffit its structural strength.

All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing sleeves, conduits, and embedments that pass through the slab must be positioned and secured before the concrete pour; otherwise they cannot be installed after the soffit is cast.
After the slab soffit concrete is poured and finished, it must cure to sufficient strength before the supporting formwork can be safely removed.

Typically, waterproofing membranes or topping screeds are applied over the cured slab soffit (or the slab top surface), but this can be scheduled with some flexibility depending on weather and subsequent trades.
The slab must be cast and cured to sufficient strength before any cutting, coring, or forming of openings can be performed, as the slab provides the structural substrate.

Reinforcement must be in place (and openings coordinated with rebar layout) before slab pouring; if openings are formed post-pour, the rebar layout must still be known and may need to be cut or relocated, but the slab must exist first.
Formwork defines the slab geometry; any formed openings (blockouts) must be placed within the formwork prior to concrete pour, or the slab must be cast and stripped before cutting openings.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems that pass through the slab require the openings to exist before their pipes, conduits, or ducts can be routed through the slab.
Waterproofing around penetrations must be applied after the opening is created to seal the gap between the penetrating element and the slab edge.
Shear stud connectors are welded onto steel beams; the beams must be in place before studs can be installed.
Shear studs are embedded into the concrete deck to create composite action; the studs must be installed before the concrete is poured over them.
In some sequences, metal decking is placed after studs are welded through the deck; however, this can vary by design, so it is a soft preference based on typical order.

predecessor: Surface Preparation / Cleaning of Steel Beam
rationale: The beam surface must be clean and free of rust, paint, or debris to ensure proper weld quality for shear stud attachment.
Load testing should occur after composite action is achieved via studs and cured concrete, but this is a quality assurance preference rather than a strict physical constraint.
Concrete must be poured and sufficiently cured to gain enough strength to support itself before the formwork can be safely removed.
Reinforcement steel must be placed and tied within the formwork before concrete is poured, and striking can only occur after the concrete has cured.
The formwork must first be installed and erected to shape and support the wet concrete; striking is the removal of this formwork after curing.
Once the formwork is struck, the slab soffit becomes accessible for any required finishing work such as patching, grinding, or coating.

The striking of slab formwork frees the area below for reuse of formwork materials and allows vertical extension above, but more importantly, the slab must be self-supporting before construction of subsequent floors can proceed.
Tendons must be placed and threaded through the ducting before they can be stressed.
Concrete must be poured and achieve sufficient strength to resist the compressive forces induced by post-tensioning stressing.
The concrete must reach its required compressive strength (typically 75-100% of design strength) before stressing can safely occur without damaging the concrete element.
After stressing, the ducts must be grouted to protect the tendons from corrosion and to bond them to the concrete section.
In some staged construction sequences, partial stressing is completed before releasing or transferring stress to other elements, though this is sequence-specific.
The structure must be post-tensioned to become self-supporting before formwork and falsework can be safely removed.
Slab curing can only begin after the concrete has been poured and placed in the formwork; curing is the process of maintaining moisture and temperature conditions immediately following placement.
Initial finishing and floating of the concrete slab surface must be completed before curing begins, as curing starts after the finishing operations are done.
Formwork must be installed and secured prior to pouring and curing the slab to contain the concrete during placement and the initial curing period.
Formwork cannot be removed until the concrete has achieved sufficient strength through proper curing, typically after a minimum curing period.
Waterproofing or sealant application must wait until the slab has fully cured and dried to the required moisture content, otherwise the coating will not bond properly.
The concrete slab must be poured and cured to sufficient hardness before grinding/levelling can commence, otherwise the surface would not be stable enough for grinding.
Grinding and levelling must be completed to create a smooth, even substrate before any floor coating or epoxy can be applied.
The concrete surface must be level and smooth before tile or stone flooring can be installed to ensure proper adhesion and avoid cracking.
Coarse grinding/levelling is the preparatory step that must be completed before the finer polishing stages can begin.

The concrete slab must be cast and sufficiently cured (gained enough strength) before non-destructive testing can be performed. If tested too early while concrete is still green, results will be unreliable and the testing equipment may not yield valid readings.
Formwork and shoring must be removed to provide unobstructed access to the slab surfaces required for non-destructive testing.

successor: Slab Surface Repair and Finishing (if required)
rationale: Test results may identify areas of delamination or voids that require remedial repairs before final finishing; however, this is a soft preference as not all NDT results necessarily require follow-up repairs.
Non-destructive testing should be completed before any destructive or load testing to establish baseline conditions and avoid confounding results.
Non-destructive testing is part of the quality assurance process that must be completed and documented before the slab can be formally inspected and handed over to the client.
Columns must be in place to provide vertical support and load-bearing structure before precast slabs can be placed on top of them.
Foundations must be fully cured and ready to transfer loads from columns and slabs to the ground before any superstructure elements like precast slabs are installed.
Support beams or girders must be in position to provide bearing surfaces and support for precast slabs.
After slabs are placed, the gaps and connections between adjacent slabs must be grouted and sealed to ensure structural continuity and waterproofing.

A topping or screed layer is often applied over precast slabs to create a level finished floor surface, but this is a preference based on design rather than a strict physical necessity for structural safety.
The rough opening (framed hole in the wall) must be prepared and sized correctly before the window frame can be set into place.
Sheathing provides structural support and a backing surface; the window frame is installed into the sheathed opening.
The weather-resistive barrier is typically installed before the window frame to ensure proper flashing integration and water tightness around the opening.
The frame structure must be securely in place before the glass panes or sashes can be inserted and sealed.
Flashing and sealant work around the window frame cannot be completed until the frame is physically installed in the opening.
Interior finishes around the window, such as drywall, plaster, and trim, require the window frame to be in place to establish finished edges and reveals.
Exterior siding is installed after the window frame so that siding can be trimmed and detailed around the frame for weatherproofing and aesthetics.
The rough opening (framed and sheathed window hole) must be prepared and structurally ready before a window sash can be installed into it.
The window frame (jambs, head, sill) must be installed in the rough opening first, as the sash is the operable part that fits within and is supported by the frame.
The weather resistive barrier (house wrap or building paper) must be applied to the exterior wall before installing the window sash to ensure proper flashing and water management integration.
Interior window trim and casing are installed after the sash is in place to cover the gap between the frame and the wall finish.
Exterior flashing, caulking, and final weather sealing around the window occur after the sash is installed to create a watertight enclosure.
The rough opening for the window must be framed and prepared (header, jambs, rough sill) before the window sill can be installed, as the sill sits on or within the rough opening structure.
The window sill is typically installed first to provide a level base and support for the window frame, which sits directly on top of or against the sill.
Flashing and weatherproofing membranes are applied around the sill afterward to seal the joint between the sill and the wall opening, preventing water infiltration.

predecessor: Exterior Wall Sheathing and Weather Barrier
rationale: The exterior wall sheathing and weather-resistant barrier must be in place before installing the window sill so that the sill can be properly integrated with the building envelope and flashed.

Interior casing and trim are typically installed after the window sill is in place to cover the gap between the sill and the interior wall finish, though this is a construction sequencing preference rather than a physical necessity.
The rough opening must be framed and prepared before the window head (the top horizontal member of a window frame) can be installed, as the window head sits within the rough opening.
The window sill (bottom horizontal member) is typically installed first to provide a base, then the jambs and head are assembled; the head closes the top of the frame.
Vertical jambs are usually installed before the head to support it; the head spans across the top of the jambs to complete the window frame.
The window head (top frame member) must be in place before the glass panes are inserted, as the head forms part of the frame that holds the glazing.
The window head must be installed before head flashing can be applied over it to prevent water infiltration at the top of the window assembly.
The rough opening must be framed before window jamb installation because the window jamb needs a structurally prepared opening to be set into.
Weatherproofing membrane or house wrap should be installed before the window jamb to ensure proper moisture management and sealing around the opening.
The window jamb forms the frame that holds the window sash; the sash cannot be installed until the jamb is in place.
Exterior trim and casing are applied around the installed window jamb to finish the opening and provide a weather-tight seal.
Interior drywall can be finished up to the window jamb after it is installed, though this is a typical sequencing preference rather than a physical impossibility.
The rough opening must be framed in the wall to provide the structural support and cavity into which the window mullion will be installed.
Mullions provide the vertical or horizontal divider between window units; window frames (sashes) are installed against or around the mullion components.
Glass panes are placed into the frame openings which are defined and separated by the mullions; mullions must be in place to support and divide the glass.
Wall sheathing provides the structural diaphragm and backing surface; mullions are typically mounted onto or within the sheathed wall opening.
Weatherproofing and flashing must be applied after mullions are installed to seal the transitions between mullion, frame, and wall opening against water intrusion.
The rough opening framing must be completed to provide the structural support and void into which the window transom will be installed.
The transom must be in place before sealing and flashing can be applied around its perimeter to ensure weatherproofing.
Interior trim and casing around the transom can only be installed after the transom itself is securely placed in the opening.
Exterior siding or façade work around the transom area must follow transom installation to properly integrate and seal the unit.
Interior painting and finishing can follow transom installation as a logical sequence, though in some schedules painting may be done beforehand and touched up later.
Window rough openings must be framed and prepared before any window hardware can be installed.
Exterior sheathing must be in place to provide a mounting surface and weather barrier for window installation.
The window frame (including sash and glass) must be installed before window hardware such as locks, hinges, handles, and operators can be mounted onto it.
After window hardware is installed, final sealing, weatherstripping, and glazing work can be completed to ensure proper operation and weather tightness.

Interior trim, drywall finishing, and painting around windows are typically done after hardware installation to avoid damaging the hardware, though this is a scheduling preference for quality and cleanliness rather than a strict physical necessity.
The window lock must be mounted onto the window frame; without the frame in place, there is no structural support for the lock.
The locking mechanism engages with the window sash; the sash must be installed before the lock can be positioned and aligned correctly.
The locking mechanism must be fully installed before testing can verify that the window opens, closes, and locks properly.
While weatherstripping can be partially installed before the lock, final fitting around the lock is easier and more effective after the locking mechanism is in place to ensure a proper seal.
Inspection of the complete window assembly, including verification that the locking mechanism functions correctly and meets security requirements, can only occur after installation is complete.
Window hinges must be attached to a stable window frame; the frame must be installed first to provide the structural support and mounting surface for the hinge.
The hinge must be mounted on the frame before the window sash (the moving part of the window) can be attached to it.
Hinges must be fully installed and secured before the window can be opened and closed for functional testing.

predecessor: Wall Framing and Rough Opening Preparation
rationale: The rough opening in the wall must be framed and ready before the window frame (and consequently its hinges) can be positioned and installed.
Hinges must be installed before final trim and weatherstripping are applied around the operable window components to ensure proper alignment and seal.
Wall sheathing provides the structural substrate onto which window flashing and window units are installed; without sheathing, there is no surface to secure the flashing to.
The rough opening must be framed and sized correctly before any window or flashing can be placed; the flashing is applied around the opening.
Window flashing is applied to the rough opening before the window unit is inserted to direct water away and prevent moisture intrusion; the window sits on top of or within the flashed opening.
Exterior cladding typically overlaps the window flashing to create a weather-tight seal; siding is installed after flashing is in place so that water shed by the siding is directed over the flashing.

While interior finishing can technically proceed after windows are installed and flashed, it is a soft preference to complete window flashing before interior work to ensure the building envelope is watertight before enclosing the interior.
Window frames and sashes must be installed and secured in the rough opening before trim/casing can be applied around them, as the casing is fastened to the window frame and the surrounding wall.
Exterior wall surfaces (sheathing, weather barrier, siding) must be complete so that the trim has a solid, finished surface to mount against and to ensure proper weather sealing.
Drywall must be hung and finished (taped, mudded, sanded) around the window opening before interior casing can be installed, as casing covers the gap between the window frame and drywall.

While painting can be done before or after casing, it is common practice to install casing first and then paint/caulk it along with the walls for a cleaner finished look; however, some painters prefer to paint walls first and then install pre-painted trim.

Casing is typically installed before flooring to allow flooring materials (especially hardwood or tile) to run slightly under the casing for a clean transition, but this is a preference as flooring can also be installed first with casing fitted over it.
Window screens are installed into window openings that must first be framed and sheathed to provide the structural support and rough opening needed to mount the screen assembly.
The window frame and glass must be installed first so the screen has a track or frame to sit into; screens are typically the last component added to a window assembly.

It is preferable but not strictly required to install screens before interior finishes to avoid damage to finished surfaces during screen installation, though screens can be installed after if careful.
Siding安装 around the window must be completed after the window screen is in place to ensure proper integration with the window assembly and to provide weather sealing and flashing continuity.
Weatherproofing and flashing around the window opening must be completed before the screen is installed to prevent water intrusion behind the screen assembly.
The window frame and rough opening must be in place to provide a mounting surface and properly sized opening for the blind/shade.
Glass must be installed to enclose the window opening; blinds/shades are mounted inside the finished window unit.
Interior walls must be finished and painted so that the blind/shade mounting brackets can be properly attached to clean, finished surfaces without later wall finishing work damaging the blinds.

While casing can often be installed before blinds, it is preferable (soft preference) to install trim first; if blinds are installed before trim, they may obstruct access for nailing and fitting the casing tightly.
Blinds and shades collect dust and can be damaged during construction; they should be among the last items installed so they remain clean and undamaged for occupancy.
Window shutters are typically mounted onto or within the window frame; the frame must be installed first to provide a stable structural support and proper alignment for the shutter.

It is often preferable to complete wall finishing after shutter installation to allow for precise cutting and neat edges around the shutter, but it is not a physical necessity as walls could be finished first then touched up.

The window glass and glazing must be in place before shutters are installed to avoid damage to the glass or interference with the glazing process, and because shutters are typically fitted around the glass assembly.
Trim work and caulking around the shutter edges must be done after shutter installation to seal gaps and provide a finished appearance.
For exterior shutters, the underlying weatherproof membrane or flashing must be applied to the wall before shutters are attached, so that the weather barrier is continuous behind the shutter.
The rough opening (framed window hole) must be completely built and sized correctly before a double-hung window can be inserted and secured into the wall structure.
The weather-resistant barrier (building wrap) must be applied to the exterior wall sheathing before window installation to ensure proper flashing integration and prevent moisture infiltration.
After the double-hung window is set in the rough opening, flashing tape and sealants must be applied around the window frame to create a watertight seal.
Interior casing and trim around the window can be installed after the window is secured, though this is sometimes done later in the finishing phase as a soft sequencing preference.
Exterior siding must be installed after the window is in place so that the siding can be cut and fitted tightly around the window frame and flanges for a weatherproof finish.
The rough opening must be framed, measured, and prepared before the window can be installed.
After the window is set in place, the perimeter must be flashed and sealed to prevent water infiltration.
Typically interior trim work follows window installation, though it could be done concurrently in some cases.
Sheathing provides the structural backing needed to support the window frame and must be completed before window installation.
Siding or cladding is installed after the window to properly interface with the window flange and create a weathertight seal.
The rough opening (framed and measured) must be ready before an awning window can be installed; the window is fitted into the opening.
The awning window unit must be fully assembled (frame, sash, hinges, and operator mechanism) before it can be placed into the opening.
After the window is installed, gaps around it must be sealed, flashed, and weatherproofed to prevent air and water infiltration.
Interior casing, trim, and paint work typically follow window installation for a clean finish, though this is a practical preference rather than a physical necessity.
Awning windows are often integrated into the building envelope; siding or cladding around the window must be completed after installation to properly overlap and secure the window flange.
The sliding window must be installed within a prepared frame opening; the window frame provides structural support and the mounting surface for the sliding window unit.
The rough opening in the wall must be framed and sized to the correct dimensions before the sliding window unit can be placed and secured.
A weather-resistant barrier (house wrap or membrane) must be applied around the rough opening before installing the window to prevent moisture infiltration.
After the sliding window is installed, all gaps between the window frame and the rough opening must be sealed with caulk or expandable foam to ensure air and water tightness.
Interior window casings and trim are typically installed after the window is in place, though this is a soft preference as trim could theoretically be fitted beforehand if carefully measured.
The window frame must be installed and structurally secured before any louvre window components can be fitted into the opening.
Weatherproofing membranes around the window opening must be applied prior to louvre installation to ensure a watertight seal and prevent moisture ingress behind the window.
The wall opening must be prepared, with proper lintels and structural supports in place, before the louvre window can be installed.
After the louvre window frame is installed, the individual louvre blades must be fitted and adjusted for correct orientation and operation.
Final sealing around the louvre window unit must occur after installation to ensure weathertightness and proper finishing.
The window frame must be installed and structurally sound before any glazing can be placed into it, as the glazing (glass panels) is physically inserted and secured within the frame.
The rough opening must be properly measured, cleaned, and prepared (including any necessary weatherproofing) before the glazing unit can be installed to ensure correct fit and seal.

After the new glazing is placed in the frame, the perimeter must be sealed with caulk or weatherstripping to prevent air and water infiltration, which cannot be done before the glazing is in position.
Interior trim and architraves are installed around the window after the glazing is in place to cover gaps and provide a finished appearance; installing trim before glazing would block access.
Hardware such as locks, handles, and hinges are typically mounted onto the window frame and sash after the glazing is installed to avoid damage to the glass and ensure proper alignment.
The rough opening (framed hole) must be prepared, including headers, sills, and cripple studs, before windows can be physically placed and secured.
Building wrap or weather-resistant barrier must be installed around rough openings to protect against moisture infiltration before windows are set.
Sheathing (e.g., plywood or OSB) must be installed on exterior walls to provide structural support and a nailing surface for window flanges.
After windows are set into the rough opening, flashing tape and sealant must be applied around the window perimeter to prevent water intrusion.
Rough-in inspections (including window placement verification) typically occur before insulation and drywall, though this is a regulatory preference rather than a physical necessity.
Siding must be installed after windows because windows are set into the wall opening and siding is cut and trimmed around the installed window frame.
Insulation and drywall cannot be installed until windows are in place, as windows define the finished openings and provide a weathertight enclosure for interior work.
Final glazing (glass panes), stops, and interior/exterior trim are installed after the window unit is set and secured in the rough opening.
The window frame must be installed in place before painting/finishing can begin, as finishing is applied to the installed frame.
Surface preparation (sanding, cleaning, priming) must be completed before painting/finishing to ensure proper adhesion and a smooth finish.
Any masonry or concrete work near the window openings should be completed to avoid damaging the freshly painted window frames.
Glass installation must occur after frame finishing to avoid paint or finish splatter on the glass and to ensure the frame is fully prepared to receive the glazing.
Interior wall finishing near windows is typically done after window frame finishing to allow for clean edges and avoid damaging the finished frame.
Window frames must be installed first to provide a substrate for waterproofing and flashing. Flashing is designed to integrate with and seal around the installed frame.
The rough opening must be framed and sheathed before window installation and waterproofing, as flashing details require the wall assembly to be complete around the opening.
Waterproofing and flashing must be complete before cladding is applied, as cladding overlaps and covers the flashing to create a weather-tight seal and direct water outward.
Waterproofing and flashing must be completed and verified before interior finishes are applied to prevent moisture damage and ensure building envelope integrity.

While often done concurrently or shortly after, it is preferable to have the waterproofing and flashing in place before installing glazing to protect the frame-to-wall interface from water intrusion during glass handling.
Scaffolding or temporary access structures must be in place to allow workers to safely reach and handle windows, especially on upper floors.
Interior finishes, trim, and surrounding wall materials may need to be removed first to access window frames and avoid damaging reusable materials.

successor: Window Opening Preparation / Rough Opening Correction
rationale: After the old window is removed, the rough opening must be cleaned, repaired, and prepared for the new window installation.
Removed window materials (glass, frames, sealants) must be cleared from the worksite to maintain safety and cleanliness before further work proceeds.
After window removal, the opening must be temporarily sealed or weatherproofed to protect the interior from water, dust, and temperature extremes until new installation.
The door frame must be installed and securely fixed in the opening before the door leaf can be hung, as the door leaf is mounted onto the frame via hinges.
The rough opening must be framed and prepared to the correct dimensions before the door frame can be installed.
The door leaf must be in place before hardware such as locks, handles, and strike plates can be fitted and aligned correctly.
While painting can be done before or after installation, it is often preferred to finish the door leaf after installation to ensure a seamless match with the surrounding frame and trim.
It is preferred to install flooring before hanging the door leaf to ensure proper clearance (gap) between the bottom of the door and the finished floor surface.
The rough opening must be framed to provide the structural support and opening dimensions required for the door sill to be properly seated and anchored.
The door sill must be installed first as it forms the bottom horizontal member of the door frame assembly, providing a level base and water seal before vertical jambs are placed.
The sill must be in place to integrate with the flashing system beneath and around it, ensuring proper water drainage and preventing moisture intrusion before wall finishing.
The subfloor must be leveled and prepared so the door sill has a stable, level bearing surface for correct installation and threshold alignment.
If the sill sits on a concrete slab or foundation, the concrete must be fully cured to provide a stable, non-settling base that won't crack or shift the sill.
The rough opening must be framed to provide the structural support and defined space into which the door jamb is installed.
The floor sheathing must be in place to provide a level surface for the door jamb to sit on and for proper alignment.
Wall framing must be completed to create the rough opening and provide the structural framework that the door jamb will be secured to.
The door jamb must be securely installed and plumb before the door itself can be hung on hinges attached to the jamb.
Casing and trim are fastened to the door jamb, so the jamb must be in place before trim can be installed around it.
The rough opening (framed wall with header) must be completed to provide the structural support and space for the door head component.
Wall framing must be in place to define the opening where the door head will be installed, as the door head sits within the framed wall opening.
The header (structural beam above the door opening) must be installed to support the load above the door before the door head trim or frame component can be placed.
The door head (top horizontal member of the door frame) must be installed first to establish the top of the frame before the side jambs can be assembled and connected.
The door head must be in place to provide the top surface and reference point for attaching the door casing or trim around the door opening.
The door stop is typically attached to the door frame or the floor/wall adjacent to the door; the frame must be in place to provide a mounting surface or reference point.
The door stop functions to prevent the door from swinging too far; the door must first be hung so the stop can be positioned correctly relative to the door swing.
While door stops can be painted before installation, it is often preferred to install the stop first then paint or touch up as a unified assembly to ensure color match and coverage of fastener heads.
If the door stop is a floor-mounted type (e.g., a rubber wedge or floor stop), the finished flooring must be in place so the stop can be secured to the final floor surface.
If the door stop is wall-mounted, the wall surface must be finished to provide a proper mounting surface and avoid damaging unfinished walls during installation.
The door frame must be installed and properly aligned before door hinges can be attached, as hinges are mounted on the frame.
Hinges must be attached to both the frame and the door before the door can be hung on them.
Door hinges must be installed and the door hung before door knobs, locks, or latches can be properly aligned and installed.
Wall framing must be complete to provide the structural support for the door frame and hinges.
The rough opening must be framed and prepared to the correct dimensions before the door frame (and hinges) can be installed.
The door handle must be mounted onto an installed door frame; without a properly positioned and secured door frame, the handle cannot be correctly aligned or attached.
The door handle is fitted onto the door leaf; the door slab must be hung and in place before the handle can be installed.
The holes and mortise for the latch and lock mechanism must be cut and prepared in the door before the handle hardware can be inserted and secured.

Although typically hardware is installed after painting to avoid damage, if painting occurs after installation, the handle must be protected or removed; this is a soft preference rather than a physical necessity.

successor: Final Door Hardware Adjustment and Testing
rationale: The handle must be physically installed before it can be adjusted for smooth operation, alignment, and security testing.
The door knob must be mounted on a door that is already hung within its frame; without the door frame installed, there is no structure to attach the door or knob.
The door must be hung on its hinges before the knob can be installed, as the knob is fitted into the door itself.
After installing the door knob, the locking mechanism must be tested to ensure it functions correctly before the door is used.

Final adjustments to the door fit and alignment are typically done after the knob is installed, but this could be done before in some sequences; it is a practical preference rather than a physical necessity.
Touch-up painting around the door hardware is often done after installation to cover any scratches, but it is a cosmetic preference, not a physical requirement.
The door lever (handle) must be mounted onto a fully installed and secured door frame; the frame provides the structural support and cutouts required for lever attachment.
The door slab must be hung on its hinges within the frame before the lever can be installed, as the lever mechanism attaches to the door itself.
After the lever is installed, the latching and locking mechanisms must be tested to ensure proper operation before the door is considered complete.
It is often preferred to install door hardware after final painting to avoid paint overspray on the lever, though some sequences paint first and install later to protect the hardware.

predecessor: Wall Framing and Rough Opening Preparation
rationale: The rough opening in the wall must be framed and the door assembly (frame + door slab) installed before the lever can be placed; the lever cannot be mounted without the complete door assembly in place.
The door frame must be installed and properly aligned before the door lock can be fitted, as the lock must align with the strike plate on the frame.
The door must be hung on its hinges before the lock can be installed, as the lock hardware is mounted onto the assembled and positioned door.
For electric or smart locks, wiring must be run through the wall and door prior to lock installation to avoid surface-mounted conduits.
Interior trim pieces like escutcheon plates and handle roses are mounted after the lock body is installed, covering the lock mechanism.
The lock must be fully installed before it can be tested for proper latching, alignment, and key operation.
The door latch must be mounted onto the door frame; the frame must be in place first to provide the structure for latch installation.
The door must be hung on its hinges before the latch can be installed, as the latch aligns with the door edge and frame.
Door handles typically connect to the latch mechanism; the latch must be in place before handles can be attached.
The striker plate must be positioned to align with the latch bolt; the latch must be installed first to ensure proper alignment.
Functional testing of the door lock requires the latch mechanism to be fully installed before operation can be verified.
The deadbolt must be mounted on a properly installed and aligned door frame to ensure correct fit and function.
The door must be hung and properly aligned within the frame before the deadbolt can be installed, as the deadbolt needs to align with the strike plate on the frame.
The door must have the appropriate holes bored (2-1/8" diameter cross bore and 1" edge bore) to accommodate the deadbolt body and latch before installation.
The deadbolt must be installed before testing the lock function, key operation, and thumb-turn operation to verify correct installation.
The deadbolt must be installed to mark the exact position for the strike plate on the door frame, ensuring proper alignment of the bolt with the strike plate hole.
The door strike plate is mounted onto the door frame; therefore, the door frame must be installed first to provide a surface for the strike plate.
The door must be hung and its latch/lock position aligned before the strike plate can be accurately positioned and installed on the frame.
The strike plate must be in place so that the lockset or latch can properly engage with it for correct alignment and function.
Final adjustment and testing of the door's latching and locking mechanism require the strike plate to be installed to verify proper fit and operation.
The recess or mortise for the strike plate must be cut into the door frame before the strike plate can be mounted flush into it.
The door closer attaches to the door frame and door leaf; the frame must be securely installed first to provide structural support for mounting the closer.
The door closer connects between the door frame and the door leaf itself; the door must be hung and properly aligned before the closer can be installed and adjusted.
After the door closer is mounted, the closing speed, latch action, and backcheck must be adjusted and tested to ensure proper operation and compliance with fire/safety codes.
While not strictly physically required, door closer function is typically verified during final walkthroughs and inspections to confirm proper operation before project closeout.
Door closer installation should occur after painting and finishing to avoid paint overspray on the closer mechanism, which can impair function and void warranties.
The door viewer must be installed into an already-installed door slab that is hung in its frame. The door frame must be in place to support the door.
The door viewer (peephole) is mounted through a hole drilled in the door slab itself. The door slab must be installed (hung) before the peephole can be fitted.
A precisely sized through-hole must be drilled in the door slab at the appropriate height before the peephole assembly can be inserted and secured.

After installing the peephole, final adjustments to door hardware (latch, closer) may be done to ensure the peephole is properly aligned and the door operates smoothly; this is a soft preference for work sequencing.

If painting or finishing is done after peephole installation, the peephole could be painted over or obstructed. Typically, painting/finishing should be completed before installing the peephole, or the peephole must be installed after painting to avoid contamination.
The door chain must be mounted on a fully installed and stable door frame to provide a secure anchoring point.
The door chain is attached to the door itself and the frame, so the door must be hung and properly aligned before the chain can be installed.
After installing the door chain, all door hardware including the chain must be tested for proper function and security before use.
The door chain installation must be completed before final inspection to verify all security hardware is properly installed and operational.
The door frame provides the structural opening and reveals that the door sweep attaches to; without the frame there is no mounting surface for the sweep.
The door must be hung in its frame before the sweep can be installed, as the sweep is attached to the bottom of the installed door slab.
It is preferable to complete floor finishes beneath or up to the door sweep to ensure a proper seal and clean appearance, but not physically required.
Inspectors often verify sweep seals after installation, but the inspection can be done concurrently or later without blocking other work.
The door frame must be installed and properly aligned to provide the structural support and recess for the glazing or vision panel to be fitted into.
The rough opening must be prepared, framed, and sized correctly to accommodate the door assembly that will receive the glazing or vision panel.
Glass or vision panel materials must be delivered to site, inspected for damage, and be on hand before glazing installation can commence.
Hardware installation should occur after glazing is complete to avoid damaging the glass during hardware fitting and to ensure proper alignment of hardware relative to the finished door panel.
Weatherstripping and perimeter sealants must be applied after the glazing is installed to ensure a complete weather-tight seal around the vision panel and prevent moisture ingress.
The door panel requires a prepared door frame opening to be installed into; without the frame, the panel has no structural support or proper fit.

predecessor: Wall Framing and Rough Opening Preparation
rationale: The rough opening in the wall must be framed and completed before any door component (frame or panel) can be installed.
Door hardware such as hinges, locks, and handles must be mounted onto the installed door panel; these cannot be properly fitted before the panel is in place.
Trim and casing are applied around the perimeter of the installed door panel and frame to cover gaps and provide a finished look; this cannot be done before the panel is hung.
Painting or applying final finish to the door surface must occur after the panel is installed to ensure even coverage and integration with surrounding surfaces.
The rough opening must be framed to provide the structural support and correct dimensions for installing the door transom.
The transom is typically installed as part of or prior to the main door frame assembly, as it sits above the door in the same frame structure.
The transom frame must be in place before glazing can be installed, as the glass units are set into the transom frame.

While not always required, wall sheathing is typically completed before transom installation to provide lateral bracing and weather protection, though installation order can vary in some construction methods.
The transom must be fully installed before interior trim and finishing work can be applied around the door assembly.
The door sidelight is installed within or adjacent to the door frame; the frame must be in place to provide structural support and proper alignment for the sidelight.
The rough opening must be framed, leveled, and weatherproofed to receive the sidelight unit; the sidelight cannot be placed without a prepared opening.
The sidelight frame must be securely installed before the glass or glazing unit is set into the frame to avoid damage and ensure proper sealing.
Interior and exterior trim or casing around the sidelight is applied after the sidelight unit is fixed in place to cover gaps and provide a finished look.
Caulking, flashing, and weather seals around the sidelight are applied after installation to prevent air and water infiltration from the perimeter.
The rough opening must be framed and prepared to the correct dimensions before a sliding door can be installed, as the door unit requires a structurally sound and properly sized opening.
The finished flooring (or at least subfloor) should be in place so that the sliding door track and threshold have a level, stable base to mount on.
After the sliding door is installed, gaps around the frame must be sealed with caulk, flashing, and weatherstripping to prevent air and water infiltration.
Interior trim and casing are installed around the door frame after the door unit is in place to cover the gap between the frame and the wall finish.

While final hardware adjustment and testing could theoretically be done later, it is a soft preference to do it immediately after installation to ensure smooth operation before other finish work proceeds.
The rough opening must be framed to provide the structural support and dimensional perimeter required for installing the folding/bi-fold door unit.
The finished floor must be in place so the bi-fold door track and bottom pivot can be set at the correct height relative to the final floor surface.
Interior wall surfaces (drywall or sheathing) need to be completed around the opening before the door frame and casing can be installed flush with the finished wall.
The bi-fold door must be installed and operating correctly before the final trim casing can be fitted around the opening to cover gaps and provide a finished appearance.
While painting can often be done before the door is installed, final touch-up painting around the door frame is best completed after the door is hung to blend the trim with the wall finish.
The rough opening in the wall structure must be framed and prepared to the correct dimensions before the revolving door unit can be set in place.
The floor area where the revolving door sits must be leveled and finished to ensure proper alignment, clearance, and smooth operation of the door assembly.
Structural supports, lintels, and overhead headers must be completed to carry the load of the revolving door and its overhead assembly before installation.
Low-voltage wiring, sensors, and control systems are connected to the revolving door after it is installed to ensure proper alignment with the door's integrated components.
Final weather seals, caulking, and gaskets around the door frame are applied after installation to prevent air and water infiltration at the perimeter.
Fire doors require a properly installed frame to mount onto; without the frame, the door cannot be hung or aligned correctly.

predecessor: Wall Framing and Rough Opening Preparation
rationale: The wall and rough opening must be framed and prepared to the correct dimensions before a fire door assembly can be installed.

successor: Fire Door Hardware Installation (hinges, locks, closers)
rationale: Hardware such as hinges, locks, and door closers must be mounted onto the installed door leaf; the door must be in place first.
Intumescent seals and smoke gaskets are fitted around the installed door and frame; the door assembly must be in place to properly install these seals.

successor: Final Inspection / Fire Door Certification Testing
rationale: A fire door must be fully installed before it can be inspected and tested for fire rating compliance and certification.
The flush door must be hung on a properly installed door frame; the frame provides the structural support and fixing points for the hinges.
Walls must be built and finished to create the opening into which the door frame and flush door are installed.
Floor finish level determines the undercut and clearance for the door; the door should be installed after the finished floor level is established.
Hardware such as locks, handles, and strike plates are mounted onto the installed flush door; the door must be in place before these components can be fitted.
While doors can be pre-finished, final painting or varnishing is typically done after installation to touch up cuts and fixings, though pre-finishing is possible if preferred.
The door opening must be framed, sized, and prepared to receive the door before the panelled door can be installed.
Structural wall framing and rough openings must be complete before any door installation can begin.
Hinges, locks, handles, and other hardware can only be mounted on the door after it is hung in its frame.
Final painting, staining, or sealing of the panelled door is performed after the door is fitted and hung to ensure proper coverage and alignment.
Architraves and casing are fitted around the door frame after the door is hung to ensure proper clearances and alignment.
Physical delivery and on-site storage must occur before installation can begin, as the door must be present at the worksite.
The rough opening must be framed and prepared to the correct dimensions before the louvred door can be fitted into place.

successor: Finish Trim and Architraves Around Door
rationale: Trim and architraves are fitted around the installed door frame to cover gaps and provide a finished appearance, which can only be done after the door is in position.

successor: Paint or Stain Louvred Door and Frame
rationale: While painting is typically done after installation to avoid damage during handling, it is a soft preference as pre-finished doors could alternatively be used.
Door hardware must be attached to the installed door; the door must be hung before handles and latches can be fitted and aligned correctly.
The rough opening must be framed and prepared to the correct dimensions before a Dutch door can be installed, as the door frame requires a structurally sound and properly sized opening.
The door frame (jamb, header, and sill) must be installed and secured in the rough opening before the Dutch door itself can be hung, as the door hinges attach to the frame.
The Dutch door must be physically hung in its frame before hardware (hinges, latches, slide bolts, and the dutch door shelf/locking mechanism) can be adjusted and fine-tuned for proper operation.
Weatherstripping must be applied after the Dutch door is installed to ensure proper fit and seal around the door edges and the split between the upper and lower halves.
Interior and exterior trim/casing around the Dutch door must be installed after the door is hung to cover the gap between the frame and the rough opening.
The rough opening must be framed and prepared to the correct dimensions before the garage door can be installed.
The track system and hardware must be mounted before the garage door panels can be placed into the tracks.
The garage door must be fully installed and operational before the automatic opener can be mounted and connected to the door.
Weather seals are applied around the installed door after the door is in place to prevent air and water infiltration.
Spring tension and door balance adjustments can only be performed after the door and all hardware are fully installed.
Rough framing (wall studs, headers, and rough openings) must be completed to create the structural opening where the door will be installed.
Exterior wall sheathing around the door opening must be in place to provide structural support and a proper nailing surface for the door frame.
Any electrical wiring that needs to run through wall cavities near the door opening must be roughed in before the door frame is installed to avoid interference.
Drywall and plaster must be installed after the door frame is in place so that the wall finish can be fitted tightly around the door frame and properly finished.
Hardware such as locks, handles, and hinges can only be installed after the door is hung and properly aligned in its frame.
Door frames are installed within wall openings. The wall framing must be complete to provide the rough opening and structural support for the door frame.
The finished subfloor provides the level surface and reference elevation upon which the door frame sits and is plumbed.
The door frame (jambs and head) must be installed and secured in the opening before the door slab can be hung on hinges attached to the frame.
Drywall is installed around the door frame; the frame must be in place so drywall can be cut to fit and taped/finished against the frame edges.
The door leaf/frame must be installed and in place before any hardware (hinges, locks, handles) can be fitted onto it.
Wall finishing around the door opening must be completed to ensure the door frame is properly set and aligned before fitting hardware.
Floor finishing must be done so the door clearance and threshold alignment are final, preventing the need to adjust hardware later.
While hardware can be fitted before painting, it is a soft preference to fit hardware after painting to avoid paint on hardware and simplify masking.
All door hardware must be fitted and operational before the final inspection and handover of the building to the client.

Doors must be installed and hung on their hinges before they can be painted or finished, as painting requires access to the full door surface in its mounted position to ensure even coverage and proper alignment with the frame.

Wall painting should be completed before door painting to avoid damaging freshly painted doors with paint drips, roller splatter, or masking tape residue from wall work, and to allow for cleaner cut-in lines at door frames.
Doors must be properly sanded, cleaned, and primed before painting to ensure proper adhesion of the paint finish; painting over unprepared surfaces leads to peeling and poor durability.

Bore holes for locksets, hinge mortises, and any hardware prep must be completed before painting so that the paint seals the exposed edges and the hardware installations do not damage a finished painted surface.

Final door hardware such as knobs, locks, and decorative hinges should be installed after painting is complete to avoid paint contamination on hardware surfaces and to ensure a clean, professional finish.

While it is preferred to complete all door finishing before final touch-ups to avoid rework, some minor trim adjustments can occur concurrently with careful protection; this is a soft preference for schedule sequencing.
The rough opening must be framed and prepared (including header, jambs, and sill) to the correct dimensions before a door can be installed.
Load-bearing walls and framing around the door opening must be in place to provide structural support before the door unit can be set.
The subfloor must be installed and leveled to provide a proper base for the door threshold and to establish correct floor-to-door clearances.
The door unit must be hung, shimmed, and secured in the opening before casing and trim can be applied around it.
The door must be installed before exterior weatherstripping, caulking, and flashing can be applied to seal the perimeter against air and water infiltration.
Locks, handles, and final hinge adjustments can only be installed and aligned after the door slab is correctly positioned and fastened in the frame.

While it is preferable to install flooring first for a cleaner threshold fit, door replacement can be done before flooring if the floor height is accounted for; thus it is a soft preference rather than a hard constraint.
Drywall can be installed before or after door replacement depending on workflow; however, it is often easier to hang drywall without a door in the way, so this is a soft preference.
The door must be physically installed in its frame before its fire rating can be inspected, as inspection evaluates the installed assembly.
The door frame must be installed to provide the supporting structure for the door; fire rating inspection covers the full assembly including the frame.
Fire-rated gaps around the door frame must be sealed before inspection to verify the integrity of the fire barrier.

While some hardware can be installed before, final inspection ensures fire-rated hardware meets requirements; it is a soft preference to install critical hardware after inspection to avoid rework if items are rejected.
Fire rating inspection is a required milestone that must be passed before the project can proceed to final closeout activities.

Mullions are vertical structural or non-structural elements that are attached to the building's structural frame (columns, beams, or slabs). The structural frame must be in place to provide a mounting surface and support for mullions.

Mullions form the vertical (and sometimes horizontal) framework that holds glass or window panels. The mullion grid must be installed first to create the openings into which glazing units are placed and secured.

Mullions serve as the supporting framework for the curtain wall or cladding system. The completion of the exterior cladding envelope depends on the mullions being in place to support panels, insulation, and weatherproofing layers.
Weather seals and caulking are applied at the gaps between mullions and glazing units or cladding panels. The mullions must be installed to define the joints that require sealing.

Interior finishes such as drywall, trim, and paint around curtain wall systems are typically installed after mullions are in place, but this can sometimes be sequenced in parallel or adjusted based on preference.
The rough opening (door/window frame) must be framed and structurally complete before a transom can be installed, as the transom sits within or above the framed opening.
Casing and trim around the transom must be installed after the transom itself is in place to cover gaps and provide a finished appearance.
If the transom includes glass panes, the glazing must be installed after the transom frame is securely mounted.
While painting can often be done before installation, final touch-up painting and finishing around the transom typically occurs after it is installed to ensure a seamless look.
The wall structure must be framed and sheathed to provide the structural support needed to hold the transom in place.
Spandrel panels are typically installed between floors on the exterior of a building, and the structural steel frame must be in place to provide support and attachment points for the panels.
Spandrel panels are often aligned with floor levels; the floor slabs must be poured to provide the structural edge and anchoring surface for the spandrel panels.

Spandrel panels form part of the curtain wall system and are installed before vision glass or window units, as they fill the opaque zones between floors and provide the backing or substrate for adjacent glazing.
Weatherproofing sealants and membranes are applied after spandrel panels are in place to seal joints between panels and between panels and other building elements.

successor: Interior Drywall / Finish Work at Perimeter
rationale: Interior finishing at the building perimeter, such as drywall installation near spandrel areas, is typically done after panel placement to allow access for panel attachment and sealing.
The vision glass panel must be installed into a supporting frame; the frame provides the structural support and mounting points required for the glass panel.
Mullions are vertical or horizontal framing members that create the grid for curtain wall systems; glass panels are installed into the openings created by mullions.
Structural silicone is often applied to the framing before the glass panel is placed to ensure proper adhesion and weather sealing of the panel.
Glazing beads are installed after the glass panel is placed in the frame to secure the panel in position and provide a finished edge.
Weather sealant is applied around the perimeter of the installed glass panel to ensure watertight and airtight integrity before further finishing work.

A stable foundation or base must be prepared before a pressure plate can be installed, as the plate requires a level, load-bearing surface to function properly and avoid cracking or uneven activation.
The subfloor or underlying structural layer must be in place to provide support and a mounting surface for the pressure plate.
The pressure plate must be physically installed and secured before electrical wiring can be connected to it, as the wiring terminates at the plate's terminals.
If the pressure plate is embedded in or covered by flooring material (e.g., tile, wood, concrete), the plate must be installed first, then the finish flooring can be laid over or around it.
The pressure plate must be fully installed and connected before calibration and functional testing can be performed to verify its sensitivity and correct operation.
The capping strip is installed on top of the roof deck to cover and protect the exposed edges; thus the roof deck must be in place first.
The capping strip must be in place before the final sealant can be applied around its edges to ensure watertight sealing.
Underlayment provides a base layer beneath the roof covering; capping strips are installed after underlayment to secure the membrane edges.
Fascia trim is often installed after capping strips to cover the exposed strip ends and provide a finished appearance.
The capping strip must be cut and prepared to the correct dimensions before it can be installed.
The anchor bracket must be placed on a prepared foundation or base surface to ensure stability and proper load distribution.
The anchor bracket serves as the base connection point; the column or post must be attached to the anchor bracket after it is secured in place.
After positioning the anchor bracket, bolts must be tightened to specified torque values to secure the bracket and attached structural elements.
The foundation or supporting structure must be prepared and cured before the dead load bracket can be installed, as the bracket transfers load to the foundation.
Steel columns or vertical supports must be erected to provide the mounting surface for dead load brackets in structural steel applications.
Dead load brackets serve as support seats for girders or beams; beams cannot be placed until the support brackets are in position.
Dead load brackets must be installed before permanent dead loads (e.g., structural deck, roofing, cladding) are applied, as the brackets are designed to support these loads.
Once dead load brackets are installed, their connections (welds or bolts) must be inspected for quality and load capacity before proceeding to subsequent loading.
Wind load brackets must be anchored to a structurally sound foundation; anchor bolts must be set and cured before bracket mounting.
Wind load brackets are typically attached to steel columns or vertical structural members; columns must be erected and plumbed first.
Brackets provide lateral support and load transfer points; tower sections rely on these brackets for alignment and stability during erection.
Wind load brackets serve as the mounting interface for exterior cladding or façade systems; panels cannot be attached until brackets are fixed in position.
All bracket connections must be completed and fully tightened before they can be inspected and torque-tested for compliance with structural standards.
The structural frame (steel or concrete) must be complete to provide the supporting structure to which the curtain wall system is anchored.
Floor slabs at each level are needed to provide working platforms and support brackets for curtain wall panels.
Primary waterproofing and air barrier systems at structural transitions must be installed before the curtain wall to ensure continuous moisture protection behind the wall system.

Interior partitions and finishes should follow curtain wall installation because the curtain wall defines the building perimeter; interior walls often align with or connect to the curtain wall mullions.
After the curtain wall framing is installed, the glass panels and weather-sealing sealants can be applied to complete the enclosure and ensure airtightness and watertightness.
Anchor brackets are typically mounted onto steel columns or embedded in concrete; steel columns must be erected to provide the structural surface for bracket attachment.
If anchor brackets are to be bolted into a concrete foundation or slab, the concrete must be poured and fully cured to achieve sufficient strength to hold the anchors.
Accurate positioning of anchor brackets requires prior layout and survey marking to ensure brackets are installed at correct locations and elevations.
Anchor brackets serve as connection points for steel beams or girders; beams cannot be placed until brackets are installed and secured.
Installing MEP systems in the area above or adjacent to brackets is more efficient after brackets are in place to avoid conflicts and rework, though not a strict physical necessity.
The structural frame (concrete or steel) must be complete to provide the supporting structure onto which glazing systems are installed.
Window and curtain wall openings must be framed, squared, and prepared to receive glazing units.
Perimeter防水 and air barriers must be in place around openings to prevent water ingress before glazing is set.
Glazing must be installed and sealed to create a weathertight envelope before interior finishes are applied, preventing damage from moisture.
While MEP rough-in can largely proceed in parallel, any electrical or mechanical work directly adjacent to or penetrating window frames should follow glazing to avoid compromising seals.
Sealant must be applied to a clean, dry, and properly prepared surface to ensure adhesion. Any dust, debris, moisture, or contaminants will compromise the bond.
Joints and gaps must be cleaned of old sealant, dirt, and debris before fresh sealant is applied to ensure proper adhesion and fill.
When required by manufacturer specifications, a primer must be applied to the substrate before sealant to improve adhesion and prevent staining.
Backer rods must be installed in deep joints before sealant application to control sealant depth, provide a backing surface, and prevent three-sided adhesion.
After sealant is applied, it must be allowed to cure or dry according to manufacturer specifications before being exposed to water, traffic, or further construction activities.
Paint or coatings over sealant must be applied only after the sealant has fully cured to avoid cracking, peeling, or incompatibility.
Water testing or inspection of the sealed joint must occur after sealant has fully cured to verify integrity and waterproofing performance.
Final clean-up of excess sealant and masking materials is typically performed after application, but some tooling and immediate clean-up can occur during application.
The structural steel frame must be in place to provide the supporting structure onto which the curtain wall mock-up can be installed and tested for fit and performance.
The curtain wall design details, including panel types, glazing specifications, and anchoring systems, must be finalized before constructing and testing a representative mock-up.

predecessor: Concrete Slab Edge Completion (at test bay)
rationale: The concrete slab edges at the designated test location must be poured and cured to provide the proper floor-to-floor height and anchorage points for the curtain wall mock-up installation.

Mock-up test results must be reviewed and approved to confirm the curtain wall design meets performance requirements (air, water, structural, thermal) before full-scale fabrication and procurement of all system components can proceed.

The mock-up test validates installation methods, sequencing, and performance standards; full-scale installation on the building cannot begin until this testing is successfully completed and signed off.
The curtain wall system must be fully installed before it can be commissioned and inspected, as inspection validates the installed work.
The building's structural frame must be complete to provide the supporting framework onto which the curtain wall is installed and subsequently inspected.
Waterproofing and air barrier systems behind or around the curtain wall must be in place before commissioning can verify the envelope's integrity.

Interior finishes adjacent to the curtain wall (e.g., drywall, trim) can ideally proceed after inspection to avoid rework if deficiencies are found, though this is a soft preference in some schedules.
