Scaffolding or access equipment used for curtain wall installation and inspection must remain in place until commissioning is complete, and can only be dismantled after sign-off.
Scaffolding, cherry pickers, or other access equipment must be in place before workers can safely reach and clean the building facade.

The facade must be fully enclosed and waterproofed before final cleaning can be performed; otherwise cleaning may be wasted effort if further construction dust or moisture intrusion will soil the facade again.
The cladding, curtain wall, or masonry must be completely installed and all surface protection removed so that cleaning and maintenance can be performed on the final surfaces.
All windows, glass panels, and glazing systems must be installed and sealed before facade cleaning to avoid damage and to ensure cleaning covers the complete facade surface.
Facade cleaning is typically one of the last exterior finishing activities; building handover and final inspection should only occur after the facade is cleaned and presentable.

It is preferred to clean the facade before installing exterior lighting and signage to avoid having to clean around fixtures and to prevent dust/debris from newly installed fixtures settling on a already cleaned facade.
Cleaning the facade before surrounding landscaping and paving work is preferable to avoid soiling the clean facade with dust and debris from earthworks and paving activities.
The structural frame (steel or concrete) must be erected to provide the load-bearing backing and support structure onto which the rainscreen cladding panels are mounted.
A weather-resistant barrier and air seal must be applied to the exterior sheathing before rainscreen panels to prevent moisture ingress into the building envelope.
The vertical or horizontal sub-framing system (aluminum or steel rails/brackets) must be installed on the structure to provide the attachment points and drainage cavity for the rainscreen panels.

Rainscreen panels are typically installed before windows to allow proper integration of window flashings with the cladding system and to ensure the cladding overlaps window frames for weatherproofing.

successor: Exterior Insulation and Finish System (EIFS) / Secondary Cladding
rationale: Any secondary cladding or finish applied to adjacent areas must follow rainscreen installation to ensure proper lapping, joint sealing, and a continuous weather-tight envelope.

The cladding substrate/sheathing board must be attached to a stable structural frame. Wall studs or structural framing provides the necessary backing and support for the sheathing boards to be fastened.

predecessor: Building Wrap / Weather Barrier (House Wrap) Installation
rationale: The weather-resistant barrier (house wrap) is typically installed directly over the sheathing or between the sheathing and the cladding; however, in some sequences the wrap goes on after sheathing. More critically, the wall cavity insulation and electrical/plumbing rough-ins must be completed before sheathing is installed, as sheathing closes the wall.

successor: Cladding / Exterior Finish (e.g., siding, brick veneer, stucco)
rationale: The sheathing board serves as the substrate onto which the final exterior cladding material is attached or applied. The final cladding cannot be installed until the substrate is in place.

Sheathing boards are typically installed around rough openings, and windows/doors are then installed into the roughed-in openings with flashing integrated with the sheathing layer for proper waterproofing.
Insulation must be placed within the wall cavities (between studs) before the sheathing is installed on the exterior side, as sheathing closes off access to the wall cavities from the outside.
Cladding brackets must be anchored to the main structural steel frame, which must be erected first to provide a stable substrate.
The foundation must be in place to support the structural frame and the cladding loads transferred through the brackets.
Cladding panels are physically attached to and supported by the brackets/anchors, so brackets must be installed first.

The weatherproof membrane is typically applied over the substrate and around brackets; brackets must be fixed first so that the membrane can be properly detailed and sealed around the anchor penetrations.
Insulation is placed around or between cladding brackets after they are fixed, as the brackets define the cavity depth and support locations for insulation boards.

The cladding rail/carrier system is typically mounted onto or supported by the structural steel frame. The steel frame must be erected first to provide the structural support and attachment points for the rail system.

predecessor: Concrete Slab / Deck Pouring and Curing
rationale: Concrete slabs or decks provide the base on which the cladding rail system is anchored. The concrete must be poured and cured to sufficient strength before rails can be bolted or fastened.
Cladding panels are attached directly to the rail/carrier system. The rails must be completely installed and aligned to serve as the substrate for panel fixing.
While some weatherproofing may be sequential, it is a soft preference to apply membranes after rails are in place to ensure continuous sealing around rail penetrations.
Thermal insulation is often placed between or over the cladding rails. The rail system must be in position to define cavities and support insulation layers.
Metal cladding panels are typically attached to or supported by the structural steel frame, which must be erected first to provide a stable mounting surface.
The roof structure must be in place before wall cladding to provide overhead weather protection and to allow cladding to be tied into the roof edge details.
Cladding panels define the final wall openings; windows and doors are typically installed after the surrounding cladding is in place to ensure proper sealing and flashing integration.
Interior finishes such as drywall or insulation often rely on the exterior envelope (cladding) being completed first to maintain a weather-tight interior environment.
Sealant and weatherproofing treatments are applied to the joints and edges of installed cladding panels to ensure watertightness and must be done after panels are in place.
The structural frame must be in place to provide a load-bearing substrate for mounting ACM panels.
A weather-resistant barrier must be installed behind the cladding to protect the building envelope from moisture ingress.
Insulation must be placed behind the cladding to meet thermal performance requirements before enclosing with ACM panels.

successor: Window and Door Installation (if flashings integrated)
rationale: ACM panels are typically installed before windows and doors when the cladding system incorporates integrated flashings and the panels define the final plane for fenestration.
Joints between ACM panels must be sealed after installation to ensure weathertightness and aesthetic finish.
Scaffolding used for cladding installation must remain in place until ACM panels are fully installed and secured, and can only be removed after the cladding work is complete.
The structural frame (e.g., steel or timber framing) must be in place to provide the load-bearing support onto which the fibre cement cladding boards are fixed.
Exterior sheathing boards (or a weather-resistive barrier) are typically installed over the frame before fibre cement cladding to provide rigidity and a drainage plane.
A weather-resistive barrier such as building wrap or felt paper must be applied to the sheathing to prevent moisture ingress behind the cladding.

While windows/doors can be installed before cladding (rough openings), final flashing and trim integration typically occurs after cladding is installed around the openings for proper weather sealing; this is a soft sequencing preference for best practice.
Fibre cement boards are often pre-primed or pre-finished, but any site-applied paint or topcoat must be applied after the boards are fully installed to ensure even coverage and proper adhesion.
The structural frame (e.g., steel or concrete frame) must be in place to provide a stable mounting surface and load-bearing support for the timber cladding board.
A weather-resistant barrier must be applied behind the cladding to protect the building envelope from moisture ingress before the timber boards are fixed.
External wall insulation (if used) must be installed prior to cladding to ensure thermal performance and a continuous substrate for the cladding system.

Although window installation can precede cladding, it is often preferable to complete cladding first to allow proper flashing integration and weather-tight sealing around openings; however, this order can vary based on detailing.
Timber cladding boards must be installed first before any final protective coating (paint, stain, or sealant) is applied to ensure complete coverage of all joints and exposed faces.
The structural wall or frame must be fully erected and stable to provide a load-bearing substrate for the stone cladding panels to be mounted or anchored onto.
A waterproofing membrane or weather barrier must be installed behind the cladding to protect the structure from moisture ingress before the stone panels are fixed in place.
The sealant and pointing work between stone panels must be applied after the panels are installed to fill joints and ensure weather-tightness.
Scaffolding that was used to access the cladding area can only be removed after the stone panels are fully installed and secured; however, this is a soft preference if partial dismantling is staged.
The stone cladding surface should be cleaned and any mortar/grout residue removed after installation is complete, though this is a workflow preference rather than a physical necessity.
Terracotta cladding panels require the building's structural frame (typically steel or concrete) to be erected first, as the cladding system is attached to or supported by the structural frame.
A waterproofing/weather barrier must be installed behind the cladding to protect the building envelope from moisture; terracotta panels are an outer rainscreen layer and require this substrate.
Thermal insulation is placed behind the cladding system and must be installed before the terracotta panels are mounted to ensure proper thermal performance of the building envelope.

Window and door frames are typically installed after the surrounding cladding system or integrated with it, but generally the cladding panels around openings are placed first to ensure proper flashing and sealing integration.

While not a hard physical constraint, interior wall finishing (drywall, plastering) is often sequenced after exterior cladding completion to avoid weather exposure damage to interior materials and to allow for coordination of wall penetrations.
The structural frame must be complete to provide the supporting substrate onto which brick slip cladding is installed.
A rigid backing wall (e.g., blockwork, plywood, or metal stud with sheathing) is required as the substrate for brick slip cladding installation.

predecessor: Damp Proof Course (DPC) / Cavity Tray Installation
rationale: Damp proofing must be in place at the base of the wall to prevent moisture ingress before the cladding is applied.
It is common practice to install cladding first and then fit windows/doors with appropriate flashings, though sequencing can vary depending on the detailing.

successor: Internal Wall Insulation / Final Internal Finishes
rationale: The cladding must be complete to seal the building envelope before internal finishes are applied to prevent moisture damage.
The metal sheet cladding is installed onto the structural steel frame. The steel frame must be fully erected and stable to provide a mounting structure for the cladding panels.

Roof structure must be completed before wall cladding can be installed, as the roof provides lateral stability to the frame and protects the work area from weather, which is important for sheet metal installation.

Cladding sheets must be installed before windows and doors are fitted, as the cladding forms the outer weatherproof envelope and openings are typically cut through the cladding for window and door frames.

The metal sheet cladding must be in place before internal insulation and vapor barriers are installed, as the cladding forms the outer protective layer and insulation is fitted against the inside face of the cladding.

Main cladding panels must be installed before flashings and trims (eaves, ridge, corner, and closure strips) can be fitted, as flashings seal the edges and transitions between cladding panels and other building elements.
The structural frame (columns, beams, and supports) must be in place to provide the load-bearing substrate onto which BIPV cladding panels are mounted.
BIPV panels are often integrated into the building envelope (roof or facade); the roof deck or structural slab must be completed before panel installation.
A weather-resistant barrier (WRB) or waterproofing membrane must be applied behind BIPV cladding to protect the building from moisture ingress.
Electrical conduits, junction boxes, and wiring for the photovoltaic system must be routed behind the cladding before panels are installed to avoid retrofitting.
Once BIPV panels are physically installed, the electrical connections between panels, inverters, and the building's electrical system can be completed and commissioned.
In some systems exterior insulation is placed over the panels; however, this is a soft preference as insulation can be installed before or after depending on the specific BIPV assembly details.
Scaffolding used for BIPV installation must remain in place until the panels are fully installed and secured; dismantling can only occur after cladding work is complete.
Interior work adjacent to BIPV-clad areas may proceed after panel installation to avoid damage, but this is a soft preference rather than a hard physical constraint.
The cladding panels must be installed first to create the cavity that the cavity closer / fire barrier will seal and protect.
The main building structure must be in place to provide support and backing for the cladding system and its cavity closer / fire barrier components.
The cavity closer / fire barrier must be installed first to contain and separate the cavity before insulation is placed, ensuring fire compartmentation and preventing fire spread through the cavity.
The cavity closer/fire barrier must be in place before internal linings are installed to maintain the integrity of the fire compartment seal from the cavity side.
It is good practice to complete the cavity closer/fire barrier prior to final weatherproofing to ensure fire safety measures are fully concealed and protected.

The parapet coping and cladding termination detail is installed on top of and terminates the parapet wall assembly. The wall structure must be built first to provide the substrate and support for the coping/cladding termination.
The roof deck provides the underlying structure adjacent to the parapet. The coping detail ties into the roof membrane and flashing, which are installed over the deck substrate.
The air barrier and vapor retarder behind the cladding must be installed before the cladding termination detail to ensure continuous airtightness and moisture protection at the parapet transition.

The roof membrane and base flashing are installed prior to the parapet coping to allow proper overlap and drainage. The coping caps and terminates the flashing, preventing water intrusion at the roof edge.
Counterflashing is installed after or integrated with the parapet coping to seal the top edge of the base flashing. The coping detail provides the anchorage point for counterflashing.

successor: Final Sealant / Caulking Application at Coping Joints
rationale: Sealant is applied at joints and seams of the coping/cladding termination after the coping pieces are fully installed to seal against water intrusion.

successor: Scaffolding / Safety System Removal at Parapet Area
rationale: Once the parapet coping and cladding termination are complete, access scaffolding and edge protection systems can be removed from the roof perimeter area as work at that elevation is finished.

The cladding panel support structure (such as furring channels, sub-girts, or brackets) must be installed before the cladding panels can be revealed or returned, as the panels are fastened to or supported by this structure.
Weatherproofing sealant is applied to the joints around the cladding panel after it has been revealed or returned to its final position, ensuring watertightness at panel edges.

successor: Install Flashing / Trim at Panel Edges
rationale: Flashing and trim pieces are installed after the cladding panel is in its revealed or returned position to cover panel edges and provide a finished appearance.
Adjacent panels can only be fully installed after the reveal or return of the current panel is complete, as panel fit and alignment depend on the preceding panel's final position.
The final inspection of the cladding installation should occur after all panels including reveals/returns are in place, though this is a quality control step rather than a physical constraint.
Cladding materials must be delivered and available on-site before they can be inspected and tested for compliance with specifications.
The structural frame must be complete to provide the support framework onto which cladding will be installed, enabling inspection of fit and anchorage points.
Cladding panels/systems must be installed before inspection and testing can be performed to verify proper installation, weathertightness, and structural integrity.
If inspection and testing identifies defects or non-compliance, remediation work must follow to correct issues before final acceptance.
Formal sign-off and acceptance of cladding work can only occur after inspection and testing has been completed and results verified as compliant.
Scaffolding or access equipment must be erected to provide safe working at height access for cladding maintenance and cleaning work.
The building's structural frame must be complete and stable before any cladding work can be performed, as cladding is attached to the structure.
Cladding must be fully installed before any maintenance or cleaning can be performed on it.

Completing the roof first reduces the risk of water ingress damaging the cladding and allows cleaning to proceed in a weather-protected environment, but is a soft preference as cleaning could be done before the roof.
Cladding must be clean and maintained before the final building inspection to ensure the building envelope is in acceptable condition for handover.
Safe access to the building facade at height is required before any cladding work can begin.
A full condition survey of the existing cladding must be completed to determine the scope of removal and necessary materials for recladding.
Dust/debris containment and protection of adjacent building elements must be in place before disturbing the existing cladding.
The underlying structure needs to be exposed and cleared of old cladding before new weatherproofing membranes can be applied.
Final cladding around window and door openings must be removed and reinstalled to ensure proper integration and sealing of new frames.

The building's structural system and load-bearing elements must be designed first, as the facade and cladding system must be anchored to and supported by the primary structure. Cladding loads, deflection limits, and connection points depend on the structural design.

The architectural design establishes the overall building form, massing, floor-to-floor heights, and aesthetic vision that informs and constrains the facade system selection, panelization, and detailing.

Foundation design depends on geotechnical data, and the facade load paths ultimately transfer to the foundation. Additionally, ground movement/settlement predictions affect allowable facade deflection and movement joint设计要求.

Facade and cladding materials (glass panels, aluminum frames, stone veneers, sealants, etc.) cannot be ordered until the facade engineering design is finalized, specifying exact quantities, sizes, performance ratings, and material specifications.

The facade engineering design produces the detailed drawings, shop drawings, and installation specifications that guide the actual installation of cladding, glazing, and waterproofing systems on site.
Coping stones are placed on top of walls or parapets to cap and protect them; the wall structure must be built and cured before the coping stone can be installed.

Coping stones provide a finished edge and weather seal; roofing or waterproofing membranes are often tied into or abutted against the coping, so the coping must be in place to form a proper watertight seal.

Coping stones are typically installed after the wall is finished but before removing scaffolding so that workers can access the top of the wall; dismantling scaffolding is safer and more efficient after all top-of-wall work is complete.
Sealant joints around coping stones (at joints between stones and between stone and wall) must be applied after the coping stones are set in place to ensure weatherproofing.
If equipment anchors or parapet flashings need to be embedded under or behind the coping, those elements should be installed prior to the coping stone to avoid rework.
Formwork provides the mold into which the parapet wall core concrete is poured. The core cannot be placed without the formwork being in position to contain and shape the concrete.
Steel reinforcement (rebar) must be installed within the formwork before concrete is poured, as the reinforcement is embedded within the concrete core to provide tensile strength.
Freshly poured concrete requires a specified curing period to achieve sufficient strength before any subsequent loads or finishing work can be applied.
Formwork can only be removed after the concrete core has gained enough strength to support itself; stripping too early could cause structural damage or collapse.

Waterproofing membranes or coatings are applied to the cured concrete surface of the parapet wall core to protect it from moisture ingress. The core must be complete and cured before waterproofing can be installed.
Parapet flashing is installed over the top of the parapet wall to weatherproof and protect the wall structure; the wall must be built first to provide a substrate for the flashing.
The roof deck provides the base level from which parapet flashing extends; the roof membrane and base flashing often tie into parapet flashing, requiring the deck to be in place.

Parapet flashing is typically installed as part of the roofing system; the base flashing of the roof membrane is often lapped over or sealed against the parapet flashing, so the parapet flashing must be in place first to allow proper watertight integration.

Counterflashing (or cap flashing) is installed over the top edge of the base parapet flashing to shed water and cover the exposed top; the base parapet flashing must be installed first to provide an overlap surface for the counterflashing.

If a stone or masonry coping is placed atop the parapet, the coping is typically set after the flashing is installed to ensure that the flashing extends under or integrates with the coping for proper drainage and waterproofing.
Through-wall flashing must be installed over the wall sheathing to direct water outward; the sheathing provides the continuous backing surface for the flashing.
Flashing must integrate with rough openings for windows and doors to create a watertight seal; openings must be framed first so flashing can be properly lapped.

Through-wall flashing is installed behind the exterior cladding to divert moisture; cladding must be installed after flashing so that the flashing's drip edge extends over the cladding or is properly integrated.
The weather-resistive barrier (house wrap or felt) is typically lapped over the through-wall flashing to ensure water flows down the WRB and over the flashing, not behind it.

While interior finishes can technically proceed after exterior walls are sealed, it is a logical sequence preference to complete exterior water management (including flashings) before enclosing interior spaces to prevent moisture damage.
The parapet cavity closer is installed within the parapet wall cavity; the wall structure must be built first to provide the cavity space.
The roof deck provides the base on which the parapet and its cavity closer sit; it must be completed before parapet cavity closer installation.
The cavity closer seals the top of the parapet cavity; coping or capping is installed over the closer to protect it and finish the parapet.
Flashing is dressed over the cavity closer to ensure watertight detailing at the parapet top; the closer must be in place before final weatherproofing.

Applying the final finish or render over the parapet is typically done after cavity closers are installed to achieve a neat appearance, but in some sequences rendering could be done before if closers are inserted from the top.

successor: Parapet Tie Bar / Wall Anchor Installation
rationale: The parapet wall and main masonry walls must be constructed first to provide the structural substrate into which the tie bars or wall anchors are embedded or attached.

successor: Parapet Tie Bar / Wall Anchor Installation
rationale: If the parapet is cast concrete, it must be fully cured to achieve sufficient strength to hold the anchors and resist pull-out forces before tie bars or anchors are installed.

predecessor: Parapet Tie Bar / Wall Anchor Installation
rationale: Wall anchors and tie bars provide the attachment points for counterflashing; the flashing is secured over or into the anchors, so anchors must be in place first.

predecessor: Parapet Tie Bar / Wall Anchor Installation
rationale: Tie bars and anchors are typically embedded in or fastened to the top of the parapet wall before the coping stone or metal coping is installed over them to conceal and protect the connections.

predecessor: Parapet Tie Bar / Wall Anchor Installation
rationale: While anchors are often installed before waterproofing to be integrated into the system, some waterproofing details require the membrane to be applied first with anchors penetrating through; however, the more common sequence is anchors first, then waterproofing lapped over the anchor flanges for continuity.
The metal capping is installed on top of the parapet wall to provide a weatherproof finish. The parapet wall must be fully constructed and cured to provide a stable substrate for the capping.

The parapet capping is part of the roof-edge assembly and typically ties into the roofing system. The roof deck and underlying structure must be in place before capping installation to ensure proper integration and flashing continuity.

Counterflashing is often installed over the top edge of the metal capping to seal the joint between the capping and the wall. The capping must be in place to provide a secure base for flashing attachment.

Metal parapet capping is typically installed prior to the final roofing membrane layer so that the membrane can be terminated or flashed against the capping, ensuring a watertight seal at the roof edge.

Sealants and weatherproofing are applied to joints and seams of the metal capping and adjoining materials after the capping is fixed, to provide a watertight finish and address any gaps or penetrations.
The foundation must be completed and cured before any brick masonry or structural wall construction above grade, including parapets, can begin to ensure structural stability.
The roof slab or structural framing that supports the parapet must be in place before the brick parapet can be constructed upon it.
Roof waterproofing or underlayment is typically installed before the parapet is built to ensure a continuous waterproof seal beneath and behind the parapet base.
The brick parapet wall must be fully laid and cured before the stone or precast concrete coping/capping is placed on top to finish and protect the parapet.

Flashing and sealant details around the parapet (base flashings, counter flashings, and sealant joints) are installed after the brick parapet is complete to seal the interface between the parapet and roofing system.
The structural steel frame must be erected to provide the primary load-bearing structure and support framework onto which the precast concrete parapet panels are installed.
The roof deck must be installed first to define the roof edge and provide a base reference for aligning and securing the parapet panels at the building perimeter.

The parapet must be in place before roof waterproofing can be installed, as the membrane typically laps up the parapet wall and is terminated/flashed at the parapet to ensure a watertight seal at the roof edge.
The precast concrete parapet panels must be erected and secured before the coping (cap) can be installed on top to provide a finished, weather-resistant top surface.

While not a strict physical dependency in all cases, the parapet is typically installed before exterior cladding reaches the roof level so that cladding panels can interface neatly with the parapet edge. This is a logical construction sequence preference to avoid rework and ensure clean junctions.
The balustrade parapet is typically cast atop the concrete deck slab; the deck must be in place to provide the structural base for the parapet formwork and reinforcement.
Deck reinforcing steel must be placed and tied before parapet starter bars can be positioned and the parapet itself cast integrally with the deck.
The vertical or dowel reinforcement (starter bars) for the parapet must be installed and tied before the concrete for the parapet is poured.
Waterproofing membranes are applied after the parapet concrete has cured to ensure a continuous seal at the parapet-to-deck interface.
Metal handrails or railings are bolted or anchored into the cured parapet concrete; the parapet must be sufficiently strong to accept fixings.
The structural deck or roof frame must be in place to provide a substrate and support for the parapet gutter system.
Roof decking creates the underlying surface onto which the parapet gutter is installed and integrated into the roof edge.
The parapet gutter must be installed first so that the roofing membrane can be lapped into the gutter, ensuring a watertight seal at the roof edge.
The gutter must be in place before downspouts or drainage outlets can be connected to it to direct water away.
The parapet gutter is typically installed prior to or concurrent with the parapet wall framing, as the gutter sits at the base of the parapet wall to collect roof runoff.
The scupper is an opening or pipe through a parapet wall; the parapet wall must be built first to provide the structural support and substrate for the scupper installation.

The scupper typically connects to the roof drainage system and penetrates through the parapet at the roof level; the roof deck must be in place to establish the correct elevation and tie-in point for the scupper.
The base layer of roof waterproofing should be installed before cutting openings for scuppers to ensure a continuous waterproof substrate; the scupper flashing is integrated into the membrane system.

After the scupper is set in place, the roof membrane must be flashed up to and sealed around the scupper opening to ensure watertight performance; the scupper must be physically present for the flashing to be terminated against.

The scupper outlet on the exterior side must be connected to downspouts or leader pipes to convey water away from the building; this connection can only be made once the scupper is installed and secured.
The roof deck must be installed to provide the substrate and surface onto which the roof-to-parapet junction flashing and detailing can be applied.
The parapet wall must be built before the junction detail can be executed, as the detail connects the roof membrane to the parapet wall.
Counterflashing is installed over the roof-to-parapet junction base flashing to cover the top edge and prevent water intrusion.
Junction completion is typically required before testing the waterproofing integrity of the roof edge system, though testing could theoretically occur partially earlier.
The junction detail at the parapet must be completed before the final layers of insulation and cover board are installed adjacent to the wall to ensure a continuous waterproof seal.
The DPC must be installed within or on top of the parapet wall structure, so the parapet wall must first be built to provide the substrate for DPC installation.

The DPC provides the waterproof barrier; coping and flashings are installed over or after the DPC to protect the top of the parapet and shed water away, ensuring the DPC is not damaged and functions correctly.
The parapet is an extension of the roof edge, so the roof structure and deck must be complete to define the parapet location and provide access for DPC installation at the parapet level.
Rendering or finishing the parapet surface is done after the DPC is in place to embed, protect, and conceal the DPC within the wall finish.
The DPC is typically laid as a continuous horizontal layer within the masonry course of the parapet; thus the brickwork or blockwork up to the DPC level must be completed first.
Parapet walls are constructed on top of roof slabs; the roof slab must be cast and cured first to provide a structural base for the parapet.
Waterproofing membrane is typically applied to the roof slab surface before parapet walls are built, as the parapet will later integrate with the waterproofing system at the roof edge.
The parapet structure must be fully built (brickwork or concrete) before any plastering, rendering, or finishing coats can be applied to its surfaces.
Coping stones or metal capping are installed on top of the completed parapet wall to protect it from weather ingress; the parapet must be fully constructed first.
Downpipes are often anchored to or routed along parapet walls; the parapet must be in place before downpipe brackets and pipes can be fixed to it.
The parapet wall must be fully constructed and cured before waterproofing can be applied to its surface; waterproofing requires a stable, complete substrate.
The parapet surface must be cleaned, dried, and free of debris, dust, or laitance to ensure proper adhesion of the waterproofing membrane.
A primer coat may be required on the substrate before applying the waterproofing membrane to promote bonding and seal the surface.
After application, the waterproofing material must be allowed to cure or dry completely before any subsequent work can proceed, to ensure its integrity and waterproof performance.

Coping or cap flashing is installed over the waterproofed parapet to mechanically protect the waterproofing membrane from weather, UV, and physical damage, and must be placed after the membrane is applied.
The coping (metal or stone cap) is installed at the edge or perimeter of the roof. A completed roof deck provides the structural base onto which the coping can be mounted.
The underlayment (or waterproofing membrane) must be in place beneath the coping to ensure proper drainage and water tightness at the roof edge.
Coping is typically installed atop parapet walls. The parapet walls must be fully built and cured before the coping cap can be set.
Base flashing and counter-flashing often integrate with the coping. Coping serves as an anchor for flashing, so it must be installed first to ensure a continuous waterproof seal.

Coping defines the finished edge of the roof/wall assembly; however, cladding can sometimes be completed before coping. Installing coping first helps create a clean termination detail, but this is a best-practice sequencing preference rather than a strict physical requirement.
Safe physical access to the parapet (typically at roof edge) is required before personnel can inspect or perform maintenance.
Working at height on or near the parapet requires fall protection (guardrails, safety lines) to be in place before any work begins.

predecessor: Roofing Membrane Installation/Repair (areas adjacent to parapet)
rationale: Roofing work adjacent to the parapet must be complete so the parapet is accessible and to avoid damaging newly installed parapet elements during roofing.
Inspection and repairs of the parapet substrate must be finished before installing the final coping, caps, or flashing to ensure the substrate is sound and ready to receive new finishes.
Any required repairs to the parapet structure must be completed before final cladding or facade finishes at the parapet level are applied, to avoid rework.
Safe access to the parapet at height is physically required before any repair or repointing work can begin.
A condition survey must identify which areas of the parapet require repair and repointing before the work commences.
Soft preference: if brickwork repairs are needed they could be done concurrently, but typically masonry stabilization is addressed before repointing to ensure a sound substrate.
Repointing and masonry repairs must be completed to provide a sound base before installing waterproof capping or flashing over the parapet.
Soft preference: cleaning or finishing work should follow repointing to avoid soiling freshly repaired masonry.
Stair stringers provide the structural support framework that stair treads are mounted onto, so stringers must be in place before treads can be installed.
Risers form the vertical backing that treads abut against, so risers must be installed first to properly support and align treads.
Handrails are typically mounted after treads are in place because the treads provide the walking surface and reference height for proper handrail positioning.
Stair nosing (the edge trim on treads) must be installed after the treads are in place as it attaches directly to the tread edge.

While treads should be installed before final finishing for a uniform appearance, some pre-finishing may be done prior to installation; this is a soft preference for work sequencing rather than a hard physical constraint.

Stair risers must be attached to stair stringers, which provide the structural support and slope for the staircase. Without stringers in place, there is no framework to which risers can be securely fastened.
In typical stair construction, treads are installed first to establish the horizontal stepping surface; risers are then fitted vertically against the back of each tread and between stringers.
The overall stair opening, floor framing, and rough structural work must be completed before any stair components like risers can be installed.

Once risers are in place, finishing activities such as sanding, painting, staining, or applying trim/nosing can proceed. This is a soft preference as some finishing could be done before risers in certain conditions.

Handrails and balusters are typically mounted onto or adjacent to the finished stair structure including risers. The risers establish the vertical plane of each step, which guides proper placement of railings.
The stringer requires a stable, level foundation or supporting structure to be placed upon; foundation preparation must be completed before stringer installation can begin.
Stringers form the structural backbone of stairs; treads and risers are attached to the stringers, so stringers must be in place before treads and risers can be installed.
Stringers must be cut, shaped, and fabricated to the correct dimensions before they can be positioned and installed on site.
Raw materials (e.g., lumber, steel) must be procured before fabrication and cutting of the stringers can commence.
The specific dimensions, angles, and quantities of stringers must be determined during design before materials can be accurately procured.
The structural frame (stairs, balconies, platforms) must be in place to provide a mounting surface for handrails.
Concrete decks or floor slabs must be cured before handrail posts can be anchored or embedded.
Any utilities that will run within or behind the handrail area must be roughed in before handrails are installed to avoid later removal/rework.
Handrails must be in place before final paint, stain, or sealant is applied to the railing and adjacent surfaces to ensure a continuous finish.
Handrail installation must be complete before safety inspections can verify proper height, strength, and graspability per building codes.

Balusters are typically installed on or between structural elements like stairs, balconies, or decks. The supporting structure (e.g., stair stringers, floor framing, railing posts) must be in place to provide a mounting surface for balusters.
For balcony or deck balusters, the deck flooring or sheathing must be installed to define the walking surface and to provide the base/footing for baluster attachment.
Although often installed after balusters, in some sequences handrails are set first to act as a guide; however, this is a soft preference as balusters can be installed independently of handrails.
Top handrails are typically mounted on top of or between balusters; balusters must be in place to support the handrail.
While finishing work is usually done after baluster installation for aesthetic continuity, it is a soft preference because balusters could be pre-finished before installation.
Newel posts require a solid structural base (framed floor with subfloor sheathing) to anchor into; they cannot be installed before the floor structure is built.

predecessor: Rough-In Electrical and Plumbing (if applicable near stairs)
rationale: Any wiring or piping that would run beneath or near the newel post location needs to be roughed in before the post is permanently anchored over those areas.
Handrails are typically connected to and supported by newel posts at landings and ends of stair runs, so the posts must be installed first to provide structural support for the handrails.
Balusters often connect into newel posts (e.g., via plowed channels or dowel holes) and run between posts; therefore, the newel posts must be fixed in place before balusters can be installed.

successor: Final Stair Trim and Finish Work
rationale: Finish carpentry around the stairway—such as baseboards, shoe molding, and stair stringer covers—is completed after the newel posts are in place to ensure tight joints and proper alignment.
The structural frame provides the supporting framework onto which balustrades are attached; without a stable structure, balustrades cannot be installed.
Balustrades are typically mounted onto finished floor or deck surfaces; the floor slab must be in place to provide the base and anchoring surface for balustrade posts.
Handrails are often mounted on top of or integrated with balustrades; the balustrade system must be in place to support the handrail.
Balustrades along staircases must be installed before final stair finishes (e.g., nosing, paint) to allow proper integration and alignment.
If balustrades are anchored into concrete, the concrete must achieve sufficient strength via curing before drilling and anchoring can safely occur.
A stable foundation must be prepared before the winder step can be installed, as the winder step requires a solid base to rest upon.
The stringers (the side supports of the staircase) must be in place before winder steps can be attached, as the winder steps are supported by the stringers.
The winder step must be installed before the handrail can be mounted, as the handrail follows the stair path and requires the completed steps for proper alignment and support.
Finishing work such as sanding, staining, or sealing is typically done after the winder step is installed, though it could be done beforehand in some cases with careful masking.
Adjacent treads that connect to the winder step must be installed after the winder step is in place to ensure proper fit and alignment at the transition point.
Nosing is typically installed at the edge of a finished floor surface, transition, or stair tread. The rough subfloor or substrate must be in place to provide a solid base for the nosing.
For stair nosing, the stair structure (stringers, risers, treads) must be framed and in place before nosing can be attached to the tread edges.
Underlayment (e.g., for laminate, vinyl, or tile flooring) must be laid before the nosing transition piece can be installed to ensure proper height alignment and moisture protection.

In some sequences, nosing is installed after the main floor covering is laid to ensure a tight fit; however in other methods nosing is installed first and flooring butts against it. This is a soft preference depending on the flooring type and manufacturer guidelines.
Baseboard and trim work at staircases and floor transitions should be installed after nosing to cover any gaps and provide a finished look.
The spiral staircase must be anchored to a structurally sound foundation; without completed foundation work there is no stable base to support the staircase load.
The staircase rests on and is secured to the ground floor slab; the slab must be poured and cured before the staircase can be erected.
The spiral staircase often connects to or is braced against upper-floor structural elements; the main structural frame must be in place to provide lateral support and define the vertical opening.
The staircase provides access to the upper level; the upper floor deck must be installed or at least framed after the staircase is in place to ensure proper alignment with the stair landing.

While not physically mandatory, it is safer and more practical to install the spiral staircase before installing adjacent railings so that the staircase's geometry is known and the railings can be aligned correctly.
The staircase must bear on a solid foundation or ground slab; the supporting floor structure must exist before the staircase can be erected.
Staircases are typically anchored to or supported by load-bearing walls or columns at each landing; these structural elements must be in place to provide lateral and vertical support.
Handrails and balustrades attach directly to the staircase stringers or treads; the staircase must be installed first to serve as the mounting surface.
Finish flooring on stair treads and risers is applied after the structural staircase is in place; installing finish materials beforehand would risk damage or misalignment.

successor: Wall and Ceiling Finishing Adjacent to Staircase
rationale: While it is possible to finish walls and ceilings before staircase installation, it is preferred to install the staircase first to allow for precise alignment of finishes around the stair opening and to avoid damaging finished surfaces during stair erection.
The staircase must be supported on a solid foundation or ground floor slab. Without a stable base, the staircase cannot be safely installed.

The staircase is typically housed between two walls or a wall and a stringer. The rough framing of these supporting walls must be in place to define the stairwell opening and provide attachment points for the staircase structure.
A quarter-turn staircase includes a landing at the turn. The floor framing for this intermediate landing must be built to support the landing platform of the stairs.
The staircase structure must be in place so that drywall can be fitted around and against the staircase stringers and finished correctly at the stairwell opening.
Handrails, balusters, and trim work such as skirting boards are installed after the staircase is fully erected and secured, as they attach directly to the finished staircase structure.

predecessor: Foundations and Ground Floor Slab Construction
rationale: The staircase must be supported on a solid foundation or ground floor slab; without the base level constructed, the stair cannot be installed or built.

The staircase lands and stringers require support from walls or structural elements at both the ground and upper floors; the ground floor walls provide lateral support and define the stairwell opening.

successor: First Floor Deck / Upper Floor Slab Construction
rationale: The staircase provides access to the upper floor; the upper floor slab or deck is typically built after the stair is in place to ensure alignment and proper landing support.
Structural installation of the staircase frame and stringers must be complete before applying finishes like handrails, balustrades, and final tread/riser coverings for safety and alignment.

Although the stair must be in place to access the upper floor for interior wall construction, this is a soft preference as walls could be built from scaffolding or temporary access; however, in typical sequences the stair is completed first for safe and efficient movement of materials and workers.

Cantilevered staircases derive their structural support from being embedded into or anchored to a load-bearing wall. The structural wall must be fully installed, cured, and capable of bearing loads before the staircase can be cantilevered from it.

The ground floor slab or foundation at the base of the staircase must be in place to provide the landing point and support for the lowest tread and to anchor the base of the stair stringer if applicable.
For cast-in-place cantilevered stairs, steel rebar or anchor bolts must be embedded into the supporting wall or structure before the stair formwork and concrete pour can proceed.

The exposed underside (soffit) of a cantilevered staircase can only be plastered, painted, or finished after the stair structure itself is fully installed and cured, as the finishing work directly applies to the completed stair surface.

Handrails and balustrades are typically mounted onto or alongside the completed cantilevered stair structure. The stair must be in its final position to take measurements, drill anchor points, and attach the railing system safely.
The structural framing (floors, beams, and load-bearing walls) must be in place to support the staircase and provide the primary structure for attachment.
The rough opening in the floor slab or framing must be cut and prepared to accommodate the staircase before it can be installed.
The main staircase structure must be installed first before any finishing elements like balusters, handrails, and treads can be added.
Electrical, plumbing, or mechanical work adjacent to or within the stairwell area is best done after the staircase is in place to avoid rework, though it is not a strict physical necessity.

successor: Wall Finishing and Painting in Stairwell
rationale: The staircase installation must be completed before final wall finishing and painting in the stairwell area, as the staircase provides access and the finishing work would be damaged or require touch-ups if done prior.
The stair core and shell must be in place before formwork can be installed, as the formwork is built within and against the existing stair structure.
Steel reinforcement must be placed and tied before formwork can be fully closed, as reinforcement needs to be positioned within the formwork cavity.
Formwork creates the mold into which concrete is poured; concrete placement cannot occur until the formwork is fully erected, aligned, and secured.

Stair finishing work such as plastering, tiling, or handrail installation can only begin after the concrete in the formwork has cured and the formwork has been stripped, revealing the final stair shape.
The formwork must first be erected and the concrete poured and cured before stripping can occur, as stripping is the removal of the formwork after the concrete has set.

The steel stair structure typically connects to or is supported by the main structural steel frame, so the frame must be erected first to establish the supporting structural grid, landings, and connections points for the stair.
Fabrication cannot begin until the stair design, shop drawings, and structural details are finalized and approved to ensure accurate material procurement, cutting, welding, and assembly.
Raw steel materials (beams, channels, plates, treads) must be delivered to the fabrication shop before any cutting, welding, or assembly operations can commence.
The fabricated stair components (stringers, treads, landings, handrails) must be fully assembled and welded in the shop before they can be transported to the site and lifted into position.
Fabrication including welding, grinding, and metal finishing must be completed before the stair can be cleaned, primed, and painted to prevent corrosion and achieve the specified finish.
The structural framing (columns, beams, floor slabs) must be fully erected and stable to provide a secure mounting surface and support for the balustrade system.
The concrete floor slab or deck onto which the balustrade will be anchored must be poured, set, and cured to achieve sufficient strength to hold anchors and resist loads from the balustrade.

Any waterproofing on balconies or roofs must be applied before balustrade posts are installed to maintain a continuous waterproof layer; pipe boots and flashings around posts are installed after but the membrane itself goes first.
Once the balustrade is fully installed, it must be inspected and load-tested to verify compliance with building codes for structural integrity, deflection limits, and safety.

It is standard practice to complete balustrade installation before applying final paint or finish coats to adjacent surfaces, as this avoids damage to finishes during installation welding or drilling; this is a logical construction sequence preference rather than a physical impossibility.
The concrete stair structure must be poured and cured to provide a rigid substrate before any finishing materials (treads, risers, or coatings) can be applied.
Rough framing or metal stair stringers must be installed to support the finished treads and risers before finishing work begins.
Any electrical conduit, plumbing, or fire sprinkler lines that run in or under the stair area must be roughed in before permanent finishes cover access.
Handrails and guardrails are typically anchored to or through the finished treads/risers; installing them after the stair finishing is complete ensures proper alignment and secure attachment.
While not a hard physical constraint, it is preferred to complete all stair finishing before final painting of adjacent walls and trim to avoid damaging finished treads with paint drips or overspray.
The staircase must be physically built and structurally installed before any inspection can take place, as there is nothing to inspect otherwise.
For concrete staircases, the concrete must reach sufficient strength before inspection to verify structural integrity.
Handrails and balustrades are part of the staircase safety system and must be in place so the inspection can verify compliance with safety codes.

While finishing works typically follow inspection to avoid covering defects, in some cases finishing can be done before final sign-off if non-structural. It is a soft preference to ensure compliance before aesthetic work.
Inspection must verify general compliance and preliminary condition before any destructive or load testing is performed on the staircase.
The ramp surface or base structure must be complete before handrails can be installed, as handrails need a stable walking surface to align to proper height and anchorage points.
The ramp's structural frame (including posts and stringers) must be in place to provide the supporting structure onto which handrails are mounted.
Once handrails are installed, they must be inspected for compliance with building codes (height, strength, graspability) and load-tested before the ramp is put into service.
It is preferred to complete handrail installation before applying final finishes or paint near the handrail mounting points to avoid damage or touch-up work.
Handrail installation must be complete before final accessibility compliance verification can be conducted, as handrails are a critical accessibility element.
The subgrade must be properly graded and compacted to provide a stable foundation for the ramp curb installation.
Formwork or curb molds must be set in place before concrete can be poured for the ramp curb.
The concrete must be batched and mixed before it can be placed into the ramp curb forms.
After the concrete is placed, finishing operations such as edging, floating, and texturing must follow while the concrete is still workable.
Curing must begin after the concrete has been placed and finished to ensure proper hydration and strength development.
The ramp guardrail must be anchored into the ramp slab. The slab must be fully cured and in place to provide a solid foundation for the guardrail posts and base plates.
The ramp's main structural frame must be completed to define the ramp geometry and provide support before guardrails can be installed along the edges.

Guardrails often serve as edge forms or barriers for the final wearing surface pour; additionally, paving equipment must work around the installed guardrails without damaging them, so guardrails are typically installed before the final surface layer.
While lighting can be installed before or after guardrails, it is often preferred to install guardrails first to define the ramp perimeter and avoid interference during lighting pole placement.
Signage is typically installed after guardrails to accurately position signs relative to the guardrail alignment and ensure proper sightlines.
The ramp nosing must be installed on a stable, properly prepared ramp base or substrate. Without the base/slope being formed and cured, there is no surface upon which to install the nosing.
The structural ramp (concrete, timber, or metal frame) must be in place before the nosing edge profile can be applied at the leading edge of each step or ramp surface.
The nosing provides the edge/transition detail; surface finishes (tiling, non-slip coating, etc.) are applied up to or after the nosing is fixed to ensure a clean transition and proper overlap.

While handrails can be installed concurrently or after nosing, it is good practice to complete nosing before final handrail positioning to ensure consistent edge alignment and fall prevention details.
If a waterproof membrane is required under the ramp surface, it must be installed before fixing the nosing to prevent moisture ingress at the edge detail.
Ramp structural supports require a stable load-bearing foundation to transfer loads safely to the ground; without completed foundation work, the ramp supports have no structural base.
The ground must be properly graded and prepared to the correct elevations and compaction before any ramp structural supports can be installed, ensuring proper alignment and stability.
The structural supports (columns, beams, or walls) must be erected and cured before the ramp deck or slab can be placed on top of them, as the deck relies on the supports for load transfer.
Handrails, guardrails, and barriers are mounted onto or anchored to the ramp structural supports and deck; the primary support structure must be in place first to provide attachment points.

Waterproofing and surface coatings are typically applied after the structural support and deck are complete, but some waterproofing could theoretically be sequenced in parallel with lower-priority scheduling flexibility.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and graded before any foundation work can begin to ensure a stable and properly prepared substrate.
The exact location, elevation, and alignment of the ramp must be surveyed and staked out before excavating or pouring the foundation to ensure correct positioning.
Any underground utilities (water, gas, electric, sewer) in the ramp foundation footprint must be relocated or protected before excavation to prevent damage and ensure safety.
The foundation must be fully cured and load-bearing before the ramp slab or deck can be poured or built on top of it to provide structural support.
Foundation/footing must be in place before masonry or concrete walls forming the ramp sides can be constructed, as walls require a solid bearing surface.
A smooth, clean, and properly graded substrate (e.g., concrete or asphalt) must be completed before tactile warning strips can be installed, as they require a stable base for adhesion or embedment.

Tactile warning strips must be in place before the final surrounding paving (e.g., concrete or asphalt) is finished and cured, so that the strip is seamlessly integrated and flush with the adjacent surface.

Curb ramps (or detectable warning surfaces) are typically constructed first to define the transition area, and the tactile warning strip is then placed at the top or along the ramp to warn of the street crossing.

After installation, the tactile warning strip should be inspected for compliance with ADA or local accessibility standards, but this is a quality assurance step rather than a strict physical constraint.
Proper grading and drainage must be established before installing tactile warning strips to ensure water does not pool around the strip and that the underlying surface is stable and sloped correctly.
The ramp must be built on a stable, level foundation or concrete slab to ensure proper load support and prevent settling or cracking.
Proper grading and drainage around the ramp location must be completed to prevent water pooling, ice formation, and erosion under the ramp.
Any underground electrical conduits for lighting or heating cables must be roughed in before the ramp surface is poured or constructed.
Handrails are attached to the ramp structure itself; the ramp must be in place to serve as the mounting surface for railings.
Final surface texturing, sealants, or non-slip coatings are applied after the ramp structure is fully cured and complete to ensure adhesion and effectiveness.
The ground must be prepared and excavated to the proper depth and grade before the vehicle ramp can be constructed, as the ramp requires a stable, graded foundation.
A compacted subbase or concrete foundation must be in place to support the structural load of the vehicle ramp.
The ramp structure must be built before its driving surface can be paved or finished with asphalt, concrete, or coating.
Safety barriers and guardrails can only be installed along the ramp edges after the ramp structure is complete.

While lighting fixtures can be partially pre-wired, final installation and mounting of ramp lights logically follows completion of the ramp structure, though this could be done concurrently in some cases.
The helical ramp requires a stable foundation to support its structural load and geometry; foundations must be completed before any superstructure elements are erected.
The helical ramp typically connects to or wraps around the building core; the core must be in place to provide structural support and alignment reference for ramp installation.
Reinforcement bars and formwork for the helical ramp's curved geometry must be prepared and positioned before concrete placement for the ramp can begin.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing work within the ramp area must follow ramp construction because the ramp structure provides the physical enclosure and support for these services.
Surface finishing, paving, or coating of the helical ramp can only commence after the ramp structure is fully cured and complete to ensure a proper substrate.
The switchback ramp requires a stable structural base; foundations and substructure elements must be completed first to support the ramp's load.
The site must be rough-graded and earthwork completed to establish the correct slope and terrain profile before the switchback ramp can be formed and poured.
The ramp provides access for material and equipment to upper levels; completing the ramp before structural steel framing in adjacent zones is a soft preference to improve logistics and crane access.
The final paving or wearing surface (e.g., concrete topping, asphalt) can only be applied after the ramp structural slab is fully cured and complete.
Guardrails and safety barriers must be installed after the ramp structure is in place to provide fall protection and comply with safety regulations.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and properly graded to provide a stable and correctly sloped base for ramp construction.
A compacted sub-base is required to support the ramp structure and prevent settling or shifting after ramp installation.
Materials such as concrete, asphalt, steel, or timber must be ordered and delivered to the site before ramp construction can begin to avoid work stoppages.
The ramp structure must be built first to provide a substrate for the final wearing surface (e.g., concrete pour or asphalt overlay).
Safety barriers and guardrails can only be installed after the ramp structure is in place to ensure proper anchoring and alignment with the ramp edges.
Reinforcement bars (rebar) must be placed and tied within the ramp structure before formwork is installed, as the formwork encases the rebar and would block access to place it afterward.

This ordering is incorrect as stated; formwork must be installed before concrete pouring, not after. However, if we consider curing/stripping: After concrete is poured and cured, formwork is stripped (removed). But formwork installation must happen first.
Formwork provides the mold that shapes and supports the wet concrete. Concrete cannot be poured until the formwork is fully installed, aligned, and secured.
Typically rebar is placed before formwork, not after. However, in some sequences, partial formwork may be installed first, then rebar, then the remaining formwork.
After concrete is poured and cured, the formwork must be stripped (removed). Formwork stripping can only begin after the formwork installation and concrete pouring/curing are complete.
Steel rebar reinforcement must be placed and tied within the formwork prior to pouring concrete to provide tensile strength.
The ground or base below the ramp must be properly graded, leveled, and compacted to provide uniform support and prevent settling or cracking of the concrete slab.
After concrete is poured, it must be screeded, floated, troweled, and then cured to achieve proper surface finish and strength development.
Formwork cannot be removed until the poured concrete has achieved sufficient strength to support itself without deformation.

The ramp surface treatment (e.g., concrete topping, asphalt overlay, or coating) requires a stable, compacted, and properly graded base or subgrade to ensure structural integrity and proper drainage. Applying surface treatment without a prepared base would result in failure.

A subbase layer (e.g., aggregate or crushed stone) provides load distribution and drainage. The surface treatment must be placed on top of a properly compacted subbase to achieve design thickness and performance.

The base course (e.g., asphalt base or concrete slab) forms the main structural layer. The surface treatment (e.g., seal coat, thin overlay, or textured finish) is the final riding surface and can only be applied after the base course has cured or gained sufficient strength.

If curbs are placed adjacent to the ramp surface, they are typically installed after the surface treatment to ensure a flush and continuous finish, or the surface treatment is applied up to the finished curb elevation.
Joints (saw-cut or formed) in concrete ramps must be cut after the surface treatment (concrete finish) has been applied and has set sufficiently, to control cracking. Joint sealing follows cutting.
The handrail must be anchored to the ramp structure; the ramp deck/slab must be in place and cured to provide a stable mounting surface for handrail posts or brackets.
Concrete must reach sufficient strength before drilling anchors or embedding handrail posts; otherwise the concrete may crack or fail to hold the fasteners.
It is preferable to install handrails before applying final surface coatings or non-slip finishes to avoid damaging the finished surface during handrail installation work.
Handrails are a critical safety component; the ramp cannot be deemed safe or ready for use until handrails are installed and inspected.
Concrete must be fully cured to achieve required strength before ramp inspection can verify structural integrity.
The formwork for the ramp must be installed and set before inspection can verify proper alignment and dimensions.
Reinforcement steel must be placed and tied before inspection can verify compliance with design drawings.
Concrete must be poured and finished before the ramp surface can be inspected for quality and finish.
Inspection must confirm structural integrity and compliance before any surface finishing or coating is applied.
Inspection must verify ramp construction meets specifications before load testing can safely proceed.
The ramp structure relies on a stable foundation; foundation work must be completed before any ramp maintenance can begin to ensure structural integrity.
After ramp maintenance is performed, a safety inspection must be conducted to verify that the ramp meets safety standards before it can be reopened for use.
General site preparation including clearing and grading must be finished before ramp maintenance activities can commence to provide a safe and accessible work area.
A structural assessment of the ramp must be carried out prior to maintenance to identify areas requiring repair or reinforcement, ensuring that maintenance addresses all necessary issues.

Surface finishing (such as sealing or coating) can only be applied after maintenance work (e.g., repairs, cleaning) on the ramp is complete, so the surface is clean and ready for finishing treatments.
The shaft enclosure wall must be supported by a stable foundation; the substructure must be completed before any vertical wall construction begins.
The base slab or floor at the shaft location provides the starting surface and support for the shaft enclosure walls.

successor: Shaft Interior Fit-Out (e.g., rails, guides, brackets)
rationale: Interior components such as elevator rails or guide brackets are mounted onto or within the completed shaft enclosure walls.
Waterproofing or lining is typically applied after the wall is erected to protect the shaft; though not always a hard physical constraint, it is best practice to apply after walls are complete.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing services running vertically within the shaft can only be installed after the enclosure walls provide the defined shaft space and support.

The lift pit provides the physical space and structural base at the bottom of the lift shaft; the lift car cannot be installed until the pit is complete as it serves as the foundation and safety clearance area.
The lift shaft (hoistway) encloses the area where the lift car travels; the car cannot be placed before the shaft structure is built to provide the vertical pathway and structural support.
Guide rails mounted inside the lift shaft define the vertical path of the lift car; the car must have these rails in place to be properly guided during installation and operation.
Lift doors on each floor interface with the lift car; the car must be positioned and aligned within the shaft before landing doors can be fitted and adjusted to match the car's position.
The lift car must be fully installed and connected before any commissioning, load testing, safety checks, and operational testing can take place to ensure safe and correct operation.
The counterweight must be physically manufactured or cast before it can be installed on-site.
The structural foundation or pit that supports the counterweight must be prepared and cured before the counterweight can be placed.
The counterweight must be installed in its intended position before it can be balanced or fine-tuned.
Mechanical or structural system testing that involves the counterweight (e.g., elevator, crane, or bridge testing) cannot commence until the counterweight is fully installed.
The main structural frame or support system must be in place before the counterweight can be mounted or suspended from it.
Guide rails must be anchored to the elevator pit floor and walls; the pit must exist before rail installation can begin.
The hoistway structure (steel beams, brackets) must be in place to support and attach the guide rails.
Overhead machine room components (deflector sheaves, hoist beam) are needed for alignment reference before rails are plumbed and secured.

successor: Mount Elevator Car Frame and Sling
rationale: The car frame runs on the guide rails; rails must be in place, aligned, and leveled before the car sling can be mounted and guided.
Car guide rails and counterweight guide rails can be installed in parallel, but typically car rails are set first as a reference; however, this is a soft preference, not a physical necessity.
The preparation work for guide rail installation, including layout marking and base inspection, must be completed before brackets can be positioned and secured.
Guide rail brackets must be installed first to provide the mounting points and support structure for aligning and leveling the guide rails.
Brackets must be in place and secured before the guide rails can be fastened onto them.

predecessor: Structural Steel or Concrete Base Completion
rationale: The structural base (steel beams or concrete foundation) where brackets mount must be fully cured and ready to support the bracket load.

predecessor: Bracket Material Inspection and Layout Marking
rationale: Incoming bracket materials must be inspected for defects and the installation layout must be marked on the base structure before brackets can be placed.
A stable foundation must be prepared before buffer assembly can be placed, as the buffer component requires a level and structurally sound base for installation.
The steel frame structure must be erected to provide the supporting framework onto which the buffer assembly will be mounted or integrated.
The buffer assembly must be fully assembled in place before welding connections can be made to join it permanently to adjacent structural elements.
Load testing can only commence after the buffer assembly is complete to verify its structural integrity and performance under design loads.
Corrosion protection coating is typically applied after assembly is complete to ensure full coverage, though in some cases pre-coated components may be used.
The shaft or hoistway must be structurally complete to provide the physical frame and support for mounting landing doors.
Landing doors must be in place to align with and interface with the lift car doors before the car can be fully installed and tested for safe operation.

successor: Shaft Door Landings Finishing (Floor Finishes at Landings)
rationale: While landing doors are often installed before final floor finishes for alignment purposes, ideally floor finishing at landings should be completed first to set the correct finished floor level; however, installation can proceed with temporary adjustments.

successor: Electrical Connection and Testing of Door Interlocks
rationale: The landing door mechanism, including its electrical interlocks and safety circuits, must be physically installed before it can be wired and tested for operation.

successor: Final Inspection and Commissioning of Lift System
rationale: All landing doors must be installed and functioning correctly before the overall lift system can be inspected and commissioned for safe public use.
The hoistway must be prepared and cleared before the landing door frame can be installed, as the frame attaches to the hoistway structure.
The landing door frame must be in place and secured before the landing doors can be hung or installed into the frame.
The door sill is typically set after or aligned with the door frame to ensure proper fit and clearance.
It is preferable to complete the door frame installation before finishing walls around the hoistway to ensure proper alignment and tolerance.
While not physically dependent, completing the landing door frame early allows for coordination of door interlocks and electrical connections during controller setup.
The speed governor must be physically mounted on its bracket before it can be secured and connected.
The speed governor is typically mounted on or driven by the engine (e.g., via gear train, belt, or shaft), requiring the engine to be assembled first.
The speed governor controls fuel delivery; fuel lines and linkages to the governor must be in place before the governor can be fully installed and connected.

successor: Governor Linkage and Control Rod Adjustment
rationale: The governor must be physically installed before control linkages (throttle, fuel rack) can be connected and adjusted to it.
Speed governing functions can only be tested and calibrated after the governor is installed and connected to the engine and fuel system.

The vehicle must be fully assembled before safety gear can be installed, as safety devices (e.g., airbags, seatbelts) are integrated into the vehicle structure and require the complete body and interior to be in place for proper mounting and connection.

Many car safety devices such as airbag control units, seatbelt pretensioners, and electronic stability sensors require electrical connections; thus the vehicle's electrical wiring must be completed before these components can be installed and connected.

Safety gear such as airbags and seatbelts are typically mounted behind or integrated into interior trim panels; installing the safety gear first allows the trim to cover and secure these components properly.

Safety devices must be fully installed before the vehicle undergoes quality control and safety testing, as these tests verify that all safety systems (airbags, seatbelts, sensors) are correctly installed and functioning.
All safety gear must be installed before the vehicle can receive final assembly sign-off, as safety compliance is a mandatory prerequisite for vehicle certification and delivery.
The shaft must be excavated and structurally prepared before the access ladder can be installed inside it, as the ladder is mounted within the shaft space.
The shaft lining (e.g., concrete segments, shotcrete, or steel rings) must be in place to provide a stable structural surface for ladder brackets and fixings.
Safety systems such as fall arrest systems, guardrails, or safety gates are often installed after the ladder is in place to ensure safe access for workers.
The shaft cannot be formally inspected or commissioned for use until the access ladder is installed, as the ladder provides the necessary means of egress and access for inspectors.
Although not a physical constraint, final cleaning and handover typically occur after ladder installation to avoid re-soiling or damaging the newly installed ladder.
Compensation ropes/chains must be anchored to a secure structural support; the anchor system provides the fixed point from which compensation lines are suspended or tensioned.
The primary structural frame (columns, beams, roof trusses) must be in place to provide attachment points and clearance for compensation rope/chains installation.
Compensation ropes/chains are used to adjust and align cladding panels; the compensation system must be operational before curtain wall panels can be fine-tuned into position.
After ropes/chains are installed, they must be tensioned to design specifications and load-tested to verify structural adequacy before subsequent loads are applied.
