Underpinning must be installed and fully cured before deflection monitoring can begin, as the monitoring measures the structural response of the underpinned foundation.
Propping removal and confirmation of stable deflection readings must be completed before backfilling, as backfilling would cover and interfere with monitoring equipment and the propping system.
Stabilization of deflections and removal of temporary propping must occur before final structural elements (e.g., slabs, walls) are constructed on the now-supported foundation.
Concrete must be placed and sufficiently cured to gain strength before propping can be safely removed and deflection monitoring can assess the structural behavior.
Monitoring and propping removal must be complete to allow unobstructed access for waterproofing membrane installation on the exposed structural surfaces.

The concrete slab must be poured and fully cured before any non-destructive integrity testing (e.g., ultrasonic, ground-penetrating radar, or hammer sounding) can be performed, as the test requires a hardened, stable concrete surface to produce valid results.
The slab surface must be smooth, clean, and free of debris, laitance, or curing compounds to ensure proper coupling of NDT sensors and accurate readings.
Formwork must be stripped and the slab fully exposed to allow access for NDT equipment operators to scan the entire slab area.
Any detected defects such as voids, delaminations, or cracks identified during NDT must be remediated before the slab can be considered structurally sound for subsequent overlays or finishes.

successor: Slab Load Testing or Final Sign-off
rationale: Integrity testing results serve as a prerequisite for load testing or final quality acceptance sign-off by the engineer, ensuring the slab meets specified strength and durability requirements before further construction proceeds.

Fire protection materials (e.g., intumescent paint, spray-applied fireproofing) are applied directly to structural steel members. The steel frame must be erected and in place before fireproofing can be applied to it.

While not always strictly required, it is preferable to complete major MEP rough-in work before applying fireproofing to avoid damaging the fire protection during subsequent MEP installations and to ensure complete coverage without obstructions.

Fire protection (especially spray-applied fireproofing and firestopping) must be completed and inspected before enclosing it behind drywall, ceilings, or other final finishes to ensure proper coverage and code compliance.

While fire alarm installation can begin concurrently or before fire protection, the final calibration, integration testing, and commissioning of detection systems often wait until fireproofing and passive fire protection are in place, as the protected structure's fire-resistance rating affects system design parameters.

Formal inspection and testing of fire protection systems (e.g., thickness testing of spray-applied fireproofing, firestop inspection, or sprinkler system hydrostatic testing) must occur after the fire protection application is complete to verify compliance with building codes and specifications.
Formwork must be installed and secured before concrete can be poured to contain and shape the wet concrete.
Reinforcement steel must be placed and tied in position prior to concrete pour so that the steel is fully encased within the concrete mass.

predecessor: Embedded Items / Conduits & MEP Rough-In (in slab)
rationale: Any embedded conduits, piping, or MEP rough-in elements must be positioned and secured before concrete is poured to ensure they are cast in place correctly.
The ground or blinding layer must be properly prepared, leveled, and compacted to provide a stable and uniform base to receive the concrete pour.
Once poured, the concrete must immediately enter its curing phase to manage hydration heat, prevent thermal cracking, and develop required strength.
Shear walls must be constructed on top of a completed foundation system (footings, base slab, or mat) to transfer lateral and vertical loads to the ground.

predecessor: Rebar Cages / Reinforcement Placement for Wall
rationale: Steel reinforcement must be placed and tied before concrete is poured to provide tensile strength as per structural design.
Formwork (shuttering) must be erected to shape and contain the wet concrete until it cures.
Floor slabs or diaphragms bearing on or connecting to shear walls must follow after the wall is cast and cured to achieve composite action for lateral load distribution.
Waterproofing coatings or finishes are typically applied after the concrete has fully cured, but in some sequences they could be done concurrently; thus a soft preference for scheduling clarity.
The foundation must be completed to provide a stable load-bearing base for the steel plate shear wall system.
The surrounding steel frame (boundary columns and beams) must be erected first to provide the structural frame into which the steel plate shear wall panels are installed and welded.

successor: Welding and Bolting of Shear Wall Connections
rationale: Once the shear wall panels are positioned, the connections (welds and bolts) to the boundary frame must be completed to ensure structural continuity.

predecessor: Welding and Bolting of Shear Wall Connections
rationale: All welded connections must be completed before NDT inspection can be performed to verify weld quality and structural integrity.

successor: Fireproofing Application on Steel Plate Shear Wall
rationale: Fireproofing material must be applied after weld inspection is approved, as covering welds before inspection would prevent quality verification.
Composite shear walls require a stable foundation to transfer their loads to the ground; the foundation must be completed and cured before wall construction begins.
Steel reinforcement cage must be placed and tied within the wall formwork before concrete is poured for the composite shear wall.
Formwork panels must be assembled and braced to define the shape and contain the concrete for the composite shear wall before concreting can occur.
Steel sections or profiles that form the composite action with concrete must be positioned and braced within the formwork before concrete placement.
The shear wall must be completed and have achieved sufficient strength to support loads from the floor slab that will bear on or connect to the wall.
Structural walls at lower levels must be finished and cured before load-bearing elements of the next story can be safely erected above them.
Finishing works such as plastering, painting, or cladding are typically performed after the wall is fully constructed and cured, though minor surface work could theoretically overlap.

Masonry shear walls require a solid, level foundation or slab to transfer vertical loads and provide a stable base for masonry construction. Without a completed foundation, the wall cannot be erected.
Vertical and horizontal reinforcing bars (rebar) must be placed and tied before masonry units are laid, as the reinforcement is embedded within the mortar joints and grouted cores of the wall.
Grouting fills the hollow cores of masonry units to bond reinforcement and create a solid structural section; this can only occur after the masonry units are laid up to the required height.

Bond beams are horizontal reinforced elements placed within the masonry wall at certain levels; they must be constructed after the masonry units are laid so that the beam block and reinforcing can be integrated.
Floor and roof diaphragms rely on completed shear walls to transfer lateral loads; the connection detailing (e.g., anchors, ledger bolts) is installed after the wall is in place and cured.
The timber shear wall requires a stable and level foundation to bear its load and transfer lateral forces to the ground. Without the foundation in place, the wall cannot be safely erected.
Timber shear walls are typically installed on top of the floor platform or subfloor, which provides the base surface for alignment, anchoring, and nailing of the bottom plate.
Shear walls provide lateral stability to the structure; upper floor or roof framing depends on the shear wall being in place to transfer vertical loads and resist lateral forces from above.
Exterior cladding and weather-resistant sheathing are applied over the shear wall assembly; the structural wall must be erected and fixed before the cladding layer can be installed.

While rough-in services can proceed after the wall is framed, in some cases partial rough-in may occur before sheathing is fully closed; however, the full wall assembly including shear panels must be in place to safely run services through stud cavities.
Shear walls require a solid foundation to transfer vertical and lateral loads into the ground; the foundation must be cured and load-bearing before any wall construction begins.

predecessor: Ground Floor Slab / Grade Beam Construction
rationale: The first lift of a coupled shear wall typically starts from the ground floor slab or grade beam, which provides the base platform for wall formwork and reinforcement.

successor: Floor Slab / Diaphragm Construction at Each Level
rationale: Floor slabs (diaphragms) bear on or interconnect with the shear walls at each story; the wall must be in place to support and tie into the slab reinforcement.

successor: Reinforced Concrete Core / Stairwell & Elevator Shaft Walls
rationale: Although core walls are often poured concurrently with coupled shear walls in monolithic construction, scheduling the core after the coupled walls allows for better alignment of coupled wall coupling beams and coordination of embedded items.
Exterior cladding and curtain wall systems require the shear wall structure to be complete and stable to serve as the supporting substrate and to establish the building envelope line.

The core shear wall must be supported by a stable foundation or mat slab to transfer its heavy vertical loads and resist overturning forces. Without the foundation in place, the wall cannot be safely constructed.

predecessor: Core Shear Wall Reinforcement (Rebar Cage) Installation
rationale: Reinforcing steel must be placed and tied before concrete can be poured to form the shear wall. The rebar cage provides the structural reinforcement needed for the wall.
Formwork molds must be erected and braced to contain the concrete and shape the shear wall before the concrete placement can occur.

successor: Core Shear Wall Concrete Curing & Stripping
rationale: After the concrete is placed, it must undergo sufficient curing time to gain strength before formwork can be safely stripped.
The core shear wall provides lateral stability and a vertical support element for adjacent floor slabs. Floor slab construction typically follows after the core wall is erected to tie into it.

Boundary elements (such as shear walls or edge columns) require a stable foundation system to transfer loads to the ground; foundation must be completed before any vertical structural element can be erected.
Boundary elements typically start from the ground floor slab or grade beam level, which provides the working platform and load distribution base for the element.

predecessor: Rebar Placement and Formwork for Boundary Element
rationale: Reinforcement steel and formwork must be installed and aligned before concrete can be placed for the boundary element.
Floor slabs or decks above rely on boundary elements as lateral and vertical supports; the boundary element must achieve sufficient strength before supporting upper floor construction.
Boundary elements often form part of the building perimeter; cladding can typically be installed after the structural element is in place, though some overlap may be possible with proper sequencing.
Wall piers require a stable load-bearing base; the foundation/footing must be completed and cured before wall pier construction can begin to support the structural load.

predecessor: Rebar / Reinforcement Installation for Wall Pier
rationale: Reinforcing steel must be placed and tied within the formwork before concrete is poured for the wall pier.
Formwork must be erected and aligned to shape and contain the concrete for the wall pier before pouring can occur.
After the wall pier is poured (the activity of placing concrete), the concrete must cure and forms must be stripped before any subsequent work can proceed.

successor: Vertical Structural Elements Above (e.g., Columns, Beams, Slabs)
rationale: Wall piers provide vertical support for upper structural elements; the pier must be complete and sufficiently cured before erecting columns, beams, or slabs atop it.

Vertical reinforcement bars in a shear wall must be installed first to form the main structural cage, after which horizontal (transverse/lateral) reinforcement can be placed around them to provide confinement and shear resistance.

Formwork provides the mold and support structure; horizontal reinforcement is placed within the formwork before concrete pour, and the formwork must be in place to position the horizontal bars correctly.
All reinforcement (including horizontal bars) must be fully installed and inspected before concrete is poured, as the reinforcement is embedded within the concrete element.
Once horizontal reinforcement is placed, an inspection is required to verify bar spacing, lap lengths, and cover before concrete placement can proceed.
Confinement ties/hoops must be placed around vertical reinforcement bars to confine them; vertical rebar must be in position first before ties can be installed around them.

Ties/hoops are installed within the formwork envelope after the formwork is set, or alternately the ties are placed before formwork; in typical sequences, vertical rebar and ties are placed before the final formwork closure, but ties cannot be placed if the main vertical bars are not already positioned.
Confinement ties/hoops must be fully installed and tied to the vertical reinforcement before concrete is poured, to ensure proper confinement of the core and seismic ductility.

Cover blocks are typically placed after rebar and ties are in position to ensure proper concrete cover; this is a soft preference as spacing can be adjusted on the fly but best practice is after tie installation.
The vertical bar cage must be assembled and stood up before confinement ties/hoops can be tied around the vertical bars at specified spacing intervals.
Excavation must be completed to reach the required bearing strata and create space for the foundation mat.
The subgrade must be properly graded and compacted to provide a stable, uniform bearing surface for the mat foundation.
A lean concrete blinding layer is often placed to provide a clean, level working surface for reinforcement placement and mat pouring.
Reinforcement steel must be tied and formwork erected before concrete can be placed for the mat foundation.
Shear wall vertical reinforcement and core walls cannot be started until the mat foundation has been poured and cured to provide a solid base and proper dowel anchorage.
Below-grade waterproofing membrane application requires the cured mat surface for proper adhesion and continuity at the foundation-to-wall interface.
Backfill against the foundation is typically done after the mat and any foundation walls are sufficiently cured, though it could be considered a soft constraint if other work is prioritized.
Hold-down anchors must be embedded into the concrete foundation; the foundation slab must be poured and cured to provide the substrate for anchor placement.
Anchor bolts are often set prior to or concurrently with the concrete pour to provide the threaded connection points or embedment for hold-down anchors.
Hold-down anchors secure the wall framing (e.g., shear walls) to the foundation; the anchors must be in place before walls can be erected and fastened to them.
Hold-down anchors are integral components of the lateral load-resisting system; shear wall panels are attached to the anchors after the anchors are installed and cured.
Concrete must reach sufficient strength before hold-down anchors are tensioned or torqued to avoid pulling out or damaging the green concrete.
Rebar cage must be installed and tied before formwork is placed, as formwork encloses the rebar and cannot be easily installed afterward.
The exact location and alignment of the shear wall must be marked on the slab/deck before formwork panels are positioned.
Formwork provides the mold that contains and shapes the wet concrete; concrete cannot be poured without erected formwork.
Before concrete is placed, the erected formwork must be checked for alignment, plumbness, and bracing adequacy to ensure structural tolerances.
Embedded conduits, sleeves, and blockouts are often installed into the formwork or rebar before concrete; however, the formwork must first be in place to locate and support these items.

The architectural floor plan defines the spatial layout, room sizes, and functional requirements of the building, which are essential to determine where shear walls can be placed without conflicting with doors, windows, corridors, and usable space.
Soil bearing capacity, seismic soil classification, and foundation recommendations from the geotechnical report directly influence shear wall sizing, reinforcement, and lateral load design.
Gravity loads (dead/live) and lateral loads (wind/seismic) must be quantified before shear walls can be rationally designed to resist these forces.
Shear wall locations and dimensions dictate slab and beam span directions, support conditions, and load transfer paths to the walls.
Shear walls transfer lateral and vertical loads to the foundation; the foundation type, depth, and reinforcement layout depend on the wall locations and the loads they impose.
Formwork must be erected first to provide the mold and support system before rebar can be placed inside the wall forms.
All rebar must be placed and tied before concrete can be poured, as the reinforcement needs to be embedded within the concrete pour.
Survey and layout marking must be completed to define the exact position and alignment of the shear wall before rebar placement begins.
The foundation or base slab must be completed to provide a stable base and to allow for proper dowel embedment and starter bar connection from the foundation into the wall rebar.

Rebar placement must be largely complete before MEP (mechanical, electrical, plumbing) rough-in work, as conduits and sleeves are often placed within or through the rebar mat, but the rebar cage must be in place first.
Rebar must be fully installed, tied, and inspected before concrete can be poured, as the reinforcement provides the structural strength for the shear wall.
Formwork must be erected, aligned, and braced to contain the wet concrete and shape the shear wall before pouring can occur.

predecessor: Shear Wall Embedment & MEP Sleeve Installation
rationale: All embedded items, conduits, sleeves, and blockouts for mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems must be placed and secured within the rebar cage before concrete is poured, as they cannot be installed afterward.
Concrete must be poured and cured to sufficient strength before formwork can be safely removed to avoid damaging the green concrete.
Final surface finishing, patching of form-tie holes, and defect repair can only be performed after concrete has been poured and forms have been stripped.
Formwork is erected around the reinforcement cage. The rebar must be in place before formwork panels can be positioned and secured.
The wall geometry and alignment must be marked on the slab/deck before formwork can be placed accurately.
Rebar inspection and approval by the engineer is required by code before closing the formwork, as it becomes inaccessible afterwards.
Concrete cannot be placed until the formwork is fully erected, aligned, braced, and checked. The formwork acts as the mold for the wet concrete.
After pouring, the concrete must cure while the formwork is still in place. Formwork stripping (removal) occurs only after sufficient curing strength is achieved.

Reinforcement (rebar) must be installed and tied before the shear wall can be inspected for compliance with structural drawings and tested (e.g., for reinforcement spacing, cover, and concrete testing).
Formwork must be erected before inspection can verify alignment, dimensions, and plumbness, and before concrete testing (e.g., slump tests) can be performed.
After the wall is poured, curing and post-pour inspections (e.g., concrete compressive strength tests, crack inspections) must be performed to verify quality and structural integrity.
Formwork removal can only commence after the concrete has achieved sufficient strength, which is verified through inspection and testing (e.g., cylinder test results).
Final surface finishing and waterproofing application must wait until the wall has passed inspection and any defects have been corrected.
Diaphragms are structural elements that transfer lateral loads to the foundation system, so the foundation must be complete to provide a stable base for load transfer.
Diaphragms (floor or roof diaphragms) typically bear on or connect to walls, so walls must be constructed first to provide support.
Columns provide vertical support for floor and roof diaphragms; columns must be erected before diaphragms can be placed.
If the diaphragm is a structural sub-component (e.g., a steel or concrete diaphragm), roof decking or topping slabs are placed over it to complete the system.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) work above a floor diaphragm typically begins after the diaphragm is complete, but this is a soft preference as MEP can sometimes be coordinated concurrently.
The collector/drag strut attaches to the main wing structure or spars; the wing structure must be in place to provide the attachment points for the strut.
The collector/drag strut is part of the internal wing structure that must be installed before the wing skin or covering is applied over it.

successor: Install Control Cables / Linkages through Wing
rationale: The drag strut provides routing points or clearance zones for control cables; while it's a soft preference to route cables after strut installation for better access, cables could theoretically be installed first and routed around.

successor: Perform Wing Structural Testing / Torque Check
rationale: The drag strut is a structural component that must be installed and properly torqued before any structural integrity testing of the wing assembly can commence.

predecessor: Fabricate / Machine Collector / Drag Strut Component
rationale: The physical component must be manufactured or fabricated before it can be installed into the aircraft structure.

The shear wall must first be constructed (poured and cured) before any openings or penetrations can be formed or cut through it. The wall mass must exist as a structural element before openings can be created.
The location, size, and reinforcement details of openings in a shear wall must be approved by a structural engineer to ensure the wall retains its structural integrity after the penetration is made.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) lines that pass through the shear wall can only be installed after the opening or sleeve is created in the wall.

After cutting or forming the opening in the shear wall, additional reinforcement (such as extra rebar or lintel beams) must be placed around the opening to restore structural capacity before final finishing.

Any final finishes such as plastering, painting, or cladding of the shear wall surface should be done after all penetrations are completed to ensure a uniform finish and to avoid damaging finished surfaces during opening work.
The seismic joint must be installed after the shear wall reinforcement is in place, as the joint accommodates movement between wall segments.
Formwork defines the wall geometry and joint location; the seismic joint material is placed within the formwork before concrete pour.
The seismic joint material (e.g., expansion joint filler) must be placed in the formwork gap before concrete is poured to create the intended separation.
After the joint is formed (post-concrete cure), waterproofing or sealant is applied to protect the joint from moisture ingress.
Connections to beams, slabs, or other walls at the joint location can only proceed after the joint is properly installed and concrete has cured.
The area must be cleared of existing walls, finishes, and debris to expose the structural elements and provide a clean workspace for shear wall installation.
Engineering evaluation is required to determine the location, size, reinforcement, and connection details of shear walls before any construction can begin.
Foundations and below-grade work must be completed to provide a stable load path for the shear walls and avoid rework or structural conflicts.
Shear walls are primary structural elements; all rough-in services that penetrate these walls must be installed after the walls are in place to ensure proper coordination and structural integrity.
Shear walls must be completed to provide the lateral load-resisting system before any non-structural framing, sheathing, or exterior cladding can be safely installed.

predecessor: Foundation or Slab on Grade Placement
rationale: Shear walls require a stable, level base to bear on; the foundation or slab must be fully cured and capable of supporting the wall's dead load and transferring lateral loads to the ground.
Vertical and horizontal reinforcing bars must be in place within the wall footprint before the shear wall panel formwork or precast panel is set, as the rebar is embedded into the wall section.
Formwork must be erected and braced to the correct alignment before concrete can be placed, as it defines the shape, thickness, and position of the shear wall.

predecessor: Shear Wall Concrete Pour (or Panel Erection)
rationale: The shear wall must be in place and have gained sufficient strength before the next-floor slab is constructed, because the slab bears on the wall and relies on it for lateral load transfer.
Backfill cannot be placed against a shear wall until the concrete has reached adequate strength to resist lateral earth pressures and avoid damage or cracking.
Core wall boundary elements require rebar to be in place before concrete is placed, as the boundary element contains additional reinforcement to resist seismic forces.
Formwork must be erected to define the shape and contain the concrete for the core wall boundary element.
The boundary element (with its reinforcement and formwork) must be complete and ready before the concrete pour for the core wall can begin.
MEP rough-in within the core area typically proceeds after the structural boundary element is complete to avoid interference, though in some cases sleeves can be cast-in-place.
The boundary element concrete must be placed and initially set before curing and formwork stripping can commence.
Formwork must be installed and secured before concrete can be poured into the wall section to contain and shape the wet concrete.
Steel reinforcement cage must be in position within the formwork before concrete is poured to ensure structural integrity of the wall.
After the concrete is poured, it must be left to cure and gain sufficient strength before any further construction loads are applied.
The poured concrete must set and achieve initial strength before formwork can be safely removed without damaging the wall section.
Waterproofing is typically applied after the concrete wall has cured, but this could be considered a soft preference if immediate waterproofing is not critical for structural sequence.
Horizontal ties are placed around and tied to the vertical rebar; vertical bars must be installed first to provide the framework.
One side of formwork is typically erected before rebar installation to provide support and positioning for the rebar cage.
The second side of formwork cannot be closed until all rebar (including horizontal ties) is placed and inspected.
Concrete cannot be poured until all reinforcing steel, including horizontal ties, is installed and inspected.

The footing or foundation concrete must be poured and at least partially cured to provide a stable base and anchorage for the vertical rebar cage. Without the foundation, there is no structural element to embed or support the rebar cage.
The rebar cage must be pre-assembled (tied and wired) on the ground or at a staging area before it can be lifted and placed into position.
Formwork is placed around the completed rebar cage to contain the subsequent concrete pour. The rebar cage must be in position before the forms can be closed around it.
Concrete cannot be placed for a vertical structural element until the rebar cage is fully installed and inspected, as the reinforcement must be inside the concrete to provide structural strength.
Horizontal reinforcement (e.g., for beams, slabs, or columns intersecting the vertical element) must be connected to the vertical cage while it is accessible, before forms are closed.
Formwork must be in place to define the concrete geometry and provide a surface to which the embed plate can be attached or positioned before concrete is poured.
Reinforcement steel must be placed and tied so that the embed plate can be secured to the rebar cage and properly positioned within the concrete section.
The embed plate must be installed, leveled, and secured in position before concrete is poured so that it becomes monolithic with the concrete element.
The concrete must cure and the plate must be embedded before any structural steel can be welded or bolted to the embed plate.
If the embed plate is cast-in-place, grouting is not typically needed; however, if it is a post-installed plate, grouting around the anchors fills any gaps after plate installation.
The ground must be cleared and excavated to the required depth and levels before any foundation work can commence.
If soil conditions are poor, ground improvement such as compaction grouting or stone columns must be completed to achieve the necessary bearing capacity before pouring the foundation.
A blinding layer of lean concrete must be placed over the excavated base to provide a clean, level, and stable working platform for reinforcement placement and formwork for the raft pedestal.
Any below-grade waterproofing system for the raft foundation must be installed on the blinding concrete before reinforcement steel is placed and concrete is poured.
The raft pedestal/foundation slab must be cast and cured to provide a solid base upon which the core wall reinforcement can be erected and formwork installed.
The foundation must be complete and sufficiently cured before the vertical core wall elements are poured to ensure structural continuity and load transfer.

Backfilling is typically done after the foundation and core walls have gained sufficient strength, but if sequencing allows it is preferred to complete walls first to avoid disturbing the fresh foundation.

The core wall must first be constructed/poured before any openings (doors, windows, MEP penetrations) can be cut or formed into it. The wall must exist physically before an opening can be created in it.
Reinforcement steel must be installed and tied before concrete can be poured and before openings are formed, as rebar must be placed around the opening area with proper lapping and detailing.
Formwork must be erected before openings can be formed; the door opening frame or blockout is typically placed within the formwork prior to concrete pour.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work through the core wall can only proceed once the door opening or wall penetration exists, providing the physical access path through the wall.
The door frame can only be installed after the rough opening in the core wall has been formed and the concrete has cured, providing the proper opening dimensions for frame placement.
Formwork provides the mold and structural support for concrete; rebar must be placed inside the formwork before concrete pouring, so formwork must be installed first.
Rebar installation for walls/columns typically requires the foundation to be poured and cured to provide a stable base and proper anchorage for vertical reinforcement.
Rebar must be fully placed, tied, and inspected before concrete can be poured, as concrete encases the reinforcement and the rebar position cannot be adjusted afterward.
Rebar installation must be inspected and approved by the engineer before concrete placement to verify correct size, spacing, and tie patterns.

While some electrical conduits and embedments can be placed concurrently, critical embedments that conflict with rebar placement are typically done after rebar is in place to avoid interference; this is a soft preference for sequencing.
Formwork must be fully installed, aligned, and inspected before concrete can be poured, as the formwork provides the mold and structural support for the wet concrete.
Steel reinforcement must be placed, tied, and inspected prior to pouring concrete so that the reinforcement is properly embedded within the concrete for structural integrity.
All embedded conduits, piping, sleeves, and other MEP services must be installed and inspected before concrete pouring, as they cannot be placed after concrete hardens.
After concrete is poured and vibrated, it must undergo curing (maintaining moisture and temperature) to achieve design strength and durability; curing cannot begin until pouring is complete.
Formwork can only be stripped after the concrete has gained sufficient strength from pouring and curing; removing forms before concrete hardens would cause structural collapse.
Concrete must be poured and sufficiently cured to gain enough strength before formwork can be safely removed without causing damage to the structure.
Reinforcement steel must be fixed in place before concrete is poured, which in turn must cure before formwork striking can occur.
Once formwork is struck, the vertical structural elements become exposed and are considered complete for that pour cycle, allowing subsequent finishing or loading.
Struck formwork panels are advanced (moved) to the next floor or bay to be re-erected for the subsequent concrete pour cycle.

Concrete cube or cylinder tests must confirm that the concrete has reached sufficient strength (typically 70-100% of design strength) before formwork removal is permitted to prevent structural failure.
The core wall must be cast and concreted first before surveying and plumb checking can be performed, as there would be no wall to measure otherwise.
Reinforcement must be placed and tied before concrete is poured into the core wall forms.
Formwork must be erected to provide the mold and support structure before rebar can be placed inside.
Surveying and plumb check must confirm the wall alignment and verticality before forms can be safely removed; if adjustments are needed, they must be made while forms are still in place.
It is preferable to complete survey checks before finishing works so that any major alignment issues are addressed first, though in practice minor finishing may proceed concurrently.
Concrete must be freshly poured and in place before curing can begin, as curing is the process of maintaining moisture and temperature conditions to allow the concrete to hydrate and gain strength.

Final surface finishing operations such as screeding, floating, and troweling must be completed before curing starts, because curing compounds or wet coverings would interfere with finishing, and curing should begin only after the surface has been properly finished and initial set has occurred.
Formwork must be erected and secured prior to pouring concrete to contain the fresh concrete in the desired shape and position.
Steel reinforcement must be placed and tied before concrete is poured, so that the reinforcement is properly embedded within the concrete section.
Formwork should remain in place during the curing period to support the concrete until it has gained sufficient strength; stripping too early can cause cracking or structural failure.

Curing must be completed and the concrete must be sufficiently dry before applying waterproofing membranes or coatings, as moisture trapped beneath these layers can cause adhesion failure or blistering.
Concrete must be adequately cured and have reached its specified design strength before it can safely support structural loads, whether from subsequent construction activities or service loads.
Concrete must be placed and sufficiently cured to achieve the design strength before any post-installed anchors or rebar couplers can be installed into the hardened concrete.
The drilled hole (including cleaning of dust/debris) must be completed to provide the cavity into which the anchor or coupler is inserted.
Post-installed rebar couplers must be set and bonded into the concrete before the adjacent reinforcement can be tied or connected to them.
Testing is a quality-assurance step that verifies the installed anchor/coupler capacity, but it could theoretically be deferred or omitted for non-critical applications.
Embedded couplers and anchors must be in place before formwork is built around them, as they protrude from the concrete surface and formwork must accommodate their position.

The exposed soffit is typically the underside of a structural roof or floor slab. The structural framing (steel or concrete) must be complete to provide the substrate to which soffit finishes are applied or to define the soffit surface itself.
For concrete structures, the roof slab or deck must be poured and cured before the underside (soffit) can be formed, finished, or treated as an exposed architectural surface.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work in the ceiling/roof cavity above the soffit must be completed before the soffit is enclosed or finished, to avoid costly demolition and rework.
The exposed soffit surface must be installed and prepared before final paint, stain, or architectural finish coatings can be applied.
While not a hard physical constraint, it is standard practice to complete the soffit before installing ceiling trim and moldings that abut the soffit edge for a clean, finished appearance.
Closed soffit requires the overhead structural framing (beams, joists) to be in place to provide a substrate for soffit attachment.
All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing work in the ceiling/soffit zone must be completed before the soffit is enclosed, as the soffit will block access to these systems.
Insulation in the soffit cavity must be installed before the soffit is closed, as it cannot be accessed afterward.
Closed soffit provides a finished ceiling surface that must be in place before final interior finishes such as taping, mudding, and painting can be applied to the soffit area.
Recessed lighting fixtures mounted in the soffit require the soffit enclosure to be complete so that cutouts can be made and fixtures can be properly secured and aligned.
Soffit panels are typically attached to the underside of roof eaves, which requires the roof framing and overhang structure to be in place first to provide the support surface.
The roof deck must be installed to define the eave overhang geometry and provide the structural base before soffit can be fitted beneath it.
Soffit connects at the intersection of the wall and roof eave; exterior wall sheathing must be in place to establish the wall plane and provide attachment points for soffit trim.

While attic insulation can be installed before soffit, it is preferable to complete vented soffit first to ensure proper venting pathways (soffit vents) are in place before blown or batt insulation is added, preventing blockage of airflow.
Soffit is typically installed before the final row of siding to allow proper interlocking and a clean finished edge at the eave line, though some sequences can overlap with careful detailing.
The stair soffit is the underside of the stair structure; the structural frame or slab must be complete to provide a substrate for soffit installation.
Finishing materials (e.g., plaster, paint, or cladding) on the underside of stairs can only be applied after the soffit itself is installed.
Any ceiling treatments, lighting fixtures, or bulkheads under the stairs depend on the soffit being in place as the finished underside surface.
Electrical, plumbing, or mechanical rough-in work in the space beneath the stairs must be completed before the soffit is enclosed.
Lighting fixtures mounted to or recessed into the stair soffit require the soffit to be in place for installation.
Beam soffit is the underside of a concrete beam. The beam must be poured and cured to sufficient strength before the soffit formwork can be stripped or soffit finishing can commence.
Reinforcement steel must be placed and tied within the beam formwork before concrete is poured, which then forms the beam soffit underside.
The formwork (including soffit panels) must be erected to shape and support the wet concrete that will form the beam soffit.
Finishing work such as plastering, painting, or applying fireproofing to the soffit can only begin after the beam soffit has been formed, cured, and formwork stripped.
While it is common practice to install false ceilings after the structural soffit is complete, it is a construction preference for sequence efficiency rather than a physical necessity.

The arch centering or falsework must be erected first to provide a temporary supporting structure for the arch soffit (intrados) to be formed or placed upon, as the intrados is the inner curved surface of the arch.
The abutments or supports at the arch ends must be completed to provide the structural bearing points before the arch soffit can be constructed between them.
The intrados (soffit) forms the inner curved surface of the arch; voussoirs (wedge-shaped blocks) are placed upon/against this soffit to build the arch ring, so the soffit surface must exist first.
The extrados (outer curved surface) is built over/after the intrados is established, as the intrados defines the arch's inner profile and the extrados follows the concentric outer curve.

The centering/falsework can only be removed after the arch soffit and the full arch ring are completed and the structure is self-supporting; removing support before the soffit is in place would cause collapse.
The main ceiling grid and support structure must be in place before a soffit or bulkhead can be dropped, as the soffit is typically suspended from or attached to the main overhead structure.
Rough-in MEP work (ductwork, piping, conduit) in the ceiling space must be completed before enclosing that space with a soffit or bulkhead, to avoid costly rework and ensure accessibility.

successor: Install Ceiling Finishes / Drywall Below Soffit
rationale: The soffit/bulkhead structure must be in place before ceiling finishes (e.g., drywall, ceiling tiles) can be installed up to or against it.
The soffit must be fully constructed before its surfaces can be painted or finished.

predecessor: Complete Framing of Walls / Studs in Area
rationale: Wall framing should typically be completed before soffit installation, as the soffit often ties into or is supported by adjacent wall framing.

Wall sheathing must be completed before soffit panels are installed because soffit panels are mounted against or adjacent to the exterior wall sheathing, which provides the structural backing and nailing surface for the soffit.

The roof decking must be in place before soffit panels are installed because the soffit is located beneath the roof overhang and requires the roof structure above to be complete for proper alignment and attachment.

Soffit panels must be installed before exterior siding because the siding typically overlaps or butts against the soffit, and the soffit provides the top termination point and weatherproofing detail for the sidewall siding.

Soffit panels must be installed before fascia boards because the fascia covers the edge of the roof deck and the outer edge of the soffit; the soffit runs into the back of the fascia, so the soffit must be in place first.

Gutters are mounted onto the fascia board, which is installed after the soffit. The soffit provides the finished ceiling under the roof overhang that gutters drain above, so soffit must be complete before gutter brackets and gutters are installed.
Soffit vents are installed into the soffit, which is the underside of the roof overhang; the roof framing must be complete to provide the structural support for the soffit area.
The exterior walls must be sheathed before soffit installation because the soffit attaches to the wall framing and the bottom of the roof eaves.

Soffit vents provide intake ventilation for the attic; blocking or covering them with insulation would defeat their purpose, so they must be installed and screened before insulation is blown or placed in the attic.
The soffit and its vents are typically installed before the final course of siding up to the eave, as the siding often butts up against or tucks under the soffit trim.

J-Channel and F-Channel trim are used around windows, doors, and wall edges to receive siding. The exterior wall sheathing must be in place to provide a nailing surface and structural backing for the trim.

J-Channel is typically installed around window and door frames to provide a clean edge and allow siding to tuck into the channel. Windows and doors must be installed first so the trim can be fitted around their perimeters.
The weather-resistant barrier (e.g., Tyvek) must be applied over the sheathing before trim is installed to ensure proper moisture management behind the trim and siding.

J-Channel and F-Channel trim serve as edge receivers that siding panels or planks slip into. Siding installation must follow trim installation so that siding ends are concealed and securely held within the channels.

successor: Corner Trim / Outside Corner Post Installation
rationale: While corner posts can be installed before or after J-Channel, it is common practice to install corner trim after J-Channel so that the J-Channel pieces can terminate neatly against the corner posts, but this is a work sequencing preference rather than a physical necessity.
The lookout rafters and soffit nailers attach to the top plate of the wall; the top plate must be installed to provide a bearing surface and attachment point.
The exterior walls must be framed and sheathed to support the roof structure and provide the attachment surface for lookout rafters.
Soffit material is fastened to the lookout rafters/soffit nailers; these framing members must be in place to provide nailing support for the soffit.
Lookout rafters support the roof edge and provide a surface for roof sheathing at the eaves; roof sheathing cannot be properly installed without the lookout framing in place.
Fascia boards are attached to the ends of lookout rafters; the lookout rafters must be installed first to provide a nailing surface for the fascia.
Soffits are installed to the underside of roof eaves; roof sheathing must be in place to provide the structural support and nailing surface for soffit panels or boards.

Fascia boards are installed along the roof edge before soffits, as the soffit typically butts into or is supported by the fascia. Fascia provides the outer trim and support for the soffit installation.
Exterior wall sheathing must be complete to provide a surface against which the soffit can be trimmed and sealed, ensuring a weather-tight connection between the soffit and the wall.

Siding is typically installed after soffits because the soffit provides the upper termination point and trim for the siding; siding panels or boards are fitted up to and under the soffit to ensure proper water shedding and a finished appearance.

successor: Exterior Trim and Soffit Vent Installation
rationale: Soffit vents (for attic ventilation) are installed as part of or immediately after the soffit is in place, and final exterior trim details that interface with the soffit must be completed afterward.
Soffit vents are installed in the soffit panels beneath roof overhangs, which require the roof structure (trusses or rafters) to be in place to provide the supporting framework for the soffit.
The soffit panels attach to the exterior walls and roof eaves, so the wall sheathing must be complete to provide a nailing surface and proper enclosure before soffit installation.
Roof decking must be installed to define the eave area and provide structural support before soffit work can proceed.

Proper attic ventilation relies on soffit vents as intake vents; ridge vents or other exhaust vents at the roof peak require soffit intake airflow to be in place, but soffit installation at the eave must precede the final roof covering to maintain weatherproofing sequence and access.

Fascia boards and gutters are installed after soffit work is complete because the soffit panels terminate at the fascia line, and gutters attach to the fascia; soffit must be finished before these trim elements are added.

While soffit and siding can often be done in tandem, it is common best practice to complete soffit first to ensure proper flashing and weatherproofing at the wall-to-eave intersection, though it is a soft preference rather than a physical necessity.
The soffit must be physically installed and in place before any painting or finishing can be applied to its surface.
The soffit surface must be cleaned, sanded, and primed to ensure proper paint adhesion and a smooth finish.
Safe working access (scaffolding, lifts, or ladders) must be erected to reach soffit areas before painting can begin.
After soffit painting is complete, a final quality inspection and minor touch-ups are needed to ensure the finish meets specifications.

It is preferable to complete soffit painting before installing exterior lights on or near the soffit to avoid paint splatter on fixtures, though fixtures could be installed earlier if properly protected.
Inspectors need physical access to the underside of roof overhangs or ceilings; scaffolding or lifts must be erected before inspection can occur.
The soffit is the underside of the roof overhang; the roof deck must be installed first so the soffit structure is in place for inspection.
The soffit must be fully installed before it can be inspected for quality, damage, or code compliance.
Any deficiencies or damage found during inspection must be addressed after inspection identifies the issues.
Typically the soffit inspection is a prerequisite before the exterior work can receive final approval or sign-off, though some jurisdictions may allow phased sign-offs.
Safe and proper access to the soffit area is physically required before any soffit work can commence.
Inspection must identify damaged sections and determine the scope of repair before replacement work can begin.
Existing damaged soffit material must be removed before new soffit can be installed.
Fascia boards support the edge of the soffit and must be in place and secure before soffit installation can proceed.
Gutters are typically mounted over or adjacent to the soffit/fascia assembly, so soffit work must be completed before gutters are installed or repaired.
While painting can follow, it is a soft preference as some finishing may be done simultaneously; however, for clean lines and protection, final painting is best done after soffit installation.
Scaffolding and access equipment cannot be removed until all elevated soffit work is fully completed.
Roof sheathing must be installed to define the roof deck and rafter bays before eave baffles can be placed at the eaves to maintain airflow channels.
Soffit vents provide the intake air path; the eave baffle must be installed to direct air from the soffit vent up into the rafter space, so soffit installation must precede baffle placement.
Eave baffles create an air gap between the insulation and roof deck, ensuring ventilation. Insulation must be installed after baffles so it does not block the airflow path.
While not a strict physical requirement, completing attic ventilation baffles before closing up ceilings prevents the need for rework and ensures ventilation pathways are fully in place.
The structural frame (columns, beams) must be erected to provide vertical and lateral support before the balcony slab can be placed.
Formwork and shuttering must be set up to define the shape and support the wet concrete of the balcony slab until it cures.
Rebar mesh and dowels must be placed and tied within the formwork before concrete can be poured for the balcony slab.
After pouring, the balcony slab concrete must undergo a specified curing period to achieve design strength before any loads are applied.
Waterproofing membrane must be applied to the cured balcony slab to protect the structural concrete and underlying spaces from water ingress.
Guardrails and handrails are anchored into the balcony slab; the slab must be completed and cured to provide a stable base for railing posts.
Floor finishes such as tiles or screed can be laid on the balcony slab after it has cured, but this is a soft preference as some finishes could be applied earlier if scheduling allows.
The balcony railing must be anchored to a completed structural floor slab or deck to provide a stable foundation and load-bearing support.
The balcony structural framing (joists, beams) must be in place before railing installation to provide the physical substrate for attachment.
Waterproofing must be applied to the balcony deck before railing posts are installed, as post bases and penetrations should be set into a waterproofed surface to prevent moisture intrusion.
The railing must be fully installed before final safety inspections can verify compliance with building codes for guardrail height, spacing, and load resistance.

successor: Exterior Finishing / Cladding Adjacent to Railing
rationale: It is often preferred to complete railing installation before adjacent exterior finishes so that cladding can be fitted neatly around or up to the railing posts for a clean aesthetic finish.
The guardrail posts must be anchored into the concrete balcony slab. The slab must be cast and fully cured to provide a solid base for post installation and achieve required anchorage strength.
Waterproofing must be applied to the balcony slab before drilling or embedding posts to maintain the waterproof integrity. Post-installed anchors would breach an unsealed waterproofing layer.
Handrails and top rails are supported by and attached to the vertical posts, so the posts must be secured first to provide the structural framework for railing installation.
Infill elements (glass panels, pickets, or mesh) are mounted between or alongside the posts, requiring the posts to be in place as the primary structural supports.

successor: Guardrail Post Caps & Finishing Trim Installation
rationale: Post caps and decorative trim are typically fitted after the post is erected; however this is a cosmetic/finishing step that can sometimes be done concurrently, making it a soft preference rather than a strict physical constraint.

The balcony handrail must be anchored to or supported by the finished balcony slab/deck. The concrete or deck structure must be cured and capable of supporting loads before handrail posts can be installed.
The main structural frame of the building (including floor levels where balconies are located) must be complete to define the balcony edge and provide support for the handrail system.

Waterproofing membranes on the balcony slab must be laid before handrails are installed, as handrail base plates and post anchors would otherwise puncture or obstruct the waterproofing layer, compromising weather tightness.
The handrail frame or top rail must be in place to serve as the upper support channel or fixing point for glass panels or infill elements between posts.

successor: Final Painting / Finishing of Balcony Area
rationale: While it is preferable to complete painting before installing handrails to avoid masking and touch-ups, in practice handrails are often installed earlier to allow other trades to work. However, if handrails are installed first, final paint touch-ups around anchor points will be needed afterward.
The balcony balustrade must be anchored to the structural concrete slab or deck. The concrete must be poured and cured before any fixings or post bases for the balustrade can be installed.
If the balustrade connects to a steel frame, the frame must be erected first to provide the supporting structure for the balustrade.
The balustrade posts penetrate the balcony deck; waterproofing around these penetrations must be completed after the balustrade is installed to ensure a watertight seal at all joints.
Handrails and top rails typically attach to or sit on top of the balustrade framework; the balustrade infill and structure must be in place before the handrail can be mounted.
The balustrade must be fully assembled and welded/bolted in position before any final surface coatings, painting, or powder coating can be applied to ensure a uniform finish.
The main structural framework (columns, main beams, load-bearing walls) must be erected first to provide support and anchorage points for balcony beams.
The floor slab adjacent to the balcony must be poured and cured to provide a stable working platform and to receive the balcony beam connection.
Balcony beams serve as the primary support structure for the balcony deck; the deck formwork is placed on and between the beams, so beams must be in place first.
Balcony beams form part of the balcony structure; waterproofing is applied over the completed structural balcony including beams, so beams must be installed and cured first.
Balustrades and railings are typically anchored to the balcony beams or the balcony slab supported by beams; the structural beam must be in place to provide a secure fixing point.
The balcony bracket physically attaches to or supports the balcony slab, so the slab must be cast first to provide a mounting surface or structural support for the bracket.
Balcony brackets are typically anchored into structural walls or columns, which must be complete to bear the load transferred through the bracket.
The railing system is often supported by or attached to the balcony brackets, so brackets must be in place before railings can be installed.
Waterproofing membrane is applied over the completed balcony structure including brackets, and any bracket penetrations must be sealed; thus brackets must be installed first.
Floor tiles or finishes are laid after all structural and bracket work is done to avoid damaging finishes during bracket installation.
The balcony door frame requires a rough opening in the wall structure, which must be framed before the door can be installed.
The rough opening must be measured, cut, and prepared (including header, sill, and cripple studs) to receive the balcony door unit.
Weather barrier should be applied to the wall sheathing before door installation to ensure proper water management and flashing integration.
After the balcony door is set in place, flashing tape and waterproofing details must be applied around the door frame to seal against moisture intrusion.
Interior trim and casing around the balcony door can be installed after the door is in place, though this is a soft preference as it could be done later during finishing stages.
The structural frame (floor slab, beams, and columns) must be in place to provide a stable base and support for the balcony threshold installation.
The primary building structure must be completed before any balcony components that attach to it can be installed, as the threshold depends on the structural support.
The threshold forms the edge frame of the balcony; the decking or finishing surface is laid after the threshold and its supports are in place.
The waterproofing layer is applied over the threshold and balcony substrate to ensure a continuous seal, so the threshold must be installed first.
Railings are often anchored into or mounted on the balcony threshold; therefore the threshold must be secured before the balustrade can be erected.
The structural frame (columns, beams, and floor slabs) must be complete to provide the load-bearing support and attachment points for the balcony glazing screen.
Waterproofing of the balcony deck must be completed before installing the glazing screen to ensure a watertight seal and prevent moisture damage behind the screen.
The balcony slab must be cast and sufficiently cured to provide a solid base and allow for anchoring of the glazing screen frame.
It is preferable to complete the glazing screen before interior finishes near the balcony to protect interior work from weather exposure and to allow for final sealing around the screen perimeter.
If the glazing screen integrates with or is mounted adjacent to the railing system, the screen must be installed first to ensure proper alignment and integration of the railing.
The balcony soffit is installed underneath the balcony slab. The slab must be in place first to provide the structural support and substrate for the soffit.
The framing structure of the balcony must be completed to provide the framework onto which the soffit is attached.
The soffit serves as the substrate or backing for the waterproofing membrane system on the underside of the balcony; the membrane cannot be applied until the soffit is in place.

Recessed lighting or light fixtures mounted on or through the balcony soffit require the soffit to be installed first; however, wiring may be roughed in earlier, so this is a soft preference rather than a hard constraint.
Safe access to the underside of the balcony is required for soffit installation; scaffolding or a work platform must be erected before workers can install the soffit.
The balcony thermal break is installed at the junction of the structural slab and the balcony. The structural slab must be in place to provide a substrate for the thermal break element.
The balcony concrete slab formwork and reinforcing steel must be in place so the thermal break can be positioned and cast into the slab connection.
The thermal break element must be installed and secured before the balcony concrete is poured, so it becomes embedded and monolithic with the slab.
The thermal break is within the structural slab; waterproofing must be applied over the cured slab (including the thermal break zone) to protect it from moisture ingress.
While not structurally dependent, it is practical to complete the structural/thermal break work before installing non-structural finishes like railings to avoid rework and access issues.
Electrical wiring, junction boxes, and conduit must be installed in the balcony before the lighting fixture can be mounted and connected.
The structural support (ceiling, soffit, or mounting surface) must be finished and load-bearing to provide a secure anchor point for the fixture.
Waterproofing must be in place before penetrating the assembly with lighting fixtures to prevent moisture intrusion and leaks.

successor: Balcony Lighting Fixture Trim and Lens Installation
rationale: The main fixture body and wiring connections must be secured before installing decorative trims, lenses, or covers.
The fixture must be physically installed before the electrical system can be energized and tested for proper operation.

predecessor: Concrete Slab or Deck Pouring & Curing
rationale: The concrete substrate must be fully poured, set, and cured to provide a stable, crack-free base for waterproofing membrane application.
Balcony drains and waste pipes must be installed and tested before waterproofing to ensure the membrane can be flashed around penetrations and water can be directed away properly.
Structural framing elements that will penetrate or abut the waterproof membrane must be in place so the membrane can be integrated and sealed at all junctions.
Waterproofing must be fully applied, cured, and flood tested before any tile, stone, or paver finish is laid; otherwise, the finish traps moisture and voids the waterproofing warranty.

Non-structural railings or glass balustrades are often installed after waterproofing to avoid puncturing the membrane; however, this is a soft preference as boots or pads can protect the membrane if installation is done carefully.
The structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) must be completed to provide the load-bearing support for balcony cantilevers and to establish the reference levels for balcony formwork installation.
Reinforcement steel must be placed and tied within the balcony formwork before concrete can be poured, as steel reinforces the concrete tensile strength.
Freshly cast concrete requires sufficient curing time to achieve design strength before any loads or subsequent finishing works are applied.
The concrete must be cast and gain adequate strength before the formwork can be safely removed to avoid structural failure or deformation.
Waterproofing membranes are applied after the balcony slab is fully cured and formwork removed, ensuring a clean, stable substrate for waterproofing.
The structural frame or balcony slab must be in place to provide a stable mounting surface for the railing system.
Waterproofing must be applied before penetrations for railing posts are made, to ensure a continuous waterproof membrane.
It is preferable to install the railing before applying touch-up paint or final coating to avoid damaging the finish during installation.
If the railing includes glass infill panels, the railing frame must be installed first to allow proper fitting and attachment of glass panels.
Permanent balcony railings provide fall protection, so temporary safety netting can be removed only after permanent railings are in place.
Waterproofing membrane must be applied and cured before tiling can proceed to ensure a watertight substrate and prevent moisture damage.
A level and properly sloped screed bed is required as the base for tile adhesive and to direct water drainage before tiles are installed.
Tiles must be fully set in place before grout can be applied to fill joints and seal the surface.

While railing can be installed before tiling in some sequences, it is generally preferred to complete tiling first to avoid damaging tiles during railing installation and to achieve a cleaner finish at the base.
The structural concrete slab or deck must be properly cast, cured, and prepared before any waterproofing or tiling work begins.
The structural frame of the balcony must be fully erected, secured, and load-bearing before any inspection can verify its integrity.
Decking must be installed so that the inspector can assess surface quality, drainage, and attachment to the frame.
Railings and guardrails must be in place to allow inspection of their height, strength, spacing, and compliance with safety codes.
Waterproofing membranes and sealants must be applied before inspection can test for water penetration and drainage performance.
Final finishes such as paint, cladding, or tile should only be applied after structural and waterproofing inspections are passed, to avoid covering defects.
Minor post-inspection adjustments to railings may be needed based on inspector findings, but fine-tuning is typically a soft preference.
Any specialized load or stress testing must follow the general inspection to verify specific load-bearing requirements.
Formal approval and handover of the balcony can only occur after all inspections and tests have been successfully completed and documented.
The structural wall must be built first to provide a load-bearing surface for the Juliette balcony to be attached to.
The floor slab at the balcony level must be completed to provide the base support and anchoring surface for the Juliette balcony structure.
Waterproofing of the wall and floor junction must be completed before balcony installation to ensure continuous moisture protection behind the balcony.

successor: Balcony Railing and Glass Panel Installation
rationale: The main Juliette balcony frame must be installed first to provide the structural support for attaching railings and glass panels.
While interior finishing can proceed in parallel, it is preferable to complete balcony installation before final interior wall and floor finishes at the doorway to avoid damage or rework.
The bracket must be manufactured and physically exist before it can be fixed or installed in place.
The bracket must be transported and available on the construction site before installation can occur.
The bracket must be securely fixed in position before any component can be mounted onto it.
Final torque-tightening of bolts is typically done after the bracket is initially fixed, though it could be done concurrently in some cases.
Quality inspection of the bracket installation follows fixing, though it is a preference to ensure workmanship rather than a physical necessity.
The substrate (e.g., concrete, metal, or wood surfaces) must be properly cleaned, dried, and prepared before applying weather sealing joint materials to ensure proper adhesion and a durable seal.
Structural elements such as walls, roofs, and decks must be fully erected and sheathed before weather sealing joints can be applied to close gaps and prevent water/air infiltration.
Some substrates require a primer coat before sealant application for optimal bonding; however, this depends on manufacturer specifications and is not always mandatory if the sealant is self-priming.
Weather sealing joints must be fully installed and cured before final cladding, siding, or exterior finishes are placed over them to ensure the seal is continuous and not damaged by subsequent work.
After weather sealing joints are completed, water penetration and air leakage tests should be conducted to verify the effectiveness of the seal before covering or enclosing the joint.
A stable foundation or prepared pad is required before any subframe or support rail can be installed, as the subframe rests on and transfers loads to the foundation.
The subframe or support rail serves as the base structure; the main chassis or frame must be mounted onto it, so the subframe must be in place first.
Equipment and components that are mounted onto the subframe cannot be attached until the subframe itself is securely installed and aligned.
While a leveling check can be performed after installation, it is recommended to verify alignment after the subframe is placed to ensure subsequent components are correctly positioned.
Any underground utilities, conduits, or cabling that will pass beneath the subframe must be installed before the subframe is placed, to avoid the need for lifting or reworking the subframe later.
Fibre cement panels are typically non-structural cladding; the building's structural frame must be in place first to provide support and attachment points for the panels.
A substrate or backing (such as plywood sheathing or stud framing) is required to mount the fibre cement panels securely.
A weather-resistive barrier or building wrap is typically installed behind fibre cement cladding to protect against moisture ingress; this must be applied before the panels are fixed.

Fibre cement panels often require painting or sealing for weather resistance and aesthetics; while it is technically possible to paint before installation, standard practice is to install first and then apply the final coating to ensure uniform coverage and protection of joints and fasteners.

In some construction sequences, fibre cement panels are installed first and then windows/doors are fitted and flashed into the cladding; however, this is a sequencing preference rather than an absolute physical requirement (panels can be cut around pre-installed openings).
HPL panels require a stable substrate or framing surface (such as plywood, MDF, or metal stud framing) to be installed and secured against before panels can be fixed in place.

Any electrical wiring, conduit, outlets, or plumbing that will be concealed behind HPL panels must be roughed-in and inspected prior to panel installation to avoid cutting or removing installed panels later.
In areas prone to moisture, a vapor barrier or moisture-resistant underlayment must be applied to the substrate before HPL panels are installed to prevent moisture damage and delamination.
Finish trims, edge profiles, joint covers, and molding pieces are installed after HPL panels are fixed in place to conceal panel edges, joints, and fasteners, providing a clean finished appearance.
Sealants, caulking at joints and perimeter edges, and any final surface cleaning or finishing can only be applied after HPL panels are fully installed and secured.
ACP panels are typically mounted onto a structural frame or substructure (such as steel or aluminum framing). The structural frame must be in place to support and fix the ACP panels.
Waterproofing membranes or sealants behind the cladding must be applied before ACP installation to prevent moisture ingress behind the facade.
After ACP panels are fixed in place, the joints between panels must be sealed with weatherproof sealants to ensure the building envelope is airtight and watertight.
Scaffolding erected for facade access can only be dismantled after the ACP cladding installation is complete, as the scaffolding is required for safe panel placement and adjustment.
The completed ACP cladding must be inspected for alignment, flatness, and finish quality before the final facade sign-off.

The structural framing system must be in place to provide the support framework onto which the terracotta rainscreen panels are mounted. The panels cannot be installed without a stable structural backing.
A weather-resistant barrier and air barrier must be installed behind the rainscreen to protect the building envelope from moisture infiltration before the rainscreen cladding is applied.
The vertical and horizontal aluminum sub-frame or support rails (the rainscreen carrier system) must be attached to the structure to provide the attachment points for the terracotta panels.

While windows can be installed before or after cladding in some sequences, installing the rainscreen first allows for proper flashing integration at window openings and avoids damage to finished windows during panel handling. This is a soft preference for sequencing efficiency.

Scaffolding used to access the facade for panel installation must remain in place until the rainscreen panels are fully installed and secured. Dismantling the scaffolding before completion would prevent access for installation work.

successor: Glass Fibre Reinforced Concrete (GRC) Panel Installation
rationale: The structural frame (steel or concrete) must be in place to provide the load-bearing support onto which GRC panels are anchored or fixed.

successor: Glass Fibre Reinforced Concrete (GRC) Panel Installation
rationale: GRC panels must be fully manufactured, cured, and quality-checked before they can be transported and installed on site.

successor: Glass Fibre Reinforced Concrete (GRC) Panel Installation
rationale: While recommended to protect the structure behind panels, GRC panels can be installed before waterproofing in some sequences, making this a soft scheduling preference rather than a hard constraint.

predecessor: Glass Fibre Reinforced Concrete (GRC) Panel Installation
rationale: After panels are mounted, the joints between them must be sealed with appropriate sealants and finished for weather-tightness and aesthetics.

predecessor: Glass Fibre Reinforced Concrete (GRC) Panel Installation
successor: Scaffolding Dismantling (if scaffolding used for installation)
rationale: Scaffolding erected for panel installation must remain in place until all panels are fixed and finished; it can only be dismantled after panel work is complete.
Structural framing (steel or wood) must be in place to provide a mounting surface and support for fire-resistant barriers such as fire-rated drywall, board, or sprayed fireproofing.

Electrical conduit, plumbing pipes, ductwork, and other mechanical systems must be routed within the wall/ceiling cavities before the fire-resistant barrier is closed up, as accessing them afterward would require cutting or demolishing the barrier.

All openings, joints, and penetrations through the fire-resistant barrier (e.g., around pipes, cables, ducts) must be sealed with approved firestop materials after the barrier is in place to maintain the required fire-resistance rating.

Although not a physical necessity, it is standard construction sequence practice to complete fire-resistant barriers before applying final finishes such as paint, texture, or decorative cladding to protect the barrier and achieve a clean appearance.

Fire-resistant barriers must be fully installed (and any firestopping completed) before inspection, as building codes require verification of fire-resistance ratings and proper installation before proceeding with enclosing finishes.
Safe physical access to the building facade is required before any inspection or testing can occur.
Inspection and testing must identify defects and conditions before cleaning/preparation can proceed, as preparation may mask underlying issues.
Test results and inspection findings are needed to determine the scope and methodology of required repairs and restoration.
The facade is supported by the structural frame; the building must be structurally complete and stable before facade inspection and testing can safely begin.
Inspection/testing may identify deficiencies in existing anchoring that must be addressed in new anchoring/ bracing design and installation.
Scaffolding or access equipment must be in place to allow workers to safely reach and work on the facade panels.
Existing damaged or old panels must be removed before new panels can be installed or maintenance performed.
The supporting structure must be inspected and deemed sound before new panels are attached to ensure safety and structural integrity.
Scaffolding cannot be removed until all facade panel replacement and maintenance work is completed, as workers still need access.
After panel replacement/maintenance is finished, a final quality and waterproofing inspection must be conducted to verify proper installation and seal integrity.
The subframe requires a stable, level foundation to be prepared and cured before installation can begin, as the subframe rests directly on the foundation.
The site must be excavated and graded to the proper elevation and soil conditions before the subframe can be positioned and anchored.
Underground utilities (drainage, electrical conduits, plumbing) must be laid in place before the subframe is installed, as access to the ground below is blocked once the subframe is in position.
The main structural frame (columns, beams, walls) is erected on top of and anchored to the subframe, so the subframe must be fully installed and secured first.
Floor decking or slab pouring typically occurs after the subframe is in place, as the subframe supports the formwork or acts as a base for the slab.
Rainwater heads are mounted to the roof structure or fascia, so the roof structure must be in place to provide a mounting surface.
Rainwater heads connect to gutters as part of the rainwater collection system. Gutters must be installed first to align with and receive water from the rainwater head.
While downpipes connect below rainwater heads, the head can often be installed first and the downpipe connected afterward, or vice versa. This ordering is a soft preference for alignment accuracy.
