The downpipe physically connects to the outlet of the rainwater head; the head must be fixed in place before the downpipe can be properly connected and sealed.
Water flow testing of the collection system requires the rainwater head to be fully installed to verify proper water capture and drainage.
The roof structure must be complete to provide a substrate for the roof drain system.
The roof deck provides the surface and support onto which roof drains are mounted and sealed.
Roof drains must be installed first so that the waterproofing membrane can be properly integrated and sealed around the drain flange to prevent leaks.
Insulation is typically laid after drain placement to ensure proper drainage flow paths and to avoid blocking drain inlets.
The roof drain body must be in place before the downstream piping can be connected to it.
The parapet outlet is a component integrated into or penetrating the parapet wall; therefore the wall structure must be built first to provide the surface and support for the outlet installation.

Roof drainage systems often coordinate with parapet outlets; the roof deck and base flashing must be installed before the parapet outlet to ensure proper drainage integration and waterproofing continuity.
The outlet must be installed before the final cladding or finish is applied to the parapet, as the cladding would otherwise block access or require cutting around the outlet.
The parapet outlet serves as the entry point for water runoff; the downspout or gutter connection must follow to direct water away from the outlet.
After the parapet outlet is installed, waterproofing must be applied around the penetration to seal the interface and prevent leaks.
The overflow outlet must be connected to the drainage or sewer pipe network, so the receiving pipes must be in place before the outlet can be installed and properly connected.
The overflow outlet typically penetrates through the foundation wall or slab, so the foundation or slab must be cast and cured before the outlet can be positioned and sealed.
After the overflow outlet is installed, the area around the penetration must be waterproofed to prevent leaks; waterproofing over the installed outlet ensures a continuous seal.
Backfilling around the structure should only occur after the overflow outlet is securely in place to avoid damage or displacement of the outlet by soil pressure.

Any interior wall or floor finishes near the overflow outlet are typically done after the outlet is installed to allow for proper trim, sealing, and aesthetic integration, though this is a logical sequence preference rather than a strict physical necessity.

predecessor: Install Roofing Material (e.g., Shingles, Metal Panels)
rationale: The gutter system is typically mounted after the roof covering is installed because the roof edge (drip edge/fascia) defines the position for the gutter and leaf guard. Without roofing in place, the correct height and alignment for the gutter guard cannot be established.
Leaf guards and gutter filters are mounted onto or inside gutters, which are attached to the fascia board. The fascia must be installed first to provide the structural support for the gutter system.

Leaf guards/gutter filters are accessories that sit on top of or inside gutters. The gutters themselves must be fully installed, secured, and tested for proper slope before adding any leaf protection system.

predecessor: Install Drip Edge (if not integrated with roofing)
rationale: The drip edge directs water into the gutter. Installing it before the leaf guard ensures proper water flow alignment and prevents water from bypassing the filter.

After leaf guards are installed, water flow tests should be performed to verify that the filters are correctly positioned and not obstructing water drainage. This inspection cannot be completed before the guards are in place.
The downpipe (vertical pipe) must be installed first to provide the connection point for the downpipe shoe at the base.
Gutters must be installed to collect water and connect to the downpipe system before the downpipe shoe can be fitted at the base.
The downpipe shoe directs water from the downpipe into the underground drainage system, so the shoe must be in place before connections to drainage pipes can be made.

Testing and inspection of the downpipe shoe connection should occur after installation to ensure proper water flow and sealing, though this is a quality assurance preference rather than a physical necessity.
Scaffolding or access equipment must be in place to safely reach the lower wall area where the downpipe shoe is installed.
The ground must be excavated and graded to the correct profile and depth before a gully (drainage channel) can be installed, as the gully sits within the excavated trench.
The gully body must be set in place before any drainage pipes can be physically connected to its outlet.
The gully must be positioned and fixed before the surrounding pavement or ground surface is poured/cast, as the gully forms part of the finished surface drainage system.
The structural roof deck must be in place to provide the load-bearing surface upon which all green roof layers, including the drainage layer, are installed.
A waterproofing membrane must be installed over the structural deck to protect the building from water intrusion before the drainage layer (which manages water flow) is placed on top.
Thermal insulation is typically installed above the waterproofing membrane and below the drainage layer to provide energy performance; the drainage layer sits on top of the insulation.
The filter fabric (geotextile) is placed directly over the drainage layer to prevent fine soil particles from clogging the drainage medium while allowing water to pass through.

The growing medium (soil/substrate) is placed on top of the filter fabric, which itself sits above the drainage layer, so drainage must be in place first to carry excess water away from the root zone.
The roof geometry, slope, and structural layout must be defined before drainage can be designed, as drainage sizing depends on roof area, pitch, and load-bearing constraints.

predecessor: Rainfall Intensity Data Collection / Local Hydrological Study
rationale: Design storm intensity and return period data are required to calculate the required gutter, downspout, and scupper sizes for the roof drainage system.

successor: Roof Drainage Pipe & Downspout Routing Layout
rationale: The sizing of gutters, downspouts, and leaders must be finalized before the routing and layout of drainage pipes can be planned to ensure adequate capacity.
The size and number of inlets or scuppers depend on the drainage design calculations; placement detailing can only commence after sizes are determined.
Material quantities and type can be ordered after sizing is complete, though ordering can sometimes be partially fast-tracked based on preliminary estimates.
Downpipes collect rainwater from the roof via gutters; the roof covering must be installed first to establish the catchment surface and positioning for gutter and downpipe connections.
Downpipes direct rainwater into tanks or drainage systems; the downpipe outlet must be installed before final connection to a rainwater tank or stormwater drain can be made.

While downpipes can be installed before or after cladding, it is often preferable to complete downpipe brackets and pipes prior to final wall finishes to allow for secure fastening and to minimise damage to finished surfaces; however, this is a soft preference rather than a strict physical necessity.
Downpipes must be installed to channel roof water to the ground-level drainage system; the stormwater connection at ground level can only be completed once downpipe outlets are in place to tie into.

The roof underlayment (felt paper or synthetic) must be laid before gutters are installed to ensure proper water shedding and to protect the roof deck. Gutters work in conjunction with the roofing system to manage water runoff.
Roof shingles must be installed first so that the drip edge and gutter system can be properly aligned with the finished roof edge to ensure correct water flow into the gutters.

Downspouts are the vertical extension of the gutter system that carry water from the gutters to the ground or drainage system. They can only be connected after the gutters themselves are mounted in place.

Gutters can be installed before or after siding, but it is common practice to install gutters after siding is complete to avoid damaging the siding during gutter installation. This is a soft preference, not a hard constraint.
Gutter guards or leaf protection systems are installed on top of or inside the gutters. The gutter system must be fully installed and secured before any guard or cover system can be added.
Underlayment is typically laid over the deck before drains are installed to ensure proper waterproofing continuity at drain flanges.
The drain body must be in place before the flashing can be installed around it to create a watertight seal.
The membrane is applied over and sealed to the drain flange; the drain must be installed first so the membrane can integrate with it.
Gutters are attached to the roof edge/fascia, so the roof structure must be in place and stable before gutters can be installed or cleaned.
Gutters are typically mounted onto the fascia board; thus the fascia and soffit must be installed first to provide the mounting surface.
The building frame must be complete to support the roof and fascia to which gutters attach.
After gutters are cleaned and maintained, the downspouts and drainage system must be checked, cleared, and connected to ensure proper water flow away from the building.

While not a strict physical requirement, water drainage from gutters should be directed away from the building before final grading and landscaping to prevent erosion or water damage to finished surfaces.

The drainage pipes and infrastructure must be fully installed before CCTV inspection can be conducted, as the inspection examines the interior of installed pipes for defects, blockages, and proper construction.
All pipe sections must be laid, jointed, and connected before a CCTV survey can traverse the pipeline to assess its condition.
Manholes and inspection chambers provide access points for CCTV equipment to enter and exit the drainage system; they must be completed for the inspection to be physically possible.
CCTV inspection must be completed first to identify any defects, blockages, or construction issues that need rectification before the system can be formally tested, commissioned, and handed over.
CCTV inspection identifies defects (e.g., cracks, misalignments, blockages) which must then be fixed before backfilling or final acceptance; remediation follows the inspection findings.
The site must be cleared of vegetation and debris to provide safe and unobstructed access for slope assessment activities.
Access roads are needed to transport assessment equipment and personnel to the slope location safely.
Slope assessment must be completed first to determine the stability and safety requirements before any excavation work can begin on or near the slope.
Assessment results provide the geotechnical data needed to design appropriate ground support and reinforcement systems for the slope.
The assessment identifies unstable areas requiring rock bolting and mesh, so the assessment must precede any installation work.
Valley gutters are installed along roof valleys where two roof planes meet; the roof decking must be in place to provide the structural surface for the valley gutter to be mounted on.
Waterproof underlayment must be laid over the roof deck before valley gutter installation to provide a moisture barrier beneath the gutter.

Roof shingles are installed overlapping the valley gutter edges to create a watertight seal; shingles must be placed after the valley gutter is in position to ensure proper water runoff into the gutter.
Valley flashing integrates with the valley gutter; flashing details around the valley are completed after the gutter is installed to ensure proper drainage and waterproofing.

Installing gutter guards or screens over valley gutters is a protective measure that can be done after gutter installation to prevent debris buildup, but is a preference rather than a physical necessity.
Box gutters are installed directly on or adjacent to the roof deck; the roof decking must be in place to provide structural support and a mounting surface for the gutter system.

The underlayment provides a waterproof barrier beneath the roofing material; box gutters integrate with the underlayment to ensure proper water drainage and prevent leaks at the gutter-roof intersection.
Box gutters must be installed before final roofing materials (shingles or metal panels) are laid, as the roofing material typically overlaps the gutter edge or flashing to create a watertight seal.
Downspouts connect to box gutters at outlet points; the box gutter must be in position to establish the proper outlet locations and connections for the drainage system.

While box gutters are often supported by the fascia board, in many construction sequences the fascia and soffit can be completed either before or after box gutter installation; however, completing them first provides a finished appearance and proper alignment for the gutter.
A stable foundation or substrate must be prepared before a cover plate can be installed, as the cover plate requires a secure mounting surface.
Cover plates are typically installed after the main structural framing is complete to protect and cover structural connections or openings.
While cover plates are often painted or coated after installation for aesthetic or protective purposes, this could be done beforehand in some cases, making this a soft preference.

successor: Electrical/conduit installation (if cover plate is for an electrical box)
rationale: If the cover plate is for an electrical outlet or junction box, the electrical wiring and box must be installed first; the cover plate is the final protective cover.
Inspections often occur after cover plates are installed to verify proper coverage and protection, but this is an administrative preference rather than a physical necessity.

The nosing profile is a finish component that attaches to the edge of the stair tread. The underlying staircase structure (stringers, treads, risers) must be installed first to provide a substrate for the nosing.
If the nosing is installed over a concrete or wood subfloor, the subfloor must be properly prepared and cured before the nosing can be securely affixed.

successor: Flooring or Tread Finishing Over Nosing
rationale: The nosing profile acts as a transition or edge trim; flooring material (e.g., carpet, tile, wood planks) is typically installed up to or over the nosing, so the nosing must be in place first to define the edge.

successor: Final Inspection / Punch List of Stair Edges
rationale: Quality checking of the nosing alignment and finish is best done after installation but is a soft preference if minor adjustments can be made later.
The groove or seat where the compression seal will be placed must be clean, dry, and properly sized/surfaced before the seal can be installed; otherwise the seal will not seat correctly.
If the compression seal is installed into a concrete joint, the concrete must be fully cured to its design strength so that the groove dimensions are stable and the seal is not displaced or damaged.
It is good practice to test the seal after installation to verify watertightness, though it is not a physical necessity.
Where a backer rod is used behind the compression seal, the seal must be in place first so that the rod can be properly positioned and compressed behind it.
Any finishing or grinding of surfaces adjacent to the seal should be done after installation to avoid damaging the seal, but this is a preference rather than a physical requirement.

predecessor: Cast-in anchor bolts or embed plates
rationale: Anchor rails must be mechanically fastened to embedded anchors (cast-in bolts or embed plates) that are placed in the concrete pour, so the embedment must be installed first.
Anchor rails are typically installed on top of a finished concrete foundation or pedestal; the concrete must be poured and sufficiently cured to bear the load before rail installation.

successor: Install rail-mounted equipment (e.g., crane or hoist)
rationale: Anchor rails serve as the mounting track for traveling equipment such as overhead cranes or hoists; the rail must be in place before the equipment can be installed on it.
After the anchor rail is positioned and bolted down, grout is typically placed beneath the rail base to fill gaps and ensure uniform bearing; this grouting step logically follows rail installation.

successor: Final alignment and torquing of anchor bolts
rationale: Once the rail is set in its final position, the anchor bolts are torqued to the specified tension; this final tightening must occur after the rail is placed and aligned.
The sliding plate joint must be installed into or onto the bridge deck structure, requiring the deck to be fabricated first so the joint has a surface and structural context for placement.
Sliding plate joints are typically installed at expansion gaps between bridge girders/beams, so the supporting girders must be erected first to establish the joint location.

The sliding plate joint must be in place and secured before the final wearing surface (asphalt or concrete overlay) is applied, as the joint accommodates thermal movement and the paving should be finished around/up to it.

The sliding plate joint's structural plates must be installed first so that any sealing elements (e.g., compression seals, gland) can be inserted into the joint gap afterward to waterproof the expansion opening.
It is advisable to verify the joint's movement capability and alignment after installation, but this is a quality assurance preference rather than a strict physical necessity.
The modular expansion joint must be installed after the bridge deck concrete is placed and cured, as the joint is embedded into or anchored to the deck structure.
Concrete must reach sufficient strength before cutting joints and anchoring the modular expansion joint system to avoid damage to the deck.
The gap for the modular expansion joint must be saw-cut and prepared to the correct dimensions before the joint assembly can be placed and anchored.
Approach slabs are typically poured after the expansion joint is installed to ensure a smooth transition and proper embedment of the joint into the approach pavement.
Final pavement layers adjacent to the joint are placed after the modular expansion joint is fully installed and anchored, allowing a smooth ride surface up to the joint.
The subgrade must be properly prepared and leveled before isolation joints can be installed to ensure a stable and uniform base.
The base course (e.g., crushed stone or gravel) must be placed and compacted before isolation joints can be positioned to provide proper drainage and support.
Formwork or edge restraints must be in place to define the boundaries and layout before isolation joint material can be installed.
Isolation joints must be installed before concrete is poured so that the joint material is embedded and can separate adjacent concrete sections as intended.
After isolation joint material is in place, joint filler (if used) can be applied to ensure proper isolation and prevent bonding between concrete slabs and adjacent structures.
Control joints are typically placed in concrete slabs. The slab must first be placed/poured before control joints can be cut or formed into it.
Control joints in concrete are often cut after the concrete has achieved its initial set but before random cracking occurs. The concrete must be firm enough to hold the cut without raveling.
Control joints must be installed before final floor finishing or treatment (e.g., sealing, coating) to ensure the joint is properly integrated and sealed.
The subgrade or base layer must be properly graded and compacted before any slab (with control joints) is placed to ensure uniform support.
Formwork must be in place to contain the concrete pour before the slab and its control joints can be installed.
Seismic joints require stable load-bearing foundations to transfer forces; the foundation must be complete before joint installation can begin.
Seismic joints are typically placed between structural segments; the primary structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) must be erected to define the locations where joints are needed.
Seismic joints allow independent movement of building sections; cladding and facade panels must be installed after joints are in place to ensure proper alignment and accommodate movement.
Interior finishes must account for seismic joint locations with appropriate trim, covers, and movement gaps; these cannot be properly detailed until the joint is installed.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems that cross seismic joints require flexible connections and expansion loops; these details depend on the joint's exact location and type being already in place.
The substrate or joint surfaces must be clean, dry, and free of dust, oil, or debris before sealant is applied to ensure proper adhesion and prevent sealant failure.
The joint must be cut or formed to the correct dimensions and geometry before sealant can be installed into the joint cavity.
Backer rod must be placed at the proper depth in the joint to control sealant depth, provide a bond breaker, and support the sealant before application.
After sealant application, sufficient curing or drying time is physically required before any subsequent activities can take place, to allow the sealant to achieve its designed properties.
Water testing or leak testing of the sealed joints must occur after the sealant has fully cured to verify the integrity of the seal.
The steel frame and its joints must be fully erected and in place before they can be inspected; inspection cannot occur on incomplete framing.
All welded or bolted connections at the joints must be completed before inspection can verify their quality and conformance to specifications.
The inspection results must be documented and accepted before subsequent construction activities (e.g., concrete encasement, cladding installation) can proceed.

successor: Corrective Work / Repair of Joint Defects
rationale: If inspection identifies defects, remediation must occur before further work; inspection triggers the corrective action process.
The joint's structural integrity must be verified through inspection before it is subjected to design loads to ensure safety.
The structural frame must be in place to provide support and attachment points for joint components in steel or concrete structures.
Concrete must be cured and set before construction joints or expansion joints can be installed, as joints are placed where concrete sections meet.
MEP rough-ins that pass through or near joint locations must be completed to avoid conflicts and allow proper joint installation.
Floor joints (expansion, control, or construction joints) must be installed before final floor finishes are applied, as joints dictate where finishes terminate or transition.
Joints in wall and ceiling assemblies must be completed before drywall finishing, taping, or painting so that joint movement is accommodated behind finished surfaces.
Foundation excavation disturbs the ground and can cause settlement or movement; baseline monitoring must begin before or immediately after excavation to capture initial movement.
Monitoring instruments (e.g., inclinometers, tiltmeters, prisms) must be physically installed and calibrated before any monitoring data can be collected.

Movement data from monitoring informs whether protective measures (e.g., underpinning, shoring) are needed for adjacent structures; monitoring must detect unacceptable movement before mitigation can be triggered.
Real-time movement monitoring must be active during excavation to provide early warning of soil or structural displacement, ensuring safety.
While not physically mandatory, monitoring data is best reviewed before final assessment to verify that movement has stabilized within acceptable tolerances.
Structural framing (steel or concrete) must be in place so that fire-stopping can seal penetrations and joints in the structural elements.
Fire-stopping must seal around pipes, ducts, conduits, and cables; therefore MEP rough-in (installation of penetrations) must be completed first.
Fire-stopping must be completed and inspected before enclosing penetrations within walls and ceilings, as access is required for proper sealing.
Fire-stopping must be in place prior to fire safety inspections to verify compliance with fire-resistance ratings and building codes.
Although painting can follow fire-stopping to avoid damaging sealed areas, it is a soft preference as minor touch-ups could still be done after painting.
The building structure and roof must be complete to provide a weathertight enclosure before installing the AHU, which is sensitive to weather damage.

predecessor: Concrete slab or equipment pad pour and cure
rationale: The AHU requires a level, cured concrete foundation or equipment pad to support its weight and ensure proper vibration isolation.

predecessor: Overhead crane or rigging plan approval
rationale: AHUs are large and heavy; a certified lifting plan and rigging equipment must be in place before the unit can be lifted into position.
Supply and return ducts must be physically connected to the AHU's openings, which can only occur after the unit is set in its final position.

successor: Chilled water and hot water piping connection to AHU coils
rationale: The AHU's heating and cooling coils must be piped to the central plant after the unit is installed, as pipe connections are made at the unit's locations.
The chiller requires a concrete foundation or equipment pad to be fully cured and load-bearing before the unit can be set in place.
The chiller unit must be delivered and rigged into position before mechanical installation and hook-up can begin.
Chilled water supply and return piping cannot be connected until the chiller is set in its final location.
Electrical wiring and power connections to the chiller require the unit to be permanently positioned first.
Hydronic piping must be fully connected and pressure-tested before the chiller can be started and commissioned.
Electrical power and controls must be fully terminated before the chiller can be energized and functionally tested.
The chiller operation must be verified and commissioned before the overall chilled water system can be balanced and optimized for building loads.
If the chiller is located indoors or under a roof, the overhead structure must be complete to protect the unit and provide clear working space; for outdoor units, weather enclosure must be ready.
Structural provisions (e.g., steel beams, roof curbs, or crane pads) must be in place before the heavy chiller can be lifted and set into position.
Cooling towers are heavy structures that require a solid foundation to support their weight and operational loads.
A reinforced concrete base or plinth must be cast and cured before the cooling tower can be set in place.
The cooling tower must be physically installed before inlet/outlet water pipes can be connected to it.

successor: Electrical Wiring for Fan Motors & Controls
rationale: Power and control cables can only be terminated at the cooling tower after the unit is in its final position.
The cooling water circuit including the tower must be complete before flushing and chemical treatment can be performed to remove debris and condition the water.
The boiler is a heavy piece of equipment that requires a structural base or foundation to bear its load. Without a properly constructed foundation, the boiler cannot be safely placed.

The boiler must be placed within an enclosed or framed space (boiler room) before final positioning; the structural frame of the building or boiler room provides support and weather protection during installation.

predecessor: Rough-in of water supply and gas piping to boiler room
rationale: The main supply lines (water and gas) need to be run to the boiler location before the boiler is set in place so that connections can be made efficiently and the boiler can be positioned relative to pre-installed piping stub-ups.
The boiler must be physically in its final position before the flue or chimney connection can be fitted and sealed to the boiler outlet.
The boiler must be set in place before the final piping connections (supply/return water lines) can be made and the system balanced.

successor: Electrical wiring and control system commissioning
rationale: Power supply wiring, control cables, and sensors are connected directly to the boiler terminals and components, requiring the boiler to be installed first.

successor: Refractory and insulation installation (if boiler is high-temperature)
rationale: Once the boiler is in place, any external insulation or refractory lining around the boiler casing can be applied safely and accurately. This must precede firing/testing to prevent heat loss and protect personnel.
The boiler must be fully installed, piped, and wired before the system can be filled, pressure-tested, and commissioned for operation.
Structural framing must be in place to support ductwork and provide attachment points for hangers and supports.
Roof must be completed to protect ductwork from weather damage during installation and to provide a weathertight enclosure.
Ductwork should be installed before electrical rough-in to avoid conflicts and allow both trades to coordinate space in ceilings and walls, though it is a preference for smoother coordination.
Ductwork installation prior to plumbing rough-in allows better access and routing coordination in confined spaces, though not strictly physically required.
The structural slab or deck provides the structural base; ductwork cannot be hung or routed until the supporting structure is in place.
Supply air diffusers must be connected to the ductwork system; the ducts must be in place to provide the air path to the diffuser.

predecessor: Install Ceiling Grid / Suspended Ceiling Supports
rationale: Supply air diffusers are typically mounted into or supported by the ceiling grid; the ceiling support structure must be installed first.

predecessor: Complete Rough-In of HVAC Piping and Electrical
rationale: Rough-in work for HVAC and electrical must be finished before installing ceiling-mounted diffusers to avoid rework and access issues.

successor: Install Ceiling Tiles / Finish Ceiling Surface
rationale: Diffusers are installed into the ceiling opening, and then ceiling tiles are placed around them to complete the finished ceiling surface.
Air diffusers must be in place to measure airflow, adjust dampers, and balance the system for proper air distribution.
Return air grilles are connected to the ductwork system; ducts must be in place to provide the physical connection point and air path for the grille.
Return air grilles are typically mounted in ceiling tiles or the ceiling grid; the grid must be installed to provide structural support and proper alignment for the grille.

While painting can be done before grille installation, it is often preferred to install grilles after painting to avoid damaging the grille finish with paint overspray and to achieve a clean, professional appearance.
The return air path must be complete (including grilles installed) before the HVAC system can be balanced and commissioned to verify proper airflow and system performance.
Building codes typically require rough-in inspection of the ductwork before concealing it with grilles and finishing work to ensure code compliance.
Electrical power supply wiring must be roughed-in and available at the fan location before the exhaust fan can be connected and installed.
The exhaust fan must be mounted to a secure ceiling or wall framing structure, so framing must be complete to provide adequate support.
The ductwork that the exhaust fan will vent into must be in place and connected to the fan housing before the fan can be fully installed and operational.
The exhaust fan housing must be installed before the ceiling finish (e.g., drywall) is completed, as the fan sits within the ceiling assembly and access is needed for mounting and connections.
After the fan is physically installed, final electrical connections such as connecting the fan to the switch and testing can be completed.
Chilled water supply and return piping must be in place to connect to the FCU for its primary heating/cooling function.

predecessor: Install Ceiling Grid / Suspended Ceiling Support
rationale: Most FCUs are concealed above a suspended ceiling; the ceiling grid supports the unit or provides access.
Power supply and control wiring must be available at the unit location to energize the fan and controls.
Condensate drain connection must be made after the FCU is positioned to ensure proper slope and removal of condensation.
Ductwork connections to the FCU plenum or collar can only be aligned and sealed once the unit is fixed in its final position.

VAV boxes are connected to the main supply ductwork and receive conditioned air from the air handler. The main supply and return ducts must be in place to provide the physical connection point and air source for the VAV box.

VAV boxes require electrical power for actuators and controllers, as well as control wiring (BACnet, MS/TP, etc.) to communicate with the building management system. These rough-ins must be complete before the VAV box is hung and connected.

VAV boxes are typically suspended from the structure above the ceiling. The structural supports, hangers, or trapeze supports must be installed to safely carry the weight of the VAV box before it can be lifted and secured.

Once the VAV box is installed, the downstream ductwork that connects the VAV box outlet to the terminal diffusers in the zone must be installed. This ductwork cannot be connected without the VAV box in its final position.

successor: Final Electrical & Controls Termination and Commissioning
rationale: After the VAV box is physically installed, electricians and controls technicians can terminate the power wiring, connect actuators, link control sensors, and perform point-to-point checkout and commissioning of the VAV box operation.
Electrical power supply must be roughed in to the HRV location before the unit can be connected and operated.
Supply and exhaust ductwork connections to the outside and to the distribution system must be in place before the HRV unit can be physically installed and ducted.
Walls, ceilings, and support structure must be framed and enclosed to provide a secure mounting location for the HRV unit.
The HRV must be fully installed and connected to ductwork and electrical before airflow balancing and performance testing can be performed.

successor: Final Mechanical Insulation of HRV Ducts
rationale: Insulating the HRV ducts after installation is preferred to ensure full access to connections and joints for sealing and inspection.
Ductwork must be installed and roughed-in before the ERV unit can be physically placed and connected to the duct system.

predecessor: Electrical rough-in / conduit to ERV location
rationale: Power supply wiring, conduit, and electrical box must be in place before the ERV unit is installed for final electrical connection.

predecessor: Structural framing and roof/wall openings complete
rationale: The building structure must be framed and weather-tight with proper openings prepared before mounting the ERV unit.

successor: Duct connection and sealing to ERV
rationale: The ERV unit must be in its final position before intake and exhaust ducts can be physically connected and sealed to the unit's collars.

successor: Final electrical connection and startup testing
rationale: The ERV must be mounted and secured before electricians can make final wiring connections and perform startup/commissioning tests.
Structural steel must be in place to provide support for hanging chilled water pipes before piping installation can begin.
Overhead electrical conduits are typically routed above chilled water pipes; installing them first allows for proper spacing and avoids conflicts in the overhead ceiling plenum.
Chilled water pipes must be installed and pressure-tested before insulation can be applied to prevent moisture condensation and thermal loss.
Chilled water piping must be roughed-in and approved before ceilings are closed to allow access for inspection and connections.
Chilled water piping must be run to the mechanical rooms and terminated at the stub-out locations before final connections to chillers and air handling units can be made.
Rough-in piping must be installed before the main hot water piping system can be connected and completed.
Piping must be fully installed and pressure-tested before insulation can be applied to prevent moisture entrapment and ensure proper coverage.
Pressure testing must be performed after piping is installed to verify system integrity before concealment.
Hot water fixtures (e.g., faucets, showers) can only be connected after the main hot water supply piping is in place and tested.
Structural walls, ceilings, and floors must be framed to provide support and routing pathways for hot water piping before installation can begin.
The structural frame and roof deck must be in place to provide support and routing pathways for refrigerant piping runs.
Outdoor condenser/compressor units and indoor air handler supports must be installed before connecting refrigerant lines.
Electrical power conduits and disconnect switches for HVAC equipment must be roughed in before refrigerant piping to allow coordinated equipment hookup.
Refrigerant piping must be fully installed, routed, and brazed before connecting to compressors, condensers, and evaporators and before charging the system with refrigerant.
Suction and liquid lines must be in place before applying closed-cell elastomeric insulation to prevent condensation and maintain efficiency.
The pump requires a stable, level foundation or slab to be mounted on, so the foundation must be completed first.
The hydronic piping system must be installed to the connection points before the pump can be physically integrated and connected to the piping network.
Pressure testing validates all connections and the pump's integrity within the system, which can only be done after the pump is installed and connected.
The pump's motor and electrical components must be physically in place before electrical wiring, control connections, and startup/commissioning can proceed.
The pump must be installed before the overall hydronic system can be balanced and commissioned to ensure correct flow rates and operation.
The expansion tank must be connected to the chiller system to accommodate water volume changes; the chiller must be in place first to establish the piping connections.
The expansion tank must be installed and connected to the closed-loop system before pressure testing can be performed to verify system integrity.
The expansion tank is part of the hydronic system; commissioning (startup and balancing) requires all components including the expansion tank to be installed.
It is good practice to insulate pipes after the expansion tank is installed to ensure proper coverage around connections, though insulation could be done before if planned carefully.
The expansion tank must be mounted on structural supports or a platform; the support framing must be installed first to provide a secure mounting location.
The air filter/media filter requires a frame, casing, or filter housing to be installed first so that the filter has a structural support and containment system to be placed into.
Ductwork must be in place so that the air filter can be installed within the duct system at the correct location (e.g., at the return air inlet or before the air handling unit).

successor: Air Handling Unit (AHU) or Fan Startup
rationale: The air filter must be in place before the AHU or fan is started to prevent unfiltered air from circulating and to protect the equipment from debris during initial operation.
Filters must be installed before final air balancing and commissioning to ensure that airflow measurements and system performance tests are conducted with the actual filtration media in place.
Installing filters before final cleanup and occupancy prevents construction dust and debris from entering the HVAC system and ensures indoor air quality is maintained.
The HVAC ductwork and housing must be roughed in before HEPA filters can be installed because the filter housing needs to be in place and accessible.
Ductwork must be tested for leaks before installing expensive HEPA filters to prevent contamination and damage from debris during testing.
HEPA filters must be installed before the cleanroom can be certified or air balancing performed, as the filters are critical to achieving required air cleanliness levels.
The HEPA filters must be in place for the final commissioning tests, which verify that the HVAC system meets design specifications for filtration and airflow.
HEPA filters are often installed above ceiling tiles in cleanrooms; once installed, the ceiling grid can be closed in and final finishes applied.
The humidifier is typically integrated into the HVAC duct system, so the ductwork must be in place to mount the humidifier and connect it to the air distribution system.
Humidifiers require a water supply connection; the water line must be roughed in before the humidifier can be connected and installed.
Many humidifiers require electrical power for operation (e.g., fan, solenoid valve, controls); electrical wiring must be in place before connecting the unit.
After the humidifier is installed, the overall HVAC system must be tested and balanced to ensure proper airflow and humidity control.
The humidifier installation must be complete before the final inspection and commissioning of the HVAC system can occur.

predecessor: Install HVAC system ductwork and air handling unit
rationale: The dehumidifier is typically integrated into the HVAC system, requiring the main ductwork and air handler to be in place to connect to.
Dehumidifiers require electrical power to operate, so wiring and circuits must be run to the installation location beforehand.
Dehumidifiers produce condensate water that must be drained away; drain piping must be ready before the unit is installed.
The unit must be physically installed before it can be powered on, tested, and commissioned for operation.

successor: Install finished ceiling or wall panels enclosing dehumidifier area
rationale: Access to the dehumidifier is needed during installation; enclosing finishes should be completed after the unit is in place to allow for connections and adjustments.
Electrical wiring must be run to the thermostat location before the thermostat can be installed and connected.
Walls must be finished and painted before mounting a thermostat to ensure a clean installation and avoid damage from finishing work.
The thermostat must be installed and wired before the HVAC system can be commissioned and tested, as the thermostat provides the control interface for temperature regulation.

successor: Building Management System (BMS) Integration and Calibration
rationale: The thermostat/sensor must be physically installed before it can be integrated into the BMS and calibrated for accurate temperature readings and control.
The VFD enclosure must be physically mounted and secured before the VFD unit can be installed inside it.
Conduit and cable trays must be in place to route power and control cables to and from the VFD.

predecessor: Main power distribution panel installation and energization
rationale: The main power source must be available to supply the VFD with incoming power.
Power cables can only be terminated at the VFD terminals after the VFD unit has been installed.
Control wiring and commissioning activities can only proceed after the VFD is installed and powered.
Motor output cables can only be connected to the VFD terminals after the VFD is in place.
The VFD must be physically installed and powered before it can be programmed.
All installation and wiring must be complete before the VFD can be functionally tested and started up.
Dampers are installed within ductwork, so the ductwork must be in place first to provide the mounting location.
Dampers must be installed and sealed before the duct system can be pressure-tested for air leakage.

successor: Fire Alarm System Integration and Testing
rationale: Fire/smoke dampers must be physically installed before they can be connected to and tested with the fire alarm control system.
Fire dampers are installed at fire-rated wall and floor penetrations; the structural framing and walls must be built first to define the fire compartment boundaries.
Dampers need to be accessible for installation and inspection; ceiling grid and finishes are installed after to avoid rework and allow access.
Structural framing must be complete to provide support and enclosure for HVAC equipment and ductwork.
Roofing must be in place to protect HVAC rooftop units and penetrations from weather damage during installation.
Exterior walls must be enclosed to create a protected environment for indoor HVAC work and to support wall-mounted components.
Electrical rough-in for HVAC units (power supply, controls wiring) can only be completed after HVAC equipment is positioned and final connections are defined.
Duct insulation and pressure testing must follow duct installation to ensure system performance and integrity.
Ceiling grid and drywall installation must occur after HVAC ductwork and diffusers are in place to avoid rework and allow proper integration.
Structural steel framework must be in place to provide support and hanging points for ductwork before ductwork can be fabricated and installed.
Overhead plumbing must be roughed-in first to avoid conflicts and ensure adequate space for ductwork routing, as ductwork is typically larger and less flexible in routing.
Ductwork must be fabricated, erected, and in its final position before insulation can be applied to the exterior of the ducts.
Ductwork must be fully fabricated, erected, and sealed before pressure testing can be performed to verify air-tightness.
Ductwork must be in place to connect to HVAC equipment such as air handling units and fans; equipment installation typically follows or is coordinated with ductwork completion.
Pipes must be installed and joined before pressure testing can be performed, as testing validates the integrity of installed joints and pipe sections.
Pressure testing must be completed and passed before pipes are insulated or coated, as testing may reveal leaks requiring repair; insulating first would hide defects.
Trenches should remain open during pressure testing so that joints and pipes are accessible for inspection and repair; backfilling is performed only after a successful pressure test.

successor: System Commissioning or Hydrostatic Test Certification
rationale: The pressure test must be completed and certified before the piping system can be commissioned and put into service.
Pipe materials and fittings must be procured, delivered, and on-site before pipes can be installed and subsequently pressure tested.

predecessor: Mechanical System Installation (HVAC Equipment, Ductwork, Piping)
rationale: All HVAC equipment, ductwork, and piping must be fully installed and connected before air balancing can commence, as TAB requires the complete mechanical system to be operational to measure and adjust airflow.
Ductwork must be installed and leak-tested to ensure system integrity before TAB can measure and balance air distribution.

predecessor: Electrical Rough-In & Power Connection to HVAC Equipment
rationale: HVAC fans, pumps, and controls require electrical power to operate; TAB cannot proceed without power to start and run the equipment.
TAB results are a prerequisite for comprehensive building commissioning, as the balanced system performance data is needed to verify that all systems meet design specifications.

successor: Final Air Filter Installation & Indoor Air Quality Testing
rationale: While TAB can be performed with temporary filters, final filters are typically installed after balancing to avoid contamination, and IAQ testing follows the balanced system operation.
All MEP rough-in work including ductwork, piping, and wiring must be physically installed before HVAC systems can be commissioned and tested.
The HVAC units (air handlers, chillers, boilers, etc.) must be physically installed and connected before they can be started and tested during commissioning.
The building must be enclosed (roof, windows, doors) to protect HVAC equipment and allow meaningful temperature control and airflow testing.
Testing, adjusting, and balancing (TAB) of air and water systems is typically performed after initial commissioning to fine-tune system performance.

successor: Building Management System (BMS) Integration and Testing
rationale: After HVAC systems are commissioned individually, they must be integrated with the BMS for centralized control, monitoring, and automated sequences.
The building enclosure must be complete to protect HVAC equipment from weather and environmental damage during maintenance and to ensure the building is weather-tight for indoor work.

The HVAC system must be fully installed before preventive maintenance can be performed on it, as maintenance activities (e.g., filter replacement, coil cleaning, lubrication) require the equipment to be in place.
Initial commissioning and startup checks must be completed to verify proper operation before routine preventive maintenance schedules can be established and implemented.

Preventive maintenance (e.g., filter changes, refrigerant charge checks, belt adjustments) must be completed to ensure the HVAC system is clean and functioning correctly before the building can be occupied and the system placed into normal continuous operation.

Preventive maintenance tasks should be completed prior to final performance verification to ensure the system is operating at peak efficiency and to avoid invalidating test results due to known maintenance deficiencies.
Trenches must be dug and excavated to provide space for laying water supply pipes below frost line.
The ground must be properly graded and leveled to establish proper drainage and stable bedding for pipe installation.
Existing underground utilities (gas, electric, telecom) must be located and marked to avoid conflicts and damage during pipe trenching.
After pipes are laid and jointed, they must be pressure-tested and inspected for leaks before backfilling.
Trenches can only be backfilled and compacted after water pipes are installed, connected, and tested to avoid re-excavation for repairs.
The building's water supply pipes must be in place before they can be tied into the municipal water main or other source.
Interior plumbing rough-in (branch lines to fixtures) can only proceed after the main water supply pipes enter the building and are stubbed up.
If pipes run under a slab, the slab can only be poured after water supply pipes are laid, tested, and inspected.

DWV pipes are typically embedded in or run beneath the concrete slab; therefore, the foundation and slab preparation (including gravel base and vapor barrier) must be complete before DWV rough-in can be laid.
DWV pipes placed below the slab require excavation and preparation of trenches prior to pipe installation.
DWV pipes that run under the slab must be fully installed and inspected before concrete is poured, as the pipes will be permanently encased.
While not physically required, it is standard sequencing to complete DWV rough-in before or concurrently with water supply rough-in to avoid rework and coordinate wall chases.
DWV pipes running through walls must be installed prior to closing up walls with framing and sheathing, as the pipes are concealed within the wall cavities.
Hot water heater requires water supply and drain lines to be roughed-in before it can be connected and installed.
Electric water heaters need electrical wiring (e.g., 240V circuit) to be run to the unit location before the heater can be wired and operated.
Gas water heaters require gas supply lines to be installed to the unit location before connection and operation.
After the water heater is installed and connected, pressure testing and leak checks must be performed to verify water/gas connections are sound before full operation.
The hot water heater must be in place before the hot water distribution lines can be connected to the outlet ports for delivery to fixtures.
The water meter must be installed after the rough-in plumbing is complete because the water meter connects to the main water supply line that is laid during rough-in plumbing.
The water meter must be installed before the water service can be connected and activated, as the meter measures flow and is required by utility companies before turning on water supply.
Inspectors typically require the water meter to be installed to verify proper water flow and pressure before approving the rough-in plumbing work.
Water meter must be in place to supply water pressure for testing and operating fixtures such as sinks, toilets, and showers during final installation.
The water meter is typically located at the property boundary or in a meter pit that requires excavation and utility trenching to be completed first.
Piping must be installed and in place before shut-off valves can be attached to the piping system.
Shut-off valves must be installed before the piping system can be pressure tested to ensure the valves are properly sealed and functional.
Valves must be in place before flow testing can verify they operate correctly and control flow as designed.
Insulation is typically applied after valves are installed, though in some sequences insulation can be applied to pipes beforehand and valves later.
All shut-off valves must be installed before the overall system can be commissioned and turned over for operation.

predecessor: Pipe Installation to PRV Connection Points
rationale: The PRV must be connected to piping at both inlet and outlet sides; pipes must be in place and terminated at the valve location before the valve can be physically installed and joined to the system.

successor: Pressure Testing and Leak Check Downstream of PRV
rationale: The PRV must be installed before any pressure testing can be conducted on the downstream piping system, as the PRV regulates the downstream pressure and must be in place to isolate and test the correct section.

The physical installation of the valve must be complete before its set-point can be adjusted and calibrated, since the valve needs to be in its final position, connected, and under system pressure to verify and set the outlet pressure correctly.
Flanges or threaded connections for the PRV must be roughed-in and prepared on the piping system so the valve can be bolted or threaded into place.

successor: Insulation Application to PRV and Adjacent Piping
rationale: While insulation can be applied after installation, it is a soft preference because it could technically be done in stages; however, best practice requires the valve to be installed and leak-tested before insulating to allow access for adjustments and verification.

predecessor: Excavate and Prepare Trench for Water Line
rationale: The trench must be excavated and prepared before the backflow preventer can be installed in the water line.
The main water supply line must be in place before the backflow preventer can be tied into the water system as a downstream component.
The backflow preventer must be installed and connected before the trench can be backfilled, to allow access for connections and testing.
The backflow preventer must be physically installed before it can be tested for proper operation and compliance.
Downstream piping must connect to the backflow preventer outlet, so the preventer must be installed first.
Excavation must be completed to create space for the sump pump pit and drainage system.
Foundation waterproofing should be applied before installing the sump pump to ensure proper water management and drainage integration.
The sump pump and its pit must be installed before the basement floor slab is poured so that the pump is embedded in/under the slab and accessible.
The sump pump discharge line must be connected to the exterior drainage system or storm sewer after installation to ensure proper water removal.
The sump pump needs electrical power, so electrical rough-in work (wiring, outlet installation) must follow sump pump installation to provide the necessary connection.
Floor drain pipes must be connected to the rough-in plumbing system before the drain body can be set in place.
The subfloor or concrete slab base must be prepared and leveled so the floor drain can be properly positioned and embedded.
The floor drain must be set in place before concrete is poured around it so it is embedded correctly in the slab.
Floor drain installation must be completed before waterproofing membranes or coatings are applied to ensure a continuous seal around the drain.

successor: Floor Tiling or Final Floor Finish
rationale: The drain must be installed and adjusted to the correct height before the finished floor surface (e.g., tile, epoxy) is laid around it.
Pipe fittings and couplings cannot be installed until the main pipe runs and rough-in plumbing are in place, as they serve as connection points for these fittings.
Pipes must be cut to length and deburred before fittings and couplings can be attached to join pipe segments.
After fittings and couplings are installed, the entire piping system must be pressure-tested to verify that all joints are leak-free and properly sealed.
Insulation is applied over completed pipe runs including fittings and couplings; installing insulation before the fittings would block access to the joints.
After all pipe connections including fittings and couplings are complete, the system must be flushed to remove debris, solder flux, or solvent residues from the joining process.
The ground must be excavated and prepared to expose the main sewer line and create a trench for the connection pipe.
Existing underground utilities must be identified and marked to avoid strikes during excavation for the sewer connection.
The trench around the newly installed sewer connection must be backfilled and compacted only after the connection is complete and inspected.
The internal building plumbing system must connect to the sanitary sewer service; the external connection to the main must be established before internal rough-in can tie into it.
Underground sewer connections must be completed before pouring concrete slabs or foundations to avoid needing to cut through the slab later.
Vent stacks terminate at or through the roof, so the roof structure and roofing membrane must be in place before the vent stack can be properly flashed and sealed to prevent leaks.

predecessor: Rough-in plumbing for drainage and waste lines
rationale: The vent stack connects to the drainage and waste plumbing system to provide air circulation; the main waste and drain lines must be roughed in first so the vent stack can be tied into the system.
Vent stacks typically run within interior wall cavities; the framing must be in place to provide support and chase space for the vertical vent pipe.
The vent stack must be fully installed and inspected before walls are closed up with drywall to ensure code compliance and accessibility for any necessary adjustments.
Individual fixture vents tie into the main vent stack; sinks, toilets, and other fixtures can only be connected to their vent branches after the main vent stack is in place and properly routed.

predecessor: Rough-in plumbing for drain waste vent (DWV) system
rationale: The drain waste vent piping and drain openings must be roughed-in and stubbed out to the correct locations before a trap can be connected to the drainage system.

successor: Connect fixture drain to trap outlet
rationale: The trap must be installed and in place before the fixture (e.g., sink, tub, shower) drain tailpiece can be connected to the trap outlet.
The trap is part of the drainage system; leak testing (hydrostatic or air test) of the entire drainage assembly can only be performed after the trap is fully installed and connected.

successor: Finish wall/floor surfacing (tile, drywall, etc.) around fixture
rationale: While it is preferable to complete all plumbing rough-in including traps before enclosing walls and floors, some trap installations occur after finishes are in place; however, best practice is to install the trap before final finishes to avoid rework.
For a P-trap or S-trap, the fixture (e.g., sink basin or bathtub) must be set in place so the trap alignment and connection to the fixture drain outlet can be accurately made.

The cleanout access point is part of the drainage plumbing system. The drainage pipes must be roughed-in before a cleanout access point can be installed, as the cleanout connects directly to the drain line.

Cleanout access points are typically located at the base of vertical drainage stacks or at floor level. The slab or foundation must be in place to support the pipe and to establish the elevation at which the cleanout fitting is installed.

The cleanout fitting provides a critical access point for introducing test plugs and water/air pressure during the drainage system pressure test. Therefore, the cleanout must be installed before the test can be performed.
The cleanout access point must be in place and visible for the plumbing rough-in inspection, which verifies that all fittings, including cleanouts, are correctly installed before walls are closed.
Cleanout access points must be installed and the plumbing rough-in approved before walls and ceilings are enclosed, so that the cleanout remains accessible and is not buried behind finishes.
The exterior wall sheathing provides the structural backing and penetration surface through which the hose bibb pipe must pass; the spigot cannot be mounted until wall sheathing is in place.
The hose bibb must be connected to the building's cold water supply line; rough-in plumbing must be completed to provide the water source before the spigot assembly can be installed.
The hose bibb must be mounted and its flange/flashing properly sealed against the weather-resistant barrier before siding or cladding is installed around it to ensure a watertight penetration.

The plumbing connection and mounting bracket for the hose bibb on the interior side must be completed and inspected before the wall is enclosed with drywall to allow access for connections and leak testing.

Ideally the hose bibb is installed before final exterior painting so that the area around the escutcheon plate can be painted or caulked for a clean finish; however this is a preference for aesthetics rather than a physical necessity.
Plumbing rough-in requires the foundation or slab to be in place so that underground pipes and drain lines can be laid and embedded in or below the slab before above-ground work begins.
The underground drain, waste, and vent (DWV) lines and water supply lines must be installed and inspected before the above-ground rough-in plumbing can proceed.
Rough-in plumbing must be complete before inspectors can verify that the piping, venting, and water supply lines meet code requirements.
Insulation is typically installed after rough-in plumbing to enclose pipes within walls, floors, and ceilings; insulating before would block access to plumbing.
Drywall cannot be hung until plumbing rough-in is complete and inspected, as the pipes and vents must be accessible for installation and inspection before being covered.

The plumbing rough-in (pipes, drains, vents, and supply lines) must be installed and pressure-tested inside the walls before fixtures can be attached to them. Trim-out connects the fixtures (toilets, sinks, faucets) to the roughed-in connections.

Walls must be closed and finished because plumbing trim-out involves installing fixtures that mount to finished wall surfaces. Backer board and tile work behind fixtures must also be complete for proper fixture installation and sealing.

Finished flooring (tile, vinyl, etc.) must be installed before setting toilets and other floor-mounted fixtures to ensure proper fit, sealing, and to avoid damaging finished surfaces during later work.

While trim-out includes installing escutcheon plates and trim rings, final painting and touch-up work around fixtures is typically done after trim-out to achieve a clean finish. However, this is a soft preference—painting can be done before trim-out with careful masking.

After all fixtures are trimmed out and connected, the plumbing system must be inspected to verify code compliance, proper operation, and leak-free connections before walls are fully closed or the building is occupied.
Pipes must be installed and connected before they can be tested for pressure integrity.
All welded joints and connections must be completed to form a closed system before pressure tests can be conducted.
Flanges, fittings, and valves must be assembled and tightened to ensure the system is sealed for pressurization.
Test pumps, gauges, and temporary connections must be installed before the actual pressure test procedure begins.
After pressure testing confirms integrity, the system must be flushed to remove test water, debris, or contaminants introduced during testing.
Pipe insulation should only be applied after pressure testing is passed to allow visual inspection of joints and to avoid trapping moisture from test water.
Final coating or painting of pipework should be done after pressure testing to avoid damage to the coating during testing and to allow access for repairs.
The system must pass pressure testing as a prerequisite before entering the commissioning phase where operational checks are performed.

Drain cleaning and descaling must occur after rough-in plumbing is installed because the drain pipes and lines need to be in place before they can be cleaned and descaled of debris and construction residues.

Plumbing fixtures such as sinks, toilets, and floor drains must be installed after drain cleaning and descaling to ensure the pipes are clear of obstructions and debris before final connections are made.

Pressure testing of drain waste and vent (DWV) systems should follow drain cleaning to verify that lines are clean, clear, and sealed properly without blockages that could cause inaccurate test results.
Underground drainage and main sewer lines must be installed and connected before cleaning and descaling can be performed on the entire drain system.
Final plumbing inspection and testing should occur after drain cleaning to confirm all lines are free-flowing and meet code requirements before walls and floors are closed up.
Pipes must be physically installed and in position before insulation can be applied around them.
Pressure testing must be completed to verify pipe integrity before covering pipes with insulation, as leaks would be undetectable after insulation.
Weatherproof cladding or jacketing is applied over the insulation material to protect it from moisture and physical damage.

Commissioning activities (system testing and startup) typically follow insulation completion to ensure thermal performance, though this is a preferred sequence rather than a strict physical necessity.
Final quality inspections are typically performed after all insulation work is complete, but insulation can be partially inspected during installation.
The system must be pressurized to detect leaks; pressure testing creates the conditions necessary for leak detection to occur.
All piping, fittings, and connections must be physically installed before leak detection can be performed on the assembled system.
All welds, threaded joints, and mechanical connections must be finished so that the complete joint system can be tested for leaks.
Leak repairs must be completed before the system can undergo final acceptance testing to verify overall integrity and performance.
Any detected leaks must be repaired before insulation is applied, as insulating over leaking joints would trap moisture and cause corrosion or system failure.
The electrical substation provides the incoming high-voltage power supply that feeds the Main Distribution Board, so it must be operational first.

The Main Distribution Board is physically housed within the main electrical room; therefore the room structure, walls, floor, and ceiling must be completed to provide a secure and enclosed space for installation.
A proper earthing system is required before energizing the Main Distribution Board to ensure electrical safety and comply with electrical codes.

successor: Feeder Cable Routing to Sub-Distribution Boards
rationale: The Main Distribution Board is the central distribution point; sub-distribution boards receive power through feeders that originate from the MDB, so the MDB must be in place first.
While meters can be installed concurrently, commissioning and verification of metering systems that interface with the MDB is typically done after the MDB is energized and operational.
The rough-in wiring (cables, conduits, and raceways) must be pulled and routed to the sub distribution board location before the board itself can be installed and terminated.
The main distribution board (MDB) must be installed and energized to provide the upstream feed to the sub distribution board (SDB). The SDB receives its power supply from the MDB.

Final circuits (lighting, power outlets, equipment connections) originate from the sub distribution board; they can only be terminated and energized after the SDB is installed and its outgoing breakers are in place.

Testing of the sub distribution board—including insulation resistance, phase rotation, and breaker functionality—can only be performed after the board is physically installed and all connections are made.

Although fire stopping around cable penetrations at the SDB is a best practice and often code-required, it is a soft sequencing preference as minor sealing work could be performed after board installation; however, ideal sequencing has it completed after all wiring is landed.
The electrical panel must be installed and wired to provide the necessary power feed and connection point for the Automatic Transfer Switch (ATS).
The ATS is typically mounted on a concrete pad or foundation; the pad must be cured and ready before the switch can be placed and secured.
The generator must be installed and its output cables run to the ATS location so that the transfer switch can be connected to both the utility and generator power sources.
The ATS must be fully installed and wired before the entire emergency power system can be commissioned and load bank tested to verify proper transfer operation.
The ATS must be in place so that the utility company can terminate their service conductors into the ATS's utility-side lugs before the system is energized.
The circuit breaker must be mounted inside the electrical panel enclosure; therefore the panel enclosure must be installed first to provide a structural housing for the breaker.
Main service conductors must be terminated at the panel lugs to provide electrical supply before branch circuit breakers can be connected.
Branch circuit wires must be connected to the circuit breaker terminals, so the breaker must be installed and secured in the panel first to receive the wiring.
The panel cover encloses and protects the circuit breakers; all breakers must be installed and wired before the cover can be secured in place.
The electrical system cannot be safely energized for testing until all circuit breakers are installed and properly seated to isolate and protect individual circuits.
The RCD must be mounted inside or adjacent to the consumer unit; the enclosure and busbar system must be in place before the RCD can be connected.
Main supply cables and incoming power must be run to the consumer unit before the RCD can be wired in series with the circuits it protects.

successor: Wire individual final circuits to RCD
rationale: Each protected circuit's phase (live) conductor must pass through the RCD's output terminals; this cannot be completed until the RCD is physically installed and secured.

successor: Test RCD functionality and trip times
rationale: Functional testing (pressing the test button and measuring trip time with a tester) must occur after wiring is complete and power available, but the RCD must be installed first.
The RCD must be in place and wired before the system can be safely energised; the RCD provides earth fault protection so it must be operational before circuits are live.
The surge protection device must be electrically connected to the main electrical panel to provide overvoltage protection.
Service entrance conductors must be in place to provide the electrical pathway for the surge protection device to be connected.
A proper grounding system is required for the surge protection device to function correctly and safely dissipate surge currents.
The surge protection device must be installed before the overall electrical system can be tested and commissioned to ensure complete protection.
The surge protection device must be in place for the final inspection to verify code compliance and proper installation.
Power cables are typically laid inside protective conduits placed in trenches; the conduit pathway must be prepared before cable pulling can occur.
Power cables need to terminate at substations or switchgear panels, which must be in place to receive and connect the cable ends.
After cables are laid, they must be terminated (connectors, lugs installed) and electrically tested (insulation resistance, continuity) before being energized.
Once cables are placed in the trench, the trench can be backfilled; backfilling cannot occur before cable placement as the cable would be buried.
Power cables must be fully installed, terminated, and tested before the electrical system can be energized and commissioned for use.
Cable trays are typically supported by structural steel members. The steel frame must be in place to provide mounting points and structural support for cable tray systems.

Large mechanical ductwork and piping that occupy overhead space must be installed first to establish the spatial layout and avoid conflicts. Cable trays are usually routed around or below major mechanical systems.

Cables are laid into or pulled through the tray after the tray sections, fittings, and supports are fully installed and secured. Attempting to pull cables without the tray in place is physically impossible.

It is preferable to apply fireproofing after cable tray installation so that the tray supports and hangers are fully encased; however, sequencing can sometimes be reversed if protection is provided for the tray.
Conduits that terminate at or enter the cable tray must be installed and connected after the tray is in place to ensure proper alignment and mechanical connections.
Conduit and trunking provide the mechanical pathway to route cables to the unit location.

predecessor: Run final circuit cables to unit location
rationale: Cables must be present and pulled through before the unit can be wired and connected.
The switched fused connection unit (SFCU) needs a mounting box fixed and flush in the wall to attach to.
The circuit must be fully connected including the SFCU before it can be energised and tested.

successor: Install appliance / equipment (e.g. extractor fan, underfloor heating)
rationale: The SFCU must be in place to provide local isolation and fused supply for the downstream equipment.
The Variable Speed Drive (VSD) requires a dedicated power supply from the electrical panel; without the panel installed, the VSD cannot be powered or safely connected.
The VSD must be connected to the motor it controls; the motor must be physically installed and positioned before the VSD can be properly wired, configured, and tested with the load.
Power and control cables between the VSD, motor, and control system need proper cable management (trays or conduits); these pathways must be in place before running cables to the VSD.
The VSD must be physically mounted, wired, and connected before it can be powered on, parameterized, and tested for correct operation.
Once the VSD is installed and connected to the motor, the motor can be started and the drive's parameters can be tuned to match the motor characteristics and load requirements.
The transformer must be placed on a stable, level concrete foundation or pad designed to support its weight. Without the foundation, the transformer cannot be safely positioned.

predecessor: Underground Conduit and Cable Trench Installation
rationale: Cable trenches or conduits for incoming and outgoing power cables must be laid before the transformer is set in place, as access to these connections is needed under or adjacent to the transformer.
High-voltage primary cables from the utility source must be connected to the transformer's bushings after the transformer is physically installed and secured.
Low-voltage secondary cables to downstream distribution panels must be connected after transformer placement.
After installation, the transformer's insulating oil must be tested for dielectric strength, moisture content, and dissolved gas analysis before energization to ensure safe operation.
Structural steel must be in place to provide mounting surfaces and support structures for electrical conduits, cable trays, and other containment systems.
Concrete slabs and decks must be poured and cured to provide the substrate for embedment of conduits and the floor/wall surfaces for routing containment.
Ceiling and wall framing must be complete to allow installation of conduit and cable tray runs within wall cavities and above ceilings before they are enclosed.
Electrical conductors and cables cannot be pulled or terminated until the conduit, cable tray, and raceway systems (containment) are fully installed and inspected.
Fire-stopping around penetrations for electrical containment must be applied after the conduit or cable tray is in place to seal openings through fire-rated assemblies.
Cables must be pulled through installed ducts, conduits, or cable trays; the pathways must be in place before any cable can be routed.
Cables are laid in or supported by cable trays/ladders; the support system must be fully installed before cable pulling commences.
The building or room where cables are installed must be weather-tight and structurally complete to protect cables from damage and environmental exposure.
Cables must be pulled and terminated before they can be electrically tested for continuity, insulation resistance, and other commissioning checks.
Power cannot be applied to the system until all cables are fully pulled, terminated, and verified; energization requires completed cable connections.
Conduits provide the physical pathways for electrical cables that will connect to the distribution board; without conduit infrastructure in place, cables cannot be routed to the DB.
The recess or mounting surface for the distribution board must be prepared and rough openings completed before the DB enclosure can be set and secured.
