The grounding electrode and main earth bonding must be in place to connect the distribution board's earth bar, ensuring safety compliance before energizing the board.
Cables are pulled from the distribution board to downstream loads; the DB enclosure and busbars must be mounted and accessible before branch circuit cables can be terminated into the breakers.
Utility meters and sub-meters are typically mounted adjacent to or integrated with the distribution board; the board must be fixed and wired before meters can be installed and energized.
All electrical wiring, conduit, and device boxes must be installed before testing can begin, as testing verifies the integrity of these installed components.
The main electrical panel and distribution boards must be installed and energized before commissioning can verify branch circuits and overall system functionality.
Proper grounding and bonding must be in place before testing to ensure safety and accurate measurement of ground resistance and continuity.
Commissioning must confirm all internal systems are safe and functional before the building can be connected to the utility grid for permanent power.
All electrical systems must be tested, commissioned, and certified before the building can be legally occupied or handed over to the owner.

A thermographic survey detects heat loss through the building envelope; the building envelope (walls, roof, windows, doors) must be substantially complete and sealed for the survey to detect meaningful thermal anomalies.

While not a strict physical dependency, it is best practice to have interior finishes at least partially in place or at a known state so that background heat signatures are consistent and do not confuse the thermal scan.

The survey results identify gaps or defects in insulation; any remediation work is dependent on knowing where the problems are, so the survey must come first. This is a soft preference because remediation may not be needed.
The thermographic survey is a quality assurance check on the building envelope; final sign-off or approval of cladding and insulation should occur after the survey confirms no thermal defects exist.
The thermographic survey is often a pre-handover quality check; ideally any thermal issues are resolved before formal handover, making this a soft preference rather than a strict physical constraint.
HVAC systems are major electrical loads. Their installation must be complete to accurately determine their electrical demand for load scheduling.
Elevators are significant electrical loads. Their installation must be finished so that their power requirements can be included in the load schedule.
Lighting is a primary electrical load. The lighting layout and fixture installation must be completed to calculate total lighting load for scheduling.
The main electrical panel size and configuration depend on the total scheduled load. Load scheduling must be completed first to determine panel specifications.
Transformer capacity is determined by the total electrical load. Load scheduling must be finished to calculate the required transformer size.
Sprinkler pipes and supply lines must be installed in the ceiling/ walls before sprinkler heads can be attached.
Electrical wiring in ceiling spaces must be completed before sprinkler head installation to avoid interference and access issues.
HVAC ducts in ceiling plenums must be in place before sprinkler heads are positioned to ensure proper clearance and coverage.
Sprinkler heads must be installed and positioned before ceiling finishes are applied so the heads penetrate or align with ceiling tiles properly.
The sprinkler system must be fully assembled (including heads) before pressure testing can verify the entire system's integrity.
The control panel must be connected to the fire suppression piping network, which needs to be installed first to ensure proper routing and connection points.
Power supply and control wiring must be roughed in before the control panel can be mounted and connected to electrical sources.
The fire suppression control panel often receives signals from the fire alarm system, so the alarm system must be in place for proper integration and communication testing.
The control panel must be fully installed and operational before the overall fire suppression system can be commissioned and tested for functionality.
Authorities having jurisdiction require the control panel to be installed before conducting final inspections and granting occupancy approvals for the fire suppression system.

predecessor: Fire Pump Foundation / Base Slab Preparation
rationale: A stable concrete foundation or base slab must be cured and ready before the heavy fire pump equipment can be set in place to ensure proper support and alignment.
The pump must be physically positioned and anchored before inlet/outlet piping can be aligned and connected to it.
Piping must be in place and pressure-tested before the electrician can safely terminate motor cables and control wiring to avoid interference and safety hazards.
Electrical power and control signals must be fully connected and verified before the pump can be operated and tested for flow, pressure, and automatic start/stop functions.

successor: Fire Pump Enclosure / House Construction (if applicable)
rationale: While the pump is typically enclosed after installation, commissioning may require temporary access for adjustments; however, completing the enclosure before testing is a soft preference for weather protection and security.

The jockey pump must be installed on a prepared foundation or base (often a concrete housekeeping pad or steel base plate) that provides structural support; without it, the pump cannot be set in place.
After the jockey pump is set in position, the suction and discharge piping can be flanged or welded to the pump nozzles; piping cannot be connected until the pump is physically located.

successor: Jockey Pump Electrical Wiring / Motor Connection
rationale: Electrical cables to the jockey pump motor should be run and terminated only after the piping is complete to avoid interference and ensure safe routing of conduit around pipework.

predecessor: Jockey Pump Electrical Wiring / Motor Connection
rationale: The pump cannot be energized and tested until its motor is wired and properly connected to the fire alarm / pump controller panel; commissioning must follow all mechanical and electrical completions.

predecessor: Fire Pump System Hydrostatic Testing & Flushing
rationale: System hydrostatic testing and flushing must be completed before final commissioning of the jockey pump to ensure the piping network is clean and pressure-tested, preventing damage to the pump internals.
Structural steel framing must be erected to provide support and attachment points for fire suppression piping, and to create the building framework through which piping will be routed.
Overhead decking must be installed before fire suppression piping can be hung from the structure above, as the piping is typically suspended from the deck or roof structure.
Fire suppression piping must be installed and pressure-tested before ceilings are closed in, to allow access for installation, inspection, and testing of the sprinkler system.
Fire suppression piping and sprinkler heads must be in place before the fire alarm and detection devices can be integrated and calibrated to respond to the sprinkler activation zones.

Fire suppression piping installation must be completed before interior finishes are applied, to avoid damage to finishes and allow for pressure testing without risk of water damage to finished surfaces.
The storage cylinder requires a stable, load-bearing foundation or mounting structure to support its weight before it can be placed.
The cylinder must be in its final position before supply and discharge piping can be connected to it.
The cylinder must be installed and connected before the system can be pressurized and tested for leaks.
Electrical and control connections (e.g., for release solenoids, pressure switches) can only be terminated after the cylinder is positioned.
The empty cylinder must be installed before it can be filled with the suppression agent.
Pipe rough-in must be completed to provide the supply and drain piping connections that the alarm check valve will be installed onto.
The sprinkler main, which connects to the alarm check valve, must be installed first as the alarm check valve is a component of the sprinkler riser assembly.
Trim components such as pressure gauges, test valves, and drains are attached to the alarm check valve body after it is in place.
The alarm check valve must be installed and connected to the system before hydrostatic pressure testing can verify the integrity of the entire sprinkler riser assembly.
The alarm check valve's flow switch and alarm port must be in place before the fire alarm system can be connected and tested for waterflow detection.

Dry pipe valves require connection to the upstream water supply piping and downstream sprinkler piping; rough-in piping must be installed first to provide the physical connection points for the valve.
The piping attached to the dry pipe valve must be properly supported; hangers and supports must be in place before the valve and connected piping can be installed.
Dry pipe sprinkler systems are pressurized with air/nitrogen; sprinkler heads must be installed to complete the downstream system before the dry pipe valve can be set to its normal operating state.
The dry pipe valve must be installed and connected before the system can be pressurized with compressed air, which holds the valve closed during normal operation.
The installed dry pipe valve assembly must be in place and connected before the entire sprinkler system can be hydrostatically tested for leaks and pressure integrity.

predecessor: Pipe installation to flow switch location
rationale: The flow switch is installed inline on a pipe; the pipe must be in place to receive the switch.

predecessor: Electrical conduit and wiring to switch location
rationale: Power and signal cables must be run to the switch location before the switch can be electrically connected.
The switch must be physically installed before it can be calibrated and functionally tested.
Flow verification and system commissioning require the flow switch to be in place and operational.

successor: Insulation of pipe at flow switch location
rationale: Insulation can be applied after the switch is installed, though in some sequences insulation may be done before; post-install insulation allows access for adjustment.
The bracket provides the physical mounting point and must be secured before the tamper switch can be attached.

predecessor: Run wiring/conduit to tamper switch location
rationale: Electrical supply and signal wiring must be present at the location before the tamper switch can be electrically connected.
The tamper switch must be physically installed before it can be functionally tested for correct operation.

successor: Connect tamper switch to alarm/control system
rationale: The switch must be in place before final wiring connections to the alarm or building management system can be completed.
The tamper switch must be mounted and wired before any protective cover or enclosure is closed, to allow access for connections and adjustment.
Structural steel framing must be in place to provide support and attachment points for fire suppression piping systems.

Other overhead rough-in work such as electrical conduit and mechanical ductwork should be completed before fire suppression piping to avoid conflicts and ensure sufficient overhead space for the piping.
Fire suppression piping must be installed and pressure-tested before ceilings or wall finishes are enclosed, as the piping is concealed above the ceiling.
The piping must be fully installed before it can be pressure-tested, flushed, and inspected for compliance with fire codes.
Main piping runs must be installed first as the foundation, then sprinkler heads (branch drops and fittings) are connected to the main lines.
A conceptual or preliminary design must be established to define basic system parameters (building layout, water demand points, expected loads) before hydraulic calculations can be performed.
Site conditions such as water table, soil permeability, and available water source pressure must be known to perform accurate hydraulic design.
Hydraulic calculations determine pipe sizes, slopes, pump capacities, and pressure requirements, which are essential inputs for creating detailed plumbing and piping layouts.
The results of hydraulic calculations (flow rates, head losses, pressure requirements) directly determine the specifications for pump selection and sizing.
Hydraulic calculations for drainage networks (pipe sizing, slopes, flow capacities) must be completed first to inform the detailed design of drainage and stormwater systems.
The suppression system must be physically installed and in place before any commissioning or testing can commence, as testing requires the complete system to be operational.

predecessor: Fire Detection and Alarm System Installation and Testing
rationale: Fire detection and alarm systems typically interface with suppression systems (e.g., releasing circuits, abort switches). The detection system must be installed and tested first to ensure proper activation signals are sent to the suppression system during commissioning.

predecessor: Electrical Power Supply and Distribution to Suppression System
rationale: Commissioning and testing of the suppression system requires electrical power (e.g., for control panels, solenoid valves, pumps). Power must be available and verified before testing can proceed.

successor: Final Fire Safety System Acceptance and Handover
rationale: The suppression system must be fully commissioned and tested before the overall fire safety system can be accepted and handed over to the client or authorities, as successful testing is a prerequisite for final sign-off.

A building cannot be occupied or operated until the life safety systems, including suppression systems, have been successfully commissioned and tested to ensure they are fully functional and code-compliant.
The suppression system must be physically installed before any maintenance or inspection activities can be performed on it.
The system must be tested and commissioned to verify it is operational before routine maintenance and inspection schedules can commence.

successor: Suppression System Repair or Component Replacement
rationale: Maintenance and inspection identifies defects or deficiencies that must be addressed through repair or replacement activities.
After maintenance and inspection, the system may need to be re-certified or re-commissioned to ensure it meets operational and safety standards.
While not a strict physical requirement, regular maintenance and inspection records inform the decision to decommission or upgrade a suppression system at the end of its service life.

Sprinkler pipes must be installed and run to the sprinkler head location before the escutcheon plate can be fitted, as the plate is the trim/finishing piece that goes around the sprinkler head where it penetrates the ceiling.
The sprinkler head itself must be installed first because the escutcheon plate fits around the head's base where it meets the ceiling finish, serving as a decorative cover.

The ceiling finish (drywall, plaster, or acoustic tile) must be completed so the escutcheon plate can be positioned flush against the finished ceiling surface, covering the gap between the sprinkler head and the ceiling opening.

Typically the escutcheon plate is installed after painting is complete to avoid getting paint on the plate, or if installed before, final touch-up painting around the plate may be needed. This is a soft preference as sequencing can vary.
Escutcheon plates must be in place before the final system testing and inspection to ensure the sprinkler system is fully trimmed and compliant with code requirements for coverage and appearance.
The traction drive unit must be installed on a stable foundation and track bed to ensure proper alignment and load distribution.
The rails must be in place and aligned so that the traction drive unit can be properly positioned relative to the rail system it will drive.

predecessor: Power supply and electrical infrastructure installation
rationale: Electrical connections and power supply infrastructure need to be available to test and commission the traction drive unit after installation.

successor: Traction Drive Unit testing and commissioning
rationale: The unit must be physically installed before any functional testing or commissioning activities can begin.

successor: Cable connection and termination to drive unit
rationale: Power and control cables can only be connected after the traction drive unit is in its final installed position.
A stable foundation must be prepared to support the weight and operational loads of the hydraulic drive unit.

predecessor: Base Frame or Mounting Bracket Assembly
rationale: The base frame or mounting bracket must be in place to provide a secure attachment point for the hydraulic drive unit.
The hydraulic drive unit must be mounted before connecting its hydraulic lines to prevent stress on fittings and misalignment.

successor: Electrical Wiring and Control System Integration
rationale: The drive unit must be physically installed before electrical connections and control signals can be routed to it.
Pressure testing and calibration can only be performed after the drive unit is fully installed and connected.
Operational testing of the full system requires the hydraulic drive unit to be installed and all connections made.

Electrical conduits provide the pathways for wiring that connects the lift control panel to the building's electrical system; without conduits in place, the control panel cannot be safely wired or powered.
The lift control panel is typically housed in or adjacent to the lift motor room; the room must be prepared, enclosed, and made weather-tight before installing sensitive electronic control equipment.
The lift control panel is part of the overall lift system; the lift shaft must be structurally complete to allow coordination between the control panel and the lift car traveling within the shaft.
The control panel must be installed and connected before the lift system can be tested, as the panel houses the logic controllers, drives, and safety circuits that govern lift operation.
The control panel must be installed and operational to control and power the lift car's movements, doors, and communications during its installation and subsequent testing.
Landing doors are installed within the hoistway openings; the hoistway structure and framing must be complete before doors can be mounted.
The door frames must be set and secured in the hoistway openings before the landing door panels and hardware can be installed.
The landing door assembly must be in place before interlock switches, wiring, and electrical connections can be installed to ensure door closure detection and safety circuits.
Final finishing, trim, and cosmetic work around the landing door assembly must occur after the doors are installed to achieve proper fit and appearance.
Safety testing and commissioning of the elevator system, including door interlock verification, requires landing doors to be fully installed and operational.
Car doors must be assembled after the car body is constructed because doors are mounted onto the body shell and need the body structure to be in place for proper fitting and alignment.
The vehicle frame must be welded and structurally complete before doors can be attached, as doors hinge onto the frame pillars.
Doors are typically painted as part of the body assembly process; painting must occur after doors are fitted to ensure color matching and uniform coating across panels and gaps.
Interior door panels, wiring, and trim cannot be installed until the door shells are mounted on the vehicle and accessible from the interior side.
Weather seals, window regulators, and glass must be installed after the doors are hung on the body to ensure proper alignment, sealing, and operation within the body aperture.
The door operator must be mounted onto a securely installed door frame; without the frame in place, there is no structural support for the operator.
The door leaf must be hung and aligned before the operator can be attached, as the operator connects to the door leaf to automate its movement.
Power supply and control wiring must be roughed in to the location before the operator can be connected and powered up.
Testing and calibration of the door operator can only be performed after the operator has been physically installed and wired.

Final adjustments to door operation and trim work are typically done after the operator is installed to ensure proper clearance and finish, though some trim work could theoretically be done beforehand.
Safety gear/governor installation requires the turbine shaft to be in place and aligned, which is done during turbine assembly.
Bearings support the shaft on which the governor is mounted; bearings must be installed before the governor can be fitted.
Overspeed trip testing requires the governor and safety gear mechanisms to be installed and operational to verify correct trip settings.
While load rejection tests ideally require the governor functional, some preliminary checks can be done without it; however full load rejection testing needs the governor to control the turbine.
The safety gear and governor must be installed and set before final commissioning of the turbine unit can proceed.
Buffers are positioned along conveyor lines to accumulate product; the conveyor system must be in place to support and align the buffers.

successor: Commission and test material handling system
rationale: Buffers must be fully installed and integrated before the overall material handling system can be tested and commissioned, as buffers are a key component of the flow path.
Buffers are often mounted on or supported by the structural steel framework; the framing must be erected to provide mounting points and load-bearing support.
Buffers typically require power and control signals for their drives and sensors; electrical infrastructure must be in place for connection.

successor: Final alignment and tuning of buffer zones
rationale: After physical installation, buffers need fine-tuning of sensors, speeds, and accumulation logic to ensure proper operation within the system.
The ground must be excavated to the required depth before the lift pit can be constructed, as the lift pit is built below ground level.
Water must be managed or pumped out from the excavation area to provide a dry and stable working environment for constructing the lift pit structure.
The lift pit structure must be fully constructed and cured before waterproofing membranes or coatings can be applied to protect it from moisture ingress.
The lift pit walls must be completed and waterproofed before soil can be backfilled around the exterior to provide lateral support.
The lift pit provides the structural base and clearance space required for the lift equipment; installation of rails, cab, and buffers can only commence once the pit is fully constructed and cured.
The site must be cleared, levelled, and prepared before any shaft construction can begin, as shaft construction requires a stable, accessible work area.
Ground conditions must be assessed to determine appropriate shaft construction methods, depth, support systems, and safety measures.
The shaft must be excavated before the lining can be installed; the lining provides structural support to the excavation.

successor: Installation of Shaft Services (ventilation, drainage, lighting)
rationale: Services such as ventilation ducts, drainage pumps, and lighting can only be installed once the shaft excavation is complete and the space is accessible.

successor: Tunnel Boring / Tunnelling (if shaft is an access point)
rationale: The shaft often serves as a launch or access point for tunnel boring machines; tunnelling activities cannot begin until the shaft is fully constructed and operational.
The lift shaft must be physically constructed to house and protect the lift equipment before any maintenance or servicing can be performed.
Lift maintenance and servicing can only commence after the lift system has been fully installed and is operational.
Power must be supplied to the lift system before any testing, maintenance, or servicing activities can be undertaken.
Maintenance and servicing work must be completed before the lift can be formally commissioned and certified for public use.
All lift systems must be serviced and verified operational before the building can be handed over to the client or occupants.

The lift shaft, pit, and machine room must be structurally complete and sound before lift modernisation works can commence, as the lift equipment needs a stable and enclosed structure for installation.
The lift shaft must be cleared of debris, rails checked/aligned, and any preparatory work finished before new lift components can be installed.
A dedicated electrical supply and control wiring must be run to the lift machine room and shaft before lift equipment can be connected and tested.
After modernisation or refurbishment is complete, the lift must be tested for safety, performance, and compliance with regulations before being put into service.
It is preferable to complete lift modernisation before finishing adjacent lobby areas to avoid damage to new finishes from heavy equipment movement, though not a physical necessity.
Smoke detectors require electrical power supply wiring to be in place before they can be connected and installed.
Smoke detectors are typically mounted on ceilings; the ceiling surface must be installed before the detector can be mounted.
The smoke detector must be connected to and communicate with the fire alarm control panel, which should be installed first.
The smoke detector must be physically installed before it can be powered on, tested, and commissioned to verify proper operation.
It is preferable to complete painting and finishing work before installing smoke detectors to avoid dust and debris contamination of the sensor, though not a strict physical constraint.
A mounting bracket or base must be securely installed at the designated location before the heat detector can be attached or mounted onto it.
Electrical conduits and wiring must be run to the detector location before the heat detector can be connected to the fire alarm system.
Ceiling or wall surfaces where the heat detector will be mounted should be finished (painted, plastered) before installation to avoid damage or contamination of the detector.
Heat detectors must be installed and wired before the overall fire alarm system can be tested and commissioned to ensure proper operation.
In suspended ceiling applications, heat detectors are often installed before the ceiling tiles are fully placed, as a soft preference for easier access during installation.
The mounting bracket must be securely fastened to the ceiling or wall before the detector unit can be attached to it.

predecessor: Run Electrical Wiring to Detector Location
successor: Connect Power to Carbon Monoxide Detector
rationale: Electrical cables must be routed and terminated at the junction box before the detector can be wired for power.
The detector must be physically installed and powered on before its alarm and sensor functions can be verified.
Final wall or ceiling finishing must be done before installing the detector's decorative cover or trim ring to avoid damage from dust and paint.

successor: Connect Power to Carbon Monoxide Detector
rationale: Electrical rough-in must pass inspection before final power connections are made to the detector to ensure code compliance and safety.

predecessor: Install electrical conduits and junction boxes
rationale: Electrical conduits and junction boxes must be in place to provide the pathway for wiring and a mounting location for the Manual Call Point.
Wiring must be pulled through conduits to the junction box before the Manual Call Point can be connected to the fire alarm system.

successor: Connect and test fire alarm control panel
rationale: The Manual Call Point must be physically installed and wired before the control panel can be fully connected and the loop/zone containing the call point can be tested.

successor: Commission and test the fire alarm system
rationale: System-wide commissioning and functional testing of the fire alarm system requires all field devices, including Manual Call Points, to be installed.

successor: Install signage and final finishes (e.g., 'Break Glass' labels)
rationale: While signage can be placed after installation for clarity and compliance, it is a soft preference as it does not physically prevent the call point from functioning.
Conduit and wiring infrastructure must be installed in walls and ceilings before the Fire Alarm Control Panel (FACP) can be mounted and connected.
The FACP requires a dedicated electrical power supply from the main electrical panel to function.
The FACP must be installed and powered before field devices (smoke detectors, pull stations, horns/strobes) can be wired into the panel.
The FACP must be fully installed and connected before the entire fire alarm system can be programmed, tested, and commissioned.

successor: Building Occupancy / Fire Alarm Acceptance Test
rationale: Code requires that the fire alarm system, with the FACP as the central controller, be fully operational and tested before a building can be occupied.
Electrical conduit and wiring must be in place to provide power and signal connections to the annunciator panel.
The enclosure or backbox must be securely mounted to the wall or structure before the annunciator panel components can be installed inside it.
The panel must be physically installed before field wiring can be terminated to its internal terminals.
All wiring connections must be completed and verified before power can be applied and functional testing performed.
The panel must be physically installed and powered before configuration or programming can be loaded onto it.
Electrical rough-in (conduit, wiring, and junction boxes) must be completed before notification appliances like strobes and horns can be installed, as they need power and signal wiring in place.
Wall and ceiling finishes (drywall, paint, ceiling tiles) must be completed before notification appliances are mounted, as these devices attach directly to finished surfaces.
All notification appliances must be installed before the fire alarm system can be tested and commissioned, as these devices are end-points that must be verified for proper operation.
Installed notification appliances must be visually inspected and verified as part of the final project punch list, though this is a quality/verification step rather than a strict physical dependency.
In some cases, ceiling-mounted notification appliances may be installed before final ceiling trim is completed to allow for alignment adjustments, though typically the sequence can be reversed.

predecessor: Install electrical wiring and control systems
rationale: The sounder/horn requires electrical power and control signals to function, so wiring and control systems must be in place before the device can be connected and tested.
The sounder/horn must be physically secured to a mounting bracket or backbox that is already installed on the wall or ceiling.

successor: Test and commission fire alarm / notification system
rationale: The sounder/horn must be installed and connected before the entire system can be tested to ensure proper audible notification.

successor: Install ceiling tiles or final finishing (if surface-mounted)
rationale: If the sounder/horn is surface-mounted on a ceiling, final ceiling finishing can be done after installation to avoid damage, though this is a preference rather than a physical requirement.

predecessor: Complete overhead cable tray and conduit rough-in
rationale: Cable trays and conduits supplying the sounder/horn location must be roughed in before the device can be connected to the cabling infrastructure.
The strobe device requires a mounted electrical backbox for secure attachment and electrical connection.

predecessor: Run Wiring for Fire Alarm System
rationale: Power and control wiring must be in place before the strobe can be connected and installed.

successor: Connect Strobe to Fire Alarm Control Panel
rationale: The strobe must be physically installed before it can be electrically connected to the control panel.
The device must be installed and connected before testing its operation and synchronization.
All visual alarm devices must be installed and tested before the overall fire alarm system can be commissioned.

predecessor: Install overhead utilities (conduit, cable tray, piping)
rationale: Beam smoke detectors are mounted to ceilings or structural beams; overhead utilities must be in place to ensure clear access and avoid obstructions or rework.

predecessor: Install structural ceiling or roof deck
rationale: The beam smoke detector's transmitter and receiver are mounted onto the ceiling or structural elements; the ceiling structure must exist to provide the mounting surface.

successor: Fire Alarm System Commissioning and Testing
rationale: Once installed, the beam smoke detector must be integrated into the fire alarm system and functionally tested to verify proper detection and signaling.
While finishing can often proceed after detector installation, it is a soft preference to protect the detector from dust and debris during finishing work.
Detector alignment across a large open space is easier before ceiling tiles are installed; however, tiles can be removed for alignment, making this a soft preference.
The duct smoke detector must be mounted on or inside the ductwork; the ducts must be in place before the detector can be physically installed.
The duct smoke detector requires electrical power and control wiring, which must be roughed in and available at the installation location before the detector can be connected and commissioned.

The duct smoke detector must be installed and wired before the HVAC system can be functionally tested, as the detector is a safety device integrated into the air handling system's control sequence (e.g., fan shutdown on smoke detection).
The duct smoke detector must be physically installed and wired before the fire alarm system can be programmed, integrated, and tested to ensure proper alarm signaling and response.

While installation before ceiling closure is preferred to avoid costly rework, it is not a strict physical requirement if access panels are provided. It is a soft preference for ease of access and reduced labor cost.
The flame detector must have a physical mounting bracket or base installed before the detector itself can be attached and secured.
Electrical cabling and conduit must be routed to the detector location before the flame detector can be wired and connected to the fire alarm system.
The detector requires electrical power to function; the power supply circuit must be available and energized (or ready to energize) before completing detector wiring.
The physical installation and wiring of the flame detector must be complete before functional testing, calibration, and commissioning can be performed.
The flame detector must be installed and wired before it can be integrated into the central fire alarm control panel and configured as part of the system.
Cable trays provide the physical pathway and support structure for routing and securing addressable loop cables, so trays must be in place before wiring can begin.
Conduits protect and route wiring; they must be installed before pulling wires through them to avoid damaging cables and to ensure proper routing.
Testing verifies the integrity and connectivity of the installed wiring; the wiring must be fully pulled and terminated before continuity tests can be performed.
Addressable devices such as detectors and modules are connected to the loop wiring; the wiring infrastructure must be complete before devices can be mounted and connected.
The loop wiring must be installed and connected to the fire alarm control panel before the panel can be programmed, configured, and commissioned for operation.
Structural steel must be in place before any wiring can be installed, as the steel frame supports the building and provides the structural paths for conduit and cable trays.
Conduit raceways must be installed and in place before wires can be pulled through them during conventional zone wiring.
Overhead mechanical systems such as ductwork must be installed first to avoid conflicts and to ensure accessible routing paths for electrical wiring.
Wiring must be completed before rough-in inspection can take place, as the inspector needs to verify that wiring is properly installed per code before walls are closed.
Ceiling grid installation typically follows wiring completion to avoid interference and so that wiring can be routed above the ceiling before the grid is installed.
The electrical room must be prepared and conduits run to the battery/standby power location before the equipment can be placed and connected.
The backup power source must be installed and operational before connecting it to the main electrical distribution panels to ensure safe power routing.
The backup battery/standby power supply must be in place before critical load testing and commissioning can proceed, as it provides emergency backup during tests.
A stable, level foundation or reinforced floor slab is required to support the weight and ensure safe operation of backup battery/standby power equipment.

successor: Fire Alarm & Life Safety System Integration
rationale: While not physically required, it is a strong safety preference to have backup power operational before integrating life safety systems to guarantee uninterrupted power for alarms.
The electrical panel must be installed and energized to provide power to the relay/interface module.
Control wiring must be run to the module location before the relay/interface module can be connected and terminated.
The relay/interface module must be installed and wired before the overall system can be tested and commissioned.
The module must be installed and all connections verified before the control panel enclosure can be closed and sealed.
Conduits and cable trays must be in place to route control and power cables to the relay/interface module location.
Fire alarm devices require power and communication cabling, which must be routed and terminated during electrical rough-in before devices can be mounted and connected.
Fire alarm control and signaling cables are typically run in conduit or cable trays; these pathways must be in place before pulling and terminating the wires.

predecessor: Ceiling Grid and Rough Openings Complete
rationale: Smoke detectors, sprinkler flow switches, and notification appliances are mounted in or on ceilings; the ceiling grid must be installed and access openings confirmed before device placement.

successor: Fire Alarm System Testing and Commissioning
rationale: A complete and fully wired fire alarm system must be in place before any functional testing, device verification, or commissioning can be performed.

Fire alarm devices such as smoke detectors and speakers are often integrated into finished ceilings; final ceiling tiles and trim should be installed after the alarm devices are fixed and wired to avoid rework.

successor: Fire Alarm System Maintenance and Inspection
rationale: Fire alarm devices require power and connectivity from the electrical rough-in before they can be installed, tested, or inspected.

successor: Fire Alarm System Maintenance and Inspection
rationale: All fire alarm components (smoke detectors, pull stations, horns, strobes, panels, etc.) must be physically installed before the system can be tested and inspected for proper operation.

predecessor: Fire Alarm System Maintenance and Inspection
rationale: The fire alarm system must be tested and certified as operational before the overall building can receive final commissioning approval and occupancy clearance.

predecessor: Fire Alarm System Maintenance and Inspection
rationale: A successfully inspected and approved fire alarm system is a life-safety prerequisite for obtaining a certificate of occupancy.

predecessor: Fire Alarm System Maintenance and Inspection
rationale: While programming may begin earlier, final verification of programming against inspection results is typically done after inspection to address any corrective actions.
Fire alarm zones must align with electrical circuitry and power distribution; electrical rough-in must be completed to define power availability and circuit layouts.
Zone planning requires finalized floor plans to determine compartmentation, egress paths, and device placement locations.
The overall fire alarm system design (device types, panel locations, signaling protocols) must be approved before detailed zone planning can proceed.
Zone plans define where each device (smoke detectors, pull stations, horns/strobes) will be placed; installation cannot proceed without zone assignments.
Cable routing and conduit plans depend on zone boundaries and device locations established during zone planning.
Panel programming requires the zone map and device assignments to configure addressable loops, zone groupings, and alarm response sequences.

predecessor: Install power supply to Central BMS Controller panel
rationale: The Central BMS Controller requires electrical power to function; power supply installation must be complete before the controller can be energized and commissioned.
The controller must have a physically installed and secured enclosure before the electronic components can be placed and connected.

predecessor: Run BMS backbone communication cabling to controller location
rationale: Communication cabling (BACnet, Modbus, etc.) must be pulled and terminated at the controller location before the controller can be wired into the network.

successor: Commission and test Central BMS Controller
rationale: The controller must be physically installed, powered, and connected before it can be programmed, configured, and functionally tested.

successor: Connect field-level BMS devices (sensors, actuators, VAVs, AHUs)
rationale: The Central BMS Controller acts as the supervisory head-end for field devices; those devices cannot be logically integrated and controlled until the controller is operational.

predecessor: Install BMS Server and Network Infrastructure
rationale: The BMS Operator Workstation relies on the BMS server and network backbone to communicate with building systems; the server and network must be operational before the workstation can be commissioned.

predecessor: Complete Electrical and Data Cabling to Workstation Location
rationale: Power and network connectivity (Ethernet or BACnet/IP) must be provided to the workstation location before the workstation hardware can be installed and powered on.

successor: Commission and Test BMS Operator Interface
rationale: The workstation hardware must be physically installed, powered up and connected to the network before software configuration, user interface setup and end-to-end testing can begin.

successor: Integrate BMS Workstation with Building Automation Controllers
rationale: All BMS field controllers and devices must be accessible via the network once the workstation is operational; the workstation serves as the central monitoring/control point, so its installation must precede system-level integration.

predecessor: Complete Room Finishes and HVAC in Control Room
rationale: While not physically required, it is strongly preferred to have a finished, climate-controlled environment to avoid dust, temperature extremes, or damage to sensitive workstation electronics during installation and commissioning.
The field control panel must be mounted on a stable foundation or structure; foundation work must be completed first to provide a secure base.
Conduits and cable trays must be in place to route power and signal cables to the field control panel location before the panel can be installed and connected.
Cables can only be terminated and connected to the field control panel after the panel is physically installed and secured in its final position.
The control panel must be fully installed and all connections made before power can be safely applied and testing can commence.
Overall system commissioning and calibration of field devices controlled by the panel require the panel to be installed, wired, and operational.
BMS control panels must be installed first because the communication network connects these panels; the network cabling and infrastructure rely on the panel locations being established.
Field devices (sensors, actuators, controllers) must be installed before the communication network can be wired and configured to connect them to the BMS.
Cable trays, conduits, and pathways for communication cables must be installed prior to pulling and terminating the network cables to provide physical routing infrastructure.
The communication network must be fully installed, terminated, and tested before system-wide integration and commissioning can begin, as all devices communicate over this network.

successor: BMS Graphics and User Interface Setup
rationale: While some GUI setup can begin in parallel, full configuration of graphics and operator interfaces depends on network connectivity being established to all controllers and devices.
Sensors and transmitters must have physical mounting points (brackets, supports) installed before they can be attached to structures or equipment.
Cable pathways must be in place before sensors and transmitters are installed so that wiring can be pulled and connected properly.
Process sensors (pressure, temperature, flow) measure conditions on or within primary equipment, so the equipment must be in place first.

successor: Instrument tubing and impulse line connection
rationale: After sensors are mounted, impulse lines and tubing must be connected to carry process media to/from the sensor for accurate measurement.

successor: Cable pulling and termination to DCS/PLC panels
rationale: Wiring from sensors and transmitters must be pulled and terminated at control system panels; this can only happen after the field device is installed and its connection point is known.

predecessor: Control valves and actuators installation preparation
rationale: Mounting brackets, base plates, and electrical conduit rough-ins must be in place before actuators and damper drives can be physically installed.

predecessor: Air handling unit (AHU) assembly and ductwork installation
rationale: Dampers and valves must be installed within the AHU and ductwork before actuators and damper drives can be mounted onto them.

predecessor: Electrical supply and control wiring rough-in
rationale: Power and control cables must be run to the actuator locations before final connection and commissioning of actuator drives.
Actuators and damper drives must be fully installed and mechanically connected before the overall HVAC control system can be commissioned, calibrated, and tested for proper operation.

successor: HVAC control system integration and BMS connection
rationale: Actuator end switches and feedback signals need to be wired and operational before the building management system (BMS) can integrate and monitor damper/valve positions.
The overall control system architecture, including communication protocols and data flow, must be designed before the HMI can be configured to interface with the correct controllers and data points.
Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs) and other controllers must be programmed and operational so the HMI can be mapped to the correct tags, variables, and control logic.
The industrial network (e.g., Ethernet/IP, Profinet) must be installed and tested to enable communication between the HMI and field devices/controllers.
The HMI hardware and software must be installed and configured before operators can be trained on the interface and before final commissioning tests can verify correct operation.

Full system integration testing, which validates that the HMI correctly displays and controls all connected devices, can only proceed once the HMI is fully deployed and connected to the control network.
The server room must be prepared with proper cooling, power, and rack mounting before the Data Historian Server can be placed and installed.
Network cabling, switches, and connectivity must be in place before the Data Historian Server can be connected to the network.
The server hardware must be physically installed before the operating system can be configured on it.
The OS must be installed and configured before the Data Historian application software can be deployed on the server.
Commissioning (testing and validation) typically follows installation, though in some cases partial commissioning could begin alongside later installation steps.
The UPS requires a primary electrical feed from the main switchboard to charge its batteries and supply bypass power, so the switchboard and its cabling must be installed and energized first.
The UPS is dedicated to powering the Building Management System (BMS) controllers and panels; therefore those BMS components must be in place so that the UPS output can be properly connected to them.
The BMS system cannot be fully commissioned and tested until its dedicated UPS is installed, wired, and operational to provide conditioned backup power during testing.
External battery banks (if separate from the UPS enclosure) must be connected after the UPS unit is in place to ensure proper physical and electrical integration.

successor: Final Electrical Safety and Load Testing
rationale: Load bank testing and verification of UPS transfer times is typically performed after installation but is a soft preference because some preliminary testing could be done with temporary power.
The gateway must be procured and delivered to site before it can be physically installed.
The BMS gateway requires electrical power to operate, so the power supply must be installed and available before the gateway can be powered on and commissioned.
The gateway needs network connectivity (Ethernet/BACnet/MS/TP cabling) to communicate with the BMS head-end and field devices, so the cabling infrastructure must be in place first.

successor: BMS Gateway / Protocol Converter Configuration and Commissioning
rationale: The device must be physically mounted and connected before software configuration, addressing, and protocol mapping can be performed.

predecessor: BMS Gateway / Protocol Converter Configuration and Commissioning
successor: BMS Head-End System Integration and Testing
rationale: The gateway must be configured and operational before it can be integrated with the BMS head-end software for end-to-end communication testing.
BMS sensors and controllers require electrical power and wiring infrastructure, which must be installed before BMS devices can be connected and commissioned.
BMS sensors (temperature, humidity, pressure, airflow) are installed within or on ductwork, so ducts must be in place before sensor mounting and wiring.

predecessor: Mechanical Equipment Installation (AHUs, chillers, boilers, pumps)
rationale: BMS controllers and actuators are physically connected to mechanical equipment, so that equipment must be installed and available for connection before BMS work can proceed.
The BMS must be operational to monitor and control HVAC equipment during testing, adjusting, and balancing of air and water systems.
The BMS must be fully installed and commissioned before the building can be handed over, as it is essential for ongoing facility management and control of all mechanical and electrical systems.

The architectural layout, room functions, and spatial zones must be defined before the BMS system can be designed, as the BMS must be tailored to monitor and control HVAC, lighting, and other systems based on the specific building layout and zone requirements.
Structural design must be complete to understand building loads, structural zones, and locations for installing BMS sensors, controllers, and cabling routes.

The BMS integrates with and controls mechanical (HVAC), electrical, and plumbing systems; therefore, the design of these MEP systems must be completed first to define the control points, setpoints, and monitoring requirements that the BMS will manage.

The BMS design and engineering phase produces the detailed specifications, schematics, and control logic that are physically implemented during installation and commissioning; installation cannot proceed without a completed design.

The electrical installation must accommodate BMS power and control cabling requirements, panel layouts, and integration points defined during BMS design; the design must precede electrical rough-in to ensure proper coordination.
The BMS must be fully installed and commissioned before operators can be trained on it, as training requires a functional system.
Operators must complete training before they can take over operation and management of the BMS system.
Trained operators are required to perform ongoing monitoring and maintenance of the BMS.
The BMS must be configured and programmed with the correct settings before operators can be trained on its operation.
While operators can begin basic energy management tasks after training, full optimization typically requires additional experience and advanced training.
BMS controllers must be physically installed and wired before integration testing can begin, as testing requires the controllers to be operational and connected to the network.

All sensors (temperature, humidity, pressure, etc.) and actuators (valves, dampers, relays) must be installed and terminated before BMS integration can verify their communication and control functionality.

The backbone network infrastructure (BACnet, Modbus, or similar protocols) must be fully installed, terminated, and commissioned to enable communication between BMS controllers, field devices, and the central BMS server.
The central BMS software platform, server hardware, and workstation licenses must be installed and configured to serve as the integration and monitoring platform during system testing.

predecessor: Electrical Power Supply and Distribution Testing
rationale: Stable electrical power supply to all BMS components (controllers, servers, network equipment) must be verified prior to integration testing to prevent damage to equipment and ensure reliable test results.
Integration and system testing must be successfully completed and all test logs approved before formal commissioning and handover to the facility management team can proceed.

BMS integration testing must verify that all HVAC subsystems (AHU, VAV, chiller, boiler) can be monitored and controlled via the BMS before performing detailed functional performance testing of the HVAC systems.

While training can partially overlap with testing, formal user training on the BMS interface and alarm management should ideally commence after integration testing is complete to ensure the system is fully operational and stable for demonstration.

The Building Management System (BMS) must be fully installed, configured, and commissioned before any preventive maintenance can be performed on it. Maintenance cannot be carried out on equipment that is not yet in place.

The BMS must be commissioned and verified as operational before routine preventive maintenance activities can begin. Commissioning ensures the system is functioning correctly and establishes baseline performance parameters for future maintenance.

After completing preventive maintenance of the BMS, a system performance verification is typically conducted to confirm that all components are operating correctly. While this is a strong logical preference for quality assurance, it may not be a physical construction necessity.

Preventive maintenance of the BMS is often completed before the building is occupied to ensure all environmental control systems function properly. However, this is generally a scheduling preference rather than a hard physical constraint, as maintenance can sometimes be performed during occupancy.

BMS (Building Management System) requires stable electrical power supply to function; electrical infrastructure must be in place before BMS controllers, sensors, and actuators can be installed and powered up.
BMS directly monitors and controls HVAC equipment (chillers, boilers, AHUs, VAVs); the HVAC systems must be physically installed before BMS integration and control wiring can be completed.
BMS typically integrates lighting control for energy management; lighting fixtures and controls must be installed as a prerequisite for BMS lighting integration and programming.

BMS must be fully installed, programmed, and operational before the overall building system commissioning can proceed, as the BMS is the central platform for monitoring, controlling, and verifying all interconnected building systems.

Facility operators and end-users must be trained on the upgraded BMS interface, controls, and alarm management procedures only after the BMS retrofit is complete and fully functional, to ensure safe and effective building operation.

The BMS (Building Management System) must be fully installed, configured, and commissioned before it can be used to collect data for energy auditing. Without a functional BMS in place, there is no system to audit or extract energy data from.

The HVAC system (heating, ventilation, and air conditioning) must be physically installed and operational because it is a primary energy-consuming system monitored by the BMS. Energy auditing analyzes HVAC performance data, which cannot be generated without the installed system.

Electrical systems, including sub-meters and power monitoring equipment, must be installed to provide energy consumption data. The BMS relies on these meters to collect electrical usage data needed for auditing.

Once energy auditing via BMS identifies inefficiencies and areas of high consumption, this data informs the planning of energy efficiency retrofits. While it is logically sequential, some retrofit planning could theoretically begin in parallel, making it a soft preference rather than a hard physical constraint.

The audit results provide the baseline data needed to optimize BMS control strategies and re-commission the system for better performance. Optimization cannot occur without first understanding current energy performance through auditing.
The ground must be excavated and prepared to the required depth and grade before a catch basin can be installed, as it sits below grade.
Inlet and outlet drainage pipes must be laid and positioned before the catch basin is set in place to connect to them.
The catch basin must be fully installed and stable before backfilling around it to avoid movement or damage.

successor: Connection of Downspout/Inlet Pipes to Basin
rationale: Inlet pipes can only be connected once the catch basin is in its final position so that pipe joints align properly with the basin openings.
Final surface grading and paving around the catch basin should follow installation so that the basin's grate is set at the correct finished grade, though minor adjustments could be made concurrently.
The trench or excavation must be dug before the storm drain pipe can be placed into it.
The trench bottom must be properly graded and compacted to provide a stable bedding for the pipe.
Pipe sections must be laid in the trench before joints can be sealed or connected.
The pipe must be installed and inspected before backfill material can be placed around it.
The main pipe run must be in place before connecting inlet structures or outlet outfalls to it.
The ground must be excavated to create space and proper bedding for the drainage inlet structure before the grate can be installed.
The concrete or precast inlet box or catch basin must be placed and cured first, as the grate sits on top of or within this structure.
The inlet piping and connections to the drainage network must be completed before the grate is installed, as the grate provides final access closure.
The grate must be securely in place before backfilling around the inlet to ensure the structure is stable and properly aligned.
Paving or final surface finishing around the grate must be done after installation to ensure the grate is flush with the finished surface elevation.
The ground must be excavated and graded to the proper slope before trench drain installation so that the trench can be cut and the drain can be placed at the correct elevation and drainage slope.
The soil subgrade must be properly compacted to provide a stable base for the trench drain system, preventing settling or shifting after installation.
Any underground utilities (drainage pipes, conduits) crossing the trench drain path must be installed first to avoid conflicts and the need to cut or disturb the completed trench drain.

Trench drains are typically set in place and leveled before the surrounding concrete slab or pavement is poured, as the drain frame becomes part of the finished surface and the concrete is cast around it.

While tile or surface finish can technically proceed after the drain is set, it is a soft preference to complete the drain installation first to ensure proper alignment and drainage integration with the finished surface.
The detention basin area must be cleared of vegetation and roughly graded to the planned subgrade levels before basin construction can begin.
Erosion and sediment controls (e.g., silt fence, inlet protection) must be in place around the basin area prior to excavation to prevent sediment runoff during construction.

successor: Fine Grading and Lining of Basin
rationale: The basin structure must be excavated and formed before final fine grading and installation of any liner (clay, geomembrane, or concrete) can be applied.
The basin excavation and grading must be completed before the outlet control structure (e.g., weir, orifice plate, riser) and associated outflow piping can be installed within the basin.
The detention basin must be excavated and shaped before incoming storm drain pipes can be connected and terminated at the basin inlet.
The site must be cleared of vegetation and rough-graded to establish the overall drainage patterns and identify the lowest area where the retention pond will be located.
Silt fences, sediment basins, and other BMPs must be in place before excavating the pond to prevent off-site sedimentation during construction.

successor: Storm Drain Piping and Outfall Installation
rationale: The retention pond serves as the discharge point for stormwater runoff; the outfall pipe directs water into the pond, so the pond must be excavated and prepared before the connecting pipe is laid to it.

successor: Permanent Landscaping and Seeding of Pond Area
rationale: Once the pond is excavated and shaped, the side slopes and bottom must be stabilized with seed, sod, or riprap to prevent erosion; this cannot happen until the pond earthwork is complete.

While not a strict physical requirement, it is good practice to have the stormwater management facility (pond) operational before major impervious surfaces are constructed, so that any runoff during subsequent construction is captured and treated.
The site must be excavated to the required depth and graded before the detention tank can be placed, as the tank is installed below grade.
A compacted, level subgrade or engineered bedding is required to support the tank structure and prevent differential settlement.
The tank must be fully installed, secured, and inspected before backfilling around it can commence.

successor: Connection of Inlet/Outlet Piping to Tank
rationale: Pipe connections to the tank structure require the tank to be in place and properly positioned before piping can be tied in.
Final surface grading, paving, or landscaping above the tank area must be done after the tank is installed and backfilled to avoid damaging the buried structure.
The ground must be excavated and graded to the proper elevation and location before a stormwater manhole can be placed, as the manhole structure requires a prepared foundation.
A compacted stone base or bedding layer must be laid and leveled to provide a stable foundation for the manhole structure before it is set in place.
Storm drain pipes entering and exiting the manhole must be connected after the manhole is set so the pipes align with the manhole openings and proper joints are formed.
Backfill around the manhole can only be placed after all pipe connections are completed to avoid disturbing pipes or compromising the connections.

The top frame and cover (adjusting rings and lid) must be installed after the manhole barrel is set and adjusted to final grade, as the lid elevation must match the finished pavement or ground surface.
The outlet control structure must be placed on stable, excavated ground at the correct elevation; excavation must be completed to provide the proper foundation and access for construction.
A properly compacted base or foundation is required before any concrete or structural elements of the outlet control structure can be placed to ensure stability and prevent settlement.

The outlet control structure serves as the terminal connection point; outlet pipes or conduits leading away from the structure cannot be fully connected until the structure itself is in place and cured.
Backfill around the outlet control structure can only be placed after the structure is complete and its concrete or components have reached sufficient strength to withstand lateral earth pressures.

While final grading can proceed after the structure is in place, it is a soft preference because partial grading could be done beforehand; however, best practice is to complete all structures before final surface restoration to avoid rework.
The headwall must be placed on a stable foundation to ensure structural integrity and proper load distribution.
The site must be properly graded and prepared to establish correct drainage and elevation before the headwall can be installed.
The headwall is typically placed at the ends of a culvert pipe to retain embankment material; the pipe must be in place first so the headwall can be properly aligned and connected.
Backfill material around the headwall can only be placed and compacted after the headwall is installed and cured to avoid displacing or damaging the structure.
Final grading and surface drainage adjustments must occur after the headwall is in place to ensure proper water flow and soil stability around the structure.
The ground must be excavated and prepared to the correct grade and alignment before the culvert structure can be placed.
The culvert must be fully installed and in position before backfill material can be placed around and over it to provide support and cover.
If the culvert is under a road or surface, the roadway structure (base and pavement) cannot be placed until the culvert is installed and backfilled.
If groundwater or surface water is present at the culvert site, dewatering must be performed to create a dry work environment before culvert installation can begin.

Culvert pipes or box sections must be delivered to the site and staged near the installation area before placement can commence, though this is a logical prerequisite rather than a physical constraint.
The area must be excavated and graded to the proper elevation and slope before the riprap apron can be placed on the prepared subgrade.
The subgrade must be compacted and smoothed to provide a stable foundation for the riprap apron stones.
A geotextile filter fabric is typically placed on the prepared subgrade before riprap to prevent soil erosion and migration of fines through the stones.
The riprap apron at the culvert outlet must be in place before or concurrently with the outlet structure to provide scour protection and energy dissipation.
Backfill around the apron edges should be placed after the riprap stones are set to lock them in position and provide lateral support.
The ground must be graded and excavated to the proper elevation and contours before bioretention cell construction can begin, as the cell requires a specific basin shape and depth to function.

The underdrain pipe network, cleanouts, and outlet structures must be installed at the base of the excavation before the bioretention media layers are placed, as they are covered by subsequent layers.
The cell liner and drainage layer (gravel) must be installed as part of the cell construction before the engineered soil mix can be placed on top.
The engineered soil media provides the growing substrate; plants and mulch are placed on top of the completed media layer.

successor: Final Erosion Control and Site Stabilization
rationale: Erosion control measures such as straw wattles, matting, or hydroseeding are installed last to protect the completed bioretention cell from runoff during establishment.

Downspouts and rainwater leaders collect water from roof gutters; the roof must be installed first to define the drainage points and provide the structural support for gutter and downspout attachment.
Downspouts are physically connected to gutters to channel water from the gutter system to the ground or drainage system; gutters must be in place before downspouts can be attached.
Downspouts are typically mounted against exterior walls; the wall cladding or sheathing must be completed to provide a finished surface for downspout brackets and to avoid damage to unfinished walls.

Downspout discharge points must be positioned before final grading and drainage work to ensure proper water flow away from the foundation; the downspout outlets define where splash blocks, drains, or grading need to be directed.

While not strictly physically required, it is best practice to inspect and verify foundation drainage systems after downspouts are in place to ensure all roof water is properly diverted away from the foundation.
Proper site grading and excavation must be completed first to establish the correct slopes and trenches needed for French drain placement, ensuring water flows properly toward the drain.
The building foundation or structure must be in place before installing a French drain around it, as the drain is typically placed adjacent to the foundation footing to intercept groundwater.
After the French drain is installed with its gravel and perforated pipe, backfilling can proceed to cover and protect the drain system while ensuring proper drainage layers remain intact.
Final landscaping, grading, or pouring of adjacent slabs must occur after the French drain is in place so that surface water is directed into the completed drainage system.

While not physically required in all cases, it is preferable to install underground utilities (water, sewer, electrical) before the French drain to avoid conflicts, digging up, or damaging the completed drain system.
Site must be mobilized with equipment, temporary facilities, and site access established before earthmoving can commence.
Existing structures, vegetation, and debris must be cleared from the site before grading and earthwork operations can begin.
Soil conditions, bearing capacity, and subsurface characteristics must be known to design proper cuts, fills, compaction specifications, and slope stability measures.
The site must be graded to rough final elevations and subgrade prepared before foundation excavation can start to ensure stable working platform and correct footing levels.
Grading establishes the surface drainage patterns and subgrade levels required before installing underground stormwater and drainage systems.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and topsoil before any underground utility work can begin, providing unobstructed access for excavation and pipe installation.
The trench must be excavated to the required depth, width, and grade before storm drain pipes can be placed in the trench.
After pipes are installed, joints must be tested for leaks and inspected to ensure proper connection before backfilling.
Backfilling and compaction of the trench can only occur after the storm drain pipes have been properly installed, aligned, and inspected.
Catch basins and inlets connect to the storm drain pipe network, so pipe runs must be in place to establish connection points for these structures.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and graded to provide a stable foundation and proper drainage slopes before constructing a catch basin.
Existing underground utilities (gas, water, electric) must be identified and marked to avoid damaging them during excavation for the catch basin.
The hole must be dug to the appropriate depth and dimensions before the catch basin structure can be installed or constructed in place.
Pipes that drain into or out of the catch basin cannot be connected until the basin structure itself is in place and cured.
The top grate and frame can only be installed after the catch basin body is fully constructed and ready to receive the cover.
The area around the completed catch basin cannot be backfilled until the structure is fully built, inspected, and approved.
Final pavement, concrete, or surface finish over the area cannot be applied until the catch basin and its connections are fully completed and tested.
The basin area must be cleared of vegetation and debris before excavation and grading can begin for the basin.
The overall site grading that establishes drainage patterns and basin location must be completed before the basin can be excavated and formed.

Erosion control measures (silt fence, sediment traps, etc.) must be in place before earth-disturbing activities like basin excavation begin, to comply with environmental regulations and prevent off-site sedimentation.
The basin structure must be formed and ready before connecting drainage pipes that route stormwater into and out of the basin.

While final landscaping typically follows basin construction, in some cases landscaping can proceed concurrently around the basin top; however, soft preference is to finish the basin first to avoid rework and ensure proper drainage integration.

Site clearing removes vegetation and debris which disturbs the soil surface; erosion and sediment control measures (such as silt fences, sediment basins, and stabilised entry/exit points) must be installed before any earthworks or construction activities begin to prevent sediment runoff.

Erosion and sediment control measures must be in place prior to major earthmoving to capture sediment generated by soil disturbance; this is a regulatory and environmental requirement to prevent off-site sedimentation.

While it is preferred to have sediment controls installed before constructing access roads to minimise tracking of mud off-site, temporary road building may in practice occur concurrently; this is a soft preference rather than a strict physical requirement.
All underground drainage pipes must be installed and connected before the system can be commissioned to ensure the physical infrastructure is in place for testing.
The complete stormwater drainage network must be finished before commissioning to verify the entire system's functionality and capacity.
Sewer connections must be installed and tied into the main system before commissioning can validate proper waste water flow and connections.
Surface paving should only be completed after drainage commissioning to ensure that drainage systems are fully functional and leak-free before covering them with permanent surfaces.
Final landscaping and grading must occur after drainage commissioning to ensure proper surface water runoff and that the drainage system handles water flow as designed.
Hydrostatic testing must be completed before flushing to ensure pressure integrity of the system; flushing is performed after the system has been pressure-tested to remove any debris or test water.
All piping must be fully installed and connected before hydraulic flushing can be performed, as flushing circulates fluid through the completed pipe network.

While some permanent instruments may need to be removed or protected during flushing, preliminary installation of sensing elements (e.g., pressure/temperature taps) should be done prior to flushing to allow verification of instrument connections.
After flushing and cleaning, pneumatic (air) testing may be performed to verify leak-tightness, but flushing must be done first to remove debris and ensure lines are clean for safe air testing.
System commissioning and start-up can only proceed after the piping system has been flushed and cleaned to prevent contaminants from damaging equipment such as pumps, valves, and heat exchangers.
The soil stack connects to underground drainage and must be installed after the underground drainage network is in place to ensure proper waste flow.
Foundation work must be completed to provide the structural support and access for vertical soil stack installation through the building.
The soil stack typically penetrates the ground floor slab, so the slab must be poured (with sleeves/penetrations) before the stack can be installed.
Plumbing fixtures such as toilets, sinks, and urinals require the vertical soil stack to be in place as the main waste drainage riser before they can be connected.
Vent pipes connect to the soil stack to allow air circulation and prevent siphoning, requiring the soil stack to be installed first.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and prepared before any structural component like the Waste Stack can be placed or erected.
A foundation or base slab must be constructed to support the Waste Stack structure before it can be built upon it.
The Waste Stack vertical pipe must be installed before waste pipes from fixtures can be connected to it.
The Waste Stack must be in place before vent piping can be tied into it for proper drainage and ventilation.
Toilets, sinks, and other fixtures that drain into the Waste Stack require the stack to be installed first for proper drainage connection.
The site must be prepared and graded before any branch drain installation can begin to ensure proper drainage slopes and stable subgrade.
Branch drains must connect into the main drain system, so the main drain line must be installed first to provide the connection point.
After branch drain pipes are laid and connected, the trench must be backfilled and compacted to protect the pipes.
Final surface finishing such as paving or landscaping must be done after branch drains are installed and buried to avoid rework.
Building drain must be installed below the building foundation, requiring excavation and site preparation to be completed first to provide access and proper subgrade.
Usually the building drain is laid after footing but before the slab pour, though some sequences may vary.
The building drain serves as the main horizontal drainage pipe that all interior waste and vent piping connects to; rough-in must connect into the building drain.
The building drain is typically embedded in or laid beneath the slab; the slab cannot be poured until the drain is installed and inspected.
Site preparation (clearing, grubbing, and rough grading) must be completed before sewer installation to provide a stable, accessible work area and proper drainage for trenching operations.
