Other underground utilities such as water lines, gas lines, and electrical conduits should be roughed-in or at least planned and coordinated before sewer installation to avoid conflicts in trench locations and depths, though sewer often has priority for gravity flow.
Building sewer connections pass beneath the foundation and slab; therefore, the sewer line and its penetrations must be installed and inspected before concrete is poured.
After sewer line installation and inspection, the trench must be backfilled and compacted before any subsequent above-ground work can proceed safely.
The building sewer connection to the municipal system or septic tank must be complete before interior plumbing rough-in can connect to the building's main drain stack and waste/vent piping.
The P-trap must connect to the drainage pipe system, so the rough-in drainage pipe must be in place before the P-trap can be installed.
The P-trap must be installed first to serve as the connection point for the trap arm leading to the drain.
The fixture connects into the P-trap, so the trap must be in place before the fixture drain is connected.
Pressure and leak testing of the drainage system can only be performed after all components, including the P-trap, are installed.

It is preferable to close up walls and ceilings after the P-trap is installed to avoid future access issues for inspection and repairs, but it can technically be done later if an access panel is provided.
The S-Trap is a plumbing component that connects to the drainage system; it requires the building's structural framework and foundation to be in place before it can be installed.
The S-Trap must connect to the main drain line, so the rough-in plumbing for the drainage system must be completed prior to installing the S-Trap.
The S-Trap is a component that must be connected to the fixture (e.g., sink) to form the P-trap or S-trap seal; the fixture is installed after the trap is in place.
While it's preferable to complete the S-Trap installation before closing up walls to avoid rework, it is not a strict physical necessity if access panels are provided.
The S-Trap is part of the drainage system; the water supply can be connected and tested only after the trap and drain lines are fully installed to ensure proper drainage and prevent leaks.
The waste pipe rough-in must be in place before the bottle trap can be connected to the drainage system.
The bottle trap must be installed first so that the basin or sink waste outlet can be aligned and connected to it.
The bottle trap must be fully installed before the drainage system can be pressure-tested or commissioned for leaks and flow.

predecessor: Mount wall bracket or support for Bottle Trap
rationale: The bottle trap requires a secure wall bracket or support to be mounted first so it can be properly positioned and fastened.

successor: Install trap connection to sewer vent pipe
rationale: Soft preference: Ideally the sewer vent pipe connection is finalised after the bottle trap is in place to ensure correct alignment, but it could be partially pre-routed beforehand.
The ground must be excavated and leveled before the grease trap/interceptor can be placed in its designated location.
A concrete pad or foundation base is required to support the grease trap/interceptor and prevent settling.
Inlet and outlet drainage pipes must be laid to and from the grease trap location before the unit is set in place.
After the grease trap is installed and connected, the surrounding excavation must be backfilled and compacted to restore grade.
Kitchen fixtures such as sinks and dishwashers must have their waste lines connected to the grease interceptor after it is in place and connected to the main drainage system.
The ground must be graded and excavated to the proper elevation and alignment before the sediment interceptor can be installed.
The sediment interceptor must be in place before other erosion and sediment control measures are fully deployed to capture runoff during construction.
The sediment interceptor should be installed prior to foundation excavation to prevent sediment-laden runoff from leaving the site.
Utility trenching generates loose soil and sediment; the interceptor must be operational before such earth-disturbing activities begin.
Sediment control measures including interceptors must be established before any major building construction commences to comply with stormwater pollution prevention regulations.
The ground must be excavated to the required depth and dimensions before the inspection chamber can be placed, as the chamber is installed below ground level.
A level concrete base or blinding layer must be poured and cured to provide a stable foundation for the inspection chamber to rest upon, preventing settlement.
Incoming and outgoing drainage pipes must be connected to the chamber after it is set in place, as the chamber serves as the junction point.
Earth must be backfilled and compacted around the installed chamber to secure it in position and restore the surrounding ground level.
The access cover and frame are fitted onto the top of the chamber after the chamber body is fully installed and aligned.
The ground must be excavated to create space for the manhole structure before it can be installed.
A compacted granular base or concrete base slab must be placed and leveled to provide a stable foundation for the manhole.
Pipes must be connected to the manhole inlets and outlets; the manhole structure must be in place first to serve as the junction point.
After the manhole is installed and connections are made, the surrounding area can be backfilled and compacted.
The cover and frame are placed on top of the finished manhole structure to provide access and surface closure.
The hole or conduit for the rodding eye must be drilled or formed before the rodding eye component can be placed or installed.
The rodding eye provides a pathway and access point for pulling cables; cables cannot be pulled until the rodding eye is in place.

successor: Inspection and Testing of Conduit System
rationale: The rodding eye must be installed to allow inspection, cleaning, and testing of the conduit run.

The cleanout plug is installed at the access point of a drainage pipe system. The drainage pipe must be in place first so that the cleanout fitting (where the plug goes) is available and properly positioned.
The cleanout plug is the removable cap that seals the cleanout fitting. The fitting (wye, tee, or cleanout adapter) must be installed first to provide the threaded or hub receptacle for the plug.
The cleanout plug seals the cleanout opening to allow the drainage system to hold pressure or water for testing. The plug must be in place and tightened before any pressure test can be performed.
The cleanout plug must be installed and secured before backfilling around the cleanout access point to prevent dirt and debris from entering the drainage system.
The cleanout plug must be in place for the drainage system to be considered complete and ready for final inspection by the building authority.
The DWV (drain-waste-vent) rough-in piping must be in place to provide the connection point where the AAV will be mounted.
The AAV must be installed before the system can be pressure-tested to verify that the valve opens/closes correctly and the vent seal is airtight.
The AAV must be in place to provide proper venting for the fixture drain when the fixture is finally connected and used.
The AAV must be installed and accessible for inspection before walls or ceilings are closed up, because the valve must be visible to the inspector per code requirements.
While it is good practice to provide an access panel for future maintenance, this is a soft preference; the valve could be left accessible without a dedicated panel.

predecessor: Rough-in underground plumbing and drainage piping
rationale: The sewage ejector pump must be connected to the underground drainage collection pit or basin, which requires the rough-in piping and drainage lines to be installed first.

predecessor: Excavation and formation of pump pit/basin
rationale: The ejector pump is physically located in a pit or basin below grade; the pit must be excavated and formed before the pump can be placed.

predecessor: Concrete slab or floor preparation (pump room area)
rationale: The pump basin is typically set into the concrete floor; the slab or floor base must be prepared to accept the basin and provide a stable mounting surface.

successor: Connection of discharge piping to building sewer main
rationale: The discharge line from the pump must be connected to the building's sewer main or septic system; this connection follows the pump being set in place.

successor: Electrical wiring and control panel connection for pump
rationale: The pump requires electrical power and control wiring (including float switches) which are connected after the pump is physically installed in the basin.
The macerator unit requires a stable, load-bearing foundation to support its weight and operational vibrations. Without a proper base slab, the unit cannot be securely mounted.
The macerator unit must first be placed and secured in its final position before inlet and outlet drainage pipes can be aligned and connected to it.

successor: Electrical Wiring & Power Connection to Macerator
rationale: Electrical connections to the macerator unit require the unit to be fixed in place so that cabling can be terminated safely at the unit's junction box or control panel.
Operational testing (including motor run tests, flow tests, and check of maceration function) can only be performed after the unit is installed and all mechanical and electrical connections are made.

predecessor: Inlet Pipework from Fixtures (e.g., toilets, sinks)
rationale: Inlet drain pipes must be roughed-in up to the unit location before the macerator is positioned, as the unit connects to these upstream pipes at its intake flange.
The ground must be excavated to the required depth and formation level before any underground drainage pipes can be laid.
Foundations must be cast and cured so that underground drainage runs can be coordinated around and through footing locations without causing structural issues.

predecessor: Underground Water Supply Piping (if crossing same trenches)
rationale: Water supply lines laid in shared trenches should be placed before sanitary drainage to maintain proper separation and avoid cross-contamination risks, though this depends on site sequencing.
All underground drain pipes must be fully installed, jointed, tested and inspected before trenches can be backfilled to avoid damage and ensure quality.

successor: Ground Floor Slab / Concrete Floor Works
rationale: Underground drainage connections (soil stacks, waste pipes, floor drains) must be roughed in and stub-ups placed before the ground floor slab is cast, as the slab will cover these connections.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and existing structures before any excavation for drainage trenches can begin, to provide unobstructed access and a safe working area.

Accurate survey and setting out of drain alignments, levels, and invert positions must be completed before trenching commences to ensure trenches are excavated in the correct location and at the correct gradient.

predecessor: Bulk Earthworks and Cut to Formation Level (rough grading)
rationale: Bulk earthworks must bring the site to approximately the correct formation level so that trench depths and drainage gradients can be properly established without excessive re-excavation.
Trenches must be excavated and the bedding layer prepared before drain pipes can be laid, as the pipes are placed directly onto the prepared bedding within the trench.
Backfilling can only take place after the trench has been excavated, bedding laid, and pipes installed; the bedding must be in place to support the pipes before any backfill is placed over them.
Drains must be physically installed and jointed before they can be tested for leaks or integrity.
Trenches must be excavated and drains laid in place before testing can be performed on the installed drainage system.
Testing must be completed and passed before trenches are backfilled, as access to drains is needed for inspection and repair of any leaks.
Testing should confirm drain integrity before connecting to the main system to avoid contaminating or pressurizing the main line with leaks.
Drains must be installed before they can be surveyed with CCTV equipment
Pipes must be laid and in place before a CCTV survey can inspect their internal condition
Access manholes must be built to allow CCTV camera entry into the drainage system
The drain survey must confirm the drainage system is clear and defect-free before it can be officially commissioned
Trenches should only be backfilled after the CCTV survey confirms there are no defects or blockages requiring rectification
CCTV survey identifies blockages, damage, and locations, guiding the rodding/jetting process for effective cleaning.

predecessor: Excavation / Trenching (to access drain access points)
rationale: Drain access points (cleanouts, manholes) must be exposed to allow insertion of rodding/jetting equipment into the drain line.
After cleaning, a follow-up CCTV survey verifies that blockages have been fully cleared and the drain is intact and operational.
Clearing the drain of debris and obstructions is necessary before any repair or relining work can be performed on the clean pipe interior.
Drain cleaning and verification must be completed before closing up excavations and restoring the surface to ensure no rework is needed.
Drains must be installed and properly positioned before backfilling can commence, as backfilling covers and embeds the drain pipes/structures.
Drains must be inspected and tested (e.g., for leaks, alignment, and gradient) before backfilling, as defects cannot be corrected once covered.
Backfilling and compaction of drain trenches must be completed to subgrade level before final surface restoration or paving can proceed.
After backfilling and compaction, final grading and landscaping can be performed over the area, though this is a soft preference as minor grading may occur concurrently.

successor: Utility Line Installation (if crossing drain trench)
rationale: Any utility lines that cross the drain trench must be installed after backfill compaction to avoid disturbing the compacted drain bedding and pipe.

successor: Pipe Sleeve and Fire Stopping Installation
rationale: Pipe sleeves are installed around pipes where they pass through walls, floors, or ceilings; therefore pipes must be in place first so the sleeve can fit around them properly.

successor: Pipe Sleeve and Fire Stopping Installation
rationale: All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-ins must be completed before fire stopping is applied, as fire stopping seals penetrations created by these services.

predecessor: Pipe Sleeve and Fire Stopping Installation
rationale: Fire stopping must be installed and inspected before enclosing walls and ceilings with drywall or plaster, as the firestop sealant needs to be accessible for inspection and cannot be buried behind finished surfaces.

predecessor: Pipe Sleeve and Fire Stopping Installation
successor: Fire Inspection and Code Compliance Sign-off
rationale: Fire stopping installations must be completed and inspected prior to obtaining fire code compliance sign-off, as they are a critical fire safety element in building construction.

successor: Pipe Sleeve and Fire Stopping Installation
rationale: The structural framing defining the wall, floor, and ceiling assemblies must be in place before pipe sleeves can be installed through those assemblies and fire stopping applied.
The water supply lines and drain line must be roughed into the location before the water heater can be connected.
Electrical supply wiring and disconnect must be run to the water heater location before the unit can be wired and energized.

successor: Connect water supply lines to water heater
rationale: The water heater must be set in place before the final water supply and drain connections can be made.

successor: Connect electrical supply to water heater
rationale: The unit must be physically installed before final electrical connections and wiring terminations can be completed.

successor: Pressure testing and commissioning of hot water system
rationale: The water heater must be fully installed and connected before the system can be pressurized, tested for leaks, and commissioned for operation.
Electrical power supply must be available at the installation location before the water heater can be connected and energized.

predecessor: Rough-in plumbing (hot and cold water lines)
rationale: Water supply lines must be installed and terminated at the unit location before the water heater can be physically connected to the plumbing system.
Gas supply line must be stubbed out at the heater location before the unit can be connected for gas-fired models.

successor: Final electrical connection and circuit breaker labeling
rationale: The unit must be mounted and in place before the final electrical connections (hardwiring) can be completed and the circuit breaker labeled.

successor: Final plumbing connections and leak testing
rationale: The water heater must be physically installed before final plumbing connections can be made to the unit and the system pressure-tested for leaks.

Heat pump water heaters require a dedicated electrical circuit (typically 240V) for operation. The electrical rough-in, including wiring, conduit, and breaker installation, must be completed before the water heater can be connected and powered.

predecessor: Plumbing Rough-In (Hot and Cold Water Lines)
rationale: The water heater requires both hot and cold water supply lines and drain connections. Plumbing rough-in must be completed to provide the necessary connections for the unit's installation.

predecessor: Floor Preparation / Concrete Pad or Stand Installation
rationale: The water heater must be placed on a level, stable surface capable of supporting its weight and managing condensation drainage. A concrete pad or stand must be installed prior to setting the unit.

Final plumbing connections, including attaching supply lines, pressure relief valve piping, and drain pan connections, are made directly to the installed water heater unit and cannot be completed before the unit is in place.
The final electrical connection (hardwiring or plug-in) and circuit testing for the water heater can only be performed after the unit is physically installed and positioned.
Water supply and return pipes must be roughed-in and in place before the boiler can be connected and installed.
If the boiler is gas-fired, the gas supply line must be run to the boiler location before the boiler can be connected.
A level, load-bearing surface or concrete pad must be prepared before the boiler can be set in place to ensure stable operation and proper drainage.
The boiler must be fully installed before the domestic hot water circulation system can be pressure-tested and commissioned.
While insulation can be done in parallel, it is preferable to insulate hot water pipes after the boiler is installed to ensure all connections are covered and accessible for inspection.

predecessor: Pipe Installation to PRV Connection Points
rationale: The inlet and outlet piping must be installed and terminated at the PRV flange locations before the PRV can be physically mounted and connected.

predecessor: Support structure / bracket fabrication and installation
rationale: The PRV must be securely supported by a dedicated bracket or support structure that is installed prior to lifting and mounting the valve into position.

predecessor: Hydrostatic/pneumatic pressure testing of connected piping (if applicable before valve installation)
rationale: Pressure testing of the pipe system is typically performed before installing the PRV to avoid damaging the sensitive valve internals with test pressures and to ensure the PRV is not used as a test plug.
After the valve is physically installed, it must be calibrated and its set-point verified in-situ (or bench-tested prior) to confirm it opens at the correct pressure.
The complete system including the PRV must undergo a final functional test under operating pressure to verify the PRV opens, relieves, and reseats correctly.

predecessor: Hot and Cold Water Pipe Rough-In
rationale: The TMV requires both hot and cold water supply pipes to be installed and in place before the valve itself can be connected and mounted.
The TMV must be connected to the hot water supply from the water heater; the water heater must be installed first to provide the hot water source.
After the TMV is installed, the outgoing mixed-water pipe can be connected to its outlet to deliver tempered water to fixtures.

successor: Pressure Testing of Hot Water System
rationale: The TMV must be in place and connected before the system can be pressure-tested to verify leak-free operation of the hot water distribution system.
While fixtures can be installed before the TMV is finalized, it is preferable to install the TMV first to ensure tempered water is available for fixture commissioning and to avoid rework.
The circulation pump must be mounted on a stable, level foundation or base slab to ensure proper alignment and support.
The suction and discharge piping must be in place to connect to the circulation pump flanges.
The pump must be physically installed before electrical supply cables can be terminated at the pump motor terminals.
The pump must be in position and connected to pipework before the entire system can be pressure-tested and commissioned.
Insulation is typically applied after pump installation to ensure all joints and connections are accessible for inspection and tightening.
The hot water source (e.g., boiler, heat pump, or water heater) must be installed and operational before distribution pipework can be connected to it.
The building structure, walls, floors, and ceilings must be in place to support, route, and enclose the hot water distribution pipework.
Insulation must be applied after the pipework is installed in its final position to ensure complete coverage and thermal performance.

successor: Hot Water Outlet Fixture Installation (taps, showers)
rationale: Outlet fixtures must be connected to the distribution pipework; the pipework must be in place before final connection of fixtures.

successor: Pressure Testing & Commissioning of Hot Water System
rationale: The pipework must be fully installed before pressure testing and commissioning can be performed to verify integrity and performance.

predecessor: Plumbing Rough-In (Hot and Cold Water Lines)
rationale: Water supply lines must be run to the installation location before the water softener can be connected to the plumbing system.
Most water softeners require a nearby electrical outlet for the control valve and timer; power must be available before installation and commissioning.
Soft preference: it is easier to install the unit after flooring is in place to ensure a level surface and avoid damaging the floor later, but the unit can be set on a bare slab if needed.
Conditioned (softened) water should be supplied to the water heater to prevent scale buildup; therefore the softener should be operational before the water heater is connected to the main supply.

successor: Final plumbing connection and fixture trim-out
rationale: Soft preference: softened water lines to fixtures can be commissioned after the softener is installed, but fixtures can also be trimmed out earlier if bypass lines are used during construction.
The anode rod must be manufactured and fabricated before it can be installed into the electrolytic cell or smelting pot.
After the anode rod is installed, the entire anode assembly (including the rod) must be baked to carbonize and strengthen the anode block.
The baked anode must be rodded (connecting the rod to the carbon block) after baking is complete. The rodding process attaches the rod to the carbon block.
After rodding, the complete anode assembly must be inspected for quality and integrity before being used in the smelting process.
The inspected anode rod assembly must pass quality checks before it can be positioned and lowered into the electrolytic smelting pot.
The hot water storage tank requires a level, load-bearing foundation to support its weight. Without proper foundation preparation, the tank cannot be safely installed.
Cold water supply lines must be run to the tank location before the tank can be connected. The tank cannot be placed without incoming water supply piping being in place.

successor: Hot Water Pipe Connection from Tank to Distribution
rationale: The hot water outlet piping from the tank to the building distribution system can only be connected after the tank is securely installed in its final position.

successor: Pressure Relief Valve and Safety System Installation
rationale: Pressure relief valves and safety devices are connected directly to the tank ports and must be installed after the tank is in place to ensure proper orientation and secure attachment.
While insulation can be applied after installation, it is a soft preference as the tank can function temporarily without full insulation, though energy efficiency demands it be done promptly.
The domestic water supply and return piping must be roughed in to the location before the indirect water heater can be connected and installed.

predecessor: Install Boiler or Primary Heat Source
rationale: The indirect water heater relies on a boiler or primary heat source to supply hot water/steam to the coil; the heat source must be in place before the coil can be connected and tested.
The support structure (bracket, stand, or pad) must be installed to provide a stable base before setting the heavy water heater tank.
The indirect water heater must be set in place before the hydronic piping connecting it to the boiler can be completed and terminated at the heater.
Insulation of hot water piping is typically done after the heater and its connections are installed, but it is a best practice for energy efficiency rather than a strict physical requirement.
The check valve must be installed within the hot water piping system, so the piping infrastructure must be in place first.

successor: Pressure Testing of Hot Water System
rationale: All components including check valves need to be installed before pressure testing can be performed to verify system integrity.

successor: System commissioning / Hot water system startup
rationale: The check valve must be installed and properly seated before the system is commissioned and hot water flow is initiated to prevent backflow.
The water supply and drain piping must be roughed in and stubbed out at the location before the water heater can be connected.
Electrical wiring and an appropriate breaker or dedicated circuit must be run to the water heater location before it can be hardwired or plugged in.
The point-of-use water heater is typically mounted on a wall; the wall framing and sheathing must be in place to provide structural support for mounting.

Although it is easier to install the heater before finishing walls to allow access for mounting and connections, it is considered a soft preference because finishing could be completed first with careful planning for access panels.
The water heater must be installed and connected to supply lines before final fixture trim-out (sinks, faucets) can be completed, as the heater provides hot water to those fixtures.
Flow meters are installed inline on pipes; the pipe network must be in place before the meter can be physically fitted.
After physical installation, the flow meter must be calibrated and tested to ensure accurate readings before being put into service.
The flow meter must be fully installed and operational before the overall system can be commissioned and turned over for use.
If the pipe is to be insulated, it is easier to install the flow meter before insulating around it, though insulation could be done after with some rework.
The flow meter must be installed before the pipe system can be pressure-tested as a complete assembly to check for leaks.
The gate/ball isolation valve must be installed into the piping system after the pipe sections are already in place and supported, as the valve connects between pipe flanges or ends.
Flange faces must be clean, aligned, and gaskets positioned before installing a flanged gate or ball valve to ensure proper sealing and avoid stress on the valve body.
The valve must be installed and fully closed (or appropriately positioned) before pressure testing the isolated pipe section to verify that the valve holds pressure and the system is leak-tight.

successor: Valve Actuator Mounting and Calibration (if automated)
rationale: If the gate/ball valve is equipped with an actuator (electric, pneumatic, or hydraulic), the actuator can only be mounted and calibrated after the valve body is securely installed in the pipeline.

Insulation or coating around the valve area is typically applied after the valve is installed and tested, but this is a soft preference as the valve could be insulated later without affecting construction sequence.

predecessor: Rough-in Plumbing for Hot Water Lines
rationale: Hot water supply lines must be roughed in to the zone location before the zone controller can be connected and operate.
Power supply wiring and control voltage cabling must be run to the controller location before the controller can be wired and energized.
The zone controller must be physically installed and wired before the overall hot water system can be commissioned, tested, and balanced for proper operation.
Zone controller must be mounted and powered before field devices such as thermostats, temperature sensors, and zone valves can be electrically connected to it.
While not physically required, it is preferable to install and test the zone controller before enclosing walls or applying insulation to avoid future access issues.
Ductwork must be in place to distribute conditioned air before a thermostat can effectively control the HVAC system.
The HVAC heating and cooling equipment must be installed and connected so the thermostat can control it.
Power supply and control wiring (low-voltage thermostat cables) must be run to the thermostat location before the thermostat can be mounted and connected.
The thermostat must be installed and wired to enable system startup, calibration, and functional testing of the HVAC system.

While the thermostat can be installed before final wall finishes, it is often preferred to complete painting and wall finishing first to avoid getting paint or debris on the device, though this is a soft sequencing preference.
The water heater must be in place to connect the flue/exhaust vent to its exhaust outlet.

successor: Vent Piping Connection to Roof/Exterior Wall
rationale: The flue/exhaust vent must be installed before connecting it to the exterior termination cap or roof penetration.
Firestop sealing around the vent penetration must be applied after the vent pipe is in place.
The exhaust vent must be fully installed and connected before the water heater can be safely operated and tested.
The water heater must be in place before the gas supply line can be connected to it.
After installing the gas supply line, pressure testing is required to check for leaks before the line is put into service.
The gas supply line must be installed before it can be connected to the water heater's gas valve.
Inspection of the gas connection must occur after the supply line is installed to verify compliance with codes.
Applying insulation or protective coating to the gas line is typically done after installation but is a best practice rather than a strict physical requirement.
The water heater unit must be physically installed and in position before electrical wiring can be connected to it.
Electrical wiring must be completed and connected to the water heater before the unit can be tested and commissioned for operation.
The main electrical panel must be installed and energized to provide the source of power for the water heater circuit.
General rough-in electrical cabling and conduit must be run to the water heater location before final connections and wiring can be made.
Electrical wiring and connections for the water heater must be completed before enclosing walls and ceilings with drywall or finishes to avoid rework.
Drain lines must be roughed-in to the location before the drain pan and floor drain can be positioned and connected to the drainage system.
The floor surface (concrete slab or subfloor) must be prepared and poured/installed to provide a stable base for setting the floor drain and drain pan.

Waterproofing membranes (e.g., around the drain pan or in wet areas) are typically applied after the drain pan and floor drain are in place to seal around the penetrations and ensure a watertight assembly.
The finished floor material (tile, epoxy, or topping) is installed after the drain pan and floor drain are set to create a continuous surface sloped toward the drain.
Hot water system installation requires connection to the building's plumbing system; rough-in pipes must be in place before the water heater can be connected.
Gas water heaters require a dedicated gas supply line to be run and terminated before the heater can be connected for fuel supply.
Electric water heaters require dedicated electrical wiring, conduit, and a circuit breaker to be installed before the unit can be wired and energized.
Hot and cold water connections to the water heater must be completed before final plumbing fixtures (sinks, showers) can be connected and the entire system pressure-tested.
Once the water heater is in place, it is preferable to complete wall finishing to avoid damage to finished surfaces during heater installation, though it is not physically required.
Pressure testing must be conducted after pipework is fully installed to verify the integrity of the installed pipework system.
Insulation should only be applied after pressure testing confirms no leaks, as insulation would conceal leaks and make repairs difficult.
System flushing and disinfection should follow pressure testing to ensure the pipework is pressure-tight before introducing cleaning or treatment chemicals.
Final connections to equipment should be made after pressure testing to avoid damaging equipment during the test and to ensure the pipework itself is sound before interconnection.
All pipe fabrication activities such as cutting, bending, and jointing must be completed before pressure testing to ensure the entire assembled system can be tested as a whole.
Plumbing rough-in must be completed to provide water supply and drain connections for the hot water system before it can be commissioned.
Electrical rough-in must be completed to provide power supply connections for the hot water system (e.g., for electric heaters or controls) before commissioning can occur.
The hot water system must be physically installed (unit set in place, connected to pipes and power) before it can be commissioned and tested.
Hot water system commissioning must be completed before final integrated building services testing, as the hot water system is a component of the overall building services.
The hot water system must be fully commissioned and verified as operational before the building can be handed over to the client or achieve practical completion.

predecessor: Building Services Design (including water system design)
rationale: The water system design must be established before a Legionella risk assessment can be performed, as the assessment evaluates the specific design features (pipework layout, dead legs, temperature control points, etc.) that influence Legionella growth risk.

The physical water system must be installed and in place before a comprehensive Legionella risk assessment and control plan can be implemented, as the assessment requires inspection and testing of the actual installed system.
The risk assessment must identify control measures and high-risk areas before targeted flushing and disinfection protocols can be developed and executed effectively.
Risk assessment determines the sampling points, frequency, and testing parameters needed to verify control measures, so sampling and testing must follow the assessment.

The Legionella risk assessment and implemented control measures must be completed and documented before the building can be handed over, as compliance with health and safety regulations regarding water safety is a prerequisite for occupancy.
The water heater must be installed and in place before any servicing or maintenance can be performed on it.
Plumbing rough-in work including water supply and drain lines must be completed before the water heater can be serviced or maintained, as these systems connect to the unit.
Electrical connections and wiring for the water heater must be roughed in before servicing, as power is required for operation and testing during maintenance.
After servicing and maintenance is completed, the system must be inspected and tested to verify proper operation and compliance with codes.
The water heater must be serviced and confirmed operational before the building can be occupied to ensure hot water supply is available and safe.
The hot water system must be isolated from power, gas, and water supplies before any decommissioning work can safely begin, to prevent electric shock, gas leaks, or flooding.
The system must be drained of all water to avoid spillage and to reduce weight before removal and decommissioning activities commence.
The decommissioning process (including isolation, draining, and disconnection) must be completed before the physical removal of the hot water system unit can take place.

successor: Disposal of Hot Water System Components
rationale: Only after the system has been fully decommissioned can its components be safely dismantled and transported for disposal or recycling.
The old hot water system must be fully decommissioned and removed before a new replacement system can be installed in its place, to avoid interference and ensure a clean installation area.
The gas meter must be connected to the mains gas supply, which requires the gas service line to be run to the building.
Gas piping from the meter to appliances must be installed before the meter is set, as the meter is the point of connection between the supply and the building's piping system.
The gas meter is typically housed in a meter box or enclosure which must be installed beforehand to provide a secure mounting location.
Appliances such as boilers, water heaters, and stoves can only be connected to the gas piping after the meter is installed to regulate the supply.
Pressure testing of the gas system and purging of air from the lines must occur after the meter is installed to ensure the system is safe and leak-free before appliances are commissioned.
The gas pressure regulator must be connected to the gas main supply line, which must already be installed and pressure-tested to provide a safe and stable gas supply source.
A manual shut-off valve is typically required upstream of the gas pressure regulator to allow safe isolation for regulator maintenance, installation, or emergency shutdown.
The gas pressure regulator must be installed and set to the correct outlet pressure before downstream gas piping to appliances is connected, to prevent over-pressurization and ensure safe operation.

successor: Gas Line Pressure Testing and Leak Check
rationale: After the regulator is installed, the entire gas system including the regulator must be pressure-tested and checked for leaks to confirm integrity before appliances are connected or gas is turned on.
Only after the gas pressure regulator is installed and the gas supply pressure is regulated properly can appliances be connected, tested, and commissioned for safe operation.
The gas supply piping must be in place to provide a connection point for the shutoff valve.
The shutoff valve must be installed before the gas system can be pressurized and tested for leaks.
The shutoff valve serves as the isolation point; appliances are connected downstream of the installed valve.
Inspection of the rough gas piping must be completed before the valve is installed to ensure code compliance and avoid rework.
The shutoff valve must be in place and operational before the entire gas system can be commissioned and turned on.
Gas distribution piping is typically installed after underground utilities such as water, sewer, and electrical conduits are placed to avoid conflicts and rework in the trench.
Gas piping entering a building through the foundation or slab requires the foundation to be complete so that wall or slab penetrations can be properly coordinated and sealed.
Gas piping runs within walls must be installed and inspected before walls are closed up with drywall or finishing materials to allow access for inspection and prevent damage.
Gas appliances such as furnaces, water heaters, and stoves require the gas distribution piping to be in place and pressure-tested to supply fuel before they can be connected and installed.
After gas piping is installed, it must undergo pressure testing and inspection by authorities before being concealed or connected to appliances, to ensure leak-free operation and code compliance.
Building foundations and substructure must be completed to provide the structural support and embedment for the gas riser pipe to be installed.
The ground floor slab must be cast and cured to allow the gas riser pipe to rise from below ground through the slab.
The gas riser pipe must be in place to connect to the gas meter box; the meter box is installed onto or adjacent to the riser pipe.
Internal gas distribution piping branches off from the riser pipe, so the riser must be installed first to serve as the supply source.
Pressure testing of the gas system can only commence after the riser pipe is fully installed and connected, to verify integrity before service.
The rigid gas piping must be installed and terminated at the appliance location before the flexible connector can be attached to bridge the gap.
The flexible connector must be installed as part of the gas supply system before the entire gas line can be pressure tested for leaks.
The flex connector serves as the final link between the gas supply piping and the appliance, so it must be installed before the appliance can be connected.
It is preferable to finish walls and ceilings before installing the flex connector to avoid damage to finishes, but it is not a physical necessity as the connector can be installed before finishing.
The flex connector must be in place as part of the gas supply circuit before the appliance can be turned on and its operation verified.
Electrical rough-in wiring must be completed to provide power and communication cabling to the sensor location before the sensor unit can be physically installed and connected.
Gas piping must be installed first so the sensor can be positioned and calibrated relative to the actual gas lines and potential leak points.
The sensor must be physically installed and wired before it can be integrated with the building's control/BMS system and undergo commissioning tests.

successor: Gas leak detection system functional testing
rationale: The sensor must be installed and connected before functional testing of the gas detection system can be performed to verify proper operation and alarm functionality.

successor: Ceiling or wall finishing (if sensor is flush-mounted)
rationale: If the sensor is flush-mounted in a ceiling or wall, the sensor installation must occur before the final finishing (drywall, paneling) to allow access for mounting and wiring.
The seismic gas shutoff valve must be installed on the main gas supply line; the gas line must be in place to provide a mounting point and connection for the device.
The shutoff device must be installed upstream of the gas meter so that it can shut off gas flow before it reaches the meter; the meter is typically connected downstream of the shutoff valve.
After the seismic shutoff valve is in place, gas piping can be safely branched off to serve individual appliances, ensuring the shutoff device can protect all downstream branches.
The gas line and shutoff device are installed after the foundation is poured and cured, as the gas line is typically run under or into the slab or along the foundation wall.

While permits are a regulatory requirement, the physical installation of the shutoff device can sometimes begin before all permits are finalized if approved by the authority having jurisdiction; however, it is strongly preferred to have permits in hand to avoid rework.
Gas piping must be in place before the relief valve can be mounted and connected to the pipeline.
The relief valve must be installed before the system can be pressurized and tested for leaks and proper relief operation.

successor: Commissioning and Calibration of Relief Valve
rationale: The valve must be physically installed before it can be calibrated and commissioned to ensure it opens at the correct set pressure.
Structural supports or mounting brackets must be in place to securely hold the weight of the relief valve before it is mounted.
While insulation can be applied after valve installation, it is a soft preference because in some sequences the valve area may be left uninsulated for access during testing.
The ground must be excavated and prepared before any underground gas service lines can be laid or installed.
Foundations and slab must be completed to allow gas pipe entry points and penetrations through the foundation to be coordinated and installed.
The external gas service line from the main must be connected to the building before internal gas piping can be run and connected to the service entry point.
The gas service line must be installed up to the meter location before the gas meter can be physically connected and set.
Gas supply must be available at the building before any gas appliances (e.g., furnace, water heater, stove) can be connected and tested for operation.
Gas lines that run beneath the slab must be installed and inspected before any above-slab rough-in work can begin, as the slab is poured over these lines.
The concrete slab must be fully cured before interior rough-in work within the building can commence, as the slab provides the base substrate.
All rough-in gas piping must be installed before a pressure test can be conducted to check for leaks in the system.
Gas pipework must be roughed in and inspected before walls and ceilings are closed up with drywall, to ensure compliance and avoid costly rework.
Gas piping must be run to appliance locations before the appliances themselves can be connected and installed.
Gas piping must be fully installed before pressure testing can be performed, as the test pressurizes the installed piping network to check for leaks.
If pressure testing identifies leaks or failures, those must be repaired immediately before the system can be certified.
Pressure testing must be successfully completed and passed before the gas system can be officially certified and commissioned for use.

The gas pipework must be physically installed and connected before any commissioning or purging of the gas system can take place, as there is no system to test or purge without the installed pipework.

All gas appliances (boilers, heaters, hobs, etc.) must be installed and connected to the gas supply before the system can be commissioned and purged, as commissioning involves testing the system with all terminal devices in place.

The gas system must successfully pass a pressure/soundness test to verify there are no leaks before purging and commissioning can proceed, as introducing gas into an untested system poses a major safety risk.

After the gas system has been purged of air/contaminants and commissioned, each appliance can be finally connected to the live gas supply and individually tested for correct operation and combustion performance.

The internal gas system must be fully purged, commissioned, and certified as safe before the utility company can register the installation, seal the meter, and activate the permanent gas supply connection.
Gas pipework must be installed, routed, and pressure-tested for leaks before any appliance can be physically connected to the gas supply.
The gas meter must be installed and commissioned to provide a controlled gas supply from the network to the premises before appliances can be connected and tested.

predecessor: Plumbing Rough-In for Appliance Supply & Drainage
rationale: Water supply lines and drainage pipework serving the appliance (e.g., for boilers, water heaters, cookers) must be roughed in before the appliance is physically set and connected.

After the appliance is connected and initial testing (e.g., gas rate, burner pressure, flue integrity) is performed, formal commissioning and certification activities must follow to verify safe operation and issue compliance documents.

Gas appliance connection and testing is one of the final mechanical works; handover inspections typically check that all gas appliances are installed and operational, but some minor finishes could proceed in parallel.
The gas piping must be fully installed (rough-in) before inspection can occur, as the inspector needs to verify the complete piping network for leaks and compliance.
Gas appliances need to be connected to the gas piping so the inspector can verify proper connections, venting, and safe operation of all gas-fired equipment.

Inspection and certification must be completed before final pressure testing and purging to ensure the system meets code requirements; the certificate is often needed before the utility company will turn on gas service.
Walls should remain open during inspection so the inspector can see all gas piping runs, joints, and connections; once certified, walls can be closed up.
After the gas system is inspected and certified, final commissioning (lighting pilot lights, adjusting burners, testing operation) can proceed safely with a certified system.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and graded before trenching can begin to provide a safe, stable worksurface and to ensure proper alignment and depth of the trench.
All existing underground utilities must be located and marked to avoid striking them during trenching, which is a critical safety requirement.
Regulatory permits for excavation must be secured before any trenching work can legally commence.
The trench must be excavated before gas pipes can be placed, laid, and joined within the trench.
After the gas pipe is installed and tested, the trench must be backfilled and compacted, and the surface restored, which can only happen after trenching and pipe placement are complete.
The gas system must be fully installed before a periodic safety check can be performed, as the check verifies the integrity and safety of an existing installation.
All gas appliances must be installed before the periodic safety check can inspect them for proper operation, leaks, and compliance with safety standards.
The gas piping system must be pressure-tested and verified leak-tight before a periodic safety check can certify the system is safe for continued use.
After a periodic gas safety check, the system may need re-commissioning or re-certification to confirm it remains safe for operation, especially if issues were found and corrected.
The gas safety certificate or record of inspection is issued after the periodic safety check is completed, documenting the results of the inspection.
The air compressor unit requires a stable, level concrete foundation to support its weight and maintain alignment during operation.
Electrical power supply lines and cooling water piping must be pre-positioned at the installation site before the compressor unit can be connected and commissioned.
The compressor must be physically set in place before the discharge and intake air piping can be connected to its ports.
Power and control cables can only be terminated at the compressor terminals after the unit is securely positioned.
All installation work including piping, electrical, and controls must be completed before the unit can be started and tested for operational readiness.
A stable foundation or base must be prepared to support the weight and operational loads of the receiver tank/air reservoir.
The receiver tank must be in place before compressed air piping can be connected to it.
Pressure relief valves are typically mounted on or adjacent to the receiver tank and require the tank to be installed first.
The entire compressed air system, including the receiver tank, must be fully installed before pressure testing can be performed to verify integrity.
Drain valves and condensate traps are typically attached to the bottom of the receiver tank and require the tank to be installed first.
The pressure relief valve must be connected to an existing piping system to properly relieve pressure; piping provides the physical conduit for flow.
The pressure relief valve protects the pressure vessel/equipment, so the vessel must be in place before the relief valve can be installed on it.
The pressure relief valve must be installed before the system can be pressure-tested to verify it will open at the correct set pressure.
Insulation can be applied after the valve is installed, but this is a soft preference as insulation could be done around the valve area later if needed.
Safety inspectors must verify the pressure relief valve is correctly installed and set before the system can be certified for operation.
A stable foundation must be prepared before the air dryer unit can be placed, as the unit needs a level, load-bearing surface to operate safely and without vibration issues.
The main compressed air supply piping must be run to the dryer location before the air dryer can be connected to the compressed air system.
Power supply conduits and wiring must be brought to the dryer location prior to setting the unit so that final electrical connections can be made.
The air dryer must be physically installed, leveled, and secured before it can be started up, tested, and commissioned for operation.

successor: Final piping connections to air dryer
rationale: The unit must be in its final position before the inlet and outlet piping can be precisely aligned and permanently connected to the dryer ports.
The coalescing filter/oil-water separator requires a stable, level foundation or concrete slab to be placed upon. The foundation must be cured and ready before the separator unit can be set in place.

Inlet and outlet drainage piping and grading for oil-water separation flow must be prepared and laid before the separator unit is installed, as the unit connects into these underground piping networks.

Electrical supply rough-in (conduit, wiring to the unit's location) is typically completed before setting the separator to avoid rework, though the unit can be installed and electrical connections made later if needed.
Once the separator unit is set in place, the inlet and outlet pipes must be connected and sealed to ensure proper flow and prevent leaks. This cannot happen until the unit is physically installed.

After the separator is installed and all pipe connections are made, the entire system must be pressure-tested and commissioned to verify proper operation and leak-tightness before being placed into service.

successor: Pressure Regulator / Pressure Reducing Valve Installation
rationale: Piping and sleeves must be installed in walls, floors, and ceilings before the valve can be mounted and connected to the piping system.

predecessor: Pressure Regulator / Pressure Reducing Valve Installation
rationale: The valve must be installed and connected before the entire piping system can be pressure tested to verify integrity and leak-free operation.

predecessor: Pressure Regulator / Pressure Reducing Valve Installation
rationale: Insulation application is typically performed after valve installation to ensure full coverage around the valve and adjacent piping, though in some cases insulation can be partially completed beforehand.

predecessor: Pressure Regulator / Pressure Reducing Valve Installation
rationale: The valve must be in place so that the system can be flushed, filled, and commissioned with the pressure regulation function active.

successor: Pressure Regulator / Pressure Reducing Valve Installation
rationale: Structural supports, brackets, or valve stands must be in place to securely mount the pressure regulator/reducing valve before installation can proceed.
Trenches and pathways for piping must be excavated before pipes can be laid and connected.
Underground piping runs beneath or through building foundations/slabs, so foundations and slabs must be completed before piping is installed.
Connection points to external main utility lines must be established before internal distribution piping can be extended from those points.
Trenches can only be backfilled after all pipes are laid, joined, and inspected to avoid crushing or damaging the piping.
The piping network must be fully installed before pressure testing and flushing can verify integrity and remove debris.

successor: Compressed Air Outlet / Service Point Installation
rationale: The compressed air piping network must be installed and routed to the location before the outlet/service point can be connected and installed.

successor: Compressed Air Outlet / Service Point Installation
rationale: Walls, columns, or structural supports must be in place to provide a mounting surface for the compressed air outlet/service point.

predecessor: Compressed Air Outlet / Service Point Installation
rationale: The outlet/service point must be installed and sealed before the overall compressed air system can be pressure tested to verify integrity.

predecessor: Compressed Air Outlet / Service Point Installation
rationale: All outlets/service points must be in place before the compressed air system can be fully commissioned, energized, and put into service.
Pipes must be cut, deburred, and prepared to the correct dimensions before an isolation valve can be fitted into the pipeline.
Pipe supports and hangers must be in place to hold the pipe and valve weight before the valve is installed in the line.
The isolation valve must be installed and connected to the pipeline before the section can be pressurized and tested for leaks.
After the valve is placed between flanges, the flange bolts must be tightened to the correct torque to ensure a leak-proof seal.
Insulation around the valve body is typically applied after installation for thermal efficiency, but can sometimes be done beforehand if pre-formed sections are used.
The condensate drain/auto-drain valve must be installed on the compressed air piping system; therefore the piping must be in place first to provide the physical mounting and connection point.
The auto-drain valve typically serves the dryer or downstream system; dryer installation provides the operational context and connection interface for the drain valve.
The drain valve must be installed and properly sealed before the system is pressurized to verify all connections, including the drain, are leak-tight.
After the auto-drain valve is installed, the outlet condensate piping can be connected to route collected condensate to the drain or collection system.

Commissioning should occur after all components, including the drain valve, are in place to verify automatic draining functionality, though some commissioning steps could begin in parallel on other subsystems.
Pressure gauges require piping connections to be in place so they can be mounted and connected to the system.

successor: Pressure test and calibration of monitoring system
rationale: The gauge must be installed before the system can be pressure-tested and calibrated to verify accurate readings.
Pressure monitoring instruments must be in place before system startup to ensure safe and monitored operation.

predecessor: Mount bracket or support structure for gauge
rationale: A secure mounting bracket or support structure is needed to hold the pressure gauge in place before it can be installed.
Insulation and protective coverings can be applied after the gauge is installed, but this is often a soft preference depending on accessibility and maintenance requirements.

The check valve must be installed after the adjacent piping is in place and aligned, as the valve is fitted between pipe flanges or couplings and requires the pipe ends to be positioned correctly for proper connection and support.

Pipe interiors must be inspected and cleared of debris, dirt, or welding slag before valve installation to prevent contamination or damage to the valve internals (disc, seat, hinge), which could cause leakage or malfunction.
Pipe supports and hangers near the valve location must be installed first to provide structural support and prevent excessive stress on the valve body and pipe joints when the valve is fitted.

Once the check valve is installed, the entire pipeline section must be pressure-tested to verify the integrity of all joints, including the valve connections, and to confirm the valve holds under rated pressure without leaks.

After valve installation, the piping system must be flushed to remove any remaining construction debris and then commissioned to ensure the check valve opens and closes correctly under actual flow conditions.
The aftercooler requires a stable, level foundation to support its weight and ensure proper alignment with connected piping systems.
The aftercooler must be installed downstream of the compressor to which it is connected, as it cools the compressed air discharged from the compressor.
Piping to the aftercooler can only be connected after the unit is set in its final position.
Condensate drain lines must be connected after the aftercooler is installed to ensure proper routing and gravity flow.
Cooling water supply and return lines can only be connected once the aftercooler is positioned and secured.
The compressor must be physically installed before its control panel can be wired up and interfaced with the BMS system, as the control panel monitors and controls compressor operations.
Electrical power supply and conduits must be run to the control panel location before the panel can be connected and energized for BMS interface commissioning.
The building management system backbone and control wiring infrastructure must be in place before the compressor control panel can be integrated into the BMS network.
The control panel must be installed, wired, and connected to the BMS before the compressor system can be commissioned and functionally tested under BMS control.
The BMS interface integration and calibration of control parameters can only be performed after the compressor control panel is installed and powered up.
A stable concrete foundation is required to support the weight of compressors, dryers, and storage tanks. The equipment cannot be properly anchored or aligned without a finished slab.
Compressed air equipment must be protected from weather during installation. The building must be enclosed to prevent rain, dust, and debris from contaminating the system components.

predecessor: Electrical Rough-In and Main Power Supply
rationale: Compressed air compressors and dryers require electrical power for operation and controls. Main electrical supply must be available to test and commission the system.

The main compressed air equipment (compressors, dryers, receivers) must be installed and connected before the distribution piping network can be tied into the system for conveying air to end-use points.
All compressed air components must be physically installed before the system can be pressurized, leak-tested, and commissioned for operational readiness.
Pipes must be fully installed and welded before pressure testing can be performed, as the test requires a complete, sealed piping system to hold pressure.
Test equipment, pumps, gauges, and temporary connections must be set up and calibrated before the actual pressure test can be conducted.
All welds and joints must be visually inspected and approved prior to pressure testing to ensure they are sound enough to withstand the test pressure.
After pressure testing, the system must be flushed and cleaned to remove any debris, test water, or contaminants introduced during the testing process.

successor: Final Connection & Tie-In to Existing System
rationale: Only after the new piping system has passed pressure testing can it be safely tied into existing live systems or placed into service.
The compressor must be physically removed from its mounting/location before any servicing or overhaul work can be performed on it.
The compressor must be disassembled into its component parts before the servicing and overhaul activities (cleaning, inspection, parts replacement, reassembly) can begin.
Servicing and overhaul must be completed before the compressor can be reassembled with refurbished or new parts.
After overhaul and reassembly, the compressor must be tested to verify proper operation before being placed back into service.
The overhauled compressor must be fully serviced and ready before it can be reinstalled in its original location and reconnected to the system.
The compressed air system must be physically installed and operational before an energy audit can be conducted to measure its performance and identify inefficiencies.
Commissioning ensures the system is functioning as designed, providing a baseline for the energy audit to assess energy performance.
The audit results are necessary to identify specific energy-saving opportunities such as fixing leaks, reducing pressure, or upgrading components.
Optimization measures (e.g., leak repairs, pressure reduction, variable speed drives) must be informed by the audit findings to be effective.
Post-implementation verification of energy savings requires the baseline audit data for comparison to measure actual savings achieved.
Pipe supports and hangers must be anchored to structural steel or concrete surfaces; these substrates must be in place before any support components can be attached or installed.
Pipes and spools rest on installed supports and hangers; the supports must be fixed in position to receive the piping.
Once supports are installed, pipes can be placed on them and aligned; alignment cannot proceed without the supports in place.
Pipes must be supported and aligned on hangers before welding can be performed to ensure correct positioning and weld quality.

Hydrostatic testing is typically performed after all piping is installed and supported, but the testing itself requires supports to hold the pipe; the ordering is a logical preference based on the construction sequence.
The card reader must be mounted on a prepared surface (e.g., wall, door frame, or pedestal); the mounting surface must exist and be ready before the reader can be physically attached.

predecessor: Run conduit and cabling to reader location
rationale: Power and communication cables (e.g., RS-485, Wiegand, Ethernet) must be pulled to the reader location before the reader can be connected and terminated.
Once the reader is physically mounted, its wiring can be connected to the access control panel and power supply.
The reader must be physically wired and powered on before it can be enrolled, addressed, and configured in the access control software/host system.
The reader must be configured in the system before credential scanning, LED response, and door unlock functions can be verified.

The biometric scanner must be mounted on a stable structural surface such as walls, door frames, or entry pylons; the building's structural framework and foundation must be complete to provide the physical support needed for secure mounting.

Biometric scanners require electrical power and data cabling (e.g., PoE or dedicated power supply). The electrical rough-in, conduit, and low-voltage cabling must be run to the scanner location before the scanner unit can be physically installed and connected.

Biometric scanners are network-connected devices that communicate with access control servers. The local network infrastructure (switches, routers, cabling to the access control panel) must be in place before the scanner can be integrated and tested.

successor: Access Control System Configuration and Calibration
rationale: Once the biometric scanner hardware is physically installed and connected, the access control software must be configured to recognize the scanner, enroll users, set permissions, and calibrate the biometric reader (e.g., fingerprint or iris template enrollment) before the system can become operational.

The biometric scanner must be installed and connected before comprehensive end-to-end testing (verifying read accuracy, response time, integration with door locks/alarms, and failover behavior) can be performed to commission the system for use.

predecessor: Rough-in electrical wiring to door frame
rationale: Power must be available at the door frame location before the electric door strike can be connected and powered.
The electric door strike is mounted into/onto the door frame; the door assembly must be in place first.

successor: Connect and test electric door strike wiring
rationale: The strike must be physically installed before final wiring connections and functional testing can be performed.
Software configuration of the access control panel can be done in parallel but logically the strike must be installed and wired before the system can verify proper signaling.

successor: Final Door Hardware Adjustment and Testing
rationale: Latch alignment and door operation must be checked with the electric strike installed to ensure proper engagement and release.
The electromagnetic lock is typically mounted on the door frame and must have the frame in place for proper alignment and anchoring.
Power wiring and conduit must be run to the lock location before the lock itself can be connected and mounted.
Data and control cables for the access control system must be pulled to the door location before terminating at the maglock.
Trim pieces, cover plates, and finishing hardware are installed after the maglock body is mounted and secured.

successor: Access Control System Commissioning and Testing
rationale: The maglock must be physically installed before the access control system can be powered on, tested for proper locking/unlocking function, and integrated with controllers.
The door frame must be built to accommodate the deadbolt strike plate and ensure proper alignment of the locking mechanism.
The door must be cut to size and have the necessary bore holes (for the deadbolt cylinder/latch and mounting screws) prepared before the deadbolt can be installed.
Electronic deadbolts require power (usually battery backup or low-voltage wiring); if hardwired, the electrical rough-in must be completed first to supply power to the lock location.
The deadbolt must be installed in the door slab before the door is hung to allow easy access for drilling, mounting, and wiring without obstruction from the frame.
After the deadbolt is physically installed, it can be connected to the access control system, programmed with user codes/credentials, and tested for proper operation.
The door position sensor is typically mounted on or inside the door frame; the door frame must be installed first to provide the physical mounting surface and correct alignment for the sensor.
Power and signal wiring for the door position sensor must be run to the sensor location before the sensor itself can be connected and terminated.

After physical installation, the sensor must be calibrated (e.g., setting open/close thresholds) and tested to verify proper operation and communication with the access control or building management system.

While it is physically possible to install the door first, it is easier to access the frame and mount the sensor before the door is hung. This is a soft preference for construction sequencing convenience.
The door position sensor must be installed and wired before it can be integrated into the broader access control system for monitoring and alarm functionality.
The REX sensor is typically mounted on or near a door frame to detect motion near the exit. The door and its frame must be installed first to provide the physical mounting surface for the sensor.

predecessor: Electrical rough-in wiring to door location
rationale: The REX sensor requires low-voltage power and signal cabling to connect to the access control system. Rough-in wiring must be completed before the sensor can be physically mounted and connected.

successor: Access control system configuration and testing
rationale: The REX sensor must be physically installed and wired before the access control panel can be programmed to respond to its signals and before end-to-end testing (e.g., triggering the sensor and verifying door unlock) can be performed.

successor: Door closer adjustment and final commissioning
rationale: It is preferred (but not physically required) to have the REX sensor installed before final door closer tuning, so that the door's motion profile does not accidentally trigger the sensor and cause false unlocks during adjustment.
Electrical conduits must be in place to route wiring for the keypad/PIN terminal before the device can be physically mounted and connected.
Rough electrical wiring must be completed to provide power and data connectivity to the keypad/PIN terminal location.
A mounting backbox or electrical box must be secured in the wall or surface before the keypad/PIN terminal can be attached.
The keypad/PIN terminal must be physically installed before the overall access control system can be tested, programmed, and commissioned.
After the keypad/PIN terminal is mounted, its data and power cables must be terminated at the device and tested for proper connectivity.
Conduit and cabling must be in place before CCTV cameras can be mounted and connected to the network and power supply.
CCTV cameras are often mounted on walls or ceilings; rough-in work (e.g., mounting brackets, backing plates) must be completed before camera installation.
Cameras must be physically installed before they can be powered on, configured, and tested for functionality and coverage.
It is preferable to install cameras after finishes to avoid dust/debris damage, but not a physical necessity if cameras are protected.
CCTV cameras must be installed and connected before the overall security system can be integrated and commissioned with recording servers and monitoring stations.
NVR requires network connectivity to receive video data from IP cameras; structured cabling must be run before NVR can be connected to the network switch.

predecessor: Mount and install IP security cameras
rationale: Cameras are the source of video input; NVR configuration and connection require cameras to be physically installed and wired.

predecessor: Install network switches and patch panels
rationale: NVR connects to the LAN via network switches; switches must be in place to provide network connectivity between cameras and NVR.

successor: Configure NVR recording schedules and retention settings
rationale: Physical installation and power-on of the NVR must be complete before any software configuration or scheduling can be performed.

successor: Connect and test video feed from cameras to NVR
rationale: The NVR unit must be physically installed and powered on before camera video feeds can be verified and tested for proper recording.
Wiring and conduit must be run to the sensor location before the sensor device can be physically mounted and connected.
The sensor is typically mounted on or flush with the ceiling surface, which must be installed and finished first.
Occupancy/vacancy sensors must be operational to enable automatic lighting control; lights are often wired through the sensor.

successor: Building Management System (BMS) / Lighting Control System Commissioning
rationale: The sensor output feeds into the control system; the sensor must be installed and connected before the control system can be tested and programmed.
Sensor functionality must be verified as part of overall electrical and lighting system testing before project completion.
The DVR unit must be physically mounted or placed on a stable surface before it can be installed; the mounting bracket provides secure attachment.
Power conduit and wiring must be run to the DVR location before the DVR can be connected to power.
Ethernet or network cabling must be pulled and terminated at the DVR location before the DVR can be connected to the network for camera communication and remote access.
The DVR must be installed, powered on, and operational before cameras can be connected to its ports and configured for recording.
Internal hard drives must be installed and formatted after the DVR is physically in place to ensure proper storage configuration before system testing.
The DVR must be fully installed and operational before the overall security system can be commissioned, tested, and verified for functionality.
The glass break detector must be physically installed and mounted before it can be connected to the security system or powered on.

successor: Connect detector to security system wiring
rationale: The mounting must be completed to position the detector before running electrical or signal wiring to it.

predecessor: Connect detector to security system wiring
successor: Power on and test glass break detector
rationale: Wiring connections must be made before power can be applied to test the device.
Rough electrical wiring must be in place (conduit, junction boxes) before the detector can be mounted and connected.
Finished surfaces (drywall, paint) should be completed before mounting the detector to avoid damage to finishes or the device.

Vibration sensors require a stable, clean mounting surface (such as concrete foundation or structural steel) to ensure accurate readings. Without a properly prepared foundation or mounting point, the sensor cannot be securely attached and calibrated.
The sensor must be physically installed in its final position before power and signal cables can be routed and connected to it, as the cable entry points and connections are part of the sensor body.
The sensor must be physically mounted and connected before any calibration, functional testing, or baseline data collection can be performed to verify it is working correctly.
The sensor must be installed and wired before it can be integrated into the building management system (BMS) or control panel for data acquisition and monitoring.

Vibration sensors are typically mounted on or near the equipment they monitor (such as pumps, chillers, fans, or generators). The equipment must be installed first so the sensor can be placed in the correct monitoring location.
The perimeter beam sensor must be mounted on a stable foundation or structural base that has been fully constructed and cured to provide proper support and alignment.
The perimeter beam sensor is typically mounted on or adjacent to structural steel beams; therefore the steel framing must be erected first to provide the mounting structure.
The sensor must be physically installed in its final position before electrical conduits and wiring can be routed to and connected to the sensor housing.
