The sensor must be physically mounted and connected before calibration and testing procedures can be performed to verify alignment and functionality.

While not a strict physical necessity, it is preferred to install the sensor before enclosing walls and ceilings to avoid difficult retrofitting, access issues, and potential damage to finished surfaces.

The Alarm Control Unit requires power and connectivity to the building's electrical system, so electrical rough-in (conduit, cabling, power supply) must be completed before the unit can be installed and connected.
The Alarm Control Unit must be physically installed and connected before the entire alarm system can be powered on, programmed, and tested for proper operation.
The wall, backboard, or panel where the Alarm Control Unit will be mounted must be framed and finished to provide a secure mounting surface before installation can occur.

successor: Connection of field devices (sensors, detectors, keypads)
rationale: Field devices such as smoke detectors, motion sensors, and keypads are typically wired back to the Alarm Control Unit, so the unit must be in place before these connections can be terminated.

successor: Integration with Building Management System (BMS) / Fire Alarm Network
rationale: Integration and communication testing between the Alarm Control Unit and the broader building management or fire alarm network requires the unit to be installed and operational first.

predecessor: Mount electrical enclosure / backbox for alarm device
rationale: The enclosure or backbox must be securely mounted to the wall or structure before the siren/audible alarm device can be installed into it.

predecessor: Run conduit and pull wiring to alarm device location
rationale: Electrical conduit and wiring must be in place before terminating wires to the alarm device.

successor: Complete fire alarm system commissioning and testing
rationale: The alarm device must be physically installed before the overall system can be tested to verify audible output and correct operation.
Audibility testing requires the siren device to be in place and connected to measure sound pressure levels across the protected area.
Conduit must be in place to route wires to the strobe/visual alarm indicator location before the device can be mounted and connected.
Power and control cables must be pulled to the device location before the strobe/visual alarm indicator can be terminated and installed.
Final wall or ceiling surfaces must be completed before mounting surface-mounted visual alarm devices, as the device is installed on finished surfaces.
All visual alarm devices must be installed and connected before the overall fire alarm system can be tested and commissioned to ensure proper functionality.
Final touch-up painting around the device mounting location may follow device installation, though this is a cosmetic/soft preference rather than a physical necessity.

predecessor: Rough-in electrical wiring to door location
successor: Video Door Phone / Video Intercom Unit installation
rationale: Electrical power and low-voltage wiring must be run to the door location before the intercom unit can be connected and powered up.

successor: Video Door Phone / Video Intercom Unit installation
rationale: The wall surface around the door must be finished and painted prior to mounting the intercom unit to ensure a clean, flush installation and avoid damage to finished surfaces.

predecessor: Conduit and backbox installation for intercom
successor: Video Door Phone / Video Intercom Unit installation
rationale: A recessed backbox or mounting bracket must be installed in the wall before the intercom unit can be securely fixed in place.

predecessor: Video Door Phone / Video Intercom Unit installation
successor: Intercom system programming and network configuration
rationale: The physical unit must be mounted and wired before it can be powered on, programmed, and connected to the building's network or intercom system.

predecessor: Video Door Phone / Video Intercom Unit installation
successor: Door strike / access control integration testing
rationale: The intercom unit must be installed and connected to the door release mechanism before door strike operation can be tested and calibrated.
Power and data conduits must be run to the turnstile locations before the units can be physically installed and connected.
Turnstiles and speed gates require a level, finished floor surface for proper anchoring, alignment, and stable operation.

predecessor: Structural Framing and Wall Construction (at mounting locations)
rationale: Any walls or structural supports that turnstiles attach to must be completed before the units can be mounted.

successor: Access Control System Integration and Configuration
rationale: Card readers, biometric scanners, or other access control devices are physically mounted on or wired to the turnstile; software configuration and testing can only occur after the hardware is in place.

successor: Final Floor Finishing and Grouting (around units)
rationale: While the turnstiles are installed first, final floor finishes or grouting around the base is a soft preference for aesthetic sealing rather than a structural necessity.

The UPS must receive input power from the electrical distribution system to function, so the main power supply lines and distribution panels must be installed and energized before UPS installation and commissioning.

predecessor: Concrete Floor Slab / Equipment Pad Construction
rationale: The UPS equipment requires a stable, level, and load-bearing foundation. The concrete floor slab or dedicated equipment pad must be poured, cured, and finished before the heavy UPS unit can be delivered and set in place.

predecessor: UPS Room / Enclosure Construction (Walls, Ceiling, HVAC rough-in)
rationale: The dedicated UPS room or enclosure must have walls, ceiling, and basic HVAC rough-in completed to provide a secure, ventilated, and environmentally controlled space before installing sensitive UPS equipment.

Security systems (access control, intrusion detection, CCTV) require clean, conditioned backup power. The UPS must be installed, wired, and commissioned to provide uninterruptible power before these critical security loads are connected and tested.

The UPS main unit must be positioned and secured before the heavy battery banks (which provide backup runtime) are placed in their racks and interconnected with the UPS DC bus, to ensure proper cable routing and physical arrangement.
Conduits and cabling for access control systems must be installed in walls and ceilings before the devices (card readers, keypads, electric strikes) can be mounted and connected.
Access control devices are typically surface-mounted on finished walls; installing them before drywall and paint would result in damage or misalignment during finishing work.

predecessor: Overhead Ceiling Installation (or Drop Ceiling Grid)
rationale: Cable pathways often run above ceilings; ceiling installation must be complete for final cable routing and device placement in finished spaces.

successor: Final Wiring and Termination of Control Panels
rationale: Physical devices must be mounted before their field wiring can be terminated at the central access control panel for integration and testing.
All hardware (readers, locks, controllers) must be physically installed before software configuration, credential assignment, and end-to-end testing can be performed.
Security system components (sensors, control panels, wiring) require electrical power and infrastructure to be installed before they can be commissioned and tested.
All security-related cabling (for cameras, card readers, door contacts, motion sensors) must be pulled and terminated before the system can be powered up and tested.
Physical installation of security hardware must be complete before commissioning can begin, as there is nothing to test without installed devices.
Security systems must be fully commissioned, tested, and verified operational before the building can be formally inspected and handed over to the owner/occupant.
End-user training on security system operation can only be conducted after the system has been commissioned and verified to be functioning correctly.

successor: Cable Pulling and Termination for Security Systems
rationale: Conduits and pathways must be installed before cables can be pulled through them, as the cables are routed inside the conduit infrastructure.

successor: Cable Pulling and Termination for Security Systems
rationale: Structural framing and overhead supports must be in place to provide cable tray supports and routing pathways before cable installation can begin.

predecessor: Cable Pulling and Termination for Security Systems
successor: Security System Device Installation and Mounting
rationale: Cables must be pulled and terminated at device locations before security devices (cameras, sensors, card readers) can be mounted and connected to the cabling.

predecessor: Cable Pulling and Termination for Security Systems
rationale: Cables must be fully installed and terminated before end-to-end system testing can be performed to verify connectivity and signal integrity.

predecessor: Cable Pulling and Termination for Security Systems
successor: Wall and Ceiling Finishing (Drywall, Plaster, Painting)
rationale: While it is preferable to complete cable pulling before enclosing walls to avoid rework, this is a soft preference as cables can sometimes be fished through finished walls if needed.
Power and communication conduits must be physically installed before security system components can be wired and integrated into the Building Management System (BMS).
A functional network backbone and IP infrastructure must be in place to enable the security system to communicate with the BMS server and controllers.
The BMS controllers and communication gateways (e.g., BACnet, Modbus) must be installed and operational to serve as the integration endpoint for the security system.

Integration of security components into the BMS must be complete before the overall BMS can be commissioned, as the security system is a subsystem that feeds data (e.g., access control events, intrusion alarms) to the BMS for centralized monitoring and control.

While the BMS dashboard and HMI can be partially configured in parallel, final configuration of security-related views and alarm handling on the user interface should occur after the security system integration is complete to ensure accurate data mapping and tag naming.
The system must be fully deployed, configured, and operational before any security testing can be performed, as penetration testing requires a live, working environment to identify vulnerabilities.
Network infrastructure must be in place to provide the connectivity and environment that the penetration test will evaluate.
Applications must be developed and integrated into the system so that they can be tested for security vulnerabilities during the penetration test.
Identification of vulnerabilities through penetration testing must occur first so that discovered issues can be remediated and patched.
The findings from the penetration test and security audit inform which security hardening measures are needed, so testing must precede hardening activities.

Security audit results are typically reviewed before granting final production go-live approval, though in some cases a conditional go-live may be granted; this is a soft preference for best practice.
The patch panel is typically mounted within a server rack; the rack must be secured in place before the patch panel can be installed.

predecessor: Run Cabling from Workstations to Patch Panel Location
rationale: Cables must be physically routed to the patch panel location before they can be terminated onto the punch-down blocks or jacks on the panel.

successor: Test Cable Continuity and Patch Panel Connections
rationale: It is a logical sequence to verify connections after installation, though testing could theoretically be interleaved; generally a soft preference to test after installation is complete.

successor: Connect Patch Cords Between Patch Panel and Network Switch
rationale: Patch cords cannot be connected until the permanent cabling is terminated on the patch panel, and the switch ports are the destination.
Labeling can be done after the panel is installed; it is a best-practice preference for documentation and troubleshooting but not physically required.
Server cabinets require a level, load-bearing structural floor to support their weight and ensure stability.
Network racks are typically mounted on or bolted to raised access floors to allow cable routing underneath.

predecessor: Overhead cable tray / ladder rack installation
rationale: Overhead cable management pathways must be in place before racks are positioned so that cables can be properly routed into the top of the cabinet.
Servers, switches, and patch panels cannot be mounted until the rack/cabinet frame is securely installed and stabilized.
Structured cabling cannot be terminated at the patch panels within the rack until the rack is in its final position.

successor: Power distribution unit (PDU) installation in rack
rationale: PDUs are mounted inside the rack after the rack is positioned to ensure proper power distribution to equipment.
Equipment grounding conductors must be connected to the rack after it is installed to ensure electrical safety.

successor: Commissioning and testing of network equipment
rationale: Network equipment cannot be tested and commissioned until the rack is installed and all equipment and cabling are in place.
The network switch must be mounted inside a rack or cabinet, so the rack must be installed first.
Cables (fiber or copper) must be pulled and terminated before the switch can be connected to the network.
The switch requires electrical power to operate; power feeds must be available before the switch can be powered on.
The physical switch must be installed and powered on before it can be configured with VLANs, IP addresses, and other settings.
Cables are often organized and labeled after switch installation for neatness and maintenance, but some labeling could be done beforehand as a soft preference.

The router typically connects to the network switch to provide routing capabilities. The switch must be installed and operational first to provide the network infrastructure that the router will connect to.
Power and network cables must be run to the router's location before the router can be physically installed and connected.
If the router is rack-mounted, the rack must be assembled and in place before the router can be mounted into it.
The router must be physically installed and powered on before software/firmware configuration, network setup, and testing can be performed.
The router must be in place and operational before firewall rules and security policies can be applied to it and tested.
Network cabling must be run to the firewall location before the firewall appliance can be physically connected to the network.
The server rack or mounting structure must be in place and power distribution must be available before the firewall appliance can be mounted and powered on.
The physical firewall appliance must be installed and powered on before its software configuration and security rule sets can be applied.
The firewall must be physically in place and operational before network security tests (e.g., penetration testing, rule validation) can be performed.
The firewall must be installed and configured as a security gateway before the network can be declared live and production traffic can flow.
WAPs require wired network connections (Ethernet/CAT6 cabling) to function; the cabling must be run to the WAP location before the WAP can be mounted and connected.
WAPs often require power (either Power over Ethernet from a switch or a separate electrical outlet); rough electrical work must be complete to provide power source.

predecessor: Install ceiling grid / suspended ceiling (if ceiling-mounted)
rationale: If the WAP is ceiling-mounted, the ceiling grid must be in place to provide the mounting structure; however some WAPs are installed above ceiling tiles or on walls, so this may vary by design.

successor: Commission and test network (including WAP connectivity)
rationale: The WAP must be physically installed and connected before network technicians can commission it, test signal coverage, and verify connectivity.

successor: Complete interior finishing (painting, ceiling tiles final placement)
rationale: While WAP installation can occur before final painting/finishing, it is a soft preference to install after finishing to avoid damage to the WAP from paint, dust, or construction debris.
Structural framing must be complete to provide support surfaces and embedments for conduit and cable tray systems.
Electrical boxes and backboxes must be installed to define termination points before conduit routing can begin.
Large mechanical ductwork and piping should be placed first to coordinate overhead space, leaving clear pathways for cable trays.
Conduit and cable trays must be fully installed before cables can be pulled through conduits or laid in trays.
It is preferable to complete cable tray installation before fireproofing to avoid damaging sprayed materials during tray installation, though fireproofing can sometimes be done afterward.
Cable trays must be installed first so that cables are routed through the planned pathways before fire stopping is applied to seal the penetrations.
All cables must be pulled through the penetration openings before fire stop materials can be applied to seal around the cables.
The structural element (wall, floor, or ceiling) must exist before any penetration can be cut or fire-stopped within it.
Fire stopping must be completed before electrical testing to ensure the integrity of fire-rated barriers and that cables are safely sealed.
Fire stop must be applied before closing up walls or ceilings with final finishes, as access to the penetration is required for proper application and inspection.
Cable trays provide the physical pathway for data cables; network outlets cannot be terminated unless the supporting cables are first routed through the installed trays.
Network outlets are typically mounted onto finished walls or partitions; the mounting surface must exist before the outlet box can be installed and trimmed.
Conduits or raceways must be placed within walls or ceilings before the outlet back boxes can be set and cables pulled to the outlet location.
The outlet body (back box and wiring termination) must be installed and secured before the decorative faceplate can be attached and the outlet made ready for use.
The outlet termination point must be physically installed at its location before cables can be terminated onto the outlet jacks and continuity/certification testing performed.

Electrical rough-in (conduits, junction boxes, power outlets) must be completed before network cables are pulled to ensure pathways and power sources are in place, and to avoid interference with electrical work.
Ceiling grid provides support structure for running network cables above drop ceilings; cables are typically laid in the plenum space before ceiling tiles are installed.
Network cables are run inside walls and through studs before drywall is fully finished and painted, allowing access for routing and avoiding damage to finished surfaces.
Cables must be pulled and terminated into patch panels before server racks and switching equipment can be fully connected and activated.
After cables are physically installed (pulled and routed), they must be terminated with connectors and tested for continuity and performance before being put into service.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and graded to provide a stable base before any underground conduit work can begin.
Trenches must be excavated to the required depth and alignment before conduits can be placed into them.
Existing underground utilities must be identified and marked to avoid damaging them during excavation and conduit installation.
Backfilling cannot occur until the conduits are fully placed, aligned, and secured within the trench.
Electrical cables or communication lines can only be pulled through conduits after the conduits have been completely installed, joined, and inspected.
Network equipment requires a stable, clean, and prepared physical environment (concrete pads, shelters, grounding) before installation and commissioning can begin.
Network equipment requires reliable electrical power (including backup power like batteries/generators) to be available before it can be powered on and commissioned.
Fiber optic or copper backbone cabling must be run to the site and terminated before network equipment can be connected and its communication links tested during commissioning.

Commissioning (including rack installation, power-up, initial configuration) must be completed before the equipment can be integrated into the broader network and end-to-end service testing performed.
Formal handover to the operations team or customer requires that commissioning is complete and equipment is verified as operational.
Cables must be physically installed and positioned before they can be tested for continuity, insulation resistance, and other electrical parameters.
All cable terminations, glands, and joints must be completed before testing, as the test verifies the integrity of the entire installed and terminated cable system.
Cable support systems (trays, ladders, conduits) must be in place before cables are laid and subsequently tested.

successor: Energization and Commissioning of Electrical System
rationale: The electrical system can only be energized and commissioned after cables have passed testing and been certified safe, to prevent short circuits, equipment damage, or personnel injury.
While tagging can partially be done during installation, final formal tagging and labeling is typically completed after testing to confirm circuit identification against test results.
Fibre cables must be laid within installed ducts/trenches before splicing and terminating the fibre ends at connection points.
The fibre optic cables must be physically pulled and placed into position before the fibre ends can be spliced and terminated at panels or splice closures.

successor: Fibre Optic Testing and OTDR Verification
rationale: Continuity, splice loss, and end-to-end attenuation testing cannot be performed until all splices and terminations are completed.
Termination of fibres into connectors and splice trays must be finished before patch panels can be fully dressed, labelled, and connected to active equipment.

successor: Fibre Optic Network Activation and Handover
rationale: The fibre link must be fully spliced, terminated, and tested before it can be handed over and activated for service delivery.
Site preparation establishes the physical layout and spatial constraints that determine where network conduits, trenches, and equipment rooms can be located.
The building's structural layout, wall locations, and ceiling spaces must be finalized to plan cable pathways, telecom rooms, and equipment mounting points.
Power requirements, outlet locations, and backup power provisions for network equipment must be known to coordinate network device placement and cabling routes.
The design and schematics for network cabling must be completed before physical installation of cables, conduits, and patch panels can commence.
Design specifications determine the types, quantities, and specifications of switches, routers, servers, and other network hardware needed for procurement.
Underground conduits must be installed first to provide the pathway for fiber optic or copper cables that will terminate at the ISP demarcation point.
Electrical power must be roughed in to the demarcation area to provide power for ISP equipment such as modems, routers, and termination panels.
The physical wall or enclosure where the ISP demarcation point will be mounted must be framed and in place before the demarcation hardware can be installed.
The demarcation point must be installed first to provide the physical termination location where ISP cables can be connected, terminated, and tested.
Internal network distribution equipment must connect to the ISP demarcation point as the source of incoming internet service; therefore the demarcation point must be in place first.

successor: Install Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS) for Network
rationale: Network racks and cabinets provide the physical mounting and structural support for network equipment; the UPS must be installed after racks are in place so it can be properly positioned and connected to the equipment it will protect.

predecessor: Run Electrical Power Cabling to Network Room
successor: Install Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS) for Network
rationale: Dedicated electrical supply circuits must be terminated at the UPS location to provide input power to the UPS unit before it can be connected and energized.

predecessor: Install Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS) for Network
successor: Connect UPS Output to Network Equipment
rationale: The UPS must be physically installed, mounted, and its output terminals ready before any network equipment can be wired to receive conditioned backup power from the UPS.

predecessor: Install Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS) for Network
successor: Configure UPS Monitoring and Management Software
rationale: While monitoring can theoretically be configured after commissioning, it is best practice to set up UPS network management and monitoring after installation and before the UPS is placed into full production service, though this is a soft preference for orderly commissioning.

predecessor: Install Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS) for Network
rationale: Full commissioning and load bank testing of the UPS can only occur after the UPS unit is installed, wired, and connected to its batteries and input power sources.
The air terminal (strike rod) must be installed on a stable foundation or structure; the foundation must be completed to provide a secure base for mounting.
The air terminal is typically mounted on the highest point of a building structure; the structural frame must be erected to provide the physical support and height for the strike rod.
Air terminals are commonly installed on rooftops; the roof deck must be in place to allow proper mounting and sealing of the strike rod base.
The air terminal must be installed first so that the lightning protection down conductors can be physically connected to the strike rod to complete the conduction path.
After the air terminal is installed, the complete lightning protection system including the strike rod must be tested for continuity and grounding resistance to ensure proper functionality.
The roof conductor network (including gutters, downspouts, and conductors) is attached to or integrated with the roof deck structure and cannot be installed until the roof deck surface is in place.
Flashing around roof penetrations and edges must be installed before gutters and conductor heads are attached to ensure proper water diversion and waterproofing integration.

While it is preferable to complete wall cladding before installing downspouts to avoid rework, downspouts can be installed alongside or after cladding; however, finishing was typically sequenced after conductor network to protect walls from water runoff.
The roof conductor network discharges water at grade; final grading and drainage systems must be in place after conductors are installed to properly direct water away from the foundation.
Landscaping and planting should follow roof conductor installation to avoid disturbing finished grading and to ensure downspout discharge locations are properly integrated with site drainage.
The down conductor must connect to the roof conductor system to provide a continuous path for lightning current to ground; therefore the roof conductor must be installed first.
The down conductor must be in place before it can be electrically connected to the grounding electrode system to complete the path to earth.
While typically the ground rod is installed first as it goes underground, the down conductor can be run and then connected to the ground rod; this is a soft preference depending on sequencing.
Continuity testing of the lightning protection system can only be performed after the down conductor is fully installed and connections are made.
Splices and connectors along the down conductor path are applied during or after the conductor is placed, but the conductor must be positioned first before these connections are made.
The ground electrode must be installed in prepared soil or excavated earth to ensure proper contact with the earth, so site clearing and excavation must be completed first.

Ground electrodes such as earthing rods or earth mats are often embedded in or placed around building foundations; the foundation concrete must be poured and set before integrating the ground electrode system.
Any underground utilities (water, gas, electrical conduits) must be laid and backfilled before the ground electrode system is installed to avoid conflicts and ensure safe separation distances.

successor: Main Earthing Conductor / Grounding Conductor Installation
rationale: The earthing conductor connects the ground electrode to the main earthing terminal; it cannot be connected until the electrode itself is in place.
Testing of ground resistance and bonding integrity must occur after the electrode is installed to verify it meets design specifications before being connected to the wider electrical system.
The main earthing terminal and bonding connections to the electrical switchboard rely on the ground electrode being installed to provide the reference earth point.
Lightning protection down conductors and air terminals must be bonded to the ground electrode system; the electrode must be in place first to provide the grounding path.
The pipe surface must be clean and prepared before installing a test clamp or inspection joint to ensure proper sealing and accurate test results.
General pre-hydrotest setup activities such as positioning and securing the pipe section must be completed before installing the test clamp or inspection joint.
The test clamp or inspection joint must be installed to seal the pipe section and provide a test access point before hydrostatic pressure testing can commence.

successor: Post-test Disassembly and Removal of Test Clamp
rationale: After testing is complete, the test clamp or inspection joint must be removed, which cannot happen until it has been installed and used for the test.
The test clamp or inspection joint facilitates the testing; only after it is installed and the test is performed can the results be inspected.
The SPD must be connected to the electrical panel's busbars or main breaker; the panel must be installed and energized to provide a proper connection point for the SPD.
The main service conductors (feeders) from the utility transformer to the main panel must be in place before the SPD can be wired in to protect the entire electrical system from incoming surges.
A low-impedance grounding path is critical for SPD operation to safely divert surge currents to earth; grounding must be completed before SPD installation.
The SPD must be physically installed and connected before the electrical system can be energized and tested for proper operation, as the SPD provides essential protection during initial power-up.
The SPD must be in place for the final electrical inspection to verify that surge protection is installed per code requirements before the building is occupied.
The bonding area must be cleaned and prepared to ensure proper electrical conductivity and adhesion before the conductive bonding clamp can be installed.
The clamp must be properly positioned in place before its fasteners can be tightened to secure it.

successor: Test Electrical Continuity of Bonding Connection
rationale: Electrical continuity testing must be performed after the clamp is installed and secured to verify the bonding connection is effective.
Corrosion protection coating is typically applied after clamp installation to protect the connection, but may be deferred or done in a different order depending on environmental conditions.

predecessor: Mount and secure main structural frame
rationale: The isolating spark gap must be mounted on or within the structural frame of the device (e.g., a lightning arrester or high-voltage equipment), so the frame must be in place first.

The spark gap must be electrically connected to the high-voltage line and ground terminals; these conductors must be terminated at the intended locations before the spark gap can be physically and electrically integrated.

successor: Connect spark gap to grounding electrode
rationale: The spark gap must be physically and electrically installed before its ground connection can be made; grounding completes the protective circuit path.
The spark gap must be fully installed to verify its breakdown voltage and isolation characteristics under high-voltage test conditions.
The spark gap must be in place and connected before the system can be safely energized, as the gap provides overvoltage protection.
The ESE terminal requires a stable mounting structure (pole, mast, or bracket) to be securely erected and anchored before the terminal itself can be attached.
A proper grounding (earthing) system must be in place before connecting the ESE terminal to ensure lightning current can be safely dissipated into the ground.
The down conductor cable leading from the ESE terminal to the ground cannot be terminated until the terminal itself is physically installed and secured at its mounting location.

Electrical testing of the complete lightning protection system, including continuity and earth resistance measurements, can only be performed after the ESE terminal is installed and all connections are made.
The formal inspection and certification of the lightning protection system can only occur once the ESE terminal is fully installed and tested.
The earth electrode ring must be installed in the excavated foundation trench before concrete is poured, so excavation must be completed first.
A level blinding concrete layer is typically required as a clean working surface before installing the ring earth electrode in the foundation.
The ring earth electrode is laid in the foundation trench before the reinforcement cage is placed, as it needs to be positioned under or within the rebar matrix.
The earth electrode must be embedded in the concrete foundation, so it must be installed and positioned before concrete is poured.
The ring earth electrode must be fully installed, connected, and inspected before the excavation is backfilled to avoid later disturbance.

The lightning protection system must be designed based on the final building geometry, including roof layout, ridge lines, and parapet walls, which are defined by the structural steelwork and roof structure.
The lightning protection system integrates with the building's earthing/grounding system; the earthing design must be established first to ensure proper bonding and dissipation paths.

Understanding the overall electrical layout helps coordinate lightning protection zones, bonding requirements, and surge protection device placement, though a preliminary design can start in parallel.
The design must be completed and approved before any installation work (air terminals, conductors, bonding) can be carried out on site.

successor: Surge Protection Device (SPD) Specification and Installation
rationale: SPD selection and placement depend on the lightning protection zones and bonding topology defined in the system design, so they cannot be finalized until the design is complete.
A stable and level foundation is physically required to support the LPS (Lightning Protection System) components, including air terminals and conductors.
The building's structural steel framework provides the physical support and attachment points for the LPS air terminals and conductors to be installed.
The roof deck must be in place so that rooftop air terminals, strike termination devices, and roof-mounted conductors can be properly installed and secured.
The LPS grounding conductors and bonding connections must be installed before the electrical system rough-in to ensure proper integration and bonding to the building's grounding electrode system.

successor: Final Inspection and Testing of LPS
rationale: The complete LPS installation must be in place before it can be tested for continuity, resistance, and compliance with standards such as NFPA 780 or IEC 62305.
Earth electrodes must be physically installed in the ground before their resistance to earth can be measured.
Earthing conductors (tape, wire, or cable) connecting electrodes to the main earthing terminal must be laid and connected before a complete earth resistance test of the system can be performed.

Trenches containing earth electrodes should remain open during testing so that additional electrodes can be driven or connections adjusted if the measured resistance is too high; backfilling only occurs after satisfactory test results are obtained.

The earthing system cannot be formally commissioned and signed off until earth resistance measurements have been taken and verified to meet the specified design criteria (typically < 1 ohm or as per local standards).

Although not a strict physical requirement, it is industry best practice to verify that the earth resistance meets manufacturer specifications before connecting sensitive electronic equipment to avoid damage from poor grounding.
The LPS (Lightning Protection System) must be designed and engineered before it can be inspected and certified, as inspection verifies the installed design meets standards.
All LPS components and materials must be procured and available on site before inspection can validate proper installation.
The lightning protection system must be fully installed, including air terminals, down conductors, and earthing/grounding, before it can be inspected and certified for compliance.
The LPS must first pass inspection and obtain certification before it can be formally commissioned and put into service.

While LPS certification is typically completed before project close-out for documentation purposes, in some phased handovers close-out may proceed in parallel; however, full certification is strongly preferred before final structural close-out.

predecessor: Installation of Metallic Services (piping, conduits, cable trays)
rationale: All metallic services must be physically installed and in place before they can be bonded together. Bonding connects these metallic components to form an equipotential zone.
The grounding electrode system provides the reference ground point to which metallic services are bonded. It must be installed first to establish the ground reference.
While not a physical necessity, inspecting metallic services prior to bonding ensures all components are properly installed and avoids rework if bonding needs to be redone.
After bonding is completed, continuity testing must be performed to verify that all metallic services are properly bonded and have low-impedance paths to ground.
Electrical systems must not be energized until all metallic services are bonded to ensure safety by preventing dangerous touch voltages and ensuring fault current paths exist.

The earth electrode is typically embedded in the foundation concrete or buried in the ground beneath the foundation, so the foundation excavation and formwork must be completed first to allow placement of the electrode.
The ground must be excavated and prepared to the required depth to allow installation of the earth electrode (e.g., copper rod driven into soil or buried conductor).
The main earthing conductor (bonding conductor) must be connected to the earth electrode after it is installed to establish the grounding path.
The main electrical panel and distribution boards require a connection to the earth electrode via the earthing conductor; this connection can only be completed once the electrode is in place.
The earthing conductor system is typically laid in the foundation trenches before concrete is poured, so excavation must be completed first to provide access.
Earth electrodes (rods, plates) must be installed and connected before the earthing conductor can be routed to them.
The earthing conductor must be laid in the foundation trench before concrete is poured, as it is embedded within or beneath the foundation.
The main earthing terminal (MET) must be connected to the earthing conductor after the conductor is installed, to establish the grounding reference point.
Equipotential bonding conductors connect to the earthing system; this bonding must follow after the earthing conductor is in place to complete the protective earthing network.
The MET must be installed in the foundation or ground-level area, so the excavation must be completed to provide access to the ground where the earthing system is placed.
The MET is often embedded in or fixed to the foundation concrete; concrete must be poured and cured to provide a stable base for mounting the MET.

successor: Main earth conductor connection to MET
rationale: The MET must be in place before any earthing conductors can be terminated or connected to it.
The MET serves as the central point for the earthing system; the main switchboard's earth connection must be made to the MET, so the MET must be installed first.

successor: Lightning protection system connection to MET
rationale: The lightning protection down conductors must terminate at the MET; therefore the MET must be installed before these connections can be made.

predecessor: Install main earthing conductor and earth electrode
rationale: The main protective bonding conductor connects to the main earthing conductor; the earthing system must be installed first to provide a bonding reference point.

successor: Bond incoming metallic services (water, gas, oil, steel structures)
rationale: The main protective bonding conductor is the means by which incoming metallic services are bonded to the earthing system; bonding cannot occur until the conductor is installed.
Continuity testing of the bonding conductor path must be performed after the conductor is installed and connected to all required services.
The main protective bonding conductor is an essential safety component that must be in place before the installation can be energized and commissioned.
The main protective bonding conductor typically terminates at the main distribution board/earthing bar, so the distribution board must be in place to provide the termination point.
The supplementary bonding conductor must be designed and specified to match the electrical system layout and protection requirements before installation can begin.
The supplementary bonding conductor must connect back to the main earthing terminal, which requires the main earthing conductor to be installed first.
After installing the supplementary bonding conductor, continuity testing must be performed to verify the integrity of the bonding connection.
The supplementary bonding conductor must be fully installed before the final inspection and certification of the electrical installation can take place.
The functional earthing conductor must be embedded in or connected to the building foundation earth electrode system, requiring foundations to be in place first.
The functional earthing conductor connects to the site earth electrode (e.g., grounding rods or grid), which must be installed before the conductor can be terminated.

The functional earthing conductor provides the reference ground point for sensitive electrical/electronic equipment; equipment cannot be safely connected to the functional earth until the conductor is in place.

successor: Testing and Commissioning of Earthing System
rationale: Continuity and resistance testing of the functional earth path must be performed after the conductor is fully installed to validate compliance with specifications.
Any trenching, conduit, or chase work for the conductor must remain open until installation is complete; concealment only occurs after the conductor is laid and tested.
The ground must be excavated to provide space for installing the earth electrode system, such as rods or grids.
The site must be graded to final levels before earth electrode installation to ensure proper depth and coverage.
Existing underground utilities must be identified and/or relocated to avoid conflicts with the earth electrode installation.
The earth electrode must be fully installed and tested before trenches or pits can be backfilled.
Resistance testing must be performed immediately after electrode installation to verify compliance with design specifications before any covering.

successor: Connection to Lightning Protection Down Conductors
rationale: Down conductors from the lightning protection system can only be bonded to the earth electrode after the electrode is installed and tested.
Earth rods must be installed in the ground near the foundation; excavation and blinding must be completed first to provide access and a stable base for the earthing system.
The earth rod must be driven and in place before the earthing conductor (e.g., copper tape) can be clamped or welded to it to form the grounding system.
The earth rod must be fully installed and connected before earth resistance testing can be performed to verify compliance with grounding requirements.
Trenches must be dug to accommodate earthing conductors and allow access for driving or placing earth rods at the required depth and location.
All earthing components, including earth rods, must be installed and connected before trenches can be backfilled to avoid re-excavation.
The ground must be excavated, leveled, and prepared before an Earth Plate (a ground-contact component like a footing or slab) can be placed.
The Earth Plate serves as the foundation or base component; vertical framing elements (walls, columns) must be anchored to it and cannot be erected until it is in place and cured.
Although utilities can sometimes be run alongside, it is best practice to complete the earth-contact base plate first to provide a stable working surface for routing pipes and conduits underneath.
Soil resistivity data is essential to design the earth grid dimensions, conductor sizing, and depth requirements before installation.
The trenches and pits must be excavated to the required depth and layout to accommodate the earth grid conductors and electrodes.
Major civil foundations should be completed first to avoid disturbing the earth mat after it is installed and backfilled.
After the earth grid conductors and electrodes are placed and connected, the trenches must be backfilled to protect and secure them.
The earth grid must be in place before any equipment or structural steel can be bonded to the earthing system.
The trench must be excavated to the required depth and length before the earth electrode tape/strip can be laid in the ground.
Backfilling can only proceed after the earth electrode tape/strip has been correctly positioned and laid in the trench.
The earth electrode must be installed in the ground before it can be electrically connected to the main earthing terminal of the building.
The earth electrode must be fully installed and connected before earth resistance testing can be performed to verify compliance with the earthing specification.

While not a strict physical dependency, site grading and soil preparation prior to installation ensures the ground conditions are suitable for proper electrode placement and reduces risk of soil contamination.
The location for the earth electrode must be determined first based on soil resistivity testing and site conditions before any chemical treatment or electrode installation can begin.
The pit or trench must be excavated to the required depth and dimensions before chemical backfill materials or enhancement compounds can be placed around the electrode.

The physical earth electrode (copper rod, plate, or strip) must be driven or placed in the ground before chemical enhancement materials (e.g., bentonite, marconite, conductive concrete) can be applied around it to reduce soil resistivity.

After chemical enhancement materials have been placed and properly saturated/tamped around the electrode, the excavation must be backfilled with native soil or specified fill and compacted to restore ground level.

The chemical enhancement must be complete and allowed sufficient time to cure/settle before conducting accurate earth resistance measurements (e.g., fall-of-potential test) to verify the enhanced grounding system meets design specifications.
The building foundation and site must be prepared before installing the ECC, as the ECC is typically embedded in or attached to the foundation and structural elements.
The main structural frame must be in place because the ECC connects to structural steel columns, rebar in concrete, or other building structural elements to provide a continuous earth path.
Trenches for underground services must be excavated before the ECC is laid, as the ECC often runs through these trenches and interfaces with the grounding electrode system.
Electrical panels and switchboards must be connected to the ECC for proper equipment grounding; the ECC must be in place first as the reference ground path.
Continuity and resistance testing of the earthing system can only be performed after the ECC is fully installed and connected to all bonding points.
The earth electrode must be physically installed in the ground before its resistance can be measured and tested.

successor: Earth Electrode Connection to Main Earthing Terminal
rationale: The resistance test must be completed and the value verified as acceptable before connecting the electrode to the main earthing system to ensure compliance with grounding resistance requirements.
Earth electrode resistance testing results are a prerequisite for overall earthing system commissioning and sign-off.
The ground must be excavated and prepared to allow installation of the electrode and access for testing equipment placement.

If test results show unsatisfactory resistance values, remediation works such as additional electrodes or chemical treatment may be required; this is a conditional soft ordering triggered only by failed tests.

Earth fault loop impedance testing measures the impedance of the fault path through installed cables and conductors. Without the cables being fully installed, terminated, and connected to the earthing system, there is no complete circuit to test.

The earthing system (earth electrodes, earthing conductors, and bonding) provides the reference point for the earth fault loop. The test measures impedance from the point of installation back to the earth source, so the earthing system must be fully installed and connected.

Each final circuit (lighting, power, etc.) must be fully wired from the distribution board to the final outlet points. The earth fault loop path exists through the entire circuit, so incomplete wiring will give inaccurate or incomplete test results.

The distribution board houses the protective devices and is the central point where supply cables, earthing conductors, and final circuits meet. It must be installed and all connections made before loop impedance testing can be performed at the board or on downstream circuits.

The measured earth fault loop impedance values are used to verify that protective devices (circuit breakers, fuses, RCDs) will operate within the required disconnection times. This verification cannot be performed without the impedance measurements.

predecessor: Installation of Protective Conductors (earthing and bonding)
rationale: Continuity testing verifies the integrity of the installed protective conductors; therefore the conductors must first be physically installed before their continuity can be tested.

predecessor: Completion of Electrical Wiring and Cable Installation
rationale: All circuits and cables that incorporate protective conductors must be in place so that the full continuity path through each protective conductor can be measured end-to-end.
Continuity testing must be performed before the electrical system is energised to confirm that all protective paths are continuous and safe, preventing shock hazards when power is applied.
Insulation resistance testing can only be carried out after continuity of protective conductors is verified, as the test equipment and procedure rely on a proven protective earthing path for safety.
Continuity testing results are a prerequisite for electrical commissioning documentation and certification, ensuring the installation meets safety standards before formal handover.
The ground surface must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and obstructions to allow access for resistivity testing equipment and to ensure accurate soil contact for electrode placement.
In some cases, minor shallow excavation or trenching may be needed to expose native soil for electrode placement, though often the survey is done on the surface.
Soil resistivity data directly determines the electrical grounding design parameters, including rod length, spacing, and configuration.
Resistivity measurements inform the design and placement of earth electrodes, which are installed during foundation work.
Soil resistivity is a critical input for designing cathodic protection systems, affecting anode placement, current requirements, and system effectiveness.
The bonding conductor is typically embedded in or laid on the concrete slab before further electrical work; the slab must be in place to provide the structural base.
Underground conduits and duct banks are installed before the bonding conductor so that the conductor can be pulled through or laid within the prepared pathways.
The grounding electrodes (e.g., ground rods, ufer ground) must be in place to connect the bonding conductor to the earth, ensuring an effective grounding path.
The bonding conductor provides the necessary grounding bond to the electrical panel; the panel cannot be properly grounded without the bonding conductor first being installed.
Equipment grounding conductors and bonds rely on the bonding conductor as the common reference point; they must be connected after the bonding conductor is in place to ensure continuity.
The earthing conductor/cable must be routed to the location before the clamp/connector can be attached to terminate or connect it.
The earth electrode (e.g., ground rod) must be driven into the ground first so the earthing clamp can secure the conductor to the electrode.
The clamp/connector must be fully installed and tightened before continuity and resistance of the earthing path can be tested.
The earthing clamp/connector establishes the earth reference point, and equipment bonding connections to that earth terminal can only be completed afterward.
The contact surface (conductor or electrode) must be clean and free of paint, rust, or corrosion to ensure low electrical resistance before the clamp is installed.

successor: Inspection Pit / Access Chamber for Earth Electrode
rationale: The earth electrode must be installed and in place before the inspection pit or access chamber can be built around or over it, as the chamber provides access to the electrode.

successor: Inspection Pit / Access Chamber for Earth Electrode
rationale: The trench or excavation for the earth electrode must be dug before the inspection pit can be positioned and constructed at the access point.

predecessor: Inspection Pit / Access Chamber for Earth Electrode
rationale: The inspection pit/chamber must be completed before backfilling the trench to ensure the chamber is properly positioned and accessible after backfill.

predecessor: Inspection Pit / Access Chamber for Earth Electrode
rationale: The inspection pit provides access for testing the earth electrode resistance; testing cannot be performed until the chamber is in place and accessible.

predecessor: Inspection Pit / Access Chamber for Earth Electrode
successor: Ground Level Finishing / Paving around Chamber
rationale: Final ground finishing and paving around the chamber lid/frame must be completed after the chamber is installed to ensure a flush, safe finish at grade.
The floor or mounting surface must be prepared and leveled before any luminaire can be safely installed.
The emergency luminaire must be physically mounted before it can be wired into the emergency lighting circuit.
The luminaire must be installed before testing its emergency backup power functionality and battery backup.
For recessed or surface-mounted emergency luminaires in suspended ceilings, the ceiling grid must be in place to provide the support and location reference.
All emergency luminaires must be installed as part of the overall electrical system before the final system-wide commissioning and testing can commence.
Earthing systems are typically integrated into building foundations; the physical structure must exist to accommodate earth electrodes and bonding conductors.
The earthing schedule/drawing must reference the as-built location and resistance of the installed earth electrode, which must be installed first.
Bonding to structural steel and reinforcement requires knowledge of the actual steelwork placement to document bonding points on the schedule/drawing.
The electrical installation must follow the approved earthing and bonding schedule to ensure all equipment and circuits are correctly earthed and bonded per design.

successor: Inspection and Testing of Earthing System
rationale: Testing verifies compliance with the earthing schedule; the schedule/document must be complete before testing can reference its requirements.
Electrical wiring and conduit must be installed in the ceiling/wall before exit signs can be physically mounted and connected to power.
Exit signs are typically mounted to or suspended from finished ceilings; ceiling grid or drywall must be in place to provide a mounting surface.
Walls must be painted and finished before exit signs are installed to avoid damage to the signage from finishing work.
Exit signs must be installed and connected before the final electrical trim-out and testing of emergency lighting systems can be completed.
Exit signs must be in place and operational before the building final inspection and life safety commissioning can be conducted to verify code compliance.
Central Battery Unit requires power from the Electrical Distribution Board to function and be tested, so the distribution board must be installed and energized first.
The Central Battery Unit supplies backup power to emergency lighting circuits; these circuits can only be connected and tested after the battery unit is in place and operational.
Full commissioning of the emergency power system requires the Central Battery Unit to be installed before any load testing and functional verification can proceed.
While integration can technically proceed in parallel, it is preferred to complete battery installation first to ensure stable backup power for fire alarm testing.
Individual battery cells must be manufactured before they can be assembled into a battery pack.
The BMS must be fabricated beforehand to integrate it into the battery pack assembly.
The enclosure or housing must be manufactured to house the cells and electronics within the pack.
The assembled battery pack must be complete before it can undergo functional and safety testing.
The battery pack must be assembled and tested before being integrated into the final device or vehicle.
The housing or mounting bracket must be physically installed before the luminaire itself can be placed and secured.
Power supply and emergency backup wiring must be pulled and terminated at the luminaire location before the unit can be connected and energized.
The emergency power source (central battery or UPS) must be in place and operational to supply the maintained emergency luminaire.
All emergency luminaires must be installed before the overall emergency lighting system can be functionally tested and commissioned.
The luminaire is typically recessed or surface-mounted; ceiling finishes can only be completed after the luminaire is fixed in place to ensure proper alignment and access.
The mounting bracket must be securely fixed to the wall or ceiling before the emergency luminaire can be attached to it.
The electrical supply conduit and cables must be run to the luminaire location before the unit can be wired and connected.
Final finishes (e.g., plasterboard, paint) must be completed before the luminaire is mounted, to avoid damage to finishes during installation.

successor: Emergency lighting circuit testing and commissioning
rationale: The luminaire must be physically installed and connected before the emergency lighting system can be functionally tested and commissioned.

successor: Final inspection and certification of emergency lighting
rationale: All emergency luminaires must be in place before the inspecting authority can certify compliance with fire safety and building codes.

predecessor: Electrical containment and cable tray installation
rationale: Sustained emergency luminaires require electrical supply cabling routed via containment (cable trays, conduits) to deliver power; containment must be in place before luminaires can be physically mounted and connected.

predecessor: Main electrical panel and distribution board installation
rationale: Sustained emergency luminaires need final circuit connections back to distribution boards/emergency supply panels; these panels must be installed and energized to test the luminaires.

predecessor: Ceiling grid and soffit installation (in finished areas)
rationale: In suspended ceiling environments, the ceiling grid provides the structural support for recessed or surface-mounted emergency luminaires; however, luminaires could be wall-mounted before ceilings are fully complete, so this is a soft preference for coordination.
All sustained emergency luminaires must be physically installed, wired, and connected before they can be functionally tested (duration test, illumination level verification, battery discharge test).

successor: Ceiling finishing and close-out (in luminaire-integrated ceilings)
rationale: Where emergency luminaires are integrated into finished ceilings, the luminaire installation should precede final ceiling panel installation and finishing to avoid rework, though this is a sequencing preference rather than a physical necessity.
The emergency lighting controller requires electrical conduit and a backbox for mounting and wiring connections, so these must be in place first.
The controller needs a mains power supply to function; cabling must be run to the controller location before it can be connected.

successor: Connect and test emergency lighting circuits
rationale: The controller must be installed and mounted before emergency lighting circuits can be terminated, connected, and tested through it.

successor: Commission and program emergency lighting system
rationale: The controller hardware must be in place and powered before it can be commissioned, configured, and programmed with addressable device settings.

successor: Perform final system integration and testing
rationale: The controller must be fully installed and operational before being integrated with the building management system or fire alarm system for final testing.
The test module must be designed based on the defined system requirements and testing criteria.
The automatic test module must interface with the physical hardware, so hardware design must be completed to define test points and connection interfaces.
The test module validates assembled PCBs; thus, the assembly process must be established and operational before the test module can be deployed for testing.
The automatic test module is used to verify and validate integrated subsystems, so it must be complete before full system integration testing begins.
The test module is typically required for production-level testing, but production ramp-up could begin with manual testing as a soft preference if the test module is delayed.
The emergency lighting distribution board must receive its main power supply from the main electrical distribution board, so the main board must be installed and operational first.
Cabling routes (conduits, cable trays, trunking) must be in place to run the supply and outgoing cables to and from the emergency lighting distribution board.
Emergency light fittings must receive their power from the distribution board; the board must be installed, terminated, and energized before the individual light fittings can be connected and tested.

successor: Emergency Lighting System Testing and Commissioning
rationale: Full testing and commissioning of the emergency lighting system can only proceed once the distribution board is installed, all circuits are terminated, and power is available.
The emergency lighting distribution board often interfaces with the fire alarm system for automatic activation during an alarm; this integration requires the board to be installed and wired first.

predecessor: Mount and secure Inhibit/Override Switch bracket
rationale: The switch must have a physical mounting bracket installed and secured before the switch itself can be attached.

successor: Route and connect wiring harness to Inhibit/Override Switch
rationale: The switch must be physically in place before its electrical wiring can be routed and terminated to its terminals.

predecessor: Route and connect wiring harness to Inhibit/Override Switch
rationale: Electrical connections must be complete before functional testing of the switch can be performed.

successor: Install adjacent panel covers or guards
rationale: The switch must be accessible during installation; adjacent covers or guards must be installed after the switch is in place to avoid blocking access.
The control system's logic for interpreting the inhibit/override signal must be configured and verified before integrated testing of the switch can confirm correct system response.
Structural framing provides the physical support and mounting points for cable trays, conduits, and support systems. Wiring cannot be installed without these structural elements in place.
Conduits must be installed within walls, ceilings, and floors before wiring can be pulled through them. This is a sequential physical requirement.
Wiring must be run and managed before it can be terminated at electrical panels and connected to breakers.
Cables must be pulled to outlet/switch locations before the devices and fixtures can be physically installed and connected.

successor: Testing and Commissioning of Electrical Systems
rationale: All wiring must be in place and properly managed before electrical testing and commissioning can verify continuity, insulation, and correct operation.
Emergency lighting fixtures require power cables and junction boxes to be installed and routed before the fixtures themselves can be mounted and connected.
Emergency lighting units are typically mounted to or recessed within ceiling grids, so the ceiling grid structure must be in place to support the fixtures.
All emergency lighting fixtures must be physically installed before they can be powered on, tested for proper operation, and commissioned.

It is preferable to install ceiling tiles and finishes after emergency lighting is in place to avoid damage to finishes during fixture installation, but tiles can be removed and reinstalled if needed.
Emergency lighting requires a dedicated power feed from the main electrical panel or emergency distribution board, which must be installed and energized before fixtures are connected.
Emergency lighting fixtures, batteries, and wiring must be physically installed before they can be energized, tested, and commissioned.

predecessor: Electrical Power Supply and Distribution Installation
rationale: Main electrical supply and distribution circuits must be in place and live to provide power to the emergency lighting system for testing.

successor: Fire Alarm System Commissioning and Testing
rationale: Emergency lighting and fire alarm systems are often interlinked; the emergency lighting must be tested to ensure it activates correctly upon fire alarm signal before the fire alarm system can be fully commissioned.
Building regulations and safety codes require that emergency lighting is tested and certified as operational before the building can be handed over and occupied.

While emergency lighting is often tested after ceiling installation, ideally testing should be done before full finishing to allow access for adjustments; however, it is a soft preference as final testing can occur after finishes are complete.
The emergency lighting system must be fully installed before it can be periodically inspected.

successor: Emergency Lighting Repair or Remedial Work
rationale: After inspection, any identified faults or non-compliances must be repaired before the system can be considered fully operational.
A certificate of testing and inspection can only be issued after the periodic inspection has been carried out and any necessary remedial work completed.

successor: Emergency Lighting Design and Lux Calculation
rationale: The electrical load assessment determines the available capacity and requirements for emergency lighting circuits, which is necessary before designing the emergency lighting layout.

predecessor: Building Floor Plan and Layout Finalization
successor: Emergency Lighting Design and Lux Calculation
rationale: Accurate floor plans showing room dimensions, exit paths, occupant density, and ceiling heights are required to perform emergency lighting layout and lux level calculations.

predecessor: Fire Safety Strategy and Exit Route Planning
successor: Emergency Lighting Design and Lux Calculation
rationale: Emergency lighting design must align with designated fire escape routes and exit signage placement, which are defined in the fire safety strategy.

predecessor: Emergency Lighting Design and Lux Calculation
successor: Emergency Lighting Fixture Selection and Procurement
rationale: The design and lux calculation outputs (required light levels, fixture types, quantities, and locations) must be completed before emergency lighting fixtures can be selected and procured.

predecessor: Emergency Lighting Design and Lux Calculation
rationale: The installation of emergency lighting fixtures and wiring cannot begin until the design is finalized and lux calculations confirm compliance with codes.
The pressurisation fan unit requires a stable structural frame to be mounted on or supported by before installation can proceed.
Electrical power supply conduits and connections must be in place to connect and power the pressurisation fan unit.
The fan unit must be installed and positioned before ductwork can be connected to it.

successor: Electrical Wiring and Control System Integration
rationale: Final electrical connections and control system integration for the fan unit can only be completed after the fan unit is physically installed.

successor: Commissioning and testing of pressurisation system
rationale: The pressurisation fan unit must be fully installed with all connections before the system can be commissioned and tested for performance.
Structural steel framing must be in place to provide support and hanging points for the air supply ductwork system.
Electrical and plumbing rough-ins must be completed before ductwork installation to avoid conflicts and ensure proper clearances within the ceiling and wall cavities.

While not a hard physical constraint, installing the ceiling grid before ductwork can make duct access and hanging more difficult; typically ductwork is installed before or concurrently with ceiling grids.
Duct insulation can only be applied after the air supply ductwork is fully installed and sealed to ensure complete coverage and thermal efficiency.
Final connection of air handling units and balancing of airflow requires the ductwork to be fully installed and sealed before system startup and testing.
Supply air grilles and diffusers connect directly to the ends of ductwork. Ductwork must be installed and in place before the grilles/diffusers can be mounted.
Supply air grilles and diffusers are typically mounted into or flush with the ceiling grid. The ceiling support structure must be in place before diffusers can be installed.
Some supply diffusers are equipped with actuated dampers or sensors requiring electrical connections; rough-in wiring should be completed before diffuser installation.
Grilles and diffusers are often installed after ceiling grid but before the final ceiling tiles/panels are placed, to allow access for adjustments and connections.
The grilles and diffusers must be fully installed before the HVAC system can be balanced and commissioned, as they are the terminal devices through which air is delivered to the space.
Pressure Relief Dampers are installed within ductwork systems; therefore the ductwork must be in place to provide structural support and connection points before the damper can be mounted.
The damper must be fully installed and sealed before pressure testing can occur to ensure the duct system including the damper is airtight and functions correctly.

successor: Fire alarm & BMS (Building Management System) commissioning
rationale: While not a strict physical necessity, the damper must be installed and connected before the BMS can verify its open/closed status and test its response to alarm signals during system commissioning.

predecessor: Structural framing and ceiling grid installation
rationale: The damper requires a stable structural framework (e.g., ceiling grid or wall framing) for secure mounting and support; installation cannot proceed without this base structure in place.
Once the damper is installed, ceiling tiles, drywall, or other enclosures can be closed up; if the damper were not in place first, access would be blocked for installation and adjustments.
The Pressurisation Control Panel requires electrical power to function, so the electrical power supply must be installed and operational before the panel can be commissioned or tested.
The control panel must be connected to building management systems and sensors via control cabling, which must be installed prior to final connection and testing of the panel.

The pressurisation control panel acts as the central controller for pressurisation fans; therefore, the panel must be installed and operational before the fans can be started and tested under controlled conditions.

successor: Smoke Extraction System Integration and Testing
rationale: The pressurisation control panel coordinates with smoke extraction systems to maintain pressure differentials; integration testing can only proceed once the panel is in place and operational.

predecessor: Pressurisation Control Panel Enclosure and Mounting
rationale: The physical enclosure, backplate, and mounting framework must be securely installed before the control panel components can be fitted and wired.
The VSD controller requires a power source and electrical connections from the panel; the panel must be installed and wired before the VSD can be connected.
The VSD controller must be wired to and configured for the specific motor it controls; the motor must be physically installed first so that cabling and parameters can be properly matched.
The physical mounting bracket, cabinet, or enclosure that houses the VSD must be in place before the VSD controller unit itself can be mounted.

predecessor: Variable Speed Drive (VSD) Controller installation and configuration
rationale: The VSD controller must be installed, wired, and have its parameters configured before functional testing and commissioning can begin.

predecessor: Variable Speed Drive (VSD) Controller installation and configuration
rationale: The motor can only be operated via the VSD controller after the VSD is installed, wired, and configured; hence operational testing of the motor-VSD system must follow VSD installation.
Electrical power and wiring infrastructure must be in place before the fire alarm interface can be connected and powered.
The communication and sensor cabling for the fire alarm system must be run to the interface location before the interface device can be installed and terminated.
Conduits and electrical backboxes must be roughed in at the interface location to provide a mounting and enclosure point for the interface device.

successor: Fire Alarm System Commissioning and Testing
rationale: The activation interface must be installed and connected before the fire alarm system can be fully commissioned, tested, and verified for proper operation.

Although the interface should be physically installed before BMS integration, this is a soft preference because integration testing could theoretically be deferred if the interface is accessible later.
The equipment must be physically manufactured and assembled before it can be tested at the factory.
Detailed design and engineering specifications must be finalized to define the testing criteria and acceptance thresholds for FAT.
All components and materials required for the equipment must be procured and delivered to the factory before assembly and testing can occur.
Equipment must pass FAT to confirm it meets specifications before it can be packed, crated, and shipped to the project site.
FAT must be completed and passed before the equipment is sent to site; SAT can only commence after FAT is successfully completed and the equipment is installed on site.

predecessor: Installation of Cooling Coil & Chilled Water Pipework
rationale: The cooling coil and chilled water pipework must be installed first because the fan unit is typically mounted downstream and connected to the coil assembly; the ductwork layout depends on the coil position.
The building structure and roof must be in place to support the fan unit and provide enclosure for ductwork routing; ductwork cannot be hung or installed without the structural framework.

successor: Electrical Connection & Commissioning of Fan Motor
rationale: The fan unit must be physically installed before electrical connections can be made to the fan motor; commissioning requires the unit to be in its final position.
Ductwork must be fully installed before insulation can be applied and before air balancing tests can be performed to verify airflow.
Terminal devices such as diffusers and grilles are connected to the ductwork ends, so the ductwork must be installed first to allow proper connection and alignment.

All fire alarm devices (smoke detectors, heat detectors, manual call points, sounders, strobes, and control panels) must be physically installed and wired before integration testing can begin, as there is nothing to integrate or test without the devices in place.
Cabling and conduit infrastructure must be completed to provide the communication backbone between all fire alarm devices and the control panel; testing requires functional signal paths.

predecessor: Fire Alarm Control Panel Installation & Power-Up
rationale: The main fire alarm control panel (FACP) must be installed, powered up, and basic verified before integration testing can coordinate device communications and cause-and-effect logic.
