Integration and cause-and-effect testing must be successfully completed before formal commissioning and acceptance by the authority having jurisdiction (AHJ), as commissioning verifies that all integrated functions work correctly.

successor: Building Fire Alarm Final Inspection & Certification
rationale: Final inspection and certification of the fire alarm system can only occur after integration testing proves that all cause-and-effect sequences (e.g., alarm activation triggering strobes, door hold-open release, elevator recall, HVAC shutdown) function as designed.
Routine maintenance and inspection can only begin after the building or facility has been fully constructed, commissioned, and handed over for operational use.
Inspections identify defects or issues that require repair; thus, repair work can only commence after the inspection has identified what needs fixing.
While inspections inform the schedule, it is a soft preference to have inspection results before planning detailed preventive maintenance tasks for optimal resource allocation.

predecessor: Install BMS Controllers and Field Devices
rationale: BMS controllers (DDC controllers), sensors, actuators, and field devices must be physically installed and wired before the BMS integration point can be established, as the integration point serves as the central hub connecting these distributed devices.

The BMS integration point (typically head-end servers, network switches, and gateway panels) requires a stable electrical power supply to operate, so electrical power distribution must be completed and energized beforehand.

predecessor: Install Structured Cabling and Network Infrastructure
rationale: The BMS integration point relies on a robust network backbone (Ethernet, BACnet/IP, or similar protocols) to communicate with field devices and the central server; structured cabling and network switches must be in place before integration can begin.

The BMS integration point must be fully configured, connected, and operational before commissioning activities (point-to-point testing, trend logging verification, alarm testing) can be performed, as commissioning validates the entire integrated system.

Although energy performance testing can begin with some manual data collection, a fully integrated BMS provides comprehensive energy data and control, making testing far more efficient and accurate; this is a strong preference rather than a hard constraint.
A stable, level concrete foundation or equipment pad must be cured and ready to support the heavy weight of the chiller unit before it can be set in place.

predecessor: Structural Steel Framing (if roof or mezzanine mounted)
rationale: For roof- or mezzanine-mounted chillers, the structural support framework must be in place to bear the chiller's operational weight.
The chiller must be set in its final position before supply and return chilled water pipes can be connected to its evaporator and condenser barrels.
The chiller must be physically installed before power cables, motor leads, and BAS control wiring can be terminated at the chiller's electrical panel.
Refrigerant lines and the charging process require the chiller to be in its permanent location, with all mechanical connections accessible.
The chiller must be fully installed, piped, wired, and charged before commissioning procedures such as leak testing, vacuum pull, oil charging, and operational testing can commence.
Chilled water pipes must be in place so that the pump can be connected to the piping system and properly aligned.
The pump must be mounted on a cured, level concrete foundation to provide adequate structural support and prevent vibration issues.
Final pipe connections (flanges, couplings) to the pump can only be made after the pump is set in its final position.
Electrical connections to the pump motor must follow mechanical installation to avoid damage during pump placement.

successor: Chilled Water Pump Commissioning and Testing
rationale: The pump must be fully installed (mechanically, electrically, and with piping) before it can be tested and commissioned for operation.
The pump requires a stable concrete foundation or housekeeping pad to be placed and cured before the pump unit can be set in position.

predecessor: Install Condenser Water Piping Main Risers
rationale: Main supply and return piping headers must be in place to connect the pump suction and discharge flanges.

successor: Align and Couple Pump to Motor
rationale: The pump must be set on its foundation before the flexible coupling and shaft alignment between pump and motor can be performed.

successor: Install Pump Piping Connections (Flanges, Valves, Strainers)
rationale: Piping connections to the pump nozzles require the pump to be in its final position for accurate fit-up and support.

successor: Commission Condenser Water System (Flushing, Balancing, Startup)
rationale: System flushing, chemical treatment, flow balancing, and pump startup testing require the pump assembly to be fully installed, wired, and coupled.
The AHU is typically installed on the rooftop or a mechanical mezzanine; the structural frame and roof must be in place to support the unit's weight and provide a weathertight enclosure.
AHUs require a level, cured concrete pad or structural base to bear their weight and maintain alignment.
Large AHU sections must be lifted into place; rigging equipment or permanent hoists need to be installed beforehand.
Supply and return ducts can only be physically connected after the AHU is set in its final position.

successor: Chilled Water / Hot Water Piping Connection
rationale: Coil piping connections require the AHU to be in place so that pipe runs can be terminated at the unit's connections.
Ductwork must be in place to connect to the fan coil unit for air distribution; FCU cannot be installed before its connecting ductwork is available.

predecessor: Complete ceiling grid and overhead structural supports
rationale: Fan coil units are often suspended from the ceiling structure; the ceiling grid and support hangers must be installed first to provide mounting points.
Electrical power supply wiring and conduit must be run to the FCU location before the unit can be connected and energized.

successor: Connect chilled water and heating water piping to FCU
rationale: Coil connections (chilled water/hot water) can only be made after the fan coil unit is physically set in place.
Functional testing, airflow balancing, and commissioning of the fan coil unit must occur after the unit is installed and all connections are made.
The structural steel frame must be in place to provide support and attachment points for condenser water piping runs, especially for overhead piping.
Underground or slab-on-grade condenser water piping requires the foundation or slab to be poured before pipe trenches or embedments can be placed.
Chillers must be set in place so that condenser water piping can be connected accurately to chiller condenser barrels and flanges.
Condenser water supply and return piping must be completed and pressure-tested before final connections can be made to cooling towers.
Insulation cannot be applied until piping is installed, pressure-tested, and approved; insulation follows piping completion.
A stable foundation and base must be prepared before the air separator unit can be set in place to ensure proper structural support and alignment.
Heavy lifting equipment must be positioned and rigged before the air separator (typically a large, heavy vessel) can be lifted and placed onto its foundation.
The air separator must be set in its final position before inlet/outlet process piping can be connected to it.
Level gauges, pressure transmitters, and other instruments can only be mounted and wired after the separator vessel is installed.
Thermal or acoustic insulation is applied after the vessel is in place to avoid damaging insulation during the lift and to ensure full coverage.

predecessor: Chilled Water Buffer Tank Foundation / Piping Sleeves Installation
successor: Chilled Water Buffer Tank Setting & Anchoring
rationale: The tank must have a completed foundation and properly placed piping sleeves before it can be set in position to ensure structural support and correct pipe connections.

predecessor: Chilled Water Buffer Tank Setting & Anchoring
successor: Chilled Water Buffer Tank Piping Connections
rationale: The tank must be securely set and anchored in place before any piping can be connected to it to avoid movement that could damage pipe joints.

predecessor: Chilled Water Buffer Tank Piping Connections
successor: Chilled Water Buffer Tank Insulation & Jacketing
rationale: Insulation and jacketing must be applied only after all piping connections are complete to ensure all joints and surfaces are accessible and properly sealed.

predecessor: Chilled Water Buffer Tank Setting & Anchoring
successor: Chilled Water Buffer Tank Electrical / Controls Wiring
rationale: Electrical and control wiring (sensors, thermostats, power connections) must be run after the tank is secured to avoid damage during installation and to ensure accurate sensor placement.

predecessor: Chilled Water Buffer Tank Pressure Testing & Flushing
rationale: The buffer tank must pass pressure testing and flushing to verify integrity and cleanliness before the overall chilled water system can be started and commissioned.
VFDs receive power from electrical panels; the panel and its wiring must be in place before the VFD can be connected and powered.
The VFD controls a specific motor; the motor must be installed, mounted, and its wiring prepared before the VFD can be configured and connected to it.

predecessor: Control system / PLC installation and programming
rationale: While the VFD can be physically mounted and wired before the control system, full commissioning and tuning typically require the control system (PLC/BMS) to be ready for communication and setpoint signals.
The VFD must be installed, wired, and configured before the motor can be started under VFD control to prevent uncontrolled operation or damage.
Physical installation and power connection must be complete before any parameter programming, tuning, and functional testing of the drive can be performed.
The chilled water piping network must be installed to provide the physical connection points and supports for the control valve.
Pressure testing of the chilled water pipes must be completed before the control valve is installed to avoid damaging the valve during testing or having to remove it for access.

The control valve must be installed in the chilled water supply line before final connections can be made to the air handling unit or fan coil unit coil piping, as the valve regulates flow to the coil.
The control valve body must be in place before the actuator can be mounted and calibrated, as the actuator is physically attached to the valve stem.

successor: Building Management System (BMS) / Controls Wiring Termination
rationale: The control valve must be installed before control wires can be terminated at the actuator, and before the BMS can be configured to control the valve position.
The differential pressure sensor is installed within or across HVAC ducts to measure pressure differences. Ducts must be in place before the sensor can be mounted and connected.
The differential pressure sensor needs a secure mounting surface or bracket, which must be installed beforehand to physically support the sensor.
Power and signal cabling must be routed to the sensor location before the sensor can be connected and terminated.
Once the sensor is physically installed and wired, it must be calibrated, zeroed, and functionally tested to ensure accurate pressure readings before the system can be commissioned.
The differential pressure sensor provides critical feedback for air balancing and system commissioning; these activities can only proceed after the sensor is installed and operational.
Temperature sensors are often mounted on or within HVAC ductwork to measure air temperature; ducts must be in place before sensor installation.
Temperature sensors require electrical power and signal wiring; conduit and wiring must be pulled to the sensor location before the sensor can be installed and connected.

successor: Commission and Calibrate HVAC Control System
rationale: The temperature sensor must be physically installed and wired before the control system can be calibrated and tested to ensure accurate readings.

successor: Install Ceiling or Wall Finishes (if applicable)
rationale: While not strictly required, it is preferable to complete sensor installation before finishing work to avoid damage to finishes or the need for rework and patching.
Rough-in inspections of mechanical, electrical, and conduit work must be passed before the sensor (a finish-level device) can be installed and closed up.
The chemical treatment system requires a stable load-bearing foundation and structural steel supports to be in place before the heavy equipment and tanks can be installed.
The chemical treatment system must be protected from weather elements; the building enclosure must be completed to provide a controlled environment for sensitive chemical processing equipment.

successor: Piping & Plumbing Connections to Chemical System
rationale: Process piping and chemical supply/return lines can only be connected after the treatment system skids and tanks are set in their final position.
Power supply wiring, control panels, and instrumentation sensors must be connected after the chemical treatment equipment is installed to ensure proper alignment and safe termination points.
Commissioning activities including leak testing, calibration, and charging with chemicals can only begin once the treatment system and all its connections are fully installed.
Pipes must be cut and beveled to the correct length and angle before installing a Y-strainer, as the strainer connects into the piping system.
Adjacent pipe sections must be fitted and aligned to ensure the Y-strainer can be properly positioned and bolted/welded in place.
After the Y-strainer is installed between flanges, the flange bolts must be tightened to the specified torque to secure the connections and prevent leaks.
The Y-strainer must be installed before the piping system can be pressure-tested to verify the integrity of all joints including the strainer connections.
The Y-strainer must be in place to capture debris during system flushing and initial operation, protecting downstream equipment during commissioning.
A stable, level concrete foundation must be fully cured to support the weight and operational loads of the plate and frame heat exchanger before it can be set in place.
The steel support structure or skid that holds the heat exchanger must be erected and secured to provide the exact mounting points and elevation required for the unit.
Main process piping headers are typically routed first so that final connections to the exchanger can be made efficiently, though in some cases pipe spools can be fitted after placement.

successor: Pipe Tie-Ins to Heat Exchanger Nozzles
rationale: The heat exchanger must be physically positioned and bolted down before its nozzles can be accurately connected to the process piping system.

successor: Tightening of Plate Pack & Pressure Testing
rationale: Once installed, the plate pack must be tightened to the specified gap dimension and the entire assembly hydrostatically tested to verify integrity before being placed into service.
A stable concrete foundation and structural slab is required to support the heavy weight of chiller units and associated equipment.
The building or plant room structure must be erected to provide weather protection and structural support before chiller plant equipment can be installed.
Water supply lines, drainage, and electrical conduits need to be in place to connect to the chiller plant after installation.
Chilled water supply and return piping can only be connected to the chiller units after the chillers are set in their final position.
Power supply cables, control wiring, and BMS connections to the chiller units can only be terminated after the chillers are installed and positioned.
Refrigerant can only be charged and system pressure tested after the chiller units are installed and all connections are made.
Chiller plant commissioning, operational testing, and balancing can only begin after all mechanical, electrical, and control connections are completed following chiller installation.
Structural steel must be in place to provide support points (hangers, brackets) for chilled water pipes before they can be installed.
The floor/ceiling slab must be cured to provide the structural base for pipe routing and supports; pipes cannot be hung from an incomplete slab.
Insulation must be applied after the pipe is installed and pressure-tested to prevent condensation and thermal loss; insulation cannot precede installation.
Pressure testing must follow pipe installation to verify the integrity and leak-tightness of the installed piping before it is concealed or insulated.

successor: Connection to Air Handling Units (AHUs) / Fan Coil Units (FCUs)
rationale: The main chilled water pipework must be installed before final connections are made to terminal units (AHUs/FCUs) so that the supply/return branches can be tied in.
Hydronic balancing requires the complete hydronic piping system to be installed and connected, as balancing involves adjusting water flow through the pipes.
All terminal units must be in place so that balancing can set the correct flow rates through each unit.
Control valves must be installed as they are the primary devices used to regulate and balance flow in hydronic systems.
The system must be balanced before it can be started up and commissioned, as improper flow will prevent proper system operation and performance verification.

successor: Building Automation System (BAS) Integration and Testing
rationale: BAS integration requires a balanced system to ensure control sequences operate correctly with proper flow conditions.

All system components (pipes, valves, fittings) must be fully installed and connected before flushing and cleaning can begin, as flushing requires a complete closed loop system to circulate cleaning agents and water.
The system must be flushed and cleaned to remove debris, dirt, and contaminants before it can be filled with final operating fluid and chemicals, ensuring the quality of the working medium.
After flushing and cleaning, the system is ready for final inspection, testing, and commissioning to verify cleanliness and readiness for operation.
Flushing and cleaning must be completed before the system is placed into active service to prevent damage to equipment and contamination of the operating environment.

Ductwork must be installed and sealed before refrigerant charging because the HVAC system needs to be fully assembled and airtight to properly hold and distribute conditioned air; refrigerant charging is performed on a completed system.

The indoor unit (evaporator coil/air handler) must be mounted and connected to the refrigerant lines before the system can be charged with refrigerant, as the refrigerant circulates through both indoor and outdoor units.

The outdoor condensing unit (containing the compressor and condenser coil) must be set in place and connected to the refrigerant piping before charging can occur, as it is the other half of the sealed refrigeration circuit.

predecessor: Refrigerant Piping and Line Set Installation
rationale: The refrigerant line sets (copper pipes connecting indoor and outdoor units) must be fully installed, brazed, and insulated before refrigerant can be introduced into the system; charging occurs after the piping loop is complete.

predecessor: Electrical Wiring and Power Connections for HVAC
rationale: Electrical power must be connected to the HVAC equipment to operate the compressor and controls during the charging procedure, and to run the system for leak testing under operating pressure.
After refrigerant is charged and leaks are verified, the HVAC system must be commissioned and tested for proper performance, airflow, temperature differential, and control operations.

successor: Final Insulation and Finish Work Around HVAC Equipment
rationale: While not a physical necessity, it is preferred to complete charging and leak testing before enclosing or finishing around HVAC equipment to ensure all refrigerant connections remain accessible for any corrective work.

The preventive maintenance programme can only commence after all construction activities are complete and the facility is handed over for operations, as maintenance plans are based on the as-built condition of the facility.
All building systems must be commissioned and verified to be operational before a preventive maintenance schedule can be established and executed.

While preventive maintenance extends equipment life, eventual replacement is typically required after the equipment's service life, but this is a soft preference as emergency replacement can occur independently.
The preventive maintenance programme runs concurrently with ongoing building operations to ensure continuous functionality and safety of building systems.
A stable foundation must be prepared before the hydraulic pump can be installed to ensure proper alignment and support for the pump and its mounting.
The hydraulic pump must be physically mounted and secured before hydraulic supply and return lines can be connected to its ports.
The pump must be in its final installed position before the drive motor can be aligned and coupled to the pump shaft.
The pump must be installed and connected before the overall hydraulic system can be pressurized and tested for leaks and performance.
The hydraulic reservoir must be in place and connected so that the pump suction line can draw fluid from it, preventing the pump from running dry.
The hydraulic cylinder requires a stable, level foundation to be properly mounted and aligned; without foundation preparation, the cylinder cannot be securely installed.
The hydraulic cylinder body must be fully fabricated and assembled before it can be installed at the job site.
Hydraulic hoses and pipes can only be connected to the cylinder after it is mounted in its final position.
The full hydraulic system, including the cylinder, must be installed before pressure testing and functional checks can be performed.
While seals are typically installed during cylinder assembly, any external sealing around the mounted cylinder should be done after installation to ensure proper fit.

predecessor: Foundation Preparation and Mounting Structure Installation
rationale: A stable foundation and mounting structure must be in place before the hydraulic motor can be securely installed and aligned.

predecessor: Hydraulic Piping and Hose Routing Preparation
rationale: Hydraulic supply and return lines must be routed to the motor location to enable connection after the motor is mounted.

successor: Hydraulic System Pressure Testing and Commissioning
rationale: The hydraulic motor must be installed and connected before the system can be pressurized, tested for leaks, and commissioned for operation.
The motor must be bolted in place before its shaft can be precisely coupled and aligned with the driven equipment (e.g., pump, conveyor, winch).

While wiring can be run in parallel, final connection of motor speed sensors, feedback devices, and control cables is typically completed after the motor is physically installed to ensure correct routing and avoid damage.

The hydraulic reservoir/tank must be placed on or within the building's structural framework. Steel erection must be completed to provide the necessary support structure and clear space for installation.
The reservoir/tank requires a stable, level foundation or base slab to bear its weight and ensure proper alignment. Foundation work must be completed before tank installation.
The reservoir/tank serves as the source and return point for hydraulic fluid. Piping connections to and from the tank can only be made after the tank is positioned and secured in its final location.
The reservoir must be installed, connected, and secured before it can be filled with hydraulic fluid. Filling and system testing can only commence after installation is complete.
Level sensors, temperature gauges, and control connections to the hydraulic reservoir require the tank to be in place before electrical and control wiring can be run and terminated.
The hydraulic control valve must be connected to the piping system; pipes must be in place before the valve can be installed.
A stable mounting base or support structure is required before the valve can be secured in its position.
The valve must be installed and connected before the system can be pressurized and tested for leaks.
The valve must be physically in place before electrical actuators or control signal cables can be connected to it.
Commissioning activities, including setting valve parameters and verifying operation, can only be performed after the valve is installed.
The directional control valve must be connected to the piping system; pipes and fittings must be installed before the valve can be placed and connected.
The valve requires a stable mounting base or support structure to be in place before it can be securely installed.
Electrical power and control wiring need to be run to the valve location before the valve can be electrically connected and tested.
After the valve is installed, the overall piping system must be pressure tested to verify all connections, including the valve, are leak-free.
The directional control valve must be physically in place before the control system can be calibrated and commissioned with the actual valve in the loop.
Check valves must be installed after the piping system is in place and properly aligned to ensure correct fit and orientation.
Pipe ends must be prepared (threaded, flanged, or welded) before the check valve can be connected to the pipe system.
The piping system must be flushed of debris, dirt, and construction residue before installing the check valve to prevent damage to the valve internals and ensure proper sealing.
The check valve must be installed before the system can be pressure tested, as the valve is part of the sealed piping circuit.
The check valve must be in place before fluid flow is initiated to prevent backflow and protect equipment such as pumps from reverse rotation or water hammer.
A stable foundation or base frame must be in place to support the weight and operational loads of the hydraulic heat exchanger/cooler.
Main hydraulic supply and return piping must be routed to the area before the cooler can be connected into the system.

successor: Hydraulic Fluid Fill and System Pressurization
rationale: The cooler must be fully installed and connected before the hydraulic system can be filled with fluid and pressurized.
The heat exchanger must be in its final position before the cooling water supply and return lines can be connected to its ports.
Leak testing and overall system commissioning can only proceed after the cooler is installed, piped, and connected on both the hydraulic and cooling water sides.

predecessor: Procurement and Delivery of Hydraulic Filter/Strainer
rationale: The filter/strainer must be procured and delivered to the site before it can be physically installed.

successor: Connection of Hydraulic Lines to Filter/Strainer
rationale: The filter/strainer must be mounted in place before hydraulic lines can be connected to it.
The filter/strainer must be installed and connected before the hydraulic system can be pressurized and tested for leaks.
The filter/strainer must be in place before filling the system with hydraulic fluid to ensure fluid is filtered upon initial fill.
The hydraulic fluid reservoir is typically installed before inline filters/ strainers to establish the fluid source pathway.
The pump is usually installed upstream of the filter/strainer to ensure proper flow direction and to protect the filter from pump debris.
The entire hydraulic system including filters must be fully installed before commissioning can begin.
The hydraulic manifold requires a stable, level foundation base to be installed upon before it can be mounted and aligned.
The manifold must be physically installed and secured before any hydraulic lines (hoses/tubes) can be connected to its ports.
Solenoid valves and sensors on the manifold require the manifold to be in place before electrical connections can be terminated.
Pressure testing of the hydraulic system can only commence after the manifold is installed and all lines are connected.
The manifold must be fully assembled and shop-tested for leaks/function before being transported to and installed in its final location.

The hydraulic fitting and connector system requires a stable, level mounting surface to ensure proper alignment and sealing. The foundation and base plates must be in place before any hydraulic components can be installed.

The main hydraulic pipeline routes and conduit pathways must be established before hydraulic fittings and connectors can be integrated, as fittings serve as junction points along these pre-routed lines.
The building's structural steel frame must be erected to provide support brackets, hangers, and attachment points for hydraulic line routing and connector mounting.

Hydraulic cylinders and actuators connect directly to the hydraulic system via fittings and connectors; the fitting network must be complete to provide pressure-tight connections for actuator operation.

successor: Hydraulic Fluid Charging and Pressure Testing
rationale: All hydraulic fittings and connectors must be fully installed and torqued to specification before the system can be charged with fluid and pressure-tested, to prevent leaks and ensure system integrity.

The hydraulic system requires a stable load-bearing foundation and substructure to support heavy equipment like pumps, tanks, and piping. Without completed foundations, the hydraulic components cannot be safely anchored or installed.

The building's main structural frame (columns, beams, roof structure) must be in place to provide overhead support, crane access, and enclosure for hydraulic system installation activities within the facility.

Electrical power supply conduits and cabling for hydraulic pump motors, control panels, and sensors must be roughed in before the hydraulic equipment is positioned, as access behind/under equipment becomes impossible after installation.

successor: Hydraulic Piping Pressure Testing and Commissioning
rationale: After the hydraulic system components (pumps, valves, actuators, piping) are installed, pressure testing and commissioning must be performed to verify system integrity, identify leaks, and ensure operational performance before covering or enclosing the system.

successor: Final Electrical Connections and Control System Integration
rationale: Final electrical termination, control wiring, and PLC/programming integration for the hydraulic system can only commence after mechanical installation is complete, ensuring all components are in place and properly aligned before power is connected.
Pipes must be installed, aligned, and properly connected before pressure testing can be performed to ensure the system is complete and ready for pressurization.
All joints must be fully welded or joined to create a sealed system capable of holding pressure during the test.
Pipe supports, hangers, and anchors must be in place to restrain the pipe against forces generated during pressurization and prevent excessive movement or damage.
Insulation must not be applied until pressure testing is complete to allow visual inspection of joints and components for leaks during the test.
Trenches must not be backfilled until pressure testing is passed, as leaks would be inaccessible for repair if buried.

Hydraulic fluid flushing requires the complete hydraulic system (pipes, fittings, pumps, valves, reservoirs) to be installed and connected first, as flushing is performed to clean the assembled system before operation.

Pressure testing of the hydraulic circuit is typically done before flushing to identify leaks or defects; flushing after pressure testing ensures cleaning is the final step before operational fluid is introduced.
After flushing removes contaminants, the system must be filled with clean, specified hydraulic fluid and commissioned for operation.
Functional testing of the hydraulic system must occur after flushing to ensure the system operates correctly with clean fluid.

It is preferred (though not physically mandatory) that flushing be completed before final area clean-up and handover to avoid re-contamination of the newly flushed system from ongoing construction dust.
The hydraulic system components (pipes, pumps, valves) are often supported by the building's structural steel framework. The structure must be in place before installing hydraulic system components.
All hydraulic pipes, hoses, and tubing must be physically installed and connected before the system can be commissioned and tested for leaks and pressure.
The hydraulic pumps must be installed and connected to the piping system before commissioning can proceed to test pump operation and system flow.
Hydraulic pumps and control valves require electrical power for operation. Electrical systems must be energized and commissioned to provide power for hydraulic system testing.
The hydraulic system must be fully tested, commissioned, and verified operational before it can be handed over to the client or operations team for use.
Detailed performance testing (flow rates, pressure levels, response times) can only be conducted after the hydraulic system has been commissioned and is operational.
While commissioning provides a basis for sign-off, the final inspection and documentation sign-off typically occurs after commissioning is complete to confirm all criteria are met.

The hydraulic system components (pumps, valves, cylinders, piping) are typically mounted on or within the structural frame. A stable, completed structure is required to support and anchor hydraulic equipment before installation or maintenance can proceed.

Hydraulic systems often require electrical power for pump motors, solenoid valves, and control panels. Electrical rough-in (conduit, wiring, and power supply) must be completed to provide the necessary power and control connections for hydraulic system commissioning and testing.

After maintenance work (e.g., replacing seals, filters, or fluids) is completed on the hydraulic system, pressure testing and full system commissioning must be performed to verify that all components are correctly reassembled, leak-free, and operating within design specifications before the system is put into service.

Hydraulic system maintenance may involve sensor recalibration or control valve adjustments. Proper control system programming and calibration can only be finalized after the physical hydraulic components have been maintained and are in known good condition to ensure accurate control logic and feedback.

Once hydraulic system maintenance (including component replacement or repair) is complete, the system must be refilled with the appropriate hydraulic fluid and air must be bled from the lines to remove trapped air pockets, ensuring proper system operation and preventing cavitation damage.
The roof structure must be complete and capable of bearing the weight of solar panels before installation can begin.
Waterproofing must be applied to the roof to prevent water ingress; solar panels are typically mounted on top of the waterproof membrane.
Electrical conduits, wiring pathways, and junction boxes must be pre-installed and routed to the roof area to connect the solar panels to the inverter and electrical system.
Solar panels must be physically installed and wired before the inverter can be connected and the photovoltaic system commissioned.
The solar array must be fully installed and connected before the entire photovoltaic system can be tested and commissioned for operation.

Thin-film PV modules require a stable mounting surface. The structural framing (e.g., roof racking or building-integrated structure) must be installed first to provide physical support and load-bearing capability for the PV modules.

Electrical conduits, junction boxes, and wiring infrastructure must be in place before modules are installed so that interconnections can be made efficiently and safely, and to avoid rework or unsafe access after modules are in position.

Once thin-film modules are physically installed and mechanically secured, their electrical leads must be terminated and connected to inverters/combiner boxes to complete the circuit and allow the system to generate power.

Commissioning (including insulation resistance testing, I-V curve tracing, and functional checks) can only proceed after all modules are installed and electrically connected, ensuring the complete system is tested as an integrated whole.
The site must be cleared, graded, and leveled, and foundations (if ground-mounted) or roof deck must be ready before any mounting structure or module installation can begin.
The roof structure must be in place to support the solar panels that connect to the inverter.
Solar panels must be installed to generate DC power before the inverter can convert it to AC power.
Electrical conduits and wiring from the solar panels must be run to the inverter location before the inverter can be connected.
The inverter's AC output must be connected to the main electrical panel to supply power to the building.
The inverter must be installed and wired before the entire solar PV system can be commissioned and tested for operation.
Microinverters are typically installed as part of or after solar panel mounting, as they connect directly to the panels.
The mounting structure must be in place to support both the solar panels and the microinverters before microinverters can be attached.
Electrical conduits and AC wiring pathways need to be prepared to connect microinverters to the electrical panel.
Microinverters output AC power that must be combined and routed through the AC combiner box before reaching the main electrical panel.
The microinverters must be fully installed and connected before the overall solar PV system can be commissioned, tested, and energized.
A stable foundation and structural support must be in place before mounting or installing power optimizers, as they are typically attached to structures such as rooftops or mounting frames.
Power optimizers are often integrated with or mounted near solar panels/racking systems, so the mounting structure must be ready to support the optimizer placement.

Power optimizers are typically connected directly to individual solar panels to perform DC-DC conversion and maximum power point tracking (MPPT), so they must be installed prior to or concurrently with panel placement.
Power optimizers feed conditioned DC power to the inverter; the inverter system cannot be fully commissioned until the optimizers are installed and connected to provide proper input voltage.
The DC power cables from power optimizers must be routed after the optimizers are mounted, as the wiring connects directly from the optimizers to the combiner box or inverter.
Charge controller must be connected to PV panels; panels must be mounted and wired first to provide the input source for the charge controller.
The structural support for PV panels and associated mounting must be in place before routing wires to the charge controller location.

predecessor: Run Conduit from PV Array to Controller Location
rationale: Conduit and wire routing must be pre-installed to bring PV input to the charge controller before it can be connected.

successor: Connect Battery Bank to Charge Controller
rationale: Charge controller must be physically mounted and wired before batteries can be connected to it; connecting batteries first could damage the controller.
The DC output from the charge controller must be established before the inverter can receive DC input from the battery/controller system.
Controller must be physically installed and powered on before its operating parameters (battery type, voltage setpoints) can be programmed.
The charge controller must be fully installed and configured before the overall PV system can be tested and commissioned for operation.
The ground or roof surface must be cleared, leveled, and graded before racking installation to provide a stable, even foundation and to avoid structural instability.
Foundations such as concrete piers, helical piles, or ground screws must be installed and cured first to bear the load of the racking system and transfer forces to the ground.

Underground conduits for DC and AC cabling, as well as grounding conductors, must be laid before racking installation to avoid digging or trenching after the racking is in place, which could undermine structural supports.
PV modules are physically attached to and supported by the racking system; racking must be fully assembled and secured before modules can be mounted.

successor: DC String Wiring & Combiner Box Installation
rationale: After racking is installed, PV modules are placed onto the racks, and then DC string wiring can be routed along the racking rails and connected to combiner boxes; wiring cannot be properly secured without the racking structure in place.

The roof must be structurally evaluated and prepared (cleaned, inspected, and load-rated) before installing a ballasted mounting system, as the ballast adds significant weight that the roof must be able to support.
The waterproof membrane must be fully installed and cured before placing ballasted mounts on the roof to avoid damaging the waterproofing layer and to ensure watertight integrity.

successor: Solar Panel Installation on Mounting System
rationale: The mounting system must be fully positioned and ballasted before solar panels can be securely attached to the rails or brackets.

While some cable trays can be pre-run, final cable connections to the panels and routing through the mounting structure should occur after the mounting system is in place to ensure proper alignment and strain relief.

Completion of the mounting system installation is a prerequisite for the final inspection and commissioning of the solar array, as the panels and electrical connections rely on the mounting structure being secure.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and compacted before any support structures can be installed to ensure stability and proper alignment.
Soil bearing capacity and ground conditions must be evaluated to determine the foundation type and depth required for the PV support structure.
While structure installation can begin before interconnection is finalized, the overall project schedule typically requires utility approval before full array commissioning.
The mounting racks or frames must be fully erected and secured before solar panels can be placed and attached onto them.
Cable trays are often integrated with the structure, but some wiring can be run after modules are installed; installing trays after structure erection is more efficient.

successor: Install DC Combiner Box Internal Components
rationale: The enclosure must be mounted and secured in place before internal components (busbars, fuses, surge protection devices, wiring) can be installed inside it.

predecessor: Install PV Panel Array and Run DC Cables to Combiner Box Location
successor: Terminate PV String Circuits at DC Combiner Box
rationale: PV panels must be installed and the DC cables routed to the combiner box location before those string circuits can be terminated inside the box.

predecessor: Mount and Enclose DC Combiner Box
successor: Terminate PV String Circuits at DC Combiner Box
rationale: The combiner box must be mounted and its enclosure closed/ready before conductors can be landed on the internal terminals.

predecessor: Install DC Combiner Box (Complete, Including All Terminations and Internal Wiring)
successor: Commission and Test DC Side of PV System
rationale: All DC circuits must be fully terminated and the combiner box complete before commissioning and testing (e.g., insulation resistance testing, string voltage/current verification) can be performed.

successor: Connect DC Combiner Box Output to Inverter DC Input
rationale: The combiner box must be fully installed and its output circuit ready before the connection to the inverter's DC input can be made to ensure safe and orderly power flow.

successor: AC Distribution Board / PV Sub-Panel Installation
rationale: The main AC distribution board must be installed and energized first to provide the primary power distribution point from which the PV sub-panel can be fed.

successor: AC Distribution Board / PV Sub-Panel Installation
rationale: The PV inverter output must be wired to the AC distribution board / PV sub-panel, so the inverter must be physically installed and positioned before the sub-panel is connected.

successor: AC Distribution Board / PV Sub-Panel Installation
rationale: Conduits and cable trays serving the sub-panel location must be in place to route incoming and outgoing cables before the sub-panel is mounted and wired.

predecessor: AC Distribution Board / PV Sub-Panel Installation
rationale: The PV sub-panel must be fully installed, wired, and terminated before the overall PV system can be commissioned, tested, and energized.

predecessor: AC Distribution Board / PV Sub-Panel Installation
successor: Branch Circuit Wiring and Load Connections
rationale: Individual branch circuits (e.g., to loads or downstream equipment) can only be wired and terminated after the sub-panel is mounted and its bus bars are ready to accept circuit breakers and conductors.
Permits and utility coordination must be completed before meter installation can begin to comply with regulations and ensure safe grid connection.

predecessor: Electrical Panel and Main Service Installation
rationale: The main electrical service panel must be installed to provide the termination point for the bi-directional meter's electrical connections.

predecessor: Solar PV or Battery System Installation
rationale: The bi-directional meter measures energy flow to/from the renewable energy system; thus the generating/storage system must be in place before the meter can be commissioned.
After the meter is physically installed, the utility company must inspect and approve the installation before officially connecting to the grid.

successor: System Commissioning and Net Metering Activation
rationale: The bi-directional meter must be installed and operational before the net metering program can be activated and the overall renewable energy system can be commissioned.
PV modules must be installed and mounted on racking before DC cables can be connected to the modules.
The racking/mounting system provides the physical support and cable management pathways; conduit and cabling runs are typically laid on or alongside racking before modules are fully wired.
DC cabling from modules must be run and terminated at the inverter input before the inverter can be electrically connected and energized.
DC conductor strings must be pulled and landed in the combiner or junction box before that enclosure can be closed, labeled, and tested.
Underground conduits must be trenched and placed before DC cables can be pulled through them, ensuring the physical raceway is ready.

The RSD must be wired and integrated with the solar panel array. Solar panels must be mounted first so that the RSD can be connected to the panel output circuits to enable rapid shutdown functionality.

The RSD is typically placed between the solar panels and the inverter. It must be installed and wired before the inverter is connected, as the RSD provides the shutdown signal path from the inverter/controller to the panels.
The RSD must be physically installed and electrically connected before the system can be energized and tested, because the RSD is a safety device that must be operational prior to any live testing.
The RSD unit requires a mounting bracket or enclosure to be secured in place before the device itself can be installed and wired.
The RSD must be fully installed, wired, and verified before the overall PV system commissioning can proceed, as rapid shutdown is a code-required safety feature (NEC 690.12).
The building structure must be analyzed and confirmed to support the additional weight of PV panels before designing the PV system layout and mounting configuration.
Permit approval establishes allowable design parameters, setbacks, and code requirements that directly inform the PV system design.
The PV system design determines the electrical capacity, inverter specifications, and interconnection requirements needed for electrical upgrades.
The finalized design specifies exact panel types, quantities, and specifications required for procurement.
The PV design defines mounting locations, penetration points, and layout that guide roof preparation work before installation.
PV panels must be installed on a structurally complete roof to provide a stable mounting surface and ensure load-bearing capacity.
Waterproofing must be completed before PV installation to prevent water ingress behind the panels and protect the building envelope.
PV panels must be physically installed before they can be electrically wired to the inverter and the building's electrical system.
The PV system must be fully installed before it can be tested, commissioned, and connected to the grid.
Safe access such as scaffolding or roof anchors must be in place before workers can perform rooftop PV installation.

The building structure must be in place to provide support for electrical conduits, junction boxes, and wiring runs; rough-in wiring cannot begin until walls, ceilings, and structural framing are complete.
Underground conduit runs and grounding systems must be laid in the foundation/slab before above-grade electrical wiring can proceed.
Electrical wiring must be completed and inspected before walls are closed up with drywall and interior finishes are applied; wiring behind walls becomes inaccessible after finishing.
Switches, outlets, and light fixtures cannot be installed until the wiring and connections (both DC and AC) are run to their respective locations.
The inverter and main electrical panel connections require completed wiring from solar arrays and building circuits before they can be energized and commissioned.
Conduit and wiring must be physically installed before inverters and batteries can be energized and commissioned, as they provide the electrical pathways required for commissioning activities.
Inverters must be physically mounted and connected before they can be powered on and undergo commissioning tests.
Battery racks must be assembled and positioned before batteries can be connected and commissioned as a system.

predecessor: DC & AC Cable Termination at Inverter
rationale: All DC and AC power cables must be terminated at the inverter terminals before the inverter can be safely energized for commissioning.

successor: System Performance Testing & Load Bank Test
rationale: Commissioning verifies that each inverter and battery unit operates correctly before the entire system can be performance-tested under load.
Commissioned inverters and batteries must be operational before they can be integrated into the monitoring and control system for remote supervision.
Inverters must be individually commissioned and verified before the system can be synchronized and connected to the utility grid.
The site must be cleared, graded, and prepared before utility inspections can occur, as inspectors need access to the prepared site to assess grid connection points.
Underground conduits, ducts, and utility runs must be installed before the grid connection inspection can verify their placement and readiness for connection.
Foundations for transformers, switchgear, and other grid equipment must be completed and cured before inspectors can verify positioning and connections.
The grid connection must be inspected and approved before internal electrical wiring and systems can be safely connected to the external utility supply.
Transformers and switchgear can only be connected and energized after the utility inspection has confirmed the grid connection point is compliant and safe.

While not a physical dependency, completing the building enclosure before or alongside utility inspection allows for coordinated weatherproofing of utility entry points, though the inspection can technically occur before full enclosure.
The PV system must be installed and operational before any operation and maintenance activities such as cleaning and inspection can be performed.
Grid connection must be completed to ensure the PV system is energized and functional, allowing O&M activities to verify performance and safety.
Commissioning and testing must be completed to confirm the system is properly configured and safe before routine O&M begins.
Cleaning and inspection activities directly affect system performance; performance data should be reviewed after O&M to assess the effectiveness of the work and detect any issues.

successor: PV System Repairs and Component Replacement
rationale: Inspection may identify defects or damage that require repair or replacement; these corrective actions naturally follow O&M inspection findings, though in some cases repairs could be scheduled concurrently.
PV modules must be installed and operational before they can be decommissioned and recycled. Decommissioning only occurs at the end of a module's useful life.
The operational phase (including ongoing maintenance) must occur before decommissioning, as decommissioning is the end-of-life process that follows the service life of the PV modules.
Final performance testing and inspection may be conducted prior to decommissioning to assess end-of-life status, but this is a procedural preference rather than a physical necessity.
After modules are removed and recycled, the site must be restored or remediated to its original condition or prepared for new use.
Non-recyclable waste materials generated during decommissioning must be disposed of properly after the decommissioning and recycling process is complete.
Corridor wall framing must be completed before the ceiling can be installed, as the ceiling typically bears on or ties into the top plates of the walls.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work (ductwork, conduit, piping) within the ceiling plenum must be completed before the ceiling is closed in.
The ceiling surface must be fully installed before any finishing work like painting or texturing can be applied.
Although flooring can sometimes be installed after the ceiling, it is preferred to complete the ceiling first to avoid dust and debris falling onto the finished floor surface.
Ceiling-mounted lighting fixtures can only be installed once the ceiling structure (e.g., grid or drywall) is in place to support and house them.
The door frame must be installed and secured in the wall opening before the door leaf can be hung on its hinges.
The door leaf must be hung in place before locks, handles, closers, and other hardware can be installed onto it.
It is a soft preference to complete floor finishes before door installation to avoid damaging finished floors, but doors can be installed afterward with protective measures.
The corridor door must be installed and adjusted before any final painting, caulking, or trim finishing around the door frame can be completed.
The corridor walls must be framed and the drywall installed (or at least roughed in) to define the door opening for the door frame to be placed.

Skirting boards are installed against finished walls. Plastering, sanding, and painting must be completed first to ensure a clean, flush fit and to avoid damaging the finished wall surface during skirting installation.

Floor coverings such as tiles, timber, or vinyl must be laid before skirting is installed, as the skirting covers the expansion gap at the wall-floor junction and sits on top of the finished floor surface for a neat finish.
Once skirting boards are installed, they need to be filled, sanded, and painted (or touched up) to match the wall finish, which is a finishing trade activity.

While electrical faceplates can be installed before skirting, it is common practice to fit them after skirting is in place so that the skirting butts neatly against the switch/socket plates for a professional appearance.
Framing provides the structural backing and mounting surface for signage installation.
Walls must be closed and MEP rough-ins completed before signage can be mounted on finished surfaces.
Final paint and wall finishes must be applied before signage installation to avoid damage and ensure clean mounting.
Signage must be installed and properly displayed before final inspection can verify compliance with wayfinding and safety signage requirements.
Signage, including exit signs and room labels, must be in place before the corridor can be occupied or commissioned for use.
Corridor partition walls are typically non-structural or semi-structural interior walls that are built on top of the finished floor slab. The floor must be poured and cured to provide a stable base.
The main structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) must be completed first so the corridor partition walls can be aligned and tied into the structure.

successor: MEP Rough-In (Electrical / Plumbing / HVAC in Corridor)
rationale: Corridor partition wall framing provides the chase and cavities for electrical conduits, plumbing pipes, and ductwork. MEP rough-in must follow wall erection before the wall is enclosed.
The partition wall framing must be fully erected and inspected before drywall or cladding can be applied to the wall surfaces.
Corridor partition walls provide the structural support for door frames; door frames can only be installed after the wall framing is in place.
The corridor structure requires a stable foundation to bear loads; without completed foundation works, corridor construction cannot proceed safely or structurally.
Corridors are often integrated with the main structural frame; the steel or concrete frame must be erected first to provide support and attachment points for corridor elements.
Electrical conduits and wiring are typically run within corridor ceilings, walls, or floor trenches; these installations must follow the corridor structure to be properly embedded or concealed.

Plumbing lines serving rooms off the corridor (e.g., fire sprinkler mains, restroom supply lines) are often routed through corridor spaces and must be installed after the corridor structure is in place.
Suspended ceilings in corridors are installed after the corridor structure, framing, and MEP rough-ins are complete; the corridor must be built first to provide the support grid and enclosure.

All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work must be completed before floor finishes are installed, as these systems run beneath the subfloor or within floor assemblies, and accessing them after flooring is installed would require demolition.

The subfloor must be cleaned, leveled, and properly prepared (including moisture mitigation if needed) to provide a sound base for the floor finish; installing on an unprepared subfloor will lead to premature failure.
Wall framing must be complete so that floor finishes can run continuously wall-to-wall without interruption; it also avoids damaging finished flooring during wall construction.
Floor finishes are typically installed before wall finishes to allow baseboards and trim to overlap the flooring cleanly, and to prevent damage to wall finishes during flooring installation.

After floor finishes are installed, final cleaning and punch-list work can proceed; this is a soft preference as some cleaning can be done concurrently but optimal sequencing protects the finished floor.
Steel stud framing must be complete to provide the wall cavities and support structure for running MEP conduits, piping, and boxes within the corridor walls.
While corridor MEP rough-in can start after main area above-ceiling rough-in is done to allow continuous workflow, some overlap is possible with proper coordination.
All MEP rough-in work within corridor walls must be completed and inspected before drywall can be installed to avoid costly rework and ensure code compliance.
Corridor MEP rough-in (including conduits, piping, and ducts above ceiling) must be finished before ceiling grid is hung to allow access for installation and inspection.
Rough-in work such as pulling wire, running conduit, and placing junction boxes must precede final trim-out activities like installing outlets, switches, and light fixtures.
Paint cannot be applied to unfinished drywall; the drywall must be taped, mudded, and sanded smooth before painting can begin.
A primer coat must be applied and dried before the final decorative paint can be applied to ensure proper adhesion and uniform color.
Ceilings are typically painted before walls to avoid dripping paint onto finished wall surfaces, but ceiling installation itself must be complete before any painting of the ceiling.
Painting must be completed before flooring is installed to prevent paint drips, spills, and dust from damaging finished floors.
After painting is complete, a final cleaning is needed to remove paint splatters, tape, and debris before occupancy or subsequent finish work.
Stair flights require stable support from the building's substructure. Foundation and ground floor slab must be completed before stair flights can be installed, as stairs bear on the structure below.
The lower end of the stair flight lands on or is supported by the ground floor slab/deck, which must be in place before stair installation.

In typical construction, stair flights are placed as part of vertical circulation before the upper floor slab is fully completed, or the upper slab must at minimum have its formwork and reinforcement ready to receive the stair connection.
Handrails and balustrades are installed after the stair flight structure is in place, as they attach directly to the stair stringers or steps.
Finish materials such as treads, risers, tile, or carpet are applied after the structural stair flight is erected and secured.
Stairwell enclosure walls require a stable load-bearing base; the foundation or slab must be completed first to support the wall.

predecessor: Rough-In Electrical and Plumbing for Stairwell Area
rationale: Underslab or in-wall mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-ins that pass through or under the stairwell area must be installed before the wall is built to avoid rework and access issues.
Stair stringers and stairs are typically anchored to or supported by the enclosure walls; the walls must be in place to provide bearing and attachment points.
Fireproofing spray or board application is applied to the completed wall surface; the wall must be fully erected and cured before fireproofing can be installed.
Door frames are installed into the rough openings of the completed stairwell enclosure walls; the walls must exist to receive door frames.
Excavation and foundation works must be completed to provide a stable structural base for stairwell construction, ensuring proper load distribution and structural integrity.
The ground slab or base slab must be cast and cured before stairwell walls and formwork can be erected, as the stairwell rests on and transfers loads to the base slab.
Formwork and reinforcement installation for the stairwell must be completed and inspected before concrete can be poured into the forms.

Stairwell formwork erection typically precedes or occurs concurrently with reinforcement steel fixing, but logically the formwork framework must be in place to support and position the reinforcement bars.
Stairwell construction is often a critical path activity; adjacent vertical elements may depend on stairwell completion for alignment and sequencing, though this can vary by design.
Balustrades and handrails are typically mounted onto structural framing or decking surfaces, which must be complete to provide the physical support structure.
Handrails for stairs must be installed after the staircase structure is in place, as the stairs provide the mounting points and the handrail follows the stair slope.
For balustrades on decks or balconies, the subfloor or deck surface must be installed first to provide the base for anchoring balustrade posts.
Handrails along walls are often installed before final painting to allow for any patching or touch-ups around the brackets, though this is a soft preference as painting could be done first.

While some balustrades are installed before finished flooring (to allow post bases to be hidden under flooring), typically the finished flooring around the post bases is completed after the balustrade is installed to achieve a clean finish.
Fire doors must be fitted into prepared door frames that are already securely installed in the wall opening.
Walls and partitions must be completed and cured to provide the proper structural opening and fire-rated enclosure for the fire door assembly.

successor: Fire Door Hardware Installation (Hinges, Closers, Locks, Panic Bars)
rationale: All hardware (hinges, door closers, locks, panic bars, signage) must be installed onto the fire door after the door leaf is hung in the frame.
Final inspection, gap measurement, and functional testing (self-closing, latching) can only be performed after the fire door and its hardware are fully installed.
Fire-rated sealant and intumescent materials around the frame perimeter must be applied after the door and frame are in place to ensure a continuous fire barrier.
Fire-resistant materials such as fire-rated drywall, firestops, and intumescent coatings must be installed before inspection can verify their proper placement and rating.
Electrical rough-in work must be completed and covered by fire-rated assemblies before the inspection can verify fire separation integrity.
Fire dampers in HVAC ducts must be installed and properly rated before the inspection can confirm compliance with fire code requirements.
Ceiling and wall cavities must remain open and accessible for the fire rating inspection to verify firestopping and compartmentation; only after passing inspection can they be closed.

successor: Obtain Fire Safety Certificate / Occupancy Permit
rationale: The fire rating compliance inspection must be passed before the authority having jurisdiction can issue a fire safety certificate or occupancy permit.
Stairwell finishing (plastering, painting, flooring, handrails) requires the structural concrete/steel staircase and landings to be fully constructed and cured before any finishing trades can begin.

Electrical conduits, junction boxes, lighting wiring, fire alarm devices, and plumbing pipes within the stairwell must be installed and rough-in inspections passed before walls and ceilings are closed up with finishes.
All through-penetration firestopping, smoke seals, and any waterproofing at stairwell exterior walls must be completed before final finishes are applied to ensure fire safety and moisture protection.

Handrails and guardrails are typically installed after wall and ceiling finishes are complete to avoid damaging finished surfaces during rail installation, and to ensure proper alignment with finished floor levels.

While generally the stairwell should be protected and cleaned after finishing, some touch-up cleaning can be done concurrently; however full final clean is preferred after all finishing is complete to avoid re-soiling.
Structural framing and concrete must be completed to provide the physical substrate and spaces (walls, floors, ceilings) into which mechanical and electrical rough-in work is installed.

Fireproofing must be applied to structural elements before rough-in to avoid damage to mechanical/electrical components and because fireproofing often coats surfaces that MEP rough-in would otherwise obstruct.

Rough-in of conduits, piping, ductwork, and junction boxes must be completed before walls and ceilings are enclosed, otherwise the MEP systems would be inaccessible and cannot be inspected or connected.
Rough-in work must be finished in order to be inspected by the authority having jurisdiction before any concealment work proceeds.
MEP rough-in must be in place and inspected before insulation is installed around pipes and ducts or within wall cavities, as insulation would conceal and impede access to rough-in work.

The concrete stairwell structure must be fully poured, cured, and finished to provide a stable substrate for waterproofing membrane application. Waterproofing cannot be applied to an incomplete or uncured concrete surface.

The stairwell surfaces must be cleaned of debris, dust, and laitance, and any cracks or defects repaired before waterproofing can be applied to ensure proper adhesion and a continuous watertight barrier.

Backfilling against the stairwell exterior walls can only proceed after the waterproofing membrane is fully installed and cured, as the backfill material would otherwise damage the exposed membrane or prevent its application.

successor: Stairwell Drainage Board / Protection Board Installation
rationale: Drainage boards and protective layers are installed directly over the waterproofing membrane to shield it from damage during backfilling and to facilitate groundwater drainage. These cannot be installed before the waterproofing is in place.

Waterproofing of external stairwell walls must be completed before interior finishing works begin to prevent moisture ingress that would damage interior finishes, and to avoid concurrent wet trades that could compromise the waterproofing system.

The heat exchanger requires a stable, load-bearing foundation or support structure (e.g., concrete pads or steel frames) to be installed first, so that the heavy equipment can be safely placed and anchored.
In many industrial plants, the heat exchanger is mounted on structural steel racks or platforms; these must be erected before the heat exchanger can be lifted into position.
Process pipes (inlet/outlet for hot and cold fluids) can only be connected once the heat exchanger is set in its final location and properly secured.
For shell-and-tube heat exchangers where the tube bundle is removable, the shell must first be placed and then the tube bundle inserted; this is a physically required sequence.

Thermal insulation is typically applied after the heat exchanger is in place and all connections are made; this is a strong preference for quality and safety, but in some modular builds insulation could be partially pre-applied.
The buffer vessel requires a stable, load-bearing foundation (typically concrete) that must be fully cured to support the weight of the vessel without settling or cracking.
The buffer vessel is often mounted on structural steel supports or skirts; these supports must be erected, aligned, and welded/bolted before the vessel can be placed.
Inlet, outlet, vent, drain, and instrument piping cannot be connected until the vessel is set in its final position and securely anchored.
Level transmitters, pressure gauges, and other field instruments mounted on or near the vessel can only be installed after the vessel is in place to ensure correct positioning and alignment.
Pressure testing of the vessel and its connected piping system must occur after the vessel is installed and all connections are made, to verify integrity before commissioning.
The pressurisation unit requires a stable, cured concrete base to be properly mounted and anchored. Installing on uncured concrete would compromise alignment and structural integrity.
The pressurisation unit must have the main water supply line available to be connected to its inlet. Without the water supply, the unit cannot be commissioned or tested.
The pressurisation unit requires electrical connections for its pump motor and control panel. Electrical conduits and cabling must be in place before the unit can be wired and energised.
The outgoing pipework from the pressurisation unit to the building's boosted water distribution network can only be connected after the unit is securely in its final position.

The control system (pressure switches, variable speed drives, BMS interface) can only be commissioned and tested after the pressurisation unit is installed and all mechanical/electrical connections are made.
The expansion vessel must be secured to a mounting bracket or support structure before it can be properly positioned and fastened in place.
The connecting pipework must be in place and prepared to receive the expansion vessel connections.
The expansion vessel must be installed and connected before the complete system can be pressure tested to ensure integrity.
The vessel must be in place before the system can be filled with water/fluid and commissioned, as the expansion vessel plays a critical role in accommodating thermal expansion.
Insulation work around the vessel area is typically done after installation to avoid obstructing access, though it could theoretically be done beforehand in sections.
Structural steel framework must be in place to provide support and mounting points for the circulating pump.
A concrete foundation or pad is required to provide a stable base for the circulating pump to rest upon and anchor to.
The connecting piping (suction and discharge lines) must be roughed-in and accessible so the pump can be installed and connected to the system.
The pump must be set in place and aligned before final connections to suction and discharge piping can be made.
The pump motor must be physically installed before electrical power wiring and control connections can be completed.
The pump must be installed and connected to the piping system before the entire system can be pressure-tested for leaks.

predecessor: Domestic Hot Water Calorifier foundation/support structure installation
rationale: The calorifier requires a level, load-bearing foundation or supports to be installed first to carry its weight safely.
Hot and cold water pipework connections cannot be made until the calorifier is in its final position.
Insulation must be applied after the calorifier is installed and before it is fully enclosed or commissioned.

successor: Electrical and control wiring to calorifier
rationale: Temperature sensors, thermostats, and any electric immersion heater connections require the calorifier to be in place.

predecessor: Domestic Hot Water Calorifier installation and pipework completion
rationale: The entire hot water system including the calorifier must be fully connected before pressure testing and commissioning can begin.
The cold water storage tank must be placed on a structurally sound, level concrete base or foundation that can support its weight when full of water.
If the tank is to be installed on an elevated platform or roof, the supporting steel structure must be erected first to provide a mounting surface.
Inlet, outlet, overflow, and drain pipes can only be connected once the tank is positioned and secured in its final location.
Thermal insulation or cladding is applied after the tank is in place to ensure full coverage and access to all surfaces.

successor: Testing & Commissioning of Water Supply System
rationale: Water supply system testing (fill test, pressure test, leak detection) can only commence once the tank is installed and all connections are made.
Plumbing rough-in work (e.g., supply and drain lines) must be completed before the water softener/treatment unit can be connected and installed.
Electrical rough-in work (e.g., wiring and outlet installation) must be completed to provide power for the water treatment unit's controls and valves.
The water softener/treatment unit must be installed and operational before final plumbing fixture connections are made, so that treated water is available to downstream fixtures.
The unit must be fully installed before water quality testing can be performed to verify the system is functioning correctly.
A level concrete slab or equipment pad must be in place to provide a stable, load-bearing foundation for the water softener/treatment unit.
Electrical ducting must be installed first to provide the pathways for cables that will connect to the MDB.
A solid foundation or concrete slab is required to mount the MDB securely and safely.
The MDB must be installed and mounted before cables can be pulled and terminated into its busbars and breakers.
Sub-distribution boards receive feeder power from the MDB, so the MDB must be in place to supply them.
Testing such as insulation resistance and trip testing can only be performed once the MDB is fully installed and connected.
Conduits and electrical pathways must be installed and routed to the UPS location before the UPS unit can be placed and connected.
The UPS requires a dedicated area with proper ventilation, temperature control, and battery room infrastructure before installation can begin.

predecessor: Concrete Floor Slab / Equipment Pad Pouring
rationale: The UPS is heavy and requires a level, load-bearing concrete floor or equipment pad to be cured and ready before the unit can be set in place.

successor: UPS Battery Bank Installation and Connection
rationale: The main UPS cabinet must be positioned and anchored before heavy battery banks can be installed and connected to the UPS internals.

successor: Electrical Final Connection and UPS Commissioning
rationale: Power cables, control wiring, and load connections to the UPS can only be finalized after the UPS unit is installed and secured.
BMS panels require power supply and control wiring pathways. Electrical conduits and rough-in wiring must be installed before the BMS panel can be mounted and connected.

successor: BMS Field Device Wiring and Termination
rationale: The BMS panel serves as the central hub for control and monitoring. Field devices (sensors, actuators, controllers) must be wired back to the panel after it is installed and terminated.
System commissioning, which includes powering up the panel, configuring controllers, and verifying communication, can only occur after the panel is physically installed and all connections are made.

predecessor: BMS Panel Enclosure and Backboard Mounting Preparation
rationale: The mounting surface (backboard, wall frame, or enclosure) must be prepared and installed prior to mounting the BMS panel to ensure secure attachment and proper alignment.
Network cabling (BACnet, Modbus, Ethernet) from the panel to the building's automation network and head-end server can only be fully connected and configured after the panel is installed.
The fuel oil storage tank requires a stable, level concrete foundation to bear its weight and prevent settling or structural failure.
Underground utilities (piping, conduits) and any secondary containment systems must be installed before placing the tank to avoid excavation damage to the tank and to ensure proper connections.
Piping, fill lines, vent lines, and fuel supply connections to the tank can only be installed after the tank is positioned and secured in place.

successor: Secondary Containment Testing / Tank Integrity Testing
rationale: Integrity testing and leak testing of the tank and its containment system must be performed after the tank is installed but before backfilling or enclosing it.
Backfilling around the tank and final grading can only proceed once the tank is installed, secured, and all connections are made.
