The hydraulic header/manifold is typically mounted on or supported by the structural steel frame. The steel structure must be in place to provide the necessary support and anchorage for the manifold assembly.
The hydraulic header/manifold often sits on a concrete foundation or base slab. The foundation must be cured and ready to bear the load and allow for anchoring of the manifold.

successor: Hydraulic Piping / Tubing Connection to Manifold
rationale: The hydraulic header/manifold must be installed and fixed in position before any hydraulic pipes or tubing can be connected to its ports, as the manifold serves as the central distribution point.

The manifold must be in place to receive and distribute hydraulic fluid from the pump system. Commissioning of the pump system typically requires all distribution components including the manifold to be installed.

successor: Hydraulic System Pressure Testing and Flushing
rationale: All hydraulic components including the manifold must be installed and connected before the system can be pressure tested and flushed to remove debris and verify integrity.
Valves must be installed into the piping system after the pipes are routed and in place, as valves are inline components that connect to pipe flanges or welded ends.
Valves require stable support or mounting structures (e.g., valve stands, concrete pads, steel supports) to bear their weight and operational loads before they can be installed.
The piping system must be fully assembled with all valves installed before hydrostatic or pneumatic pressure testing can be performed to verify system integrity and leak-tightness.
Actuators (electric, pneumatic, or hydraulic) are mounted onto control valves after the valve body is installed, and then calibrated for proper stroke and positioning.
After valves are installed, the completed piping system can be flushed to remove debris, weld slag, and contaminants that could damage valve seats and sealing surfaces.
The electrical panel must be installed to provide the connection point and circuit protection for the energy meter array.
The main service conduit must be in place to route the electrical feed from the utility to the meter array location.
The mounting bracket or enclosure for the meter array must be installed first to physically support the meters.
The energy meter array must be installed before current transformers can be wired to the meters for accurate current sensing.
The meters must be physically installed before they can be calibrated, tested, and commissioned for operation.
The structural frame must be complete to provide support and enclosure for the flue and exhaust components.
Flue and exhaust ducts typically penetrate the roof; the roof structure must be in place to allow proper flashing and weatherproofing around flue terminations.
Fireproofing must be applied over the flue and exhaust components to ensure fire-rated enclosures meet code requirements.
Flue and exhaust ductwork must be installed and tested before enclosing them within finished ceilings and walls to allow access for inspections and repairs.
Flue and exhaust system must be fully installed and connected before the overall mechanical system can be commissioned and tested for proper airflow and emissions.
The plant room must be structurally complete (walls, floor, roof) before any commissioning activities can begin to ensure a safe and enclosed environment.
All mechanical and electrical rough-in work (pipework, ductwork, cable trays, conduits) must be installed before commissioning to allow testing of systems.
All major plant equipment (boilers, chillers, pumps, air handling units, electrical panels) must be physically installed and connected before commissioning can commence.
Commissioning must be successfully completed and signed off before the plant room can be handed over to the client or operations team for use.

While not strictly required as a hard constraint, it is strongly preferred that plant room commissioning precedes building-wide systems integration testing to verify individual plant performance before full system integration.
Structural framing (columns, beams, slabs) provides the physical support and enclosure for M&E systems. Ducts, conduits, pipes, and cables cannot be installed until the structural frame is in place.
Roofing and waterproofing must be completed to protect the building interior and M&E equipment from weather damage before sensitive M&E installations begin.
M&E services (ductwork, piping, conduits, cables) must be installed and tested in ceiling voids before ceilings are closed up, as they would be inaccessible afterward.
M&E rough-in work within walls (conduits, wiring, pipes) must be completed before walls are finished with plasterboard or plaster to allow access for installation and inspection.
Underfloor M&E services (conduits, heating pipes, cables) must be laid and tested before floor screeds or finishes are applied over them.

successor: Plant Room Fit-Out and Builder's Work
rationale: The plant room must be structurally complete (walls, slab, roof) before any fit-out and builder's work can commence, as the structural shell provides the enclosure and load-bearing capacity required for installing plant equipment, partitions, and finishes.

successor: Plant Room Fit-Out and Builder's Work
rationale: Waterproofing must be completed to prevent moisture ingress that would damage plant equipment, electrical installations, and builder's finishes during and after fit-out.

predecessor: Plant Room Fit-Out and Builder's Work
rationale: Builder's work such as plinths, chases, floor screeds, and wall finishes must be completed before heavy MEP plant equipment (chillers, boilers, pumps, AHUs) is installed, to avoid damage to finishes and to provide the prepared surfaces and supports for equipment mounting.

predecessor: Plant Room Fit-Out and Builder's Work
successor: Electrical and Plumbing Rough-In in Plant Room
rationale: Builder's work including wall and floor preparation must be completed before electrical conduits, cables, and plumbing pipework can be roughed-in, as these services are installed into or onto the finished building fabric.

predecessor: Plant Room Fit-Out and Builder's Work
successor: Plant Room Ceiling and Wall Finishes
rationale: The primary builder's fit-out (screeds, blockwork, plastering) must be completed before applying final decorative finishes such as painting, tiling, or ceiling installation, as these are the final surface treatments.
The building must be fully constructed and enclosed before an energy audit can be performed, as the audit assesses the actual building envelope, systems, and performance.
All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems must be installed so that their energy consumption and efficiency can be measured during the audit.
The HVAC system must be commissioned and operational to allow testing of its energy performance and verification against design specifications.
The audit results and verified performance data serve as the basis for issuing an official energy performance certificate or rating.
While not physically mandatory, it is best practice to complete the energy audit first to identify inefficiencies before undertaking any optimization or retrofit work, ensuring targeted improvements.
Structural columns require stable foundations to transfer loads to the ground; excavation and foundation work must be completed before any column erection can begin.
Reinforcement steel (rebar) must be placed and tied within the column formwork before concrete is poured, as the rebar is integral to the column's structural integrity.
Formwork (molds) must be in place to contain and shape the concrete pour for a structural column; concrete cannot be placed without proper formwork.
Beams and slabs typically bear on or are supported by columns; the columns must be in place and cured to provide support for the horizontal structural elements.

successor: Concrete Curing and Stripping of Formwork
rationale: After the column is poured, the concrete must cure to reach sufficient strength before formwork can be safely removed and subsequent loads can be applied.
The foundation must be prepared and cured to provide a stable, level base for precast concrete planks or slabs to be placed upon.
Underground utilities (drainage, plumbing, electrical conduits) must be installed before the slab is placed, as they would be inaccessible afterward.
After precast planks are placed, a concrete topping or grout layer is applied to bond the planks together and create a monolithic surface.
Waterproofing is applied over the completed precast slab surface to protect the structure from moisture ingress.
Precast slabs provide the working platform and structural diaphragm needed before vertical elements can be safely erected on top of them.
Formwork must be erected to provide the mold and temporary support for the wet concrete before the slab can be poured.
Reinforcement steel (rebar) and post-tensioning tendon ducts must be placed and secured within the formwork before concrete is poured to ensure structural integrity.
Post-tensioning tendons are housed in ducts that must be accurately profiled and positioned before pouring concrete so they are embedded correctly.
After the concrete slab is poured, it must undergo a curing period to achieve sufficient strength before any stressing or further construction loads are applied.
The concrete must be poured and reach adequate compressive strength before the post-tensioning tendons can be tensioned (stressed) to introduce compressive forces into the slab.
The structural frame must be erected and stabilized to provide the load-bearing support system onto which the anti-glare screen or mesh façade panels can be mounted.
Fixings, brackets, and sub-framing attachments must be secured to the structural frame before the screen or mesh elements can be attached or clipped into place.
The façade must be completed and weathertight to protect interior works from weather ingress before internal fit-out, drywall, and finishes commence.

Perimeter seals, gaskets, and final weatherproofing at the screen-to-structure interface must be applied after the mesh/screen panels are fully installed to ensure a continuous airtight and watertight envelope.

The vehicle restraint barrier (e.g., guardrails, crash barriers) is typically anchored into or placed adjacent to the finished road pavement or base. The road surface must be at its final grade and compacted to provide the proper alignment and anchorage for the barrier.

For barrier types that require footings or embedded posts (e.g., concrete barriers, metal beam guardrails with posts), the foundation trench, post holes, or base slab must be prepared, excavated, and formed before the barrier elements are placed and concreted.

Reflectors, delineators, and pavement markings adjacent to or on the barrier are applied after the barrier is fully installed and aligned, as the barrier defines the exact edge line and clearance envelope.

In some sequences, the final asphalt wearing course is laid after barrier installation to seal around the base of the posts/barrier. However, this is often a preference to avoid damage to the new surface during barrier installation and to ensure a clean seal.

Subsurface drainage systems, edge drains, and culverts that run beneath or adjacent to the barrier line must be installed and backfilled before the barrier is placed, to avoid excavation/damage to the completed barrier.
Speed bumps and ramps require a properly graded and compacted subgrade to ensure uniform thickness and structural integrity.
A stable base layer must be in place to support the speed bump/ramp and prevent differential settlement.
Any underground utilities (drainage, conduits) in the area must be installed before paving over them with the speed bump/ramp structure to avoid excavation after construction.
Warning signs, pavement markings, and reflective markers for the speed bump/ramp must be applied after the bump/ramp is fully constructed and cured.
If the speed bump/ramp is part of an integrated paving operation, the final surface course can be placed after the bump/ramp formwork and concrete/asphalt have been set.

predecessor: Concrete Slab / Pavement Placement and Curing
rationale: Wheel stops must be anchored into or placed on top of cured concrete or asphalt pavement. The pavement or slab must first be placed and sufficiently cured (if concrete) to support the anchoring or adhesive bonding of the wheel stop.

successor: Concrete Slab / Pavement Placement and Curing
rationale: A properly graded and compacted sub-base is required before any pavement or slab can be poured, which in turn supports the wheel stop.

While wheel stops can be installed before striping, it is preferred to complete layout and striping first to ensure the wheel stops are aligned with parking stall markings for proper vehicle positioning.

successor: Parking Lot Striping Touch-Up / Final Striping
rationale: Once wheel stops are installed, any striping that was damaged during installation or that needs to be adjusted around the stops can be completed. This is a soft preference as it depends on whether striping was done before or after.
Wheel stops must be installed, aligned, and anchored before the parking lot can be signed off as complete. This is a logical project sequence rather than a strict physical necessity.
The surface must be prepared, leveled, and the base course laid before bay markings and lines can be painted, as paint requires a clean, stable, and even substrate to adhere properly.
Freshly laid concrete or asphalt must be fully cured before painting to ensure paint adhesion and prevent cracking or peeling due to moisture or surface instability.

successor: Final Inspection / Handover of Parking Area
rationale: Line painting is a finishing activity; the completed markings must be in place before the area can be inspected and handed over for use.

While signage is often installed after markings to ensure alignment with painted bays, it can sometimes be done concurrently; however, it is preferred to install signage after painting to ensure accurate placement.
Interior wall finishes must be completed before signage can be installed, as signage is mounted on or adhered to finished walls.
Ceilings must be in place before suspended or ceiling-mounted signage can be installed.
Flooring must be complete to allow proper positioning and installation of floor-mounted or wall-mounted signage at correct heights relative to finished floor levels.
Electrical work must be complete, especially if signage requires illumination or power connections, to avoid rework or damage after signage is installed.
Signage installation must be completed before final clean and punch list walkthrough, as signage is one of the last finish elements and needs to be in place for final inspection and occupancy.
The height restriction bar/gauge requires a stable, level foundation and base to be installed onto; without a proper base, the structure cannot be securely anchored.

The height restriction bar/gauge must be installed before the final pavement or surface finishing around the gate or roadway entrance, as the bar's base and supports need to be embedded or integrated before the surface is completed.

While the height restriction bar/gauge itself is the primary physical barrier, proper signage and warning markings are typically added after installation to alert drivers; this is a soft preference as signs could theoretically be installed beforehand.

Any underground utilities, drainage lines, or conduits near the installation location must be laid before the height restriction bar/gauge is installed, to avoid digging up or disturbing the newly installed structure.

successor: Testing and Commissioning of Height Restriction System
rationale: After physical installation, the height restriction bar/gauge must be tested to verify its correct height setting, structural integrity, and any sensor/alert functionality before the area is opened to traffic.
The ground must be cleared and excavated to the required depth and alignment before drainage channels can be installed, as they need a prepared sub-grade.
A compacted sub-base provides a stable foundation for drainage channels and prevents settlement; cannot be laid directly on loose soil.

successor: Pipework / Drainage Connection to Main Sewer/Outlet
rationale: Channels and gullies collect surface water and must be installed before the outlet pipework can be connected to them to form a continuous drainage path.

successor: Surfacing / Pavement Laying (e.g., asphalt, concrete, block paving)
rationale: Surface finishes are laid up to the finished level of drainage channels and gullies; installing them after would risk damaging the new surface or requiring re-cutting.
After channels are placed, the sides must be backfilled and compacted to lock them in position before any further construction above or adjacent.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated to the required depth before any structural framing can commence, as the frame requires stable foundations and a prepared substrate.
Foundations (e.g., footings, piles, or raft slabs) must be fully cured and load-bearing before the structural frame can be erected, as the frame transfers all loads to the foundation system.
Drainage, water, sewer, and electrical conduits that run beneath the building footprint must be laid before the frame goes up; otherwise, access for installation would be blocked by the structure.
The roof structure (trusses, rafters, or decking) typically bears directly on the frame's columns and beams, so the frame must be complete and stable to support roof loads.
Exterior cladding, masonry, or curtain walls are attached to or supported by the structural frame; the frame provides the primary structural backing for these envelope systems.
Foundations must be prepared and cured to provide a stable base for precast elements.
A crane or lifting equipment must be set up on stable ground before precast elements can be lifted and placed.
Precast elements must be delivered to site and inspected for damage/quality before installation can begin.
After precast elements are placed, connections must be grouted and finished to secure them permanently.

successor: Structural Steel or Topping Slab Placement
rationale: Any subsequent structural elements (e.g., topping slabs, steel beams) resting on or connecting to precast elements can only be installed after the precast elements are in place.

Post-tensioning tendons must be installed and stressed after the concrete has been poured and has reached sufficient strength (typically after curing) to withstand the compressive forces from tensioning.

The post-tensioning tendons, ducts, anchorages, and sheathing must be placed and secured within the formwork before concrete is poured, and these form the system that is tensioned during post-tensioning works.
Formwork must be erected and reinforcement steel (rebar) placed prior to installing post-tensioning tendons and before concrete pouring, as the tendons are integrated into the reinforcement cage.
After the tendons are tensioned to the required force, the ducts must be grouted to bond the tendons to the concrete and protect them from corrosion.
Formwork and falsework can only be removed after post-tensioning is complete because the structure gains its self-supporting capacity through the applied compression from the tensioned tendons.
The ground must be cleared and excavated to expose the subgrade and provide a working area for laying drainage pipes and systems.
Existing underground utilities must be located and marked to avoid conflicts and damage during drainage excavation and pipe laying.
Drainage pipes and structures must be fully installed and inspected before trenches can be backfilled and compacted.
Proper drainage must be in place to manage groundwater and surface water before concrete foundations or slabs are poured to prevent water damage and ensure structural integrity.
Drainage systems must be operational before road base layers are placed to ensure water is properly directed away from the pavement structure.
Floor coating requires a smooth, cured concrete or screed substrate to bond properly. The slab must be fully cured (typically 28 days for concrete) and dry before any coating can be applied.
The concrete surface must be mechanically profiled (ground or shot-blasted) to remove laitance and create a proper mechanical bond for the coating system.
Any structural cracks, joints, or surface defects must be repaired and sealed before coating to prevent reflective cracking and ensure a uniform finished surface.

Floor coating and line marking are near-final finishing activities. After the coating is fully cured and markings are applied, no other wet trades should be active. The area is then ready for protection, final cleaning, and project handover.

While not a physical necessity in all cases, it is strongly preferred to complete overhead M&E rough-in work (piping, conduit, ductwork) before coating the floor to avoid damage to the finished floor from scaffolding, dropped tools, or material spills during overhead work.
The structural frame provides the load-bearing support and attachment points for the façade and screening systems; without a completed frame, there is no structure to mount the façade onto.
Roof completion and waterproofing must precede façade installation to ensure weather-tight conditions for below work and to integrate roof-to-wall flashing details properly.
Internal partition walls and finishes rely on the façade being in place to establish the building envelope, control environmental conditions, and provide datum points for internal layouts.
Primary façade and screening systems must be installed first to create the structural openings and sub-frames into which glazing units and windows are fitted.
External building services such as drainage downpipes, HVAC grilles, and electrical conduits must be routed after the façade is in place to ensure proper integration and sealing through the envelope.

The structural frame must be complete to provide the physical enclosure and support systems (e.g., floors, ceilings, walls) into which M&E services are installed. Without the structure in place, there is no substrate for conduit, ductwork, piping, or cable trays.
The building must be weathertight before sensitive M&E equipment (e.g., electrical panels, controllers, ductwork insulation) is installed to prevent water damage and ensure a dry working environment.
Enclosure of the building envelope provides security, weather protection, and containment for internal M&E works, and allows the building to be temporarily sealed for dust-sensitive activities.

M&E services such as conduits, pipes, and ductwork are typically installed within wall cavities and ceiling voids; partition framing and boarding must follow to enclose these services. Installing partitions before M&E would require cutting or coring through framing for service runs, which is inefficient and may compromise fire stopping.

Suspended ceiling grids and tiles are installed after M&E services (e.g., sprinkler pipes, HVAC ducts, lighting conduits) are run above the ceiling plane. Ceilings conceal and protect these services; installing ceilings first would block access for M&E routing and testing.

While it is preferable to install floor finishes after M&E rough-in (e.g., underfloor conduits, drainage pipes) to avoid cutting or chasing finished floors, this is a soft preference because careful coordination and 'first-fix' scheduling can allow some floor finishes to be laid before M&E final connections.

It is generally preferable to complete painting and decoration after M&E is installed to avoid damage to finished paintwork from M&E installation activities, but this is a soft preference as painting can be phased (e.g., first coat before M&E, final coat after).
Interior finishes such as painting, wall covering, and ceiling installation must be completed before signage can be mounted, as signage is applied onto finished surfaces.
Flooring must be installed before wayfinding floor graphics or floor-mounted signs are placed, as the signage would be affixed to the finished floor surface.
Suspended or ceiling-mounted signage requires the ceiling grid and tiles to be fully installed to provide the structural support for hanging signs.
Electrical rough-in work must be complete to provide power connections for illuminated signage, and lighting must be installed to ensure proper visibility of wayfinding elements.
Signage installation is one of the last finishing trades; after signage is in place, final cleaning and commissioning can occur without risk of damage from subsequent finishing work.
Office partitioning systems require a finished, level floor slab to be installed upon. The partitions must anchor to the structural floor.

Electrical outlets, data ports, and cabling for workstations must be roughed into the floor slab before partitions are installed, as the partitions may cover or obstruct floor boxes and access to underfloor wiring.

predecessor: Overhead MEP Rough-In (HVAC ducts, sprinklers, main electrical)
rationale: Major overhead mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work (ductwork, sprinkler mains, conduit) must be completed before partitions are framed, as partitions define room layouts and final MEP device placement; installing overhead systems after partitions would require cutting through finished walls.
The partition framing and panels must be fully installed before drywall, paint, or decorative wall finishes can be applied to partition surfaces.

While partition installation can occur before final floor finishes, it is a soft preference that final flooring be completed after partitions to avoid damaging new flooring during partition installation and to achieve a cleaner finished appearance at partition bases.
Modular furniture and workstations are typically installed after partitions define the office layout and spatial divisions, ensuring proper alignment and fit within partitioned zones.
A structural slab provides the load-bearing floor surface required to support the weight of workstations and desks. Without a completed slab, desks cannot be placed safely.
Electrical outlets and data ports must be roughed in and available in the floor or walls before workstations can be positioned and connected to power and network services.
Network cabling must be run to the workstation locations prior to desk installation so that connectivity can be established without having to move or partially disassemble installed desks.

In some sequences, workstations are placed first and floor finishes like carpet tiles are installed around or under them, which is a soft preference for scheduling efficiency rather than a physical necessity.

successor: Workstation / Desk Electrical & Data Connection & Testing
rationale: Desks must be physically installed before final plug-in of power strips, cable management, and testing of electrical outlets and data ports at the workstation.
The chair frame (base, gas lift, seat pan, backrest structure) must be fully assembled before adding ergonomic components like lumbar support, armrests, and cushioning.
The structural assembly must be complete before applying foam padding, mesh backing, and fabric/leather upholstery to the frame.
The main chair structure must be assembled before installing and calibrating the tilt mechanism, tension control, and lock functions.
All assembly and upholstery work must be finished before the chair undergoes ergonomic testing for lumbar support, seat height range, armrest adjustability, and recline functions.
All individual components (casters, gas cylinder, tilt mechanism, armrests, lumbar pad, mesh back, seat cushion, upholstery) must be procured and inspected for quality before assembly begins.
The storage pedestal/filing cabinet must be placed on a finished, level floor surface to ensure stability and proper alignment.
The exact location for the storage pedestal/filing cabinet must be marked out according to the floor plan before installation can proceed.
Storage pedestals/filing cabinets often support or are positioned underneath work surfaces/desk tops, so they must be installed first to provide support.
It is easier to route cables around or behind the storage unit after it is in place, but this could also be done before if the unit is easily movable.
The installation of storage units is typically completed before final decorative touches are added to the space, though this is a preference for workflow order rather than a physical necessity.
Acoustic panels require a structural support framework (wood or metal studs) to be fixed to. Without the underlying framework, there is no substrate to attach the panels to.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing services within walls/ceilings must be roughed-in before enclosing them with acoustic panels, as access behind panels would be difficult or impossible later.
Sound-absorbing insulation within wall/ceiling cavities is typically installed before acoustic panels are fixed, as the panels would block access to the cavity.
Acoustic panels are a finished surface element; any surrounding paint, trim, or final finishes are completed after the panels are in place to ensure clean edges and proper integration.
Acoustic performance testing (e.g., reverberation time, sound absorption) must be conducted after all panels are fully installed to measure the actual completed acoustic environment.
Window frames must be installed and secured before any window blinds or solar shading devices can be mounted onto them, as they provide the structural support and attachment points.
Glass panes must be installed in the window frames before blinds or shading are added, as the shading devices are typically mounted adjacent to or over the glass to control light and solar gain.
It is a soft preference to complete wall finishing before installing window blinds to avoid damaging the blinds with paint splatter or dust from wall work, and to ensure clean aesthetic lines.
Soft preference: installing trim and molding around the window after the blind/shading allows for precise fitting and a finished look, but the blind can be installed first if needed.
Soft preference: final cleaning and floor finishing should be done after blind installation to avoid dust and debris settling on the newly installed blinds and to prevent damage during floor work.
Raised floor panels require a level, cured concrete subfloor as a stable base. The subfloor must be finished and set before pedestals and panels can be installed.
Cabling infrastructure (data, power, cooling pipes) must be laid in the underfloor plenum before the floor panels are placed, as the panels will cover and restrict access to the subfloor zone.

predecessor: Raised Floor Pedestal and Stringer Grid Layout
rationale: The adjustable pedestals and stringer support grid must be fully installed and leveled first, as the raised floor panels are placed directly on top of this support structure.
Heavy equipment like server racks and workstations must be placed on the completed raised floor surface, not before, to avoid damaging loose panels or requiring re-leveling.

While often done after, some finishes like anti-static tiles or carpet tiles can technically be installed concurrently, though it's standard practice to complete all raised panel placement before applying final floor finishes to avoid contamination or damage.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work (ductwork, conduit, piping) must be installed above the ceiling grid before ceiling tiles are placed, as access to the plenum space is blocked once tiles are installed.
Fire sprinkler heads and piping must be positioned and tested in the ceiling plenum before tiles are installed; once tiles are in place, the sprinkler system cannot be easily accessed or modified.
The metal T-grid suspension system (main runners, cross tees, and wall angles) must be fully installed and leveled before ceiling tiles can be laid into the grid.
Any insulation laid above the ceiling tiles must be placed before the tiles are installed; otherwise, the insulation cannot be added without removing tiles.

successor: Final Flooring and Wall Finishes (Painting, Trim)
rationale: While not always strictly required, ceiling tile installation is often completed before final wall painting and floor finishes to prevent dust and debris from the ceiling work from soiling finished surfaces.
Electrical wiring, outlets, switches, plumbing pipes and fixtures must be roughed-in within walls before partitions are installed and enclosed.
The floor must be level and prepared to provide a stable base for partition walls and to ensure proper alignment and attachment.
The main structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) must be complete to define the building envelope and support the non-load bearing partitions.
Partitions must be installed and surfaces prepared before final trim-out of electrical switches/outlets, plumbing fixtures, and application of wall finishes like drywall or paint.
Partition frames and openings must be in place to receive doors and windows; the rough opening is created by the partition framing.
The structural concrete slab must be fully cured and finished before any raised floor system can be installed, as it provides the load-bearing substrate and base surface for the pedestals and panels.

predecessor: Overhead MEP Rough-In (Electrical, Plumbing, Fire Protection)
rationale: Major overhead mechanical, electrical, and plumbing work above the ceiling (e.g., ductwork, conduit, sprinkler piping) should be completed before the raised floor is installed to avoid damage to the floor system and prevent access issues for overhead installations.

Cable trays supporting data and power cables are often mounted directly to the raised floor pedestals or installed after the grid is set, requiring the floor structure to be in place to support and route cabling systems.

successor: Floor Covering & Sealing (Carpet, Tile, ESD Finish)
rationale: Final floor coverings, anti-static finishes, or carpet tiles must be applied on top of the completed raised floor panels to provide the finished walking surface and protect the underlying system.
Heavy IT equipment and server racks can only be positioned after the raised floor is fully installed, leveled, and load-tested to ensure stable support and proper weight distribution.
Structural framing (including ceiling joists and roof structure) must be in place to provide the support system from which the suspended ceiling grid is hung.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) runs that go above the suspended ceiling (e.g., ductwork, conduit, piping) must be installed and inspected before the ceiling grid and tiles are put in place, as they become inaccessible afterward.

Fireproofing spray-applied to structural members and any overhead insulation must be completed prior to enclosing the ceiling space, as these materials are applied to the deck above and cannot be easily applied after the suspended ceiling is installed.

successor: Final MEP Trim-Out and Light Fixture Installation
rationale: After the suspended ceiling grid is installed, light fixtures, diffusers, sprinkler heads, and other ceiling-mounted devices can be placed into the grid openings and connected to the rough-in services.

Although surface finishing of ceiling tiles is typically done during manufacturing, any on-site painting or touch-up of the ceiling grid or tiles should occur after installation but is a soft preference sequence based on workflow efficiency rather than a physical necessity.
The ground slab or substructure must be completed to provide the base for M&E services installation, including underfloor conduits and drainage connections.
The main structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) must be in place before M&E risers, conduits, and pipework can be installed within the building structure.
The building must be weather-tight (roof and external cladding completed) before commencing M&E first fix to prevent water damage to electrical and mechanical installations.
M&E first fix (cables, conduits, pipework in walls and ceilings) must be completed before walls and ceilings are closed up with plasterboard or plaster finishes.
M&E second fix (socket outlets, switches, sanitaryware, radiators) should be substantially completed before final floor finishes to avoid damage and allow access for connections.

A level, clean, dry, and structurally sound subfloor (e.g., concrete slab, plywood underlayment) must be prepared before any flooring material (tile, hardwood, laminate, vinyl) can be installed. Installing on an unprepared surface leads to unevenness, adhesion failure, and premature flooring damage.

Rough-in work for electrical wiring, plumbing pipes, and HVAC ductwork that runs beneath the floor must be completed before flooring is laid. Access to the subfloor is blocked once flooring is installed, making later modifications extremely costly.

The building must be fully framed (walls, roof structure) and enclosed to protect flooring materials from weather exposure and to establish the final floor layout and elevations based on wall positions.

While flooring is often installed before baseboards and trim (so trim sits on top of the finished floor for a clean look), painting and wall finishing can be done before or after. However, installing flooring first avoids paint drips on the new floor and allows baseboards to be cut precisely to the finished floor height. This is a strong preference but not a physical impossibility.

Flooring must be installed before kitchen cabinets, built-in appliances (dishwasher, stove), and heavy vanities are placed. These fixtures sit on top of the finished floor; installing them first would trap flooring beneath them, leaving unfinished edges and preventing future floor replacement without removing the cabinets.

Plastering and drywall finishing creates a smooth, sealed surface that is necessary for paint adhesion. Painting over unfinished plaster or exposed drywall would result in poor finish quality and potential paint failure.
Floor screeding generates significant dust and debris that would contaminate freshly painted walls and decorations. The screeding process also requires access to the full room space.

Electrical first fix (running cables, installing back boxes) involves cutting into walls and chasing channels, which would damage completed paintwork. All wall-disturbing work must be finished before painting.
Plumbing first fix requires chasing walls and floors for pipe runs, creating dust and damaging surfaces. This must be completed before any decorative finishes are applied.
First fix carpentry (door frames, window boards, skirting grounds) must be installed before painting so that the gaps between joinery and walls can be filled and painted over for a seamless finish.

Floor coverings must be installed after painting to avoid paint drips, splashes, and dust settling on finished floors. Painters need full access to walls without risking damage to expensive floor finishes.

successor: Electrical Second Fix (Sockets, Switches, Light Fittings)
rationale: Electrical second fix (fitting sockets, switches, and light fixtures) is done after painting so that these items sit neatly on top of the finished paintwork. Installing them first would require painting around them, resulting in an untidy finish.
Final cleaning and snagging rectification is done after painting to remove any paint splashes, dust from sanding, and to touch up any minor defects before handover.

While final cabinet installation is typically done after painting for a cleaner finish, pre-painted or factory-finished kitchens can be installed earlier. This is a soft preference for quality rather than a hard physical constraint.
Flooring must be fully completed and cured before furniture can be placed to avoid damaging floors and to ensure stable, level installation.
Wall finishing and painting must be done first to prevent dust, paint splatters, or damage to installed furniture and to allow access for wall work without obstruction.
Electrical rough-ins behind walls and floors must be completed before furniture is installed, as furniture placement can block access to wiring and outlet locations.
Ceiling work (grid, tiles, lighting fixtures) must be completed before furniture to avoid dust/debris falling on finished furniture and to ensure unobstructed access for ceiling installation.

Furniture installation must be fully complete before final cleaning can be performed, as debris and packaging from furniture installation need to be cleaned, and the space must be in its final state for handover.
The building must be substantially complete (all major works finished) before snagging inspections can commence, as snagging identifies only minor defects and incomplete items.
After snagging inspection identifies defects, those defects must be rectified before formal handover can proceed.
The snagging inspection is a prerequisite step before the building can be formally handed over to the client or owner.
The defects liability period typically begins after the snagging inspection and formal handover are completed.
The WC pan must be connected to the building's drainage and water supply systems, which must be roughed-in before the pan can be installed and connected.
The WC pan needs a stable, prepared subfloor (typically waterproofed and screeded) to sit on securely and to ensure proper drainage connections.

successor: Tiling / floor finishing around WC pan
rationale: The WC pan must be fixed in position before the final floor finishing (tiles, waterproofing upstand) can be completed around it to ensure a neat and watertight interface.

successor: Connection of flush mechanism and toilet seat
rationale: The WC pan must be in place before the flush mechanism (cistern, flush pipe) and toilet seat can be physically connected to it.
After the pan is installed, final connections to water supply and drainage can be made, pressure tested, and verified for leaks.
The ground must be excavated to create space for the cistern structure before it can be installed.
A stable, level foundation (e.g., compacted gravel or concrete base) must be prepared to support the weight of the cistern before placing it.
Inlet and outlet pipes can only be connected to the cistern after it is set in place and leveled.
Soil must be backfilled around the installed cistern to secure it and provide lateral support; this cannot be done before the cistern is in position.
Overflow and drain lines must be connected to the cistern after it is installed to ensure proper drainage away from the structure.
The flush mechanism depends on the water supply and drainage pipes being in place, as it connects directly to the plumbing system for flushing and refilling.
The flush mechanism is typically installed as part of or after the toilet bowl is set, as it mounts inside or onto the toilet tank which sits atop the bowl.
The flush mechanism (fill valve, flapper, flush valve) must be installed inside the toilet tank before the tank is placed and secured onto the bowl.
The flush handle or push button connects to the flush mechanism internally; the mechanism must be in place before the handle can be attached and linked.
The water supply line connects to the fill valve of the flush mechanism; thus the mechanism must be installed first, then the supply line can be attached and water turned on for testing.
The toilet seat and lid must be mounted on a fully installed toilet bowl, as they physically attach to the bowl.
Plumbing connections for the toilet must be in place and the wax ring/seal installed before the toilet bowl and seat can be placed.
All bathroom fixtures including the toilet seat and lid must be installed before the final inspection can be completed.
While not physically required, it is standard practice to confirm toilet seat and lid installation as part of the completion checklist before project sign-off.
It is preferable to place the toilet paper holder after the toilet seat is installed to ensure proper alignment and clearance, though it could technically be done beforehand.
The drain pipe must be in place before the washbasin can be connected and mounted, as the basin's drainage outlet must connect to the waste pipe.

predecessor: Install water supply lines (hot and cold)
rationale: Water supply lines for faucet connections must be roughed-in before the washbasin is installed so that the faucet can be properly connected.
The wall structure and finished surface (tile, drywall, etc.) must be completed before mounting a washbasin, as the basin attaches to and is supported by the wall.
The washbasin must be mounted in place before the faucet and supply lines can be connected to it.

successor: Connect drain trap and waste line
rationale: The washbasin must be secured before its drain assembly and P-trap can be connected to the waste piping.
Urinals require a stable load-bearing floor to be installed upon; the floor slab or subfloor must be in place before any plumbing fixtures can be mounted.

predecessor: Rough-in Plumbing (Drain and Water Supply Lines)
rationale: The concealed drain waste pipe (DWV) and water supply lines must be roughed in within the wall/floor before the urinal can be connected.
Urinals are wall-hung or wall-mounted; the wall framing with proper blocking/backing must be completed to support the fixture's weight.
Once the urinal is installed and connected, the surrounding wall finish (e.g., tile, waterproof membrane) must be completed up to and around the fixture to seal and finish the wall surface.

After the urinal body is mounted and connected, final trim (flush valve, handle/sensor, supply stops) and water supply pressure testing / flush testing must occur to verify proper operation before the restroom is put into service.
The bracket must be securely mounted to the wall or counter before the soap dispenser can be attached to it.
Plumbing supply lines must be in place behind the wall before the dispenser can be connected.
Soap can only be added after the dispenser unit is physically installed, but this is a logical sequence rather than a hard physical constraint.
Functional testing can only occur after the dispenser is fully installed and connected.
For counter-mounted dispensers, the countertop must be installed first so the dispenser can be mounted through the pre-drilled hole.
The water supply pipes (hot and cold) must be roughed-in and terminated at the wall or floor before the basin tap can be connected to them.
The basin itself must be mounted and secured on the vanity or countertop before the tap/faucet can be fixed onto the basin deck or wall, as the faucet physically mounts to the basin.

successor: Plumbing Waste Connection to Basin Trap
rationale: The tap must be installed to allow proper alignment and connection of the waste outlet and trap beneath the basin; the tap handles and spout position affect the waste assembly routing.

successor: Water Supply Connection to Flexible Hoses
rationale: The tap body must be fixed in place before flexible supply hoses can be connected from the tap tails to the isolation valves on the supply pipes.

successor: Final Testing and Commissioning of Basin
rationale: All water and waste connections can only be tested for leaks and function after the tap/faucet is fully installed and connected to both supply and drainage.
Power supply wiring must be run to the hand dryer location before the unit can be connected and mounted.
Hand dryers are mounted on finished walls; the wall surface must be in place to support the unit.
Final wall finish should be completed before mounting the hand dryer to avoid damage from finishing work and to ensure proper aesthetics and sealing around the unit.
Hand dryer must be installed before the overall restroom systems can be tested, including power-on verification and functional checks.
Installing the hand dryer early allows inspectors to confirm it meets code requirements before project closeout, though it is a scheduling preference rather than a physical necessity.
The paper towel dispenser must have a secure mounting surface or bracket attached to the wall before it can be installed.

predecessor: Rough-in plumbing (if connected to water supply)
rationale: If the dispenser is a hands-free or automatic model requiring a fixed water line, the plumbing rough-in must be completed before installing the unit.
The dispenser must be physically installed and secured before it can be loaded with paper towel rolls.

successor: Final inspection / commissioning of restroom fixtures
rationale: The dispenser installation must be complete before the overall restroom fixture commissioning and inspection can be finalized.

predecessor: Wall finishing (tiling, painting, or drywall completion)
rationale: Wall surfaces must be finished before mounting the dispenser to avoid damaging finished surfaces or having to work around an already-installed fixture.
The toilet roll holder needs to be attached to wall studs or framing for structural support.
The toilet roll holder requires a solid wall surface (e.g., tile backer board or drywall) to be installed onto.
If the toilet roll holder is recessed or surface-mounted on a tiled wall, tiles must be cut around or installed after the holder is positioned to ensure proper fit and waterproofing.
Soft preference: It's easier to position the toilet roll holder at the correct height and distance from the toilet before the toilet bowl is installed, though not physically required.
Soft preference: Painting or finishing the wall before installing the holder avoids the need to cut in around the fixture and provides a cleaner finish.
Grab rails need a solid structural backing to be securely mounted; wall framing provides the necessary support structure.
Sheathing creates the finished wall surface into which grab rails are anchored.
Pipes must be installed behind the wall before grab rails are mounted to avoid interference and re-work.
Electrical wiring must be run behind walls before grab rails are installed to prevent obstruction and ensure safety.

In some sequences, grab rails can be installed before final wall finishes to allow for proper sealing around penetrations; however, it's often a soft preference to install after tiling for aesthetic alignment.
Grab rails must be installed and secured before the space can be considered safe for occupancy and pass final building inspection.
Mirrors need to be attached to wall framing; the framing must be complete to provide structural support.
Drywall provides the finished surface onto which mirrors are mounted or adhered.
Drywall joints and screw heads must be finished smooth before mounting mirrors to ensure a flat mounting surface.
Paint or wall finish behind the mirror should be complete before mirror is installed, as the mirror would block access to paint afterwards.
Trim around mirrors is typically installed after the mirror is in place to achieve a clean finished edge, though it could be done beforehand with careful measuring.
The sanitary bin must be placed on a finished, stable floor surface to ensure proper support and alignment.
Wall finishing (tiling, painting, etc.) must be completed before mounting or positioning the sanitary bin to avoid damaging finished surfaces or requiring rework.
Plumbing connections for water supply and drainage must be roughed in before the sanitary bin is placed and connected.
If the sanitary bin has electrical components (e.g., automatic lid, sensor), electrical connections must be made after the bin is physically installed.
The sanitary bin must be fully installed and operational before the final inspection of the sanitary fixtures can be completed.

Cubicle partitions must be installed on a finished floor surface to ensure proper alignment, stability, and level placement. Installing partitions before floor finishing would damage or trap flooring materials.
Overhead cabling for power, data, and telecom must be routed above the ceiling grid before cubicle partitions are installed, as partitions can obstruct access to ceiling spaces and cable trays.

The ceiling grid and any overhead infrastructure must be completed before partitions are erected, since partitions define the layout below the ceiling and must align with ceiling grid and light fixture positions.
Desks, work surfaces, and other furniture components are typically attached to or fitted within the cubicle partition system. The partition panels must be in place to support these components.

successor: Final Power/Data Outlet Trim-Out and Connection
rationale: Power and data outlets are often integrated into the cubicle partition system (e.g., raceways in the panels). Final trim-out, cover installation, and plug-in connections can only be completed after the partitions are fully assembled and positioned.
Electrical power supply wiring must be installed to the fan location before the fan unit can be connected and mounted.
Exhaust ductwork must be in place so that the fan can be physically connected to the duct system.
Fan mounting requires structural support such as ceiling joists or a soffit frame to be completed first.
Drywall must be installed after the fan is mounted so that the fan can be properly integrated and access panels can be cut.
Final power connection, commissioning, and functional testing of the fan must occur after the fan is physically installed.
The foundation and ground slab must be completed before soil and waste pipes can be laid underground, as the pipes are embedded in or run beneath the slab.
The oversite concrete or ground floor slab provides the base upon which soil and waste pipe runs are laid; without it, pipework has no stable bedding.
Soil and waste stacks and underground drainage branches must be in place before above-ground sanitary pipework (WCs, basins, baths) can be connected to them.
Once underground soil and waste pipes are laid and tested, the final floor screed or topping can be applied to encase and protect the pipework.
Soil and waste pipes must be fully installed before formal drainage testing and inspection can be carried out to verify watertightness and compliance.
Ground must be cleared and excavated to expose the installation area and provide access for laying water supply pipes.
Building foundations must be completed before pipework can be installed through or under the structure to avoid rework and ensure structural integrity.
Underground drainage pipes should be laid before water supply pipes to coordinate trenching and avoid cross-contamination or conflicts in underground services.
The main water supply line must be connected to the building before internal branch plumbing and fixture connections can be undertaken.
Once pipework is installed and connected, pressure testing must follow to verify integrity and leak-tightness before concealing or finishing walls.
Pipework must be embedded or enclosed before floor screeds and wall finishes are applied to avoid damage and ensure the pipes are concealed.
Water supply must be fully run and terminated at stub-outs before toilets, sinks, and other fixtures can be connected and installed.
Structural framing provides the primary support structure (walls, floors, ceilings) that fixtures must be attached to or mounted on.
Plumbing rough-in (pipes, drains, supply lines) must be installed behind walls and in floors before fixtures like sinks, toilets, and showers can be connected.
Electrical wiring, junction boxes, and outlets must be run and positioned within walls/ceilings before light fixtures, switches, and powered fixtures can be installed.
HVAC ductwork and vents must be installed in ceilings and walls before ceiling-mounted fixtures or diffusers can be placed.
Drywall must be completed and finished before most wall-mounted fixtures (mirrors, grab bars, towel racks) can be installed, as fixtures mount onto the finished wall surface.

While painting can be done before fixture installation for some applications, typically finishing touches around fixtures are done after installation; this is a soft preference as fixtures can be installed after painting to avoid damage.
Final connection of supply lines and drain assemblies to fixtures (e.g., connecting faucets to water supply, attaching P-traps) must occur after the fixture bodies are physically installed in place.

Certain floor-mounted fixtures (e.g., toilets) are typically installed after flooring is complete, but this is a preference sequence; some fixtures may need to be set before final flooring for proper fit.
Tiling requires a clean, level, and cured substrate. Concrete slabs or subfloors must be fully set and prepared before tiles can be laid.
Wall tiles are applied onto finished wall surfaces. The wall framing and plasterboard/backer board must be installed and finished before tiling can begin.
In bathrooms, showers, and other wet areas, waterproof membranes must be applied and tested before tiling to prevent moisture damage.
Grouting and sealing can only be applied after tiles are fully installed and the adhesive has set.
Plumbing fixtures such as toilets, basins, and shower bases are installed over or adjacent to tiled surfaces; tiling must be complete to allow proper fit and waterproofing.
Electrical wiring and first fix must be installed within walls, ceiling voids, and structural cavities that must already be framed and enclosed.
Structural rough-in inspection must be passed before electrical work begins to ensure the building frame is safe and ready for MEP installations.
Electrical first fix (cables, back boxes) should be installed before plumbing rough-in to avoid clashes and to allow electrical to be embedded within walls before pipes are run.
Electrical wiring must be installed and inspected before insulation is placed to ensure cables are properly routed and not covered prematurely.
First fix electrical cables, back boxes, and conduits must be in place and tested before walls are closed up with plasterboard.

predecessor: Floor slab installation at reception area
rationale: The reception desk must be installed on a completed, level floor slab to provide a stable foundation and proper alignment.

predecessor: Rough-in electrical wiring at reception zone
rationale: Electrical outlets, data ports, and lighting connections need to be roughed-in behind or beneath the reception desk location before the desk is placed, as access would be blocked afterward.
Any concealed plumbing (for sinks) or data conduit routing must be installed in walls/floors before the desk is positioned and fixed in place.
The main desk structure must be fully installed before the countertop can be fitted, sealed, and finished.

successor: Reception area decorative cladding and trim
rationale: Decorative panels, trims, and front cladding are applied to the desk frame after it is positioned, so the desk must already be installed.
The turnstile/security gate must be mounted on a stable, level finished floor; the concrete slab must be poured and cured before any gate anchoring can occur.

predecessor: Underground Conduit and Rough-In Electrical Work
rationale: Power and data cabling for the electronic lock, access controller, and intercom must be run in conduits beneath or within the floor/wall before the gate frame is installed.
The turnstile is typically mounted between finished walls or integrated into a wall opening; drywall/plaster must be completed to provide the proper finished opening dimensions and anchoring surface.

successor: Access Control System Wiring and Configuration
rationale: The card reader, biometric scanner, and electronic latch hardware are physically mounted on or inside the turnstile; they cannot be cabled and programmed until the gate is in place.

successor: Final Floor Finishing and Sealing (around gate)
rationale: While final floor coating can be applied before gate installation if the area is masked, it is better practice to complete floor sealing after the gate base plate is set to avoid gaps and ensure a clean finished appearance.
The structural framing and roof structure must be complete to provide the overhead support system to which the suspended ceiling grid is attached.
HVAC ductwork and other mechanical rough-ins above the ceiling line must be installed before the ceiling is closed in, as they are inaccessible once the suspended ceiling is installed.
Electrical conduits, junction boxes, and wiring that run above the ceiling must be completed before ceiling installation to ensure accessibility and code compliance.
Plumbing pipes, sprinkler lines, and other wet rough-ins routed above the ceiling plane must be installed and pressure-tested prior to enclosing them with the ceiling.
Recessed lighting fixtures, speakers, and other ceiling-mounted devices are typically installed into the ceiling grid after the grid is in place, as they attach to the ceiling system.
Power and control wiring must be run behind walls/ceilings before signage can be physically mounted and connected.
Signage (especially overhead or suspended wayfinding signs) requires complete ceilings to be in place for proper mounting and alignment.
Wall-mounted signage requires finished wall surfaces to be installed cleanly; painting and patching must be completed to avoid damaging signage or requiring rework.
Signage must be in place for final code compliance inspection and system testing of public address and wayfinding functionality.

successor: Interior finishing touch-ups and punch list
rationale: It is preferred to complete signage before final touch-ups so that any minor damage around mounted signs can be addressed in one pass, though not physically required.
The rough opening must be framed and dimensioned correctly to accommodate the automatic sliding door system, including header support for the door track.
Automatic sliding doors require electrical power for the motor, sensors, and control system; wiring must be roughed-in before the door unit can be connected.
The door track and bottom guide require a finished, level floor surface to ensure proper alignment and smooth operation.
The door unit must be physically installed before electrical terminations can be completed and the system can be tested and commissioned.

successor: Wall finishing and trim around door frame
rationale: Although it is preferable to finish walls after installation to achieve clean transition details, it is a soft preference as the door can be protected and walls can be finished later with careful masking.
The structural frame must be complete to provide the load-bearing support and attachment points for the curtain wall system.
Floor slabs are required at each level to provide the horizontal structural support and anchorage for curtain wall mullions and transoms.
It is preferable to complete the facade enclosure before interior finishes to protect interior works from weather exposure, though not physically mandatory.
The curtain wall installation must precede final waterproofing and air sealing of the building envelope to ensure continuity of the weather-resistant barrier.
External scaffolding used for facade installation cannot be removed until the curtain wall is fully installed and secured.
The wall requires a stable foundation to bear its load and prevent settlement or collapse.
The floor slab provides the base surface upon which the wall is constructed or installed.
The main structural frame must be erected to define the building envelope and provide support for non-load-bearing walls.
While some MEP rough-in can precede the wall, final routing and outlet placement should occur after the wall is in place to ensure accurate positioning.
Surface finishes and cladding are applied after the wall structure is fully erected to achieve a uniform and complete appearance.
The flooring must be fully installed and cured before placing furniture on top to prevent damage to the floor and ensure stability of furnishings.
Wall finishes, paint, and wall coverings must be completed to avoid dust and debris settling on new furniture, and to allow access for wall work without obstruction.

Ceiling work, overhead lighting installation, and any overhead MEP rough-ins must be finished to prevent dust and debris falling on furniture and to avoid needing to move furniture for overhead access.
Decorative accessories, artwork, and final styling elements are placed after furniture is in position to ensure proper spacing, visual alignment, and to avoid interfering with furniture placement.

Final cleaning and punch list walkthroughs are conducted after all furniture and soft furnishings are in place to perform a complete inspection and clean the space without needing to work around ongoing furniture delivery.
A stable, level foundation must exist before the kiosk structure can be installed or built upon it.
Power, network, and data lines must be run to the kiosk location in the rough-in phase before the kiosk is enclosed or finished.
The kiosk structure and workstations must be fully installed before IT equipment, computer systems, and communication devices can be mounted, connected, and tested.
The kiosk installation must be complete so that final cleaning, touch-ups, and readiness for public use can occur in proper sequence.
The ground must be excavated and graded to the proper elevations and slopes before the ramp and entrance can be constructed, as the ramp requires a stable, graded base.
The foundation or slab adjacent to the entrance must be poured and cured to provide a structural base and tie-in point for the ramp and entrance framing.
Drainage provisions must be in place to prevent water accumulation at the base of the ramp, ensuring safety and long-term durability.
The ramp and entrance landing must be complete to provide the structural support and threshold for the entrance door frame and door installation.
Handrails are mounted on the ramp structure; therefore the ramp must be fully constructed before handrails can be installed.
It is preferable to complete the ramp first so that the connecting walkway can align precisely with the ramp landing, but minor adjustments can be made if sequencing varies.
Interior wall finishes must be completed before planting to avoid damage from paint, dust, and debris settling on plants.
Ceilings must be finished to prevent dust, debris, and overhead work from falling onto and damaging new plantings.
Flooring must be installed before plants are brought in, as flooring work involves heavy materials, adhesives, and dust that would harm plants and impede access.
After planting, a final cleaning is needed to remove soil, debris, and packaging from the landscaping work, and any remaining punch-list items can be addressed without dirtying the new plants.

Landscaping and planting are among the final aesthetic and functional installations; commissioning and handover occur after all interior work, including planting, is complete and the space is ready for occupancy.
Interior walls must be finished (painted, textured) before installing artwork or sculptures to provide a clean mounting surface and avoid damage to the artwork from ongoing finishing work.
Flooring must be completed to provide a stable, clean base for the installation of heavy sculptures or for setting up scaffolding and lifts needed for wall-mounted artwork.
While not always physically required, installing lighting first is a strong preference to allow the artwork to be positioned and oriented correctly relative to the intended lighting design.
Final cleaning and touch-up painting must be done after artwork installation to clean dust and debris from the installation process and perform any necessary repairs to surrounding finishes.
Protective floor coverings can only be removed after heavy sculptures and artwork are in place, to avoid damaging the finished floor during the installation process.
Columns require a stable load-bearing foundation to transfer vertical loads to the ground; without completed footings, columns have no support base.

predecessor: Rebar Cage / Reinforcement Installation for Column
rationale: Steel reinforcement must be placed and tied before concrete is poured to ensure the column has tensile strength.
Formwork molds must be erected and braced to contain and shape the wet concrete during column construction.
Floor slabs and decks are typically supported by columns; columns must be cured to sufficient strength before slab formwork and pouring can proceed above.
Beams transfer loads to columns; columns must be in place and cured to receive beam ends and provide vertical support.
While shear walls and columns often work together laterally, columns are typically erected first to define the grid, but some sequencing can overlap.
Structural shell and core walls must be completed to provide the enclosure and substrate for lobby finishes such as drywall, cladding, and ceiling installation.
Ductwork, conduit, piping, and wiring within walls and ceilings must be installed before they can be covered by interior finishes like gypsum board, ceiling tiles, and wall panels.
Floor slabs must be leveled and screeded to provide a smooth substrate for lobby floor finishes such as tiles, marble, or carpet.
After finishes are complete, electrical outlets, light fixtures, switches, plumbing fixtures, and HVAC grilles can be installed as trim-out without damaging finished surfaces.
Final paint and decorative touches are applied after all other interior finishes are installed to ensure a uniform, undamaged finish.
Excavation must be completed to expose and prepare the ground/subgrade before any structural slab and columns can be poured or erected.
A blinding layer of concrete is typically required to provide a clean, level working surface and to protect the reinforcement and slab from contamination before pouring the main structural slab.

predecessor: Rebar & Formwork Installation for Lobby Slab
rationale: Reinforcement steel (rebar) must be placed and formwork erected to define the slab shape and support the wet concrete; these are preparatory steps that must precede the actual concrete pour/structural works.
After pouring the slab and columns, a curing period is physically required for the concrete to gain strength before any further loads are applied.
Waterproofing membrane or coating is applied to the cured structural slab to protect it from moisture ingress; this cannot be done before the slab is cast and cured.

MEP (Mechanical, Electrical, Plumbing) rough-in works such as conduit and pipe embedment are often done in conjunction with or immediately after the slab pour before finishes; however, some MEP can be cast-in-place, so this is typically a soft preference rather than a hard constraint.
MEP rough-in work for lobby services requires that the slab/ foundation is in place (building has a base floor) before any underground or in-slab conduit, piping, or sleeves can be placed.
Lobby MEP rough-in (ductwork, piping, conduits) cannot start until the structural frame is erected to provide support and clear working space.
After MEP rough-in is complete, wall and ceiling framing can be built around the installed mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems.
Interior finishes (drywall, ceiling tiles, paint) must follow MEP rough-in because the rough-in work is concealed within walls and above ceilings.
Trim-out and final connections (fixtures, outlets, diffusers) must occur after rough-in because they terminate the rough-in systems.
The building's structural frame must be complete to provide the load-bearing support for curtain wall systems, which are typically hung from or attached to the structural skeleton.
Roof completion and waterproofing are necessary to protect the interior and the curtain wall system from weather exposure during installation; curtain walls often interface with roof flashings.
Floor slabs must be poured and cured to provide working platforms and anchorage points for curtain wall mullions and support brackets at each floor level.
Interior partitions should follow curtain wall installation to ensure proper alignment with the building envelope's interior face and to allow for perimeter sealant and thermal break continuity.

successor: Building Envelope Air/Water Barrier & Insulation (Interior Side)
rationale: After the curtain wall is installed, the interior side of the envelope can be completed with air barriers, vapour retarders, and insulation to achieve the designed thermal and moisture performance.
All lobby systems (lighting, HVAC, access control, audio/visual, etc.) must be physically installed before they can be commissioned and tested.
Electrical wiring, conduits, and connections must be completed and energized before systems can be powered on and tested.
Low voltage/data cabling for security, AV, and building automation systems must be run and terminated before system testing can occur.
Systems must be verified as operational before enclosing them with ceiling tiles, wall panels, and decorative finishes to avoid costly rework.
The lobby cannot be occupied or handed over to the client until all systems have been successfully commissioned and tested to ensure functionality and safety.
The structural roof deck and steel framing must be in place to provide support and a substrate for skylight and glazing installation.
Roof sheathing and underlayment must be installed to create a weather-tight base before cutting openings and installing skylight units.
Rough openings must be framed to the correct dimensions to receive the skylight or glazing unit.
Flashing must be installed after the skylight is in place to seal the joint between the skylight and the roof membrane, preventing leaks.
Interior ceiling finishing, such as drywall and painting around the skylight well, must follow after the skylight is installed to ensure a clean transition and proper sealing.
The atrium floor cannot be placed until the foundation and substructure elements (footings, slab-on-grade, or structural slab) are complete, as the floor requires a stable load-bearing base.
If the atrium is bounded by structural columns or walls, these support elements must be erected before the floor slab is poured to provide edge support and embedment connections.
The atrium floor must be in place to provide a working platform and base for installing atrium curtain walls or glazing systems, and to anchor bottom tracks.
Floor installations (e.g., concrete topping, tile, stone, or raised access floor) must be completed before final wall finishes, ceiling work, and millwork can begin in the atrium space.

Electrical conduits, plumbing chases, and HVAC ductwork located beneath the atrium floor slab require the floor to be poured before rough-in can be completed above it; conversely, MEP rough-in within the floor slab itself (embedded conduits) must be done prior to the pour, but overhead MEP requires the slab as a floor.
The foundation must be completed to provide structural support and load-bearing capacity before the atrium wall/façade can be erected.
The ground floor slab provides the base surface on which the atrium wall/façade is installed or anchored.
The wall/façade structure must be in place to support and receive the glazing or window panels that enclose the atrium.
Interior finishing work such as drywall, painting, and trim can begin after the façade is closed in to protect interior spaces from weather, though some sequencing flexibility may exist.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in within the atrium walls typically follows the wall structure but can sometimes be coordinated in parallel with façade installation.

The steel space frame roof structure requires a stable and level foundation or substructure to bear its weight and transfer loads. The substructure must be fully cured and capable of supporting the heavy steel components before erection can begin.
Steel space frames are typically supported by columns or vertical supports. These vertical elements must be in place and secured before the roof structure can be erected upon them.

The roof cladding or decking material is applied onto the completed steel space frame. The frame provides the structural support surface for the cladding, so it must be fully erected and stable first.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) systems that run within or above the ceiling space can only be installed after the roof structure is in place, as the structure provides the support points and spatial enclosure for these services.

Interior finishes such as ceiling installation, painting, and fixtures depend on the roof structure being complete to provide a weathertight enclosure and to prevent damage from ongoing structural work.
Smoke and fire curtains require a structural support framework (e.g., steel beams, tracks, or channels) to be in place to anchor and suspend the curtain assembly.
Fire/smoke curtains are typically mounted to the overhead structure or ceiling. The ceiling grid or soffit must be complete to provide the mounting surface.
Motorized smoke/fire curtains require electrical power connections for the motor and control panel; rough-in wiring must be run before curtain installation.

successor: Fire Alarm / Smoke Detection System Integration
rationale: Fire/smoke curtains must be physically installed before they can be wired to and electronically integrated with the fire alarm and smoke detection systems for automatic deployment.

It is safer and more efficient to install the curtain before enclosing the area with finished ceiling panels or cladding, though in some sequences the curtain can be installed through an access panel after finishes.
The balustrade/guardrail must be anchored to a completed concrete slab or deck structure that provides the necessary structural support and fixity.
Where balustrades attach to steel framing, the structural frame must be erected and stable to receive the guardrail system.
Handrails are typically mounted on top of or integrated with the balustrade/guardrail structure, so the balustrade must be in place first.

successor: Final Finishing / Painting of Balcony Areas
rationale: While finishing work can often be done after the guardrail is installed, it is preferable to complete painting and surface coatings as early as possible to avoid damage to the completed guardrail.
The guardrail system must be fully installed before it can be inspected and load-tested to verify compliance with safety codes and structural integrity requirements.
The building structure must be complete to provide the physical support surface (walls, frames) onto which green walls or landscaping elements are installed.
Waterproofing must be in place behind green walls and before soil/planting to prevent moisture damage to the structure.
Proper drainage behind green walls and in planter areas must be installed before adding soil and plants to ensure water can escape and prevent root rot or structural water damage.
The planting medium and vegetation must be in place before the irrigation system can be fully tested and commissioned to ensure it delivers water correctly to the plants.

Landscaping and green walls are typically among the final finishing activities, and their completion is preferred before final clean and handover to avoid soiling or damage, though not a strict physical prerequisite.
The elevator/lift core requires a solid foundation to support its structural load and ensure vertical alignment.
The lift core must be constructed on top of the finished slab to provide a level base and proper load distribution.
