The elevator core often serves as the primary lateral stability element (shear wall/core) for the building; the steel frame is erected around and tied into the core.
While some MEP work can run concurrently, the core must be complete before running vertical risers, conduits, and ductwork through the core shafts.
The elevator car, rails, and machinery cannot be installed until the concrete lift shaft is fully constructed, cured, and structurally ready.
The open staircase must be supported by the structural frame; the frame provides the load-bearing structure onto which the staircase is anchored.
The floor slabs at each level must be in place to define the landing points and support the staircase structure.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work adjacent to the stairwell can only be accurately positioned after the staircase is installed to avoid clashes.

While not physically impossible, finishing work such as painting, railing installation, and tread covering is typically sequenced after the structural staircase is in place to protect finishes and ensure accurate fit.
Fireproofing materials are applied directly to the exposed steel or concrete components of the open staircase after it is fully installed and inspected.
Steel frame requires stable, cured foundations to bear the structural load and provide anchor points for columns.
The site must be leveled and compacted to provide a stable working platform for cranes and steel erection equipment.
Ground slab must be poured and cured before steel erection to allow safe crane access and material staging.
The roof structure relies on the steel frame as its primary support; the frame must be complete before roof trusses and panels can be installed.
Wall panels and cladding systems are attached to the steel frame structural members and cannot be installed until the frame is erected.
While not physically impossible, it is standard practice to run conduit and wiring through the steel frame after erection to avoid interference and ensure proper routing.
HVAC ductwork and piping are typically suspended from or routed through the steel frame; installation is far more efficient after the frame is complete.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and compacted before scaffolding can be safely erected to ensure stable base and load-bearing capacity.
Foundations must be completed and cured to provide a solid structural base on which scaffolding can be supported or tied into the building structure.
The main structural frame must be in place to provide anchorage points for scaffolding ties and to define the working heights that the scaffolding will serve.
Scaffolding must be erected to provide safe access and a working platform at height before masons can begin laying bricks or blocks on upper building levels.
Scaffolding must be in place to support workers, materials, and equipment needed to install exterior cladding panels, curtain walls, or façade systems at height.
The atrium's structural frame (steel or concrete) must be complete to provide the load-bearing support and enclosure for fit-out activities such as ceiling installation, glazing, and finishes.
The building envelope, including roof and exterior wall waterproofing, must be in place to keep the atrium dry and weather-tight before interior finish work commences.

Overhead ducts, piping, conduit, and electrical rough-in must be installed before ceiling grids, drywall, and decorative finishes are placed, as they would be inaccessible or require destructive rework otherwise.

Atrium fit-out activities such as partition framing, glazing installation, and ceiling grid placement must be completed before final surface finishes like paint, wallcoverings, and flooring are applied.

Commissioning of HVAC, lighting, fire alarm, and other building systems in the atrium area can only proceed after the fit-out is substantially complete, as the systems are embedded within the finished ceilings, walls, and floors.

The overall building concept, use, and layout must be defined before a fire strategy can be developed, as the strategy depends on occupancy types, compartment sizes, and escape routes determined during concept design.
Spatial zoning, floor plans, and compartmentation must be established to serve as the basis for smoke modelling and fire engineering analysis.

The fire strategy determines fire severity, duration, and temperature-time curves that dictate the required fire resistance rating for structural elements; structural fire protection cannot be designed without these inputs.
Smoke modelling results (e.g., smoke layer height, extraction rates, flow paths) are required to size and locate smoke control systems such as natural or mechanical smoke vents.
HVAC systems must incorporate fire mode operation (e.g., pressurization, smoke purge) based on the smoke modelling outputs, though some parallel design is possible with later verification.

The thermal stratification study requires a fully enclosed building to accurately measure and analyze temperature gradients and air stratification within the conditioned space. Without the enclosure in place, external weather conditions would interfere with the internal thermal profile.
The HVAC system must be installed and operational to create the controlled temperature conditions necessary for studying thermal stratification patterns within the building.

Data from the thermal stratification study informs the adjustments needed for HVAC balancing and commissioning, ensuring supply and return airflows are optimized for the actual stratification conditions observed.
Temperature sensor placement and control system calibration rely on the thermal stratification analysis to determine optimal setpoints and sensor locations for accurate comfort control.

The architectural design (building geometry, orientation, window placement, and shading elements) must be defined before daylighting analysis can be performed, as the analysis evaluates the daylight performance of the designed spaces.

predecessor: Site Analysis and Solar Orientation Study
rationale: Site context including surrounding buildings, obstructions, and solar orientation data must be established to provide accurate input for daylight simulation models.

predecessor: Building Envelope Design (Glazing and Shading Selection)
rationale: Window types, glazing properties, and shading device specifications must be selected to model accurate light transmittance and daylight performance.

Daylighting analysis results inform the electric lighting design by determining where and when daylight is sufficient, allowing optimization of artificial lighting layout, controls, and dimming zones.
Daylighting analysis outputs (daylight factors, illuminance levels, solar heat gain) are critical inputs for whole-building energy modeling to calculate heating/cooling loads and energy consumption.

The BMU (Building Maintenance Unit) gantry system is typically mounted on the roof or upper structure of the building. The structural steel frame must be in place to provide the support and anchoring points for the gantry rails and trolley system.
The BMU tracks and base supports are often installed on the roof slab. The roof must be structurally complete and waterproofed before the heavy BMU equipment can be placed and operated on it.

The BMU is designed to clean and maintain the building facade. The curtain wall or exterior cladding must be installed so that the BMU's cleaning path, reach, and interface with the facade can be properly aligned and tested.

After the BMU gantry system is fully installed, it must undergo load testing and safety commissioning to verify its structural integrity, hoist operation, and emergency systems before being put into service.

The BMU provides the means of access for final cleaning of the glass panels and exterior detailing of the facade. These finishing activities cannot be performed safely or efficiently until the BMU is operational.
The dock bumper must have a stable foundation or base structure to be mounted onto before installation can begin.
Dock bumpers are typically mounted onto dock walls or edges; the wall structure must be in place before bumper installation.
Safety inspection of completed dock installations, including bumpers, must occur after the bumper is fully installed to verify proper placement and function.

successor: Apply Protective Coating/Finish to Dock Area
rationale: While not physically required, it is preferable to finish coatings and sealants around the dock area after bumper installation to avoid damaging the bumper or needing touch-ups.
The dock cannot be operational and open for use until all safety components including dock bumpers are installed to prevent damage to vehicles and the dock structure.
Dock levelers must be installed first to establish the proper height and alignment of the loading dock platform, which determines the positioning requirements for the dock seal or shelter.

predecessor: Dock Wall Construction / Rough Opening Framing
rationale: The dock wall and rough opening must be fully constructed and finished to provide a structurally sound mounting surface and proper opening dimensions for the dock seal or shelter frame.
Dock bumpers should be installed before the seal/shelter to establish the stop point for backing trucks and to ensure the seal/shelter is positioned correctly relative to the bumper face.

successor: Dock Pit / Approach Slab Paving (if applicable)
rationale: While the seal/shelter is typically installed after the approach slab is complete, if any final paving or grading adjustments are needed near the dock face, they should be done after the seal/shelter is in place to ensure a tight fit and avoid damaging the seal.
The dock seal/shelter must be installed and fastened before final commissioning and testing can verify proper truck interface, compression, and weather sealing performance.
The rough opening (including header, jambs, and sill) must be framed and prepared to the correct dimensions before the overhead sectional door can be installed.
The overhead sectional door must be installed and properly balanced before the automatic door opener can be mounted and connected.
Weatherstripping and seals around the door are applied after the door frame is installed to ensure a proper fit and prevent air/water infiltration.
Interior or exterior trim around the door frame is typically completed after door installation to cover gaps and provide a finished appearance.
The track, springs, cables, and rollers must be aligned and tensioned after the door panels are hung to ensure smooth operation.
The dock door frame must be anchored to a finished concrete slab or foundation. The concrete must be cured and load-bearing before the frame can be set in place and fastened.
The wall structure surrounding the dock door opening must be framed to provide the rough opening dimensions and structural support for the door frame.
Any conduit, piping, or sleeves that pass beneath the slab must be installed and inspected before concrete is poured, as they cannot be placed afterward.
The door frame must be installed, plumbed, and secured in the opening before the actual dock door (panel, track, rollers, hardware) can be mounted onto it.

The dock door frame defines the door opening location, and the dock leveler pit and mounting must be coordinated with the finished opening and adjacent slab edge. Typically the door frame is set before forming the leveler pit.

predecessor: Receiving and Inspection of Truck Restraint / Wheel Chock System
successor: Installation of Truck Restraint / Wheel Chock System
rationale: The system must be received and inspected for damage or defects before installation can begin.

predecessor: Installation of Truck Restraint / Wheel Chock System
successor: Testing and Commissioning of Truck Restraint / Wheel Chock System
rationale: The system must be installed before it can be tested and commissioned for functionality.

predecessor: Foundation and Anchoring Preparation for Loading Dock Area
successor: Installation of Truck Restraint / Wheel Chock System
rationale: The concrete foundation and anchor bolts must be in place to securely mount the truck restraint system.

predecessor: Installation of Truck Restraint / Wheel Chock System
rationale: The restraint system must be fully installed and operational before any truck docking and loading/unloading activities can safely occur.

predecessor: Utility Rough-In (Electrical/Control Wiring) at Loading Dock
successor: Installation of Truck Restraint / Wheel Chock System
rationale: Electrical power and control signal wiring must be roughed in to allow connection of the restraint system's control unit and warning lights.
The mounting bracket must be in place to physically support the dock light fixture.

predecessor: Run electrical conduit to dock light location
rationale: Electrical wiring and conduit must be in place before the light can be connected and powered.
Rough electrical work (cabling, boxes) must precede final fixture installation.

successor: Connect and test dock light electrical supply
rationale: The fixture must be physically installed before it can be wired, connected, and tested for operation.
The light must be installed and operational before the overall dock lighting system can be commissioned and verified.

successor: Install Dock Safety Light / Traffic Signal
rationale: The dock leveler must be in place before the safety light/traffic signal can be installed, as the signal needs to be positioned relative to the leveler to indicate when it is safe for truck loading/unloading.

successor: Install Dock Safety Light / Traffic Signal
rationale: Dock bumpers must be installed first to define the truck parking position, so the safety light/traffic signal can be positioned at the correct height and location for truck drivers to see.

successor: Install Dock Safety Light / Traffic Signal
rationale: Electrical conduit and wiring must be roughed in before the safety light/traffic signal can be connected to power and control systems.

predecessor: Install Dock Safety Light / Traffic Signal
successor: Test and commission dock safety system
rationale: The safety light/traffic signal must be physically installed before it can be tested and commissioned to verify proper operation and interlock with dock equipment.

predecessor: Install Dock Safety Light / Traffic Signal
rationale: Although training can partially proceed with other dock features, full operational training including use of the traffic signal is best performed after the signal is installed and functioning.
The dock canopy structure requires a stable foundation or pile support to bear its load; the piles/foundation must be installed first to provide structural support.
The canopy structure is typically mounted on or anchored to the dock deck/platform, so the deck must be completed before the canopy can be erected.
The structural frame of the canopy must be in place before roofing or cladding materials can be applied to it.
Electrical conduits and wiring for canopy lighting can only be run after the canopy structure is erected, as they are attached to or routed through the structure.

While finishing work like painting can be done after structural completion for convenience and to avoid damage, it is a soft preference as some finishing could theoretically be done prior to erection in a modular approach.

predecessor: Slab on Grade / Concrete Floor Pour
rationale: Dock levelers require a concrete slab to be poured, cured, and prepared with proper pit dimensions before the leveler can be set in place.

predecessor: Rough-In Electrical Conduit to Dock Area
rationale: Electrical rough-in and conduit for dock leveler controls must be placed in the slab or wall before the leveler is installed.
Dock bumpers protect the building wall and must be mounted before or concurrently with dock levelers to ensure proper alignment and protection during loading operations.
Testing of hydraulic or mechanical functions, safety features, and load ratings can only occur after the dock leveler is fully installed and connected.
While dock seals/shelters can sometimes be installed concurrently, it is preferred to install them after the leveler to ensure proper fit and clearance around the dock opening.
The rough opening must be properly framed and sized before the dock door and frame can be installed, as the door frame requires a structurally sound and correctly dimensioned opening.
The concrete slab or foundation at the dock area must be poured and cured to provide a level base for the dock door frame and to ensure proper elevation and anchoring.
Dock levelers are typically installed after the dock door frame is in place to ensure proper alignment and integration with the doorway and pit.
Dock seals or shelters mount around the dock door opening, so the door frame must be installed first to provide the correct mounting surface and dimensions.

While interior finishes can be completed after the door is installed for a cleaner appearance, it is a soft preference because the wall finish could also be done beforehand if the door opening is carefully protected.
The dock wall must be constructed to provide a structural surface for mounting the dock seal or shelter.
The concrete apron must be poured and cured to provide a level base and proper elevation for dock seal/shelter installation.
The dock door must be installed first so the dock seal/shelter can be aligned and fastened around the door opening.
Dock levelers are typically set after the seal/shelter to ensure proper coordination between the leveler pit and the seal positioning.
It is preferable but not strictly required to complete seal installation before final floor coating to avoid damaging fresh seal materials from coating application.

The dock leveler provides the structural reference and anchoring point for the truck restraint system; the restraint must be aligned with the leveler to ensure proper engagement with the truck's ICC bar.
A stable, cured concrete slab is required to bolt and anchor the truck restraint hardware; installation on uncured or unprepared foundation would compromise structural integrity.
Dock bumpers define the stopping position of the truck and protect the dock face; restraints are positioned relative to the bumpers so the hook engages the ICC bar correctly.
The door opening must be installed after the restraint so that the restraint hook path and sensor positioning are unobstructed and the door seals align properly.
Electrical connections for the restraint's warning lights and control system must be completed after the mechanical unit is fixed in place to ensure correct wiring length and conduit routing.

The dock structure and concrete works must be completed to provide the physical platform and mounting surfaces for safety system components such as guardrails, bumpers, lighting fixtures, and signage.

Safety systems such as dock leveler controls, warning lights, safety barriers, and emergency stop systems require electrical power; the electrical supply must be installed and energized before commissioning can proceed.
Dock levelers and lifts must be physically installed so that safety interlocks, limit switches, and edge-of-dock sensors can be calibrated and tested during commissioning.

Commissioning must verify that all safety systems (alarms, barriers, lighting, interlocks) function correctly before the dock can be declared operationally ready and subjected to live loading/unloading tests.
The safety system commissioning is a prerequisite for final inspection and handover to operations, as regulatory and safety compliance must be confirmed before the dock is accepted for use.
Excavation must be completed to expose and prepare the subgrade before the basement floor slab can be poured.
Foundation footings must be in place to support the structure before the basement floor slab is cast, as the slab often ties into or bears on the footings.
Foundation walls (or retaining walls) must be erected to enclose the basement area before the interior slab is poured.
All underground plumbing, drainage pipes, and electrical conduits that run beneath the slab must be installed and inspected before the concrete slab is poured.
Compacted granular fill and a vapour barrier (or rigid insulation) must be placed over the subgrade prior to pouring the slab to provide drainage and moisture protection.
Interior partition walls and framing in the basement can only be built after the slab is cured to provide a stable, level floor surface.
Finished flooring materials (tile, vinyl, or coatings) are typically applied after the slab has fully cured, though this is a soft preference as some finishes can be delayed.
The site must be cleared of debris, vegetation, and existing structures before any foundation work can begin.
The ground must be excavated to the required depth and dimensions before footings can be placed.
Proper survey and staking of footing locations are required to ensure correct positioning and alignment before pouring concrete.
The bearing capacity of the soil must be verified and the subgrade must be compacted to support the footing without excessive settlement.
Footings provide the load-bearing base; foundation walls are constructed directly on top of them after the footing concrete has cured.
Waterproofing membrane and drainage systems around the foundation are installed after footings are in place and the concrete has cured.
Rebar for foundation walls is typically anchored into the footing after the footing has been poured and set.

Backfilling around footings typically occurs after any foundation walls are built, though it is a sequential preference rather than a physical impossibility to backfill directly against footings alone.

The basement window well is attached to or installed around the foundation wall opening, so the foundation wall must be constructed first to provide the structural support and opening for the window well.
The area around the foundation where the window well will be placed must be excavated first to provide space for the window well assembly and proper drainage.
Window wells must be installed before backfilling against the foundation, as backfill material would cover and block access to the window well area if placed first.
The window well cover (if specified) is installed after the window well itself is in place to provide protection from debris and water.
Proper drainage (gravel or drain tile) at the base of the window well is typically placed before the window well is set in position to ensure water management.
Rough framing must be completed to provide the structural opening and support for the egress window installation.
After the egress window is installed, flashing and sealing must be applied around the window to prevent water intrusion and air leakage.
Interior wall finishes, trim, and drywall around the window rough opening can only be completed after the window is installed and secured.
Exterior siding around the window opening must be installed after the egress window is in place to ensure proper integration and weatherproofing.
For basement egress windows, the foundation wall and subfloor must be complete to define the window well and opening dimensions before window installation.
The foundation and subfloor must be prepared and structurally sound to provide a stable base for installing the bulkhead/cellar door frame and threshold.
The rough opening framing for the bulkhead/cellar door must be built into the foundation or floor structure before the door assembly can be installed.
Waterproofing and flashing around the bulkhead/cellar door must be installed after the door is in place to seal the perimeter and prevent water infiltration.
Backfilling and final grading around the exterior of the bulkhead cannot be completed until the cellar door is installed, as the door assembly defines the finished grade interface.
Interior or exterior stairs/ramps leading to the bulkhead door must be built after the door is installed to ensure proper alignment and safe egress.
The ground must be excavated, leveled, and compacted before formwork can be placed and concrete poured to ensure a stable foundation.
Steel reinforcement bars must be tied and placed within the formwork before concrete is poured to structurally reinforce the concrete element.
After concrete is poured, it must be allowed to cure and gain sufficient strength before the formwork can be safely stripped/removed.
Concrete elements must be fully set, cured, and formwork removed before waterproofing membranes or coatings can be applied to the concrete surface.
Concrete foundations and slabs must be fully cured to design strength before heavy structural steel columns and beams can be erected on them.

The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and obstructions before shoring and temporary support systems can be installed, as these systems require a clean, accessible working area to be properly positioned and anchored.

Shoring systems are installed to support the sides of excavations and trenches; therefore, initial excavation and grading must occur to create the void that requires shoring, though shoring often proceeds concurrently with deeper excavation.
Accurate surveying and layout are required to mark the exact locations and depths where shoring systems must be placed to ensure they align with foundation and structural requirements.
Shoring and temporary support systems must be in place to protect the excavation and support adjacent structures before foundation construction can safely begin within the excavated area.
Deep foundation installation requires stable, shored excavations to ensure worker safety and structural stability during pile driving or caisson drilling operations.
The ground must be cleared and excavated to expose the existing foundations before underpinning can commence.
Temporary support structures must be installed to safely carry the load of the existing structure while underpinning is carried out.
Soil bearing capacity and ground conditions must be assessed to design the appropriate underpinning method and depth.
After underpinning is complete and the new foundation has cured, the excavated areas around the foundation must be backfilled and compacted.
The building's superstructure or wall construction can only begin once the underpinned foundation is complete and load-bearing capacity is achieved.
Structural deck requires a stable base from the foundation to support its loads.
Columns or load-bearing walls must be in place to support the structural deck above.
Formwork provides the mold into which concrete for the structural deck is placed.
Upper walls or additional vertical framing rely on the structural deck as their working platform and support surface.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in above the deck is sequenced after deck completion, though some coordination may allow parallel work.
Excavation must be completed to create the space for the drainage layer installation.
The subgrade must be properly graded and compacted before placing the drainage layer to ensure proper drainage and stability.
Any underground utilities that will run below the drainage layer must be installed first to avoid disturbance or damage to the drainage layer.
The drainage layer provides a stable base; a geotextile or filter fabric is often placed on top to prevent fine soil migration into the drainage medium.
The drainage layer must be fully in place before the base or subbase course is laid above it, forming the next structural layer in the pavement or foundation system.
Overflow drains and scuppers are installed through the roof deck or structural slab, which must be in place to provide the structural support and opening for the drain body.

The roof membrane or waterproofing layer is typically installed up to the scupper/drain location, and the overflow drain integrates with this membrane to ensure watertightness. The membrane provides the base flashing surface against which the drain connects.
After the overflow drain or scupper body is installed, flashing and counterflashing are applied around the opening to seal the penetration and prevent water intrusion at the drain-roof interface.
The overflow drain or scupper outlet must be in place before downspouts or conductor pipes can be connected to carry water away from the drain.

Insulation is typically installed before the drain to maintain consistent roof assembly levels, but in some sequences the drain can be installed first and insulation fitted around it; this is a soft preference for orderly construction.
The pedestal support system requires a stable, level foundation slab to bear the load and provide a mounting surface; excavation and base slab must be completed first.

successor: Pedestal Anchor Bolt Embedment & Alignment Check
rationale: Anchor bolts are cast into or mounted onto the pedestal support structure, so the pedestal must be in place before bolts can be accurately positioned and aligned.

successor: Formwork & Concrete Pour for Pedestal Column
rationale: If the pedestal support system is a precast or pre-assembled component, its installation must be completed before the surrounding pedestal column can be formed and poured to encase or integrate it.

The primary purpose of the pedestal support system is to provide a raised, stable base for equipment (e.g., pumps, compressors, turbines); equipment can only be mounted after the support system is fully installed and cured.

After installing the pedestal structure, non-shrink grout must be applied under the baseplate and leveling adjustments made to ensure a flat, load-bearing interface before any superstructure or equipment is placed on top.
The structural frame or deck must be in place to provide a supporting surface and anchorage points for the balustrade/railing installation.

successor: Floor / Deck Finishing (e.g., waterproofing, screed, tiling)
rationale: Balustrades/railings are typically installed before final floor finishes to allow proper fixing through the finish layers and to protect finished surfaces from damage during installation.
Permanent balustrades must be in place to provide edge protection before temporary scaffolding or edge protection can be safely removed.

Parapet coping sits on top of the parapet wall, which is constructed above the roof deck. The roof deck must be installed to provide the base and structural support for the parapet walls and subsequent coping.
Parapet coping is the cap or cover installed on top of the parapet wall. The wall must be fully constructed and cured before the coping can be installed to cover and protect the wall top.
Base flashing and counterflashing are typically integrated with the parapet wall before the coping is installed, as the coping often covers or secures the top edge of the flashing system.

In some systems, the roof membrane may be installed before or after coping. However, it is often preferred to install coping after the membrane to allow the membrane to be dressed up the parapet and then capped by the coping for waterproofing integrity.
Exterior finishes near the parapet may be installed after coping, but this is often a soft preference to ensure a clean transition and avoid damaging finishes during coping installation.
The ground must be leveled, cleared, and foundation footings (or concrete pads) must be poured and cured before any pergola structure can be erected to provide a stable, load-bearing base.

Any electrical conduits, lighting wiring, or plumbing that will run beneath or through the pergola footprint must be installed before the structure is built to avoid digging or trenching under the completed pergola.

Overhead lighting fixtures, ceiling fans, or outlets mounted on or within the pergola can only be installed after the structural frame and roof/shade are complete to provide a finished surface for attachment.

While the pergola can be built before the final decking or patio surface is laid, it is often preferable to complete the surface first to avoid working around posts; however, the pergola can serve as a guide for the finished grade and surface layout.
Soft landscaping, planters, and decorative elements around the pergola are best installed after the structure is complete to ensure proper spacing, alignment, and access for final touches.
The ground must be leveled, cleared, and prepared before building a planter box to ensure stability and proper drainage.
Any underground irrigation lines or drainage pipes that will serve the planter box must be installed before the planter box is built to avoid excavation through the finished structure.
The planter box structure must be complete before soil is added, as the walls contain the soil and prevent spillage.
Plants cannot be placed until the planter box is fully constructed and filled with soil to provide a stable growing medium.
Surrounding decorative elements like mulch, edging, or paving adjacent to the planter box are typically done after the box is built, though some overlap may be possible with careful sequencing.
The structural frame of the building must be in place to support the roof access stair/hatch and provide the load-bearing structure it attaches to.
The roof deck must be installed to provide the surface and opening through which the roof hatch is mounted and accessed.
Flashing and waterproofing around the roof hatch must be completed after the hatch is installed to seal the penetration and prevent water ingress.
Insulation around the hatch area is typically installed after the hatch is in place to ensure a continuous thermal envelope, though some sequencing flexibility exists.
Interior finishing of the stairway leading to the roof hatch (e.g., handrails, treads, drywall) must follow the structural installation of the stair/hatch assembly to allow proper alignment and fit.

The lift overrun and elevator penthouse are structural extensions above the elevator shaft, requiring the concrete core and shear walls of the shaft to be fully constructed to provide vertical support and load transfer.
The lift overrun is built directly atop the completed elevator shaft, providing the necessary vertical enclosure and structural base for the penthouse structure.
The lift overrun typically projects above the main roof level; the roof slab must be completed to define the transition point and provide structural integration and waterproofing continuity.

The elevator machine room equipment (hoist machines, controllers, etc.) is housed within the lift overrun/penthouse; the structure must be enclosed and weathertight before installing sensitive mechanical and electrical equipment.

The elevator penthouse provides the overhead space for the hoist beam, sheaves, and overspeed governor mechanisms; these components must be in place before the elevator car and counterweight can be rigged and installed in the shaft.

The windbreak screen requires a stable, level base or foundation to be installed upon; site preparation (clearing, grading) and foundation work (footings or slab) must be completed first to provide structural support.
The windbreak screen is a permanent or semi-permanent structure; once installed, surrounding landscaping, paving, or finishing work can be completed around it without risk of damage or rework.

Any underground electrical, drainage, or irrigation lines that would pass under or near the windbreak screen's footprint must be trenched and installed before the screen is erected to avoid digging up or undermining the finished screen structure.

successor: Attachment of Privacy Slats or Louvers
rationale: The main structural frame of the windbreak screen must be erected first to provide the supporting framework onto which infill elements such as slats, louvers, or screening mesh are subsequently attached.

While sealing can be done after installation for weatherproofing, it is a soft preference because some coatings may be applied to components before assembly; however, final touch-up coating typically follows installation for complete coverage.

Waterproofing requires a clean, dry, and fully cured concrete substrate to adhere properly and function effectively. Installing waterproofing before the slab has cured can lead to adhesion failure, blistering, or cracking.

The surface must be free of debris, dust, oil, laitance, and loose particles to ensure proper bonding of the waterproofing membrane. Without this preparation, the waterproofing system will not adhere correctly and may delaminate.
Any cracks, joints, honeycombing, or surface defects in the concrete must be patched, filled, or repaired before waterproofing is applied to prevent water intrusion through those points.

A protective layer (e.g., protection board, drainage mat, or insulation) must be installed immediately after the waterproofing membrane is fully cured to shield it from mechanical damage during subsequent construction activities.
Backfilling against foundation walls can only occur after the waterproofing system is fully installed and cured to avoid damaging the membrane and to maintain a continuous water barrier.

Penetration sleeves are cast into or set into the structural slab or wall before concrete is poured. The sleeve must be positioned and secured before the concrete placement so that it becomes an integral part of the structure.
The exact location, elevation, and size of each penetration must be marked and coordinated on formwork or rebar before the sleeve can be positioned and fixed.
Reinforcing steel must be installed and the sleeve must be placed between rebar bars (or rebar cut/reframed per approved detail) before concrete is poured.
Once the sleeve is cast in place, mechanical, electrical, and plumbing pipes and conduits can be threaded through the sleeve for continuous MEP routing.

successor: Firestop / Smoke Seal Application at Sleeve
rationale: After the sleeve is installed and the service pipe is passed through, a firestop sealant or wrap must be applied around the annular gap to maintain fire-resistance rating and smoke barrier integrity.
The roof slab provides the structural substrate upon which insulation and drainage boards are installed; they cannot be placed until the concrete has cured and the surface is ready.
The waterproofing membrane must be laid and fully bonded to the substrate before insulation boards are installed, as the insulation protects and sits atop the membrane.
The geotextile filter fabric is placed directly on top of the insulation/drainage boards to prevent soil ingress into the drainage layer.

successor: Green Roof Growing Medium / Soil Placement
rationale: The growing medium or soil layer is placed above the insulation and drainage boards; it cannot be installed until the insulation/drainage layer is complete.
Roof pavers or protective finishes are typically installed after the insulation and drainage boards to provide a walking surface or final finish, though in some designs the order may vary slightly.
The ground must be properly excavated, leveled, and compacted before any paving or decking can be installed, as unstable ground will cause settlement and failure of the paving or decking structure.

Subsurface drainage pipes, French drains, and stormwater management systems must be installed before paving to ensure water is properly channeled away from the paved surface, preventing water damage and pooling.

All underground utilities (electrical conduits, water lines, gas pipes, communication cables) must be laid in trenches prior to paving, as paving over these would require costly demolition to access utilities later.
A proper base layer of crushed stone or aggregate must be placed and compacted to provide a stable, load-bearing foundation for the paving material or decking supports.
After paving stones, tiles, or decking boards are installed, joint sand, sealants, and protective coatings must be applied to protect the surface and lock the paving/decking elements in place.

Landscaping around paved areas (planting grass, shrubs, flower beds adjacent to paving) is typically done after paving is complete to avoid damaging new plants and to achieve clean edges, though it is a preference rather than a strict physical necessity.

The structural framing and deck surface must be in place to provide a stable base and support for the balustrade and parapet system. Balustrades and parapets are typically fastened to the structural deck or floor slab, so the structure must be complete first.
Where parapets are built as extensions of concrete or masonry walls, those walls must be constructed first to provide the substrate and structural connection for the parapet.

Waterproofing must be applied to the deck or balcony surface before balustrade posts are installed, as post bases and flashings integrate with the waterproofing layer to ensure water tightness and prevent leaks.
After installation, the balustrade and parapet system must be inspected to verify compliance with building codes, safety requirements, and structural integrity before the area is put into service.

While not a strict physical constraint, it is common practice to complete balustrade installation before applying final floor finishes (e.g., tiles, pavers) adjacent to the balustrade to allow for neat edge detailing and avoid damage to finishes during installation.
Site must be cleared of debris, existing structures, and obstructions before any landscaping and planting can begin.
Grading, leveling, and contouring of the site must be completed to establish the final topography and drainage patterns before planting and landscaping.
All underground pipes, cables, drainage systems, and utility connections must be installed before landscaping to avoid digging into and damaging newly planted areas.
Structural elements, paved paths, retaining walls, and other hardscape features must be completed before soft landscaping to prevent construction traffic and materials from damaging plants and soil.
Landscaping and planting are among the final finishing works; once complete, the site can be presented for final inspection, snagging, and handover to the client.
The roof deck or structural slab must be fully constructed and cured before waterproofing can be inspected, as the waterproofing membrane is applied directly onto the structural substrate.
Parapet walls form the vertical terminations of the waterproofing system; they must be built so that the waterproofing can be lapped up the walls and properly detailed at penetrations.
The waterproofing membrane must be installed before it can be inspected. Inspection verifies the quality and integrity of the applied membrane.

Inspection of the waterproofing must be completed and approved before covering it with drainage layers, insulation, or protective screeds, as these would conceal defects and make remediation impossible without costly removal.

successor: Roof Terrace Paving / Finish Layer Installation
rationale: Final paving, tiles, or decking can only be laid after the waterproofing has been inspected and signed off, to ensure no leaks exist beneath the finished surface.
The structural framework and load-bearing elements must be completed before terrace work can begin to ensure a stable base and safe working conditions.
Proper waterproofing and insulation of the roof or terrace slab must be finished before terrace maintenance to prevent water damage and ensure the terrace is protected from moisture ingress.
Drainage systems (gutters, downpipes, floor drains) must be installed prior to terrace cleaning to allow water and debris to be properly channeled away during and after maintenance.
The terrace must be cleaned and prepared before final surface finishes like paving stones, tiles, or deck boards are installed to ensure adhesion and a level substrate.
Cleaning and maintenance of the terrace must be completed before the final project inspection and handover to present a finished, clean, and safe outdoor area to the client.

The raised access floor system requires a solid, level structural slab to serve as its base and support. The pedestals and panels cannot be installed without the underlying slab being fully cured and ready.

Cables, conduits, piping, and ductwork that will run beneath the raised floor must be installed and tested before the floor panels are placed, as access to the sub-floor space is severely restricted after the raised floor is completed.
The raised access floor panels provide the substrate for final floor finishes; carpet tiles, vinyl, or other coverings are installed directly on top of the raised floor panels.

While it is preferable to complete all underfloor connections before closing the floor, some final plug-in connections to floor-mounted outlets can be done after panels are installed by lifting individual tiles. This is a soft preference for efficiency.
Workstations, partitions, and furniture are typically placed on top of the finished raised floor surface, and any floor-mounted outlet boxes should already be accessible through the floor panels.
The CRAC unit requires a level, load-bearing floor surface (often a raised access floor or structural slab) to be installed and cured before the heavy unit can be placed.
Dedicated electrical power supply (feeder cables, disconnect switches, and conduit) must be roughed in to the unit's location before the CRAC unit can be connected and commissioned.
For water-cooled CRAC units, the supply and return chilled water piping must be installed and pressure-tested to the unit location before the unit can be connected.
Supply and return air duct connections can only be made to the CRAC unit after it is set in its final position, and air balancing must follow to verify proper airflow.
The condensate drain line must be connected to the unit's drain pan outlet after the unit is installed to ensure proper gravity drainage of condensate water.
Final power wiring termination, control wiring, and startup testing can only be performed after the CRAC unit is mechanically installed and secured in place.

While IT equipment can be placed beforehand, optimal practice is to have the cooling system operational before energizing critical servers to maintain environmental control, though racks may be physically installed before CRAC startup.

predecessor: Install Overhead Cable Trays and Raceways
rationale: Cable trays and raceways for power and data must be in place before CRAH units are positioned, as the CRAH units will obstruct overhead access once installed.

predecessor: Complete Structural Floor Slab and Waterproofing
rationale: The CRAH unit requires a level, finished structural floor that is waterproofed to protect against potential condensate leaks, preventing water damage to lower levels.

successor: Connect Chilled Water Supply and Return Piping
rationale: Chilled water piping connections to the CRAH unit require the unit to be precisely placed and anchored so that piping can be aligned with the unit's connection points.

successor: Install Underfloor Cabling and Power Distribution
rationale: While underfloor work can technically begin before CRAH placement, it is preferable to install the CRAH first to avoid moving the heavy unit over vulnerable cabling and to ensure accurate floor tile layout around the unit.
The CRAH unit must be installed and fully connected (chilled water, power, controls) before system-level testing and commissioning can verify airflow, temperature control, and cooling capacity.

predecessor: Install Electrical Switchgear & Main Distribution Panels
rationale: PDUs receive power from upstream switchgear and main distribution panels; these must be installed and energized first to provide the input power source.
PDUs are heavy floor-mounted units requiring a cured concrete slab to support their weight and allow proper anchoring.

predecessor: Install Overhead Cable Trays / Conduit Pathways
rationale: Cable trays and conduits must be in place to route power cables from the switchgear to the PDU and from the PDU to downstream loads.

successor: Terminate & Connect PDU Feeders and Branch Circuits
rationale: Cable terminations and branch circuit connections can only be performed after the PDU is physically mounted, grounded, and ready for wiring.
System commissioning including load bank testing, voltage checks, and insulation resistance tests requires the PDU to be fully installed and connected.
Server racks require a level, stable, and load-bearing floor surface. Foundation and floor slab must be completed and cured to support the heavy weight of populated server racks.
Overhead cable trays and conduits must be in place before racks are positioned, so that cables can be dropped down into the racks. Installing trays after racks would be difficult and disruptive.
Data and power cables are run to and terminated at the racks only after the racks are securely positioned in their final location.
Servers, switches, and other IT equipment are physically mounted into the rack only after the rack itself is installed, leveled, and secured.

successor: Power distribution unit (PDU) installation in rack
rationale: PDUs are mounted inside the rack after the rack is in place, to allow proper positioning and cable routing within the cabinet.

Electrical conduits, junction boxes, and outlet boxes must be installed before cable trays and cable management pathways can be secured in place, as cable management systems often attach to or coordinate with electrical rough-in locations.
Structural supports, ceiling grids, and wall framing must be complete to provide mounting surfaces and anchor points for cable trays, ladder racks, and other cable management components.
Large mechanical ducts and major piping must be installed first to avoid spatial conflicts and ensure that cable trays can be routed around these existing systems with proper clearance.

Cable trays, raceways, conduits, and pathways must be fully installed and inspected before any cables (power, data, or control) can be pulled through them to prevent damage to cables and ensure proper support.
Cable management pathways that penetrate fire-rated walls or floors must be in place before firestop sealants can be applied around the cables and pathways to maintain fire-resistance ratings.
Electrical power and data cabling must be roughed-in and terminated before IT equipment can be connected and powered on.
Ceilings, wall coverings, and painting must be completed to avoid dust and debris damaging sensitive IT equipment.
Raised access flooring or finished flooring must be in place to support server racks, cabling trays, and equipment.
IT equipment must be physically installed and racked before it can be configured, connected to the network, and tested.
A light clean-up after installation is preferred but the building can technically be commissioned with equipment in place but not yet fully operational.

ATS requires a dedicated, clean, and properly sized electrical room or enclosure with adequate ventilation, lighting, and working space clearances per NEC and local codes before installation can begin.

ATS units (especially larger floor-standing models) must be installed on a level, cured concrete pad or foundation to support their weight and maintain alignment, preventing mechanical stress and ensuring safe operation.

predecessor: Primary power supply installation (utility service entrance)
rationale: The ATS must be connected to the primary (normal) power source, so the utility service entrance conductors, metering, and main disconnect must be in place and energized for the ATS to receive its primary feed.
The ATS connects both the utility and the backup generator; the generator and its output circuit breaker must be installed and ready for connection to the ATS secondary (emergency) side.

successor: Cable pulling and termination to ATS
rationale: Conductors from utility, generator, and downstream loads can only be pulled and terminated into the ATS after the unit is securely mounted and its lugs/terminals are accessible.

successor: Control wiring and communication cable installation
rationale: Remote monitoring, start/stop control signals to the generator, and building management system (BMS) connections require the ATS to be in its final position before control wiring is run and terminated.

Critical or emergency load panels (e.g., life safety, fire alarm, medical equipment) must receive power through the ATS; the ATS must be installed and tested before these downstream panels can be safely energized from the backup source.

successor: ATS commissioning and load bank testing
rationale: Full functional testing, including transfer under load, timing verification, and simulated power failure sequences, can only be performed after the ATS is installed, wired, and all power sources are available.
Authority having jurisdiction (AHJ) inspection of the emergency power system requires the ATS to be fully installed, wired, and ready for demonstration before approval can be granted.
Cooling towers must be physically installed and connected before the cooling system can be commissioned, as they are a key component of the overall system.
Chillers must be installed, connected to piping and electrical systems, and ready for operation before commissioning can test and validate the cooling system.

predecessor: Cooling Piping Installation and Pressure Testing
rationale: All chilled water and condenser water piping must be installed, flushed, and pressure-tested to ensure leak-free operation before the system can be commissioned.

predecessor: Electrical Power Supply to HVAC Equipment
rationale: Electrical connections, switchgear, and power supply to all cooling equipment (chillers, pumps, cooling towers) must be complete and energized before commissioning can proceed.
The cooling system must be fully commissioned (tested, balanced, and verified) before the overall HVAC system can undergo final acceptance testing and handover.
A commissioned and functional cooling system is typically required before the building can be occupied to ensure occupant comfort and safety.

successor: BMS (Building Management System) Integration and Testing
rationale: While ideally the BMS is integrated during commissioning, final BMS integration and testing can sometimes overlap or follow initial commissioning activities.

The power infrastructure must be physically installed (cables, transformers, switchgear, panels, etc.) before any Factory Acceptance Testing (FAT) or Site Acceptance Testing (SAT) can be performed, as testing validates the installed system.
The electrical rooms, substations, or enclosures housing the power equipment must be built and enclosed before SAT can proceed, to provide a safe, weather-protected environment for testing.

Testing (FAT/SAT) must be successfully completed before full commissioning activities (e.g., energization, load testing, integrated system tests) can begin, to verify equipment works correctly and safely before putting it into service.
Connection to the main electrical grid or to downstream loads can only occur after SAT has verified the installed power infrastructure meets specifications and safety requirements.

predecessor: Civil / Structural Works for Power Equipment
rationale: Foundations, cable trenches, and structural supports for power equipment must be completed and cured before installation and subsequent testing can take place.
The sprinkler system must be fully installed before testing can begin, as testing verifies the functionality of the installed components.
Fire alarm integration and triggering mechanisms must be in place to test the suppression system's response to alarm signals.
Power supply to pumps, panels, and control systems is required to energize and test the suppression equipment.
Testing must be completed and passed before the building can receive final approval and commissioning sign-off.

successor: Ceiling and Wall Finishing (in tested areas)
rationale: It is preferable but not strictly required that testing be done before enclosing ceilings and walls, as leaks or failures discovered later would require costly rework.

The building geometry, envelope design, and spatial layout must be defined before a thermal/CFD analysis can be performed, as the survey simulates airflow and heat transfer based on the architectural design.
Preliminary HVAC and mechanical system layouts are needed as inputs for CFD modeling to assess thermal comfort and air distribution.
External environmental conditions such as solar radiation, wind patterns, and ambient temperatures must be gathered to serve as boundary conditions for the CFD simulation.
CFD survey results inform the sizing, placement, and ductwork design of HVAC systems, so the detailed MEP design must follow the thermal analysis.

While CFD outputs often feed into whole-building energy models for validation, the energy model can be started in parallel with simplified assumptions; however, best practice uses CFD results for accuracy.
All systems must be safely shut down before any decommissioning or data sanitisation activities can commence to prevent data corruption or loss.
A detailed decommissioning plan must be approved before execution to ensure compliance with legal, regulatory, and organisational requirements.
All critical data must be backed up and archived prior to sanitisation to prevent permanent loss of important information.
Data sanitisation must be completed before physical hardware disposal to ensure no sensitive data remains on devices that are sent for recycling or disposal.
A formal certification verifying that all data has been securely erased must follow the sanitisation process to provide audit evidence.
The MSB is a heavy piece of equipment that requires a stable, level floor foundation to support its weight and ensure proper alignment.
The MSB must be installed within its designated electrical room; walls, ceiling, and overhead protection must be in place before bringing in the sensitive switchboard.
The MSB must be connected to a completed grounding grid to ensure personnel safety and equipment protection before power is brought to the board.

successor: Incoming Main Feeder Cable Pulling and Termination
rationale: The MSB must be physically set in place and secured before the large incoming feeder cables from the transformer or generator can be pulled and terminated onto its lugs.
Sub-feeders from the MSB to downstream distribution boards cannot be connected until the MSB is installed and its busbars are ready to accept the outgoing circuits.
Electrical conduits and wiring must be run to the DB location before the DB can be connected and mounted, as the DB serves as the central distribution point for incoming cables.
The earthing and grounding system must be in place before the DB is installed, because the DB enclosure and neutral/earth bars require bonding to the main earth.
The mounting surface (wall, recess, or enclosure) must be ready and roughed-in before the DB can be securely fixed and aligned.
Circuit breakers and MCBs are installed directly into the DB's internal busbars and din rails; the DB enclosure must be mounted and wired first.
All final sub-circuits (lighting, power outlets, appliances) are connected from the DB; this cannot occur until the DB is installed and energized.
The busbar chamber connects directly to the main switchboard to distribute power; the switchboard must be in place first to provide the mounting and connection point.
Branch circuit cables terminate at the busbar chamber; the chamber must be installed and secured before cables can be connected to its terminals.
The busbar chamber must be fully installed and connected before the system can be energized and tested for continuity and insulation resistance.
The busbar chamber is housed within the enclosure frame; the frame must be erected to provide structural support before the chamber can be positioned and fixed.
Main feeder cables supply power to the busbar chamber; they must be routed and terminated prior to connecting to the busbar chamber's incoming terminals.
PFC units need to be connected to the main electrical distribution panel to monitor and correct power factor; the panel must be installed first to provide the connection point.
The PFC unit must connect to the main switchboard to monitor total facility power factor and inject capacitive reactance; switchboard must be in place before PFC cabling and integration.

The transformer steps down utility voltage to facility voltage; PFC units are typically installed on the secondary side of the transformer and require transformer to be operational for load-side power factor correction.
The PFC unit must be physically installed and connected before the overall electrical system can be commissioned and tested to verify power factor correction performance.

While load balancing can begin before PFC installation, the final balancing should account for the PFC unit's reactive power compensation to optimize system performance; this is a preference for optimal operation rather than a physical necessity.
Metering panels are typically mounted on walls or concrete slabs; the slab must be cured and ready to support the panel.
Conduits, cables, and electrical pathways leading to the metering location must be installed before the panel can be connected.
Individual branch circuits and final wiring connections cannot be terminated until the metering panel is mounted and its bus bars are energized-ready.
The utility meter and service disconnect can only be installed and energized after the metering panel is securely in place and all upstream connections are complete.
Drywall and finishing work around the metering area must be completed after the panel is installed to allow access for mounting, conduit connections, and inspection.
The mounting base or frame must be securely fixed to the panel or enclosure before the fuse disconnector unit can be installed onto it.
Incoming power cables must be pulled and terminated at the line-side terminals of the fuse disconnector before the unit can be fully wired and closed.
Fuses can only be inserted after the disconnector body is mounted and wired, to avoid damage during installation and to ensure safe handling of live parts.
The disconnector must be fully installed and connected before any labels are applied and electrical testing (e.g., continuity, insulation resistance) can be performed.
The fuse disconnector must be completely installed, fused, and closed before the circuit can be safely energized and commissioned.

The RCD is typically mounted inside or adjacent to the distribution board, which serves as the central hub for electrical distribution. The DB must be installed first to provide the physical enclosure and busbar connections for the RCD.
The RCD requires a proper earth connection to function correctly and safely. The main earthing conductor must be run from the earth electrode to the DB before the RCD can be connected.

Final subcircuit cables (lighting, power points, etc.) must be terminated on the load side of the RCD so that they are protected by it. The RCD must be in place and wired to the busbar before downstream circuits can be connected.
The RCD must be installed and wired before the electrical system can be safely energised and tested. Testing of RCD trip times and functionality is part of the commissioning process.

successor: Install Socket Outlets and Final Points
rationale: Socket outlets and other final points are protected by the RCD. While rough-in wiring may occur earlier, the final connection and fitting of outlets should occur after the RCD is in place to ensure proper circuit protection from the start.
The building structure (steel framework and concrete floors/walls) must be in place before switchroom fit-out can commence, as the switchroom is housed within the building envelope.
The roof and cladding must be completed to provide a weathertight environment before sensitive electrical switchroom equipment and fit-out works begin.
The switchroom must be installed and fitted out to provide the mounting infrastructure and terminations points before HV cables can be laid and terminated into the switchgear.
The switchroom equipment must be fully installed and fitted out before electrical commissioning and testing can begin, as switchgear energisation and testing is part of the commissioning sequence.
While not a strict physical dependency, it is common practice to complete the switchroom early to allow main electrical distribution before finishing other MEP services fit-out works.
Cable trays and ladders provide the physical support pathway for cables; cables cannot be pulled and laid without the tray system in place.

predecessor: Duct Bank Installation / Underground Conduit Laying
rationale: Underground ducts and conduits must be installed before cables can be pulled through them.
Cable pulling into substations or switchrooms requires that the building/civil works (walls, floors, cable trenches) are finished to provide access and containment.
Cables must be pulled, laid, and terminated before insulation resistance testing, hi-pot testing, and other commissioning tests can be performed.

successor: Cable Tray / Ladder Final Covers & Firestopping
rationale: Firestopping and final tray covers are typically installed after cables are pulled, but in some sequences they can be partially done beforehand (soft preference for post-installation to avoid rework).
The switchboard must be manufactured and assembled before it can be tested for acceptance. Testing cannot occur on a non-existent or incomplete assembly.
The design and engineering specifications must be finalized and approved before FAT can be performed, as the test criteria and acceptance standards are based on the approved design.
All components (circuit breakers, relays, meters, busbars, enclosures, etc.) must be procured and delivered to the factory for assembly before the assembled switchboard can undergo FAT.
The switchboard must pass FAT to confirm it meets specifications before it can be packed, shipped, and dispatched to the project site. Failed FAT would require rework before dispatch.

FAT must be successfully completed at the factory before the switchboard is transported to site for installation and commissioning activities, ensuring only tested and approved equipment is installed.
The facility or area must be shut down or access restricted to ensure safety before maintenance work can begin.
All energy sources must be isolated and locked out to prevent accidental energization during maintenance activities.
A valid work permit (e.g., hot work, confined space) must be issued before scheduled maintenance can proceed.
After completing scheduled preventive maintenance, inspection and testing must be performed to verify the work was done correctly and equipment is functioning.
The system can only be re-energized or returned to service after all scheduled maintenance tasks are completed.

Thermographic inspection detects heat anomalies in electrical systems; therefore, the electrical system must be fully installed and energized before thermal imaging can capture temperature patterns under load.

Thermographic inspection for building envelope thermal performance requires the building enclosure (roof, walls, windows) to be complete so that air sealing and insulation are in place to detect thermal bridging or air leakage.
HVAC systems must be installed and running to create temperature differentials needed for thermographic inspection to identify pipe blockages, duct leakage, or equipment overheating.

Findings from thermographic inspection (e.g., hot spots, insulation gaps) dictate where corrective work is needed; remediation cannot be rationally planned or executed before inspection results are available.

While commissioning can partially proceed in parallel, final sign-off often depends on satisfactory thermographic inspection results to confirm systems are defect-free, making this a soft preference for sequential ordering.
Accurate arc flash hazard assessment requires complete electrical system design, including single-line diagrams, equipment ratings, protective device settings, and fault current calculations.
Actual equipment nameplate data, manufacturer specifications, and installed component ratings are needed for precise arc flash calculations.
The assessment must be performed on the as-built configuration with all electrical equipment installed and properly connected to determine incident energy levels accurately.

successor: Arc Flash Labeling and Warning Installation
rationale: Arc flash labels specifying incident energy levels, shock boundaries, and required PPE must be produced from the assessment results before they can be affixed to equipment.

successor: Safety Training and Work Practice Development
rationale: The findings of the arc flash assessment determine the required PPE levels, approach boundaries, and safe work practices that must be incorporated into training programs and procedures.

The protection relay coordination study requires the electrical design (single-line diagrams, equipment ratings, relay types) to be already completed, as the study determines relay settings based on the electrical system configuration.
The relay settings determined by the coordination study must be finalized before they can be programmed into the actual protection relays.
The short circuit analysis provides fault current magnitudes at various points in the system, which are essential input data for determining proper relay coordination settings.
Relays must have their coordination settings determined and programmed before they can be tested and commissioned in the field.
Load flow results indicate normal operating currents and voltage profiles that inform the pickup and time-dial settings for protective relays.

predecessor: Lift shaft preparation and structural works
rationale: The lift shaft must be structurally complete, including the machine room or overhead structure, to provide a safe and stable mounting location for the traction machine before it can be installed.

predecessor: Machine room civil works and overhead beam installation
rationale: The traction machine is heavy and must be mounted on a reinforced concrete plinth or steel beams in the machine room; these must be constructed and cured before the machine can be lifted and bolted into place.
The traction machine sheave must be in place and secured before hoist ropes can be threaded over it and tensioned.

successor: Electrical power supply and control wiring to motor
rationale: The motor unit must be physically installed before electricians can connect the main power cables, control wiring, and encoder/sensor cabling to the motor terminals.

successor: Machine room commissioning and load testing
rationale: Commissioning procedures including the no-load and load tests of the traction machine can only commence once the motor unit is fully installed, aligned, and connected.

predecessor: Electrical room preparation and power supply installation
rationale: The lift controller panel requires a stable power supply and electrical connections from the main electrical room before it can be operational.

predecessor: Lift shaft construction and pit preparation
rationale: The lift controller panel is typically located adjacent to the lift shaft or machine room; the shaft and machine room must be structurally complete before installing the controller.

successor: Lift motor and drive system installation and commissioning
rationale: The controller panel provides the control logic and power distribution to the lift motor; the motor cannot be connected and tested until the controller is installed and wired.

successor: Lift car wiring and control signal testing
rationale: All lift car functions (doors, buttons, indicators) are controlled by signals from the controller panel; car wiring must follow controller installation to ensure correct termination and testing.

successor: Safety system integration and testing (overspeed governor, brakes, sensors)
rationale: Safety devices rely on the controller for monitoring and emergency response; they must be integrated after the controller is in place and programmed.
The governor device requires a stable, level foundation or mounting pad to be installed upon, which must be constructed first to support its weight and ensure proper alignment.
The governor must be installed and fixed in place before the turbine or prime mover can be aligned with it, as the governor controls the speed and must be mechanically coupled to the prime mover.

successor: Control Linkage and Hydraulic System Connection
rationale: The governor device must be physically installed before control linkages, hydraulic lines, or actuator connections can be attached to it.
The governor must be physically in place and connected before it can be calibrated and tested for speed regulation performance.
Electrical conduits, cables, and instrumentation wiring paths must be roughed in and available up to the governor location before the device is mounted, to allow connections to be made efficiently.

The main drive sheave requires a stable, cured concrete foundation to support its massive weight and operational loads. Installing before the concrete has fully cured could cause foundation failure or misalignment.

The main drive sheave is typically mounted on the headframe structure at the top of the mine shaft. The headframe steel must be erected and structurally complete to provide the support platform for the sheave.
The hoist ropes must pass over the main drive sheave to connect the skips or cages. The sheave must be in place and rotating freely before ropes can be threaded over it.
After installation, the sheave must be precisely aligned with the headframe and drum, and dynamically balanced to ensure smooth operation and prevent excessive wear on ropes and bearings.
The main drive sheave is an integral part of the hoisting system. Full system commissioning, including test runs with loads, can only begin once the sheave is installed, aligned, and secured.
The sheave support bracket provides the structural mounting point for the deflector sheave; the sheave cannot be installed without its support bracket already in place.
The cable or rope must pass through the sheave groove to function; threading can only occur after the sheave is securely mounted in its final position.
Proper alignment and tensioning of the cable system requires the deflector sheave to be in place so the cable path is fully defined.
The brake components (rotors, calipers) mount onto the axle hub or spindle. The axle must be in place to provide the structural mounting point for the brake assembly.

While brake lines can be routed before the mechanical brake parts are installed, it is often more convenient to run the lines after the calipers and wheel cylinders are mounted, but not a strict physical dependency.
The steering knuckle or upright that carries the brake caliper bracket must be installed first, as the brake caliper mounts directly to the knuckle.
The wheel mounts over the brake rotor/drum and is bolted to the hub; the brake assembly must be in place before the wheel can be fitted.

Bleeding the brake system to remove air requires all calipers and wheel cylinders to be connected and sealed. This can only be done after the brake assembly (including calipers and lines) is installed.
The encoder/pulse generator must have a stable mounting bracket installed before it can be securely attached.

successor: Connect encoder signal cables to control system
rationale: The encoder/pulse generator must be physically installed before signal cables can be connected to it.

successor: Calibrate encoder/pulse generator with drive system
rationale: Calibration can only be performed once the encoder is installed and wired to verify proper alignment and signal output.

successor: Align encoder shaft with motor/drive shaft
rationale: Mechanical alignment of the encoder shaft must be done after the encoder is installed to ensure accurate rotation sensing.
The encoder/pulse generator requires a stable power supply to be available for testing after installation, so the power supply should be installed and verified beforehand.
The rope must be fabricated before the tension equaliser can be installed on it.
Anchor points must be prepared and fixed in place before the tension equaliser can be attached.
The equaliser must be fully installed before load testing can be performed to verify its integrity.

The concrete foundation must be fully cured and leveled to provide a stable, load-bearing surface for the bedplate; installing the bedplate before the foundation is ready would cause misalignment or structural failure.

The bedplate serves as the precision reference surface; all machine tool components (e.g., spindle, guide rails) must be mounted and aligned relative to the installed bedplate for accurate positioning.

After placing the bedplate onto the foundation, precision leveling and epoxy grouting must be performed to fill gaps and ensure uniform support under the entire bedplate before any machinery is loaded onto it.

While coolant pipes and drains can be roughed in earlier, final connections to the bedplate's integrated coolant channels should be made after the bedplate is set in its final position to avoid stress on connections.

successor: Electrical Grounding & Conduit Routing to Machine
rationale: Grounding cables and power conduits are best routed and terminated after the bedplate is fixed in place to ensure correct grounding paths and avoid rework from positional changes.
The machine room structure (walls, floor, ceiling) must be in place before the access door can be installed, as the door is integrated into the structural opening.

Large mechanical equipment (e.g., elevator machinery, HVAC units) must be moved into the machine room before the access door is fully closed/framed, or the door must be installed first and opened to allow equipment entry. Typically, the door frame and rough opening are prepared, equipment is brought in, then final door installation is completed. However, if the door must be fully operational first, equipment comes after.
The door frame must be properly anchored and leveled within the rough opening before the door panel and hardware can be mounted.

successor: Machine Room Fire Rating and Insulation Work
rationale: Fire-rated access doors must be installed before fire caulking, sealing, and insulation around the door assembly can be completed to maintain the fire-resistance rating.

successor: Machine Room Final Inspection and Commissioning
rationale: The access door should be installed and operational before the final inspection of the machine room, as inspectors need to verify secure access, fire rating compliance, and proper operation of the door.
Cables for CCTV cameras and remote monitoring must be routed through cable trays and conduits before the terminal equipment can be connected and powered.
The CCTV and remote monitoring terminal requires a stable electrical power source to be available before it can be energized and commissioned.
Network cabling (e.g., Ethernet, fiber) must be run and terminated to support data transmission from cameras and monitoring devices to the terminal.
After the terminal hardware is physically installed, the software, user interfaces, recording parameters, and network settings must be configured before operational use.
Full system testing—including camera feeds, recording, alarm verification, and remote access—can only be conducted after the terminal is installed and configured.
