The lift must be installed and in place before maintenance and inspection can begin, as you cannot inspect or maintain equipment that has not yet been installed.
Electrical power supply and control wiring must be completed to enable functional testing and inspection of the lift system during maintenance activities.
Maintenance and inspection must be completed to verify all components are functioning correctly before commissioning the lift for operational use.

Although not a strict physical dependency, it is strongly preferred that lift maintenance and inspection be completed prior to building handover to ensure safe vertical transportation is available for occupants.
The lift shaft and hoistway must be structurally complete and safe to access before maintenance personnel can perform inspection and servicing of the lift system.

The building must be substantially complete (enclosed, with major systems installed) before commissioning and load testing can proceed, as testing requires a finished environment and operational systems.
HVAC and mechanical systems must be fully installed before they can be commissioned and load tested to verify performance.
Electrical systems including power distribution and backup generators must be in place before load testing can be performed.
Plumbing and fire suppression systems must be installed before they can be tested and commissioned.
All systems must be commissioned and load-tested before the final inspection and certification can occur, as the inspection verifies that systems perform as designed.
Electrical safety requires that power to the controller be isolated and locked out before any upgrade or modernisation work begins on the controller to prevent electrocution or equipment damage.
The old or existing controller must be physically removed from its mounting location before the new or upgraded controller can be installed in its place.
After the upgraded controller is installed, it must be commissioned and tested to verify proper operation, configuration, and integration with the system before being placed into service.
Power can only be restored after the new controller is fully installed, as re-energising before controller installation would create an unsafe condition and could damage equipment.
System-level integration testing must follow controller installation to confirm the upgraded controller communicates correctly with other systems and devices.
Hydronic piping must be installed before sprinkler control valves to ensure there is a pressurized water supply line available for the sprinkler system to draw from.

predecessor: Rough-In Electrical for Fire Alarm System
rationale: Electrical rough-in for fire alarm and detection systems must be completed before control valve installation to allow for proper integration of valve position monitoring and flow switches.
Control valves must be installed first to serve as the isolation point before branch piping is run downstream, ensuring the system can be properly shut off for maintenance.
Control valves must be in place and operational before sprinkler heads are installed to allow for system pressure testing and flushing without damaging the heads.

successor: Fire Alarm System Testing and Commissioning
rationale: Control valves must be installed to enable flow switch and tamper switch connections to the fire alarm system, which are verified during commissioning.
The fire suppression piping network must be physically installed before control systems can be wired and integrated with the piping, valves, and suppression agents.
Fire suppression controls often interface with and receive signals from the fire alarm system for automatic activation; the alarm system must be in place for proper integration.
Control panels and devices require electrical power; rough electrical work including conduit, wiring, and dedicated circuits must be completed to supply power to the controls.

successor: Fire Suppression System Testing and Commissioning
rationale: The controls must be installed and operational before the overall suppression system can be tested, calibrated, and commissioned to verify proper response to alarms and manual activation.

Control panels, pull stations, and indicating devices are typically mounted in or on walls and ceilings; final finishes must be installed after the controls are placed to allow access for wiring and mounting.

The PA/VA system requires electrical power to operate. Conduits, wiring, and power outlets must be roughed in and a dedicated power supply installed before the system components can be connected and energized.

Speaker mounting brackets, back boxes, and cable pathways are installed within ceiling plenums and wall cavities. These structural supports and concealed pathways must be in place before speakers, amplifiers, and control panels can be mounted.

The PA/VA system must be installed and operational before it can be integrated with the fire alarm system for emergency voice evacuation commands, as the VA system is a slave to the fire alarm control panel.

Speakers and control panels must be installed prior to final ceiling tiles and wall finishing to allow access for mounting, wiring, and adjustment. Final finishes then cover and trim around the installed components.
The complete PA/VA system must be installed and wired before comprehensive testing, sound level calibration, intelligibility testing, and formal acceptance/commissioning can be performed.

predecessor: Electrical backbone installation and cable tray routing
rationale: Fire telephones require dedicated wiring and cabling infrastructure; electrical backbone and cable trays must be installed first to provide pathways for the intercom cables.
The firefighter's intercom system is typically connected to and powered by the fire alarm control panel, which must be installed and operational beforehand.

predecessor: Conduit and backbox installation for intercom points
rationale: Conduits and backboxes for intercom handset locations must be embedded or mounted in walls/structures before the intercom units themselves can be installed.
The main intercom infrastructure (cabling, control panel connection) must be in place before individual handsets can be connected, terminated, and tested.
The fire telephone system must be fully installed before it can be commissioned, integrated with the fire alarm system, and tested for functionality and compliance.

predecessor: Install electrical conduits and cabling for CCTV
rationale: CCTV monitoring stations require power supply and data cabling to function; electrical and network infrastructure must be in place before the station equipment can be installed and connected.
The monitoring station room or enclosure must be structurally complete with finished walls, flooring, and ceiling to provide a secure, clean environment for mounting sensitive electronic equipment.

predecessor: Complete HVAC installation in monitoring room
rationale: CCTV monitoring equipment generates heat and requires controlled temperature/humidity; HVAC must be operational before installing sensitive electronic equipment to prevent overheating and damage.

successor: Configure and test CCTV video management software
rationale: The monitoring station hardware (servers, monitors, workstations) must be physically installed and powered on before software can be installed, configured, and tested on that hardware.
The monitoring station must be fully installed and operational as the central hub before the complete security system can be commissioned, tested, and handed over to the client.
The EPSU must be placed on a stable, load-bearing foundation and floor slab to ensure proper support and alignment.
Electrical conduits, cabling pathways, and grounding systems must be installed before the EPSU can be connected to the building's electrical infrastructure.

successor: EPSU Connection to Main Switchboard / ATS
rationale: The EPSU must be physically installed and positioned before final electrical connections to the automatic transfer switch (ATS) and main switchboard can be completed.

successor: Testing and Commissioning of Emergency Power System
rationale: All load bank testing, transfer switch testing, and full system commissioning can only proceed after the EPSU is fully installed and connected.

successor: Final Fire Alarm and Life Safety System Integration
rationale: While integration can begin beforehand, final verification and acceptance testing of life safety systems powered by the EPSU typically occurs after EPSU installation and is a soft preference for sequence optimization.
The smoke control system panel requires electrical power supply and connections, which must be roughed in before the panel can be installed and wired.
The fire alarm system backbox or enclosure must be mounted in the wall before the smoke control panel can be placed and connected, as the panel integrates with fire alarm components.
Conduit runs and cable trays for smoke control wiring must be installed prior to panel installation to allow for proper cable routing and termination at the panel.

successor: Smoke Control System Panel Testing and Commissioning
rationale: The panel must be fully installed, wired, and powered before any testing, commissioning, or functional performance verification can take place.

successor: Smoke Damper Actuator Connection and Testing
rationale: Smoke dampers throughout the building are controlled by the smoke control panel; their actuators can only be connected and tested after the panel is operational to send control signals.

predecessor: Electrical Conduit & Wiring Installation to Lift Shaft
rationale: Power and control cables must be run to the lift shaft and control panel location before the panel can be installed and connected.

predecessor: Lift Machine Room / Controller Cabinet Installation
rationale: The main lift controller in the machine room must be in place and operational to interface with the control panel.
The control panel provides signals and power that must be terminated at the lift car before car wiring is completed.
The panel must be physically installed and connected before software configuration, testing, and calibration of floor recall and control logic can be performed.
The control panel must be operational to integrate with the fire alarm system for floor recall during emergencies.
Conduits and wiring pathways must be installed before the panel can be mounted and connected to the electrical system.
The emergency lighting control panel requires a dedicated power feed from the main electrical distribution panel, which must be installed and energized first.
The control panel must be installed, wired, and operational before emergency lighting fixtures can be connected and tested for functionality.

Final testing and commissioning of the emergency lighting system requires the control panel to be fully installed and operational to verify proper switching, battery backup, and circuit functionality.
Walls and structural supports must be completed to provide a mounting surface and enclosure for the panel, ensuring it is securely anchored.
The booster pump controls require electrical power to operate, so the electrical supply must be installed and energized before controls can be commissioned.

predecessor: Firefighting Water Booster Pump Mechanical Installation
rationale: The pump and associated mechanical equipment must be physically installed before control wiring and control panels can be connected.
A water source (tank) must be in place before the booster pump system can be tested and controlled.

successor: Firefighting Water Booster Pump Commissioning and Testing
rationale: The controls must be fully installed and wired before the system can be commissioned, tested, and verified for proper operation.
The booster pump controls must be operational before they can be integrated with the broader fire protection system (e.g., fire alarm panel, sprinkler system interfaces).
The hazardous materials survey identifies all hazardous substances present on site; the register display itemizes and communicates those findings, so survey data must exist first.
The register must be compiled and finalized before it can be physically displayed or posted.
Workers should be informed of hazardous materials via the displayed register before starting work, though this is a safety best practice rather than a physical construction dependency.
The register must be displayed to inform personnel of hazards before any handling or removal activities commence to ensure safety compliance.
Inspectors typically require the register to be posted before signing off, but the inspection itself can sometimes occur concurrently; this is a regulatory preference.
As-built plans document the actual construction; they cannot be stored until construction is complete and all changes are known.
The as-built drawings must be prepared and finalized before they can be archived or stored in a repository.
Final inspection verifies construction matches the as-built conditions; inspection sign-off typically precedes plan storage as a record.
Stored as-built plans are a key deliverable handed over to the facility management team for ongoing operations and maintenance.
Storage of as-built plans is a prerequisite step in the project closeout process before final documentation can be considered complete.

predecessor: Install Master Key Cabinet / Key Safe
rationale: Keys must be stored and organized in the key safe before they can be distributed to building occupants.

successor: Install Master Key Cabinet / Key Safe
rationale: Door locks and cylinders must be installed and keyed before the master key cabinet can be populated with the corresponding keys.

successor: Install Master Key Cabinet / Key Safe
rationale: Electrical work near the key safe location should be finished to avoid dust and debris damaging the cabinet, though the safe could be installed earlier if protected.

predecessor: Install Master Key Cabinet / Key Safe
rationale: The master key cabinet must be installed and all keys accounted for before the building can be formally handed over to the owner/occupant.

successor: Install Master Key Cabinet / Key Safe
rationale: Dust and debris from finishing work could contaminate the key safe; it is preferable to install after finishes are complete, though not physically mandatory.

successor: Fire Control Room Door (Self-Closing, Fire-Rated) Installation
rationale: The door frame must be installed into a completed wall opening; the wall structure provides the support and surrounding enclosure for the fire-rated door assembly.

predecessor: Fire Control Room Door Frame Installation
successor: Fire Control Room Door (Self-Closing, Fire-Rated) Installation
rationale: The self-closing fire-rated door leaf must be hung on its frame; the frame must be securely anchored and aligned before the door can be fitted.

predecessor: Fire Control Room Door (Self-Closing, Fire-Rated) Installation
successor: Fire Control Room Door Hardware Adjustment and Self-Closing Mechanism Calibration
rationale: The door must be installed before the closing mechanism (e.g., spring hinge or door closer) can be adjusted and calibrated to ensure proper self-closing operation and latching.

predecessor: Fire Control Room Door (Self-Closing, Fire-Rated) Installation
successor: Fire Control Room Door Fire Seal and Intumescent Strip Installation
rationale: Perimeter fire seals and intumescent strips are applied after the door is hung to ensure continuous fire-rated integrity around the door-to-frame gaps.

predecessor: Fire Control Room Door (Self-Closing, Fire-Rated) Installation
successor: Fire Control Room Door Final Inspection and Fire-Rating Certification
rationale: The complete door assembly including hardware and seals must be in place before a certified fire inspection can verify compliance with fire-rating requirements.
The fire control room must be fully constructed, finished, and ready before signage and wayfinding elements can be installed within or for it.

predecessor: Electrical Rough-In for Fire Control Room
rationale: Electrical conduits, wiring, and power supply for illuminated signage and wayfinding must be roughed-in before signage can be installed and connected.
While not physically required, it is preferable to have the fire detection and alarm system operational first to ensure safe installation conditions for signage.
Signage and wayfinding must be fully installed and verified before the fire control room can be commissioned and handed over for operational use.
Signage and wayfinding installation must be complete as part of the finishing works before the final inspection and regulatory approval of the fire control room.
The structural shell and building enclosure must be completed to provide a weather-tight and secure environment for the sensitive fire control room fitout, including walls, slab, and roofing.

predecessor: Fire Control Room Slab / Base Preparation
rationale: The floor slab for the fire control room must be poured and cured before any fitout activities such as wall framing, MEP rough-ins, or floor finishes can commence.

predecessor: MEP Rough-in Works (Electrical, Data, HVAC, Fire Services)
rationale: All Mechanical, Electrical, Plumbing, and fire services rough-in (conduits, cables, ductwork, piping) within the fire control room must be installed in the walls and ceilings before fitout finishing works (plasterboard, ceilings, painting) can begin.

successor: Fire Detection and Alarm System Commissioning
rationale: The fire control room fitout (including installation of fire indicator panel, consoles, and operator workstations) must be complete before the fire detection and alarm system can be fully commissioned and tested.
The fire control room must be fully fitted out and operational before the building can be handed over or occupied, as it is a critical life-safety facility.
The structural framing (studs, tracks, and runners) must be in place to provide the substrate for attaching fire-rated partition assemblies.
Concealed conduits, pipes, and ducts within the partition cavity must be installed and inspected before the partition is closed up with fire-rated board.
After the partition boards are installed, all gaps, joints, and penetrations must be sealed with firestop materials to maintain the fire-resistance rating.
The fire-rated board surfaces must be fully installed before joint compound, tape, and surface finishing can be applied.

successor: Wall-Mounted Fixture Installation (e.g., doors, frames, hardware)
rationale: Partition must be complete and rigid before door frames, hardware, or other heavy fixtures can be mounted onto it.
All fire services equipment (sprinklers, fire alarms, extinguishers, hose reels, etc.) must be physically installed and connected before they can be commissioned and tested.
Electrical supply and wiring connections to fire alarm panels, pumps, and detection devices must be completed to provide power for commissioning and testing.
Water supply piping and connections to sprinkler systems and fire hydrants must be installed before flow testing and pressure testing can be performed.
Signage indicating fire equipment locations and emergency exits is typically installed after systems are commissioned to reflect the final verified locations.
Regulatory and safety compliance requires that fire services be fully commissioned, tested, and certified before the building can be handed over and occupied.
Individual subsystems must be integrated and verified to work together before full system-level integrated testing can commence.
All electrical and data cables must be installed and terminated to enable communication and power flow between subsystems during integrated testing.
All physical equipment, panels, sensors, and controllers must be mounted and installed in their designated locations before system-wide testing can be performed.
Main power supply and distribution systems must be commissioned and verified to safely provide power to all subsystems before integrated testing can proceed.
Integrated Systems Testing must be successfully completed and signed off before the system can be formally accepted and handed over to the client or operations team.
Integrated testing results inform final calibration, tuning, and adjustments needed before the system is fully commissioned for operational use.

While training can partially begin earlier, final operator and maintenance training based on actual system behavior is best conducted after IST is complete, though this is a soft preference depending on project schedule.

predecessor: Construction HIRA (Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment)
rationale: The HIRA identifies all potential hazards and risks on the construction site; the ERP must be based on these identified risks to ensure appropriate emergency procedures are in place.

The physical layout of the construction site (including access roads, laydown areas, and facilities) determines evacuation routes, muster points, and emergency equipment placement, which are essential inputs for ERP development.

predecessor: Project Safety Plan / Safety Policy Development
rationale: The overall safety plan establishes the safety management framework and protocols that the ERP must align with and complement.

successor: Emergency Response Drills / Mock Drill Execution
rationale: The ERP must be fully developed and documented before drills can be planned and executed to test its effectiveness.
All workers must be trained on the emergency response procedures contained in the ERP before they are allowed on site, so the ERP must be finalized first.
All fire control room equipment (panels, detectors, communication systems) must be physically installed before they can be inspected and certified for proper operation.
The room structure, walls, ceiling, flooring, and fire-rated construction must be fully completed before inspection can occur to ensure the room meets fire safety and building code requirements.
All fire alarm system wiring, cabling, and connectivity to detection and alarm devices must be completed so the inspector can test end-to-end system functionality.
The fire control room must be certified as operational before the overall fire suppression system can be activated, as the control room manages and monitors suppression responses.
Regulatory authorities require certified fire control room inspection as a prerequisite for issuing a building occupancy permit, ensuring fire safety systems are verified before occupancy.
Conduit pathways must be installed to house and protect the intercommunication cabling before the WIP unit itself can be placed and connected.
The main communication backbone cables must be run to the WIP location prior to installing the unit so that terminations can be made immediately.
Cables can only be terminated and tested at the WIP after the physical unit is mounted and in place.
The WIP must be installed and connected before it can be integrated into the wider communications system and commissioned for operation.

successor: Ward Area Fit-Out Completion (finishes, painting, ceiling)
rationale: It is preferable to complete fit-out works around the WIP after installation to avoid damaging finished surfaces during unit placement, though not a physical necessity.

successor: Firefighter Access Panel / Indicator Board installation
rationale: Electrical supply and control wiring must be run to the panel location before the panel can be physically mounted and connected.

successor: Firefighter Access Panel / Indicator Board installation
rationale: The main fire alarm control panel and system backbone must be in place so the indicator board can interface with the overall fire alarm system.

predecessor: Firefighter Access Panel / Indicator Board installation
successor: Fire Alarm System Commissioning and Testing
rationale: The panel must be installed and connected before the entire fire alarm system can be tested for proper operation.

predecessor: Firefighter Access Panel / Indicator Board installation
successor: Fire alarm system final inspection and approval
rationale: Authorities having jurisdiction require the panel to be fully installed before conducting final inspections and granting system approval.

predecessor: Firefighter Access Panel / Indicator Board installation
rationale: All life safety systems including the firefighter access panel must be fully operational before the building can be commissioned and handed over to the owner.
The gym equipment requires a level, cured concrete slab to be properly installed and anchored without risk of shifting or damage.
Gym equipment must be placed in its final position before rubber flooring can be cut and fitted tightly around it for a seamless finish.
Heavy equipment should be moved into the space before installing wall padding and mirrors to avoid damage to finished wall surfaces during equipment maneuvering.
While final electrical connections to equipment can technically be done simultaneously, it is preferred to have equipment in place first so outlet and cable locations are confirmed.

predecessor: Structural framing and ceiling grid installation
rationale: The ceiling grid and overhead structural supports must be in place to provide the track system and structural anchorage that operable partitions slide along and attach to.
Any power, data, or low-voltage cabling that will serve the partition area must be roughed in before walls are installed to allow access to ceiling and floor chases.

The bottom track or floor guide for the operable wall must be set before finished flooring is laid so flooring can be installed flush against or over the track to avoid tripping hazards and ensure proper alignment.
The partition panels and frames must be in place to allow seamless finishing of adjacent walls and to paint or touch up the partition itself, avoiding damage to finished surfaces during installation.
Perimeter seals, gaskets, and trim components must be fitted after the main partition panels are hung and aligned to ensure proper acoustic performance and a finished appearance.
Electrical rough-in, including wiring and junction box installation, must be completed before any lighting fixtures can be physically mounted and connected to the power supply.
The ceiling structure must be framed and the drywall installed and finished to provide a stable mounting surface and to conceal wiring before the lighting fixture can be attached.

After the feature lighting fixture is physically installed, final connections, trim adjustments, and electrical testing (e.g., verifying proper voltage, dimming function) must be performed to ensure safe and correct operation.
Once the fixture is mounted, any minor paint touch-ups around the fixture perimeter or ceiling area can be completed to achieve a clean aesthetic finish.
Wall framing and drywall must be completed to provide a finished, flat surface against which cabinets and millwork can be properly installed and anchored.

Electrical wiring, outlets, and plumbing rough-ins must be installed behind the walls before cabinetry is placed, as accessing these after installation would require removing or cutting into the millwork.
Flooring must be installed first so that cabinets sit on top of the finished floor surface, ensuring proper fit, leveling, and alignment without later having to cut or trim around the cabinetry.
Base cabinets must be fully installed and leveled before countertops can be templated, fabricated, and placed on top of them.

While final painting can technically proceed before cabinetry, it is preferable to install millwork first so that painters can caulk and blend seams between the millwork and the wall in a single finish coat, avoiding mismatched paint lines.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) rough-in work must be completed before ceiling installation because acoustic ceiling panels are suspended from the overhead structure and would block access to all above-ceiling systems.

predecessor: Install Overhead Structural Framework / Suspension Grid
rationale: The suspension grid (T-bar or furring channels) must be installed first to provide the support system onto which acoustic ceiling panels are laid or clipped.
Fireproofing (spray-applied fire resistive materials) on steel beams must be completed before enclosing the ceiling space, as the ceiling panels would obstruct application and inspection.

It is a soft preference to complete wall finishing after ceiling installation to allow for a clean transition line at the wall-ceiling interface and to avoid damaging finished walls during overhead panel work.

Although not a hard physical constraint, it is preferred to install the ceiling before flooring to prevent dust and debris from ceiling work (e.g., cutting panels) from settling on and damaging finished floor surfaces.
The ground must be properly graded and prepared before any outdoor structures can be installed to ensure a level, stable foundation and proper drainage.
Concrete pads or foundations for shade structures (e.g., pergolas, gazebos) must be cured and set before the structures can be erected on them.
Any underground electrical conduits (for lighting near shade structures) or plumbing (for outdoor kitchens/fountains) must be buried before footings or posts are installed.

It is logistically easier to install large furniture and shade structures before planting delicate flowers, shrubs, or laying sod, to avoid damaging new plantings with heavy equipment and foot traffic.

Applying sealants to adjacent hardscape surfaces (e.g., stamped concrete, stone patios) is preferably done after shade structures are in place so that the sealant application can abut the structure cleanly.
Sauna enclosure requires a level, structurally sound base to sit on; the floor must be prepared before any walls or framing can be erected.
Drain lines and water supply for potential sauna shower or steam unit must be roughed in beneath the floor before the enclosure is built over them.

predecessor: Rough Electrical (Conduit & Wiring to Sauna Location)
rationale: Electrical wiring for the sauna heater, lights, and controls must be run in the walls/ceiling before the enclosure is closed up with vapor barrier and interior finishes.
The sauna enclosure must be fully framed and the heater mounted before the vapor barrier and insulation can be installed over/inside the enclosure walls and ceiling.
The structural enclosure and heater mounting must be complete before interior cedar paneling or other wall finishes can be applied to the inside of the sauna.

The structural steel frame must be erected to provide the building envelope and load-bearing support before any interior fit-out work, including amenities (toilets, kitchens, changing rooms), can commence.
Floor slabs, stair cores, and lift shafts must be completed to create the physical floors and vertical circulation needed to access and build out amenity areas.
The building must be weathertight (roof, external cladding, windows installed) to protect interior finishes, plumbing, and electrical fit-outs from weather damage during amenity construction.
Main risers, ductwork, conduit, and plumbing rough-ins must be installed before amenity fit-out so that distribution runs can be concealed above ceilings/within walls and final fixtures connected.

Amenity fit-out (tiling, vanity units, toilet partitions, kitchen joinery) must be fully installed before final painting, floor finishing, and systems commissioning to avoid rework or damage to completed finishes.

The excavation and grading must be completed to create the proper hole and base for the pool shell. The pool shell cannot be constructed without first having the excavated pit prepared to the correct dimensions and elevation.
The excavated soil must be properly compacted and the base prepared to provide a stable, load-bearing foundation for the pool shell. Without this preparation, the shell may crack or settle unevenly.

Any underground plumbing (drains, returns, skimmer lines) and electrical conduits that will pass beneath or through the pool shell must be roughed in before the shell is poured or installed, as they would be impossible to add later without demolition.
The pump, filter, heater and all above-ground circulation plumbing can only be installed after the shell is complete and waterproofed, as they connect to fittings cast into or mounted on the shell.

Interior tile, plaster, pebble, or other finish surfaces cannot be applied until the shell structure is fully cured and waterproofed, as the finish bonds to the shell substrate and would be damaged or impossible to apply beforehand.

Structural framing must be complete before MEP rough-in can begin because MEP systems (electrical, plumbing, HVAC) are typically installed within walls, floors, and ceilings that are framed by the structural components.
The concrete slab or deck must be poured and cured before MEP rough-in can commence, as MEP systems are embedded in or run beneath/within the slab.
MEP rough-in must be completed before insulation is installed, because insulation is placed around and over MEP lines, and any subsequent MEP work would damage or require removal of insulation.
MEP rough-in must be completed and inspected before drywall can be hung, as drywall permanently encloses the MEP systems within wall cavities.
MEP rough-in (concealed piping, wiring, ducts) must be installed and inspected before trim-out work (fixtures, outlets, switches) can begin.
The site must be cleared, graded, and properly leveled before any landscaping or planting can begin to ensure proper drainage and soil preparation.
Underground utilities such as irrigation lines, drainage pipes, and electrical conduits must be installed before landscaping to avoid disturbing newly planted areas.
Major building construction must be complete to prevent heavy equipment and construction debris from damaging newly planted landscaping.
Hardscape elements like walkways, patios, and retaining walls should be installed first to define planting areas and avoid soil compaction or damage to plants.

Landscaping is typically one of the final finishing activities, after which a final cleanup and inspection of the site is performed, though this is a logical preference rather than a strict physical necessity.

All amenity systems (HVAC, electrical, plumbing, fire protection, etc.) must be fully installed before they can be tested, commissioned, and handed over. Commissioning cannot commence without installed equipment and systems to test.

Interior finishes such as ceilings, walls, and floor coverings must be in place for amenity spaces to be in a ready state for commissioning, and to ensure that systems can be tested under final conditions without risking damage to finishes.

Occupants or end-users can only take possession and begin using amenity spaces after the systems have been successfully commissioned, tested, and formally handed over. This ensures all systems are fully functional, safe, and compliant.
Final inspection and certification authorities require proof that all amenity systems have been commissioned and are operating correctly before issuing final occupancy certifications or sign-offs.

While punch list and defect rectification can begin in parallel, formally the commissioning and handover process identifies deficiencies that feed into the punch list. In practice, minor defects may be resolved after handover, but major system issues should be resolved before or during commissioning.
Flooring must be fully installed and finished before FF&E is brought in to prevent damage to both the flooring and the furniture, and to ensure a clean, stable surface for placement.
Wall finishes must be completed before FF&E installation to avoid dust, paint splatter, or damage to newly placed furniture and fixtures from ongoing wall work.
Overhead work such as ceiling tiles, painting, and light fixture installation must be finished to prevent debris falling on FF&E and to ensure ceiling access is not obstructed by furniture.
Electrical outlets, switches, and final trim work must be in place before FF&E is installed so that furniture can be positioned relative to power and data connections.
After all FF&E is placed, a final clean-up and punch list walk-through is required to remove packaging, adjust placements, and address any last defects before project handover.
Fire dampers are installed within HVAC ductwork at fire-rated barriers; the ductwork must be in place to provide the mounting structure and penetration for the damper sleeve.
Fire dampers are required at fire-rated wall, floor, or partition penetrations; the rated barrier must be constructed before the damper can be installed within it.
After the fire damper is installed, the penetration around the damper sleeve must be firestopped and the adjacent ductwork insulated to maintain the fire rating.
Dampers must be fully installed and operable before the HVAC system can be balanced and commissioned to ensure proper airflow control.

successor: Fire Alarm and Smoke Detection System Testing
rationale: Fire dampers are often linked to fire alarm/smoke detection systems for automatic closure; testing of the alarm system integration requires the dampers to be in place.
Smoke dampers are installed within ductwork, so the duct system must be in place to receive and support the damper.
Duct leakage testing must occur after dampers are installed to ensure the entire duct system including damper seals is airtight.
Smoke dampers are typically integrated with fire alarm systems for automatic closure; testing can only be done after the damper is installed and wired.
Structural framing must be complete to support the ductwork and provide mounting points for smoke damper assemblies.
Electrical wiring for actuator power and control signals must be roughed in before the damper is installed and connected.
Access panels are typically installed within or onto ceiling grid systems; the grid must be in place to provide structural support and proper alignment for the panel.

Access panels provide access to mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems above ceilings or within walls; those services must be roughed-in before the access panel location can be finalized and installed.
The rough opening or framed aperture must be constructed to the correct dimensions to receive the access panel frame.
Access panels are often set into place before the surrounding finish surface is applied so that the panel flange can be flush with or covered by the finish material.
While painting is typically done after installation to achieve a uniform finish, the panel itself may be painted separately, making this a soft preference rather than a strict physical requirement.
The shaft structure must be constructed first to provide the opening and frame into which the shaft door is installed.
Shaft doors must be physically in place before wiring the control systems that interface with the door mechanisms (e.g., sensors, locks, and open/close controls).
While finishing can be done after installation, it is a soft preference to complete installation before finishing to protect the finish from damage during other construction activities.
Cable ladders are typically supported by structural steel members; structural steel must be in place to provide support and attachment points for the cable ladder system.
Large mechanical ducts and major piping should be installed before cable ladders to avoid conflicts and ensure accessible routing space; cable ladders are more flexible in routing around obstacles.
Cables must be laid or pulled onto/into the cable ladder; the ladder structure must be fully installed and secured before any cables can be placed in it.

Firestop compounds and wraps are applied after the cable ladder and its cables are in place; however, if the ladder itself requires intumescent coating, that would be done after installation but before cable loading. Typically firestopping around penetrations is done after cables are installed.
Cable pulling and termination at equipment can only proceed once the supporting cable ladder pathway is fully installed and accessible.

Underground conduits and rough-in work (e.g., sleeves, stub-ups) must be placed in the ground or slab before above-ground conduit installation can begin, as conduit systems often connect to these underground entry points.
Conduit is typically mounted to or embedded within walls, ceilings, and structural supports; thus the framing must be in place to provide the attachment surface and routing pathway for conduit runs.
Conduit acts as a protective raceway for electrical wires and cables; wires cannot be pulled through a conduit until the conduit system is fully assembled, secured, and inspected.

Inspection of the installed conduit system (for proper support, bending, connections, and grounding) must occur before the conduit is enclosed by wall finishes or wires are pulled, as required by building codes.
Conduit must be fully installed, secured, and inspected before walls and ceilings are closed up; otherwise, the conduit would be inaccessible for future wiring modifications or repairs.
Busbar trunking systems typically connect to or are fed from the main distribution board; the MDB must be installed first to provide the source connection point.
Cable trays and ladders provide the primary support and routing pathway for busbar trunking runs; they must be in place before trunking can be mounted and secured.
Busbar trunking requires robust structural supports (brackets, hangers, steelwork) to bear its weight; these supports must be installed and anchored before the trunking can be lifted into place.
Electrical connections (tap-off units, joint packs, end feeds) and continuity/insulation testing can only be performed after the busbar trunking sections are fully installed and mechanically joined.
Firestop materials must be applied around busbar trunking penetrations through walls and floors after the trunking is in place to ensure a complete seal and maintain fire compartmentation integrity.
Excavation must be completed to expose the area where pipe sleeves will be placed in foundation walls or slabs.
Pipe sleeves are typically placed within formwork before concrete is poured, so formwork must be in place to support and position the sleeve.
Reinforcement steel is placed prior to positioning pipe sleeves, as sleeves must be tied or secured within the rebar mat before concrete pour.
Pipe sleeves must be securely installed and positioned within formwork before concrete is poured, as they are embedded elements that become fixed in place once concrete cures.
The pipe sleeve must be installed (embedded in concrete or wall assembly) before any pipe can be routed through it, as the sleeve provides the passageway.

predecessor: Electrical and Mechanical Rough-Ins (e.g., conduits, cables, pipes, ductwork)
rationale: Electrical and mechanical services (conduits, cables, pipes, ductwork) must be routed through wall/floor penetrations before fire-stopping materials are applied to seal those openings.

predecessor: Structural Wall/Floor Construction (including drywall, masonry, or concrete placement)
rationale: The substrate (wall, floor, or ceiling assembly) through which penetrations pass must be fully built and cured before fire-stopping can be installed around the penetrating items.

successor: Fire Resistance Testing / Inspection of Compartmentation
rationale: Fire-stopping seals must be fully installed and cured before the fire-resistance rating of the compartment can be verified through inspection or testing.

successor: Final Painting / Finishing of Walls and Ceilings
rationale: While fire-stopping can be painted over, it is preferred to complete sealing before final finishes to avoid damaging the sealant during finishing work.
All passive fire protection, including intumescent seals, must be fully installed and verified before the building can be occupied to ensure life safety compliance.

predecessor: Install Cold Water Main Supply Line
rationale: The cold water main supply line must be run to the building base before the vertical riser pipe can be connected to it, as the riser depends on a pressurized water supply source.
Vertical riser pipes run through structural shafts and chases; the building's core framing and floor penetrations must be complete to provide the physical pathway for the riser.
Branch lines for each floor tap off the vertical cold water riser; they cannot be connected until the riser is in place and pressurized.
The riser must be fully installed and joined before the overall cold water system can be pressure-tested for leaks.
Insulation is applied after the riser pipe is installed and tested to prevent condensation and maintain water temperature; applying it earlier would block access to joints and valves.
The structural framework (columns, slabs, and walls) must be in place to provide support and routing paths for vertical riser pipes.
Holes or sleeves through floor slabs must be drilled or set before riser pipes can be run vertically through the building.
Insulation must be applied directly to the installed hot water riser pipe to contain heat and prevent heat loss.
After installation, the riser pipe must be pressure-tested to verify leak-free joints before being concealed or insulated.
Branch lines supplying hot water to individual floors or fixtures can only be connected after the main riser is installed and tested.
The primary heating circuits must be installed first to establish the main distribution network that the riser pipes will connect to.
The building's structural framework must be in place to provide support and vertical routing paths for the riser pipes.

successor: Connection to Terminal Units (Radiators / Fan Coils)
rationale: The riser pipes must be installed and in place before terminal units can be connected to the vertical heating distribution system.
Riser pipes must be fully installed and pressure-tested before thermal insulation can be applied to them.
The riser pipes must be complete and connected before the entire heating system can be flushed and commissioned.
The soil and waste stack must be anchored to or pass through the ground slab; the slab must be in place to provide structural support and proper drainage connection points.
The underground drainage network must be installed before the soil and waste stack can connect to it, ensuring proper waste flow from the stack into the below-ground drainage system.
The soil and waste stack typically runs within or adjacent to structural cores; the vertical framing and core walls must be erected to provide support brackets and vertical chase space for the stack.
Branch waste pipes from fixtures (toilets, sinks) connect into the main soil and waste stack; the stack must be in place to serve as the vertical collection point for these branch connections.

The soil and waste stack requires a vent pipe to maintain atmospheric pressure and prevent siphoning; the vent connection must be installed after the stack is erected to tie into the top of the stack or its vent branch.

The building's structural frame and core must be erected first to provide vertical pathways (shafts, chases, and sleeves) through which chilled water riser pipes are routed. Without the structural shell, there is no support or enclosed space for the riser pipes.

successor: Pressure Testing & Flushing of Chilled Water Risers
rationale: After the riser pipes are installed and jointed, they must be pressure-tested and flushed to verify integrity, identify leaks, and remove debris before they can be connected to downstream equipment or concealed.

Branch piping that takes off from the vertical riser to serve air handling units or fan coil units on each floor can only be connected once the main riser is installed, as the riser is the source and distribution backbone for chilled water flow.
Insulation must be applied after the riser pipe is installed, tested, and approved to prevent condensation and thermal loss. Insulating before testing would conceal potential leaks.

While riser pipe installation often precedes other mechanical rough-ins in the same shaft for coordination and access, it is a soft preference — some trades can work concurrently in different zones if access is carefully managed and sequencing is agreed upon.
Structural steel framing must be in place to provide support and attachment points for the compressed air riser piping.
Foundations and floor slabs must be completed to provide a stable base and to allow for riser penetrations through the slab.

successor: Compressed Air System Testing and Commissioning
rationale: The riser must be fully installed and connected before the overall compressed air system can be pressure-tested and commissioned.
Branch piping that distributes compressed air to individual workstations or equipment can only be connected after the main riser is in place.
Fire-stopping around riser penetrations through floors and walls can only be applied after the riser piping is installed.
The sprinkler riser connects to the underground or rough-in piping; the piping infrastructure must be in place before the riser can be installed.

successor: Sprinkler branch line piping and head installation
rationale: Branch lines feed off the riser; the riser must be installed to provide water supply to downstream sprinkler branches and heads.

predecessor: Concrete slab / floor deck placement (if riser is floor-mounted)
rationale: A stable concrete slab or structural floor must be in place to support and anchor the riser assembly.

successor: Pressure testing and flushing of sprinkler system
rationale: The riser is a central component of the system; it must be installed before the entire system can be tested for leaks and flushed.

predecessor: Fire alarm rough-in (if riser includes flow/pressure switches)
rationale: Electrical rough-in for alarm devices on the riser should ideally be prepared in advance, though minor coordination adjustments are possible on site.

successor: Final fire alarm device connection and commissioning
rationale: Once the riser is installed, flow switches, pressure gauges, and tamper switches can be connected and the fire alarm system can be commissioned.
Coordination of overhead utilities is a soft preference to avoid interference, but the riser can proceed with minor adjustments if needed.
The structural frame and floor decks must be in place to provide the vertical shaft pathways and support points for ductwork risers before any duct sections can be installed.
The building core walls and slab penetrations (sleeves/chases) must be roughed in to define the vertical shaft openings through which the duct riser will pass.
Main horizontal duct trunks feeding into or out of the riser must be roughed in so that the riser can connect to them at each floor level.

successor: HVAC Ductwork Branch Installation & Diffuser Connection
rationale: Branch ducts must tie into the completed vertical riser at each floor; the riser must be fully installed to serve as the supply/return source for all downstream branch runs.

successor: Firestop & Smoke Seal Installation at Penetrations
rationale: Firestopping and smoke sealing can only be applied around duct riser penetrations after the ductwork is permanently in place through the floor slabs, to ensure a proper seal.

The flue/exhaust riser is typically installed within a dedicated structural shaft or chase. The structural core (walls, slabs, and shaft openings) must be constructed first to provide the physical enclosure and support for the riser.

Once the flue/exhaust riser is installed through floor and wall openings, all penetrations must be firestopped to maintain the fire-resistance rating of the building elements and prevent the spread of fire and smoke between floors.

successor: Connection to Mechanical Equipment (Boilers, Generators, Fireplaces)
rationale: The flue riser must be in place before mechanical equipment such as boilers, emergency generators, or fireplaces can be connected to it, as the riser provides the vertical exhaust pathway.
Thermal insulation and/or protective cladding around the flue riser can only be applied after the riser itself is fully installed, as the insulation wraps around the installed pipe or ductwork.

successor: Commissioning and Smoke Testing of Exhaust System
rationale: The complete flue/exhaust riser system must be installed before commissioning activities such as smoke testing, draft testing, and system balancing can be performed to verify proper exhaust flow and integrity.
The steel shaft frame requires a stable, load-bearing foundation (concrete base/foundation) to be cast and cured before the steel frame can be erected on top of it.
Accurate survey and layout marking of anchor bolt locations and column centerlines must be completed to guide the placement of the steel shaft frame.
Once the steel shaft frame is erected, its vertical alignment (plumbness) and overall positioning must be checked and adjusted before proceeding with further connections.
The main shaft frame columns and beams must be in place to serve as the attachment points for cross-bracing, girts, and secondary steel members.
The structural steel shaft frame provides the supporting skeleton onto which cladding, siding, or enclosure panels are fastened.
The slab must be structurally complete and cured to provide a stable substrate before any openings can be cut or formed through it.
Reinforcement steel must be in place and tied before the slab is poured (and thus before openings are cut), as openings affect the structural reinforcement layout.
Formwork must be erected to define the slab geometry, including any blockouts or sleeves for planned penetrations, before the concrete is placed.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) services can only be routed through the slab after the penetration opening has been created.
Firestop sealants and collars must be applied after the opening is formed and any MEP services are in place, to restore the slab's fire-resistance rating.
The pipe riser must be installed before its clamp or support can be attached, as the clamp physically fastens around the installed riser pipe.
The clamp/support needs a structural backing (steel beam, column, or embedded anchor) to be mounted to; that structure must be in place first.
Pressure testing of the riser pipe can only be performed after the pipe is fully installed and supported/clamped in position to prevent movement or damage during pressurization.

Insulation work typically follows clamp/support installation as a logical sequence, though it is a soft preference because insulation could theoretically be installed prior to clamping if access is arranged.

successor: Firestopping / Penetration Sealing at Floor Slabs
rationale: Firestopping around riser penetrations through floors must be applied after the riser and its support/clamp are in their final position to ensure a complete seal around the pipe and clamp assembly.

Cable tray support brackets are typically mounted on or anchored to structural steel members (columns, beams, or struts). The structural steel frame must be erected and secured before any bracket can be attached.

If brackets are to be anchored to an overhead concrete slab (e.g., using expansion anchors or drop-ins), the concrete must be poured and fully cured to develop the designed anchorage strength before brackets can be installed.

predecessor: Electrical Room Rough-In / Tray Routing Layout
rationale: The layout and routing of the cable tray system must be predetermined and marked, including bracket locations and spacing, to ensure correct positioning before any brackets are permanently affixed.
Cable tray sections are placed onto and secured to the installed support brackets. The brackets must be in place and fastened to provide the structural support for the trays.
Cables are laid into or pulled through the cable tray system only after the tray sections and their supporting brackets are fully installed and secured, providing a continuous safe pathway.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and obstacles before any excavation or shaft construction can begin, as physical access and a clear working area are prerequisites.
Accurate ground surveys and setting out of shaft locations are required before excavation commences to ensure correct positioning and alignment.
Understanding ground conditions (soil type, groundwater, obstructions) through geotechnical investigation is essential to design the shaft support system and method of construction.

As shaft excavation proceeds, the lining or primary support (e.g., shotcrete, ring beams) must be installed immediately to maintain ground stability and worker safety; this is a sequential dependency.
The base slab or sump at the bottom of the shaft can only be constructed once the shaft excavation has reached its design depth.
Tunnelling operations frequently launch from or pass through the shaft; the shaft must be fully excavated and lined to provide a stable launch chamber or access point for tunnelling activities.

successor: Testing and Commissioning of Riser Services
rationale: Riser services must be physically installed before they can be tested and commissioned, as testing requires the complete system to be in place.

successor: Testing and Commissioning of Riser Services
rationale: Individual pressure testing of riser pipes must be completed before the overall system commissioning to ensure pipe integrity and leak-free operation.

successor: Testing and Commissioning of Riser Services
rationale: Electrical power and control connections must be finalized to enable functional testing of pumps, valves, and monitoring systems during commissioning.

predecessor: Testing and Commissioning of Riser Services
rationale: Testing and commissioning must be successfully completed and signed off before the riser services can be formally handed over to the client or building management.

predecessor: Testing and Commissioning of Riser Services
successor: Final Inspection and Approval of Riser Systems
rationale: Commissioning results and documentation are required for the final inspection and approval process to verify compliance with specifications and standards.
The shaft must be excavated before it can be inspected and surveyed, as inspection requires physical access to the completed excavation.
Temporary or permanent support systems (e.g., shotcrete, rock bolts, steel sets) must be installed for safety and stability before personnel can safely enter and inspect the shaft.
Groundwater ingress must be managed and dewatering completed to provide a dry, safe working environment for inspection and survey teams.
Inspection and survey must be completed to verify shaft geometry, alignment, and condition before the shaft is formally commissioned or handed over for operational use.

successor: Shaft Concrete Lining / Final Lining Works
rationale: Final lining (e.g., cast-in-place concrete) should only proceed after the shaft has been fully inspected and surveyed, as inspection results determine whether remedial works or adjustments to final lining design are needed.
The structural frame (ceiling grid or support structure) must be in place to support the FFU, which is typically mounted in a ceiling grid system.
Ductwork connecting the air handling system to the FFU location must be installed before the FFU can be connected and integrated into the HVAC system.
Electrical wiring and junction boxes must be roughed in to provide power to the FFU motor and controls.
The FFU is typically installed within a cleanroom ceiling grid system; the grid must be complete before FFU placement.
After FFU installation, the ceiling system can be sealed and the cleanroom can be certified for particulate cleanliness, as the FFUs are critical to maintaining air cleanliness.
FFU installation must be complete before HEPA/ULPA filters (if integrated into the FFU) can be tested for proper sealing and performance.
FFUs must be operational before the overall cleanroom pressurization and airflow balancing process can be performed.
The ceiling grid must be fully installed and in place before the flush ceiling grid can be applied, as the flush grid is a finish layer attached to the supporting grid.
All MEP rough-in work (ductwork, conduit, piping) above the ceiling must be completed before installing the flush ceiling grid, as the grid will conceal access to these systems.

All overhead electrical wiring, data cables, and other low-voltage cabling must be run and terminated before the flush ceiling grid is installed, to avoid the need to remove or cut through the finished ceiling.
Fire sprinkler heads and piping must be installed and tested before the flush ceiling grid is placed, as the grid integrates with or accommodates sprinkler head locations and access.
The flush ceiling grid serves as the support framework; ceiling tiles or panels are placed into the grid after it is fully installed and secured.
The cleanroom ceiling grid must be installed first to provide top support and alignment reference for the wall panels.
Raised access flooring must be completed to establish the base level and allow wall panels to be mounted securely on the finished floor.
All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work behind the walls must be completed before enclosing the space with cleanroom wall panels.

successor: Cleanroom Wall Panel Sealing and Cove Base
rationale: After wall panels are installed, all joints, seams, and corners must be sealed and coving applied to maintain cleanroom air tightness and cleanliness standards.

successor: Cleanroom Ceiling Trim and Light Fixture Installation
rationale: Ceiling trim and flush-mounted light fixtures can only be installed after wall panels define the final cleanroom perimeter dimensions.
A stable foundation or base slab must be completed before the pass-through chamber can be installed or constructed upon it.
The main structural enclosure or shell of the facility (e.g., hot cell walls) must be erected before the pass-through chamber can be integrated into the wall penetration.
After the pass-through chamber is installed, all penetrations must be sealed and leak-tested to ensure containment integrity before any radioactive materials are transferred.
Electrical, control, and mechanical connections to the pass-through chamber (e.g., interlocks, ventilation) must be completed after the chamber is physically in place.
The pass-through chamber must be fully installed and connected before the overall system can be commissioned for transfer operations.
The ceiling grid provides the structural support and mounting framework for cleanroom lighting fixtures; fixtures cannot be installed without a completed overhead support system.
HVAC ductwork occupies ceiling plenum space; lighting fixtures must be placed after ducts to avoid interference and ensure proper clearance.
Electrical supply wiring and junction boxes must be in place before lighting fixtures can be connected and powered.
Ceiling panels are installed around or after fixtures to provide a sealed, cleanable finished ceiling surface; fixtures must be in place first so panels can be cut to fit.
Fixtures must be physically installed before they can be energized, tested for proper operation, and validated for cleanroom light levels and contamination control.

Before any decontamination can occur, the specific hazardous materials present must be identified and assessed to determine appropriate cleaning protocols, PPE requirements, and decontamination methods.

The contaminated area must be isolated and containment measures (e.g., negative pressure enclosures, barriers, warning signs) established to prevent the spread of contaminants during decontamination activities.

Decontamination generates contaminated wastewater, used cleaning materials, and removed residues that must be properly packaged, labeled, and disposed of as hazardous waste after cleaning is complete.

After cleaning and decontamination, verification sampling and visual inspection must be conducted to confirm that contaminant levels have been reduced to acceptable thresholds before the area can be declared safe.
Only after decontamination is complete and verified can the area be restored (e.g., rebuilding structures, repainting) and reoccupied for normal use.

Physical construction and installation must be fully completed before any commissioning or qualification activities can begin, as IQ/OQ/PQ validates that the facility and equipment are installed and functioning as designed.
Mechanical completion ensures all equipment is physically installed and connected, which is a prerequisite for performing Installation Qualification (IQ) and Operational Qualification (OQ).
All piping, wiring, and electrical connections must be in place before commissioning can validate system functionality and performance.

IQ/OQ/PQ must be successfully completed and approved before formal process validation or production startup can commence, as it verifies that equipment and systems are qualified for their intended use.
The facility and systems cannot be formally handed over to the operations team until commissioning and qualification are complete and all documentation is approved.
ISO Classification Testing requires physical samples to be collected first, as testing cannot be performed without material to classify.
Samples must be prepared (e.g., dried, sieved, or conditioned) before they can undergo ISO classification testing to ensure standardized and accurate results.
Material certification relies on the ISO classification test results to confirm the material meets specified standards.
A quality control review typically follows testing to verify that the classification was performed correctly, though in some workflows it could be concurrent.
Testing equipment must be properly calibrated before performing ISO classification testing to ensure accurate and valid measurements.

The structural shell (walls, roof, and floor slab) must be completed and watertight before any cleanroom fit-out can begin, as the cleanroom environment requires a sealed, stable envelope to install sensitive finishes and HEPA filtration systems.

Bulk MEP rough-in such as ductwork mains, piping risers, and cable trays must be installed before cleanroom walls and ceilings are erected, because once the cleanroom envelope is sealed, access for major distribution runs becomes extremely difficult and would compromise contamination control.

After the cleanroom walls, ceiling grid, flooring, and lighting are fully installed, the space must undergo certification testing (airborne particle counts, airflow velocity, pressure differentials) to verify it meets the required ISO class specification before being placed into operation.

The cleanroom envelope must be completely built and sealed prior to installing terminal HEPA/ULPA filters and final commissioning of the HVAC system, as the filters are delicate and must not be exposed to construction dust generated during fit-out activities.

It is strongly preferred that cleanroom fit-out (walls, ceiling, flooring, lighting) be completed before process equipment is moved in, to protect equipment from construction debris and to allow proper cleaning and pass-through procedures, though in some cases equipment can be installed concurrently if strict segregation protocols are followed.

The physical and chemical properties of aggregates and cement (e.g., gradation, specific gravity, moisture content, compressive strength) must be known before the mix proportions can be scientifically calculated and designed.

The required concrete compressive strength (f'c), exposure conditions, and workability requirements defined by the structural engineer are mandatory inputs for designing the appropriate mix proportions.
The mix design provides the approved proportions of cement, aggregates, water, and admixtures; batching cannot proceed without these specified ratios.
A trial batch must be prepared from the designed mix to verify its workability, strength, and durability before full-scale production is approved.

Although bulk material procurement may begin earlier based on estimates, final material procurement quantities and specifications are confirmed only after the mix design is complete, to avoid waste or shortage.
Formwork (molds) must be built and properly positioned before concrete batching can begin, as the batched concrete will be poured into these forms.
Steel rebar must be placed and tied within the formwork before concrete is batched, because the concrete is poured around the reinforcement to create reinforced concrete.
Raw materials such as cement, sand, gravel, water, and chemical admixtures must be available on-site or in silos before batching operations can commence.
Once concrete is batched (mixed) at the plant, it must be immediately loaded into truck mixers for transport to the pour site before it begins to set.
Batched concrete must be poured into formwork promptly after batching to ensure it is placed before initial setting occurs.
Formwork molds must be built and ready before concrete mixing can begin, as the mixed concrete needs to be poured into prepared formwork immediately to prevent premature setting.
Reinforcement steel must be placed and tied within the formwork before concrete mixing, as the rebar provides structural strength and must be embedded within the concrete pour.
All concrete ingredients (cement, sand, gravel, water, admixtures) must be sourced, delivered, and stored on-site before mixing can commence.
Freshly mixed concrete must be poured immediately after mixing (within the initial setting time) to prevent loss of workability and ensure proper curing.
Slump and quality tests must be performed immediately on the freshly mixed concrete batch before pouring to verify consistency and workability meet specifications.
Formwork creates the mold into which concrete is poured; concrete cannot be placed without a form to contain it.
Steel reinforcement must be positioned and tied within the formwork before concrete is placed to ensure structural integrity.
Concrete finishing (screeding, floating, troweling) must occur while the concrete is still fresh/plastic, immediately after placement.
Curing can only begin after concrete has been placed and finished; it is the process of maintaining moisture for hydration.
Forms cannot be removed until the placed concrete has gained sufficient strength (set and cured).
Concrete must be placed/poured into formwork before compaction can be applied, as vibration is used to consolidate freshly placed concrete and remove air voids.
Formwork must be in place to contain the concrete during pouring and subsequent compaction.
Reinforcement bars must be positioned before concrete is poured and compacted, as they are encased in the concrete.
Initial surface leveling and screeding is typically performed immediately after compaction while the concrete is still workable, before initial set begins.

Curing can only begin after concrete placement, compaction, and finishing are complete. Proper curing requires the concrete to have been compacted and finished first to achieve desired strength and durability.
The foundation or substructure must be complete to provide a stable and level base for erecting concrete formwork, ensuring proper load distribution and alignment.

Reinforcement steel must be placed and tied before formwork installation because the rebar cage needs to be positioned within the formwork; however in practice rebar often precedes formwork erection for columns/beams, while for slabs formwork may precede rebar placement. Typically, for vertical elements, rebar is installed first then formwork is erected around it.
The ground must be excavated and prepared to the required levels and dimensions before formwork can be laid out and assembled.
Formwork must be fully erected, aligned, braced, and inspected before concrete can be poured, as the formwork provides the mold that shapes and supports the wet concrete.

Concrete must be placed and cured within the formwork before the forms can be stripped; however stripping is a direct successor activity, preceded by concrete curing time. The formwork removal cannot occur until after concrete placement and sufficient strength gain.
Formwork provides the mold and support structure into which concrete is poured, so it must be fully installed and secured before concrete pumping can begin.
Steel reinforcement must be placed and tied within the formwork before concrete is pumped, as the rebar provides structural reinforcement and cannot be placed after concrete has been poured.
The concrete mix must be properly designed, batched, and tested for slump and workability to ensure it can be pumped through the equipment without clogging or segregation.
Freshly pumped concrete must be spread, leveled, and finished (screeding, floating, troweling) immediately after placement before the concrete sets and hardens.
After concrete is placed via pumping, it must undergo controlled curing (moisture and temperature management) to achieve proper strength development and prevent cracking.
Concrete must be designed and batched before samples can be taken for testing to verify mix proportions and workability.
Formwork must be erected and secured to receive concrete for casting test specimens (e.g., cylinders, beams) under field conditions.

Reinforcement is typically placed before concrete is poured; while testing of concrete itself does not strictly require rebar, representative structural element casting for strength tests often includes reinforcement.
Fresh concrete tests (slump, temperature, air content) must be performed on the batch before it is placed into forms to ensure compliance with specifications.

Compression test cylinders are cast from the same concrete batch and must be cured under controlled conditions to determine if the in-situ concrete has achieved required strength before curing begins.
Test results (e.g., 7-day or 28-day compressive strength) must be verified before formwork can be safely removed to prevent structural failure.
Concrete must achieve a minimum compressive strength (verified by testing) before post-tensioning tendons can be stressed to avoid crushing or cracking the concrete.
While some finishing occurs before testing, major remedial work (grinding, patching) is often informed by test results indicating strength or surface quality issues.
Rebar reinforcement must be installed and tied before concrete can be poured into the column formwork to provide tensile strength.
Formwork (molds) must be erected and secured to contain the wet concrete and shape the column before pouring can occur.
Concrete must be poured and achieve sufficient initial set strength before formwork can be safely removed without causing deformation or collapse.
After pouring, the concrete column must undergo curing (moisture and temperature control) to develop its design strength and durability.
Columns must be fully cured and at design strength before they can safely carry axial loads from beams, slabs, or upper floors.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and all obstructions removed before demolition equipment can access and safely operate on the concrete structures.

All electrical, water, gas, and telecommunications lines embedded in or near the concrete must be disconnected and isolated to prevent electrocution, explosion, flooding, or utility damage during demolition.

A structural engineer must assess the concrete element to determine its load-bearing status, reinforcement layout, and the safest demolition method (e.g., selective removal vs. full demolition) to avoid uncontrolled collapse.
Asbestos, lead paint, or other hazardous materials must be removed from concrete surfaces prior to demolition to prevent airborne contamination and comply with health and safety regulations.
Once concrete is demolished, the resulting rubble and debris must be cleared, sorted, and disposed of or recycled before the next construction phase can begin on that area.
After demolition, exposed rebar, foundations, or adjacent structures must be inspected for damage or integrity issues before proceeding with new construction.
New formwork for replacement concrete can only be installed after the old concrete is removed to provide the correct space and geometry for the new pour.
The ground must be excavated, leveled, and prepared with a compacted sub-base before any concrete slab can be poured to ensure stable support and proper thickness.
Formwork (wooden or metal forms) must be built and secured around the slab perimeter and any openings before concrete can be placed, as the forms define the shape and contain the wet concrete.
Steel reinforcing bars or welded wire mesh must be positioned and tied within the formwork before concrete is poured to provide structural tensile strength to the slab.
Any electrical conduits, plumbing pipes, or mechanical sleeves that pass through the slab must be placed and secured before pouring, as they cannot be installed after concrete hardens.
A vapor barrier (e.g., polyethylene sheet) must be laid over the sub-base before concrete placement to prevent moisture migration from the ground into the slab.
The ground must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and topsoil, and graded to the proper elevation before any foundation work can begin to ensure a stable and level base.
Soil bearing capacity, composition, and groundwater conditions must be assessed to design the foundation correctly and determine if soil improvement is needed.
The ground must be excavated to the required depth and dimensions for the foundation footings and slab before any concrete can be placed.
Formwork or molds must be constructed to contain and shape the wet concrete until it cures and gains sufficient strength.
Steel reinforcing bars (rebar) must be positioned and tied within the formwork before concrete is poured to provide tensile strength to the foundation.
After the concrete is poured, a curing period is required to allow the concrete to hydrate and reach its design strength before any loads are applied.
Foundation walls must be fully cured and clean before waterproofing membranes or coatings can be applied to prevent moisture intrusion.
After the foundation is cured and waterproofed, soil can be backfilled around the foundation to provide lateral support and prepare for further construction.
The superstructure (walls, columns, beams) requires a fully cured and load-bearing foundation to anchor and support the vertical loads of the building.

Plumbing drains, conduits, and other utilities that run beneath the slab must be installed and inspected before the slab is poured, but the slab (foundation) must be complete before above-slab rough-ins can proceed; actually this predecessor/successor ordering is reversed: under-slab utilities must be done before the slab pour.

The subgrade (soil or base layer) must be properly graded, compacted, and prepared to provide a stable and uniform foundation for the concrete pavement; otherwise, the concrete will crack or settle unevenly.
A granular or stabilized base course is typically placed over the subgrade to distribute loads and provide drainage support before concrete can be poured.
Forms (wood, metal, or slipform) must be set in place to contain and shape the wet concrete before pouring can begin.
Freshly placed concrete pavement requires a controlled curing period (moisture and temperature maintenance) to achieve proper strength and durability before being subjected to traffic or loads.
