Contraction/expansion joints must be cut into the cured concrete pavement to control cracking, and then sealed to prevent water infiltration.
Timber roof structure requires load-bearing walls or columns to be completed first, as they provide the structural support needed to bear the roof loads.
Where a primary structural frame exists, it must be completed to provide the supporting members and connections for the timber roof structure.
The roof covering (tiles, shingles, membrane, etc.) cannot be installed until the underlying timber roof structure (trusses, rafters, decking) is fully erected to provide a substrate.
Gutters fix to the roof edges/fascia boards which are part of the timber roof structure; installation must follow the structural roof completion.
Internal ceilings are typically fixed to or suspended from the underside of the timber roof structure/trusses, requiring the roof structure to be in place first.
Steel columns provide the vertical support structure upon which timber trusses are mounted; trusses cannot be installed without underlying column support.
Foundations must be completed to provide a stable base for columns and load-bearing walls that support timber trusses.
The concrete deck provides the working platform and bearing surface; trusses are erected after the deck is cured.
Roof sheathing (plywood/OSB) is applied directly onto the timber trusses; trusses must be fully erected and braced before sheathing can be installed.
Insulation and waterproof membranes are placed on top of or between the trusses after the truss structure is in place.
A stable foundation must be prepared and cured before any vertical structural element like a timber column can be erected to ensure structural integrity and load distribution.
Beams must be supported by columns; thus columns must be in place and secured before beams can be installed on top of or between them.
Columns serve as primary vertical supports; wall framing often attaches to or is aligned with columns, requiring columns to be erected first.
Timber must be treated with preservatives, fire retardants, or other coatings before installation to protect against moisture, pests, and fire, as post-installation treatment is less effective.
The roof structure relies on columns (and beams) for support; columns must be erected and stable before roof loads can be placed upon them.

Structural framing and walls must be erected before timber joinery (windows, doors, architraves, skirting boards) can be installed, as joinery is fitted into the prepared openings and onto finished wall surfaces.

The roof structure and covering must be completed to provide weather protection before installing timber joinery, as joinery components are susceptible to water damage and require a dry environment for proper installation.

External cladding and weatherproofing must be completed before installing external timber joinery (e.g., windows, doors) to ensure proper sealing and integration with the building envelope, preventing moisture ingress.

Timber joinery such as door frames, window reveals, architraves and skirting boards must be installed prior to plastering and internal wall linings, so that the plasterboard can be fitted neatly against the joinery elements and the junctions can be finished properly.

While painting can start once joinery is installed, this is more of a soft preference—joinery surfaces must be prepared and installed before final painting and staining to achieve a seamless finish, though paint work could theoretically be done in parallel with careful masking.
Forest management plans must be in place to identify which areas are authorized for timber harvesting before any procurement can begin.
Environmental approvals and assessments must be completed to ensure legal compliance and sustainable harvesting before timber can be procured.
Timber must be procured (harvested or purchased) before it can be transported to the construction site.
Procured timber needs to be stored and conditioned (e.g., drying) before it is ready for use in construction.
After procurement, timber must undergo quality inspection to verify it meets project specifications before being used in construction activities.
The specific timber elements must be selected, procured, and delivered to the treatment facility before any fire-retardant chemical treatment can be applied to them.
Timber must be cut, planed, and shaped to final dimensions before treatment, as applying fire retardant to oversized stock and then cutting it would expose untreated surfaces.
Timber must be dried to the specified moisture content (typically below 19%) before treatment, as excessive moisture prevents proper penetration and fixation of fire-retardant chemicals.
After chemical impregnation, treated timber must undergo controlled drying/curing to stabilize the chemicals and reach the required moisture content before further handling or installation.

successor: Quality Control Testing of Treated Timber
rationale: After treatment, samples must be tested for fire-retardant penetration depth, chemical retention levels, and fire performance ratings to verify compliance with specifications and building codes before the timber is approved for use.

Treated timber must be stored in a dry, protected environment to prevent moisture re-absorption and damage to the fire-retardant coating/impregnation before it is delivered to the construction site for installation.
The treated timber components must be installed in the final building structure only after the fire-retardant treatment process is fully complete, cured, and tested.
Raw timber logs must be harvested from forests and transported to the processing site before any cutting or machining operations can be performed on them.
Cut and machined timber pieces must be produced before they can undergo drying and seasoning to reduce moisture content.
After cutting and machining, timber must be graded and inspected for quality, dimensions, and defects before being approved for use.
Cut and shaped timber must be machined to final dimensions before any chemical treatment or preservation processes can be applied effectively.
Finished cut and machined timber products must be completed before they can be stored in inventory and dispatched to customers or construction sites.

The timber frame requires a stable, level base to be erected upon, which is provided by the completed foundation. Without a foundation, the timber frame has no structural support and cannot be safely or accurately positioned.

The ground floor slab or base must be cast and cured before timber frame erection begins, as the frame typically sits on and is anchored to this slab. Erecting timber on an unfinished base would compromise stability and alignment.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and properly prepared before any structural work. Uneven ground or debris would prevent correct placement and alignment of the timber frame.
The roof structure (trusses, rafters, roofing) is typically installed directly onto the timber frame, so the frame must be fully erected and braced to support the roof loads.
External wall cladding and sheathing boards are fixed to the timber frame structure. The frame must be erected first to provide the substrate for cladding attachment.
Timber must be milled and cut to precise dimensions before jointing can be performed, as joints require accurate sizing to fit.
Timber must be conditioned to appropriate moisture content before jointing to prevent joints from opening or distorting due to shrinkage after assembly.
Individual timber members must be jointed and connected into sub-assemblies before the frame can be erected on site.
Load testing of timber connections should follow joint completion to verify structural performance, though in some cases partial testing may occur during fabrication.
Jointing and connections must be completed before final surface finishing and treatment to ensure all surfaces, including joint interfaces, are properly coated.
The subfloor must be level, clean, and dry before timber flooring or cladding can be installed to ensure proper adhesion, prevent uneven surfaces, and avoid moisture damage.
A moisture barrier must be laid down before timber flooring to protect the wood from ground moisture or concrete slab moisture, which can cause warping, mold, or decay.
For timber cladding, the structural framing and sheathing must be complete to provide a secure mounting surface and weather-tight backing before external timber cladding is applied.

All rough-in electrical wiring, plumbing pipes, and other services that run under floors or within walls must be completed before timber flooring or cladding is installed, as accessing them afterward would require damaging the finished timber.
While painting can be done before flooring, it is generally preferred to install timber flooring after wall painting is complete to avoid paint drips, dust, and damage to the finished timber surface.
Baseboards and trim are installed after timber flooring to cover the expansion gap between the floor and the wall and to provide a clean finished edge.

successor: Final Electrical and Plumbing Fixture Installation
rationale: Final fixtures such as switch plates, outlets, and plumbing fittings should be installed after timber cladding on walls to ensure proper fit and to avoid damaging the timber during fixture installation.
Timber must first be installed, laid, or fixed in place before any maintenance, sealing, staining, or refinishing can be applied to it.
Structural timber framing must be complete before the finishing work of timber maintenance and refinishing can be performed on visible surfaces.
Sanding and surface preparation of timber is a necessary prerequisite to applying stains, oils, varnishes, or sealants as part of the refinishing process.
Timber refinishing is a finishing trade that must be completed before the final inspection and handover of the building, as it affects the aesthetic appearance and protection of timber elements.

If timber flooring is being refinished, other floor coverings like carpet or tile in adjacent areas are typically installed after to avoid damaging the finished timber surface, though this can sometimes be re-sequenced.
A comprehensive forest management plan must be in place before certification can be assessed, as certification bodies evaluate the plan's alignment with sustainability standards.
Certification requires documented proof that all forestry operations comply with local, national, and international laws; this review must be completed before certification can proceed.
An EIA must be conducted to identify and mitigate environmental risks; certification auditors require this documentation as evidence of responsible forest management.
Certification must be obtained before timber harvesting can be marketed or sold as certified sustainable wood; the certification credentials authorize the harvesting and chain-of-custody labeling.
Forest-level certification is a prerequisite for establishing a chain of custody system, which tracks certified material from the forest through processing to the final product.
Timber must be delivered and received on site before its moisture content can be tested, as testing requires the physical presence of the timber materials.

Storing timber in a covered, dry area prior to testing helps ensure moisture readings reflect stable conditions rather than recent weather exposure, but testing could technically be done directly after delivery if needed.
Moisture content must be tested first to determine if timber requires conditioning or equalisation to reach acceptable moisture levels before use.
Timber must be tested and confirmed to have acceptable moisture content before being used in framing installation to prevent future shrinkage, warping, or structural issues.

While it is strongly recommended to test moisture before machining to ensure dimensional stability, cutting could theoretically proceed without testing if moisture is assumed acceptable, making this a soft preference.
The steel I-beam must be supported on a structurally sound foundation or footing that can bear its load; the foundation must be in place before the beam is erected.
Anchor bolts are embedded in the foundation to secure the base plate of the steel column or beam; they must be installed before the beam can be placed and bolted down.
Metal decking is often laid over and supported by the steel beams; the beams must be in place to provide the structural framework for the decking.
After the beam is positioned, its connections to other structural members (e.g., columns, girders) must be welded or bolted to achieve structural continuity and stability.
Fireproofing material (such as spray-applied fire-resistive material) is applied to the exposed steel surfaces after the beam is fully installed and connections are complete, to protect it from fire.
Steel columns require a stable foundation base to transfer loads; columns cannot be erected without completed footings or pile caps.
Steel columns are bolted to anchor bolts embedded in the foundation; the bolts must be placed and set in concrete before the column can be erected.
Column base plates must be fabricated and delivered to site to allow for bolting or welding the column to the foundation.
Steel beams frame into columns; columns must be erected and plumbed before beams can be connected.
Bracing provides lateral stability; braces connect to columns and cannot be installed until columns are in place.
Steel trusses must first be fabricated from raw steel components before they can be installed or placed on site.
The building foundations or support columns/pilasters must be completed and cured to provide a load-bearing surface for steel truss placement.
The site must be graded and prepared to allow access for cranes and delivery vehicles needed to erect steel trusses.
Roof decking (metal deck, plywood, or insulation board) is placed directly onto or between steel trusses, so trusses must be erected first.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems that run through or above the truss space cannot be installed until the supporting truss structure is in place.
Steel members must be fabricated, cut, and prepared before they can be joined together at connections.
Raw steel materials must be delivered and available on site before any connection work can commence.
Steel members must be positioned, aligned, and fitted up into their correct positions before connections (bolting or welding) can be made.
After connections are completed, they must be inspected and tested (e.g., ultrasonic, visual inspection) to verify integrity before further work proceeds.
Connections and joints must be finished and inspected before protective coatings or paint are applied to the steel structure.
Steel decking requires the structural steel frame to be in place as a supporting structure to bear on and be fastened to.
Concrete topping over metal deck requires the steel deck to be installed first as a form and reinforcement for the concrete slab.
Shear studs are typically welded through the metal deck to the supporting steel beams after the deck is placed.
MEP work below the deck (sprinkler piping, conduit, ductwork) can be installed after the deck provides a working platform, though some rough-ins may start before decking in certain areas.
The roofing membrane requires a completed metal roof deck substrate to be installed and properly prepared before waterproofing can be applied.
The concrete foundation must be poured and cured to provide a stable, level surface for the steel base plate. The base plate cannot be placed on uncured or nonexistent concrete.
Anchor bolts must be embedded in the concrete foundation before the steel base plate can be lowered onto them. The base plate's holes align with these bolts for secure fastening.
The concrete foundation must reach sufficient strength before bearing the load of the steel base plate and subsequent structural steel. Premature loading could damage the foundation.
The steel base plate serves as the anchoring interface between the foundation and the steel column. The column must be welded or bolted to the base plate, which must already be in place and leveled.

After the base plate is positioned and leveled, the gap beneath it must be filled with non-shrink grout to ensure full load transfer to the foundation. Grouting cannot be done before the plate is installed.
Steel sections, plates, and other raw materials must be ordered, delivered, and available at the fabrication shop before any cutting, welding, or assembly can begin.
Approved shop drawings, connection details, and engineering specifications are required to define the exact dimensions, hole locations, weld types, and member sizes for fabrication.

While fabrication can start in a shop off-site before foundations are ready, the final fit-up, trial assembly, and any adjustments dependent on site-measured anchor bolt locations require foundation completion for accurate alignment.
Steel members must be completely fabricated (cut, drilled, welded, painted, inspected) before they can be transported to site and erected into place.

Fabricated steel components must undergo non-destructive testing (e.g., ultrasonic testing of welds, dimensional checks) to verify compliance with specifications before they are accepted and released for installation.

Steel columns and frames require load-bearing foundations (concrete piers, footings, or pile caps) to be fully cured and ready to receive the steel loads. Erecting steel on unprepared ground or uncured concrete would lead to instability and structural failure.

The site must be cleared, leveled, and compacted to provide a stable working platform for cranes, delivery trucks, and steel storage. Uneven or soft ground creates safety hazards and prevents accurate placement of steel members.

predecessor: Anchor Bolt Setting and Concrete Curing
rationale: Anchor bolts must be accurately set into the foundation concrete and allowed to cure to sufficient strength before base plates of steel columns can be bolted down. Premature erection could pull out under-strength bolts or misalign the structure.

The structural steel frame (columns, beams, bracing) must be fully erected, plumbed, and stabilized before cladding panels, roofing sheets, or curtain walls can be attached to it, as the frame provides the support and attachment points for the envelope.

While some MEP rough-in can begin once the steel frame is in place, it is a soft preference rather than a hard constraint because overhead conduits, cable trays, and ductwork are typically hung from or supported by the steel structure. Starting before the steel is complete would risk interference with ongoing erection work and lack proper support points.
Steel members must be erected and positioned in place before any welding can be performed to join them.
Steel components must be inspected for quality and prepared (cleaned, beveled if needed) before welding can commence to ensure proper weld integrity.
Components must be temporarily fitted and tack-welded into position to hold alignment before full structural welding is performed.
Welds must be completed before they can be inspected via NDT methods (ultrasonic, radiography, etc.) to verify quality and structural integrity.
Welding must be finished and allowed to cool before surface preparation (grinding, cleaning) and protective coating or painting can be applied.
A stable foundation or base is required before steel bolting can be performed, as bolting connects steel members that must be placed on a prepared surface.
Steel columns must be erected and positioned before bolting can be used to secure connections between columns and other steel members.
Steel beams must be placed/lifted into position before they can be bolted to columns or other supporting members.
Temporary bolting is often used to align and hold steel members in place before permanent structural welding is applied.
Bolting must be completed on all connections before a structural steel frame inspection can verify the integrity and torque of the bolted connections.
The steel structure must be fully erected and assembled before surface treatment can begin, as painting requires access to the completed steel framework.
The steel surface must be cleaned and prepared (e.g., abrasive blasting to remove mill scale, rust, and contaminants) to ensure proper adhesion of paint/coating.
All welding, bolting, and connection inspections must be completed before painting, as paint would hide defects and make re-inspection or rework difficult.

successor: Final Inspection / Commissioning of Steel Structure
rationale: Painting is part of the finishing works; final inspection and commissioning should occur after the coating is applied and cured.

While cladding can be installed after painting, it is a soft preference to complete painting before enclosing the structure to avoid having to work around installed panels and to ensure full coating coverage.
The intumescent coating is applied to steel members that must first be erected and installed in their final positions. Coating cannot be applied to steel that is not yet in place.
Steel surfaces must be blast-cleaned and primed to the required surface profile and cleanliness standard before intumescent coating can be applied, otherwise the coating will not adhere properly.
A compatible primer must be applied to the prepared steel surface before the intumescent top coat, as per coating system specifications for adhesion and corrosion protection.
Services such as conduits, ducts, and pipes are typically installed after fire protection coating is complete to avoid damaging the coating and to allow full inspection of the fire protection system.
Fire-rated ceilings are installed after intumescent coating to enclose and protect the coated steelwork, and to avoid having to work around or damage the finished coating.
Steel components must be fabricated, welded, and assembled before they can be inspected and tested for quality and defects.
Steel members must be erected and positioned in place before NDT testing (e.g., ultrasonic testing of welds, magnetic particle testing) can be performed on the installed connections.
All welding and bolting connections must be completed before NDT methods (ultrasonic, radiographic, MPI, DPI) can inspect weld integrity and connection quality.
NDT testing (e.g., MPI, DPI) must be completed before surface preparation and coating, because coatings can mask surface defects and interfere with NDT inspection results.
The final inspection and NDT testing results must be documented and approved before the steel structure can be formally signed off and handed over for subsequent construction phases.
Steel cannot be recycled or deconstructed from a structure until the building has been demolished and structural components have been removed and made accessible for processing.
After steel is deconstructed and collected, it must be sorted and graded by type and quality before being sent to recycling facilities.
Hazardous materials (e.g., asbestos, lead paint) must be safely removed from steel components before deconstruction to protect workers and prevent contamination of recycled material.
After deconstruction, the salvaged steel must be transported to a recycling or processing facility for further treatment.
Non-structural interior elements (walls, ceilings, MEP systems) should be removed first to expose the structural steel frame for safe deconstruction.

Structural glass panels (e.g., curtain wall or structural glazing) require the building's main structural steel frame to be erected and stabilized first, as the glass panels are typically anchored to the frame.
Floor slabs must be in place to provide working platforms and support for glass panel staging, and to allow for anchor points at each floor level.
The building envelope (glass) must be sealed and weathertight before interior finishes can be installed; otherwise, moisture damage may occur.

successor: HVAC & Electrical Rough-In Adjacent to Envelope
rationale: It is preferable to complete the glass enclosure before running final connections near the perimeter to avoid damaging the glass or requiring rework, though some adjacent rough-in can be done beforehand.
After structural glass panels are installed, the joints and perimeter must be sealed and waterproofed to ensure a weathertight building envelope.

Spandrel glass panels are typically mounted on or between structural steel members of the building frame. The steel frame must be fully erected and stable to provide the supporting structure for the glass.
Spandrel glass is often installed as infill panels within a curtain wall framing system (mullions and transoms). The frame must be in place to receive and support the glass panels.

Once spandrel glass panels are set into the frame, all perimeter joints and gaps must be sealed with weatherproofing sealants to prevent air and water intrusion. The glass must be in place before the sealant can be applied to the joints.
Interior drywall, insulation backing, or fire-stop materials installed behind spandrel glass areas must wait until the glass is in place to ensure proper alignment and closure of the wall assembly.

successor: Final Cleaning and Protective Wrap Removal
rationale: While protective films or coverings on spandrel glass are ideally removed after installation and before final cleaning, this is a soft preference because it can be done later or in stages without affecting structural sequence.
The structural frame must be complete to provide the supporting structure onto which the glass balustrade is mounted.
The floor slab must be in place to provide the base anchorage point for the glass balustrade system.
The glass panels must be installed first to define the line and support points before the handrail can be fixed on top.
The balustrade glass panels must be in position before final seals, gaskets, and silicone joints can be applied.

The structural framing (e.g., curtain wall mullions, window frames, or structural supports) must be erected to provide the load-bearing substrate onto which the glazing frame will be attached or installed.
Waterproofing and air/vapor barriers around the rough opening must be applied before the glazing frame is set to ensure the building envelope remains watertight and airtight.
The glazing frame must be fully installed and secured before glass panels or infill panels can be placed into the frame openings.
Sealants, gaskets, and weatherstripping around the glazing are applied only after the frame and glass are in place to ensure a complete weather seal.

While interior finishing can proceed in parallel, it is often preferred to complete the glazing frame first to avoid damage to interior finishes during frame installation and to allow for proper integration of window returns and trim.
The glass door requires a structurally sound frame to be mounted into, as the door hinges and locking mechanism attach to the frame.
The rough opening must be framed, leveled, and properly sized to accommodate the glass door unit before installation can begin.
Weatherstripping, caulking, and sealants around the glass door can only be applied after the door is properly installed and fitted in its frame.
Hardware such as handles, locks, and decorative hinges must be attached to the door after it is hung and aligned within the frame.
While trim can sometimes be partially installed beforehand, final trim work around the door is typically completed after the door is fitted to ensure proper alignment and reveal.
The steel frame provides the structural support onto which the glass roof or skylight system is mounted. Without the primary structure in place, the glass panels cannot be installed.
The roof deck provides the substrate and opening framing into which the skylight or glass roof system is set. The skylight curb or frame must be installed on a completed deck.
Base flashing and waterproofing layers under and around the skylight curb must be in place before the glazing is installed to ensure a watertight seal.
The glass roof/skylight must be installed and weather-sealed before interior finishes such as drywall, painting, or ceiling work can commence beneath it, to avoid water damage to finished surfaces.

successor: MEP Rough-In (above ceiling in skylight area)
rationale: While MEP rough-in can largely proceed in parallel, final connections and fixtures near the skylight well are often sequenced after glazing to allow access and avoid damaging the glass during mechanical work.
Spacer bars are typically attached to or integrated within rebar cages to maintain proper concrete cover; the rebar cage must be fabricated first before spacer bars can be installed on it.
The raw steel bar must be cut to length and bent into shape before it can be placed as a spacer bar in the reinforcement assembly.
Spacer bars must be in position to ensure proper concrete cover and reinforcement positioning before concrete is poured.

While spacer bars are often tied at the same time as the rebar cage, typically the spacer bar positioning helps maintain alignment during final tying; this is a soft preference as sequencing can vary.
The foundation or slab layout must be surveyed and marked to know exact positioning for spacer bars that maintain cover relative to formwork or ground.
The structural frame must be in place to provide support and attachment points for glass panels and curtain walls.
Window openings, sills, and framing must be prepared and measured before glass panes can be set into them.
Weather barrier, flashing, and sealant systems must be installed around openings to prevent water intrusion once glass is placed.
Interior finishes near glazed areas should be completed after glass is installed to avoid damage and to allow for proper sealing and trim work.
Final exterior sealants and caulking around glass edges must be applied after glass panels are securely positioned.
The window or door frame must be installed first to provide a structural opening and support for the glass panels to be placed into.
After the glass is placed into the frame, glazing beads or stops must be installed to secure and hold the glass in place.
The exterior perimeter must be sealed and caulked after the glass is installed to ensure weatherproofing and prevent water infiltration.

Interior trim work around the window or door can begin after glass replacement, though it could also be done concurrently in some cases; typically it follows as a soft preference for cleanliness and access.
Existing broken or old glass must be removed and the opening cleaned before new glass can be installed.
Glass must be cut to the required size and shape before tempering, as tempering alters the glass's internal stress and makes post-tempering cutting or modification impossible without shattering.

All edges and surfaces must be ground, seamed, and polished before tempering because any surface damage, chips, or sharp edges will cause stress concentrations that lead to breakage during the heating and quenching process.

Any holes, notches, or cutouts required in the glass must be drilled or machined before tempering, as the tempering process creates high compressive surface stress, making any post-tempering drilling impossible without destroying the glass.

Glass must be thoroughly cleaned and washed to remove dust, oil, fingerprints, and any contaminants before entering the tempering furnace, as impurities can cause surface defects, uneven heating, or thermal shock during tempering.

Tempered glass is often used as a component in laminated glass or insulating glass units (IGUs); assembly of these composite units can only occur after tempering is complete, as the tempering furnace cannot process assembled units.

Final quality inspection for tempering quality, including checking for roller wave, distortion, bow, and verifying fragmentation pattern (particle count per ASTM C1048 or EN 12150), must occur after the tempering process is complete.
Tempered glass must be carefully handled, stored, and packaged after tempering to prevent edge damage or surface scratching before installation, as the glass is in its final strengthened state.
Glass cleaning should only occur after window frames are fully installed to avoid soiling or damaging the glass during frame installation work.
All glass panels must be installed and the building envelope sealed before cleaning can commence, as cleaning exposed or unsealed glass is ineffective and unsafe.
It is preferable to clean glass before interior finishing work to avoid dust and debris from finishing operations settling on cleaned glass surfaces, though it is not a physical necessity.
Glass must be cleaned and maintained prior to final inspection and handover to present the building in a finished, clean state for the client.
Cleaning should be performed while scaffolding or access equipment is still in place (or before its removal), so that all glass surfaces can be safely and thoroughly accessed.
Glazing beads are typically installed after the window or door frame is in place because they secure the glass or panel within the frame.
The glazing bead serves to hold the glass or infill panel in position within the frame, so the glass/panel must be placed before the bead can be snapped or screwed into place.
Sealant or caulking around the glazing bead is applied after the bead is installed to ensure a weathertight seal and prevent water ingress.
Interior or exterior finishing work such as painting or trim installation is typically sequenced after glazing beads are in place to achieve a clean, finished appearance.
Inspection of the glazing assembly (glass security, seal integrity, bead fit) must occur after the bead is installed to verify that the assembly meets specifications.
Ducts must be installed and in place before they can be insulated, as insulation wraps around or is applied directly to the installed ductwork.
The overall HVAC rough-in, including ductwork placement and support, must be completed before insulation can be applied.

In some sequences, ducts are first insulated and then sealed/taped at joints; however if leak testing is done prior, insulation would block access. Typically, duct leakage testing must be completed BEFORE insulating. So this relation is context-dependent. For correct sequencing: duct leakage testing must precede insulation so that leaks can be repaired.
Leakage testing must be performed on bare ducts to identify and seal air leaks before insulation covers the joints and makes repair inaccessible.
Insulated ducts must be fully enclosed within ceiling or wall cavities; drywall or cladding cannot be installed until insulation is in place and inspected.
The cavity wall must be structurally built (both inner and outer leaves) before insulation can be installed into the cavity space.
Damp proof courses must be in place to prevent moisture bridging before cavity insulation is installed, as insulation can trap moisture against walls.

successor: Wall Ties Installation (if not already in place)
rationale: Wall ties may need to be installed or adjusted during or after insulation placement to ensure cavity width is maintained.
Plastering or drylining the inner face of the cavity wall must follow insulation installation to enclose the insulation and provide a finished interior surface.

While windows/doors can be installed before insulation, it is often preferable to complete cavity insulation first to avoid gaps around frames, though this is a practical preference rather than a strict physical necessity.
The ground must be excavated and graded to the proper level before any under-slab work can begin, as the insulation sits directly on the prepared subgrade.
A compacted gravel or stone base layer is required to provide a stable, well-drained surface for the insulation to be placed upon.
A vapor barrier (polyethylene sheet) is typically laid over the gravel base to prevent moisture migration; the under-slab insulation is then placed on top of the vapor barrier.

successor: Radiant Floor Heating (if applicable) / Slab Reinforcement
rationale: Under-slab insulation must be in place before any in-slab utilities (such as radiant heating tubes) or reinforcing mesh/rebar are installed, as the insulation provides the thermal break beneath these systems.
The concrete slab is poured directly over the insulation layer; therefore, all under-slab components (including insulation) must be fully installed before the concrete can be placed.
The roof deck or sheathing provides the structural base upon which the insulation layer is installed. Without a completed deck, there is no surface to support the insulation.

A vapor barrier (if specified in the design) must be placed beneath the insulation to prevent moisture migration into the insulation layer. Insulation must be installed after the vapor barrier is in place.
The underlayment (e.g., synthetic felt or self-adhered membrane) is installed over the insulation to provide a weather-resistant barrier before final roofing materials are applied.
Flashing details around penetrations, edges, and transitions must be installed after the insulation layer is in place to ensure proper integration and sealing against water intrusion.

The final roofing material (shingles, tiles, metal panels, etc.) is applied over the insulation layer. The insulation must be fully installed and any protective layers placed before the final roofing can be laid.

The breather membrane is typically installed over the structural sheathing (e.g., OSB or plywood) or directly over the frame, so the structural frame and any sheathing must be in place first to provide a substrate for the membrane.

The breather membrane is installed behind windows and doors to provide a continuous weather-resistive barrier; openings must be wrapped before window/door frames are placed to ensure proper flashing integration.
The breather membrane serves as a secondary weather barrier behind the finished cladding material (brick, siding, render); cladding must therefore be installed after the membrane is fully in place.

While some taping occurs concurrently, the primary taping and sealing of membrane overlaps, penetrations, and edges is performed as part of the membrane installation process before subsequent trades cover it.
If an external insulation layer is specified (e.g., in EIFS systems), it is placed over the breather membrane; therefore the membrane must be installed first as the inner weather barrier.
The substrate must be clean, dry, and free of debris to ensure proper adhesion and mechanical fixing of insulation anchors.
The structural frame or wall surface must be in place to provide a mounting surface for insulation fixings and anchors.
Vapor barriers are typically installed behind insulation; fixings and anchors are then driven through or applied over the vapor barrier.
Fixings and anchors must be installed first to provide the mechanical support onto which insulation boards or blankets are secured.
After fixings secure the insulation, an outer weatherproof layer or cladding is applied over the insulation system to protect it.
Plumbing and electrical lines must be installed within wall cavities before insulation is blown or sprayed, as insulation would block access to these cavities for future installation.
Interior walls must be framed to create the cavities that will receive blown or sprayed insulation material.
The exterior sheathing and air barrier must be in place to contain the insulation material when it is blown or sprayed into wall cavities.
Insulation must be installed before drywall is hung, as drywall encloses the wall cavities and permanently conceals the insulation.
In many assemblies, a vapor barrier is applied over the insulation before drywall, so insulation must be in place first.

The structural substrate (walls, floors, or roofs) must be in place before thermal bridging mitigation elements (such as insulation wraps, thermal break strips, or cladding brackets) can be installed, as the mitigation element is applied onto or into the structural assembly.

A continuous air barrier or weather-resistant barrier is typically installed prior to thermal bridging mitigation to ensure that moisture control and airtightness are established before adding thermal break layers, preventing condensation within the assembly.

Thermal bridging mitigation elements such as insulation boards, thermal break brackets, or continuous insulation layers must be fully installed before exterior cladding (brick veneer, metal panels, rainscreen) can be applied over them, as they form the intermediate layer between structure and finish.

While interior finishes can technically proceed concurrently or even before exterior thermal bridging work, best practice and sequencing typically have the thermal mitigation element in place before interior finishes on the same wall assembly to ensure continuous thermal performance and avoid rework; this is a soft preference for quality control.

successor: Window/Door Installation (if perimeter thermal break applied)
rationale: If the thermal bridging mitigation element includes perimeter thermal break strips or insulation around window/door openings, these must be installed before the windows and doors themselves to ensure proper sealing and thermal continuity at the interface.
A hazardous material survey (e.g., for asbestos) must be completed before removing insulation to identify dangerous materials and ensure safe handling procedures.
If insulation is in a confined space, confined space entry procedures and permits must be established before removal work begins.
After insulation is removed, the underlying surfaces must be cleaned and prepared for the next step (e.g., new insulation application or coating).
Removed insulation materials must be properly disposed of and documented as part of waste management procedures following removal.
Old insulation must be completely removed and disposed of before new insulation can be installed in the same area.
The building envelope (walls, roof, windows, doors) must be fully closed and air-sealed before thermal testing can measure actual heat transfer and air leakage accurately.
Heating, ventilation, and air conditioning systems must be installed and operational to create controlled temperature conditions required for thermal performance testing.
All insulation materials must be fully installed and inspected to ensure proper coverage before thermal testing can assess the effectiveness of the thermal envelope.

If thermal testing identifies deficiencies such as air leaks or insulation gaps, corrective weatherization work typically follows the test results, though this is conditionally required rather than an absolute physical constraint.

Thermal performance validation is a prerequisite input for final commissioning of the building's energy systems, but some commissioning activities can proceed in parallel or before testing is complete.

The wall assembly design (including material layers and thicknesses) must be established before its thermal transmittance (U-value) can be calculated, as U-value depends on the thermal resistance of each layer.
The thermal conductivity (k-values) of each building material must be known before the overall U-value can be computed, as material properties directly influence the calculation.
Calculated U-values for building envelope elements are essential inputs for whole-building energy modeling and simulation, as they define heat loss rates through opaque surfaces.
Preliminary U-values of baseline assemblies are needed before detailed thermal bridge analysis can be performed to determine linear thermal transmittance at junctions.

Detailed cross-section drawings showing the exact layer build-up of walls, roofs, and floors are required to measure layer thicknesses and verify construction sequencing for accurate U-value calculation.

The building envelope design must be finalized to define the thermal enclosure boundaries, cavity depths, and assembly types, which directly dictate the required insulation materials, thicknesses, and R-values.
The structural frame must be in place to establish actual cavity dimensions and substrate conditions before insulation can be accurately specified and procured in correct quantities.

HVAC system design determines duct routing, plumbing chase locations, and mechanical penetrations through insulated assemblies, which must be known to specify insulation that accommodates these elements without thermal bridges.

Insulation materials must be specified, ordered, and delivered to site before any installation work can commence, as installation crews require the actual materials and approved specifications on hand.

The type and location of vapor retarders depend on the insulation material chosen (e.g., faced vs. unfaced batts), so insulation specification must precede vapor retarder procurement and installation.
The subgrade must be prepared and compacted to provide a stable, uniform base before placing the drainage layer, otherwise the dimple mat may deform or settle unevenly.
If a concrete slab or foundation is poured as the base, it must be fully cured before the drainage layer is installed so that the dimple mat has a solid, level substrate.
A vapor barrier is typically laid directly on the prepared subgrade and beneath the drainage layer to prevent moisture migration; thus it must be installed first.
After the dimple mat is rolled out, a filter fabric or protection board is placed over it to prevent soil or backfill from clogging the drainage channels.

Backfill material is placed against the drainage layer to cover and protect it, but only after the dimple mat and any filter fabric have been installed to ensure the drainage system remains functional.
The protection board is typically laid on or against the foundation structure (e.g., on blinding concrete or retaining walls), so foundation works must be completed first to provide a stable base.
Protection board is installed directly over waterproofing membranes to shield them from damage during backfilling or subsequent construction, so the membrane must be in place first.
In some designs, a drainage layer is placed before the protection board; this is a soft preference as sequence can vary by system design.
Protection board must be in place to protect the waterproofing before backfill soil is placed and compacted against the structure.
While protection board is primarily for below-grade waterproofing protection, above-grade work can proceed after; this is a soft preference as scheduling may allow concurrent activities.

Termination bars are typically installed at the interface between different wall or floor assemblies (e.g., at expansion joints or where a wall meets a column). The structural concrete element must be in place to provide a substrate for the termination bar.
Termination bars are often used to secure and terminate waterproofing membranes at roof edges, parapets, or wall bases. The membrane must be applied first so the bar can clamp and seal its edge.
Termination bars serve as a mechanical anchor for flashing; the bar must be secured before the flashing is dressed over it and sealed.
Termination bars at wall base or window perimeters provide a clean edge and drainage point; cladding or siding is installed after to overlap or abut the bar.
The surface where the termination bar is attached must be clean, dry, and free of debris to ensure proper adhesion or fastening.
The excavation must be completed to expose the area where waterstop will be installed, typically at construction joints in foundation slabs or walls.
Formwork must be in place to define the joint where the waterstop will be embedded before installation.
Reinforcement steel must be placed and tied before waterstop installation so the waterstop can be properly positioned around the rebar at the construction joint.
Waterstop must be securely installed in the joint before concrete is poured so that it becomes embedded and forms a continuous watertight barrier.
After waterstop installation, adjacent joint sealing can follow, though this is often done after concrete curing; it is a soft preference as it can be deferred.
The surface must be inspected and assessed for defects, contamination, and condition before preparation begins, to determine the required preparation method and extent.

Any structural repairs to the substrate (e.g., concrete crack repair, rust removal on steel) must be completed before surface preparation, as preparation would need to address the repaired areas uniformly.
Initial cleaning to remove loose debris, dirt, and gross contamination must precede fine surface preparation steps like abrasive blasting or chemical etching.
Primer must be applied to a properly prepared surface to achieve adhesion; surface preparation (cleaning, profiling, dust removal) is a prerequisite for any coating or primer application.

All surface preparation steps including achieving the correct surface profile, cleanliness, and dust-free condition must be completed before any paint or coating is applied to ensure proper bonding and finish quality.

A clean, smooth, and properly prepared substrate (e.g., concrete slab or deck) is physically required before membrane installation; the membrane must adhere to a sound surface free of debris, protrusions, or moisture.

If the substrate is a concrete slab, it must be fully cured (typically 28 days) before membrane installation to prevent trapped moisture from blistering the membrane and to ensure dimensional stability.
A protection layer or cover board is placed immediately over the installed membrane to shield it from UV exposure, foot traffic, and damage during subsequent construction activities.
After membrane installation, a flood test or leak test must be performed to verify the integrity and watertightness of the membrane before covering it with subsequent layers.

In inverted roof systems or certain waterproofing assemblies, insulation boards are placed on top of the membrane after it has been installed and tested to provide thermal protection without compromising the waterproofing layer.
Panels must be positioned and temporarily tack-welded in place before continuous seam welding can be performed to join them permanently.
Surfaces must be cleaned of dirt, oil, rust, and mill scale to ensure proper weld penetration and sealant adhesion; welding on contaminated surfaces leads to defects.
Seam welds and seals must be completed before leak testing can verify their integrity; testing cannot be performed on incomplete welds.
Welding and sealing must be finished before painting or coating is applied, as coatings would be damaged by welding heat and would interfere with weld quality.
Seam welds must be completed before non-destructive examination (such as radiographic or ultrasonic testing) can be performed to verify weld quality.
Flood testing requires the structure to be built and waterproofed; the foundation and substructure must be complete to contain water for testing.
Waterproofing membranes and systems must be installed before flood testing to ensure the test checks the effectiveness of the waterproofing.
Drainage systems (floor drains, gutters, piping) must be in place so that water can be drained after testing and to verify drainage works as intended.
Interior finishes (drywall, flooring, painting) must not be installed until flood testing is complete to avoid water damage to finished surfaces.
Electrical and mechanical equipment (especially below-grade or in wet areas) must be installed after flood testing to prevent water damage to sensitive equipment.
The membrane must be installed before it can be inspected and subjected to quality assurance checks.
Inspection may reveal defects that require repair or correction work before final acceptance.
The inspection and QA process must be completed and passed before the installation can be formally accepted and signed off.

successor: Overlying Works (e.g., drainage layer, protection course, surfacing)
rationale: Although typically the inspection must be passed before covering, in some sequences limited overlying works can begin in parallel; however, full coverage should wait for QA sign-off to avoid burying defects.
The membrane must be fully installed and in place before backfilling can occur, as backfilling covers and protects the membrane system.
The integrity of the membrane must be verified (e.g., via leak detection or visual inspection) before it is buried, to avoid having to excavate and repair later.

Once backfilling is complete, final grading, compaction, and surface restoration (e.g., topsoil placement, revegetation) can proceed, though this order is not a physical impossibility but a logical construction sequence.
Compaction testing of the backfill material can only occur after the backfill has been placed and compacted over the membrane.
The membrane must first be installed or existing delamination issues addressed before patching and repair can take place, as patching is performed on the installed membrane surface.
The area to be patched must be cleaned and prepared (removing debris, dirt, and loose material) to ensure proper adhesion of the patch to the membrane.
After patching, the repair material must be allowed to cure and dry properly before any subsequent loads or waterproofing layers are applied.
Once patching is complete, testing (e.g., flood testing or vacuum testing) must be performed to verify that the patch is watertight and the repair is effective.

Applying a protective layer or topping over the repaired membrane is beneficial after patching to protect the repair from physical damage, though in some sequences it could be deferred depending on design.
Wall sheathing provides the structural base and weather-resistant barrier that brick veneer is anchored to. The brick veneer cannot be installed without this underlying support surface.
Flashing must be installed around window and door openings before brick veneer to direct water away from the building and prevent moisture intrusion behind the brick.
Windows and doors need to be installed first so that brick veneer can be laid around the openings with proper clearances, flashing integration, and sealing details.

While brick itself does not require painting, any adjacent exterior surfaces (trim, siding) are typically finished after brick veneer to avoid damage to finishes during brick installation and mortar clean-up.
Scaffolding erected for brick masonry work cannot be fully dismantled until the brick veneer installation is complete and the mortar has sufficiently cured.
A stable foundation is required to support the weight and lateral forces of the brick arch before construction can begin.
The brick arch typically spans between two supporting walls or piers; these must be built first to provide the abutments for the arch.
Temporary formwork or centering must be erected to support the bricks during arch construction until the keystone is placed and the mortar sets.
The arch must be fully completed, including placement of the keystone and initial mortar curing, before the temporary centering can be safely removed.
The structural brick arch ring must be completed before any backing material or infill above the arch can be placed.
Brick walls require a solid, level foundation or footing to bear the load and prevent settling or cracking.
The substrate or floor where the brick wall will be built must be prepared and cured before wall construction begins.
A damp-proof membrane or course must be laid on the foundation before brickwork starts to prevent moisture rising into the wall.
Door and window frames are typically installed after the brick wall is built, as the brickwork defines openings and provides support for frames.
Load-bearing brick walls must be completed to support roof beams, trusses, or rafters before the roof structure can be erected.
Plastering and rendering are applied onto the completed brick wall surface and cannot be done before the wall is built.
Chasing for conduits and pipes inside the brick wall can only be performed after the wall is fully constructed and cured.

successor: Wall Tying / Cavity Wall Insulation Installation
rationale: In cavity wall construction, the inner leaf brick wall must be completed before cavity insulation and wall ties are installed.
A brick column requires a solid foundation to distribute its load and prevent settlement. The foundation must be completed and sufficiently cured before any vertical masonry can be started.
Vertical reinforcement bars (rebar) must be placed and tied within the foundation prior to laying bricks around them, as the rebar provides structural reinforcement for the brick column.
Lintels or ring beams that bear on brick columns require the columns to be completed and cured to support the load above openings or at slab levels.
Plastering or rendering over a brick column can only begin after the brickwork is fully completed, pointed, and the mortar has cured sufficiently.
While conduits or pipes can be chased or embedded during brick laying, the main rough-in work is typically done after the column is erected to ensure proper alignment and accessibility.
The brick lintel spans openings in masonry walls; the wall must be built up to the height of the lintel before the lintel can be placed across the opening.
The lintel supports the masonry above an opening; bricks or blocks above the lintel cannot be laid until the lintel is in place to bear the load.
The entire wall system, including the lintel, requires a stable foundation; the foundation must be completed and cured before any masonry wall construction, including lintel placement, begins.
The lintel creates the structural opening; window or door frames are typically installed after the lintel is in place and the surrounding wall has been constructed.

The mortar in the wall below the lintel should have sufficient initial set to support the additional load of the lintel; while not always a strict physical necessity, it is good practice to allow some curing time.
Brick coping is installed on top of masonry walls to provide a finished, protective cap; the wall must be built first to provide structural support.
The mortar in the masonry wall must sufficiently cure to bear the weight of brick coping and resist displacement during installation.
Flashing is often integrated with or applied after brick coping is in place to ensure watertight seals at the wall top.
Finishes such as capping or sealant over the coping joint are applied after brick coping is fully set to protect the interface.
Coping installation may require scaffold access; once complete, scaffolding can be removed, though scheduling may allow some overlap.
A stable, compacted subgrade is physically required to support brick pavement, otherwise bricks will settle unevenly.
The aggregate or gravel base layer must be placed and compacted to provide drainage and structural support before bricks are laid.
Edge restraints (e.g., curbs, edging) must be installed before brick laying to contain the bricks and prevent lateral movement.
Sand must be swept into the joints only after bricks are fully laid and aligned to fill gaps and lock the paver surface.
After bricks are laid, a plate compactor must be used to vibrate and settle the bricks into the bedding sand for proper interlock.
The foundation must be completed and fully cured before any brick bonding can begin, as the brick wall relies on the foundation for structural support and load distribution.
Mortar must be prepared and available before bricks can be laid in any bond pattern, as mortar is the binding material that holds bricks together.
Bricks must be selected, sorted, and inspected for quality and consistency before laying them in a bond pattern to ensure structural integrity and uniform appearance.
Reinforcement such as rebar or wire mesh is typically installed as the brick bond progresses or immediately after, to ensure the wall's tensile strength and stability.
Pointing (tooling the mortar joints) must be done after the bricks are laid in the bond pattern but before the mortar fully hardens, to achieve the desired finish and weather resistance.
A solid foundation is physically required to support the weight of brick walls and ensure structural stability.
The floor slab or base must be cured and in place before load-bearing brick walls can be erected on top.
A damp-proof membrane/course must be laid at the base to prevent rising damp from wicking up into the brickwork.
Scaffolding is strongly preferred for safe bricklaying at height, though small-scale work could theoretically use ladders.
Openings must be formed and lintels placed during bricklaying; frames are then installed into the prepared openings.
Load-bearing walls must be fully constructed and cured to support the roof structure above.
Wiring, conduits, and pipes must be run through wall cavities after walls are built but before plastering or cladding.
Brick surfaces must be complete before any plaster or render is applied to the walls.
Raw clay must be extracted, ground, and blended before it can be cut into brick shapes, as cutting requires prepared clay mixture.
The clay must be tempered (mixed with water) and matured to achieve the correct plasticity before it can be cut into brick shapes.
Freshly cut green bricks must be dried to remove moisture before firing; cutting must precede drying.
After cutting, bricks are typically stacked onto drying racks or pallets to prepare for the drying process.

Brick pointing is the process of finishing and repairing mortar joints between bricks. The brick wall must first be constructed (laid with mortar) before the pointing work can be performed on the joints.
The mortar mix must be prepared and available before pointing can begin, as pointing requires fresh mortar to be applied to the joints.
Brick pointing on upper wall sections requires safe access via scaffolding, which must be erected before pointing work at height can commence.
After pointing mortar is applied, it requires a curing/drying period to gain strength and hardness before any subsequent work that might disturb the joints.

After pointing is complete, the brick surface is typically cleaned to remove any excess mortar smears. This is a soft preference as cleaning could be done at other times but is most effective immediately after pointing.

Brick cleaning (usually with acid or chemical solutions) must be done after mortar has been mixed and applied, but before the mortar cures fully, to remove excess mortar from brick faces without damaging set mortar.
Bricks must first be laid in place and mortar joints struck before cleaning can begin, as cleaning removes mortar smears and stains from the brick surfaces after installation.
Sealants or waterproofing coatings must be applied to clean brick surfaces to ensure proper adhesion; dirt, mortar residue, or efflorescence would prevent sealant from bonding correctly.
It is preferable to have brick cleaning completed before final inspection to present clean, finished work, but inspection can occur after cleaning as a soft preference for quality presentation.
Any pointing or repointing of mortar joints must be done after brick cleaning to ensure the joints are free of debris and cleaning chemicals do not damage fresh pointing mortar.
Scaffolding must be erected to provide safe access and working platform for workers to perform brick demolition at height.
Temporary shoring or bracing must be installed to support adjacent structures and prevent collapse before demolition of load-bearing brick walls begins.
All electrical, gas, water, and other utility lines serving the brick structure must be disconnected or isolated to prevent hazards during demolition.
Demolished brick and mortar waste must be removed from the site after demolition to clear the work area for subsequent construction activities.
New structural steel framing can only be erected after the existing brick structure has been demolished to create an open working area.
Fresh mortar must be prepared and mixed to the correct consistency before it can be applied to joints during repointing.
Damaged or deteriorated mortar must be removed from the joints (typically to a depth of 2-3 times the joint width) before new mortar can be packed in.
Brick faces should be cleaned of loose debris, dust, and efflorescence so that new mortar bonds properly and adjacent brick surfaces remain unstained.
After new mortar is packed into the joints, it must be tooled (compressed and shaped with a jointer) to the desired profile before it sets hard.
Freshly repointed mortar must be kept moist and protected from rapid drying (cured) to achieve full strength and prevent cracking.
Aggregates (sand, gravel) must be extracted and processed before they can be mixed with binder to form mortar.
The binder component (e.g., lime, cement, or other binding agent) must be manufactured or sourced before it can be used in mortar mixing.
Water is essential for hydrating the binder and achieving workable mortar; a clean water supply must be available before mixing.
Fresh mortar binder must be prepared and applied before bricks, blocks, or stones can be laid and bonded together.
Mortar binder is used as the base coat for plastering or rendering; the binder mix must be ready before application to surfaces.
A stable, level foundation surface is required before mortar joints can be started, as the mortar must bond with the substrate.
The concrete slab or foundation must be fully cured (typically 28 days) before mortar can be applied, otherwise the moisture and shrinkage of green concrete will crack the mortar joints.
Mortar joints are formed between masonry units (bricks, blocks, stones) during their placement; thus the units themselves must be positioned first so the mortar fills the gaps between them.
After the mortar joint is formed, it must be tooled (struck or finished) while still pliable to achieve proper compaction, weather sealing, and aesthetic appearance.
The freshly applied mortar joint must be allowed to cure and harden before any subsequent loads (e.g., additional courses of masonry or wall bracing) can be applied.
Bed joint cannot be formed without prepared mortar to lay between masonry units.
Bed joint is formed by spreading mortar on top of the previously placed course of masonry units; units must be placed first to provide the surface for the bed joint.
The next course of masonry units is laid onto the fresh bed joint, so the bed joint must be spread first to receive the units.

Tooling of the bed joint for weatherproofing and aesthetics can be done after the mortar has set slightly but before it hardens; this is a recommended sequence best practice but not an absolute physical necessity.
Perpend joints in masonry require fresh mortar to be placed between bricks or stones; mortar must be mixed and prepared before it can be applied to form the perpend joint.
The perpend joint is the vertical joint between bricks or stones in adjacent courses; the lower course must be laid first so that the vertical joint can be formed above it.

Bed joints (horizontal mortar joints) in the same course are typically finished and tooled after the perpend joints are filled, as the vertical perpend joints must be consolidated before the horizontal bed joints are fully completed and struck.
The perpend joint must be formed and filled for the current course before the next course of bricks or stones can be laid on top, providing proper vertical alignment and load transfer.

After the perpend joint is filled with mortar, tooling or pointing of the joint (to compress and shape the mortar) must occur before the mortar sets, to achieve a weathertight and aesthetically finished joint.

The collar joint is constructed at the base of a structure like a shaft or chimney. The excavation or subgrade preparation for the collar must be completed first to provide a stable foundation and proper geometry for the collar joint.

The collar joint often ties into or sits on top of a concrete base slab or footing. The base slab/footing must be poured and sufficiently cured to provide a solid bearing surface before the collar joint can be formed and poured.
Reinforcing steel (rebar) for the base structure must be placed and tied before the collar joint is formed, as the collar joint's reinforcement typically laps or ties into the base reinforcement.

The collar joint serves as the transition or starter element between the base and the vertical walls. The shaft or chimney walls above rely on the collar joint for proper alignment, load distribution, and connection; therefore they cannot start until the collar joint is complete and cured.

Waterproofing membranes or sealants at the base-to-wall transition are applied after the collar joint is fully cured, since the joint must be intact and sound to provide a continuous substrate for waterproofing.
Sand, cement, and water must be procured and delivered to the site before mortar can be mixed, as these are the essential raw ingredients.
Cement and sand must be properly stored (e.g., kept dry) before mixing; wet or contaminated materials cannot be used.
Freshly mixed mortar must be used promptly before it sets; bricklaying and blockwork require wet mortar as the binding agent.
Plaster and render coats require freshly mixed mortar to be applied; the mortar must be prepared immediately prior to application.
Pointing work to finish masonry joints must be done while the mortar is still workable but after initial brick/block placement.

The surface must be clean, sound, and properly prepared (e.g., cured concrete or masonry laid out, joints raked) before mortar can be applied; mortar will not bond correctly to unprepared or dirty surfaces.
Dry ingredients and water must be mixed to the proper consistency before the mortar can be troweled or applied; application cannot begin without prepared mortar material.

Although mortar can sometimes be applied from ground level, for most wall heights scaffolding must be in place to safely reach the work area; this is a safety-driven preference but in practice almost always required.

After mortar is applied between masonry units, the joints must be struck or tooled while the mortar is still plastic (partially set) to achieve proper compaction and weatherproofing; this finishing step physically cannot occur before the mortar is in place.

Fresh mortar must be allowed to cure and gain strength before any subsequent loads (such as installing lintels, roof plates, or further wall sections) are applied; disturbing mortar before it sets would compromise the bond and structural integrity.
Scaffolding must be erected to provide safe access to the masonry walls at height before repointing work can begin.
The existing mortar joints must be inspected to determine the extent of deterioration, mortar composition, and required repointing approach before work commences.
Freshly repointed mortar requires adequate curing time to gain strength and weather resistance before any subsequent work can be done on or against the wall.
Scaffolding must remain in place until repointing work is complete to ensure worker safety and access; dismantling can only begin after repointing is finished.
After repointing is complete, the wall surface must be cleaned of excess mortar and debris to achieve the final finished appearance.
Mortar must be mixed and applied before it can begin curing; curing is the process of hydration and hardening that starts after the mortar is placed.
Mortar is used to bond masonry units; the mortar must be placed between bricks/blocks before the curing process begins.
Tooling of mortar joints must be completed before curing progresses to an advanced stage; once mortar stiffens, joints can no longer be effectively shaped or compacted.
While not a strict physical necessity, it is a soft preference to allow mortar to gain sufficient strength before removing scaffolding that may impose loads or require access to the cured wall.
Waterproofing coatings should be applied only after mortar has fully cured to avoid trapping moisture or causing adhesion failure.
Mortar must be mixed and prepared before it can be tested for properties such as consistency, workability, and strength.
Sand, cement, lime, water, and admixtures must be proportioned and batched before mixing and subsequent testing of the mortar.
The mortar must be tested and approved (e.g., for workability, setting time, strength) before it can be used in masonry construction to ensure quality and compliance with specifications.
Test results inform quality records, but documentation can be completed partially in parallel or after testing is underway.
Grouting is often used to seal or stabilize the soil around piles; piles must be installed first to define the locations needing treatment.
Excavation exposes the surfaces or cavities that require grouting to stabilize soil, seal joints, or fill voids.
Grout is injected into pre-drilled holes; drilling must be completed first to create the injection points.
Grouting must seal cracks and voids before waterproofing membranes are applied to ensure a stable substrate.
In many sequences, grouting is done to fill anchor bolt holes or base plates before secondary concrete or grout caps are placed.
The main vertical and horizontal rebar cage for columns or walls must be assembled first because helical/spiral reinforcement is tied around the longitudinal bars of the cage, providing confinement.
Helical/spiral reinforcement must be fully placed and tied before formwork is closed up, as the formwork encloses the reinforcement cage and cannot be installed afterward.
All reinforcement including helical/spiral wraps must be in position before concrete is poured, as the reinforcement is embedded within the concrete element.
Cover blocks (spacers) are placed after the spiral reinforcement to ensure proper concrete cover, though in practice this may be done concurrently or after the spirals are tied.

While helical/spiral reinforcement typically constitutes the transverse reinforcement, any supplemental ties or hoops may be placed after the spiral is installed, though this order can vary by design preference.
Stirrups/links are placed around the main longitudinal reinforcement bars to provide shear resistance and confinement, so the main reinforcement must be in position first.
Formwork provides the mold and support structure; stirrups/links are tied within the formwork onto the main reinforcement cage.
All reinforcement including stirrups/links must be fully placed and tied before concrete is poured to encase the reinforcement.
Cover blocks are placed after stirrups/links to maintain proper concrete cover between the reinforcement and the formwork face.

Transverse reinforcement bars (stirrups/ties) are placed around the main longitudinal reinforcement bars to confine them and provide shear resistance. The main bars must be in position first to establish the framework around which transverse bars are wrapped or placed.

While formwork can be partially set up before transverse reinforcement, in typical construction sequences, the formwork for beams and columns is often prepared so that rebar cages (including transverse bars) can be placed inside. This is a soft preference as prefabricated cages can be lifted into existing formwork.

Concrete cannot be poured until all reinforcement, including transverse reinforcement bars (stirrups/ties), is fully placed and tied in position. The transverse bars must be in place to ensure structural integrity and proper concrete cover.

Cover blocks (spacers) are typically placed after the transverse reinforcement is positioned to ensure adequate concrete cover between the rebar and the formwork face. The transverse bars define the outer perimeter of the reinforcement cage.
The transverse reinforcement bars must be fully placed and tied before the final side of formwork is closed, as access to the reinforcement cage is needed for proper installation and inspection.
Rebar must be placed and positioned in the forms before lap splices can be created, as the lap splice involves overlapping and tying together the reinforcing steel bars.
Rebar must first be cut to length and bent according to design specifications before the bars can be overlapped and spliced together.
Lap splices must be completed and properly tied before concrete is poured, as the spliced rebar assembly becomes embedded in the concrete and cannot be adjusted after pouring.
After lap splices are tied, the rebar assembly (including splices) must be inspected before concrete placement to verify splice lengths, tie spacing, and overall compliance with structural drawings.

In some sequences, formwork may be partially erected before lap splicing begins, but typically lap splicing of rebar is performed within or adjacent to completed forms; however, this is a soft preference depending on construction method.
The foundation or base must be prepared and cured before any mechanical coupling device can be installed, as the coupler typically mounts onto or is embedded into the base structure.
Rebar must be cut, bent, and positioned prior to installing the mechanical coupler, because the coupler joins reinforcing bars end-to-end and the bars must be ready for connection.
Mechanical couplers for prestressed or post-tensioned applications must be fully installed before tensioning forces are applied, as the coupler transfers the tensile load between bars.
Concrete can only be poured after the mechanical coupler and connected rebar are in place, since the coupler becomes embedded within the concrete element.

After installing the mechanical coupler, it must be inspected and tested (e.g., torque checks, pull-out tests) before being covered by subsequent construction activities to ensure compliance with specifications.
Rebar spacers / cover blocks are placed onto rebar to maintain proper concrete cover; the rebar must first be installed in position before spacers can be attached.
Cover blocks are typically secured before formwork is closed, but in some sequences formwork can be partially erected first; this is a typical preference for quality assurance.
Cover blocks ensure the correct concrete cover depth; concrete cannot be poured until all cover blocks are in place on the rebar to prevent rebar exposure or corrosion.
While inspection follows pouring, proper placement of cover blocks before pour directly affects inspection outcomes; this is a soft precedence since inspection is a later quality control step.
The bar top must be installed before bar chairs can be positioned, as chairs are placed relative to the bar counter height and location.
Floor finishing (tiling, polishing, or flooring) must be completed before placing bar chairs to avoid damaging finished surfaces or having to move chairs.
Chairs must be manufactured or procured before they can be delivered and placed on site.
Final cleaning should ideally be done after all furniture including bar chairs are in place to ensure a clean final state, but this is a soft preference.
Final decorative touches and styling are often completed after all furniture is placed, but chairs could be moved if needed.
Rebar must first be cut to the required lengths before it can be bent, as bending happens on individual pre-cut bars.
Steel reinforcement bars must be delivered and received on site before any bending operations can be performed.
Rebar must be bent into its required shape (stirrups, hooks, etc.) before it can be placed and tied in the formwork.
