Bent rebar must be inspected for dimensional accuracy and proper bend angles before being used in structural placement.
Although formwork is often installed before rebar placement, bent rebar assembly must be complete before closing/shuttering the formwork. This is a soft preference when formwork is partially open.

Formwork provides the mold and support structure into which rebar is placed; rebar cannot be fixed in position before the formwork is erected because there is no framework to hold it in place and define the concrete shape.
Rebar must be cut and bent to the specified dimensions and shapes before it can be placed and tied into position at the construction site.
Concrete must be poured after rebar is fixed in place so that the reinforcement is embedded within the concrete matrix to achieve the desired structural strength.

While inspection of the formwork often occurs before rebar placement, a final check of both formwork and placed rebar before concrete pouring is a standard quality control step; this ordering reflects a soft preference for sequential workflow coordination.

Some embedded items can be placed concurrently with rebar, but if conduits or sleeves must pass through rebar cages, it is often preferable to position them during or after rebar fixing to avoid rework, though this is a soft preference depending on design.
Rebar must be cut and bent to the required shapes and lengths before they can be tied together into a reinforcement cage or mat.
Rebar bars must first be placed and positioned in their designated locations before they can be secured by tying wire at intersections.
The rebar cage/mat must be fully tied and stable before formwork is installed around it, as formwork encloses the reinforcement.
All rebar tying must be completed and inspected before concrete is poured, so that the reinforcement remains in its correct position during pouring.

predecessor: Delivery and Storage of Reinforcement Steel
rationale: Reinforcement steel must be delivered and stored on site before welding can commence, as the material is physically required for the welding activity.
Reinforcement bars must be cut and bent to the required shapes and dimensions before they can be welded together into cages or assemblies.

While often formwork is installed before reinforcement placement, in some construction methods reinforcement cages are welded in place before formwork. However, typically formwork provides the support and alignment for reinforcement welding.
The reinforcement components must be welded into their final assembled configuration (e.g., beam or column cages) before they can be placed into the formwork.
All reinforcement welding must be completed and inspected before concrete is poured, as welding after concrete placement would be impossible and would compromise the structural integrity.
Rebar fabrication requires detailed shop drawings and bending schedules derived from structural engineering designs before any cutting or bending of rebar can commence.
The raw steel rebar materials must be ordered, delivered, and available at the fabrication yard before off-site fabrication operations can begin.
Fabricated rebar cages and assemblies must be completed off-site before they can be loaded and transported to the construction site.
Prefabricated rebar components must be produced off-site before they can be installed and tied into position within formwork on-site.
The entire rebar cage must be fabricated and placed before concrete can be poured, as rebar provides the tensile reinforcement essential to the structural element.
Reinforcement bars must be fabricated, cut, and bent to design specifications before they can be inspected and tested for compliance.
Reinforcement must be fully placed, tied, and positioned in the formwork before inspection of spacing, cover, and alignment can be performed.
Formwork must be erected so that reinforcement can be placed within it; inspection of rebar is typically done prior to final formwork closure or concreting.
Concrete cannot be poured until reinforcement has been inspected and approved to ensure it meets design and quality requirements, as it will be concealed by the concrete.
Side or top formwork is often closed only after reinforcement is inspected; inspection is a prerequisite before final formwork closure and subsequent concreting operations.
Concrete cover refers to the distance between the rebar surface and the outer face of the concrete. Therefore, rebar must be installed and in place before the concrete cover can be checked.
Formwork defines the outer boundary of the concrete element; the concrete cover is measured from the rebar to the formwork face, so formwork must be installed before checking.
Concrete cover must be verified and approved before pouring concrete, as the cover ensures durability and reinforcement protection; once concrete is poured, cover cannot be adjusted.
If the cover check reveals non-compliance, rebar must be repositioned to achieve the required cover before proceeding to concrete pouring.
Reinforcement quantities, bar sizes, and layout details must be finalized in structural design before a bar schedule can be produced.
The bar schedule specifies the types, quantities, and lengths of reinforcement bars needed, which must be known before ordering materials.

successor: Fabrication of Reinforcement Cages / Cutting & Bending
rationale: Fabrication requires the bar schedule as the instruction set for cutting, bending, and tagging each reinforcement bar.

While formwork can often be set up in parallel, final placement of reinforcement may depend on formwork readiness, but scheduling the bars typically precedes formwork design adjustments for cover and spacers.

successor: Steel Reinforcement Laying / Fixing on Site
rationale: The bar schedule is the instruction document used by steel fixers to place the correct bars in the correct positions; laying cannot begin without the finalized schedule.
Individual steel plates must be cut, beveled, and prepared to the required dimensions before they can be assembled into a built-up girder. This is a fundamental fabrication prerequisite.
Plate edges must be beveled and prepared for welding to ensure proper weld penetration and joint strength before girder assembly can begin.
The web and flange plates must first be positioned, aligned, and tacked together to form the built-up girder shape before permanent structural welding of the seams can be performed.
The main built-up girder cross-section must be assembled and welded before intermediate transverse and longitudinal stiffeners can be attached to the web.

The complete built-up girder must be fully welded and inspected before surface preparation (abrasive blasting) and protective coating application can be carried out, as coating on incomplete welds would be wasted.
Steel braces require a stable foundation to anchor and support the structural loads they will transfer.
Steel braces typically connect between columns or from column to floor; columns must be in place to provide connection points.
Braces provide lateral stability to the frame; concrete slabs should not be poured until the bracing system is installed to prevent collapse under load.
Exterior cladding is attached to the structural frame; steel braces must be in place to ensure the frame is stable and correctly aligned before cladding is applied.
While not physically required, coordinating MEP rough-in after bracing avoids conflicts and rework since braces may occupy space needed for ductwork or piping.
The ground must be excavated and leveled to provide a stable foundation before placing the base plate.
A concrete foundation must be poured and fully cured to support and anchor the base plate.
Anchor bolts must be set into the foundation (or positioned beforehand) to allow the base plate to be bolted down securely.
The base plate provides the mounting surface and connection points for the vertical columns or steel frame members.
After the base plate is positioned and leveled, grout must be injected underneath to fill voids and ensure full bearing on the foundation.
Gusset plates are used to connect steel beams and columns at joints; the main structural members must be erected and in place before the gusset plates can be bolted or welded to them.

successor: Bolting and Welding of Joint Connections
rationale: The gusset plate must first be positioned and temporarily secured at the joint before permanent bolting or welding of the connection can be completed.

predecessor: Connection Plate / Gusset Plate Fabrication and Delivery
rationale: The plates must be manufactured, cut to size, hole-punched, and delivered to the construction site before they can be installed on the structure.
The building foundation with embedded anchor bolts must be cured and ready to support the steel columns before any steel structure erection begins, which is prerequisite to gusset plate installation.

successor: Structural Steel Inspection and Load Testing
rationale: Once gusset plates are installed and connections are made, the completed steel frame including all joint connections must be inspected and load-tested before proceeding to subsequent construction activities such as decking or cladding.
Stiffener plates are welded onto steel girders; the girder must be fabricated first to provide the base structure for stiffener attachment.
The steel girder surface must be cleaned and prepared (e.g., removed of mill scale, rust, and debris) prior to welding stiffener plates to ensure weld quality and adhesion.
The stiffener plates themselves must be cut, shaped, and prepared to their final dimensions before they can be positioned and welded onto the girder.
After stiffener plates are welded in place, non-destructive testing (e.g., ultrasonic or magnetic particle inspection) must be performed to verify weld integrity and compliance with specifications.
Any protective coating or paint system must be applied after all welding of stiffener plates is completed, as welding after painting would damage the coating and create safety hazards.
Bolted connections physically join steel members together, so the steel columns and beams must first be erected and positioned in place before their connections can be bolted.
The foundation and base plates must be set and anchored to provide a stable support for steel columns before any bolted connections can be made at column bases.
Bolt holes in steel members must be aligned and temporarily fitted (e.g., with drift pins or erection bolts) before permanent bolting can proceed; otherwise bolts cannot be inserted.
Bolts must be installed and hand-tightened first before final torqueing, tensioning, or preloading to achieve the required clamping force.
The bolted connections must be fully installed before structural frame inspections and quality checks can be performed to verify connection integrity.

While some bracing can be installed concurrently, final bracing elements often rely on bolted connections being completed first to stabilize the frame; this is a preference for sequential work to avoid rework.
Structural steel columns and beams must be erected and positioned before they can be welded together to form permanent connections.
Steel members must be properly fitted, aligned, and tack-welded or bolted temporarily before permanent structural welding can be performed.
Steel materials and weld joints must be inspected for compliance with specifications, cleanliness, and fit-up tolerances before welding commences.
Non-destructive testing of structural welds must be performed after welding is complete to verify weld integrity and compliance with code requirements.

successor: Surface Preparation and Painting / Coating (Structural Steel)
rationale: Final surface preparation, priming, and painting or fireproofing of structural steel connections must be done after welding is finished, as welding would damage any previously applied coatings.
Steel must be erected and framed in place before surface preparation and priming can begin, as the coating work is performed on the installed structural steel members.
All welding, bolting, and connection work must be completed before surface preparation to avoid damaging the primer with sparks, heat, or physical interference from connection work.
Fireproofing materials must be applied over the primer; surface preparation and priming are required to ensure proper adhesion of fireproofing to the steel.
The primer coat serves as the base layer for the finish/topcoat painting system and must be completed and cured before the topcoat can be applied.

Although often sequenced after priming to avoid contaminating the primer, it is a soft preference because cladding can be installed concurrently if the primer is fully cured and protected from damage.
Spray-applied fire-resistive materials (SFRM) must be applied to structural steel members after they are erected, as the steel frame needs to be in place to receive fireproofing.

Metal decking is typically installed before fireproofing is applied to ensure the substrate for fireproofing and flooring is in place, and to allow SFRM application to proceed without decking interference.

Concrete slabs or toppings are poured over metal decks before SFRM is applied; the slab must cure and be in place to provide the finished floor system before fireproofing work begins on the underside.

While MEP rough-in can technically start before fireproofing is complete, it is preferable to apply SFRM first to avoid damaging or covering fireproofing with MEP installations, and to ensure continuous coverage without obstructions.
Ceilings and drywall must be installed after SFRM application because fireproofing needs to be fully applied and inspected on the structural members before they are enclosed by ceiling systems.
Steel members must be erected before they can be surveyed for plumbness and alignment.

predecessor: Bolting and Welding of Steel Connections
rationale: Connections must be completed to stabilize the steel frame before checking vertical and horizontal alignment.
Survey results may identify misalignments that require adjustment before bolts are finally torqued.
Floor decking and concrete slabs should only be placed after steel frame alignment is verified to avoid embedding misalignments.
While preferred to wait for alignment verification before installing stairs and facade to ensure fit, some installation may proceed in parallel with minor adjustments.
Shear studs are welded onto steel beams or columns; the steel structural member must be erected and in place before studs can be welded to it.
Shear studs are often welded through metal decking to the steel beam below; the metal deck must be installed and positioned before stud welding can occur through it.
Shear studs must be welded and in place before concrete is poured so that the studs become embedded in the concrete slab, creating the composite action between steel and concrete.
After installation, shear studs must be inspected (e.g., bend testing or visual inspection) before any further work such as concrete placement to ensure weld quality.

If rebar is placed after stud welding, the studs must be in place first; however, rebar can also be placed before studs in some sequences, so this is a soft preference for typical order where stud welding occurs before rebar mats are tied.
Corner bead requires a framed surface (stud walls) to attach to; framing provides the structural backing.
Sheathing (e.g., gypsum board, drywall) must be installed first because corner bead is applied over the sheathing to protect and reinforce corners.
Corner bead is installed onto drywall boards at external and internal corners; the drywall must be in place to provide a substrate.
Joint compound is applied over corner bead to embed it and create a smooth finish; taping/mudding cannot start until corner bead is fixed in position.
Once corner bead is installed and covered with compound, sanding and final finishing of corners occurs to achieve a smooth surface for painting.
Metal stud framing requires a stable, level concrete slab or foundation to anchor the bottom track and ensure proper alignment and structural integrity.
Wall layout lines and reference marks must be transferred from the structural slab to accurately position the metal stud tracks before any studs are installed.
Any mechanical, electrical, or plumbing work that runs below the slab or within the floor must be completed before framing walls, as access will be blocked once studs are erected.
Vertical MEP rough-ins (conduit, piping, ductwork) are installed through the stud cavities after the metal stud walls are framed but before drywall or insulation is placed.
Insulation batts or spray foam are placed within the cavities of the completed metal stud walls to provide thermal and acoustic performance before the walls are enclosed.
The resilient bar must be manufactured from steel before it can be installed on-site.
Resilient bars are typically attached to wall studs or framing, so the framing must be completed first.
Resilient bars serve as a mounting base for drywall to create sound isolation, so drywall must be installed after the bars are in place.
While not physically required, inspecting the resilient bar installation before enclosing it with drywall is a standard quality assurance practice.
It is generally preferred to complete rough-in work behind the wall before installing resilient bars to avoid having to cut through or disturb the sound isolation system.
Plasterboard (drywall) is typically attached to the structural framing (studs, joists) of walls and ceilings. The framing must be complete to provide a surface for the plasterboard.

All electrical wiring, outlet boxes, plumbing pipes, and HVAC ducts must be installed within the walls and ceilings before they are closed up with plasterboard, otherwise costly rework would be required.
Insulation batts must be placed inside wall and ceiling cavities before plasterboard is fixed over them, as it would be impossible or destructive to install insulation afterward.
Once plasterboard sheets are installed, the joints between sheets must be taped and finished with joint compound to create a smooth surface. This cannot be done before the boards are fixed.
Plasterboard must be installed, taped, and finished before any painting or decorative wall finishes can be applied to the surface.
Plasterboard sheets must be fixed to the framing before any taping and jointing can occur, as jointing compounds are applied over the seams between installed boards.
Taping and jointing must be completed and dried before sanding can take place, as sanding smooths the dried joint compound.
Surface preparation including taping, jointing, and sanding must be finished before any paint or primer can be applied to achieve a smooth finish.
Cornices are typically installed after wall and ceiling sheets are taped and jointed, as the jointing provides a flush surface for moulding alignment.
The structural framing must be complete to support plasterboard sheets; however, this is an indirect prerequisite as plasterboard installation is the immediate predecessor to taping and jointing.
Plasterboard sheets must be installed, fixed, and jointed before any sanding and finishing can occur, as sanding prepares the installed and jointed surface for painting or decoration.
All joints between plasterboard sheets must be taped and the compound must be applied and dried before sanding can smooth the surface.

successor: Priming and Painting of Plasterboard Surfaces
rationale: Sanded and finished plasterboard surfaces must be smooth and clean before primer and paint can be applied to achieve a quality finish.
After sanding and finishing is complete, the surfaces must be inspected for defects and any necessary touch-ups performed before final decoration.

successor: Installation of Wall and Ceiling Fixtures (e.g., cornices, architraves, skirting)
rationale: Sanding generates fine dust, so it is preferable to complete sanding before installing trim and fixtures to avoid dust contamination on finished elements, though not a physical impossibility.
Plasterboard must be cut to fit the framed wall layout; the stud positions define the dimensions and locations for plasterboard sheets.
Plasterboard sheets must be delivered and stored on site before they can be cut to size.
Plasterboard sheets must be cut to the required dimensions before they can be lifted into position and fixed to the framing.
Once cutting is complete, waste offcuts and dust should be cleared to maintain a clean worksite, though this is a soft preference rather than a physical necessity.
Dot-and-dab requires a solid substrate wall (either studwork/plasterboard backing or masonry blockwork) to fix plasterboard onto.
Cables, conduits, pipes and back boxes must be chased into or routed within the wall before the plasterboard is fixed, otherwise the services cannot be installed behind the finished wall surface.
Once the plasterboard is dot-and-dabbed onto the wall, the joints and board surface are skimmed with plaster to create a smooth finish.
Tiling should be applied onto the plastered and set wall surface after dot-and-dab and skimming are complete to provide a flat substrate.
Final paint finishes are applied only after plastering (and any drying/curing) is complete; painting before dot-and-dab would be impossible.
Plasterboard waste is generated during installation (cutting, trimming, damaged boards). Waste management cannot commence until there is waste material to manage.
All plasterboard waste must be collected, sorted, and disposed of/recycled before the site can be declared clear and ready for final handover.
Structural framing must be finished before plasterboard installation begins, and plasterboard waste management follows installation.

While it is preferable to complete waste documentation after all waste is processed, some documentation can be done in parallel. However, final certification typically requires evidence that all waste has been managed.

Screed joints (expansion/control joints) can only be cut or formed after the screed concrete has been poured and has achieved initial set; otherwise the joint cannot be created in the hardened material.
Proper curing of the screed must begin after the joints have been cut/formed to allow the curing process to proceed without interfering with joint formation.
The sub-base or underlying floor layer must be prepared and compacted before any screed is poured, and consequently before screed joints can be installed.
Final floor finishing (e.g., polishing, sealing, covering) can only commence after the screed joints have been formed and the screed has cured adequately, to avoid damaging the joints.
Screed is typically poured over underfloor heating pipes to encase and protect them; heating must be installed and pressure-tested before screeding.
A clean, level, and cured subfloor is required as the base onto which the screed is poured; the subfloor must be fully prepared beforehand.

predecessor: Moisture Barrier / Damp Proof Membrane Installation
rationale: A damp proof membrane or moisture barrier must be laid before screeding to prevent rising moisture from damaging the screed and subsequent floor finishes.

successor: Floor Covering Installation (e.g., tiles, wood, vinyl)
rationale: Screed must be fully cured and dried before any floor finish can be applied on top, as the finish requires a stable, level substrate.
After screeding, the floor level must be checked and verified for tolerance compliance before proceeding with subsequent trades.
Raw materials like cement, sand, aggregate, and water must be procured and delivered to the site before screed mixing can commence.
The subfloor or base surface must be cleaned, leveled, and prepared prior to screed mixing and laying.
For screed applied over a structural slab, the concrete slab must be poured and sufficiently cured before screed mixing and application.
A damp proof membrane must be laid on the subfloor prior to screeding to prevent moisture migration.
Screed must be mixed before it can be laid, spread, and leveled on the substrate.
Screed must be mixed and laid before the curing/drying process can begin.
Final floor finishes (tiles, wood, vinyl, etc.) can only be installed after the screed has been mixed, laid, and fully cured.
The sub-base must be prepared and compacted to provide a stable, level foundation before the screed can be applied.
A damp-proof membrane must be laid prior to screeding to prevent moisture migration from the sub-base into the screed.

predecessor: Installation of Edge Insulation / Perimeter Strip
rationale: Edge insulation strips around the perimeter must be in place before screeding to allow for thermal expansion and to isolate the screed from walls.

successor: Floor Covering Installation (e.g., Tiles, Vinyl, Carpet)
rationale: The finished screed must be fully cured and levelled before any final floor covering can be installed to ensure a smooth, durable substrate.
After screeding, a proper curing period must be allowed to achieve the required strength and prevent cracking before any subsequent loads or finishes are applied.

Screed (the levelled concrete layer) must be poured and finished before curing can begin, as curing is the process of maintaining moisture and temperature conditions to allow the freshly placed concrete to hydrate and harden.
The screed must be properly floated, trowelled, and levelled to the correct grade and surface finish before curing starts, as curing locks in the final surface condition.

Curing should begin after the concrete has achieved initial set (typically when it is hard enough to resist surface damage), so that the curing compound or water application does not wash away or damage the fresh surface.

Floor coverings (tiles, vinyl, timber, etc.) can only be installed after the screed has completed its specified curing period and reached adequate strength and dryness, to avoid cracking, debonding, or moisture-related failures.
Moisture content testing of the screed can only be performed after curing is substantially complete, to verify that the slab is dry enough for subsequent floor coverings.
Screed must be installed before it can dry and be tested for moisture content.

successor: Floor Covering Installation (tiles, wood, vinyl, carpet)
rationale: Floor coverings can only be installed after screed has dried to the required moisture level; otherwise trapped moisture causes adhesion failure and mold.
Any subsequent leveling layers require the base screed to be fully dry and tested to ensure compatibility and prevent delamination.

successor: Underfloor Heating Commissioning (if screed is the thermal mass)
rationale: Underfloor heating system embedded in screed must only be commissioned after the screed has sufficiently dried and been moisture-tested to avoid cracking from thermal shock and trapped moisture.

successor: Final Floor Finishing / Sealing (polishing, sealing, coating)
rationale: Surface treatments and sealants require a fully dry and tested screed substrate to bond correctly and avoid blistering or failure.

The screed must be pumped and finished to its final shape and level before grinding can commence, as grinding is a surface refinement process that removes irregularities from the already-placed screed.
The screed needs sufficient curing time to develop adequate strength and hardness; grinding too early could damage the soft surface and cause delamination or excessive dust.
Surface preparation creates a clean, properly profiled substrate for the hardener/sealer to bond effectively; applying sealer before grinding would seal in imperfections and prevent proper adhesion.

After grinding and surface preparation, the area should be cleaned and inspected to verify surface tolerances and readiness before subsequent finishing steps, though this is a quality assurance step rather than a physical necessity.
The concrete substrate must be cleaned, sound, and free of contaminants before screed repair and patching can be applied, otherwise the repair material will not properly bond.
Excess moisture in the substrate can cause screed repair materials to debond or fail; moisture levels must be verified as acceptable before patching.
After placing the repair or patching material, a curing period is required to allow the material to reach sufficient strength before further trades work on top.
Any final surface levelling or smoothing (e.g., grinding, power floating) must occur after the patched areas have been placed and initially set.
Floor finishes such as tiles, vinyl, or carpet can only be installed after the screed repairs are fully cured and the surface is sound.
The screed must be mixed, poured, and allowed to set/harden before it can be inspected and tested for quality and compliance.
The screed requires adequate curing time to reach sufficient strength and dryness before inspection and testing (e.g., moisture tests, hardness tests) can be performed.

Inspection and testing of the screed (e.g., moisture content, surface flatness, strength) must be completed and approved before any final floor covering (tiles, vinyl, wood, etc.) can be installed on top.

If inspection and testing identify defects or non-compliance, remedial works (grinding, patching, re-screeding) will follow; this is a conditional soft sequencing based on test results rather than a mandatory physical constraint.

Formal sign-off of the screed quality through inspection and testing is a prerequisite for progressing to the next stage or handover, ensuring that the substrate meets specification before subsequent trades commence.
The joint must be clean, dry, and free of debris before backing rod can be inserted to ensure proper adhesion and sealant performance.
Backing rod serves as a bond breaker and depth control for sealant; sealant must be applied directly over the installed backing rod before it cures or becomes dislodged.
After backing rod is placed, the sealant can be tooled and finished to the correct profile; the backing rod provides the necessary backer to achieve proper sealant shape and depth.
The area must be cleaned and prepared to ensure the sealant removal tools can access the joints and the new sealant can bond properly.
Proper access and fall protection equipment must be in place before workers can safely perform sealant removal at height.
Old sealant must be completely removed before primer is applied to the exposed joint surfaces for new sealant adhesion.
The removal of old sealant must be completed to create clean joint voids before fresh sealant can be installed.
Sealant removal and replacement must be finished before the curing period begins and final inspection can take place.
Pipes must be cut to the required length before the joint ends can be prepared (beveled, cleaned) for welding or joining.
Bevelling creates the angled edge on the pipe end, which is an essential part of joint preparation before welding.
The joint must be properly prepared (cleaned, beveled, aligned) before welding can take place to ensure weld quality and penetration.
Joint preparation includes cleaning and beveling pipe ends; pipes must then be aligned and fitted together before welding can commence.
Pipes and fittings must be inspected for defects, dimensions, and material compliance before joint preparation work begins to avoid rework.
Surfaces must be cleaned, primed, and properly prepared before sealant is applied and subsequently inspected.
The sealant must be fully applied before inspection can take place to verify correct installation, coverage, and adhesion.
Sealant must be allowed to cure for the manufacturer-specified time before inspection can assess its final condition and integrity.
If sealant fails inspection, any subsequent joint backing installation must wait until the sealant is repaired and re-inspected.
It is preferred that sealant inspection is completed before final finishing to avoid rework, though not physically required.
Tooling (smoothing and shaping the sealant) can only begin after the sealant has been applied to the joint or surface, as there is no material to tool otherwise.
The substrate must be cleaned and prepared before sealant application and subsequent tooling to ensure proper adhesion and finish quality.
Once the sealant has been tooled to its final shape and profile, the curing/drying period must follow before any further finishing or handling, as tooling disturbs the surface.
While excess material is often removed during tooling, a final cleanup pass after tooling is preferred to remove smears and achieve a clean finish, but it is a soft preference as it can overlap.
Surfaces must be clean and dry for caulk to properly adhere; applying caulk to unprepared surfaces will fail to bond.
Masking tape is often applied along joints before caulking to create clean lines, but it is a preference for finish quality rather than a physical necessity.
After applying caulk, masking tape should be removed before the caulk skins over to avoid tearing the bead, but this is a finish preference.
Freshly applied caulk must be tooled (smoothed) immediately after application to press it into the joint and create a uniform seal before it begins to cure.
After application and tooling, the caulk must be left undisturbed to cure before any painting or water exposure occurs.
The surface must be clean, dry, and free of debris for the sealant to properly adhere.
Masking tape must be applied to adjacent surfaces before sealant application to ensure clean, straight sealant lines and prevent over-spread.
The sealant must be applied before it can be tooled or smoothed into the joint.
Masking tape must be removed after the sealant is applied and before it fully cures to avoid pulling or damaging the sealant bead.

predecessor: Sealant Cartridge Preparation (Cutting Nozzle / Puncturing Seal)
rationale: The cartridge nozzle must be cut and the inner seal punctured before the sealant can be dispensed from the cartridge.
The raw gasket material must be selected and acquired before any cutting or fabrication can begin.
The flange faces must be clean, smooth, and free of debris or damage before the gasket can be placed, otherwise the seal will be compromised.
The gasket must be correctly positioned between the flanges before bolts are tightened to achieve proper compression and sealing.
The two flanges must be aligned properly before inserting the gasket; misalignment can damage the gasket or prevent a proper seal.
The gasketed joint must be assembled and bolted before pressure testing can verify the seal integrity.
Surfaces must be cleaned, degreased, and properly prepared (e.g., abraded or primed) to ensure adequate adhesion. Contaminants or improper surface conditions would compromise bond strength.
The parts or substrates to be bonded must be correctly positioned and secured in fixtures before adhesive is applied to ensure proper joint geometry and alignment.
For multi-component adhesives (e.g., epoxy resins), the components must be mixed in correct proportions and degassed if necessary prior to application to ensure proper curing.

After the adhesive is applied and the joint is assembled, a curing period (with controlled temperature, pressure, and/or humidity) is physically required to allow the adhesive to reach full structural strength.

Once bonding and curing are complete, the bond line must be inspected (e.g., visual inspection, ultrasonic testing) to verify bond integrity, detect voids, and ensure the joint meets specifications before subsequent handling or loading.
The substrate must be inspected for contaminants, moisture, and structural soundness before surface preparation begins, as preparation methods depend on substrate condition.
Safety barriers and containment zones (e.g., dust control) must be established before abrasive or chemical surface preparation to protect workers and surrounding areas.
The prepared surface must be clean, dry, and at the correct profile before any bonding agent or adhesive can be applied; otherwise, bond failure will occur.
Surface preparation quality directly affects bond strength; verification testing can only occur after preparation and before covering or further work.
While curing naturally follows bonding, some curing processes (e.g., moisture curing) might begin during or immediately after surface preparation in staged workflows; typically a soft sequence.
Surfaces must be clean, dry, and free of dust, oil, or debris for adhesive to bond properly.
The substrate or base material (e.g., drywall, concrete, wood) must be in place before adhesive can be applied to it.
Primer may be required on porous surfaces to ensure proper adhesion, but is not always necessary depending on the adhesive type and surface conditions.
The finishing material (e.g., tiles, flooring, veneer) must be placed while the adhesive is still wet or tacky to achieve proper bonding.
After application, the adhesive must be allowed to cure or dry before any loads or stresses are applied to the bonded materials.

Concrete must be poured before its curing process can begin, as curing is the process of maintaining adequate moisture and temperature conditions for freshly placed concrete to develop its desired properties.
Final finishing operations (such as troweling, brooming, etc.) must be completed before curing starts, as curing begins immediately after finishing is complete to prevent moisture loss.
Forms cannot be removed until the concrete has achieved sufficient strength through proper curing, typically requiring a minimum curing period as specified in the structural design.
Surface coatings or sealants can only be applied after the specified curing period is complete and the concrete has reached adequate maturity and dryness.
Structural loads (construction equipment, subsequent building elements) must not be applied to concrete until its curing period is complete and it has achieved the design strength.
Surfaces must be cleaned, dried, and possibly roughened or primed before adhesive can be applied to achieve proper bond strength.
After the adhesive joint is formed, a designated curing or setting period must be allowed for the adhesive to reach its designed strength before any load is applied.
The adhesive joint must be completed before its quality can be inspected for coverage, alignment, and bond integrity.
The structure or component must not be subjected to design loads until the adhesive joint has fully cured and achieved required strength.
Finishing coatings over the adhesive joint area should typically wait until the adhesive is fully cured to avoid interfering with bond strength or causing cosmetic defects.
The surface must be clean, dry, and free of debris for the adhesive or caulk to bond properly. Applying adhesive on unprepared surfaces will lead to adhesion failure.
Multi-component adhesives or caulks must be thoroughly mixed before being loaded into the dispenser gun, otherwise the material will not cure or perform correctly.
After dispensing the adhesive or caulk bead, the materials (e.g., panels, trim, sealant joint) must be immediately positioned and pressed into place before the adhesive skins over or cures.
The dispenser gun and any nozzles must be cleaned promptly after use to prevent the adhesive or caulk from hardening and ruining the tool.
Surfaces must be properly cleaned, filled, sanded, and primed before paint can be applied to ensure adhesion and a smooth finish.
Drywall must be hung, taped, mudded, and sanded smooth before painting can occur, as painting over unfinished drywall would ruin the finish.
Plaster must be fully dried and cured before paint can be applied to avoid cracking, bubbling, or adhesion failure.
Primer must be applied and dried before the final paint coats to ensure proper coverage, adhesion, and uniform color.
While painting before flooring is a common soft preference to avoid getting paint on new floors, it is not a strict physical requirement; some projects paint after flooring with proper protection.
After painting is complete, final cleaning, touch-ups, and inspection must occur to address any drips, splatters, or missed spots before the space is considered finished.
It is conventional to paint walls before installing cabinets to achieve a cleaner finish behind them, though not a strict physical requirement.
If trim is pre-finished, it can be installed after painting; if it requires on-site painting, it should be installed first. This is a sequencing preference rather than a hard constraint.
Surfaces must be cleaned, sanded, and primed before spray painting to ensure proper paint adhesion and a smooth finish.
Areas not to be painted must be masked off with tape and protective coverings before spray painting begins to prevent overspray.
Paint must be properly mixed, thinned, and filtered before being loaded into the spray gun to ensure correct viscosity and atomization.
Spray painting must be completed before the painted surface can be allowed to dry and cure to achieve the final hard coating.
The painted surface can only be inspected for defects, runs, or coverage issues after spray painting is complete and the paint has settled.
The surface must be cleaned of dirt, grease, and loose debris before paint stripping can be effectively applied, ensuring the stripper can penetrate the existing paint layers.
Safe access (scaffolding, ladders, or lifts) must be erected before workers can reach all painted surfaces to perform stripping.
Floor coverings, dust barriers, and containment measures must be installed before paint stripping to protect adjacent areas from chemical drips, dust, and debris.
Damaged or rough substrate revealed after paint removal must be repaired and patched before any new coating is applied.
A primer coat must be applied to the stripped bare surface to ensure proper adhesion of the topcoat; the old paint layer must be fully removed first.
Touch-up paint must be applied over a properly primed surface to ensure proper adhesion and uniform color. Primer seals the substrate and provides a uniform base for the topcoat.
The surface must be clean, dry, and smooth before any paint is applied. Dust, dirt, grease, or rough patches will cause the touch-up paint to peel, bubble, or have an uneven finish.

Touch-up painting is typically performed after the main coat of paint has been applied and dried, to cover minor imperfections, missed spots, or damages that occurred after the main painting was completed.
A final inspection and quality check must occur after touch-up painting is complete to verify color consistency, coverage, and finish quality before the area is considered finished or handed over.

While not a strict physical requirement, it is a soft preference to complete touch-up painting before installing final fixtures and trim to avoid splattering paint on finished hardware and to minimize the need for masking.
Surface must be properly cleaned, abraded, and prepared before paint can be applied and inspected; paint will not adhere properly to unprepared surfaces.
Primer must be applied and cured before the final paint coat is applied and inspected; primer provides adhesion and corrosion protection.
Paint materials must be mixed, thinned, and conditioned to the correct viscosity and color before application and inspection can occur.
The paint top coat must be applied and allowed to cure to the necessary stage before inspection of film thickness, color, gloss, and defects can be performed.

If inspection identifies defects such as runs, sags, holidays, or insufficient coverage, touch-up and repair work should follow; this is a soft preference as inspection may also result in acceptance without need for repairs.
The painting work cannot be accepted or handed over until the quality control inspection has been completed and all defects have been resolved or signed off.
Plastering must be completed before colour scheduling because colour scheduling involves final paint/colour selection and application, which requires a smooth plastered surface.
Ceilings must be fixed and finished before colour scheduling, as ceiling colour/painting is typically coordinated with wall colours and must be done first to avoid drips.
Wall framing must be completed and lined before any colour scheduling can occur, as the colour is applied to finished wall surfaces.
Floor finishing must follow colour scheduling to prevent damage to finished floors from paint drips, spills, and scaffold movement during painting work.
Final cleaning is done after all painting and colour work is complete to remove paint splatters, dust, and debris from the painting process.
The paint brush must be manufactured before it can be used to apply paint.
Bristle material must be selected before the brush can be assembled.
The brush must be fully assembled before it can undergo quality inspection.
The brush must pass inspection before it can be packaged for distribution.
Packaging must be completed before the product can be shipped.
The paint roller cannot be used until the wall surface has been properly prepared (cleaned, sanded, and primed) to ensure paint adhesion and a smooth finish.
After paint is applied with the roller, the paint must be allowed to dry and cure before any subsequent activities can take place on the painted surface.
A second coat is typically applied after the first coat has dried, though this is a preference for quality rather than a physical necessity.
Large surface painting with a roller is usually completed before cutting in or painting trim and details to avoid smudging and ensure clean edges.
Drop cloths and floor protection should remain in place until all painting (including roller work) is complete, though this is a cleanup preference rather than a physical constraint.
The paint tray must be physically manufactured before it can be installed on the construction site.
The paint tray must be installed or placed in position before paint can be poured into it.
Paint must be poured into the tray before a roller can be dipped into the paint for application.
The surface must be clean, dry, and properly masked before paint can be applied; otherwise, contaminants will cause adhesion failure and defects in the coating.
Paint must be properly mixed, strained, and thinned to the correct viscosity before being loaded into the spray gun, or the gun will clog and produce an inconsistent spray pattern.
The applied coating must be allowed to dry and cure after spraying before any subsequent handling, recoating, or finishing steps can occur.
The spray gun and fluid lines must be flushed with solvent immediately after use to prevent paint from hardening inside the equipment, which would ruin the gun.

predecessor: Airless Spray Gun Setup (tip selection, pressure test)
rationale: The correct spray tip must be installed and the system pressure must be tested and set before production spraying begins, otherwise the spray pattern and flow rate will be incorrect.
Resilient channels are typically attached to structural framing (studs or joists) to provide a sound-dampening separation, so the structural framing must be in place first.

Resilient channels serve as a furring support system for drywall; gypsum board is screwed directly into the resilient channels, so the channels must be fastened to the structure before drywall can be applied.

While insulation can be installed before or concurrently with resilient channels, it is common practice to place insulation in the cavity before securing the resilient channels for ease of access; however this ordering is often a soft preference rather than a physical necessity.
Any MEP rough-in work within the wall or ceiling cavity must be completed before resilient channels are installed, as the channels would block access to the cavity.
All surface finishing work (tape, mud, paint, trim) occurs after drywall is hung on the resilient channels, so these finishing activities cannot begin until the channel-supported drywall is in place.
Electrical wiring must be completed in the ceiling plenum before ceiling tiles are installed, as access to the plenum is required for running wires and installing junction boxes.
HVAC ducts, diffusers, and mechanical systems in the ceiling plenum must be installed and tested before ceiling tiles are placed, as they need access above the ceiling grid.
Any plumbing pipes, sprinkler lines, or fire suppression systems running in the ceiling plenum must be installed and pressure-tested before the ceiling tiles are installed.
The suspended ceiling grid (main tees, cross tees, and wall angles) must be fully installed and leveled before acoustic ceiling tiles can be laid into or clipped onto the grid.

Ceiling tiles are typically installed before final floor finishes (e.g., carpet, tile) to avoid damaging finished floors from ladders and scaffolding; however, this is a soft preference for work sequencing rather than a physical necessity.

The structural opening (e.g., rough opening in wall) must be framed, sized, and prepared before the acoustic window assembly can be installed, as the window unit needs a complete and properly dimensioned opening to be placed into.
The primary window frame (or sub-frame) must be set and secured in the opening first, since the acoustic window assembly typically nests into or attaches to this pre-installed frame.
Weather-resistant barriers and flashing around the opening must be applied before installing the acoustic window to ensure a continuous water and air seal behind and around the assembly.

After the acoustic window assembly (including its frame and sealed glazing units) is placed, perimeter sealants, glazing compounds, and acoustic caulking must be applied to finalize the air-tight and sound-proof seal around the assembly.

Interior trim, architraves, or acoustic panel surrounds can only be installed after the acoustic window unit is fully set in place, as these finishes conceal the gap between the window frame and the wall finish.

predecessor: Installation of MEP Services (Mechanical, Electrical, Plumbing)
rationale: MEP services (ductwork, piping, conduits) must be installed first as acoustic insulation is often placed around or between these services, and access to MEP routes is needed before enclosing them with insulation.

predecessor: Completion of Wall and Ceiling Framing
rationale: Wall and ceiling framing (studs, joists) provides the structural cavity into which acoustic insulation is fitted; without the framing there is no support or cavity for the insulation material.

successor: Installation of Interior Wall and Ceiling Linings (Drywall/Plasterboard)
rationale: Acoustic insulation must be placed within the wall/ceiling cavities before they are enclosed by linings; once drywall is installed the insulation becomes inaccessible.

successor: Electrical and Data Cabling Rough-In (if not already completed)
rationale: While cabling is typically roughed-in before insulation, some low-voltage or data cabling may be run after insulation to avoid damaging the insulation; this is a soft preference depending on sequence planning.

predecessor: Structure/Frame Completion and Weatherproofing (Building Envelope Closed)
rationale: The building envelope must be sealed (roof, walls, windows) to prevent moisture ingress before installing acoustic insulation, as insulation must remain dry to maintain its acoustic and thermal performance.
The architectural layout, room volumes, and spatial adjacencies must be established before acoustic design can commence, as these determine the fundamental acoustic requirements and constraints.
Structural framing plans and slab configurations are needed to assess flanking paths, vibration transmission, and structural-borne noise control strategies.
The facade design and glazing specifications must be known to evaluate external noise ingress and determine necessary sound insulation performance for the building envelope.

HVAC duct sizing, air handling unit locations, and mechanical noise control (silencers, attenuators, vibration isolators) depend on the room noise criteria (NC/RC curves) established during acoustic design.

Specifications for acoustic ceiling tiles, wall linings, sound-absorbing panels, partition construction, and floor finishes are derived from the acoustic design and must be implemented during fit-out.
The building structure must be complete to provide the enclosed spaces necessary for acoustic testing; otherwise, sound leakage and uncontrolled ambient noise would invalidate results.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work must be finished because running pipes, ducts, and conduits after acoustic testing could damage installed acoustic treatments or introduce new noise paths.

Acoustic performance depends on final finishes such as drywall, ceiling tiles, flooring, and acoustic panels being installed; testing before finishes are complete would not represent the actual acoustic environment.

predecessor: Installation of Acoustic Treatments (Panels, Insulation, Seals)
rationale: All dedicated acoustic treatments (soundproofing insulation, acoustic panels, door seals, and gaskets) must be in place before testing, as the test measures the effectiveness of these installed treatments.

While acoustic sign-off is typically required before final handover, some minor punch-list items (aesthetic touch-ups, non-critical adjustments) could theoretically proceed in parallel or be deferred; however, full handover usually awaits successful acoustic commissioning.

Occupancy must not begin before acoustic testing is complete because testing requires quiet, unoccupied conditions and the results are needed to certify that noise levels meet regulatory or contractual requirements for safe/comfortable occupation.
The site must be prepared and cleared before flanking path inspection can commence, as inspection requires access to the paths.
The subgrade must be compacted to provide a stable base before the flanking paths can be inspected for proper formation.
Drainage systems must be in place to ensure paths are not waterlogged during inspection, allowing accurate assessment of path integrity.
Inspection must verify that the base and subgrade are acceptable before any paving or surface material is applied.
Edge restraints cannot be installed until the path alignment and base have been inspected and approved.
Fire-resistant boards (e.g. cement board, gypsum board) are mounted onto wall or ceiling framing; the structural frame must be in place to provide a substrate for attachment.

predecessor: MEP Rough-In (Electrical, Plumbing, HVAC rough wiring/piping)
rationale: All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work within the wall cavity must be completed before installing fire-resistant boards, as subsequent access to the cavity would require damaging the board.
Gaps, seams, and penetrations between fire-resistant boards must be sealed with firestop compounds or joint tape/mud after the boards are placed to maintain the fire-resistance rating.

successor: Fire-Resistant Board Final Finish (Painting / Tiling / Cladding)
rationale: The board surface must be fully installed to receive the final decorative or protective finish layer such as paint, tile, or cladding.
Board installation and joint sealing must be complete before the fire-resistance assembly can be inspected for code compliance.
The fire-resistant boards are fixed onto the steel frame or studwork, so the frame must be in place before boards can be installed.
After boards are fixed, the joints between boards must be taped and finished with joint compound to create a seamless fire-resistant surface.
While priming and painting typically follow board installation, some systems may allow for alternative wall finishes; however standard practice is to finish the surface after boarding.
All electrical conduits, cables, and boxes must be run within the stud cavity before it is enclosed by the fire-resistant boards, as access is impossible after boarding.
Thermal/acoustic insulation within wall cavities must be placed before the boards are fixed, as the boards will seal off the cavity.
Steel frame must be in place to provide the structural support and attachment surface for fire-resistant boards.

All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work within walls/ceilings must be completed before boarding, as accessing these services after board installation would require cutting and removing the boards.
Fire-resistant boards must be installed first to provide the substrate for joint treatment, taping, and finishing of seams and fastener heads.
Fire caulking and sealing of all penetrations (pipes, conduits, ducts) through the fire-rated assembly must be done after boards are installed and joints are accessible.

While painting typically follows board installation and finishing, in some cases paint may be applied before board installation in off-site prefabrication, but for on-site work the boards must be installed and finished before final paint coating is applied.
Fire-resistant boards must be installed and fixed in place before jointing (taping, compounding) and finishing can begin, as jointing is applied to the seams between installed boards.
Jointing compound must be fully cured, sanded, and finished to a smooth surface before any priming or painting can be applied to achieve a proper fire-rated finish.

Board jointing and finishing creates continuous sealed surfaces; fire-rated sealants around penetrations (e.g., pipes, cables) are applied after the board joints are finished to ensure continuous fire integrity.
The metal stud framework must be completed to provide the substrate for fire-resistant board installation, which is a prerequisite for jointing and finishing.
All jointing, finishing, and surface preparation must be complete before the final inspection can verify the integrity and continuity of the fire-rated system.
Fire rating testing must be performed on completed wall assemblies to accurately assess their fire resistance performance.
Fire rating testing applies to completed floor and ceiling assemblies to measure fire resistance ratings.
Fireproofing materials (e.g., intumescent coatings, spray-applied fire-resistive materials) must be installed and cured before testing their fire rating performance.
Fire rating testing results must be confirmed and approved before the building can pass final inspection and receive occupancy clearance.
If fire rating testing reveals deficiencies, remedial work may follow; however, this is a contingent soft preference as it depends on test outcomes rather than a mandatory sequence.
Fire stopping seals gaps around penetrations through fire-rated walls and floors. The structural framing must be in place to define these compartments before fire stopping can be applied.
Fire stop materials are installed within and around completed fire-rated walls, floors, and partitions. These assemblies must be built first to provide the substrate for the fire stopping.

Fire stopping seals the annular space around pipes, conduits, ducts, and cables that pass through fire-rated barriers. These penetrations must be installed first so that the fire stop material can be applied around them.
While fire stopping is typically completed before full enclosure to allow access, it is a soft preference; some exterior work can proceed concurrently in non-fire-rated areas.
Fire stopping must be completed and inspected before finishes are applied, as finishes would conceal the fire stopping and prevent verification and future access for maintenance.
The fire-resistant boards must be physically present on site before they can be inspected.
Boards need to be properly stored and handled after delivery to ensure they are in inspectable condition.
Inspection must confirm boards meet quality and specification requirements before they can be installed.
The inspection outcome determines whether boards are approved for use or rejected, which is a direct procedural follow-up.
If inspection identifies the need for further testing (e.g., fire rating verification), testing may follow; this is a soft constraint as not all inspections require additional testing.
A hazardous material assessment must be completed to identify if the existing fire-resistant boards contain asbestos or other hazardous materials before any removal work can begin.
After removing and replacing fire-resistant boards, the new installation must be inspected to verify fire compartmentation integrity and compliance with fire safety standards.

successor: Surface Finishing and Fire-Rated Coating Application
rationale: Fire-rated coatings and surface finishes can only be applied after the new fire-resistant boards are installed and properly fixed in place.
Structural fire protection certification must occur after the replacement of fire-resistant boards to verify that the new installation meets required fire resistance ratings.
Tiles must be firmly installed and set in place before grout can be applied between them; grouting is performed on installed tiles.
The thinset or adhesive holding the tiles must be fully cured to prevent tiles from shifting during grouting.
Grout must be applied before it can cure; sealing and final cleaning occur after grout has set.
Excess grout must be removed and the tile surface cleaned only after grouting is complete to avoid disturbing fresh grout.
The substrate (e.g., concrete slab or backer board) must be properly prepared, clean, and level before tile installation and subsequent grouting.
Anchor bolts must be set and aligned in the foundation before base plates are placed and grouted, as the base plate sits on and aligns with the anchor bolts.
The concrete foundation must be sufficiently cured to support the base plate and grout without cracking or settling.
The base plate must be positioned and leveled over the anchor bolts before grout can be placed underneath.
After grout is placed under the base plate, adequate time must be allowed for the grout to cure and reach design strength before any loads are applied.
Steel columns must be erected on top of base plates only after the grout has set and the base plate is firmly fixed to the foundation.
Anchor bolts need to be embedded in the foundation concrete before grouting can take place. The concrete must be poured and initially set to provide a stable base.
Anchor bolts must be physically positioned and aligned in the foundation formwork or embedment prior to grouting to secure them in place.
After grouting the anchor bolts, the grout must cure to develop sufficient strength before any loads are applied.
Steel columns or equipment cannot be mounted on the anchor bolts until the grout has been placed and cured to ensure proper load transfer and alignment.
Base plates for columns or equipment are aligned and leveled immediately after grouting while the grout is still adjustable, or after curing to finalize the bearing surface.
CMU blocks must be fully laid and mortar cured before grout can be poured into the cores; otherwise the grout would leak out or the wall would not have structural integrity.
Vertical reinforcing bars must be placed and positioned inside the CMU cores before grout is poured; grouting encapsulates the rebar and cannot be added after the cores are filled.
After grouting, sufficient curing time and inspection (e.g., core sampling or NDE) must occur before any load-bearing or subsequent work proceeds to verify grout integrity.
Grouting must fill the vertical cores before bond beams or top closure elements are placed to ensure continuous load path and lateral reinforcement encapsulation.

While rough-ins can often be embedded in grouted cores, it is preferable to complete grouting first to avoid blocking core voids; however, conduits can be placed prior to grouting if planned, so this is a soft sequencing preference for quality and access.
Drilling must be completed to create the borehole or cavity that will receive the grout material during injection.
The borehole must be cleaned of debris, cuttings, and drilling fluids to ensure proper grout adhesion and penetration.
The grout material must be mixed to the correct consistency and formulation before it can be injected under pressure.
After injection, the grout must be allowed sufficient time to set and cure to achieve design strength and sealing properties.
Post-grouting pressure testing (e.g., packer tests or water tightness tests) can only be performed after grout has been injected and cured to verify effectiveness.
Grout is used to bond tendons to the concrete; tendons must be in place before grout can be mixed and injected.
Cement is a primary ingredient of grout; the silo must be erected and filled before mixing can begin.
Water is required for the grout mix; the water supply must be ready before mixing operations start.
The grout must be mixed to the proper consistency before it can be injected into the tendon ducts.
Samples for quality control (flow cone test, bleed test) must be taken from the freshly mixed grout before or during injection.
Grout must be mixed to the correct consistency before it can be placed and begin curing.
Grout must be placed or injected into the intended void or space before the curing process can commence.
Formwork or containment must be in place to hold the grout during placement and the initial curing period.
Grout must achieve sufficient strength during curing before formwork can be safely removed without damaging the grout.
Curing must be complete to allow the grout to reach its design strength and durability before any inspection or strength testing is performed.
Tiles must be installed and set in place before grout can be applied to fill the joints between them.
After the grout float is used to press grout into the joints, the excess grout must be cleaned and the joints finished with a sponge.
Grout must be mixed to a proper consistency before it can be applied using the grout float tool.
After grout is applied with the float, it must be left to cure and dry before any further finishing or sealing.
The thin-set mortar beneath the tiles must be fully cured before grouting to prevent tile movement and ensure proper grout adhesion.
A stable foundation must be prepared before installing the grout pump to ensure proper alignment and structural support.
The grout pump must be installed and operational before it can be used to mix and deliver grout materials to the application point.
Formwork and reinforcement must be in place before grouting so that the grout pump can inject grout into the prepared cavities.
The grout pump must be set up, connected to hoses, and calibrated for the correct pressure and flow rate before actual grouting operations can commence.
Grout materials must be mixed and prepared to the correct consistency before being loaded into the grout pump for delivery.
Mortar or grout material must be prepared and mixed before it can be loaded into a grout bag or pointing bag for application.
The bricks, blocks, or stones must first be laid in place to create the joints that will later be filled or pointed using the grout bag.
After grout is applied via the bag, the joints must be tooled and finished while the material is still workable to achieve the desired profile and seal.
Once pointing is complete, excess grout or mortar smeared on the masonry faces must be cleaned off before it hardens.
After pointing is applied, the grout must be allowed to cure and dry properly to gain strength and durability before any further loads or finishes are applied.
Grout spacers are placed between rebar layers to maintain consistent spacing for grout flow; rebar must be installed first to provide the framework around which spacers are positioned.
Formwork creates the enclosed cavity into which grout will be poured; spacers must be placed within the formwork before grouting to ensure proper alignment and cover.
Grout spacers maintain uniform gaps for grout distribution; grout can only be poured or injected after spacers are properly positioned to ensure even flow and complete filling.
In post-tensioned construction, grout spacers ensure ducts are properly aligned before tensioning; post-tensioning must follow spacer placement to avoid displacing spacers.
Grout is applied into the gaps between tiles/paver stones; tiles must be in place first to create the joints that will be filled with grout.
Freshly applied grout must be allowed to cure/harden before any further work can proceed on the surface.
After grout is applied and partially set, excess grout and haze must be cleaned from tile surfaces to achieve the final finish.
Grout joints must be fully cured before applying sealant to ensure proper adhesion and protection against moisture.
A stable, clean, and properly prepared substrate is necessary before any tile or grout work to prevent cracking or failure of the grout joints.
Rough-in inspection of ductwork must be completed and approved before installing grout ducts, as grout ducts are typically embedded in concrete or masonry and cannot be accessed after grouting.
Primary HVAC ductwork must be roughed in before grout ducts are installed, as grout ducts often interface with or are supported by the main duct system.
Grout ducts must be in place before concrete or grout is poured, as they create pathways within the grout/concrete for post-tensioning cables or future duct runs.
Grout ducts serve as conduits for post-tensioning tendons; they must be installed before tendon insertion and tensioning can occur.
Structural framing or concrete formwork must be in place to provide support and alignment for grout duct installation before ducts are placed.

The grout vent/vent port is typically installed on or after the casing is in place, as the vent port allows for grout to be injected and air/water to escape from the annular space between the casing and the ground.

The grout vent/vent port must be installed and functional before grout injection begins, as the vent port serves as the exit point for displaced air, water, and excess grout during the grouting process.
After grouting is complete, the vent port area is used to verify grout take and confirm that the grout curtain is properly formed, so vent port installation must precede testing.
The borehole must be drilled to the required depth and diameter before any vent port or grouting components can be installed within or at the borehole.
After grouting operations are completed and verified, the vent port may be sealed or abandoned as part of final closure, but this may be a soft preference depending on site requirements.
The concrete substrate must be cleaned, dried, and free of debris before applying bituminous waterproofing membrane to ensure proper adhesion and prevent delamination.
A primer must be applied to the prepared substrate to promote bonding of the bituminous membrane; without primer, adhesion failure can occur.
Cracks, holes, and surface defects must be patched and smoothed prior to membrane installation to prevent punctures and ensure a continuous waterproof layer.

successor: Protection Board or Geotextile Layer Installation
rationale: A protective layer (e.g., protection board, geotextile, or rigid insulation) must be installed over the bituminous membrane to shield it from mechanical damage during backfilling or subsequent construction activities.
Backfilling against foundation walls can only commence after the waterproofing membrane and its protective layer are in place to avoid damaging the membrane with soil and rocks.

The DPC must be laid on a stable, prepared foundation base. Excavation and foundation preparation (including leveling and blinding concrete) must be completed first to provide a solid, even surface for the DPC membrane.

predecessor: Concrete Foundation / Strip Foundation / Raft Foundation
rationale: The concrete foundation must be fully cured and in place before the DPC is applied, as the DPC is installed on top of the foundation to prevent moisture rising from the ground into the wall structure above.

successor: Brickwork / Blockwork Wall Construction (First Course Above DPC)
rationale: The DPC must be installed before any masonry wall construction above it, as it acts as a moisture barrier. The first course of bricks/blocks is laid directly on or above the DPC layer.

While the floor slab can technically be placed after the DPC in the walls, it is often a soft preference to complete the DPC first to ensure continuity of the damp-proofing system at the junction between walls and floor.
It is preferable to complete the DPC before applying internal render or plaster near the base of walls, so that the moisture barrier is fully in place and the finishes are protected from rising damp.

The concrete substrate must be fully cured, clean, dry, and free of laitance or debris before hot-applied bitumen can be applied; otherwise, the waterproofing membrane will not properly bond to the surface and may delaminate.
A primer must be applied and allowed to dry/cure prior to hot-applied bitumen to ensure proper adhesion of the bitumen membrane to the substrate.

A protection board or insulation layer must be installed immediately after the hot-applied bitumen membrane has been applied and inspected to protect the waterproofing from physical damage during subsequent construction activities.
Backfilling against waterproofed walls can only proceed after the hot-applied bitumen waterproofing is fully installed, inspected, and (if required) protected, to avoid damaging the membrane.

successor: Pouring of Concrete Topping Slab or Wearing Surface
rationale: Concrete topping slabs or wearing surfaces over hot-applied bitumen waterproofing must be placed after the membrane is fully installed and protected, as pouring concrete directly onto uncured or exposed waterproofing can damage the membrane and compromise watertightness.

The substrate (typically plywood or OSB decking) must be clean, dry, smooth, and free of debris before torch-on membrane can be applied. Any moisture, dirt, or unevenness will compromise adhesion and the integrity of the membrane.
A compatible primer must be applied and fully cured on the prepared substrate before torching the membrane. The primer ensures proper bonding of the modified bitumen membrane to the substrate.
Metal edging at the perimeter is typically installed prior to the membrane so that the membrane can be torched over and adhered to the metal, creating a watertight seal at the edges.
After the membrane is fully applied and cooled, walkway pads, ballast, or protective layers are typically placed over high-traffic areas to protect the membrane from punctures and UV degradation.

After the torch-on membrane is fully installed and seams are welded, a flood test or electronic leak detection should be performed to verify watertightness before any subsequent roofing layers or final close-in.
The surface must be clean, dry, and properly prepared (e.g., swept, cleared of debris, and any existing cracks filled) before cold bitumen can be applied to ensure proper adhesion.
A primer (e.g., bitumen emulsion or tack coat) must be applied to the prepared surface to promote bonding before the cold bitumen layer is placed.

successor: Top Coat or Wearing Course Application
rationale: Any final wearing course, seal coat, or top layer (e.g., asphalt overlay or surface dressing) can only be placed after the cold bitumen has been applied and cured.
Traffic (vehicular or pedestrian) should not be allowed on the cold bitumen surface until it has sufficiently cured to avoid deformation and damage.
Bituminous tanking requires a clean, smooth, and cured concrete surface to adhere properly and form a continuous waterproof membrane.
The concrete substrate must be fully dry before bituminous coating is applied, as moisture trapped beneath the membrane can cause blistering and failure of the waterproofing system.
A primer is typically required on the prepared concrete surface to ensure proper adhesion of the bituminous tanking membrane.
A protection board or drainage layer must be installed over the cured bituminous tanking to shield the waterproof membrane from damage during backfilling and subsequent construction activities.
A drainage layer is often placed over the waterproofed surface to direct water away; while not physically mandatory, it is best practice to protect the tanking system.
The surface must be clean, dry, and free of dust, dirt, or loose particles before bitumen primer can be applied to ensure proper adhesion.
Any cracks, holes, or uneven areas in the substrate must be repaired and leveled prior to priming to achieve a uniform primer coat and prevent future failure.
The substrate moisture level must be verified to be within acceptable limits before primer application to avoid blistering or poor bonding.
Bitumen primer must be applied and allowed to cure/tack-dry first to provide a bonding layer for the subsequent bitumen membrane or waterproofing sheets.
Priming creates the adhesive base necessary for torch-on or self-adhesive membrane installation; the membrane cannot bond directly to an unprimed substrate.
The roof deck or substrate must be clean, dry, smooth, and structurally sound before any waterproofing membrane can be applied, otherwise the membrane will not bond properly and may fail.
Any thermal insulation or slope-forming layers beneath the waterproofing must be installed first, as the waterproofing layer is typically placed on top of these to protect the building interior.

predecessor: Parapet Wall Construction (up to required height)
rationale: Parapet walls must be built before the waterproofing layer so that the membrane can be lapped up the walls to form a continuous watertight seal at the perimeter.

The waterproofing membrane must be in place before gutters and downpipes are installed, as the drainage components are fixed onto or over the finished waterproofed roof edge and must integrate with the membrane for water runoff.
A protective layer (e.g., concrete screed, paving slabs, or gravel ballast) must be placed after the waterproofing membrane to shield it from UV radiation, foot traffic, and mechanical damage.
The subgrade must be properly graded, compacted, and stable to provide a uniform foundation for the asphalt layers; otherwise, the asphalt will crack or settle unevenly.
A base course (e.g., crushed stone or gravel) must be placed and compacted over the subgrade to distribute traffic loads and provide drainage before asphalt can be laid.
The binder course (intermediate asphalt layer) must be laid and compacted prior to the final surface course to provide structural strength and a smooth base for the wearing course.

Road markings (lane lines, crosswalks) and signage must be applied after the final asphalt surface is laid and cured, as markings adhere to the finished surface and would be damaged or obscured by asphalt placement.
The road cannot be opened to vehicular or pedestrian traffic until the asphalt surface course is completed, compacted, and sufficiently cooled/cured to withstand loads without deformation.
A stable, level foundation is required to support the weight of the bitumen boiler/melter and prevent tipping or structural damage during operation.
Proper drainage around the boiler area is required to prevent water accumulation that could cause safety hazards or damage to the equipment.
Fuel/gas supply lines and electrical connections must be roughed in before the boiler can be connected and commissioned.
The boiler must be installed, connected, and tested before it can be used to heat and melt bitumen for application.
