A functional boiler/melter is the upstream source that supplies heated liquid bitumen to downstream applicators (e.g., for roofing, waterproofing, pavement work).
Polystyrene foam sheets must be installed on a clean, debris-free surface to ensure proper adhesion and prevent uneven surfaces or bonding failure.
The concrete substrate must be fully cured before installing polystyrene foam sheets to avoid moisture entrapment, adhesion failure, and dimensional instability of the foam.
A vapor barrier (e.g., polyethylene sheeting) is typically laid down before rigid foam insulation to prevent ground moisture from migrating into the foam and building assembly.

successor: Taping / Sealing of Foam Board Joints
rationale: After foam boards are placed, all joints and seams must be taped or sealed to create a continuous air and vapor barrier, which cannot be done before the sheets are in position.
Polystyrene foam sheets serve as a thermal insulation layer beneath floor finishes or a topping slab; subsequent layers cannot be placed until the foam is fully installed.
Reinforcement steel (rebar) must be placed and tied in the slab area before polystyrene void formers can be positioned, as the void formers sit within or above the reinforcement cage.
Polystyrene void formers must be fully installed and secured in position before concrete is poured, as they create the voids in the concrete slab and must be encapsulated by the pour.
After placing polystyrene void formers, the top layer of reinforcement mesh or steel is laid over them to maintain structural integrity before concrete pouring.
Formwork edges and boundaries for the concrete slab must be set up before void formers can be accurately placed within the defined pour area.
Polystyrene void formers must be in place before concrete is poured; once poured, the concrete must cure, and the void formers remain embedded, so curing follows the pour.
Polystyrene ceiling tiles require a supporting ceiling grid (typically T-bar grid) to be installed first, as the tiles are laid into or clipped onto the grid structure.

All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing work above the ceiling (ductwork, conduit, piping) must be completed before ceiling tiles are installed, as access to the plenum space is blocked once tiles are in place.
Any fireproofing or insulation work in the ceiling plenum must be finished before tiles are installed, as polystyrene tiles are combustible and access for fireproofing application would be hindered.
While not a hard physical constraint, it is preferred to install ceiling tiles before final flooring to avoid dust, debris, and potential damage to finished floors from ceiling work.

Typically ceiling tiles are installed before final wall painting or finishing to allow for any touch-ups needed where walls meet the ceiling, though this is a soft preference rather than a physical necessity.

predecessor: Wall Surface Preparation (e.g., plastering, drywall finishing)
rationale: Coving and moulding need a smooth, clean, and fully dried wall/ceiling surface for proper adhesion. Any plastering or drywall finishing must be completed and set/cured before installation to ensure the adhesive bonds correctly and the moulding sits flush against the surface.
Ceiling boards must be fixed in place before coving can be applied to the ceiling/wall junction, as the coving bridges the wall-to-ceiling corner and requires a stable ceiling substrate.

Although coving is often installed before final painting (to blend caulking and paint seamlessly), it is a soft preference because the coving can also be painted separately off-site or after wall painting if carefully masked; however, best practice is to install first, then paint both walls and coving together for a uniform finish.

successor: Flooring Installation (if coving meets floor skirting)
rationale: If the moulding includes skirting/coving near the floor, flooring should follow to avoid damaging installed moulding during floor fitting; this is a soft preference because flooring can be completed before moulding with careful gap management.

predecessor: Electrical and Plumbing First Fix (cables, pipes in walls/ceilings)
rationale: All first-fix services (electrical cables, plumbing pipes) that will be concealed in walls or ceiling voids must be run before coving is installed, as the moulding would obstruct access and would need to be removed if services are added later.
The polystyrene insulation boards must be applied onto a stable, completed structural wall surface. The structure provides the substrate for fixing the insulation.

The wall surface must be clean, dry, and reasonably flat before insulation boards can be adhered or mechanically fixed. Debris, dust, or unevenness would compromise adhesion and overall installation quality.
A base coat adhesive (cementitious or polymer-based) must be applied to the wall or to the back of the insulation boards to bond the polystyrene to the substrate.
After positioning the insulation boards, additional mechanical fixings (e.g., plastic dowels with screw pins) are driven through the boards into the wall to secure them, especially at heights.

successor: Application of Base Reinforcement Layer (Mesh + Render)
rationale: Once insulation is fixed, an alkali-resistant mesh embedded in a base render coat must be applied over the polystyrene to provide impact resistance and a substrate for the finish.

While frames can be installed before or after insulation depending on detailing, best practice often has insulation installed first to minimize thermal bridging, though it is not a strict physical necessity.
The final textured or colored render coat (e.g., silicone, acrylic, or mineral render) is applied over the reinforced base layer; it cannot be applied before the insulation is installed.
A stable, level concrete slab or foundation must be in place to support the polystyrene formwork system and provide a base for assembly.
Steel reinforcement bars must be positioned within the formwork area before the polystyrene blocks are assembled, as the blocks are placed around the rebar cage.
Once the polystyrene blocks are assembled into walls, concrete is poured into the hollow cores; concrete cannot be placed before the formwork is complete.
Temporary bracing is often installed after assembly to ensure alignment and stability before concrete pour, though some bracing may be integrated during assembly.
MEP rough-ins are typically done within the polystyrene formwork before concrete pour, but they can occur concurrently with or slightly after the assembly is complete.

Polystyrene surface rendering requires a clean, stable, and properly prepared substrate (e.g., masonry, concrete, or existing render) to ensure proper adhesion. Without substrate preparation, the render will not bond correctly.
Safe access at height is required before applying render to elevated surfaces. Scaffolding must be in place for workers to perform the rendering work safely.
After the polystyrene render layer is applied and has set, a primer or base coat is typically needed to prepare the surface for the final finish coat.
The final decorative or protective finish coat (e.g., acrylic, silicone, or mineral render) can only be applied after the base render coat has cured sufficiently.
Scaffolding must remain in place until all rendering work, including finish coats, is completed. Dismantling too early would prevent access for finishing and inspection.
Polystyrene blocks must be fully prepared (foamed, molded, and cured) before they can be cut or shaped, as the material needs to be stable and dimensionally sound for accurate cutting.
Inspection must confirm the polystyrene blocks meet density and quality standards before cutting and shaping, to avoid wasting work on defective material.
If cutting or shaping is done using custom molds or templates, those molds must be designed and fabricated before shaping can commence.
Surface treatments (e.g., sealants, fire retardant coatings) can only be applied after the polystyrene has been cut and shaped to its final geometry.
Individual shaped polystyrene pieces must be cut and shaped before they can be assembled or bonded together into larger components.
Polystyrene waste must first be generated from demolition and site clearance activities before it can be collected, sorted, and processed for disposal or recycling.
Polystyrene waste must be segregated and sorted from other waste streams before it can be directed to the specific disposal or recycling process.
Removal of polystyrene waste from the site through disposal or recycling must be completed before the site can be remediated and backfilled to a clean state.
All waste materials including polystyrene must be removed and processed before final grading and landscaping can commence to ensure a clean building site.
Recycled polystyrene may be processed into new construction materials such as SIPs; while not a hard requirement, using recycled content for SIPs is a preferred sustainable sequencing approach.
Aluminium Composite Panels require a stable structural substrate (e.g., steel studs, curtain wall framing, or existing wall surface) to be fully installed and secured before panels can be mounted.
A weather-resistant barrier and air seal must be applied to the substrate before installing ACP panels to prevent moisture ingress and ensure building envelope integrity.
Panels must be pre-cut, routed, and fabricated to precise dimensions off-site or on-site before they can be installed onto the substrate.
After panels are fixed in place, all joints, edges, and penetrations must be sealed with appropriate sealants and gaskets to ensure watertightness and weatherproofing.
Protective film removal, surface cleaning, and final quality inspection are performed after all panels are installed to verify alignment, finish, and defect-free surfaces.
The substrate must be clean, dry, and free of debris for the adhesive to bond properly with polystyrene insulation boards.
Any cracks, unevenness, or structural defects in the wall must be repaired before applying adhesive to ensure a flat, stable base for fixing polystyrene boards.
Priming the substrate is recommended to improve adhesion and prevent suction, though in some systems it may be optional depending on substrate type.

After fixing the polystyrene boards with adhesive, sufficient curing time is required for the adhesive to achieve full bond strength before any subsequent loads (such as mechanical fixings or render application) are applied.
Mechanical fixings are typically installed after the adhesive has cured, though in some systems they may follow immediately; it is a common sequence to allow adhesive to set first.
The base coat and reinforcing mesh are applied over the fixed polystyrene boards to create a rigid impact-resistant surface; this cannot be done until the boards are securely fixed in place.
The final decorative and protective render coat is applied over the reinforced base coat, which itself depends on the polystyrene boards being fixed first.
Window frames require structural openings to be formed and cured before installation can begin.
The rough opening must be measured, framed, and prepared with appropriate sills and flashings to receive the window frame.
Weather-resistant barriers and sill flashings must be in place before window frame installation to prevent water ingress behind the frame.
Glass panels or glazing units can only be installed after the aluminium frame is securely fixed and level within the opening.
Perimeter seals, weatherstripping, and sealants are applied after the frame is installed to ensure airtightness and watertightness.
The rough opening must be framed and sheathed to provide the structural support and defined aperture into which the aluminium door frame is fitted and secured.
The subfloor and waterproof membrane at the door threshold must be completed before installing the aluminium door frame to ensure a watertight seal and proper drainage at the base of the frame.
The door frame must be set, leveled, and anchored in place before the door leaf can be hung on hinges and locks/handles installed, as the frame provides the mounting points for these components.

Once the aluminium door frame is installed, gaps between the frame and the rough opening must be sealed with backer rod, sealant, and/or foam to achieve the building envelope's air and water tightness.

successor: Interior Wall Finishing (Plasterboard / Cladding around Frame)
rationale: Interior wall finishes are applied up to the installed door frame to create a clean junction; the frame must be in place to define the edge of the finished wall surface.
The aluminium roof panels require a stable structural frame (steel or truss) to be erected first, as the panels are fixed directly onto the roof framing.
Insulation is typically laid over the roof structure before cladding to provide thermal performance and a flat substrate for the aluminium panels.
Flashings, ridge caps, and edge trims are installed after the main roof panels to seal joints and provide weatherproofing at panel ends.
Gutters and downpipes must be installed after the roof panels in place to correctly align with the roof edge and collect runoff.
The internal ceiling lining is installed after the roof is closed in to protect it from weather and to allow access for roof fixings from above.
The structural frame (steel or concrete) must be fully erected and stable before aluminium cladding panels can be attached, as the panels are mounted onto the frame or its supporting sub-structure.
Wall brackets, rails, or sub-frames must be installed on the structural frame to provide a mounting surface and alignment for the aluminium cladding panels.

A weather-resistive barrier (e.g., building wrap or membrane) is required behind the cladding to protect the building envelope from moisture ingress. This must be installed before the cladding panels are fixed.

successor: Window and Door Installation (in cladded areas)
rationale: In typical curtain wall or rainscreen systems, the aluminium cladding panels are installed first, forming the outer skin, and windows/doors are then fitted into the prepared openings within or adjacent to the cladding system.
Once the aluminium panels are fixed in place, all joints, seams, and penetrations must be sealed with appropriate sealants and gaskets to ensure weather-tightness and aesthetic finish.

Aluminium structural sections are typically non-load-bearing or secondary structural elements that are installed after the primary steel frame is erected, as the steel frame provides the main structural support and attachment points.
Aluminium structural sections often serve as frames or support elements for cladding, curtain walls, or glazing systems, so they must be installed first to provide the supporting framework.
A stable foundation or ground slab is required to support any structural elements, including aluminium sections, and to provide a level working platform.

predecessor: Aluminium Structural Section Fabrication/Cutting to Size
successor: Aluminium Structural Section Surface Treatment (Anodising/Powder Coating)
rationale: Aluminium sections must be cut and fabricated to their final dimensions before surface treatments are applied, as cutting after treatment would damage the coating.

predecessor: Aluminium Structural Section Surface Treatment (Anodising/Powder Coating)
rationale: Surface treatment must be completed before installation to ensure corrosion protection and aesthetic finish are in place, and to avoid damaging the treatment during handling and installation.
The structural frame (e.g., concrete slab, steel beams, or staircase stringers) must be in place to provide a stable substrate and anchor points for the aluminium handrail brackets and posts.

predecessor: Rough-in for MEP Services (Electrical/Plumbing in adjacent walls)
rationale: Rough electrical, plumbing, or mechanical work near handrail locations must be completed before handrail installation to avoid interference, rework, or access issues.

predecessor: Wall & Ceiling Finishes (plaster/drywall/painting) in handrail area
rationale: Wall and ceiling finishes should be completed before handrail installation to prevent damage to finished surfaces during handrail attachment and to allow clean alignment with finished wall surfaces.
The handrail must be fully installed to allow for final safety inspections, load testing, and punch-list verification of the completed railing system.

successor: Flooring & Stair Tread Finishes (if handrail installed after flooring)
rationale: While ideally flooring/treads are completed before handrail to set accurate height, handrail can be installed first and flooring fitted around posts; this is a soft preference sequence depending on project phasing.
The structural frame (floor slabs, beams) must be in place to provide a stable mounting surface for balustrade posts and handrails.
Waterproofing must be completed on balconies, terraces, or roof edges to prevent water ingress behind the balustrade fixings and flashings.
Glass panels are typically fitted into the aluminium frame channels or clamped to the balustrade structure after the frame is fixed in position.
The top handrail is often the final component, bolted or screwed onto the installed balustrade posts and glass/cladding infill.
While touch-up painting can be done after balustrade installation, final finishes are preferably applied after to avoid damaging the powder-coated aluminium surface during other works.
Aluminium louvres are typically mounted onto the structural frame of the building; the frame must be in place to provide support and attachment points for the louvre system.
Aluminium louvres are often installed before the glazing system, particularly when louvres form part of the façade or window wall system, to allow for proper integration and sealing.
Louvre installation should be completed before final cladding finishes to ensure proper alignment, weatherproofing integration, and to avoid damage to finished surfaces.
Waterproofing must be in place before louvre installation to prevent water ingress at the interface between the louvre frame and the building envelope.
MEP rough-in adjustments (e.g., ductwork alignment with louvre openings) can be done after louvres are installed to fine-tune connections, though ideally they are coordinated beforehand.
The aluminium soffit panels are typically fixed to the underside of the structural steel frame or roof structure, so the supporting steelwork must be in place before soffit panels can be installed.
Soffit panels are installed beneath roof overhangs and eaves; the roof decking must be completed first to define the eave geometry and provide the upper fixing substrate.

Fascia gutters are mounted to the fascia board along the roof edge, and soffit panels are fitted underneath them; the gutter/fascia assembly must be in place to establish the alignment and trim interface for the soffit.

Soffit panels close off the eave area from below, and external wall cladding is typically installed after the soffit is complete so that the cladding can be neatly terminated or trimmed against the underside of the soffit panel.

While electrical rough-in can be done before soffit closure, it is often more practical to run wiring and mount light fixtures after the soffit panel is in place to ensure accurate placement and secure attachment to the panel substrate.
Aluminium gutters are typically mounted onto the fascia boards which are attached to the roof structure. The roof structure must be in place to provide a surface for gutter attachment.
Aluminium gutters are directly fixed to fascia boards. Fascia boards must be installed before gutters can be mounted.
Downpipes connect to the gutter outlets to channel water downward. Gutters must be in place to determine the position and connection points for downpipes.
Gutters collect rainwater and direct it to downpipes which feed into rainwater harvesting systems. Gutter installation must precede connection to collection systems.
While soffits can technically be installed before or after gutters, installing gutters first allows soffits to be fitted neatly against the gutter profile for a cleaner finish.
The aluminium downpipe collects rainwater from the roof gutters, so the roof structure must be in place to define the roof edge and gutter positions before downpipes can be installed.
Downpipes connect directly to gutters to channel water downward; gutters must be installed first to provide the connection point for downpipes.
The bottom outlet or shoe of the downpipe that diverts water away from the foundation can only be fitted once the downpipe itself is in place.
The downpipe must be installed to route water into the stormwater drainage system; the final connection to drainage pipes occurs after the downpipe is fixed.

While downpipes are often installed after wall cladding for aesthetics and secure bracketing, it is a soft preference rather than a physical necessity, as downpipes can be fixed to the structure before cladding in some sequences.
Aluminium flashing must be installed over a solid substrate (e.g., plywood sheathing or existing wall surface) to provide proper attachment and weatherproofing.
Head flashing and sill flashing above windows/doors must be integrated with or installed after the window/door frames are in place to ensure proper drainage and sealing.
For roof flashing applications (e.g., valleys, chimneys), the underlayment must be installed first so that flashing can be integrated into the waterproofing layers.
Flashing must be installed before siding or cladding so that it can be properly lapped over the flashing, directing water away from the building envelope.

successor: Exterior Insulation and Finish Systems (EIFS) or Stucco Application
rationale: Flashing must be in place prior to finish plaster or EIFS to ensure termination bars, weeps, and water diversion details are correctly integrated.
The structural frame (steel or concrete) must be in place to provide the load-bearing substrate onto which aluminium decking panels are fixed or supported.
A waterproof membrane or underlayment must be laid on the deck substrate before aluminium decking to prevent moisture ingress and protect the structure below.
After aluminium decking is installed, surface treatments such as anti-slip coatings, sealants, or protective finishes are applied to enhance durability and appearance.
Handrails and balustrades are typically fixed onto or adjacent to the finished deck surface; installing them after decking ensures proper alignment, secure anchoring, and safety compliance.
Once the decking is fully installed, a final inspection and any required load testing must be performed to verify structural integrity and compliance before the area is put into service.
The aluminium profile must first be extruded into its basic shape before any thermal break can be inserted or applied.
Aluminium billets must be sourced and available before the extrusion process can commence, which precedes thermal breaking.
The thermally broken profile must be fully formed and cured before it can be cut or machined to specific dimensions.
Surface treatment must be applied after the thermal break is complete to avoid damaging or contaminating the thermal break material during coating processes.
The final assembly of windows or doors requires the thermally broken profiles to be ready as the primary framing components.
Structural steel framework must be in place to provide the supporting structure onto which aluminium cladding, curtain walling, and other aluminium elements are attached.
Concrete slabs and floor decks must be completed and cured to provide stable working platforms and anchor points for aluminium facade and structural framing installation.
Aluminium window frames and curtain wall systems must be fabricated and installed before glass panels can be fitted into them.
Aluminium cladding panels and aluminium composite material (ACM) installation must be completed before the final external cladding and weatherproofing can be finished.

While not a strict physical requirement, it is preferable to complete aluminium ceiling grids and bulkhead framing before MEP services are roughed in within those zones to avoid rework and ensure proper integration.
Aluminium sections must be cut to size, deburred, and cleaned of oxides/oils before welding to ensure proper joint fit-up and weld quality.
The components to be welded must be positioned, clamped, and aligned correctly before welding can commence; otherwise, distortion or misalignment will result.
For thicker aluminium sections, preheating may be needed to reduce thermal shock and prevent cracking; this is a soft preference as thin sections may not require preheating.
After welding, slag, spatter, and oxidation residues must be removed from the weld zone before any inspection or further treatment can occur.
Welds must be visually inspected and non-destructively tested (e.g., dye penetrant, radiography) after welding to verify integrity before accepting the joint.
The structural frame must be completed to provide a stable substrate and support for aluminium structural elements and framing systems.

predecessor: Concrete Slab / Deck Pouring and Curing
rationale: Concrete slabs must be fully cured to serve as a level base for aluminium curtain walls, window frames, and cladding supports.
Waterproofing must be in place to protect the building envelope before installing aluminium cladding and window assemblies.
Aluminium window and curtain wall frames must be installed first to receive glass panels and glazing units.
All aluminium assemblies must be fixed in position before weatherproof sealants and gaskets are applied to ensure continuous envelope integrity.
Aluminium materials must be delivered and stored on site before any surface treatment can commence, as treatment requires the physical aluminium components to be present.

Aluminium profiles or sheets must be cut to required dimensions before surface treatment, as treatment is typically applied to final-sized components to avoid damaging treated surfaces during cutting.
Quality inspection of the treated aluminium surface must occur after treatment to verify coating/ treatment quality, adhesion, and finish acceptability.
Assembling and installing aluminium components should only occur after surface treatment is complete, to prevent damage to the treated finish and ensure corrosion protection is fully applied.
Aluminium surfaces must be cleaned, degreased, and pre-treated (e.g., etching or conversion coating) before the main surface treatment to ensure proper adhesion and uniform finish.
Aluminium waste must be collected before it can be processed in the recycling facility.
Aluminium must be sorted and separated from other materials to ensure proper recycling input and avoid contamination.
Aluminium scrap must be cleaned of impurities and shredded into manageable pieces before being fed into the recycling furnace or remelting process.
After recycling/remelting, the output aluminium must be inspected for quality and composition before it can be used in new products.

successor: Casting or extrusion of recycled aluminium
rationale: The recycled molten aluminium must be cast into ingots, billets, or extruded into shapes before further manufacturing processes can take place.

The aluminium surface must be cleaned and free of contaminants (dirt, grease, oxides) before applying corrosion protection coatings to ensure proper adhesion and effectiveness of the protective layer.
Aluminium components must be installed and fixed in their final position before corrosion protection is applied, as the protection coating is typically applied to the installed elements.

successor: Final Inspection / Quality Control of Aluminium Works
rationale: After corrosion protection is applied, a quality control inspection must be carried out to verify the coating integrity, thickness, and coverage before the aluminium components are considered complete.
Sealants and gaskets should be installed after corrosion protection to avoid damaging or interfering with the protective coating and to ensure proper sealing over the protected surface.

Adjacent finishing works can be done after corrosion protection is complete, but in some cases they may be done concurrently with care. It is a soft preference to avoid contaminating or damaging the freshly applied corrosion protection layer.
The concrete slab or surface must be properly cleaned, dried, and free of debris before applying bituminous membrane to ensure proper adhesion and waterproofing performance.
A primer must be applied to the prepared surface to improve bonding between the substrate and the bituminous membrane, as the membrane will not adhere properly without it.
A protection layer or insulation boards are placed over the completed bituminous membrane to protect it from physical damage, UV exposure, and to provide thermal insulation.
Leak testing and inspection of the waterproofing system can only be performed after the bituminous membrane has been fully applied and cured to verify its integrity and effectiveness.

Backfilling against foundation walls can only commence after the bituminous membrane waterproofing is fully applied, cured, and protected, to avoid damaging the membrane during backfilling operations.
The concrete substrate must be properly prepared (cleaned, repaired, and roughened) to ensure adhesion of the cementitious waterproofing coating.
A scratch coat or mortar bed may need to be applied and cured to provide a suitable base for cementitious waterproofing on certain surfaces.
Cementitious waterproofing must be fully cured before tile or stone can be applied over it to prevent damage to the waterproof membrane.
Any plaster or render finish applied over waterproofed areas must wait until the cementitious coating has cured sufficiently.
Backfilling against waterproofed walls should only proceed after the cementitious waterproofing has fully cured to avoid dislodging or damaging the membrane.
The concrete surface must be cleaned, dry, and free of contaminants for epoxy to properly bond.
Cracks must be widened and routed out to create a proper entry path for the epoxy injection.
Holes must be drilled along the crack at specific spacings to install injection ports before epoxy can be introduced.

predecessor: Installation of Injection Ports and Surface Seal
rationale: Injection ports must be installed and the crack surface sealed with an epoxy cap compound to contain the injected epoxy.
After injection, the epoxy must be allowed to cure (harden) to its full structural strength before any subsequent loads are applied.
The subgrade must be properly graded, compacted, and prepared to provide a stable and level base for the drainage layer, ensuring proper water flow and structural support.
Any underground utilities that run beneath the drainage layer must be installed and inspected before the drainage layer is placed, to avoid disturbing the completed drainage system.

Typically a filter fabric is placed over the drainage layer to prevent fines migration while allowing water to pass; however, in some designs the fabric goes below the drainage layer, so this ordering may vary.
The drainage layer serves as a foundation for the base course or subbase, which is placed directly on top to support the final pavement or structural slab.

successor: Waterproofing Membrane Application (if above drainage layer)
rationale: If a waterproofing membrane is required above the drainage layer (e.g., on a green roof or below-grade wall), it must be applied after the drainage layer is installed to ensure drainage function is not compromised.
The basement walls must be excavated and exposed before waterproofing can be applied to the exterior surface.
Waterproofing is applied to the completed foundation walls; the walls must be fully constructed, cured, and ready to receive the waterproofing membrane or coating.
Footing drains and perimeter drainage systems are typically installed at the base of the foundation before the waterproofing membrane is applied up the wall surface.
Backfilling around the foundation can only occur after the waterproofing membrane or coating has been fully applied and cured, to avoid damaging the waterproofing layer.
Rigid exterior insulation boards are installed over the waterproofing membrane, so waterproofing must be completed first to provide the protective and moisture barrier layer.
The concrete podium deck must be installed and fully cured before waterproofing can be applied, as waterproofing requires a stable, clean, and dry substrate that has reached sufficient strength.
The deck surface must be cleaned of debris, dirt, and laitance, and any cracks or defects must be repaired prior to waterproofing to ensure proper adhesion and a continuous waterproof membrane.
After applying the waterproofing membrane, it must be allowed to cure and should be tested (e.g., flood testing) for leaks before any subsequent trades or coverings are placed over it.
The waterproofing membrane must be fully installed, cured, and verified watertight before the drainage board, insulation, or protection board can be placed over it.

The waterproofing system (including membrane, protection layer, and drainage) must be complete before the final paving stones, tiles, or other deck finishes are installed to avoid damaging the waterproofing and to ensure proper drainage above the membrane.

All plumbing pipes, drains, and rough-in work within wet areas (showers, bathrooms) must be installed before waterproofing is applied; otherwise, waterproofing would be punctured or interrupted for later plumbing installation.

The concrete slab or structural substrate must be properly cured, cleaned, and leveled to receive waterproofing membrane; applying waterproofing over unprepared or uncured concrete leads to adhesion failure.
Floor wastes and drain flanges must be set at their correct heights and sealed into the slab before the waterproofing membrane is applied around them to ensure a watertight seal.

successor: Tile / Floor Finishing in Wet Areas
rationale: Tiling, floor screeding, and all finished floor coverings in wet areas can only be laid once the waterproofing membrane has cured and been tested, as the waterproofing layer provides the necessary water barrier beneath the finish.

A mandatory inspection and flood-testing of the waterproofing membrane must occur before any covering is applied, to verify there are no leaks; this logically follows immediately after the waterproofing is cured.
The concrete substrate must be fully cured, clean, and dry before any waterproof membrane can be applied and tested. Applying membrane to uncured or damp concrete will cause adhesion failure.
The substrate must be primed or mechanically prepared to ensure proper bonding of the waterproof membrane. Testing before surface prep would be meaningless.
The waterproof membrane must first be fully installed (applied, cured/dried) before any testing such as flood testing, electronic leak detection, or adhesion testing can be performed.
Waterproof membrane integrity must be verified before covering it with screed or tiles; otherwise, leaks would be impossible to repair without costly demolition.
The test results must be documented and formally approved before proceeding to subsequent construction stages. This is a quality assurance hold point.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and graded before shoring can be installed, as shoring systems require a stable, accessible work surface and cleared area to be placed effectively.
Soil conditions and groundwater levels must be known to design and select the appropriate shoring system (e.g., sheet piles, soldier piles, lagging, secant piles).

Existing underground utilities in the shoring area must be located, marked, and relocated or protected before driving or installing shoring elements to avoid damage, safety hazards, and service disruptions.
The shoring system must be fully installed and verified before excavation begins, as shoring provides earth retention and prevents collapse of the excavation walls during digging.
Foundation work (such as footing or mat placement) typically occurs after the excavation is complete and shoring is in place to ensure a safe, open, and stable working area below grade.
Falsework requires a stable, load-bearing base. Foundation work must be completed to provide the ground support and footing for falsework legs and supports.
The physical materials (timber, steel props, formwork panels, scaffolding) must be procured and delivered on-site before falsework can be assembled.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and the falsework layout marked out to ensure correct positioning and stability before assembly begins.
Formwork panels are placed and supported on top of the falsework structure. The falsework frame must be fully erected and stable before formwork can be installed.

Steel reinforcement bars for the concrete element are typically placed after the formwork is installed on the falsework. However, the falsework must be in place first to support both the formwork and the reinforcement.
Layout lines and markings must be established on the slab or beam surface to indicate exact positions where formwork panels will be placed, ensuring accuracy and alignment.

Vertical shores or falsework towers must be erected to provide load-bearing support before formwork panels are positioned, as the panels cannot be safely placed without a supporting structure underneath.
Reinforcement bars are placed after formwork is in position because the formwork defines the shape and containment boundaries within which rebar must be placed.
Concrete can only be poured once all formwork panels are securely placed, aligned, and braced, as the formwork acts as the mold that contains and shapes the wet concrete.
After initial placement, formwork panels must be adjusted, aligned, and leveled to meet design specifications before being locked in place for concreting.
Formwork must be installed in its rough position before it can be aligned and levelled to precise tolerances.
Formwork must be correctly aligned and levelled before placing reinforcement steel, so that reinforcement is positioned within the correct concrete cover and geometry.
Concrete cannot be poured until formwork is properly aligned, levelled, braced, and stable to ensure the final structure meets dimensional tolerances.
Excavation and shoring must be completed to expose the soil face and provide a stable working surface for installing tie rods and anchors.
Soil nail walls or initial ground support systems are typically required before tie rod and anchor installation to stabilize the excavation and provide a reference surface.
Accurate survey and layout of anchor locations must be completed to ensure tie rods and anchors are installed at correct positions, angles, and elevations.
Tensioning and load testing can only begin after tie rods and anchors are fully installed and grout has cured to required strength.
Final shotcrete or facing concrete is placed after tie rods and anchors are installed to embed and tie back the structural face system.
Concrete must be poured and allowed to reach sufficient strength before formwork can be safely removed without damaging the structural element.

Concrete requires a minimum curing period to achieve the specified initial strength (striking strength) before formwork can be stripped, as per structural design requirements and safety considerations.
After formwork is removed, exposed concrete surfaces often need patching, grinding, or finishing to address surface imperfections, tie-hole filling, and form-joint treatment.
Waterproofing membranes or coatings for retaining walls and below-grade structures can only be applied after the formwork has been stripped and the concrete surface is fully exposed and accessible.
Formwork must be stripped and reshored (if required) before subsequent floor cycles can proceed, as the formwork system needs to be released and reinstalled at the next level.

Formwork cannot be cleaned and oiled before it has been used for concrete pouring. The formwork must first have concrete poured and cured so that it can be stripped, revealing the surfaces that need cleaning and oiling.
Formwork must be physically removed/stripped from the cured concrete element before it can be cleaned, repaired and re-oiled for reuse in subsequent pours.

Cleaned and oiled formwork is the prerequisite for re-assembling and erecting the formwork panels for the next concrete pour. Oil acts as a release agent to prevent concrete from bonding to the form surface.

While steel fixing can technically begin before oiling is complete in some areas, it is preferable to complete cleaning and oiling first to avoid contamination of the release agent by steel fixing debris and to provide a clean working surface.
Formwork must be fully installed and erected before it can be inspected and signed off. Inspection cannot occur without the physical formwork in place.
The reinforcement steel must be placed and tied within the formwork before inspection, as the inspector needs to verify rebar coverage, spacing, and cover prior to concrete pour.

Concrete can only be poured after the formwork has been inspected and signed off, ensuring the formwork is stable, properly aligned, and the reinforcement is correctly placed. This is a critical quality and safety hold point.
The ground must be excavated and prepared to the required level and bearing capacity before slip forming can commence, as the slip form structure relies on a stable foundation.
A concrete footing or foundation slab is required to support the slip form rig and the structure being poured; slip forming initiates on top of completed foundations.
Vertical and horizontal reinforcing steel must be placed and tied before concrete is poured, as the reinforcement is embedded within the slip-formed concrete wall.
After the slip form passes, the freshly placed concrete must undergo initial curing and gain sufficient strength before any subsequent loads are applied or formwork is stripped.
Post-tensioning of vertical tendons can only be performed after the slip-formed concrete has reached the required compressive strength, which occurs after the slip forming is complete.
Jump forming is a system used for vertical concrete construction that requires a stable foundation or base slab to be cast first before the jump form system can be erected and anchored.
Reinforcement steel must be placed and tied before jump forms are positioned, as the forms encase the rebar and the concrete is poured around it.
Jump forms serve as the mold for the concrete; therefore the concrete pour for that lift must occur immediately after the forms are set and aligned.
After concrete is poured and gains sufficient strength, the jump form system can be stripped from the hardened wall and lifted/jumped to the next level.
Once the jump forms are stripped and moved up, the exposed rebar from the previous pour is spliced/extended for the next lift before the forms are reset.
The tunnel must be excavated to create the void space before forming the tunnel structure; you cannot form a tunnel in solid ground without first removing the earth.
Immediate ground support (e.g., rock bolts, shotcrete) must be installed after excavation to stabilize the tunnel opening before any permanent tunnel forming or lining can be safely placed.
After the tunnel formwork is placed and concrete is poured, the concrete must cure to gain sufficient strength before any subsequent activities can proceed.
The tunnel lining formed by concrete must be complete and cured before waterproofing membranes or systems can be applied to the interior surface.
MEP systems installation within the tunnel requires the tunnel structure to be formed and stable before mounting conduits, pipes, cables, and fixtures.
Excavation must be completed before formwork can be installed to provide a stable, prepared surface and proper working space.
Foundation must be poured and cured to provide a solid base for formwork panels to be erected upon.
Steel reinforcement must be placed before formwork panels are closed, as the rebar cage needs to be accessible for tying and inspection.
Formwork panels must be fully assembled, aligned, and secured to contain and shape the wet concrete during pouring.
Formwork panels must be in place to contain concrete; stripping can only occur after concrete has cured sufficiently.
Waler (Strongback) components are mounted onto or supported by shoring frames/towers; the shoring system must be erected first to provide the structural support for the waler.
Vertical shore jacks are typically placed beneath the waler to provide vertical support; they must be installed before the waler is placed onto them.
Horizontal shore jacks are often installed between the waler and the wall/slab to provide lateral bracing; the waler must be in place before these jacks can be connected.
Waler (Strongback) acts as a horizontal support beam that backs formwork panels; formwork panels are placed against or attached to the waler after it is installed.
The waler must be fully installed and braced to support the formwork system before concrete can be poured against the formed surface.
The adjustable steel prop must be placed on a stable, level foundation slab that has been properly prepared and cured to support the load transferred through the prop.
The adjustable steel prop is used to support formwork; therefore the formwork panels or beams must be in position before the prop can be placed underneath to provide temporary support.
The acrow prop provides temporary support for the formwork during concrete pouring and until the concrete gains sufficient strength; pouring cannot commence without the propping system in place.

Any load from fresh concrete, construction materials, or equipment on the supported element can only be applied after the prop is installed and adjusted to the correct height to transfer loads to the ground.

The acrow prop must remain in place until the supported concrete element has cured and reached sufficient structural strength to be self-supporting; premature removal could cause collapse or structural failure.
Workers need safe access to the building perimeter at height to install tie rods through column formwork; scaffolding must be in place first.
Tie rods connect to or brace against steel columns; columns must be erected to provide anchorage points.
Tie rods are often embedded or anchored in cast-in-place columns; concrete must be cured to sufficient strength to resist pullout forces.
The tie rod and wing nut assembly must first be installed and connected before any tensioning or post-tensioning operations can be performed on the rod.
Tie rods often serve as support or anchorage for façade panels; cladding installation must wait until the tie rod system is secured in place.
Concrete must be poured and allowed to gain sufficient strength before formwork can be safely removed; stripping too early can cause slab collapse or structural damage.
Concrete needs adequate curing time to reach the required compressive strength (typically 70-100% of design strength) before formwork is stripped to prevent cracking or failure.
Slab formwork is typically stripped first to allow access for stripping supporting beam formwork below; beams support the slab, so slab forms must be cleared first.
The slab surface must be exposed and accessible after formwork removal for waterproofing membrane application.
After formwork is stripped, the underside of the slab becomes visible and can be inspected for defects, honeycombing, or curing quality.
Concrete must be poured and gain sufficient initial set strength before formwork can be safely removed without causing deformation or collapse.
Concrete needs adequate curing time to reach the required compressive strength to be self-supporting when formwork is stripped.
Formwork must first be installed, aligned, and secured before it can later be stripped after concrete placement.

successor: Inspection of Column Surface and Repair
rationale: After formwork is removed, the exposed concrete surface must be inspected for defects (honeycombing, bug holes) and repaired before any subsequent finishing work.
Column formwork must be stripped to free up the column area and provide access for installing shoring and formwork for the slab and beams above.
Concrete must be poured and gain sufficient strength before formwork can be safely removed; otherwise the beam would not be self-supporting.
Concrete must be cured to achieve the required strength (typically 70% of design strength) before formwork stripping to prevent structural damage or collapse.
Reinforcement steel must be placed and tied in position before concrete can be poured into the formwork.
The formwork mould must be erected first to provide the container and shape into which reinforcement is placed.

successor: Curing and Finishing of Beam Surface
rationale: Once formwork is removed, the exposed concrete surface becomes accessible for final curing treatment, patching, and finishing works.
Concrete must achieve sufficient strength (cure) before formwork can be safely removed to prevent structural damage or collapse.
Concrete must be placed and allowed to harden before the formwork that shapes it can be stripped.
Formwork must be removed to expose the concrete surface before waterproofing membranes or coatings can be applied.
Formwork removal is necessary to allow access for backfilling material against the foundation walls.

While stripping should precede inspection for quality control, inspections can sometimes be performed partially before full stripping; however, best practice is to strip first for complete visual and physical access.
Concrete must reach sufficient strength through curing before formwork can be safely removed to prevent structural damage or collapse.
Formwork must be removed to expose the concrete surface for visual and physical inspection of quality and finish.
Formwork removal is required to access the staircase surfaces for application of plaster, render, or other finishes.
Concrete must be poured and set within the formwork before the formwork can be stripped; stripping is the demolding step after pouring.
Handrails are typically installed after the staircase structure is exposed and finished; formwork must be removed to provide a clear working area.
Concrete must reach sufficient strength before props and shoring can be safely removed; premature removal can cause structural failure.
Backfilling around a structure provides lateral support and may be preferred before removing shoring, but it is not always a physical necessity depending on design.
Removing props and shoring clears access for surface finishing, but finishing can sometimes proceed in other areas while shoring remains in place.
Props and shoring obstruct wall and ceiling spaces; they must be removed to allow full MEP rough-in work in those areas.
Load testing of a concrete structure must be performed after shoring is removed so that the structure bears loads independently without temporary support.
Concrete must reach sufficient strength (curing) before falsework (formwork supports) can be safely removed; premature dismantling can cause structural collapse.
Concrete must be poured and in place before the falsework supporting it can be dismantled.
Falsework must first be erected to support formwork and wet concrete; dismantling is the reverse operation and cannot occur before erection.

Surface finishing (e.g., patching, grinding) is often easier after falsework is removed to access the concrete surface, but could theoretically be done partially before; this is a soft preference for work sequencing.
Backfilling around foundations or abutments typically cannot begin until falsework is removed, as the falsework occupies the space needed for backfill material.
Formwork must be fully erected and in place before it can be inspected prior to striking/de-stripping.
Concrete must be poured and allowed to reach sufficient initial set before the formwork can be inspected for striking readiness.
A minimum curing period is required for the concrete to gain adequate strength before formwork can be struck; inspection must occur after sufficient curing time has elapsed.
The inspection must be completed and passed before formwork can be safely removed/struck; striking prematurely could cause concrete damage or collapse.

Following inspection, strength testing (e.g., cube tests) may be performed to verify concrete has reached required strength before full striking; this is a soft preference if the inspector can visually confirm adequacy.
Concrete must be poured and in place before its strength can be tested; testing cannot occur without the concrete being present.
The concrete must undergo initial curing and reach a sufficient set state before strike-off testing can be performed to measure its strength.
Strike-off strength testing determines whether concrete has reached adequate strength to allow safe removal of formwork; forms must not be removed before the required strength is verified.

Further construction loads (e.g., placing upper floors or heavy equipment) must only be applied once the concrete's in-situ strength has been confirmed through strike-off testing to prevent structural failure.

While some surface work can be done earlier, applying final coatings or finishes is typically deferred until strength testing confirms the concrete is sound enough to support the finish without damage.
Formwork panels cannot be cleaned until after concrete has been poured and cured because the formwork is still in place, holding the wet concrete. Cleaning occurs after formwork stripping.
The panels must first be removed/stripped from the cured concrete structure before they can be accessed and cleaned.
Cleaning must be completed before panels can be inspected and repaired to ensure a clear surface for assessment.
Cleaned panels must be stored only after cleaning is done to prevent dirt/debris from being introduced into storage areas.
Panels must be cleaned before they can be reassembled and reused for the next concrete pour cycle.

The formwork must be fully manufactured and assembled into its final shape before oil or release agent can be applied to its surfaces; otherwise the oiling would be damaged or disrupted during assembly.

The formwork surface must be clean and free of debris, old concrete residue, or dirt so that the release agent can adhere evenly and effectively; oiling a dirty surface would result in poor concrete finish and potential bonding issues.

Release agent must be applied to the formwork surface before concrete is poured so that the concrete does not bond permanently to the formwork; this enables easy stripping of the formwork after the concrete cures.

Release agent should be applied before reinforcement steel is placed inside the formwork to avoid contaminating the reinforcement bars with oil, which could reduce bond strength between steel and concrete.

While oiling is typically completed before the final inspection of formwork, this is a procedural preference rather than a physical necessity; inspection can sometimes be done concurrently or in a different order depending on site practices.
Formwork can only be stripped and stored after the concrete has achieved sufficient strength during curing; otherwise, the structure could be damaged.
Formwork must be removed from the cured concrete before it can be transported to a storage area and stacked.
Formwork should be cleaned and inspected for damage before being stored to ensure it is ready for future reuse.
Formwork must be properly stored and organized before it can be retrieved and reassembled for the next pour cycle.
It is preferable to have formwork stored in an organized manner before final site cleanup to keep the area tidy, but this is a soft preference rather than a physical necessity.
Formwork must first be stripped and dismantled from the cured concrete before it can be inspected, cleaned, and repaired for reuse.
Formwork should be inspected and cleaned to identify damages and defects before any repair work can be carried out.
After repair and refurbishment, the formwork must be properly stored and stacked to protect it from damage and keep it organized for future use.
Repaired and refurbished formwork panels must be ready before they can be re-assembled and re-erected for the next concrete pour cycle.
The formwork must be repaired, refurbished, re-assembled, and in place before concrete can be poured in the next construction cycle.
Concrete must be poured and allowed to set before the formwork can be stripped and the surface inspected.
The formwork must be removed (stripped) to expose the concrete surface so that post-strip inspection can be performed.
Inspection must identify surface defects (e.g., honeycombing, bug holes, fins) before any remedial patching or repair work can be undertaken.

Ideally curing begins immediately after stripping, but inspection may need to happen first to ensure the surface is acceptable before applying curing compounds or covers; this is a soft preference as some curing methods can be applied concurrently.
The inspection results must be recorded and approved before the concrete element can be formally accepted and documented in quality records.
Concrete must first be placed/poured so that it can cure and be inspected for defects; patching repairs defects in already-placed concrete.
Concrete must reach sufficient strength through curing before patching work can be performed without damaging the substrate.
Inspection is needed to identify the locations and extent of defects (e.g., honeycombing, spalls, voids) that require patching.
Patched areas must be finished and leveled before final surface preparation (e.g., grinding, coating application) can proceed over the entire concrete surface.
Waterproofing membranes require a sound, smooth, and defect-free concrete substrate; patching ensures all holes and cracks are sealed before membrane installation.
Concrete must be fully cured and hardened before tie holes can be sealed, as sealing uncured concrete would trap moisture and compromise integrity.
The formwork must be removed to expose the tie holes so they can be accessed and sealed.
Tie holes must be sealed first to provide a continuous surface before waterproofing membranes or coatings are applied, preventing water ingress through unsealed holes.
Tie holes must be sealed and patched before final surface finishing or plastering to achieve a smooth, uniform finish.
While not physically required, inspection is best performed after sealing is complete to verify all holes are properly sealed before waterproofing is applied.
Concrete must be poured and initially set before stripping forms can occur, and curing continuation happens after stripping.
Stripping (removal of formwork) must be completed before curing continuation can proceed, as the exposed concrete surface needs to be accessible for continued curing.
The continued curing process after stripping must be completed before final curing is considered finished and the concrete reaches its design strength.
Curing continuation must be finished before any surface treatments or waterproofing are applied, as these coatings require a properly cured substrate.
Backfilling against concrete structures should only occur after sufficient curing has taken place post-stripping to avoid damaging the immature concrete.
Hazardous materials (e.g., asbestos, lead, chemicals) must be removed first to ensure worker safety during general debris and waste removal.
The primary demolition or dismantling work must be completed to generate the debris and waste that will then be removed from the site.
The site must be cleared of all debris and waste before grading and earthwork can begin to avoid burying debris or interfering with soil preparation.
Debris and waste must be cleared from the site prior to excavation for foundations to prevent obstructions and ensure clean excavation work.
The site must be fully cleared of demolition debris and waste before any new construction activities can commence.
Soldier piles and walings are typically installed in excavated trenches or along excavation walls; excavation must create the space before soldier pile and waling installation can begin.
Walings are horizontal beams that connect soldier piles; soldier piles must be installed first so that walings can be attached to them.
Lagging (horizontal timber or concrete panels) is placed between soldier piles after the waling and soldier system is in place to retain soil.
Cross-lot bracing or raker braces are typically installed after the waling/soldier system is in place to provide lateral support to the excavation walls.
The waling and soldier system supports excavation walls, allowing deeper excavation to proceed safely below the current level.

Formwork props (acrow props) are used to support formwork for concrete slabs and beams. The concrete slab/beam must be cast first so that the props can be placed underneath to provide temporary support during curing and after stripping.
Acrow props are installed as temporary supports for formwork. The formwork cannot be removed until the props are in place to safely support the concrete structure during curing.
Acrow props support the wet concrete and formwork during the curing period. Curing must occur after props are installed to ensure the concrete gains strength without excessive deflection or collapse.
Acrow props must remain in place until the concrete has achieved sufficient strength. Props can only be removed after the concrete has cured enough to be self-supporting.

Once acrow props are removed, the area becomes free for subsequent finishing works such as plastering, painting, or ceiling installation. This is a soft preference/logical sequence as some finishing could theoretically be done around props, but it's standard practice to remove props first.
Plastic cones / tie cones are typically placed onto exposed reinforcement bars (rebar) after concrete has been poured and is setting, to protect workers and materials from sharp rebar ends.
Plastic cones or tie cones are fitted onto the ends of reinforcing steel bars after the rebar cage/mat has been installed and tied, as the cone caps are placed directly on the protruding rebar ends.
While not a strict physical dependency, tie cones are often used as spacers or formwork tie components, so they should be in place before formwork is stripped to maintain cover and alignment.
Once cones are installed on protruding rebar, the area becomes safer for workers, so subsequent safety inspections of the reinforcement zone would logically follow installation.
Tie cones used as formwork ties must be installed before the next concrete lift is poured, as they provide the connection between formwork panels and maintain correct spacing.
Formwork cannot be struck (removed) until the concrete has been poured and has gained sufficient strength to support itself and any imposed loads.
Concrete must undergo adequate curing to achieve the required compressive strength before formwork can be safely removed. Striking too early can cause structural failure or surface damage.
The decision to strike formwork is governed by achieving a minimum concrete strength (often specified as a percentage of design strength). Test results confirm this condition is met.
After formwork is struck, the exposed concrete surfaces must be inspected for defects (e.g., honeycombing, surface voids) and the formwork panels cleaned and stacked for reuse or disposal.
Waterproofing membranes or coatings are typically applied to concrete surfaces only after the formwork has been removed, providing access to the structural element.
Formwork provides the mold and support structure into which reinforcement steel is placed; without the formwork in place, there is no defined area or support for the rebar.
The surface where the reinforcement will be placed must be clean and free of debris, mud, or laitance to ensure proper bonding between concrete and steel.
Accurate layout marks and survey points are needed to position reinforcement steel correctly according to the structural drawings.
Concrete cannot be poured until all reinforcement steel is properly placed, tied, and inspected because the steel must be encased in concrete for structural integrity.
After steel placement, an inspection (spacing, cover, tying, bar size) must occur before concrete pouring; this is a quality assurance step that is physically tied to the placement being complete.
Concrete must be mixed/batched before it can be transported to the construction site; fresh concrete cannot be transported before it is prepared.
Fresh concrete must be tested for workability (slump) before being dispatched to ensure it meets specification requirements.
Concrete must be transported to the pour location before it can be placed/poured into formwork.
Concrete must arrive at the site via transportation before it can be pumped to the point of placement.

Formwork should ideally be installed and ready before concrete is transported to the site to avoid delays and concrete setting before placement, though it is a soft preference as concrete can be held temporarily in trucks.
Concrete must be poured and achieve sufficient strength before formwork can be safely removed; otherwise the concrete may not be self-supporting and could collapse or be damaged.

Concrete must undergo adequate curing to reach the required compressive strength (e.g., typically 70% of design strength) before formwork can be stripped, preventing structural failure or surface defects.
Formwork must first be erected and installed to shape and support the wet concrete; striking/removal can only occur after the concrete has set and the formwork's function is complete.
Once formwork is removed, the exposed concrete surfaces can be inspected, patched, and finished (e.g., rubbing, grinding, or applying coatings) as required for quality and appearance.

Formwork removal is a prerequisite before full design loads can be applied to the structural element, though some partial loading may be permitted earlier; this is a soft preference as phasing may allow staged loading.
Concrete must be poured and allowed to set before any surface finishing (such as troweling, smoothing, or applying coatings) can begin, as surface finishing requires a stable, semi-hard substrate.
Structural framing (walls, floors, ceilings) must be completed to provide the surfaces that will receive finishing work such as plastering, drywall finishing, or painting.
All conduits, pipes, and wiring within walls/ceilings must be installed before enclosing them with surface finishes like drywall, plaster, or paneling.
Surface finishing (e.g., plastering, drywall jointing, sanding) must be complete and dry before paint or protective coatings can be applied to achieve a smooth, durable finish.
Surface finishing of walls and ceilings should be completed before floor and tile work to prevent dust and debris from damaging finished floors and to allow clean installation.
The ground must be excavated, leveled, and compacted to provide a stable base for the concrete pump and the subsequent concrete placement.
Formwork molds must be in place before concrete can be pumped into them to create the desired structural shapes (e.g., slabs, columns, walls).
Steel reinforcement must be positioned and tied inside the formwork before concrete is pumped, as the concrete encases the rebar for structural strength.
After concrete is pumped and placed, it must be left to cure (harden and gain strength) before any loads can be applied or subsequent work proceeds.
Formwork cannot be removed until the pumped concrete has set and achieved sufficient strength to support its own weight and any applied loads.
Concrete must first be placed/poured before a concrete vibrator can be inserted to consolidate the mix and remove air voids.
Vibration/consolidation must be completed before final surface finishing (screeding, floating, troweling) begins, as vibration brings finer materials to the surface and settling must occur first.
Formwork (molds) must be assembled and secured before concrete is poured and vibrated, as the vibrator consolidates concrete within the formed cavity.
Steel reinforcement must be positioned and tied before concrete is poured and vibrated, so that the vibrator can consolidate concrete around the rebar.
Concrete must be properly consolidated and allowed to gain sufficient strength before formwork can be removed; vibration is part of the placement and consolidation phase.
Concrete must be poured and in place before any post-pour inspection can be performed, as the inspection evaluates the poured concrete.
Initial finishing operations (screeding, floating, troweling) must be completed before the post-pour inspection can assess the final surface condition and quality.
Concrete must have reached initial set (sufficient hardness) before inspection can be safely conducted without damaging the fresh concrete surface.
Post-pour inspection must confirm that the concrete has achieved adequate strength before formwork and shoring can be safely stripped.
Inspection identifies any defects (honeycombing, spalling, surface imperfections) that must be repaired; remediation typically follows inspection findings, though scheduling flexibility exists.
Formwork must be in place to define the shape and boundaries of the concrete surface at the construction joint location.
Reinforcement bars must be installed and tied before forming the joint to ensure structural continuity across the joint.
The first concrete lift/pour must be completed so that the construction joint can be formed at the interface between the existing and new concrete.
After the joint is formed, the exposed surface typically needs cleaning, roughening, or application of bonding agents before the next concrete pour.
Waterstops are installed at construction joints to prevent water ingress; this can only be done once the joint location and profile are established.

predecessor: Material Cooling (e.g., chilled water, ice, liquid nitrogen)
rationale: Concrete ingredients must be cooled before batching and mixing to reduce the initial concrete temperature, preventing rapid setting and loss of workability in hot weather.

predecessor: Moist Curing Setup (e.g., wet burlap, fogging, curing compound)
rationale: Curing materials and equipment must be prepared in advance so that curing can commence immediately after concrete placement to prevent moisture loss and cracking due to high temperatures.
Erecting temporary shades or windbreaks before placement reduces concrete temperature and evaporation rate, but is a preference rather than a physical necessity.
Curing must start immediately after finishing to keep the concrete surface moist and cool, preventing plastic shrinkage cracking and ensuring proper hydration.
An evaporation retarder must be applied right after placement and finishing to reduce water loss from the surface until curing can be fully established.
Excavation must be completed to expose the foundation/substructure where waterstops are placed, providing access and proper subgrade conditions.
The concrete foundation or slab must be prepared (cleaned, leveled) and initial pour complete to embed or position waterstops at construction joints.
Formwork for the first concrete pour must be in place to define the joint location where waterstops will be installed.
Waterstops must be embedded in the first pour and properly positioned before the subsequent concrete placement to ensure they function as a continuous waterproof barrier at the joint.

Backfilling against waterproofed structures can only commence after waterstops are installed and the adjacent concrete has cured to prevent damage to the waterstop system and maintain integrity of the waterproofing.
Curing compound must be applied to freshly placed concrete after finishing, so concrete must be placed first.
Concrete surface must be finished (screeded, floated, troweled) before curing compound can be sprayed or applied to seal moisture.
Curing compound should be allowed to cure and form a membrane before other trades work on top to avoid damaging the curing layer.
Joint cutting must be performed after curing compound application to ensure proper curing before creating control joints.
Moisture or hardness testing should be done after curing compound is applied and cured to obtain accurate results.
Steam curing is applied to freshly poured concrete to accelerate strength gain; concrete must be poured and in place before steam curing can begin.
Formwork must be set up and secured to contain the concrete during pouring and curing; steam curing cannot start until forms are in place.
The concrete mix must be prepared, transported, and placed before steam curing can be applied to the fresh concrete.
Steam curing accelerates the early strength development of concrete; formwork should only be stripped after the concrete has achieved adequate strength through the curing process.
Steam curing must be completed to ensure concrete has reached sufficient hardness and surface dryness before any finishing or coating work can be applied to the concrete surface.

Concrete must be poured before curing can begin, as curing is the process of maintaining moisture and temperature conditions in freshly placed concrete to ensure proper hydration and strength development.
Concrete finishing operations (screeding, floating, troweling) must be completed before curing can start, as curing begins after final finishing is complete to prevent surface damage.
Formwork must be installed and secured before concrete placement and subsequent curing monitoring, as forms contain the concrete during initial setting and curing.
Curing duration monitoring must be completed to verify that concrete has achieved sufficient strength before formwork can be safely removed without damaging the structure.
Curing must be completed and verified before applying surface treatments, coatings, or sealants, as these would trap moisture or interfere with the curing process if applied too early.
Temperature monitoring during curing can only begin after concrete has been placed, as curing is the process of maintaining moisture and temperature conditions in freshly placed concrete.

Temperature monitoring typically begins after the concrete has reached initial set, as before that point the concrete is still in its plastic state and monitoring during finishing operations would be premature.

Temperature monitoring data informs decisions about when concrete has gained sufficient strength for formwork removal; removing forms too early before proper curing temperatures are verified can cause structural damage.

Curing temperature data is essential for interpreting concrete strength test results, as temperature history affects the rate of strength gain; testing before monitoring is complete would not represent properly cured concrete.

It is preferable to complete the curing period and temperature monitoring before applying surface treatments, but in some cases waterproofing can begin once minimum curing duration is achieved even if monitoring is still underway.

Cold-weather curing can only begin after concrete has been poured and placed, as curing is the process of maintaining moisture and temperature conditions after placement to ensure proper hydration and strength development.

Concrete finishing operations (screeding, floating, troweling) must be completed before curing begins, as curing protects the finished surface and finishing cannot be performed once curing measures are applied.

Weather conditions must be forecasted and preparations (e.g., insulating blankets, heating enclosures, additives) must be in place before cold-weather curing procedures are initiated to protect concrete from freezing.

Formwork removal should only occur after the cold-weather curing period is complete and the concrete has achieved sufficient strength, as premature stripping can damage concrete that has not adequately cured in cold conditions.

In cold weather, concrete strength development is slowed; strength testing must be performed after the curing period is complete to verify that the concrete has reached the required strength before proceeding with subsequent construction activities.
Hot-weather curing is performed on freshly placed concrete to prevent rapid moisture loss; concrete must first be placed and finished before curing begins.
Finishing operations (screeding, floating, troweling) must be completed before curing starts, as curing involves applying water, coverings, or compounds to the finished concrete surface.
Curing must be completed to ensure concrete has achieved sufficient strength before formwork is removed; premature stripping can lead to surface damage or structural failure.
Curing covers (wet burlap, plastic sheeting, curing compounds) must remain in place for the specified curing period before removal to ensure proper hydration and strength development.

While it is generally preferred to complete hot-weather curing before starting subsequent work (e.g., waterproofing, coatings, or loading), this can sometimes be partially overlapped depending on specifications and is a best practice rather than an absolute physical requirement.

The concrete substrate must be tested for moisture vapor emission rate (MVER) and prepared (cleaned, dried) before epoxy can be applied, otherwise the epoxy will not bond properly and may blister or delaminate.

predecessor: Concrete Slab Placement and Curing (Initial Concrete Cure)
rationale: Fresh concrete must be poured and reach sufficient maturity (typically 28-day cure) before epoxy coating can be applied, as epoxy cannot bond to uncured or green concrete.
The epoxy must be fully cured before any additional topcoats, sealers, or floor finishes are applied to avoid damaging the coating or causing adhesion issues.
Epoxy requires a minimum curing period (typically 12-24 hours) before it is hard enough to support light foot traffic without marking or indentation.
Full chemical cure (typically 5-7 days) is required before the epoxy can withstand heavy loads, forklift traffic, or equipment installation without being damaged.

Masonry units (bricks, blocks, or stones) must be laid and mortared in place before curing can begin, as curing is the process of maintaining moisture and temperature conditions to allow the mortar to properly hydrate and gain strength.

Joint tooling and finishing should be performed after the mortar has begun to set but before it becomes too hard; however, the curing process must commence immediately after initial set to prevent moisture loss, making curing the overarching process that starts after laying and continues through and beyond joint finishing.
Mortar must be properly cured for a specified period (typically 7, 14, or 28 days) before compression testing can be conducted to verify that the mortar has achieved its design strength.

While waterproofing is typically applied after curing is substantially complete to ensure the mortar is fully hydrated and stable, some waterproofing systems may be applied earlier; however, it is best practice to allow full curing to prevent trapping moisture within the wall assembly.
