Backfilling against masonry foundation walls must not occur until the mortar has sufficiently cured to withstand lateral earth pressures; backfilling too early can displace or crack the masonry before the mortar has gained adequate strength.
Joints must be cleaned, dried, and free of debris/dust before sealant is applied; sealant cannot cure properly on contaminated surfaces.
Primer must be applied to joint substrates and allowed to become tacky before sealant is applied, to ensure adhesion.

successor: Subsequent Construction Activities (e.g., painting, waterproof testing, traffic)
rationale: Sealant must be fully cured before being disturbed by other trades, painting over it, exposure to water, or load-bearing to avoid compromising the seal.
The surface must be clean, dry, and properly prepared (e.g., sanded, degreased) to ensure proper adhesion of the resin; contaminants or moisture can prevent curing or cause bond failure.
Resin and hardener must be thoroughly mixed in the correct ratio before curing can begin; the curing reaction starts upon mixing.
The mixed resin must be applied to the target surface (e.g., via brushing, rolling, or injection) before the curing process can proceed; curing begins once the resin is in place.
Any secondary finishing operations such as sanding, painting, or applying topcoats must wait until the resin has fully cured to avoid damaging the uncured material or trapping solvents.
Concrete must first be poured into the formwork before the formwork can be retained for curing; the curing process begins only after concrete placement is complete.
The formwork must be fully installed and in place to retain the poured concrete during the curing period.
Formwork must be retained in place for the required curing duration to allow concrete to gain sufficient strength before it can be safely stripped and removed.

While curing compound can sometimes be applied immediately after finishing, it is typical to apply after formwork retention begins; this is a soft sequencing preference rather than a physical necessity.
Surface finishing or repair work on the concrete element can only be performed after the formwork is removed, which requires completion of the formwork retention/curing period.

Post-tensioning stressing must be completed before the curing hold begins, as the curing hold period starts after the tendons have been stressed to allow the concrete to achieve full strength under compression.

The curing hold must be completed before grouting can begin, as the concrete needs sufficient time to cure and gain strength to withstand the grouting pressure and to ensure the bond between tendon and concrete.

Curing hold must be completed before formwork and shoring can be removed, as the concrete requires adequate curing time to develop enough strength to be self-supporting without the temporary support system.

Concrete must be placed and initially set before the post-tensioning curing hold can begin; the curing hold is part of the post-tensioning sequence that follows concrete placement and initial tensioning.
Curing inspection can only occur after concrete has been poured and has begun the curing process.
Surface finishing must be completed before curing inspection to ensure the concrete surface is properly prepared for curing evaluation.
Inspection of curing must be completed before formwork can be removed to ensure concrete has achieved sufficient strength.
Curing inspection must confirm adequate curing before any subsequent surface treatments or coatings are applied.
Structural loads from subsequent construction stages can only be applied after curing inspection confirms concrete has reached required strength.
Concrete must be poured and in place before accelerated curing can begin, as accelerated curing applies to fresh concrete to speed up hydration and strength gain.
The concrete must reach its initial set before accelerated curing methods (such as steam or heat curing) can be safely applied to avoid damaging the concrete structure.
Accelerated curing allows the concrete to gain sufficient early strength more quickly, enabling earlier removal of formwork.
After accelerated curing is complete, concrete strength tests are conducted to verify that the desired strength has been achieved before proceeding with subsequent construction activities.

Autogenous curing is an internal curing process that occurs during concrete hydration. Concrete must first be placed and consolidated before internal curing can begin, as autogenous curing relies on the water already within the concrete mixture.

predecessor: Mixing of Concrete with Internal Curing Agents
rationale: For autogenous curing to be effective, internal curing agents such as lightweight aggregates or superabsorbent polymers must be incorporated into the concrete mix during batching. These materials release water internally during hydration, which is the mechanism of autogenous curing.

Autogenous curing must reach a sufficient degree of hydration before final finishing operations (e.g., troweling, texturing) can be performed, as the concrete needs adequate strength and surface hardness to withstand finishing without damage.

Sufficient autogenous curing is required for the concrete to develop enough strength to be self-supporting before formwork can be safely removed. The internal curing process must progress to achieve the required early-age strength.

successor: External Moist Curing or Water Curing
rationale: While autogenous curing provides internal water supply, supplementary external moist curing may follow to continue hydration if the internal water supply is depleted. This is a soft preference as external curing may not be strictly necessary if the internal agents provide sufficient moisture.
Timber must first be harvested from trees before it can be seasoned or cured.
Logs must be debarked and cut into rough lumber or baulks before seasoning to allow proper moisture evaporation.
Timber must be seasoned (dried) to a stable moisture content before it can be planed to final smooth dimensions without warping.
Seasoned timber is dimensionally stable and less prone to shrinkage or movement, making it suitable for precise joinery work.
While treatment can sometimes occur on green timber, seasoning before treatment allows better penetration of preservatives and prevents trapping moisture.

Green lumber must be milled to remove rough surfaces and shape the wood before drying, as the milling process requires the wood to be in its undried (green) state for optimal cutting and to prevent excessive wear on equipment.

Different wood species and grades require specific drying schedules (temperature, humidity, duration). Sorting must occur before kiln drying to ensure appropriate drying parameters are applied to each batch.
Lumber must be properly stacked with stickers (spacers) between layers to allow air circulation and uniform drying. This preparation is essential before placing the lumber into the kiln.

After the main drying cycle, lumber needs conditioning to equalize moisture content throughout the pieces and relieve drying stresses. This can only occur after the kiln drying process brings the wood to the target moisture range.

After kiln drying stabilizes the lumber at the target moisture content, the wood can be planed to final dimensions. Planing green lumber would result in dimensional changes as the wood dries, so planing must follow drying.
Curing record documentation can only begin after concrete has been poured, as curing is the process of maintaining moisture and temperature conditions for freshly placed concrete.
Formwork removal typically requires that concrete has achieved sufficient strength through proper curing, which must be documented before stripping can be authorized.
Surface finishing or coating application often requires that the concrete curing period is completed and documented to ensure the surface is ready for subsequent treatments.
Strength testing is performed after or during the curing period to verify that the concrete has reached specified strength, and curing records provide the environmental context for test results.
Surfaces must be clean, smooth, and free of dust, oil, or debris for paint to adhere properly.
Drywall must be installed, taped, and mudded before painting to provide a finished surface.
Primer must be applied to seal surfaces and ensure proper paint adhesion and uniform finish.
Rough-in work inside walls must be completed before painting, as painting seals wall cavities.
While painting can be done before flooring, it is preferred to paint first to avoid drips and splatter on new floors.
Painting must be finished before final cleaning to allow for touch-ups and avoid re-soiling cleaned surfaces.
Preference is to paint walls before installing trim to achieve clean edges, though some trim may be pre-finished.
The structural frame must be complete to provide the support framework onto which plasterboard/dry lining is fixed.
External walls must be in place to enclose the building before internal dry lining can be installed, providing weathertightness and defining internal spaces.
The roof must be completed to provide overhead weather protection; dry lining materials are moisture-sensitive and must be kept dry.

predecessor: MEP First Fix (First Fix Electrical, Plumbing, HVAC)
rationale: First fix services (cables, conduits, pipes, ductwork) must be run within walls and ceilings before they are enclosed by plasterboard.

successor: MEP Second Fix (Second Fix Electrical, Plumbing, HVAC)
rationale: After plasterboard is installed, second fix works such as fitting sockets, switches, light fixtures, sanitaryware, and grilles can be completed, as these are surface-mounted or penetrate the finished boarding.
Structural framing (walls, floors, roof) must be complete to provide the supporting structure onto which joinery (cabinets, doors, window frames, etc.) is installed.
Electrical rough-in wiring and outlet boxes must be in place before joinery is installed, as joinery often conceals or is fitted around these elements.
Plumbing rough-in pipes must be in place before installing joinery like kitchen cabinets or vanities that will be fitted around plumbing connections.
Wall and ceiling finishing must be completed before joinery installation to ensure a clean substrate and to avoid damage to finished joinery from wet trades.
Floor base preparation must be complete so that base cabinets and other floor-supported joinery sit on a level, finished surface.
Final painting and touch-up work is typically done after joinery installation to blend wall finishes with the newly installed joinery and cover any gaps or marks.

While flooring is often installed before joinery, in some sequences floor coverings like tiles or hardwood are laid after joinery to allow a clean finish around cabinet bases; this is a soft preference depending on project staging.
Final installation of lighting fixtures, switches, and outlets is done after joinery is in place so that fixtures align correctly with the finished joinery and no rework is needed.
Plumbing fixtures such as sinks, faucets, and appliances are installed after joinery (e.g., kitchen cabinets and vanities) to ensure proper fit and connection.
Doors and windows require completed structural wall openings to be fitted into. The walls must be built and cured to provide the rough openings with proper dimensions and structural support.
The structural frame (studs, headers, lintels) around door and window openings must be in place before the doors and windows can be installed.
Rough openings must be properly measured, framed, and prepared (with sill pan flashing, etc.) before doors/windows can be inserted.

Drywall and plastering must be done after doors and windows are installed so that the wallboard can be fitted neatly around the frames, and so that door/window jambs and casings can be properly integrated.
Exterior cladding is installed after windows and doors to allow proper flashing and water-tight integration around the openings.
While flooring can technically be done before door fitting, it's standard practice to install doors after flooring to ensure proper clearance and to avoid damaging finished floors during fitting.
Building envelope waterproofing (house wrap, flashing) around openings should be applied before doors and windows are installed to ensure a watertight seal.
While not strictly required, it is preferable to install doors and windows before final electrical trim and switch/outlet covers near openings to avoid damaging sensitive finish work.
Electrical rough-in work must be completed before cabinetry installation to allow wiring to be placed within walls and avoid obstruction by cabinets.
Plumbing rough-in for sinks, dishwashers, and other fixtures must be completed before cabinet installation so that pipes are in place behind cabinets.
HVAC ductwork and vents must be roughed in before cabinetry to ensure proper airflow and avoid conflicts with cabinet placement.
Drywall must be installed, taped, mudded, and sanded before cabinetry is hung to provide a finished wall surface and allow for proper alignment and mounting of cabinets.
Floor underlayment or subfloor must be prepared prior to cabinet installation to ensure a level base and proper cabinet placement.
Countertops must be installed after cabinetry is set in place because countertops are fabricated to fit the specific cabinet dimensions and are mounted on top of the cabinets.
Final painting and touch-up work is often performed after cabinetry is installed to address any wall damage or gaps created during installation, though some prefer to paint walls before cabinets.
Built-in appliances such as dishwashers, ranges, and refrigerators are installed after cabinetry to ensure proper fit within cabinet openings and to connect to utilities.
In some construction sequences, finished flooring is installed after cabinetry to avoid damaging flooring during cabinet installation, though this can vary depending on the flooring type.
Wall and floor framing must be complete to provide the structural support needed for mounting cabinets and millwork.
Structural framing must be complete to provide the load-bearing support and backing for feature wall installation.
Base wall sheathing or backing board must be installed before applying feature wall treatments such as cladding, panels, or finishes.
Electrical rough-ins such as wiring, outlets, and switch boxes must be in place behind the wall before feature wall treatment is applied, to avoid cutting into finished surfaces.
The feature wall treatment must be installed before final painting or finishing of adjacent surfaces to ensure clean edges and seamless integration.
While trim and molding can be installed after feature wall treatment for best fit and finish, it is a soft preference as some trims could be fitted beforehand with careful detailing.

Cornice and coving must be installed onto smooth, finished walls. Plastering/skimming must be completed to provide the proper surface for adhesive and to ensure a seamless joint between the wall and the cornice.

Cornice and coving is fixed at the junction of walls and ceilings. The ceiling surface must be finished first so that the cornice can be properly aligned and bonded to both the wall and ceiling surfaces.
Painting should be done after cornice and coving installation so that the paint covers the cornice/coving itself and any filler or joint compound used at the seams, ensuring a uniform finish.

While not a strict physical necessity, it is preferable to install cornice and coving before final electrical fit-out to avoid damaging newly installed light fittings or switches during the coving installation process.

Soft preference: installing cornice/coving before flooring avoids dust and debris from coving installation falling onto finished flooring, and prevents the need for working around floor protection. However, it is not physically required.
Walls must be smooth, clean, and dry for wallpaper adhesive to bond properly; wallpapering over unprepared surfaces causes bubbles, peeling, and poor adhesion.
Primer seals the wall surface, prevents the wall from absorbing adhesive too quickly, and ensures uniform adhesion of wallpaper.
Electrical boxes and outlets must be installed and trimmed out before wallpapering, as wallpaper is applied around and over these fixtures; doing electrical work after would damage the wallpaper.

Soft preference: wallpaper is typically installed before trim so that the wallpaper edge can be neatly tucked behind molding for a clean finish, though trim can be installed first with careful cutting.
Soft preference: painting ceilings and trim before wallpapering prevents drips on new wallpaper; however, if wallpaper is installed first, painters must take care not to get paint on the wallpaper.
The concrete slab or subfloor must be fully cured, clean, and level before applying screed or self-levelling compound to ensure proper bonding and a stable base.
Underfloor heating pipes or cables must be installed and pressure-tested before the screed is poured over them to encase the heating system.

predecessor: Damp Proof Membrane (DPM) / Vapour Barrier Installation
rationale: A damp proof membrane must be laid prior to screeding to prevent moisture migration from the substrate into the screed layer.

successor: Floor Covering Installation (e.g., tiles, vinyl, hardwood, carpet)
rationale: The screed/self-levelling compound must be fully cured and dried before any final floor finish is installed to prevent cracking, delamination, or moisture damage.

successor: Skirting Board / Wall Base Trim Installation
rationale: Skirting boards are typically installed after screeding so they sit neatly above the finished floor level, though this can sometimes be done earlier with careful allowance for floor height.
A clean, smooth, and cured concrete slab or substrate is required for waterproofing membranes to properly bond and adhere without defects.
Concrete must be fully cured (typically minimum 28 days) to avoid moisture trapped within the slab causing blistering or delamination of the waterproofing membrane.
Any required screeding to achieve falls or smooth surface must be completed and cured before waterproofing is applied.
Tiles and floor finishes must be installed over the waterproofed surface to protect the membrane and provide the final wearing surface.
Backfilling against waterproofed walls or basements must only be done after the waterproofing membrane is fully installed and cured to prevent damage to the system.
Surfaces must be clean, dry, and free of dust, dirt, grease, or debris for sealant to properly adhere and bond.
Where specified, primer must be applied to the substrate before sealant to ensure proper adhesion and prevent sealant failure.
Backer rod must be placed into joints to control sealant depth, provide a backing for proper tooling, and prevent three-sided adhesion before sealant is applied.
After sealant is applied and tooled, a visual inspection should be performed to check for voids, gaps, or defects, though this can sometimes occur concurrently.
Sealant must be fully cured (per manufacturer specifications) before paint or coatings are applied over it to avoid adhesion issues, cracking, or discoloration.
Epoxy coating requires a cured, clean concrete slab as a substrate for proper adhesion.
Concrete must be fully cured (typically 28 days) to ensure moisture levels are low enough for epoxy to bond and not blister.
The concrete surface must be mechanically profiled (grinding or shot-blasting) and cleaned to remove contaminants and create a mechanical bond for the epoxy.
Moisture vapor emission tests (e.g., ASTM F2170) must be performed and pass requirements; excessive moisture will cause epoxy to delaminate.
After epoxy application, the coating must cure undisturbed for the manufacturer-specified time (typically 24-72 hours) before any foot or vehicle traffic is allowed.
All floor coating work must be completed and fully cured before furniture, equipment, or personnel can occupy the space.
While ideally overhead work is done before flooring to prevent debris falling on wet epoxy, it is a soft preference; some sequencing can be managed with protective coverings.
The concrete slab must be placed and allowed to cure before any polishing can begin, as polishing requires a hardened, stable surface.

Sufficient curing time (typically 28 days for full cure, but at least 7 days minimum) is required to achieve the necessary hardness and moisture content for polishing. Polishing green concrete can cause surface damage and poor results.
The surface must be ground and leveled to remove imperfections, expose aggregate if desired, and create a flat substrate before the final polishing steps can be applied.
Moisture vapor emission rate (MVER) and relative humidity testing must be completed to ensure the concrete is dry enough for polishing and any sealers or densifiers to properly bond.
Once polishing is complete, the finished concrete surface must be protected with temporary coverings (e.g., ram board, masonite) to prevent damage from subsequent construction activities.
Polished concrete is often a final finish; detailed cleaning and inspection for the owner walk-through occurs after polishing is fully completed.

Some interior finishing (painting, millwork, etc.) can be done before polishing in certain sequences, but it is generally preferred to complete polishing early to avoid contaminating the porous unpolished concrete. However, polishing should ideally precede dust-sensitive finishes to avoid airborne dust settling on new surfaces.
The structural frame must be completed to provide a substrate for the external render application.
Roofing must be completed to ensure the building envelope is weathertight before applying external render, and to provide top-down finishing sequence.
Insulation boards must be fixed to the walls before render can be applied as a protective and decorative top coat over the insulation system.
Render must be fully cured before any paint or decorative finish is applied to ensure proper adhesion and finish quality.
External rendering work is typically performed from scaffolding; the scaffolding can only be dismantled once all render application is complete to allow access to all facade areas.
The structural staircase (concrete/reinforcement) must be complete to provide a stable base for finishing works such as plastering, tiling, or painting.
Surrounding walls and partitions must be in place to define the staircase enclosure and allow proper finishing alignment and edge detailing.
Stair treads and risers must be finished (tiled, carpeted, or painted) to establish the final dimensions and fixings for handrails and balustrades.
Staircase finishing is typically completed before final painting to avoid damaging freshly painted surfaces, though this is a preference for quality and efficiency rather than a physical necessity.
Finishing the staircase first allows adjacent floor finishes to be laid up to the staircase edge for a clean transition, but is a sequencing preference to minimize rework.
The window frame and rough opening must be fully installed and prepared before the IGU can be placed, as the IGU sits within the frame.
Weatherproofing and flashing around the frame opening must be completed to prevent moisture ingress before installing the IGU.
The surrounding structural wall must be complete and stable to provide the necessary support and anchorage for the window frame and IGU.
Interior trim, drywall finishing, and paint around the window cannot be completed until the IGU is installed, as the IGU defines the final position and edge conditions for finishes.
Air leakage and water penetration testing must be performed after IGU installation to verify the complete window assembly (frame + IGU) performs as designed.
The structural frame (including lintels and supports above openings) must be in place to provide the supporting structure for the shopfront glazing system.
The rough opening must be framed, sized, and prepared to receive the shopfront glazing unit and its frame.
Waterproof membranes and flashing at the sill and jambs must be installed before the glazing to prevent water ingress behind the shopfront.
Sealing the shopfront creates a weather-tight enclosure, allowing interior finishes such as drywall, painting, and trim to proceed without weather damage.
Signage is often attached to or aligned with the glazing frame; while not physically mandatory, installing signage after glazing ensures accurate fit and alignment.
Double glazing units must be installed into prepared window frames; frames need to be in place and secure to receive the glazing.
Walls must be fully constructed and cured to provide the structural opening into which window frames and glazing are installed.
Window openings must be measured, cleaned, and prepared (e.g., flashing installed, sill prepared) before glazing units can be fitted.
Interior finishes around windows require the glazing to be in place to properly seal, trim, and finish the window reveals and edges.
External cladding and weatherproof membranes must be installed after windows are in place to create a continuous weather-tight seal around the openings.
Glass panels must be delivered and stored on-site before they can be cut and sized to required dimensions.
Cut glass pieces must first be sized correctly before their edges can be ground and polished for safety and installation.
Glass must be cut to final dimensions before undergoing tempering, as tempered glass cannot be cut or resized.
Cutting and sizing must be completed first to establish the final glass piece dimensions before drilling holes or notching edges.
Individual glass layers must be cut to size before being laminated together into a composite unit.

predecessor: Window Opening Preparation / Rough Opening Inspection
rationale: The window opening must be properly framed, measured, and prepared to receive the triple-glazed unit. Installing the glazing into an unprepared or incorrectly sized opening would be physically impossible or would result in improper fit and sealing.

The building's structural frame and walls must be in place to provide the rough opening that houses the triple glazing. Without the structural support, there is no opening to install the glazing into.

The weather-resistant barrier (building wrap) around the window opening must be installed before the glazing to ensure proper integration of flashing and waterproofing membranes with the window frame, preventing water ingress.
Once the triple-glazed window unit is physically placed and secured in the opening, the perimeter must be sealed with caulk, backer rod, and flashing to make the installation airtight and watertight.

Interior finishes such as drywall, plaster, and window trim are installed after the window unit is in place. Finishing the wall surface before window installation would require cutting and rework to expose the opening.
Frame materials (timber, steel, or aluminum) must be sourced, delivered, and on-site before any preparation or priming work can begin.
The building site must be cleared, leveled, and foundations poured/cured before frame components are prepared and primed, as the frame is erected on the foundation.
Frame components must be prepared (cut, drilled, notched) and primed with protective coatings before they can be assembled and erected into the structural framework.
Once frame components are prepared and primed, they must be inspected for dimensional accuracy, coating quality, and defects before being cleared for erection.
Glazing units (windows, curtain walls, etc.) must be physically installed before they can be inspected and tested for performance, water penetration, and structural integrity.
The supporting frames, gaskets, and seals must be properly prepared and set to receive the glazing before inspection of the completed assembly can occur.
If inspection reveals defects (e.g., leaks, cracks, seal failures), remediation cannot be identified as needed until after inspection and testing are complete.
Formal acceptance or sign-off of the glazing work by the client or authority requires successful completion of inspection and testing.

Interior finishes near glazed areas (e.g., drywall, painting, trim) can proceed more safely and cleanly after glazing is inspected and sealed, but this is a preferred sequence rather than an absolute physical necessity.
The rough opening must be framed, blocked, and prepared to the correct dimensions before fire-rated glazing units can be installed.
After the fire-rated glass is placed in the frame, glazing beads or stops must be installed to secure the glass in position.
Fire-rated sealant and perimeter firestopping must be applied after glazing installation to maintain the fire-resistance rating of the assembly.
The primary structural frame and supports must be in place to carry the load of the fire-rated glazing assembly before it can be installed.
After installation is complete, the assembly must be inspected and certified to verify it meets the required fire-resistance rating.
The frame must be in place to provide a structural support and enclosure for the acoustic glass panels.
Vertical and horizontal framing members must be installed to create the grid that will hold the acoustic glass units.
After the glass is installed, seals and gaskets must be applied around the perimeter to achieve the acoustic insulation performance.
Interior trim work typically follows glazing to cover gaps and provide a finished appearance, though in some sequences trim may be partially installed beforehand.
Sound transmission tests can only be performed once the glazing system is fully installed to verify it meets acoustic performance specifications.
A stable, level foundation must be prepared to support the block; setting a block on unprepared ground would cause instability.
Formwork defines the boundaries and shape for the concrete or block placement; blocks cannot be set without the formwork in place to contain them.
If the foundation slab or blinding concrete is poured, it must cure sufficiently to bear the weight of the block without deformation.
After each block is set, mortar must be applied and the block leveled before the next course can be laid.
Reinforcement bars or ties are inserted into the hollow cores or between blocks after they are positioned, as they cannot be placed through an already-solid wall section.

The structural steel frame provides the primary load-bearing support and attachment points for curtain wall panels. Without the completed steel frame, there is no structural substrate to anchor the glazed panels to.
Floor slabs provide lateral support and the finished edge conditions (slab edges) that curtain wall systems are typically anchored to or aligned with at each floor level.

successor: Interior Wall Finishes (Adjacent to Curtain Wall)
rationale: The curtain wall panels must be installed and fully sealed before interior finishes can be applied adjacent to them, to prevent water ingress damage and to establish the final interior boundary conditions.

Permanent window cleaning systems (e.g., davits, anchors, or tracks) are designed to interface with the installed curtain wall geometry and must be installed after the panels are in place to ensure proper alignment and load distribution.

successor: Air and Water Barrier Testing & Commissioning
rationale: The curtain wall assembly must be fully installed to create the building envelope before air leakage and water penetration tests can be meaningfully performed on the completed façade system.
Structural framing must be complete to provide the rough openings and structural support necessary for window installation.
Weather-resistant barrier and sheathing around window openings must be installed before windows to prevent moisture intrusion and ensure proper sealing.
Windows must be in place before interior wall finishes are applied to allow for proper trimming, sealing, and integration of window frames with walls.
Window units must be installed so that interior trim and casings can be fitted around them for a finished appearance.
Windows are set into the wall openings before the final exterior cladding is applied to ensure proper flashing and waterproofing integration.
The surface must be properly prepared (cleaned, smoothed, and primed) to ensure topcoat adhesion and a uniform finish.
Primer must be applied and fully cured before topcoating to provide a suitable base, improve adhesion, and prevent substrate contamination.
The topcoat paint or coating must be properly mixed, thinned, and prepared to the correct viscosity before application.
After the topcoat is applied and dried/cured, it must be inspected for defects such as runs, sags, orange peel, or incomplete coverage.
The applied topcoat must undergo a specified curing or drying period before any subsequent handling, recoating, or service.
The handle must be manufactured before it can be assembled with bristles to form the paintbrush.
Bristles must be produced before they can be attached to the handle during paintbrush assembly.
The paintbrush must be fully assembled before it can undergo quality inspection.
The paintbrush must pass quality inspection before it can be packaged for distribution.
The ferrule (metal band) must be crimped onto the assembled paintbrush to secure bristles to the handle; this is part of the assembly process before the brush is complete.
The spray gun requires a clean, prepared surface to ensure proper paint adhesion; spraying onto unprepared or dirty surfaces would result in poor coating quality and defects.
The paint must be properly mixed and thinned to the correct viscosity before being loaded into the spray gun; otherwise the gun will clog or produce an uneven spray pattern.
The spray gun must be fully assembled, connected to the air compressor, and adjusted for fluid and air flow before painting can begin.
Paint must be applied via the spray gun before it can dry or cure; the drying process can only commence after the coating has been deposited on the surface.
The spray gun must be cleaned immediately after use to prevent paint from hardening inside the nozzle and fluid passages; cleaning cannot occur before painting is complete.
The surface must be prepared (e.g., cleaned and dried) before using a paint scraper to remove old paint, as dirt and moisture can prevent effective scraping.
After scraping off loose paint with the paint scraper, sanding must follow to smooth the surface and prepare it for new paint.
Scraping removes old, loose paint; primer must be applied to the bare surface after scraping to ensure proper adhesion of the new paint.
The paint scraper removes flaking or peeling paint; new paint can only be applied after the old, loose paint has been removed and the surface smoothed.
Personal protective equipment (gloves, goggles, dust mask) must be in place before scraping to protect the worker from paint chips, dust, and debris.
Wall framing must be completed before painting to provide the structural surface for paint application.
Drywall must be installed and finished (taped, mudded, and sanded) to create a smooth surface before painting can begin.
Plastering must be completed and cured before painting to ensure a smooth, sealed substrate for paint adhesion.
Primer must be applied and dried before the final paint coat to ensure proper adhesion, coverage, and durability.
Painting is typically completed before flooring to avoid paint drips on finished floors, though it's a soft preference as drop cloths can be used.
Baseboards and trim are usually installed after painting to allow for clean edges and to avoid getting paint on the trim, though some prefer painting trim first.
Final cleaning and touch-up work must occur after painting is complete to address any paint splatters, drips, or missed spots.
Drywall must be installed and finished before painting can begin, as paint requires a smooth, sealed surface to adhere properly.
Taping and mudding joints must be completed and sanded smooth before painting to ensure an even finish on the ceiling surface.
Primer must be applied to the ceiling surface to seal the drywall and provide proper adhesion and uniform absorption for the paint.
Soft preference: Painting is typically done before flooring to avoid paint drips and spills damaging finished floors; however, with proper protection, flooring can be installed first.
Ceiling painting must be completed before installing trim and baseboards so that paint lines are clean and trim can be cut and fitted without damaging freshly painted ceilings.
Trim and skirting surfaces must be properly prepared (cleaned, sanded, filled) and primed before painting to ensure proper paint adhesion and a smooth, durable finish.
Main wall painting should be completed before trim and skirting painting to avoid overspray and drips on freshly painted walls, and to allow for cleaner cutting-in along edges.

Ideally flooring is installed before skirting painting to allow skirting to be painted after flooring is in place, providing a neat finish; however skirting can be painted before flooring with careful masking.
The steel structure must be fully erected and in place before painting can commence, as painting is applied to the installed structural steel members.
The steel surface must be cleaned and prepared (e.g., abrasive blasting to remove mill scale, rust, and contaminants) to ensure proper adhesion of the paint system.
Primer coats must be applied to the prepared steel surface before the main structural steelwork paint coats can be applied, as part of the multi-coat painting system.
Inspection of the completed paint system (e.g., dry film thickness, adhesion, pinhole testing) must be performed after painting is finished to verify quality and compliance with specifications.

successor: Subsequent Trade Works (e.g., Cladding, Services Installation)
rationale: Other trades such as cladding installation, electrical, and mechanical services typically begin after structural steelwork painting is complete to avoid damaging the painted finish, though this may be partially overlapped in some sequences.

Floor painting requires a clean, dry, and stable substrate. The concrete slab must be poured and fully cured to ensure the paint adheres properly and does not crack or peel due to moisture or movement.
Any leveling compound or screed must be applied and dried before painting to create a smooth, even surface for the paint to bond to.
Dust, dirt, grease, and debris must be removed and the floor may need grinding or etching to ensure proper paint adhesion. Painting over an unprepared surface will lead to delamination.
After application, the paint needs a designated period to dry and cure to achieve its final hardness and durability before any traffic or further work can take place on the floor.

A clear topcoat or sealer is often applied over painted floors for protection. While sometimes combined, if separate, painting must be done first. This is a soft preference if the sealer is applied wet-on-wet, but hard if the paint must dry first.

The surface (e.g., asphalt, concrete, or flooring) must be clean, dry, smooth, and fully cured before line markings can be applied to ensure proper adhesion and durability of the paint or thermoplastic material.
Any base layers such as asphalt paving, concrete pouring, or floor screeding must be completed and fully set before line marking to provide a stable substrate.

Fresh concrete or asphalt must be allowed to cure for the specified period (typically 7–28 days for concrete, 24–48 hours for asphalt) before marking to prevent marking defects and ensure long-term performance.

If a clear protective sealant or anti-graffiti coating is to be applied over markings, it should be done after line marking is fully dry. However, this is optional and depends on design specifications.
The area (road, parking lot, sports court, warehouse floor) can only be opened to traffic or put into use after line markings have been applied and have fully dried/cured to avoid smudging or damage.
Surface preparation (cleaning, sanding, priming) ensures proper paint adhesion; paint cannot be applied or cured on unprepared surfaces.
Paint must be applied (sprayed, rolled, or brushed) onto the surface before the curing process can begin; curing is the chemical process that occurs after paint is applied.
The paint must be fully cured before inspection or testing of the finish, as uncured paint is fragile and would be damaged by contact.

successor: Final Assembly or Installation of Adjacent Components
rationale: Adjacent components (trim, fixtures, hardware) should only be installed after paint is fully cured to avoid damaging the finish or trapping solvents.
Masking tapes and protective covers must remain in place during curing; removing them before curing is complete can ruin the paint edge or finish.
Surface preparation (cleaning, sanding, priming) must be completed before paint is applied, and Paint Quality Inspection assesses the final painted surface.
Primer must be applied and dried before the final paint coat; inspection verifies the quality of the paint over the primer.
All paint coats must be fully applied and cured before inspection can assess the final finish quality.
Paint must be allowed to cure or dry to its specified hardness and finish before inspection can be performed; otherwise, the inspection could damage the wet paint or yield inaccurate results.

If inspection identifies defects, touch-up or repair work is needed. This is a soft preference because if no defects are found, touch-up may not be required; however, as a logical workflow, any rework follows inspection.

predecessor: Installation of all mechanical and electrical equipment
rationale: Pre-commissioning checks can only begin after all mechanical and electrical equipment (pumps, motors, valves, instruments, etc.) are physically installed and in place, as there is nothing to check otherwise.

predecessor: Completion of piping and wiring connections
rationale: All piping, tubing, electrical wiring, and cable connections must be completed so that pre-commissioning checks can verify continuity, tightness, and proper termination.

predecessor: Flushing and cleaning of piping systems
rationale: Piping systems must be flushed and cleaned of debris, weld slag, and construction dirt before pre-commissioning checks to avoid damaging sensitive equipment during initial testing.

Pre-commissioning checks (visual inspections, alignment checks, continuity checks) must be completed before applying pressure for leak tests, as unsafe conditions or incorrect setups would be dangerous without prior verification.
Formal commissioning and initial system startup can only proceed after pre-commissioning checks verify that all equipment is correctly installed, aligned, and ready for energized operation.
The building structure must be complete to provide a load-bearing framework for performance testing such as structural load tests and vibration analysis.

predecessor: Installation of Building Systems (HVAC, Electrical, Plumbing)
rationale: Building systems must be installed before performance testing can evaluate system integration, energy efficiency, and overall building performance.
Performance testing must be completed to verify that all systems meet design specifications before the building can be commissioned and handed over to the client.
The building must pass performance testing to ensure safety, functionality, and compliance before occupants can move in and begin normal operations.
Performance testing results are required documentation for final inspection and certification by regulatory authorities.
Pipes and joints must be fully welded and prepared before leak testing can be performed to ensure that the system is closed and can hold pressure.
All piping components must be assembled and connected before leak testing can verify the integrity of the complete system.
The pressure testing equipment (pumps, gauges, hoses) must be connected and set up before leak testing can be conducted.
Insulation should only be applied after leak testing is completed to avoid covering leaks and to allow access for repairs if leaks are found.
The system can only be commissioned or started up after leak testing has confirmed that there are no leaks, ensuring safe operation.

successor: Fire and Life Safety System Testing
rationale: Fire protection rough-in (piping, sprinkler heads, alarm wiring, ductwork for smoke control) must be physically installed before any testing can be performed. Testing validates installed components.

successor: Fire and Life Safety System Testing
rationale: Fire alarm control panels, smoke detectors, and notification appliances require permanent electrical power to operate during testing.

successor: Fire and Life Safety System Testing
rationale: Fire-rated barriers and penetration seals must be in place to ensure compartmentation integrity can be verified during smoke control and containment tests.

predecessor: Fire and Life Safety System Testing
rationale: Successful completion of all fire and life safety system tests is a mandatory prerequisite for obtaining regulatory occupancy approval and building handover.

predecessor: Fire and Life Safety System Testing
rationale: While integrated commissioning can overlap, formal sign-off of fire and life safety testing typically precedes full integrated systems commissioning to ensure life safety systems are verified before broader building automation testing.

All HVAC equipment (air handlers, chillers, boilers, pumps, variable air volume boxes, etc.) must be physically installed, connected, and in place before balancing and commissioning can begin, as there is nothing to balance or commission without installed equipment.

All supply, return, and exhaust ductwork must be fully installed, sealed, and pressure-tested before air balancing can be performed, as air distribution is physically impossible without a complete duct system.
Hydronic piping systems for chilled water, hot water, and condenser water must be fully installed, pressure-tested, and flushed before water-side balancing and commissioning can occur.

All electrical connections, motor starters, variable frequency drives, and control wiring for HVAC equipment must be complete and energized to allow equipment operation during balancing and commissioning procedures.

The building automation system (BAS) controllers, sensors, actuators, and software must be installed and operational to enable monitoring, control, and verification of HVAC system performance during commissioning.

HVAC balancing and commissioning must be completed and verified before the building can be handed over to the owner or occupants, as it is a prerequisite for ensuring proper environmental conditions, energy efficiency, and system functionality.

Proper HVAC balancing and commissioning ensures that ventilation rates, airflow patterns, and temperature controls are functioning correctly, which is necessary before meaningful IAQ testing can be conducted to verify air quality meets design specifications.

successor: LEED or Green Building Certification Review
rationale: While commissioning documentation is typically required for LEED certification and green building ratings, this is a procedural/administrative preference rather than a physical construction constraint.

Although it is preferable to complete the building envelope and insulation before balancing to achieve accurate thermal load conditions, partial commissioning can begin in conditioned spaces before full envelope completion is achieved.
Electrical power and cabling must be installed and roughed-in before BMS controllers and panels can be powered up and commissioned.
The physical BMS hardware (controllers, panels, sensors) must be installed before they can be commissioned and programmed.
All field devices such as temperature sensors, pressure sensors, valves, and damper actuators must be physically installed before the BMS can be tested and calibrated.
While sensors can be installed after drywall, it is often more efficient to complete ceiling and wall finishes before installing certain room-level sensors to avoid damage.
The BMS must be commissioned and operational before the HVAC system can be started up and tested, as the BMS controls the HVAC equipment operation.
Full commissioning and verification of BMS control logic must be completed before the energy management system is declared operational.
BMS commissioning is a prerequisite subsystem commissioning activity that must be completed prior to overall building systems commissioning and handover to the owner.
All rough-in plumbing pipes, fittings, and drainage lines must be installed before testing can be performed, as testing is used to verify the integrity of the installed system.

Underground plumbing drainage lines are typically embedded in or run beneath the foundation slab; the slab must be poured and cured before above-ground rough-in plumbing and subsequent testing can proceed.

successor: Wall and Ceiling Cladding / Drywall Installation
rationale: Plumbing and drainage systems must be tested and approved before walls and ceilings are closed up, to avoid costly removal of drywall for leak repairs after finishing.
Testing must be completed to confirm the drainage and supply systems are leak-free and code-compliant before fixtures (sinks, toilets, showers) are connected and installed.
Drainage testing is typically performed before the full water supply system is pressurized and connected, ensuring the waste lines are sound before introducing permanent water flow.
Elevator and escalator units must be physically installed and assembled before any testing can be performed on them.
A permanent electrical power supply must be connected to the elevator and escalator systems to operate them during testing.

predecessor: Structural Completion of Shafts and Wells
rationale: The elevator shafts and escalator wells must be structurally complete and safe to contain the equipment before testing can commence.
Testing must be successfully completed to verify safety and functionality before the systems can be formally commissioned and handed over.
Elevators and escalators must be tested and deemed safe for public use before the building can be occupied and the systems used by occupants.
Concrete must reach its specified design strength through proper curing before load testing can be performed, otherwise the test could damage or fail the uncured structure.
Formwork and temporary shoring must be in place to support the structural element during concrete placement and initial curing before testing can commence.
Reinforcement must be fully placed, tied, and inspected prior to concrete pour and subsequent testing to ensure the structural element meets design specifications.
Load testing must verify that the structure can support its design loads safely before formwork and shoring can be struck and removed.

The load and deflection test results must be reviewed and accepted to confirm structural performance before the element or structure can be formally accepted and handed over for subsequent works or occupancy.

The air barrier system must be fully installed before testing can commence, because the test measures the integrity of the installed air barrier. Testing cannot be performed without the barrier in place.
All penetrations through the building envelope (windows, doors, ducts, pipes, etc.) must be sealed so that the test can accurately measure the overall air leakage of the envelope.
The test identifies specific leakage locations; those leaks must be located before they can be repaired. Remediation logically follows the diagnostic test.

successor: Installation of Interior Finish Layers (e.g., drywall, insulation)
rationale: While it is physically possible to install interior finishes after testing, it is strongly preferred to complete air-tightness testing before covering the air barrier with finishes, as this allows access for sealing any discovered leaks without damaging finished work.

Air-tightness testing is typically a prerequisite step before overall building commissioning and occupancy to verify that the envelope meets performance specifications, though some commissioning activities could theoretically proceed in parallel.

Acoustic testing requires the physical partitions (walls, ceilings) to be in place so that sound transmission paths are fully established and can be measured accurately according to standards like ASTM E90 or E336.
All gaps, penetrations, and joints must be sealed to ensure the assembly's true acoustic performance is tested; unsealed leaks would invalidate the test results.
Acoustic-rated doors and windows are integral parts of the sound-isolating assembly and must be installed before testing can measure the complete system's performance.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-ins that penetrate acoustic barriers (e.g., ductwork, conduit, pipes) must be complete and sealed so that flanking paths are accounted for in the test.

If acoustic testing reveals deficiencies, remediation (e.g., adding sealant, upgrading insulation, installing backer rods) is typically performed afterward; this is a soft preference because sometimes remediation is done during construction before final testing.
Power and control wiring must be installed before lighting control systems can be energized, connected, and commissioned.
Lighting fixtures must be physically installed and connected before their controls can be tested, programmed, and commissioned.
Electrical panels providing power to lighting circuits must be installed, terminated, and energized before commissioning can proceed.
Ceiling installation should occur after lighting commissioning to allow access to wiring and controllers above the ceiling for adjustments and troubleshooting.

successor: Building Occupancy and Final Punch List
rationale: While commissioning can extend into occupancy, complete commissioning is preferably finished before occupancy to ensure functional lighting and avoid disruptions.

Security and access control systems (card readers, electronic locks, alarms, intercoms, CCTV cameras) require electrical power to operate and be tested. Electrical installation must be complete to supply power to these devices.
Security and access control systems rely on network connectivity for data communication, remote monitoring, and centralized control. Network cabling must be installed before testing these systems.

Access control devices such as magnetic locks, card readers, and door contacts are physically mounted on doors and frames. Doors and windows must be installed before access control hardware can be fitted and tested.

Security and access control systems must be fully tested and verified to be operational before the building can be commissioned, handed over to the client, or occupied. Testing validates system functionality and compliance with specifications.

successor: Final Inspection and Punch List Completion
rationale: While not a strict physical dependency, completing security and access control testing early is advisable so that any deficiencies identified can be addressed before the final project inspection and punch list walkthrough.
The water system must be fully installed and operational before water quality testing can be performed, as testing requires a functioning water distribution system to collect samples.
Plumbing rough-in work (pipes, fixtures) must be completed to provide the physical infrastructure through which water flows, enabling representative water samples to be taken.
Regulatory authorities typically require satisfactory water quality test results before issuing a certificate of occupancy, as potable water safety must be verified for building habitation.
Water quality testing results are usually a prerequisite for final plumbing inspection sign-off, confirming that the water meets health and safety standards.
While building commissioning can begin before water quality results are available, it is preferable to have water quality verified early to avoid rework in HVAC and other water-dependent systems.
Electrical systems must be fully installed and operational before thermal imaging can detect heat patterns, hot spots, or electrical faults under load conditions.
Roofing must be complete so thermal imaging can detect moisture intrusion, insulation gaps, and thermal bridging in the building envelope.
HVAC systems need to be operational to perform thermal imaging of ductwork, refrigerant lines, and to assess system performance under load.
Interior finishes (drywall, insulation) must be in place so thermal imaging can identify defects in insulation coverage, air leaks, and thermal anomalies in finished walls and ceilings.
Thermal imaging results identify issues (e.g., moisture, electrical hot spots, insulation gaps) that typically require remediation; while preferred, some minor findings may be deferred.
Concrete must be placed and cured before witness testing of concrete strength or integrity can be performed.
Witness testing often serves as a quality hold point; subsequent work (e.g., backfilling, coating, or structural loading) typically proceeds only after witnessed tests are passed.
Equipment must be installed and ready before witnessed functional or pressure tests can be conducted on that equipment.
Witness testing results are typically reviewed and approved prior to formal system acceptance or handover to the client.
All test instrumentation, safety measures, and procedures must be prepared and verified before witnessed testing can commence.

Retesting and Remediation cannot begin until initial testing has been completed, because retesting is a follow-up process that checks whether issues identified during initial testing have been resolved.
Defects must first be identified and documented before remediation and retesting can occur, as the remediation targets the specific defects found.
Final acceptance testing can only proceed after retesting and remediation are complete to ensure all defects have been addressed before final sign-off.
The system should not be deployed until retesting and remediation have been completed, ensuring that all known defects are resolved before moving to production.

Defect identification and snagging can only commence after the contractor has achieved substantial or practical completion of the works, as snagging lists are generated to identify remaining defects before final completion.
Systematic inspections and testing of completed works must be carried out first to identify any deficiencies, which then form the basis of the snagging list.
Defects must first be identified and logged through the snagging process before any rectification work can be planned and executed.
All identified defects must be documented and subsequently rectified before the project can achieve final completion and be formally handed over to the client.
The snagging list and defect identification process provides the necessary documentation to support the issuance of the practical completion certificate.
Commissioning can only begin after construction is substantially complete, as commissioning involves testing and verifying installed systems.
Mechanical completion ensures all mechanical equipment is installed and ready for testing before commissioning begins.
Electrical systems must be complete and energized to support commissioning activities.
The commissioning schedule defines the sequence and timing for all system startup activities.
Performance verification follows the commissioning schedule to validate that systems meet design specifications.
O&M manuals document how to operate and maintain the completed facility/systems; they cannot be compiled until construction is substantially complete and final as-built conditions are known.
Manufacturer O&M documentation, warranties, and spare parts lists for installed equipment are essential inputs that must be received before the consolidated manual can be compiled.
Final commissioning results, test reports, and verified system performance data must be included in the O&M manual to reflect actual operating parameters.
The completed O&M manual is a key deliverable for handover; the owner cannot be formally trained on operation and maintenance until the manual is finalized and approved.
Submission and approval of the O&M manual is typically a contractual requirement that must be fulfilled before the project can be formally closed out and final payments released.
Users must be trained on installed and operational systems, not before installation is complete.
All systems must be commissioned and verified as operational before training can be delivered to end users.
Training materials and systems should reflect the final, tested configuration; training on a system that hasn't passed QA would risk teaching incorrect procedures.
The facility or system cannot be handed over for operational use until all relevant personnel have been trained.
Formal project handover to the client requires that training has been completed and the facility/system is ready for operation by the client's team.
Post-occupancy seasonal commissioning can only occur after the building is occupied and operational, as it involves fine-tuning systems under real occupancy conditions across different seasons.
The building must be substantially complete and have undergone initial commissioning to ensure all systems are installed, started up, and functioning before seasonal fine-tuning can begin.
After completing seasonal commissioning across all seasons, the final optimized settings and documentation are handed over to facility management as the last step before full operational phase.
Seasonal commissioning must be completed to verify occupant comfort levels across all seasons before formally closing out the commissioning process.
The electrical system must be installed to provide the necessary infrastructure and power connections for testing renewable energy systems.
Solar panels, wind turbines, or other renewable energy components must be physically installed before they can be tested for functionality and performance.
The control and monitoring software must be programmed and configured to enable proper operation and testing of the renewable energy system.
Grid connection must be approved and established to allow the renewable energy system to export or import power as part of testing protocols.
Testing of the renewable energy system must be completed and successful before the overall system can be commissioned and handed over for operational use.
The building's physical structure must be complete to provide a secure environment for IT infrastructure, including server rooms and cabling pathways.
Reliable power supply must be available to run IT servers, networking equipment, and testing tools during infrastructure testing.
Cooling and ventilation systems must be operational to prevent overheating of IT equipment during testing.
IT infrastructure must be tested and verified before it can be integrated with building management systems and fully commissioned.
IT systems must be tested and proven operational before the building can be handed over to occupants for use.
Gas pipework must be physically installed before it can be tested for leaks and pressure integrity.
All gas appliances such as boilers, cookers, and heaters must be connected to the gas supply before the overall gas installation can be tested.
Testing must be completed and passed before a formal gas safety certificate can be issued.
The gas meter is typically installed after the system has been tested to ensure there are no leaks that could be hazardous when the meter is first opened.

successor: Purging and Commissioning of Gas System
rationale: After successful testing, the system can be purged of air and commissioned by introducing gas into the system for the first time.

The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and existing structures before bulk excavation can commence, as excavation equipment needs unobstructed access and the cut/fill volumes must be calculated from a cleared datum.
Accurate survey control points, grid lines, and reduced levels must be established so that excavation depths, side slopes, and boundaries are correctly followed during bulk earthworks.

Soil classification, groundwater conditions, and bearing capacity must be known beforehand to select appropriate excavation methods, batter slopes, and dewatering requirements; unforeseen ground conditions can cause collapse or delays.

Bulk excavation removes the majority of overburden to within ~150–300 mm of final design levels; only after this mass removal can the precise trimming and levelling of formation surfaces be carried out.
After bulk excavation exposes the founding plane, the exposed subgrade must be inspected, tested for compaction, and if necessary improved or stabilised before any fill or foundation works proceed.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and topsoil before any excavation can begin to ensure unobstructed access and proper working conditions.
The exact location and boundaries of the pit must be surveyed and staked out on the ground before excavation starts to ensure the pit is dug in the correct position and to the correct dimensions.
All underground utilities (gas, water, electric, telecom) must be located and marked before excavation to prevent damage to existing infrastructure and ensure worker safety.
Required permits and approvals from local authorities must be secured before any excavation work commences to comply with regulations and avoid legal violations.
Once the pit is excavated, the excavated walls must be immediately shored or stabilized to prevent collapse and ensure worker safety before any personnel enter the pit.
If groundwater or rainwater accumulates in the excavated pit, dewatering must be performed after excavation to provide a dry work environment for subsequent activities.
The base of the excavated pit must be prepared, leveled, and compacted before any foundation work or structure can be placed within the pit.

After excavation is complete, the exposed soil and bearing capacity must be inspected and tested by a geotechnical engineer to verify it meets design requirements before proceeding with foundation work.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and existing structures to provide unobstructed access for rock excavation equipment and to expose the rock surface that needs to be excavated.
Accurate layout and staking of the excavation boundaries, grades, and depths must be completed before rock excavation begins to ensure the excavation is performed to the correct lines and levels.
Rock must be excavated to the required depth and elevation before foundation preparation activities such as trimming, cleaning, and pouring mud mats or concrete can commence.
Rock excavation must be completed first to create the void or trench that will subsequently be backfilled with engineered fill material and compacted to specification.
The rock excavation must be finished to create the trench or pathway before underground utilities such as water pipes, sewer lines, conduits, or ducts can be placed in the excavated area.

Site mobilization (setting up site offices, utilities, access roads, and laydown areas) must be completed before any earthwork like topsoil stripping can commence, as it provides the necessary infrastructure and logistics for construction equipment and personnel.

Accurate surveying and staking of the site boundaries, clearing limits, and reference points must be completed before topsoil stripping to ensure the correct areas are stripped and to avoid encroachment or environmental damage.

Trees, shrubs, brush, and other vegetation must be cleared and grubbed (root removal) before topsoil stripping, because topsoil stripping equipment cannot effectively remove large debris, and leaving vegetation would contaminate the salvaged topsoil.

Erosion and sediment control measures (e.g., silt fences, sediment basins, check dams) must be installed before any soil-disturbing activity such as topsoil stripping to comply with environmental regulations and prevent sediment runoff.

Topsoil stripping must be completed before subgrade excavation and grading begins, because topsoil is unsuitable for structural support and must be removed to expose the underlying competent subgrade material for subsequent earthwork.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and topsoil before excavation can begin to provide unobstructed access and prevent organic material from mixing with bearing soils.
Accurate layout and staking of the building footprint and excavation limits must be completed to guide the excavation equipment and ensure proper location and dimensions.
Existing underground utilities must be located and marked to avoid damaging them during excavation and to plan for any required utility relocations or protection.

Geotechnical analysis of soil bearing capacity, groundwater conditions, and soil classification is required to determine excavation slopes, shoring needs, dewatering requirements, and foundation design before excavation proceeds.

predecessor: Environmental Permitting and Erosion Control Installation
rationale: Erosion and sediment control measures (silt fencing, sediment basins) must be installed and environmental permits obtained before disturbing soils to comply with regulations and prevent off-site sedimentation.
The excavation must be completed to the required depth and grade before foundation footings can be formed, reinforced, and poured, as footings bear directly on the excavated subgrade.
If required by depth or soil conditions, shoring systems must be installed after excavation begins but before deep excavation is complete to prevent collapse of adjacent soils.
If groundwater is encountered during excavation, dewatering systems (wellpoints, sump pumps) must be installed to lower the water table before further excavation and foundation work can proceed.
The excavated subgrade must be trimmed, leveled, and compacted after excavation is complete to provide a uniform bearing surface for the foundation system.
A blinding layer or mud slab is often placed over the excavated subgrade after excavation to provide a clean, level working surface for rebar placement and foundation concrete.
Spoil disposal cannot begin until excavation has generated the spoil material to be disposed of.
In some sequences, spoil disposal (removal of excess material) must be completed before backfilling can occur, as backfilling uses suitable imported material after spoil is cleared.
Spoil must be removed from site before final grading can shape the site to its finished contours.
Vegetation clearance and topsoil stripping must be completed before spoil disposal can begin, as these activities generate the initial spoil material for disposal.
Final landscaping and revegetation can only begin after spoil has been disposed of and the site is cleared of excess material.
Excavation must be completed to create the trench or area where sheet piles will be installed, providing access and proper depth for piling.
Site preparation (clearing, grading, surveying) is necessary to establish a stable and level working platform for sheet piling equipment.
Underground utilities must be located and relocated if necessary to avoid damage during sheet pile driving and to ensure safe working conditions.
Sheet piles form a watertight barrier; once installed, dewatering can be performed inside the enclosed area to create a dry work environment for subsequent excavation and foundation work.
After sheet piles are driven and form a retaining wall, excavation can safely proceed inside the shored area without risk of cave-in or soil collapse.
The ground must be cleared and graded before soldier piles can be installed, as soldier piles require a stable, prepared ground surface for proper placement and alignment.
Surveying and layout marking must be completed before soldier pile installation to ensure accurate positioning of the piles at the correct locations and elevations.
Underground utilities must be located and protected before driving or drilling soldier piles to avoid damaging existing services and to ensure worker safety.
Lagging boards or panels are placed between soldier piles as excavation progresses; soldier piles must be installed first to provide the vertical support elements between which lagging is placed.
Excavation between soldier piles can only proceed after the piles are installed because the soldier piles serve as the primary shoring system that supports the excavation walls.
The ground must be excavated and prepared to the required elevation and configuration before ground anchors can be installed, as anchors require access to the subsurface for placement and drilling.
For tied-back anchors or those embedded in foundation elements, the foundation concrete must be placed and sufficiently cured to provide a structural connection point for the anchor head.
Ground anchors must be fully installed and grouted before tensioning and load testing can commence, as testing applies design loads to verify anchor capacity.
Ground anchors must be in place and secured before backfilling against the retained structure, as anchor heads and bearing plates would otherwise be inaccessible or buried.

While not always physically mandatory, it is standard practice to complete ground anchor installation (tieback system) before erecting superstructure above to ensure lateral stability of the excavation support system.
Geotechnical survey data (soil type, stratification, groundwater conditions) is required as input before bearing capacity can be calculated or assessed.
The site must be cleared of vegetation and topsoil removed to expose the subgrade for testing and observation.
The allowable bearing capacity determined from the assessment is a critical design parameter for sizing foundations.
If bearing capacity is insufficient, ground improvement (e.g., compaction, grouting, soil replacement) must be designed and executed before foundation construction.
The bearing capacity result dictates whether the natural ground is adequate or needs improvement; excavation can only proceed once the assessment confirms the soil conditions.
Vegetation and topsoil must be cleared before batter/slope excavation can commence to expose the ground surface and prevent organic material from being mixed into slope soils.
Survey control points and batter peg lines must be set out to define the exact alignment, width, and gradient of the slope before excavation begins.

General mass excavation to approximate levels is typically done first so that batter trimming can be performed as a final shaping operation, though in some sequences batter excavation may proceed concurrently.
The batter slope must be cut to its final profile before erosion control measures such as hydroseeding, jute matting, or shotcrete are applied to the exposed slope surface.
Surface and subsoil drainage systems along the batter slope can only be installed after the slope has been excavated to final design levels and shape.
Excavation must be completed to create the space and stable ground surface where benching (cutting steps into earth or rock) can be performed.
Vegetation, topsoil and debris must be removed before benching to expose the underlying soil or rock surface for step cutting.
Survey markers and slope geometry must be established to guide the correct elevation, width, and angle of each bench.
Benching creates the stepped slope surface; subsurface drains or ditch liners are placed on or behind the benches to control water runoff and prevent erosion.
After benches are cut, retaining walls or stabilization measures (e.g., soil nails, shotcrete) are built against or on the benched slope to secure it.
Site clearing removes vegetation, debris, and topsoil, providing a clean and stable surface for compaction to occur on native soils.

Excavation removes unstable or unsuitable soils and creates the required subgrade levels; compaction cannot begin until the excavation has reached the design depth and exposed the proper base material.

Any underground utilities, drainage pipes, or conduits must be laid in trenched areas before final compaction to ensure the compacted fill properly encases and supports these elements; compacting after trenching would disturb the trench backfill.

A well-compacted subgrade is essential to provide uniform bearing capacity for concrete slabs and foundations; pouring concrete over uncompacted soil would risk differential settlement and structural failure.
Compaction provides the stable, dense base layer required to support pavement structures; paving over inadequately compacted subgrade leads to premature cracking and rutting.
The construction site must be prepared, boundaries marked, and access roads established before any excavator can be brought onto site for operation.
The excavator must be delivered to site, assembled, and undergo pre-operation checks before it can begin its digging or earthmoving work.
Excavation by the excavator is a prerequisite for creating trenches or foundation pits that are needed for subsequent construction steps.
The material excavated by the excavator must be removed or stockpiled before backfilling or disposal operations can commence.
Once all excavation work is complete, the excavator must be decommissioned, cleaned, and removed from site to allow subsequent construction activities to proceed without obstruction.

The site must be cleared, levelled, and excavated before dumpers/tipper trucks can access and begin hauling materials. Earthmoving and site preparation create the initial cut/fill conditions that dumpers transport material for.
Dumpers and tipper trucks require stable, well-constructed haul roads and access routes to safely travel and deliver materials to designated areas. Without roads, trucks cannot navigate the site.

The primary function of a dumper/tipper truck is to transport and dump materials (soil, aggregate, debris) at designated locations. This cannot occur until the truck itself is operational and on-site.
Dumpers deliver fill materials (e.g., soil, gravel) that are then spread and compacted by compaction equipment. The dumping operation must precede compaction activities.
Tipper trucks often deliver aggregates and raw materials to concrete batch plants, or transport ready-mix concrete to pour locations. Concrete placement depends on timely delivery by tippers.
The area must be cleared, leveled, and graded before compaction can begin, as uneven ground or debris would prevent effective compaction.

All underground utilities (pipes, conduits, cables) must be laid and backfilled before compaction of the surrounding soil can be performed, otherwise compaction would damage or crush buried utilities.
Concrete slabs, asphalt paving, or floor toppings must only be placed on properly compacted subgrade/base material to prevent differential settlement and cracking.

Compaction quality control tests (e.g., nuclear density gauge, sand cone test) must be performed immediately after compaction to verify that the required density is achieved before proceeding with subsequent layers or covering.

The next layer of aggregate (sub-base or base course) can only be placed and compacted after the previous layer has been compacted to specification, ensuring structural integrity of the pavement or foundation system.
