Soil conditions, groundwater levels, and bearing capacity data from site investigation are essential inputs for designing temporary works such as shoring, falsework, and excavations.
The permanent structure's geometry, loads, and layout dictate what temporary supports, formwork, and falsework are needed; temporary works cannot be designed without knowing the permanent design.
Materials such as beams, props, and shoring components cannot be ordered until the temporary works design specifies quantities, sizes, and specifications.
Construction and erection of temporary works on site cannot proceed without an approved design detailing arrangement, connections, and safety requirements.

successor: Permit / Approvals (e.g., Building Control, Temporary Works Coordinator Check)
rationale: Regulatory and independent design checks (e.g., by a Temporary Works Coordinator) require the completed design documentation before approval and permitting can be granted.
A detailed site assessment and investigation must be completed to identify the type, extent, and distribution of contaminants before any remediation strategy can be designed and implemented.
The remediation approach (e.g., excavation, bioremediation, soil washing) must be selected and designed based on site investigation findings before physical remediation work can commence.
Environmental regulatory approvals, permits, and a remediation action plan must be obtained from authorities before any remediation works can legally begin.
After remediation activities are completed, validation sampling and testing must be performed to confirm that contamination levels have been reduced to acceptable standards.
The site can only be backfilled, re-graded, and restored to its intended use (e.g., construction platform, landscaping) after contaminated material has been removed or treated.
Topsoil stripping exposes the archaeological horizon, which the watching brief then monitors for archaeological features or finds.

General site clearance (removal of vegetation, debris, surface obstructions) must be completed before the watching brief can commence to ensure the ground surface is visible and accessible for archaeological monitoring.
The watching brief identifies and records archaeological features; if significant remains are found, full archaeological excavation may need to follow to recover data before construction proceeds.

The watching brief must be completed (or at least be ongoing) before ground disturbance works (e.g., trenching, foundation digging) can proceed, as the brief is intended to monitor and record any archaeological finds during such works.
Archaeological monitoring must be completed before permanent foundation construction begins to avoid destroying unrecorded archaeological remains.
Site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and obstructions before piling equipment can access and operate on site.
Accurate survey and marking of pile positions is required before piling can commence to ensure piles are placed in correct locations.
Piles must be installed and cured before integrity testing can be performed to verify their quality and load-bearing capacity.
Pile caps are constructed on top of completed piles to distribute loads from the superstructure; piles must be in place first.
Bored piles provide deep foundation support; general excavation for ground beams or raft foundations proceeds only after piles are installed to avoid destabilizing uncured piles.
The site must be cleared of debris, vegetation, and topsoil, and rough grading completed to provide a level working platform for piling rigs.
Pile positions must be accurately marked on the ground based on the structural drawings before the piling rig can commence drilling.
Soil conditions and ground strata must be known to determine pile depths, diameters, and reinforcement requirements.
Pile caps are structural elements cast on top of completed piles to distribute loads; they cannot be formed until the piles are installed and concrete has cured.
Quality assurance tests (e.g., sonic logging, static or dynamic load tests) are performed after piles are installed to verify their integrity and load-bearing capacity.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and access routes established before micro piling equipment can be positioned and operated safely.
Accurate survey and marking of pile locations are required before drilling or installing micro piles to ensure correct positioning and alignment.
Underground utilities must be located and diverted if necessary to avoid damaging existing services during micro piling operations.
Micro piles must be installed and cured (if grouted) before load testing can be performed to verify their load-bearing capacity.
The micro piles must be fully installed before pile caps can be cast over them to transfer structural loads from the superstructure to the piles.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and surveyed before any piling can begin to ensure proper placement and alignment of screw piles.
Underground utilities must be identified and marked to avoid striking gas, water, electrical, or communication lines during pile installation, which could cause safety hazards and project delays.
Pile caps are structural elements that sit on top of the completed screw piles to distribute loads; they cannot be installed until the piles are fully driven and tested.
Load testing must be performed after pile installation to verify that the screw piles meet the required bearing capacity and design specifications before proceeding with further construction.
Ground beams (or foundation beams) tie the pile caps together and form the base for the superstructure; they can only be constructed after screw piles are installed and approved.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and existing structures before ground investigation can commence to ensure unobstructed access for drilling and testing equipment.
Initial topographic and boundary surveys are needed to define the site layout and locate safe access points and investigation positions before ground investigation begins.
Underground utilities must be identified and marked or diverted before ground investigation to prevent service strikes, which are a major safety hazard.
Borehole logs, soil test results, and groundwater data from ground investigation are essential inputs for foundation and geotechnical design.
Foundation type, depth, and reinforcement design depend on soil bearing capacity and stratification data obtained from ground investigation.
Piles must be driven/installed into the ground first before they can be cropped or cut to the required level.
Pile heads must be cropped/cut to expose reinforcement and achieve the correct level before pile caps can be constructed on top.
Pile cropping is typically done before integrity testing (e.g., sonic logging or dynamic testing) to expose the pile head, though in some sequences testing may occur before cropping.
Cropped piles at the correct cut-off level are required before ground beams connecting pile caps can be constructed.
The pile concrete must have cured and achieved sufficient strength before cropping/cutting can occur to avoid damaging the pile.
The ground must be surveyed, cleared, and leveled before any piling work can commence to ensure proper placement and stability.
Steel tubes must be fabricated, delivered, and inspected on site before they can be driven or installed as piles.
The exact positions for each pile must be marked on the ground based on engineering drawings before pile driving begins to ensure correct alignment.
After pile installation, load tests (e.g., dynamic or static) must be performed to verify the pile's load-bearing capacity before proceeding to superstructure construction.
Pile caps that distribute loads from the superstructure to the pile group can only be constructed after the steel tube piles are fully installed and cut to the required elevation.
If piles need to be extended by welding additional sections, this splicing operation can only occur after the initial pile segment is driven into the ground.
Casing is installed into a pre-drilled borehole or foundation pit; the foundation excavation must be completed to provide the space for casing installation.
The ground surface must be cleared and leveled before any drilling or casing placement can occur.
Accurate positioning and alignment must be established before casing installation to ensure correct placement.
Casing acts as a form or liner for the foundation; concrete is poured inside the casing after it is in place.
Reinforcing steel is placed inside the installed casing before concrete is poured, so casing must be in place first.
The ground must be cleared, graded, and excavated to the required elevation before pile installation can begin, as piles are driven into undisturbed or prepared soil.

Soil properties (bearing capacity, soil type, depth to competent strata) must be known to determine the required pile length, helix configuration, and torque requirements for helical screw pile design.
The exact positions of each helical screw pile must be marked out on site before installation begins to ensure proper alignment with structural loads and foundation layout.
After installation, discrete piles must be load-tested (compression/tension/lateral) to verify capacity meets design specifications before proceeding with further foundation work.
Pile caps or grade beams that transfer loads from the structure to the piles can only be constructed after the helical screw piles are installed and their cut-off elevations are verified.
The pile shoe must be designed and selected based on the pile type, soil conditions, and load requirements before it can be fabricated or installed.
The physical pile shoe component must be manufactured or procured before it can be attached to the pile for driving.
The pile shoe must be attached to the tip of the pile before pile driving begins, as the shoe protects the pile tip and aids penetration during driving.
Pile driving with the shoe must be completed before load testing can be performed on the installed pile.
The pile (with its driving shoe attached) must be fully driven and installed before the pile cap is constructed on top of it.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and obstructions before pile boring equipment can access and operate on the ground surface.
Pile locations must be accurately marked and surveyed before boring/excavation begins to ensure piles are placed in the correct positions as per design drawings.
The borehole/excavation must be completed before the steel reinforcement cage can be lowered into it.
Concrete cannot be poured until the borehole/excavation is fully formed and ready to receive the concrete.
Pile integrity testing (e.g., sonic logging or load testing) can only be performed after the pile borehole has been excavated, reinforced, and concreted.
The ground must be cleared and excavated to the required depth before pile installation can begin, as piles are placed into the ground.
Pile locations must be accurately surveyed and marked on site before drilling or driving piles to ensure correct alignment and positioning.
Understanding soil conditions and load-bearing capacity is essential before designing and installing piles to ensure adequate foundation depth and safety.
Pile caps are constructed on top of completed piles to distribute loads from the superstructure to the pile group; piles must be installed first.
Load testing (e.g., static or dynamic) on completed piles must be performed before proceeding with further foundation works to verify design capacity.
Ground beams or foundation slabs are cast after piles are installed and connected via pile caps, as they transfer structural loads to the piles.
The site must be cleared of debris, vegetation, and existing structures before ground improvement work can begin, as vibro-compaction equipment needs unobstructed access to the treatment area.
Accurate survey and setting out of column locations is required to ensure stone columns are installed at the correct positions and spacing as per design.
Plate load testing or other ground verification must follow stone column installation to confirm that the ground improvement has achieved the required bearing capacity and settlement criteria.
Foundation excavation must only proceed after ground improvement is complete, as the improved ground provides the uniform bearing stratum for foundation construction.
Depending on the construction sequence, if excavation occurs before stone column installation, backfilling and re-compaction may be needed after columns are placed to restore working grade levels.
The ground surface must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and uneven terrain to provide a level, stable working platform for the heavy pile rig to traverse and operate safely.
Pile positions must be marked out according to engineering drawings before the rig can begin drilling or driving piles at the correct locations.
Underground utilities (gas, water, electrical, telecom) must be located and marked to avoid striking them during pile installation, which could cause dangerous service disruptions or accidents.
The pile rig is the equipment that performs the pile installation and driving work; the rig must be set up on site before driving operations can commence.
Pile caps are constructed on top of the completed piles to distribute loads; the piles (installed by the rig) must be finished before pile cap construction can begin.
The site must be cleared of obstructions, debris, and existing structures to provide a clean, accessible area for accurately marking out pile positions.
A control grid and survey benchmarks must be established first so that the pile layout can be accurately set out from known reference points.
Temporary access routes and working platforms need to be in place to allow survey and piling equipment to reach and operate at the pile layout areas.
The exact positions of each pile must be physically marked on the ground before any piling rig can commence drilling or driving piles.
Setting out pile positions allows the team to verify that no underground utilities intersect with pile locations, enabling utility marking and protection before drilling begins.

Rebar scheduling depends on finalized structural engineering drawings and rebar detailing (including bar bending schedules) that specify the sizes, shapes, quantities, and placement of reinforcing steel.
While rebar ordering can begin before scheduling is complete, detailed scheduling optimizes cutting lists and reduces waste, making prior procurement planning a soft preference.
Fabrication of rebar (cutting, bending, tagging) requires the bar bending schedule and cutting lists produced during scheduling as its direct input.
Rebar cannot be delivered until it has been scheduled, fabricated, and the delivery quantities/locations are known from the schedule.
While formwork can sometimes start independently, coordinating rebar placement with formwork sequencing is easier once the rebar schedule is finalized, so this is a soft preference.
Formwork provides the mold and support structure for concrete; rebar must be placed inside the formwork before concrete is poured, so formwork must be in place first.
For slabs and walls, the footing or foundation must be prepared and cured to provide a clean, level base for rebar placement.
Post-tensioning tendons are often placed after or concurrently with rebar, but rebar cage must be in place before tensioning operations begin.
Rebar placement must be inspected for correct spacing, size, and ties before concrete is poured to ensure structural integrity.

Formwork provides the mold or containment structure into which rebar is placed and tied. Rebar tying cannot begin until the formwork is installed because the rebar needs to be positioned within the forms.
Individual rebar bars must be placed and roughly positioned in the formwork before they can be tied together with wire. Tying is done after bars are laid out.
If post-tensioning tendons are used, they are typically installed and stressed after the rebar cage is fully tied and in place, as the tied rebar cage provides the structural framework.
Concrete cannot be poured until the rebar is fully tied into a stable cage. The tied rebar provides the tensile reinforcement within the concrete; pouring must wait for rebar completion.

While inspections can partially overlap, it is preferred to complete rebar tying before MEP rough-in so that conduit and embedments can be placed and tied to the rebar cage, and so that inspectors can verify rebar placement without obstruction.
Cables must be cut, stripped, and cleaned before mechanical splicing can be performed to ensure proper fiber alignment and connector fit.
The outer protective sheath of the cable must be removed to expose the individual fibers for splicing.
Fibers must be cleaned of debris and inspected for damage before splicing to ensure low-loss connections.
After the mechanical splice is made, a protective sleeve or housing must be placed over the splice point to shield it from environmental damage and stress.
The integrity and quality of the mechanical splice must be verified through optical loss testing after splicing is complete.

predecessor: Cleaning and Preparation of Steel Surfaces
rationale: The steel surfaces must be cleaned of rust, mill scale, dirt, and grease to ensure proper weld penetration and joint quality. Welding on contaminated surfaces leads to defects like porosity and weak bonds.

predecessor: Cutting and Beveling of Steel Members
rationale: Steel members must be cut to the correct length and the ends must be beveled to create the proper weld groove geometry that allows full penetration welding for a structurally sound splice.

predecessor: Alignment and Fit-Up of Steel Sections
rationale: The two steel sections being spliced must be aligned, leveled, and properly gapped (fit-up) before welding can begin. Misalignment would result in structural eccentricities and unacceptable welds.
Tack welds are required to temporarily hold the aligned sections in position before full welding proceeds. Without tacking, the sections would shift during the welding process.

After welding is complete, the splice must be inspected visually and via NDT methods (ultrasonic, magnetic particle, or radiographic testing) to verify weld integrity, penetration, and absence of defects before the connection is encased or covered.

While coating can be applied after welding, it is a soft preference because the weld area may need to cool and be cleaned before painting. However, painting is not strictly necessary for structural integrity of the splice itself, but it is needed for corrosion protection.
Cover blocks are placed on top of the steel reinforcement to ensure proper concrete cover; therefore, the steel reinforcement must be installed first.
Formwork provides the mold into which concrete is poured; cover blocks are placed inside the formwork against the reinforcement, so formwork must be in place first.

Cover blocks maintain the correct spacing between reinforcement and formwork; concrete is poured after cover blocks are positioned to ensure the reinforcement is properly encased with the required cover.
Concrete curing is part of the post-pouring process; pouring must occur after cover block installation, and curing follows pouring. Cover blocks ensure correct cover depth before concrete hardens.
Steel rebars must be cut and bent to the required dimensions and shapes before they can be assembled into a reinforcement cage.
The reinforcement cage must be fully assembled before it can be lifted and placed into the designated position (e.g., pile bore or column formwork).
The reinforcement cage must be in place before concrete can be poured around it to form the reinforced concrete element.
Spacers or chairs must be placed on the rebars during assembly to ensure proper concrete cover is maintained.
Typically formwork is installed after or simultaneously with cage placement, but in some sequences formwork may partially precede cage positioning; this ordering depends on the construction method.

The substrate (e.g., roof deck or wall surface) must be clean, dry, and properly prepared before starter bars can be installed, as starter bars are typically the first layer of a system that attaches directly to the substrate.

Proper layout lines and reference marks must be established on the substrate to ensure accurate alignment and positioning of starter bars, which define the starting point for subsequent panel or cladding installation.
Starter bars serve as the anchoring base for the first row of panels or cladding; panels cannot be installed until the starter bar is securely fastened in the correct position.
Starter bars often incorporate or align with drip edges and base flashings; the starter bar must be installed first so that flashings can engage properly and provide weatherproofing continuity.
All subsequent rows of cladding or panels interlock with or rest upon the starter bar installation; the starter bar establishes the level and alignment for every row above it.
Vertical reinforcement bars must be in place first so that shear links/stirrups can be tied around them to form the reinforced cage.
Stirrups and shear links must be fully tied and secured around vertical reinforcement before formwork is erected around the reinforcement cage.
Concrete cannot be poured until the full reinforcement cage (vertical bars + shear links/stirrups) is in position and inspected.
Cover blocks are placed after stirrups are tied to ensure proper concrete cover between the reinforcement and the formwork.
In beam construction, bottom reinforcement is often placed before stirrups are slid into position, though sequence can vary by method.
The formwork must be in place to shape and contain the concrete or material that forms the anchorage and hook.
Steel reinforcement bars must be placed and tied within the formwork before the anchorage and hook can be formed, as the reinforcement provides structural integrity to the anchorage.
The substructure or base concrete must be sufficiently cured to provide a stable foundation for forming the anchorage and hook element.
The anchorage and hook must be fully formed and cured to provide the fixed end for post-tensioning tendons to be stressed against.
The formed anchorage and hook serve as the bearing point for hydraulic jacks during the stressing operation; this can only proceed after the anchorage is complete.
Rebar must be cut and bent to the designed shapes and sizes before it can be inspected for compliance with drawings and specifications.
All reinforcement bars must be placed, positioned, and tied in their final locations before inspection can verify cover, spacing, and alignment.
Formwork must be set and braced in position before reinforcement is placed and inspected, as the rebar is placed inside the forms.
Concrete can only be poured after the reinforcement has been inspected and formally signed off, to ensure structural integrity and compliance before embedment.
Final closure and adjustment of formwork (e.g., closing side forms) often occurs after rebar inspection is complete, just before concrete placement.
Concrete cover spacers are placed on or around rebar to ensure proper concrete coverage. Therefore, the rebar must be installed first before spacers can be attached or positioned.

Formwork defines the outer boundary of the concrete element; spacers are placed within the formwork to maintain the correct distance between rebar and the form face. The forms must be in place to properly position the spacers.

Cover spacers ensure the rebar is positioned at the correct depth within the concrete section. Concrete must be poured after spacers are installed to lock the rebar in its designed position and achieve the required cover.
Curing can only begin after concrete has been poured over the spacers. The spacers are embedded in the concrete pour, which must be completed before curing starts.
The foundation must be prepared and cured before any mechanical bar coupler can be installed, as the coupler requires a stable base.
Rebar must be cut, shaped, and positioned before mechanical bar couplers can connect them together.
Mechanical bar couplers must be fully installed and secured on the rebar before concrete can be poured, as the couplers become embedded in the concrete.
If post-tensioning is part of the design, the mechanical bar couplers must be in place to join the tendon segments before tensioning forces are applied.
Rebar placement must be inspected and approved prior to installing mechanical bar couplers to ensure correct alignment and spacing for the couplers.
Bar Bending Machine requires steel reinforcement bars (rebar) as input material; therefore, rebar must be delivered, unloaded, and stored on site before bending operations can commence.
A stable, level foundation or concrete plinth is required to install and anchor the bar bending machine securely, preventing vibration and misalignment during operation.
Bar bending machines are electrically powered; the electrical panel, wiring, and appropriate circuit breakers must be installed and energized to operate the machine.
The bar bending machine must be operational to produce bent reinforcement shapes (stirrups, hooks, bends) which are then used in assembling reinforcement cages for columns, beams, and slabs.

While bending and cutting are often integrated, if cutting is a separate step, bars should be cut to length before or after bending depending on workflow; this is a soft preference as sequence can vary by site practice.
Rebar must be placed and aligned in position before tying can begin, as the tying tool is used to secure already-positioned rebar.
The rebar tying tool is the implement used to perform the tying operation; tying cannot commence without the tool being available and ready.
Rebar must be cut and bent to the required shapes before it can be placed and subsequently tied with the tying tool.
Once rebar tying is complete (using the tool), formwork can be installed around the finished rebar cage; this is a logical sequence but formwork may be partially installed earlier in some methods.
Concrete cannot be poured until the rebar cage is fully tied and secured using the tying tool, as the rebar must be in its final bound configuration to receive concrete.
A stable, level foundation and prepared site are physically required to support the heavy bar cutting machine and ensure accurate cutting operations.
Electrical power supply must be available at the machine location before the bar cutting machine can be connected, tested, and operated.
Reinforcing steel bars (rebar) must be staged and accessible near the cutting machine to enable continuous cutting operations once the machine is installed.
In rebar fabrication workflows, bars are typically cut to length first on the cutting machine before being transferred to the bending machine for shaping; this is a physically required sequence.
Cut reinforcing bars are a prerequisite for assembling and tying rebar cages; the cutting operation must supply the individual bar lengths before assembly can commence.

Concrete cover verification must be performed after rebar is placed and tied, as it measures the distance from the rebar surface to the formwork (or finished concrete surface), ensuring sufficient protective cover before concrete is poured.
Formwork defines the outer boundary of the concrete element; concrete cover (distance from rebar to the form face) cannot be verified until the formwork is in position.

Concrete cover must be verified and accepted before concrete is poured, because once concrete is placed, the cover cannot be adjusted; inadequate cover compromises durability and reinforcement protection.

If cover verification identifies insufficient or excessive cover, rebar adjustments (spacers, chairs, repositioning) must be made before concrete placement; this is a sequential dependency within the quality control process.
Formal inspection sign-off (by engineer or QA/QC) typically occurs after cover verification is documented, and before proceeding to pour concrete.
Anti-crack reinforcement (such as steel mesh or fibers) must be placed or detailed over the fresh or hardened concrete slab/pavement to control cracking; thus the concrete base must be poured first.
A stable, compacted subgrade is required before any concrete working surface is placed and before anti-crack reinforcement is detailed on top.
Formwork defines the shape and edges of the concrete element; anti-crack reinforcement is placed within the formwork prior to concrete pouring.
The anti-crack reinforcement (e.g., wire mesh or rebar) must be fully positioned and tied down before concrete is poured over it to ensure it is embedded correctly.

While joints are typically cut after concrete placement, detailing of anti-crack reinforcement influences joint layout; however joint installation after detailing is a soft preference as joints can be adjusted independently.
Formwork must be in place and aligned to provide the correct geometry and support for tendon placement within the concrete member.
Rebar cage must be partially or fully assembled to define the tendon duct paths and provide anchorage zones before tendons can be threaded.
Ducts or sheathing must be placed to create the void through which the pre-stressing tendons will be threaded; tendons cannot be installed without ducts in place.
Tendons must be installed inside the ducts prior to concrete placement so they become embedded and bonded (or remain unbonded) within the structural element.
Once tendons are positioned within the ducts, they can be tensioned (stressed) either before pouring (pre-tensioning) or after concrete gains sufficient strength (post-tensioning).
Rebar must be placed and fixed in position before any corrosion protection coating or treatment can be applied to the reinforcement bars.
Corrosion protection treatment must be applied to rebar before concrete is cast around it, as the concrete encasement makes later access to the reinforcement impossible.

predecessor: Reinforcement Surface Cleaning (e.g., wire brushing, abrasive blasting)
rationale: The reinforcement surface must be cleaned of rust, dirt, oil, and mill scale to ensure proper adhesion of the corrosion protection coating.

In some sequences, formwork can be pre-installed before corrosion protection is applied; however, where the coating needs unobstructed access, formwork is best erected after protection is complete. This is a soft preference based on access requirements.
If corrosion protection involves applying an epoxy coating or galvanizing, the coating itself must be allowed to cure/harden before subsequent handling or concrete placement.
Architectural design must be approved before structural drawings can be interpreted, as the structural design is based on the architectural layout and loads.
Soil conditions and site data are required to properly interpret structural foundation and framing requirements.
The structural drawings must be interpreted to understand the reinforcement layout and formwork dimensions before placing them on site.
Concrete cannot be poured until the structural drawings are interpreted to ensure correct dimensions, reinforcement, and placement.
Steel members must be fabricated and erected based on the interpretations of the structural drawings to ensure proper fit and load paths.
The formwork must be erected and stable before wire mesh can be fixed onto it, as the mesh is laid over the formwork surface.
Wire mesh panels or sheets need to be cut and prepared to the required dimensions before they can be positioned and fixed onto the formwork.
Concrete cannot be poured until the wire mesh reinforcement is properly fixed in place within the formwork, as the mesh provides structural reinforcement within the concrete.

Additional steel bars (e.g., main reinforcement) are typically placed after or concurrently with wire mesh fixing, but in some sequences bars may be placed first; this is a soft preference based on typical workflow.
Inspection of the fixed wire mesh and overall reinforcement must occur after fixing and before concrete pouring to ensure compliance with design specifications.
Steel columns require a stable, cured concrete foundation or footing to bear the load and provide anchorage; columns cannot be installed without a finished base.
Anchor bolts must be accurately positioned (surveyed and set) into the foundation before steel column base plates can be bolted down.
Foundation concrete must reach sufficient compressive strength before it can safely support the steel column loads and bolt tightening torques.
Steel beams and girders connect directly to columns; the columns must be plumbed, aligned, and temporarily braced before beams can be placed between them.
Permanent or temporary bracing between columns is installed as soon as columns are erected to ensure structural stability before additional loads are applied.
Steel beams must be supported by columns and foundations; the structural vertical elements must be in place before beams can be erected.
Concrete columns must achieve sufficient strength before they can support steel beam loads; otherwise structural integrity is compromised.
Accurate positioning marks and alignment checks must be completed to ensure beams are placed at correct coordinates and elevations.
Metal decking and formwork for concrete slabs are placed on top of steel beams; the beam framework must be in place first.

successor: Steel Beam Connection Welding and Bolting
rationale: Final bolting and welding of beam-to-beam and beam-to-column connections can only be completed after beams are positioned and temporarily secured.

Steel decking is installed on top of and supported by the structural steel frame. The steel beams and columns must be erected first to provide the structural support for the decking to be placed upon.
Steel decking serves as the formwork and reinforcement for the concrete slab. The concrete is poured over the completed steel decking, so the decking must be fully installed and secured first.
After steel decking is laid, reinforcing steel bars or welded wire mesh are placed on top of the decking before concrete is poured. The decking must be in place to support the reinforcement.

Conduits, pipes, and electrical boxes that are embedded in the concrete topping slab must be roughed-in on top of the steel decking before the concrete pour. The decking provides the working surface for this rough-in work.

While fireproofing can be applied after decking installation, it is often a soft preference to spray fireproofing on the underside of the steel deck after installation but before ductwork and ceilings are installed, to avoid later access issues.
Foundation must be in place to support and anchor the moment frame, which transfers loads to the foundation.
Moment frames consist of columns and beams rigidly connected; columns must be erected first to provide vertical support for beam connections.

successor: Bolt Tightening and Welding of Connections
rationale: After moment frame members are assembled into position, the connections must be permanently tightened/welded to achieve the rigid joint behavior required by the frame design.
Floor decks and slabs are typically placed after the moment frame structure is erected to allow the frame to support the formwork and wet concrete.

Exterior cladding can be installed after the frame is assembled to enclose the building, though in some sequences cladding may start earlier on lower floors; this is a preferred sequence for safety and access.
Braced frames require a stable foundation to support and anchor the steel members; the foundation must be cured and ready before any frame assembly can begin.
Braced frames typically rely on columns being erected first so that beams and bracing members can be connected between them to form the lateral load-resisting system.

predecessor: Concrete Slab or Floor Deck Placement
rationale: While often done after frame assembly for access, in some sequences a working platform or slab is placed beforehand; this is a soft preference depending on staging.
Cladding systems are attached to the structural frame; the braced frame must be fully assembled to provide the support structure for exterior walls and facades.
The roof structure typically bears on or connects to the braced frame; the frame must be complete to support roof loads and provide lateral stability during roof installation.
Steel columns provide the vertical support structure that trusses rest upon; trusses cannot be erected without columns in place to bear their load.
Foundations must be completed to anchor the columns and ultimately support the load from the trusses.
Cranes and rigging equipment must be in place to lift and position truss members safely.
Roof decking is installed on top of the trusses to create the roof surface; trusses must be in place first.
Permanent bracing and stability connections between trusses must be installed after trusses are erected to ensure structural integrity.
High-strength bolting connects steel members that must first be erected and positioned before bolts can be installed.
Steel members must be properly aligned and fitted together before bolts can be inserted and torqued.
Bolted connections must be fully installed before they can be inspected for torque and tension compliance.
Structural loads can only be applied after bolted connections are completed to ensure proper load transfer through connections.
Fireproofing is typically applied after bolting is complete, though in some cases fireproofing of some areas may proceed before all bolting is finished.
Pipe spools must be fabricated in the shop before they can be brought to the field for welding into place.
The pipe materials and weld consumables must be procured and delivered to the site before any field welding can commence.
The trench or area where pipes will be laid and welded must be excavated and prepared before field welders can access and join pipe sections.
Welds must be completed before they can be inspected and tested (e.g., radiography, ultrasonic testing) to verify integrity.
Field weld joints must be completed and cooled before applying corrosion coating or wrapping over the weld area.
Shear studs are welded through the metal deck to the steel beams below. The metal deck must be installed first to provide the surface and access for stud welding.
Shear studs are welded directly to the top flange of steel beams. The steel beams must be erected and in place before shear studs can be installed.
Shear studs are embedded within the concrete slab to create composite action. The concrete cannot be poured until the shear studs are installed.
While typically rebar is placed after studs, in some sequences welding studs through rebar mats is possible. However, standard practice places studs first to avoid welding near or through rebar.
Welded shear studs must be inspected (e.g., bend testing, visual inspection) before concrete is placed, as the studs become inaccessible after pouring.
The foundation must be fully cured and structurally complete before plumbing systems can be installed, as plumbing pipes are often embedded in or run beneath the foundation slab.
The ground must be excavated and prepared before any underground plumbing lines (drainage, water supply) can be laid and aligned.
Wall and floor framing must be in place to provide structural support and chase cavities for running plumbing pipes, vents, and drain lines through the building.

While electrical and plumbing can sometimes be run concurrently, it is typically preferred to complete plumbing rough-in first to avoid conflicts in wall cavities and to coordinate pipe and conduit placement.

successor: Slab on Grade or Under-Slab Inspection
rationale: All plumbing lines laid under the slab must be inspected and approved before concrete is poured, making the plumbing installation a necessary predecessor to slab pouring.
Plumbing pipes, fixtures, and rough-in work must be completely installed, tested, and inspected before walls are closed up with drywall or plaster to avoid costly future access issues.
Final plumbing fixture installation requires that the rough-in plumbing (pipes, drains, supply lines) is already in place, aligned, and connected to the main system before fixtures can be mounted.
Steel connections require a stable and level foundation to anchor and support the structural steel elements.
Steel members must be fabricated, cut, drilled, and delivered to site before connections can be assembled and bolted or welded.
Steel connections (e.g., bolting or welding of beams to columns) must be completed before the overall steel frame erection and alignment can progress to subsequent tiers or bays.
Completed steel connections must be inspected (e.g., torque checks, weld inspection) before any load is applied or subsequent construction proceeds.
Steel connections must be fully tightened and approved before metal decking and concrete slabs are placed over the steel frame, as the connections provide structural support for the deck.
Anchor bolts are embedded in concrete foundations; foundation excavation must be completed to form and pour the footing or foundation where bolts are placed.
Formwork must be in place to define the shape and position before anchor bolts are set into the wet concrete.
Anchor bolts must be positioned and secured in the formwork before concrete is poured so they become embedded in the cured foundation.
Anchor bolts provide the connection point for steel columns; columns can only be erected once bolts are set and concrete has cured enough to support the load.

successor: Leveling and Alignment of Base Plate
rationale: The anchor bolts must be in place to receive the base plate and allow final leveling and alignment of the structural steel.
Steel girders must be fabricated, inspected, and delivered to the construction site before they can be installed. This is a physical prerequisite as the girder must exist on-site.
The supporting piers or abutments must be fully cured and ready to bear load before a steel girder can be placed on them. The girder cannot be installed without a stable support structure.
The steel girders must be in place and properly connected to serve as the structural support framework before concrete deck slabs can be poured or formwork can be placed on top of them.

successor: Cross Bracing and Lateral Bracing Installation
rationale: Cross bracing and lateral bracing are typically installed after the main girders are positioned to stabilize the structure and resist lateral loads. The girders must be erected first to provide the framework onto which braces are attached.

Final welding, bolting, and connection detailing between girder segments and to piers must occur after the girders are placed in their designated positions to ensure proper alignment and structural continuity.
Foundation must be prepared and cured before erection bolts can be installed to ensure stable anchorage.
Anchor bolts must be set in the foundation to provide the base for erection bolts to be mounted.
Erection bolts must be in place and secure before steel columns can be erected and bolted to them.
The structural frame assembly depends on erection bolts being installed as the primary connection points.
Design development must be sufficiently complete to establish the general design intent, specifications, and performance criteria before shop drawings can be prepared and submitted for review.
A submittal log tracking all required shop drawings must be established before any individual shop drawing can be formally reviewed and tracked through the approval process.
The subcontractor or supplier responsible for fabricating the component must be under contract before they can prepare and submit shop drawings for review.
Shop drawings must be prepared by the subcontractor/fabricator showing detailed fabrication and installation information before they can be submitted for review and approval by the design team.

Fabrication and manufacturing of the component cannot begin until the shop drawings have been reviewed and approved, as they contain the detailed dimensions, materials, and methods required for fabrication.
Procurement of component-specific materials (e.g., steel beams, ductwork, piping) often depends on approved shop drawings to confirm exact quantities, sizes, and specifications.
Steel columns and frame require a stable, cured concrete foundation to bear on; without foundations, steel cannot be erected safely or accurately.
Access roads, staging areas, and crane pads must be prepared before steel deliveries arrive to enable safe unloading, storage, and handling.
Steel members must be delivered and sorted in the correct erection sequence before they can be lifted, positioned, and bolted into place.
Steel frame must be erected first to provide the supporting structure upon which metal decking is placed.
Welding and quality inspection of steel connections can only occur once steel members are delivered, sequenced, and erected.
Bolts must be installed in place before their tension can be verified; verification is impossible without installed bolts.
Tension verification ensures bolts are properly tightened to design specifications before the structure can safely bear loads.
The joint cannot be accepted as complete until bolt tension has been verified to meet required specifications.
If verification reveals insufficient tension, corrective torqueing or adjustment must follow as a subsequent step.
Proper surface preparation and cleaning of bolt threads and contact surfaces must be completed before accurate tension verification can be performed.
The site must be prepared and accessible before any safety planning specific to steel erection can be conducted, as planning requires knowledge of site conditions, layout, and access points.
The steel erection plan and safety planning depend on the finalized engineering designs, including member sizes, connections, and lifting points, which are established during the design phase.

predecessor: Procurement and Delivery of Structural Steel
rationale: Safety planning must account for the specific materials, their weights, dimensions, and handling requirements; thus, procurement and delivery information is needed before detailed safety planning can occur.
The physical erection of structural steel cannot commence until the safety plan has been fully developed, reviewed, and approved to ensure all hazards are identified and controls are in place.
Crane placement, lifting plans, and equipment selection are directly informed by the safety planning outputs, including load calculations, fall protection measures, and exclusion zone requirements.
The area must be excavated to expose the adjacent earth faces or below-grade construction zone before shoring can be installed to support those faces.
Existing utilities must be located, marked, and protected or relocated before excavation and shoring work begins to avoid damage and ensure worker safety.

Shoring provides the lateral support needed to safely excavate and form foundations adjacent to existing structures or deep excavations; foundations cannot be safely poured until the excavation is secured.

While dewatering can sometimes begin before shoring, it is typically more effective to install and operate dewatering after shoring is in place to control groundwater inflow into the shored excavation.

Waterproofing of below-grade walls can only begin after the shoring system is installed and the excavation is complete, as the waterproofing membrane is applied to the shoring or retained wall surface.
Brick walls require a solid, cured foundation to bear their weight and prevent settlement cracking.
The concrete slab or footing must be fully cured to provide a stable base before brickwork commences.
A damp-proof membrane must be laid on the foundation before brick laying to prevent moisture rising through the brickwork.
Fresh mortar must be prepared and available to bond the bricks as they are laid.
Scaffolding is typically erected before brick laying for elevated work to provide safe working platforms, though ground-level courses may start without it.
Freshly laid brickwork must be left to cure and gain strength before being loaded.
Lintels are placed over openings after the brick courses on either side are complete to support the brickwork above.
Electrical conduits can be chased into walls after brickwork is complete, but pre-planning avoids unnecessary cutting.
Internal plastering or external rendering must follow brick laying so that the brick surface is fully available for bonding.
Window and door frames are generally installed after brickwork reaches the appropriate openings, allowing the brickwork to frame the openings precisely.
Concrete block walls must be built on a solid, cured foundation. The foundation must be poured and fully cured to gain sufficient strength to support the load of the blockwork.
After laying concrete blocks, the mortar joints between blocks need time to cure and gain strength before any further loads are applied or subsequent work begins.
Lintels are placed over openings as the block laying progresses or immediately after; the block walls must be laid up to the required height before lintels can be positioned.
Chases, conduits, and pipes are installed within or against the block walls after the walls are erected, as the blockwork provides the structural backing.
Internal and external wall finishes are applied only after the block walls are fully laid, aligned, and the mortar has cured sufficiently to provide a stable surface.
Mortar must be properly mixed and prepared before it can be applied for jointing and pointing work.
The masonry units must be laid in place before their joints can be pointed or finished with mortar.
After the mortar is applied for pointing, the joints must be tooled and profiled while the mortar is still workable.
Once joints are pointed, the mortar needs proper curing to achieve strength and durability.
Excess mortar smears on the masonry face should be cleaned off after pointing, though in some cases cleaning can be done concurrently or delayed.
Reinforced masonry walls and structures require a stable, level foundation to bear the load. The foundation must be fully cured and ready before any masonry work begins.
Load-bearing reinforced masonry walls must be completed to support the roof structure above them.
External plaster or render is applied over finished reinforced masonry surfaces for protection and aesthetics; it cannot be applied before the masonry is complete.
While some conduits can be embedded during masonry, the bulk of first-fix services typically follow after walls are erected to allow chasing and installation within the completed masonry.
Window and door openings are formed within reinforced masonry walls; frames are installed after the masonry around the openings is complete and cured.
Masonry veneer requires a structural backing or framed wall sheathing to be installed first in order to provide a stable, load-bearing surface for attachment.
The weather-resistive barrier (house wrap) must be applied over the sheathing before masonry to protect the structure from moisture infiltration and provide drainage behind the veneer.
Foundation and footings must be completed and inspected to ensure they can support the additional load of the masonry veneer before veneer installation begins.
Flashing and weep holes at the base of the veneer are installed concurrently or immediately after the first course of masonry to direct moisture outward and prevent water damage.
Adjacent exterior finish systems typically begin after the masonry veneer is in place to ensure a clean interface, proper overlapping, and a weathertight seal between materials.
The foundation provides the structural base and load-bearing support for the cavity wall; walls cannot be built without a solid foundation in place.
A damp proof course must be laid on the foundation before wall construction begins to prevent moisture rising through the wall via capillary action.
The ground floor slab or oversite concrete must be prepared to provide a stable working platform and to establish floor levels before wall construction commences.

Wall ties are installed progressively as the cavity wall is built up to connect the inner and outer leaves, but the overall process of tie installation is part of the wall construction sequence and continues after the basic wall structure is started.
Lintels are installed above doors and windows once the cavity wall reaches the height of those openings, providing structural support for the masonry above.
Cavity wall insulation is installed after the wall is built up to a certain height, typically as the construction progresses or after completion, to fill the cavity space.
The roof structure is erected after the cavity walls are built to their full height to provide support for roof trusses or rafters and to enclose the building.
Windows and doors are installed after the cavity wall and lintels are in place, as the openings are formed within the wall structure.
Fresh mortar must be prepared and available before tuckpointing can begin, as the process involves applying new mortar to raked joints.
Old deteriorated mortar must be removed from joints to a sufficient depth (typically 3/4 to 1 inch) before new mortar can be applied during tuckpointing.

predecessor: Joint cleaning (wire brushing and blowing out dust)
rationale: Joints must be free of dust, debris, and loose particles to ensure proper bond between the new mortar and the substrate.
Safe working access at height must be established before tuckpointing work can commence on elevated wall sections.
After tuckpointing mortar is applied, it must be left to cure properly (typically 2-7 days depending on conditions) before any further work that could disturb it.

successor: Final cleanup and pointing tool finishing
rationale: After the tuckpointing mortar has been placed, the joints must be tooled and finished to match the historic profile before the mortar sets.

While often recommended after tuckpointing, sealants can be applied after the mortar has fully cured; however, many preservationists prefer to avoid sealants, so this is a soft preference rather than a hard constraint.
Masonry walls and structures must be fully constructed and cured before any waterproofing or damp-proofing can be applied to them.
Foundations and slabs must be poured, cured, and set before waterproofing is applied, as waterproofing often extends from the foundation to the masonry walls.
Waterproofing and damp-proofing of below-grade masonry must be fully applied and cured before backfilling against the foundation/walls, to avoid damaging the waterproofing layer.
Interior finishes are best done after waterproofing is complete to prevent moisture damage, though this is a soft preference as interior work can proceed in dry conditions.
Exterior cladding and siding are installed over or after waterproofing is complete to ensure the building envelope is properly sealed against moisture intrusion.
The arch abutments and foundations must be built to support the arch's lateral thrust and vertical loads before arch construction can begin.
Temporary centering or falsework is required to support the arch stones (voussoirs) during construction until the keystone is placed and the arch becomes self-supporting.
Stones or bricks must be cut to precise wedge shapes (voussoirs) as per the arch geometry before they can be laid in the arch ring.
The falsework can only be removed after the arch is fully constructed and the keystone is set, allowing the arch to become self-supporting.
The arch ring must be completed before backfilling over the arch or building spandrel walls above the arch haunches to avoid applying unbalanced loads during construction.
Lintels are structural elements installed over openings (doors, windows) in masonry walls; the supporting masonry walls must be built first to provide the bearing surface for the lintel.
The building foundation and footings must be complete to support the walls that will receive the lintels.
Lintels transfer loads from the structure above (roof or upper floor slabs) to the surrounding walls; thus the lintel must be in place before the slab or roof above is poured or constructed.
Finishing work around openings typically follows lintel installation; though not physically mandatory, it is the logical sequence to achieve a finished appearance.
Scaffolding requires a stable, level base to ensure safety and structural integrity; uneven or unprepared ground would pose significant risks.
Scaffold for masonry work is typically erected adjacent to the building structure, which must have its foundations completed to provide the necessary support and reference points.
Masonry work requires scaffolding to provide safe access at height; walls cannot be safely or efficiently built without the scaffold in place.
It is more efficient to lift bricks, blocks, and mortar to scaffold platforms after the scaffold is erected, though materials could theoretically be staged beforehand in some cases.
A formal inspection must occur after erection and before any workers use the scaffold to ensure it meets safety regulations and load-bearing requirements.
Wall ties and masonry anchors are embedded into or attached to the masonry as it is laid; the masonry wall must be partially erected to receive the ties/anchors.
Masonry walls require a stable foundation or slab to bear on; foundation work must be complete before masonry wall construction (and thus wall tie installation) can begin.
Many masonry anchors tie the brick veneer back to the structural steel frame; the steel frame must be erected to provide the backing structure for anchors.
Wall ties are installed as the masonry is laid; once the wall reaches full height and ties are placed, pointing and finishing work can proceed.
Sealant joints at masonry interfaces (e.g., shelf angles, expansion joints) are finished after the masonry and its anchors are fully installed.
The masonry walls must be built up to the lintel level first, as the lintel is installed to span openings (doors/windows) within or on top of the masonry walls.
Temporary formwork and shoring must be placed beneath the lintel location to support the wet masonry/mortar and the lintel itself until it gains sufficient strength.
Reinforcing bars (rebar) must be positioned within the formwork before pouring concrete or placing masonry lintel blocks to ensure structural integrity.
The lintel must be fully cured and capable of bearing load before any roof, floor slab, or upper wall loads are applied above the opening.
The lintel provides the structural header over the opening; window or door frames are installed after the lintel is in place and cured to ensure proper fit and load transfer.
A stable, level foundation or concrete slab must be fully cured and prepared before any masonry work begins, as the bond pattern is laid upon this base.
Fresh mortar must be mixed and ready to use for laying bricks or blocks according to the bond pattern; the mortar is the binding material applied during the process.
After laying bricks/blocks in the specified bond pattern, the mortar joints must be allowed to cure and gain strength before any further loads are applied.

While some reinforcement can be placed as masonry progresses, final reinforcement such as bond beams or vertical rebar installation typically follows the completion of the bond pattern up to a certain height.

Final tooling and pointing of mortar joints (e.g., concave, V-joint, flush) should be done after the masonry bond pattern is laid but while the mortar is still slightly plastic to ensure proper finish and weather resistance.
Bolts must be fully tightened before grout filling to ensure that the grout does not interfere with the bolt tensioning process and that the connection is secure.
Grout must be filled before it can begin curing; curing is a time-dependent process that starts after the grout is placed.
Surface finishing after grout filling is preferable to ensure smooth and even surfaces, but in some cases finishing can be done beforehand if grout is applied carefully.
Anchors must be installed and positioned correctly before grout is poured to encase and secure them in place.
Formwork must be erected and sealed to contain the grout during the filling operation; without formwork the grout would not be held in place.

Masonry units (bricks, blocks, stones) must be fully installed, mortared, and set before any surface treatment or cleaning can be applied. Cleaning before installation is complete would damage fresh mortar and interfere with the construction process.
Safe access at height is required for workers to perform surface treatment and cleaning of masonry walls, especially on upper elevations.
Mortar joints must be sufficiently cured (typically 7-28 days) before chemical cleaning or pressure washing to avoid washing out fresh mortar or causing damage to the joints.
Surfaces must be clean and free of dust, efflorescence, and debris before waterproofing or sealant can be applied, otherwise sealants will not adhere properly.

successor: Final Inspection & Quality Control of Masonry
rationale: Surface treatment and cleaning should be completed before final inspection, as the cleaned surface allows for accurate visual assessment of masonry quality, joint condition, and overall finish.
Structural steel framing must be in place to provide the supporting structure onto which the roof deck is installed.
Load-bearing walls that will support the roof deck must be completed to provide proper bearing and anchorage.
The roof deck provides the structural substrate required before any waterproofing or membrane layers can be applied.
Insulation is installed over the completed roof deck to provide thermal performance and a base for the roofing system.
Mechanical equipment, rooftop ducting, and electrical conduits are typically installed after the deck is in place, though some prep work can run in parallel with careful coordination.

The concrete substrate must be fully cured (typically 28 days) and properly prepared (cleaned, patched, and primed) to ensure proper adhesion of the waterproofing membrane. Applying membrane to uncured or unprepared concrete can cause delamination and failure.
A primer coat must be applied to the prepared concrete surface to promote bonding of the waterproofing membrane. Without primer, the membrane may not adhere correctly, leading to voids and leaks.

Sub-slab drainage pipes and French drains must be installed before the membrane is applied, as the membrane will cover and seal the slab, making post-installation impossible without damaging the waterproofing layer.

A protective layer (e.g., drainage board, geotextile fabric, or rigid insulation) must be placed over the cured waterproofing membrane to shield it from puncture during backfilling and subsequent construction activities.
Backfilling against foundation walls or slabs can only proceed after the waterproofing membrane is fully applied and cured, to protect the membrane from damage and ensure a continuous water barrier.
Insulation is typically applied onto or within structural walls, roofs, or decks. The structural substrate must be in place to provide a stable base for insulation installation.
A weather-resistant barrier or air barrier is often installed before insulation to protect the building envelope from moisture intrusion, which could compromise insulation performance.
Electrical wiring, conduits, outlet boxes, and plumbing pipes that run within walls must be roughed-in before insulation is placed, as insulation would obstruct access to these installations.
A vapor retarder/barrier is typically applied over the insulation layer (on the warm side of the wall) to prevent moisture diffusion, requiring insulation to be in place first.
Interior finish materials like drywall are installed after insulation to enclose the insulation within the wall cavity and provide a finished interior surface.

Underlayment must be installed over a clean, dry, smooth deck surface. The deck sheathing (e.g., plywood or OSB) must be fully installed, fastened, and free of debris or moisture to provide a stable base.

predecessor: Ice and Water Shield Installation (in valleys/eaves)
rationale: In cold-climate applications, ice and water shield membrane is typically applied directly to the deck before synthetic or felt underlayment to prevent ice-dam water intrusion at eaves and valleys.

Underlayment provides the first waterproof layer; flashings for roof penetrations (plumbing vents, chimneys, skylights) are installed over the underlayment to properly shed water onto the underlayment surface.

successor: Roof Covering Installation (shingles, metal panels, tile)
rationale: The primary roof covering (shingles, metal, or tile) must be installed over the underlayment to protect it from UV degradation and wind uplift, and to provide the final weatherproof layer.

Drip edge is often installed before underlayment (at eaves) and after underlayment (at rakes); where it is installed after, it must wait for underlayment to be in place to be properly fastened and sealed.
Shingles require a solid, continuous roof deck (typically plywood or OSB sheathing) as a nailing surface; without the deck, there is no structural substrate to attach shingles to.
Ice and water shield or felt underlayment must be laid over the roof deck before shingles to provide a secondary moisture barrier; shingles are installed directly on top of the underlayment.
Drip edge flashing is installed along roof eaves and rakes before shingles to direct water away from the fascia and prevent rot; shingles overlap the drip edge.

Valley flashing, pipe boot flashing, and other roof penetrations must be integrated as shingles are laid (step flashing interleaved with shingle courses), but after the base shingle layer is installed the final flashings and counter-flashings are completed. However, the primary ordering is that roof-integrated flashings are installed concurrently with or directly after shingle courses.

Ridge cap shingles and ridge vents are the final step on the roof ridge, installed only after all field shingles on both slopes have been applied, to ensure proper overlap and weatherproofing at the peak.
The structural steel frame provides the load-bearing support system onto which metal roofing panels are attached. Roof panels cannot be installed without the underlying structural framework in place.
A roof deck (typically steel decking, plywood, or OSB) must be installed over the structural framing to provide a solid substrate for the metal roofing panels to be fastened to.
Water-resistant or vapor-permeable underlayment must be laid over the roof deck before metal panels are installed to provide a secondary moisture barrier and protect the deck from condensation.
Flashing, ridge caps, gable trim, and other edge trims are installed after the metal panels are in place to seal joints, edges, and penetrations against water intrusion.

While gutters are typically installed after roofing is complete to ensure proper alignment with the roof edge, this can sometimes be done concurrently or in slightly different order depending on design. It is a strong preference for quality and alignment, but not a strict physical impossibility if done otherwise.
Tile roofing requires a solid, continuous roof deck or sheathing surface to be installed first, as tiles must be fastened to a stable substrate for structural integrity and waterproofing.

A waterproof underlayment (e.g., felt paper or synthetic membrane) must be installed over the roof deck before tiles are placed to provide a secondary moisture barrier and protect the structure from water ingress.
Drip edge metal flashing must be installed along eaves and rakes prior to tiling to direct water away from the fascia and into the gutters.
Field tiles must be installed first to establish the roof plane, after which ridge and hip tiles can be set to cap the intersections and complete waterproofing.

Gutters are typically installed after tiling to ensure proper alignment with the roof edge and drip edge; however, this is a soft preference as gutters could occasionally be installed before tile work if careful coordination is used.
The roof deck provides the structural base and substrate that the membrane is applied onto; without a completed deck, the membrane cannot be installed.
Insulation boards are typically placed over the roof deck and beneath the membrane; the membrane must be installed after the insulation to create a continuous thermal and waterproofing layer.
Proper sloping or tapered insulation must be in place to direct water toward drains before the membrane is applied, ensuring positive drainage and preventing ponding.

Membrane installation creates the waterproof barrier; drainage components (e.g., roof drains, scuppers) must be integrated into and flashed to the membrane, requiring the membrane to be installed first for proper watertight connections.
Edge flashings, counter-flashings, and metal trims are installed over and sealed to the membrane to provide weatherproof terminations; the membrane must be in place to receive these flashings.

Sheathing provides the structural base and weather-resistant barrier upon which flashing is installed. Flashing must be applied over properly installed sheathing to ensure a continuous water-resistive barrier.

predecessor: Window and Door Rough Opening Preparation
rationale: Rough openings for windows and doors must be framed and prepared before flashing can be installed around them to direct water away from the openings.
Flashing is integrated into the weather-resistive barrier system and must be in place to direct water outward before siding or cladding is applied over it.
Flashing around rough openings must be installed before windows and doors are placed to ensure that the pan flashing and sill flashing are properly integrated behind and under the units.

Step flashing, counterflashing, and base flashing at roof-to-wall intersections must be installed before the final roofing materials (shingles, tiles, etc.) are laid to ensure water is directed properly.
The ridge cap sits at the peak of the roof and requires a complete, stable roof deck to be installed as the underlying structural support.
Roof underlayment (felt or synthetic) must be laid over the roof deck before ridge caps are installed to provide a waterproof barrier beneath the ridge.
Ridge cap shingles are the final roofing layer at the peak; all field and hip shingles must be installed first so that ridge caps can overlap and seal the topmost edge.
The ridge cap completes the roof assembly; the final roof inspection must occur after ridge caps are in place to verify proper installation and weatherproofing of the roof system.

While gutters can technically be installed before ridge caps in some cases, it is standard practice to complete all roofing work including ridge caps first to avoid damaging gutters with falling debris or tools.
The roof deck provides the structural base onto which ventilation components (fans, ducts, vents) are mounted; without a deck, there is no surface to attach the system.
Roof framing defines the cavity spaces where ventilation ducts and equipment must be routed; ventilation work cannot begin until the roof structure is in place.
Sheathing provides the enclosed plane through which roof vents penetrate and to which flashing boots attach; ventilation components cannot be installed on an open-framed roof.
Underlayment is laid over the sheathing and around vent penetrations; vent hoods and stacks must be in place and flashed before underlayment can be properly sealed around them.

Finished roofing materials (shingles, tiles, or metal panels) are installed over the underlayment and terminate at vent openings; vents must be fully installed and flashed before the finish layer is applied to ensure watertight integration.
Gutters are attached to the roof fascia or edge, which requires the roof sheathing to be in place to provide structural support and proper alignment.
The underlayment prevents water ingress behind the gutter system and must be installed before gutters to ensure proper waterproofing integration at the roof edge.
Gutters are directly mounted onto fascia boards, so fascia boards must be installed first to provide the mounting surface and ensure correct gutter alignment.

successor: Downspout Drainage System / Drainage Pipe Connection
rationale: Downpipes must be installed before connecting them to underground drainage pipes or splash blocks to ensure water is properly channeled away from the building foundation.

While gutters are often installed after siding is complete, in some sequences gutters can be installed before upper wall cladding to allow behind-gutter flashing integration; however, it is generally preferred to install siding first to avoid damaging gutters during siding work.
The roof structure must be framed to provide the structural support and opening for skylight and roof light installation.
Roof decking must be installed to create the substrate and opening through which skylights are mounted.
Underlayment must be applied before skylight installation to ensure proper flashing integration and weatherproofing around the skylight curb.
Skylight flashing must be installed immediately after the skylight is placed to seal the gap between the skylight and the roof, preventing water intrusion.
Roofing materials like shingles or tiles are installed up to and around the skylight after it is in place, with flashing integrated properly.

The vertical load-bearing walls or columns must be completed to provide support for the roof trusses and structural frame. Roof loads transfer down through the frame to the walls and foundations, so walls must be in place first.
Roof trusses or structural framing must be erected before any roof decking or sheathing can be installed, as the sheathing is attached directly to the top chords of the trusses or frame.
Roof underlayment is laid over the roof sheathing, which itself requires the trusses/frame to be in place. The structural frame provides the substrate for all subsequent roof layers.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work in attic or above-ceiling spaces is typically easier after the roof trusses are installed to allow access from above, though some work could be done from below. This is a practical sequencing preference rather than a strict physical requirement.

Soffit and fascia are exterior trim components that attach to the edges of the roof structure. The roof frame and trusses must be complete to define the roof edge geometry and provide attachment points.
Roof flashing is installed on top of the roof deck or sheathing to seal joints and transitions; the deck provides the structural base required for flashing attachment.

Roof underlayment (e.g., felt or synthetic membrane) is laid over the roof deck before flashing to provide a water-resistant barrier; flashing is then installed over or integrated with the underlayment for proper drainage and sealing.
Flashing must be installed at roof penetrations, valleys, and edges before the final roofing material is applied, as the shingles/tiles are laid over the flashing to create a watertight overlap.
Drip edge flashing along eaves must be in place before gutters are installed, as gutters attach below or integrate with the drip edge to direct water flow.
While insulation can technically be installed before or after, it is often preferred to complete flashing and roofing first to ensure a dry interior environment before insulation work commences.
Ridge vents are installed along the ridge line of the roof, which requires the roof framing (rafters or trusses) to be in place to provide structural support.
The roof deck (sheathing) must be installed to provide the surface onto which the ridge vent is mounted and to define the ridge gap opening.
Ridge vents are installed at the roof peak before the final ridge shingles or cap shingles are applied, as the vent is covered by the cap shingles for weatherproofing.

While ridge vent installation typically precedes final ridge flashing/cap installation, in some roof systems the vent and flashing are integrated; however, it is a strong preference that ridge vent goes before final cap shingles.

Proper attic ventilation design requires intake vents (soffit vents) to be installed before or concurrently with exhaust vents (ridge vents) to ensure balanced airflow, though the ridge vent can technically be installed first.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and topsoil, and excavated to the required depth before the substrate (subgrade) can be accessed and prepared for construction.

Underground utilities (water, sewer, gas, electrical conduits) must be relocated or installed in the rough before substrate preparation, as disturbing the prepared substrate to install utilities would compromise its compaction and grade.

The prepared substrate (compacted soil, gravel base, or vapor barrier) serves as the load-bearing surface directly beneath the concrete slab or foundation; concrete cannot be poured until the substrate is properly graded, compacted, and approved.

Rigid insulation boards or other under-slab insulation materials are placed directly on top of the prepared substrate before any floor slab is poured, so insulation placement requires a complete and level substrate.

Vapor retarders or waterproofing membranes are laid directly onto the prepared substrate to prevent moisture migration; these materials cannot be installed until the substrate is smooth, compacted, and free of sharp debris that could puncture the membrane.
Framing requires a stable, level base; the foundation or concrete slab must be fully cured and set to provide the structural support for wall and floor framing.
Any plumbing lines that run beneath the slab must be installed before the slab is poured and certainly before framing begins, as they cannot be accessed afterward.
Termite pre-treatment of the soil under the slab must be completed before any wood framing is placed to prevent future infestation.
The roof structure (rafters or trusses) is part of the framing system; roof sheathing and roofing materials are applied directly onto the roof framing after it is erected.
Exterior wall coverings (plywood, OSB, siding) are attached to the exterior side of the wall framing and cannot be installed before the frame is in place.
Electrical wiring is run through the cavities of walls, floors, and ceilings after the framing is complete, as the wires are secured to the studs and joists.
Plumbing pipes for supply and waste are installed within framed walls and floors after the framing is erected.
Insulation is placed into the wall and ceiling cavities created by the framing; the framing must be complete to define these cavities.
Drywall is attached directly to the framing members (studs, furring strips); the framing must be in place to provide the nailing surface.

The weather-resistive barrier (WRB) must be applied directly over the structural sheathing (such as plywood or OSB) to protect the building from moisture infiltration. Sheathing provides the nailable substrate and structural backing required for WRB attachment.
