Wall framing must be completed and inspected before sheathing is installed, which in turn supports the WRB. Framing provides the structural skeleton to which sheathing is attached.

WRB is installed before windows and doors so that the barrier can be integrated with proper flashing details at rough openings, ensuring a continuous water-resistant layer behind and around fenestrations.
The WRB serves as the secondary moisture barrier behind the exterior cladding. Siding or cladding is installed over the WRB to provide the final exterior finish and primary weather protection.

If exterior rigid insulation is used, it is typically applied over the WRB. However, some wall assemblies place insulation behind the WRB — this ordering is a soft preference based on the specific assembly design, not a physical necessity.
The cladding panels are attached to the structural frame; therefore, the frame must be erected first to provide a supporting structure.
The roof structure must be in place before cladding panels are installed to ensure weather protection and proper alignment of the building envelope.

Cladding panels form the outer skin of the building; windows are typically installed into prepared openings within the cladding system or after the cladding provides the final geometry and weatherproofing.
Cladding panels serve as the primary weather barrier; subsequent insulation and weatherproofing layers are applied over or between the cladding panels to complete the building envelope.

Once cladding panels are installed, the external scaffolding is no longer needed for facade work; however, other trades may still require access, so this is a soft preference rather than a hard constraint.
The cladding sub-frame attaches to or is supported by the main structural steel frame, so the steel frame must be erected first to provide a stable mounting structure.

predecessor: Base Building Structure (Concrete/Steel) to Floor Level
rationale: The main building structure must be complete at least up to the floor/level where cladding sub-frame will be installed to provide the supporting framework.
Cladding panels are directly attached to the sub-frame; the sub-frame must be in place to receive and support the panels.

successor: Weatherproof Membrane / Air Barrier Application (if on sub-frame)
rationale: The weatherproofing layer is typically applied over or integrated with the sub-frame before final cladding to ensure building envelope integrity.
In unitized or stick curtain wall systems, windows/glazing units are installed into or onto the cladding sub-frame after the sub-frame is erected.
The structural frame must be in place to provide the supporting structure onto which mechanical components can be fixed.
The building must be enclosed (roof and walls) to protect mechanical fixings and equipment from weather during installation.
Electrical wiring and conduit connections to mechanical equipment (e.g., fans, pumps) require the mechanical units to be fixed in place first.
Mechanical units such as air handlers and pumps must be firmly mounted before ducts, pipes, and fittings can be connected to them.
All mechanical equipment must be fully installed and fixed before the commissioning process (testing, balancing, and verification) can begin.
Corner and edge trim requires smooth, clean wall surfaces for proper adhesion and alignment. Without surface prep, the trim will not sit flush.
Trim must be installed before final paint or coating so that paint can overlap onto the trim edges for a seamless finish and to cover any fasteners.
Corner and edge trim is installed after drywall is hung, taped, and mudded to protect corners and provide a clean edge.
Ideally, corner trim is installed prior to final inspection so any defects can be corrected, but this is a scheduling preference rather than a physical necessity.
Concrete must be fully cured and the joint surfaces must be clean, dry, and properly prepared (e.g., sandblasted or wire-brushed) before any sealant can be applied to ensure proper adhesion.
Formwork must be stripped to expose the joints and gaps between concrete panels or slabs where sealant will be placed.

predecessor: Installation of Joint Backer Rod / Bond Breaker
rationale: Backer rod must be inserted into the joint before sealant application to control sealant depth, provide a backing support, and prevent three-sided adhesion.
Sealant must be fully cured before any adjacent painting or surface finishing occurs, though this is a soft preference if finishes do not directly contact the joint.
Sealant in expansion/control joints must be completed and cured before applying continuous waterproofing membranes over those joints to ensure a watertight system without trapping moisture.
The rough opening framing must be completed to provide the structural cavity and dimensions into which window and door surrounds can be integrated and fastened.
Windows and doors must be physically installed in the rough openings before the surrounds (trim, casing, flashing) can be integrated around them.
Flashing and weatherproofing around the window/door frame must be applied to the rough opening before the surround integration to ensure a watertight seal behind the trim.
Surround integration must be completed before interior wall finishes (drywall, plaster) are applied, because the surrounds define the finished edge and reveal around the window/door opening.
Exterior siding and cladding must be installed after the window/door surrounds are integrated so that the siding can be cut and trimmed neatly against the surround pieces.
Fire cavity barriers are installed within wall and floor cavities; structural framing provides the supporting framework and defines the cavities in which barriers must be placed.
MEP services running through cavities must be in place before fire barriers are installed so that the barriers can be properly sealed around penetrations, maintaining fire compartmentation.
Any gaps around penetrations through cavity barriers must be fire-stopped after the barrier is in place to ensure a continuous fire-resistant seal.
Cavity barriers must be installed and inspected before enclosing walls or ceilings are lined, as the barriers become inaccessible once linings are fixed in place.

successor: Final Inspection / Commissioning of Fire Compartmentation
rationale: The completed fire cavity barrier installation must be inspected and signed off as part of the overall fire compartmentation commissioning process.
The cladding materials must be selected and procured before they can be inspected and checked for fire safety compliance.
The cladding system must be installed before a compliance check can be performed on the installed system.

predecessor: Fire Stop Installation at Cladding Penetrations
rationale: Fire stopping measures at penetrations through the cladding must be in place to verify overall fire safety compliance.
The compliance check must be completed and passed before the cladding system can be formally approved or signed off by authorities.
If scaffolding was used for cladding work, it should remain until the fire safety compliance check is completed to allow access for inspection; dismantling should follow after the check.
All construction work must be substantially completed before quality inspection can commence, as inspection verifies the finished work.
The site must be cleaned and prepared for inspection so that inspectors can safely and accurately assess the quality of work.

predecessor: Submission of Required Documents and Test Results
rationale: Documentation (e.g., material certifications, test reports) must be submitted prior to inspection to allow inspectors to verify compliance with specifications.
After inspection, any deficiencies identified must be documented and rectified before final acceptance can be granted.
Inspection sign-off is a prerequisite for releasing final payments and closing out the project, confirming all work meets quality standards.

The panel layout and setting-out marks positions on a prepared, level substrate. Without completed foundation works or slab preparation, there is no stable surface on which to set out panel positions.

While not a strict physical prerequisite, the structural frame often defines gridlines and reference points that guide panel placement. In typical sequences, the frame is erected first to establish the building envelope.
Accurate panel layout requires a surveyed reference grid or control points to ensure correct positioning. Without these benchmarks, setting-out cannot achieve required tolerances.
The layout marks define exactly where each panel must be placed. Panel installation cannot begin until the positions have been set out on site.

Once panel positions are marked, any embedded services or blockouts within or behind panels must be positioned relative to those marks. Setting-out provides the spatial reference for MEP coordination in panels.
Structural steel must be in place before fire protection (fireproofing) can be applied to steel members.
Concealed electrical and plumbing rough-ins must be completed before sprinkler piping and fire alarm devices are installed in ceilings/walls to avoid conflicts.
HVAC ductwork must be installed before fire sprinkler piping to ensure proper routing and clearance for both systems.
Fire sprinkler heads, piping, and fire alarm devices must be installed before ceilings and drywall are closed up.

successor: Fire Alarm and Detection System Testing
rationale: The fire protection system must be fully installed before it can be tested and commissioned for functionality.
The foundation must be in place to provide a stable base and to allow for the placement of underground plumbing pipes and drainage systems before any above-ground plumbing work begins.
Rough framing establishes the structural walls, floors, and cavities through which plumbing pipes, vents, and drain lines can be routed and securely mounted before walls are enclosed.
Site excavation is needed to create trenches for underground water supply and sewer lines before any plumbing installation can commence.
Plumbing pipes and fixtures must be in place before electricians run wiring to avoid conflicts and ensure proper clearances around water lines as per code.
Plumbing rough-in must be completed and inspected before insulation is installed, so that pipes are fully accessible for inspection and any leaks can be detected before walls are sealed.
All plumbing pipes, fixtures, and connections within walls must be installed and pressure-tested before drywall can be applied to enclose them permanently.

Plumbing rough-in for floor drains and supply lines should be completed before flooring is laid, though temporary access could be arranged; this is a practical sequencing preference to avoid cutting or damaging finished floors.
Electrical rough-in work, including conduit installation and power wiring, must be completed to provide power infrastructure for BAS controllers, panels, and devices.
HVAC ductwork must be in place so that BAS sensors (e.g., temperature, humidity, pressure sensors) and actuators (e.g., damper actuators) can be installed within or adjacent to the ductwork.

All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work overhead must be complete to avoid interference and to allow BAS installers to access ceiling spaces for mounting sensors, controllers, and running low-voltage control cabling.

BAS commissioning, including point-to-point verification, sensor calibration, and control logic testing, can only begin after all BAS hardware (controllers, sensors, actuators, panels) is physically installed and wired.
HVAC system startup and air/water balancing require the BAS to be installed and operational so that control signals can be sent to equipment and system performance can be monitored and adjusted.
The building structure (walls, floors, roof) must be in place to provide physical support and enclosure for gas pipes and equipment.
Underground gas main lines and service connections must be laid before interior gas piping can be tied in.
After installation, all gas piping must be pressure-tested to verify there are no leaks before any gas is introduced or appliances connected.
Gas appliances (boilers, cooktops, heaters) can only be connected to the gas supply system after the pipes and valves are fully installed.
Building inspection authorities require proof of proper gas system installation before signing off on the project.
The building must be fully framed and enclosed (roof, walls, windows, doors) before installing hydronic heating components to protect them from weather damage and provide structural support.
Electrical supply lines and plumbing connections for the boiler, pumps, and manifolds must be roughed in before the hydronic system is installed to ensure proper utility connections.

predecessor: Slab or Subfloor Preparation (including insulation & radiant tubing embedment)
rationale: For in-floor radiant systems, the subfloor or slab must be prepared and insulation placed before the PEX tubing is laid and connected to the manifold.
Flooring materials must be installed after the hydronic radiant tubing or panels are in place to cover and protect the heating system.
The boiler, pumps, expansion tanks, and piping must be installed before the mechanical room walls are finished and closed up to allow access for connections and testing.
Structural steel must be in place to provide support and hanging points for chilled water pipes and equipment before installation can begin.
The building envelope (roof, walls, windows) must be weathertight to protect chilled water equipment and piping from weather damage during installation.
Floor slabs must be cured and ready to support the weight of chillers, pumps, and associated equipment before installation begins.
Pipe insulation must be applied after the pipes are installed to prevent condensation and thermal loss; insulation cannot be installed before piping is in place.

successor: Air Handling Unit (AHU) Connection and Commissioning
rationale: AHUs require chilled water supply and return connections to be installed before they can be connected, tested, and commissioned.
Pressure testing and flushing of the chilled water system can only occur after all pipes, fittings, and equipment are fully installed.

successor: Ceiling and Wall Finishing (in areas with overhead piping)
rationale: Overhead chilled water piping must be installed and tested before ceiling grids and finishes are closed up to avoid costly rework and access issues.
Plumbing pipes and connections must be in place before the hot water system can be connected to the building's water supply lines.
Electrical wiring, conduit, and dedicated circuit must be installed to provide power to the hot water system before it can be connected and operated.
The building structure must be framed, and the designated mechanical room or installation area must be fully enclosed and structurally ready to support the water heater.
Hot water supply lines and fixtures cannot be finalized until the hot water system is installed and connected to distribute hot water throughout the building.
Insulation and drywall work around the mechanical area should occur after the hot water system is installed to allow access for connections, venting, and inspection.
Structural framing (columns, beams, floor decks) must be in place to provide support and hanging points for overhead ventilation ducts.

predecessor: Roof Deck or Top Slab Installed
rationale: The roof or top slab must be installed to create a weathertight envelope, preventing water damage to ductwork and insulation during installation.

predecessor: Rough-in Electrical and Plumbing Above Ceiling
rationale: Electrical conduit, cable trays, and plumbing pipes that run above ceilings should be installed first to avoid conflicts and rework when ductwork is already in place.
Insulation and vapor barrier wrap must be applied after duct sections are installed and joined, as it wraps around the completed ductwork.

successor: Fire Dampers and Smoke Dampers Installation
rationale: Fire and smoke dampers are installed within or at the termination of duct runs after the main ductwork is in place.
Suspended ceilings and drywall ceilings are installed after all overhead MEP rough-in, including ductwork, is completed, to allow access for connections and inspections.
System airflow measurement and balancing can only begin once all ducts, terminals, and diffusers are installed and connected.
The pump requires a stable and level foundation or base to be installed upon; without the foundation, the pump cannot be properly mounted or supported.
Piping and plumbing connections to the pump can only be made after the pump is physically installed in its designated location to ensure correct alignment and fit.
Electrical connections and power supply wiring to the pump motor must be done after the pump is secured in place to avoid hazards and ensure proper cable routing.
Testing and commissioning of the pump can only occur after the pump is installed, connected to piping, and wired to verify its operational performance.
While it is preferable and more efficient to clear and prepare the site before pump installation, in some cases minor site work could be done concurrently or after.
Pipework must be installed, flushed, and pressure-tested before thermostatic radiator valves (TRVs) can be fitted, as the valve connects directly to the radiator and the heating pipework system.
The TRV must be mounted onto a pre-installed radiator; the radiator must be positioned and secured on wall brackets before the valve can be attached.
All valves including TRVs must be fitted before the heating system can be filled with water, vented, and commissioned, otherwise water leakage and system damage could occur.
After TRVs are installed, the system must be balanced to ensure correct flow rates and heat distribution across all radiators.
Once TRVs are fitted and operational, final system testing, customer demonstration of valve operation, and handover documentation should be completed.
VAV boxes receive conditioned air from the main supply ductwork; the main ducts must be in place to provide a connection point for the VAV box inlet.
VAV boxes require electrical power for their actuators and controllers; rough-in wiring must be completed to provide power connections at the box location.
While VAV boxes are often installed before the ceiling grid to allow access, in some sequences the grid is installed first to mark exact positions; this is a soft preference for coordination.

successor: Duct Branch Connection to VAV Box
rationale: The branch ducts that distribute air from the VAV box to the zone must be connected after the VAV box is mounted and secured in place.

successor: VAV Box Controller Programming and Commissioning
rationale: The VAV box must be physically installed and wired before its digital controller can be programmed, calibrated, and commissioned for proper airflow control.
Site must be prepared and equipment mobilized before any extraction activity can begin.
The exact location of the fan must be surveyed and marked to guide the extraction process.
The fan must be de-energized and electrically isolated to ensure safe working conditions during extraction.
The fan must be extracted before it can be inspected for condition assessment.
The extracted fan must be moved to a storage or workshop area for further handling or repair.
Removal of the existing fan creates space and access for preparing and installing a replacement unit.
Grilles and diffusers are the terminal ends of ductwork; they cannot be installed until the ductwork is in place and terminated at the correct locations.
Grilles and diffusers are typically mounted in or on the ceiling; the ceiling grid or finished ceiling surface must be installed first to provide the support and opening for the grille/diffuser.
If the grille or diffuser includes motorized dampers or integrated sensors, the rough-in wiring and control cabling should be in place prior to installation for ease of connection.
Air balancing and commissioning require all diffusers and grilles to be installed and adjusted to measure and set proper airflow rates.

Final painting and touch-up work around ceiling penetrations is typically performed after grilles and diffusers are installed to blend the edges seamlessly, though this is a finishing preference rather than a physical necessity.
Insulation cannot be applied until the pipes and ducts themselves are physically installed and in place, as insulation wraps around or covers the installed pipework and ductwork.
Pressure testing must be completed before insulation to allow for detection and repair of any leaks; insulating over untested pipes would conceal defects and make repairs difficult and costly.

After insulation is applied, it typically requires a protective cladding or finishing layer (e.g., aluminum jacketing, vapor barrier wrapping) to protect the insulation material from damage and environmental exposure.
Insulated pipes and ducts must be enclosed within ceilings or walls only after insulation is complete, as enclosing them beforehand would prevent access for insulation application and inspection.

While commissioning can partially proceed before insulation, full system performance testing (especially thermal efficiency tests) is best conducted after insulation is in place to ensure the system operates under design conditions.
Mechanical systems (HVAC, piping, pumps, fans, etc.) must be physically installed before they can be tested, balanced, and commissioned.
Electrical power supply and control wiring must be in place to run mechanical equipment during commissioning tests.
Plumbing connections to mechanical equipment (condensate drains, water supply, chilled water lines) must be complete to allow proper operation and testing.

predecessor: Completion of Structural and Enclosure Work
rationale: Building must be enclosed (roof, walls, glazing) to protect installed mechanical equipment and permit controlled testing of HVAC systems under enclosed conditions.
After commissioning identifies system performance, final adjustments (air balancing, water flow balancing, control tuning) are performed to meet design specifications.
Mechanical systems must be fully commissioned and verified operational before the building can be handed over to the owner and occupied.
BMS programming, sensor calibration, and control logic verification depend on the mechanical systems being tested and commissioned first.
Structural steel must be in place to provide support for mechanical services such as ductwork, piping, and equipment.
Concrete slabs form the floor base where mechanical equipment will be placed and through which penetrations for services will be made.
Coordination of mechanical services layout must be finalized before ductwork can be installed to ensure correct routing and avoid conflicts.
Coordination is required to determine pipe routes and locations before plumbing rough-in work begins.
Electrical conduits must follow coordinated routes established for mechanical services to avoid clashes with ductwork and piping.
Electrical rough-in (conduit, wiring, and backboxes) must be installed before power distribution boards can be mounted and connected to the building's electrical system.
Power distribution boards (e.g., panelboards, switchboards) must be energized and operational before branch circuit wiring can be connected and distributed to loads.
Final connection, termination, and testing of electrical circuits can only occur after the power distribution boards are installed and ready to distribute power.

The electrical room or designated area must have completed civil works (flooring, walls, conduits, openings) and be clean, dry, and structurally ready to support the weight and anchoring of the main switchgear.

predecessor: Main Power Cable Tray / Conduit Installation
rationale: Cable trays, conduits, and underground ducts feeding into the switchgear must be installed and aligned before the switchgear is placed, so incoming and outgoing cables can be properly terminated.
All main power and distribution cables can only be terminated and connected to the switchgear components (busbars, breakers) after the switchgear is securely installed and leveled.
High-potential testing, insulation resistance testing, breaker functional tests, and relay calibration can only be performed after the switchgear is fully installed and all connections are made.

Downstream distribution boards, motor control centers, and sub-panels receive their supply from the main switchgear; their installation and cable pulls must follow the main switchgear's position and feeder assignments.
The Sub-Distribution Board receives its power supply from the Main Distribution Board (MDB). Therefore, the MDB must be installed and energized first to provide the upstream feed for the sub-board.
Cable trays, trunking, or conduits must be routed to the sub-board location to allow cables to be pulled and terminated into the board. Without these pathways, cables cannot reach the board.

Branch circuit wiring (e.g., lighting, power socket, and equipment circuits) originates from the Sub-Distribution Board. The board must be mounted and terminated first to provide the termination point for outgoing branch circuits.

successor: Final Termination and Testing of Sub-Board Circuits
rationale: All final terminations of cables, tightening of connections, and commissioning tests (insulation resistance, polarity, loop impedance) for the sub-board's outgoing circuits can only be performed after the board itself is installed and securely fixed.

The sub-board must be physically installed, terminated, and tested dead before it can be safely energized and commissioned live. Energization is the final step after all installation work is complete.
Conduits must be installed before pulling wires through them for final circuit connections.
Rough-in wiring (running cables, installing junction boxes) must be completed before making final circuit terminations and connections.
The main electrical panel and subpanels must be installed and energized before final circuit wiring can be connected to breakers.
Final circuit wiring must be completed before the electrical inspection can verify all connections are correct and safe.
Final circuit wiring must be run to each box before outlets, switches, and fixtures can be installed and terminated.

Containment structures require a stable, level foundation to support their weight and ensure structural integrity. The foundation must be fully cured and load-bearing before containment installation can begin.
The base mat provides the structural base upon which the containment vessel or structure rests. It must be poured, cured, and inspected before containment installation.
Embedded anchor bolts, sleeves, and other connection hardware must be placed in the foundation/base mat before the containment structure can be erected and secured to the foundation.

After the containment structure is installed, it must be pressure tested and leak tested to verify its integrity and ability to contain contents under design conditions before further construction proceeds.

Thermal insulation and protective lagging are typically applied after the containment is in place to protect it and maintain thermal performance, though this can sometimes be staged depending on access requirements.
Cable trays and conduits provide the physical pathways and support systems through which cables are pulled and laid. These must be installed first to define the cable routing.
Underground duct banks form the protective enclosures for buried cables. Ducts must be in place before cables can be pulled through them.
Electrical rooms, switchgear rooms, and panel locations must be ready (walls, floors, main equipment placed) to receive cables for termination.
Cables must be pulled and laid in their final positions before they can be cut to length, stripped, terminated, and connected to equipment.
Cables must be pulled, laid, and terminated before insulation resistance tests, continuity tests, and high-potential testing can be performed to verify integrity.
Cables must be physically laid and positioned before they can be terminated and connected to equipment.
The equipment (switchgear, transformers, panels) must be installed and fixed in place before cable terminations can be made to their connection points.
Cable support systems and conduits must be in place to route and protect cables prior to termination activities.
All terminations and connections must be completed before electrical testing and commissioning can commence, as testing verifies the integrity of completed connections.
While tagging can be done concurrently, final identification labelling is typically completed after terminations are made to ensure accurate labelling of connected circuits.

The LV switchgear must be placed in a dedicated electrical room that is fully enclosed, weatherproof, and structurally complete to protect the equipment from environmental damage and unauthorized access.

predecessor: Foundation & Floor Slab for Electrical Room
rationale: The switchgear is heavy and requires a level, load-bearing concrete floor slab to support its weight and maintain proper alignment.
The LV switchgear receives incoming power from the main transformer via bus ducts or cables; the transformer must be in place to define the exact connection points and voltage parameters.

successor: Cable Pulling & Termination to LV Switchgear
rationale: Cables from downstream loads (distribution panels, MCCs) cannot be terminated until the switchgear is set and its connection points are fixed and accessible.
Distribution boards receive their supply from the LV switchgear; they cannot be energized or functionally tested until the switchgear is installed, connected, and ready to supply power.
The standby generator must be installed on a stable, cured concrete foundation pad before any electrical or fuel connections can be made to it.
The physical generator unit must be set in place and secured on its foundation before electrical wiring, fuel lines, and exhaust connections can be started.
Conduits for feeder cables between the generator and the main electrical switchboard or transfer switch must be installed in the ground or structure before the cables can be pulled and terminated.
The main switchboard and automatic transfer switch (ATS) must be installed and ready to accept incoming generator feeder connections for proper electrical integration.
All electrical, fuel, and exhaust connections must be complete and verified before the generator can be started, load-tested, and commissioned to ensure it operates correctly under load.
Power factor correction equipment must be connected to the electrical distribution system via the main electrical panels; therefore electrical panel installation must be completed beforehand.
The main power supply must be installed and energized to provide the necessary electrical input for power factor correction equipment to function and be tested.
Cable trays and conduits provide the physical pathways for power cables connecting to the power factor correction equipment; these must be in place before equipment installation.

successor: Electrical System Commissioning and Load Testing
rationale: Power factor correction equipment must be installed before the overall electrical system can be commissioned and load-tested, as it is an integral part of the power distribution system.
Installation of power factor correction equipment must be completed before final close-out of the electrical room, including sealing walls, labeling, and final inspections.
Conduit runs and electrical rough-in must be installed to provide pathways for metering equipment wiring and connections.

predecessor: Main Electrical Service Entrance / Switchgear Installation
rationale: The main service entrance and switchgear must be in place to provide the power feed that the metering equipment will monitor and measure.
Utility company must review and approve metering specifications and location before the equipment can be installed to ensure compliance with grid requirements.
Metering equipment must be installed and energized to supply power to downstream distribution panels and load centers.
Metering equipment must be in place and operational before overall electrical system testing, load verification, and commissioning can proceed.
Walls must be finished (plastered and painted) before socket outlets are installed, as the sockets need to be mounted on and flush with the finished wall surface.
Conduits for electrical wiring must be embedded in the walls during rough-in stage before socket installation, as the wiring runs inside these conduits to reach the outlet positions.
The electrical cables must be pulled through conduits to the outlet box locations during rough-in stage before the socket outlets themselves can be wired and mounted.
After installing socket outlets, the entire electrical circuit must be tested (continuity, polarity, insulation resistance) to verify safe and correct installation before the system is energized.
While technically independent, installing socket outlets before light fixtures allows a logical top-down electrical finish-out sequence and reduces risk of damaging fixtures during outlet work.

Electrical rough-in (running cables, installing junction boxes, and routing conduits) must be completed before lighting fixtures can be installed, as the wiring infrastructure needs to be in place to connect the lighting circuits.
Ceiling framing or the ceiling structure must be complete to provide a mounting surface and support for recessed lighting fixtures and ceiling-mounted light fittings.

The lighting circuit wiring must be installed and connected before final trim-out, bulb installation, and switch plate covers can be fitted, as the electrical connections need to be complete and tested.
While lighting circuit wiring must be roughed in before drywall, the final installation of decorative fixtures is often done after ceiling finishing to avoid damage from dust, mud, and paint.

After lighting circuits are installed, final connections to the panel, circuit breaker installation, and full system testing (voltage, continuity, ground fault checks) must be performed to ensure safe and code-compliant operation.
Structural framing (walls, ceilings, floors) must be in place to provide mounting surfaces and support for wiring accessories such as outlets, switches, and junction boxes.

Rough-in wiring (cables, conduit, and boxes installed within walls) must be completed before installing the final wiring accessories (outlets, switches, cover plates) that connect to and terminate those circuits.
Wiring accessories such as outlet and switch boxes must be installed and positioned before drywall is hung so that the drywall can be cut around the boxes and finished flush with them.
Cover plates, switches, and receptacle outlets should be installed before final painting or trim work so that these finishing elements can be applied up to the accessories for a clean appearance.
All wiring accessories must be fully installed before the electrical system can be tested, energized, and commissioned to ensure proper function and safety.
The electrical room must be cleared, clean, and have all necessary mounting foundations and floor drains in place before the MCC can be delivered and installed.

predecessor: MCC Foundation and Mounting Steel Installation
rationale: Concrete pads, anchor bolts, and structural steel supports must be set and cured before the heavy MCC can be offloaded and bolted into position.

predecessor: Main Power Cabling Routing to MCC Room
rationale: While rough-in of conduits and cable trays can happen before the MCC arrives, final termination cannot occur until the cabinet is in place; this ordering is a soft preference to avoid rework.
Incoming power cables and motor feeder cables can only be terminated at the MCC terminals after the unit is physically installed, leveled, and grounded.

successor: Electrical Room Lighting and Finish Work
rationale: Final painting, lighting fixture installation, and ceiling work are best completed after the large MCC is brought in to avoid damage to finishes; this is a soft preference for worksite logistics.

The VSD must be connected to an electrical power source; the panel installation provides the main electrical supply, disconnects, and overcurrent protection required before any VSD can be safely powered.

The VSD controls the speed of a specific motor; the motor must be physically installed and its nameplate data (voltage, current, frequency) confirmed so the VSD can be properly sized and configured for that motor.
Power and control cables between the electrical panel, VSD, and motor require cable trays or conduits to be installed first to provide the physical routing pathway.
The VSD enclosure must be mounted and in place before power and control cables can be pulled to its terminal blocks and correctly terminated.
The VSD must be physically installed and all electrical connections made before the unit can be powered up, parameters configured, and the drive commissioned for operation.
All rough electrical wiring, conduit, outlet boxes, and junction boxes must be installed before they can be inspected to verify code compliance.
The main electrical panel and subpanels must be installed and connected to rough wiring before inspection can verify proper installation.
Electrical inspection must be completed and certified before insulation can be installed, as insulation would cover electrical boxes and wiring, making them inaccessible for inspection.
Once electrical is inspected and certified, drywall can be installed covering the wall cavities; inspection must happen first to avoid costly removal of drywall if corrections are needed.
After the rough-in inspection is passed, final connections such as switches, outlets, fixtures, and appliances can be safely connected to the certified wiring system.
The transformer requires a solid, level concrete foundation or pad to support its weight and ensure proper alignment before installation can begin.
Incoming medium-voltage primary cables must be routed and terminated at the transformer primary compartment before the transformer is fully installed and energized.
Secondary low-voltage cables can only be connected to the transformer's secondary terminals after the transformer is set in place and secured.
All electrical tests (insulation resistance, turns ratio, winding resistance) and commissioning procedures must be performed after the transformer is physically installed and connected.
The transformer must pass all acceptance tests and commissioning checks before it can be safely energized and connected to the electrical load.
Transformer requires a stable concrete foundation to support its weight and ensure proper alignment before installation can proceed.
Crane or lifting equipment must be positioned and rigged on site before the heavy transformer can be lifted and placed onto its foundation.
The area around the transformer pad must be graded and drainage installed to prevent water accumulation that could undermine the foundation.
The transformer must be delivered to site and undergo receiving inspection (checking for shipping damage, verifying nameplate data) before it can be installed.
Primary and secondary cables can only be terminated and connected to the transformer bushings after the transformer is securely positioned on its foundation.
Bushings and surge arresters must be mounted onto the transformer tank after the unit is installed and leveled to ensure proper alignment and clearances.
Transformer oil filling, filtering, and degassing can only be performed after the transformer is installed and all bushings/accessories are in place.
Ground grid connections and bonding to the transformer neutral must be completed after the transformer is placed to ensure proper grounding system integration.
All electrical tests (insulation resistance, turns ratio, power factor, etc.) and commissioning procedures must follow after the transformer is fully installed and connected.

Type 1 or Type 2 SPDs are typically installed at the service entrance or main distribution panel. The main service equipment must be in place to define the point of common coupling where the SPD will be connected.

SPDs require a low-impedance ground path to safely divert surge currents to earth. The grounding electrode system must be complete and tested before SPD installation to ensure proper surge protection performance.
The SPD must be physically installed and connected before the panel can be fully energized and tested for final commissioning, as the SPD is a safety device that protects downstream equipment.
SPD installation is part of the complete electrical system that must be inspected for code compliance and operational readiness before the building can be commissioned or occupied.
The electrical system design must be completed to define the system configuration, equipment ratings, and protective device settings, which are essential inputs for the arc flash study.
Equipment specifications and nameplate data from procured electrical equipment are required for accurate arc flash hazard calculations.
Arc flash hazard labels and mitigation requirements identified in the assessment must be implemented during equipment installation to ensure worker safety.

Arc flash boundary distances, incident energy levels, and required PPE identified in the assessment must be used to create and install proper warning labels and safety signage on electrical equipment.
The arc flash study results inform safe work practices and protective device coordination settings that must be verified during commissioning.
Cable trays and ladders must be installed before cables are run and labelled, as they provide the physical support and routing infrastructure for the cables.
Cables must be physically pulled and installed before they can be labelled and scheduled, as labelling is applied to the installed cables.
Cables must be terminated and tested to confirm continuity and functionality before final labelling and schedule documentation can be completed accurately.
Labelling and schedules must be complete before system commissioning, as commissioning requires identified and documented cable routes and connections for testing and verification.
Labelling and schedules feed into as-built documentation, which records final cable identifications and routing for future maintenance and operations.

MEP rough-in work (pipes, ducts, conduits, cables) must be installed before fire-stopping can be applied around the penetrations, as the sealant is applied to the annular space between the penetrating item and the opening.

predecessor: Structural Wall and Floor Construction / Drywall Installation
rationale: Fire stopping is applied to gaps, joints, and penetrations in walls, floors, and ceilings. The substrate (gypsum board, concrete, masonry) must be in place before sealants and firestop materials can be installed.

Firestop sealants and caulking must be applied and fully cured before final finishes like paint are applied, as painting over uncured firestop can compromise its performance and hide visual inspection indicators.

successor: Building Pressure and Smoke Control Testing
rationale: Containment sealing ensures compartmentation; pressure and smoke leakage tests can only yield valid results after all fire-stopping and air-sealing work is complete.

successor: Final Inspection / Commissioning of Passive Fire Protection
rationale: Inspection and commissioning of fire-stopping systems must occur after all containment seals are installed to verify compliance with fire-resistance ratings and building codes.
A clean, properly prepared substrate (e.g., concrete slab, masonry, or lath) is required for the scratch coat to bond. The surface must be clean, dampened, and free of debris.
Metal or wire lath must be securely installed over the substrate before the scratch coat is applied, as the scratch coat is troweled into the lath to create mechanical bond for stucco systems.
Building paper, felt, or a weather-resistive barrier must be installed behind the lath to protect the sheathing from moisture before the scratch coat is applied.
The scratch coat must be applied and allowed to partially cure (usually 24-48 hours) before the brown (second) coat of stucco can be applied over it.
After the scratch coat is applied, it must be kept moist and allowed to cure properly (typically 24-48 hours) before subsequent coats are applied, to ensure strength and prevent cracking.
The surface must be properly prepared (cleaned, smoothed, and primed) before applying the finish coat to ensure proper adhesion and a smooth final appearance.
A primer coat must be applied and fully cured before the finish coat to ensure proper adhesion, uniform absorption, and maximum durability of the finish coat.
In multi-coat systems, the base coat must be applied and dried before the finish coat can be applied to achieve the desired color, texture, and thickness.
After the finish coat is applied, a curing or drying period must be observed before any subsequent activities can proceed to avoid damaging the fresh coating.
The finish coat must be fully applied and cured before a quality inspection can be performed to assess the final appearance and integrity of the surface.
Plaster materials (cement, sand, water, additives) must be procured and delivered to the site before mixing can commence.
Cement and sand must be properly stored in dry conditions to prevent moisture damage before being used in the plaster mix.
A reliable water supply must be established on site as water is an essential component of the plaster mixture.
Mortar mixer, measuring buckets, and mixing tools must be cleaned, assembled, and ready before batch mixing begins.
Fresh plaster mix must be applied to walls/surfaces while still workable before it begins to set and harden.
A sample of the prepared mix must be tested for consistency, slump, and setting time before full-scale application proceeds.
The surface to be plastered must be prepared (cleaned, moistened, and keyed) before plaster can be applied, but this typically occurs concurrently or just after mixing begins.
Masonry walls must be fully constructed before surface preparation can begin, as plastering is applied onto masonry surfaces.
Concrete surfaces must be adequately cured (typically 7–28 days) before any plastering preparation to ensure proper bonding and prevent cracking.
All embedded conduits, pipes, and boxes must be installed within walls before surface preparation, as plastering would cover these elements and make later installation destructive.
Surface preparation—including cleaning, dampening, and applying a bonding agent or scratch coat—must be completed before the main plastering application can begin.

successor: Installation of Plaster Beads / Corner Beads
rationale: Corner beads and plaster stops are typically fixed to the prepared surface during or immediately after surface preparation, prior to the full plaster coat application.
Lath must be attached to a structural frame (wood or metal studs), which must be fully erected and braced before lath application.
Electrical boxes and wiring must be roughed in behind the lath and within the stud cavities before the lath is installed over them.
Plumbing pipes and fittings within walls must be installed inside the stud cavities before the lath covers them, preventing costly rework.
HVAC ducts and vents within wall/ceiling spaces must be installed before lath is placed, as lath would block access to these areas.
Plaster must be applied over the lath, which serves as the mechanical key and substrate for the plaster layers to bond to.
While trim can be installed after plastering, it is logically sequenced after lath and plaster complete; however, this is a soft preference as trim work order can sometimes vary.
Painting typically occurs after plaster has cured, not directly after lath; but paint cannot be applied until plaster substrate exists, making this a derived soft preference.
Metal lath requires a structural frame (studs, joists, or beams) to be in place for attachment and support.
Metal lath serves as a substrate and reinforcement for plaster or stucco; the plaster cannot be applied until the lath is securely fastened.

successor: Metal Lath Trim / Corner Bead Installation
rationale: Trim and corner beads are typically attached directly to the lath or its supporting structure after the lath is in place to define edges and corners for plastering.
While rough-in inspections often occur before concealing work, if lath is applied over open studs, rough-in should precede lath; however, this is not a physical dependency of the lath itself.
For exterior applications, a weather-resistant barrier or sheathing should be installed behind the metal lath to provide drainage and moisture protection.
Plaster beads cannot be installed until wall framing is in place, as they attach to the framed corners and edges.

predecessor: Sheathing / Board Installation (Drywall or Base Layer)
rationale: Plaster beads are installed over the corner edges of the base layer (e.g., drywall or cement board), requiring the sheathing or board to be installed first.
Plaster beads serve as a guide and reinforcement for plaster, so the first plaster coat must be applied after beads are securely attached.
Final plaster finishing cannot occur until beads are installed, as beads define the corners and edges that are finished over.
Plaster stop beads are attached to metal stud framing to provide a termination point for plaster; without the framing in place, there is no substrate to attach the bead to.

All rough-in services (electrical, plumbing, HVAC) must be complete before plaster stop beads are installed, as these services run within the wall cavity and the bead installation would be damaged or obstructed if trades need to access the cavity later.

Plaster stop bead defines the edge boundary for plaster application; the scratch coat of plaster is applied directly up to the bead, so the bead must be in place first to act as a screed guide and termination edge.
The brown coat (second coat of plaster) is applied over the scratch coat and must also terminate at the plaster stop bead; the bead provides a straight edge and thickness guide.
The final finish coat of plaster is travelled smooth and terminates at the plaster stop bead, which provides a clean, straight edge and protects the plaster edge from chipping or cracking.
Plaster must be mixed and prepared before it can be applied using a plastering trowel.
The wall or surface must be cleaned, dampened, and prepared before plaster can be troweled onto it.
A scratch coat is typically applied first to provide a key for the subsequent finish coat applied with the finishing trowel.
The trowel is used to apply and spread plaster, after which smoothing and final leveling of the applied plaster occurs.
The trowel must be cleaned immediately after use before the plaster dries and hardens on the tool.
Mortar or plaster must be mixed and prepared before a hawk can be used to hold and apply it.
A stable work platform must be in place before a plasterer can safely stand and use the hawk to apply plaster to walls or ceilings.
The wall or ceiling surface must be clean and free of debris before plaster is applied using the hawk.
The hawk is used to hold and carry the plaster; the plaster must be transferred from the hawk to the trowel and then applied to the surface.
Plaster must first be applied (using the hawk and trowel) before it can be finished, textured, or left to cure.

The floating rule / darby is used to smooth and level the concrete surface after it has been placed. The concrete slab must first be poured and have a stable base (the foundation/slab on grade) before floating can begin.
Concrete must be poured into the forms before any floating or darby operation can be performed to finish the surface.
Screeding (striking off) the concrete to the correct grade must be completed before floating, as the darby/float is used after the initial screeding to further flatten and smooth the surface.
After floating with a darby or bull float, once the concrete has further set, steel troweling is performed to create a denser, smoother finish. Floating must precede troweling.

If a broom finish or other surface texture is desired, it is applied after floating and often after troweling. However, this is a design preference rather than a physical necessity—the broom finish could theoretically be skipped.
Sheathing provides the structural base and substrate for stucco application; stucco cannot be applied directly to framing without sheathing.
A weather-resistant barrier (building paper) must be installed over sheathing before stucco to prevent moisture infiltration and protect the structure.
Metal lath must be attached over the weather barrier to provide a mechanical key for the stucco to adhere to; without lath, the stucco will not bond properly.
After stucco is applied, it requires a controlled curing and drying period before any further work can proceed; the material must set and harden.
A finish coat (textured or colored layer) can only be applied after the base coat(s) of stucco have cured sufficiently.
Skimming (plastering/finishing) cannot begin until formwork is removed and the concrete/masonry surface is exposed and accessible for plastering.
The structural concrete walls/ceilings must be poured, set, and sufficiently cured to provide a stable substrate for skimming/plastering.
Internal blockwork or brick walls must be fully constructed before skimming can be applied to them.
First-fix electrical cables, conduits, switch boxes, and plumbing pipes must be embedded in walls/ceilings before plastering covers them up.
Window and door frames must be installed and properly positioned so that skimming can be finished neatly around their reveals and edges.
Skim coat plaster must be fully dry and smooth before paint, wallpaper, or decorative finishes can be applied.
While skimming walls/ceilings is typically done before floor finishes to avoid damaging new floors, it is a soft preference as floors can be protected if needed.
Skimming before kitchen cabinets or built-in joinery allows for neater finishes behind units, but joinery can be installed first if accurately measured, so this is a soft preference.

Venetian plaster requires a smooth, continuous substrate. Drywall must be installed and all tape joints, fastener depressions, and seams must be fully finished before any plaster application to prevent cracking and ensure proper adhesion.

A properly primed and sealed surface is required to prevent the drywall from absorbing moisture from the plaster too quickly, which would cause uneven drying, cracking, and poor workability of the Venetian plaster.

successor: Final Finish Coating/Sealing of Venetian Plaster
rationale: The Venetian plaster must be fully applied, troweled, dried, and cured before any final protective sealer or wax coating can be applied to the surface.

successor: Paint Grade Trim and Millwork Installation
rationale: While it is physically possible to install trim after plaster, it is a strong preference to complete Venetian plaster first to avoid damaging the finished plaster surface during trim installation and to achieve a cleaner edge where trim meets the plaster wall.

successor: Final Electrical and Lighting Fixture Installation
rationale: It is preferable to complete Venetian plaster before installing final light fixtures and switch/outlet covers to prevent dust from the plastering process settling on fixtures and to avoid damaging the finished plaster when mounting fixtures.
Plaster must be mixed to the correct consistency before it can be applied and begin curing.
The plaster must first be applied to the surface before the curing/hardening process can begin.
The substrate (e.g., wall, ceiling) must be clean, dry, and properly prepared (e.g., lath or base coat applied) before plaster is applied and cured.
Plaster must be fully cured and dried before any paint, wallpaper, or decorative finish can be applied; otherwise, moisture trapped in the plaster will cause finish failure.
Plaster must be fully cured to provide a stable, rigid substrate for tile installation; tiling over uncured plaster can lead to cracking and adhesion failure.
Ceiling boarding must be complete to provide a surface for the plaster cornice to be applied and adhered to.
The supporting walls and framing must be in place to define the perimeter where the cornice will be installed.
Plaster cornice must be installed and allowed to set before final painting and finishing of the ceiling and walls to achieve a clean, continuous finish.
Cornice installation creates a junction between walls and ceiling that must be finished and sealed before wall decoration to avoid damaging the fresh cornice work.
While recessed lighting can be roughed-in earlier, final trim and fitting is typically done after cornice is in place to ensure alignment and clean visual appearance.
The structural framing must be in place to provide a substrate for plaster or drywall. Plaster cannot be applied without a supporting structure.
Electrical wiring and boxes must be installed within walls before the walls are closed up with plaster or patching compound, otherwise the walls would need to be cut open again.
Plumbing pipes and fittings must be run inside walls before they are sealed with plaster patching, or the walls would need to be reopened.
HVAC ducts and registers must be installed within walls and ceilings before those surfaces are plastered or patched.
Insulation must be placed inside wall and ceiling cavities before they are sealed with plaster or patching compound.
Surfaces must be smooth and fully repaired before primer and paint are applied; painting over unpatched or unsealed plaster leads to poor finish and adhesion.

It is preferable to complete patching and any dusty plaster work before installing finished flooring to avoid dust and debris damaging the new floor, though this can be sequenced differently with protection.
Plaster repair and patching should be completed before trim and baseboards are installed, so that the plaster extends cleanly behind and under the trim pieces for a tight fit.
Tile spacers are placed between tiles during installation to maintain consistent gaps; therefore tile installation must begin before spacers can be placed.
Tile spacers create the uniform gaps needed for grout; grout cannot be applied until the tiles are set with spacers in place to ensure proper joint width.
Tile spacers must be removed after the tile adhesive has cured before grouting can be completed in some methods, or after grout has set partially; the spacers cannot be removed before being placed.
The substrate (floor/wall surface) must be properly prepared, cleaned, and leveled before any tiling work (and thus spacer placement) can begin.
Thin-set mortar or tile adhesive must be applied to the substrate before tiles are set and spacers are inserted between them.
Structural framing and rough carpentry must be complete to provide the underlying support structure and substrate for plaster mouldings and ornamental work.

predecessor: Rough Electrical / Rough Plumbing / Rough Mechanical (MEP Rough-In)
rationale: All rough MEP work must be completed before plaster moulding, as these services run within walls and ceilings that will be covered or enclosed by ornamental plaster, and accessing them later would damage the finished plasterwork.

Exterior wall sheathing and cladding must be finished to ensure the building envelope is weathertight before interior ornamental plasterwork begins, preventing moisture damage to delicate plaster finishes.
Ornamental plasterwork must be complete and fully cured before painting and finishing can begin, as paint is applied directly onto or adjacent to the plaster surfaces.

Plaster moulding work involves overhead and wall work that can generate significant debris and dust; flooring should be installed after plasterwork to avoid damage and soiling of finished flooring surfaces.

While some finish carpentry can be done concurrently, final trim pieces (such as baseboards and crown moulding interfaces) are best installed after ornamental plasterwork to ensure tight joints and proper alignment, though this is a soft preference for quality rather than a strict physical constraint.
Tile trim and edge profiles are installed after the main tile field is set, as they are used to finish and protect the exposed edges of the installed tiles.
The substrate must be properly prepared (clean, level, primed) before any tiling or trim can be applied.
Grouting is done after edge profiles are installed to seal the joints and embed the profile flanges beneath the grout line.
Typically, painting and finishing work should be completed after edge profiles are installed to avoid damaging finished surfaces and to allow clean caulking/sealing at edges.

Movement/expansion joints must be installed after the foundation or substructure is complete because the joints are designed to accommodate movement in the superstructure, and the substructure provides the stable base.

Expansion joints are typically placed at intervals within the structural frame to accommodate thermal expansion, contraction, and settlement; the main structural elements (columns, beams, slabs) must be erected first so that joint locations can be coordinated.
Exterior cladding panels and curtain walls must be installed after expansion joints are in place so that the joints can properly separate building sections and prevent stress transfer to the façade.

Interior finishes such as drywall and ceilings must be installed after expansion joints to allow for proper detailing of joint covers, control joints, and movement accommodation within finished surfaces.

Floor coverings and waterproof membranes must be installed after expansion joints to ensure that the joint system is continuous and that movement is properly accommodated without damaging the finished flooring.
The site must be cleared of obstructions, debris, and vegetation before layout and setting out can begin, as the surveying marks and pegs need to be placed on clean, accessible ground.
Accurate site survey data and soil investigation results are required to establish reference points, levels, and grid lines before setting out the building footprint.

While not strictly a physical prerequisite, having temporary site offices, storage, and welfare facilities in place enables surveyors and engineers to operate effectively before commencing layout work.
Excavation for foundations, trenches, and earthmoving operations can only begin after the building lines, grid positions, and excavation limits have been accurately marked out on site.
Foundations cannot be constructed until the exact locations, orientations, and dimensions of footings and foundation elements are established through layout and setting out.

The substrate (concrete slab or subfloor) must be clean, flat, dry, and structurally sound before any tile leveling system components can be placed. An unprepared substrate would prevent the leveling system from achieving proper alignment and could lead to failure.
The tile layout pattern and starting point must be determined before installing leveling clips or straps, as their placement depends on the grout joint positions defined in the layout.

The tile leveling system components (clips, straps, wedges) are installed concurrently with or immediately after the thin-set mortar bed is laid; however, the leveling system must be positioned before tiles are fully set so that clips/straps sit between tiles and wedges can be driven to level.

The tile leveling clips or straps must be placed under the edges of the tiles as they are being set. Tiles cannot be installed without the leveling system in place because the leveling mechanism requires the clips to be embedded in the mortar under adjacent tiles.

All tile leveling wedges and clips must be removed (typically after the mortar has cured for 24 hours) before grouting can commence. Grouting over leveling components would trap them permanently and ruin the finish.
The surface must be prepared (cleaned, leveled, and smoothed) before tiles can be cut to fit the specific dimensions of the prepared area.
The subfloor must be installed and set before tiles are measured and cut, as tile dimensions depend on the subfloor layout and dimensions.
Tiles must be selected and delivered to the site before any cutting can occur.
Tiles must be cut to size before they can be installed or adhered to the prepared surface.
Tiles must be cut and installed completely before grout can be applied to fill the joints between tiles.
The substrate must be clean, dry, and free of dust, grease, or debris to ensure proper adhesion of the adhesive or mortar.
The surface must be level and primed (if required) to provide a uniform base for adhesive/mortar application; otherwise, bonding may be compromised.
The adhesive or mortar powder must be mixed with water or additive to the correct consistency before it can be applied to the substrate.
Tiles or stones must be placed into the freshly applied adhesive/mortar bed while it is still workable to achieve proper bonding.
After application, the adhesive/mortar must be allowed to cure for a specified period before any subsequent loads or further finishing work can be applied.
A smooth, clean, level, and structurally sound subfloor or underlayment is physically required before any tile can be set, as tile cannot be laid directly on an unprepared or uneven surface.
In wet areas such as bathrooms or showers, a waterproof membrane must be installed and cured before tile bedding is applied to prevent moisture damage to the substrate.
Freshly poured concrete must be fully cured (typically 28 days) before tile is set to prevent cracking due to ongoing shrinkage and moisture release.
Grout can only be applied after tile bedding has cured sufficiently and tiles are firmly set in place, as the grout fills the joints between fixed tiles.
Sealers are applied after both tile installation and grouting are complete and fully cured, as sealing before tiles are set would be ineffective.
Surfaces must be clean, dry, and free of dust, oil, or debris for sealant to properly adhere and form a durable bond.
Primer must be applied and cured before sealant to ensure adhesion on porous or non-porous substrates.
Backer rods or bond-breaker tape must be installed in joints to control sealant depth and prevent three-sided adhesion.
Sealant must be allowed to cure undisturbed for the manufacturer-specified time before being exposed to stress, water, or paint.

Painting or finishing of adjacent surfaces should ideally be done after sealant is applied and cured to avoid contaminating the sealant surface, but this is a soft preference as painting can be done beforehand if carefully masked.
Tile sealing is applied after tiles are installed to protect the tile surface and grout from moisture and stains.
Grout must be applied and allowed to cure before sealing, as sealant applied before grouting would prevent proper grout adhesion and could get trapped under grout lines.
Grout must be fully cured and dried (typically 24-72 hours depending on product) before sealing; sealing wet grout can trap moisture, cause discoloration, and prevent proper sealant penetration.
Tile and grout surfaces must be thoroughly cleaned of dust, debris, and any construction residues before sealant application to ensure proper adhesion and uniform coverage.
Caulking at perimeter and movement joints is typically done after sealing, as sealant on uncured caulk can cause adhesion failure, and some sealers can discolor fresh silicone.
The work area must be cleared of furniture, debris, and obstacles before tile demolition can begin to ensure safe and unobstructed access.
Utilities such as water or electricity serving the area with tiles must be safely disconnected to prevent hazards during demolition.
Old tiles must be completely removed to expose the subfloor, which can then be inspected, repaired, and leveled before new flooring is installed.
Demolition generates significant dust and debris that must be cleaned and disposed of before any subsequent finishing trades can proceed.
After tile removal, the underlying surface must be prepared, repaired, and made ready for new tile or other flooring materials.
Wall tiling requires a stable substrate. Wall framing provides the structural support and nailing surface for backer board or tile backing, so framing must be completed first.
Electrical wiring and outlet boxes must be installed within the wall cavity before tiling, as tiles cover the wall surface and accessing wiring after tiling would destroy the tile work.
Plumbing pipes and shower valve bodies must be installed in the wall before tiling, since tiles permanently cover the wall surface and any plumbing work after tiling would require removing tiles.
Grout is applied to the joints between tiles after tiles are set and the adhesive has cured. Tiling must be complete before grouting can begin.

Items such as towel bars, soap dishes, mirrors, and toilet paper holders are mounted onto or through the finished tiled surface. Tiling must be complete to provide the finished backing and to avoid damaging tiles during installation of fixtures.
Floor tiling requires a stable, level, and cured substrate. Concrete slabs or subfloor underlayment must be prepared and cured before tiles can be laid to prevent cracking and ensure adhesion.
In wet areas (bathrooms, kitchens), a waterproofing membrane must be installed over the subfloor before tiling to prevent moisture damage and mold.

predecessor: Rough-in Plumbing and Electrical (below floor level)
rationale: Any plumbing pipes, drain lines, or electrical conduits that run beneath the floor must be installed and inspected before tiling, as tiling permanently covers the subfloor.
Although often a preference, some tilers prefer to complete floor tiling before wall tiling to allow wall tiles to overlap and cover the floor tile edges for a cleaner waterproof finish.
Floor tiling must be completed before installing cabinets and vanities that sit on top of the finished floor to ensure proper fit, leveling, and to avoid damaging the tiles.
The structural frame must be completed to provide a stable substrate for facade tiling attachment.
The roof must be completed to protect the facade area from weather during tiling work and to define the top edge condition.
Scaffolding can only be removed after facade tiling is completed to allow access and ensure all tiling work is finished.
Windows and glazing are typically installed after facade tiling to avoid damaging the finished tile surface and to allow proper sealing interfaces.
While internal finishes can technically start before facade tiling is complete, completing the external envelope first helps maintain clean and dry conditions for internal finishing work.
Waterproofing must be completed before tiling to ensure the substrate is watertight and prevents moisture damage to the structure.
A properly prepared, cured, and level concrete slab or substrate is required as a stable base for tile installation.
All drainage, circulation, and water supply pipes must be roughed in before tiling to avoid cutting or damaging finished tiles later.
Tiles must be fully installed and set before grouting and sealing can be applied to fill joints and protect the surface.
Tile work must be completed around fixture openings before pool fittings can be mounted and sealed in place.
The structural frame (roof trusses/rafters) must be erected to provide the underlying support structure for the roof tiles.
Roof decking (plywood/OSB) must be installed over the trusses to create a solid base for underlayment and tiles.
Waterproof underlayment (felt/synthetic) must be laid over the decking before tiles are installed to provide weather protection.
Gutters are installed after tiling because they need to be fitted along the roof edges (eaves) where tiles terminate, ensuring proper water runoff.
Interior ceiling work and attic insulation should follow roof tiling to ensure the building is watertight before enclosing interior spaces.
Tiles must be fully installed and set before they can be inspected for proper alignment, level, spacing, and adhesion quality.
Grouting must be completed so that the inspection can assess the finished tile work including grout lines, uniformity, and cleanliness.
A properly prepared substrate (clean, level, dry, and primed) is required before any tile installation can begin.

successor: Final Cleanup and Protection of Tile Surfaces
rationale: After inspection and sign-off, the tile surfaces can be cleaned, sealed if needed, and protected before subsequent trades work or occupancy.
Deficiencies identified during inspection must be corrected before the tile work can be considered complete and accepted.
The screed bay former is installed on top of a prepared concrete slab. The slab must be clean, level, and cured sufficiently to support screed rail installation.
Screed bay formers are set between screed rails to define the bay dimensions and guide the concrete finishing process. The rails must be in place first.
The screed bay former acts as a formwork or guide within the bay; concrete is poured and screeded after the former is positioned and secured.
Once the concrete has been poured and screeded to the bay former's level, surface finishing (trowelling, floating) can proceed.
After the concrete has set sufficiently, the screed bay former can be removed to expose the joint or edge it created.

Screed depth gauges/pins are used to set and verify the thickness of fresh concrete. Concrete must be placed and spread first so that the pins can be inserted to the correct depth and used to guide the screeding process.

The screed depth gauges/pins provide the reference height markers needed to perform the screeding operation. Screeding cannot begin until the depth pins are set to the proper elevation to ensure the correct slab thickness and surface flatness.
The subgrade must be properly prepared, leveled, and compacted before any concrete work including setting screed pins, as the pins' reference elevation depends on a stable, properly graded sub-base.

Formwork establishes the perimeter boundaries and elevation reference for the concrete slab. Screed depth gauges/pins are set relative to the forms to ensure the correct slab thickness and surface profile.
The ground must be excavated and leveled before any surface preparation can begin to ensure a stable and proper base for subsequent layers.
Underground utilities (drainage, water, electrical conduits) must be laid before surface preparation to avoid disturbing the prepared surface with trenching later.
All existing structures, debris, vegetation, and obstructions must be removed from the site before surface preparation can proceed to provide a clear work area.
A properly prepared and compacted sub-base is required before pouring concrete to ensure uniform support, prevent cracking, and achieve correct slab thickness.
The surface must be graded, compacted, and leveled before asphalt or paving materials can be applied to ensure a smooth, durable, and properly draining final surface.
A stable, compacted sub-base is required to support the screed layer and prevent cracking or uneven settlement.
Abutments and retaining walls define the boundaries of the area to be screeded and must be in place before screed is laid.
Drainage pipes and systems must be installed before screeding to avoid later excavation and damage to the finished screed.
Screed must be pumped and laid before the curing and drying process can begin.
Any final floor finish or topping can only be applied after the screed has been laid and properly cured.
Screed compaction and tamping can only be performed after the concrete or asphalt mix has been placed/spread on the surface, as the screed works the material that is already in place.
Formwork or edge rails must be set up to define the boundaries and guide the screed before compaction and tamping can begin.
The sub-base or underlying layer must be properly prepared, graded, and compacted to provide a stable foundation before placing and compacting the screed layer.

After the screed has been compacted and tamped to the required density and level, final surface finishing (e.g., floating, troweling, or texturing) can follow to achieve the desired surface smoothness and texture.
Proper curing of concrete or asphalt must begin after compaction and tamping are complete to ensure adequate strength development and durability.
Concrete must be poured and placed before it can be screeded and finished, as screeding levels and smooths the freshly placed concrete surface.
After floating and finishing the concrete surface, curing must begin to allow the concrete to properly hydrate and gain strength without moisture loss.
Control or contraction joints are cut after the concrete has been finished and has achieved initial set, typically after floating and finishing operations are complete.
The subgrade or base layer must be properly compacted and prepared before concrete is poured and screeded, ensuring uniform support and preventing settlement.
Formwork must be set up to contain the concrete pour and define the slab edges before the concrete can be placed, screeded, and finished.
The screed must be fully installed, spread, and leveled before the curing process can begin, as curing refers to the controlled hardening and moisture retention of the freshly laid screed.

successor: Application of Floor Finishes (e.g., tiles, wood, vinyl, epoxy)
rationale: The screed must be fully cured to achieve sufficient strength and low residual moisture before any floor finishes are applied. Premature finishing can cause adhesion failure, cracking, or moisture damage.

successor: Installation of Underfloor Heating (if screed is poured over heating pipes)
rationale: If underfloor heating pipes were embedded in the screed, commissioning/heating of the system should typically wait until after curing is substantially complete. This is a soft constraint because some phased heating may begin during curing to aid drying, but full operation only after curing.

Allowing heavy loads, scaffold, or construction traffic on the screed before curing is complete can cause permanent deformation, cracking, or surface damage. The screed needs to reach design strength during the curing period.

predecessor: Moisture Barrier / Damp Proof Membrane (DPM) Installation
rationale: A damp proof membrane must be laid prior to screed installation (and thus prior to curing) to prevent rising moisture from the substrate from affecting the screed's water-cement ratio and curing conditions.
The area around the crack must be cleaned and prepared (removing loose debris, dust, and contaminants) before any repair material can be applied to ensure proper adhesion.
The crack must first be widened and undercut (chased) using a grinder or saw to create a sound substrate and a mechanical key for the repair material.

After the repair material (e.g., epoxy or polymer-modified mortar) is applied into the crack, it must be left undisturbed to cure and gain sufficient strength before any subsequent loads or finishes are applied.
