Once the crack repair has fully cured, the repaired area may need to be ground smooth or finished to match the surrounding screed surface level.
The underlying concrete or screed must be sufficiently dry before applying repair materials (especially if using moisture-sensitive epoxy or resin-based products) to prevent bonding failure.
The floor flatness and surface regularity survey must be performed on the finished concrete slab after it has been poured and cured, as the survey measures the final surface condition.
If a separate screed or levelling layer is applied, the survey can only be conducted after that layer has been placed and set, since the survey measures the final walking surface.

successor: Floor Covering Installation (tiles, vinyl, carpet, epoxy coating)
rationale: Floor coverings must not be installed until the flatness/surface regularity survey has been completed, because non-compliant areas may require grinding, patching, or re-screeding before covering.

successor: Final Floor Finishing / Polishing (if exposed concrete)
rationale: Any final polishing or finishing of an exposed concrete floor must follow the survey, as the survey identifies areas needing correction before the final finish is applied.

It is a soft preference to complete the floor flatness survey before placing heavy equipment, because equipment placement can be done later but surveying access is easier prior to equipment installation.

The structural slab or subfloor must be constructed and prepared (e.g., cleaned, leveled, primed) before screed thickness can be designed, as the screed is applied on top of this substrate and its thickness depends on the existing surface conditions and structural load capacity.

Any underfloor heating pipes, electrical conduits, or plumbing must be laid and pressure-tested before screed thickness is determined, because the screed must cover and embed these services, requiring minimum cover depths that influence the overall screed thickness.

predecessor: Level Survey or Floor Flatness Assessment
rationale: A survey of the existing floor levels and flatness is required to determine the minimum and maximum screed thicknesses needed to achieve the desired finished floor level while meeting structural and material limitations.

The specific screed thickness dictates the required material properties (e.g., compressive strength, shrinkage characteristics, aggregate size), so the mix design and material ordering cannot be finalized until the thickness is designed.
The physical installation of the screed cannot begin until the thickness design is completed, as the design defines the application depth, slope requirements, and placement technique.
The base floor surface must be prepared, cleaned, and leveled before any heated screed system can be installed or commissioned.
Thermal insulation boards or layers must be laid beneath the heated screed to prevent heat loss downwards; commissioning cannot start without this insulation in place.
The underfloor heating pipes or electric mats must be fully installed, fixed, and connected to the manifold before screed can be poured and commissioned.
Once the heated screed is poured and commissioned, a controlled curing and drying period must be observed before any floor finishes can be applied or the system can be operated at full temperature.
Final floor finishes such as tiles, wood, or vinyl can only be installed after the heated screed has fully cured and been commissioned to avoid damage to the finish from residual moisture.
Electrical wiring must be installed in walls before insulation is placed, as insulation would block access to wall cavities for wiring.
Plumbing pipes must be run through wall cavities before insulation is installed, as insulation would obstruct access to plumbing routes.
HVAC ducts and vents must be installed within walls and ceilings before insulation is placed, since insulation would cover and block access to these systems.
Exterior walls must be enclosed (sheathing installed) before insulation is placed to provide a backing for the insulation and to protect it from weather.
Insulation must be placed inside wall cavities before drywall is installed, as the drywall permanently seals the wall and covers the insulation.
Electrical wiring must be installed before spray foam insulation because the foam will encapsulate and seal around the wires, making post-foam wiring impossible without cutting out the cured foam.
Plumbing pipes and fixtures must be in place before spray foam is applied, as the foam will seal around them and any subsequent plumbing work would require removal of cured foam.
HVAC ducts and vents must be installed before spray foam so that the foam can seal around the ducts; adding ducts after foam would require cutting into the cured insulation.
Spray foam insulation must be fully cured and in place before drywall is installed, as the drywall closes off the wall cavities and makes the insulation inaccessible.

While inspections can technically occur before insulation, it is standard practice to inspect the framed walls before they are covered by drywall; however, if inspection was already done pre-insulation, this can be a soft preference rather than a hard constraint.
Blown-in loose fill insulation requires an enclosed cavity or framed space to be blown into. Without framing (walls, attics, ceilings), there is no structural containment for the insulation material.
Electrical wiring must be run through wall and ceiling cavities before insulation is blown in, as accessing wiring after insulation is extremely difficult and would require removing the insulation.
Plumbing pipes must be installed within walls and attics before insulation is added, since the insulation would block access to plumbing work and repairs.

Blown-in insulation must be completed before drywall is installed because the insulation is blown into open wall cavities; once drywall is up, the cavities are enclosed and inaccessible for loose fill insulation application.
While air sealing is ideally done before insulation, final inspection of vapor barriers and air sealing effectiveness can only be confirmed after insulation is in place to verify complete coverage.

Rigid board insulation must be installed over a continuous, flat surface. Exterior sheathing (e.g., plywood or OSB) provides the necessary substrate for attaching and supporting the rigid insulation boards.
The wall framing and sheathing must be inspected and approved before any insulation work begins to ensure the structural integrity and compliance with building codes are verified.
An air barrier (e.g., building wrap or weather-resistant barrier) is typically installed over the sheathing before rigid foam insulation to control air leakage and moisture intrusion.

Windows and doors are typically installed after rigid insulation to allow the insulation to be cut and fit tightly around rough openings, and to ensure proper flashing integration between the insulation layer and the window/door frames.
The rigid board insulation serves as a continuous thermal break and substrate for the exterior cladding (siding, brick veneer, stucco, etc.), which is installed over the insulation layer.
The radiant barrier must be installed directly onto or above the roof deck/sheathing, which provides the structural base.
The roof framing must be complete to provide the structural support onto which the roof deck and subsequently the radiant barrier can be installed.
The roof underlayment (e.g., felt or synthetic) is installed over the radiant barrier to provide waterproofing and protection.
The final roofing material (shingles, metal panels, tiles, etc.) must be installed over the underlayment and radiant barrier to complete the roof assembly.

Attic insulation is typically installed after the radiant barrier to avoid compressing or damaging the barrier, though in some designs insulation may be placed before; it is a soft preference for best thermal performance.
Pipes and ducts must be physically installed and in place before insulation can be wrapped around them, as insulation is applied to the exterior surface of installed pipes and ducts.

Pressure testing must be completed to verify the integrity and leak-tightness of pipes and ducts before they are covered with insulation, as accessing leaks after insulation would require costly removal and reinstallation.
Insulation wrapping must be applied first before any external cladding, jacketing, or protective covering is installed over the insulation to protect it from weather and mechanical damage.

While not a physical necessity, it is standard practice to complete insulation wrapping before final commissioning to ensure the system is fully finished, thermally efficient, and ready for operational testing.
Insulation must be in place before fire-stopping seals are applied around pipe and duct penetrations through fire-rated walls and floors, as the insulation forms part of the fire-rated assembly.

Vapor barrier must be installed over a clean, smooth, and cured concrete slab or subfloor to ensure proper adhesion and sealing. Installing before the slab is cured or prepared would trap moisture and cause failure.
In below-grade applications, a compacted gravel base must be placed and leveled before the vapor barrier to provide a stable surface and prevent punctures from sharp stones.
Any plumbing pipes, conduits, or electrical lines that will run beneath the slab must be installed and inspected before the vapor barrier is placed, as the barrier will cover them.

The vapor barrier must be fully installed and sealed before concrete is poured over it; pouring concrete directly on unprepared ground without a vapor barrier would allow moisture migration through the slab.

Interior flooring materials must not be installed until the vapor barrier is in place to prevent moisture damage from below, especially on concrete slabs where moisture vapor can cause flooring failures.
Framing must be complete to access wall cavities and gaps that need sealing.
Exterior sheathing provides the structural base; air sealing is applied to seams and gaps in the sheathing.
Windows and doors must be installed so that gaps around their frames can be air-sealed.
The roof deck must be in place to seal attic floor or ceiling plane air barriers.
Air sealing must be completed before insulation to prevent air movement that would bypass or compromise insulation effectiveness.
Air sealing must be done before enclosing walls with drywall, as access to seal joints is lost.
All air sealing must be finished before interior finishes (paint, trim) as those would cover and block access to seal points.
Thermal bridging mitigation materials (e.g., insulation wraps, thermal breaks) are typically applied directly to the structural frame; the frame must be in place to serve as the substrate.
Exterior sheathing provides the surface onto which continuous insulation or thermal break layers are applied; sheathing must be installed before thermal bridging treatments can be placed.

Thermal break strategies often involve wrapping or insulating around window and door openings; the frames must be installed first so that thermal bridging materials can be integrated and sealed at penetrations.

Continuous insulation and thermal break layers are placed behind the exterior cladding; cladding must be installed after the thermal bridging mitigation layer is complete to avoid trapping moisture and to ensure proper thermal performance.

While air barriers can be installed concurrently or after thermal bridging mitigation in some sequences, it is typical best practice to complete the thermal break layer first to ensure continuity and seal the assembly before applying the air barrier system.
R-value testing must be performed after insulation materials are installed to verify that the installed insulation meets the specified thermal resistance requirements.
Air sealing must be completed before R-value testing to ensure the thermal envelope is properly sealed, as air leakage can significantly reduce the effective R-value of insulation.
Framing must be completed to create cavities for insulation placement before insulation materials can be installed.
R-value testing and verification must be completed before enclosing the insulation behind drywall, as testing may require access to insulation for inspection or thermal imaging.
R-value verification results are typically required documentation for final building code compliance certification, though some inspections may proceed in parallel.

Fire blocking requires walls to be closed, but trades must complete their rough-in work (wiring, pipes, ducts) before fire blocking is installed, as fire blocking seals penetrations and gaps around these elements.
Framing must be inspected and approved before fire blocking is installed, as the fire blocking work covers framing elements and would need to be removed if framing corrections are required.

Fire blocking and draft stopping must be completed before insulation is installed, because fire blocking creates the required fire-resistant compartments and seals gaps that would otherwise be concealed by insulation.
Fire blocking must be completed before drywall is installed, as drywall will cover and permanently enclose the fire blocking, making it inaccessible for inspection or correction.

Fire blocking and draft stopping work must be fully in place and visible before the final framing inspection can be conducted, as building codes require verification that all fire blocking is properly installed.
The horizontal DPC layer is installed on top of the completed foundation wall to prevent moisture rising from the ground into the wall structure.
The ground must be excavated and the sub-base prepared and compacted before any foundation or DPC work can commence.
A concrete blinding layer provides a clean, level working surface for laying the DPC and subsequent foundation wall construction.
The horizontal DPC must be in place before the ground floor slab is poured, to act as a moisture barrier between the ground and the slab.
Wall construction above the DPC level can only proceed after the DPC layer has been laid, ensuring the damp-proof barrier is continuous.

The vertical DPC membrane is applied to substructure walls (e.g., foundation or basement walls) to prevent rising damp. The substructure must be fully constructed and cured before the DPC can be applied.
The concrete or masonry wall surface must be fully cured, clean, and dry to ensure proper adhesion of the DPC membrane.
The DPC membrane must be fully installed and protected before backfilling can commence, as backfill would otherwise damage the wall and compromise the damp-proofing.
Vertical DPC must be lapped and sealed with the horizontal DPC or floor slab membrane. The slab should be poured after the vertical membrane is in place to create a continuous damp-proof barrier.
Internal finishes must not be applied until the DPC is fully installed and tested, as the DPC is essential to prevent moisture ingress that would damage plaster and finishes.
Cavity trays and DPC (damp proof course) must be installed on top of completed foundation walls or substructure to bridge the cavity and prevent moisture ingress.
The DPM from the substructure must overlap with the cavity tray DPC to form a continuous damp-proof barrier.

successor: Brickwork / Masonry outer leaf (above DPC level)
rationale: Cavity trays and DPC are built into the masonry as the outer leaf is constructed; the DPC is laid on the brick course and then the next brick course is laid on top.
The cavity tray DPC must be installed at the base of the cavity before inner leaf blockwork continues above that level to ensure proper drainage and water tightness.
Cavity insulation should be installed above the DPC level; the DPC must be in place to prevent moisture bypassing the insulation.
The trench must be excavated to the required depth and width before the stepped damp-proof course can be installed at the correct level.
The concrete foundation must be poured and cured to provide a stable, level base upon which the stepped DPC can be laid.

The stepped DPC must be installed first to form a continuous water-resistant barrier; brickwork or blockwork above DPC level cannot commence until the DPC is in place to ensure proper damp protection.
Soft preference: While blinding can sometimes be placed before DPC, it is typically done after DPC to coordinate ground floor slab levels with the stepped DPC profile.
Backfilling against the external face of walls must only occur after the stepped DPC is complete to avoid bridging the damp-proof course and compromising its effectiveness.
The Chemical Injection DPC (Distribution Point Can) must be installed after the pipe spools are in place to ensure proper alignment and connection of chemical injection lines.
Structural steel supports must be erected before mounting the Chemical Injection DPC to provide the necessary structural support framework.
Concrete foundations or pads must be cured and ready prior to installation of the Chemical Injection DPC to provide a stable, level base.
The DPC must be installed first to serve as the termination point before running chemical injection tubing from the DPC to the injection points.
Instrumentation connections (e.g., flow meters, pressure gauges, control valves) at the DPC must be completed before wiring and calibration can proceed.
Masonry walls require a stable, level foundation to bear their weight. Without footings or a foundation slab, there is no structural base on which to lay masonry units.
If the masonry wall sits on a concrete slab, the slab must be fully cured to provide adequate support and avoid cracking or settling of the masonry.
Proper grading and drainage must be in place to prevent water accumulation around the base of the masonry wall, which could compromise stability and cause moisture damage.
Preparation includes layout, mortar mixing, tool staging, and material delivery. Actual laying of masonry units cannot begin until these preparatory steps are complete.
A damp-proof course (DPC) is typically installed at the base of the wall during the early stages of masonry work, after preparation but before full wall height is built.
The DPC material must first be laid in its primary position before lapping and jointing can be performed to ensure continuous waterproofing at joints and overlaps.

predecessor: Masonry Work (Brick/Block Laying) up to DPC Level
rationale: Walls must be built up to the DPC level so that the DPC layer can be lapped and jointed into the masonry for proper integration and sealing against moisture.
Masonry above the DPC level cannot commence until the DPC lapping and jointing is complete, as the DPC must form a continuous barrier beneath the upper wall to prevent rising damp.
The DPC must be properly lapped and jointed into floor construction to prevent moisture ingress at the wall-floor junction; floor works follow DPC completion.

Internal finishes at the DPC level are typically done after DPC lapping and jointing to avoid damaging the DPC and to ensure a clean finish, though it can be considered a soft preference if temporary protection is provided.
The damp-proof course (DPC) must be installed first as the continuity connection bridges the DPC to the damp-proof membrane (DPM).
The damp-proof membrane (DPM) in the oversite slab/concrete floor must be laid before the continuity connection can link the DPC in the wall to the DPM in the floor.
The continuity connection between DPC and DPM must be established before the concrete slab is poured, so that the membrane connection is continuous and not bridged or broken by the concrete.
The DPC and its continuity connection to the DPM must be complete before building the wall above DPC level, to ensure the damp-proofing continuity is not compromised.

Floor finishes such as screed or floor coverings should be installed after the DPC-to-DPM connection is verified, though this is a work sequence preference to avoid covering up the damp-proofing before inspection, not a strict physical necessity.
The concrete foundation must be fully cured and stable to provide a solid base before cutting into the masonry for the DPC slot.
The masonry wall must be constructed first so that the DPC slot can be cut into the existing brickwork or blockwork.
Accurate survey and setting out of DPC levels must be completed to guide the correct cutting depth and position.
The DPC slot must be cut before the damp proof course membrane can be inserted into the prepared slot.
After cutting, debris and dust must be cleaned out from the slot before applying mortar or inserting the DPC material.
The ground must be excavated, leveled, and properly prepared before any membrane can be laid to ensure a stable, even substrate.
A clean, smooth blinding concrete layer is typically poured over the hardcore to provide a proper working surface for the DPM and to prevent sharp stones from puncturing the membrane.

successor: Concrete Slab / Ground Floor Slab Pouring
rationale: The DPM must be laid and sealed beneath the concrete slab to provide a continuous moisture barrier before the structural slab is poured on top.
The DPM is lapped and sealed with the DPC in the walls to create a continuous damp-proof barrier; this integration occurs as wall construction begins above slab level.

Where a reinforced slab is specified, rebar is typically placed on top of the DPM (using concrete spacers/chairs) before pouring the slab, but this is a soft preference as the membrane must first be down to protect against ground moisture.
A site inspection is needed to identify visible signs of dampness and assess access conditions before a detailed rising damp assessment can be conducted.
Moisture readings from the surface must be taken to confirm the presence and extent of damp before a comprehensive rising damp assessment can be performed.
The assessment identifies the type and severity of rising damp, which determines the appropriate damp proof course (DPC) installation method and materials.
The assessment determines the extent of plaster and render damage; affected areas must be identified before any remedial plastering can proceed.
Findings from the rising damp assessment inform the design of any structural waterproofing solutions needed to address moisture ingress.
Wall ties are installed to connect masonry walls to other structural elements; the masonry wall must be partially or fully constructed to provide a surface for embedding or affixing the wall ties.
Wall ties often connect masonry walls to the building's structural frame (concrete columns/beams or steel), so the frame must be in place to receive the ties.
Wall ties span the cavity between inner and outer leaves of a cavity wall; insulation boards are typically impaled on or placed between the ties after the ties are installed.

successor: Inner Leaf Blockwork / Second Leaf Construction
rationale: In cavity wall construction, wall ties are embedded into the outer leaf first, then the inner leaf is built up engaging with the exposed ties.

While it is preferable to install cladding after wall ties are in place to ensure proper support and alignment, some cladding systems may be installed concurrently with tie placement depending on the specific construction method.
Weep holes are formed in masonry walls to allow water drainage; the wall structure must exist before weep holes can be created within it.
Weep holes are typically placed above or in conjunction with flashing; however, the weep holes must be formed first to create openings, then flashing can be integrated around them.
Weep holes must be formed and left open before final pointing and finishing of the wall joints, as closing them prematurely would block drainage paths.
Weep holes provide drainage; insulation should be installed after weep holes are formed to ensure proper water evacuation paths are not obstructed.
A stable foundation or substrate must be prepared before the wall (and thus weep holes) is constructed, as weep holes are part of the wall system.
Mortar joints must be fully formed, set, and partially cured before sealing can be applied; sealing cannot proceed until the masonry units are laid and mortar joints are in place.
Mortar joints need to be tooled or raked to the proper depth and profile before sealant can be applied into the joint.
Joints must be clean, dry, and free of dust, debris, and loose particles to ensure proper adhesion of the sealant.

Backer rod is typically installed after the sealant is applied to control sealant depth and shape; however in some sequences backer rod goes in first. The more common sequence is: backer rod installed first then sealant. So this should be reversed. Let me correct: Backer rod installation must precede sealant application.

Building regulation compliance inspection must occur after construction works are substantially complete to verify that all building work meets the required standards and regulations before the building can be occupied or used.
The structural framework must be erected and complete so that inspectors can assess the structural integrity and compliance with building regulations regarding structural safety.
All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems must be installed so that the compliance inspection can verify they meet safety and performance standards as per building regulations.
Fire safety systems such as alarms, sprinklers, and fire doors must be in place before the compliance inspection can verify fire safety regulation compliance.

The building regulation compliance inspection must be completed and passed before a certificate of occupancy can be issued, as the certificate confirms that the building meets all regulatory requirements for safe occupation.
While some final finishing works can proceed after inspection, certain cosmetic finishes may be delayed until after the inspection to avoid covering up elements that need to be checked.
The building cannot be handed over to the client or owner until the compliance inspection has been successfully completed and any identified issues have been resolved.
Site mobilization must occur first to bring equipment, materials, and personnel to the site before wellpoint installation can begin.
Site survey and layout are required to identify the locations for wellpoints, groundwater conditions, and discharge points before installation can proceed.
All existing underground utilities must be located and marked to avoid damage during wellpoint installation and to ensure safe excavation.
The wellpoint system must be fully installed and connected before dewatering pumps can be operated to lower the groundwater table.
The wellpoint system must be installed and operational to dewater the area before excavation can begin in dry conditions.
Site must be cleared and graded before dewatering wells can be installed.
Accurate survey and marking of well locations is required before drilling and installation of deep wells.
Groundwater must be lowered and controlled by dewatering before safe excavation can commence below the water table.
Dewatering must be active to keep the excavation dry and stable for foundation pouring and curing.
Dewatering reduces hydrostatic pressure on shoring systems, so dewatering should be operational before installing and relying on shoring for excavation support.
The sump pit and drainage system must be excavated before sump pumping can be installed and operated.
Waterproofing membranes and drainage boards around the foundation must be in place to direct water to the sump pit before the sump pump system can function effectively.
A gravel or stone base must be laid in the sump pit area to provide proper drainage and filtration before installing the sump pump.
The sump pump system must be fully installed and operational before the concrete floor slab is poured, as the pump and pit need to be accessible and embedded beneath the slab.
While backfilling can often proceed alongside sump pump installation, it is preferable to have the sump pump discharge lines and drainage complete before backfilling to avoid re-excavation.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and prepared before any well system installation can begin, as the eductor/ejector well requires a stable and accessible foundation.

The eductor/ejector well system needs connection to process and utility lines (e.g., motive fluid supply, discharge piping) that are laid in the utility corridors; these must be trenched and piped first to allow tie-in.
After the eductor/ejector well system is installed, the wellhead connections must be made and pressure/flow tested to verify integrity before operation.
Surface piping and valves that connect to the eductor/ejector system can only be installed after the well system is in place to ensure correct alignment and fit.
Commissioning activities require the eductor/ejector well system to be fully installed and connected before initiating operational checks and startup procedures.
Vacuum dewatering is a process applied to fresh concrete immediately after pouring and initial compaction, so concrete must first be placed.
The concrete surface must be screeded and roughly leveled before the vacuum dewatering mat can be placed and the process initiated.
After vacuum dewatering removes excess water, the concrete surface is stiffened and ready for power troweling and final finishing operations.
Vacuum dewatering must be completed before curing begins, as curing is the final stage of moisture retention after the surface has been finished.
Joint cutting (sawing control joints) is typically performed after vacuum dewatering and finishing, though timing can be slightly flexible depending on concrete stiffness.
Initial dewatering must be performed to remove bulk groundwater before electro-osmosis can be applied to further reduce the moisture content in fine-grained soils.
The site must be excavated and prepared to expose the soil mass requiring electro-osmotic treatment.
Electrodes must be placed into the soil in the required geometric pattern before electrical current can be applied to induce electro-osmotic flow.
After electro-osmosis treatment, the dewatered and stabilized soil must be tested and verified to confirm that moisture content and strength meet design specifications.

The treated soil area must complete the electro-osmosis dewatering process before final backfilling and earthworks can proceed, as the ground must be stable and dry enough for compaction and construction activities.
The ground must be excavated and prepared to the required levels and grades before drainage pipes can be laid, ensuring proper fall and subgrade stability.

Vertical drainage elements (e.g., vertical drains or wellpoints) are typically installed first to dewater the site and manage groundwater, creating dry conditions necessary for horizontal drainage pipe installation.
After horizontal drainage pipes are laid and connected, a granular drainage blanket is placed over them to protect the pipes, provide filtration, and distribute water flow into the drainage system.
Trenches containing horizontal drainage pipes must be backfilled and compacted once the pipes are installed and inspected, to restore ground stability and support subsequent construction layers.
The drainage system must be fully operational before final subgrade preparation and capping layers are placed, to ensure that the ground is properly drained and stable for structural loads.
The site must be cleared and prepared before monitoring wells can be installed and baseline groundwater sampling can begin.
Monitoring wells must be drilled, constructed, and developed before any groundwater level measurements or water quality sampling can be performed.
Groundwater data (levels, quality parameters) must be collected in the field before it can be analyzed, interpreted, and reported.
While remediation design can begin based on initial site characterization, detailed design often benefits from baseline monitoring data to confirm contaminant levels and flow directions.
Groundwater levels and quality must be characterized before dewatering systems are designed and operated to ensure proper handling and discharge compliance.
Settlement monitoring measures ground movement caused by structural loads, so the foundation must be installed first to generate the loads that cause settlement.
Settlement data must be collected and analyzed to confirm foundation stability before proceeding with vertical construction, preventing structural damage from ongoing settlement.
The site must be cleared and graded to establish baseline ground conditions and install monitoring instruments before settlement readings begin.
Monument pins, inclinometers, or survey markers must be physically installed before any monitoring readings can be taken.
It is preferred but not strictly required to complete the monitoring period before final grading, as ongoing settlement could distort finished surfaces.
The water treatment system must be physically installed and operational before discharge water treatment can commence, as treatment requires the equipment to be in place.
A collection or containment system (e.g., pipes, sumps, tanks) must be in place to channel water to the treatment system before discharge treatment can begin.

successor: Water Quality Testing and Compliance Verification
rationale: After water is treated, its quality must be tested to verify it meets discharge permit requirements before it can be released.
Treated water can only be discharged to the environment or municipal sewer after the treatment process is complete.
It is preferable to complete discharge water treatment before flushing and shutting down the water treatment system, but this is a soft operational preference rather than a hard physical constraint.
The site must be excavated and prepared before dewatering pumps can be placed, as pumps are installed in the lowest points of the excavation to remove groundwater.
A perimeter drainage system (e.g., French drains, sump pits) must be in place to collect groundwater and direct it to the pump intake location.
Dewatering pumps must operate continuously to keep the excavation dry before and during concrete foundation placement to prevent water contamination and ensure proper curing.
Continuous dewatering is required until backfilling is complete to prevent hydrostatic pressure buildup and soil instability.
While utilities can technically be installed concurrently, keeping the excavation dry via dewatering improves working conditions and prevents water damage to pipes and conduits.
Header pipes require structural supports (e.g., hangers, brackets, or stanchions) to be in place before the pipe itself can be installed, as the pipe must be secured to these supports.
The building's structural frame and foundations must be completed to provide the anchorage points for pipe supports and to define the routing envelope for the header pipe.
Branch pipes tap off from the header pipe; therefore, the header must be installed first to serve as the source for branch connections.
Flanges, valves, and fittings that attach directly to the header pipe cannot be installed until the header pipe is in place and aligned.
Pressure testing (hydrostatic or pneumatic) of the piping system must follow header pipe installation to verify the integrity of all joints and connections within the system.
The wellpoint riser pipe is installed inside the dewatering well; the well must first be drilled and cased before the riser pipe can be placed.
Excavation support (e.g., soldier piles and lagging or sheet piling) must be in place to provide stable ground conditions before installing wellpoint riser pipes within the excavation perimeter.
The riser pipe must be fully installed and seated at the correct depth before connecting it to the above-ground wellpoint header or pump system.
All riser pipes and wellpoints must be in place before the dewatering system can be tested, primed, and commissioned for continuous operation.
The riser pipes are required for active dewatering; excavation below the water table can only proceed after the dewatering system (including riser pipes) is operational to keep the excavation dry.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated to the appropriate depth before well casing can be installed, as the casing is placed into the excavated borehole.
The borehole must be drilled to the target depth before the well casing can be inserted, as the casing is placed inside the pre-drilled hole.
Once the casing is in place, the annular space between the casing and the borehole wall must be filled with cement or grout to seal the well and prevent contamination.
The well must be fully cased and sealed before development (e.g., surging, pumping) and testing procedures can begin, as these processes verify the integrity and performance of the completed well.
The casing provides the structural conduit for the well; screens and pumps are installed inside or attached to the casing after it is securely placed and cemented.
The well screen must be placed into a drilled borehole; drilling must occur first to create the hole.
A gravel pack is placed around the outside of the installed well screen to filter sediment and stabilize the formation.
Well development (surge/air lift/pumping) removes fines from the formation and screen to improve yield; this cannot be done before the screen is in place.
The pump is typically lowered into the casing above or inside the screen section; the screen must be installed first to provide the intake zone.
The annular space above the screen and gravel pack is sealed with grout to prevent surface contamination; this is done after the screen and pack are in place.
A borehole must be drilled to the required depth before a piezometer can be installed, as the piezometer is placed inside the borehole.
Casing or protective tubing must be placed in the borehole before inserting the piezometer to maintain hole integrity and allow proper seating of the instrument.
A sand or gravel filter pack must be placed around the sensing zone before the piezometer is positioned to ensure proper hydraulic connectivity and filtration.
After the piezometer is installed in the borehole, a bentonite seal must be placed above the filter pack to prevent vertical water migration along the borehole annulus.
The remaining annular space above the bentonite seal must be grouted after piezometer installation to complete the borehole abandonment and ensure long-term stability.
Geotechnical data (soil permeability, groundwater levels, stratigraphy) from site investigation is essential input for designing the dewatering system and understanding the hydrogeological regime.
Accurate ground elevation data from topographical survey is needed to determine groundwater flow directions, hydraulic gradients, and optimal locations for dewatering wells or sumps.
Understanding the existing environmental conditions, including nearby water bodies and sensitive receptors, is required to design a dewatering plan that avoids adverse environmental impacts.
The dewatering system (wells, pumps, piping) cannot be installed until the dewatering design is completed, as the design specifies well locations, pump capacities, and system layout.
Excavation in water-bearing ground cannot safely proceed until dewatering measures are designed and implemented to lower the groundwater table and prevent flooding or instability of the excavation.
Site characterization data (soil types, groundwater levels, permeability) is required to determine dewatering needs, design the system, and support permit applications.
Environmental assessment findings are needed to evaluate potential impacts of dewatering on surrounding ecosystems and groundwater resources, which regulators require before issuing permits.
Dewatering permits must be obtained before commencing site preparation and mobilization activities that involve groundwater handling or discharge.
Regulatory permits are a legal prerequisite before installing dewatering wellpoints, pumps, and discharge infrastructure.
Excavation in water-bearing ground requires active dewatering, which cannot legally commence without the necessary regulatory permits in place.
The dewatering system must first be installed and operational before it can be decommissioned, as decommissioning is the reverse process of removal and termination of the system.

The dewatering system is typically used during foundation and substructure construction to keep the excavation dry; once foundation construction is complete, the need for dewatering ceases and the system can be decommissioned.
The dewatering system pipes and pumps must be removed or decommissioned before backfilling the excavation, otherwise they would be buried and inaccessible.
Removal of dewatering equipment is necessary before final grading, restoration and landscaping can be completed to ensure the site is clear of temporary systems.
Legal access rights must be secured before the survey team can physically enter the property to perform topographic measurements.
Survey equipment must be transported to site and basic site logistics established before field survey work can commence.
Topographic maps and ground surface data are needed to identify suitable borehole locations and access routes for geotechnical drilling equipment.
Existing ground elevations and contours from the topographic survey are essential inputs for designing cut/fill requirements and grading plans.
Accurate surface elevation data from the topographic survey is required to establish foundation elevations and slab-on-grade designs relative to existing grade.
The property boundaries must be legally defined and the site must be acquired before a boundary survey can be performed, as the survey establishes the precise legal property lines.

The boundary survey provides the accurate property lines and legal limits needed to develop a site plan, ensuring buildings and improvements are placed within the correct setbacks and property bounds.
While often performed concurrently, a boundary survey is typically completed first to establish the property limits within which the topographic survey data is collected.
The boundary survey establishes the exact property corners and lines needed to stake out building locations, utility routes, and other improvements on the site.

Most building permit applications require a recorded boundary survey as part of the submission documents to verify that proposed construction falls within legal property limits and meets setback requirements.
The site must be cleared and graded before any survey markers or control points can be established, as debris or uneven terrain would prevent accurate placement of survey monuments.
Borehole locations and soil test positions are often tied into the control network, so the geotechnical survey must be completed first to inform the placement of control points.
The control network provides the reference points (benchmarks and baselines) that guide all subsequent earthmoving and grading operations to the correct elevations and alignments.
Foundations must be laid out using the established control network to ensure correct positioning, orientation, and leveling of structural elements.
Road alignments, curbs, and pavement layers rely on the control network for correct horizontal and vertical geometry.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and prepared before any benchmark or survey marker can be placed, as benchmarks require stable, undisturbed ground.
The primary survey control points and reference network must be established first so that the benchmark can be accurately positioned relative to the overall coordinate system.
Benchmarks serve as fixed reference points for elevation and alignment control; foundation excavation must not start until benchmarks are in place to guide depth and positioning.
The building layout and staking of column lines and walls rely on the installed benchmarks for accurate horizontal and vertical control.

While benchmarks are ideally installed before monitoring begins, in some fast-track projects monitoring equipment may be set up provisionally; however, permanent benchmarks should be installed first for reliable baseline data.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and obstructions before grid lines can be accurately set out on the ground.
A topographical survey provides the reference points, benchmarks, and existing ground levels needed to accurately establish the grid lines.

While soil investigation is typically done beforehand to inform foundation design, grid setting out can technically begin if temporary benchmarks are established; however, it is standard practice to complete soil investigation first.
Excavation for foundations cannot commence until the grid lines have been physically marked on site to define the exact locations and boundaries of excavation.
Foundation concrete cannot be poured until the grid lines are set out to ensure precise positioning of footings and columns.
The site must be cleared, graded, and prepared before any layout or offset lines can be established on the building footprint.
Accurate survey control points and property boundary stakes must be in place to reference when establishing offset lines for the building.
Offset lines define the exact building perimeter and setbacks; excavation for foundations cannot begin until these reference lines are established.
The foundation footprint and forms are laid out based on the offset lines, so foundation work must follow the establishment of offset lines.
Formwork for footings and walls is positioned according to the offset lines, requiring the lines to be set first.

Profile boards are set up to mark the layout of the building on site, which requires that the foundation and substructure work (or at minimum the excavation and leveling) be completed or at least started to establish the proper reference points.
The site must be cleared and leveled before profile boards can be accurately positioned to mark the building outline and excavation limits.
Profile boards serve as reference guides for excavation; trenches and footings are dug based on the string lines and markings established by the profile boards.
The positioning of concrete footings and foundation walls follows the layout lines transferred from the profile boards, ensuring accurate placement.
Profile boards establish the building's footprint and alignment, which must be set before any vertical wall construction can begin to ensure correct positioning on the foundation.
The site survey must be completed to establish the reference points and boundaries before the datum peg can be accurately positioned as a fixed reference marker.
The datum peg provides the vertical and horizontal reference level from which all excavation depths and earthworks are measured, so it must be in place before any digging begins.
Building footings and foundations are set out using the datum peg as the primary reference point for alignment and levels.
The site must be cleared of vegetation and debris before the datum peg can be installed, so that accurate survey measurements can be taken on exposed ground.
Foundation concrete is poured to specified levels relative to the datum peg, ensuring correct finished floor levels and structural alignment.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and obstructions before setting out excavation works to ensure accurate measurement and marking of excavation boundaries.
A detailed topographic survey is required to establish existing ground levels, contours, and reference points that are essential for correctly setting out excavation positions.
Temporary utilities (water, electricity, sanitation) must be in place to support the surveying and marking equipment used during excavation setting out.
Excavation cannot begin until the boundaries, depths, and alignments have been accurately set out and marked on the ground to ensure the excavation is positioned correctly.
The setting out must be inspected and approved by the engineer or surveyor before any excavation work proceeds, to verify accuracy against design drawings.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and existing structures before foundations can be set out, as there must be a clean, unobstructed area to accurately mark foundation positions.
A detailed topographical survey is needed to establish existing ground levels, site boundaries, and reference points before setting out foundation positions.
Soil investigation and borehole tests must be completed to confirm ground bearing capacity and soil conditions, which influence the final foundation design and layout before setting out can proceed.
The structural engineer's foundation design and drawings must be reviewed and approved before setting out can begin, as the setting out is based on these approved dimensions and positions.

Excavation cannot start until the foundation lines, corners, and levels have been precisely marked on the ground through the setting out process, as the excavation coordinates and depths are defined by the setting out.
As-built surveys document the actual constructed conditions; construction must be complete before measurements can be taken.
The building or system must be substantially complete to accurately capture as-built conditions.
As-built survey data is the source information needed to produce final record drawings and documentation.
As-built surveys can identify deviations from design that may need to be addressed; however, some deficiency resolution may happen concurrently or before survey.
The as-built survey documentation is typically a prerequisite deliverable for project closeout and final owner acceptance.

predecessor: Site Preparation and Survey Control Establishment
rationale: The total station requires stable, pre-surveyed control points and a cleared site to set up and establish accurate reference measurements before any layout can begin.
The total station must be set up, leveled, and calibrated to provide accurate angular and distance measurements before any building layout or stakeout can be performed.
Accurate excavation boundaries and depths are determined using total station measurements; therefore the instrument must be ready before excavation guidance begins.
Verification of verticality and alignment of structural elements relies on total station sightings, so the instrument must be operational before these checks.
The total station is used to capture final as-built positions of constructed elements; this can only be done after the total station itself is set up and ready for measurement.
The construction site must be cleared and leveled before setting up a dumpy level so that the instrument can be placed on stable ground and provide accurate readings.
The tripod must be assembled and set up at the desired location before the dumpy level can be mounted onto it.

predecessor: Optical Level (Dumpy Level) calibration and leveling
successor: Initial site survey and elevation readings
rationale: The dumpy level must be properly calibrated and leveled using its bubble vial before any accurate survey measurements or elevation readings can be taken.

predecessor: Optical Level (Dumpy Level) setup and calibration
rationale: Reference points and benchmarks can only be accurately established after the dumpy level is set up and calibrated to ensure correct elevation data.
Excavation depths and cut/fill volumes depend on the elevation data obtained from the dumpy level survey, so excavation must follow the leveling survey.
A theodolite requires a stable, prepared base with known reference points; the survey marks the locations and elevations needed for theodolite positioning.
The theodolite must be mounted on a leveled tripod to ensure accurate angular measurements; leveling must be done before mounting the instrument.
The theodolite must be set up and calibrated before it can be used to measure horizontal and vertical angles.
Once the theodolite is operational, it is used to sight reference points and mark out building lines, column centers, or other alignment features on site.
The theodolite is essential for establishing the primary control network (baselines, grid lines) from which all subsequent layout and construction measurements are derived.

predecessor: Set up Automatic Level / Theodolite / Total Station
rationale: The automatic level or theodolite must be set up and leveled before the levelling rod can be used for reading measurements.
The telescope must be functional and focused on the staff to take readings.
The tripod must be firmly set up to support the level or theodolite before staff measurements can be taken.
Room must be darkened for certain survey observations.
The site must be excavated and prepared before any leveling instruments can be set up to measure elevations and establish benchmarks.
Temporary benchmarks must first be established from known reference points so that the digital level can be used to transfer and verify elevations accurately.
The digital level is used to set out elevation and alignment marks for foundation excavation and formwork; therefore these activities can only begin after leveling is complete.
The digital level provides the precise height references needed before concrete can be poured and finished to the correct level.
Column and wall positions must be marked using the digital level's alignment data before construction of vertical elements can commence.

predecessor: Manufacturing/Procurement of Measuring Tape / Steel Band
successor: Quality Inspection of Measuring Tape / Steel Band
rationale: The measuring tape/steel band must be procured or manufactured before it can undergo quality inspection.

predecessor: Quality Inspection of Measuring Tape / Steel Band
successor: Calibration of Measuring Tape / Steel Band
rationale: Inspection must verify the tape/band is free from defects before it is calibrated for accurate measurements.

predecessor: Calibration of Measuring Tape / Steel Band
rationale: The tape must be calibrated to ensure accurate measurements before it can be used for layout or marking on construction sites.

successor: Storage/Maintenance of Measuring Tape / Steel Band
rationale: After use, the tape should be cleaned and stored properly to maintain accuracy and prolong lifespan, though this is a maintenance best practice rather than a physical necessity.
Measurements taken during construction using the tape/band are essential for verifying that completed work meets specifications during post-construction surveying.
A theodolite traverse requires established control points or reference stations from which to measure angles and distances; the instrument must be set up over known points to begin traversing.
The survey area must be cleared and roughly graded to allow access to traverse stations and ensure line-of-sight between successive traverse points.
The traverse provides the precise horizontal and vertical control framework needed to locate and stake out building corners, column centers, and other construction elements with accuracy.
Traverse control points serve as the backbone for subsequent topographic detail surveys; theodolite traversing establishes coordinates that enable accurate mapping of terrain features.
Accurate traverse control is required before excavation can commence to ensure cut/fill lines, footing locations, and building offsets are correctly positioned in plan and elevation.

The levelling run establishes the vertical datum and reference heights for the entire structure; excavation must be completed first to expose the ground levels that need to be referenced for foundation depths.

predecessor: Setting out of building lines and pegs
rationale: Setting out marks the horizontal position of the building; the levelling run uses these established pegs and reference points to transfer and verify the required elevations.
The levelling run provides the precise height benchmarks and datums needed to ensure the foundation concrete is poured at the correct levels and uniform depth.
The levelling run establishes the datum from which all vertical masonry and wall heights are controlled, ensuring walls are built level and to correct elevation.

successor: Installation of drainage and underground services
rationale: While not a strict physical dependency, completing a levelling run before laying drains allows the correct gradients and invert levels to be accurately set, avoiding costly rework.
Raw field survey data (points, angles, distances) must be collected before any COGO computations can be performed to calculate coordinates, bearings, and distances.
Known control points and benchmarks are required as reference geometry for all coordinate calculations.
COGO-calculated coordinates must be finalized before field crews can use them to physically stake out building corners, road alignments, or utility locations.
Grading plans rely on calculated coordinates and elevations from COGO to determine cut/fill volumes and surface slopes.
Exact building corner coordinates must be computed before foundation forms can be laid out and excavated.
The site must be cleared and accessible before any setting out can commence, as RTS requires unobstructed lines of sight and a prepared ground surface to establish control points and markers.
A primary survey control network (with known coordinates and benchmarks) must exist on site for the RTS to reference when setting out secondary points and building geometry.

predecessor: Review and Approval of Construction Drawings/Setting Out Plans
rationale: Accurate setting out requires finalized, approved dimensional plans and coordinates; without these reference documents the RTS operator cannot determine where to place markers.
Setting out marks the exact positions of foundations, columns, and building outlines; excavation cannot begin until these markers are placed to guide digging and avoid errors.
Foundation formwork and reinforcement must be positioned according to the set-out points; the concrete pour relies on the RTS-established grid and levels for correct placement.
The scanning area must be cleared of debris, obstructions, and large equipment to provide clear line-of-sight for the LiDAR scanner and ensure safe, unimpeded data collection.

predecessor: Establishment of Control Points / Survey Network
rationale: A network of surveyed control points (targets) must be established in the field prior to scanning so that individual scans can be accurately registered and georeferenced in post-processing.
Raw scans captured during the field session must be processed by aligning overlapping scans and tying them to the control points before any further modeling or analysis can commence.

The registered point cloud from the LiDAR survey is the foundational dataset required to create as-built 3D models, BIM elements, or CAD drawings; these modeling activities cannot begin without the completed scan data.
A formal flight plan must be submitted and approved by relevant aviation authorities before any drone can be legally operated in the airspace.
The drone operator and support crew must be on-site and have completed a safety briefing prior to commencing flight operations.
The drone, camera, GPS, and batteries must be inspected, calibrated, and verified to be in working order to ensure safe and accurate data capture.
Wind speed, precipitation, visibility, and lighting conditions must be confirmed suitable for flight before the survey can commence.

successor: Point Cloud Generation and 3D Model Reconstruction
rationale: The raw aerial imagery captured by the drone survey is the prerequisite input for photogrammetric processing steps such as georeferencing, orthorectification, and 3D reconstruction.
Concrete must be poured and sufficiently cured before checking verticality, as the check verifies the alignment of the poured structural elements (columns, walls, cores).
Formwork defines the initial position of concrete elements; the verticality check assesses whether the erected formwork and subsequently poured concrete are within tolerance.
Rebar must be placed and tied before concrete is poured; the verticality check occurs after concrete is in place to confirm that the finished element is plumb.
Verticality must be verified and accepted before formwork removal, as any misalignment needs to be documented and potentially corrected while forms are still in place.
Final verticality confirmation of the current level is required before proceeding with the next level to ensure cumulative tolerances do not exceed limits.
Floor level monitoring can only begin after the concrete slab or deck has been poured and has achieved sufficient initial set, as the monitoring process measures the finished floor elevation.
The concrete must have reached initial set so that workers can safely walk on the surface and take accurate level measurements without damaging the fresh concrete.

Accurate floor level data is required before cutting trenches or placing sleeves for mechanical, electrical, and plumbing runs to ensure proper depth and alignment relative to the finished floor elevation.
The final floor topping or finishing compound is applied only after level monitoring confirms that the substrate meets the required elevation tolerances.

While not a strict physical necessity, it is best practice to have verified floor levels before laying out partition wall positions to ensure consistent floor-to-ceiling heights and avoid fit-out issues.
The physical site survey and measurement data collection must be completed before the quality assurance review and close-out of the survey process can begin.
Survey data must be validated and closed out before it can be used as a basis for foundation design and engineering work.
Accurate survey data must be finalized and assured before any earthmoving or site preparation activities can commence, as they rely on verified survey benchmarks and levels.
The survey must be closed out with QA approval before the building layout can be staked out on site.
The site must be cleared of obstructions and existing structures before utility surveys can be accurately conducted to locate buried services and utilities.

predecessor: Temporary Site Access / Haul Route Setup
rationale: Survey equipment and personnel need safe access to the site, so temporary access routes must be established before the survey can begin.
Excavation cannot safely commence until all existing underground utilities and services have been identified and marked to prevent damage and ensure worker safety.
Foundation design and excavation depend on knowing the locations of existing utilities to avoid conflict and plan for any necessary utility relocations.
Temporary utility connections must be routed around or connected to existing services, which requires survey data to plan safe and compliant connections.
Site must be cleared of obstructions, debris, and dense vegetation to allow GPR equipment to access the survey area and to prevent signal interference or physical damage to the equipment.
A survey grid and reference markers must be laid out on site to guide systematic GPR data collection and ensure accurate spatial positioning of radar readings.
Existing known underground utilities must be identified and marked to protect them during the survey and to help differentiate known features from GPR-detected anomalies.

successor: Data Processing and Interpretation of GPR Results
rationale: Raw GPR data must be collected in the field before it can be processed, filtered, and interpreted to generate subsurface profiles and identify anomalies.

GPR survey results identify subsurface anomalies; while often followed by targeted excavation to verify findings, this is a soft preference as some surveys are conducted for non-intrusive assessment only and may not require follow-up excavation.
Crew, equipment, and drilling rigs must be mobilized and have site access established before any ground investigation can commence.
Surface vegetation and obstructions must be cleared to provide access to borehole and test pit locations for the ground investigation.
Soil and rock samples collected during the field survey must be sent to a laboratory for classification, strength, and compaction testing before results are available.
Subsurface soil/rock parameters, bearing capacity, and groundwater data obtained from the investigation are essential inputs for designing foundations.
Geotechnical data informs slope stability, excavation support requirements, and suitability of on-site materials for reuse, so bulk earthworks must wait for survey results.

Monitoring surveys for settlement and movement can only begin after site preparation and excavation are complete, as these initial ground-disturbing activities establish the baseline conditions and the structure must be in place before any meaningful settlement monitoring can occur.

Foundation construction must be completed before settlement monitoring surveys can begin because the survey measures movement of the foundation and the structure above it. Without a completed foundation, there is nothing to monitor for settlement.

Initial settlement monitoring must be conducted before structural framing proceeds, to establish baseline settlement readings and ensure the foundation is stable enough to support the superstructure loads.

While final grading can technically proceed without completing all settlement monitoring, it is preferable to complete monitoring surveys first to avoid disturbing monitoring instruments and to have accurate final settlement data before finishing site surfaces.

It is preferred to complete settlement monitoring before paving hardscape areas, as covering the ground with pavement would obstruct access to settlement monitoring points and make ongoing measurements difficult.
The site must be cleared and prepared before survey prisms/targets can be installed, as debris, vegetation, or uneven ground would prevent accurate placement and measurement.
The survey prism/target must be physically installed and in place before any surveying measurements can be taken using it as a reference point.
Survey instruments (e.g., total stations, theodolites) must have the prism/target in place to be sighted and calibrated properly before use.
The overall control network (benchmarks, control points) must be established first so that survey prisms/targets are positioned correctly relative to known coordinates.
Survey targets/prisms serve as reference points for layout; construction staking and positioning of building elements rely on these references being established first.
The device must be physically produced or acquired before it can be used on a construction site.
The device must be transported and received at the construction site before it is available for use.
The device requires sufficient power to operate; batteries must be charged or installed beforehand.
The measurement activity cannot begin until the laser distance meter is available, powered on, and ready for use.
Measurement data can only be recorded and documented after the distance measurement activity has been performed using the device.
The site must be cleared of obstructions, debris, and existing structures to provide unobstructed access for surveyors to mark the ground accurately.
Rough grading and earthworks establish the basic ground levels; survey pegs are then placed to mark precise locations, levels, and boundaries based on the final graded surface.
Excavation requires the survey pegs to be in place to mark exact excavation limits, building corners, and depths as per the construction drawings.
Formwork and rebar are positioned according to the reference lines and levels established by the survey pegs to ensure structural alignment.
Underground utility trenches must follow the alignment and offsets marked by survey pegs to avoid conflicts with building foundations and property boundaries.
The trench must be excavated before it can be backfilled; backfilling cannot physically begin without an open trench to fill.
All pipes, conduits, or utilities must be installed and inspected in the trench before backfilling can cover them.
Any utility connections (water, sewer, electrical, gas, telecom) placed in the trench must be completed and tested prior to backfilling to avoid future excavation.
Proper bedding material must be placed and compacted around pipes/utilities before the main backfill material is added to provide support and protect the installed elements.
Regulatory or quality inspections of the trench, bedding, and installed utilities must be completed and approved before backfilling can proceed to ensure compliance with specifications.
The backfilled trench must be compacted and leveled before any surface restoration (asphalt, concrete, or topsoil) can be applied to restore the ground surface.
After backfilling is placed, compaction testing is performed to verify that the fill material meets density requirements before final surface restoration.
The backfill must be completed to grade before final fine grading and landscaping can be done to ensure proper drainage and surface finish.
The excavation must be completed to create the space for foundation installation before backfilling can occur.
Concrete foundations must be poured and cured to sufficient strength before backfill can be placed against them to avoid damaging the structure.
Waterproofing membranes or coatings must be applied to the foundation walls before backfilling, as they become inaccessible once soil is placed.
Perimeter drains, French drains, and drainage boards must be installed around the foundation before backfill material is placed to ensure proper water management.
Final grading and compaction of the site surface can only be completed after backfilling is done, as backfill brings the ground level up and provides the base for final grading.

While rough-in utilities are installed before backfill, final connections from the building to external utility lines (e.g., sewer, water, electric conduits) must occur after backfill to avoid damage and allow proper trenching from the building outward.
Interior floor slabs and slab-on-grade work typically proceed after backfilling is complete to ensure the sub-base is properly compacted and drainage is established.

The retaining wall structure (including its footing, reinforcement, and concrete curing) must be completed and sufficiently cured before backfilling can begin, as backfill material and compaction forces would otherwise destabilize or damage the unfinished wall.

Drainage components such as weep holes, perforated drain pipes, and granular drainage aggregate must be placed against the back of the wall before bulk backfilling, because they cannot be installed effectively after the backfill is in place.

Waterproofing membranes or coatings on the back face of the retaining wall must be applied and cured before backfilling to protect the wall from moisture, as they cannot be applied after backfill material is placed.

successor: Final Compaction and Grading of Backfill
rationale: The backfill material must be placed behind the wall before final compaction and grading can be performed to achieve the required fill density and surface finish.

successor: Surface Drainage / Swale or Pavement Construction atop Backfill
rationale: Surface improvements such as pavements, sidewalks, or drainage swales atop the backfill area should generally follow backfilling and compaction to avoid settlement issues, though in some sequences these could be partially concurrent if compaction is staged.
Excavation must be completed to create the trench where pipe bedding material will be placed.
The trench bottom must be graded and prepared to receive the bedding material for proper pipe support.
Bedding material provides a stable, uniform foundation; pipes must be laid onto the prepared bedding.
Pipes are aligned and graded on top of the bedding layer to ensure proper slope and positioning.
Backfilling over pipes can only proceed after bedding is placed and pipes are installed.
Basement walls must be fully constructed, cured, and waterproofed before backfilling can commence, as backfilling places lateral earth pressure against the walls.
The basement floor slab or footing must be in place to provide structural support and prevent the backfill material from entering the basement area.
Waterproofing and damp-proofing membranes must be fully applied and cured on exterior walls before backfilling to protect the basement from moisture intrusion.
Perimeter drainage systems (e.g., French drains, weepers) must be installed and connected before backfilling to ensure groundwater is properly diverted away from the foundation.
After backfilling is complete, final site grading and shaping can be performed to establish proper drainage slopes and prepare for landscaping.
While many utilities are installed before backfill, some exterior connections (e.g., final gas, water, or electrical service lines) may be completed after backfilling as a soft preference.
Backfilling should ideally be completed before above-grade exterior cladding and insulation to provide a stable base, though in some sequences cladding may start simultaneously.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and obstructions before selecting fill placement to ensure the fill is placed on a clean, prepared surface.
Initial excavation and rough grading must be completed to define the areas where fill is needed, establishing the subgrade elevations and limits for fill placement.

Soil borings, laboratory tests, and geotechnical analysis must be performed to determine the suitability of existing soils and the required fill material properties before selecting fill placement locations and depths.
The fill placement areas, lifts, and material specifications must be selected and planned before the actual placing and compacting of fill material can commence.

successor: Perform Quality Control Testing of Fill
rationale: After selecting fill placement locations and specifications, quality control testing (e.g., compaction tests, moisture content checks) can be scheduled and performed during and after fill placement operations.
Moisture conditioning prepares concrete for subsequent finishes; concrete slab must be placed and have reached initial set before moisture conditioning can begin.
The concrete must undergo its initial curing period to develop sufficient strength and stability before moisture conditioning (such as damp curing or membrane curing) is applied.
Moisture conditioning must be completed to achieve the proper moisture content and surface condition required for the adhesion and performance of floor finishes or coatings.
While not a physical necessity, it is best practice to complete moisture conditioning before testing to ensure accurate vapor emission readings; this is a quality control preference.
Moisture conditioning is preferably completed before final slab inspection to ensure the slab meets moisture specifications, though inspection can theoretically occur without it.
Nuclear density testing measures the in-situ density and compaction of soil; the soil must be placed and spread before its compaction can be tested.
The soil typically needs to be at or near optimum moisture content before compaction testing; moisture conditioning ensures the soil is prepared for proper compaction and density testing.
Nuclear density testing is performed after compaction to verify that the soil has achieved the required density; testing before compaction would not reflect the final compacted state.
The compaction test results must be reviewed and approved before fill work can be accepted and subsequent layers placed; this ensures quality control compliance.
The next layer of soil can only be placed after the current lift has been tested and approved for density to avoid burying non-compacted material.
The ground surface must be graded, cleared of debris, and compacted before geotextile can be laid to ensure uniform support and prevent puncture or uneven settlement.
The alignment and extent of geotextile placement must be marked on the ground based on design drawings before deployment begins.
Cover material (e.g., granular fill, riprap, or soil) must be placed immediately after geotextile rollout to protect the fabric from UV degradation, wind uplift, and displacement.
Adjacent geotextile sheets must be overlapped and sewn, heat-bonded, or pinned after placement to ensure continuity of separation/filtration function before covering.

Final cover placement is preferred after geotextile is in place to complete the lining system, though this may be a design preference rather than a strict physical necessity if temporary cover is used.
The ground surface must be cleared, leveled, and graded before compaction can begin, as the plate compactor requires a smooth and stable base to operate effectively.
Trenches must be dug and utilities (pipes/cables) laid before backfilling and compacting the soil over them to ensure proper embedment and protection.
Compacted subgrade provides the necessary load-bearing foundation for pavement or concrete slabs; pouring or paving over uncompacted soil would lead to settlement and cracking.
Final grading and sod/turf installation is typically done after compaction is complete to achieve a uniform, settled surface, though some minor regrading may occur afterward.
Compaction quality (density/moisture) testing must be performed immediately after compaction while the soil is still in its compacted state to verify compliance with specifications before covering.
The sheepsfoot roller is used for compacting soil in earthfill applications, so bulk earthwork and rough grading must be completed first to provide the soil layer to be compacted.
Soil must be at optimal moisture content before compaction with a sheepsfoot roller to achieve the desired density.

successor: Smooth drum roller or final grading
rationale: After sheepsfoot roller compaction, the surface is uneven and rough; a smooth drum roller or final grading pass is needed to seal and smooth the surface.
Compaction density and soil quality tests must be performed after the sheepsfoot roller pass to verify that required compaction specifications are met before proceeding with subsequent layers.

successor: Placement of subsequent soil lift or base layer
rationale: Each lift of soil must be compacted by the sheepsfoot roller before the next lift can be placed to ensure proper layer-by-layer compaction.
The ground must be excavated to the required depth and trench prepared before any drainage pipe can be placed and installed.
A layer of granular bedding material (e.g., gravel) must be placed and compacted at the bottom of the trench to provide a stable, uniform support for the pipe and facilitate drainage flow.
Individual pipe sections must be laid in position before they can be connected and jointed together to form a continuous sub-drain line.
The pipe must be fully installed, jointed, and inspected before the trench can be backfilled to protect the pipe and restore the ground surface.
The sub-drain pipe run must be completed to the point of connection before it can be tied into the main drainage system or outfall structure.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and existing structures before soil stabilization can begin, as stabilization needs a clean working surface.
Topsoil must be removed to expose the subgrade that requires stabilization; stabilization cannot be effectively performed on topsoil.
