Engineering design and survey stakes establish the required depths, limits, and specifications for stabilization work.
Foundations require a stable, load-bearing subgrade; soil stabilization must be completed first to achieve the required bearing capacity.
Stabilized ground provides a uniform working platform and prevents soil movement during trenching and utility installation.
Control joints must be formed in fresh or hardened concrete, so the concrete slab must first be placed.
Control joints are typically created after initial finishing (e.g., floating) but before final curing, to control cracking.
Curing must begin after joint formation so that the joints are properly established and can function to control cracking during the curing process.
If additional surface treatments (e.g., brooming, troweling) are specified, they are typically done after joint cutting but before final curing starts.
Expansion joints must be placed within or between concrete slabs; the slab must be in place (or at least formed and poured) before the joint can be physically installed.
For expansion joints that are cut or tooled into concrete, the concrete must have reached its initial set to support cutting without damaging the slab.
The subgrade or base layer must be compacted and leveled before placing any concrete and its accompanying expansion joints.
After expansion joints are installed (whether pre-formed strips or tooled grooves), the surrounding concrete surface is finished and floated to integrate the joint.
Once the expansion joint is in place and the concrete has cured, joint filler or sealant is applied to protect the joint from debris and moisture.
Weatherstripping requires a framed structure with rough openings (windows and doors) to be in place, as weatherstripping is applied to the edges of these openings.
Exterior sheathing must be installed to provide a backing surface for weatherstripping and to ensure the building envelope is prepared.
Windows and doors must be fully installed before weatherstripping can be applied around their frames to seal gaps and prevent air leakage.
Weatherstripping should be completed before interior finishes like drywall to ensure the air barrier is sealed and to avoid damaging drywall during weatherstripping work.
Weatherstripping is part of the air sealing process which should be completed before insulation to ensure the building envelope is airtight for optimal insulation performance.

predecessor: Rough-in of Mechanical, Electrical, and Plumbing (MEP) Services
rationale: All MEP penetrations through fire-rated assemblies (pipes, ducts, conduits, cables) must be installed before fire-stopping can be applied, because the fire-stop sealant is applied around the completed penetrations to maintain the fire-resistance rating.

predecessor: Fire-Rated Wall or Floor/Ceiling Assembly Construction
rationale: The fire-rated barrier (drywall, concrete, masonry) must be fully in place before fire-stopping can seal the openings, as fire-stop material is applied to gaps and penetrations within that already-constructed assembly.
Fire-stop sealants and putties must be fully cured and inspected before they are covered by finishes, to ensure the integrity of the fire-stop system is verifiable and not concealed prematurely.

Fire-stop sealing must be completed prior to the formal inspection and certification of fire-rated assemblies, so that the inspector can verify all penetrations are properly sealed before signing off.

successor: Ceiling Installation / Suspended Ceiling Grid Closure
rationale: Fire-stopping around penetrations in fire-rated ceilings or above-ceiling barriers must be finished before the ceiling tiles or boards are installed, to allow full access and visual inspection of the fire-stop application.
The building frame must be in place before acoustic sealing can be applied, as acoustic sealing is installed onto or within the structural framework.
Acoustic sealing is applied to finished wall and ceiling surfaces; sheathing or boarding must be installed first to provide a substrate for sealing.
Electrical, plumbing, and HVAC rough-in work must be completed before acoustic sealing, as sealing around penetrations is done after services are installed and before final finishes.

Acoustic sealing must be complete before final interior finishes (paint, wallpaper, decorative coatings) are applied, as sealing can damage finished surfaces and finishing over seals would compromise their effectiveness.

While acoustic sealing at wall-floor junctions is ideally done before flooring, in some sequences flooring can be installed first with sealant applied at the joint afterward; however, best practice is to seal before flooring to ensure continuous seals.
The substrate must be clean, dry, and free of debris, dust, or moisture to ensure proper adhesion of the waterproofing joint treatment material.
The structural substrate (e.g., concrete slab or wall) must be fully placed and sufficiently cured to provide a stable, sound surface for joint treatment application.
Control joints, construction joints, or expansion joints must be cut, grooved, and formed in the substrate before the waterproofing joint treatment can be applied into or over them.
The joint treatment (e.g., joint tape, sealant, or reinforcing layer) must be installed first so the subsequent waterproof membrane layer can bond over and integrate with the treated joint.

In some systems a primer is applied over the joint treatment before the main membrane; however, some systems combine these steps, so this is a soft preference depending on the specific product specification.
The joint must be clean, dry, and free of debris, dust, laitance, or contaminants to allow proper adhesion and placement of the backer rod.
Correct joint dimensions must be confirmed to select the appropriately sized backer rod (typically 25-50% wider than the joint width) before insertion.
Concrete or masonry substrates must be fully cured to ensure dimensional stability and prevent moisture-related issues before backer rod installation.

Masking tape adjacent to joints is typically applied after backer rod placement to protect adjacent surfaces from sealant smearing, though this is a workmanship preference rather than a physical necessity.
The base slab must be installed and cured before joint preparation can begin, as joint preparation involves cleaning and preparing the joints on the installed slab surface.
Concrete must be properly cured before joint preparation and cleaning can take place, as working on uncured concrete can damage the slab and compromise joint integrity.
Joints must be prepared and cleaned before joint sealant can be applied, as sealant will not properly adhere to dirty or unprepared joint surfaces.
Joints need to be properly prepared and cleaned before filler material can be installed to ensure proper bonding and performance.
The expansion joint itself must be installed first to create the gap and substrate that the cover plate will mount over.
The structural slab or deck must be in place and cured so the expansion joint and cover plate have a stable supporting surface.
The cover plate is typically set flush with the finished floor level; floor finishes are applied up to or over the plate edges only after the plate is securely fastened.
Sealant around the cover plate edges should be applied after the plate is fully installed to ensure a watertight and finished joint.
It is easier to install cover plates before surrounding wall finishes to avoid damaging those finishes, but it is not a physical necessity.
Preformed joint tape must be applied onto clean, dry, and properly prepared joint surfaces to ensure proper adhesion and seal integrity.
After the preformed joint tape is embedded in the joint compound or adhesive, the first taping coat of joint compound must be applied over the tape to cover it and ensure a smooth finish.

Finishing and sanding typically follow after the joint tape and initial compound layers have been applied and dried, though this is a standard sequencing preference rather than a strict physical necessity if alternative sequences are used.

Priming and painting cannot begin until the joint tape is installed and all joint finishing (compound, sanding) is complete, as painting over unfinished joints would cause visible defects and poor adhesion.
Drywall panels must be installed and fastened to the framing before any joint tape can be applied to the seams between panels.
Surfaces must be clean, dry, and primed before sealant application to ensure proper adhesion and prevent contamination.

predecessor: Joint / Gap Formation (concrete curing, panel installation)
rationale: The joint or gap into which sealant is applied must already be formed and fully cured/set before sealant can be applied.
Backer rod must be placed in the joint to control sealant depth and provide a backing surface before sealant is injected.
After applying sealant with the gun, it must be tooled and smoothed immediately to ensure proper contact, shape, and adhesion before it skins over.
Sealant must be fully applied before the curing/drying period can begin; no disturbance is allowed during cure time.
Joint design requires knowledge of forces, moments, and loads acting on the structure to determine the type, size, and capacity of joints needed.
The materials being joined (e.g., steel, concrete, timber, composite) must be known before designing joints, as joint configuration, fasteners, and connection methods depend on material properties.
The dimensions and cross-sectional properties of structural members must be finalized before joints can be designed, as joint geometry and connection details depend on member sizes.
Shop drawings, welding details, bolt patterns, and fabrication instructions for connections cannot be prepared until the joint design is complete and specified.

While erection sequencing can be preliminarily planned, detailed lifting and assembly procedures that account for specific connection methods require finalized joint specifications to ensure proper fit-up and installation sequence.
Sealant must be fully applied and installed before it can be inspected and tested for quality and performance.
If inspection identifies defects, repairs must follow; however, if the sealant passes inspection, this step may be skipped, making it a soft preference rather than a hard constraint.
Inspection and testing must be completed and passed before the sealant work can be formally accepted and signed off.
Surfaces must be properly cleaned and primed before sealant can be applied to ensure adhesion and performance.
After application, sealant requires sufficient curing or setting time before it is ready for inspection and testing.
Inspection and testing must occur after the sealant has fully cured to obtain accurate and valid results.
The surface must be properly cleaned and prepared (e.g., filling cracks, removing debris) before re-sealing can be applied to ensure adhesion and a smooth finish.
Any damaged joints or cracks must be repaired first so that the re-sealing material can be applied over a sound, stable substrate.
Oil spots and stains must be chemically cleaned and removed prior to re-sealing to prevent bonding failure and discoloration of the new sealcoat.
Parking lot or pavement markings are applied after the final sealcoat has cured to ensure the paint adheres properly and markings remain crisp and visible.
After re-sealing, the pavement requires a specified curing/drying time before it can be opened to traffic or subjected to further surface treatments.

Intumescent collars are installed around pipes and cables that pass through fire-rated compartments. The pipes, sleeves, or conduits must be in place first so the collar can be fitted around them at the penetration point.
The fire-rated partition (wall or floor slab) must be built before the collar can be installed, because the collar wraps around the service penetration through that rated assembly.

After the collar is fitted around the pipe/sleeve, the annular space around the pipe and between the collar and the wall opening must be sealed with firestop sealant or caulk to complete the fire-rated seal.

If the pipe requires insulation or a protective casing, this can proceed after the collar is installed, though in some sequences insulation may be pre-installed and the collar placed over it. Preferential order is to install collar first to ensure proper fit and fire rating.

Final inspection of the fire-rated penetration seal, including verifying that the intumescent collar is correctly installed and tight around the pipe, must occur after installation is complete and before the penetration is concealed.

Fire stopping systems (such as firestop pillows, collars, or boards) must be installed before applying fire-rated sealant, as the sealant is often used to cover and seal these systems to complete the fire barrier.

All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing penetrations through fire-rated walls and floors must be roughed-in before fire-rated sealant can be applied around those penetrations to seal gaps and maintain fire integrity.

Fire-rated sealant is applied at joints, gaps, and penetrations in completed drywall assemblies; the drywall must be installed, taped, and finished first to provide the substrate surface for sealant application.

Fire-rated sealant must be fully cured and in place before final painting and finishing work begins, as painting over uncured sealant can compromise its fire-resistive properties and the sealant application must be inspected prior to concealment.

Fire-rated sealant application must be completed before fire safety inspections can verify the integrity of fire barriers and sealant installations, as inspectors need all sealant work finished to assess compliance with fire codes.
Firestop pillows are placed within or around sleeves/penetrations to seal openings; the sleeve or conduit must be installed first to provide the structural opening and support for the pillows.

Firestop pillows are used to seal around cables, cable trays, or conduits passing through fire-rated barriers; these mechanical/electrical elements must be in place before the pillow can be packed around them.

After pillows are placed, a firestop sealant or caulk is often applied over the pillows to ensure an airtight seal and maintain the fire-resistance rating; the pillows act as a base for the sealant layer.
Inspection and testing of firestop installations must occur after the pillows are fully installed to verify proper placement, density, and compliance with firestop specifications.
The opening or penetration through the fire-rated wall/floor must be created before firestop pillows can be placed to seal it.
Steel surfaces must be cleaned, primed, and free of debris/rust before intumescent wraps can be applied to ensure proper adhesion and fireproofing performance.
The structural steel frame must be fully erected and stable before intumescent wraps are installed onto the steel members.

Any conduit, piping, or ductwork that will be enclosed by or run adjacent to the wrapped steel should be roughed in first to avoid damaging the intumescent wrap during later mechanical/Electrical installations.
Penetrations and gaps around the wrapped steel members must be firestopped after the wrap is in place to maintain fire-rated assembly integrity.
Suspended ceilings or architectural closures that conceal the wrapped steel should be installed after wrap placement to avoid rework; preference-based as access can be staged.
Fire rated boards are typically screwed onto metal studs or furring channels. The stud framing must be fully erected, plumb, and braced to provide the structural substrate for board attachment.

All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work within the wall cavities must be completed and inspected before enclosing them with fire rated boards, as retrofitting after board installation would require removal and reinstallation.

predecessor: Fire Caulking and Penetration Sealing (First Pass)
rationale: Firestop sealants and through-penetration firestop systems around conduits, pipes, and ducts passing through rated partitions should be applied at the rough-in stage prior to boarding, though additional sealing at board joints will follow.

Once boards are installed, the joints between boards (and at corners) must be taped and finished with joint compound to create a continuous fire-resistive membrane and achieve the required fire rating.

successor: Firestop Sealant Application at Board Joints
rationale: After boards are in place, specific fire-rated sealants or intumescent caulks must be applied at board joints, edges, and around any penetrations to maintain the fire-resistance rating of the assembly.
Mineral wool packing is typically applied around ductwork for thermal and acoustic insulation. Ductwork must be installed first so that mineral wool can be packed around it.
Mineral wool is packed around pipes for insulation. Pipes must be in place before the insulation material can be wrapped or packed around them.
Once mineral wool is packed around ducts or pipes, an outer cladding or protective wrapping is applied over the insulation to protect it from moisture and mechanical damage.

Mineral wool packing often serves as a firestop material. However, additional fireproofing sealants or coverings may be applied after packing. This is typically required but could be considered a soft preference if the mineral wool itself provides sufficient fire resistance.
The structural supports, brackets, or hangers for ducts and pipes must be in place before mineral wool can be packed around those services.
The fire rated duct wrap is applied directly onto the installed and positioned ductwork. Ductwork must be in place before any wrapping can occur.
Duct surfaces must be clean, dry, and free of dust, oil, or debris to ensure proper adhesion and performance of the fire rated wrap material.
The installed fire wrap must be inspected and approved by the site supervisor or fire protection engineer before any subsequent work that could conceal or damage it.

Leakage testing typically occurs before wrapping, but if testing is scheduled after, the wrap must be complete first. However, wrapping before testing may hinder leak detection, so this is a soft preference depending on project sequencing.

Fire rated duct wrap must be fully installed and cured before enclosing the ducts within ceilings, walls, or shafts, as the wrap provides required fire resistance and must not be damaged during enclosure work.
After the fire damper is installed within the duct, the remaining ductwork sections and airtight seals can be completed to ensure system integrity and proper airflow.
Firestop sealants must be applied around the damper assembly at the penetration of the fire-rated barrier to restore the fire-resistance rating after the damper is physically in place.

Although system balancing can begin before all dampers are installed, final balancing and testing of airflow should be performed after all fire dampers are in place to account for their presence and position in the duct system.
Smoke seals are typically installed onto or around door frames; the frame must be in place to provide a mounting surface and alignment for the seal.
Smoke seals require a finished wall surface to create an effective seal; gaps around the door opening must be properly prepared before seal application.
Smoke seals are usually fitted to the frame or floor before the door leaf is hung, as the leaf's fit and gap tolerances depend on the seal already being in place.
All smoke seals must be fully installed prior to performing fire and smoke door tests to verify compliance with building codes.
Regulatory inspections require smoke seals to be installed and functional before the building can be certified for occupancy.
Firestop sleeves or devices must be installed first to provide the containment boundary and support structure for the mortar application.

predecessor: Penetrating Item Installation (Pipe, Cable Tray, Conduit)
rationale: The pipes, cables, or conduits that penetrate the fire-rated assembly must be in place before mortar can be applied around them to seal the opening.
The mortar must be fully applied before it can cure and harden to achieve its fire-resistive rating.
The mortar application must be completed before inspectors can verify that the firestop system is properly installed per the approved design.
In some firestop systems, a sealant or caulk is applied over the cured mortar as a final finish layer; the mortar base must be in place first.
Third-party inspection occurs after construction works are completed to verify that the built structure conforms to the design and regulatory requirements.
Material test reports and quality control documentation are required as evidence for the third-party inspector to review and certify compliance.
The building cannot be handed over or occupied until it has been certified by an independent third-party inspector confirming it meets all safety and code requirements.
Contractual conditions typically require third-party certification before the final payment milestone is released to the contractor.
All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems must be fully installed so the third-party inspector can verify system functionality and code compliance.
Primer must be applied to ensure proper adhesion of the firestop spray material to the substrate.
Substrates must be clean, dry, and free of dust, grease, or loose material to ensure firestop spray bonds correctly.
Firestop spray must be fully applied and cured before inspection can be performed to verify thickness, coverage, and integrity.

successor: Backer Rod or Firestop Sealant Installation (if required)
rationale: In some sequences, sealant or backer rod may go over or adjacent to spray-applied firestop; however, this is sequence-dependent and not always a hard physical requirement.
Finish paint or intumescent overcoating must be applied only after the firestop spray has cured to avoid damaging the firestop layer.
The opening in the wall/floor slab must be formed and ready before the intumescent collar can be fitted around the pipe.
The pipe must be in place so the intumescent collar can be positioned around it.
The intumescent collar must be secured around the pipe before the remaining annular space can be firestopped and sealed.

successor: Apply fire-rated covering/insulation over collar area
rationale: Final fire protection covering is typically applied after collar installation to ensure continuity, though in some sequences covering could be done earlier around the penetration.
Inspection of the complete firestop system including the intumescent collar must occur after the collar is installed to verify correct positioning and compression.
Firestop pillows are typically placed within firestop sleeves or openings that contain penetrating items; the sleeve or opening must be prepared first to house the pillow.

predecessor: MEP Penetration Installation (e.g., pipes, cables, conduits)
rationale: Firestop pillows are installed around penetrating items (pipes, cables, conduits) to seal the opening; the penetrations must be in place before the pillow can be positioned around them.
Some firestop pillow installations require a final sealant or caulk layer over the pillows to ensure an airtight smoke seal; this must be applied after pillows are placed.
Inspection and testing of the firestop assembly (including pillows) must occur after installation is complete to verify compliance with fire ratings.

successor: Final Wall / Ceiling Finish (e.g., drywall, paint)
rationale: Firestop pillows are installed within wall or ceiling openings before the final finish is applied to conceal or complete the assembly.
The smoke seal must be applied to the completed structural frame to ensure proper sealing and alignment.
Firestopping must be in place to create the base fire-resistant barrier before smoke seals are applied at joints and penetrations.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-ins must be completed before smoke seals are installed to avoid damaging the seal around penetrations.
Smoke seals are applied to the substrate before final finishes (drywall, paint, etc.) so they are concealed and protected.
Smoke seals must be fully installed and cured before smoke control system testing can verify compartmentalization integrity.
Penetration sleeves are cast or embedded into concrete walls, floors, or slabs; the wall/floor structure must exist before a sleeve can be placed within it.
The exact routing of pipes, conduits or cables determines the sleeve size and location; rough-in layout must be completed to position the sleeve correctly.
Penetration sleeves create openings that require firestopping to maintain fire resistance ratings; firestop materials are applied after the sleeve is installed and fixed in place.
The sleeve provides a protective passage through the structure; the actual pipe, conduit, or cable can only be routed through the opening after the sleeve is securely installed.
Exterior or below-grade penetration sleeves must be sealed against water ingress; this sealing step (e.g., link-seal, waterproof boot) occurs after the sleeve is embedded and concrete has cured.
Safety gear (such as guardrails, safety nets, and edge protection) requires a stable structural base to be anchored to, which is provided by completed foundations.
Many safety gear components (e.g., fall arrest systems, guardrails) need to be attached to the structural frame once it is in place.
Roofing activities require edge protection and fall arrest systems (safety gear) to be installed beforehand to protect workers at height.
Exterior cladding work at heights requires safety nets and guardrails to be in place to prevent falls.
Interior finishing work on upper floors is safer with guardrails and fall protection installed, but lower-level interior work may proceed without all safety gear completed.
Shaft excavation must be completed before any structural works can begin, as the structural lining requires an excavated void to be placed in.
Ground conditions must be understood before designing and executing the shaft structural lining to ensure appropriate support and stability measures.
Structural works (e.g., lining installation) must be completed before waterproofing can be applied to the shaft surface.
The structural lining must be in place before backfilling or grouting the annular space between the lining and the ground.

successor: Shaft Equipment Installation (e.g., ladders, pipes, pumps)
rationale: Shaft structural works provide the finished stable environment required before installing fixed equipment within the shaft.
The pit must be fully excavated to expose surfaces requiring waterproofing treatment.
A smooth, clean concrete blinding layer is typically required as a base for applying waterproofing membranes or coatings.
Waterproofing must be installed and cured before placing reinforcement bars to avoid damaging the waterproofing layer and to ensure continuity.
Waterproofing acts as a barrier behind or beneath the structural concrete; concrete is placed after waterproofing is complete and inspected.
A protective layer is often placed over waterproofing membranes before backfilling to prevent mechanical damage, though this is a best practice rather than a physical necessity in all cases.
Rail brackets are mounted on steel columns or beams; the structural frame must be erected first to provide the mounting surface.
Bracket locations must be marked on the steel members based on survey control before brackets can be welded or bolted in place.
Crane rails are placed directly onto and fastened to the installed rail brackets; brackets must be in position to support the rails.
After brackets are installed and rails are set, final alignment adjustments and grouting of bracket base plates are performed to lock in the correct rail elevation and alignment.

While ideally the rail and bracket system should be complete before installing crane electrical systems, some electrical rough-in work can proceed in parallel. However, final connections require the brackets and rails to be firmly in place.
The lift pit must be constructed and waterproofed before any ladder or access components can be installed inside it.

Ladder and access components must be installed in the lift pit before the lift system can be installed and commissioned, as the ladder provides essential access for installation and maintenance personnel.

Electrical wiring is typically installed within walls, ceilings, and structural cavities. The building's structural frame and shell must be in place to provide the physical substrate for running conduits, cables, and junction boxes. Additionally, working before structural completion would risk damage to wiring and pose safety hazards.

Plumbing rough-ins (water supply lines, drain pipes) are usually installed in wall cavities before electrical wiring to avoid conflicts in space routing and to ensure proper separation between electrical and plumbing systems as required by building codes.

Electrical wiring must be fully installed, inspected, and approved before insulation is placed over it. Insulation applied before wiring would conceal un-inspected electrical work, violate code, and require costly removal of insulation to access wiring later.

All electrical wiring, outlet boxes, switch boxes, and conduit must be in place before walls are closed up with drywall or cladding. Once drywall is installed, access to add or modify wiring becomes extremely difficult without demolition.

While it is technically possible to do some painting before electrical fixtures (switches/outlets) are fully trimmed out, best practice and efficiency dictate that wiring and outlet/switch installations be completed first to avoid paint work around unfinished electrical boxes and to allow for a single coordinated finishing pass.
The steel structure must be in place to provide support and attachment points for the hoisting and lift removal equipment.
Concrete foundations need to be cured and ready to support the lift removal and hoisting equipment before it can be installed or mobilized.
The lift removal and hoisting equipment must be set up and operational before it can be used to lift or place heavy components.
Mechanical systems installation often requires hoisting of heavy machinery into place, which depends on the availability of the lifting equipment.
Roofing materials may need to be hoisted to roof level, but this is a soft preference as alternative lifting methods may exist.
Expansion joints must be established and the structural frame must be complete before expansion joint covers can be installed, as the covers bridge the gap between structural segments.
The expansion joint opening/gap must be formed (via pour strips, backer rod, etc.) before a cover can be placed over it.
Concrete adjacent to expansion joints must be sufficiently cured to support the anchoring or attachment of expansion joint covers.
Expansion joint covers are typically installed flush with the finished surface; final floor finishes or wall finishes are applied up to or around the installed cover.
Installing expansion joint covers before partitions allows for a clean interface, but partitions can be cut around covers if needed (soft preference).
The fire-rated separation wall must be supported by a stable foundation or concrete slab to bear its load and maintain structural integrity.
If the fire-rated wall is non-load-bearing, the primary structural frame must be in place to provide lateral support and connection points before the wall can be installed.

successor: Rough-In of Electrical / Plumbing / MEP Services
rationale: MEP rough-ins can only be installed after the wall is built because certain fire-rated walls require specific sleeves, firestopping, and sealing around penetrations, which must be coordinated during wall erection.

successor: Fire Stopping / Fire Caulking at Joints and Penetrations
rationale: Fire stopping must be applied after the wall is fully erected to seal all gaps, joints, and penetrations to maintain the required fire-resistance rating.
Finish work typically follows wall installation to achieve the final aesthetic surface; this is a logical construction sequence preference but not a strict physical requirement.
Acoustic partitions require structural support; the framing provides the structural grid or support system onto which acoustic partitions are mounted or within which they are placed.

predecessor: MEP Rough-In (Electrical, Plumbing, HVAC conduits in wall)
rationale: Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work within partition cavities must be completed before enclosing them with acoustic partitions to avoid costly rework and damage to finished surfaces.
Acoustic partitions are typically installed on a finished or prepared floor surface; the floor slab or subfloor must be in place to provide a level base and support.
Acoustical insulation and sealants are placed within or around the partition assembly after the partition framework is installed; this cannot logically precede the partition structure.
Final interior finishes such as drywall, cladding, or surface treatments are applied over the acoustic partition assembly; the partition must be in place as the substrate.
Blast walls require a stable foundation or substructure to bear their load and resist blast forces. The foundation must be completed first to provide the necessary structural support.
Backfilling can only occur after the blast wall is fully erected and cured, as the backfill material is placed against the completed wall.
Any final cladding, coating, or finishing applied to the blast wall must occur after the main structural wall construction is complete.
Blast doors and other penetrations through the wall are installed after the wall structure is in place, as they fit into prepared openings within the completed wall.
Paving or hardstanding adjacent to the blast wall should be completed after the wall is built to achieve proper interface detailing and drainage.

The seismic separation gap is typically formed between adjacent building structures or sections. The supporting substructure (foundations, base slabs) must be completed first to provide the base on which the separation gap is created.

The seismic separation gap physically separates adjacent structural frames or building sections. The frames on either side must be erected up to the relevant level before the gap can be formed between them.
Flexible MEP connections, expansion joint covers, and utility crossings that traverse the seismic gap must be installed after the gap is formed to ensure proper alignment and accommodate movement.

successor: Exterior Cladding / Facade Installation (at gap location)
rationale: Facade elements, weatherproofing seals, and expansion joint covers adjacent to the seismic separation gap must be installed after the gap is formed to properly bridge and seal the opening.

successor: Fire Stop Installation in Seismic Gap
rationale: Fire-rated sealants and firestop systems installed within the seismic separation gap to maintain fire compartmentation must be applied after the gap is fully formed and cleared.
Demising walls require a stable base support; the foundation or slab must be in place to bear the wall load and provide a level surface for construction.
If the demising wall is not load-bearing or is infill, the primary structural frame must be erected first to provide attachment points and establish spatial boundaries.
Demising walls define separate tenant spaces; mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in within the wall cavities and adjacent areas cannot proceed until the wall framing is in place.
The demising wall must be fully erected and inspected before applying finishes such as drywall, taping, painting, or trim to achieve a finished surface.
Firestopping around penetrations through demising walls can only be applied after the wall is built and any MEP penetrations are in place, to properly seal fire-rated separations between units.
The rough opening (door frame opening in the wall) must be framed, sized, and prepared before the fire door assembly can be installed, as the door unit fits into this opening.
The door frame (buck/jamb) must be installed and properly anchored before the fire-rated door leaf can be hung, as the door hinges attach to the frame.
Fire-rated hardware such as hinges, locks, closers, and panic bars must be installed after the door assembly is in place, as they are mounted directly onto the door leaf and frame.
Fire-rated caulking and intumescent seals around the door frame perimeter must be applied after the door assembly is installed to complete the fire-resistive barrier.
The fire door assembly must be fully installed before final inspection and fire door labeling/certification verification can be performed to confirm compliance with fire codes.
Structural framing (walls, floors, ceilings) must be in place to provide the physical substrate onto which smoke barriers are installed.
Smoke barrier doors are installed into the barrier openings and must fit precisely within the constructed barrier frame.
Penetrations through the smoke barrier (for ducts, pipes, cables) can only be sealed after the barrier itself is built to ensure a continuous smoke-tight seal.
Smoke control system testing can partially commence earlier but final integrated testing requires the smoke barriers to be complete to verify compartmentalization effectiveness.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work above ceilings must be completed before closing in the smoke barrier, as the barrier often extends through ceiling spaces to create a continuous smoke compartment.
The site must be cleared and prepared before boundary surveys can be accurately conducted, as debris or vegetation would obstruct survey measurements.
An initial assessment of site conditions is needed to understand the terrain and any existing features before defining zone boundaries.
The exact boundary lines and limits of the construction zones must be established before foundation layouts can be set out on the ground.
Zone boundaries define the areas where utilities can be routed, so the survey must be completed before utility routing can be planned.

While erosion controls can theoretically be installed in some areas before all boundaries are set, completing the zone boundary survey first ensures erosion control measures are placed within the correct zones and comply with permitting requirements.

The structural frame must be in place before fire compartmentation can be designed, as compartmentation boundaries (walls, floors) are defined by and rely on the structural grid and load-bearing elements.
The building envelope and primary subdivision of spaces must be completed to establish the physical compartments that will receive fire-rated separations.
The design of compartmentation must be finalized before constructing fire-rated walls and floors, as these elements are built according to the compartmentation plan.
Fire doors and dampers are selected and installed based on the compartmentation design specifications, including required fire resistance ratings and locations.

successor: Passive Fire Protection Inspection and Testing
rationale: Inspection and testing of passive fire protection systems can only occur after fire compartmentation has been fully designed and constructed to verify compliance.

Acoustic modelling requires the physical structure of the building (walls, floors, ceilings) to be in place so that sound transmission paths, room volumes, and boundary conditions can be accurately defined.
Finalized room layouts, materials, and geometry specifications from architectural design are needed as inputs to perform acoustic analysis and modelling.
Acoustic modelling results determine noise control requirements, which inform HVAC system sizing, ductwork layout, and vibration isolation design.
Installation of acoustic panels, baffles, insulation, and other sound-absorbing materials is based on the specifications derived from the acoustic model.

While not a strict physical necessity, completing acoustic modelling first ensures A/V system design (speaker placement, reverberation control) aligns with the acoustic environment for optimal audio performance.

The architectural floor plan defines the spatial layout, room sizes, and functional zones that form the basis for thermal zone assignment. Without a finalized floor plan, thermal zones cannot be properly delineated.
Envelope properties (wall, roof, window types, insulation levels) significantly influence thermal loads and must be known to define zone boundaries and load characteristics.

predecessor: Climate Data Analysis / Site Weather Selection
rationale: Outdoor design conditions and weather data are required as inputs to calculate heating/cooling loads per zone and to define zone conditioning strategies.
The thermal zoning analysis outputs the heating and cooling load for each zone, which is the fundamental input for sizing HVAC equipment and selecting air handling unit configurations.
Zone boundaries and load requirements determine the number, location, and capacity of diffusers, grilles, and duct runs, making the zoning analysis a prerequisite for distribution design.
Fire stopping materials must be installed in all penetrations and joints before inspection can verify their correct placement and integrity.
Fire doors are a critical component of compartmentation and must be installed before inspection to verify compliance with fire ratings and closure mechanisms.
The compartment walls and barriers must be fully constructed and finished before inspection can confirm their fire-resistance ratings and integrity.
Ceiling voids must remain open for inspection access so that fire stopping and compartmentation within ceiling spaces can be verified before being sealed.
Final finishes should not be applied until compartmentation inspection is complete, as inspection may require access to walls and surfaces for verification of fire-stopping and barrier integrity.
Movement joints in concrete slabs must be installed after the concrete has been placed/poured but before it cures fully, as the joints create controlled cracking planes in the setting concrete.

The ground or sub-base must be properly prepared, leveled, and compacted before any slab or movement joint installation can occur, as movement joints are placed within or beneath the slab on the prepared subgrade.

Formwork defines the slab perimeter and pour location; movement joints must be laid out relative to the formed area, and some pre-formed joint materials are placed before concrete is poured within the forms.

After movement joints are installed (whether saw-cut after initial set or pre-formed), the concrete surface must be finished, and proper curing must begin; joints create weak planes so finishing and curing can proceed after their installation.
Sealants are applied into the joint gap after the joint has been formed (cut or pre-formed) and after the concrete has cured sufficiently; the joint must exist before it can be sealed.

predecessor: Penetration Creation (e.g., drilling holes for pipes/cables)
rationale: Fire-stopping can only be applied after the penetrations (holes, openings) have been created in walls, floors, or ceilings to accommodate building services such as pipes, ducts, or cables.

predecessor: Installation of Mechanical, Electrical, and Plumbing (MEP) Services
rationale: Fire-stopping seals the gaps around installed MEP services (pipes, cables, ducts) after they have been routed through the penetrations, ensuring the fire-resistance rating of the compartment is restored.

successor: Final Inspection and Testing of Fire-Stopping
rationale: Once fire-stopping is complete, inspections and testing (e.g., visual checks, pull tests, smoke testing) must follow to verify compliance with fire safety standards before the area is enclosed or covered.

successor: Cladding / Finishing Works (e.g., drywall, plaster, painting)
rationale: Fire-stopping must be finished and inspected before walls, ceilings, or floors are closed up with finishing materials, as the fire-stopping needs to remain visible and accessible for inspection.

While not always physically required, pressure or smoke testing is typically performed after fire-stopping to ensure the compartment is airtight and the fire seal performs correctly; this is a quality assurance preference.

The core and shell (base building structure, exterior envelope, central MEP systems, common areas) must be substantially complete before tenant fit-out can commence, as fit-out work occurs within the shelled spaces and depends on the building being weather-tight and structurally ready.

Main mechanical, electrical, and plumbing risers and base building systems must be roughed-in to the floor level so that tenant-specific branch distribution and connections can be designed and installed during fit-out.

The tenant lease agreement must be signed to define the scope, layout, and finish standards for the fit-out; this is a contractual/administrative prerequisite, though some pre-leasing coordination may begin earlier.

Coordination activities (design approval, permit applications, material procurement, and trade scheduling) must be completed before physical interior construction work (demolition, framing, drywall, finishes) can begin on the tenant's demised premises.

Final tenant-specific mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and finish installations cannot start until the coordination process has resolved conflicts, secured permits, and established the installation sequence through detailed shop drawings and submittals.
Site survey and land acquisition must be completed before zoning can begin, as zoning decisions depend on the physical boundaries, topography, and ownership of the land parcel.
Environmental constraints and sensitive areas identified in the EIA must inform the zoning designations to avoid inappropriate land uses.
The overarching city or regional master plan provides the strategic vision and broad land-use categories that the detailed zoning plan must conform to.
A legally adopted zoning plan is a prerequisite for any building permit application, as permits must comply with the designated zoning district and permitted uses.
Infrastructure networks must be designed around the approved zoning layout to ensure roads, water, sewer, and power align with the designated development zones.

Accurate topographic and geodetic surveys of the land are required before any grid layout can be established, as the grid must conform to existing terrain contours, property boundaries, and legal survey markers.

predecessor: Land Acquisition and Legal Zoning Approval
rationale: The legal right to use the land and approved zoning regulations must be in place before the urban grid can be designed and staked out, as the grid layout depends on parcel boundaries and permitted land uses.
Understanding soil bearing capacity and underground conditions is necessary to determine optimal street and block orientations within the grid layout.
The paved road network follows the grid layout; streets cannot be constructed until the grid pattern, block dimensions, and street alignments have been finalized and staked.

successor: Utility Trenching and Underground Infrastructure Installation
rationale: Water, sewer, gas, electrical and telecom conduits are typically laid within the rights-of-way defined by the grid; the grid layout must be established before trenching can begin along those alignments.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and excavated before any building foundation work can begin.
Foundations must be poured and cured before the superstructure (building) can be erected.
Underground water, sewer, electrical, and data conduits must be installed before slab or foundation is placed, as they are buried beneath the building.
The building structure must be enclosed (roof, walls, windows) before interior drywall, flooring, painting, and finishes can be installed to protect materials from weather.
Structural framing must be complete before running HVAC ducts, electrical wiring, and plumbing pipes through walls and ceilings.
Regulatory permits (e.g., environmental, land disturbance) must be obtained and site access established before any ground disturbance can begin.
Accurate site survey, boundary staking, and grade stakes are required to define the limits of clearing, grading, and earthmoving operations.
Existing underground utilities must be located and marked to avoid damage during excavation and to plan for any required utility relocations.
The building pad must be rough-graded and compacted to specification before foundation excavation can begin to ensure a stable, level substrate.
Underground drainage, water, sewer, and conduit networks are installed in open trenches after site grading and before final slab/floor construction.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and compacted before any road pavement layers can be laid, otherwise the road structure will lack a stable foundation.

All underground utilities (water, sewer, gas, electrical conduits, telecom ducts) must be installed or relocated before the road sub-base and pavement are placed, to avoid cutting into the finished road surface.
The base and sub-base layers of the road structure must be completed before the final asphalt wearing course can be laid.
Road markings, traffic signs, and signals can only be applied or installed after the finished road surface is in place and cured.
Street lighting poles and roadside landscaping are typically installed after the road structure is complete to avoid damage from construction equipment, though some planting can be done in parallel.

The site must be cleared, leveled, and graded before any underground utility lines (water, sewer, gas, electric, telecom) can be trenched and installed, as uneven ground or debris would hinder excavation and damage equipment.

Soil conditions must be assessed to determine trenching requirements, shoring needs, and backfill materials before installing underground utilities; unknown soil conditions could cause trench collapse or improper pipe bedding.

Underground utility lines (water supply, sewer drainage, electrical conduits, gas lines) must be in place before pouring foundations and concrete slabs, as these utilities need to run beneath or into the building footprint.

Water, sewer, gas, and electrical conduits that run under roads and parking areas must be installed and backfilled before paving can begin, otherwise roads would need to be torn up later to install utilities.

While not a strict physical necessity, completing underground utility connections before starting above-ground mechanical rough-in allows the building to have temporary power and water during construction, improving efficiency.
The project scope, location, and basic design must be defined before an EIA can be conducted, as the EIA evaluates environmental impacts of a specific proposed project.
The specific site location must be chosen before environmental impacts can be assessed, as different sites have different ecological and environmental conditions.
Basic design parameters (scale, footprint, layout) are needed to evaluate potential environmental impacts and propose mitigation measures.
EIA findings and mitigation requirements may impose design constraints that must be incorporated into the detailed design phase.
The EIA report is typically a prerequisite document required by regulatory authorities before construction permits, environmental licenses, or development approvals can be issued.
Physical construction activities cannot commence until the EIA has been completed, reviewed, and approved, as the EIA determines whether the project can proceed and under what conditions.
Legal and regulatory framework must be established to permit increased density, including zoning changes, height allowances, and density bonuses before any densification projects can commence.
Evaluation of existing water, sewer, electricity, transportation, and other infrastructure must be completed to determine if upgrades are needed to support higher population density.
Parcels of land must be assembled and acquired before redevelopment at higher densities can physically occur on the site.
Existing structures on the site must be removed and the site cleared before new denser construction can begin.
The densified buildings must be completed before people can move in and occupy the new residential or commercial spaces.
Transit routes and frequencies may need to be adjusted to serve the increased population, though this can sometimes be planned in parallel; ideally it follows completion to accurately match demand.
A thorough environmental site assessment (Phase I/II ESA) must be completed to identify the type, extent, and location of contamination before any remediation plan can be designed and executed.
Remediation cannot legally commence without obtaining necessary permits and approval from environmental regulatory agencies (e.g., EPA, state DEQ).
A detailed remediation strategy and engineering design must be developed based on site assessment results before field remediation work begins.
After remediation activities conclude, confirmatory soil/groundwater sampling and testing must be conducted to verify that cleanup goals have been achieved.
Brownfield remediation must be completed and the site certified as clean before redevelopment activities such as excavation, foundation work, or building construction can safely proceed.
Land must be acquired and regional zoning plans approved before interface infrastructure (connecting urban and rural zones) can be sited and constructed.
An environmental assessment is required to identify sensitive ecological transition zones and obtain permits before disturbing the urban-rural boundary area.

predecessor: Utility Trunk Line Installation (Water, Power, Gas)
rationale: While not strictly required in all cases, it is highly preferred to have main utility trunks laid to the edge of the development zone before building the interface connectors, to avoid re-excavation.
The interface infrastructure (e.g., gateway roads, fencing, checkpoints) must be complete before paving rural access roads that connect to it, to ensure proper alignment and drainage integration.
Utility connections from the rural side cannot be energized or activated until the interface infrastructure (substations, tap points, metering stations) is fully installed and tested.
The site must be cleared, graded, and excavated before any superstructure construction can begin, as the foundation and substructure work require a prepared ground.
Foundations (including piles, footings, and ground beams) must be completed to provide structural support for the mixed-use building block before above-ground construction can commence.
Underground utility mains and service connections need to be installed before slab-on-grade or ground-floor construction to avoid costly rework and ensure service availability.
Structural and envelope completion is necessary before interior partitioning, MEP rough-in, and finishes can be installed, as these depend on the enclosed, weathertight shell.
The main structural frame must be complete to safely apply external cladding, glazing, and curtain wall systems.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and prepared before any recreational facility construction can begin to ensure a stable foundation and proper drainage.
Underground utility lines and connections to water, power, and sewage systems must be installed prior to building the facility to avoid costly retrofitting and disruption.
The main recreational facility structure must be completed before final landscaping, turf installation, and planting can be done to prevent damage from construction equipment.
Access paths, walking trails, and hardscape connections to the facility should be installed after the facility is built to ensure proper alignment and integration with building entrances.
Playground equipment, benches, picnic tables, and other site furnishings can only be installed once the facility structure is complete and surrounding areas are stable.

A comprehensive site assessment and feasibility study must be completed before urban densification can begin to evaluate existing infrastructure capacity, zoning regulations, environmental constraints, and structural viability of adding density to the area.
All necessary zoning changes, planning permits, and regulatory approvals must be secured before commencing urban densification to ensure legal compliance and avoid construction violations.
Any existing structures on the site that are incompatible with the densification plan must be demolished or deconstructed to clear the site for new construction.

After completing urban densification (new residential/commercial units), the local infrastructure such as water supply, sewage, electrical grid, and transportation networks must be upgraded or expanded to accommodate the increased population and demand.

Soft preference: Landscaping, green spaces, and public amenities are typically finished after densification to enhance the urban environment, though they could theoretically be phased in parallel in some cases.

A thorough site assessment and conservation planning must be completed to identify ecological values, sensitive areas, and appropriate conservation strategies before any green wedge conservation work can begin.
The land designated as a green wedge must be formally acquired or zoned for conservation purposes to establish legal authority and protection status before conservation activities commence.
Engaging with local communities, landowners, and environmental groups early helps ensure support and reduce conflicts, though conservation could theoretically begin without full agreement.
Ongoing ecological monitoring and maintenance (such as weed control, replanting, and access management) must follow conservation actions to ensure long-term success and adaptive management.

Developing trails, signage, and visitor facilities can follow conservation work to allow public enjoyment, but this is a soft preference as access may be restricted depending on conservation sensitivity.
A specific site must be selected and acquired before zoning and masterplanning can begin, as the location, size, and boundaries of the parcel are fundamental inputs to any land-use plan.
Initial environmental evaluation of the site must be completed to identify any contamination, wetlands, or protected habitats that would constrain permissible land uses and zoning designations.
Knowledge of existing topography, soil conditions, and subsurface characteristics is required to inform realistic land-use allocations, building envelopes, and density planning.
Understanding community需求和market demand helps shape appropriate land-use mix and density, but masterplanning can begin with preliminary assumptions before formal assessments are finalized.
The masterplan establishes zoning districts, density limits, land-use allocations, and overall site layout, which form the binding framework within which individual building designs must comply.
The masterplan determines the spatial distribution of land uses, road networks, and development parcels, which dictates where utilities, water mains, sewers, and power lines must be routed.
The approved masterplan and zoning designation are prerequisite documents that must be submitted as part of formal development permit applications to local authorities.
The masterplan defines parcel boundaries, lot sizes, and circulation patterns; subdivision into individual plots cannot proceed until these spatial allocations are finalized.

Regional transportation and transit network planning must be completed first to determine where transit stations and corridors will be located, which defines the anchor points around which TOD is built.
Existing zoning codes and land use regulations must be reviewed and revised to permit higher-density, mixed-use development around transit stations before TOD can proceed.
Environmental reviews and impact assessments must be conducted to identify constraints, mitigate risks, and obtain necessary permits before construction can begin.

The transit station and core transit infrastructure must be built or at least substantially underway to serve as the anchor for TOD, ensuring that development is oriented around existing or imminent transit service.

Public input and stakeholder buy-in should be obtained before TOD design and construction to align the development with community needs and reduce opposition, though this is a procedural best practice rather than a physical necessity.
The overall TOD master plan and site preparation must be complete before individual mixed-use buildings (residential, retail, office) within the TOD zone can be constructed.
The TOD layout, including street grids and block patterns, must be established before installing sidewalks, bike lanes, and pedestrian pathways to ensure proper integration.
The TOD site grading and core infrastructure placement must be completed before installing or upgrading utilities (water, sewer, electricity) to serve the new development.

successor: Public Realm and Open Space Landscaping
rationale: While landscaping and public spaces can begin after core TOD construction, they are often sequenced afterward as finishing work; however some soft landscape elements could theoretically be installed concurrently.
The base TOD buildings and common areas must be substantially complete before individual tenants can install interior finishes, fixtures, and commence occupancy.

The ground must be cleared, leveled, and prepared before any infrastructure extension (e.g., laying pipes, cables, or roads) can begin, as the new infrastructure requires a stable and unobstructed base.
Soil analysis, load-bearing capacity testing, and site surveying must be completed to determine the appropriate design and foundation requirements for the infrastructure extension.
Existing underground utilities (water, gas, electricity, telecom) must be located and marked to avoid damage during excavation and construction of new infrastructure.

After the physical infrastructure (e.g., pipes, cables, road segments) is extended, it must be tested for leaks, continuity, load capacity, and proper integration with existing systems before being put into service.

Once the extension work (laying conduits, pouring concrete, installing structures) is complete, trenches and excavated areas can be backfilled and the surface restored to its original or finished condition.
Environmental impact assessments must be completed to identify sensitive ecological areas and justify the need for greenbelt protection legislation.
Existing land use plans and zoning regulations must be analysed to determine where greenbelt boundaries should be drawn and what land uses need to be restricted.
Public input, particularly from landowners, farmers, and environmental groups, should be gathered before enacting greenbelt laws to ensure community support and reduce opposition.
Greenbelt legislation must be in place to legally empower authorities to acquire or designate protected greenbelt lands.
Enforcement mechanisms and legal frameworks must be established before compliance monitoring and auditing of greenbelt regulations can begin.
An urban growth boundary must be established first to define the limit beyond which sprawl prevention measures (fingers) are to be enforced.
Zoning must be in place to identify areas designated for growth versus those to be protected from sprawl, guiding where finger prevention measures apply.
Assessing environmental impacts beforehand helps tailor sprawl prevention strategies to protect sensitive ecosystems, though not a strict physical prerequisite.
Green infrastructure (e.g., parks, greenbelts) can only be developed after sprawl prevention measures have designated and protected the open spaces.
Transport corridors should be planned after sprawl prevention to ensure they align with the desired finger-shaped growth pattern, though some preliminary planning can occur simultaneously.
The ground must be graded and excavated to the proper slopes and elevations before a drainage ditch can be constructed, as the ditch relies on the final contouring to function correctly.
Any underground utilities (e.g., water, sewer, gas lines) that cross the ditch path must be installed first to avoid conflicts or the need to dig up the completed ditch later.
The drainage ditch must be completed before building adjacent road layers to ensure proper drainage away from the road structure and prevent water damage.
Final landscaping and topsoil placement should occur after the ditch is finished to avoid sediment runoff into the ditch and to allow for clean, finished edges.
Culverts or outlet pipes that connect to the drainage ditch must be installed after the ditch is formed to ensure correct alignment, elevation, and hydraulic connection.
The levee must be built on properly graded and prepared ground to ensure structural stability and uniform compaction.
The levee requires a compacted and stable foundation to prevent differential settlement and potential failure under flood loads.
Internal drainage systems must be placed before levee embankment construction to manage seepage and prevent water pressure buildup within the levee.
Erosion protection such as riprap or revetment must be placed on the finished levee slopes to protect against scour during flood events.

successor: Levee Crown Paving & Access Road Construction
rationale: Paving and access roads on the levee crest are typically done after the levee is completed to provide maintenance access, though in some cases staging can overlap.
A stable reinforced concrete foundation is required to support the heavy weight of the grain storage silo and its contents before the silo structure can be erected.
The ground must be properly leveled and drainage systems installed to prevent water accumulation around the silo base, which could compromise structural stability.
Grain handling conveyors and bucket elevators must be attached to and aligned with the silo structure, requiring the silo to be in place first.
Aeration ducts, fans, and drying equipment are installed into and around the silo structure, which must be completed before these systems can be fitted.
The bottom discharge hopper and gates are mounted to the silo's outlet structure, requiring the silo to be fully erected before these components are attached.
Vegetation and surface debris must be removed from the road alignment before any earthwork or road construction can begin to ensure a clean working surface.
Erosion control measures such as silt fences and check dams must be in place prior to earth disturbance activities to comply with environmental regulations and prevent sediment runoff.
The subgrade of the road must be prepared and compacted before placing the aggregate base course to provide a stable foundation.
The base course and geometric formation of the road must be completed before any final wearing surface (gravel, stone, or pavement) can be applied.
Cattle guards are typically placed after the road subgrade and base are formed to ensure proper integration with the road profile and drainage.
Soil conditions, drainage patterns, and site-specific factors must be assessed to determine optimal tree/shrub species selection and planting layout for the windbreak.
The planting area must be cleared of debris, weeds, and obstacles, and the ground must be graded to ensure proper drainage and a suitable planting bed.
If topsoil stripping is required for the site, it must be completed before planting to ensure that quality topsoil is preserved and available for backfill around root balls.

It is preferable to install the main irrigation lines after the windbreak layout is finalized to avoid damaging the newly planted trees/shrubs, though trenching could be done before planting with careful planning.
The shelterbelt must be established (planted and mulched) before final landscaping and decorative finishes are applied to avoid disturbing the newly planted vegetation.
The ground must be properly graded and cleared before trenching for irrigation lines can begin, ensuring proper drainage and stable base.
All existing underground utilities must be located and marked to avoid damaging them during trenching for irrigation pipes.
Main water supply lines and connection points to the irrigation system must be in place before irrigation laterals and sprinkler heads can be connected.
After irrigation pipes and components are installed in trenches, the trenches can be backfilled and final grading completed.
Irrigation system must be fully installed, tested, and operational before planting turf or landscape plants so they receive adequate water immediately.
The site must be cleared of all vegetation, debris, and existing structures before soil can be prepared and tilled, as tilling requires an unobstructed work area.
Boundaries and grading stakes must be set to define the area where soil preparation and tilling will occur, ensuring the work is confined to the correct zone.
Soil testing must be completed first to determine if amendments (lime, fertilizer, organic matter) are needed; tilling incorporates these amendments, so the testing results must be known beforehand.
Underground utilities must be located and marked to avoid damage during tilling operations, as deep tilling can strike buried lines.
Erosion controls (silt fences, sediment basins) must be in place before soil is disturbed by tilling, to prevent sediment runoff as required by environmental regulations.
Tilling breaks up and loosens the soil; final grading and leveling must follow to create a smooth, even surface at the desired elevation for subsequent construction.

If soil amendments (compost, lime, fertilizer) are added, tilling must occur first to aerate and loosen the soil, allowing amendments to be thoroughly mixed in during a second pass or subsequent operation.
Tilled soil provides a stable, compactable subgrade; the aggregate base course for pavements, slabs, or foundations is placed on top of the prepared and compacted subgrade.
For landscaping, tilling is the first step in soil cultivation; seeding or sodding of grass and plants can only be done after the soil has been tilled and smoothed.

Soil borings, bearing capacity tests, and subsurface exploration must be completed first to determine the foundation conditions, soil type, and groundwater levels necessary for designing stable levee and embankment slopes.
The ground surface must be cleared, stripped of topsoil, and graded to proper elevations before placing fill material to ensure proper bonding and prevent differential settlement.
Underdrains, toe drains, and dewatering measures must be installed prior to embankment placement to control seepage and prevent water from weakening the fill during construction.

After each lift of fill is placed, compaction tests (e.g., Proctor tests, nuclear density gauge) must be performed to verify that the specified density and moisture content requirements are met before proceeding with subsequent lifts.
Embankment shaping must be completed before turf establishment, riprap placement, or erosion control blankets can be applied to protect the slopes from surface runoff and wave action.
Site survey and assessment must be completed first to identify topography, soil conditions, drainage patterns, and slope gradients that determine the terracing and grading design requirements.

All vegetation, trees, stumps, and topsoil must be cleared from the construction area before terracing and grading can begin to expose the native soil/subgrade and ensure proper cut and fill operations.
Any existing structures, foundations, or debris must be fully demolished and removed to provide a clear work area for earthmoving equipment during terracing and grading.
After terracing and grading are complete, the prepared subgrade must be compacted and stabilized to achieve the required soil density and load-bearing capacity before any subsequent construction.
Terracing creates flat, level building platforms; foundations and footings can only be excavated and poured after the terraced benches are graded to final elevations.

The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and obstructions before any drainage work can begin to provide unobstructed access to the ground surface and ensure proper grading for drainage systems.

Rough grading establishes the required slopes and elevations needed for drainage systems to function correctly; drainage pipes and structures must be installed into the prepared subgrade at the proper grades.
Existing underground utilities must be located and marked to avoid damage during excavation for drainage infrastructure and to plan safe routing of new drainage lines.
After drainage pipes and structures are installed, the excavated trenches must be backfilled and compacted to restore ground support and prevent future settlement.
Drainage systems must be fully installed and operational before paving layers are placed, to ensure proper subsurface drainage and avoid having to cut into finished pavement for drainage corrections.
The subgrade must be prepared, leveled, and compacted to provide a stable foundation before any kerb or edging can be installed.
The road base or sub-base course must be laid and compacted to establish the correct pavement profile and support for the kerb.
Underground drainage pipes and catch basins must be installed below the kerb line before kerbing to avoid later excavation that would disturb the kerb.
Kerb and edging act as a formwork and guide for asphalt or pavement layers, which are placed flush against the kerb after it has cured.
Footpaths are typically constructed after kerbing is complete, as the kerb defines the edge of the roadway and provides a boundary for the sidewalk.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and obstructions, and the ground must be graded before hedgerow planting can begin to ensure proper soil conditions and access.

Soil must be tested for pH, nutrients, and drainage capacity, and any necessary amendments (lime, fertilizer, organic matter) must be applied before planting hedgerow species to ensure healthy establishment.
Any sub-surface drainage systems must be installed before hedgerow planting to prevent waterlogging of roots and ensure long-term viability.

Fencing is often installed after hedgerow planting to protect young plants from livestock and wildlife, though it can also be done before; it is a soft preference to plant first then fence to avoid damaging newly installed posts during planting operations.
Mulch and weed control fabric or herbicide should be applied immediately after planting to suppress competition from weeds and retain soil moisture, which is critical for establishment.
While irrigation can be installed before planting, it is often preferred to plant the hedgerow first and then lay drip irrigation along the row to ensure proper alignment with the planted root zones.
A stable foundation (compacted soil or levelled ground) must be prepared before the first stones are placed, otherwise the wall will settle unevenly or collapse.
A trench is required to set the larger base stones (footings) below frost line or topsoil; the wall cannot be built without this supporting trench.
Stones must be gathered, sorted by size and shape, and delivered to site before construction can begin; no wall can be built without the raw materials.
Coping or capstones are placed on top of the completed wall to finish it; they require the full wall structure beneath to be complete for proper seating and stability.
If the wall is retaining or freestanding, backfill material and drainage aggregate can only be placed after the wall is built to prevent collapse or shifting of stones during backfilling.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and marked before posts can be set to ensure proper alignment and stable footing for the fence structure.
Property boundaries and fence lines must be surveyed and staked out to ensure the fence is erected in the correct location and along the proper alignment.
Holes for the timber posts must be dug before posts can be placed and set in concrete or compacted earth.
Once posts are positioned vertically in the holes, gravel must be added and backfill compacted to secure the posts in place before rails can be attached.
Rails cannot be fastened to posts until the posts are set, plumb, and adequately secured in their holes.
Road markings must be applied on a completed, stable, and clean paved surface. Applying markings before paving is physically impossible as the base would be unstable or non-existent.
Curbs define the road edge and drainage boundaries; markings must align with the curb lines. Installing curbs after markings would disrupt or cover them.
Road markings and signage provide essential guidance, warnings, and regulatory information for drivers. The road cannot be safely opened to traffic without these visual cues in place.
It is preferable to complete markings and signage before the final inspection so the inspector can verify all markings meet specifications, though inspection could theoretically occur without them.
The planting area must be cleared, leveled, and properly graded before trees can be planted to ensure proper drainage and root establishment.
All underground utilities such as water, sewer, gas, and electrical lines must be installed before tree planting to avoid digging near or damaging newly planted trees and their root systems.

Curbs, sidewalks, and paved street surfaces must be completed first so that tree pits or planting strips are properly located and aligned with the hardscape, and to prevent soil compaction or damage from construction equipment after planting.
Irrigation lines and drip emitters must be placed after trees are planted to ensure they are positioned correctly around each tree's root ball for efficient watering during establishment.
Final grading, mulching, and surface landscaping around the tree pits can only be completed after the trees are in place to ensure proper finish grading and aesthetic integration.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, structures, and debris before earthworks can begin to ensure a clean working area and prevent organic material from being buried under road foundations.

Accurate topographical surveys and staking out of road alignments, levels, and boundaries must be completed before earthmoving and grading can commence to ensure the road is built to correct specifications and alignments.

Soil bearing capacity, compaction characteristics, and ground conditions must be assessed before earthworks to determine whether ground improvement, stabilization, or special foundation treatments are needed for the road subgrade.
The subgrade must be graded, compacted, and shaped to design levels before any pavement layers (sub-base, base course) can be placed on top of the prepared earthwork formation.

Earthworks must be completed to create the road profile and cross-section before installing drainage ditches, culverts, and sub-drains, as these are integrated into the earthwork formation and road prism.
A stable, compacted and graded sub-base or base layer is physically required to support the surfacing material (asphalt, concrete, etc.). Surfacing cannot be laid on unprepared ground.
