Drainage systems (culverts, stormwater pipes, kerbs and gutters) must be installed and operational before final surfacing, otherwise water damage would require cutting and patching the new surface.
Underground utility lines (water, gas, electricity, telecoms) must be laid in trenches and backfilled before surfacing to avoid excavating through the finished surface.

Road markings, signage, and surface-mounted furniture (bollards, reflectors) must be applied after the final surface course is placed, as they adhere to or are installed on top of the finished surface.
Joint sealing in concrete pavements or crack sealing in asphalt must be done after the surfacing material has been placed and initially set/cured to ensure proper adhesion and performance.
Site must be cleared of vegetation and debris before any kerb installation can commence to provide a clean working area and proper alignment.
The subgrade must be properly graded and compacted to provide a stable foundation for kerb and edging, preventing future settlement or misalignment.
Bulk earthworks and cut/fill operations must be completed so that the final surface levels are established for accurate kerb line and grade installation.
Subsurface drainage pipes and catch basins must be installed before kerbing so that drainage infrastructure is in place and kerb inlets can be correctly tied in.
Kerb forms the edge restraint for pavement; asphalt or paving must be placed after kerbs are set to achieve proper abuttment and finished surface elevation.
Site must be graded and leveled before any street furniture can be placed to ensure stable foundations and proper alignment.
Underground utilities (water, gas, electric, telecom) must be laid before street furniture is installed to avoid digging up or damaging finished furniture.
Road base and pavement must be completed so that street furniture (e.g., benches, bollards, signs) can be anchored on a finished surface.
While planting can sometimes be done concurrently, it is generally preferred to install furniture first to avoid damaging new plants and to ensure proper spacing and access.
Street furniture must be installed before final surface finishes (e.g., decorative paving, joint sealing) around the furniture bases to create a neat, integrated appearance.

Street furniture (such as benches, bollards, signposts, lighting poles) is typically anchored to or placed on the finished road surface or pavement. Installing street furniture before the final pavement course would result in the furniture being at the wrong height, damaged during paving, or requiring removal and reinstallation.

Underground utility ducts, cables, and pipes must be laid before street furniture is installed, because many items of street furniture (e.g., lighting columns, traffic signals, EV charging points) require a direct underground connection to utility networks. Installing furniture before utilities would necessitate excavation beneath or around the already-placed furniture.

Curbs and gutters define the edge of the roadway and footway, establishing the exact boundary lines and levels where street furniture (bollards, signs, benches) must be placed. Without curbs in place, furniture positions cannot be accurately set relative to the road edge.

Soft preference: While planting can be done after furniture installation, it is often more efficient to complete final landscaping after furniture is in place so that planting beds and grass are not trampled by installation equipment. However, some landscaping activities (e.g., tree planting) must be done before certain furniture (e.g., tree grilles and guards).

successor: Street Lighting and Traffic Signal Commissioning
rationale: The physical installation of lighting columns and signal poles must be completed before electrical commissioning (testing, energizing, and adjusting light beam angles or signal timing) can take place. Commissioning requires the equipment to be mechanically installed and connected.
The site must be cleared, graded, and excavated to the required levels before any bridge or culvert foundation work can begin.
Soil bearing capacity, subsurface conditions, and foundation design parameters must be determined before designing and constructing bridge/culvert foundations.
Traffic must be diverted away from the construction area to ensure safety and provide a clear workspace before bridge or culvert construction commences.
Any underground or overhead utilities (water, gas, electrical, telecom) in the bridge/culvert footprint must be relocated or protected before excavation and construction can start.
The bridge/culvert structure must be completed and cured before the road pavement and wearing course can be laid across or adjacent to it.
Safety barriers and guardrails on the bridge and approach roads can only be installed after the bridge structure is complete and stable.
While preferable to mark after structure completion to ensure alignment, markings could theoretically be applied beforehand but would risk damage during construction.
The completed structure must undergo load testing and structural inspection before being opened to traffic to verify safety and compliance with design specifications.

Traffic calming features such as speed humps, raised crosswalks, or chicanes must be installed on a properly prepared and compacted road base/subgrade to ensure structural stability and load-bearing capacity.
The road surface must be paved to the correct grade and finish before traffic calming features (e.g., speed humps, raised tables) can be formed or installed integral to the pavement.
Drainage systems (curbs, gutters, inlets) must be in place to manage water flow around traffic calming features, preventing ponding or erosion that could compromise the feature.
Warning signs, pavement markings, and delineators alerting drivers to the traffic calming feature can only be applied after the physical feature is constructed and in its final position.

While not strictly physically required, it is strongly preferred to install or adjust street lighting after the traffic calming feature is in place to ensure the feature is properly illuminated for nighttime visibility and safety.
The ground must be graded and prepared to ensure proper drainage and a stable base before installing the gate and access point.

predecessor: Foundation / Concrete Works for Gate Posts
rationale: Concrete footings or post bases must be poured and cured to anchor the gate posts securely before the gate structure can be installed.

predecessor: Underground Utility Installation (if crossing access point)
rationale: Any water, electrical, or communication lines that run under the access way must be installed before the gate to avoid excavating later and damaging the finished gate.
The field gate provides the opening in the fence line; perimeter fencing on either side is typically tied into the gate posts, requiring the gate to be in place first.
The access drive surface (e.g., gravel, asphalt, concrete) should be laid after the gate is installed to achieve a smooth transition and avoid damaging new pavement during gate installation.
A level, stable ground surface is physically required before constructing a grain silo or bulk storage facility to ensure structural stability and proper foundation placement.
The concrete foundation (including ring foundations or mat slabs) must be cured and ready to support the heavy loads of the silo structure before erection of the silo itself can begin.
Drainage systems, grounding grids, and electrical conduits beneath the silo must be installed prior to silo construction as they would be inaccessible once the silo is built.

successor: Mechanical Conveying and Aeration System Installation
rationale: Conveyors, bucket elevators, augers, and aeration fans are installed into the silo structure after the silo shell is complete, as they attach to and pass through the silo walls and roof.
Temperature monitoring cables, level sensors, and motor control wiring can only be run and terminated once the silo structure is in place and the conveying equipment is mounted.
The water tower requires a stable foundation; excavation and ground preparation must be completed before any vertical structure can be erected.
The concrete foundation must be poured, cured, and set to support the weight and anchoring of the water tower structure.
The steel tank components must be fabricated off-site or on-site before they can be lifted and assembled into the water tower structure.
The water tower must be fully erected and stable before pipes can be connected from the tower to the water distribution network.

successor: Water Tower Painting and Corrosion Protection
rationale: While painting is typically done after erection for access, some coatings could theoretically be applied before assembly; however, final coating is best applied after the structure is complete to cover weld joints and field connections.
The verandah structure requires a stable foundation or slab to bear its load; building the structural frame before the foundation is complete would be structurally unsound.
The timber verandah frame must be erected to provide the structural support for roofing materials; roof cannot be installed without the underlying frame.
The structural frame of the verandah (posts, beams, joists) must be in place before decking boards or flooring can be laid on top.
Balustrades and handrails are mounted onto or between the verandah posts and frame; the main structure must exist to act as the substrate for these safety elements.

While painting typically follows construction, it is a soft preference because the structure could theoretically be painted in sections before full completion, though standard practice is to finish erection first.
A Heritage Impact Assessment must be completed before any conservation works begin to identify heritage values, constraints, and required protection measures.
Detailed site surveys and documentation of existing conditions are necessary to plan conservation works accurately and to establish baseline records.
Statutory heritage approvals and permits from relevant authorities must be secured before any physical conservation works can legally commence.
Conservation works must be complete before installing interpretive signage or displays, as these elements are sensitive and should not be subjected to construction disturbance.
A final inspection and certification process must occur after conservation works are finished to verify compliance with heritage specifications and approval conditions.
The underlying structure must be sound and any structural defects repaired before cosmetic façade work begins, otherwise the restoration could be applied to a failing substrate.
Safe access to the façade at height is required before any restoration work can commence on the shopfront.
Adjacent footpaths, doorways, and neighboring properties must be protected from dust, debris, and falling materials before façade work begins.
New or restored signage should be installed only after the façade surface is fully restored and finished to avoid damaging or soiling the signage during restoration work.
Final cleaning and cosmetic touch-ups should occur after all major restoration work is complete to ensure a uniform finish and to remove any construction dust or marks.

Site survey and soil testing must be completed to determine ground conditions, load-bearing capacity, and identify any underground utilities or obstacles before any construction or upgrade work can begin.
Legal land rights and necessary construction permits must be secured before physical upgrade work can commence to ensure compliance with regulations and avoid legal disputes.

Upgrades to underlying infrastructure such as drainage, water pipes, or electrical conduits must be completed before the final road surface is paved to avoid needing to tear up the completed surface for underground work.

After infrastructure upgrades are physically completed, a formal quality inspection and commissioning process must be carried out to verify that all work meets specifications and safety standards before the infrastructure is handed over for use.

Engaging with the local community and obtaining their input or approval is a soft preference that ensures smoother project execution and reduces resistance, but construction could technically proceed without it.
The construction site must be cleared, graded, and leveled before any building foundation work can begin to ensure structural stability and proper drainage.
The concrete foundations and footings must be poured and cured before the superstructure (walls, columns, roof) of the hall can be erected, as the entire building load rests on these foundations.

Underground utility connections for water supply, sewerage, and electrical conduits must be laid before slab pouring and wall construction to avoid costly post-construction trenching and structural damage.

The main structural shell (walls, roof, doors, windows) must be fully completed and weather-tight before interior finishing works such as plastering, tiling, painting, and false ceiling installation can commence, to protect materials from weather damage.

The building structure must be complete before internal electrical wiring, switchboard installation, plumbing fixtures, and sanitary fittings are installed, as these systems are integrated into the walls and floors.
Geotechnical data such as soil bearing capacity, permeability, and subsurface stratigraphy are essential to design levee foundations and select appropriate materials before construction can begin.
Regulatory permits (e.g., Clean Water Act Section 404, local floodplain permits) and environmental clearance must be obtained before any earthmoving or construction activities can commence.
Flood frequency analysis, storm surge modeling, and hydraulic design criteria determine levee height, alignment, and freeboard requirements, which must be finalized prior to construction.
Construction staging areas and the levee footprint must be free of legal encumbrances and physically cleared of vegetation and obstructions before earthwork can proceed.

successor: Embankment Compaction Testing and Quality Control
rationale: After levee fill is placed and compacted in lifts, field density tests (e.g., nuclear gauge or sand cone) must be performed to verify compaction meets specifications before subsequent lifts or final acceptance.

successor: Drainage System and Outlet Structure Installation
rationale: Internal drainage systems (e.g., toe drains, relief wells, flap gates) and culvert outlets must be installed after the levee embankment is constructed to integrate properly with the completed levee cross-section.

successor: Vegetative Stabilization and Erosion Control Seeding
rationale: Final grading and shaping of levee slopes must be completed before seeding, sodding, or placing erosion control blankets to protect the earthen structure from rainfall and runoff.

A formal inspection and certification (e.g., by USACE or local levee board) verifying the levee meets design standards must occur after all construction is finished before the system can be placed into operational service.
Land must be legally acquired and appropriately zoned before it can be subdivided and released for development.
Accurate survey data and soil analysis are required to determine subdivision boundaries, lot layouts, and land viability before release.
Environmental approvals and impact assessments must be completed to ensure subdivision design complies with regulations before land can be released.
Land must be subdivided and released so that infrastructure installation can proceed on designated lots and road corridors.
Once subdivided lots are released, they can be marketed and sold to developers or individual buyers, though this is a commercial step rather than a physical construction requirement.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated before any foundation work for the memorial can begin.
A stable concrete foundation or base must be in place to support the weight and structure of the war memorial or cenotaph.
The memorial structure must be erected first before surrounding paths, gardens, paving, and decorative landscaping can be completed around it.
The physical monument must be fully constructed and set in place before names, inscriptions, or commemorative plaques can be added or affixed to it.
While typically the memorial is completed before its official unveiling or dedication ceremony, this is a ceremonial preference rather than a physical construction necessity.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and prepared before hedgerow planting can begin to ensure proper soil conditions and layout.
Nutrient-rich topsoil must be spread over the planting area to provide a suitable growing medium for hedgerow plants.
Proper drainage systems must be in place before planting to prevent waterlogging and ensure healthy root development for the hedgerow.
Fencing is often installed after hedgerow planting to protect young plants from livestock or wildlife, though it could be done before if carefully planned.
Final landscaping and finishing work (e.g., mulch, edging, final grading) should follow hedgerow planting to complete the area without disturbing the newly planted vegetation.
The grain silo requires a stable, level foundation (typically reinforced concrete) to support its significant weight and prevent differential settlement, which could compromise structural integrity.
A reinforced concrete pad or ring foundation must be poured and fully cured before the silo structure can be erected on top to provide adequate load-bearing capacity.
The aeration fans and ductwork are integrated into the silo's base or walls and must be installed after the silo structure is complete to ensure proper sealing and air distribution.
Inlet and outlet connections for grain conveyors, bucket elevators, and augers are attached to the silo after its erection to align precisely with the silo's openings and achieve proper grain flow.
The silo roof, including vents and hatches, is installed after the main cylindrical shell is erected to enclose the structure and protect stored grain from weather and pests.
Site must be accessed, cleared, and basic facilities established before survey teams can safely and efficiently operate on site.

predecessor: Desk Study and Preliminary Site Reconnaissance
rationale: A desk study reviewing existing geological maps, historical records, and site history is needed to plan the scope, locations, and methods for the ground investigation.
Permits for intrusive ground investigation (e.g., borehole drilling permits, environmental agency consents, land access agreements) must be obtained before physical work can commence.
Soil and rock samples recovered during the ground investigation must be sent for laboratory testing (e.g., moisture content, shear strength, consolidation) to characterize material properties.
Ground investigation provides essential subsurface soil parameters (bearing capacity, stratification, groundwater conditions) that inform the selection and design of foundation systems.

A site survey and assessment must be completed to identify property boundaries, existing utilities, environmental constraints, and the extent of vegetation/obstructions before any clearing or grubbing can commence.
Environmental, tree removal, and land disturbance permits (e.g., NPDES stormwater, local clearing permits) must be secured prior to any land disturbance activities to ensure regulatory compliance.
Vegetation, stumps, roots, and topsoil must be removed before rough grading can begin, as grading requires a clear, unobstructed surface to achieve proper cut/fill elevations.
Erosion control measures (silt fences, sediment basins, etc.) must be implemented immediately after clearing to manage stormwater runoff and prevent soil erosion on the exposed, disturbed ground.
While demolition can sometimes overlap with clearing, it is generally more efficient and safer to remove vegetation and underbrush first to provide clear access to structures targeted for demolition.
The land must be cleared and graded before any rural infrastructure (such as roads, drainage, or utility poles) can be installed.
Main water, sewer, and power trunk lines need to be in place before rural infrastructure like local distribution networks and service connections are installed.
Subsurface drainage, culverts, and base layers installed as part of rural infrastructure must be completed before the final road surface is paved.
Rural infrastructure (roads, water supply, power supply) must be operational to support the construction of buildings and structures in the rural area.
While not a strict physical necessity, it is standard practice to complete all underground infrastructure before final landscaping to avoid rework and damage to finished surfaces.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and graded before any building construction can begin to ensure a stable foundation and proper drainage.
Foundation plans and engineering must be completed before construction starts so that footings and slabs can be properly placed.
Building permits and regulatory approvals (zoning, environmental, agricultural) must be obtained prior to construction to comply with legal requirements.
Arrangements for water, electricity, and other utilities need to be secured before construction to allow for proper installation of service lines.
Interior work such as installing milking systems, feeding equipment, ventilation, or storage racks can only commence after the building shell is complete and weather-tight.
Regulatory inspections and occupancy approvals occur after construction is finished to verify that the building meets all safety and building codes.
While often done after construction to avoid damage, some landscaping may be done earlier; however, final grading and restoration typically follow building completion.
Training farm staff on the new building's systems (ventilation, feeding, waste management) and formal handover can only occur after construction is fully complete.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and obstructions before fencing can be laid out and erected, otherwise the fence line cannot be accurately established.
Boundary lines and fence positions must be surveyed and pegged out before any fencing posts are installed or trenches dug.
Major ground shaping and leveling must be completed to final grades so that fence lines follow the correct topography and are not disturbed by subsequent earthmoving.

Fencing defines the perimeter, so landscaping, planting, and topsoil placement adjacent to the boundary must occur after the fence is in place to avoid damage to plants and to work up to the fence line.
While perimeter fencing is a key element of site security, it is a soft preference to install full security systems/gates after fencing is complete as temporary measures can be used beforehand.
The site must be properly graded and shaped for drainage and planting beds before any landscaping or planting can commence.
Drainage systems must be in place to prevent waterlogging and ensure healthy plant growth before planting occurs.
Underground utility services must be installed before landscaping to avoid disturbing newly planted areas and root systems.
Hardscape elements such as paths, patios, and retaining walls must be completed before planting to prevent construction traffic damage to plants and to ensure proper layout.
Final clean-up and commissioning activities can only proceed after planting is complete to avoid soil compaction, debris damage, and disturbance to newly installed vegetation.

Before submitting a formal planning application in rural areas, it is typically required to conduct pre-application consultation with the local planning authority and community to identify issues early.
A site survey and feasibility study must be completed to determine the viability of the proposed rural development before applying for planning permission.
Proof of land ownership or landowner's consent is a mandatory requirement for submitting any planning application.
Full detailed design and engineering drawings can only be developed once planning permission is granted, as the permission sets the parameters for what is approved.
Physical construction work cannot legally begin on site until planning permission has been granted by the local planning authority.
The wall or surface must be properly prepared, cleaned, and primed before any mural or art panel can be applied to ensure proper adhesion and a smooth finish.
The supporting wall or substrate must be fully built and structurally sound before the mural or art panel can be installed or painted onto it.
If the mural is at height, scaffolding may need to be erected beforehand; however, some murals are done at ground level, making this optional rather than mandatory.
A protective clear coat or anti-graffiti sealant can only be applied after the mural or artwork is fully completed and dried to protect it from weather or vandalism.
Final project inspections typically occur after all finishes including murals are complete; however, inspections can be done in phases, making this a soft preference rather than a physical necessity.
The display area must be cleared, measured, and planned before any modular fixture can be positioned, as the fixture layout depends on available floor space and traffic flow.
Flooring must be completed to provide a level and finished surface for the modular display fixtures to sit on and be anchored to, preventing instability or damage.
Any power or data conduit needed beneath the fixture location must be roughed in before the fixture is placed, as the fixture would block access to the floor.
Products cannot be placed on shelves or hanging bars until the modular fixture frame and shelves are fully assembled and secured.

While signage can technically be installed concurrently, it is standard practice to install the primary display structure first so that header signs and graphics align precisely with the fixture dimensions.
The ground must be prepared and excavated to the proper depth and elevation before any gate structure can be erected.
The concrete foundations or footings that will support the gate pillars must be poured and fully cured to achieve sufficient strength before the gate structure can be mounted.

successor: Architectural Detailing and Finishing of Gate
rationale: The primary gate structure must be erected and stabilized before any decorative cladding, cultural carvings, paint, or surface finishes can be applied.
While landscaping could be done partially in parallel, final paving and planting around the gate should occur after the gate is installed to ensure alignment with the entrance path.
Any underground electrical conduits for gate lighting or automatic opening mechanisms must be laid before the gate foundations are poured to avoid re-excavation.
The bleacher structure requires a stable, level foundation and properly prepared ground to bear the load and ensure safety and structural integrity.
If the bleachers are supported by or attached to a structural steel frame, the frame must be erected first to provide the support structure for the seating system.

predecessor: MEP Rough-In (if applicable to bleacher area)
rationale: Any underground or in-slab electrical conduit, plumbing, or drainage that runs beneath the bleacher area must be installed before the bleacher footprint is covered.
The bleacher frame structure must be in place before individual seats, handrails, aisles, and finishing touches can be installed onto the frame.
The complete bleacher system including its moving/flexible mechanisms must be installed and operational before safety inspections and occupancy approvals can be conducted.

Acoustic baffle panels are typically suspended from or attached to a ceiling grid or substructure. The support framework must be installed first to provide the physical mounting points for the panels.
Mechanical ducts, electrical conduits, and plumbing lines that run above the ceiling must be roughed in before acoustic baffles are installed, as the baffles would obstruct access to these systems.
Large overhead ductwork and piping that will be hidden or run above the acoustic baffles must be in place prior to the baffles; otherwise, the baffles would have to be removed or worked around.
After acoustic baffle panels are installed, final ceiling finishing work such as painting, trim, or touch-ups can proceed without risk of damaging the baffle panels.

While lighting can be installed before or concurrently in some designs, it is often preferred to install acoustic baffles first so that lighting fixtures can be precisely positioned relative to the baffle layout for optimal acoustic and aesthetic effect.
The raised access floor plinth must be installed on a completed structural slab or floor deck to provide a stable, level base for supporting the pedestal system.

Main underfloor services such as data cables, electrical conduits, and HVAC piping must be laid out before plinth installation so that the pedestals and floor panels do not obstruct access to these services.
Plinths (pedestal bases) must be fixed and leveled on the slab before floor panels can be placed onto them.
The plinth forms the base of the pedestal; the adjustable head and support stringers are mounted onto the plinth before panels are laid.

predecessor: Cultural Space Needs Assessment & Community Engagement
rationale: The needs assessment and community engagement must be completed first to establish what cultural programming is desired and required, informing the design parameters.
The site must be selected and acquired to define physical constraints and opportunities that shape the cultural space design.
Zoning approvals define allowable uses, density, and setbacks that directly impact the programming and design of cultural spaces.
The overall project master plan provides the framework (massing, circulation, adjacencies) within which cultural spaces are programmed and designed.
Detailed design and engineering require the approved cultural space program and design concepts as a starting point for technical development.
Accurate cost estimation depends on the defined program and design scope for cultural spaces.
Permit applications require completed design documents including cultural space layouts and specifications.

successor: Specialty Consultant Engagement (Acoustics, Theater Planning, Museum Design)
rationale: Specialty consultants for cultural spaces require the defined program and spatial design to begin their detailed analyses and designs.

predecessor: Site Preparation and Floor Flatness Verification
rationale: The floor surface must be level, clean, and prepared before adaptive partitions can be installed, as these partitions require a precise and stable base for proper alignment and functionality.
All overhead and in-wall mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work must be completed before partition installation to avoid rework and damage to the finished partitions.
The overhead support tracks or grid system for the adaptive partitions must be installed first to provide the structural anchor and guidance system for the partition panels.
Final flooring finishes (such as carpet, tile, or polished concrete) must be completed after partition installation to avoid damaging the floor finishes or requiring cutting around partition bases.

Final electrical, data, and other utility connections to the partitions (such as power/data modules integrated into the partition system) must be completed after the partitions are fully installed and aligned.
Electrical rough-in work (conduit, wiring, junction boxes) must be completed to provide the necessary infrastructure and power pathways for cultural lighting systems before commissioning can begin.
Ceiling and wall finishes must be installed as the mounting surfaces and backdrop for cultural lighting fixtures; commissioning lighting without finished surfaces would be premature.
All cultural lighting fixtures must be physically installed before they can be commissioned, tested, and calibrated.
Commissioning of cultural lighting is a prerequisite for project close-out activities, as the lighting system must be verified operational before final inspections and handover.
The building cannot be handed over or occupied until the cultural lighting system has been fully commissioned to ensure it meets design intent and safety requirements.
The overhead crane is needed to lift and position the heavy base frame of the Agile Workstation into place before any workstation assembly can begin.

successor: Bolt and level Agile Workstation base frame
rationale: The base frame must be positioned in its final location before it can be bolted down and leveled.

predecessor: Bolt and level Agile Workstation base frame
rationale: Vertical columns must be mounted onto a leveled and secured base frame to ensure structural stability and alignment.
Crossbeams connect the vertical columns; columns must be in place first to serve as attachment points.
The work surface/platform is supported by the crossbeam structure, so the frame must be complete before the platform can be installed.

A community needs assessment must identify key issues, concerns, and priorities before engaging the community in a co-design workshop, ensuring that the workshop has a clear problem statement and scope to work from.
Relevant stakeholders, community members, and participants must be identified and invited before the workshop can be scheduled and conducted.
A physical or virtual venue, materials, and logistical arrangements must be secured prior to the workshop taking place.

The workshop generates community input, ideas, and preferences that inform the development of design concepts; while some preliminary concepts could exist, the co-design outputs ideally feed directly into concept development.
Workshop outcomes, participant feedback, and design suggestions must be compiled and documented after the workshop for use in subsequent planning phases.
Electrical and data wiring for power outlets, switches, or motorized screens must be roughed-in within walls/ceilings before partition installation to avoid surface-mounted conduits or rework.

predecessor: Complete overhead structure and ceiling grid
rationale: Movable partitions suspend from or attach to the overhead structure/framing; ceiling grid and support tracks must be installed before the partition panels can be hung or tracked.
Floor-mounted tracks or bottom guides for movable partitions require finished flooring to be in place for proper alignment, clearance, and anchoring.

successor: Final wall and ceiling finishing (paint, trim)
rationale: Partition installation may require touch-ups around tracks and edges; however, major painting and finishing should be substantially complete before partition installation to avoid overspray and damage to partition surfaces.
Movable partitions must be fully installed and operational before the final building commissioning and inspection process can verify their functionality and compliance.

Flooring (carpet, tiles, hardwood) must be fully installed and cured before placing loose furniture and soft seating to avoid damage to finished floors and to prevent furniture from blocking access during installation.

Wall finishes such as painting and wallpapering must be completed before furniture is brought in to avoid dust, splatters, and obstructions that would damage or dirty the soft seating and loose furniture.

Ceiling work (painting, acoustic tiles) and overhead lighting installation must be finished before placing furniture to prevent dust falling on upholstery and to allow unimpeded access for ceiling work.

Once all loose furniture and soft seating are placed, the site can undergo final cleaning, touch-ups, and inspection to prepare for occupancy, as furniture placement is one of the last finishing steps.
The building can only be occupied or handed over after all loose furniture and soft seating are installed, as they are essential for the functional use and habitation of the space.

Wayfinding and zone signage must be installed after interior finishes are completed because signage is typically surface-mounted on finished walls, floors, or ceilings. Installing signage before finishes would require removal and reinstallation.

Overhead or suspended signage often attaches to ceiling structures or is coordinated with lighting layouts. Ceiling and lighting work must be complete to provide the mounting surface and proper illumination for signage.

Electrical rough-in provides the necessary power supply and conduit for illuminated or electronic signage (e.g., digital wayfinding displays). Electrical infrastructure must be in place before signage is installed.

Wayfinding and zone signage is a critical component for building navigation and must be fully installed and verified before the building can be commissioned and occupied, as occupants and visitors rely on signage to navigate the space.

While signage installation is ideally completed before final inspections to avoid re-inspection, it is a soft preference because inspections can still occur and signage can be addressed as a punch-list item afterward.
Structural framing and roofing must be completed to create a weathertight enclosed shell before interior finishes can be installed, preventing water damage and providing a stable substrate.
MEP rough-in work (conduits, ducts, pipes within walls/ceilings) must be installed and inspected before walls are closed up with drywall and interior finishes are applied.
Interior fit-out including partitioning, ceiling grids, and substrate preparation must be complete before final decorative finishes such as paint, wallcoverings, and floor coverings are applied.
Permanent fixtures (cabinetry, countertops, toilet partitions) and equipment must be installed after interior spaces are framed and finished to ensure proper fit and alignment.
All interior fit-out work must be substantially complete before final inspection and commissioning can verify that spaces meet design specifications and building codes.
The building must be fully constructed, commissioned, and handed over before occupants can move in and the building can be evaluated in use.
POE assesses the building's performance while it is occupied and in use; thus, occupants must have moved in and been using the building for a sufficient period before evaluation can begin.
Findings from the POE often identify performance gaps or occupant dissatisfaction, which may lead to retrofit or remedial work to improve building performance.
The POE generates data and insights about building performance that must be captured and documented to inform future design and construction projects.
The structural steel frame provides the primary load-bearing support system. The Landmark Facade must attach to and be supported by the completed steel frame, making it a physical prerequisite.
The building foundation and substructure must be in place to provide structural stability and load transfer before any above-grade facade work can commence.
Floor slabs provide lateral bracing for the facade and establish the floor-to-floor geometry that the facade panels must align with.
The facade must be fully enclosed and weather-tight before interior finishing work such as drywall, painting, and flooring can proceed, to protect materials from weather damage.
The primary facade structural support system and panel frame must be installed first to provide the mounting framework for glazing units and window systems.
A stable, level foundation and cleared site are physically required before any art installation can be placed to ensure structural integrity and safety.

Interactive public art often requires power and data connections; underground conduits and electrical rough-ins must be completed before the installation to avoid re-excavation or damage to the artwork.
Any supporting steelwork, mounting brackets, or anchor points must be in place before the art piece itself is installed, as they provide the physical attachment points.
The physical installation must be in place before sensors, actuators, and interactive software can be programmed and calibrated on-site to match the actual configuration.
Comprehensive safety and functionality testing of the interactive elements can only occur after the artwork is fully mounted, wired, and physically complete.
The site must be excavated and prepared to create the proper base and substrate for the water feature structure and water basin.
A concrete foundation or slab is required to provide a stable, level base to support the weight of the water feature, fountain, and water.
Underground water supply lines, return lines, and drainage pipes must be installed before the fountain structure is built above them.
Electrical conduits and wiring for the fountain pump, lighting, and controls must be roughed-in before the water feature is permanently installed.
The water feature must be fully assembled and structurally complete before waterproof membranes and decorative finishes (e.g., tile, stone cladding) are applied to its surfaces.
Final landscaping and planting around the water feature can begin after it is installed, though this is a logical sequence preference to avoid damaging plants during construction.
The fountain pump, lighting, and controls can only be tested and commissioned after the water feature is fully installed and connected to utilities.
The site must be cleared of debris and existing structures before any street furniture can be placed to ensure a clean, safe, and level installation area.
Underground utilities (water, gas, electric, telecom) must be laid before street furniture installation to avoid digging up or moving newly placed furniture and to ensure utilities are accessible.
Paving, sidewalks, and hardscape surfaces must be completed to provide a stable, finished base upon which street furniture can be anchored or placed.
Street furniture should be installed before final landscaping and planting to avoid damage to new plants and to allow proper spacing and alignment around furniture elements.
Street furniture installation is a near-final finishing step; after installation, only final cleanup, inspection, and handover activities remain.
Structural steel frames require stable load-bearing foundations to transfer structural loads to the ground; steel columns cannot be erected without completed footings and foundation systems.
A level working surface (slab or mud mat) is needed for crane access, material staging, and safe erection of steel columns and beams.
Steel members must be designed, procured, fabricated, and delivered to site before erection can commence.
The roof structure (trusses/rafters) bears directly on the steel frame; the frame must be in place to support roof loads.
Wall cladding panels are typically attached to or supported by the structural steel frame; the frame provides the structural backing.

The architectural design of the facade defines the geometry, surfaces, materials, and aesthetic intent that lighting design must work with. Without a finalized facade design, lighting placement, fixture types, and light distribution cannot be determined.
The structural framework of the facade must be in place to know where lighting fixtures can be physically mounted, routed, and supported.
The lighting design must be completed to generate fixture schedules, specifications, and quantities before fixtures can be ordered.
The electrical and mounting installation of facade lighting cannot begin until the design is finalized, including fixture locations, wiring routes, and control systems.
Control system logic and zone configuration depend on the completed lighting layout design to define which fixtures are grouped and how they are controlled.
The site must be properly graded, cleared, and prepared before any placemaking elements (e.g., plazas, seating, art installations) can be installed to ensure a safe and stable ground surface.
Underground utilities such as water, sewer, electrical, and data conduits must be installed and buried before paving, landscaping, and permanent above-ground placemaking features are constructed.
Base paving, sidewalks, and hardscape surfaces must be completed to provide the foundational floor for programming elements like kiosks, stages, seating, and activity zones.
The placemaking elements (art, furniture, signage, programming infrastructure) must be fully installed and ready before the public opening or activation event can occur.

While major landscaping can proceed in parallel, final fine-grain planting and decorative green elements are often done after placemaking installations to avoid damage, though this is a soft preference.

The building must be enclosed and weathertight before exterior site work begins to avoid damage to interior finishes and to allow scaffolding and construction debris to be cleared from the building perimeter.
Underground utility lines (water, sewer, electrical, gas) must be installed before paving, planting, and hardscape elements are placed, otherwise the landscape would need to be dug up again.
Site grading and drainage systems must be established before landscape and hardscape work begins to ensure proper water runoff and stable ground conditions for pavers, planters, and structures.
Landscape and hardscape work is typically completed before the final project inspection and punch list walk-through, though this is a soft preference as some minor landscaping can be deferred.

After landscape and hardscape construction is finished, heavy equipment and leftover materials can be removed from the site, but this is a soft preference since clean-up can overlap with finishing touches.

The building's structural frame (steel or concrete) must be complete and stable to provide the support framework onto which facade and cladding systems are attached. Cladding cannot be installed on an incomplete structure.

Floor slabs provide the necessary working platform and load-bearing support for scaffolding, masts, or suspended access equipment used during facade installation. Without completed slabs, safe access for cladding work is not possible.

While not strictly required, completing the roof waterproofing early prevents water ingress that could damage interior finishes and cladding components. This is a strong preference to protect weather-sensitive facade materials.

The cladding system creates the primary weather barrier and establishes the wall openings. Windows and glazing units are typically installed into the prepared openings within the completed cladding framework to ensure proper sealing and integration.

Interior wall framing and drywall should follow facade completion to ensure the building envelope is weather-tight, protecting interior materials from moisture damage during installation. The closed envelope also allows for proper environmental control.
The bus stop shelter must be placed on a stable, paved surface; road base and asphalt/concrete paving must be completed first to provide a solid foundation.
Signage and route maps are typically mounted on or adjacent to the shelter structure; the shelter frame must be in place before signs can be attached.

If the shelter includes lighting or digital displays, electrical rough-in may occur during or after shelter installation, but final connection and testing must happen after the shelter is securely installed. This is a soft constraint because not all shelters have electrical components.
Benches or seats are often integrated into or bolted to the shelter foundation; the shelter structure must be erected before internal seating can be installed.
Proper drainage and site grading must be completed before placing the shelter to prevent water pooling and ensure the shelter pad remains level and stable.
The ground must be leveled, cleared, and properly compacted before any cycle hire station infrastructure can be installed.
A stable concrete foundation or paved base is required to support the cycle hire docking stations and terminals.
Electrical power and data cabling must be run to the site to power the payment terminals, docking mechanisms, and communication systems before station installation.

After the physical installation of docking stations, terminals, and signage, the entire system must be tested for functionality, including payment processing, bike locking/unlocking, and network connectivity.

Informational signage and directional wayfinding for the cycle hire station can be installed after the station is in place, though this is a soft preference as signage could theoretically be installed concurrently.

Real-time passenger information displays require electrical power to operate; therefore, power supply infrastructure (cabling, conduits, connections) must be installed and energized before the display units can be installed and tested.

The displays need data connectivity (e.g., Ethernet, fiber optic, or wireless backbone) to receive real-time schedule and arrival information from the central system; network cabling and switches must be in place before display commissioning.
Displays must be securely mounted on dedicated brackets, poles, or structural frames which need to be installed first to provide a stable attachment surface.

After physical installation of the display units, the system must be commissioned — including software configuration, network integration, and signal testing — to ensure correct operation before public use.

While not a physical necessity, it is practical to finalize other static signage and wayfinding elements after the real-time displays are installed to ensure visual consistency and accurate position referencing across all information points.
The ticket vending machine must be placed on a stable, finished platform or floor area within the station, so the base structure and platform must be complete before installation can begin.
The ticket vending machine requires electrical power supply; conduit and wiring must be run to the installation location before the machine can be connected and powered on.
The ticket vending machine requires network connectivity for transaction processing and remote monitoring; data cables must be laid and terminated before the machine can be commissioned.

After the machine is physically installed and connected, it must undergo integration testing with the central ticketing system, payment processing, and fare validation systems before being put into service.

successor: Station finishing works (flooring, wall cladding, signage)
rationale: Although finishing works can proceed around the machine, it is preferred to install the machine early to coordinate cutouts, align signage, and avoid rework, but this is a soft preference rather than a physical necessity.
Turnstiles must be mounted on a level, finished floor slab. The base surface must be prepared and cured before any equipment can be set in place.
Turnstiles require electrical power for operation. Conduit runs and junction boxes for power and data must be roughed-in below the floor or in the slab before the turnstile units are positioned.
Turnstile fare gates connect to the central access control and fare collection system. Network and data cabling must be run to the location before the units are permanently installed.
After the turnstile units are mechanically set in place, final electrical connections can be made from the rough-in conduits to the internal terminal blocks of each unit.
The fare gates must be physically installed and wired before they can be powered on, programmed, and tested for proper operation, card reading, and gate swing/motion control.
The ground must be cleared, levelled, and compacted before any ramp or kerb cut can be formed, as the ramp base requires a stable subgrade.
Any drainage, water, sewer, electrical or communication lines beneath the ramp or kerb location must be laid before the ramp is constructed to avoid excavation through finished concrete.
The ramp ties into the roadway; the road base layers must be compacted to the correct level so the ramp can be formed to match the road profile.
Footpaths typically connect to the ramp landing; the ramp provides the transition from road to footpath level, so the footpath is poured after the ramp is set.
Warning tiles at the top and bottom of the ramp must be placed on the finished ramp surface and adjoining footpath; they are installed after the ramp concrete has cured.
The canopy/roof structure must be supported by the main steel or timber frame, which provides the structural load path and attachment points before the roof system can be installed.
Foundations and substructure must be complete to support the columns/frame that in turn carry the roof; without a stable base, the roof structure cannot be safely erected.

Mechanical, electrical and plumbing rough-in work in the ceiling/roof zone is preferably completed before enclosing with the roof canopy to avoid costly rework, though some work can be done afterward if access is maintained.
The waterproofing layer must be applied over the completed roof deck structure to seal the building from moisture ingress.
Interior ceiling finishes (e.g., drywall, suspended ceiling systems) are installed after the roof structure is complete to provide the overhead enclosure and support.
The site must be cleared of debris, vegetation, and existing structures before perimeter fencing can be erected, as fencing needs a clear boundary line and unobstructed access along the perimeter.
The exact property boundaries, building lines, and fence alignment must be surveyed and marked out before installing perimeter fencing to ensure the fence is placed on the correct legal boundary.

predecessor: Temporary Site Access / Haul Road Construction
rationale: While not strictly mandatory, establishing temporary site access roads before hoarding allows delivery vehicles and machinery to enter the site efficiently during fence installation; however, fencing can proceed from other accessible sides first.

Security gates, turnstiles, guard booths, and CCTV cameras can only be installed once the perimeter fencing/hoarding is in place to provide the physical barrier and structure to mount or integrate these security elements.

Temporary site offices, welfare facilities, material storage, and laydown areas should be established only after perimeter hoarding is erected, as the hoarding defines the secured construction zone and prevents unauthorized access to these facilities.
The ground must be properly graded and prepared before installing the bicycle rack to ensure a stable, level surface.
If the bicycle rack requires anchoring, a concrete foundation or pad must be poured and cured before the rack can be securely mounted.
Any underground utility lines (electrical, plumbing, drainage) in the rack area must be installed before the rack is placed to avoid digging around the installed rack.
The bicycle rack should be installed before the final surface finishing (e.g., asphalt or paving stones) to embed or integrate it properly.
It is preferable to install the rack before final landscaping to avoid damage to new plants and soil, though landscaping can be done around an existing rack if needed.

predecessor: Electrical infrastructure installation (main distribution board, conduits, wiring)
rationale: The EV charging point requires a dedicated electrical supply from the main distribution board. Wiring and conduits must be installed first to provide power to the charging unit.

The physical location of the charging point must align with designated parking spaces to ensure vehicles can reach the charger. Parking layout defines where the charger pedestal or wall unit will be positioned.
For ground-mounted EV chargers, a concrete foundation or pedestal mounting base must be poured and cured before the charging unit can be installed and anchored.

successor: Commissioning and testing of EV charger
rationale: Once the charging point hardware is physically installed, it must be electrically tested, commissioned, and connected to the network/backend system before it is put into service.

successor: Pavement restoration and finishing around charging bay
rationale: After the charger unit is installed and cabling is complete, the surrounding pavement or ground surface can be restored and finished to provide a safe, tidy environment for vehicle access.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and existing structures to provide a clean, level work area for constructing the platform/hard standing.
Accurate surveying and marking out of the platform boundaries and levels is required before any earthworks or construction can begin.
Soil bearing capacity and ground conditions must be assessed to inform the design of the sub-base and pavement thickness.
Any temporary shoring, drainage, or access arrangements must be designed and approved before excavation or construction commences.
The platform/hard standing provides the stable working area and crane pad required to construct the turbine foundation.

successor: Erection of Wind Turbine Tower & Nacelle
rationale: The hard standing serves as the crane lifting area and laydown zone essential for turbine erection.
The crane can only be mobilised and assembled once the hard standing is constructed and cured to bear the crane loads.
Turbine components require a level, stable hard standing area for temporary storage and staging before installation.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and graded before any shelter can be erected to ensure a stable, safe foundation and proper drainage.
A concrete foundation (slab, piers, or footings) must be fully cured and in place to provide a load-bearing base for the shelter structure.
Underground plumbing, electrical conduits, and other buried utilities must be installed before the shelter is erected, as they run beneath the foundation or slab.
The structural frame and walls of the shelter must be erected before the roof can be installed, as the roof depends on the wall framing for support.

successor: Interior Finishing (Drywall, Insulation, MEP Rough-In Above Grade)
rationale: Interior work such as installing insulation, running electrical wiring, plumbing lines, and hanging drywall can only begin after the shelter structure is enclosed and weathertight.
Signage cannot be installed until the building structure (walls, facades, ceilings) is complete, as signage requires a finished surface for mounting and structural support.
Illuminated or electronic signage requires electrical wiring and power source rough-ins to be completed before signage can be connected and installed.
Interior wall surfaces must be finished (painted, wallpapered, or clad) before signage is mounted to avoid damage to signage or needing to work around installed signs during finishing.
Suspended or ceiling-mounted signage requires the ceiling grid or structure to be in place for attachment and proper alignment.
The ground must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and rough-graded before trenches can be excavated, otherwise obstructions will prevent accurate trenching.
It is often preferable to rough-grade first and finish grading after utilities are in place, so final grading is typically a successor, not predecessor.
After ducts and conduits are laid in the trench, the trench must be backfilled and compacted to protect the utilities and restore the surface.
Underground utility ducts that pass beneath foundations must be installed and inspected before concrete is poured, otherwise access to the ducts would be permanently blocked.
All underground ducting must be completed and covered before pavement or final surface finishes are applied to avoid re-excavation.
A stable, compacted sub-base is physically required to support the pavement layers and prevent settlement or failure of the finished surface.
Drainage pipes and systems must be installed beneath or adjacent to the paved area before surfacing, otherwise the pavement would have to be torn up to install drainage later.

predecessor: Utility Service Installation (water, gas, electricity,通信)
rationale: Underground utilities must be laid and backfilled before paving, as paving over them would block access and require breaking the surface for future connections.
Line markings and signage must be applied on top of the finished paved surface; they cannot be installed before the paving is complete.

While curbs can sometimes be installed before paving, best practice is often to complete paving first to ensure a clean joint between pavement and curb, though this is a preference rather than a strict physical necessity.
The structural frame must be complete to provide the basic building envelope and support systems before accessibility features like ramps, lifts, and accessible routes can be installed.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work must be completed before accessibility installations to avoid conflicts with accessible pathways, grab bars, and clearances.
Floor slabs and subfloors must be finished to provide a stable, level base for accessibility features such as accessible routes, threshold ramps, and level landings.

While not physically required, it is a soft preference to complete accessibility installations before final finishes to avoid damaging completed paintwork and to allow for seamless integration of accessibility features.

Accessibility features such as tactile indicators, grab bar bases, and accessible route components must be installed before final floor coverings to allow proper embedment and avoid cutting or compromising finished flooring.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated to proper depths before any foundation work can begin, as the foundation requires a stable, prepared subgrade to bear structural loads.
Underground utilities such as drainage, water supply, and electrical conduits must be placed before concrete foundations are poured, to avoid cutting or coring through the hardened foundation later.
Soil bearing capacity and subsurface conditions must be assessed to design the correct foundation type and depth; construction cannot proceed without this data.
The foundation and structural frame (footings, grade beams, slab-on-grade) must be fully cured and load-bearing before any vertical structural elements can be erected on top.
Waterproofing membranes are applied directly onto the cured foundation walls and slab; this cannot proceed until the foundation concrete is placed and sufficiently cured.
The structural frame must be complete to provide a stable load-bearing support for the external envelope and façade cladding.
The roof structure provides overhead rigidity and a waterproof tie-in point; façade work often proceeds top-down from the roof level.
The building envelope must be enclosed and weathertight before interior mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work can begin to protect materials and equipment from weather damage.
Interior finish work requires a dry, weathertight enclosure to prevent moisture damage to drywall, paint, and flooring materials.

Although windows are part of the façade, primary structural glazing and window units are typically installed as the envelope is erected; final seals and trim follow the main cladding installation to ensure a continuous weather barrier.

A feasibility study and site analysis must be completed before masterplanning begins to understand site conditions, constraints, opportunities, and regulatory requirements that inform the master plan.
Land must be legally secured and due diligence completed before masterplanning can proceed, as the master plan is specific to the acquired site boundaries and ownership.
The project's vision, goals, and key performance indicators must be established first to guide the masterplanning process and ensure alignment with stakeholder objectives.
Detailed architectural design of individual buildings and spaces depends on the master plan's layout, zoning, plot divisions, density, and urban design guidelines.
Infrastructure planning (roads, water, power, drainage) must follow the master plan as it defines the spatial layout and demand points that infrastructure must serve.
Subdivision of the site into individual plots or parcels is derived from the master plan's block layout and land use allocations.
Public realm and landscape design must follow the master plan as it defines open space locations, street hierarchies, and public amenity areas.

Site mobilization (setup of site offices, access roads, and utility connections) must be completed before ground investigation can begin, as survey teams need site access and basic facilities to operate.

A desk study review of existing site records, geology maps, and historical data must be completed beforehand to define the scope, locations, and depth of ground investigation boreholes and trial pits.
Soil and rock samples obtained during ground investigation must be collected before they can be sent to a laboratory for geotechnical and environmental testing.
All field data, borehole logs, and survey measurements must be completed before they can be compiled into a factual ground report for design use.
Ground conditions revealed by the site survey and investigation are essential input data for designing foundations, retaining walls, and substructures; design cannot proceed without this information.

The site must be cleared, leveled, and graded before any underground utilities (water, sewer, gas, electrical conduits) can be installed to ensure proper drainage, load-bearing capacity, and alignment.
Trenches and pits for utility lines (water mains, sewer pipes, electrical ducts) must be excavated before the pipes and conduits can be laid and connected.

Foundations for buildings and major structures must be completed before connecting utility lines to the building entry points, as underground utility stubs are typically brought in after footings are poured.

Once all underground utility pipes, conduits, and cables are laid and inspected, the excavated trenches must be backfilled and compacted to restore ground stability and prepare for further construction activities.
Roads and paved surfaces are typically constructed after underground utilities are installed to avoid cutting and reinstating pavement, which is costly and disruptive.
Above-ground building construction can commence only after utility connections (water, power, sewer) are available at the site to support construction activities and permanent building services.

Hard construction activities (building structures, foundations, superstructure) must be substantially complete before public realm and landscaping works commence, to avoid damage to finished landscaping from heavy plant, material storage, and ongoing construction traffic.
Underground services, drainage, and foundations must be installed before finishing ground surfaces and planting, to prevent re-excavation and reinstatement of landscaping.
All buried utilities, service trenches, and connections must be completed and tested before hardscape and softscape finishes are applied, to avoid digging up completed landscaping.
Landscaping and public realm finishes are typically among the last major site activities, completed before final clean and handover to present the finished environment to the client and end users.
Public realm and landscaping must be complete before site hoardings are removed and demobilisation occurs, ensuring the site is fully finished and safe for public access.
The physical location and legal ownership of the land must be secured before any construction activities can begin on the site.
Soil conditions must be analyzed to determine foundation design requirements and ensure structural safety before construction starts.
Complete building plans, structural calculations, and engineering specifications are required before physical construction can commence.
Building permits, zoning approvals, and environmental clearances must be obtained legally before construction can begin.
The building site must be cleared, graded, and leveled before foundation and structural work can proceed.
The main structural shell and building envelope must be completed before interior finishing work such as drywall, flooring, painting, and ceiling installation can begin.
While some rough-in work may occur concurrently, full MEP system installation and connection depends on the structural framework being in place.
All building systems (HVAC, electrical, fire safety, elevators) can only be tested and commissioned after construction is substantially complete.
Regulatory inspections and occupancy certification can only occur after construction is fully complete and all systems are operational.

While landscaping can ideally follow construction to avoid damage from heavy equipment, it is a soft preference as some preliminary planting or grading could occur alongside final construction stages.
Substantial completion (or practical completion) must be achieved before any phased handover can occur, as it certifies that the building is safe and sufficiently complete for occupation.
All final inspections, commissioning, and system testing must be completed and signed off to ensure building systems are operational and safe before occupants can take possession.
Outstanding defects and snagging items for the phase being handed over must be resolved to a satisfactory standard before handover can proceed.

The project cannot be fully closed out until all phases have been handed over and occupied, as closeout requires final documentation, as-built records, and financial settlement based on full occupation.
Post-occupancy evaluation typically begins after occupants have moved in and the building is in use, though this is a soft/preferred sequence rather than a hard physical constraint.

A feasibility study and project initiation must be completed first to define the project scope, objectives, and key parameters before engaging the community, so that meaningful consultation can take place with clear proposals to discuss.
Community feedback gathered during consultation must inform the design process, so design development cannot begin until consultation is complete and input has been collected and analyzed.
Many regulatory approval processes require evidence of community consultation and input as part of the application package, so consultation must be completed before permit applications are submitted.
While procurement can begin in parallel, finalizing tender documents typically benefits from incorporating community feedback that emerges during consultation, making it a soft preference.
Community concerns and agreements regarding construction impacts (noise, traffic, hours of operation) must be addressed before physical site works commence, making this a hard constraint.
A stable foundation or substructure is required before installing a threshold marker, as the marker needs a solid base to be properly positioned and anchored.

predecessor: Floor Slab / Deck Pouring and Curing
rationale: The threshold marker is typically placed at the transition between floor surfaces or at door openings; the floor slab must be poured and cured to provide the finished surface level the marker will align with.
Wall framing and door openings must be roughed in to define the exact location and width where the threshold marker will be installed.

The threshold marker serves as a transition or edge between different flooring materials; finished flooring on both sides of the threshold must be installed after the marker is in place to abut it properly.
Doors are installed to close against or over the threshold; the threshold marker must be in place to provide the correct reveal, seal, and clearance for the door leaf.
The foundation or base slab must be prepared and cured before the gate structure can be mounted, as the gate requires a stable, level surface for proper alignment and anchoring.
Power and data conduits for the gate's electrical system must be laid in the ground before the gate posts are set, to allow cable routing without later excavation.
The gate must be physically installed and anchored before final electrical connections (motor, sensors, card readers) can be made and tested.
The gate posts define the opening width; perimeter fencing must align with the installed gate to ensure continuous security barrier without gaps.
While paving can be done before gate installation, finishing pavement after gate placement avoids damage to new pavement from heavy equipment during gate installation, though it is a soft preference.
The ground must be properly graded and prepared before any planter or landscape screen can be installed, as these elements sit on the ground and require a stable, level surface.
If the planter or landscape screen is adjacent to a building or hardscape, the foundations and slabs must be completed first to define the edges and ensure proper drainage and support.
All underground utilities (irrigation lines, drainage pipes, electrical conduits) must be installed before planters are placed, to avoid digging up or damaging the completed planter.
The planter structure or screen must be fully constructed before soil, mulch, and plants are added, as the planter contains and defines the planting area.

While clean-up typically occurs after all major work is done, it is a soft preference because some final touches could be done concurrently; however, it is logical to complete the planter before final cleaning to avoid re-soiling the area.
The fire separation wall requires a stable, level base. The foundation or slab must be poured and cured before any load-bearing wall construction can begin.
Fire separation walls often tie into the main structural frame. The primary structural columns and beams must be in place to provide support and anchorage points for the wall.

Fire separation walls must be fully constructed before mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) rough-in work can proceed, as these services need to penetrate or be routed around the fire-rated assembly.

Any penetrations through the fire separation wall (for MEP services) must be sealed with approved firestop materials after the wall is built and MEP rough-in is complete, to maintain the fire-resistance rating.
Fire separation walls serve as a substrate for interior finishing. Gypsum board or other finishes cannot be applied until the fire-rated wall assembly is fully erected and inspected.
A stable foundation is physically required before any zone installation can begin to ensure structural integrity and proper alignment.
The structural frame must be in place to provide support and attachment points for zone installation components.
Rough mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems must be installed in the structural cavities before zone installations can enclose or finish those spaces.
Zone installation often includes partition framing and rough-in work that must be completed before final interior finishes are applied.

Soft preference: While zone installation should ideally be completed before commissioning to ensure all systems are in place, some parallel commissioning activities can begin before all zones are fully installed.
Electrical power and wiring infrastructure must be in place before access control devices (controllers, readers, locks) can be connected and integrated.
Conduits and cable trays must be installed to provide the physical pathways for access control cables before any cabling can be run.
Doors and frames must be installed so that electronic locks, magnetic door holders, and door position sensors can be mounted directly on them.
The access control system must be fully integrated and wired before it can be powered on, programmed, and tested for proper operation.

Access control devices including readers, keypads, and controllers are typically surface-mounted or recessed into walls; final finishing work must occur after installation to avoid damaging finishes and to allow patching around devices.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and obstructions before demolition of boundary walls or fences can begin, ensuring safe access and clear delineation of the work area.

Existing boundary structures must be removed before excavation can proceed along the property perimeter, as the demolition debris must be cleared and the new boundary line established to define the excavation limits.
The old boundary must be demolished and the site reconfigured before new boundary walls or fences can be erected on the realigned property lines.

Any utility lines (gas, water, electricity, telecom) running along or through the boundary must be disconnected, capped, or relocated before demolition to prevent damage, leaks, or electrocution hazards.

Final grading and landscaping of the boundary area is typically performed after demolition and reconfiguration, though in some sequences grading may begin elsewhere on site before boundary work is fully complete.

The building's floor plan, circulation paths, and spatial layout must be established before wayfinding elements (signage, maps, directories) can be designed and positioned to guide users through the space.
Walls, ceilings, corridors, and interior surfaces must be in place before installing wayfinding signage, digital displays, or mounted directories.

Power outlets, data cabling, and network connections for electronic wayfinding systems (e.g., digital kiosks, interactive maps, LED signage) must be installed before those systems can be implemented and activated.

Wayfinding systems must be fully installed and operational before the building can be commissioned and handed over, as functional signage and navigation aids are required for safe and efficient building use.

External wayfinding and monument signs are often coordinated with landscaping for aesthetic integration, but interior wayfinding can be completed independently; this is a soft preference for visual continuity.
Smoke curtains are typically suspended from the overhead structure; structural steel must be in place to provide support and attachment points for the smoke curtain track or housing.

predecessor: Rough-In Electrical and Fire Alarm Wiring
rationale: Many smoke curtain systems require electrical power for the motor/drive unit and integration with the fire alarm system for automatic deployment; rough-in wiring must be completed before the curtain assembly is installed.
Smoke curtains are installed prior to enclosing ceilings or soffits so that the curtain housing can be concealed within the ceiling plenum and final finishes applied around the curtain slot.

successor: Fire Alarm System Testing and Commissioning
rationale: The smoke curtain must be fully installed and connected to the fire alarm system before integrated testing of automatic drop/retract functionality can be performed.

successor: Final Interior Fit-Out and MEP Trim-Out
rationale: While not physically required, it is standard practice to complete the smoke curtain assembly before final trim-out of adjacent mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems to avoid damage or rework.
The privacy screen panels require a structural support framework (posts, rails, or brackets) to be installed first, as the panels themselves are not self-supporting.
Ground preparation such as digging post holes, pouring concrete footings, or installing ground anchors must be completed before the posts can be erected and secured.

successor: Apply protective finish or sealant to screen
