rationale: It is preferable to seal or stain wooden privacy screens after installation to protect the material, but this can also be done pre-installation; hence it's a soft preference for post-assembly finishing.
Planting shrubs or placing decorative elements near the screen is easier once the screen is in place to define the space, but landscaping could also precede installation with careful planning.

predecessor: Verify property boundaries and obtain permits
rationale: Legal and regulatory compliance (boundary surveys, permit approvals) must be secured before any ground disturbance or construction begins to avoid legal issues and rework.
The landmark building requires a stable foundation to support its structural load; foundation construction must be completed before any vertical building can commence.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and excavated before building construction can begin to ensure proper ground conditions and access.
Underground utility lines such as water, sewer, electrical, and data conduits must be laid before the building footprint is established to avoid retrofitting under the completed structure.
The building structure must be fully erected and enclosed before interior finishing work such as drywall, painting, flooring, and fixtures can begin.
The main structural frame of the landmark building must be complete before the external facade (cladding, glass curtain walls, decorative elements) can be installed.
The site must be cleared, levelled, and prepared before any residential block construction can begin, as the foundation and structural works require a stable, prepared ground surface.
The building foundations (footings, slabs, drainage) must be completed before the residential block typology (superstructure) can be erected, as the block rests on these foundations.
Underground utility lines and connections to the plot must be laid before or concurrent with foundation work, as the block's internal services depend on these external hookups being in place.

The structural shell (residential block) must be complete before interior finishing (plastering, flooring, electrical/plumbing fittings) can commence, as finishing works require enclosed, weather-tight spaces.

The block's structural frame and walls must be erected before external cladding, insulation, rendering, or other façade treatments can be applied, as these materials attach to the completed structure.
The site must be graded and leveled before any streetscape furniture (benches, bollards, planters, etc.) can be installed to ensure stable and level placement.
Water, drainage, electrical, and communication lines must be laid underground before installing streetscape furniture to avoid digging up or moving furniture later for utility access.
The road base and pavement sub-base must be completed to define the final surface levels and provide a stable foundation for anchoring furniture like bollards and signposts.

Streetscape furniture that is bolted or anchored into the ground (e.g., bollards, bike racks) must be installed before the final paving or surface finish is laid so that fixings can be embedded neatly and the finish can be worked around them.

Furniture such as planters, benches, and litter bins should be in place before final landscaping and planting occurs so that planting beds are defined and soil grading can be completed around the installed items.
The site must be graded and prepared before any trees can be planted to ensure proper drainage and soil conditions.
All underground utilities (water, sewer, gas, electrical, telecommunications) must be installed before tree planting to avoid damaging tree roots or requiring future excavation near trees.
Sidewalks and curbs define the tree planting locations and tree pits must be formed within the sidewalk zone before trees can be planted.
Street trees must be planted and in place before final paving to allow for proper tree pit adjustments, root protection measures, and to avoid damage to newly paved surfaces during tree installation.

While street lighting can theoretically be installed before trees, it is preferable to plant trees first to coordinate light pole placement with canopy clearance and avoid conflicts between tree branches and light fixtures.
A stable foundation and prepared site are physically required before any superstructure construction can begin.
The building structure must be complete before interior work such as electrical, plumbing, and finishing can be installed.
The completed building must be inspected and commissioned before it can be occupied or used.
While landscaping can begin after the building is up, it is a soft preference as some exterior work could theoretically overlap with final construction stages.
The building must be fully constructed, inspected, and approved before it can be opened to the public or occupied.

The wall, pavement, or structural surface where the art will be mounted or placed must be fully finished (e.g., plastered, painted, tiled) so the artwork has a clean, permanent backing and does not need to be removed or disturbed for later finishing work.

All structural framing, electrical conduits, plumbing, and HVAC ducts behind or near the art location must be completed before installing the artwork; otherwise, the art would block access or need to be removed for utility work.
Accent or display lighting must be aimed and calibrated after the artwork is in its final position so the illumination properly highlights the art without shadows or glare.

successor: Final Flooring / Polishing (if art is floor-mounted)
rationale: If the art is a floor sculpture, it is often placed before final floor polishing so workers can finish around it; however, this is a soft preference because the art could be installed after polishing if carefully protected.
Adequate rigging, scaffolding, or crane access must be in place to safely lift and position the artwork before the installation activity begins.
Land must be legally acquired and owned before any masterplanning can begin, as the planning applies to specific parcels of land.
Accurate site data including topography, boundaries, utilities, and existing conditions are essential inputs for developing a neighborhood masterplan.
Understanding existing zoning regulations, land use designations, and legal constraints is necessary to inform the masterplan design parameters.
The masterplan sets the overall layout and land use distribution; detailed design of roads, utilities, and drainage systems must follow the approved plan.
While an EIA can begin during masterplanning, the finalized plan is needed to assess cumulative impacts and propose mitigation measures accurately.
Individual lot boundaries and subdivision layouts are derived directly from the approved masterplan's block and land use configuration.
The completed masterplan document must be submitted for formal review and approval before any subsequent detailed design or construction can proceed.

A thorough site assessment must be completed to evaluate soil conditions, existing infrastructure, zoning restrictions, and environmental constraints before any infill development can proceed, as these factors determine whether and how the site can be developed.

If the infill site contains contaminated soil, groundwater, or hazardous materials (common on previously developed urban land), remediation must be completed before construction begins to ensure health and safety compliance.
Existing buildings or structures on the infill site must be demolished and cleared to provide a clean, unobstructed area for new construction.

Landscaping, paving, and site amenities can only be installed after the main infill building or development structure is complete, as construction equipment and activities would damage finished landscaping.

Final connection of the new infill building to municipal water, sewer, electricity, and gas systems, as well as system commissioning, must occur after the structure is built and internal systems are installed.

A thorough site investigation and assessment must be completed before heritage conservation works begin to understand the existing condition, historical significance, and structural integrity of the heritage asset.
The structure must be stabilized to ensure safety before any conservation or restoration work can be performed on the heritage asset.
Non-heritage elements, debris, and hazardous materials must be removed from the site before heritage conservation can commence to provide clear and safe access.

Heritage conservation (including facade restoration, structural repairs, and heritage fabric treatment) must be completed before interior finishes and mechanical/electrical/plumbing systems are installed to avoid damaging the conserved heritage elements.
All heritage conservation activities must be fully completed and inspected before the final project handover and occupancy can take place.
A project must be initiated and planned before engaging the community, as the community needs to know the project scope, purpose, and preliminary plans to provide meaningful input.
Community feedback gathered during engagement must inform design decisions, so design development proceeds after community input is collected.
Many regulatory permits require documented community engagement and feedback as part of the approval process.

While community engagement ideally occurs before construction begins to address concerns early, in some projects engagement may continue during early construction phases; however, it is a strong preference to complete major public outreach before mobilization.

Underground utilities such as water, sewer, gas, and electrical lines must be relocated before streetscape work begins to avoid digging up newly paved surfaces and to ensure all subsurface work is complete.
The base pavement layer must be laid and cured before streetscape elements like curbs, gutters, sidewalks, and landscaping can be installed on top.
Stormwater drainage systems including pipes, catch basins, and subgrade drainage must be installed before surface-level streetscape features to ensure proper water management.
The final road surface wearing course is applied after streetscape elements like curbs, gutters, and landscaping are completed to achieve a clean finished edge and avoid damage.
Street lighting poles and fixtures are installed after streetscape upgrades (curbs, sidewalks, planters) are complete to ensure proper placement relative to finished streetscape elements.
The transit node requires a stable and level foundation to be properly installed; foundation work must be completed before any structural components are placed.
Electrical power and data cabling must be run to the transit node location before the node is physically installed, as access to conduit and connection points is needed behind or beneath the node.
The transit node must be physically in place and connected before end-to-end system tests can verify its communication with other transit nodes and the central control system.
Calibration of displays, ticketing interfaces, and passenger information systems cannot occur until the transit node hardware is installed and powered on.
Security cameras, sensors, and access control systems at the transit node depend on the physical installation of the node structure before they can be mounted and integrated.
Edge treatment (such as joint cutting, edging, or forming) can only be performed after concrete has been poured and sufficiently cured to hold its shape and support the finishing work.
Formwork defines the edges and boundaries of the concrete slab; edge treatment works along the perimeter require the forms to be in place to guide the finish and prevent uncontrolled concrete flow.
The concrete surface must be screeded to the correct level and roughly leveled before edge tools (such as edgers or joint cutters) can be applied to define clean, uniform edges.

Edge treatment (edging, jointing) is typically performed as an intermediate step after initial leveling but before final troweling and finishing, so that edges are defined first and then blended into the final surface finish.
Final curing compounds or membranes should be applied after all edge finishing and joint cutting are complete to ensure the curing agent seals the entire surface including the treated edges.
The exact boundaries and layout of the perimeter fence must be established through site survey before the fence can be installed.
The ground along the fence line must be cleared of vegetation and debris and graded to a stable, level surface before fence posts can be set and panels erected.
All underground utilities must be located and marked before any digging for fence posts to avoid damage to existing services and ensure worker safety.
The perimeter fence must be completed and secure before the site can be locked down and access control measures implemented to protect the construction area.
The perimeter fence establishes the site boundary and secures the area, which is necessary before major earthworks and foundation excavation can begin within the protected site.
The site must be surveyed and soil conditions assessed to determine the exact boundary lines and foundation requirements for the wall.
The site area must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and obstacles, and levelled to provide a stable working surface for wall construction.
The exact boundary lines must be marked on the ground using survey pegs and string lines to guide excavation and wall placement.
While not physically required, the boundary wall is often built early to secure the site perimeter before main construction begins, providing security and demarcation.
The boundary wall must be completed to serve as a secure perimeter barrier before establishing controlled site access and security measures.
The ground must be excavated and leveled before any gate structure can be installed to ensure proper foundation support.
Gate posts or track foundations require cured concrete to bear the load and anchor the gate securely.
Any electrical conduits for gate operators, intercoms, or lighting must be laid underground before gate posts are set to avoid re-excavation.
The physical gate structure must be in place before motors, sensors, and control systems can be mounted and connected.
The entry gate serves as the access point in the perimeter; the adjacent fencing should align with and connect to the installed gate posts.
While the gate can be installed before final paving, it is preferable to complete driveway surfacing up to the gate area to avoid damaging new pavement during gate installation.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and graded before any building construction can begin, including the gatehouse/guard post.
The concrete foundation for the gatehouse must be excavated, formed, and poured before the gatehouse structure can be erected.
Underground utility lines (electrical, water, communication/data) must be roughed-in to the gatehouse location before slab pouring or wall construction to avoid later trenching and disruption.
The gatehouse structure must be completed before the main entrance gates and automatic gate operators can be installed, as they are physically anchored to or adjacent to the guard post.

successor: Security System Installation (Cameras, Intercom, Access Control)
rationale: Security equipment such as cameras, intercoms, and access control panels are typically mounted on or inside the gatehouse; the structure must be in place before these systems can be installed.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and prepared before bollard installation can begin.
Concrete footings or foundations for the bollards must be poured and cured before the bollards themselves can be installed.
Bollards must be installed before the final surface paving or finishing around them to ensure proper embedment and alignment.
Permanent bollard installation defines lanes and boundaries, which must be in place before painting traffic lines around or between them.
The site must be cleared and prepared before boundary signage can be installed, as signage posts and foundations require a stable, cleared surface.
A professional boundary survey must be completed first to determine the exact property lines where boundary signage will be placed.
Regulatory approvals and permits for signage installation must be obtained before any physical installation of boundary signs can proceed.
Boundary signage marks the property lines that guide where fences should be erected; fencing must follow the marked boundaries to ensure proper alignment.
While the site can be secured before signage, boundary signage is often used to demarcate the perimeter and is therefore best installed before full security fencing or access control is established.
Site mobilization must be complete to enable survey crew access to the site and establish control points.
Boundary markers and survey reference points must be established before any clearing begins to prevent accidental removal of markers and ensure work stays within property lines.
Boundary survey provides the baseline reference from which all building and utility stakeout locations are measured.
Knowing precise property boundaries helps target geotechnical borehole locations and environmental sampling within the correct parcel.
Finalized boundary lines allow the design team to confirm setbacks and building placement before issuing final construction drawings.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and graded before boundary walls or fences can be erected to ensure a stable, even foundation and accurate alignment along property lines.
Accurate survey and setting out of boundary lines and wall/fence positions must be completed first to ensure the structure is built on the correct property limits and alignment.
Boundary walls/fences are often built first to secure the site perimeter, mark property boundaries, and prevent encroachment before main building works commence.
While not physically required, it is preferable to complete boundary walls/fences before final landscaping to avoid damaging new planting and to define the finished site edges.
Gates and automated entry systems are physically mounted onto or integrated with the boundary wall/fence structure, so the wall/fence must be complete before gates can be installed.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and properly graded before any gate or access point structures can be installed, as uneven ground or debris would prevent proper foundation work and alignment.
Gate posts, pillars, and supporting structures require concrete footings or foundations to be poured and cured before the gate hardware and panels can be mounted.
Utilities such as electrical conduits, data cables, and drainage pipes must be laid beneath the gate area before gate installation to avoid digging up completed work or damaging gate components.
The perimeter fence line must be established so that the gate aligns with the fence opening and integrates properly with the overall boundary system.
Driveway pavement or entrance hardscaping should be laid after gate installation to ensure proper alignment with gate swing or slide paths and to avoid damaging fresh pavement.
Access control devices, intercoms, card readers, and sensors are mounted on or integrated with the gate structure, so the gate must be installed first before these systems can be fitted and wired.
The gate operator/motor must be connected to the power supply after the gate is installed and aligned, as the operator is mounted to the gate structure.

Final landscaping, planting, and decorative finishes around the entrance area are typically completed after gate installation to avoid damage, though this is a logical sequence preference rather than a strict physical necessity.
The site must be graded and leveled before any perimeter security components (fencing, barriers, sensors) can be installed to ensure proper alignment and foundation.
Concrete foundations for perimeter walls, fence posts, or security bollards must be cured and set before the security system components can be mounted on them.

Electrical conduits, data cables, and piping for powering security sensors, cameras, and lighting must be installed underground before above-ground perimeter structures are erected, to avoid re-excavation and damage.

Security sensor cables, detection loops, and mounting brackets for cameras are typically installed first along the perimeter route, and then physical fencing and barriers are built over or around them to conceal and protect the sensing elements.
All perimeter security hardware (sensors, cameras, alarms) must be physically mounted and connected before the system can be powered on, calibrated, and tested for proper operation and coverage.
Site boundaries must first be cleared and accessible before boundary maintenance and inspection can take place.
The property boundaries must be formally surveyed and staked before any boundary maintenance or inspection can be performed.
Boundaries must be verified and maintained before excavation work begins to ensure construction stays within property lines.
Permanent fencing around the property should only be installed after boundary inspection confirms the correct alignment.
While boundary inspection is ideally completed before final grading and landscaping to ensure the site perimeter is accurate, it is not a strict physical necessity.
All debris, vegetation, and existing structures must be removed before any new landscaping can be installed to ensure a clean working surface and prevent damage to new plants.
Bulk earthworks, grading, and soil preparation must be completed to establish proper contours and drainage before landscape planting can commence.
All buried pipes, conduits, and drainage systems must be installed and backfilled before planting to avoid disturbing new landscaping with subsequent trenching.

Fence posts and gates are typically installed after or concurrently with boundary landscaping so that finished ground levels and plant locations are known and to avoid damaging new plants during fence erection.

Landscaping is one of the final finishing activities; site handover or final inspection logically occurs after all landscaping is complete, though it is a soft preference as handover could technically proceed with minor landscape punch-list items.
A site survey and title search are required to determine existing property boundaries, ownership, and any prior easements before a new easement can be legally defined and registered.
Boundary staking physically marks the property lines, which is necessary to precisely identify the location and extent of the easement area for legal registration.
A signed legal agreement between the grantor and grantee defining the easement terms must be completed before the easement can be formally registered with the land registry office.
The easement must be legally registered to grant lawful right of entry and use before any construction or utility work can begin within the easement area.
The easement must be registered on title to be legally binding on subsequent property owners before the property can be sold or transferred to a new owner.
The platform structure requires a stable base; foundation construction must be completed to provide load-bearing support before the platform can be erected.
The platform structure is typically mounted on or integrated with the steel frame; the frame must be in place to support the platform.
The deck or flooring system is placed directly onto the platform structure, so the platform must be complete to serve as the supporting base for deck installation.

Safety railings are typically installed after the platform is in place, though they could theoretically be pre-assembled; however, standard practice requires the platform to be erected first for safe access and positioning.
Mechanical or electrical equipment mounted on the platform requires the platform structure to be complete and stable before installation can proceed.
The canopy or platform shelter requires a stable foundation or footing to be installed first to support its structure and ensure safety.
If the canopy is supported by a steel frame, the frame must be erected first to provide the structural support onto which the canopy is mounted.
Electrical wiring and lighting fixtures for the canopy area must be installed after the canopy structure is in place to ensure proper routing and mounting.
If the canopy includes a roof or weatherproof membrane, this can only be applied after the canopy structure is fully erected to ensure complete coverage and sealing.
The canopy or platform shelter must be fully installed and completed before final inspection and project handover can take place.

A stable, compacted subgrade is physically required to support the track bed, ballast, and rails. Without proper earthworks and subgrade compaction, the track structure would lack the necessary load-bearing capacity and drainage.
Proper drainage (culverts, ditches, sub-surface drains) must be in place before track laying to prevent water accumulation that could undermine the track bed, cause erosion, or lead to frost heave.
Bridges and major culverts must be completed to provide continuous support for the track route. The rail cannot be laid over gaps where structures are still missing.

After the rails and sleepers are placed, ballast must be distributed around and under the sleepers and then tamped to stabilize the track geometry. This physical process cannot occur before the track components are in position.

Signaling equipment (signals, track circuits, cables) and electrification components (catenary masts, overhead wires) are mounted alongside or above the track. The track must be in place to establish correct alignment and clearances for these systems.
The road base or substrate must be compacted and leveled before the accessibility ramp can be constructed to ensure proper structural support and ADA-compliant slope.
Curb cuts and adjacent curbs must be in place to define the ramp boundaries and transition height before ramp pouring or paving begins.
All buried utilities (storm drains, water, electrical) beneath the ramp area must be completed to avoid excavation after the ramp is built.
Tactile warning strips (detectable warning surfaces) are placed at the ramp landing edges and must be installed after the ramp surface is finished.
The adjoining sidewalks are typically paved after the ramp to ensure a seamless flush transition, but could precede with careful planning.
Regional transportation plans establish the overall travel demand, corridor needs, and funding framework that define the scope and parameters for transit network planning.
Existing and planned land use patterns determine where transit demand will be generated, influencing route alignment and station location decisions.
Travel demand models provide ridership projections and origin-destination data needed to design the transit network's route structure, frequencies, and capacities.
The specific transit network alignments, station locations, and design features must be defined before environmental impacts can be assessed and mitigated.
Network-level decisions about route alignments and modal choices provide the framework within which detailed engineering design of guideways, stations, and systems can proceed.
Understanding ground conditions, soil/rock properties, groundwater levels, and potential hazards is essential before selecting the tunneling method and designing the tunnel boring machine (TBM).
The tunnel alignment, cross-section, lining design, and construction methodology must be fully designed and approved before excavation can commence.
Launch shafts, access roads, staging areas, and utility connections must be prepared to provide the TBM with a point of entry and support operations.
Once the TBM advances, the excavated tunnel must be immediately supported with segmental lining or shotcrete to prevent ground collapse and ensure structural stability.
After excavation, gaps between the tunnel lining and surrounding ground must be filled with grout to prevent water ingress and ground settlement.

A stable, compacted and graded subgrade is physically required to provide the foundation for the track ballast and rails; without proper earthworks, the track would lack the necessary support and drainage.
Proper drainage (e.g., culverts, side drains) must be in place to prevent water accumulation that would undermine the ballast and subgrade, compromising track stability and safety.
The ballast layer must be laid and compacted on the prepared subgrade to provide the elastic support, load distribution, and drainage medium onto which the sleepers and rails are directly placed.

successor: Rail Welding and Continuous Welded Rail (CWR) Formation
rationale: Individual rail sections must first be laid and positioned onto the sleepers before they can be welded together into continuous lengths for smooth, joint-free track.
The track must be laid first so that tamping machines can then adjust the ballast beneath the sleepers to achieve the correct alignment, level, and geometry of the finished track.
The structural frame, slabs, walls, and columns must be completed before any fitout and finishing works can begin, as the fitout activities require a stable, enclosed structural shell to work within.
The building envelope must be watertight and waterproofed to protect interior finishes (plasterboard, paint, flooring, ceilings) from water damage before fitout commences.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in works (conduits, ducts, pipes in walls/ceilings) must be installed before finishing works cover them up with wall linings, ceilings, and floor finishes.

Final installation of fixtures, fittings, switches, sockets, and commissioning of MEP systems can only occur after ceiling, wall, and floor finishes are complete to avoid damage and to allow proper mounting.
All finishing works (painting, tiling, flooring, joinery) must be completed before final cleaning and handover can take place, as cleaning is the last step before project closeout.

All individual subsystems (e.g., HVAC, electrical, plumbing, fire alarm, security, BMS) must be installed and fully tested in isolation before they can be integrated together into a unified building system.
Rough-in of mechanical, electrical, and plumbing services must be complete to provide the necessary infrastructure connections for integrated system testing.
The building envelope (roof, walls, windows, doors) must be weathertight to protect sensitive electronic and mechanical equipment during commissioning activities.
While soft preferences may allow some interior finishes to proceed concurrently, formal commissioning sign-off is ideally completed before tenant fit-out to avoid disruptions and rework.
Integrated systems must be fully commissioned, tested, and verified as operational before the building can be handed over to the owner and occupants.
The Central Island structure requires a stable foundation. Excavation and piling must be completed first to provide the necessary load-bearing support for the central island component.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and graded to create a suitable base before the Central Island component can be constructed.
Underground utilities must be laid before the Central Island is built to avoid later excavation and disruption of the completed structure.
The raw structural construction of the Central Island must be completed before any finishing work such as paving, landscaping, or surface treatments can be applied.

successor: Connection of perimeter bridges/pathways to Central Island
rationale: Access structures such as bridges, walkways, or tunnels that connect to the Central Island can only be installed after the island is constructed, as they require precise alignment and anchoring to the completed structure.

The splitter island is typically a raised concrete curb or barrier that separates traffic lanes. Foundation and subgrade preparation must be completed before installing the island to ensure structural stability.
Once the splitter island is constructed, lane markings, signage, and reflective markers can be applied to guide traffic around the island.
Landscaping around the splitter island is typically done after the island structure is complete to avoid damage during construction, though in some cases it could be done concurrently.
The exit lane path must be excavated and have a stable base/foundation before the lane surface can be laid.
Any underground utilities crossing the exit lane path must be relocated or protected before lane construction to avoid conflicts and rework.
Subsurface drainage along the exit lane route must be completed prior to paving to ensure proper water management and pavement longevity.
Lane markings, directional arrows, and exit signs can only be applied after the exit lane surface is fully constructed and cured.
Light poles and fixtures along the exit lane are installed after the lane is built to ensure proper alignment with the roadway geometry.
Final landscaping adjacent to the exit lane is typically completed after paving to avoid soil and debris contamination on the new surface.
A stable, level foundation must be prepared before the mountable apron can be installed to ensure proper load distribution and structural integrity.
The mountable apron must be fully installed in its final position before any surface finishing or sealing treatment can be applied to ensure a continuous, protected surface.
The mountable apron serves as a transition or edge element; adjacent paving or flooring should be laid after the apron is in place to achieve a flush, aligned joint.
The mountable apron component must be fabricated or pre-assembled before it can be physically installed on site.
If the apron incorporates any embedded utilities or drainage, connections should ideally be made after installation, but this may be possible concurrently in some designs.
The ground must be excavated and leveled to the required formation level before kerb and edging can be installed, as kerbs need a stable, prepared subgrade.
The sub-base or road base layer must be compacted and finished to the correct profile so that kerbs can be set at the correct height and alignment.
Any underground drainage pipes or services beneath the kerb line must be laid and backfilled before kerb installation to avoid excavating through newly placed kerbs.
Kerbs act as a formwork and edge restraint for asphalt or pavement layers; paving is placed up to the finished kerb line.
Topsoil and landscaping finishes are placed after kerbs are installed so that soil can be neatly graded up to the back face of the kerb without soiling the new kerb face.
Road markings must be applied to a finished, stable surface. Asphalt paving must be completed first to provide the substrate for the paint or thermoplastic markings.
The entire pavement structure (base, subbase, and surface course) must be compacted and completed before the final wearing surface is ready for line marking.
Road markings and lane lines are one of the final surface finishes before the road can be opened to traffic, as they provide essential guidance and safety information to drivers.
Final adjustments or installation of barriers and guardrails near the roadway can be aligned with the marked lanes, so this activity benefits from markings being in place first.

Road pavement must be fully constructed and cured before traffic signs and gantries are installed, as the gantries' foundations require stable pavement and the signs need to be positioned relative to the finished road surface and lane markings.
The road base and sub-base must be prepared and compacted to provide a stable foundation for gantry footings and sign posts, ensuring structural stability.
Underground utilities such as cables, pipes, and ducts must be relocated away from planned gantry foundation locations before excavating and pouring foundations to avoid service strikes.

Traffic signs and gantries must be installed before final road markings are applied because the positioning of signs and overhead gantries determines lane configurations and regulatory markings that must align with the installed infrastructure.

All traffic signs and gantries must be fully erected, tested, and verified before the road is opened to traffic, as these are critical safety devices that provide regulatory and directional guidance to motorists.
The road base must be prepared and compacted to provide a stable foundation before pedestrian crossing infrastructure such as crosswalks, ramps, and refuge islands can be installed.
Any underground or overhead utilities (e.g., drainage, gas, electrical) that conflict with the crossing location must be relocated before crossing infrastructure can be constructed.

While lighting can be installed after, ideally it is in place to ensure visibility and safety during and after crossing construction; however it is a soft preference as the crossing can function without immediate lighting.

The final road surface course must be laid after the crossing is installed to ensure a seamless, flush finish between the road surface and the crossing elements (e.g., raised crosswalks, textured pavers, ramps).

Crosswalk markings, pedestrian warning signs, and regulatory signage can only be applied once the crossing infrastructure (pavers, ramps, refuge islands) is physically in place to ensure accurate alignment and placement.
Site must be cleared of debris, existing structures, and obstructions before any landscape grading or planting can occur.
Rough grading and earthworks must be completed to establish final site topography and drainage patterns before detailed landscape works begin.
All buried services (stormwater drainage, irrigation mains, electrical conduits for landscape lighting) must be laid and tested before topsoil placement and planting to avoid disturbance.

predecessor: Foundation and Slab Works (for adjacent structures)
rationale: Building foundations and ground-floor slabs must be completed and cured to prevent landscape areas being used as construction access routes or being damaged by heavy plant/materials.
All planting, turfing, mulching and soft landscaping must be finished before the final clean and project handover to avoid soiling or damaging newly completed landscape areas.

successor: External Paving and Hardscape Finishes (final surfacing)
rationale: While some hardscape can be done concurrently, final paving adjacent to planted areas is often sequenced after planting to avoid heavy traffic damage to new plants; this is a soft preference rather than a strict physical constraint.
Planting must be in place before the irrigation system can be fully commissioned and tested for coverage and performance, as the system is designed around the planted areas.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and existing structures before any earthmoving or grading can begin, as obstacles would prevent access and proper grading.
Survey stakes and grade markers must be set to define cut/fill areas, slopes, and final elevations before earthwork equipment can operate.

predecessor: Temporary Site Utilities and Erosion Control
rationale: Erosion control measures (silt fences, sediment basins) and temporary water supply must be installed before grading disturbs the soil to prevent sediment runoff.
After rough grading and cutting/filling to design elevations, the soil must be compacted and stabilized to achieve the required bearing capacity before further construction.
The site must be graded to final subgrade elevations and properly drained before precise foundation excavations can be laid out and dug.

The subgrade must be properly prepared, graded, and compacted to provide a stable and uniform foundation before any pavement layers can be placed, otherwise the pavement will crack or settle unevenly.

Drainage pipes, underdrains, and sub-base drainage systems must be installed before pavement construction to remove water from the subgrade and base layers, preventing water damage and pavement failure.

predecessor: Utility Installation (water, sewer, gas, electrical conduits)
rationale: All underground utilities and conduits must be laid and backfilled before pavement construction to avoid cutting or excavating through the completed pavement, which would compromise its structural integrity.

successor: Installation of Pavement Markings and Signage
rationale: Pavement markings (lane lines, crosswalks, arrows) and signage must be applied only after the final pavement surface is complete and cured to ensure proper adhesion and durability.
Curbs and gutters adjacent to the pavement are typically installed after the base pavement layer to ensure proper alignment and drainage flow between the pavement surface and the curb.
Road markings must be applied on top of the finished pavement surface. The pavement provides the stable, smooth base required for marking adhesion and durability.
The entire road structure including base layers must be compacted and finished before the final pavement surface is laid and subsequently marked. This ensures a stable foundation.

It is preferable (soft preference) to have road markings in place before installing signals so that signal pole and sensor placements can be coordinated with lane markings, but signals can be adjusted after marking if needed.

Road markings are essential for safe traffic guidance and are typically the final surface treatment before a road is opened to traffic. The road should not be opened to uncontrolled traffic without markings in place.
Installing street signs can be done before or after markings, but it is often more efficient to place signs after markings to ensure proper alignment with lane configurations.

The construction site must be prepared and mobilized (including setting up perimeter fencing, signage, and material laydown areas) before traffic management plans can be implemented, as the physical site layout dictates where traffic control devices and detour routes are positioned.

Traffic management measures (e.g., lane closures, detours, temporary barriers) must be in place before any road construction or paving work begins, to ensure the safety of workers and the public by redirecting traffic away from active work zones.

While utility relocation can sometimes be sequenced independently, setting up traffic management first helps control access to utility work zones and reduces conflicts with ongoing traffic, making it a preferred sequencing order.

Demolition work adjacent to roadways poses significant safety hazards; traffic management (lane closures, barriers, diversions) must be established first to protect both road users and demolition crews from falling debris and construction equipment.

Traffic management measures must remain fully operational until all construction activities are complete; only after final inspections and removal of construction equipment can the full road be opened to traffic and temporary traffic controls be demobilized.
Site mobilization (establishing site access, temporary facilities, and safety perimeters) must precede any utility work to ensure a safe and organized worksite for diversion activities.

A comprehensive survey of existing underground utilities and surface marking-out is required before any diversion work can begin, to identify the locations, depths, and types of utilities that need to be relocated or protected.

Traffic control measures and road closures must be in place before utility diversion begins, as excavation in roadways or footpaths for ducting work poses safety risks to the public and requires controlled access.

Utility diversion and installation of new ducting must be completed before bulk earthworks commence, because undisturbed utility runs need to be protected and newly diverted utilities must be in their final positions before large-scale grading and cut/fill operations occur.

All utility diversions and ductwork must be completed and verified before foundation excavation begins, to ensure no active utilities are encountered during deep excavations and that duct routes are clearly established and protected.

The building structure must be fully erected and stable before any specialist learning furniture can be installed, as the furniture often requires precise positioning within completed rooms and relies on structural supports.

All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work (conduits, pipes, wiring) must be completed before installing furniture that may be fixed in place or integrated with building services, to avoid rework or damage.
Interior partitions and drywall must be finished to define room layouts; specialist learning furniture (e.g., fixed desks, lab benches) is placed against or attached to walls.
Floor surfaces must be level and prepared before heavy or fixed learning furniture is installed to ensure stability and alignment.
It is preferable to complete painting and final finishes before installing furniture to avoid damage, but touch-up painting can be done after installation if needed.
The wall bracket or mounting frame must be securely attached to the wall before the smartboard/display can be hung on it.

predecessor: Run electrical conduit and wiring to mounting location
rationale: Power and data cables must be in place behind the wall or at the mounting point before the display is installed, as it is difficult or impossible to add wiring afterward.

predecessor: Complete ceiling and wall finishing (painting, drywall)
rationale: Wall finishing and painting should be completed before mounting expensive equipment to avoid dust, debris, and damage.

successor: Connect and test audio-visual and network cables to display
rationale: Once the display is physically mounted, the final cable connections (HDMI, network, USB) can be made and the system can be powered on for testing.

successor: Calibrate touch interface and configure software
rationale: Touch calibration and software configuration can only be performed after the display is installed and powered on.

The structural frame or opening (e.g., stud wall, timber frame, or metal frame) must be installed and prepared before the glazed screen or vision panel can be fitted, as the panel requires a stable support structure.
After the glazed screen panel is placed, sealants, gaskets, or glazing beads must be applied to secure the panel and ensure airtightness and watertightness.

Decorative trims or architraves around the screen are typically installed after the glazed panel is in place to cover gaps and provide a finished appearance, though this is a preference for work sequence rather than a physical necessity.

predecessor: Rough-in Electrical / Services (if vision panel includes integrated lighting or sensors)
rationale: If the glazed screen or vision panel incorporates electrical components (e.g., integrated lighting, electrochromic glass controls), rough-in electrical work must be completed prior to panel installation.

While painting can be done before installation, it is often preferred to install glazed screens after painting to avoid damage to the finished wall surface, but this is a soft preference rather than a hard constraint.

The educational vision and curriculum define the specific teaching methods, class sizes, and learning activities that must be supported; space planning cannot proceed without knowing what pedagogical functions the spaces need to accommodate.
Site constraints, dimensions, orientation, and context influence the building footprint and spatial organization, which must be understood before programming specific spaces.
Stakeholder input on space requirements, user numbers, and functional needs must be gathered to inform the space program parameters before detailed planning begins.
The spatial program (room types, sizes, quantities, adjacencies) provides the direct brief for architects to begin schematic design; design cannot start without the program of spaces.
The types and sizes of spaces defined in the program determine what furniture and equipment are needed; FF&E specifications depend on room dimensions and functions.
The building elements (walls, floors, ceilings) must be fully constructed before acoustic testing can measure their sound insulation properties.
Doors and windows are critical paths for sound transmission and must be installed to test overall acoustic separation between spaces.
All gaps, penetrations, and joints must be sealed to ensure the tested assembly represents the final soundproofing performance.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-ins must be complete and any penetrations sealed so they don't compromise acoustic results.
Once acoustic testing validates the sound isolation, interior finishes can be applied without risking damage or rework to tested assemblies.
Acoustic testing should precede ceiling finish work to allow access to plenum spaces if remedial soundproofing is needed.
Building must be acoustically certified before permanent occupancy or furniture layout to ensure regulatory compliance.

predecessor: Rough-in & conduit installation for electrical & low-voltage systems
rationale: Power and data cabling infrastructure (conduit, cable trays, backboxes) must be installed before any AV/IT equipment can be placed or terminated.

predecessor: Ceiling & wall finish completion (drywall, painting, flooring)
rationale: AV/IT equipment should not be installed until ceiling grids are in place and final finishes are complete to avoid dust and debris contamination of sensitive electronic components.
Dedicated power circuits must be run and terminated before AV racks, displays, and IT servers can be connected and powered up for commissioning.
AV/IT system commissioning must be complete and verified before the building can be handed over to the owner/operator.

While not a hard physical constraint, AV/IT commissioning is typically sequenced before final furniture placement to allow technicians unobstructed access to wall outlets, ceiling projectors, and equipment racks.
Rough carpentry (stud walls, framing) must be completed before partition installation begins, as partitions are attached to or aligned with the rough framing.
All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work within walls and ceilings must be finished before partitions are enclosed or furniture is installed, to avoid costly rework.
Flooring and underlayment should be installed before fixed partitions and furniture to ensure a consistent finished floor surface and avoid damage to new flooring.
Partitions must be in place before final painting and wall finishing can be applied, as the partitions define the surfaces to be painted.
Final installation of electrical outlets, switches, plumbing fixtures, and HVAC grilles occurs after partitions are installed, as these fixtures are mounted into or onto the completed partitions.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated before any structural framing can begin, as the frame requires a stable and properly prepared foundation base.

The structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) must be erected on top of completed foundations to transfer loads safely to the ground. Foundation concrete must be cured and strong enough to support frame loads.

predecessor: Underground Utility Installation (Drainage, Plumbing, Electrical Conduits)
rationale: Underground utilities beneath the slab must be laid and backfilled before the structural frame is built, otherwise excavation and pipe laying would be impossible or extremely costly under the completed frame.
The roof structure rests directly on the mall's structural frame (columns and beams); the frame must be complete to provide vertical supports and lateral stability for the roof.

successor: Exterior Wall Cladding and Facade Installation
rationale: Exterior cladding panels and facade elements are attached to the structural frame; the frame must be in place to provide the mounting points and structural backing for the building envelope.
The steel frame provides the primary structural support that the skylight/atrium roof will be attached to and rest upon. Without the structural frame in place, the skylight cannot be installed.
The roof deck forms the substrate / base around the skylight opening. The skylight frame sits on and is sealed to the roof deck, so the deck must be completed first.
The atrium walls and support structure must be built to the full height before the roof-level skylight can be craned into position and installed at the top of the atrium.

The waterproofing around the skylight perimeter can only be applied after the skylight frame and glazing are installed, as the membrane must lap up onto the skylight frame to create a continuous weather seal.

successor: Interior Ceiling Finishes & Atrium Wall Cladding
rationale: While not physically required, completing the skylight first allows interior finishes below to be protected from weather and allows natural light for finishing work. Some overlap may be possible with temporary weather protection.
The structural steel frame provides the primary load-bearing support and fixing points for the shopfront glazing system; without the frame in place there is nothing to attach the glazing to.
The shopfront glazing system sits on the finished floor slab which provides a level, stable base; the slab must be poured and cured to support the weight and provide accurate alignment.

predecessor: Weatherproof Membrane / Waterproofing to Rough Opening
rationale: Waterproofing must be applied to the structural opening before the glazing is installed to prevent moisture ingress behind the shopfront frame, which could cause corrosion, mould, or water damage.

successor: Internal Fit-out / Finishing Works (e.g. plasterboard, painting)
rationale: Once the shopfront glazing is installed, the building envelope is weathertight, allowing sensitive internal finishing works to proceed without risk of weather damage; the glazing also defines the interior boundary.

While signage can technically be installed before glazing, it is typically sequenced after to avoid damaging the glazing panels during sign fixing and to ensure the shopfront appears as a finished backdrop for sign alignment.

The structural frame, including the openings (trusses/shafts) for escalators and travelators, must be in place before any escalator or travelator components can be installed, as the units are placed into these structural openings.
Floor slabs and the building core must be constructed to provide the physical support and bearing points for the escalator and travelator trusses.
Fireproofing application to the escalator/travelator structure can only proceed after the units are installed and secured in their final position.
Glass panels, balustrades, skirting and other cladding components are installed onto the escalator/travelator structure after the main framework is in place.
Final tuning of steps, handrails, and overall commissioning of the escalator/travelator system must occur after all mechanical and electrical components are installed and aligned.
The passenger lift core requires a stable foundation to transfer its vertical loads to the ground; without completed foundation works, the lift core would lack structural support.
The lift core must be constructed on a waterproofed slab to prevent moisture ingress into the lift shaft and pit, which is critical for lift equipment and long-term durability.
Lift rails are physically fastened to the lift core walls; the core structure must be fully erected and cured before rails can be installed.
The lift car and counterweight operate within the lift shaft formed by the core; the core must be complete to provide the enclosed vertical pathway for safe assembly.
Landing doors are installed into the openings of the lift core at each floor level; the core walls and floor slabs must be in place to receive the door frames.
The building structure (walls, ceilings, floors) must be complete before any signage or wayfinding elements can be mounted or installed.
Wall surfaces must be finished before signage can be attached to avoid damage to finishes and ensure proper adhesion/fastening.
Power supply lines and conduit must be in place to provide electricity for illuminated signage and digital wayfinding displays.
Signage and wayfinding must be operational before tenant move-in and merchandising to ensure proper customer navigation and brand presentation.
All signage and wayfinding elements must be installed and functional before the final building commissioning and inspection can verify compliance with codes and design intent.
The slab on grade or structural floor must be in place to provide a level and stable substrate upon which partition walls can be framed and erected.
Overhead mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work must be completed before partitions are framed to avoid interference, rework, and to allow unobstructed access for overhead installations.

successor: Partition Wall Inspection (Frame & MEP Rough-In Inspection)
rationale: Partitions must be framed and standing before inspection of the wall framing and any embedded MEP rough-in within walls can be performed.
Partition framing and installation of studs/tracks must be fully complete before drywall or gypsum board can be hung and attached to the framework.

Although finishes typically follow partition installation, in some phasing scenarios limited finishes in non-partitioned zones can proceed concurrently; however, a hard physical dependency is that the partition system provides the backing and support for many finishes.
The structural slab must be completed, cured, and leveled before any raised access floor system can be installed, as the access floor pedestals and panels require a stable, level base substrate.

All underfloor cabling, conduit, piping, and ductwork must be roughed-in and inspected before the raised access floor is installed, as these services will be concealed beneath the access floor and cannot be accessed without removing finished panels.

successor: Floor Covering Installation (Carpet Tile or Vinyl)
rationale: The raised access floor panels must be fully installed and leveled before any final floor finish (carpet tile, vinyl, etc.) can be applied, as the finish is laid directly on top of the access floor panels.

Partition walls, workstations, and interior fit-out activities depend on the raised floor being in place to establish finished floor levels and to allow partition tracks to be anchored to or aligned with the access floor grid.

While final mechanical, electrical, and plumbing trim-out and suspended ceiling installation often occurs after the raised floor is in place to coordinate floor-to-ceiling heights and MEP drops, some overhead work can proceed in parallel; this is a soft preference sequence for coordination efficiency.

predecessor: Overhead MEP Rough-In (Electrical, Plumbing, HVAC Ductwork & Pipes)
rationale: All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) rough-in work including ductwork, piping, conduit, and wiring must be completed before installing the suspended ceiling grid, as the ceiling conceals these systems and must remain accessible during rough-in. Installing the ceiling first would block access to overhead MEP systems.

Fire sprinkler piping and heads must be roughed-in and tested before ceiling grid installation because sprinkler heads must penetrate the ceiling tiles and the piping is typically routed above the ceiling. Ceiling installation would obstruct sprinkler work.

Interior wall framing and any wall-mounted MEP rough-ins should be completed first, as bulkheads often tie into wall framing and the ceiling grid must align with finished wall locations. Installing ceiling before walls would create alignment issues.
The suspended ceiling grid (carrying channels, tees, hangers) must be fully installed and leveled before ceiling tiles or panels can be placed into the grid system.

successor: Final MEP Trim-Out (Lighting Fixtures, Diffusers, Sprinkler Heads, Sensors)
rationale: Lighting fixtures, HVAC diffusers, sprinkler heads, and other ceiling-mounted devices are installed after the ceiling grid is in place, as the grid provides the support structure and penetrations are coordinated with the grid layout.

While painting of bulkhead surfaces can occur after bulkhead installation, it is a soft preference because some painting may be done beforehand. However, typically painting is completed after the ceiling/bulkhead framework is installed to achieve a clean finish without taping/transition issues.
The site must be cleared of debris, vegetation, and existing structures to provide unobstructed access for piling rigs and to ensure accurate pile positioning.
Accurate surveying and setting out of pile positions is required before any piling can commence to ensure piles are installed in the correct locations as per engineering drawings.
Temporary access roads and working platforms for piling rigs should be prepared beforehand to provide stable ground conditions and safe access for heavy piling equipment.
Pile caps are structural elements that transfer loads from the superstructure to the piles; they cannot be constructed until the piles themselves have been installed and tested.
Ground beams and other foundation elements typically bear onto pile caps or piles, so they require completed piling works before they can proceed.
Structural framing, roofing, and exterior enclosure must be completed to provide a weather-tight shell before MEP rough-in work can begin, protecting materials and equipment from weather damage.
In-slab conduits, under-slab drainage, and foundation penetrations for MEP services must be installed during or after slab/foundation placement but prior to above-grade rough-in work.
MEP rough-in (piping, ductwork, conduit, wiring) must be installed within wall cavities and above ceilings before they are enclosed by insulation and drywall.
Regulatory authorities require inspection of rough-in MEP work (plumbing, electrical, mechanical) before walls and ceilings are closed up.
MEP first fix (pipes, cables, ducts) must be in place before second fix activities such as installing fixtures, outlets, switches, and trim can proceed.

The structural frame (columns, slabs, core walls) must be complete before the shell and core can be handed over, as the structure provides the physical substrate for all subsequent fit-out and MEP systems.
The building envelope (façade, roofing, glazing) must be weathertight before handover to protect interior works and meet contractual shell-and-core scope.

Main risers, primary ductwork, and central plant connections for the core areas must be installed before handover, as they are part of the landlord's shell-and-core scope and are prerequisites for tenant fit-out connections.
Tenants cannot begin their interior fit-out works until the shell and core space has been formally handed over, providing legal possession and a finished base building ready for customization.

While common area finishes often follow shell handover, in some projects they can run concurrently with tenant fit-out; however, handover typically marks site access turnover, making this a strong preference rather than a hard physical constraint.
The building structure must be completed to define the final site boundaries, grades, and access points required for landscaping design and external works coordination.

All underground drainage, water, gas, electrical, and telecommunications utilities must be laid and backfilled before topsoil placement, planting, and hardscape installation to avoid excavation damage to finished landscaping.
External wall finishes, cladding, and building envelope works must be completed to allow for accurate grading, drainage connections, and finishing details around building perimeters.
Landscaping and external works are the finishing activities on site; once complete, the site can be cleaned up and handed over to the client or end user.

While external lighting and signage can conceptually be installed after landscaping is complete to avoid damage, in practice these are often coordinated concurrently; however, final adjustments and finishing touches on lighting/signage may be done after landscaping to ensure proper alignment.

The building's structural frame (columns, slabs, and beams) must be complete to provide a safe and stable enclosure before any internal fit-out can commence. Fit-out activities like partition walls, ceilings, and finishes rely on the structural grid being in place.

External cladding, roofing, glazing, and doors/windows must be installed and sealed to protect interior works from weather damage (rain, wind, dust) before sensitive fit-out materials like drywall, insulation, flooring, and finishes are installed.

Core mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) risers, main ductwork, main electrical panels, and plumbing stacks must be rough-installed to the floor level before tenant fit-out can connect and extend branch runs within the tenanted space.

All fit-out installations (partitions, ceilings, MEP branch work, finishes) must be complete so that inspectors and commissioning agents can verify compliance with building codes, fire safety, accessibility standards, and functional performance of systems.

Furniture, fixtures, and equipment installation and tenant move-in activities can only occur after the fit-out construction (walls, floors, ceilings, lighting, power outlets) is finished to avoid damage, dust, and interference with finishing trades.
The property must be legally acquired and zoned for retail use before any management activities can begin.
The physical retail building must be constructed, completed, and fitted out before property management operations (leasing, maintenance, tenant coordination) can commence.
Essential utilities (electricity, water, sewage, HVAC) must be connected and operational before the property can be managed and occupied by tenants.
A certificate of occupancy from local authorities is a legal prerequisite before retail spaces can be leased, occupied, or managed.
Property management must be in place to coordinate lease agreements and oversee tenant fit-out activities before individual retail stores can open.

successor: Ticket Booth / Fare Collection Point Installation
rationale: A stable foundation and level site must be prepared before the ticket booth structure can be erected, as it is a physical building component.

successor: Ticket Booth / Fare Collection Point Installation
rationale: Power and data cabling must be laid in the ground beneath or leading to the booth before the booth is placed, otherwise retrofitting would require destructive work.

predecessor: Ticket Booth / Fare Collection Point Installation
rationale: The ticket booth must be physically in place and its internal wiring terminated before electrical power can be connected and fare collection systems can be tested.

predecessor: Ticket Booth / Fare Collection Point Installation
rationale: While it is logical to install queue barriers and directional signage after the booth is positioned, this is a soft sequencing preference; signage could theoretically be placed beforehand and adjusted later.

predecessor: Ticket Booth / Fare Collection Point Installation
rationale: The ticket booth must be fully installed and all its fare collection equipment operational before a final inspection and acceptance test can be performed to verify compliance with specifications.
The foundation or base must be completed to provide a stable and level surface for constructing the canopy or roof shelter structure.
The main structural frame (columns, beams, or walls) must be in place to support the roof or canopy structure.
The canopy or roof shelter structure must be completed before installing roofing materials or weatherproofing membranes on top of it.
Electrical and lighting work is typically done after the roof is in place to protect wiring and fixtures from weather, though some rough-in work can be done concurrently.
Interior ceiling finishes, insulation, and interior cladding cannot be installed until the roof structure is complete and weathertight.
Walls and surfaces must be finished (painted, wallpapered, etc.) before signage can be mounted or adhered to them; otherwise, installation would damage or interfere with finishes.
Suspended and overhead signage requires a completed ceiling structure for secure mounting and alignment.
Floor-mounted signage, floor decals, and wayfinding markers require completed flooring to be installed correctly without damage or later disruption.
Illuminated and electronic signage requires electrical power supply and lighting context to be in place for connection, testing, and proper visibility.
All signage must be installed before final inspection and commissioning to verify that wayfinding and informational signage are correctly placed and compliant with codes and design specifications.
Complete wayfinding signage is essential for occupant safety, navigation, and regulatory compliance before the building can be occupied or handed over to the client.
Benches require a stable, level base. The concrete slab or foundation must be cured and ready to support the weight and anchoring of seating elements.
Proper grading and drainage must be completed so that the area where benches are placed does not collect water, preventing deterioration and ensuring stable placement.
It is easier to install benches before surrounding soft landscaping and planting to avoid damaging new plants and to allow machinery access for bench placement.
Benches are a finishing element; once installed, the final cleanup and detailing can proceed around them without risk of damage from other construction activities.

The subgrade must be properly prepared, graded, and compacted to provide a stable foundation before kerb and channel installation. Without a compacted and correctly graded subgrade, the kerb would lack proper support and drainage alignment.

The road base or pavement layers are typically placed and compacted prior to kerb installation so that the kerb can be set at the correct finished level relative to the pavement surface and to ensure the kerb integrates properly with the road structure.

Underground stormwater drainage infrastructure (pipes and catchment pits) must be installed and tested before kerb and channel construction to ensure that the channel outlets connect correctly to the drainage system and to avoid excavating through newly placed kerb work.

The kerb and channel must be completed and cured before final asphalt or pavement surfacing is laid, as the kerb acts as a vertical formwork/edge restraint for the asphalt and defines the finished pavement edge level.

Footpath and pedestrian paving works adjacent to the roadway typically follow kerb and channel installation because the kerb defines the edge boundary and finished level for the adjoining footpath, ensuring proper water drainage and transition.
The ground surface must be properly graded and compacted to provide a stable, level base for the ramp foundation, ensuring proper drainage and structural support.
A concrete slab or foundation must be poured and cured to serve as the structural base onto which the ramp system is anchored.
Any underground electrical conduits for lighting or drainage pipes must be installed prior to ramp construction to avoid cutting into the finished ramp.
Handrails and guardrails are mounted onto the ramp structure itself and must be installed after the ramp framework is complete to ensure proper alignment and anchorage.
While not a strict physical dependency, it is preferable to complete the ramp before final paving of adjacent walkways to achieve a seamless, flush transition and avoid damaging new pavement.
The subgrade must be properly graded, compacted, and prepared to provide a stable foundation before any pavement layers can be placed.
Subsurface drainage systems (e.g., perforated pipes, French drains) must be installed before pavement to prevent water accumulation beneath the pavement structure that could cause premature failure.
The aggregate base or sub-base course must be laid and compacted to provide a load-bearing layer between the subgrade and the pavement surface.
After pavement (especially concrete pavement) is placed, a curing period is physically required to allow the material to gain sufficient strength before traffic loads are applied.
Road markings, lane lines, and striping must be applied after the pavement surface is complete and cured to ensure proper adhesion and visibility.
The structural frame (walls, columns, roof trusses) must be erected and braced before roofing can be applied, as the roof deck depends on the frame for support.
A solid roof deck or sheathing (e.g., plywood, OSB, metal decking) must be in place to provide the substrate for roofing membranes, underlayment, and waterproofing layers.
Roof overhangs and flashing are typically installed before wall cladding to allow proper weatherproofing integration and prevent water ingress behind cladding panels.
Roofing and waterproofing must be completed to protect the interior from weather before installing ceiling finishes and drywall, which are moisture-sensitive.

While rough-in can technically proceed before roofing, completing the weather-tight envelope first protects exposed wiring and pipes; however, this is a soft preference rather than a hard physical constraint.
Site must be cleared of obstructions, vegetation, and existing structures before any drainage or civil earthworks can commence, as debris would interfere with excavation, grading, and pipe laying.

Rough grading and cut/fill operations establish the required slopes and levels; drainage pipes and subgrade preparation must follow the final earthwork contours to ensure proper water flow and stable foundations.

Underground drainage and civil infrastructure (stormwater pipes, culverts, subsoil drains) must be installed and tested before road pavement layers and kerbing are constructed, to avoid later excavation that would damage the pavement.

External drainage systems (stormwater, subsoil drainage) around building footprints must be completed to prevent water accumulation, before pouring concrete slabs or footings, ensuring structural stability and water management.

While utility trenches can be coordinated with drainage, it is standard practice to complete primary drainage networks first to avoid conflicts in trench sequencing and to ensure stormwater management is operational before other services are buried.
Line markings must be applied on a finished, clean, and properly cured paved surface. The pavement/base layer must be complete and cured before any markings can adhere correctly.
Curbs define the roadway edges and boundaries; line markings must align with these permanent features, so curbs must be in place first.

Final grading and landscaping establish the finished site contours and drainage; line marking is a finishing operation that should only occur after all earthmoving and landscaping is complete to avoid damage.

Line marking and signage are among the final finishing activities. Once markings are applied and signs are erected, the site can be cleaned up and inspected for handover; no major construction should follow that could damage markings.
Roads and parking areas must be fully marked and signed before they can be opened to traffic for safety and regulatory compliance.

The building must be substantially complete (all major construction work finished, systems installed) before commissioning can begin, as commissioning tests require the building to be in a finished state.
All MEP systems (HVAC, electrical, plumbing, fire protection) must be fully installed before they can be commissioned and tested.
The building envelope must be sealed and weathertight before indoor commissioning activities can proceed, to protect equipment and ensure valid test conditions.
The building cannot be occupied or handed over to the owner/tenant until commissioning is complete and all systems have been verified as operational.
The warranty period and post-occupancy phase formally begin only after commissioning, handover, and acceptance of the building by the owner.

The foundation and substructure must be completed to provide a stable base before any vertical structural elements defining inter-story height can be erected. Without a completed foundation, floor-to-floor heights cannot be established.

The vertical columns and horizontal beams that define the structural frame must be in place to set the clear floor-to-floor height dimensions. Inter-story height is physically determined by the spacing between successive floor slabs and the beam/column depths.

The lower floor slab must be completed to serve as the reference datum from which the inter-story height is measured upward to the next floor. The inter-story height is the vertical distance between successive finished floor levels.

Ceiling systems are installed at a specific height below the upper floor slab, and the inter-story height (floor-to-floor dimension) determines the available plenum space and the finished ceiling elevation. Without establishing the floor-to-floor height, ceiling height and layout cannot be accurately set.

Interior partition walls are built to the full floor-to-floor height. The vertical stud length and the top/bottom track positions depend on the precise inter-story height measurement. Wall framing cannot proceed until the floor-to-floor dimension is known and established.
The site must be surveyed and graded to establish a reference elevation before the building height datum can be set.
Excavation to the designed depth is required to establish the correct vertical reference for the building height datum, typically tied to the foundation level.
The building height datum must be established first so that all vertical control points (columns, floor levels, etc.) can be laid out relative to a common reference.
The height datum defines the top-of-footing or top-of-foundation elevation, which is the reference for pouring concrete to the correct level.
The vertical alignment of columns, walls, and subsequent floors depends on an established height datum to ensure storey heights and overall building elevation are correct.
Columns and shear walls provide vertical support for the floor slab; the slab cannot be placed without completed vertical structural elements beneath it.
Formwork creates the mold and temporary support structure into which concrete for the slab is poured; it must be erected before the slab can be cast.
Steel reinforcement bars must be placed and tied within the formwork before concrete pouring to provide the slab's tensile strength.
After the slab is poured, sufficient curing time is required for the concrete to gain strength before any loads can be applied or subsequent work can proceed.
Columns and walls on the next level must be built on top of the completed floor slab, which acts as their working platform and load-bearing base.
The staircase core transmits significant vertical loads to the ground, requiring a completed foundation system to support its structural weight and maintain alignment.
The staircase core is typically erected on top of the ground or basement slab, which provides a level working platform and base for the core's structural walls.
Floor slabs that bear on or connect to the core require the core walls to be in place first to provide vertical support and lateral stability.
