The stair flights and landings are physically supported by, or anchored into, the core walls; the core structure must therefore be complete before stairs are installed.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing risers running through the core require the core's vertical shafts and wall openings to be formed and cured before conduits, pipes, and ducts can be pulled through.
Elevator shaft must be supported by a structural foundation that can bear its load.
The elevator shaft is typically framed within the building's structural steel or concrete frame, which must be in place to define the shaft envelope.
The physical shaft enclosure, including walls and structural supports, must be complete before elevators, rails, and cars can be installed inside it.
Electrical conduits, wiring, and control panels for the elevator system are installed within the shaft after its structure is complete.
Fireproofing materials (e.g., fire-rated drywall or spray-applied fireproofing) are applied to the shaft interior after its structural completion to meet fire code requirements.
The fire egress stairway requires a structural support platform (floor slab or landing) to be in place before stair stringers and treads can be anchored.
Fireproofing spray or intumescent coating must be applied after the stair structure is erected to protect the steel or concrete from fire exposure.
Handrails and guardrails physically attach to the stair stringers and landings, so the stair structure must be in place first.

successor: Stairway Lighting and Exit Signage Installation
rationale: While electrical rough-in can precede stairs, final installation of stair lighting and exit signs is typically done after the stairway is complete to position fixtures correctly and avoid damage.
Building codes require the fire egress stairway to be fully installed and functional before the building can receive occupancy approval, as it is a critical life-safety component.
The site survey and zoning analysis must be completed first to determine the applicable height restrictions and maximum building height allowed on the property before compliance can be assessed.
A preliminary architectural design that includes the proposed building height must be developed so that it can be reviewed against zoning height restrictions for compliance.
Detailed structural engineering depends on the approved/verified building height envelope from zoning compliance to accurately calculate loads, wind forces, and structural system requirements.

Zoning height compliance must be confirmed before the building permit application can be submitted, as permit applications require evidence that the proposed structure meets all zoning height limitations.

Excavation and foundation work cannot begin until the building's approved height and overall design (including basement depth relative to grade) are confirmed compliant, as these affect the finished floor elevations and total building height.
The building must be physically constructed before its story count can be verified through a survey.
Before an occupancy permit can be issued, the story count must be verified to ensure compliance with zoning and building codes.
The story count survey must be completed as part of the documentation needed before final inspection of the building.
The structural frame must have a stable, level base from the foundation to support the loads transferred from each floor being erected.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and excavated before any foundation elements (footings, piles, slabs) can be installed.
Structural columns, beams, and vertical elements must be erected first to provide the load-bearing framework onto which floor slabs/decks are placed.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work (conduits, piping, ductwork embedded in or running above the slab) must be installed before the slab is fully finished or enclosed.
The building's structural frame must be in place to provide attachment points and support for the facade or curtain wall system.

The structural frame (slabs, columns, beams) must be completed to provide a stable mounting surface and load-bearing support for the facade panels. Installing facade without the structure in place would be unsafe and physically impossible.
The concrete floor slab at each level must be sufficiently cured to support the weight of facade panels, installation equipment, and workers. Premature loading could cause structural failure.
The facade framing and structural panel system must be in place to provide the supporting framework into which windows and glazing units are installed.

While interior framing can theoretically start before facade is fully complete, it is strongly preferred to complete facade first to protect interior works from weather exposure and to establish the building envelope.
The facade panels must be installed before the waterproofing and air-sealing membranes can be applied to the joints and connections between panels to ensure a continuous building envelope.

The building program (occupancy type, use groups, intended functions) must be defined before the code story-count classification can be determined, as the applicable building code and its story-count thresholds depend on the occupancy classification.

Site conditions, including soil bearing capacity, seismic zone, and flood zone designations, influence whether a building is classified as a high-rise or low-rise under code definitions, which directly affects story-count classification.

Local zoning ordinances often impose maximum height and story-count limits that must be known before the applicable building code story-count classification can be finalized, as the zoning constraints may restrict the allowed number of stories.

The structural system (e.g., moment frame, shear wall, braced frame) and its design parameters are directly dependent on the building's story count classification, as code-defined seismic and wind load requirements scale with building height and number of stories.

The number of stories determines required egress components such as number and width of stairs, maximum travel distances, and fire-resistance ratings of exit enclosures, which must be designed after the story-count classification is established.

Code-required fire protection systems (sprinklers, standpipes, fire alarms) vary based on whether the building is classified as low-rise, mid-rise, or high-rise, which is determined by the story-count classification.
The ground must be cleared, graded, and excavated to proper elevations and compaction before any foundation or ramp structure can be constructed.
Concrete footings and foundation systems must be in place to support the vertical and lateral loads of the parking ramp structure.
Underground utility lines (storm drainage, water, electrical conduits) must be installed before slabs and structural columns are placed to avoid costly rework and conflicts.
Structural concrete decks and ramps must be fully cured and complete before waterproof membranes and traffic-bearing coatings are applied to protect the structure from moisture and chemical damage.

While some finishes can be phased, typically the ramp structure must be enclosed and structurally complete before final finishes, elevator installation, and lighting fixtures are installed to protect materials and ensure safe access.
The ground must be excavated, graded, and compacted before bollard foundations can be poured or barriers installed.
Any underground utilities (drainage, electrical, etc.) must be laid and backfilled before bollard footings are installed to avoid excavation damage to utilities.
Bollards require concrete footings or sleeves to be poured and cured before the bollard posts can be set or mounted.
Bollards and barriers are typically installed prior to the final surface layer (asphalt, concrete, pavers) so that surface material can be finished flush around the posts.
While it is preferable to stripe and sign after barriers are in place to ensure proper alignment of spaces and traffic flow, this is a logical sequence rather than a physical impossibility.

The parking layout and zoning study requires accurate site boundary, topography, soil conditions, and utility locations as base input data; without a site survey, the parking layout cannot be dimensioned or located correctly.

The overall site plan establishes building footprints, main access points, circulation routes, and land-use zones that define the area available for parking; the parking design must conform to the master plan.

Applicable parking ratios, setback requirements, fire lane clearances, and local zoning ordinances (e.g., minimum number of spaces, stall dimensions, accessibility requirements) must be known before the layout can be designed to ensure compliance.

successor: Detailed Parking Lot Grading & Drainage Design
rationale: The parking geometry (aisle widths, stall layout, drive lanes) determines the surface flow paths, catch basin locations, and grading contours; drainage design cannot proceed until the parking layout is finalized.
The parking layout defines traffic patterns (e.g., car-only vs. occasional truck/emergency vehicle loading) and load distribution areas, which inform pavement thickness and material specifications.

The Traffic Impact Study provides the baseline traffic generation and modal split data that feeds into parking demand calculations; without understanding overall traffic patterns, parking demand cannot be accurately estimated.
The existing site conditions survey establishes current parking inventory, land use data, and physical constraints that must be known before analyzing parking demand and ratios.
Zoning regulations specify minimum/maximum parking ratios that the analysis must comply with; the analysis cannot proceed without knowing the applicable parking code requirements.
The parking demand analysis determines the required number of parking spaces and stall count, which directly drives the physical layout and dimensions of the parking lot design.
The number of parking spaces and demand ratios determine the required driveway widths, aisle widths, and circulation patterns needed to serve the projected parking volume.
The ratio analysis establishes the mix of parking types (standard, compact, accessible, EV) which defines the dimensional requirements for stall and aisle geometric design.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and compacted before any structural foundation work for the parking deck can begin.
Soil bearing capacity and subsurface conditions must be assessed to design proper foundations for the parking deck structure.
All necessary building permits and engineering approvals must be secured before commencing structural construction of the parking deck.

successor: Concrete Curing and Waterproofing of Deck
rationale: The structural frame and deck slab must be completed before curing, sealing, and waterproofing can be applied.
Structural components (columns, beams, slabs) must be in place before electrical conduits, lighting fixtures, and wiring can be installed within the parking deck.
The concrete substrate must be fully cured, clean, dry, and free of debris before any waterproofing membrane or sealant can be applied to ensure proper adhesion and prevent moisture entrapment.
All structural concrete elements (beams, slabs, walls) must be in place and finished before waterproofing can be installed to provide a continuous substrate.

In roofing and below-grade applications, a base sheet or underlayment is typically installed prior to the primary waterproofing layer for added protection; this is a preferred sequence but may vary by system.
Protective boards, drainage mats, or rigid insulation over below-grade waterproofing must be applied after the waterproofing membrane has cured to avoid damaging the membrane.
Backfill against foundation walls can only proceed after waterproofing is fully cured and protected, otherwise the membrane will be punctured or dislodged by the soil and equipment.
Line markings must be applied on a cured, stable asphalt surface. Asphalt paving and compaction must be completed first to provide the substrate for markings.
The surface must be clean, dry, and free of debris, dust, or loose material before any line marking paint can be applied to ensure adhesion.
Freshly laid asphalt or concrete must be fully cured before marking to prevent paint from bonding poorly or being damaged by residual moisture.

successor: Parking Area Usage / Opening to Traffic
rationale: The parking lot or roadway cannot be opened for use until all line markings and bay demarcations are complete and markings have dried/set.
It is preferable to complete line markings first to guide the positioning of signs and bollards, though some signage installation can occur concurrently if carefully coordinated.
The subgrade must be properly graded and compacted to provide a stable, uniform foundation that supports the pavement layers and prevents differential settlement.
The base course (aggregate base) provides structural support, drainage, and a working platform upon which the pavement (asphalt or concrete) is placed.
Subsurface drainage such as edge drains or underdrains must be installed before paving to ensure water can be properly channeled away from the pavement structure, preventing water damage.
Traffic markings, lane stripes, and pavement legends must be applied after the pavement surface is completed and cured to ensure proper adhesion and durability.
Curbs and gutters are typically placed after the pavement is constructed so that they align properly with the finished pavement edge and provide proper drainage confinement.
The electrical system design must be completed to determine load requirements, panel capacity, conduit paths, and breaker specifications before EV chargers can be installed.

predecessor: Main Electrical Panel Installation or Upgrade
rationale: The main electrical panel must be in place and capable of supporting the additional load from EV chargers before any charger units are connected to the building's electrical system.
Conduit pathways from the electrical panel to the EV charging locations must be installed prior to pulling cables and mounting chargers, as the conduit is a physical infrastructure prerequisite.
After EV chargers are physically installed, they must be tested for proper voltage, current, grounding, and communication functionality before being put into service.

successor: Parking Lot Paving and Striping (Final Layer)
rationale: It is often preferable to install EV chargers and their pedestals before the final asphalt or pavement layer is laid, to avoid cutting into fresh paving; however, this is a sequencing preference for a cleaner finish rather than a strict physical impossibility.
The parking guidance system (sensors, signage, control units) must be physically installed before it can be powered on, tested, and commissioned.
The commissioning process requires electrical power to test and calibrate all system components, so power supply must be in place beforehand.
The parking guidance system relies on a data network to communicate between sensors, controllers, and display signs; the network backbone must be ready before system integration testing can begin.

Final finishing works such as painting, marking, and cleaning in the parking area should be completed after commissioning to avoid damage from testing activities and to allow final adjustments based on system calibration.
Commissioning is a prerequisite for formal acceptance testing and handover to the client, as it verifies that the system operates according to specifications before acceptance can be granted.
The subgrade must be properly graded and compacted before the median strip can be constructed to provide a stable foundation and ensure proper drainage.
The base course (aggregate base) must be laid and compacted to the required level before constructing the median strip, as the median strip sits on top of the base layer.
The median strip must be constructed before the adjacent road pavement is laid, as the paving typically abuts the median and the curb/gutter interface must be established first.

Landscaping and planting within the median strip can begin only after the median structure (curbs, base, and soil fill) is completed, though this is a logical sequence rather than a physical necessity.
Signage or lighting poles mounted in the median require the median to be constructed first to provide a stable base, though signage could theoretically be installed later with some rework.

The subgrade must be graded, compacted, and prepared to the correct line and level before kerb and gutter can be laid, as the kerb and gutter requires a stable, properly compacted foundation to prevent settlement and cracking.

Stormwater drainage pipes, pits, and connections must be installed and tested before kerb and gutter construction, as the kerb and gutter integrates with the drainage system (e.g., inlet pits, grated drains) and the drainage infrastructure must be in place before concrete is poured.

Kerb and gutter must be cured and completed before asphalt or pavement can be laid, because the pavement abuts the kerb and uses it as a formwork edge and channel for drainage; paving up to the completed kerb ensures proper surface water runoff and edge restraint.

Footpath construction typically follows kerb and gutter, as the kerb defines the boundary between the roadway and footpath, and the footpath is laid flush against the back of the kerb to achieve correct levels and drainage.

While line marking usually occurs after all pavement and kerb works are complete to avoid damage, it is a soft preference rather than a strict physical constraint; marking could theoretically be done prior but would risk being damaged during kerb construction.

Road markings must be applied onto a finished, stable, and cured road surface. The substrate (asphalt or concrete) must be laid, compacted, and fully cured before any paint, thermoplastic, or tape markings can be applied, otherwise the markings will not adhere properly or will be damaged.

The structural layers of the road (sub-base and base course) must be completed and the final wearing surface laid before road markings can be applied. Markings are the final surface treatment and cannot be installed on unfinished structural layers.

successor: Traffic Signal Installation and Road Opening
rationale: Road markings provide essential visual guidance for traffic flow, lane delineation, and pedestrian crossings. Traffic signals and road opening to public use must follow marking completion to ensure safety and regulatory compliance.

Road markings and signage are complementary; however, markings often define lane configurations and turning movements. Final signage placement (e.g., lane arrows, stop bars) should be coordinated after markings are complete to ensure alignment and consistency.

The road marking system must be in place and fully cured before final quality inspection and handover can occur, as markings are a critical safety element that must be verified for compliance with road design specifications.

Traffic signs are typically installed on or adjacent to the final road surface. The pavement or base course must be completed to provide a stable foundation and correct elevation for sign posts and supports.
Though often done in parallel, it is preferable to have road markings completed before installing signage to ensure sign placement aligns with lane markings and regulatory zonal layouts.
All traffic signs must be in place and visible before a road can be opened to public traffic to ensure driver safety, regulatory compliance, and proper guidance.
A safety inspection or audit of the completed installation verifies that all signs are correctly positioned, visible, and compliant with standards before the road is operational.
Final grading and earthworks must be completed so that the ground surface is at its design level, ensuring sign posts are set to correct height and alignment without subsequent earth movement.

Vegetation, topsoil, and surface obstructions must be removed before earthworks can begin to expose suitable bearing material and prevent organic matter from being incorporated into the embankment fill.
The alignment, centerline, and grade stakes must be set out by surveyors to define the exact footprint and elevation of the embankment before any earthmoving operations can commence.
Temporary surface water drainage and sedimentation controls must be installed prior to earthworks to manage runoff, prevent erosion, and maintain site stability during embankment construction.

After each lift of embankment fill is placed and compacted, in-situ density and moisture content tests must be performed to verify that compaction meets specification before the next lift or subsequent pavement layers are placed.
The final embankment surface must be trimmed and compacted to the specified formation level before any sub-base or base course materials can be placed on top as part of the pavement structure.
The site must be cleared of existing structures, vegetation, and debris before trenching can commence, as obstructions would prevent safe access and excavation for utility installation.

Accurate surveying and marking of utility routes and trench alignments must be completed before excavation begins to ensure trenches are dug in the correct locations and avoid existing buried services.
Temporary site facilities, power, and water supplies need to be established to support the trenching operations and provide welfare facilities for workers.
Utility pipes, ducts, and cables must be laid and the trench backfilled before final connections to the network can be made and pressure/continuity testing performed.

Trench reinstatement (backfilling, compaction, and temporary or permanent surface restoration) must be completed before final road base, asphalt, or pavement layers are laid to avoid re-excavation and to ensure a stable subgrade.
Traffic data and site conditions must be understood before designing traffic management measures.
The timing and phases of construction activities must be known to plan traffic disruptions and detours accordingly.
Regulatory approvals for road closures or lane restrictions are required before finalizing the traffic management plan.
The approved traffic plan must be in place before mobilizing equipment and setting up site access and barriers.
Physical implementation of closures and diversions cannot proceed without the finalized traffic management plan.
The ground must be properly graded and prepared to provide a stable, level foundation for the noise barrier wall footings and base.
Excavation and formation of concrete footings or pile caps must be completed before the noise barrier wall panels or posts can be erected.
Any underground or overhead utilities within the wall alignment must be relocated or protected before construction to avoid conflicts and safety hazards.
After the wall panels and posts are in place, the excavated trench area must be backfilled and compacted to restore the grade and provide lateral support to the wall.
The noise barrier wall structure must be fully erected before final grading, seeding, and landscaping work can be completed adjacent to the wall.

predecessor: Bridge Deck Concrete Pouring and Curing
rationale: The guardrail and safety barrier system is typically mounted on or anchored to the bridge deck. The concrete deck must be poured and fully cured to provide a stable, load-bearing surface for guardrail post installation and anchorage.
Waterproofing is applied to the bridge deck surface before barriers are installed, as the barriers would obstruct continuous membrane application and proper detailing at the barrier-deck interface.
Any temporary scaffolding, formwork, or falsework beneath or beside the deck must be removed to provide clear access for guardrail installation along the bridge edges.

The final road surface is typically laid after barrier installation because the barrier serves as a reference edge for paving equipment and prevents asphalt from spilling over the deck edge. Also, paving after barriers ensures a tight seal at the barrier-pavement joint.

Guardrails and safety barriers are critical safety components that must be fully installed, inspected, and tested before the bridge is opened to traffic. Final load testing and safety checks cannot proceed until barriers are in place.
Proper site grading and drainage systems must be completed to ensure water flows away from structures and planted areas, preventing erosion and water damage to new landscaping.
All underground utilities (water, sewer, gas, electrical, communications) must be installed before landscaping to avoid digging up or damaging newly planted trees and landscaping features.
Building exterior and facade work (including scaffolding) must be complete to prevent damage to landscaping from construction debris, material drops, and heavy equipment access.

Street paving, sidewalks, curbs, and driveway aprons must be installed before street trees and landscaping to ensure proper alignment, avoid soil compaction from paving equipment, and prevent damage to new plantings.

successor: Final Site Cleanup and Punch List
rationale: Landscaping is typically one of the final finishing activities; after it is complete, only final cleanup, touch-ups, and inspections remain to avoid soiling or damaging the new landscape work.
The altar must have a solid, level foundation to ensure stability and structural integrity.
The location for the altar must be chosen and cleared of debris before construction can begin.
Stones or materials for the altar must be prepared and shaped before they can be assembled into the structure.
The altar must be physically complete before any religious consecration or dedication ceremony can take place.
The altar structure must be in place before the surrounding pavement can be laid, as pavement typically abuts the base.
The bell tower or campanile requires a solid foundation and base structure to support its weight and height. Without a proper foundation, the tower cannot be safely erected.

In many construction sequences, the bell tower is attached to or integrated with the main building structure. The main building must be sufficiently advanced (or completed) to provide lateral support and integration points for the tower.
The bells and their mounting hardware can only be installed after the tower structure is complete and stable enough to bear the weight and dynamic loads of the bells.

successor: Exterior Cladding and Weatherproofing of Tower
rationale: Exterior finishing (cladding, roofing, weatherproofing) must occur after the structural frame of the tower is erected to protect the interior and ensure durability.
Interior staircases, ladders, or elevator access within the tower can only be installed after the structural framework is complete to provide safe access to upper levels.
The dome requires a stable base; foundation must be built first to support the structural load of the dome.
The dome must be installed onto a completed structural framework that provides support and anchorage points.
The dome forms part of the roof structure; waterproofing and sealing can only be applied after the dome is fully installed to ensure a continuous weatherproof envelope.
Interior ceiling finishes, cladding, or acoustic treatments below the dome must be installed after the dome structure is complete to provide a substrate and access.
Running electrical conduits and wiring through the dome area is typically done after dome completion, though it could be coordinated concurrently in some designs.
The window opening must be framed and roughed into the wall structure before the stained glass window can be installed, as there must be a prepared opening to receive the window assembly.
The load-bearing walls must be constructed to provide the structural support necessary for the window frame and to define the opening dimensions before the stained glass window can be placed.
The stained glass panels must be fully fabricated, assembled, and cured (if lead came or copper foil method) before they can be installed into the prepared opening.
Interior finishes around the window opening should be completed after the window is installed to ensure a proper seal and to finish neatly against the window frame.
After the stained glass window is set in place, weatherproof sealants and glazing compounds must be applied to protect the window from moisture and air infiltration.
The pulpit must be supported by a stable foundation; without it the structure cannot be safely erected.
The pulpit sits on the floor slab; the slab must be cured and load-bearing before installing the pulpit.
Electrical wiring, outlets, or lighting integrated into or near the pulpit cannot be completed until the pulpit is in its final position.
Final surface treatments, staining, varnishing, or decorative elements are applied after the pulpit is installed in place.
Microphone placement and audio tuning often occur after the pulpit is positioned, but could theoretically be done before if the pulpit location is known.

predecessor: Slab on Grade / Floor Slab Construction
rationale: The pews or seating system must be installed on a finished, stable floor surface. The slab on grade provides the structural base and level surface required for seating layout and anchorage.

Any electrical conduits, floor boxes, or junction boxes serving seating areas must be roughed in and stubbed up before seating is placed, as access to the floor beneath pews becomes inaccessible after installation.

Perimeter wall finishes (including base trim, wainscoting, and wall receptacles) must be completed before seating is installed to avoid damage to new walls and to allow unobstructed access for wall finishing.

The final floor finish (e.g., carpet installation, tile grouting, or concrete sealing) should be completed after seating is installed in sections, or seating must be temporarily removed; however typically in fixed pew installations, floor finishes under and around seating are completed before pew placement, but any touch-up finish work or aisle carpet must follow pew installation to ensure a clean fit around pew bases.

Final adjustment of speaker placement, projector throw distances, and sightline testing for screen visibility must be performed after seating is installed and fixed in position, though this is a soft preference in that rough cabling can precede seating; the precise tuning depends on actual seated eye heights.
The font must be placed on a stable, level floor surface; the foundation and slab must be completed first to support the weight and ensure proper installation.
If the baptismal pool requires water supply and drainage, rough-in plumbing pipes must be installed in the slab or wall before the font is placed and finished.
Floor finishes around the font area must be installed after the pool is placed so that the finishes can be properly cut, fitted, and sealed against the pool structure to ensure waterproofing.

Soft preference: It is easier to paint or plaster walls before the font is installed to avoid having to work around the pool, but the font can be installed first if needed to protect finished walls from damage.
After the font/baptismal pool is fully installed, it must be tested for leaks and waterproofing integrity before any surrounding finishes are completed or the pool is put into use.
Electrical wiring must be roughed in behind the confessional booth walls before the booth structure is finalized and enclosed.
The confessional booth is typically a built-in or prefabricated unit that requires the surrounding wall framing to be complete for proper fit and anchoring.
After the confessional booth is installed, finish carpenters can trim around it, seal gaps, and integrate it seamlessly with surrounding finishes.
Painting and finishing of walls adjacent to or part of the confessional booth must occur after the booth is installed to avoid damaging finished surfaces during installation.
Confessional booth doors, hinges, latches, and privacy hardware must be installed after the booth frame is in place to ensure proper alignment and fit.
The physical location must be chosen and legally obtained before any construction can begin.
The land must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and leveled before foundation work for the sacred site can start.
Stone, timber, and other building materials must be sourced and transported to the site before construction can proceed.
A stable foundation is physically required before any superstructure (walls, columns) of the sacred site can be erected.
The sacred site must be physically complete before religious ceremonies can consecrate and dedicate the space for worship.

successor: Interior Decoration and Installation of Artifacts
rationale: While typically done after construction, some decorative elements like frescoes can be done during construction; however, structural completion generally precedes detailed interior work.
Landscaping can sometimes overlap with final construction phases, but the primary structure is usually completed first to coordinate with surrounding layout.

A thorough understanding of the site's historical significance, existing conditions, and any environmental hazards is required before any conservation or restoration work can begin, ensuring that the intervention is appropriate and does not cause inadvertent damage.

The building or structure must be structurally sound and safe for workers to access before conservation and restoration activities can commence; otherwise, there is a risk of collapse or further deterioration during sensitive restoration work.
All conservation and restoration work must be completed before a final inspection can be conducted to verify that the work meets heritage standards and regulatory requirements.

While some interior finishes may be installed after restoration, typically any new interior fit-out work should follow heritage restoration so that original fabric is not damaged by subsequent construction activities.
The conserved or restored heritage asset must be fully completed before opening to the public, to ensure visitor safety and that the interpretive elements are properly integrated.

The building structure must be complete and stable before any liturgical furnishings, altars, screens, or decorative elements can be installed, as these fixtures depend on finished walls, floors, and ceilings for proper placement and attachment.

The building must be weathertight (roof, windows, doors installed) before beginning liturgical fit-out to protect sensitive materials like wood carvings, textiles, paintings, and plasterwork from water damage.

Electrical conduit, wiring, and plumbing rough-ins for lighting, sound systems, and any liturgical water features (fonts, lavabos) must be completed before walls are finished and liturgical fixtures are installed.

The church cannot be consecrated or dedicated until all liturgical furnishings (altar, ambo, cathedra, iconostasis, etc.) are permanently installed and in their proper positions as required by liturgical norms.

While not a strict physical constraint, it is standard practice to complete all liturgical fit-out work before final interior inspection and handover, as inspection verifies that all elements meet specifications and liturgical requirements.
The site must be acquired or access granted before any physical investigation can take place on the land.
Archaeological investigation must be completed before site clearance to ensure any historical artifacts or remains are documented and preserved, and to avoid destruction of archaeological evidence.
Archaeological investigation must be completed prior to any major ground disturbance or excavation to ensure compliance with heritage regulations and to recover any archaeological finds.

Results of the archaeological investigation may inform foundation design decisions (e.g., avoiding sensitive areas, adjusting foundation depths), so the investigation must be completed before finalizing foundation designs.
Heritage or historical permits and approvals must be obtained before commencing the archaeological investigation to ensure legal compliance and authorized access.
Acoustic commissioning requires the building envelope and interior partitions to be completed so that sound transmission paths are fully established and measurable.
HVAC systems must be installed and balanced to assess background noise levels and HVAC-related sound transmission during acoustic testing.
Acoustic commissioning must be completed and verified before the space can be deemed ready for occupancy, ensuring acoustic performance meets design specifications.
While not physically required, it is typical to complete acoustic testing early in closeout so that any remedial work can be addressed before final handover.

predecessor: MEP System Installation (Electrical, Plumbing, Fire Protection)
rationale: All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems must be installed to evaluate structure-borne and airborne noise from these systems during acoustic commissioning.
Stained glass panels require a structurally complete opening (frame, rough bucks, headers) to be installed into; without the supporting frame, the stained glass cannot be physically mounted.
The building envelope (sheathing, flashing, moisture barrier) must be in place before installing stained glass to prevent water damage to the delicate glass and lead came during installation.

Interior wall finishes around the stained glass window must be completed after the glass is installed so that the finishes can be properly terminated against the window frame, covering gaps and ensuring a clean aesthetic seal.
Exterior perimeter sealants, glazing compounds, and weatherproofing around the stained glass unit can only be applied after the glass is securely positioned in its opening.

Interior accent or backlighting for stained glass is best installed after the stained glass is in place to ensure correct positioning and light diffusion, though it could technically be pre-wired before; this is a soft preference for quality control.
Relics and artifacts must first be uncovered and extracted from the site before they can be conserved and treated.
Artifacts must be physically retrieved from the excavation area and transported to the conservation lab before conservation work can commence.
Artifacts must be documented in situ (photographed, mapped, and recorded in their original context) before they are moved or treated, to preserve archaeological data.
Conserved artifacts must be stabilized and treated before they can be safely placed into long-term storage or shelving.
Artifacts must undergo conservation treatment to be stabilized and preserved before they can be safely exhibited in a museum setting.
Site must be cleared of debris and existing structures before any landscaping or grounds maintenance can begin.
Underground utilities (water, electrical, drainage) must be installed before topsoil, planting, and hardscaping to avoid disturbing finished landscape work.
Building foundations and slabs must be completed before final grading and landscaping around the structure.
Rough grading to establish site drainage and elevations must be done before fine grading and landscape installation.
Building exterior (walls, roof, gutters) must be finished to prevent construction debris and material drops from damaging newly installed landscaping.
Landscaping and grounds maintenance are typically among the final finishing activities, completed before final project walkthrough and closeout.
While landscaping enhances the site, occupancy can sometimes begin before full landscaping is complete; however, it is preferred to have finished grounds for safety and aesthetics.
The water supply pipes must be in place and terminated at the fixture location before the faucet can be connected to the water supply.
The drain line must be installed to receive wastewater from the faucet; however, the faucet installation primarily requires supply lines.
The faucet is mounted on the sink deck or countertop, so the basin or countertop must be in place to provide the mounting surface.
After the faucet body is mounted, the flexible supply hoses can be connected and the system can be pressure-tested for leaks.
While it is common to install the faucet before other deck-mounted accessories to avoid interference, this is a soft preference as sequence can be reversed with care.
The stopcock/isolation valve must be installed onto the pipework, so the pipes must be in place first to provide the physical connection point.

successor: Pressure testing of water supply system
rationale: The stopcock/valve must be installed and closed to isolate sections for pressure testing; testing cannot be performed without the valve in place to control flow.
The stopcock serves as the main shut-off point; downstream fixtures (taps, toilets, appliances) must connect after the isolation valve so the supply can be isolated for maintenance.
For underground stopcocks, the trench must be excavated first to access the water main and provide space for valve installation.

successor: Commissioning and inspection of plumbing system
rationale: The stopcock must be installed to allow full commissioning, as inspectors need to verify the valve's correct operation and accessibility before signing off the plumbing system.

predecessor: Rough-in plumbing for water supply and drainage
rationale: Water supply and drain pipes must be roughed into the wall or floor before the fountain can be connected.
The fountain is typically mounted to a finished wall; wall surface must be complete to support the fixture and provide a finished appearance.

predecessor: Electrical rough-in (if fountain has chiller or light)
rationale: If the fountain includes a refrigerated water chiller or lighting, electrical conduit and wiring must be installed prior to connecting the unit.

successor: Final plumbing trim-out and fixture testing
rationale: After the fountain is mounted and connected, plumbers can install trim pieces (e.g., covers, handles) and test water flow and drainage to verify proper operation.

successor: Floor finishing (e.g., tile, VCT, polishing) near fountain area
rationale: While not physically required, finishing floors after fountain installation risks damaging the fountain with dust, moisture, or heavy equipment; typically preferred to install fountain after rough-in but before final floor finish to avoid rework.
Water supply lines must be roughed in and stubbed out to the exterior wall location before a hose bib can be connected to them.
The exterior wall sheathing provides the structural surface and mounting point for the hose bib, which needs to be securely fastened to the wall structure.
The hose bib must be installed and flashed before exterior cladding or siding is applied, so the cladding can be cut and fitted around the bib and a proper weatherproof seal can be achieved.
The hose bib connection must be completed to be included in the plumbing system pressure test, ensuring no leaks exist at the outdoor tap connection before walls are closed.

The interior connection of the hose bib to the water supply should be accessible and completed before interior walls are finished, to allow for any necessary adjustments or leak repairs without damaging finished surfaces.
Floor slab must be poured and rough-in plumbing (drain, water supply lines) must be stubbed out before the sink can be positioned and connected.
Sink is typically installed before adjacent wall finishes so that wall materials can be cut and finished neatly around the sink and backsplash.
The sink must be set in place before supply lines, traps, and faucet trim can be permanently connected.
If the sink includes an electrical component (e.g., a garbage disposal, hot water dispenser, or soap dispenser), electrical rough-in must be completed first to provide power at the sink location.
Floor finishes around the sink area are typically applied after the sink is installed so that the sink base can be sealed against the floor and any water-proofing details can be completed.
The water pressure regulator must be connected to the main water supply line, which must first be installed and pressurized to provide the water source for the regulator.
Rough-in plumbing (piping, fittings, and shut-off valves) must be in place before the pressure regulator can be installed as part of the plumbing system.
Pressure testing of the plumbing system can only be performed after the pressure regulator is installed to ensure the regulator is functioning and system pressure is within safe limits.

All downstream plumbing fixtures (faucets, toilets, water heaters) must be connected after the regulator to ensure they receive water at the correct reduced pressure, preventing damage from overpressure.
While not a strict physical necessity, final inspection and system commissioning is typically scheduled after regulator installation to verify proper pressure settings and overall system compliance.
Trenching and excavation must be completed to expose the water main and create access for the service connection installation.
The main water line must be installed and in place before a service connection can be tied into it.
Rough grading must be completed to establish proper drainage and elevations before underground utility connections are made.
Backfilling can only occur after the service entry pipe and connections are fully installed and inspected.
The water meter is installed downstream of the service entry connection and cannot be placed until the service line is connected to the main.
The tank requires a stable, load-bearing foundation or base slab to support its weight and prevent settlement or structural failure.
If the tank is elevated, the supporting steel frame or structural supports must be erected first to provide the mounting platform for the tank.
Inlet, outlet, overflow, and drain piping can only be connected after the tank is set in its final position to ensure proper alignment and fit.

successor: Pressure Testing / Leak Testing of Tank System
rationale: The tank must be installed and all connections made before hydrostatic or leak testing can be performed to verify integrity.

Thermal insulation or weatherproof cladding is typically applied after the tank is installed, though it could theoretically be done in sections before installation; this is a practical sequencing preference.

Water tanks must be installed and connected to the plumbing system before water quality testing can be performed, as the testing requires a complete and operational water storage and distribution system.
The complete plumbing system (pipes, fixtures, and fittings) must be installed to enable water flow and circulation needed for representative water quality sampling and testing.
Water treatment equipment (filters, softeners, disinfection units) must be installed so that the testing verifies overall water quality as delivered by the full treatment train.
Water quality testing and commissioning must be completed and water quality verified as safe before the building can be handed over for occupancy and use.
Regulatory approval of the plumbing system depends on successful water quality testing results, so testing must precede final inspection sign-off.
Construction cannot begin without finalized architectural and engineering plans, permits, and regulatory approvals.
The land must be cleared, leveled, and excavated for foundations before any structural construction work can commence.
While some materials can be ordered during construction, critical long-lead items (e.g., structural steel, concrete) should ideally be procured before construction starts to avoid delays.
After construction work is completed, inspections, testing, and quality checks must be performed to verify compliance with specifications and building codes.
Interior work such as drywall, painting, flooring, and installation of fixtures can only begin after the main structural construction (walls, roofing, utilities rough-in) is complete.
All rough-in inspections (electrical, plumbing, mechanical) must be completed and approved before commissioning can begin, as they verify that the underlying systems are correctly installed per code.
The building must be substantially complete with all major systems installed and ready for testing before the formal commissioning process can start.
Heating, ventilation, and air conditioning equipment must be fully installed before commissioning can verify their performance and calibration.
Complete electrical system installation is required before commissioning can test power distribution, lighting controls, and emergency systems.
Plumbing systems including water supply, drainage, and fixtures must be installed before commissioning can verify water quality, flow rates, and pressure.
Fire sprinkler systems, alarms, and detection devices must be installed and inspected before commissioning can test their functionality and integration.
The BAS controllers, sensors, and network infrastructure must be in place before commissioning can verify control sequences and system integration.
Commissioning must verify all building systems perform as designed before the building can receive final occupancy approval and be used for its intended purpose.

Commissioning provides the baseline documentation and system insights that inform operator training, but training could theoretically begin concurrently; however, best practice is to complete commissioning first.
Commissioning must be completed to formally close out the construction phase and trigger the start of the warranty period.
While punch list items can be addressed concurrently, commissioning often identifies deficiencies that feed the punch list, making it preferable to complete commissioning first.
The commissioning report and verified systems performance documentation are prerequisites for formal building handover from contractor to owner.

A structural assessment must be completed before refurbishment to ensure the building's framework can safely support any planned modifications and to identify any structural weaknesses that need addressing.
Interior demolition and strip-out of existing finishes, partitions, and utilities must be completed before refurbishment work can begin to provide a clean working surface.
Hazardous material surveys and removal (e.g., asbestos) must be completed before refurbishment to comply with safety regulations and protect workers.

Final inspection, testing, and commissioning of building systems can only begin after refurbishment works are substantially complete to verify that all renovations meet specifications and are fully functional.

Interior finishing such as painting, flooring, and decorative elements can only proceed after the core refurbishment (structural work, MEP installations) is complete to avoid damage to finished surfaces.

Corrective maintenance is a reactive process; the specific fault or defect must first be identified (through inspection, monitoring, or user report) so that the maintenance team knows what needs to be repaired.

Once a fault is identified, a work order must be created and planned (including procurement of necessary spare parts, allocation of skilled labor, and scheduling of downtime) before corrective maintenance activities can commence.
The affected equipment or area must be isolated from energy sources and secured via lockout/tagout procedures to ensure the safety of maintenance personnel before hands-on corrective work begins.
After the corrective repair is completed, the equipment must be tested to verify that the fault has been resolved and that the asset is functioning correctly before being returned to service.

The corrective maintenance intervention must be fully finished (including cleanup, removal of lockout/tagout devices, and close-out of the work order) before the equipment or system can be safely returned to normal operational status.
Demolition must be completed before renovation can begin to clear out existing structures and debris, providing a clean slate for renovation work.
A structural assessment must be performed before renovation to evaluate the integrity of existing elements and determine what can be renovated safely.
Renovation permits must be obtained before work begins to comply with legal and regulatory requirements.
Interior finishing such as painting, flooring, and trim installation can only begin after the main renovation work (structural changes, drywall, rough-ins) is complete.
The final building inspection must occur after renovation is complete to verify that all work meets code requirements before the space is occupied.
The existing building must be evaluated for structural integrity and stabilized before any reuse work can begin to ensure safety and establish load-bearing capacity for new uses.
Hazardous materials such as asbestos, lead paint, or mold must be removed or abated before construction activities can safely commence in the existing structure.
Documentation of existing conditions and approvals from historic preservation authorities must be completed before alterations to a historically significant building can begin.

Structural modifications and spatial reconfiguration (the core adaptive reuse work) must be completed before new mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems can be routed through the renovated spaces.
The core structural and envelope work of adaptive reuse must be finished before interior finishes, partitions, and tenant fit-out can be installed to avoid damage and ensure proper sequencing.
A building or facility must be fully constructed and operational before it can be decommissioned at the end of its lifecycle.
The facility must have gone through its operational phase and reached the end of its useful life before decommissioning activities can begin.
Decommissioning involves dismantling and removing structures, after which the site must be remediated and cleaned up to meet environmental and safety standards.
Decommissioning generates waste materials (hazardous and non-hazardous) that must be properly disposed of or recycled after removal from the site.
After decommissioning is complete and the site has been cleared of all structures and hazards, it can be handed over or closed out for future use or redevelopment.

A detailed deconstruction plan, including safety protocols, waste management strategies, and structural analysis, must be completed before any physical dismantling begins to ensure worker safety and project efficiency.

Hazardous materials such as asbestos, lead paint, or mold must be identified and removed prior to deconstruction to prevent exposure to workers and environmental contamination during the dismantling process.
All utilities (gas, electricity, water, sewer) must be safely disconnected and capped before deconstruction begins to eliminate risks of electrocution, gas leaks, explosions, or flooding.
As materials are removed during deconstruction, they must be immediately sorted into salvageable, recyclable, and waste streams to maximize reuse and minimize landfill disposal.
The site must be completely deconstructed (structures removed down to the foundation or ground level) before final site clearance and grading can occur to prepare the land for its next use.
Site preparation including securing permits, utility disconnection, and site surveys must be completed before demolition can begin to ensure safety and legal compliance.
Hazardous material surveys and abatement must be completed prior to demolition to protect workers and the environment from exposure to harmful substances.
All utilities (gas, water, electricity, sewer) must be disconnected and capped before demolition to prevent accidents such as explosions, electrocution, or flooding.
After demolition is complete, debris removal and site grading can begin to prepare the land for new construction.
Excavation for foundations or underground work can only proceed once the existing structures have been demolished and the site is clear.
A Waste Management Plan must be developed during the planning and design phase, before construction begins, to establish waste reduction, reuse, and disposal strategies.

The Waste Management Plan must align with local, regional, and national regulations regarding waste handling, so relevant permits and regulatory approvals should be obtained or at least understood before finalizing the plan.
Understanding the site conditions (e.g., existing contamination, soil type, access routes) is necessary to tailor waste management strategies for the specific site.
Demolition and site clearance generate significant waste streams; the Waste Management Plan must be in place to guide how demolition waste is sorted, reused, recycled, or disposed of properly.

While not a strict physical necessity, having the Waste Management Plan finalized early helps guide procurement decisions (e.g., specifying materials with recyclable content, minimizing packaging waste), which is a best practice for sustainability.
The site must be cleared and prepared for access before any building condition assessment can be performed to ensure safety and accessibility for inspectors.
The condition assessment identifies existing defects and deterioration, which are critical inputs needed before structural analysis can determine load capacities and repair needs.
Assessment findings directly inform the scope and type of repairs required; repair designs cannot be developed without knowing the current condition.
Accurate cost estimation relies on the detailed list of defects and required interventions identified during the condition assessment.
While assessments typically precede permit applications to document existing conditions, some jurisdictions may allow concurrent or pre-application activities; thus this is a soft preference.

A feasibility study defines the project scope, objectives, and constraints, forming the basis for any cost analysis. Without initial requirements and concept definition, a whole-life cost analysis lacks the contextual inputs needed to be meaningful.

Whole-life cost analysis requires at least a preliminary design or concept design to evaluate material choices, system options, and long-term operational costs. Without a defined design concept, cost parameters such as construction methods, maintenance needs, and energy consumption cannot be estimated.

Initial capital cost estimates are an essential input to whole-life cost analysis, which combines upfront construction costs with operation, maintenance, and disposal costs. The capital cost data must be available before the whole-life assessment can be compiled.

Whole-life cost analysis informs design decisions and material selection. The analysis results provide cost-benefit comparisons (e.g., higher upfront cost for lower operational cost) that guide the detailed design phase. Therefore, detailed design proceeds after the cost analysis is complete to incorporate its findings.

While not a hard physical dependency, value engineering and formal cost-benefit approval typically follow whole-life cost analysis to validate that the design achieves optimal lifecycle value before moving to procurement or construction. This is a logical/preferential sequence to ensure informed decision-making.
The old or faulty component must be physically removed from its location before a replacement cycle can begin.
After the replacement cycle is complete, verification is needed to ensure the new component is correctly installed and functioning.
System-level testing can only begin after the component replacement cycle is finished to validate overall system performance.
The replacement component must be procured and available on-site before the replacement cycle can commence.
Commissioning typically follows replacement to bring the system into service, though it may overlap in some cases.

Post-Occupancy Evaluation (POE) requires a completed, occupied building to assess its performance in use. The building must be fully constructed and occupied before any evaluation of its performance, occupant satisfaction, or operational efficiency can take place.

Building commissioning ensures all systems (HVAC, lighting, electrical, plumbing) are installed and functioning correctly. POE requires these systems to be operational and in use so that their real-world performance can be measured and evaluated.

POE by definition analyzes a building after occupants have moved in and are using the space. The building must be occupied for a sufficient period (typically 6-12 months) to allow for meaningful data collection on occupant comfort, satisfaction, space usage, and operational performance.

While not a strict physical dependency, findings from POE typically inform recommendations for building improvements, retrofits, or operational changes. The evaluation should precede planning for modifications so that decisions are data-driven and address actual performance gaps.

POE results should be documented and shared with the design and construction team before future projects begin, so that insights from building performance are incorporated into the design of subsequent buildings. This is a soft dependency as it relates to organizational learning rather than physical construction.
The end-of-life strategy must be informed by the design for deconstruction principles, which dictate how the building can be disassembled and materials recovered.
The choice of materials directly impacts recyclability, reusability, and disposal methods, so material selection must precede the end-of-life strategy definition.
A life cycle assessment provides environmental impact data that informs optimal end-of-life decisions, though it is a soft preference as an LCA is not always strictly required.
The waste management plan must align with the end-of-life strategy to ensure proper segregation, handling, and disposal or recycling of materials at project conclusion.
The specific deconstruction or selective demolition procedures must be based on the end-of-life strategy to determine which materials are salvaged, recycled, or sent to landfill.

predecessor: Plumbing Rough-In for Toilet Drains and Water Supply
rationale: Water supply lines and drain waste pipes must be roughed in within the wall cavities and floor before toilet stall framing and fixtures can be installed, as the plumbing must be embedded behind the walls and below the floor slab.

predecessor: Floor Slab / Subfloor Preparation and Waterproofing
rationale: The floor must be structurally complete, leveled, and waterproofed (especially in wet areas) before toilet cubicles are anchored to the floor to ensure proper drainage and avoid water damage.

predecessor: Wall Framing and Backer Board Installation
rationale: Support walls and partition anchors must be framed and sheathed before cubicle panels can be securely attached to walls and to each other.

Toilet bowls cannot be set until the cubicle partition walls and support rails are in place, because the toilet is positioned relative to the cubicle dimensions and the partition provides anchoring for the toilet if wall-mounted, or defines the clearance envelope.

While not physically required, it is a soft preference to install cubicles before overhead access panels so that the cubicle layout can be finalized and access panel positioning aligned with the stall geometry.

predecessor: Rough-in plumbing for water supply and drainage
rationale: The water supply lines and drainage/waste pipes must be roughed-in behind the wall and through the floor before the toilet can be physically connected to them.
The toilet must be set on a finished subfloor or tile underlayment that provides structural support and a stable base; installing the toilet before the subfloor is complete is not possible.

successor: Toilet Flange and Wax Ring Sealing
rationale: The wax ring is compressed between the toilet base and the closet flange during installation, creating the watertight seal; the toilet must be set in place to compress the wax ring.

successor: Final Tiling or Flooring Around Toilet Base
rationale: It is preferable to set the toilet after the finished floor is laid to avoid damaging the toilet or having to work around it, but if necessary flooring can be cut and fitted afterward.

successor: Connection of Supply Line and Shut-off Valve
rationale: The flexible supply line from the shut-off valve must be connected to the toilet fill valve once the toilet is in its final position.

predecessor: Plumbing Rough-In (Hot & Cold Water Supply Lines)
rationale: Water supply lines must be run inside the wall before the sink can be connected and mounted.
The waste pipe and P-trap connection must be roughed into the wall or floor before the sink can be installed and drained properly.
The wall must be framed, sheathed, and finished before the sink can be mounted or attached to the wall structure.
For drop-in or undermount sinks, the sink must be set into the countertop before the countertop is fully installed or sealed.
After the sink is physically installed, the faucet, trap, and supply line connections can be finalized and trimmed out.
Backsplash tiles often need to be cut and fitted around the sink basin after it is set in place.

successor: Wall Finishing / Painting (touch-up in sink area)
rationale: While painting is typically done before fixture installation, final touch-ups around the sink edge are common after the sink is mounted.
Baby changing stations are typically wall-mounted units that require a framed wall to attach to securely.
If the baby changing station includes a built-in diaper disposal or adjacent handwashing sink, rough-in plumbing must be completed before wall finishes and fixture installation.
Any electrical wiring for lighting or outlets near the baby changing station must be roughed in before wall closure and station mounting.
Proper structural backing (plywood or blocking) must be installed within the wall to support the weight of the changing station and a child.

While typically the station is installed after painting to avoid damage, if the station has a backsplash it may be installed before final wall finishing; this is generally a soft preference to avoid getting paint on the unit.

Plumbing rough-in must be completed before installing restroom accessories such as toilet paper dispensers, grab bars, and soap dispensers, as the plumbing stub-outs and waste lines need to be in place within the walls.
Wall surfaces must be finished (tiled or painted drywall) before mounting accessories like mirrors, shelves, and dispensers to ensure a clean installation and proper sealing.
Flooring must be installed before placing floor-mounted accessories such as toilet partitions or waste bins to avoid damaging new flooring or having to work around unfinished surfaces.
Accessories like grab bars and toilet paper holders must be installed before final plumbing fixtures to avoid interference and allow unobstructed access for fixture placement.
It is standard practice to complete all accessory installation before the final walkthrough to ensure the restroom is fully functional and compliant with accessibility codes before inspection.
Rough-in plumbing (drainage and vent pipes) must be installed before sanitary fixtures (toilets, sinks, etc.) can be connected to the waste system.
Water supply lines must be run to fixture locations before fixtures can be physically connected to the water supply.

Floor finishes, especially waterproof membranes and tile, must be completed before installing fixtures like toilets and floor drains to ensure proper waterproofing and finished appearance under fixtures.

successor: Trim & Accessory Installation (faucets, toilet seats, etc.)
rationale: Sanitary fixtures must be securely installed before trim items like faucet handles, toilet seats, and supply stops can be attached.
Fixtures must be installed before the drainage system can be fully tested for leaks and proper flow using the fixtures as test inputs.
The wall framing must be complete to define the rough opening for the door frame.

successor: Hang Restroom Door with Privacy Hardware
rationale: The door frame must be installed and secured before the door slab can be hung.

successor: Install Restroom Door with Privacy Hardware
rationale: Wall finishes around the door opening must be completed so the door casing and hardware align properly with finished surfaces.

successor: Install Restroom Door with Privacy Hardware
rationale: While not physically blocking, it is standard sequencing to complete all rough MEP work before installing doors to avoid damage and access issues.

predecessor: Install Restroom Door with Privacy Hardware
rationale: The door must be hung before the privacy lock and latch hardware can be installed and adjusted for proper operation.

predecessor: Install Restroom Door with Privacy Hardware
successor: Final painting and touch-up of door and frame
rationale: The door must be hung to allow final painting, touch-up, and adjustment of all surfaces.

predecessor: Install Restroom Door with Privacy Hardware
successor: Install restroom accessories (towel bar, mirror, etc.)
rationale: Doors are typically installed before finishing accessories to avoid damaging them during door installation, though this is a soft preference based on workflow.
Rough-in plumbing must be installed over the foundation slab or within the slab before walls are closed up, requiring the foundation to be in place first.
Plumbing pipes run through wall cavities and floor/ceiling assemblies, so the framing must be complete to provide access for running pipes and installing drains and vents.
Plumbing and electrical rough-ins are often done in parallel, but it is common practice to complete plumbing first to avoid conflicts and allow inspection before electrical work begins.
Insulation is installed after rough-in plumbing is complete because insulation would block access to plumbing pipes and must be placed around (not behind) them.
Drywall closes up the wall cavities; rough-in plumbing must be fully installed and inspected before walls are closed to allow access for plumbing work and inspection.

Tile installation requires a smooth, level, and cured base surface to ensure proper adhesion, flatness, and long-term durability. Any unevenness or uncured screed would compromise the tiling quality and lead to cracking or detachment.

All concealed plumbing pipes, drains, and fittings must be installed and pressure-tested before tiling and waterproofing, as these services are embedded within the floor or wall structure and cannot be accessed once tiles are laid.

predecessor: Electrical Conduit and Wiring Rough-In (for floor/wall zones)
rationale: Any electrical conduits, back boxes, or wiring that pass through floor or wall zones to be tiled must be installed beforehand, as they would be covered by waterproofing and tile finishes and become inaccessible.

Wall finishes (plaster, paint, or wall cladding) adjacent to tiled areas are typically completed after tiling to avoid damaging finished painted surfaces during tile cutting, adhesive application, and grouting. Tiling also defines the final alignment for wall finish edges.

Sanitary fixtures are mounted onto the finished tiled and waterproofed surfaces. Tiles provide the final finished surface and waterproof membrane must be continuous behind fixtures; installing fixtures before tiling would disrupt the waterproofing layer and require removal/reinstallation.
The structural frame must be complete to provide support and mounting points for ventilation ducts and equipment.
Roof must be installed to protect ventilation equipment and ductwork from weather damage during installation.
Exterior walls must be enclosed to create a weather-tight environment before installing ventilation systems.
Ventilation units must be installed first so that electrical connections can be run directly to the equipment locations.
Ductwork must be installed before insulation can be applied to the ducts.
Fire dampers are installed within ductwork and require the ducts to be in place first.
The building must be structurally complete (shell constructed) before accessibility inspections can be performed, as accessibility features are part of the finished interior and envelope.

predecessor: Installation of Interior Walls and Doors
rationale: Interior walls and doors define pathways, door widths, and room configurations that must meet accessibility standards (e.g., ADA clearances) before inspection.
Flooring surfaces must be installed to verify slope, levelness, and slip-resistance requirements for accessible routes.

predecessor: Installation of Restroom Fixtures and Grab Bars
rationale: Restroom accessibility (toilet heights, grab bar placement, sink clearances) must be fully installed to be evaluated during inspection.
The certificate of occupancy is contingent upon passing all required inspections, including accessibility compliance.
While inspections typically precede closeout, some minor punch-list items could be completed simultaneously; however, major accessibility issues must be resolved before final closeout.
The offset core shaft requires a stable foundation to support its structural load before construction can begin.
The excavation for the basement must be completed to provide the space and access for constructing the offset core shaft structure.
Floor slabs around the core area depend on the core shaft being in place for load transfer and structural continuity.
Elevator shafts and stair cores are housed within the offset core shaft, so the shaft structure must be complete before circulation elements can be installed.

The cantilevered floor plates require a central core or vertical support structure to be in place first, as they cantilever out from the core and need that structural anchor for stability and load transfer.
Foundations must be completed to provide a stable base for the entire structure, including the cantilevered floor system, ensuring load paths are properly established.
The lower-level structural frame must be erected up to the point where the cantilevered floor plates begin, as they typically extend from a completed section of the building frame.

Once the cantilevered structural steel or precast concrete plates are in place, the decking (e.g., metal deck or formwork) and concrete topping slab can be installed to create the finished floor surface.

The cantilevered plates define the outer building envelope geometry; exterior cladding and curtain wall systems can only be installed after the cantilevered structure is in place to attach to and follow the building profile.
Outrigger frames connect the core to perimeter columns; the core must be constructed first to provide the central structural support and connection points for the outrigger.
Outrigger frames span between the core and perimeter columns; perimeter columns must be in place to receive the outrigger connections and transfer lateral loads.
Floor slabs at outrigger levels often incorporate the outrigger within them; the structural steel outrigger frame must be erected before concrete deck placement can proceed.

Belt trusses are frequently installed at the same or adjacent levels as outriggers to distribute loads around the perimeter; outrigger placement typically precedes or is concurrent with belt truss installation.

successor: Facade/Curtain Wall Installation at Outrigger Zones
rationale: While not physically impossible, installing the curtain wall before outrigger erection would require rework or removal to access the outrigger connections; best practice is to complete the outrigger frame before enclosing the facade at those levels.
The fire escape stairwell must be supported by the building's foundation and structural slabs; the stairwell cannot be constructed without a stable base.
The stairwell enclosure is typically integrated with the building's structural core and shear walls, which must be erected first to provide support and lateral stability.
Pressurization fans and ductwork are installed after the stairwell volume is enclosed to ensure correct air balancing and smoke control performance.
Fire-rated doors are hung and adjusted after the stairwell walls and frames are in place to ensure proper fit and fire-tight seals.

successor: Interior finishing and painting of stairwell
rationale: While finishing can be done after the structure is erected, it is a soft preference to sequence it after major construction debris is cleared to avoid damaging finishes.
The ground must be cleared of obstructions, vegetation, and topsoil, and excavated to the required level before piling can commence, as piles need a clear and stable working platform.
Soil bearing capacity, ground conditions, and pile design parameters must be determined through site investigation to select the appropriate pile type, length, and installation method.
Accurate positioning of each pile location must be marked out on site based on engineering drawings before piling equipment can begin installation.
Pile caps transfer loads from the superstructure to the pile group and can only be cast after the piles are installed, cut to level, and tested for integrity.
Ground beams spanning between pile caps rely on the completed pile group for support and cannot be constructed until the piles are in place and load-bearing.
Reinforcement steel must be in place before formwork is erected around it, as formwork encases the rebar cage.
Formwork must be fully assembled and braced before concrete can be poured into it to shape the core walls.
Formwork must be constructed and concrete poured and set before formwork can be stripped away.
Higher-level rebar installation typically follows after lower-level formwork is complete, though some overlap may be possible with careful sequencing.
The building site and foundation must be prepared and leveled before any core formwork can be assembled on it.
Concrete must reach sufficient design strength through curing before load testing can be performed, otherwise the structure would fail under test loads.
All steel members must be erected and bolted/welded in place to form a complete load path before applying test loads.
Temporary supports must be removed so that the structure bears loads independently as designed, making the load test valid.
If load test results indicate insufficient capacity, remedial strengthening work may be required, but this is a conditional dependency not a strict requirement for all projects.
Load testing validates structural performance and must be completed and documented before the structure can be formally inspected, accepted, and commissioned for occupancy.
A stable, level crane pad must be prepared to support the outrigger loads and provide a solid foundation before outriggers can be positioned and deployed.
The ground must be graded and compacted to proper bearing capacity to prevent outrigger settlement or tipping during crane operations.
The crane must be moved into its approximate working location before the outriggers can be extended and set.
Once outriggers are installed (deployed and placed on cribbing/pads), the crane can be leveled and stabilized using the outrigger jacks.
The crane must be fully supported on its outriggers and stable before the boom can be safely assembled and erected.
The structural frame (walls, floors, ceilings) must be erected to provide the physical substrate for running MEP conduits, ducts, and piping.
