The building must be weathertight to protect MEP materials from water damage during installation.
Insulation is installed after MEP rough-in to wrap around pipes, ducts, and conduits; insulating before would block access to MEP runs.
Drywall encloses the MEP rough-in work; all electrical boxes, piping, and ductwork must be in place before walls are closed up.
Interior finishes are applied after MEP rough-in and after wall/ceiling enclosure to avoid damage and to ensure all rough MEP work is complete.
Structural assessment must be completed first to determine the existing condition, load paths, and deficiencies of the core before any retrofit design and construction can proceed.

Any existing non-structural elements, deteriorated concrete, or inadequate reinforcement within the core must be removed before new retrofit work (e.g., jacketing, new rebar, shotcrete) can be installed.
Temporary shoring and bracing must be installed to safely support the building loads during core retrofit, preventing collapse or instability while structural elements are modified.
After the retrofit is installed (e.g., new concrete, grout, or epoxy), sufficient curing time and strength verification are required before the core can be loaded or subsequent work can commence.
Shoring and temporary bracing can only be removed after the retrofitted core has achieved full design strength and can independently carry the building loads.
Perimeter columns require a foundation system (such as footings or a mat foundation) to transfer structural loads to the ground; the foundation must be in place before any column erection can begin.
The subgrade and ground slab provide a stable working platform for setting out and erecting perimeter columns and for crane access around the perimeter.
Accurate setting out of column centre lines and grid lines must be completed before columns can be positioned and erected.
Perimeter spandrel beams connect perimeter columns laterally; they cannot be installed until the columns are in place and secured.
Exterior cladding and curtain wall systems attach to or between perimeter columns; the column grid must be erected first to provide the structural support and attachment points.
A clean, flat, and properly prepared substrate (e.g., silicon wafer or glass slide) is physically required before any thin-film layers or density boundaries can be deposited or formed.
The underlying base layer or first material film must be deposited to provide the foundation upon which the density gradient will be introduced or formed.
Any subsequent material layers (e.g., capping layers, additional films) can only be deposited after the density gradient boundary region has been established to maintain proper interfacial integrity.

Thermal processing may be performed after the density gradient boundary is formed to stabilize the gradient or relieve interfacial stresses, but this is a process preference rather than a physical impossibility.
Inspection and measurement (e.g., XRR, TEM) of the density gradient region typically occurs after its formation to verify gradient profile and thickness.
The podium block requires a stable foundation system (footings, mat slab, or piles) and subgrade drainage to support the heavy structural loads of the mixed-use podium.
All underground utilities (water, sewer, storm drainage, electrical conduits, gas lines) must be installed and backfilled before the podium slab is poured to avoid digging up the slab later.
The structural podium deck (reinforced concrete slab) must be cast and cured to design strength before any vertical construction or wall framing can begin on top of it.
The podium block serves as the structural base and transfer slab for the upper residential tower; tower columns, walls, and floors cannot be erected until the podium is complete and cured.

While fit-out can begin in phases after podium completion, it is a soft preference because some interior work could theoretically start earlier on lower floors if the slab is partially complete, but full fit-out requires the entire podium block to be enclosed and weathertight.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated to the required depth before any foundation work for the mid-rise mixed-use block can begin.
The concrete foundation and ground slab must be poured and cured to provide a stable base before the mid-rise structure can be erected.
Underground water, sewer, electrical, and data conduits must be laid before the slab is poured and vertical construction begins.
The structural shell and roofing of the mid-rise block must be complete and weathertight before interior drywalling, flooring, and finish work can proceed.
The building's main structure must be completed before installing the exterior cladding, curtain wall systems, and architectural facade elements.

The ground must be excavated and load-bearing foundations (piles/mat/footings) installed before any superstructure elements of the tower can be erected, as the tower requires a stable base to transfer its immense vertical and lateral loads into the soil.

A fixed tower crane is typically erected directly on the tower's core foundation or embedded within the structure as it rises; however, conceptually the tower's base/foundation must be complete before the crane can be installed on that foundation, and crane installation is a prerequisite for vertical construction. Alternatively, if a mobile crane is used initially, the permanent tower structure must still be sufficiently progressed to support climbing operations.

predecessor: High-Rise Residential Tower Structural Frame Completion
rationale: The structural concrete or steel frame of the tower must be erected to the required floor levels before the curtain wall or cladding panels can be attached, since the cladding system is supported by and enclosed around the frame.

The building envelope (roof, exterior walls, windows) must be weathertight before interior finishes such as drywall, flooring, painting, and mechanical/electrical/plumbing installations can commence, to prevent water damage and allow climate-controlled conditions.

predecessor: High-Rise Residential Tower Core & Shear Walls
rationale: The concrete core of the tower, which contains elevator shafts and stairwells, must be cast and cured to the full height before elevator rails, cars, and machinery can be installed within the shaft, as the shaft structure provides the support and enclosure for the elevator system.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated for foundations before any building structure can be erected.
Concrete foundations and ground slabs must be poured and cured to provide a stable base for the load-bearing walls and structure of the courtyard housing.
Below-grade piping for stormwater, sewer, water supply, and electrical conduits must be laid before slab pouring or wall construction to avoid later excavation under the building.
The building structure (walls, columns, slabs) must be completed to provide a substrate for roof installation and waterproof membrane application.
The structural shell and weatherproof enclosure must be complete before interior finishes can be applied without risk of weather damage.
Accurate topographic and boundary surveys must be completed before any masterplan layout can be established, as the layout depends on site dimensions, contours, and existing features.
Soil bearing capacity and subsurface conditions must be known to determine allowable building densities and foundation strategies, which inform the masterplan layout.
Environmental constraints such as protected areas, wetlands, or buffer zones must be identified before the density ring layout can be planned, to ensure regulatory compliance.
Individual block and parcel boundaries are derived directly from the masterplan density ring layout; detailed subdivision cannot proceed without the overarching layout.
Major utility and road corridors must follow the density ring layout to ensure service coverage matches the planned density zones.
Formal permit applications and zoning approvals require a finalized masterplan layout as the basis for review and approval.
Urban density modelling requires accurate demographic data (population counts, household sizes) as foundational input parameters to estimate density distributions.
Existing land use classifications (residential, commercial, industrial) must be mapped first to define zones and constraints for density modelling.
Digital terrain models, parcel boundaries, and infrastructure networks are essential spatial inputs that must be compiled before density modelling can proceed.
Density models determine population and employment distribution patterns that serve as key inputs for predicting transport demand and trip generation.

successor: Zoning Regulation Review / Land Use Planning
rationale: While density modelling can proceed independently, zoning and land use planning often incorporate density model outputs to adjust or validate proposed zoning changes.
A site survey is required to collect data on existing conditions, which forms the basis for assessing infrastructure capacity needs.
Existing utility layouts must be mapped to understand current infrastructure capacity and constraints before an assessment can be performed.
Geotechnical data on soil and subsurface conditions is essential to determine load-bearing capacity and infrastructure support requirements.
Capacity assessment results inform design parameters (e.g., pipe sizes, road widths, electrical loads); design cannot proceed without knowing existing capacity.
Identified capacity gaps determine which upgrades are needed; upgrade planning depends on assessment findings.
While not always a hard physical dependency, understanding infrastructure capacity helps scope environmental impacts; typically performed in parallel or after capacity is known.
The ground must be properly prepared, cleared, and excavated to create a stable foundation and workspace before densification construction can begin.
Structural foundations or piles must be installed first to support the densification loads and prevent settlement issues.
Soil conditions must be assessed and treated (e.g., grouting, compaction) to ensure the ground can withstand densification without failure.
After construction, structural integrity tests and inspections are needed to verify that densification meets design specifications.
Surface finishing typically follows densification, but in some sequences partial finishing may occur concurrently; thus it is a soft preference rather than a strict physical requirement.

A comprehensive site survey is required to identify hazardous materials (e.g., asbestos, lead), structural conditions, underground utilities, and environmental constraints before any demolition can safely begin.
All gas, electricity, water, and telecommunications services must be disconnected and capped to prevent accidents, electrocution, gas leaks, or flooding during demolition activities.
Regulatory approvals and permits from local authorities are legally required before any demolition work can commence, ensuring compliance with safety and environmental regulations.
Hazardous materials such as asbestos, lead paint, and chemical contaminants must be removed by licensed professionals before demolition to prevent airborne contamination and health risks.
The site must be cleared of all structures and debris before grading and earthmoving equipment can safely access and reshape the land for subsequent construction.

While some soil testing may be done before demolition, comprehensive geotechnical investigation is most effective after the site is cleared of structures, though it is a soft preference if pre-demolition test pits were sufficient.
Foundation excavation for new construction can only proceed after existing structures have been demolished and debris removed to provide a clean working area.

Temporary power, water, and sanitation for the construction phase are best installed after demolition is complete to avoid damage to temporary services, though portions could theoretically be set up earlier.

Site preparation (clearing, grading, and soil compaction) must be completed before any landscaping or green infrastructure installation can begin, as these activities establish the required ground conditions and topography.

All underground utilities (drainage, water, gas, electrical conduits) must be installed before landscaping to avoid digging up finished landscaping work and to ensure proper soil conditions for planting.
Building foundations and structural elements must be completed before final grading and landscaping around the structure to prevent damage to landscaping from heavy construction equipment.

Landscaping and green infrastructure are typically among the final finishing activities on a construction site, and must be completed before the project can be formally inspected and handed over to the client.

While paving and hardscape finishes can be done before or after landscaping, it is often a soft preference to complete them after landscaping to prevent soil compaction and damage to plantings from paving equipment.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated before any foundation or structural work for the parking structure can begin.
Concrete footings, slabs, and subgrade drainage must be installed first to provide a stable base for the parking structure.
Underground electrical, plumbing, and drainage lines serving the parking structure must be laid before the slab is poured or structure erected.
Structural framing and decks must be complete to mount conduit, junction boxes, and lighting fixtures within the parking structure.
The structural frame must be finished before applying top coatings, sealants, striping, or any final driving/parking surface finishes.
The barrier must have a physical mounting point or base installed prior to being attached.

predecessor: Run Conduit / Wiring to Barrier Location
rationale: Electrical power and control wiring must be in place before connecting the barrier unit.
Wiring connections can only be completed after the barrier is physically installed.
Operational testing cannot occur until the barrier is mechanically and electrically installed.
Software and system integration requires the physical barrier to be in place and operational.
The foundation must be laid and cured before the counter can be installed on top of it.
Electrical conduit and wiring must be roughed-in within walls/floors before the counter can be placed over those utilities.
Data cables for scanners, computers, and security equipment must be pulled to the location before the counter encloses the area.
The counter serves as the mounting surface and housing for fixed security equipment, so it must be in place first.

successor: Connect Electrical and Data to Counter Equipment
rationale: Final connections for power and data to the counter's built-in equipment can only be made after the counter is installed.
The structural steel framework (columns, beams, floor slabs) must be in place to support the floor area where the concierge desk will be located.
The floor slab must be poured and cured to provide a stable, level surface for installing the concierge desk.
Electrical, data/IT, and HVAC rough-in work in the vicinity is required before installing the desk to avoid rework and ensure services can be connected.
After the desk is physically installed, power outlets, data ports, and communication lines can be terminated and connected at the desk location.
The desk installation should be completed before final wall finishes and painting in the lobby to allow for touch-ups and a clean finish around the desk.
The structural shell and framing must be completed before seating and soft furnishing installation can begin, as these require a weathertight and structurally sound enclosure.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work must be finished before installing soft furnishings and seating to avoid damage to finished surfaces and allow access for service runs.

While final touch-ups often occur after all major installations, some finishing work may be done concurrently; however, it is preferable to complete seating and furnishing installation before final paint/trim to prevent damage to new furnishings.
Decorative elements and detail trim should be installed after seating and soft furnishing placement to ensure proper alignment and fit around the installed furnishings.

Flooring and subfloor work must be completed before installing seating and soft furnishings, as these items are placed on top of finished floors and would need to be moved or protected if flooring work were done afterwards.

The site must be cleared, graded, and excavated to create stable ground conditions before any landmark or feature element can be installed, as these elements typically require a level, compacted base or foundation.
A structural foundation or substructure (e.g., concrete footing, pile cap, or anchor block) must be completed to provide a secure load-bearing base for the feature/landmark element.

Any underground utilities (drainage, electrical, water lines) that might pass beneath or adjacent to the feature area must be installed and backfilled prior to placing the feature to avoid future excavation and disturbance.
Any integrated lighting, signage, or electrical components that are part of or adjacent to the feature can only be connected and commissioned after the feature element is fully installed and secured.
Electrical conduit must be installed in the ceiling/structural slab to provide the pathway for wiring before lighting fixtures can be mounted and connected.
The ceiling grid or support structure must be in place to provide the mounting framework for the lighting fixture array.
The structural slab or deck must be fully cured and load-bearing before any ceiling-mounted fixtures can be installed.
The lighting fixture array must be physically mounted and in place before final wiring connections from the junction box to the fixture terminals can be completed.
The lighting fixtures must be installed before the control system can be programmed, tested, and commissioned to ensure proper operation.
A stable, level foundation and prepared site are physically required before any kiosk can be placed or anchored.

predecessor: Underground Electrical Conduit and Data Cabling
rationale: Power and network connectivity must be run to the kiosk location before the kiosk is physically installed and connected.
The kiosk hardware must be physically in place and connected before it can be powered on and its software configured.
The digital display and touch interface must be installed and operational before content can be loaded and user-interaction testing can occur.
While not physically required, final landscaping around the kiosk is typically done after installation to avoid damage to finishes; this is a soft preference for sequencing.

The site must be cleared of all obstructions, debris, and vegetation before layout and setting-out can begin, as survey markers and reference points need a clean, unobstructed surface to be accurately established.

Accurate topographic data, boundary information, and soil conditions from the survey and geotechnical investigation are required to determine the correct positioning and alignment of the building layout.
While not physically mandatory, having temporary power, water, and site facilities in place supports the survey team's equipment and workflow, improving efficiency during setting-out.
The layout marks (stakes, strings, pins) define the exact footprints and reference lines for excavation; digging cannot begin until these control points are established.
Setting-out provides the precise reference lines, offsets, and levels that guide the placement of formwork panels and reinforcing steel within the excavated areas.
The ground must be cleared, graded, and compacted before any raised floor or podium can be built upon it, as the podium requires a stable, prepared subgrade.
The main building foundation (footings, foundations walls) must be completed to support the podium slab or raised floor structure.

All underground utilities and conduits that will run beneath the raised floor or podium must be installed and inspected before the slab or raised floor deck is placed, otherwise they would be inaccessible.
The raised floor or podium slab provides the base (working platform or load-bearing surface) upon which the vertical structural elements for upper levels are erected.
Waterproofing membranes are typically applied to the top of the podium slab before any overlying finishes or upper construction, to protect the structure from moisture ingress.

Feature ceiling installation typically requires the structural framing (including ceiling grid supports, trusses, or furring) to be completed first so that the ceiling system has a stable mounting surface.

All mechanical ducts, electrical conduits, wiring, and plumbing lines that will run above the ceiling must be roughed-in before the ceiling is installed, as access to these systems becomes restricted or impossible once the feature ceiling is in place.
HVAC ductwork, diffusers, and equipment located above the ceiling must be fully installed and tested before the ceiling is closed in, to avoid costly rework and ensure proper air distribution.
Recessed lighting fixtures, ceiling-mounted light fixtures, and other ceiling-integrated electrical components can only be installed or trimmed out after the ceiling structure is in place.

While painting can be staged differently, it is standard practice to complete feature ceiling installation before final painting and finishing of the ceiling surface to avoid damage to finished paint during installation work.
The subfloor (concrete slab or plywood underlayment) must be clean, level, dry, and structurally sound before tile can be adhered; otherwise tiles will crack or debond.
Any plumbing or electrical runs beneath the slab must be completed and inspected before the tile goes down, as accessing them afterward would require demolition of the finished floor.
A waterproof membrane or vapor barrier must be installed on the subfloor (especially in wet areas or on-grade slabs) before tiling to prevent moisture damage and mold growth.
Grout cannot be applied until the tile adhesive (thinset) has fully cured and tiles are firmly set in place; grouting too early will dislodge tiles.
Baseboards and trim are fitted after the finished flooring is installed so they can sit flush on top of the tile, covering the expansion gap at the perimeter.

Backboxes, conduits, and rough-in wiring for low-voltage systems (e.g., data, security, AV) must be installed within the wall, ceiling, and floor cavities before the finished fit-out of devices, equipment racks, and final connections can commence.

General MEP rough-in work, including primary electrical and mechanical services, must be completed to clear the ceiling and wall spaces and provide necessary power and environmental conditions before low-voltage and AV fit-out begins.

predecessor: Overhead Ceiling Grid & MEP Rough-In Sign-Off
rationale: All overhead rough-in (conduit, cable trays, ductwork) must be inspected and signed off before ceiling grids are closed, as low-voltage and AV fit-out involves running and terminating cables that must tie into these pathways.

After the low-voltage and AV systems are fitted (cabling terminated, equipment mounted), the final trim-out of outlets, faceplates, jacks, speakers, and control panels can be installed to complete the finished appearance.
The low-voltage and AV fit-out must be fully installed and terminated before system commissioning, programming, signal testing, and performance verification can be performed.
The site must be cleared of debris, vegetation, and existing structures before any new planting can be installed to provide a clean, safe work area.
Rough grading and excavation must be completed to establish the final ground levels and contours before planting beds can be prepared and plants installed.
All subsurface drainage pipes, French drains, and soakaways must be installed and backfilled before planting to prevent soil disturbance and root damage later.
Buried services (water, gas, electric, data cables) must be laid and tested before planting to avoid excavation through finished landscapes and to comply with safety regulations.

Hard surfaces such as paving, patios, paths, and retaining walls should be completed first to prevent damage to soft landscape areas from heavy machinery and material deliveries, and to define the exact planting boundaries.
Large shrubs, trees, and specimen planting must be installed before turf or lawn seed is laid to avoid trampling or damaging the new grass during planting operations.
Plants must be placed in the ground first, after which final topsoil dressing and mulch can be applied around them to retain moisture and suppress weeds.

successor: Irrigation System Final Connection and Testing
rationale: Planting must be completed so that the drip lines, sprinklers, and irrigation zones can be precisely positioned around the installed plants and then tested for coverage.
Once all planting is done, the site can be cleaned of soil spills, plant debris, and packaging, and any final touch-ups can be completed, though some clean-up can occur concurrently.
Physical installation of the node must be completed before commissioning and occupancy trials can begin, as there is no system to test or occupy without proper setup.
All electrical, data, and control cabling must be terminated and verified before node commissioning, as power and signal integrity are prerequisites for functional testing.
Individual node commissioning must be completed before system-level integration testing can proceed, as integrated tests require each node to be verified as functional first.
Occupancy trials demonstrate that the node is ready for use, and formal handover/acceptance requires successful completion of commissioning and trial results.

While commissioning may reveal defects that need rectification, some minor punch-list items can be addressed concurrently or after occupancy trial begins, making this a soft preference rather than a hard constraint.
Underground utilities and trenches must be completed before tree planting to avoid soil disturbance that could damage tree roots or require replanting.
Sidewalks and curbs define the tree pit location and boundaries; trees are typically planted after these hardscape elements are formed.
Street trees are planted before the final surface layer (e.g., asphalt or concrete) is applied around them to ensure proper integration and avoid damaging the tree.
While street trees can be planted before or after general landscaping, it is usually preferable to plant trees first to avoid damage from landscaping equipment and to establish a clear layout.
Street lighting is typically installed after trees are planted to coordinate pole locations with tree canopy and avoid conflicts, though it is a soft preference.
The ground must be excavated and prepared to create the physical pit cavity before any tree pit structure or grate can be installed.
Any underground utilities that conflict with the tree pit location must be relocated before excavation and installation of the tree pit to avoid damage or safety hazards.
Proper drainage layers (e.g., gravel, drainage pipes) must be placed at the bottom of the excavated pit to prevent waterlogging before the tree pit structure is completed.
The tree pit structure (including root barriers, soil medium, and grate frame) must be fully installed before the tree can be planted into the prepared pit.
The tree grate and frame must be in place to set the final grade and edge condition before adjacent paving, sidewalk, or hardscaping is completed around the tree pit.
A stable, level foundation or slab must be in place before installing benches or seating elements to ensure structural stability and proper alignment.
The ground surface must be graded and prepared to the correct elevations and drainage slopes before seating elements are placed, to avoid积水 and uneven settling.
Soft preference: planting around seating areas is often completed after bench installation to avoid damage to new plants from foot traffic or material delivery, but this is not a physical necessity.
Soft preference: final paving or surface finishes around bench areas are often completed after bench installation to achieve a neat finish and avoid damaging the paving during bench placement.
Soft preference: final clean-up and inspection typically occur after all furniture including benches are installed, but this is a logical sequence rather than a physical constraint.
The ground must be excavated, leveled, and prepared before the lighting column's foundation can be laid and the pole installed.
Electrical supply conduits and cabling must be laid underground before the column base is cast and the column erected, to avoid digging up finished foundations.
The concrete foundation for the lighting column must be poured and adequately cured to achieve sufficient strength before the column itself can be mounted and secured.
The lighting column must be installed and physically secure before electrical wiring can be terminated, connected to the mains, and tested for functionality and safety.
The lamp post must be erected in its final position before the light fixture (luminaire) can be mounted on top of it.
The structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) must be in place to provide the primary support and attachment points for the balustrade system.
Balustrades are typically mounted onto finished floor slabs, decks, or stair treads; the floor surface must exist to anchor the railing base.
For stair balustrades, the stair structure (stringers and treads) must be constructed first to define the handrail path and provide mounting points.
Final paint or decorative finishes are applied after balustrade installation to avoid damaging the railing during finishing work and to ensure a continuous coating.
Balustrades are safety-critical components that must be fully installed and secured before the building can be certified and handed over to the client.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and properly graded before any bollard can be installed to ensure a stable foundation.
Bollards typically require a concrete footing or foundation to be excavated and poured first to provide structural anchorage.
Any underground pipes, cables, or conduits must be laid and backfilled before bollard installation to avoid conflicts and rework.
Bollards are often installed before the final surface finish (paving, concrete slab) so that the surface material can be poured/cast flush around the bollard base for a neat finish.
Bollards should be in place before final landscaping, planting, and decorative elements are added to ensure proper alignment and integration with the finished site layout.
Water supply and drain pipes must be roughed into the wall before a drinking fountain can be connected.
The wall must be framed to provide structural support and mounting surface for the drinking fountain.
If the drinking fountain includes a chiller or refrigeration unit, electrical wiring must be roughed in before the unit is installed.
Floor finishes such as tile or vinyl should be installed after the drinking fountain to allow for proper fit and sealing around the base of the unit.
While it is easier to paint behind the fountain before installation, touch-up painting can be done after; this is a soft preference for efficiency.
The ground surface must be cleared, leveled, and graded to the correct slope before any ramp or accessible path can be constructed on it.
Any supporting foundations (e.g., for elevated ramp sections or retaining walls along the path) must be in place before the ramp structure is built.
Drainage pipes, electrical conduits, or other utilities beneath the path location must be installed before paving or constructing the accessible path to avoid later excavation and damage.
Once the ramp structure and base course are in place, the final surface layer (e.g., concrete, asphalt, slip-resistant coating) can be applied.
Handrails and guardrails are mounted onto the ramp structure after the ramp itself is constructed, as they require the ramp framework for attachment and alignment.

The waste/recycling bin is often integrated into cabinetry (e.g., pull-out drawer or under-sink unit). Cabinetry and countertops must be installed first to provide the structural housing and clearance for the bin system.
If the bin is located under a kitchen sink, the sink drain and supply plumbing must be roughed in before positioning the bin to ensure proper fit and access.
Flooring must be installed before placing a heavy waste/recycling bin to prevent damage to the floor surface and to ensure the bin sits level on the finished floor.

successor: Final interior finishing and trim work
rationale: It is preferable (soft preference) to complete painting, trim, and other finish work after bin installation to allow easy access and avoid moving the bin multiple times, but the bin can be temporarily placed earlier if needed.
The waste/recycling bin must be installed and operational before occupants move in, as waste management is essential for daily habitation and cleanliness.
A compacted and level sub-base is structurally required to support paving units; without proper sub-base preparation, paving will settle unevenly or fail.
Edge restraints (kerbs or haunching) must be in place to contain paving units and bedding material, preventing lateral movement during and after installation.
Drainage channels, gullies or pipework beneath or adjacent to paved areas must be installed before paving to avoid excavation and disturbance of completed paving.
Joint filling with sand or mortar can only be applied after paving units are laid and bedded in their final position to ensure joints are properly formed and aligned.
Final compaction and surface finishing (e.g., plate compaction, brushing in joint sand) must follow laying and bedding to consolidate the paving and lock the units in place.
Steps and staircases must be supported on a stable, completed foundation or substructure to prevent settlement or structural failure.
The structural frame (walls, floors, landings) must be in place to define the geometry and provide anchorage for stair stringers and step supports.
The floor slab or deck at each level must be poured/completed to provide the landing and support points for the staircase.
Finish flooring materials (tile, hardwood, carpet) on landings and steps are applied after the stair structure is built and stable.
It is preferred to install stair railing and steps before routing electrical or plumbing lines that run beneath or alongside the stairs, to avoid rework, though not physically required in all cases.
Drywall and plaster finishes adjacent to the stairway are installed after the stair structure is in place, so that the finishes can be fitted and taped to the stair frame.
Handrails and guardrails are physically attached to the completed stair structure and cannot be installed before the steps are in place.
The site must be cleared of debris, rubbish, and existing vegetation, and earthworks such as grading must be completed to create a proper planting surface before any landscape planting can commence.
A layer of quality topsoil must be spread and prepared to provide a suitable growing medium for plants, trees, and shrubs before planting can take place.
Underground drainage, irrigation pipelines, and any other buried services must be installed and tested before planting to avoid disturbing root systems and newly planted vegetation.
After planting is completed, mulch must be applied around the newly planted vegetation to retain moisture, suppress weeds, and provide a finished appearance.

While soft landscaping is often one of the final activities, a final inspection and handover of the project can only occur after all landscape planting works are complete to ensure the entire site is in its finished state.
The ground must be excavated and prepared before any underground utility ducts and services can be installed, as ducting is laid within prepared trenches.
Underground utility ducting must be laid and roughed-in prior to pouring the concrete slab or foundation, to embed necessary conduits and service entries.
Backfilling and compaction of trenches can only occur after the utility ducts and services have been properly installed and inspected.

While internal rough-in can proceed concurrently in some cases, the main underground service entry points need to be established before internal distribution can be connected; this is a logical dependency but may allow some parallel work.
Roads and pavements should be installed only after all underground utilities and ducts are in place, to avoid cutting or breaking finished surfaces for later utility access.
The display window frame must be installed to provide structural support and define the opening into which the display window unit is placed.
Wall framing around the window opening must be completed to create the rough opening that accommodates the display window assembly.
Weatherproofing measures such as flashing and waterproof membranes must be applied to the opening to prevent moisture intrusion once the display window is set.
Interior trim, sill, and surrounding finishes around the display window can only be installed after the window unit is in place to ensure proper fit and alignment.
Exterior caulking and sealant around the display window perimeter must be applied after installation to create a weathertight seal between the window and the surrounding wall.
A level and stable ground surface is physically required before any modular or prefabricated kiosk structure can be placed and secured.
The kiosk must be anchored to a proper foundation or concrete slab to ensure structural stability and prevent movement or sinking; the foundation must be cured before kiosk installation.
Underground conduit, water supply lines, and drainage pipes must be laid before the kiosk is placed, as the kiosk will sit on top of these connections.
Interior work such as shelving, countertops, and displays can only begin once the kiosk shell is erected and enclosed.
Final connection of electrical fixtures, lights, and plumbing fixtures to the kiosk requires the structure to be fully in place and the internal walls/ceiling accessible.
The building structure must be complete to provide a stable mounting surface for signage and fascia boards.
External wall surfaces must be finished before signage can be securely mounted and fascia boards installed.
Roofing must be completed so that fascia boards (which form part of the roof edge) can be properly installed and sealed.
Electrical conduits and wiring for illuminated signage must be roughed in behind wall surfaces before signage can be connected and fascia boards cover the access.

Signage and fascia installation is typically one of the final finishing works; however, final inspection can technically proceed without signage in some cases, though it is preferred to have all visible elements complete prior to sign-off.
Scaffolding and temporary access equipment must remain in place until high-level fascia and signage installation is complete, as they are needed for safe access.
The road base and pavement must be constructed first to provide a stable foundation for the pedestrian crossing surface and markings.
Site must be cleared and graded before any pedestrian crossing installation can begin.
Drainage systems must be in place to prevent water accumulation around the pedestrian crossing area.
Road markings and signage for the crossing can only be applied after the pedestrian crossing surface is completed.
Traffic signals and lighting for the crossing must be installed after the crossing area is prepared, but may be coordinated to avoid rework.
The structural steel frame must be erected to provide the primary support structure onto which the covered arcade/glazed roof system is installed.
The roof deck or substrate provides the base surface and structural diaphragm needed before the glazed roof and arcade components can be assembled and sealed.
The arcade/roof structural framing and support rails must be in place before glazing panels can be installed, fitted, and weather-sealed onto the framework.
The covered arcade/glazed roof assembly must be substantially complete before final weatherproofing membranes, flashings, and sealants are applied to ensure watertightness at joints and transitions.
The glazed roof and arcade structure overhead must be in place before interior ceiling/soffit finishes below can be installed, as they are applied to the underside of the completed roof assembly.
A stable and properly compacted subgrade is required to support the pavement layers and prevent differential settlement or failure of the surface.
The base and sub-base layers provide structural support and drainage; paving cannot be laid directly on unprepared ground and requires these load-bearing layers to be in place.

predecessor: Drainage System Installation (subsurface drains, French drains)
rationale: Subsurface drainage must be installed before paving to ensure water is properly channeled away from the base layers, preventing water damage and extending pavement life.
Curbs and gutters adjacent to paved surfaces are typically installed after paving to match the finished surface elevation and ensure proper water runoff.
Traffic markings, road lines, and signage are applied to the finished paved surface; they cannot be installed before the pavement is complete.
Site must be established with temporary facilities, fencing, and access roads before any utility diversion work can commence to ensure a safe and organised working environment.
Accurate site survey and setting out of existing utility locations is required to identify the exact positions of services to be diverted and plan the diversion route.
All existing underground and overhead utilities must be located, marked, and verified (e.g., using GPR, potholing) before any excavation or diversion work begins to avoid damaging active services.
Utilities must be diverted and new ducting laid before large-scale earthworks commence, otherwise active services would be damaged or obstruct the earthmoving operations.
Ducting for future services (power, water, communications) must be installed beneath the building footprint before foundations are poured to avoid the need for later breaking through concrete.
Structural steelwork for the canopy/arcade requires completed foundations and substructure to provide a stable load-bearing base for erection.
The ground slab provides the working platform and base level from which steel columns and frames are erected; steelwork cannot be placed on unprepared ground.
Underground services must be installed and backfilled before steel columns are placed to avoid excavation and access conflicts under the canopy footprint.
The structural steel frame must be erected and stable before roof decking and cladding panels can be fixed to it.

successor: Canopy / Arcade Lighting and Electrical Rough-In
rationale: Electrical conduits, junction boxes, and lighting fixtures are mounted to or routed through the steel structure, requiring the steelwork to be in place first.

The stage or performance platform requires a solid, level foundation to bear the dynamic loads from performances and audience movement. Substructure must be completed before any superstructure or platform framing begins.
The stage platform is often supported by a structural steel frame or primary structure. The main structural frame must be erected to provide support for the platform decking and framing members.

Stage lighting fixtures, cabling, and power outlets are mounted on or integrated into the stage platform structure. The platform must be in place to serve as the substrate for electrical rough-in work.

While the structural platform must be complete, the final performance floor surface (e.g., sprung floor, dance floor, or finished timber deck) is typically installed after the platform framing is fully erected and secured.
Acoustic panels, speakers, and sound equipment are often installed after the stage deck is complete to ensure proper mounting and integration with the performance surface.
The bar framing provides the structural support and backing for the millwork and counter installation.
Plumbing rough-in for sinks and drains must be completed before the bar top and millwork can be installed, as access to wall/floor cavities is needed.
Electrical wiring for outlets, lighting, and appliances behind/in the bar must be roughed in before millwork covers the walls and cavities.
Millwork and base cabinetry must be installed first to provide support for the bar top surface.
Sinks and fixtures are mounted into or onto the bar counter and millwork, so the counter must be in place first.
The ground must be stable, level, and free of debris before barriers can be installed to ensure they sit securely and do not tip over.
Underground utilities must be located and marked to avoid damaging them when driving stakes, anchors, or base plates into the ground for barrier installation.
Signage directing crowd flow and queue lines should be installed after barriers are in place to ensure signs are positioned correctly relative to the defined pathways and queuing zones.
Security checkpoints must be placed within or at the entrance of the barrier system; therefore barriers defining the queue lanes and access points must be installed first.

While not physically required, it is preferable to install barriers before final decorative elements so that decorations can be added to barrier surfaces and the layout is clearly defined for aesthetic treatment.

The building's structural shell (walls, roof, floor slab) must be fully erected and weathertight before any interior finishing works, including themed fit-out, can commence, as interior finishes require a protected environment.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work (conduits, piping, ductwork within walls/ceilings) must be installed before themed finishes are applied, to avoid damaging or having to cut through themed surfaces.

successor: Installation of Themed Fixtures and Props
rationale: The base themed surfaces (wall finishes, painted backdrops, scenic elements) must be completed before attaching fixed props, fixtures, or detailed thematic decorations that rely on those surfaces for support or alignment.

After themed finishes are in place, final installation of light fixtures, switches, outlets, HVAC grilles, and other trim items can be completed and the systems commissioned, ensuring these elements integrate cleanly with the themed environment.

Themed fit-out should precede final cleaning and snagging (punch-list) to avoid re-soiling or damaging completed work; while not a physical impossibility to reverse, it is a standard sequencing preference for quality and efficiency.
The building structure and envelope must be complete to provide a contained environment that supports acoustic isolation before testing can commence.

predecessor: Installation of Mechanical, Electrical & Plumbing (MEP) Systems
rationale: MEP systems can generate background noise and vibration that could interfere with baseline acoustic measurements; they need to be installed and possibly operational to assess real-world conditions.
Interior finishes such as acoustic panels, ceiling tiles, and floorings significantly affect the acoustic properties of the space and must be in place for accurate testing results.
Acoustic and vibration test results inform the calibration and tuning of audio systems, vibration dampers, and other performance systems; commissioning should leverage baseline data.
Testing results must be documented and verified before final certification or occupancy approval can be issued, ensuring the facility meets required acoustic and vibration standards.
The physical building structure must be substantially complete before any fit-out work begins, as the fit-out occurs within the completed shell of the building.
Zoning and land use approvals must be secured before liquor license applications and regulatory fit-out can proceed, as the premises must be legally designated for commercial/bar use.

The liquor license application must be submitted and basic approvals obtained before commencing fit-out that is specific to liquor service requirements, to ensure the fit-out meets regulatory standards.
Regulatory fit-out (e.g., bar counters, service areas, drainage) must be completed before general interior finishing and furnishing can be installed.
The fit-out must be completed to the required regulatory standards before the final inspection can be conducted and the liquor license officially issued.
Foundation design must be completed first to determine the load paths and structural support points that the dynamic load reinforcement will integrate with.
The dynamic loads (e.g., wind, seismic, vibration) must be analyzed and modeled to quantify their magnitude, frequency, and direction before designing and placing the corresponding reinforcement.
Steel rebar, fiber-reinforced polymers, dampers, or other reinforcement materials must be procured and delivered to site before installation can commence.
Reinforcement must be fully placed, tied, and inspected before concrete can be poured, as the reinforcement is embedded within the concrete element.

While it is preferable to install damping devices (e.g., tuned mass dampers, base isolators) after the main structural reinforcement is in place to avoid rework, some dampers can be installed concurrently; thus this is a soft preference rather than a hard physical constraint.
The steel structure and support framing must be in place to provide the structural anchorage points and load-bearing capacity required to suspend the rigging and truss system.
Overhead cranes or permanent lifting equipment must be installed first to facilitate the safe lifting and positioning of heavy truss sections and rigging components.
Overhead electrical and data cables should be routed before the truss system is closed in, as the truss grid would obstruct cable pulling and access.
Lighting fixtures are typically mounted directly to or supported by the truss system, so the truss must be fully installed and secured before lighting can be attached.
Audio speakers and PA systems are often flown from or attached to the overhead truss, requiring the truss grid to be complete before rigging audio equipment.
The canopy structure requires a stable foundation to support its weight and resist wind loads; without completed foundations, the canopy cannot be safely erected.
The canopy structure is typically mounted on or supported by the main steel frame; therefore the frame must be erected first to provide the structural attachment points.
The canopy structure serves as the underlying support framework for roof cladding; cladding cannot be installed until the canopy framing is complete.

While it is possible to run some electrical conduit before the canopy is installed, final routing and fixture mounting within the canopy area is more efficiently completed after the canopy is in place.
The canopy structure must be fully erected and secured before official structural inspections can verify compliance with design specifications and safety standards.
The structural frame (steel or concrete) must be complete and fully cured to provide a stable load-bearing platform for the glazed facade system to be anchored to.
Perimeter slab edges and any spandrel beams must be finished to receive the curtain wall anchoring brackets and perimeter seals.
The exterior enclosure must be weathertight before interior drywall, insulation, and finishes are installed to prevent water damage and allow proper sealing at facade junctions.

Permanent window washing anchors, tracks, or davit systems are typically installed after or concurrently with facade completion, as they mount to the facade structure and must align with the finished glazing.

successor: Final Commissioning of HVAC (zones near facade)
rationale: While HVAC rough-in can proceed earlier, final balancing and commissioning of perimeter zones is ideally done after the facade is sealed to accurately model solar heat gain and infiltration rates.
Design and engineering approvals must be obtained before any site work begins to ensure compliance with regulations and to have approved plans for site layout and preparation.
The site must be legally acquired and all land clearance permits obtained before enabling works can commence on the property.
Environmental assessments and necessary permits are legally required before any ground disturbance or site clearing activities can begin.
Foundation excavation and construction cannot begin until the site has been cleared, leveled, and prepared with necessary temporary access and services.
Bulk earthmoving and excavation activities depend on completed site clearing, demolition (if any), and establishment of site access.

The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and obstructions before any excavation or foundation work can begin, as the ground needs to be accessible and safe for construction equipment and workers.
Soil bearing capacity, groundwater conditions, and soil type must be determined to design appropriate foundation types and depths before any foundation construction can commence.
Accurate positioning of the building footprint, grid lines, and foundation layout must be established on site before excavation and foundation construction can begin.
The foundation must be complete, cured, and load-bearing before any above-ground structural elements (columns, walls, slabs) can be erected upon it.
Foundation pour must be complete before drainage pipes and waterproofing membranes are installed around and under the substructure to protect the foundation from water ingress.

The structural steel frame provides the primary support structure for the canopy and roof system. Without the steel frame erected, there is no structural骨架 to attach the roof panels or canopy elements to.
Foundations and ground slabs must be fully cured and in place to support the steel columns and walls that carry the roof loads. Roof installation cannot proceed without stable foundation support.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work that runs through the roof or ceiling plenum must be completed before the roof is closed in. Once the roof/canopy is installed, access for overhead rough-in becomes significantly more difficult and costly.

Interior finishes such as ceiling installation, drywall, and painting must be protected from weather and are typically done after the building is enclosed. The roof/canopy must be in place to provide a dry and enclosed environment for these finishes.

successor: Roof-Mounted Equipment Installation (HVAC units, solar panels)
rationale: Roof-mounted equipment must be installed on top of or integrated with the completed roof/canopy structure. The roof system must be fully installed to provide the base surface and structural support for such equipment.
The platform substructure or subgrade must be compacted, levelled, and prepared to provide a stable base before the surface layer (e.g., concrete, asphalt, or paving) can be laid.
Drainage pipes, channels, and sub-drains must be installed beneath or around the platform before the surface is laid to ensure proper water runoff and prevent future water damage.

Any electrical conduits, communication cables, or utility ducts that run under the platform surface must be placed before the surface covering is applied to avoid later excavation and surface disruption.

After the main platform surface is laid (e.g., concrete pour or asphalt compaction), finishing works such as tiling, anti-slip coating, edge trimming, or marking can only be applied once the base surface has cured or set.

Fixtures such as benches, shelters, lighting poles, signage, or ticket machines must be installed after the platform surface is completed to ensure proper anchoring and avoid surface damage during installation.
The structural frame must be complete to provide the physical support and enclosure for mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (M&E) installations.
The building must be weathertight (roof and envelope complete) to protect sensitive M&E equipment and materials from water damage during installation.
M&E services (conduits, ducts, pipes) are typically run within wall cavities and ceiling voids, so partition framing must be in place before routing these services.
All M&E services (wiring, ductwork, pipes) must be installed and pressure-tested before they are concealed behind ceiling and wall finishes.

successor: Floor Screeding and Final Floor Finishes
rationale: While some floor finishes can be installed concurrently, sensitive flooring is typically laid after M&E rough-in to avoid damage from heavy equipment and to allow access for underfloor services.
Individual components must be verified to work correctly before they can be integrated and tested together as a system.
All subsystems and components must be physically installed and assembled before the integrated system can be tested and commissioned.
Power, data, and control cables must be run and connected between components before the integrated system can be functionally tested.
Control software, firmware, and configuration settings must be loaded and set up on all relevant components before the system can be tested as a whole.
The integrated system must be successfully tested and commissioned before it can be formally accepted by the client and handed over for operational use.
It is preferable that operators and maintenance staff receive training after the system is commissioned so they can train on the fully functional system, though it could start earlier in parallel.
The system must pass integration testing and commissioning before it can be put into live operation or transitioned from an old system.
The floor slab must be in place to provide a stable base and support for the internal partition walls.
The main structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) must be completed to define the building envelope and provide support before non-load-bearing partition walls are installed.
Under-slab or in-floor conduits, pipes, and sleeves must be placed before walls are built to avoid cutting or coring through the finished slab.
Partition walls must be fully erected, framed, and braced before any wall finishes (plaster, drywall boarding) can be applied to their surfaces.

Electrical cables, outlet boxes, switch boxes, and plumbing pipes that run inside the partition walls must be installed after the wall framing is complete but before the wall is closed up with finishes.
Loadbearing walls require a stable foundation to transfer vertical loads safely to the ground; without the foundation, the wall would have no structural support and would settle or fail.

predecessor: Slab on Grade / Ground Floor Slab
rationale: The ground floor slab or substructure must be completed to provide a level bearing surface and to anchor the bottom of the loadbearing wall.
Foundation concrete must reach sufficient strength before loadbearing walls can be erected on top; premature loading can cause cracking or structural failure.
Upper floor slabs or decking require the loadbearing walls below to be in place to support their weight and transfer loads to the foundation.
Roof trusses, beams, and roofing materials bear directly on loadbearing walls; the walls must be completed and cured to support roof loads.
The foundation must be completed to provide a stable load-bearing base before any floor structure or slab can be cast or placed.
Ground must be excavated, leveled, and compacted to the required bearing capacity before pouring or installing a floor slab.
Underground plumbing, drainage pipes, and conduits must be laid and inspected before the slab is poured to avoid breaking the slab for later installations.
Columns and walls are typically erected on top of the completed floor slab, which provides the working platform and load distribution.
Screeding and floor finishes require the structural slab to be fully cured and stable before applying toppings or leveling layers.
Roof structure requires load-bearing walls or columns to be completed in order to provide support for the roof framing and transfer loads to the foundation.
Roof sheathing or decking material is installed directly on top of the roof structure (trusses/rafters), so the structural framing must be in place first.
Insulation is typically installed after the roof structure is complete and before the final roofing material to provide thermal performance.
The final waterproof roofing layer (shingles, tiles, or membrane) is applied after the roof structure and decking are in place to provide weather protection.
Interior ceiling finishes and drywall are installed after the roof structure is complete, as the roof framing supports the ceiling assembly.
Internal doors require framed openings within walls to be installed; without wall framing, there is no structural support or opening for the door.
The rough opening (with header, studs, and cripples) must be framed to the correct dimensions before the door unit can be fitted.
Door casing and trim are fastened around the installed door frame; the door must be in place and plumb before trim can be applied.
Hardware such as hinges, locksets, and handles are fitted onto the installed door leaf and frame; the door must be hung first.
While painting can be done before installation (pre-finishing), it is a soft preference to paint after installation to ensure touch-ups and uniform finish with surrounding trim and walls.
The rough opening must be framed and prepared (with proper header, jack studs, and sill) before an external door can be installed.
Weather-resistant barrier should be applied to the exterior wall before door installation to ensure proper flashing integration and water management.
The subfloor must be in place to provide a stable threshold base and proper elevation reference for the door frame.
The door frame must be securely installed before exterior trim or casing can be applied around it.
The door must be hung and aligned in its frame before locks, handles, and final hinge adjustments can be made.

successor: Insulation and Air Sealing Around Door
rationale: After the door frame is installed, gaps between the frame and rough opening can be foamed or sealed and insulated to prevent air infiltration.

Interior wall finishing can proceed after the door is installed, though some sequencing may allow drywall before door installation to be possible; it is a practical preference to install the door early to avoid finishing work around an empty opening.
Door is typically installed before the final siding around it to allow proper flashing and integration, but siding can in some cases be fitted afterward; it is a preferred sequence.
The staircase structure must be supported on a solid foundation; without poured foundations, the staircase cannot be safely anchored or structurally supported.
Staircases typically connect between floors; the floor slabs or structural decking must be in place to define the vertical levels and provide bearing points for the staircase.
Staircase installation must be completed before finishing walls around the stairwell, as the stair structure defines the finished opening and allows wall finishes to be installed flush against it.
Railings and balustrades are attached directly to the assembled staircase structure; the staircase must be in place to provide the mounting surface and alignment for safety barriers.

While not a physical impossibility, floor finishes on stairs (e.g. stair treads, carpeting) are typically applied after assembly to avoid damage; this is a standard sequencing preference to protect finished surfaces during construction.
Cabinetry must be installed against finished wall and ceiling surfaces. Installing cabinets before drywall and paint would require removal and reinstallation during finishing.
Cabinets must be set on a level, stable subfloor. The floor substrate must be fully prepared to support cabinet loads and ensure level installation.

predecessor: Plumbing Rough-In (Water Supply & Drainage in Walls)
rationale: Plumbing lines that will serve the kitchen sink and appliances must be roughed in behind walls and floor before cabinets are placed, as access to these areas is blocked once cabinets are installed.

Electrical wiring and junction boxes for kitchen counter outlets, appliance connections, and lighting must be installed within the walls before cabinets are mounted, since cabinet placement covers wall surfaces.
Countertops are fabricated and installed directly on top of base cabinets, and final plumbing hookups for the sink and appliances require the cabinets to be in place to position fixtures correctly.
Plumbing rough-in (water supply and drainage pipes) must be installed and pressure-tested before sanitary fixtures (toilets, sinks, showers) can be connected.
Floor and wall finishes (e.g., tiles, waterproof membrane) in bathrooms and toilets must be completed before installing sanitary ware, as fixtures are mounted on finished surfaces.
Electrical wiring for lighting, exhaust fans, and power outlets near sanitary fixtures must be roughed-in before fixtures are installed to avoid interference.
After sanitary ware is placed and anchored, the final connections of supply lines, drain traps, and shut-off valves are completed.
Soft preference: installing sanitary ware early allows final paint touch-ups and caulking around fixtures, but minor touch-ups can also be done after installation.
The site must be legally acquired and all necessary permits/approvals obtained before any physical site work or demolition can begin.
Detailed site surveys and soil testing must be completed to understand ground conditions, utility locations, and site boundaries before demolition and preparation work commences.
Asbestos, lead, or other hazardous material surveys must be conducted prior to demolition to ensure safe removal and compliance with regulations.
Gas, electricity, water, and communications lines must be disconnected, capped, or relocated before demolition to prevent hazards and service disruptions.
Demolition and site clearing must be fully completed before excavation can begin, as debris and existing structures would obstruct earthmoving operations.
Temporary power, water, and sanitation facilities for construction crews are typically installed after the site is cleared and leveled.
All demolition debris must be removed and the site graded before foundation work can commence, as foundations require a clean, stable subgrade.

successor: Site Security Fencing & Erosion Control Installation
rationale: While ideally done after clearing to establish the perimeter, some temporary fencing may be installed before full demolition; however, permanent site security and erosion controls are best placed after site preparation is complete.
The ground must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and topsoil, and leveled before any excavation or foundation work can begin to ensure a stable working surface and proper load distribution.
Soil bearing capacity, groundwater levels, and soil composition must be determined to design the foundation type and depth; construction cannot proceed without this data.
The ground must be excavated to the required depth and shape as per engineering drawings before concrete or footings can be placed.
Waterproofing membranes and coatings are applied directly onto the cured foundation surfaces to protect against moisture ingress; this cannot be done before the foundation is constructed.
After the foundation walls and footings are complete and cured, the excavated areas around them must be backfilled with soil and compacted to provide lateral support and prevent water accumulation.

successor: Slab on Grade / Floor Slab Construction
rationale: The foundation walls or perimeter footings must be in place to support and contain the concrete floor slab, which is poured after the foundation is complete.
Columns, beams, and load-bearing walls of the building's superstructure require a completed foundation to transfer loads safely to the ground.
The structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) must be complete to provide a stable load-bearing surface for roof installation.
Load-bearing walls must be in place to support roof trusses and roofing materials.
Roof trusses or rafters must be erected to form the structural skeleton onto which roofing materials are applied.
Electrical wiring in attic/roof spaces is typically done after roofing but before ceiling finishes; however, this is a soft preference as wiring can be done before roof closure in some cases.
Gutters and downpipes are physically attached to the roof edge and require the completed roof surface to be in place for proper installation and drainage alignment.
The structural frame must be complete to provide a stable supporting substrate for the external cladding and rendering system to be applied.
Roof completion ensures weather-tightness from above, preventing water ingress that could damage cladding before or during installation.

Cladding and rendering define the final finished wall plane; windows and doors are typically installed into the prepared openings within the completed envelope to achieve proper weather sealing and flashing integration.
Final decorative and protective coatings must be applied onto the completed rendered or cladded surface to ensure adhesion, uniformity, and durability.
While scaffolding can be partially removed earlier, full dismantling typically waits until cladding and rendering are finished to maintain safe access for the envelope work.
The structural frame must be complete to provide the load-bearing support and defined spatial volumes within which internal partitions and drylining can be safely installed.
The roof must be completed and weathertight to protect interior works, including drylining materials, from water damage and moisture ingress before commencing internal finishes.
External wall enclosure must be in place to create a weathertight shell and define the building envelope before internal partitions are laid out and constructed.

predecessor: Rough-in Mechanical, Electrical & Plumbing (MEP) First Fix
rationale: First-fix MEP services (conduits, cables, pipes, ductwork) must be routed within walls and ceilings before they are enclosed by drylining, otherwise retrofitting would require cutting into and damaging finished partitions.
After drylining is complete, final MEP installations (sockets, switches, fixtures, terminal units) can be fitted through the finished wall surfaces, and wall/ceiling finishes can be applied.
Paint and decorative finishes are applied onto the completed drylined surfaces; painting must follow after jointing, taping, and sanding of drywall is finished.

While flooring and ceiling finishes can technically be done before or after drylining in some sequences, standard practice prefers completing drylining first to avoid damaging finished floors and to allow partition walls to sit directly on subfloor or structure.
All internal partition and drylining works must be fully completed and inspected before the building can be handed over to the client or tenant.
Walls and blockwork must be in place before M&E services (cables, pipes, conduits) can be installed within or through them.
The structural frame must be complete to provide support for M&E services and to allow safe access for installation.
The roof must be watertight before first fix M&E to protect electrical components and sensitive equipment from weather damage.
M&E services must be installed within walls/ceilings before they can be closed up with plasterboard and plaster.
First fix M&E (cables, conduits, pipe runs) must be completed before second fix (switches, sockets, fixtures) can be installed and connected.
All MEP rough-ins must be installed within walls before plastering and screeding, as these services will be hidden behind the plaster.
Wall framing and stud partitioning must be completed to provide the substrate onto which plasterboard or plaster is applied.
Ceilings and roof enclosure must be in place to create an enclosed environment and provide the overhead structure for ceiling plastering.
Tiling requires a smooth, level substrate provided by screeding and plastering; plaster must be fully set before tiles can be applied.
Paint and decorative finishes require a fully cured, dry plastered surface to adhere properly and achieve a quality finish.

While joinery can technically be installed before plastering, it is standard practice to plaster first so that joinery fits neatly against finished walls; this is a soft preference for quality and aesthetics.

successor: Final Fixing of Electrical & Plumbing Fixtures
rationale: Light switches, sockets, and sanitary fixtures are installed after plastering to sit flush against the finished wall surface.
The security checkpoint must be built on a stable foundation and concrete slab, requiring the foundation work to be completed first.
Electrical wiring, data cabling, and network infrastructure for screening equipment (X-ray machines, metal detectors, CCTV) must be run before walls and checkpoint barriers are installed.
Any plumbing for洗手 stations, water fountains, or drainage near inspection areas must be in place before finishing the checkpoint area.

successor: Commissioning and Testing of Security Equipment
rationale: Screening machines, metal detectors, and access control systems can only be installed, powered on, and tested after the checkpoint physical structure is complete.
While signage and paint can be done after the checkpoint is erected, it is a soft preference as some signage may be installed concurrently with final touches.
The structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) must be in place to provide support and anchorage for the glazed partition system.
The floor slab must be leveled and finished to provide a stable base and accurate alignment for the glazed partition track/channel.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work in the ceiling/overhead zone must be completed to avoid rework once glazed partitions are installed below.
The partition frame (channels, studs, mullions) must be erected first before glass panels can be inserted and secured.

Final electrical outlets, switches, and trim work near the partition can proceed after the partition is in place, though this is a soft preference for work sequence efficiency rather than a physical necessity.

Door access hardware (such as locks, latches, strikes, and electronic access controls) is mounted on or within the door frame. The frame must be installed and secured first to provide the structural support and alignment required for hardware attachment.

Electronic door access hardware requires power and/or data cabling (e.g., for maglocks, card readers, or electric strikes). Rough-in electrical wiring to the door location must be completed before the hardware can be connected and terminated.

The door slab must be hung on the frame before door access hardware (such as handlesets, deadbolts, or electronic trim) can be installed onto the door itself, as the hardware interfaces with both the door and the frame.

After the physical door access hardware (locks, readers, controllers) is installed, the system must be programmed, configured, and tested to ensure proper communication and functionality with the building's security system.

Once access hardware is installed, final adjustments to door fit, latch alignment, and strike plate positioning are needed to ensure smooth operation. Trim-out and cosmetic covers are also installed after the core hardware is in place.
A stable, level foundation or footing must be in place to support the privacy screen/enclosure structure.
Any underground electrical, data, or irrigation lines that will serve the privacy screen area must be roughed in prior to installing the enclosure to avoid digging up finished work.
Planting beds, ground cover, or decorative hardscape around the privacy screen should be completed after the enclosure is installed to avoid damage during installation.
While not strictly required, mounting exterior light fixtures on or near the privacy screen is easier and safer once the screen structure is fully assembled and anchored.
The privacy screen/enclosure must be fully installed before the final inspection can verify its compliance with design plans and building codes.

The structural framework (load-bearing walls, columns, slabs) must be in place to provide support and define the spaces where acoustic separation elements (such as acoustic partitions, soundproof walls, or acoustic insulation) will be installed.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in works (ductwork, piping, conduits) should be completed before installing acoustic separation elements, as these services often run within or through walls and partitions, and retrofitting after acoustic installation can compromise the acoustic seal and integrity.

Acoustic separation elements (e.g., acoustic insulation within partitions, soundproof barriers) must be fully installed and sealed before being enclosed by finished surfaces such as drywall, plaster, or paint.

Tiling is typically a finishing task; while it is preferred to complete acoustic separation elements first to avoid sound leaks through unfinished gaps, tiling can occasionally proceed concurrently with careful detailing.
Acoustic separation elements must be fully installed before acoustic performance testing can be conducted to verify that sound transmission requirements (e.g., STC ratings) are met.
Users must be registered in the system before access rights can be assigned to them.
Roles must be defined before access rights can be assigned to those roles.
The system must be installed and operational before access rights can be managed within it.
Access rights must be configured before testing whether users can access the system as intended.
Access rights management must be completed before the system can go live to ensure only authorized users have access from the start.
The building's foundation must be completed before spatial zoning can be laid out, as zoning defines interior spaces that rest upon the structural base.
The primary structural frame (columns, beams, load-bearing walls) must be in place to define the physical boundaries within which spatial zones are organized.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and prepared before any spatial layout planning can be meaningfully executed on the construction site.
Interior partitions and walls are built according to the spatial zoning plan; the layout must be finalized before physical partition construction begins.
MEP systems are routed based on the spatial zoning and room layout; the zoning must be complete to determine where ducts, pipes, and conduits should run.

A security risk assessment requires a defined scope, objectives, and project parameters established during project initiation and planning to identify what systems, assets, and processes need to be evaluated.
Identifying and classifying all assets (hardware, software, data) is a prerequisite for a risk assessment, as risks are defined in terms of threats and vulnerabilities to specific assets.
