Threat modeling identifies potential threat actors and attack vectors, which provides essential input to the risk assessment process for analyzing likelihood and impact of threats.
Security controls (safeguards and countermeasures) must be selected and designed based on the identified risks from the assessment to mitigate the prioritized risks appropriately.
A formal risk treatment plan that defines how to accept, avoid, transfer, or mitigate each identified risk can only be developed after the risk assessment has identified and prioritized all risks.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and graded before any boundary fencing or wall can be erected to ensure proper alignment and stable foundations.
Accurate property boundary lines must be surveyed and staked out to guide the correct placement of the fence or wall along the legal property line.
Underground utilities (water, gas, electric, telecom) must be located and marked before digging post holes or footings to avoid damage and ensure safety.

Landscaping and planting along the boundary is best done after the fence or wall is complete to avoid damaging new plants during construction and to allow proper grading against the finished structure.
Gates are typically installed as part of or immediately after the boundary fence/wall is erected to ensure proper fit, alignment, and structural integration with the fence or wall.
The shared roof structure typically requires the main structural steel frame to be erected first to provide the support framework onto which the roof can be installed.
Concrete cores (e.g., stair/elevator shafts) provide lateral stability and vertical support needed before the roof structure can be placed.
The roof membrane and waterproofing system can only be applied after the structural roof deck is in place to provide the substrate.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work at the roof level (e.g., ductwork, conduit, rooftop unit supports) must follow the structural roof completion since they mount to or penetrate the roof structure.

While interior finishes can technically begin earlier on lower floors, completing the roof enclosure first protects upper-floor interior work from weather, making this a strong practical preference to avoid weather damage and delays.
Site selection must be completed first because the masterplan and layout design depend on the specific site's topography, dimensions, boundaries, soil conditions, and access points.
Feasibility studies and needs assessments define the functional requirements, budget constraints, and space needs that drive the masterplan layout.
Detailed architectural design requires the overall masterplan and layout as a framework to locate specific buildings, roads, and infrastructure.
Infrastructure design must follow the masterplan because utility routes, road alignments, and drainage networks are determined by the overall site layout and building placements.

While EIA can begin in parallel with preliminary design, final permitting submissions often require the approved masterplan to show how the project addresses environmental concerns on the specific layout.
A site must be selected and acquired before planning permission can be sought, as the application requires specific site details including location, boundary, and ownership documentation.

Feasibility studies assessing site constraints, zoning, environmental impact, and development viability must be completed to inform the planning application and demonstrate compliance with local regulations.
Preliminary architectural designs and community consultations are required to develop the proposal that will be submitted for formal planning approval.

Detailed engineering and architectural design development depends on approved planning conditions and parameters, ensuring designs comply with planning consent requirements before proceeding to construction-level drawings.
Physical construction work cannot legally begin without obtaining formal planning permission and approval from the local planning authority, as it is a statutory requirement.
Superstructure requires a stable foundation to bear loads and transfer them to the ground; building cannot proceed without completed foundation.
The ground floor slab or substructure provides the working platform and base on which the superstructure columns, walls, and frames are erected.
The roof depends on the completed superstructure frame and vertical supports to be placed and secured.
Exterior walls and cladding attach to the superstructure frame and cannot be installed until the frame is in place.

While some MEP rough-in can begin in parallel, vertical risers and major ductwork routing through the superstructure are best installed after the structural frame is complete to avoid conflicts and rework.
The site must be cleared of debris, vegetation, and existing structures before any excavation or foundation work can begin.
Accurate site levels, boundaries, and foundation locations must be surveyed and marked before excavation and groundwork can commence.
Soil bearing capacity, groundwater levels, and ground conditions must be assessed to determine the appropriate foundation design and depth before any groundwork begins.

predecessor: Temporary Site Services and Welfare Facilities
rationale: While work can theoretically start without full welfare facilities, providing temporary site services (water, power, toilets) is a practical and regulatory requirement for safe construction operations.
The damp proof membrane/course is laid directly on top of or within the foundation walls before any superstructure walls are built to prevent rising damp.
The ground floor slab is poured after foundations and any necessary hardcore fill and insulation are in place.
Below-ground drainage runs and service ducts are typically laid within the foundation phase before backfilling and before any above-ground construction.
After foundation walls and underground services are complete, the excavation must be backfilled and compacted before proceeding with further ground slab or landscaping works.
Load-bearing walls and the entire above-ground structure can only be built once the foundation is fully cured and capable of supporting the imposed loads.

The building's main structural elements (frame, roof, enclosure) must be in place before shared services such as electrical, plumbing, HVAC, and data cabling can be installed, as these services are typically mounted within or on the structure.
Underground conduits, water lines, and drainage must be installed before internal shared service distribution begins, as they form the supply and waste connections for the building's systems.

Interior finishes such as drywall, ceiling tiles, flooring, and painting must follow the installation of shared services because these services are concealed within walls, above ceilings, and below floors.
Commissioning of electrical, mechanical, and plumbing systems can only begin after all shared services are installed and connected, to verify proper operation.

While it is strongly preferred that all shared services are fully installed and tested before final inspection, partial inspections could theoretically occur. However, in standard practice, inspection follows installation completion.

The project must reach substantial or practical completion status (all major works finished, systems commissioned, and statutory approvals obtained) before the formal handover and snagging process can commence, as snagging identifies minor outstanding defects after the building is deemed complete.
The site must be cleaned and prepared so that the snagging inspection can be carried out unobstructed and the condition of finishes can be properly assessed.
All building services (MEP, fire safety, lifts, etc.) must be commissioned and tested to ensure they are operational before handover; snagging then addresses any minor adjustments or defects.
The formal handover and resolution of all snagging items must be completed before the final account can be agreed and the project closed out, as outstanding defects affect contractual completion.
The client can only take beneficial occupancy or begin moving into the building after handover is formally executed and all critical snags are resolved.

The Residents Management Company (RMC) is established to manage and oversee the completed building. Therefore, the building's physical construction must be finished before the RMC can begin its operations.

Legal completion and registration of the building (e.g., obtaining completion certificates, title registration) must occur before the RMC can be formally constituted and take over management responsibilities.
The RMC must be established first to have the legal authority to collect service charges from residents for building maintenance and operations.
The RMC is responsible for overseeing and commissioning building maintenance and repairs, so it must be in place before such activities can be formally managed.

While the RMC often appoints a managing agent for day-to-day operations, this could theoretically be done in parallel or by the developer initially. However, typically the RMC is formed first to make the appointment.
The front facade requires a stable foundation and structural base to be built upon; without proper foundation work, the facade cannot be safely supported.
The structural frame of the building must be erected before the front facade can be attached, as the facade is mounted onto or integrated with the load-bearing frame.
The roof structure must be in place before the front facade is installed to ensure proper alignment, weatherproofing integration, and structural continuity at the top of the facade.
Windows and doors are typically installed after the facade structure is in place, as the facade provides the openings and mounting points for these elements.
Final exterior finishing, cladding panels, or decorative elements are applied after the main facade structure is erected to ensure proper attachment and seamless integration.
A stable foundation is required to support the weight of a load-bearing masonry wall; the wall cannot be built without a finished foundation.
Concrete footings or slabs must be fully cured to reach sufficient strength before masonry loads can be applied.
Any starter bars or dowels for the masonry wall must be embedded in the foundation before the wall is laid.
Load-bearing masonry walls provide vertical support for floor joists, beams, or roof trusses; these structural elements cannot be placed until the supporting wall is built and cured.
Waterproofing membranes and damp-proof courses are applied to the completed masonry surface; they cannot be installed before the wall exists.
Chimney stack requires a solid foundation to bear its weight and ensure stability; without footings/foundation, the stack cannot be safely built.
The flue lining must be installed inside the completed chimney stack structure; the stack provides the structural enclosure for the flue.
Roof flashing around the chimney can only be properly installed after the chimney stack has been constructed and penetrates through the roof.
The chimney cap or crown is placed on top of the completed stack to protect it from weather; it requires the stack to be fully built.

While the fireplace is often built concurrently or after the chimney, the chimney stack must be structurally complete to connect to the fireplace flue; this is a soft preference as sequencing can vary by design.
The roof must be framed and opened to create the structural opening where the dormer window will be installed.
The dormer window must be in place before the roof sheathing is installed around it to ensure proper flashing and weatherproofing.
Flashing around the dormer window can only be properly installed after the window is set in place to seal the roof penetration.
Exterior cladding or siding around the dormer area must be installed after the window is placed to ensure proper fit and sealing.
Interior wall finishing around the dormer can only be completed after the window frame is installed to allow for proper trimming and sealing.
The ground must be excavated and leveled before any foundation or damp proof work can begin, as the DPC is installed at a specific height above ground level within the wall structure.
The foundation or footings must be completed to provide a stable base on which the DPC layer and subsequent wall construction can be placed.
If a ground floor slab is present, it must be cast and cured before installing the DPC to ensure proper continuity of the damp proof membrane.
The DPC layer must be laid on top of the foundation or footing before the main wall construction above it can commence, as the DPC acts as a barrier to prevent rising damp.
Internal floor screeds and finishes should be applied only after the DPC is installed to ensure that the damp proof membrane is continuous with the floor damp proofing, preventing moisture ingress.
Fire stopping seals gaps around structural elements; the structural frame and steelwork must be in place and often fire-protected before compartmentation sealing can be applied.

predecessor: Service Rough-Ins (MEP rough-in, conduits, ductwork, piping)
rationale: Fire stopping is installed around penetrating services (cables, pipes, ducts). All rough-ins must be complete so that fire-stop sealants, collars, and wraps can be applied around the actual installed services.
Fire stopping is typically applied at joints, gaps, and penetrations in lined walls and ceilings. The linings must be installed to expose the edges and openings that require fire-stop treatment.

successor: Final Finishes (painting, wall coverings, ceiling tiles)
rationale: Fire-stop sealants and materials must be fully cured and inspected before final finishes are applied, as finishes would cover and obstruct access to fire-stop work.

successor: Commissioning & Testing (smoke control, fire alarm, pressurization tests)
rationale: Compartmentation integrity must be verified before commissioning tests that rely on compartment boundaries (e.g., smoke control, pressure differentials).

A site survey is necessary to understand the existing structures, boundaries, and conditions before a Party Wall Award can be drafted, as the award must account for the physical relationship between adjoining properties.
Detailed design drawings are required to show the proposed works affecting the party wall, which must be included in the Party Wall Award notice and agreement process.
Planning permission should be obtained first so that the scope of permitted works is known, which then informs the Party Wall Award process with certainty.

successor: Demolition / Soft Strip (adjacent to party wall)
rationale: Works affecting the party wall, such as demolition adjacent to it, cannot commence until the Party Wall Award is in place to legally protect the adjoining owner's rights and define the scope of work.

Excavation near or below the foundation level of adjoining properties requires a Party Wall Award to be in place first, as it legally governs the notification, schedule of condition, and protection measures.
A structural survey must be completed to determine if the existing roof structure can support the loft conversion, and to identify any necessary reinforcements before work begins.
Statutory building regulations approval must be obtained before commencing structural alterations to the roof and loft space to ensure legal compliance.

Planning permission must be secured prior to construction if the loft conversion changes the roof shape, increases volume beyond permitted development limits, or alters the external appearance of the dwelling.
After clearing and preparing the loft space, structural steel beams (RSJs) must be installed to support the new floor and redistribute loads from the removed roof structure.

Thermal insulation must be installed after the structural framing is in place but before plasterboarding to meet building regulation requirements for thermal efficiency in the converted habitable space.
A new staircase providing access to the loft must be installed after the structural floor is completed and before internal finishing can proceed.
Electrical wiring, outlets, lighting points, and any plumbing runs must be installed within the loft structure after framing but before insulation and plasterboard are applied.
Plasterboarding of walls and ceilings can only commence after all structural work, insulation, and services rough-in are complete within the converted loft space.
The site must be cleared of existing structures, debris, and obstructions before any new construction can begin.
Geotechnical surveys and foundation design must be completed to determine load-bearing requirements before excavation and foundation work can commence.

predecessor: Planning Permission and Building Regulations Approval
rationale: Statutory approvals from local authorities are legally required before any construction work can start.
Service routes and connection points must be designed and coordinated prior to foundation works to avoid later disruption.
The structural shell and roof of the extension must be weathertight before interior finishes can be applied.

successor: Electrical and Plumbing First Fix Installation
rationale: Cabling, conduits, and pipework for electrical and plumbing systems must be installed after the structure is in place but before walls are closed up.
Structural openings must be formed and ready before windows and doors can be fitted into the extension.
The roof structure and waterproof membrane must be completed to protect the interior from weather damage.
The roof structure (trusses or rafters) must be fully installed and secured to provide the framework that supports the roofing materials.
Roof decking (e.g., plywood or OSB) must be laid over the framing to create a solid substrate for the roofing membrane or shingles.
A waterproof underlayment (e.g., felt paper or synthetic membrane) must be installed over the roof deck to provide a secondary moisture barrier before the final roof covering is applied.
Gutters and downspouts are typically installed after the roofing material is in place so they can be properly secured to the roof edge and integrate with the roof's drainage system.

Work along the roof-wall interface (e.g., siding, fascia, or trim) is often completed after roofing to ensure flashings are properly integrated and finished appearance is achieved without damaging new roofing.
Scaffolding must be erected to provide safe access to the facade before any restoration work can begin.
A thorough inspection is required to identify damaged areas, assess structural integrity, and plan the restoration scope before work commences.
Dirt, grime, and biological growth must be removed from the facade surface before repairs, repointing, or coating can be applied effectively.
After the facade is restored (repaired, repointed, and surfaces prepared), a protective sealant or waterproofing coating can be applied to protect the restored work from moisture ingress.
Scaffolding can only be dismantled once all facade restoration work is complete, as the scaffold provides essential access and safety for the restoration activities.
The green roof layer must be installed on top of a structurally sound roof deck that can support its weight and provide a stable base.
A waterproofing membrane must be applied before the green roof layer to protect the building structure from water infiltration and root damage.
A root barrier must be placed before the green roof layers to prevent plant roots from damaging the waterproofing membrane and roof structure.
The drainage layer must be installed before the green roof growing medium to allow excess water to drain away from the root zone and roof structure.
Filter fabric must be placed between the drainage layer and growing medium to prevent fine soil particles from washing into and clogging the drainage system.
The green roof growing medium layer must be in place before vegetation can be planted, as plants require the soil/substrate for rooting and nutrient uptake.

While irrigation can be conceptually planned earlier, testing and final commissioning of the irrigation system typically occurs after the growing medium is in place to verify proper coverage and water distribution.

The building's foundation and substructure must be completed before facade work begins because the facade requires a stable structural base to be anchored to, and the building's load-bearing elements must be in place.
The main structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) must be erected before facade installation, as the facade panels or cladding are typically attached to or supported by the structural frame.
Floor slabs provide lateral support and diaphragm action for the structure, and the facade elements often align with floor levels for attachment and sealing.
Interior finishes (drywall, flooring, ceilings) should begin after the facade is enclosed to protect interior work from weather exposure and to ensure the building envelope is watertight.
Windows and glazing are installed as part of or immediately after the facade framing to complete the building envelope and provide weatherproofing before interior systems are activated.

Vegetation, topsoil, and debris must be removed from the foundation area before earth embankment construction can begin to ensure proper compaction and bonding between fill layers and the natural ground.

Soil bearing capacity, groundwater conditions, and subsurface stratigraphy must be assessed prior to embankment design and construction to ensure stability and prevent differential settlement or slope failure.
The base area must be excavated to competent material, benched if on a slope, and compacted to provide a stable foundation for the earth embankment fill.

Subsurface drainage systems such as blanket drains or toe drains must be placed at the foundation level before fill placement to control pore water pressures and prevent embankment saturation and instability.
The earth embankment fill must be completed, compacted to specification, and shaped to final grade before any pavement layers or surface courses can be placed on top.
Embankment side slopes must be constructed to final profile before erosion control measures such as riprap, turf reinforcement, or hydroseeding can be applied to protect the slopes.
Utilities such as conduits or pipes that traverse the embankment zone cannot be installed until the embankment has been raised to the required elevation to provide proper cover and support.

Although not always a strict requirement, it is good practice to allow a period of monitored settlement after embankment completion before constructing sensitive structures on top, to verify that post-construction settlement is within tolerable limits.
Formwork provides the mold into which concrete is poured, so it must be fully installed and braced before concrete placement.
Steel reinforcement bars must be tied and positioned within the formwork before concrete is poured to provide structural strength.
Any embedded plumbing, electrical conduits, sleeves, or anchor bolts must be placed and secured within the formwork before concrete is poured, as they cannot be added afterward.
Freshly poured concrete must undergo a designated curing period to develop its design strength before any loads are applied or subsequent work is performed.
Formwork cannot be removed until the poured concrete has gained sufficient strength (typically after curing) to be self-supporting.
The building structure must be evaluated and potentially reinforced to support the additional weight of the green roof system, including saturated growing medium, drainage layers, and vegetation.
A watertight roof deck with proper waterproof membrane and insulation must be installed before any green roof components to prevent water leakage into the building.
A root barrier layer must be placed over the waterproofing to prevent plant roots from penetrating and damaging the waterproof membrane.
The drainage layer (e.g., drainage mats, gravel, or plastic drainage panels) must be installed prior to the growing medium to manage excess water and prevent waterlogging of the vegetation.
The irrigation system must be tested and commissioned after the green roof components (growing medium and plants) are in place to ensure proper water distribution across the installed vegetation.
After installation, a period of establishment and monitoring is required to ensure the plants take root and thrive in the new growing medium.
A final inspection of the completed green roof system must occur after full installation to verify all layers are properly placed and the system is functioning before project handover.
Grab rails must be mounted on finished wall surfaces to ensure proper anchoring and to avoid damaging wall finishes during installation.
Safety signs indicating grab rail locations and weight capacities should be placed after grab rails are installed so they can be positioned correctly relative to the rails.
The underlying wall framing or substructure must be in place to provide structural support for grab rail anchoring points.
Grab rails must be installed before the final inspection can verify compliance with accessibility codes and standards.
Any plumbing rough-ins behind walls near grab rail locations must be completed before grab rail installation to avoid interference with mounting points and anchors.

predecessor: Structural assessment and floor loading verification
rationale: The stairlift requires adequate structural support, so a structural assessment must confirm that the staircase and surrounding floor can bear the load before installation begins.

predecessor: Electrical rough-in and wiring near staircase
rationale: Stairlifts require a power source (typically a nearby electrical outlet or hardwired connection), so electrical wiring must be in place before the unit can be connected and tested.
After physical installation, the stairlift must be tested for safe operation, including rail alignment, seat movement, and emergency stop functionality, before it can be placed into service.

successor: Handrail and guardrail adjustment or installation
rationale: While stairlifts often occupy the staircase space, adjusting or adding handrails/guardrails in remaining areas is easier after the stairlift is in place to ensure proper clearance, though this is a preferred sequence rather than a strict requirement.

Installing stairlift rails and brackets before final stair surface finishes prevents damage to the finished material and allows for proper alignment, though this is a construction best practice rather than an absolute necessity.
The lift shaft and supporting structure must be built before the elevator can be installed, as the elevator components are housed within the structural core.
The lift shaft must be waterproofed and sealed before elevator installation to protect mechanical and electrical components from water ingress.
Elevator car, guide rails and machinery must be in place before landing doors are installed and finished to ensure proper alignment and clearance.

successor: Electrical Supply & Control Wiring for Lift
rationale: The elevator must be physically installed before final electrical connections and control wiring can be terminated and tested.
The elevator must be fully installed and connected before it can be commissioned, tested and certified for safe operation.
Signage must be mounted on finished wall surfaces to ensure proper adhesion, alignment, and visual clarity.
Flooring must be in place so that signage placement can be coordinated with floor patterns, color contrast, and navigation cues that assist dementia wayfinding.
Signage visibility depends on proper lighting conditions; electrical and lighting work must be complete to ensure signs are illuminated or positioned correctly relative to light sources.
Wayfinding signage must be fully installed before final inspection so the entire navigation system can be tested, verified for accessibility compliance, and approved.

While furniture can technically be placed before signage, optimal workflow places signage first so that furniture layout can be arranged to respect clear sightlines and wayfinding paths for dementia users.
Structural framing, roofing, and external envelope must be completed to provide a weathertight and structurally sound environment before internal fitout works commence.
All concealed rough-in services (pipework, conduits, wiring within walls/ceilings) must be installed before fitout works such as wall lining, flooring, and cabinetry can proceed.

Age-in-place fitout includes installation of grab rails, shower seats, accessible cabinetry, and non-slip flooring; final painting and surface finishing must follow to avoid damage to finished surfaces and to achieve a seamless appearance.

Specialised age-in-place fixtures such as adjustable-height benches, wall-mounted fold-down seats, and accessible shelving can only be installed after the underlying fitout (walls, floors, supports) is complete and prepared for their attachment.

The age-in-place fitout must be fully installed and finished before commissioning activities and final handover inspections can verify compliance with accessibility standards and operational readiness.
The ground must be excavated, leveled, and compacted before ramp construction can begin to provide a stable foundation and ensure proper slope.
A concrete or gravel sub-base must be poured and cured to support the ramp structure and prevent settling or cracking.
Underground utilities must be located and clearly marked to avoid damage during excavation and ramp installation.
Handrails and guardrails must be installed after the ramp structure is in place to ensure proper alignment, anchoring, and code compliance.
Anti-slip surface treatments or textured finishes must be applied after ramp installation to ensure safe pedestrian access and ADA compliance.
The completed ramp must be inspected for slope compliance, width, landings, and railing safety before it can be opened for public use.
Electrical rough-in (wiring, conduit, power outlets) must be installed before the nurse call system can be commissioned, as the system requires power and physical cabling to function.
The nurse call system hardware (stations, pull cords, lights, control panels) must be physically installed before it can be tested and commissioned.
Commissioning validates that the system is operational, which must occur before formal acceptance testing by the client or authorities.

Commissioning is often completed before final finishes (e.g., wall trim, painting touch-ups) to allow access to devices and wiring for adjustments if needed, though this is a soft preference for workflow efficiency.
Modern nurse call systems often rely on network connectivity (data cabling, PoE switches) which must be installed prior to commissioning to enable communication between system components.

The subfloor must be properly prepared (cleaned, leveled, dried, and primed) to provide a stable, clean, and moisture-controlled base for specialist flooring materials such as vinyl, laminate, engineered wood, or epoxy coatings.

Underlayment (e.g., moisture barrier, acoustic underlay, or thermal insulation layer) must be laid prior to the specialist flooring to ensure correct performance, moisture protection, and sound insulation as per manufacturer specifications.

All rough-in work behind walls and below floors (electrical conduit, plumbing pipes, HVAC ductwork) must be completed and inspected before flooring is installed, as accessing these services after flooring would require destructive removal.

It is strongly preferred to complete wall plastering and painting before flooring to avoid damaging the finished floor surface with paint drips, plaster dust, or scaffolding marks, though it is not a physical impossibility to do it after.
Baseboards and skirtings are installed after the flooring is laid so they cover the expansion gap around the perimeter and provide a clean finished edge against the floor surface.

It is preferred to install flooring before built-in cabinetry and kitchen units are placed so that the flooring runs continuously underneath, allowing easier future replacement and avoiding visible cut lines, though cabinets can be installed first and flooring worked around them if necessary.

Doors must be hung after the finished floor level is established to ensure proper clearance at the bottom of the door based on the final floor height, preventing doors from dragging or having excessive gaps.

If the flooring is on a ground-bearing concrete slab, the slab must be fully cured (typically 28 days) and moisture-tested to ensure moisture vapor emissions are within acceptable limits for the specialist flooring adhesive and material.
The building must be fully enclosed and structurally complete to provide a weathertight, secure environment before commencing infection control finishes that require clean, controlled conditions.

All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work (ductwork, conduits, piping) must be completed behind walls and ceilings before infection control surfaces are installed, as accessing these systems afterward would damage the sterile finishes.
Fire suppression piping and sprinkler heads must be roughed in prior to ceiling grid and infection-control ceiling tile installation to avoid disrupting the sealed environment later.

The sealed, gasketed finishes (airtight walls, seamless flooring, sealed penetrations) must be in place before the HVAC system is balanced and pressure differentials are verified, as the room pressurization depends on the integrity of the infection control envelope.

All infection control surfaces, antimicrobial flooring, wall cladding, sealed fixtures, and cleanable trim must be fully installed before the terminal cleaning and sterilization process can be performed, as the cleaning protocol is designed for the finished infection control surfaces.
The structural floor slab must be in place to provide a stable load-bearing surface for the hot-desking station installation.
In-floor and in-wall power and data cabling must be roughed in before desks are placed, as running cables afterward would require moving or drilling through workstations.
Overhead mechanical and ceiling systems must be installed before furniture placement to avoid obstructions, dust fallout, and rework.
Final connection and trim-out of power/data outlets integrated into the desks can only be performed after the desks are positioned and anchored.

While furniture is typically placed before finish flooring to avoid damage, some projects install flooring first. Generally, placing desks before final carpet is a soft preference to protect the flooring from scratches and heavy loads.
Locker units require a level, finished slab on grade as their base support surface; the slab must be prepared and cured before lockers can be placed.
Electrical and data rough-in work (conduit, outlet boxes) must be completed in the walls and floor behind/under lockers before locker units are installed, as access is blocked afterward.
Locker units must be set in position before they can be aligned, leveled, and permanently anchored to the floor and walls.
While lockers can be painted before installation (pre-finished), final touch-up painting and finishing typically occur after installation to cover field damage and ensure uniform appearance.

Final floor finishes such as vinyl composition tile or ceramic tile are laid up to the locker base; lockers must be installed first so that flooring can be trimmed tightly against them for a clean edge.

Acoustic partitions and demountable walls require a completed rough-in framing (e.g., stud walls, track systems) and a solid substrate to be mounted onto or between. Without the structural frame in place, the partition cannot be installed.
Many demountable wall systems attach to overhead structures or ceiling grids for top support and stability. The ceiling grid or overhead structure must be in place before the wall can be set.

predecessor: MEP rough-in (electrical, plumbing, HVAC) within wall zones
rationale: Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-ins that run within or behind the partition zone must be completed before enclosing those runs with the acoustic partition, to avoid rework and allow access.
After the partition is installed, surface finishes such as joint compound, taping, painting, or trim can be applied to achieve the final aesthetic and acoustic seal.

successor: Final MEP trim-out and device mounting
rationale: Electrical outlets, switches, data ports, and HVAC grilles that penetrate or mount onto the partition must be installed after the wall is in place for proper alignment and fit.
The building's foundation must be excavated and prepared before any conversion work can begin, as the structural base needs to be in place.
The primary structural frame (steel or concrete) must be erected before internal fit-out and conversion work can commence, as the building's skeleton defines the spatial volumes to be converted.
After the shell and core conversion, the first fix of mechanical, electrical, and plumbing services can be installed within the newly configured spaces.
Once the Cat-A to Cat-B conversion reconfigures the base building layout, internal partition walls can be built to define individual rooms and zones.
After the conversion work reconfigures the spatial layout, finishing works such as flooring installation, ceiling installation, and painting can be applied to complete the interior.

Structural works (concrete frame, beams, columns, slabs) must be completed to provide the building envelope and load-bearing structure before any interior finishing can commence, as interior fit-out depends on a structurally sound and enclosed space.
The roof and building envelope must be made watertight before interior finishes are installed to prevent water damage to sensitive materials like drywall, flooring, and paint.
External walls and windows/glazing must be installed to enclose the building and provide weather protection before interior work proceeds.

Electrical conduits, plumbing pipes, HVAC ductwork, and other mechanical rough-ins must be installed within walls, ceilings, and floors before they are closed up by interior finishes (e.g., drywall, ceiling tiles, flooring).
Interior fit-out (partition walls, ceiling grids, subflooring) provides the substrate upon which final decorative finishes such as paint, wallpaper, and decorative coatings are applied.
Once interior partitions and rough-ins are complete, final flooring (tiles, hardwood, carpet, vinyl) can be installed over the prepared subfloor.
Cabinetry, built-in furniture, doors, and trim work are installed after the basic interior partitions and MEP rough-ins are complete, as they require precise measurements of finished spaces.
After interior fit-out creates the finished wall and ceiling surfaces, electricians and plumbers complete the final installation of outlets, switches, fixtures, and trim plates.

Although painting typically follows fit-out, in some sequences painting of ceiling and wall surfaces may begin before all joinery is installed, making this a soft preference rather than a hard constraint.
A feasibility study must be completed to determine project viability, budget, and high-level requirements before detailed space planning can begin.
The site must be selected and acquired because space planning requires knowledge of the physical dimensions, zoning constraints, and site conditions.
User needs, functional requirements, and space needs must be documented first to inform the programming of spaces.
Space programming defines the room sizes, adjacencies, and functional relationships that form the basis for schematic design development.
Accurate cost estimating requires knowledge of the programmed square footages and space types before detailed budgets can be prepared.
A workplace strategy defines the goals, requirements, and parameters for how space will be used, which must be understood before studying actual occupancy patterns.
The occupancy study provides data on space utilization and occupant density that directly informs the design program and space allocation decisions.
Findings from the occupancy study are essential inputs for comparing current usage against requirements and identifying space surpluses or deficits.
While not strictly required, understanding the physical condition of existing facilities provides helpful context for interpreting occupancy patterns.
Occupancy data such as headcounts, utilization rates, and activity patterns are fundamental inputs that drive workplace design concepts and layouts.

Decommissioning and strip-out cannot begin until the initial demolition and soft strip of interior finishes, fixtures, and non-structural elements has been completed, as these activities clear the space and prepare it for deeper strip-out work.
Hazardous materials such as asbestos and lead-based paint must be removed prior to decommissioning and strip-out to ensure worker safety and regulatory compliance before disturbing building systems.

All active utility services (electrical, gas, water, sewer, telecom) must be disconnected and isolated before strip-out work can safely commence to prevent electrocution, gas leaks, flooding, or other hazards.

Once decommissioning and strip-out is complete (removing all interior systems, equipment, and non-structural elements), structural demolition of remaining building elements can proceed safely and efficiently.

successor: Waste Sorting & Recycling of Salvaged Materials
rationale: After strip-out, salvaged materials (metal, timber, fixtures) should be sorted and recycled to maximise resource recovery and minimise landfill waste, though this is an environmental best practice rather than a physical necessity.
The chair frame provides the structural foundation that all other components attach to.
The wheeled base and casters must be attached to the frame before the chair can be considered assembled.
The seat cushion must be mounted onto the frame before the chair is complete.
The backrest must be secured to the frame for the chair to be functional.
The fully assembled chair must be completed before it can be packaged for shipment.
The overall office layout and desk placement must be determined before installing individual sit-stand desks to ensure proper spacing, power/data access, and workflow organization.
Flooring must be completed before placing desks to avoid damage to the flooring material and to ensure the desk sits on a finished, level surface.
Electrical outlets and wiring for desk power must be roughed in before the desk is positioned, as sit-stand desks often require access to power for motorized height adjustment.
Network and data cabling infrastructure must be in place before desks are installed so that connectivity can be provided to the workstation.
The desk must be physically installed and stable before computers, monitors, and other peripheral equipment can be placed on it.
While the desk must be installed first, the ergonomic assessment is a soft preference step that can occur after desk placement to fine-tune desk height and user setup for comfort.
The whiteboard/writable surface must be mounted on a stable wall surface; wall framing provides the structural backing needed for secure attachment.
Drywall provides the smooth, finished wall surface required before the whiteboard can be mounted; mounting directly to unfinished framing is not structurally appropriate for this component type.
Electrical rough-in for overhead lighting near the whiteboard area should be completed before the whiteboard is installed to avoid damaging the writable surface during electrical work.

While painting can be done before installation, final touch-ups around the mounted whiteboard edges are easier after installation to ensure clean lines; this is a soft preference for aesthetic quality.
Furniture such as collaborative seating and tables should only be placed after the whiteboard is installed to ensure proper spacing, sightlines, and accessibility to the writable surface.

The saw-tooth roof structure requires a stable structural frame to support its weight and transfer loads. The vertical columns and primary roof beams must be in place before the saw-tooth roof trusses or frames can be installed.
The structural frame that supports the saw-tooth roof depends on completed foundations for load bearing and stability.
The roof cladding (sheets, panels, or membranes) is applied directly onto the completed saw-tooth roof frame. The structure must be fully erected before any weatherproofing layers can be installed.

successor: Installation of Glazing / Windows (North-facing saw-tooth slopes)
rationale: The glazed sections or windows that are characteristic of saw-tooth roofs (typically on the steeper, north-facing slope) require the roof frame to be in place as their supporting structure.

Overhead mechanical, electrical, and plumbing services within the saw-tooth roof cavity (such as lighting fixtures, ventilation ducts, and sprinkler lines) can only be routed and installed after the roof structure is complete and accessible from below.
The structural frame and roof must be in place to provide the supporting structure onto which the clerestory glazing band is installed.
The roof deck provides the vertical support and weatherproof base against which the clerestory glazing band is positioned and sealed.
Interior finishes such as ceiling installation must follow glazing to avoid damage from glass installation and to allow proper integration with the glazing system.
Weatherproofing and flashing details around the clerestory band must be completed after the glazing is in place to achieve a watertight seal.

While exterior cladding can technically be sequenced before or after, it is typically installed after the clerestory glazing to ensure proper alignment and continuity of the building envelope, though this is a soft preference.
The portal frame columns require anchor bolts and concrete foundations to transfer loads to the ground; steel cannot be erected without completed foundations.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and compacted before crane access and steel erection can safely commence.
Underground services (drainage, conduits) must be laid before steel columns are placed to avoid excavation conflicts under the frame.
Roof purlins are supported directly by the portal frame rafters; the main structural frame must be in place to provide the supporting structure.
Wall girts and cladding panels are attached to the portal frame columns; the frame must be erected to act as the supporting substructure.
The crane rail must be mounted on a stable and level foundation or substructure (e.g., crane beams, support columns, or runway girders) which must be constructed and cured first to bear the load.

predecessor: Steel Structural Steelwork / Building Frame Erection
rationale: The overhead crane rail is typically supported by the building's structural steel columns and roof girders; the main steel frame must be erected before the crane runway beams and rails can be installed.

successor: Overhead Travelling Crane Installation / Trolley Mounting
rationale: The crane rail must be completely installed, aligned, and fixed before the overhead travelling crane itself (bridge, trolley, and hoist) can be placed onto the rails.
Load testing and commissioning of the overhead crane can only be performed once the rail is installed and the crane is mounted on it.

The electrical supply system (busbar or conductor rail) for the crane is typically mounted parallel to the crane rail and must be installed after the rail is in its final position to ensure proper alignment and clearance.
The ground must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and topsoil, and excavated to the required formation level before any slab concrete can be placed.
A well-compacted granular or lean-mix sub-base layer is required to provide a uniform bearing surface and prevent differential settlement under the slab.
A damp-proof membrane must be laid over the sub-base to prevent moisture migration from the ground into the concrete slab.
Freshly placed concrete requires controlled curing to achieve design strength and minimize shrinkage cracking; curing starts immediately after finishing the slab surface.
Ground-bearing slabs serve as the base for load-bearing walls; walls cannot be started until the slab has gained sufficient strength to support construction loads.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and any existing structures before excavation and foundation work can begin, as groundworks require unobstructed access to the soil.
Accurate surveying and marking of building positions, levels, and boundaries is required before any excavation or foundation construction to ensure correct positioning.
Foundations must be complete and cured before floor slabs can be poured, as the slab rests on or ties into the foundation system.
Foundation trenches and excavations provide access for laying drainage pipes, water mains, and other underground services that must be routed through or around the foundation footprint.
The load-bearing foundations must be fully completed and cured before the steel or concrete structural frame can be erected on top of them.

The structural steel frame provides the primary load-bearing support and attachment points for cladding and roofing panels; without the frame in place, there is no structure to attach the cladding and roofing to.

The concrete slab or deck forms the working platform and base for walls and roof structure; cladding and roofing installation requires a stable, completed floor/deck to work from and to ensure proper alignment.

Roof trusses or rafters define the roof geometry and provide the substrate onto which roofing materials (e.g., sheeting, tiles, membrane) are directly fastened; they must be erected before any roof cladding can be applied.

Cladding and roofing enclose the building envelope; windows and doors are typically installed after the cladding is in place so that the cladding can be properly flashed and sealed around openings to ensure weathertightness.

While not a strict physical necessity (internal linings can technically proceed in parallel), it is standard practice to have the building envelope closed and weathertight before installing interior finishes to protect them from moisture and weather damage.
The ground must be excavated, leveled, and compacted before a concrete slab can be poured to provide a stable, uniform sub-base and prevent differential settlement.
Formwork (shuttering) must be erected to define the slab edges, thickness, and shape; without it, the wet concrete would not be contained and would not achieve the correct dimensions.
Steel reinforcement bars or welded wire mesh must be positioned and tied within the formwork before pouring concrete to provide tensile strength and control cracking in the finished slab.

All underground plumbing pipes, drainage lines, and electrical conduits must be laid and inspected before the slab is poured, as they cannot be accessed after the concrete is in place without breaking the slab.

A vapour barrier (e.g., polyethylene sheet) must be placed over the sub-base and beneath the slab to prevent moisture migration from the ground into the concrete, which can cause dampness and flooring failures.

After the concrete is poured, it must undergo a controlled curing period (typically 7–28 days) to achieve design strength and prevent shrinkage cracks before any loads or subsequent work can be applied.
The formwork can only be removed after the concrete has sufficiently hardened and gained enough strength to support its own weight and any incidental loads.
Load-bearing walls and partitions are built on top of the finished slab; the slab must be completed and hardened to provide a level, stable working platform and structural base for the walls.

While it is physically possible to start finishing work after the slab is laid, it is typically delayed until curing is complete and the building envelope is closed to protect the finish; this is a soft preference for quality and durability rather than a strict physical requirement.
The kiosk foundation and utility connections (power, data) must be roughed in at the site location before the kiosk unit can be placed and connected.
The kiosk structure must be fully installed and enclosed before interior shelving, displays, refrigeration, and merchandise can be stocked inside.
The kiosk must be set in place before final connections to power and data networks can be completed at the unit.

While signs can theoretically be installed earlier and attached later, it is standard practice to place exterior signage and branding only after the kiosk is fully positioned to ensure proper alignment.
All systems (POS, lighting, refrigeration) can only be tested after the kiosk is fully installed, connected, and stocked.
The modular partition walls require a level, cured floor slab or deck as a stable base for installation and anchoring.

predecessor: Overhead Structural Grid / Ceiling Grid Completion
rationale: Head tracks for modular partitions must be fastened to the overhead structure or ceiling grid, which must be in place first.

predecessor: Mechanical, Electrical, Plumbing (MEP) Rough-In Above Ceiling
rationale: Overhead conduit, ductwork, and piping must be installed before partition walls are erected, as the walls will block access to overhead spaces.
Finish coatings and trims are applied to the completed partition surfaces; the walls must be fully erected and stable to receive finishes.
Electrical outlets, switches, and data ports are integrated into the modular wall panels; these can only be installed once the wall system is in place and aligned.
Raised access flooring requires a clean, level structural slab or subfloor as its base. The floor panels cannot be installed until the underlying substrate is complete and properly prepared.
Electrical cables, data cables, HVAC ductwork, and piping that run beneath the raised floor must be installed before the access floor panels are laid, as the panels cover and enclose these services.
The final floor finish (e.g., carpet tiles, vinyl, or other surface covering) is typically applied on top of the raised access floor panels after they are fully installed and leveled.

While partition walls can be built on top of raised access floors, it is generally preferred to complete the floor first to ensure a level base for wall framing and to avoid damaging the floor system.

After the raised access floor panels are installed, final leveling and adjustment of the pedestal system must be completed to ensure a uniform, stable walking surface before any furniture or equipment is placed.

The building must be structurally complete (slabs, columns, walls) before any interior fit-out work can commence, as the furniture installation requires a fully enclosed and structurally stable environment.

All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-ins (conduits, piping, wiring) must be installed behind walls and in ceilings before furniture placement, otherwise furniture would block access and require costly rework.

Flooring, ceiling tiles, and wall finishes must be fully installed and cured before furniture is brought in, to avoid damaging finished surfaces and to ensure proper alignment of furniture with floor and wall layouts.

Once all furniture and loose fit-out items are in place, the space must be thoroughly cleaned and all building systems commissioned/balanced, as furniture installation generates dust and debris and final adjustments require the space to be fully furnished.
End users cannot occupy the building until all furniture, workstations, and loose equipment are installed and ready for use, as the fit-out provides the functional workplace environment.

The mounting bracket or support structure must be securely installed and anchored to the wall or structure before the digital display screen can be attached, as the screen physically depends on the bracket for support.

Electrical conduit, wiring, and power outlets must be roughed in and brought to the display location before the screen can be connected to power, as the screen requires a finished electrical supply to function.
Data cabling (Ethernet, HDMI, or other signal cables) must be pulled and terminated at the display location before the screen can be connected to the building's network and content management system.

The physical screen must be installed and powered on before software configuration, content uploading, and calibration can be performed, as the system needs to be operational to test and load the wayfinding content.
The digital display must be mounted and aligned in its opening before any decorative bezels, trim pieces, or flush-mount covers can be installed around it to achieve a finished appearance.

Structural framing, slabs, columns, and load-bearing walls must be completed before interior fit-out begins, as the structural shell provides the physical enclosure and load-bearing support for all interior partitions, finishes, and MEP systems.

The roof, exterior walls, windows, and doors must be weathertight to protect interior finishes, materials, and equipment from weather damage during fit-out activities such as drywall, painting, flooring, and cabinetry installation.

Rough-in work for ductwork, plumbing pipes, electrical conduits, and wiring within walls and ceilings must be completed before interior finishes (drywall, ceiling tiles, flooring) are installed, as these systems need to be embedded within the structure and accessing them later would require demolition.

Interior fit-out such as partitions, ceiling grids, flooring, cabinetry, and trim must be installed before final finishes (painting, wall coverings, decorative elements) and systems commissioning can occur, as these delicate final steps require the interior surfaces to be fully prepared and ready.

Interior construction including wall completion, ceiling installation, and floor preparation must be finished before installing trim-out elements such as light fixtures, switches, outlets, diffusers, thermostats, and plumbing fixtures, as these devices mount onto or into completed surfaces.
The structural frame and core must be completed to provide the physical space and support for MEP systems; MEP rough-in cannot proceed without walls, floors, and structural openings in place.
The building envelope must be weathertight to protect MEP rough-in work (electrical, plumbing, HVAC) from water damage and environmental exposure.
MEP rough-in (conduit, piping, ductwork inside walls/ceilings) must be completed before walls and ceilings are enclosed with drywall, plaster, or ceiling tiles.
Rough plumbing and electrical rough-ins must be in place before floor and wall finishes are applied, as finishes would cover access points and need to be cut around penetrations.
Rough-in work (conduit, piping, ductwork) must be installed prior to trim-out (switches, outlets, fixtures, registers) since trim-out connects to and finishes the rough-in systems.
The structural steel frame must be fully erected and stabilized to provide the load-bearing support onto which the curtain wall and facade system is anchored.
Floor slabs must be poured and cured to establish the horizontal structural diaphragms and tie-in points required for facade alignment and anchoring.
The roof structure must be in place to provide the top anchoring point and weather seal for the curtain wall system, and to allow for overhead crane access for panel installation.
Window glazing and weather seals are installed directly into the curtain wall framing after the facade panels and mullions are in place to ensure a watertight and airtight building envelope.
Interior partitions and drywall must follow facade installation to allow for proper alignment with the exterior wall system and to avoid weather intrusion damage to interior finishes.
All systems and equipment must be physically installed before they can be commissioned and tested for proper operation.
Electrical connections and rough-in work must be completed to provide power for systems testing during commissioning.
Plumbing systems must be roughed in and connected before they can be pressure-tested and commissioned.
HVAC ductwork and components must be installed before the system can be balanced, tested, and commissioned.
Commissioning and testing of all building systems must be successfully completed before final inspections can be conducted and the project closed out.

Structural and building works must be substantially complete before landscape and public realm works begin, as heavy machinery, material deliveries, and construction traffic would damage finished landscape surfaces, planting, and paving. Landscape works are typically the final finishing phase after all major building and infrastructure is in place.

All underground drainage, water, gas, electrical, and telecom services must be installed and covered before landscape works commence, otherwise the landscape would need to be dug up and reinstated, causing rework and damage.

The sub-base and preparation for hard landscaping elements such as paving, kerbs, and footpaths must be completed before the final surface laying and soft landscape planting can proceed, as they form the structural foundation for the public realm.

Landscape and public realm works are typically the last external finishing activities before project handover, as they provide the final aesthetic and functional environment around the building. The project cannot be considered complete until these finishing touches are in place.

The main landscape and public realm installation (including planting beds, trees, turf) must be completed before the establishment/maintenance period can begin, during which plants are watered, nurtured, and monitored to ensure they thrive.

A thorough structural assessment and existing conditions survey must be completed before any adaptive reuse work begins to understand the building's current state, identify deficiencies, and determine feasibility of the proposed new use.
Asbestos, lead paint, and other hazardous materials must be identified and removed/abated before construction work commences to ensure worker and occupant safety.
Architectural and engineering designs, including structural modifications, MEP upgrades, and code compliance strategies, must be finalized before construction activities can proceed.
After refurbishment is complete, building systems (HVAC, electrical, plumbing, fire protection) must be commissioned and tested to verify proper operation before occupancy.
Upon completion of all adaptive reuse and refurbishment work, a final inspection by authorities and issuance of a certificate of occupancy are required before the building can be used.

predecessor: Concrete Slab Foundation for Council Chamber
rationale: The raised dais requires a stable, level concrete slab foundation to be poured and cured before any framing or platform construction can begin on top of it.

predecessor: Rough Electrical and Data Rough-In for Dais
rationale: Electrical conduit, data cabling, and junction boxes must be installed within the slab or subfloor before the dais platform is fully enclosed and finished.

successor: Finish Flooring and Carpet Installation on Dais
rationale: The structural platform of the dais must be fully built to provide a substrate before finished flooring materials (carpet, tile, or wood) can be laid.
Custom millwork (front panels, railings, built-in lectern surrounds) attaches to the completed dais structure, so the platform must be erected first.

successor: Installation of Dais Seating and Podium
rationale: Chairs, the presiding officer's podium, and any fixed seating on the dais must be placed after the raised platform is fully constructed and finished to ensure proper anchoring and alignment.
Acoustic panels require a structural frame (stud wall or furring channels) to be mounted on. Without the frame, there is no support structure to attach the panels to.
All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work within walls must be completed before acoustic panels are installed, as once the panels are in place, access to wall cavities is blocked.
Acoustic insulation (e.g., mineral wool bats) must be placed in wall cavities before acoustic panelling is installed to achieve the desired sound absorption performance.
It is preferable to complete painting and finishing of adjacent walls, ceilings, and trim before installing acoustic panels to avoid damaging the delicate panel surfaces.
Flooring is often installed after acoustic panelling to allow for neat transitions at the base of the panels and to avoid damaging finished floors during panel installation.
The flag mast requires a stable foundation (concrete base) to be constructed first to support the structural load of the mast.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and prepared before the flag mast foundation can be excavated and poured.
Typically, the flag mast is installed before surrounding landscaping is completed to avoid damaging finished landscaping during installation.
The flag and mast must be fully installed and operational before any formal ceremony or public unveiling can take place.
Any underground electrical conduits for lighting the flag must be laid before the mast foundation is poured, to embed conduits properly.
The structural frame must be supported on properly designed and constructed foundations; excavation and foundation work must be completed before any steel or concrete frame erection can begin.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and prepared before any structural work can commence to provide a stable working platform and access for cranes and equipment.

Underground piping, conduits, and utilities that pass beneath the building footprint must be installed and backfilled before the frame is erected to avoid conflicts and the need for later excavation under the structure.
The roof structure requires the completed frame to provide support; the frame must be in place before roof trusses, decking, and roofing materials can be installed.
Exterior walls, cladding, and curtain walls depend on the structural frame for attachment and support; the frame must be complete before enclosure can proceed.

The building's structural frame (steel or concrete) must be complete to provide the load-bearing support and attachment points for the curtain wall system. Without the primary structure in place, there is no substrate to anchor the facade.
Floor slabs must be cast or installed at each level to provide working platforms, slab edge anchorage, and fire-stopping support for the curtain wall.

While interior walls can begin before full glazing, completing the facade first seals the building envelope, protecting interior work from weather and allowing environmental control. This is a strong preference but not a physical impossibility.

MEP work can begin before facade completion, but final connections near the perimeter and coordination with curtain wall penetrations benefit from the facade being in place. This is a logical sequencing preference.
The building envelope must be watertight and weather-sealed before installing finished flooring, ceiling tiles, and interior finishes to prevent water damage, mold growth, and material degradation.
The ground must be excavated, leveled, and compacted to provide a stable foundation before ramp foundations and lift pits can be constructed.
Concrete footings, slab, or lift pit must be poured and cured to provide a structural base for mounting ramps and lifts.
Any electrical conduits, drainage pipes, or other utilities that will run beneath the ramp or lift area must be installed before the ramp/lift structure is placed to avoid rework.

Ramp surfaces, landings, and lift surrounds must be installed so that final paving, coatings, slip-resistant finishes, and edge trims can be applied seamlessly up to the installed ramp and lift components.
Railings are typically anchored into the ramp structure or alongside the lift platform; the ramp/lift must be in place to set rail post locations and ensure compliance with accessibility codes.
A structural assessment must be completed before refurbishment to ensure the building can safely accommodate the planned renovations and to identify any necessary structural repairs.
Hazardous materials like asbestos must be identified and removed before any refurbishment work begins to ensure worker and occupant safety.
The refurbishment design and plans must be reviewed and formally approved by relevant authorities before construction work can commence.

successor: Reinstatement of Council Chamber Furniture and Equipment
rationale: After the refurbishment (painting, flooring, lighting, etc.) is complete, furniture, audiovisual equipment, and other fittings can be reinstalled.

successor: Final Inspection and Handover of Council Chamber
rationale: A final quality inspection and official handover of the refurbished chamber can only occur after all refurbishment activities are finished.
Scaffolding must be erected to provide safe access to the facade for conservation and restoration work.
The facade must be cleaned to remove dirt, pollutants, and biological growth before conservation treatments can be applied effectively.
Any structural repairs or stabilization (e.g., fixing cracks, anchoring loose elements) must be completed before cosmetic/conservation restoration begins to ensure safety and durability.
Waterproofing or protective coatings should be applied after restoration work is complete to seal and protect the conserved surfaces.
Scaffolding can only be dismantled after all facade conservation and restoration work is finished, as it provides the necessary access platform.
Structural integrity must be verified before installing accessibility features like ramps, lifts, or handrails to ensure they can be safely supported.
Existing non-structural elements that obstruct accessibility upgrades (e.g., narrow door frames, non-compliant toilets, steps) must be removed before new accessible features can be installed.
Plumbing and electrical rough-ins for accessible toilets, sinks, automatic door openers, and emergency call systems must be in place before final accessibility fixtures are installed.
Accessible routes, ramps, and tactile indicators must be installed before final floor finishes are applied to ensure seamless transitions and proper alignment.
All accessibility features (ramps, handrails, accessible washrooms, door widths) must be fully installed before the building inspector or accessibility consultant can certify compliance with codes.
The location and quantity of asbestos-containing materials must be identified before remediation can be planned and executed.
Surveyors and remediation crews need site access, utility disconnections, and safety perimeters established before entering the building.
Asbestos must be removed prior to any demolition or soft strip to prevent airborne contamination and protect workers.
Renovation and finishing work must occur in an asbestos-free environment to meet health and safety regulations.
HVAC systems should not be installed or operated until asbestos abatement is complete to avoid spreading fibers through ductwork.

The building structure and fabric (roof, walls, floors) must be in place and watertight before M&E installation can begin, as M&E equipment and cabling need to be mounted on or within the structure, and exposure to weather could damage sensitive electrical and mechanical components.

Conduits, sleeves, and chases for wiring and piping must be embedded in the structure (e.g., in slabs or walls) before the main M&E equipment and cabling are installed, as these pathways are part of the primary building fabric and cannot be added easily once M&E fit-out is underway.

M&E services (ductwork, pipes, cables) are typically concealed above ceilings, within partitions, or under raised floors. Therefore, M&E installation must be completed and tested before finishing works close off access to these spaces.
All mechanical and electrical systems must be fully installed and operational before they can be tested, commissioned, and handed over to the client for use.

Inspection and approval of M&E rough-in work (concealed conduits, wiring, piping) must occur before finishing works cover them up, but this inspection logically follows the rough-in portion of the M&E upgrade; however, the full M&E upgrade completion is needed before final commissioning.
Power conduits, cables, and outlets for AV and digital systems must be roughed in before the actual AV equipment can be installed.
Ductwork, piping, and electrical trunk lines running above ceilings must be completed before installing ceiling-mounted AV components like speakers and projectors.
Walls and structural supports must be framed to provide mounting surfaces and enclosed pathways for low-voltage cabling and equipment.

successor: Ceiling and Wall Finish (Drywall, Painting, Cladding)
rationale: AV cabling, back boxes, and mounting brackets must be installed within the wall and ceiling cavities before they are enclosed by finishes.
All AV hardware (screens, speakers, processors) must be physically installed and connected before software configuration, network integration, and system testing can begin.

Security systems require power and data cabling infrastructure which is typically installed during electrical rough-in. The security system components cannot be installed or connected until the electrical wiring and conduits are in place.

Security systems (cameras, access control, alarms) depend on low voltage cabling (Cat6, alarm wiring) for communication and power. The cabling must be run before security devices can be mounted and connected.

predecessor: Interior Wall Framing and Drywall (Rough Stage)
rationale: Security cables and sensors are typically installed within wall cavities before drywall is closed up. Conduit and junction boxes for security devices must be placed during wall rough-in stage.

Security devices such as motion sensors, keypads, and cameras are surface-mounted or flush-mounted; final interior finishes should be applied after all security hardware installation to avoid damage, paint overspray, or requiring rework.

After security devices are physically installed and connected, the entire system must be tested and commissioned to verify functionality, coverage, and integration with other building systems before building occupancy.
A condition survey establishes the current state and significance of the listed building, providing essential baseline documentation and justification required to support the consent application.

A Heritage Impact Assessment must be completed to evaluate the effect of proposed works on the building's special architectural or historic interest. This assessment is a mandatory supporting document for the consent application.
Detailed drawings, specifications, and design proposals for the proposed works must be prepared first, as these form the core submission required for the consent application.

successor: Consent Decision Issued by Local Authority
rationale: The local planning authority must receive and process the consent application before they can issue a formal decision (grant or refusal) on the proposed works.

Physical works to a listed building must not begin until listed building consent has been granted, as proceeding without consent is a criminal offense under the Planning (Listed Buildings and Conservation Areas) Act 1990.

The noticeboard structure requires a stable, level base. Site preparation including clearing, grading, and pouring a concrete foundation or setting posts must be completed before the noticeboard frame can be installed.
All lumber, hardware, fasteners, glass/acrylic panels, and weatherproofing materials must be acquired and cut to size before assembly of the noticeboard structure can begin.

The protective transparent panels (glass or acrylic) that cover the posted notices must be installed after the main structural frame is fully assembled and securely mounted to ensure proper fit and protection from the elements.

Weatherproofing sealants, caulking, and any protective coatings should be applied to the completed noticeboard structure to seal joints and prevent moisture damage before the unit is put into service.

Painting, staining, or applying community signage/decals to the noticeboard is aesthetically best done after the structure is fully assembled, though it could theoretically be done on pre-assembled components as a soft preference for quality and finish consistency.
The shade canopy structure requires a stable, level foundation (such as concrete footings or slab) to be cast and cured before canopy posts or columns can be anchored.
Any electrical, plumbing, or drainage lines that must run beneath the canopy area need to be installed and backfilled before the canopy footings are poured to avoid future excavation conflicts.
Lighting fixtures, fans, or outlets mounted to or within the canopy structure cannot be installed until the structural frame and roofing of the canopy are in place.
While flooring can technically be installed before the canopy, it is preferable to complete the canopy first to protect the finished surface from weather and debris during overhead work.
Final landscaping, planting, and decorative elements around the canopy base should be performed after the structure is complete to avoid damage during construction and to allow accurate grading.
Floor slab/deck must be in place to provide a stable, level surface for installing seating and rest furniture.
Interior walls define the spatial boundaries and room layouts required before placing seating and rest furniture.
Electrical wiring and outlet boxes must be installed in walls/floors before furniture placement to avoid rework.

successor: Final Floor Finishing (if furniture is loose)
rationale: If seating is loose (not built-in), final floor finishing like carpet or tile can be installed before bringing in furniture to avoid damage.
Soft preference: painting and trim finishing can be done before furniture to avoid splatter, but in some sequences furniture may be installed first to protect floors.

The project team must be assembled and project scope defined before engaging the community, as the team needs to prepare materials, logistics, and have a clear understanding of project goals to facilitate the workshop effectively.
Key community stakeholders and participants must be identified, mapped, and contacted in advance to ensure their attendance and meaningful participation in the co-design workshop.
A preliminary site analysis must be completed so that the workshop can present relevant site context, constraints, and opportunities to inform community input during co-design activities.

Feedback, ideas, and priorities gathered from the community during the workshop directly inform and shape the initial design concepts; design development cannot meaningfully proceed without this input.
The outputs and findings from the workshop must be documented, analyzed, and reported before they can be used to guide subsequent design decisions and be shared with broader stakeholders.
The ground must be graded, leveled, and compacted before any paving can be laid, otherwise the pavement will crack and settle unevenly.
