All underground pipes, conduits, and drainage lines must be installed before paving to avoid cutting or disturbing the finished pavement later.
A crushed stone or granular base layer must be compacted to provide a stable foundation for the paving material.
Curbs and gutters are typically formed and poured after the base paving is installed to ensure proper alignment and drainage transitions.
Landscaping is often done after paving to avoid soil and mud being tracked onto the new pavement, but it is a soft preference as some planting can be done before paving in certain sequences.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated to provide a stable foundation base before any structural erection can begin.
Concrete foundations (footings, piers, or slab) must be poured and cured to support the structural loads of the pavilion before steel or timber framing can be erected.

Underground electrical conduit, water lines, and drainage pipes must be laid beneath the slab or within the foundation footprint before the structure goes up, as retrofitting would require costly excavation.
The primary structural frame (columns, beams, trusses) must be fully erected and braced to provide the supporting framework for roof panels and wall cladding.

While some MEP routing can begin once the frame is up, it is a soft preference because wiring and ductwork could theoretically be installed concurrently if carefully coordinated; however, standard practice waits for the structure to be enclosed.
Vegetation and debris must be cleared from the site before any planting can occur to provide a clean, workable surface for landscape installation.
The soil must be graded to final contours and properly prepared (e.g., tilled, amended) to create a suitable growing medium for plant materials before planting can begin.
All buried utilities (water, sewer, gas, electrical, irrigation lines) must be installed first to avoid digging up and damaging newly planted landscapes.
Drainage systems, French drains, and subsurface preparation must be completed before planting to ensure proper water management and prevent soil erosion or waterlogging around new plants.
Final cleanup, mulch application, and finishing touches occur after all planting is complete to avoid soiling or damaging newly installed landscape materials.
Final inspections and walkthroughs for project closeout must occur after landscape planting and establishment are finished to verify all work is complete.

successor: Erosion and Sediment Control Final Measures
rationale: Once vegetation is established, final erosion control measures (e.g., hydroseeding, permanent stabilization) can be applied, though temporary measures may already be in place; this is a logical sequencing preference for project phasing.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and obstacles before trenching can begin to allow unimpeded access and accurate utility layout.
Rough grading establishes the proper elevations and drainage patterns needed to set trench depths and align utilities correctly before final grading.
Temporary power, water, and sanitation must be available on site to support trenching equipment and worker safety during excavation.
Trenches must be backfilled and compacted immediately after utility installation to protect buried services and restore safe working surfaces.
Underground utility connections must be laid and inspected before any concrete foundations or slabs are poured to avoid re-cutting concrete for service entry points.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and graded before artwork can be installed to ensure a stable, safe foundation and proper drainage.
Any underground foundations, footings, conduit, or utility connections needed to support or power the artwork must be in place before the artwork is installed.
Walkways, plazas, and other paved surfaces that serve as the setting or base for the artwork should be completed before artwork installation to avoid damage and ensure proper alignment.

Landscaping around the artwork should be done after installation to avoid damage to plants from equipment and to ensure the artwork's placement is accurately integrated with the surrounding vegetation.
Final cleanup activities should follow artwork installation to remove any debris, packaging, or protective coverings from the artwork and its surroundings.

A community engagement and activation strategy must be planned before ongoing programming can commence, as the planning defines the objectives, target audiences, and initial schedule for activation activities.

predecessor: Site Preparation and Activation Infrastructure Setup
rationale: Physical infrastructure such as gathering spaces, seating areas, event platforms, signage, and utility connections must be in place before ongoing community activation events and programs can be held on site.
Key community partners, vendors, volunteers, and facilitators must be identified and contracted before recurring activation programming can be launched.
The structural frame must be complete to provide a stable mounting surface and support for the shopfront facade system.
The ground floor slab must be cast and cured to provide a level base and anchorage point for the shopfront facade system.
Waterproofing at structural interfaces (e.g., slab edges, beam faces) must be in place before the facade is installed to prevent water ingress behind the finished facade.

successor: Internal Finishes (Plasterboard/Wall Linings) Adjacent to Shopfront
rationale: Internal wall linings that abut or tie into the shopfront facade system should be installed after the facade frame is in place to ensure proper sealing and finishing at the interface.
The facade frame and structural supports must be installed first to provide the framework into which glazing panels and windows are set and sealed.
The structural frame and floor slabs must be complete to provide the supporting structure and substrate onto which demountable partition walls are installed.
Electrical and data cables that run within or behind the partition walls must be roughed-in before the walls are erected, as access to routing paths becomes restricted after wall installation.
HVAC ductwork that passes through or above the partition zone must be installed before walls are placed to avoid cutting or rework of the partition system.
Final finishes such as paint, wallpaper, or panel cladding are applied after the partition wall frame and panels are fully installed, as the wall must exist as a substrate for these finishes.

Electrical outlets, switches, and data ports must be installed into the finished partition wall surface after the wall is erected, as the wall provides the mounting surface for these trim-out components.
The ground must be prepared, leveled, and graded before the pylon foundation can be poured or the pylon structure erected, ensuring a stable base.
The concrete foundation footing for the pylon must be excavated, formed, and poured, then cured sufficiently to bear the load before the pylon structure can be mounted.

predecessor: Electrical Conduit and Underground Wiring Installation
rationale: Electrical supply conduits and underground wiring must be laid in the trench to the pylon base before the foundation is poured or the pylon is set, to allow internal illumination.
The pylon structural frame must be erected and anchored before sign panels, cabinet faces, or vinyl graphics can be attached to the structure.
The pylon must be fully installed and wired before electricians can connect the internal lighting fixtures, test illumination, and commission the sign.
The structural frame (e.g., building columns, walls, or roof structure) must be in place to provide a mounting surface and load-bearing support for the canopy or awning.
Roofing and waterproofing where the awning meets the building envelope must be completed to prevent water intrusion behind or above the canopy/awning.
It is often easier to install cladding and finishes up to the awning after the awning is in place to ensure a clean interface and weather seal, though in some sequences cladding could be done first.

If the canopy/awning includes integrated lighting or electrical components, the electrical rough-in (conduit, wiring) must follow after the canopy structure is installed to route wiring through the awning frame.
Signage attached to or suspended from the awning should be installed after the awning is fully secured and load-tested to ensure proper support.
The roller shutter is typically mounted onto or within a window frame or structural opening. The frame/opening must be in place to provide a secure fixing surface.

predecessor: Rough electrical wiring to shutter location
rationale: Electrical supply must be roughed in to the shutter location so that the motorized shutter can be connected and powered during installation.

successor: Final electrical connection and testing of shutter
rationale: After the shutter is physically mounted, electrical connections can be finalized and the motor/controls tested for proper operation.

successor: Install shutter controls and automation system
rationale: Control switches, remote receivers, or building automation interfaces are installed and configured after the shutter body is in place to ensure proper integration and wiring.

Finishing work such as plastering, painting, or cladding around the shutter can be done after installation, but this is often a soft preference as some finishing may be completed beforehand to avoid damage to the shutter.
The roof structure requires the main building frame and walls to be completed first to provide structural support and attachment points.
Roof covering materials (sheets, tiles, or membranes) can only be installed after the roof structure/framework is in place.
Ceiling installation typically follows roof structure completion, though it could theoretically be sequenced differently depending on design.
Electrical work at the roof level is often easier after the structure is in place, but could be partially pre-installed.
Gutters, downspouts, and drainage systems physically require the roof structure to be present for attachment and routing.
Public seating furniture requires a stable, level base. The concrete slab or foundation must be completed and cured before benches, seats, or fixed seating can be installed on top.
The surrounding ground must be graded and drainage installed to prevent standing water and erosion around seating areas. Installing seating before grading risks instability and water damage.
Soft preference: Landscaping can be done before seating, but it is often easier to install seating first to avoid damaging new plantings, then complete final landscaping around the furniture.
Seating furniture is typically anchored into or placed on finished paving surfaces. The paving surface must be completed first to provide the mounting surface, so seating must come after paving.
The space cannot be opened for public use until seating furniture is installed, secured, and inspected for safety.
The roof structure requires the building's structural frame (walls, beams, columns) to be in place to provide support and attachment points for roof trusses, rafters, and decking.
Wall sheathing provides lateral bracing for the structure and is needed before roof installation to ensure the building envelope is properly supported.
Roof overhangs and flashings must be installed before exterior siding to ensure proper weatherproofing and to allow siding to be fitted against roof elements for a watertight seal.
While not physically required, completing the roof first protects interior work from weather damage, making it a strong soft preference to avoid delays and material damage.
Ceiling drywall or ceiling finishes require the roof structure to be complete so that overhead support and attachments are in place before enclosing the space below.
Structural frame must be in place to provide support and define the building envelope before shopfronts and partitions can be installed.
External walls must be completed to enclose the building before internal shopfront and partition work can commence.
Roof must be watertight to protect interior works, including partition installation, from weather damage.
MEP rough-ins (conduits, pipework, ductwork) must be installed within walls/ceilings before partitions are closed up, to avoid costly rework.
Partitions and shopfronts must be in place to define surfaces that require painting, plastering, and final finishing.
Flooring is typically laid after partitions are installed to achieve clean edges and avoid cutting around installed partitions.

successor: Joinery and Fit-Out (Shelving / Counters / Display Units)
rationale: Fixed joinery and retail fit-out elements are installed against completed partition walls and shopfront frames.

successor: Final Electrical / Lighting / Data Point Installation
rationale: Final electrical fit-out (switches, sockets, light fixtures) occurs after partitions are in place so that devices can be correctly positioned on finished walls.

Structural works such as framing, slab pouring, and load-bearing wall erection must be completed before any fit-out and finishing work can begin, as finishes are applied to the completed structural shell.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in (conduits, pipes, ducts, wiring) must be installed within walls, ceilings, and floors before these are enclosed by finishes like drywall, plaster, or ceiling tiles.
Waterproofing of roofs, basements, wet areas, and exterior envelope must be completed before interior finishes are applied to prevent moisture damage to finished surfaces.

All finishing work such as painting, flooring, tiling, ceiling installation, and trim must be complete before final inspections, testing, and commissioning can occur, as inspectors need the finished environment to verify compliance.

successor: Installation of Final Fixtures and Fittings
rationale: Final fixtures such as light fittings, sanitary ware, kitchen cabinets, door handles, and electrical faceplates are typically installed after finishes like painting, tiling, and flooring are complete to avoid damage to finished surfaces during installation.
The building must be structurally complete and enclosed (shell & core) before tenants can take possession and begin their fit-out work.
Essential MEP (mechanical, electrical, plumbing) services including HVAC, power, water, and fire protection must be installed and operational before the space is handed over to tenants.
The building systems must be tested, commissioned, and inspected to ensure they meet safety and performance standards before tenants can occupy the space.
Tenants can only begin their interior fit-out works (partitioning, finishing, custom installations) after they have formally taken possession of the space through the handover process.
The building can only be officially occupied and used for its intended purpose after tenants have taken possession of their leased spaces through the handover process.
Plumbing supply and drain rough-in pipes must be installed in the wall before the hand-wash station can be mounted and connected.
The wall must be framed, enclosed, and finished (e.g., with tile or moisture-resistant board) to provide a solid mounting surface for the hand-wash station.
If the hand-wash station requires an electrical connection (e.g., for automatic faucets, soap dispensers, or sensors), conduit/wiring must be roughed in behind the wall before the unit is installed.
After the hand-wash station is physically mounted, the final plumbing connections (supply lines, drain, trap) can be made to complete the installation.
It is often preferred to install the hand-wash station first and then tile up to it or install a backsplash behind/around it for a clean, finished appearance and proper sealing against moisture.
The structural wall framing (studs) must be erected first as they form the supporting skeleton onto which acoustic partition wall boards are mounted.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work within the wall cavity must be completed before the acoustic partition is enclosed, as accessing these services after wall closure would require demolition.

Sound insulation material (e.g., mineral wool or acoustic batts) must be placed within the wall cavity before the partition boards are fixed, as this is the primary acoustic treatment that cannot be installed after closure.
Once the acoustic partition boards are installed, joints and fastener heads must be taped, jointed, and finished to create a continuous airtight surface essential for acoustic performance.
Final decorative finishes such as paint or wall coverings can only be applied after the partition wall boards are installed and joint finishing is complete.

predecessor: Rough-in Electrical and Data Wiring for Door
rationale: Electrical power and low-voltage control/data cables must be run and terminated at the door location before the door unit can be connected and tested.

predecessor: Install Door Frame and Rough Opening Preparation
rationale: The structural door frame, headers, and jambs must be in place to provide the mounting surface and alignment for the automatic sliding door system.

successor: Infection Control Sealant and Gasket Application
rationale: After the door is installed, all perimeter gaps must be sealed with hospital-grade sealant and antimicrobial gaskets to maintain the infection control barrier.
Motion sensors, presence detectors, and touchless activators must be calibrated only after the door panel and frame are fully installed and aligned.

successor: Final Testing and Commissioning of Door Operation
rationale: Operational testing including open/close cycles, safety stop, and emergency breakaway must be performed after installation is complete to verify compliance with infection control and life safety standards.

predecessor: Plumbing rough-in and water supply piping
rationale: The eyewash and safety shower requires a dedicated water supply line for operation; plumbing rough-in must be completed before the fixture can be installed and connected.

predecessor: Floor slab preparation and drainage installation
rationale: The safety shower typically requires a floor drain beneath it to handle water discharge; the floor slab must be prepared and drainage piping installed before the shower unit is placed.
After the eyewash/shower unit is physically mounted and positioned, the final water supply connections and flow testing must be performed to verify proper operation.
It is a soft preference to complete wall finishing after the unit is installed to avoid damaging finished surfaces during equipment mounting; however, touch-ups can be performed later if needed.
The eyewash and safety shower must be fully installed and operational before the final safety/plumbing inspection and commissioning of the facility can be completed.

successor: Sharps Disposal and Waste Management Unit
rationale: The sharps disposal and waste management unit requires a stable, level base for installation. Foundation and slab work must be completed first to provide structural support.

successor: Sharps Disposal and Waste Management Unit
rationale: Waste management units require plumbing connections for drainage and flushing systems. Rough-in plumbing must be installed before the unit can be placed and connected.

successor: Sharps Disposal and Waste Management Unit
rationale: Electrical power may be needed for automatic waste handling or disposal equipment. Electrical conduits and wiring must be roughed in before unit installation.

predecessor: Sharps Disposal and Waste Management Unit
rationale: The waste management unit must be fully installed before final interior finishes are applied around it to ensure proper sealing, accessibility, and to avoid rework.

predecessor: Sharps Disposal and Waste Management Unit
successor: Final Plumbing and Electrical Connections and Commissioning
rationale: Once the unit is in place, final connections to plumbing and electrical systems and commissioning/testing can be completed to ensure proper operation.
The ground must be excavated and leveled before the ramp foundation can be laid to ensure proper slope and stability.
A concrete base or slab must be poured and cured to provide a stable substrate for the ramp structure.
The ramp structure must be fully constructed before non-slip coatings or surface treatments can be applied for safe pedestrian use.
The ramp frame must be in place to serve as the anchor point for handrails and to allow proper alignment and secure fastening.

successor: Final Inspection and Accessibility Compliance Check
rationale: The full ramp and handrail assembly must be complete before inspectors can verify compliance with accessibility codes (e.g., ADA or equivalent standards).

predecessor: Rough-In of Mechanical, Electrical, and Plumbing Services
rationale: MEP rough-in (conduits, pipes, ductwork within walls and ceilings) must be installed before enclosing them with joinery and clinical fit-out finishes to avoid costly rework and ensure access for inspections.
Finished wall surfaces (drywall) must be in place to provide a stable substrate for mounting clinical joinery, cabinets, and other fit-out elements, and to define room geometry.
Floor screeding/leveling must be completed prior to installing base cabinets, reception desks, and other clinical joinery to ensure stable, level foundations and avoid damage to finished floors.

After joinery is installed, final connections of MEP services (sinks, medical gas outlets, power/data sockets on joinery) can be trimmed out and commissioned without interfering with joinery installation.
It is generally preferred to complete painting before joinery to achieve cleaner lines, but painting can be done after if carefully masked; sequence may vary based on contractor preference.

successor: Medical Gas System Installation and Testing
rationale: The building structure (walls, ceilings, floors) must be in place to provide the physical substrate for mounting medical gas piping, outlets, alarms, and manifolds.

successor: Medical Gas System Installation and Testing
rationale: Medical gas alarm panels and zone valve box assemblies require electrical power and sometimes data/communication cables; rough-in electrical work must precede gas pipe installation to avoid conflicts and enable coordinated routing.

successor: Medical Gas System Installation and Testing
rationale: HVAC ductwork occupies ceiling and wall spaces that must be installed before medical gas piping to prevent access issues and ensure proper clearance around gas lines.

predecessor: Medical Gas System Installation and Testing
successor: Ceiling and Wall Finishing (Drywall and Plaster)
rationale: Medical gas piping, outlets, and zone valves must be fully installed, pressure-tested, and approved before enclosing them behind drywall or ceiling tiles to allow inspection and prevent future access problems.

predecessor: Medical Gas System Installation and Testing
successor: Final Medical Gas Certification and Commissioning
rationale: The installed system must be pressure-tested, purged, and verified for purity and flow before formal certification and handover; commissioning cannot occur until installation and preliminary testing are complete.
Radiation shielding (e.g., lead-lined walls, concrete encasements) must be installed after the structural frame is complete, as the shielding is integrated into the building's permanent structure.
The foundation must be finished to provide a stable base for heavy radiation-shielding materials such as dense concrete or lead sheets.
MEP rough-in (conduits, ducts, pipes) must be installed after shielding to avoid cutting or penetrating the shielding layer, which would compromise its integrity.
Interior finishes (plaster, drywall, cladding) are applied after the shielding is in place to cover and protect the shielding materials.
Specialized radiation-shielded doors and windows must be installed after the surrounding shielding is complete to ensure continuity of the protective envelope.
The building must be verified as clean before infection control commissioning can begin, as infection control measures require a clean baseline environment to be effective.
Proper plumbing and sanitary systems must be installed to support hand hygiene stations, drainage, and other infection control infrastructure before commissioning can proceed.

Heating, ventilation, and air conditioning systems, including filtration and pressure differentials, must be in place and balanced to support infection control requirements such as air changes and pressurization.
Non-porous, cleanable surfaces, sealed joints, and antimicrobial finishes must be fully installed to allow for infection control verification and testing.
Infection control commissioning must confirm that the environment meets hygiene and contamination standards before sensitive clinical equipment is brought in and validated on-site.
The types, volumes, and categories of clinical waste generated must be classified and assessed before a management plan can be developed to address specific waste streams.
Applicable regulations, licenses, and compliance requirements from environmental and health authorities must be reviewed to ensure the plan meets all legal obligations.

predecessor: Waste Storage Area Design and Construction
rationale: Physical storage infrastructure for clinical waste must be in place before the plan can specify operational procedures for waste handling, segregation, and temporary storage.

successor: Clinical Waste Collection and Transport Scheduling
rationale: The management plan must define collection protocols, segregation procedures, and transport requirements before scheduling can be arranged with waste contractors.

successor: Staff Training on Clinical Waste Handling
rationale: Training programs must be based on the approved management plan so that staff are instructed in the correct segregation, packaging, and disposal procedures specified in the plan.
The transfer slab distributes loads from upper columns to foundation elements; therefore, the foundation must be completed to support the transfer slab.

predecessor: Column and Core Wall Construction (Lower Levels)
rationale: Vertical support elements such as columns and core walls below the transfer slab must be in place to carry and transfer the loads from the slab.
The transfer slab provides the structural base and load redistribution platform for columns and walls above; they cannot be erected until the slab is cured and load-bearing.

successor: Vertical Zoning and Floor Construction Above Transfer Level
rationale: All floors above the transfer slab depend on it for support and load transfer; construction above cannot commence prior to completion of the slab.

While waterproofing and MEP services directly under the transfer slab are typically sequenced after slab completion to avoid damage, they could theoretically be partially installed in advance if designed for access, making this a soft preference.
The bridge/gallery structure requires a stable foundation or substructure to bear its load before erection can commence.
Vertical supports or columns must be in place to carry the gallery/corridor bridge structure before it can be installed.
The bridge/gallery structure must be in place before the walking surface or floor finishing can be applied to it.
The main structural element (bridge/gallery) must be complete before safety railings and handrails can be installed along its edges.
The bridge/gallery structure must be fully erected before waterproofing membranes can be applied to protect it from moisture.
Demountable walls require a completed floor slab to provide a stable, level base for installation and to anchor the bottom track.
Ceiling grids must be in place so that demountable walls can be precisely aligned and anchored to the overhead structure, ensuring proper fit and stability.
All rough-in work for ductwork, conduit, and piping must be completed before demountable walls are installed, as walls enclose and conceal these services and access would be blocked.
Demountable wall panels must be fully installed and aligned before any finishing treatments such as painting, joint sealing, or surface cladding can be applied.
Electrical outlets, switches, data ports, and other fixtures installed within demountable walls require the walls to be in place for mounting and termination.

Structural steel provides the primary support framework and attachment points for interstitial services such as HVAC, electrical, and plumbing systems; these services cannot be installed without the structural frame in place.

The concrete slab or deck forms the floor surface within interstitial spaces; interstitial services are routed above ceilings and below floors, requiring the structural slab to be cured before installation.
Dedicated overhead supports, hangers, and trapeze assemblies must be anchored to the structure before any mechanical, electrical, or plumbing lines can be suspended.

All interstitial services (ductwork, piping, conduits) must be completely installed, tested, and approved before the ceiling grid or drywall is closed in, to avoid costly rework and ensure accessibility for inspection.

successor: Final Inspection / Commissioning of MEP Systems
rationale: Commissioning and final inspection of mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems require the interstitial installations to be fully in place to verify functionality, pressure tests, and code compliance.
A stable foundation is physically required to support the plug-in unit. The unit cannot be placed or installed without a prepared base.
Utility connections (water, electricity, sewer) must be roughed in at the site before the plug-in unit can be connected and installed.
If the plug-in unit is attached or adjacent to the main dwelling, the main structure must be completed to provide structural support and weatherproofing before the secondary unit is added.
Interior finishing work (drywall, flooring, trim) must follow after the unit's shell is in place and weather-tight, to avoid damage from exposure.
Final connection of plumbing, electrical, and HVAC to the unit can only be done once the unit is physically installed and in its final position.
The ceiling structure (joists, beams, deck) must be in place to provide a mounting surface and support for the baffle suspension system.

Ductwork, plumbing pipes, and electrical conduit that run above the finished ceiling must be installed before baffles are hung, as access after baffle installation is extremely difficult and would require removal of baffles.
Sprinkler heads, piping, and other fire suppression components must be in place and pressure-tested before ceiling baffles are installed to avoid interference and ensure safety compliance.

Installing baffles first allows trim carpenters to work around the fixed ceiling elements and ensures clean sightlines, though this is a logical sequencing preference rather than a physical necessity.

successor: Flooring and Wall Finishing (if ceiling mounted first)
rationale: Completing overhead baffles before final floor finishes protects the flooring from dust and debris that would fall during baffle installation, but this is a protective sequencing preference rather than a hard constraint.
Structural framing must be complete to provide the enclosed space and load-bearing support required before any fit-out work such as partitioning, ceilings, and finishing can commence.
The building envelope must be weathertight to protect interior fit-out materials and work from weather damage during the fit-out phase.
MEP rough-in (conduits, ductwork, piping) must be installed within walls, ceilings, and floors before they are enclosed by fit-out finishes such as drywall, ceilings, and flooring.
Fit-out activities like partitioning, ceiling grids, and built-in joinery must be completed before final finishing works (painting, floor coverings, and systems commissioning) can proceed.
All fit-out, finishing, and building services must be complete and inspected before the facility can be handed over for occupancy and use by the community or end users.
A stable, compacted road base is physically required to support the installation of a traffic calming device such as a speed hump or raised crosswalk.
The road surface must be paved and finished before a traffic calming device can be constructed or mounted on top of or integrally with the pavement.
Any underground utilities, drainage systems, or manhole covers must be adjusted or relocated prior to device installation to avoid conflicts and future access issues.
Warning signs, pavement markings, and speed limit signage specific to the traffic calming device must be installed after the device is in place to ensure accurate placement and visibility.
The road can only be reopened to traffic after the traffic calming device is fully constructed, cured (if concrete), and all safety measures are in place.
Signage and line marking are typically final finishing items that require the building structure and surfaces to be complete before installation.
Line marking must be applied onto finished floor surfaces; rough or unfinished floors cannot hold permanent markings.
Wall-mounted signage requires finished, painted wall surfaces for proper adhesion and placement.
Illuminated signage and line markings that require lighting conditions necessitate completed electrical rough-in and lighting fixtures.
Overhead signage and hanging signages require the ceiling structure to be fully installed.
Signage and line marking are among the last finishing items; once complete, the area is ready for final cleanup and project handover.
Signage and markings must be in place for safe navigation and compliance before occupants can use the facility.
Final inspections require all signage and markings to be installed to verify compliance with safety and accessibility codes.
The area must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and existing structures before subgrade preparation can begin to ensure a clean working surface.
Soil testing and subsurface investigation must be completed to determine soil type, bearing capacity, and moisture content to inform subgrade treatment requirements.
Road alignment, centerline, and grade levels must be marked out by surveyors before earthworks can commence to ensure the subgrade is prepared to the correct alignment and elevation.
The subgrade forms the foundation of the road pavement; the sub-base layer must be placed directly on top of the prepared and compacted subgrade.
Subsurface drainage pipes and French drains are typically installed after subgrade preparation but before or concurrently with sub-base to manage groundwater within the pavement structure.
A stable, well-compacted subgrade is required to provide uniform support for the pavement layers above; without proper subgrade preparation, the pavement would settle unevenly and fail prematurely.

The base course acts as the load-bearing foundation directly beneath the pavement; it must be compacted and leveled before the pavement can be laid on top to ensure structural integrity and proper drainage.
Any underground utilities, drainage systems, or conduits must be installed and backfilled before pavement is laid to avoid cutting or disturbing the completed pavement later.

Once the pavement material (asphalt or concrete) is laid and compacted, surface finishing (texturing, troweling) and proper curing must follow immediately to achieve the specified surface properties and strength.
In concrete pavements, joints must be cut after the pavement has been laid and compacted but before traffic loading begins, to control cracking and ensure long-term performance.
The subgrade (earthwork base) must be properly graded, compacted, and stable before kerb and channel can be laid to ensure adequate foundation support and correct alignment/drainage falls.

Lower pavement layers (e.g., road base or sub-base) are typically placed and compacted before kerb installation so that the kerb can be set at the correct finished road level and tied into the pavement structure.

The kerb and channel must be completed and cured before the final asphalt or concrete wearing course is laid, as the wearing course is placed up against the kerb line to achieve a flush, sealed joint.
Footpath construction typically abuts the back of the kerb; the kerb must be in place to define the edge and level for the footpath pavement.
Channel outlets and pit connections to the stormwater drainage system must be installed after the kerb and channel is formed, as the channel directs stormwater flow into drainage inlets or pits.
The site must be cleared and rough grading completed to expose the ground and provide a clean working area for stormwater trenching and pit placement.
Existing underground utilities must be located and marked to avoid clashes or damage when excavating for stormwater pits and pipes.
Erosion and sediment controls (e.g., silt fences, sediment basins) must be in place before any earth disturbance to comply with environmental regulations and contain runoff during stormwater works.
After stormwater pipes and pits are laid and connected, the trenches must be backfilled and compacted to restore ground stability and allow subsequent surface works.

Stormwater drainage infrastructure must be in place and connected to kerb inlets before concrete kerbing and road pavement can be poured, as the drainage system needs to be operational beneath the paved surfaces.

Road markings must be applied on a clean, cured, and finished pavement surface. Asphalt or concrete paving must be completed and fully set before any markings can be applied, otherwise the markings will not adhere properly or will be damaged by ongoing paving operations.

The structural road layers (subbase, base, and binder course) must be completed and the final surface course placed to provide a stable, smooth platform for the markings. Signage also requires stable ground/foundations for post installation.

Curbs and gutters define the road edge geometry. Markings such as edge lines and gutter markings depend on the final curb alignment being in place. Signage placement also references curb lines for setback distances.

successor: Traffic Management / Road Opening to Public
rationale: Road markings and signs provide essential guidance, warning, and regulatory information to road users. The road cannot be safely opened to traffic until all markings and signage are installed, verified, and legible to ensure safe navigation and compliance with traffic laws.

successor: Final Inspection and Punch List Completion
rationale: The final inspection of the roadway must verify that all markings are correctly placed and all signs are installed per the design drawings before the project can be accepted. Markings and signage are among the last finishing items to be inspected.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and properly compacted before any concrete or paving for the driveway crossover can be laid to ensure a stable base.

predecessor: Underground Utility Installation (water, sewer, drainage, gas, electrical)
rationale: Underground services must be laid and connected before the driveway crossover is constructed to avoid digging up and damaging the finished crossover later.
Regulatory approval of the crossover design and location must be obtained before construction to ensure compliance with road authority standards and avoid costly rework.

successor: Driveway/Pavement Construction (main driveway slab or paving)
rationale: The crossover (the transition from the public road to the property) must be built first so that the private driveway can tie into it seamlessly at the property boundary.

successor: Landscaping and Final Finishes (lawns, gardens, pathways)
rationale: Landscaping is typically done after the crossover is completed to avoid soil and debris being tracked onto the new crossover surface, though it is a soft preference as some planting can occur concurrently with care.
The ground must be excavated and graded to the proper slope before the kerb ramp can be formed and poured.
A stable, compacted subgrade is required to support the concrete or paving of the kerb ramp.
Formwork must be set in place to shape and contain the concrete pour for the kerb ramp.
Any underground drainage pipes or utility conduits beneath the ramp area must be installed prior to pouring the ramp to avoid future excavation and damage.
The kerb ramp must be completed before the surrounding pavement or asphalt is laid, so the paving can be finished flush against the ramp.
Tactile warning indicators are installed on top of the completed kerb ramp surface to alert visually impaired pedestrians of the curb edge.
Adjacent curb and gutter sections can be installed after the ramp is in place to ensure continuity and proper alignment, though this is a sequencing preference.
The ramp must be fully constructed and cured before it can be inspected for ADA compliance and slope tolerances.
The road design must be completed before a safety audit can be performed, as the audit reviews the design for safety issues.
Traffic data (volumes, speeds, accident history) is needed input for the safety audit to assess potential hazards.
The road must be physically constructed before a post-construction safety audit can inspect the actual built environment.
Findings from the safety audit must be identified before remediation actions can be planned and implemented.
The safety audit report is typically reviewed before a road is opened to traffic, though in some cases a road may open with temporary measures pending audit completion.

As-Constructed Survey captures the final built conditions of the project; it must be performed after Substantial Completion when all major construction work is finished and the structure is essentially ready for occupancy.
Final site grades and elevations must be established before the as-constructed survey can accurately document the finished ground levels and drainage patterns.
The building's structural elements and exterior enclosure must be fully erected so that the survey can capture accurate final positions of columns, beams, walls, and roof elements.

All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems must be installed and rough-ins completed so that the as-constructed survey can record the actual locations of pipes, conduits, and equipment for future maintenance records.
The as-constructed survey provides the definitive record of actual built conditions, which is required before the final punch list can be verified and project closeout documentation can be completed.
The junction box provides the electrical connection point and mounting support; the lighting fixture cannot be installed without a secured junction box in place.

predecessor: Run Electrical Wiring to Junction Box
rationale: Electrical wiring must be routed and terminated at the junction box before the lighting fixture can be connected and energized.
Ceiling framing, drywall, and rough openings must be finished to provide a stable surface and opening for the fixture housing.
The fixture must be physically installed and connected before the circuit can be energized and tested for proper operation.
Lamps are typically inserted after the fixture housing is mounted and wired to avoid damage during installation.
Decorative trim or finish ring is attached after the fixture body is secured and wiring is complete.
Corner wall reinforcement requires the wall framing to be in place so that corner studs, blocking, and reinforcement anchors can be properly installed within the frame.
A solid foundation or slab is necessary to anchor the corner wall reinforcement, especially if it involves dowels or anchor bolts embedded in the concrete.

Wall sheathing (e.g., plywood or OSB) is installed after corner reinforcement is complete because the reinforcement adds structural rigidity and must be fully in place before sheathing is applied over the corner area.
Drywall cannot be installed until corner reinforcement is finished, as the reinforcement may include metal corner beads or blocking that must be flush with the finished wall surface.
Exterior cladding (siding, stucco, brick veneer) depends on the corner reinforcement being in place to ensure structural integrity and a proper corner substrate for the cladding system.
Emergency exit signage must be mounted on completed walls; walls provide the structural surface for sign placement.
Electrical wiring for illuminated exit signs must be run within walls/ceilings before the sign can be connected and installed.
Exit signage must be installed and operational before the building can pass final safety inspection and be approved for occupancy.
Regulatory codes require all emergency exit signs to be in place and functioning before occupants can safely use the building.
Many exit signs are ceiling-mounted or suspended from the ceiling grid; ceilings must be installed first to provide a mounting point.

predecessor: Rough-in piping for fire suppression system
rationale: Sprinkler heads must be connected to the fire suppression piping network; the piping must be installed and roughed-in before sprinkler heads can be mounted and connected.

predecessor: Ceiling grid or overhead structure installation
rationale: Sprinkler heads are typically mounted to or through ceiling systems; the supporting ceiling grid or overhead structure must be in place to provide attachment points and proper positioning.
Sprinkler heads must be installed before ceiling finishes are completed so that the heads can be properly positioned through the finished surface and aligned with ceiling panels or openings.

successor: Pressure testing and inspection of fire suppression system
rationale: Sprinkler heads must be installed before the system can be fully pressure-tested and inspected to verify proper operation, coverage, and leak-free connections.

successor: Painting and final finishing of ceiling
rationale: While painting can be done carefully around sprinkler heads after installation, it is a soft preference because painting before installation may cover or damage the heads, and painting after allows for clean edges and proper masking.
The fire door frame must be installed first to provide the structural support and mounting surface for the junction fire door assembly.
Walls must be framed and drywall installed to define the opening and provide the proper fire-rated enclosure before the fire door assembly can be fitted.
The fire door assembly must be in place before hardware such as hinges, handles, locks, and closers can be installed onto the door.
After the door assembly is installed, the gaps around the junction must be sealed with fire-stop materials to maintain the fire rating integrity.

successor: Inspection and Testing of Fire Doors
rationale: The fire door assembly must be fully installed before inspections and functional testing (e.g., self-closing operation, latch engagement) can be performed.

A site assessment must be completed before traffic flow planning can start, as planners need to understand the existing road network, topography, and surrounding infrastructure to design effective traffic patterns.

Traffic flow planning must be completed before road construction begins, as the road layout, lane configurations, intersection designs, and traffic control measures are determined by the traffic flow plan.
Traffic signal placement and timing configurations are dependent on the traffic flow plan, so signal installation cannot proceed until traffic flow planning is finalized.
Lane markings, directional signs, and traffic signs must follow the traffic flow plan specifications, making this a hard precedence constraint.

While not a physical necessity, obtaining necessary permits and regulatory approvals before detailed traffic flow planning ensures the plan complies with local regulations and avoids costly redesigns.
The subgrade must be properly prepared, graded, and compacted to provide a stable and level surface before any layout marking can be applied to define junction geometry.
Underground drainage pipes and culverts must be installed before junction layout marking to ensure markings align correctly with the final surface and drainage infrastructure.

All underground utilities (water, gas, electricity, telecommunications) must be laid before marking the junction layout to avoid rework and ensure accurate positioning of surface markings relative to utility access points.

Junction layout marking defines the geometry and boundaries of the junction, which serves as a guide for subsequent pavement laying and ensures the pavement is placed within the correct alignment and limits.

The junction layout must first be marked on the prepared surface to establish turning paths, lane widths, and island locations before final road surface markings (e.g., lane lines, arrows, stop lines) can be applied.
The structural frame must be erected to provide the load-bearing support and attachment points for wall partitions at junctions.
The floor slab must be poured and sufficiently cured to provide a stable base for wall partition installation at junctions.
MEP rough-in work such as conduit, piping, and ductwork routing behind walls must be completed before partitions are installed to avoid rework or access issues.
Wall partitions must be fully installed and secured at junctions before finishing work such as plastering, drywall taping, or painting can begin.
Wall partitions at junctions provide the structural openings and framing required for installing door and window frames.
The structural steel frame must be in place to support the ceiling grid system at the junction area.
MEP conduits, ducts, and pipes must be routed above the ceiling before the grid is installed, or access would be blocked.
Ceiling tiles are laid into the grid after the grid framework is fully installed and secured.
Lighting fixtures are typically mounted to or supported by the ceiling grid, so the grid must be in place first.
Fire alarm devices and sprinkler heads are integrated into or positioned relative to the ceiling grid, requiring the grid to be installed beforehand.
Wayfinding design must be based on the overall architectural layout and the designated locations for signage, which are determined during architectural design and signage strategy development.
Wayfinding elements (colors, materials, typography) must align with interior design themes and finishes to ensure visual consistency and integration.
Accurate floor plans showing all corridors, rooms, exits, and amenities are required to map routes and place directional signage correctly.
Signage cannot be fabricated or installed until the wayfinding design (including sign content, layout, and specifications) is finalized.

successor: Construction of Common Areas & Circulation Paths
rationale: Wayfinding design defines where signs, maps, and other guidance elements will be placed; construction of these areas must accommodate the designed locations.
Design plans must be sufficiently developed to evaluate against accessibility codes and standards such as ADA, IBC, or local requirements.
Detailed architectural drawings are needed to verify that door widths, ramp slopes, restroom layouts, path of travel, and other accessibility features meet code requirements.
Structural framing is typically complete before detailed accessibility checks are performed on interior spaces to ensure clearances and pathways are physically achievable.
Accessibility compliance approval is often required as part of the building permit application package before construction can legally proceed.
Accessibility compliance sign-off is a prerequisite to beginning construction to ensure the design meets all legal accessibility requirements before work starts.
A stable, compacted sub-base is required to support the tactile ground surface indicators and prevent uneven settlement or displacement.
Tactile ground surface indicators are typically embedded into or applied onto a finished walking surface such as concrete or paving slabs; the base surface must be in place first.

successor: Curing and finishing of surrounding surface
rationale: If tactile indicators are cast into wet concrete, the concrete must be finished around them and then cured; however, if they are applied as adhesive tiles, the surface must be prepared first. In typical cast-in-place installation, the tactile indicator is placed before final surface finishing and curing.

successor: Site inspection and accessibility compliance check
rationale: While inspection can begin before full installation is complete, a formal compliance check typically occurs after all tactile indicators are installed to verify correct placement, spacing, and color contrast.
The ground must be excavated and graded to the correct levels before any surface layer or tactile indicators can be installed.
Electrical wiring and conduit must be installed before security cameras can be mounted, as cameras require power and data cabling that runs through walls and ceilings.
Ceilings (or mounting surfaces) must be fully installed before camera brackets can be attached to them, ensuring a stable structural base.
The camera mount must be physically installed before wiring connections to the camera unit can be completed, as the mount provides the attachment point for the camera and cable routing.
Camera mounting must be finished before the camera can be powered on, configured, and tested, as the physical installation is a prerequisite to functional testing.
Mounting cameras before final paint touch-ups allows painters to work around the mounts, though this is a soft preference as touch-ups can be done carefully after installation.
The corner protection column must be anchored to a stable, level foundation or slab. Without a properly prepared base, the column cannot be securely installed.
Reinforcement steel (rebar cage) must be placed and tied before concrete for the column can be poured, as it provides the structural strength required for the corner protection element.
After the column is poured or placed, sufficient curing time is physically required before any loads are applied or subsequent construction activities proceed.
The corner protection column provides the structural interface for adjacent wall panels or cladding systems; those elements cannot be installed until the column is in place and stable.
The ground must be properly graded and prepared before excavating a tree pit to ensure proper drainage and stable soil conditions.

All underground utilities (water, gas, electricity, telecommunications) must be installed before digging tree pits to avoid conflicts, damage to utilities, and ensure safe placement of trees away from utility lines.
The tree pit must be excavated and prepared before the tree can be planted into it.
Tree pits are typically formed or framed before the surrounding sidewalk or pavement is poured, so the pavement can be finished around the pit with proper edging and tree grates.
The tree pit structure must be in place before tree grates, guards, or protective covers can be installed around the tree.
Ground must be leveled and prepared before installing the tree grate to ensure proper drainage and structural stability.
The tree must be planted in the ground before the grate can be placed around it to protect the root zone.
Any underground utilities near the tree pit must be completed before installing the grate to avoid digging up the grate later.
The tree grate must be installed so that surrounding paving or concrete can be finished flush with the grate frame for a seamless surface.
Topsoil and decorative mulch can be placed after the grate is installed to fill in around the tree, though this could also be done concurrently.
The site must be properly graded and prepared to provide appropriate drainage, soil conditions, and topography before any planting can occur.
Soil must be amended (e.g., with compost, pH adjustment) to create a suitable growing medium for native and adaptive plants to establish.
Irrigation infrastructure (pipes, drip lines, sprinklers) must be installed prior to planting to ensure plants receive adequate water immediately upon installation.
Erosion control blankets, silt fences, or other measures should be in place to protect newly planted areas from washout during establishment.
Hardscape elements like walkways, retaining walls, and boulder placement must be completed first to avoid damaging new plantings during construction.
Mulch is applied immediately after planting to retain soil moisture, suppress weeds, and protect plant roots.
A regular watering regimen must begin right after planting to support root establishment during the critical first growing season.
Monitoring for plant health, pest issues, and irrigation effectiveness begins after planting to ensure successful establishment.
Landscaping completion is typically a prerequisite for final project inspection, though in some phased projects this may be a soft preference.
Underground utilities (water, sewer, gas, electric, telecom) must be installed or relocated before street construction to avoid digging up newly paved streets, which is costly and dangerous.
Existing structures, vegetation, and debris must be cleared from the street alignment area before any earthwork or paving can commence.
The ground surface must be graded, compacted, and brought to proper elevation to provide a stable subgrade for the pavement layers.
Catch basins, storm sewer pipes, and drainage systems must be placed below the street surface before road base and pavement are laid.
Traffic markings, lane stripes, and signs are applied only after the final pavement surface is complete to ensure proper adhesion and alignment.

While curbs and sidewalks can be built after the street, they are often constructed concurrently or slightly after; however, final sidewalk finishing typically follows street paving to avoid damage from paving equipment.
The subgrade (soil or base layer) must be properly graded, compacted, and prepared to provide a stable foundation for the pavement surface.
A base course (aggregate or bound base layer) must be laid and compacted on the subgrade to provide structural support and drainage before the pavement surface can be applied.
Subsurface drainage pipes, culverts, or edge drains must be installed before paving to ensure water can be diverted away from the pavement structure.
Road surface markings (lane lines, symbols, etc.) can only be applied after the pavement surface is fully laid, cured, and clean.

While curbs are often placed before paving to serve as forms, in some sequences they can be installed after surfacing; however, for proper alignment and finish, it is generally preferred to install curbs before the final pavement surface.

The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and topsoil before stormwater infrastructure can be installed to provide a clean, stable work area and proper subgrade for pipes, inlets, and retention/detention systems.
Rough grading establishes the general drainage patterns and elevations needed to properly design and place stormwater infrastructure such as catch basins, piping networks, and outfall structures.

Erosion and sediment control measures (e.g., silt fences, sediment basins, inlet protection) must be in place before commencing stormwater work to prevent sediment runoff during excavation and installation activities, as required by environmental regulations.
All existing underground utilities must be located and marked before excavation for stormwater infrastructure to avoid utility strikes, service disruptions, and safety hazards.

Final grading and compaction work must occur after stormwater pipes, structures, and drainage systems are installed, as the stormwater infrastructure is buried and the surface is then shaped to direct water flow properly to the installed inlets and systems.

Stormwater drainage infrastructure (e.g., culverts, underdrains, catch basins) must be installed before road base and pavement are placed, so that drainage is operational beneath and adjacent to the roadway.

Stormwater management systems around building footprints and site drainage networks must be installed before foundation work to ensure proper drainage away from structures and to avoid re-excavation around foundations.

Landscaping, topsoil placement, and seeding are typically done after stormwater infrastructure is in place since trenching and heavy equipment work would disturb finished landscaping; however, this is a logical sequencing preference rather than a strict physical impossibility.

The guard rail and barrier system is typically installed on the edges of the bridge deck. The bridge deck must be completed to provide a stable surface and structural support for the guard rail installation.
Approach slabs connect the bridge deck to the roadway; guard rails and barriers must extend across this transition zone, requiring the approach slab to be in place first.
While not a physical necessity, pavement markings are typically applied after barriers are installed to ensure accurate placement and alignment relative to the barrier positions.
Guard rail and barrier installation is one of the final construction activities; site cleanup and demobilization logically follow its completion.

Traffic signs are typically mounted on the finished road surface or on posts anchored beside the road; the road base and surface must be completed to establish final elevations and positions for sign placement.
A stable, compacted road base is needed before any roadside furniture (including signposts) can be securely installed.
Underground utilities (water, gas, electrical, telecom) must be laid and backfilled before digging post holes for traffic signs to avoid conflicts and rework.
While often done concurrently, typically signs are installed first to provide fixed reference points; however, this is a soft preference as line painting can be adjusted around existing signs.
All traffic signs must be in place before a road is opened to public traffic to ensure driver guidance, regulatory compliance, and safety.
The road base must be prepared and compacted before installing pedestrian crossing components such as markings, signals, or tactile paving.
Any underground utilities (drainage, conduits, cables) beneath the crossing area must be installed and covered before the crossing surface is constructed.
Pedestrian crossing surface and tactile paving must be in place before installing pedestrian push buttons and crossing signals to ensure correct positioning.
The crossing surface must be finished and cured before applying crosswalk thermoplastic or paint markings.
The pedestrian crossing surface must be completed to the correct level before installing curb ramps that transition from the sidewalk to the crossing.
The Speed Control Device requires electrical power and connections to operate; the electrical system must be in place before the device can be installed and connected.
The Speed Control Device is typically installed on or connected to a motor/engine to regulate its speed; the motor must be present before the controller can be mounted and interfaced.

predecessor: Control panel or mounting structure fabrication
rationale: The device needs a secure mounting location (e.g., control panel, chassis, or bracket) to be physically attached; this structure must be ready beforehand.

successor: Calibration and tuning of speed controller
rationale: Once the physical device is installed and wired, it must be calibrated and tuned to ensure correct speed regulation for the specific application.

successor: Load or driven equipment connection and testing
rationale: The driven equipment (e.g., conveyor, pump, fan) is connected after the speed controller is in place, so the system can be tested under load conditions.
A stable concrete foundation or slab must be poured and cured to provide a level, load-bearing surface for mounting the charging station equipment.
Underground or surface-mounted electrical conduits and feeder cables from the main electrical panel must be installed and routed to the charging station location before the station can be connected.
The main electrical panel must be upgraded (if needed) with a dedicated circuit breaker and sufficient capacity to handle the EV charger's load before the station can be powered.

After physical installation of the charging unit, commissioning activities such as electrical testing, software configuration, and network connectivity verification must be performed before the station can be placed into service.
Parking space markings, directional arrows, and EV charging signage are typically applied after the charging station is installed to ensure accurate alignment with the unit's position.
The subgrade must be properly graded, compacted, and prepared to provide a stable and uniform foundation before pavement can be laid, otherwise the pavement will crack or settle unevenly.
The base course (aggregate or crushed stone layer) must be placed and compacted above the subgrade to distribute traffic loads and provide drainage before the pavement surface layer can be applied.

Subsurface drains, culverts, or edge drains must be installed before pavement laying to ensure proper water runoff and prevent water accumulation beneath the pavement which would cause premature failure.
Freshly laid pavement (especially concrete or asphalt) requires a designated curing period to gain strength and durability before it can be opened to traffic or have subsequent work performed on it.
Road markings, lane stripes, and signage must only be applied after the pavement surface is fully laid, compacted, and cured to ensure the markings adhere properly and remain visible.
Traffic management (cones, signs, diversions) must be in place before any road work begins to ensure worker and motorist safety.
A thorough inspection is needed to identify damage, cracks, potholes, and determine the extent of resurfacing required before work can commence.
Underground utilities (gas, water, electricity, telecom) must be located and marked to avoid striking them during milling or excavation.
The old road surface must be milled, cleaned, and prepared (e.g., crack sealing, patching base failures) before new asphalt or surface layer can be laid.

successor: Road Line Marking and Signage Installation
rationale: New road markings (lane lines, arrows, crosswalks) and signage can only be applied after the fresh resurfaced pavement is completed and cured.
The road can only be reopened to normal traffic after resurfacing is fully complete and the surface has sufficiently cooled/cured.
Post-construction testing (density, smoothness, thickness checks) must occur after resurfacing is finished to verify compliance with specifications.
Security turnstiles require electrical power for operation, so electrical infrastructure must be in place before installation.
Security turnstiles typically connect to access control systems via network cables, requiring data cabling to be installed first.

predecessor: Pour and cure concrete floor slab
rationale: Turnstiles are heavy and require a level, load-bearing concrete floor for secure anchoring and stable operation.
The physical turnstile hardware must be installed and connected before the access control system can be programmed and tested.
End-to-end testing of turnstile operation (card readers, biometrics, emergency unlocking) requires the physical unit to be fully installed and connected.
The canopy structure requires a stable foundation or structural support to be in place before it can be erected.
The entrance canopy is typically mounted onto or supported by the main structural frame or dedicated columns, which must be erected first.
The canopy must be installed before final finishes, cladding, and weatherproofing that tie into or abut the canopy can be completed.
The canopy provides overhead protection and structural integration above the entrance; doors are typically installed after the canopy framework is in place.
While some electrical work can be done concurrently, installing fixed lighting fixtures under or on the canopy is easier and safer after the canopy is fully erected.
The rough opening must be framed and prepared to the correct dimensions before the door frame can be installed, as the frame fits into the prepared opening.
A completed subfloor is required to provide a stable base for the threshold, which sits on the finished floor surface.
Load-bearing and partition walls must be framed to define the doorway opening before the door frame can be set in place.
The door frame and threshold must be securely installed and leveled before the door leaf can be hung on hinges within that frame.
Door frame installation must be completed before wall finishing around the opening, since the frame establishes the final reveal and the wall finish butts against the frame.

The curtain wall surround requires a stable structural frame to which it can be anchored and supported. The steel frame must be erected and fully connected before the non-structural curtain wall can be installed.

Concrete slab edges or spandrel beams provide the perimeter support and anchorage points for the curtain wall system. These must be cast and cured to sufficient strength before the curtain wall surround can be mounted.
Sealants and gaskets are applied to the joints between curtain wall panels and the surrounding structure after the panels are installed, to ensure airtightness and watertightness.

successor: Interior Drywall / Finishing Adjacent to Curtain Wall
rationale: Interior finishes (e.g., drywall, insulation, trim) around the perimeter of the curtain wall are completed after the curtain wall is in place, to conceal connections and achieve a finished appearance.
The curtain wall surround frame (mullions and transoms) must be erected first to create the structural grid, after which the glass infill panels are installed into the frame.
Signage and wayfinding panels are typically mounted on finished walls or surfaces; therefore, interior finishes and wall cladding must be completed first to provide a suitable substrate.
Many signage panels require electrical power for illumination (e.g., backlit signs); electrical rough-in and wiring must be installed before panels are mounted and connected.
Signage and wayfinding panels must be fully installed before final inspection and commissioning to verify that all directional and informational signs are correctly placed and functional.
Wayfinding systems must be in place prior to occupancy to ensure occupants and visitors can navigate the building safely and efficiently.
While not always a strict physical dependency, completing ceiling work before installing wall-mounted signage avoids dust, debris, and access issues that could damage or obstruct new signs.
The foundation must be completed to provide a stable base for the portal frame columns and lintel supports.
The floor slab provides the working platform and base level from which portal frames are erected and braced.
The portal frame forms the primary structural support for the roof; roof members and cladding cannot be installed until the frame is in place.
Wall panels and façade elements are typically supported by or attached to the portal frame and lintels; the frame must be erected first.

Overhead crane rails are often mounted on portal frame brackets; though the crane can be installed after the frame, it is a logical sequence to complete the frame first to provide support for the crane runway.
The ground surface must be graded and compacted to the required slope and elevation before the ramp/threshold can be formed or installed to ensure proper drainage and a stable base.
The concrete slab or foundation substrate that the ramp and threshold tie into must be poured and cured to provide a solid anchoring surface and to achieve the correct finished floor elevation.
Any drainage pipes, electrical conduits, or other utilities routed beneath the ramp/threshold area must be installed and inspected before the ramp is formed/poured to avoid cutting or patching later.

successor: Surface Finish Application (e.g., broom finish, sealant, anti-slip coating)
rationale: The ramp and threshold structure must be fully formed, poured, and cured before any final surface treatment is applied to ensure a clean, durable finish.
Handrails and guardrails are mounted onto or adjacent to the ramp; the ramp must exist in its final position to locate anchor points, set post heights, and verify clearances per accessibility codes.
The ground must be excavated and prepared to accommodate the foundation and base for bollards and vehicle barriers.
Any underground electrical, plumbing, or data lines that may intersect with bollard locations must be installed before bollard footings are poured to avoid conflicts and rework.
Bollards are typically anchored into concrete foundations or slabs, so the concrete must be poured and cured before bollard installation can begin.
Final paving, asphalt, or surface finishes around bollards should be completed after bollard installation to ensure seamless integration and a clean finished surface.
Landscaping around bollards is typically done after installation, though in some cases temporary landscaping could precede it; this is a soft preference for better workflow.
The gate leaf must be anchored to a stable structural base; the foundation or plinth must be completed to support and secure the gate.
The gate leaf hinges are mounted on the gate frame or pillars; the supporting structure must be in place before the leaf can be hung.
Locks, handles, and closing mechanisms can only be installed after the gate leaf itself is positioned and aligned on its hinges.

successor: Decorative Finishing / Surface Treatment of Gate
rationale: While some finishing can be done pre-installation, final touch-ups, painting, or gilding often occur after the leaf is hung to ensure seamless appearance and alignment.

The gate leaf can be installed before the adjacent wall is fully complete, but typically the wall is built up to the gate opening first for proper integration, though this order may be flexible depending on site logistics.
Rough openings must be framed and prepared with proper dimensions before doors and frames can be installed.
Floor surfaces must be completed or prepared to the proper level so door frames can be installed at the correct height and alignment.
Walls must be framed and sheathed to provide the structural support and rough openings into which door frames are set.
It is preferable to install door frames before running electrical wiring near doorways to avoid interference, though wiring can sometimes be routed around frames.
Door frames must be installed and secured before drywall or wall paneling can be applied, as the frames define the finished opening edges and provide attachment surfaces.
The door frame must be in place before hinges, strike plates, and other hardware can be mounted to the frame and door.
The frame must be fully installed, plumbed, and secured before the door slab can be hung and adjusted for proper fit and operation.

Openings (such as door/window openings, chases, or penetrations) can only be formed after the concrete or masonry has been poured, placed, and sufficiently cured. Cutting or forming openings in green concrete can cause structural damage or cracking.

For masonry walls, the block or brick work must be laid and the mortar must have set before openings can be precisely cut or formed. Forming openings during laying would compromise wall integrity and alignment.

successor: Rough-In for Mechanical, Electrical, and Plumbing (MEP)
rationale: MEP rough-in work (running pipes, conduits, and ducts) through walls and slabs requires completed openings or chases to pass through. The openings must exist before MEP trades can install their systems through those penetrations.

Door and window frames are installed directly into the rough openings left in concrete or masonry walls. The opening must be fully formed (cut/created) prior to setting frames to ensure proper fit and anchoring.

successor: Firestopping and Sealant Application at Penetrations
rationale: Firestopping and sealants around penetrations through concrete/masonry walls can only be applied after the openings have been formed and the penetrating items (pipes, conduits) are in place, but the opening creation itself must precede any firestop work.
Access control hardware such as controllers, readers, electric locks, and door strikes must be physically installed and wired before they can be tested and commissioned.
Cables for access control devices (door controllers, card readers, REX devices) must be pulled and terminated at both ends before commissioning can verify connectivity and device function.
Dedicated power supplies or power-over-ethernet (PoE) switches must be energized to provide power to access control panels and field devices during commissioning tests.
After commissioning validates the electronic access control functions, doors may need final hardware adjustments (latch alignment, closer speed) to ensure proper operation under electronic control.
Commissioning must be complete and all access control devices verified operational before formal system acceptance testing with the owner or general contractor can proceed.
Steel columns and structural frames require completed concrete foundations (including bolt pockets and base plates) to be set and cured before erection can commence.
The steel frame must be erected and stabilised before roof and wall cladding panels can be installed onto the structure.

While some touch-up painting can be done later, final protective coating application is typically performed after erection to avoid damage during handling, though this is a practical preference rather than a physical necessity.
A level, compacted and prepared ground surface is required to provide stable temporary works access and cranage positioning for steel erection activities.
The structural steel members must be fabricated, inspected, tested, and delivered to site before any erection can physically take place.
Doors and windows must be installed first so that hinges, handles, locks, and other hardware can be fitted onto the installed frames and leaves.
Ironmongery is typically fitted after painting to avoid paint contamination on hardware and to achieve a clean finish around fittings.
After fitting hardware, final adjustments (e.g., latch alignment, door closer calibration) and snagging inspections are performed to ensure correct operation.
Hardware must be fully installed before functional testing of door and window operation (open/close, locking, security) can be carried out.
Timber frames, architraves, and joinery must be in place to provide the substrate for screwing and fixing ironmongery items.
A stable, compacted subbase is required to support the kerb ramp and prevent settlement or cracking after installation.
Underground drainage must be installed before kerb works to avoid excavating through newly placed concrete and to ensure proper drainage connection at the ramp.
The kerb ramp forms the edge transition; footpath surfacing is laid up to the kerb ramp to ensure a flush, continuous surface.
Tactile indicators are installed on the ramp surface at the transition point to warn visually impaired users; the ramp must exist first.
