Final road surface is typically laid after kerb installation to create a clean seal; however, sequencing can vary, so this is a soft preference for quality and appearance.
The pedestrian signal head must be mounted on a supporting pole or mast arm; the structure must be in place before the signal head can be attached.
Electrical conduit must be installed to provide the pathway for wiring to the pedestrian signal head location.

predecessor: Install Traffic Signal Controller Cabinet and Base
rationale: The controller cabinet must be installed to house the signal control equipment that will operate the pedestrian signal head.
Signal cables must be pulled through the conduit to provide electrical connection from the controller to the pedestrian signal head before it can be wired and operational.
The pedestrian signal head must be installed and wired before the overall signal system can be tested and commissioned to verify it functions correctly.

predecessor: Install pedestrian signal poles and foundations
successor: Install Audible / Tactile Pedestrian Push Button
rationale: The push button must be mounted on a pedestrian signal pole, so the pole and its foundation must be installed first to provide a supporting structure.

predecessor: Run conduit and wiring to push button location
successor: Install Audible / Tactile Pedestrian Push Button
rationale: Electrical wiring and conduit must be in place before the push button can be connected and mounted.

predecessor: Install Audible / Tactile Pedestrian Push Button
successor: Test push button functionality and audible/tactile feedback
rationale: The push button must be physically installed and wired before its operation, including audible tones and tactile vibration, can be verified.

predecessor: Install Audible / Tactile Pedestrian Push Button
successor: Configure traffic signal controller with push button inputs
rationale: The push button must be installed and connected to the signal controller before the controller can be programmed to respond to its activation.

predecessor: Install Audible / Tactile Pedestrian Push Button
successor: Perform final inspection and acceptance testing of pedestrian crossing equipment
rationale: The push button must be fully installed before the overall pedestrian crossing system can be inspected and accepted.
Excavation must be completed to create the foundation hole for the signal pole base before the pole can be installed.
The concrete foundation or base must be poured and cured to provide a stable mounting point before the signal pole or mast arm can be erected.
Underground conduits for electrical and signal cables must be in place before the pole is installed so that cables can later be pulled through without re-excavating.
Signal heads, lanterns, and light assemblies must be mounted onto the pole or mast arm, which requires the pole/arm structure to be in place first.
Electrical and signal cables are pulled from the controller cabinet through the pole to the signal heads; the pole must be installed to provide the vertical raceway for cable routing.

predecessor: Excavate and prepare foundation for traffic signal pole
rationale: The pole must have a stable foundation before it can be erected.
The pole structure must be in place to support the signal head mounting hardware.
The mounting bracket or mast arm must be installed before the traffic signal head can be physically attached.

predecessor: Run underground conduit and pull wiring to pole base
rationale: Electrical wiring must be in place at the pole base to later connect to the signal head.

successor: Connect electrical wiring to signal head and controller cabinet
rationale: The signal head must be physically mounted before its internal wiring can be connected to the power and control system.

successor: Align and aim signal head lenses
rationale: The signal head must be installed before its lenses can be adjusted for proper visibility to approaching traffic.

successor: Test signal head operation (light sequencing, visibility)
rationale: The signal head must be physically installed and wired before functional testing can be performed.
The ground must be graded and prepared to provide a stable foundation before guard rails or barriers can be installed.
Guard rails and pedestrian barriers are typically anchored into or alongside finished road surfaces or sidewalks, so the pavement or road base must be in place first.
Many guard rails and pedestrian barriers require concrete curbs, footings, or foundations to be poured and cured before the barrier posts can be secured.
Road markings and signage are often aligned with the installed barrier locations and should be applied after barriers are in place to ensure correct positioning and visibility.
Final surface layers adjacent to barriers are typically completed after barrier installation to create a clean transition and avoid damaging the barrier during paving operations.

The timer module (including the microcontroller and timing circuitry) must be assembled and functional before the display can be connected, as the display receives its input signals from the timer module.
The printed circuit board with the display driver circuitry must be fabricated and tested before the display components can be mounted and soldered onto it.
The countdown timer display must be assembled and tested before it can be mounted into its final enclosure or housing, as the enclosure is designed around the display assembly.

The countdown timer display must be fully installed and operational before system-level integration testing can begin, as the display is a critical output component that must be verified during testing.
The display hardware must be in place and functioning before software calibration and UI adjustment can be performed to ensure correct timing values are shown accurately.
Excavation must be completed before installing signage posts/foundations at the crossing location.
Concrete footings must be cured and set before the sign posts and signs can be mounted on them.
The road base and approaching road surfaces need to be prepared so that the signage location is accessible and the surrounding work is complete.
Warning signs must be installed before pavement markings (e.g., crosswalk lines, warning symbols) are applied, as signs establish the formal crossing zone.
Signage installation should precede final surfacing to ensure signs are properly positioned and not damaged by paving equipment, and to allow for final grade adjustments.
Conduit must be in place to terminate at the junction box; the box serves as a connection or pull point in the conduit system.

predecessor: Mount Junction Box / Pull Box Support Bracket or Hanger
rationale: The support structure (bracket, strut, or hanger) must be installed first to securely hold the box in place.

successor: Pull Electrical Conductors / Cabling Through Conduit
rationale: The junction/pull box provides access for pulling cables; conductors cannot be pulled through a conduit segment without an accessible pull box at intermediate or termination points.
Conductors must be pulled into the box before they can be spliced, terminated, or connected to devices within the box.
The cover can only be installed after the box is mounted, conductors are pulled, and terminations are completed, to provide access during wiring.

Road markings must be applied on a stable, finished pavement surface. Asphalt paving must be completed and cured before markings can be applied, as the markings need a clean, smooth substrate to adhere properly.
The road surface must be cleaned of debris, dust, dirt, and moisture before applying road markings to ensure proper adhesion and durability of the marking material.

While traffic signals can be installed before markings, it is more practical to mark lanes and stop bars first so signal placement can be coordinated with marked pavement layout. This is a soft preference for workflow efficiency.

Road markings provide essential guidance, lane delineation, and safety information for drivers. A road cannot be opened to public traffic without proper markings in place, as this would create a safety hazard and violate traffic regulations.
Signals are positioned relative to the track alignment and must be installed after the track is laid and aligned to ensure correct positioning and sighting distances.
Signals require stable ground for foundations and cable routing, which must be completed after the ballast and sub-ballast layers are placed and compacted.
Signal cables must run through dedicated ducts and trenches that are installed before signal equipment can be connected and commissioned.
Signals must be installed and fully commissioned (tested and calibrated) before any train testing or trial runs can safely occur, as signals are critical for safe train movement.
Signal systems must be operational before overall system integration testing can commence, as signalling is a core subsystem that interacts with train control and safety systems.
The ground must be graded and levelled to the required formation level before any kerb or ramp can be laid, as kerbs require a stable, shaped subgrade to achieve correct alignment and drainage falls.

Subsurface drainage pipes and catchpits must be installed before kerb construction, because kerbs often form part of the drainage channel and the drainage network must be in place to receive runoff collected by the kerb and gutter system.
Kerbs and ramps define the edge of the paved area and act as a formwork/restraint for asphalt; pavement must be laid up to the kerb line after kerbs are fixed.

While line marking can technically be done after pavement is laid, it is standard practice to complete kerbs first because kerb alignment defines the roadway edge and parking boundaries, and marking without completed kerbs may require rework.
Ramps (e.g., pram/disabled ramps) connect the footpath to the roadway; the footpath surface must be finished after ramp construction to ensure smooth transition and correct gradient at the interface.
Existing pavement surface must be removed or milled to provide a clean, even substrate for new resurfacing material to bond properly.
Any defects or instability in the road base must be repaired before resurfacing, otherwise the new surface will fail due to underlying structural issues.
Proper drainage (gutters, drains, culverts) must be in place or repaired before resurfacing to prevent water damage to the new surface.
Kerbs and channels define the road edge and drainage path; they must be installed first so resurfacing can be laid flush against them to the correct profile.
Line marking, road studs, and signage are applied on top of the finished new road surface; resurfacing must be complete to provide a clean surface for markings.
The road can only be opened to traffic after resurfacing is finished and has sufficiently cured/hardened to withstand vehicle loads.
A stable, compacted sub-base is physically required to support the tactile paving slabs or tiles, preventing uneven settlement and ensuring a level walking surface.
Kerb edges define the boundary of the footpath and provide a physical abutment against which tactile paving is laid, ensuring proper alignment and drainage.
A wet concrete or mortar bedding layer must be placed and leveled to receive the tactile paving slabs, providing a firm setting bed for correct height and alignment.
Grout must be applied after paving slabs are laid to fill joints, lock slabs in position, and prevent water ingress and weed growth.
Any finishing touches, cleaning, and curing of mortar/bedding must occur after tactile paving is installed to protect the newly laid surface from disturbance and achieve design strength.

Structural framing must be erected to provide the building skeleton and support points for electrical conduits, cable trays, and ductwork; electrical and ducting works cannot commence without an established structural framework.

Floor slabs or decking must be poured/cast to create the substrate where electrical conduits are embedded and ducting routes are laid out; work on embedded conduits and underfloor ducting requires the slab to be in place.

Internal wall partitions define the rooms and vertical pathways for electrical wiring and duct risers; rough-in for outlets, switches, and duct penetrations depends on partition framing being complete.

Insulation and fireproofing materials are applied after electrical cables and ductwork are in place to avoid covering or fireproofing over unfinished MEP services; access for inspection and testing of electrical and ducting must occur prior to encapsulation.

Ceiling grids and drywall are installed after overhead electrical conduits, cables, and ducting are complete to allow permanent closure of ceiling spaces; installing ceilings first would block access for MEP rough-in and create rework.
The ground must be cleared, stripped of topsoil, and excavated to the required depth and dimensions before any footing concrete can be placed or forms installed.
Accurate staking and layout of the building corners and footing locations must be completed before excavation or forming of footings can begin.
Soil bearing capacity and ground conditions must be verified prior to designing and placing footings to ensure structural adequacy.
Footings provide the load-bearing base; foundation walls cannot be constructed until the footings have been poured and cured.
Underslab utilities such as drain lines and water pipes are installed after footings are in place but before the slab is poured, as footings define the perimeter and elevation.

Support columns and piers require a stable load-bearing foundation to transfer vertical loads to the ground. The foundation must be fully cured and capable of supporting the column loads before column construction can begin.
Column starter bars or anchor bolts must be embedded in the footing or base slab. The footing provides the structural base and connection point for column reinforcement.
Vertical rebar cages and dowels must be placed and tied within the column formwork before concrete can be poured for the columns/piers.
Beams and girders bear directly on columns or piers. Columns must be in place and have achieved sufficient strength to carry the beam loads before beam installation can proceed.
Upper floor slabs or decks are typically supported by beams that rest on columns. The column support system must be complete to provide vertical support for the slab framework.
Guardrails are mounted to or anchored in the bridge deck; the deck must be in place to provide a mounting surface for guardrail installation.
Guardrails define the edge of the roadway, and paving must be completed up to the guardrail line; installing guardrails first ensures precise alignment for the paving operation.

While markings could theoretically be applied before guardrails, it is standard practice to install guardrails first to avoid running over fresh markings and to ensure accurate edge-line placement relative to the barrier.
For bridge-mounted guardrails, the steel superstructure and any parapet or curb must be completed before guardrail post-anchoring or bolting can occur.
Guardrail systems must be fully installed before final safety inspections and any required crash-test verification or acceptance testing can be performed on the barrier.

The foundation and slab provide the base support and load-bearing surface upon which the structural framing (joists and beams) must be erected. Without a completed foundation, the framing has no stable base to attach to.
Columns or vertical support members must be in place before joists and beams can be installed, as beams typically span between columns to transfer loads vertically.
Joists and beams form the horizontal structural framework that supports the decking or subfloor. The decking material is laid directly on top of or attached to the joists.

MEP rough-in work such as running ductwork, conduit, and piping often occurs after the structural framing is in place, as these systems are routed through and supported by the floor/ceiling framing cavities.
In multi-story or roof-bearing applications, the floor/ceiling joists and beams must be completed to provide the working platform and load path before the roof structure can be erected above them.
The bracing system requires a stable foundation to anchor against, as braces transfer lateral loads to the ground.
Steel frame erection must be completed first to provide the structural members that the bracing system connects to and stabilizes.
Bracing system installation must be complete before concrete floor slabs are poured, as the braces provide temporary or permanent lateral stability needed during slab placement and curing.
The bracing system must be in place to ensure structural stability before non-structural cladding or curtain walls are installed.
While not a strict physical necessity, completing the bracing system before interior fit-out avoids rework and ensures the building is stable for interior trades.
The staircase must be supported on a stable foundation or substructure before it can be installed; a structural base is required to bear its load.
The structural frame provides the vertical support and landings onto which the access stair is attached; stairs cannot be installed without the main structural skeleton in place.

Interior finishes around the stairwell (e.g., plastering walls, painting, final flooring) should be done after the staircase is installed to ensure a seamless finish and avoid damaging finished surfaces during stair installation.
Handrails and balustrades are typically installed on the completed staircase structure to provide safety and code compliance; they cannot be fitted before the stair itself exists.

successor: MEP Rough-In (Electrical, Plumbing, HVAC) within Stairwell
rationale: While MEP rough-in can partially proceed before stairs, final routing of conduits, pipes, or ducts that pass through the stairwell should be completed after the stair is installed to avoid clashes and ensure proper alignment.

Expansion joints are typically installed at planned locations within concrete slabs or decks; the slab must be poured and partially cured before expansion joint materials can be properly placed and bonded.

While expansion joints are primarily associated with concrete, structural steel frames often require coordination; however, steel erection is not a strict prerequisite for all expansion joint installations.
Waterproofing over expansion joints must be applied after the expansion joint assembly is complete to ensure continuity of the waterproofing system across the joint.
Floor finishes such as tiles or screeds over expansion joints must be installed after the joint filler and sealant are in place to allow proper movement and prevent cracking.
Fascia boards are installed along the edges of the roof structure; roof trusses or rafters must be in place to provide the structural support onto which fascia boards are fastened.
Roof sheathing is typically installed before fascia to create a solid roof deck; fascia boards are then attached at the eaves and gable ends of the sheathed roof.
Gutters are mounted directly onto or under the fascia board; the fascia must be in place first to provide the mounting surface and proper alignment for the gutter system.

Soffits are installed beneath the fascia board to enclose the underside of the roof overhang; the fascia board defines the outer edge and must be installed first to allow proper soffit fitting and drainage.

While painting can be done after installation, it is a soft preference to complete painting or finishing of the fascia board after installation to protect the material from weather and achieve a uniform appearance.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and existing structures before any excavation can begin to provide a clear and safe working area.
Temporary support systems such as shoring, dewatering, and ground stabilization must be designed and installed before deep excavation to prevent collapse and ensure worker safety.
Accurate site surveying, grid layout, and peg setting must be completed first to mark the exact excavation boundaries, footing locations, and levels before digging commences.
Existing underground utilities (water, gas, electricity, telecom) must be located and either diverted or protected before excavation to avoid damage, service disruptions, and safety hazards.

After excavation and footing construction, a layer of blinding concrete must be poured and waterproofing applied to provide a clean, level, and watertight base for subsequent reinforcement and concrete works.

Excavation and footing construction must be completed before steel reinforcement can be placed and formwork erected for the foundation slab or raft, as the reinforcement sits within the excavated footprint.
Once footings are cast and cured, backfilling around the substructure can only proceed after excavation and footing works are finished to provide lateral support and prepare for slab-on-grade works.
Columns and piers require a stable load-bearing base; footings/foundations must be completed first to provide structural support and proper load transfer.
Reinforcement steel within the foundation must be placed and tied before columns can be erected, as column dowels are typically embedded into the foundation concrete.
Foundation concrete must reach sufficient strength (curing) before columns/pier installation can begin to bear the imposed loads without cracking or failure.
Beams and girders span between columns/piers and rely on them as vertical supports; columns must be in place before any beam/girder can be erected.
Elevated slab formwork is typically supported by beams and columns; columns must be installed to provide the vertical framework before slab formwork can proceed.
A stable, level, and compacted subgrade or foundation is required to support the deck structure; installing decking on uneven or unprepared ground would lead to structural instability and failure.
The decking boards are fastened directly to the underlying joists/frame; the frame must be fully installed, level, and secured before any decking boards can be laid.
Railings and guardrails are typically mounted on top of or through the finished deck surface; installing rails first would interfere with the decking layout and fastening.

While stairs can sometimes be constructed concurrently, it is standard practice to complete the main deck surface first to establish the finished floor elevation from which stair stringers and treads are measured and attached.

Protective finishes (sealant, stain, paint) must be applied after decking is fully installed to ensure all board surfaces and gaps are treated; applying finish before installation would damage the coating during fastening and leave uncovered areas.
Guardrails and handrails are typically anchored into concrete slabs or decks; the concrete must be poured and sufficiently cured to provide a stable substrate and achieve required anchorage strength.
Where guardrails attach to steel columns or beams, the structural steel frame must be erected and stabilized before railings can be welded or bolted in place.
Handrails are installed alongside or on top of stair stringers and landings; the stair structure itself must be complete to provide the supporting surface and geometry for railing layout.
Guardrails and handrails are life-safety components; inspectors must verify railing height, strength, and compliance with building codes, which can only occur after installation is complete.

successor: Flooring / Deck Surface Finishing (if painting or coating overlaps)
rationale: Finishing crews often prefer to complete floor coatings or sealants before railings obscure access; however, this is a soft preference as touch-up work can be done after railing installation.
Concrete must be placed and cured to achieve sufficient strength before structural inspection and load testing can be performed.
Steel structural members must be erected and fully connected to form a stable frame before load testing can evaluate structural integrity.
Formwork and falsework must be installed to support uncured concrete, and inspection occurs after this temporary support is in place.

successor: Subsequent Finishing Works (e.g., cladding, MEP rough-in)
rationale: Load testing must confirm structural adequacy before enclosing or loading the structure with finishes and mechanical systems.
Inspection and load testing identify deficiencies that must be rectified before proceeding to later construction stages.
The ground must be excavated and prepared before any structural component like a bicycle rack can be installed.
The bicycle rack typically requires a stable concrete foundation or slab to be cured in place before the rack can be anchored or bolted down.
Underground utility lines and rough-in work must be completed before installing any anchored structure to avoid interference or rework.
The bicycle rack anchors need to be set before the final pavement or surface finish is laid to ensure the rack is flush and securely integrated.
While not physically required, it is best practice to complete landscaping and site cleanup after the rack is installed to avoid damaging new plants or finishes during installation.
The bike rack must be anchored to a stable, cured concrete surface or slab; without the foundation, the rack cannot be secured in place.
All buried utilities must be located and marked before any excavation or concrete pouring to avoid damage and ensure safety.
Proper grading and drainage must be established before the slab is poured so that water runs away from the rack area.
Signage indicating bike parking location should be installed after the rack is in place to ensure correct positioning relative to the installed rack.
Surrounding landscaping, asphalt, or paving around the bike rack must be finished after the rack is bolted down to ensure a clean, flush finish and avoid damaging the rack.
A stable, level concrete slab or foundation must be in place to support the bike locker structure before the locker can be installed.
Any underground electrical conduits or power supply needed for lighting or security features of the bike locker must be roughed in before the slab is poured or the locker is placed.
Installation of the bike locker must be complete before final finishes (painting, sealing, etc.) are applied to avoid damage to finishes and ensure proper integration.
Surrounding paving, pathways, and landscaping around the bike locker should be completed after the locker is installed to ensure proper alignment, accessibility, and fit within the site design.
Electronic access control systems, keypad readers, or security cameras intended for the bike locker area must be installed after the locker is physically in place for proper mounting and wiring.

Bike lane markings must be applied on a clean, smooth, and properly prepared pavement surface to ensure adhesion and visibility. Any base preparation such as sweeping, patching, or priming must be completed first.
The structural pavement layer (asphalt or concrete) must be fully laid, compacted, and cured before any surface markings can be applied to ensure a stable and durable substrate.

While signs can technically be installed before markings, it is standard practice and preferable to apply pavement markings first to ensure proper alignment and placement of signs relative to the marked lane boundaries.
The bike lane markings are a final surface treatment that must be completed and cured before the roadway is opened to cyclists and vehicular traffic to ensure safety and marking durability.
The road surface must be prepared, cleaned, and ready before any markings or signage can be applied to ensure proper adhesion and visibility.

Pavement markings for the bike lane (such as lane lines, symbols, and stencils) should be laid down before installing vertical signage to ensure the lane layout is clearly defined and signage is correctly positioned.
Bike lane signage must be fully installed and verified before the road or bike lane can be opened to traffic or pass final inspection.
Although not always a physical necessity, it is good practice to verify that signage is correctly placed and visible before conducting any user acceptance testing or safety audits.
A level, stable concrete slab or foundation is required to support the Bike Repair Station equipment and provide a safe working surface.
Proper drainage around the repair station area must be established before installation to prevent water pooling and damage to the station.
If the repair station includes an air pump or wash station requiring water/power, utility rough-ins should be completed before final installation.
The repair station must be anchored and installed before the surrounding pavement or pathway surface is finished to ensure proper integration and a seamless appearance.
Directional or informational signs for the repair station should be installed after the station is in place to ensure accurate positioning.
Final landscaping and placement of adjacent site furniture (benches, bike racks) can be completed after the repair station is installed to avoid damage during construction.
The ground must be cleared, levelled, and excavated before the bike shelter foundation can be laid.
A stable concrete slab or foundation pad is required to anchor the shelter structure.
Any underground drainage or electrical conduits for lighting must be placed before the slab is poured to avoid cutting/excavating later.

successor: Installation of Bike Racks / Parking fixtures
rationale: Bike racks and parking fixtures are typically installed on or anchored to the shelter slab/floor after the shelter structure is erected.
Surrounding paving, pathways, and landscaping are completed after the shelter is built to ensure clean edges and proper grading around the structure.
The ground must be leveled and cleared of debris before installing a bike rack to ensure a stable and secure foundation.
If the bike rack requires a concrete base or is being set into pavement, the concrete must be poured and cured before the rack can be anchored.
Any underground utilities (power, water, gas) must be identified before digging or drilling anchor points to avoid damage and ensure safety.
If the bike rack is installed in an area that will later be paved, the rack must be in place before the final paving layer is applied to ensure proper integration.

Final landscaping, planting, and decorative elements around the bike rack area are typically done after installation to avoid damage, though this is a soft preference as landscaping could precede if done carefully.

successor: Subbase and Paving Works for Bike Paths
rationale: The ground must be cleared, graded, and rough-graded before any subbase or paving can be placed to ensure a stable, properly prepared surface.

predecessor: Installation of Underground Drainage and Utilities
successor: Subbase and Paving Works for Bike Paths
rationale: All underground drainage pipes, conduits, and utility services must be installed and backfilled before subbase and paving to avoid trenching through the finished pavement.

predecessor: Subbase and Paving Works for Bike Paths
successor: Application of Surface Seal Coat or Protective Treatment
rationale: The paving works must be completed and cured before any surface seal coat or protective treatment can be applied to ensure proper adhesion and finish.

predecessor: Subbase and Paving Works for Bike Paths
successor: Installation of Bollards, Signage, and Road Markings
rationale: Paving must be finished and set before bollards can be anchored, signs can be erected, and permanent road markings can be painted on the surface.

predecessor: Subbase and Paving Works for Bike Paths
rationale: While landscaping can sometimes be done alongside paving, it is generally preferred to complete paving first so that topsoil and planting are not disturbed by construction traffic and to achieve a clean interface between hard and soft surfaces.
Bike lockers require a stable, level concrete surface for proper anchoring and stability. The foundation must be cured and ready before lockers can be mounted.
Proper drainage and site grading must be completed to ensure water does not pool around the bike lockers, preventing rust and structural damage.
While bike lockers can function without immediate signage, clear markings and directional signs should be placed after installation to guide users to the locker location.
The bike lockers must be fully installed and anchored before a final inspection can verify that all components are secure and compliant with design specifications.
If the bike lockers require electronic locking mechanisms or lighting, electrical rough-in should be completed prior, though not strictly required for basic locker installation.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and graded before fencing can be installed to ensure a stable and even base for fence posts and barriers.
Fence posts for child-safe barriers often require concrete footings or foundations to be set, which must be installed before the fence panels and gates are erected.
Any underground utilities (water, gas, electrical) along the fence line must be located and rerouted if necessary before digging post holes to avoid damage and safety hazards.
The fence must be in place before playground equipment is installed to ensure the play area is securely enclosed and children cannot wander off during or after installation.

Fencing and barriers must be completed before laying soft fall surfacing (e.g., rubber mulch, sand, or synthetic turf) and landscaping to avoid disturbing the finished surfaces and to allow proper grading against the fence base.
Wall surfaces must be finished and waterproofed before sanitary fixtures are mounted to ensure proper sealing and to prevent moisture damage behind fixtures.
Floor levels and waterproof membranes must be completed prior to installing sanitary fixtures to establish correct drainage gradients and a watertight base.
Underground and in-wall waste pipe connections and vent stacks must be roughed-in so that sanitary fixtures can be connected directly to the drainage network.
After fixtures are set in place, final connection of supply lines, trap assemblies, and water pressure/leak testing must be performed to verify proper operation.

Minor grouting, caulking, and touch-up painting around installed fixtures are typically done after fixture placement to achieve a clean finished appearance, though this is a soft sequencing preference.

Rough carpentry and framing establish the structural walls and cavities into which child-scale furniture and casework are installed; without framed spaces, casework has no mounting surface or enclosing structure.
Electrical outlets, plumbing stub-outs, and HVAC ductwork concealed within walls must be roughed in before casework is permanently installed, as the casework would block access to these services.

Wall surfaces must be finished (taped, mudded, sanded, and painted or primed) before casework is installed so that the casework sits flush against a complete, level wall surface and to avoid damaging newly installed casework during drywall finishing.

Flooring and base moldings are typically installed after fixed casework so that the flooring can be run up to or slightly under the casework toe-kick, creating a clean finished appearance and avoiding gaps that would result if flooring were laid first.

While it is physically possible to paint after casework, it is a soft preference to complete final painting before casework installation to avoid overspray on finished surfaces and tedious cutting-in around cabinet edges; however, touch-up painting inevitably follows casework installation.
A level, stable, and properly graded surface is required to securely anchor shade structures and canopies.
Shade structures typically require concrete footings or anchor foundations to be set and cured before the structure can be erected.
Any underground electrical, water, or data lines serving the shade area must be installed before footings and posts are placed to avoid conflicts.
Final landscaping, planting, and surface finishes around the shade structure are completed after the structure is in place to ensure proper fit and avoid damage.
The shade structure must be fully installed and stable before the final project inspection and punch-list walkthrough can be performed.
The spatial layout, room functions, and circulation paths must be fully designed before signage locations and wayfinding routes for children can be determined.
Walls and surfaces must be finished and prepared to allow proper mounting, adhesion, or installation of signage elements.
Any illuminated signage, digital displays, or interactive wayfinding elements require electrical supply which must be roughed in before final signage installation.
After signage and wayfinding elements are installed, a safety and accessibility audit must verify they are properly placed, at correct heights, and free of hazards for children.
Signage installation should be completed before final cleaning to avoid dust and debris settling on signs, though cleaning could technically be done around signage if needed.

The building's structural frame (columns, slabs, beams, walls) must be complete before interior finishing can begin, as fit-out works require stable enclosed spaces and structural load-bearing elements to be in place.
The building envelope must be weathertight (roof and external waterproofing completed) to protect interior finishes from water damage during fit-out activities.
External walls, windows, and glazing must be installed to enclose the building, providing weather protection and security before interior finishing works can proceed.
All interior installation works (ceilings, partitions, floor finishes, doors, carpentry, etc.) must be completed before final cleaning, snagging, and handover activities can take place.

successor: MEP (Mechanical, Electrical & Plumbing) Fixtures, Fittings & Equipment (FF&E) Installation
rationale: While rough-in MEP work happens before or concurrently with fit-out, the final installation of fixtures (light fixtures, sanitaryware, switches, outlets, HVAC grilles) typically occurs after or at the final stage of interior fit-out to avoid damage and ensure alignment with finished surfaces.

A stable, compacted and properly graded base is physically required before any safety surfacing (e.g., rubber mulch, poured-in-place rubber, synthetic turf) can be installed. Without a prepared sub-base, the surfacing will not be level, stable, or meet fall-height safety standards.

Proper drainage (e.g., French drains, sub-surface drainage layers) must be in place before safety surfacing is installed, otherwise water will become trapped beneath the surface, causing degradation, mold, and loss of impact-attenuation properties.

Play equipment posts, footings, and anchors must be installed and concrete cured before safety surfacing is placed, because the surfacing is laid around and up to the equipment supports. Installing after would require cutting through the safety surface.
Border edging (e.g., timber curbs, rubber borders) must be installed after the safety surface is placed to contain it properly and provide a clean finished edge.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and graded before playground equipment can be installed to ensure a stable, safe foundation.
Any underground utilities (drainage, electrical, water lines) must be laid before playground equipment is erected to avoid digging near installed structures or having to relocate equipment.
Concrete footings or anchoring pads must be poured and cured before the playground equipment can be bolted or set onto them for structural stability.

Safety surfacing (e.g., rubber mulch, poured-in-place rubber, or engineered wood fiber) must be installed after the equipment is erected so it can be placed flush against posts and around the structure's footprint.
While fencing can be installed before or after, it is often done after equipment erection to precisely align gate locations and setback distances from play structures.
The building must be substantially complete and handed over before child safety audits can be conducted, as the audit inspects completed facilities and installed safety features.
Children cannot occupy or use the building until child safety audits and commissioning have verified that all safety measures, equipment, and systems are properly installed and functioning.

predecessor: Installation of Safety Equipment (e.g., window guards, childproof locks)
rationale: All child safety equipment must be installed before the audit can verify its presence and correct installation.
While ideally all defects are resolved before audit, any safety issues identified during the audit may require follow-up remedial work, though this is a soft preference for a clean sequence.
Fire detection, alarm, and suppression systems must be commissioned and operational before child safety audits can verify overall building safety for children.
The ground must be prepared and excavated to the required depth and slope before installing any water play feature, as the feature requires a stable, level base and proper drainage.

Water supply lines and drainage pipes must be laid and connected underground before the water play feature is installed above ground, as the feature requires water input and proper drainage to function.
A concrete base or foundation pad is needed to anchor the water play feature securely and provide a flat, stable surface; this must be poured and cured before the feature is placed.

Safety flooring (e.g., rubber pour-in-place, turf, or mats) must be installed after the water play feature is in place, as the flooring needs to be laid flush against the feature edges to create a seamless, tripping-hazard-free surface.

After the water play feature is physically installed, final plumbing, electrical, and control system connections must be made and the entire system tested for leaks, pump operation, and water quality before opening to users.
A stable foundation is required to support the Ticket Booth structure before it can be built.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and prepared before any construction of the Ticket Booth can begin.
Underground conduits for electrical power and data cabling must be laid before the Ticket Booth floor and structure are built.
Interior finishing (painting, flooring, counter installation) can only commence once the Ticket Booth structure is fully erected and enclosed.
Wiring and data cables can only be terminated and tested inside the Ticket Booth after its walls and structure are in place.
Signage is typically mounted after the booth is complete, though it could be prefabricated and installed concurrently; this is a strong preference for sequencing.
The physical queue barriers and rails must be positioned relative to the Ticket Booth's final location and orientation, requiring the completed booth as a reference point.
The entrance gate must be anchored to a stable foundation; without foundation preparation (excavation, concrete footing), the gate structure would lack structural support and stability.
Proper grading and drainage must be completed before installing the entrance gate to ensure water flows away from the gate area, preventing erosion, soil settling, and long-term structural damage.

Electrical wiring for gate automation (motors, sensors, lights, intercom) must be run after the gate structure is in place to ensure proper routing through gate posts and connection to moving components.

The entrance road or driveway should be paved after the gate is installed so that the pavement aligns precisely with the gate opening and gate posts, avoiding misalignment or the need for cutting/demolition of newly laid pavement.

While security cameras, card readers, and intercoms can be partially installed beforehand, final installation and calibration of security components at the gate is best done after the gate is fully constructed to ensure proper positioning and integration with gate hardware.

The Ferris Wheel requires a stable, level foundation to support its massive weight and dynamic loads. Site preparation including ground leveling, concrete foundation pouring, and anchor bolt placement must be completed before any assembly can begin.

predecessor: Structural Steel Framework Assembly (Base & Support Legs)
rationale: The A-frame support legs and central axle mounting structure must be erected and secured to the foundation before the wheel hub, spokes, and passenger cabins can be attached.
The central axle/hub is the core rotating element around which the entire wheel is built. It must be installed on the support structure before spokes, rim, and cabins are added.

The drive motors, control panels, wiring, and operating mechanisms for the Ferris Wheel can only be installed after the wheel structure is fully assembled, as these systems are integrated into the wheel's mechanical components.
Gondolas/cabins are attached to the outer rim of the wheel along its perimeter. The wheel structure must be fully erected and secured before cabins can be hung from the rim attachment points.
The carousel requires a stable, level foundation to support its weight and rotating mechanism. Without a properly poured and cured foundation, the carousel structure cannot be safely mounted.
Power supply conduits and wiring for the carousel's motors, lights, and control systems must be run underground and to the base location before the carousel structure is placed on top.
The central support column and structural framework of the carousel must be erected first to provide the anchor point and support structure for the canopy roof assembly.
The rotating platform and drive mechanism must be installed and operational before individual ride vehicles (horses, chariots, etc.) can be mounted onto the platform.

While decorative painting, trim, and themed lighting can be partially installed before the carousel is completed, final decorative finishing and rigorous lighting tests are best done after the structure is fully assembled to ensure alignment and electrical continuity.
The roller coaster track must be mounted on top of the support structure (columns, footers, and beams). Without the foundation and supports in place, there is nothing to attach the track sections to.

successor: Roller Coaster Train Assembly and Installation
rationale: The train (roller coaster cars) must be placed onto completed track to run. Track must be fully installed and aligned before trains can be loaded onto it.

While some electrical work can be done in parallel, final wiring of block brakes, sensors, and station controls along the track requires the track to be in its final position so that sensors and signaling components can be precisely mounted.
Safety testing (e.g., clearance checks, load testing, brake testing) cannot be performed until the track is fully installed and secured.

successor: Station Platform and Queue Line Construction
rationale: While station structure can be built earlier, precise alignment of the loading platform with the track cannot be finalized until the track is in place.
The ground must be leveled and cleared of debris to provide a stable, flat surface for tent installation and to ensure proper anchoring.
The precise footprint and anchor point locations must be marked on the ground to guide the correct placement and orientation of the tent structure.
Any underground electrical, water, or data lines intended to service the tent must be laid before the tent is erected, as installing them afterward would require lifting or moving the structure.
Interior finishing, flooring, and partition walls can only be installed after the tent frame and fabric are fully erected and weather-tight.
Overhead electrical cabling, lighting fixtures, and HVAC ducting within the tent must be installed after the structure is complete to allow proper attachment to the frame.
The grandstand seating must be mounted on a stable foundation and support structure; without it, the seating cannot be safely installed.
The structural frame of the grandstand must be in place to provide the tiers and framework onto which seating is attached.
Safety railings are installed after seating to ensure proper alignment with seating rows and to maintain safe egress paths.
Seating must be fully installed before final inspection and load testing can verify the complete grandstand assembly meets safety standards.
Signage indicating row/seat numbers is typically placed after seating installation to align precisely with seat positions, but could theoretically be pre-installed in some configurations.

The stage platform requires a solid foundation to bear the load of the stage structure, performers, and equipment; pouring concrete foundations must be completed before any platform assembly can begin.
The supporting steel framework or structural columns that will hold the stage platform must be erected first to provide a mounting point for the platform.
The stage platform structure must be complete before the finished stage flooring (e.g., wood, vinyl, or dance surface) can be installed on top of it.
Safety railings around the stage edges can only be attached after the platform is fully assembled and in its final position.

While lighting rigging can theoretically be done concurrently, it is preferred to complete the stage platform first to provide a safe work surface and reference elevation for positioning overhead lighting trusses.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and graded before fencing can be installed to ensure a stable base and correct alignment of fence posts.
Any underground utilities (water, electric, data lines) that will cross the fence line must be installed first to avoid digging up or damaging the newly installed fence.

successor: Main Gate and Access Control Installation
rationale: Gates and access control systems (card readers, keypads, turnstiles) are physically mounted onto or integrated with the perimeter fence, so the fence structure must be in place first.

While not strictly required, landscaping (planting, mulching, sodding) is typically easier and neater after the fence is installed to avoid damaging plants during fence construction and to work right up to the fence line.

Security cameras, motion sensors, and intrusion detection systems are often mounted on fence posts or poles along the fence line, requiring the fence to be erected first to serve as the mounting infrastructure.
The ground must be properly prepared, leveled, and compacted before constructing the waste management station to ensure a stable foundation and proper drainage.
A concrete foundation or slab must be poured and cured before the waste management station structure can be erected on top of it.
Water supply lines and sewer/drainage connections must be installed and roughed in before the waste management station can be connected to these services.
Electrical conduits, wiring, and panels must be roughed in to the waste management station location before the station's electrical systems can be finalized.
The waste management station structure must be complete and enclosed before heavy waste processing equipment like compactors, balers, or shredders can be installed inside.
The station must be structurally complete before designated waste storage areas, bins, and segregation zones can be set up within it.
Final connections of plumbing fixtures and electrical outlets/fixtures within the waste management station can only be completed after the station structure is in place.

While not a strict physical requirement, it is preferred to have the waste management station in place first so that access roads and paving can be aligned precisely to the station's loading/unloading areas.
The waste management station must be fully constructed and all equipment installed before final inspection, testing, and commissioning can take place to verify operational readiness.
Ride assembly requires a stable, level foundation and structural steel framework to support the ride components and ensure safety during installation.
Electrical power and mechanical utility connections (e.g., compressed air, hydraulics) must be roughed-in to the ride location before assembly and commissioning can proceed.
Theming elements (scenery, props, decorative cladding) are installed after the ride structure and mechanical systems are in place to avoid damage and allow accurate fitment.
Full ride testing, load testing, and safety certification can only occur after the ride is fully assembled, commissioned, and all systems are operational.
Project handover and final inspections require the ride to be completely assembled, commissioned, and operational before the client accepts the installation.
Legal ownership and required permits (environmental, grading, building) must be secured before any site disturbance or earthwork can legally begin.
Accurate boundary, topographic, and utility location surveys are needed to establish grading limits, cut/fill areas, and ensure work stays within property lines.
All existing underground utilities (gas, electric, water, sewer, telecom) must be located and marked to avoid damage during excavation and grading operations.
Erosion control measures, silt fences, and protected tree zones must be established before any clearing or grading to comply with environmental regulations.
After grading to design elevations, the prepared subgrade must be tested for compaction density and stability before subsequent foundation work can commence.
The site must be rough-graded to final subgrade elevations and properly compacted before foundation excavation can begin to ensure a stable working platform.
Grading establishes proper drainage slopes and subgrade elevations; underground water, sewer, and storm drainage pipes are installed after grading is complete to maintain design grades.
Site grading establishes road subgrade and drainage patterns; paved roads, curbs, and gutters follow once final earthwork grades are achieved.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and prepared before any temporary structures (such as site offices, storage sheds, or scaffolding) can be erected on it.
Underground or overhead utilities must be identified and relocated if necessary to avoid interference with temporary structure foundations or placement.

Soil bearing capacity should be assessed to ensure safe foundation design for heavy temporary structures such as tower cranes or hoardings, though in some cases temporary structures may proceed with assumed values.

Temporary structures (e.g., site offices, material storage, scaffolding, hoardings, tower cranes) must be in place to support and enable the main construction activities such as excavation, concreting, and steel erection.
Erection of temporary structures is a key part of site mobilization; work cannot commence until temporary facilities (power supply, fencing, welfare units) are operational.
Rough-in electrical work (conduit, wiring, boxes, and cables) must be installed in walls, ceilings, and floors before hook-up and testing can begin, as the hook-up connects to these pre-run systems.
Mechanical equipment (HVAC units, pumps, etc.) must be set in place before electrical hook-up can connect power and control wiring to them.
Plumbing systems must be roughed in before electrical hook-up of water heaters, pumps, and other electrically-powered plumbing equipment can proceed.

Electrical hook-up and testing must be completed before enclosing walls with drywall and applying finishes, so that all wiring connections can be verified and any faults corrected without needing to tear out finished surfaces.
Electrical hook-up and testing is a prerequisite for full building commissioning, as all electrical systems must be energized and verified before integrated system testing and start-up can occur.
Signage and theming elements require a completed structural shell to provide mounting surfaces and structural support for installation.
Wall surfaces must be finished and painted before signage and decorative theming can be mounted to achieve proper adhesion and appearance.
Electrical wiring and outlets must be in place to power illuminated signage, digital displays, and interactive theming elements.
Flooring must be completed before floor-mounted signage, wayfinding elements, or themed floor graphics are installed to avoid damage or rework.
All signage and theming must be fully installed before the final inspection can verify completeness, accuracy, and compliance with design specifications.
The ride must be fully operational and maintained up until the point of decommissioning; decommissioning cannot begin while the ride is still in active service.
After dismantling the ride structure and equipment, the site must be cleared, cleaned, and remediated to prepare it for future use.
The old ride must be completely removed and the area cleared before any new ride construction or installation can commence on the same footprint.
All electrical power to the ride must be isolated and safety lockout/tagout procedures completed before any physical dismantling work can begin to ensure worker safety.
The dismantled components, materials, and debris from the ride must be processed, sorted, and disposed of or recycled after removal from the site.
A solid foundation or ground preparation is needed before installing the rear fence to ensure stability and proper anchoring.
The rear fence structure must be in place before gates can be hung or attached to the fence posts.
Final landscaping and finishing work around the fence area is typically done after the fence is installed to avoid damage and ensure clean edges.
The building must be substantially complete and legally occupiable before final site restoration can begin, as all major construction work that could disturb the site must be finished.
All earthwork, grading, and drainage installations must be completed before site restoration, as restoration would cover or be damaged by further grading.
Underground utilities and service connections must be fully installed before restoring surfaces, to avoid re-excavation.
Landscaping, pavement, and hardscape elements are typically installed as part of site restoration; major landscaping work must precede final clean-up operations.
The site must be fully cleaned and restored before the final project inspection and close-out can occur, as inspectors need to review the completed site condition.
The ground must be leveled and prepared before installing any gate structure to ensure stability and proper alignment.
Gate posts or supporting fence posts must be set in concrete and fully cured before hanging a gate, as the gate hinges attach directly to these posts.
Concrete used to secure gate posts must cure (typically 24-48 hours minimum) to achieve sufficient strength to bear the weight of the gate.
The gate must be hung in place before latches, handles, or locking mechanisms can be aligned and installed, as their positioning depends on the exact final location of the gate.

While not physically required, it is preferable to complete landscaping such as planting, mulching, or paving near the gate after installation to avoid damaging new plants or finishes during the heavy gate installation work.
The ground must be cleared and excavated to the required depth and width before the acoustic barrier foundation or posts can be installed.
Concrete footings or bases must be poured and cured to provide a stable structural support for the acoustic barrier panels and posts.
Once the acoustic barrier panels and posts are in place, the excavated area around the base must be backfilled and compacted to secure the barrier and restore ground level.
Landscaping and surface finishing around the barrier can proceed after installation but this is a soft preference as some minor finishing could be done concurrently.
All buried utilities (gas, water, electric, telecom) must be identified, located, and if necessary, diverted before excavation for the barrier foundation begins to avoid damage and ensure safety.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and properly graded before a fence can be installed to ensure a stable and even foundation.
Underground utility lines must be identified and relocated if necessary to avoid damage during fence post excavation and to comply with safety regulations.
Concrete footings or piers for fence posts must be poured and cured before the fence panels and posts can be erected.
Final landscaping, topsoil placement, and seeding/sodding should be done after the fence is installed to cover post holes and blend the fence into the finished site.

The completed noise fence should be inspected for compliance with noise mitigation specifications and structural integrity before the project is signed off, though this is a procedural preference rather than a physical necessity.
The rear elevation (rear wall) must be built on top of a completed foundation to provide structural support and stability.
The ground floor slab provides the base upon which the rear elevation wall is erected.
The roof structure bears on the completed rear elevation wall, so the wall must be in place before roof framing can begin.
Windows and doors in the rear elevation require the wall structure to be erected before they can be installed into the rough openings.
Exterior finishes such as brickwork, siding, or render are applied onto the completed rear elevation wall structure.
Foundations must be completed before any superstructure work like a rear extension can begin, as the extension requires a stable base.
The ground floor slab provides the working platform and structural base for the rear extension walls and structure.
The existing rear wall must be removed (or openings created) to allow the new extension to be structurally connected to the existing building.
The walls and structure of the rear extension must be erected before the roof can be installed.
The structural openings in the extension must be built before windows and doors can be fitted.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and excavated before any foundation work for the outbuilding can begin.
The concrete foundation or slab must be poured and cured before the outbuilding structure can be erected on top.
Any underground electrical, plumbing, or drainage lines serving the outbuilding must be installed and inspected before the floor slab is poured or structure is built.
The structural frame and walls of the outbuilding must be completed before roof trusses, sheathing, and roofing materials can be installed.
The outbuilding frame must be erected and sheathed before exterior siding or cladding can be applied.
The structure must be enclosed and weathertight before interior drywall, flooring, and trim work can commence.
While not physically required, it is standard sequencing to complete the outbuilding structure before doing final landscape grading and planting around it to avoid rework and damage to new plantings.
All debris, existing structures, and vegetation must be removed from the site before soft landscaping can begin, to provide a clean, safe working area and prevent damage to new planting.
The site must be brought to final levels and contours before topsoil placement and planting, as soft landscaping follows the established grades.
All buried pipes, cables, drainage runs, and service connections must be installed and backfilled before topsoil is placed and planting occurs, to avoid digging up finished landscaping.
Hard surfaces such as paths, patios, retaining walls, and kerbs must be completed before soft landscaping is undertaken, as these define the boundaries and beds for planting.

The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and obstacles before any boundary walls, fences, or enclosures can be erected, as obstruction-free ground is physically required for marking and building the foundation.

Footings and foundation trenches for the boundary wall or fence posts must be excavated and prepared before the actual enclosure elements (walls, panels, posts) can be installed, as they provide the structural base.

Final landscaping, grading, and aesthetic finishing work around the perimeter should occur after the boundary enclosure is complete to avoid damaging newly installed walls or fences and to ensure proper alignment of soil and planting against the enclosure.

Installing perimeter security elements (sensors, cameras, alarms) is typically done after the physical enclosure is in place so that the devices can be mounted directly onto the structure; however, wiring can be pre-run, so this is a soft preference rather than a hard constraint.

The boundary enclosure defines the property limits and provides site security, which is essential before internal building work begins to prevent unauthorized access and to demarcate the construction zone clearly.
The acoustic assessment requires the building structure to be in place to measure actual sound transmission paths and structural vibrations.
The building must be weather-tight (roof, windows, exterior walls sealed) before acoustic testing to avoid external noise interference and to test the actual acoustic performance of the enclosure.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-ins must be installed so that acoustic testing can evaluate noise from HVAC ducts, pipe vibrations, and potential flanking paths.
Acoustic test results inform any needed remedial soundproofing (e.g., additional insulation, resilient channels) before finishing layers are permanently enclosed.
The acoustic assessment must be completed and any issues rectified before the building can be formally commissioned and handed over to the client.
Accurate surface water management design requires knowledge of existing ground levels, slopes, drainage patterns, and site topography to properly design drainage systems and flow paths.
Soil permeability, infiltration rates, and ground conditions must be understood to design appropriate surface water drainage solutions such as soakaways or infiltration basins.

predecessor: Conceptual Site Layout and Earthworks Design
rationale: The overall site grading, building footprints, road alignments, and earthworks strategy define catchment areas and flow paths that the surface water drainage system must accommodate.
Detailed drainage construction drawings are developed based on the surface water management design philosophy, pipe sizes, gradients, and outfall locations established during the design phase.
The surface water management design forms the basis of the SuDS approval submission to regulatory authorities, demonstrating compliance with drainage standards and flood risk requirements.
Site survey establishes property boundaries, existing adjacent structures, and natural sightlines needed to determine required setback distances for privacy protection.
Building codes and zoning regulations define minimum privacy setback distances; these requirements must be known before the setback can be implemented.
The building footprint must be established before the privacy setback from the building edge can be measured and enforced.
The setback line must be defined and verified before vertical construction begins, to ensure the building envelope does not encroach into the required privacy zone.
Window placement and overlooking sightlines are controlled by the privacy setback; windows must be positioned to respect the setback line to prevent overlooking of adjacent properties.
The ground must be properly graded and drainage systems installed to ensure a stable, sloped foundation that meets accessibility requirements before pathway construction.
A compacted aggregate base layer is required to provide structural support and prevent settling or cracking of the accessible pathway surface.
Any underground electrical, plumbing, or data conduits that will run beneath the pathway must be installed and inspected before the pathway is constructed to avoid later excavation and disruption.
After the pathway material (concrete, asphalt, or pavers) is placed, it must be finished with a slip-resistant texture and allowed adequate curing time before use.

Signs indicating accessible routes and directional arrows are best installed after the pathway is complete so they can be precisely positioned relative to the final pathway alignment, though they could theoretically be installed concurrently.
A stable, level foundation must be prepared before the Adaptive Seating Unit can be installed, as the unit requires a solid base for structural support and alignment.
The main building frame or primary structure must be erected to provide the supporting framework and mounting points for the Adaptive Seating Unit.

Electrical rough-in work (conduit, wiring, outlets) must be completed before installing the Adaptive Seating Unit to avoid rework or damage to the unit and to allow proper integration of any powered seat adjustments or controls.
Final finishing, trim work, and cosmetic detailing around the seating area can only begin after the Adaptive Seating Unit is fully installed and positioned.
The final inspection and functional testing of the adaptive seating system must occur after installation to verify proper operation, safety, and compliance with specifications.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and properly graded to provide a stable, well-drained base for constructing the raised planting bed.
Underground utilities (gas, water, electric, telecom) must be located and marked before any digging or earthwork to avoid damage and ensure safety during bed construction.
The structural frame, walls, or containment system of the raised bed must be fully constructed and secured before any soil or growing medium can be placed inside it.

Drip lines or irrigation components can be installed after the bed is built and filled, though in some designs irrigation is laid prior to soil fill; typically it follows bed completion for ease of access and layout.
Plants or seeds cannot be placed until the raised bed structure is complete and filled with growing medium, as the bed provides the container and soil environment for the plants.
The water supply and drain piping must be installed in the wall before the drinking fountain can be connected and mounted.
The wall structure must be in place to provide support for mounting the drinking fountain and to house the plumbing connections.
If the fountain includes a cooler or requires power, electrical wiring must be installed and boxes set prior to fountain installation.
The drinking fountain must be installed before the wall finish is applied around it so that the finish can be properly trimmed and sealed to the fountain.
The drinking fountain itself must be mounted and connected before final trim, valve installation, and pressure testing of the plumbing system can be completed.
The ground must be properly graded, leveled, and compacted to provide a stable, safe, and accessible foundation for installing inclusive play equipment, ensuring it meets ADA and safety standards.

Any underground electrical, drainage, or water lines needed for the play area (e.g., for nearby lighting or accessible fountains) must be installed before heavy equipment placement to avoid excavation conflicts and rework.

predecessor: Concrete or Rubberized Safety Surfacing (Base Layer)
rationale: The poured-in-place rubber or concrete safety surfacing that supports the play structure and provides accessible ground surface must be installed before the play equipment is anchored into it.

successor: Final Safety Surfacing and Border Installation
rationale: After inclusive play equipment is erected and anchored, the surrounding engineered wood fiber or rubber safety surfacing can be filled, leveled, and bordered around the equipment to complete fall protection.

Installing perimeter fencing, shade structures, and landscaping around the play area is typically done after equipment installation to avoid damaging the equipment during construction; however, fencing could theoretically be installed earlier as a soft preference for workflow efficiency.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and properly graded to provide a stable base before constructing the planting bed.
Subsurface drainage must be installed first to ensure proper water management and prevent waterlogging of the planting bed.
Irrigation supply lines and any underground utilities serving the bed must be laid before the soil and planting layers are placed to avoid excavation damage later.
The bed structure (edging, soil layers, substrate) must be fully constructed before any plants can be installed into it.
Once the bed is built and plants are installed, applying mulch and finishing touches is the logical next step, though some mulching could be done concurrently.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and excavated before boundary fencing can be installed, as fence posts need to be set into the ground and the perimeter must be defined on a prepared surface.

Boundary fencing establishes the site perimeter and secures the construction area, which is necessary before pouring foundations to prevent unauthorized access and to clearly demarcate the working zone.

While not physically mandatory, it is preferred to have boundary fencing and controlled gate access in place before setting up temporary site facilities (site office, storage, welfare units) to secure materials and equipment from theft.

Boundary fencing and a secure gate should be installed before bulk material deliveries arrive to ensure the site is secure, controlled, and that materials can be stored safely within the demarcated perimeter.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and graded to the correct elevations before pathway sub-base and paving can be laid to ensure proper drainage and stability.
Any underground utilities (water, electrical, drainage) that will run beneath the pathway must be installed before the pathway is constructed to avoid excavation and damage after paving.

Landscaping beds, sod, and decorative planting adjacent to the pathway should be installed after the pathway is completed to avoid soil, mud, and debris being tracked onto the finished walking surface.
Signage posts, directional markers, and wayfinding elements are typically anchored beside or into the pathway; the pathway surface must be complete to correctly position and install signage.

While pathway lighting can technically be installed concurrently, it is preferable to complete the pathway first so that light pole bases and conduit runs are aligned precisely with the finished edge of the accessible route.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and graded before irrigation pipes and sprinklers can be installed to ensure proper drainage and pipe layout.
Main water supply lines and any underground electrical conduits must be laid before irrigation trenching to avoid conflicts and allow coordinated underground work.
Irrigation pipes, sprinkler heads, and drip lines must be in place before planting turf, ground cover, or other vegetation to ensure they can be watered immediately after planting.
After irrigation lines are laid and tested, trenches must be backfilled and the surface restored (soil, topsoil) before any finish grading or paving.
Once all irrigation components are installed, the system must be tested for leaks, coverage, and proper operation before being covered or put into service.

The physical building or renovated space must be fully constructed and finished before an accessibility compliance audit can be conducted, as the audit evaluates the completed structure against accessibility standards.
Relevant building permits and approvals must be secured before construction is completed, and the accessibility audit verifies that the built work complies with those permits and codes.

The architectural design (including accessibility features such as ramps, door widths, and accessible routes) must be finalized before the audit can check if the as-built condition matches the design intent and code requirements.

The accessibility compliance audit must be completed and passed before a certificate of occupancy can be issued, as the audit confirms that the building meets mandatory accessibility codes for safe public or tenant use.

If the audit identifies non-compliance issues, any necessary corrective construction work (e.g., widening doorways, adding grab bars, adjusting ramp slopes) can only begin after the audit results are known, so that the specific deficiencies are identified and addressed.
The play equipment requires a level, stable, and properly graded surface for safe installation. Without site preparation, the ground would be uneven and unstable.
Many play equipment structures require concrete footings or foundations to anchor posts securely. These must be poured and cured before equipment can be mounted.
Any underground electrical, drainage, or irrigation lines must be installed before play equipment to avoid digging near completed structures and to ensure safety.

Safety surfaces (rubber mulch, poured-in-place rubber, engineered wood fiber) must be installed after the equipment is in place so that the surface seamlessly surrounds the equipment's footprint and supports fall zones.
Fencing is often installed after play equipment to ensure proper alignment and access for equipment assembly, though in some cases fencing can be installed prior as a soft preference.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and prepared before any planting beds can be installed.
Proper drainage systems must be in place before soil and planting beds are added to prevent waterlogging and root damage.
Underground utilities must be located and marked before digging to avoid damage and ensure safety.
Irrigation pipes and emitters are typically laid after planting beds are formed so they can be positioned correctly around the plants.
Mulch is applied after planting to retain moisture and suppress weeds around the newly placed plants.
Lighting fixtures are typically mounted on or recessed into ceilings, so the ceiling structure must be in place before fixtures can be installed.
The electrical wiring, junction boxes, and conduit must be run and terminated before lighting fixtures can be connected and mounted.
After fixtures are installed, any gaps around them must be patched and the ceiling finished for a clean appearance.
Painting is typically done before installing light fixtures to avoid paint on the fixtures, but if fixtures are installed first, they can be masked off; however, convention is to paint first.
Lighting fixtures must be installed to test, commission, and verify proper operation before project closeout.
The ground must be properly leveled and prepared before benches can be installed to ensure stability and proper placement.
If benches require anchor footings or concrete bases (e.g., for permanent park benches), the foundation work must be completed first so benches can be securely mounted.

It is preferable to install benches after landscaping is done, but if benches are installed first, planting around them can still be done with care; however, typically benches are placed after hardscape and softscape to avoid damage.
Benches are often among the final furnishing installations before project completion, but inspection can happen before or after; soft preference for benches to be in place for final walkthrough.
The ground must be excavated and leveled before bollards can be installed to ensure proper footing and alignment.
