Any underground pipes, conduits, or cables must be laid before bollard installation to avoid digging around or damaging newly installed bollards.
Bollards require a concrete footing or foundation to be poured and cured to provide structural stability and impact resistance.
Bollards must be installed before the final paving or surface finish (e.g., asphalt, concrete slab, pavers) is laid around them for a clean, flush finish.
Typically bollards are installed before final landscaping and cleanup to avoid damage to finished landscaping, though this is a soft preference as it can be done in reverse order with care.

Structural framing and core construction must be complete to provide mounting surfaces and structural support for signage elements such as wall-mounted signs, directional markers, and overhead signage.
Interior walls must be framed and finished with drywall before permanent wall-mounted signage can be installed, as signs require a finished surface for proper attachment and alignment.
Flooring and ceiling finishes must be in place to ensure that floor-mounted and suspended signage can be accurately positioned and aligned with the finished interior surfaces.
Electrical rough-in and lighting must be complete to provide power connections for illuminated signage and wayfinding elements, and to ensure adequate ambient lighting for sign visibility.

Signage and wayfinding elements must be installed before final inspection and commissioning to verify that all egress signs, directional markers, and informational placards comply with building codes and accessibility requirements.
Steps and ramps must be supported on stable foundations; the foundation and substructure must be completed first to provide a solid base.
Steps and ramps typically connect to the ground floor slab; the slab must be in place to establish the finished floor level that steps and ramps abut.
Handrails and balustrades are installed on or alongside steps and ramps for safety; the steps/ramps structure must be complete to provide the mounting surface.
While paving can often proceed independently, it is preferable to finish steps and ramps before adjacent paving to ensure a clean transition and consistent levels.
Steps and ramps must be complete before final inspection can verify accessibility compliance, slip resistance, and overall safety.

The ground must be cleared and excavated to the required depths and grades before retaining walls can be constructed, as retaining walls require a stable, prepared subgrade for proper foundation and structural support.
Retaining walls typically require reinforced concrete footings or foundations to be poured and cured first, providing the load-bearing base upon which the wall elements are placed.

Proper drainage (e.g., perforated pipes, gravel backfill, weep holes) must be installed behind or at the base of the wall before or concurrently with wall construction to prevent hydrostatic pressure buildup; however, the drainage medium is often placed as the wall is built. If a drainage blanket/pipe is needed below the wall, it must precede the wall.
Backfill material behind the retaining wall can only be placed and compacted after the wall structure is sufficiently constructed and cured to withstand lateral earth pressures.

Final surface grading, topsoil placement, and landscaping around the retained area typically follow retaining wall completion, but this is partially a logical sequence preference rather than a strict physical necessity, as some planting could theoretically be done before the wall is fully finished.
A stable foundation or concrete slab must be in place to support the structural columns and posts of the canopy/pergola.
Any electrical conduits, drainage pipes, or water lines that will pass beneath the pergola must be roughed in before the slab is poured and the structure is erected.
If the canopy/pergola supports a solid roof or shade structure, the roofing membrane or weatherproofing layer can only be installed after the structural frame is complete.
Any wiring for ceiling fans, lights, or outlets mounted to the canopy/pergola must be run after the frame is erected but before finish materials are applied.
While finishing is typically done after the structure is built, some components may be pre-finished; however, final touch-ups and site-applied coatings require the structure to be fully erected.
The site must be graded and prepared to provide a stable, level foundation and clear space for the sculpture installation.
Public art and sculptures typically require a concrete pad or foundation base to be poured and cured before the artwork can be securely anchored or placed.
Any underground electrical, water, or data lines for lighting or fountain features must be installed before the sculpture is placed to avoid disturbance or rework.
Final landscaping, planting, decorative gravel, and site amenities around the sculpture must be completed after installation to avoid damaging the artwork or interfering with placement.
Accent lighting fixtures aimed at the sculpture should be installed and connected after the sculpture is in place to ensure proper positioning and focus.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and properly graded before any pathway construction can begin to ensure a stable and properly sloped base for accessibility.
Any underground utilities (water, electrical, data lines) must be installed before pathway construction to avoid digging up and damaging the completed accessible pathway.
A compacted aggregate base or subbase layer must be placed and compacted prior to the final pathway surface to provide adequate load-bearing capacity and drainage.

Landscaping, topsoil placement, and final site finishes adjacent to the pathway must be completed after the pathway is installed to avoid soiling or damaging the new surface and to ensure proper grading transitions.

The accessible pathway must be completed and inspected for compliance with accessibility codes (e.g., ADA) before the building or site can be occupied and used by pedestrians, as it provides the required accessible route.
The subgrade (soil or base layer) must be properly graded, compacted, and stabilized before paving can be laid to ensure a stable foundation and prevent uneven settling or cracking.
The aggregate base course must be placed and compacted over the subgrade to provide structural support and drainage before the paving layer can be installed.
Underground drainage pipes, culverts, or subdrains must be installed before paving to avoid cutting into or damaging the finished pavement surface later.
Underground utilities (water, sewer, gas, electrical conduits) must be laid and inspected before paving to prevent the need for future trenching through the finished pavement.

While curbs can be installed before paving in some sequences, typically paving is placed first and curbs/gutters are formed against or after the pavement edge to ensure a tight joint and proper drainage alignment.
Flooring must be fully installed before furniture and fixtures are placed to prevent damage to the finished floor surface and to allow for seamless installation without obstruction.
Wall finishes such as painting or wallpapering must be completed before furniture and fixtures are brought in to avoid dust, paint splatter, or damage to the installed items.
Ceiling work including drywall, acoustical tiles, and painting/finishing must be done before furniture placement to prevent debris and dust from falling on finished items.

Final electrical work such as outlet installation, switch plate covers, and light fixture mounting must be completed before furniture and fixtures are positioned, as these may require wall or ceiling access.

While final cleaning can theoretically be done before furniture placement, it is preferable to perform a final clean-up after furniture and fixture installation to remove dust, debris, and packaging materials, though this is a soft preference rather than a hard constraint.

Hard landscaping elements such as paths, patios, and paved areas must be constructed before soft landscaping and planting, as heavy machinery and material deliveries for hardscaping would damage newly planted vegetation and soil.
Soil must be graded, leveled, and prepared with proper topsoil before any planting can occur, as plants require a suitable growing medium and properly contoured ground to establish roots.
Subsurface drainage systems must be installed before planting to ensure excess water is properly managed, preventing waterlogging and root rot in new plants.
Underground utilities (water, gas, electricity, telecom) must be laid before planting to avoid excavation damage to established plants, trees, and root systems.

While irrigation pipes are often laid before planting, the final above-ground sprinkler heads, drip emitters, and system commissioning must occur after planting to ensure precise water delivery to the specific locations of plants.
Mulch is typically applied after planting to retain soil moisture and suppress weeds, but this is a soft preference as the timing can vary depending on seasonal conditions and planting methods.

Soft landscaping and planting are among the final finishing works on a construction site, and the project can only be handed over to the client after all planting is complete, as vegetation is a key aesthetic and functional deliverable.
Structural framing and roofing must be completed to provide the physical enclosure and support structure for running electrical conduits, cables, and mounting lighting fixtures.
Rough-in plumbing is typically completed before electrical rough-in to avoid interference and to coordinate routing of utilities within walls and ceilings.
Foundation and slab must be in place to provide the base for running underground electrical conduits and to support electrical equipment placement.
Electrical wiring, boxes, and fixtures must be installed before walls are enclosed with insulation and drywall, as these would otherwise block access.

Electrical rough-in, outlet boxes, switch boxes, and light fixture mounting must be completed before interior finishing work such as painting or tiling, as these finishes would be damaged or obstructed by later electrical work.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated to the required depth and shape before any water feature structure can be installed.
Underground water supply lines, drainage pipes, and electrical conduits for pumps must be laid and connected before the water feature basin or structure is built over them.
A stable concrete foundation or compacted sub-base is required to support the weight of the water feature structure (e.g., pond liner, fountain base, pool shell) and prevent settling or cracking.
Once the water feature shell or basin is constructed, waterproof membranes or liners must be applied to seal the structure and prevent water leakage.
The water feature structure must be in place before pumps, filters, pipes, and water jets can be mounted and connected to the water circulation system.
The ground must be leveled and prepared before placing waste and recycling bins to ensure stability and proper drainage.
A concrete pad or durable base is required to support the weight of waste and recycling bins and to prevent them from sinking into the ground.
If the waste area includes compactors or wash-down systems, underground utilities should be roughed in before bin placement, though this is not always required for standard bins.
Final landscaping around the bin enclosure should be completed after bins are placed to ensure proper alignment and access.
Waste and recycling bins must be installed and in place before the building can be occupied and used, as waste services are essential for daily operations.
Site must be cleared of existing structures, debris, and vegetation before tree pits can be excavated.
Rough grading establishes the general site topography and drainage patterns, which must be in place before tree pits are dug to appropriate depths.

predecessor: Underground Utility Installation (Sewer, Water, Storm Drain, Electrical)
rationale: Underground utilities must be installed first to avoid conflicts with tree root zones and to ensure root barriers do not obstruct utility lines.
Tree pits must be excavated and root barriers installed before final grading and topsoil are placed, as topsoil would need to be removed again if pits were dug afterward.
Trees cannot be planted until their pits are excavated and root barriers are in place to direct root growth.
Root barriers must be installed around tree pits before adjacent hardscape surfaces are constructed, to prevent future root damage to pavements and curbs.
While irrigation can be installed concurrently in some cases, it is typically preferable to install root barriers first to avoid damaging irrigation lines during pit excavation.
The elevator shaft requires a stable load-bearing foundation to support its vertical structure, so foundation and substructure work must be completed first.

predecessor: Core Wall Construction (Ground Floor to Lower Levels)
rationale: The elevator shaft is typically integrated into the building's core and lower-level walls provide the base alignment and structural support needed before shaft construction begins.

successor: Elevator Car Installation and Rail Mounting
rationale: The shaft enclosure must be fully constructed to provide the vertical pathway and mounting surfaces for elevator car guide rails and cabin installation.

successor: Elevator Door Frame Installation at Each Floor
rationale: Elevator shaft walls and openings must be in place before door frames can be installed and aligned at each floor landing.

successor: Vertical Cable and Electrical Conduit Routing
rationale: Cables and conduits run inside the shaft and require the completed shaft enclosure for proper routing, support, and protection.
BMU tracks must be anchored to the building's structural steel frame, which needs to be in place to provide support and load-bearing capacity.
BMU tracks are typically installed on or near the roof area; the roof deck provides the working surface and base for track mounting.

successor: BMU system assembly and trolley installation
rationale: The BMU trolley and carriage system must ride along the installed tracks; tracks must be in place before the moving components can be mounted.

BMU tracks support window washing and facade maintenance equipment; while not physically mandatory, installing facade panels after BMU track installation allows for coordinated access and protection of finished surfaces.

Electrical connections for the BMU system (power, controls, and safety systems) need to be routed to the track area after the track structure is in place to ensure proper alignment and termination points.
The rooftop steelwork must be supported by the main structural steel frame, which must be erected first to provide a stable base.

Rooftop steelwork components (e.g., roof trusses, purlins, or steel joists) are installed on top of or in conjunction with the roof deck, which must be in place to provide the working surface and structural support.
Waterproofing is applied over the completed rooftop steelwork and deck to protect the structure from water ingress; the steelwork must be fully installed before the waterproofing layer can be laid.
Heavy HVAC units are placed on the rooftop steelwork; the steel support frame must be completed to bear the loads before equipment can be set.

Solar panels are typically mounted on rooftop steel racking/frame systems; installing the steelwork first ensures proper anchoring, though in some designs panels could be installed concurrently with minor coordination.
Formwork must be erected and secured to provide the mold that shapes and supports the wet concrete until it cures; without formwork, concrete cannot be placed at height.
Rebar must be positioned and tied within the formwork before concrete is poured to ensure the structural reinforcement is embedded correctly within the slab or beam.
Safe working platforms and temporary support structures must be in place to support workers, equipment, and the fresh concrete load at elevated levels.
Once concrete is placed, it must be allowed to cure (harden) and finishing operations (screeding, troweling) commence immediately after placement before the concrete sets.
Formwork cannot be removed until the placed concrete has gained sufficient strength to be self-supporting; stripping is a subsequent activity that follows concrete placement and curing.
The structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) must be erected and stable to provide a mounting surface and load-bearing support for the facade panels or curtain wall system.

predecessor: Floor Slab Construction at Each Level
rationale: Floor slabs must be cast or installed to create working platforms and to anchor the facade at each level; without slabs there is no intermediate support or safe access for installation.

predecessor: Scaffolding or Mast Climbing Platform Erection
rationale: Safe access at height requires erected scaffolding, suspended cradles, or mast climbing work platforms before workers can reach the facade zone.
The main facade structure (framing, cladding panels) must be in place to receive windows, glazing units, or curtain wall infill panels.
The building envelope must be enclosed to protect interior works from weather; interior drywall, insulation, and finishes cannot proceed until the facade is sealed against rain and wind.

predecessor: Structural Concrete Work / Roof Slab Casting
rationale: The roof slab must be cast, cured, and structurally complete to provide a solid, stable substrate for the waterproofing membrane to be applied.
Screed or slope-to-fall must be laid and cured first to ensure proper drainage away from the waterproofing layer, preventing ponding water.

successor: Waterproofing Protection Layer / Insulation Board Installation
rationale: A protective layer (e.g., rigid insulation, protection board) is installed immediately over the cured waterproofing membrane to shield it from mechanical damage during subsequent trades.
Final floor finishes (tiles, pavers, or screed topping) are laid after waterproofing is fully cured and tested, as they cover and protect the waterproofing system.
Rainwater outlets and drain connections must be completed after the waterproofing membrane is integrated with the drainage system to ensure watertight seals at penetrations.
All low-level MEP systems (e.g., wiring, piping, ductwork within walls/ceilings) must be physically installed before high-level commissioning can verify and test system-wide performance.
Rough-in inspections must be completed and approved to confirm that concealed MEP work meets codes before commissioning can proceed.
Full commissioning of high-level MEP systems must be finished before formal acceptance testing and handover to the owner can occur.
Commissioning ensures that all major MEP systems (HVAC, electrical, plumbing, fire protection) are fully operational and safe before occupants can use the building.
While commissioning typically precedes closeout, some minor punch-list items can run concurrently; however, substantial completion requires commissioning sign-off.
Steel structures must be erected to provide the anchor points and structural framework before fall-protection systems (e.g., guardrails, safety nets, lifelines) can be installed on them.
Elevated work surfaces such as concrete decks need to be poured and fully cured to bear loads before fall-protection systems can be installed and used on those surfaces.
Scaffolding provides the working platform and access needed to safely install elevated fall-protection components at height.
Fall-protection systems (e.g., guardrails, safety lines) must be in place to protect workers during subsequent roof installation and waterproofing activities performed at height.
Workers installing exterior cladding or curtain walls at height require fall-protection systems to be fully installed and certified before they begin work on the building envelope.
A stable, leveled ground surface is required before any platform can be erected; otherwise the structure will be unstable.
The platform needs a load-bearing base or foundation to support its weight and the subsequent loads from stage equipment and personnel.

It is preferable to complete underground utilities before installing the platform to avoid cutting through or dismantling the platform later, though not physically mandatory if access remains available.
The structural frame or platform base must be fully erected before any decking or finished flooring can be laid on top of it.
Safety barriers, guardrails, and scaffolding around the stage rely on the platform structure as their supporting base and cannot be installed before the platform exists.

successor: Road Barrier / Crowd Control Barrier Installation
rationale: The ground must be properly graded and prepared before installing barriers to ensure they sit level and stable.

successor: Road Barrier / Crowd Control Barrier Installation
rationale: Barriers are typically anchored to or placed on the finished roadway surface; pavement must be complete to provide a solid foundation.

predecessor: Road Barrier / Crowd Control Barrier Installation
rationale: Road markings and signage often need to reference the barrier positions (e.g., no-parking zones, lane delineation), so barriers must be in place first.

predecessor: Road Barrier / Crowd Control Barrier Installation
rationale: Barrier installation should not occur before the pavement has cured, as the barrier could settle or shift on uncured asphalt/concrete.

predecessor: Road Barrier / Crowd Control Barrier Installation
rationale: Barriers must be fully installed and secured before traffic is allowed to use the roadway to ensure safety and proper lane separation.

Electrical rough-in work including conduit, wiring, and junction boxes must be completed before the Power Distribution Unit (PDU) can be installed, as the PDU needs to connect to these pre-run electrical systems.
The main transformer that steps down incoming utility voltage must be installed and operational before the PDU can receive its primary power feed.
The main switchboard or main distribution panel must be in place to provide the upstream breaker and connection point for the PDU.
Server racks and IT equipment cannot be installed until the PDU is in place, as the PDU provides the critical power distribution to the racks and must be positioned and connected first.
While cable trays can be partially installed before, final routing of cables from the PDU to equipment is typically done after the PDU is set, making this a soft ordering preference for efficiency.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and graded before a tent or canopy can be safely erected to ensure stable footing and proper layout.
Underground utilities (power, water lines) must be installed before the tent footprint is established, as it would be extremely difficult or impossible to trench after the tent is erected.
If the tent requires anchor points or a permanent slab foundation, the concrete must be poured and cured before tent installation.
Interior furnishings (tables, chairs, flooring, lighting, décor) can only be placed after the tent structure is fully erected and weather-tight to protect them from the elements.
Final landscaping around the tent is typically performed after the tent is in place to ensure proper alignment; however, it could technically be done before with careful coordination.

Legal and regulatory compliance requires that all necessary permits (e.g., road closure permits, traffic management plans) are approved before any road closure or traffic diversion can be implemented.
While not a strict physical necessity, it is operationally prudent to have site facilities and personnel mobilized before closing roads to ensure efficient transition to active construction.
Road closure is a physical prerequisite to ensure worker and public safety before any excavation or earth disturbance can begin on or adjacent to the roadway.
Utility relocation within the road corridor requires the area to be closed to traffic to safely expose and relocate underground or overhead utilities.
Demolition near or within the roadway envelope requires road closure to protect the public from falling debris and heavy equipment operations.
The event must be fully set up and installed before it can be dismantled; dismantlement is the reverse process of installation.
After dismantlement and reinstatement of the space to its original condition, the area must be cleaned and restored to complete the process.
The space must be reinstated to its pre-event condition before a final inspection and handover can take place.
All structural concrete work must be completed and fully cured before surface preparation can begin, as the concrete provides the base substrate that needs to be prepared.
Rough framing and sheathing must be finished to create the surfaces (walls, ceilings, floors) that will be prepared and cleaned before finish work.
The building must be weather-tight with roofing completed to protect prepared surfaces from water damage before preparation work begins.
Windows and doors must be installed to enclose the building envelope before interior surface preparation, preventing debris and weather from affecting prepared surfaces.
Surfaces must be cleaned, sanded, and prepped before any primer or paint can be applied to ensure proper adhesion and a smooth finish.
The subfloor must be cleaned and prepared before any finished flooring materials (tile, hardwood, carpet) are installed to ensure a level, debris-free base.
Wall surfaces must be properly prepared, smooth, and clean before any decorative wall finishes can be applied for proper adhesion.

Acoustic treatment materials (e.g., acoustic panels, insulation, barriers) are typically installed onto or within the structural framing and wall assemblies. The structural support must be in place to physically attach or house the acoustic treatment.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work (conduits, ducts, pipes) must be completed before enclosing walls with acoustic barriers, as accessing these systems after acoustic treatment installation would require damaging the finished acoustic surfaces.

Often a base layer of drywall or sheathing is installed before specialized acoustic barriers or treatments are applied on top, providing a flat substrate. However, in some systems the acoustic barrier itself serves as the base layer, making this a soft preference rather than a hard constraint.

Acoustic panels and barriers are often considered part of the finish work, but some final finishes (e.g., painting acoustic panels, installing trim around them) must occur after the acoustic treatment is in place. This is generally a soft preference as final finishes can sometimes precede if the treatment is recessed or protected.

successor: Final Inspection / Commissioning of Acoustic Performance
rationale: Testing and commissioning of acoustic performance can only occur after all acoustic treatments are fully installed, as any missing treatment would invalidate the test results.
The ground must be cleared, graded, and leveled before waste management facilities (such as waste sorting areas, bins, or litter receptacles) can be placed or installed on stable ground.
Underground drainage and sewer connections are required to handle leachate and wastewater from waste storage areas before the above-ground waste infrastructure is installed.
Waste receptacles and storage areas must be in place before final landscaping is completed, so that they are integrated into the site design and accessible without disturbing finished surfaces.
Waste management facilities must be fully installed and operational before the site can be commissioned for occupancy, as waste collection is a critical ongoing operational service.
Concrete pads or foundations for waste bins, compactors, and enclosures must be poured and cured before the waste management infrastructure can be mounted or placed upon them.
Excavation must be completed to create space for pool shell and skimmer box placement.
The skimmer box is typically integrated into the pool wall structure, so the pool shell or liner must be in place first.
Plumbing lines (suction line to pump) can only be connected after the skimmer box is physically installed in the pool wall.

successor: Install Pool Pump and Filter System
rationale: The skimmer box feeds water into the pump/filter system, so it must be in place before pump and filter connections are finalized.
The skimmer box opening and faceplate must be installed before the final plaster or interior finish is applied around it to ensure a watertight seal.
The pool coping sits on top of and is anchored to the pool shell structure, so the shell must be fully constructed and cured before coping can be installed.
Waterproofing membranes and coatings must be applied to the pool shell before coping is installed, as the coping edge caps and seals the waterproofing system.
The interior finish (plaster, tiles, or liner) is typically installed after coping because the coping forms the top edge and trim that the interior finish works up to.

Pool coping serves as the transition between the pool structure and the surrounding deck or paving, so the coping must be in place before adjacent decking is laid to ensure proper drainage and alignment.

While sealing and grouting the coping joints is typically done immediately after installation, it is a soft preference because the coping is already structurally in place; however doing so promptly prevents water ingress and staining.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and prepared before any drainage infrastructure can be installed.
Trenching and excavation must be completed to create the pathway for the main drain pipe installation.
The main drain must be in place and secured before backfilling the trench can occur.
Lateral drains from buildings and other areas connect into the main drain, so the main drain must be installed first to serve as the collection point.
Proper drainage must be established before foundation construction to prevent water accumulation and ensure stable ground conditions.
The pool shell must be fully constructed and cured before the ladder and handrail can be mounted, as they attach to the pool structure.
The ladder and handrail should be installed before the final decking or surrounding surface is completed to ensure proper integration and secure anchoring.
Safety equipment like ladders and handrails must be in place before the final inspection can verify compliance with safety codes.
Concrete footings or anchor points must be set and cured to provide a stable foundation for bolting or embedding the ladder and handrail.
The ladder and handrail should be installed before the pool is filled to allow for safe access during filling and to avoid installing hardware in a filled pool.
The weir wall requires stable ground conditions; foundation excavation, compaction, and concrete blinding must be completed before any wall construction can begin.
The base on which the weir wall sits must be reinforced and leveled to ensure uniform load distribution and structural integrity of the wall.
Formwork must be erected and braced prior to concrete placement for the weir wall to shape and support the wet concrete.
The concrete weir wall must be cast and set before curing can commence and waterproof membranes can be applied to protect against water ingress.
Backfilling against the completed wall provides lateral support and can only be performed after the wall has achieved sufficient strength to withstand soil pressures.
Excavation must be completed to create space and proper grade for the basin/tank installation.
A stable, level foundation or base slab is required before setting the catch basin or balance tank structure.
Preliminary drainage provisions (e.g., sub-drains) must be in place to manage water during and after basin installation.

successor: Piping Connections to Catch Basin / Balance Tank
rationale: Inlet and outlet pipes can only be connected after the basin/tank is set in its final position.
Backfilling around the structure must wait until the basin/tank is fully installed and secured.
Waterproofing or lining applications should follow after the tank/basin structure is in place and stable.
Functional testing of the basin/tank can only occur once it is fully installed, with all connections made.
The ground must be excavated and leveled to create a stable foundation for the waterfall structure, preventing settlement or shifting.
A concrete footing or foundation is required to support the weight of the waterfall structure and prevent uneven settling.
Water supply lines and electrical conduits for pumps and lighting must be run underground before the structure is built to avoid destructive retrofitting.
After the waterfall frame/rockwork is constructed, waterproof membranes or liners must be applied to prevent water leakage.
The pump, filter, and recirculation plumbing can only be installed and connected once the waterfall structure is in place.
Surrounding plants, decorative rocks, and aesthetic finishes are typically applied after the main structure is complete, though some overlap may be possible.
The fountain jet nozzle must be installed within the fountain basin; the basin must be constructed first to provide a stable mounting foundation and water containment area.
The jet nozzle requires connection to the water supply system; plumbing lines must be run to the nozzle location before the nozzle can be attached and sealed.
The pump provides pressurized water to the jet nozzle; the pump must be installed and connected to the water supply before the nozzle can function and be tested for proper spray pattern.
After the nozzle is physically installed, it must be aligned, adjusted, and aimed to achieve the desired water spray pattern and coverage.
The complete fountain system, including the jet nozzle, must be installed before final commissioning, testing of flow rates, spray patterns, and leak checks can be performed.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and graded before excavation can begin to provide a stable, accessible work area and to mark utility lines.
Engineering drawings, structural calculations, and building permits must be approved before any ground disturbance occurs to ensure compliance with codes and safety standards.
All underground utilities (gas, electric, water, sewer, telecom) must be located and marked to avoid accidental strikes during excavation.
Excavation must be complete to expose the soil subgrade, allowing steel rebar cages to be placed and all return/suction lines to be laid in the trench before concrete is poured.
After excavation, the floor must be shaped and compacted, and a gravel base or bond beam poured to provide a stable foundation for the pool shell.
The ground must be excavated and leveled before the pool shell can be formed and poured, as the shell rests directly on the prepared subgrade.
Pool plumbing lines (main drain, returns, skimmers) are embedded within or pass through the pool shell, requiring the shell to be in place before pipes can be connected through and around it.
The interior surface finish such as plaster, pebble, or tile is applied directly onto the cured concrete or gunite shell, so the shell must be complete and cured before any finish can be installed.
The coping (edge trim) and surrounding deck are cast or placed against and on top of the pool shell's bond beam, requiring the shell to be finished first to provide a structural edge.
Waterline tile is adhered to the set and cured pool shell walls at the water level, necessitating a completed shell surface for proper adhesion and alignment.
The pool shell must be fully constructed and cured before any tiling can begin, as tiles need a stable, cured concrete substrate to adhere properly.
Plumbing lines must be installed within the pool shell before tiling, as tiles cover and conceal these pipes; retrofitting plumbing after tiling would require destructive removal of tiles.
Waterproofing membranes must be applied to the pool shell before tiling to ensure a watertight substrate; tiles are installed over the waterproofing layer.
Coping (the cap or edge around the pool) is installed after the wall tiles are finished, as the coping typically overlaps and seals the top edge of the wall tiles.
Grouting of tile joints and caulking of expansion joints can only occur once all tiles are set in place and the thinset/adhesive has cured.
The pool shell must be fully constructed and cured before any equipment (pumps, filters, heaters) can be mounted or connected to the structure.
Equipment such as pumps and filters must be installed and in place before final plumbing connections (pipes, return lines, skimmer lines) can be made to the equipment pad.
Pool equipment (pump motor, heater, controller) must be physically installed and anchored before electricians can run conduit, wire, and bond the equipment to the grounding system.
The concrete or crushed stone equipment pad must be poured and cured before heavy equipment like pumps, filters, and heaters can be set on it.
All pool equipment must be installed and connected before the system can be pressure-tested, primed, and started for initial operation.
The pool structure must be physically built and in place before a safety fence can be installed around it, as the fence perimeter directly follows the pool's edge and shape.
The coping, tile work, and surrounding pool deck must be completed to provide a stable, finished surface onto which fence posts can be anchored and the fence line properly established.
Underground plumbing and electrical conduit work must be finished before any fence posts are set or concrete is poured to avoid digging into or obstructing these buried utilities.

The fence provides a secure barrier that restricts access to the pool area, which is important for safety while the interior finish is applied and cured — keeping unauthorized personnel and debris out of the freshly finished pool surface.
Building codes and safety regulations typically require the pool safety fence to be installed and inspected before the pool can pass final inspection and receive a certificate of compliance for use.
The pool shell must be structurally complete and waterproof before any water can be introduced for commissioning and balancing.
All circulation, filtration, and drainage plumbing must be installed and pressure-tested before the pool can be filled and the water chemistry balanced.
Pump, heater, chlorinator, and lighting electrical connections must be in place and bonded before equipment can be energized during commissioning.
Finish work around the pool edge must be completed to prevent water damage or leaks when the pool is filled to its operating level.
The pool must be filled and water chemistry balanced before the heater and automation system can be calibrated and tested with actual water flow.
While decking can sometimes occur concurrently, it is preferred to complete water balance first so that any leaks or issues from deck installation do not contaminate the balanced water.
The pool structure must be fully constructed before leak testing can begin, as leak testing requires a complete and sealed pool shell to hold water for testing.

All plumbing pipes, fittings, and circulation system connections must be installed and connected to the pool before leak testing, as the test checks for leaks in both the structure and the plumbing system.

The interior surface finish (such as plaster, pebble, or tile) must be applied and cured before introducing water for leak testing, as the finish provides the waterproof membrane and filling the pool prematurely could damage uncured surfaces.

Leak testing must be completed before installing pool decks and surrounds, because if a leak is detected after decking is in place, access for repairs would require demolition of the finished decking.
The water treatment/filtration system should only be commissioned after leak testing confirms the pool is watertight, avoiding potential water damage or operational issues if leaks are present.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and obstacles before stream course landscaping can begin to ensure a safe and unobstructed workspace for shaping the stream channel.
Proper grading and drainage must be established prior to stream course landscaping to ensure water flows correctly through the designed stream channel and prevents erosion or flooding.
The stream course must be fully shaped and constructed before any riparian or bank vegetation is planted, so that plants are placed correctly along the finished stream banks.
Stream course landscaping should be completed before final inspection to verify that the work meets design specifications, though this is a procedural preference rather than a physical necessity.
Erosion control blankets, matting, or rock armoring are typically installed immediately after or concurrently with stream course shaping to stabilize the banks and bed before water is introduced.
The birthing bed frame must be assembled first to provide the structural base for attaching other components
The mattress foundation or support platform must be installed before the bed can be considered functional
Mattress pads, sheets, and protective covers are typically placed after the bed is fully assembled, but this could be done in parallel
Safety rails for the birthing bed must be attached after the main bed structure is complete to ensure proper alignment and secure mounting
The bed must be fully assembled before electrical and hydraulic adjustments can be tested for position changes and patient comfort
The structural framework and core shell must be complete to provide the enclosed space and support systems before any infection control finishes can be applied.

All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work (ductwork, conduit, piping) must be installed within walls and ceilings before infection control finishes are applied, as these systems are hidden behind the finished surfaces.
The underlying wall and ceiling substrates must be erected and prepared to receive infection control finishes such as cleanroom panels, antimicrobial coatings, or seamless flooring.

Infection control rooms require HEPA filtration, pressure differentials, and other HVAC balancing that can only be finalized once the sealed fitout is complete to achieve proper air tightness and cleanroom classification.

The infection control fitout (sealed surfaces, antimicrobial finishes, seamless flooring) must be fully installed before formal cleanroom certification, particle count testing, and pressure validation can be performed.

predecessor: Install Neonatal Resuscitation Station mounting bracket
rationale: The mounting bracket provides the structural support needed to hold the Neonatal Resuscitation Station in place, so it must be installed before the station can be mounted.

successor: Connect medical gas supply lines to Neonatal Resuscitation Station
rationale: The station must be physically mounted and positioned before gas supply lines from the central medical gas system can be connected to its inlet ports.

successor: Install electrical wiring to Neonatal Resuscitation Station
rationale: Electrical power connection requires the station to be in its final mounted position so that wiring can reach the unit's power inlet without excessive slack or strain.

predecessor: Complete rough-in of medical gas piping in ceiling/ wall
successor: Connect medical gas supply lines to Neonatal Resuscitation Station
rationale: The medical gas piping infrastructure must be roughed-in before final connections can be made to the station's gas inlet valves.

predecessor: Complete rough-in of electrical conduit to station location
successor: Install electrical wiring to Neonatal Resuscitation Station
rationale: Electrical conduit rough-in must be completed so that wiring can be pulled through to the station's location.
Electrical power supply must be roughed-in and available at the ceiling grid before surgical lighting can be connected and mounted.
The overhead ceiling support structure or mounting grid must be in place to provide a secure attachment point for surgical lights.
HVAC ducts are typically routed above the ceiling and must be installed before lights are mounted to avoid interference and rework.
Surgical lights are mounted to the structure above; once lights are in place, the ceiling around the light fixtures can be finished and sealed for cleanroom conditions.

successor: Surgical Room Commissioning and Light Calibration
rationale: After installation, the lights must be calibrated for proper illumination levels, focus, and positioning as part of the room's final commissioning process.
The curtain track system must be securely mounted to the ceiling structure; the ceiling must be in place to provide a support substrate for the track.
Any electrical wiring for curtain controls or nearby lighting must be roughed in before the track is installed to avoid interference or rework.
Curtain panels must be hung on the track; the track must be installed and secured first to support the panels.
It is easier to paint and finish ceiling and walls before the track is in place, but touch-up can be done after; thus a soft preference to finish painting before track installation rather than after.
Flooring installation can be done before or after track installation, but it is preferable to install flooring after to avoid damaging new flooring with scaffolding or ladders.
Plumbing supply and drain lines must be roughed in before the pool/tub can be positioned and connected.
The floor area must be leveled, waterproofed, and structurally ready to support the weight of the filled pool/tub before placement.
Electrical supply for pump, heater, and control systems must be pre-wired to the location before final tub installation.
The pool/tub must be set in place before final plumbing connections to supply lines, drains, and jets can be completed.
Decking, tile, or surrounding waterproof finishes cannot be installed until the tub/pool is positioned and its rim/flange is set for watertight integration.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated before any foundation work for the maternity unit can begin.
The concrete foundations and footings must be laid and cured before the structural framework of the maternity unit can be erected.
The load-bearing columns, beams, and slabs must be completed before enclosing the building and proceeding with internal works.
Electrical wiring, conduit, and plumbing pipes are installed within the walls and ceilings after the structure is built but before wall finishing.
Walls cannot be plastered and finished until the structural shell and rough-in services are complete.
Medical gas piping (oxygen, vacuum, etc.) is installed within the building structure after the unit is enclosed and before final commissioning.

successor: Installation of Doors, Windows, and Roofing
rationale: The building must be weathertight with its roof, doors, and windows installed to protect interior work from environmental damage.
Rough-in inspection must be completed before medical gas rough-in to ensure that the building's structural and mechanical systems are properly installed and ready for medical gas piping.
Medical gas rough-in must be completed before final connections can be made to ensure that the piping network is properly installed, tested, and ready for terminal unit connections.
Medical gas rough-in must be completed before walls and ceilings are closed in to allow access for inspection, testing, and verification of the medical gas piping system.
Medical gas piping installation must be completed as part of the rough-in process before the rough-in can be considered complete and ready for final connections.
Medical gas rough-in must be completed before pressure testing can be performed to verify the integrity and leak-tightness of the installed piping system.

predecessor: Rough-In of Electrical and Mechanical Services
rationale: Electrical and mechanical rough-ins (conduit, wiring, ductwork, piping) must be installed within walls and above ceilings before sterile room finishes (clean panels, sealed surfaces) are applied, as accessing these services after sterile finishing would breach the cleanroom integrity.
The building structure and exterior enclosure must be in place to provide a weathertight shell before the sterile fit-out commences, preventing contamination and moisture ingress.
A level, cured floor slab with appropriate subfloor sealing and coving must be completed as the substrate for sterile flooring systems (e.g., seamless epoxy or vinyl sheet).

successor: HEPA Filter and Terminal HEPA Box Installation
rationale: The sterile room ceiling grid and wall panels must be in place to support and seal the HEPA filter housings, and the cleanroom must be prepared to receive the final filtration system.

All sterile finishes (walls, floors, ceilings, sealed penetrations) must be installed before the room can undergo formal certification testing for particle counts, pressure differentials, and air changes, as any unfinished surfaces would compromise test results.

The neonatal ward must be structurally complete (walls, flooring, ceilings, and doors) before any sensitive neonatal equipment can be brought in, to protect it from dust, debris, and construction hazards.

Neonatal equipment (incubators, ventilators, monitors) requires dedicated, stable electrical circuits and backup power (UPS/generator) to be in place and tested before equipment can be connected and commissioned.

predecessor: Medical Gas System Installation and Testing
rationale: Oxygen, compressed air, and vacuum systems must be installed, tested, and certified before neonatal respiratory equipment can be connected to them.

predecessor: HVAC and Environmental Control System Completion
rationale: Temperature and humidity control systems, along with HEPA filtration, must be operational to maintain the strict environmental conditions required for neonatal equipment and patient safety.

successor: Calibration and Functional Testing of Neonatal Equipment
rationale: After installation, all neonatal equipment must be calibrated, tested for proper function, and validated against clinical specifications before being put into clinical use.

While ideally training occurs after installation so staff can practice on the actual installed units, some training can begin beforehand using simulators or manuals; therefore this is a soft preference.

successor: Final Clean and Sterilization of Neonatal Ward
rationale: Once equipment is installed, a final terminal cleaning and sterilization of the ward must be performed to achieve infection control standards before patients can be admitted.
The ward can only admit patients after all neonatal equipment is installed, tested, calibrated, and the environment is verified to meet clinical safety standards.
The building envelope (walls, windows, doors, roof) must be complete to create a sealed environment for accurate acoustic testing, as external noise leakage would invalidate results.
All internal partition walls, including their acoustic-rated construction, must be finished before testing sound transmission between rooms and spaces.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-ins must be complete as penetrations through walls and floors can create acoustic flanking paths that affect test results.
Any remedial acoustic sealing or treatment identified during testing must be completed before final finishes are applied, as finishes can cover access to acoustic seals and corrections.
Acoustic certification is typically a regulatory or contractual requirement that must be satisfied before the building can be formally handed over or occupied.
The maternity ward must be physically built and enclosed before its systems can be commissioned and tested.
All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems must be installed before commissioning can verify their functionality.
Commissioning must verify all systems are operational before the ward can be formally handed over to the clinical team.
Ideally staff training occurs after commissioning so they can train on fully verified systems, though some training could start earlier if needed.
The ward cannot safely accept patients until all systems have been commissioned and proven operational.
The steeple or spire typically sits atop the main roof structure, requiring the roof to be completed first to provide a stable base and waterproof enclosure.
The steeple/spire is usually supported by a tower or structural frame that must be erected and stabilized before the spire can be installed.
Lightning rods and protection systems are often installed on or integrated with the steeple/spire after it is in place to protect the highest point of the building.
The spire marks the uppermost completion; upper-zone cladding and decorative finishing around the tower base are finalized after the spire is erected to ensure proper alignment and sealing.
In church construction, bells are typically hoisted and installed in the bell chamber of the tower after the spire framework is complete, as the spire provides the top anchor point.
Pews must be placed on a finished, level floor surface; the floor slab or subfloor provides the necessary stable substrate for seating installation.
The building envelope and structural walls must be in place to define the interior space where pews will be located before seating can be installed.

If pews are installed before final floor finishing (e.g., polishing, sealing), the seating may protect finished floors from construction traffic, but typically flooring should be completed first as a soft preference to avoid damaging pews.
It is preferable to complete painting and wall finishes before installing pews to avoid dust, paint splatter, and damage to the seating; however, pews can be protected if painting must occur after.
Electrical outlets and wiring in floors or walls near seating areas must be roughed in and inspected before pews are placed, as access behind or beneath seating would be blocked.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and graded before any boundary wall or fence can be erected to ensure proper foundation and alignment.
Property boundaries must be surveyed and staked out to establish the exact alignment and location for the perimeter wall/fence.
Soil testing informs foundation design for walls; though not always mandatory, it is a strong preference to avoid settlement issues.
Erecting the perimeter wall/fence first enhances site security by controlling access, though temporary fencing could be used earlier as a soft preference.
The perimeter boundary should be established before major interior excavation begins to clearly define the construction site limits and prevent boundary disputes.
The gate structure requires stable ground and foundations; site grading, compaction, and foundation work must precede any above-ground construction.
The gate defines the entry point; paths and roads should align with and lead up to the completed gate structure for proper spatial coordination.

successor: Fencing or boundary wall installation adjacent to gate
rationale: The gate serves as an access point in the perimeter; adjacent fencing/walls should connect to the gate's sides for a continuous enclosure.

successor: Signage and wayfinding installation at entrance
rationale: Signage is typically mounted on or near the completed gate, but could be installed separately; it is a logical rather than strictly physical dependency.

predecessor: Utility trenching and underground services routing
rationale: Any underground electrical, lighting, or data cables serving the gate must be laid before the gate structure is erected to avoid digging under or through the completed foundation.

successor: Foundation Pouring for Fountain / Ablution Basin
rationale: The ground must be excavated and leveled before any concrete or foundation work for the fountain/ablution basin can begin.

predecessor: Foundation Pouring for Fountain / Ablution Basin
rationale: The concrete foundation must be cured and set before the basin structure can be built upon it.
Water supply lines and drainage pipes must be laid underground before the basin is constructed to avoid breaking up finished work for retrofitting.
The basin structure must be complete before waterproofing membranes or sealants can be applied to prevent leaks.
Waterproofing must be done and tested before decorative tiles or final surface finishes are applied.
The physical basin must exist before the pump, nozzles, and mechanical components can be installed in their correct positions.
Pumps and plumbing fixtures must be in place before connecting water supply and testing for leaks and flow.
It is preferable to complete water testing before installing surrounding paving, planters, or decorative landscaping to avoid damage if leaks occur.
The window openings (frames and rough openings) must be built first to provide the physical structure into which the stained glass panels are installed.
The building's structural framing must be finished to support the weight of stained glass windows and to provide the load-bearing openings.
Flashing, sealants, and weatherproofing membranes around window openings should be installed prior to stained glass to prevent water damage to the finished artwork.
Interior wall finishes around the window openings must be applied after the stained glass is installed to allow for proper integration, sealing, and trim work.

successor: Final Glazing and Protective Glazing Installation
rationale: Exterior protective glazing (if specified) is often installed after the stained glass to shield it from weather and impact, though this is a design preference rather than a strict physical necessity in all cases.
The structural framework (walls, ceiling, and floor) must be complete to provide a stable mounting surface and secure environment for placing heavy or delicate statues and iconography.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-ins must be completed before installing statuary to avoid damage to finished iconography from dust, debris, or structural modifications.
Wall finishing including plastering and painting must be done first as installing statuary onto unfinished walls would require rework or cause damage to the iconography.
Lighting is positioned and focused to highlight the iconography and statuary; therefore, the statues must be in place first to achieve proper illumination angles and effects.
While preferable to install flooring after heavy statuary to avoid carrying materials over finished floors, this is a soft constraint as protective coverings can be used to mitigate risk.
The organ must be installed after the building structure and roof are complete to protect it from weather and construction debris during building construction.
The organ must first be fully installed and assembled before it can be voiced and tuned to the acoustics of the room.
Ideally, organ installation should occur before final painting or wall finishes in the organ chamber area to avoid damaging finished surfaces, though this is a soft preference.
The organ must be completely installed, voiced, and tuned before it can be played in worship services or performances.
The organ's wind supply system (bellows, reservoirs, blowers, and wind trunking) must be installed and operational before the pipes can be connected and the organ made playable.
The specific plot of land must be identified, measured, and legally designated before any consecration rituals or ground preparation can commence, as the exact boundaries define the sacred space.
Ownership and legal permissions for the land must be secured before consecrating the ground, as consecration is a permanent dedication that requires lawful control of the property.

Any required environmental impact assessments and archaeological investigations must be completed before ground disturbance or consecration, to ensure no protected sites or contaminants are disturbed.

The ground must be ritually purified, blessed, and consecrated before any foundation stone can be laid or cornerstone ceremony performed, as the consecration sanctifies the earth for sacred construction.
Physical excavation and earthmoving can only begin after consecration rituals are complete, as disturbing the consecrated ground without proper rites would violate the sanctity of the site.

The building site must be cleared of all obstacles, vegetation, and existing structures before any earth moving or foundation excavation can begin. This is a hard physical constraint as earthworks cannot proceed on an uncleared site.

Accurate survey and setting out of building lines, levels, and reference points must be completed before excavation and earthworks commence, as the foundation position depends on precise site measurements.
Temporary water, power, and site access roads must be in place before earthworks begin to support construction equipment and provide necessary utilities for the works.

The earthworks, including excavation, compaction, and preparation of the formation level, must be complete before concrete blinding, reinforcement, and slab pouring can commence, as the concrete is placed directly onto the prepared ground.

The excavation for foundations must be completed before underground drainage pipes, sewers, and service ducts are laid within the foundation trenches, as these services are installed at the base of the excavation before backfilling.
Masonry and stonework require a stable, level foundation to build upon; the foundation must be fully cured and set before masonry loads can be applied.
The site must be cleared, excavated, and graded before any masonry walls or stone structures can be erected.
Load-bearing masonry walls must be completed to support roof framing and trusses.
While plumbing rough-in can be partially done in parallel, complete masonry walls are needed before finalizing wall-penetrating plumbing runs to avoid rework.
Similar to plumbing, electrical conduit runs embedded in or passing through masonry walls must wait until those walls are constructed.

Stained glass panels require a solid structural frame or support system (e.g., steel armature, stone tracery, or wooden framework) to be installed and anchored into before the glass can be set. Without the frame, the stained glass has no physical support.

The rough openings must be prepared with weatherproof membranes, flashing, and sealants before stained glass installation to prevent moisture ingress that could damage the glass, lead came, or solder joints.

predecessor: Glass Panel Assembly & Leading Shop Work
rationale: The individual stained glass pieces must be cut, leaded or foiled, soldered, and fully assembled into panels in a studio or workshop before they can be transported to the site and installed into the prepared openings.

After the stained glass panels are set into the frame, the perimeter must be glazed (putty, silicone, or glazing compound applied) and fully weather-sealed to lock the panels in place and prevent air and water infiltration.

Interior trim, moldings, and decorative coverings around the stained glass window should be installed after the stained glass is in place to properly cap the edges and provide a finished aesthetic appearance without damaging the glass.
The structural framing (walls, ceilings, niches) must be complete to provide stable surfaces and supports for mounting religious art, icons, and heavy artwork.
Wall surfaces must be finished and painted before installing art and iconography to avoid damaging artwork with dust, paint splatter, or construction debris.
Electrical conduits, junction boxes, and lighting fixture mounts must be in place so that accent lighting for art can be installed or coordinated with artwork placement.
Flooring should be installed after art installation to prevent dust, debris, and heavy foot traffic from damaging finished floors during the delicate art mounting process.
Art installation generates dust, packing materials, and debris; final cleaning must occur after all artwork is in place to ensure the space is pristine for worship or display.
The ground must be cleared, graded, and compacted before any pavement or surface layer for the cycle path can be laid.
A stable sub-base (e.g., crushed stone or gravel) is required to support the cycle path surface and prevent settling or cracking.
Drainage pipes, gullies, or culverts must be placed beneath or alongside the path to prevent water accumulation and damage to the pavement structure.
Surface markings (e.g., cycle symbols, lane lines) and signs can only be applied or installed after the cycle path surface is completed and cured.
Soft landscaping, verges, and planting along the path edges typically follow surface completion, though some planting could technically occur concurrently with minor inconvenience.
The site must be graded and prepared before any gate structure can be erected, as the gate foundation requires a level, stable base.
Concrete footings and foundations for the gate support pillars must be poured and cured before the gate structure can be assembled and installed.
Electrical and data conduits for gate automation (motors, sensors, intercoms, card readers) must be laid underground before the gate is installed to avoid rework.
The entrance gate defines the main access point and must be in place before perimeter fencing can be tied into it to ensure proper alignment and security.

While paving can technically be done before or after, it is preferable to pave the entry road after the gate is installed to avoid damaging fresh pavement with heavy equipment during gate construction.
Any underground utilities (water, electrical for lighting near play areas) must be installed before play equipment is placed to avoid excavation near installed equipment.
Play equipment posts and anchors require cured concrete footings to be in place before equipment can be bolted or set into position.
Engineered wood fiber, rubber mulch, or poured-in-place rubber safety surfacing must be installed after the play equipment structure is in place to ensure proper fit around and under the equipment.

Safety fencing or border curbing around the play area is typically installed after equipment placement to accurately define the use zone boundaries, though in some cases it could be done simultaneously.

The ground must be cleared of debris, vegetation, and topsoil, and excavated to the required levels before any hard landscaping features such as patios, paths, or driveways can be installed on a prepared sub-base.

Underground drainage pipes, cables, and other utility services must be laid and backfilled before hard surfaces are placed, to avoid digging up completed hard landscaping or compromising its integrity.
A stable, compacted sub-base (e.g., MOT Type 1 aggregate) is required beneath paving, slabs, or concrete to prevent settlement, cracking, or uneven surfaces in the hard landscaping.

Hard landscaping elements such as patios, walls, and edging must be fully installed first so that soil, turf, and planting can be placed accurately up to the finished hard edges without damaging newly laid surfaces.

Once hard landscaping is complete, the site can be cleaned of debris, jointing sand swept in, sealants applied, and final quality checks carried out without interference from ongoing construction work.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and graded before fencing can be installed to ensure proper fence alignment, post depth, and stability.

All underground utilities (water, gas, electrical, communications) must be installed before digging fence post holes to avoid damaging buried lines and to ensure proper coordination of utility easements with fence locations.

Final landscaping, planting, and surface finishes should be completed after fencing is installed to avoid damaging finished landscaping during fence construction and to ensure proper grading and drainage against fence lines.

It is preferable to complete fencing and gates before finishing building exteriors to secure the site, control access, and prevent theft or vandalism of exterior materials, though not a strict physical dependency.

While foundation work typically precedes fencing as a soft preference to allow heavy equipment access, it is not a strict physical requirement since fencing can be installed around poured foundations.

Electrical rough-in work, including conduit runs, junction boxes, and wiring pathways, must be completed before external lighting fixtures can be installed, as the fixtures need to connect to the pre-installed electrical infrastructure.
Final site grading and drainage must be completed to ensure proper ground levels and stable footing for light pole foundations and base installations.
Wall-mounted external lighting fixtures require finished exterior wall surfaces for proper mounting, sealing, and weatherproofing.
It is preferable to complete external lighting installation before final landscaping and hardscaping to avoid damaging newly planted areas, turf, or paving during lighting installation work.
Final touch-up painting and coating work is typically done after external lighting is installed because the fixtures may mar or scratch wall surfaces during installation.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and topsoil before drainage works can commence to expose the subgrade and ensure proper drainage installation.
Bulk excavation and grading to achieve formation levels must be completed before drainage trenches are dug and pipe runs are laid to ensure correct falls and alignment.
Drainage pipes and SuDS features must be installed and tested before placing the capping layer or sub-base to avoid the need for future excavation through the pavement layers.
All underground drainage and SuDS infrastructure must be in place and backfilled before the road pavement layers are constructed, as the pavement cannot be laid over unfinished drainage works.

While utilities can sometimes be installed concurrently with drainage, it is generally preferred to complete drainage first to avoid conflicts and to ensure drainage falls are not compromised by later utility trenches crossing drainage runs.
The ground must be properly graded and prepared to provide a stable, level base for constructing the enclosure and to ensure proper drainage away from the structure.
A concrete slab or foundation must be poured and cured before the enclosure walls, posts, or structure can be erected on top of it.
Any underground drainage, electrical, or water utilities that need to serve the enclosure area must be installed before the slab and enclosure are built over them.
The structural frame or walls of the enclosure must be in place before cladding, siding, or exterior finishes can be applied.
The enclosure structure must be complete before gates, doors, or access hatches can be hung and fitted to the frame.
Ground must be prepared, leveled, and excavated before installing EV charging infrastructure to ensure a stable base and proper cable routing.
Electrical supply cables must be laid in underground ducts before the charging unit can be connected to the grid.
The main electrical distribution board and supply must be in place to provide power to the EV charging unit.
Final surface finishing around the charging point must be completed after installation to avoid damaging new paving and to ensure a flush, finished appearance.
The charging unit must be physically installed before it can be electrically tested, commissioned, and certified for safe operation.
The building must be watertight and enclosed before exterior signage can be installed to ensure signage has a stable mounting surface and to prevent damage from weather exposure.
Exterior wall finishes must be completed to provide the final surface onto which signage is mounted; installing signage before finishes could result in damage or misalignment.
Electrical conduit and power supply to illuminated external signage must be roughed-in and connected before the signage units are installed.
Pedestrian pathways and plazas must be finalized to ensure wayfinding signage is correctly positioned relative to walking routes and that sign bases are anchored into finished hardscape.

While landscaping can be done concurrently, it is preferable to install wayfinding signage before final planting and topsoil to avoid disturbing new plantings during sign installation and to ensure signs are aligned with final site grading.
All external signage and wayfinding must be in place before the final inspection and issuance of a certificate of occupancy, as signage is a required life-safety and egress element.
A stable, level floor surface must be in place before installing the Sensory Play Station to ensure structural integrity and safety.
Electrical rough-in for any lighting, sound, or interactive components near the Sensory Play Station must be completed before installation to avoid rework or damage.
The wall or structural backing where the Sensory Play Station may be mounted or abutted must be framed and finished before the station can be secured in place.
Trim, baseboards, and final finishes around the Sensory Play Station must be installed after the station is placed to ensure clean edges and proper fit.
Any lights, sensors, or sound modules integrated into the Sensory Play Station must be calibrated and functionally tested only after the station is fully installed and connected.
The climbing structure requires a stable, level foundation (concrete pad or compacted base) to ensure structural integrity and safety; without this base, the structure cannot be properly anchored.
Proper drainage must be in place around the climbing structure area to prevent water accumulation, erosion, and destabilization of the foundation or the structure's base.

Impact-absorbing safety surfacing (e.g., rubber mulch, poured rubber) must be installed after the climbing structure is erected so that the surfacing can be placed flush against and around the structure's support posts and base components.

Once the climbing structure is fully assembled and all components are fastened, a formal safety inspection must be conducted to verify structural stability, proper hardware torque, and compliance with safety standards before the equipment is opened for public use.

Although not physically required for the structure itself, perimeter fencing is typically placed after the climbing structure is in position to ensure proper setback distances and to enclose the play area; this is often a regulatory or design preference rather than a hard physical constraint.
Power and data cabling must be run to the play panel location before the panel can be connected and mounted.
The play panel requires a finished wall surface for proper mounting and alignment.
Flooring is typically completed before wall-mounted fixtures to avoid damage, but the panel could be installed before flooring if careful protection is provided.
The panel hardware must be physically installed before software can be loaded, calibrated, and integrated with building systems.

successor: Final commissioning and user acceptance testing
rationale: Testing of the interactive panel's touch, display, audio, and connectivity functions requires the panel to be fully installed and powered.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and prepared before any fencing can be erected to ensure a stable and level base for fence posts.
Any concrete footings or post foundations required for the fence posts must be poured and cured before the fence structure can be installed.
Underground services (water, gas, electricity, data) must be located and any trenching completed prior to fence post installation to avoid damaging utilities or having to redo fencing work.
The play area boundary must be physically enclosed by fencing before installing soft-fall surfaces or synthetic turf to contain materials and define the work zone.
Fencing should be completed first to secure the site, prevent unauthorized access, and establish the perimeter before bringing in play equipment and undertaking assembly.

successor: Storage Unit for Play Equipment Installation
rationale: The storage unit requires a stable, level base or foundation to sit on; the base must be prepared and cured before the unit can be installed.

successor: Storage Unit for Play Equipment Installation
rationale: It is preferable to install the play surface before placing the storage unit so that the unit sits on top of the finished surface, but if needed the surface can be cut and fitted around the unit later.

predecessor: Storage Unit for Play Equipment Installation
rationale: The storage unit is often positioned adjacent to or within the play area; major play equipment installation should wait until the storage unit is in place so that access and layout are not obstructed.

predecessor: Storage Unit for Play Equipment Installation
rationale: It is easier to install fencing after the storage unit is placed to ensure proper alignment and gate placement around the unit.

predecessor: Storage Unit for Play Equipment Installation
rationale: Final landscaping and grading should be completed after the storage unit is installed to blend the unit into the surrounding terrain and avoid damaging landscaping during installation.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and properly graded before any play equipment or surfacing can be installed to ensure a stable, safe foundation.
Any concrete slabs or footings for play structures must be poured and cured before the play equipment can be anchored and installed.
Underground drainage must be in place before play surfacing and equipment are installed to prevent water accumulation and ensure long-term stability and safety.
All buried electrical, water, or data conduits serving the play area (e.g., for lighting or water features) must be laid before surface-level construction begins to avoid re-excavation.

The play structures and equipment must be fully installed and in place before the safety surfacing (e.g., rubber mulch, poured-in-place rubber) is applied around and beneath them to ensure proper fit and coverage.

While final landscaping around the play area is typically done after equipment installation to avoid damage, some planting can be done beforehand if carefully coordinated; however, complete landscaping is best performed after play space installation.

Perimeter fencing is often installed after play equipment to ensure access for construction equipment, though it can be done before if gates are wide enough; it is a soft preference to install fencing after play space construction.
Equipment must be procured and delivered to site before it can be commissioned and tested. Without the physical equipment on-site, commissioning cannot begin.
Equipment must be properly installed, assembled, and connected before commissioning and testing can occur. Commissioning validates that installed equipment functions correctly.
Power supply, control wiring, and mechanical connections must be completed before the equipment can be powered up and functionally tested.
Individual equipment must be commissioned and verified as functioning correctly before it can be integrated into the broader system for comprehensive integration testing.
