Commissioning and testing must be successfully completed and signed off before the system or equipment can be formally handed over to the client or declared practically complete.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and obstructions before grading can begin to ensure a clean working surface and proper soil handling.
Rough grading establishes the general site slopes and drainage patterns, which must be completed before fine grading of the play space area can achieve final contours.
All underground utilities (water, drainage, electrical conduits) must be installed prior to final grading to avoid disturbing the finished grade surface during trenching and backfilling.
The graded and compacted subgrade must be complete before any engineered wood fiber, rubber mulch, or synthetic turf safety surfacing can be placed over it.
Footings and foundations for play structures require precise grading and compaction to ensure proper load-bearing capacity and level installation.

The building must be fully constructed, commissioned, and handed over before routine maintenance can begin. Maintenance activities cannot be performed on a structure that is not yet built or operational.
All outstanding deficiencies and punch list items from construction must be resolved before transitioning to routine maintenance, ensuring the facility is in a complete and acceptable condition.
Building systems (HVAC, electrical, plumbing, fire protection) must be started, tested, and verified operational before routine maintenance schedules can be established and executed.

Routine maintenance and inspections ensure that the building systems are fully functional, safe, and code-compliant before tenants can occupy the space. Occupancy should only occur after maintenance protocols are in place.

While routine maintenance programs feed into larger capital repair planning, this is more of a soft preference — routine inspections may identify issues that lead to deferred maintenance projects, but capital repairs can also be planned independently.
The subgrade (soil or base layer) must be compacted and graded to proper elevations before any hardscape or plaza floor can be installed, to ensure stability and proper drainage.
All underground piping, conduits, and drainage systems beneath the plaza area must be installed and inspected before the hardscape floor is placed, to avoid costly demolition and rework.
Perimeter curbs, retaining walls, or foundation walls that border the plaza area must be constructed first to define the boundary and provide support for the hardscape flooring system.
The structural hardscape floor (e.g., concrete slab, paver base) must be fully placed and cured before any surface finishing treatments such as sealing, staining, or joint fillers can be applied.

While site furnishings like benches, planters, and bollards can ideally be installed after the hardscape floor is complete for a clean workflow, they could technically be anchored during floor placement, making this a soft preference rather than a strict physical constraint.
The seating wall requires a stable, level foundation or base slab to bear its load and prevent settling or cracking.
Steel reinforcement must be placed and tied before concrete (or masonry) is poured/laid to form the structural integrity of the seating wall.
If the seating wall is cast-in-place concrete, the formwork must be erected before concrete placement.
Backfill against the seating wall can only be placed after the wall has cured sufficiently to withstand lateral earth pressures.
The top cap or coping stone is installed after the main wall structure is complete to provide a finished, weather-resistant top surface.
Structural framing and building envelope must be complete to provide the load-bearing support and waterproof backing required for green wall installation.
Roof waterproofing and drainage systems must be finished to prevent water infiltration that could damage the green wall and to manage water flow.
Plumbing lines for irrigation and electrical conduits for lighting/fans must be roughed in before the green wall is installed to avoid rework and wall damage.

While the green wall must be in place before final ground-level landscape finishes like mulch and decorative stone can be placed around its base, this is a soft preference as these finishes could be done before if careful coordination occurs.
The green wall planting must be fully installed before the integrated irrigation system can be tested and commissioned to ensure it properly waters all plants.
The ground must be excavated and prepared to create a stable base and accommodate plumbing and electrical lines before a water feature can be installed.
Water supply lines, drainage pipes, and electrical conduits for pumps and lighting must be run underground before the water feature structure is built on top.
A concrete slab or foundation pad is typically required to support the weight of the water feature basin, structure, and water volume.
Final grading, planting, paving, and decorative elements around the water feature should be installed after the water feature is complete to ensure proper fit and avoid damage.
After the water feature is constructed, it must be tested for leaks and waterproofed to ensure long-term functionality before being put into full operation.
Wiring, conduit, and junction boxes must be installed and in place before outdoor lighting fixtures can be mounted and connected.
The exterior wall cladding, siding, or masonry must be completed so that fixture mounting brackets can be properly secured to the finished surface.
After fixtures are mounted, final connections, switch installation, and circuit testing can be performed as part of electrical finish work.
While not physically required, installing lighting before final landscaping avoids damage to new plants and allows for precise placement of landscape lighting.
All outdoor lighting must be fully installed and operational before the final electrical inspection and system commissioning can be completed.
The site must be graded and prepared to ensure proper drainage and soil conditions before trees can be planted.
All underground utilities (water, gas, electric, sewer) must be installed before tree planting to avoid digging up newly planted trees or damaging root systems.
Sidewalks and curbs define the tree pits or planting strips; trees must be planted after these are in place to ensure proper alignment and spacing.

If paving occurs after tree planting, heavy equipment and hot asphalt can damage tree trunks, roots, and soil compaction; however sometimes trees are planted after rough grading but before final pavement to allow for tree pit adjustments.

It is generally easier to plant trees before final lawn seeding or sodding to avoid damaging new grass with foot traffic and tree planting equipment, though this is a soft preference as sod can be laid around existing trees.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and graded before building a planter box or raised bed so that the structure sits on stable, well-drained soil.
A level base or foundation (e.g., compacted gravel, concrete pad, or landscape fabric) is required to support the planter box and prevent uneven settling or rot.
Any underground pipes, irrigation lines, or drainage systems that will run under or near the planter must be installed first to avoid excavation damage later.
The planter structure must be fully assembled and in place before it can be filled with soil or planting mix.
Plants, seeds, or seedlings can only be placed into the planter after the box is built and filled with growing medium.
The ground area must be leveled and prepared before placing outdoor furniture to ensure stability and proper positioning.
Outdoor furniture is typically placed on a finished hardscape surface like a patio, deck, or paved area; the hardscape must be fully cured and installed first.
Surrounding landscaping, plantings, and sod should be completed before furniture is placed to avoid damage from landscaping equipment and to allow for final grading around the area.
While furniture placement is often one of the final steps, it is a soft preference that final cleaning occurs after furniture is installed so that the area is fully finished for occupancy.
The space cannot be used for its intended purpose (seating, dining, etc.) until the furniture is installed and secured in place.
The ground surface must be excavated, graded, and compacted to provide a stable, level base for installing the bike rack foundation.
If the bike rack requires a concrete base or embedded sleeves, the concrete must be poured and cured before the rack can be anchored or bolted in place.
The bike rack should be installed before the final paving or surface finish to avoid damaging the finished surface and to allow proper integration of the rack's base into the pavement.
Soft preference: completing the rack installation first prevents heavy equipment or materials from damaging newly planted vegetation, but landscaping can be done concurrently with care.
All underground utilities and conduits must be installed and backfilled before digging or setting posts for the bike rack to avoid conflicts and rework.
The ground must be excavated and prepared before the pylon foundation can be poured and the pylon installed.
The concrete footing or foundation must be cured and in place to provide a stable base for mounting the pylon structure.
Power and data conduits must be run underground to the pylon location before the pylon is set, so connections can be made internally.
Landscaping and paving around the pylon should generally be completed after the pylon is installed to avoid damage to finished surfaces and to allow precise grading around the base.
The pylon must be physically installed before electricians can make final connections from the internal wiring to the building power system and test illumination features.
The ground surface must be graded and excavated to the proper slope and elevation before the accessible ramp structure can be built to ensure correct transition grades and ADA compliance.
A compacted subbase or foundation layer is required beneath the ramp to provide stable support and prevent settlement before ramp installation.
If underground utilities run beneath the ramp area, they should be roughed in beforehand to avoid excavation or disturbance after the ramp is in place.

successor: Ramp Surface Finishing (e.g., concrete curing or paving)
rationale: The ramp structure must be fully installed before any surface finishing, curing, or paving can be applied to the ramp surface.
Handrails and guardrails require the ramp structure to be in place as a mounting surface and to ensure proper alignment and code-compliant heights.
The site must be graded and rough earthwork completed to establish the correct elevations and drainage patterns before excavating and constructing the bioretention cell.

Erosion and sediment controls (e.g., silt fence, inlet protection) must be in place before any earth disturbance to prevent sediment from entering the bioretention area or downstream drainage systems.
Any underground stormwater conveyance pipes or underdrain connections that tie into the bioretention cell must be installed prior to placing the filter media and planting layers.

The bioretention cell must be fully constructed, including planting media and vegetation, before final fine grading and landscaping of the surrounding area can be completed to avoid soil compaction and disturbance to the cell.
Adjacent pavement, curb, and gutter work should occur after the bioretention cell is built to ensure proper sheet flow drainage into the cell and prevent construction debris from clogging the cell.
Underground conduit must be in place to route electrical and data cables to the outdoor outlet location before the outlet can be installed.
Electrical cabling and wiring must be pulled and terminated at the outlet box location before the outdoor outlet can be mounted and connected.
The wall or structure where the outdoor outlet is mounted must be framed and in place to provide physical support for the outlet box.
The outlet must be mounted and wired before a weatherproof cover or enclosure can be fitted over it to protect against moisture and debris.
The outdoor outlet must be fully installed before electrical testing (e.g., GFCI test, voltage check, continuity test) can be performed to verify safe operation.
Electrical power and data cabling must be run to the camera locations before the camera mounts can be installed, as the mounts attach over the wiring access points.
For ceiling-mounted cameras, the ceiling grid or structure must be in place to provide a mounting surface for the CCTV mount brackets.
Mounting to finished walls ensures the mount sits flush against a completed surface and avoids damage to wet paint or unfinished drywall.
The camera mount must be securely fixed to the structure before the camera unit itself can be attached to the mount and its cables terminated.
Mounts must be in place with cameras attached before the system can be powered on, aligned, and tested for proper operation.
The ground must be properly graded, compacted, and prepared before any hardscape elements (like pavers, patios, or walkways) can be installed to ensure a stable, level base and proper drainage.

Electrical conduits, irrigation lines, drainage pipes, and other buried utilities must be placed before hardscape surfaces are laid, otherwise the hardscape would need to be torn up to access underground services.

predecessor: Foundation & Slab Work (if adjacent to building)
rationale: Building foundations, footings, and adjacent concrete slabs must be completed before hardscape elements are installed against the structure to ensure proper connection, expansion joints, and avoidance of settlement issues.

Hardscape surfaces such as patios, walkways, retaining walls, and driveways must be in place before soil, mulch, plants, and turf are installed, to avoid soil compaction on finished hardscape, damage to plants during hardscape construction, and to achieve clean edge transitions.

While it is generally easier to install outdoor structures after hardscape so that posts anchor into the finished surface, some structures can be built concurrently with careful coordination; the preference is to complete hardscape first to avoid damaging new structures with heavy equipment.
Proper site grading and drainage systems must be in place to ensure water flows away from planted areas and to prevent soil erosion or waterlogging before planting begins.
All underground utilities (e.g., irrigation lines, electrical conduits, drainage pipes) must be installed before planting to avoid digging up newly planted vegetation for utility access.
Final grading, soil amendments, and topsoil placement must be completed to provide a suitable growing medium and proper bed conditions for plant installation.
Irrigation system testing typically occurs after planting to verify that all zones adequately water the newly installed plants before the system is put into regular operation.
Mulch is typically applied after planting to retain soil moisture and suppress weeds, but this is a soft preference as some projects may mulch before planting.
Underground conduits and power cables for outdoor lighting must be laid and buried before lighting fixtures can be installed above ground.
Concrete pads or foundations that will support light poles or bollards must be poured and cured before the lighting fixtures can be mounted.
Final site grading ensures that lighting poles and fixtures are installed at the correct elevations and that drainage around bases is properly established.
Outdoor lighting fixtures need to be in place before final landscaping, sod, pavers, and decorative site features are installed to avoid rework and damage.
All outdoor lighting fixtures must be physically installed before the electrical system can be energized, tested, and commissioned for proper operation.
The site must be graded and cleared before any underground irrigation pipes or trenching can be installed, as uneven ground would compromise pipe slopes and proper coverage.
Existing underground utilities (gas, electric, water, telecom) must be located and marked to avoid striking them when trenching for irrigation lines.
A water supply connection (e.g., tap into main line) must be established to provide the source of water for the irrigation system before any sprinklers or drip lines can be commissioned.

Irrigation pipes and sprinkler heads must be installed and tested before final landscaping, sodding, or seeding is laid, so that the irrigation system is operational to water the new plantings and to avoid disturbing the irrigation system after landscaping is complete.

Commissioning of the irrigation system is typically completed before final project inspections to ensure the system operates correctly, though inspections could theoretically occur simultaneously or before commissioning in some sequences.
The site must be prepared, graded, and stable before public art can be installed to ensure a level, safe foundation and proper integration with the landscape.
Concrete footings, slabs, or structural foundations must be poured and cured before mounting or anchoring permanent public art pieces to ensure structural stability.
All underground utilities (electrical, plumbing, drainage, data) must be laid and inspected prior to art installation to avoid the need for excavation that could damage the artwork.

Final landscaping, planting, paving, and decorative hardscaping around the artwork should be completed after the art is installed to avoid damage to plants or finishes during the installation process.

successor: Final Site Cleanup and Punch List
rationale: Any debris, packaging, or construction materials from the art installation must be removed, and final touch-ups completed, only after the artwork is fully in place.
The site must be graded and earthworks completed to establish proper drainage slopes and stormwater flow paths before the stormwater system can be tested under designed conditions.
All stormwater pipes, culverts, and conveyance structures must be installed and connected before the system can be tested for flow capacity and leak-tightness.

predecessor: Stormwater Inlet and Catch Basin Construction
rationale: Inlets, catch basins, and manholes must be constructed and connected to the pipe network to allow water entry and system pressurization during testing.
Detention or retention basins must be completed to test the full system's storage and discharge performance.
Testing must be successfully completed and results documented before the system can be formally accepted by the client or regulatory authority.
It is preferable to complete testing before final landscaping to avoid damage to finished surfaces if excavation or repairs are needed due to test failures.

The initial landscape installation (planting, sodding, hardscaping) must be completed before any ongoing maintenance can begin, as maintenance activities such as pruning, watering, weeding, and mowing presuppose the existence of the installed landscape elements.

Site grading and earthworks must be completed prior to landscape installation and therefore before ongoing maintenance, as the topography and drainage patterns must be established for landscape features to be properly installed and maintained.

The irrigation system must be installed and operational before the ongoing landscape maintenance programme can commence, as maintenance includes watering schedules and irrigation system checks that require the system to be in place.

While seasonal replanting and renovation typically occur as part of the maintenance cycle, it is a soft preference that routine maintenance precedes major renovation work to establish baseline conditions, though in practice these activities may overlap.

A full landscape replacement or redevelopment project cannot begin until the ongoing maintenance programme has ceased for that area, as redevelopment involves removing existing landscape elements that were being maintained.
The burial vault must be placed within an excavated pit or foundation area; excavation provides the necessary space and stable base.
A level concrete base or slab is typically poured before the vault is set to provide a stable, level foundation for the vault structure.
Below-grade waterproofing must be applied to the foundation/excavation surfaces before the vault is placed to prevent groundwater ingress.
The burial vault serves as the containment structure; the casket is lowered into and placed inside the vault after the vault is in position.
The vault lid or cover is sealed onto the vault body after the vault is in place and the casket has been inserted, enclosing the contents.
The grave must be excavated to create space before a grave liner can be installed.
The grave liner must be in place before the casket or outer burial vault can be placed inside it.
Backfilling cannot occur until the grave liner and its contents are fully installed.
While ideally the marker is placed after all burial work is complete, it could theoretically be installed before the liner in some sequences, but convention follows after completion.
Grading and landscaping must prepare the ground before excavation and liner installation can begin.
The grave site must be excavated and the foundation prepared (e.g., concrete base or plinth) before the headstone can be placed on a stable surface.
The exact plot location, orientation, and boundaries must be surveyed and marked before the headstone can be installed in the correct position.
The burial or interment of remains must be completed before the permanent headstone or grave marker is set, as the marker is placed over the grave.
Final landscaping around the grave (sodding, gravel, planting) must follow headstone installation to ensure the marker is properly positioned and graded around its base.
While inscription can be done on the stone before placement, any final on-site touch-ups or additions to the inscription are performed after the headstone is set in place.
The ground must be excavated and prepared before the footstone can be placed as it sits at the base of the foundation.
Formwork for the footing must be in place to contain and shape the concrete or masonry for the footstone.
The footstone forms the lowest part of the foundation upon which the wall or superstructure is built; walls cannot be started until the footstone is set and cured.
A damp-proof membrane or course is typically applied on top of the footstone/footing to prevent moisture rising into the walls above.
Backfilling against the foundation can only proceed after the footstone and any associated footing concrete have sufficiently cured.

The grave surround or kerb set must be installed on a stable, level foundation. Without proper base preparation (e.g., compacted soil, concrete footing), the kerb units would settle unevenly or shift.
The grave must be excavated to the correct depth and dimensions before any above-ground surround or kerb can be positioned around the grave opening.
Backfilling around the kerb or surround stabilises it in place and completes the ground-level finish; this cannot occur until the kerb units are installed.
Headstones or memorial plaques are often mounted onto or within the kerb set / surround; the surround must be fixed in position before the memorial can be securely attached.
Final landscaping and turfing around the grave area is typically done after the kerb is in place to achieve a neat finish, though it could theoretically be done beforehand with careful work.
The building or wall surface must be structurally complete to support the memorial plaque.
The surface where the plaque will be mounted must be finished (plastered, painted, or faced) before the plaque can be affixed.
Final landscaping, paving, and cleanup around the plaque area must occur after the plaque is installed to avoid damage or soiling.
The ceremonial unveiling or official commissioning logically follows installation, though it is a soft preference rather than a physical necessity.
The physical plaque must be manufactured, engraved, and delivered to site before it can be installed.
The grave must be excavated to the required depth and dimensions before the cover slab can be placed over it.
A burial vault or liner must be installed around the casket before the grave cover slab is placed on top to seal the grave.
The casket must be lowered into the grave before the cover slab can be positioned over the burial space.
The cover slab must be in place before backfilling soil over the grave can commence, as the slab provides structural separation.
Final landscaping and turfing over the grave area can only begin after the cover slab is installed and backfilling is complete.
Raw materials like wood, metal, or composite materials must be sourced and prepared before coffin construction can begin.
The specifications and dimensions for the coffin must be determined before fabrication can start.
The interior fabric, padding, and lining can only be installed after the coffin shell structure is fully assembled.
External paint, stain, varnish, or polish application must occur after the coffin structure is built.
Casket hardware such as handles, hinges, and closure mechanisms can only be attached to a fully constructed coffin body.
Final inspection and testing of the coffin's structural integrity and finish must be performed after complete assembly.
The clay must be properly prepared (mixed, wedged, and de-aired) before it can be shaped into an urn, as the urn cannot be formed from unprepared clay.
The urn body must be physically formed through wheel throwing or hand building techniques before it can be considered a complete urn structure.
The formed urn must be completely air-dried to remove moisture before it can undergo firing, as wet clay would crack or explode in the kiln.
The dried urn must undergo its first (bisque) firing to transform the clay into a permanent ceramic state before glazing can be applied.
The bisque-fired urn must be complete as a ceramic vessel before glaze can be applied to its surface; glazing cannot be done on unfired or wet clay.
The niche is a recess or cavity within a wall or column structure; the supporting wall/column must be constructed first to provide the structural backing and defined space for the niche.
The overall structural shell of the building (including load-bearing walls) must be completed before any detailed interior components like a columbarium niche can be installed or built into the wall.
It is preferred that the niche is installed or formed before applying final interior finishes such as plaster and paint, so that the finishes can be applied seamlessly around the niche opening.
The niche structure must be fully built and ready before urns (containing cremated remains) can be placed inside it, as the niche provides the designated storage compartment.
The niche must be completed before a plaque or nameplate can be affixed to seal or identify the niche, since the plaque attaches to the niche face/frame.
The site must be cleared of debris, vegetation, and existing structures before accurate surveying and layout can occur, as obstructions would prevent proper measurement and staking.
Legal ownership of the land and necessary permits must be secured before site surveying begins, as surveyors require authorized access and regulatory approvals to mark boundaries.
The survey and layout must define exact building footprints, grades, and reference points before any excavation or earthmoving can commence.
Foundation construction requires precise positioning established by the survey layout, including column locations, foundation lines, and elevation benchmarks.
Underground utility runs (water, sewer, electrical, gas) must follow the surveyed layout to avoid conflicts with building foundations and to ensure proper alignment.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and obstacles before any excavation can begin to provide unobstructed access for digging equipment and to define the grave boundaries.
The exact position, orientation, and dimensions of the grave must be surveyed and marked on the ground before excavation starts to ensure accurate digging to the required specifications.
The grave must be fully excavated to the required depth and dimensions before the coffin or casket can be lowered into it, as there is no physical space for placement until excavation is complete.
A grave liner or burial vault can only be installed into the excavated pit after the excavation is finished, as it requires an open hole of the correct size.

Backfilling (replacing soil over the buried coffin) can only commence after the coffin has been placed and any vault/lid installed, and it directly follows from the existence of the excavated hole that needs to be refilled.
The ground must be excavated to the proper depth and width to accommodate the burial vault before the vault can be placed in the ground.
A level, compacted base layer (often crushed stone or concrete) must be prepared at the bottom of the excavation to provide a stable foundation for the vault.

In some designs, a perimeter drainage system or sump may be installed at the base before the vault is placed to prevent water accumulation; though not always required, if specified it must precede vault placement.
The vault body must be set in place and leveled before the lid or cover can be positioned on top of it.
The burial vault must be fully installed in the ground before the casket can be lowered into the vault.
After the vault (with lid) is in place and the interment is complete, the excavation must be backfilled and the site graded to restore the ground surface.
The grave or burial pit must be excavated before the body or remains can be placed into it.
The deceased must be prepared (e.g., embalmed, washed, dressed) before being placed in the grave.
Typically a funeral or memorial service precedes the burial, but this is a cultural or religious preference rather than a physical construction constraint.
After the casket or remains are placed in the grave, the excavation must be backfilled and the grave capped or covered.
A headstone or grave marker is typically placed after burial, but this can be delayed and is a cultural preference rather than a physical requirement.
A stable, level concrete foundation or base must be cured and ready before the headstone can be placed on it, otherwise the headstone would sink or shift.
The burial plot area must be excavated, graded, and compacted to provide proper drainage and support before the headstone base is laid.
The burial or interment of remains must be completed before the headstone is permanently installed, as the headstone marks the grave location and would obstruct burial access.
While landscaping can be done after headstone installation for a clean finished look, it is a soft preference because landscaping could theoretically be done beforehand and patched around the stone.
The headstone must be in place before the grave site can be fully cleaned, dressed, and formally dedicated, as the headstone is the central feature of the completed grave.
The grave must first be excavated to create the void space before it can be backfilled and compacted.
The coffin or urn must be placed in the excavated grave before backfilling can occur, as backfilling covers the burial container.
The grave must be fully backfilled and compacted to provide a stable base before installing a headstone or monument.
Backfilling and compaction must be completed before the surface can be restored with sod or turf, as the final grade must be established first.
While typically done after backfilling, final grading could theoretically occur concurrently in some cases, but best practice dictates backfilling first for proper compaction.
The base or surface of the monument must be prepared, smoothed, and finished before any inscription or engraving can be applied to ensure a clean, stable substrate for text and designs.
The raw stone or material must be quarried and selected before it can be inscribed or engraved with memorial text.
The rough stone must be cut and shaped into the memorial form (e.g., slab, headstone, panel) before inscriptions can be added on the finished surface.

The completed inscribed memorial must be finished with all engravings before it can be transported and erected at its final location, as adding inscriptions after placement is far more difficult and impractical.
After engraving, the recessed letters are often painted or gilded to enhance readability; this is a soft preference because some memorials may be left with raw engraved stone.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and obstructions before any fencing can be installed to ensure clear access and proper alignment.
Accurate boundary lines must be surveyed and staked out to define exactly where the fence should be constructed.
All underground utilities must be located and marked before digging post holes to avoid damage to utility lines and ensure worker safety.
While some landscaping can be done simultaneously, final grading, seeding, and aesthetic finishing around the fence line is typically completed after the fence is erected to avoid damage.
Gates are typically installed as part of or after the fence structure is in place, as the gate posts and hardware integrate with the completed fence line.
The recirculation pump requires a stable, level foundation or base slab to be installed upon; without the base, the pump cannot be mounted or aligned properly.
Inlet water piping to the pump must be in place before the pump is installed, so the pump can be connected to the water supply system.
After the pump is mounted, the outlet piping that connects the pump to the recirculation loop or distribution system must be installed and connected to the pump discharge flange.
The pump motor requires electrical power; wiring, conduit, and motor connections can only be run to the pump once it is physically in place.
The recirculation system, including the pump, must be fully installed before the system can be flushed of debris and commissioned for operation.
A stable foundation is physically required before constructing the overflow weir to ensure structural integrity and proper load distribution.
The spillway channel must be excavated before the overflow weir is built, as the weir forms part of the spillway system and must align with the excavated channel geometry.
The overflow weir must be completed before constructing downstream energy dissipation structures, as these structures are designed based on the weir's discharge characteristics and hydraulic profile.
The overflow weir must be fully constructed and cured before the still water basin can be filled, as the weir controls water levels and prevents uncontrolled flooding of upstream areas.
Concrete curing of the weir body structure must be sufficiently advanced before the overflow weir can be considered operational and ready for subsequent hydraulic testing or water impoundment.
Pipe supports must be in place to hold and align the piping system before inlet fittings can be installed.
Pipes must be cut and beveled to the correct dimensions and angles before fittings can be attached.
Pipe ends must be cleaned and deburred to ensure a proper seal and fit before installing the inlet fitting.
After the inlet fitting is installed, the system must be pressure tested to verify the integrity of the connection and ensure no leaks.
Once the inlet fitting is securely in place, the overall system can be flushed to remove debris and then commissioned for operation.
Rough-in plumbing pipes must be installed and stubbed out before drain fittings can be attached, as the outlet/drain fitting connects directly to the rough-in piping system.
The concrete slab or subfloor must be poured and cured (or prepared) before drain fittings can be embedded or mounted, as they are typically set into the slab or floor structure.
In wet areas such as bathrooms or showers, waterproofing membranes should be applied before drain fittings are installed to ensure a watertight seal around the drain.

The outlet/drain fitting must be installed and its height set before floor finishes and tile work are applied, as the finish material is laid up to and around the drain flange to achieve proper drainage slope.

successor: Fixture Connection (e.g., sink, toilet, shower pan)
rationale: The drain fitting must be in place and connected to the rough-in plumbing before fixtures can be attached, as the fixture waste outlet connects directly to the installed drain fitting.
The construction site must be cleared, graded, and prepared before any aquatic planting can take place, as planting cannot occur on an unprepared or unstable substrate.

For constructed water bodies (ponds, wetlands), the waterproof membrane or liner must be installed and tested before aquatic plants can be placed, to ensure water retention and a stable growing environment.
The water body must be filled or partially filled with water to the appropriate level before aquatic plants can be installed, as they require an aquatic environment for survival.

After aquatic planting, water quality parameters (pH, nutrient levels, turbidity) should be monitored and stabilized to support plant establishment, though this is a soft preference as some adjustment can occur concurrently.
Final bank stabilization, erosion control mats, or riprap along water edges must be completed after aquatic planting to avoid disturbing or burying newly installed plants.
The UV steriliser must have a stable mounting bracket installed first to securely hold the unit in place before it can be attached.
Electrical wiring and conduit must be roughed in to the steriliser location to provide power connections before the unit can be wired and energised.
The UV steriliser must be physically installed before inlet and outlet plumbing can be connected to it.
Final electrical connections and testing of the UV steriliser can only be performed after the unit is fully mounted and in place.

successor: System Commissioning and Water Flow Test
rationale: The UV steriliser must be installed and connected before the overall system can be commissioned and water flow tested to ensure proper operation.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and graded to provide a stable, accessible work area before any excavation can begin.
All existing underground utilities (gas, electric, water, sewer) must be located and marked to avoid damage during excavation and ensure worker safety.
Erosion control measures (silt fencing, sediment basins) must be in place before earth disturbance begins to comply with environmental regulations and prevent sediment runoff.
After excavation is complete the exposed subgrade must be inspected, trimmed, and compacted to provide a uniform bearing surface for the water feature base or liner.
Drainage pipes and aggregate layers must be placed directly onto the excavated subgrade to manage groundwater and prevent hydrostatic pressure buildup beneath the water feature.
Excavation must be completed to create the basin cavity before any formwork can be placed and concrete poured into it.
The basin floor must be properly graded and compacted to provide a stable, level base for formwork installation and concrete placement.
After concrete is poured into the basin formwork, sufficient curing time is required before formwork can be safely stripped without damaging the green concrete.
Waterproofing membranes or coatings must be applied only after the basin concrete has fully cured and gained sufficient strength to prevent damage to the waterproofing system.

Pipe penetrations, drains, and plumbing fixtures within the basin structure can only be installed or cast-in after the basin concrete is poured and set, or must be embedded during the pour itself, with any subsequent plumbing work following the concrete placement.
The liner must be installed before coping and surround can be placed, as the coping and surround typically secure the liner in place at the pool edge.
The pool shell (concrete/gunite) must be fully cured and complete before coping and surround materials can be attached or installed around the perimeter.
Coping and surround must be in place before tile work begins, as tile often abuts or is set against the coping, and the coping provides the finished edge reference.
Decking or paving around the pool is typically installed after coping and surround are complete, as the coping forms the transition between the pool structure and the surrounding deck.
While not a strict physical requirement, final plumbing connections and equipment setup are often sequenced after coping installation to avoid damage to the coping from heavy equipment or materials.
Pipes must be installed and connected before they can be tested for leaks and pressure integrity.
All welded joints and connections must be completed and cooled before pressure testing to ensure the system is fully sealed.
Pipes must be properly supported and anchored to withstand the forces during pressurization without movement or damage.
All valves, flanges, fittings, and instrumentation necessary for the test must be in place to allow controlled pressurization and monitoring.
Pressure testing must be completed before flushing to avoid introducing debris into newly tested systems and to ensure test pressure integrity is confirmed before cleaning.
Thermal insulation should only be applied after successful pressure testing to allow visual inspection of joints and to avoid insulating over leaks or defects.
Final coatings and painting should follow pressure testing to avoid covering weld defects or test-related damage.
System commissioning requires confirmed pressure integrity from testing before introducing operational fluids and startup procedures.
Trenches must remain open during pressure testing for visual inspection of pipe joints and for detection of leaks; backfilling occurs only after successful testing.
The physical structure of the water feature must be constructed before it can be commissioned, as commissioning involves testing and activating the built system.

predecessor: Water Supply and Drainage Piping Installation
rationale: Water supply lines, recirculation pipes, and drainage piping must be installed and pressure-tested before the water feature can be commissioned to ensure proper flow and drainage.
Electrical power supply, pump wiring, and control system cabling must be in place before commissioning to allow pumps, lights, and controls to be tested.

successor: Landscaping and Final Finishes Around Water Feature
rationale: While some landscaping can proceed in parallel, final hardscape and softscape finishes directly adjacent to the water feature are typically done after commissioning to avoid damage during testing and to allow access for adjustments.

successor: Water Feature Handover and Client Training
rationale: The water feature must be fully commissioned and verified to be operating correctly before it can be handed over to the client or owner for use and operation.

Site preparation (clearing, grading, drainage installation) must be completed before seasonal drainage and winterisation can begin, as the drainage system and winterisation measures rely on a properly prepared and graded site to function correctly.

The permanent underground drainage network (pipes, catch basins, sumps) must be installed before seasonal drainage and winterisation activities, as winterisation includes protecting, insulating, and temporarily adjusting these drainage elements for cold weather conditions.

Foundations must be in place prior to seasonal drainage and winterisation because winterisation includes protecting foundation drains, waterproofing, and ensuring frost protection around foundation perimeters.

While winter concrete pouring can technically proceed independently, it is preferable to complete seasonal drainage and winterisation first to ensure the site drainage is functional and the work area is protected from frost, reducing the risk of frost heave damaging fresh concrete.

Seasonal drainage and winterisation must be completed before final landscaping and grading because winterisation activities include installing temporary drainage channels, covering exposed soils, and applying frost protection measures that would be disturbed or undone by subsequent landscaping work.

Site preparation (clearing, grading) can generate sediment runoff that must be captured before baseline water quality monitoring, otherwise the monitoring data would reflect construction-induced turbidity rather than natural conditions.

predecessor: Installation of Erosion and Sediment Control Measures
rationale: Erosion and sediment controls (silt fences, sediment basins, check dams) must be in place before water quality monitoring begins to ensure that construction site runoff is properly managed and monitored for effectiveness.

Baseline water quality must be established prior to major earth-disturbing activities to have a reference point for assessing construction impacts and to comply with environmental permitting requirements (e.g., NPDES Stormwater permits).
Concrete pouring can introduce alkaline runoff and sediment; water quality must be monitored beforehand to establish baseline pH and turbidity levels for impact assessment.

Post-construction water quality monitoring is typically performed after landscaping and revegetation are complete to verify that stormwater runoff meets regulatory standards, but this is a soft preference as monitoring could be conducted earlier for compliance checks.
A stable foundation must be completed before spectator stands can be erected to ensure structural safety and load distribution.
The site must be leveled and prepared to provide a proper base for the bleacher foundations and seating layout.
Primary structural columns and beams that support the bleacher tiers must be in place before standalone spectator stands can be installed.
The bleacher structural platform must be fully erected before seats or bench components can be attached or placed onto it.
Safety railings are mounted onto the completed bleacher structure and cannot be installed until the stand itself is in place.
The scoreboard must be mounted on or supported by the structural steel framework; the steel structure must be in place to provide a secure attachment point.
Power and data cables for the scoreboard must be run through conduits behind the mounting surface before the scoreboard is installed, otherwise wiring would be inaccessible.
The physical scoreboard unit must be mounted and in place before electricians can connect power and data lines and test the display.
Software configuration, display calibration, and commissioning can only occur once the scoreboard hardware is physically installed and powered.

successor: Final Finishes and Signage Around Scoreboard
rationale: If the scoreboard is installed early, surrounding aesthetic finishes can be completed around it; however if schedule flexibility allows, finishing work could also be done before mounting the scoreboard.
The field sub-base must be prepared and leveled before goal posts can be installed to ensure proper anchoring and stability.
Concrete footings or anchor points for goal posts must be set and cured before the posts can be erected and secured.
Proper site grading and drainage systems must be completed to prevent water pooling around goal post foundations and ensure long-term stability.
Goal posts must be installed before field markings are painted to ensure correct alignment of lines with the goal positions.
Goal posts should be installed before the final surface layer (artificial turf or natural grass) is laid so that post bases can be properly concealed and integrated into the field.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and properly graded before any sports facility can be built to ensure a stable foundation and proper drainage for the playing surface.

Underground utilities such as water supply, sewer lines, and electrical conduits must be installed before the facility is constructed to avoid digging up completed structures and playing surfaces later.

A proper foundation or sub-base layer (e.g., crushed stone, concrete slab) is required to support the structural loads of the facility, seating, and playing surfaces before above-ground construction begins.

successor: Installation of Sports Equipment (Goals, Nets, Scoreboards)
rationale: Permanent sports equipment and fixtures must be installed after the facility shell, playing surface, and structural components are completed to ensure proper anchoring and alignment.

successor: Interior and Exterior Finishing (Painting, Seating, Lighting)
rationale: Finishing work such as installing seating, painting lines on the playing surface, and mounting lighting fixtures logically follows the completion of the main structure and surface to avoid damage and allow precise placement.
A stable, well-compacted base and sub-base layer is required to support the playing surface, prevent uneven settling, and ensure proper drainage.
Proper drainage must be installed and tested before the playing surface is laid to ensure water can be effectively removed from beneath the surface.
Game lines and field markings must be applied on top of the completed playing surface for accuracy and durability.
Fixed equipment such as goal posts, sockets, and anchors must be installed after the playing surface to ensure proper alignment and anchorage.
While inspection often occurs after surface completion, it is a soft preference because some pre-installation checks (e.g., sub-base approval) can be done earlier.
A stable foundation base must be prepared and cured before floodlight poles/masts can be erected to ensure structural stability and safety.
Underground power and control cables must be laid in ducts before floodlight poles are installed, so that cables can be routed into the poles from below without requiring re-digging.
Floodlight fixtures must be physically mounted and securely in place before electricians can connect power supply cables and perform energization testing.
The floodlight units must be installed and fixed to their mounts before they can be precisely aimed and calibrated to achieve the required illumination pattern.
Final landscaping and surface finishing works are typically performed after floodlight installation to avoid damage to new landscaping during pole erection and heavy lifting operations.
A stable foundation or substructure is physically required before any grandstand or seating structure can be erected, to provide load-bearing support and ensure structural stability.
The main steel frame or structural support system must be in place before seating can be attached or installed, as the seating is typically mounted onto or supported by the frame.
The grandstand and seating must be fully erected and completed before final inspection and handover of the facility can occur, as it is a major component of the venue.

While some MEP (mechanical, electrical, plumbing) rough-in work may occur beforehand, final MEP fit-out and finishes (e.g., lighting installation under seats, power outlets) are typically done after seating is in place to avoid damage and ensure proper alignment.
Concrete slabs or terraced steps that form the base of the grandstand must be poured and cured before seating can be installed upon them.
The site must be cleared and excavated to the required levels before drainage pipes and trenches can be dug, ensuring the ground is prepared and free of obstructions.
The subgrade must be graded and compacted to provide a stable base and correct falls for drainage systems to function properly.
Existing underground utilities must be located and marked to avoid damaging them during drainage trench excavation and pipe laying.
Drainage pipes and structures must be installed and tested before trenches can be backfilled and compacted to final levels.
Drainage must be completed to ensure proper groundwater and surface water management before pouring concrete foundations, preventing water accumulation and soil instability.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and graded before fence posts can be set to ensure proper alignment, stability, and drainage.
All buried utilities (gas, water, electrical, telecom) must be located and marked before digging post holes to avoid damage, service disruption, and safety hazards.
Property boundaries must be officially surveyed and staked before fence placement to ensure the fence is built within legal property lines and to prevent boundary disputes.
It is often preferred to complete fencing first so that landscaping, sod, or decorative elements can be installed flush against the fence line, but it is not a strict physical requirement.

successor: Gate Installation and Access Control Setup
rationale: The main fence structure must be in place before gates can be hung on hinges or automated access control systems (e.g., keypads, card readers) can be mounted and wired to the fence posts.
The climbing frame must be anchored to or installed on a stable, level concrete slab foundation to ensure structural stability and safety.
The ground must be excavated, leveled, and prepared before the foundation and frame can be installed.
Safety surfacing (e.g., rubber mulch, synthetic turf, or poured rubber) must be installed after the climbing frame is erected to ensure the surface is flush around the posts and covers the fall zone.
The climbing frame must be fully assembled, anchored, and secure before a final safety inspection and certification can be conducted.

Additional playground components (slides, swings, etc.) are often connected to or positioned adjacent to the climbing frame, so it is preferable to install the frame first to ensure proper alignment, though it is not always a strict physical necessity.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and prepared before assembling or placing a swing set to ensure stability and safety.
A proper base (e.g., gravel, concrete footings, or rubber matting) must be in place before the swing set is installed to provide structural support and impact absorption.
Safety surfacing (e.g., rubber mulch, wood chips, or poured rubber) around the swing set must be installed after the frame is erected to ensure proper coverage and fall protection.
All bolts and fasteners must be fully tightened and torqued to specification after assembly to ensure structural integrity before use.
A comprehensive safety and stability inspection must be conducted after installation is complete and before the swing set is used by children.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and prepared before slide installation can begin.
A stable foundation or base structure must be built to support the slide's anchoring and structural integrity.
Safety surfacing (e.g., rubber mulch, poured-in-place rubber) around and under the slide must be installed after the slide is in place to ensure proper coverage and fall protection.
Final safety and structural inspections must occur after slide installation to verify secure attachment and compliance with safety standards.
Rope material must be fabricated or prepared before it can be used to build the bridge.

predecessor: Set Anchor Points on Both Banks
rationale: Anchor points (trees, stakes, or rock fixtures) must be secured on both sides of the gap before the rope can be tensioned and attached.
People or loads can only cross the bridge after it is fully constructed and secured.
Final tensioning and stabilizing (adding handrails, tightening slack) must happen after the main rope is in place.
The ground area must be cleared, leveled, and prepared before installing the mud kitchen to ensure a stable and safe foundation.
A solid base or foundation (e.g., concrete pad, paving stones, or compacted gravel) must be in place to support the mud kitchen structure and prevent sinking or movement.
If the mud kitchen includes a water supply (tap/sink), the kitchen structure must be in place before connecting pipes and fittings to ensure proper alignment.
The mud kitchen must be fully installed before a safety inspection can be carried out to check for sharp edges, stability, and overall safety compliance.

While landscaping can be done partially before or during installation, final decorative elements such as bark mulch, edging, or planting around the mud kitchen are best done after installation to ensure a neat finish and access for construction.
The balancing beam must be mounted on a solid, level foundation or base structure to ensure stability and safety. The foundation provides the necessary support and anchoring points.
Safety mats or padding around the beam can only be placed after the beam itself is installed, as the matting must conform to the beam's final position and dimensions.
A final safety and quality inspection of the beam must occur after installation to verify proper alignment, stability, and compliance with standards before the equipment is used.
The installation area must be leveled and prepared to provide a stable, flat surface for the beam's foundation, preventing uneven stress or tipping.

Other nearby gymnastics equipment like floor mats or bars may be positioned after the beam is installed to ensure proper spacing and safe clearance distances, though this is a soft preference for workflow efficiency.

The anchor foundations (concrete footings or ground anchors) must be installed and cured before the zip line cables and hardware can be attached, as the zip line's structural stability depends on secure anchor points.
The support towers or poles that suspend the zip line cable must be fully erected and secured before the zip line cable can be strung between them.
The zip line cable must be procured, delivered to site, and inspected for defects before it can be installed as part of the zip line system.
The zip line must be fully installed (cable, trolley, braking system) before safety testing can be conducted, as testing validates the complete assembly's performance and safety.

successor: Platform Decking and Landing Area Construction
rationale: The zip line cable alignment and termination points must be established first so that the launch platform and landing/deceleration area can be positioned and built accurately relative to the cable path.

Shade sail and canopy structures require a stable, load-bearing base such as a concrete slab, deck, or footings to anchor posts or support columns. The foundation must be fully cured and ready before any above-ground structural framing can begin.

Any underground electrical conduits, water lines, or drainage that pass beneath the shaded area or near support posts must be installed and covered before post holes are dug or footings are poured, to avoid excavation conflicts and rework.

It is generally preferable to complete the shade structure before installing final surface finishes (e.g., pavers, tiles, deck boards) to avoid damaging finished surfaces during post installation, but this is a soft preference as the surface can be worked around with care.

Final landscape planting and irrigation should be completed after the shade structure is in place so that plant locations, sun exposure patterns, and irrigation heads can be accurately adjusted relative to the installed canopy, and to avoid disturbing freshly planted beds during structure erection.

Installing exterior lighting (e.g., string lights, downlights, or post lights) is easier after the shade structure is up, as light locations can be aligned with the canopy and support posts. This is a soft preference since lighting can be retrofit, but sequencing it after avoids rework.
A stable, level foundation is required before installing the timber deck platform to ensure structural integrity and prevent uneven settling.
The underlying support structure (joists, beams, or bearers) must be installed and fixed to the foundation before decking boards can be laid on top.
Sealing, staining, or oiling the timber surface can only be applied after the deck boards are fully installed and secured.
Handrails and balustrades must be mounted onto or after the deck structure is complete, as they rely on the deck platform for support and alignment.

While deck lighting can often be retrofitted, it is more efficient and aesthetically preferable to install integrated lighting after the deck platform is complete to avoid damaging boards during electrical work.

The ground must be prepared, cleared, and excavated to the required depth before an embankment slide (a movable or adjustable embankment component) can be placed or formed. A stable foundation is a physical prerequisite.
Any underlying base or subbase layers must be compacted to design density before the embankment slide material is placed, to prevent differential settlement.

predecessor: Drainage System Installation (if required under embankment)
rationale: Subsurface drainage (e.g., perforated pipes, geocomposite drains) must be installed and backfilled before the embankment slide is constructed, as they cannot be placed effectively afterwards.
The embankment slide forms the final grade or sliding surface; any top pavement, asphalt, or protective wearing course can only be laid after the slide is complete and compacted.

It is best practice (soft preference) to install erosion control and revegetation after the embankment slide is fully placed, but in staged construction some temporary erosion measures could be applied earlier.
The ground must be leveled, cleared of debris, and properly graded before playground equipment can be safely installed on a stable surface.
Any underground electrical, water, or drainage lines must be laid before the playground area is developed to avoid excavation after installation.
Anchor footings and concrete bases for playground posts and structures must be poured and fully cured before equipment can be mounted on them.

The playground equipment must be fully erected and anchored before rubber mulch, poured-in-place rubber, or engineered wood fiber safety surfacing is installed around it to ensure proper fit and coverage.
All playground structures and components must be completely installed and assembled before a certified inspector can verify compliance with safety standards (e.g., ASTM F1487, CPSC guidelines).

The aquarium tank requires a level, load-bearing concrete foundation or slab to support its immense weight when filled with water; installing the tank before the foundation would lack structural support.
The building's structural frame must be in place to provide the support structure and load paths for the heavy aquarium tank; the tank cannot be installed without the surrounding framework.
The tank must be physically positioned in its final location before any water supply, drainage, or circulation plumbing lines can be connected to it.
The tank must be fully installed and all seals verified before water can be introduced to prevent leaks and structural failure.
Filtration, heating, aeration, and other life support equipment must be connected to the installed tank before they can be commissioned and tested.

The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and existing structures before excavation can begin, as obstacles would prevent access for earthmoving equipment and compromise the accuracy of ground levels.
Accurate survey stakes, benchmarks, and layout markings are needed to guide the excavation equipment to the correct depths, slopes, and boundaries; without this, excavation would be uncontrolled.

Soil tests and groundwater assessments are required to determine excavation methodology, shoring requirements, and dewatering needs; excavating without this data risks collapse or unsuitable conditions.
Foundations must be placed on properly prepared, level, and compacted subgrade; excavation and levelling create the correct bearing surface and dimensions for foundation work to proceed.

Drainage pipes, utility conduits, and gravel drainage layers are installed directly on the prepared subgrade after excavation is complete and before concrete slabs are poured, as they must be buried beneath the final floor level.
The ground must be leveled and cleared of debris before fence posts can be installed and fencing stretched.
Underground utilities must be identified and marked before post-hole digging to avoid strikes and ensure safety.
Concrete footings or post anchors must be set and cured before fence panels or wire mesh can be attached to the posts.
Animals cannot be placed into the enclosure until the fencing is fully installed, secured, and checked for gaps or weaknesses to prevent escape.
Fence runs should be completed before gates are hung, as gate posts and hinges align with the finished fence line.
The feeding trough requires a stable, level base that can only be provided by a properly installed foundation.
The feeding trough is typically anchored to or placed upon a concrete slab, which must be poured and cured before the trough can be installed.
Livestock cannot be introduced to the feeding area until the feeding trough is securely installed and ready for use.

If the feeding trough has an integrated watering system or requires plumbing, the water line connection should follow trough installation, though this may be a soft preference if the trough is manually filled.
The ground must be properly graded and prepared before any equipment or trough installation can take place to ensure proper drainage and stability.
The ground must be properly graded and prepared before installing a biosecurity barrier to ensure proper drainage and stable foundation for the barrier structure.
Any concrete footings or foundation elements that the barrier attaches to must be completed first to provide a stable base for the barrier installation.
Any underground utility lines (water, power, data) that cross the barrier line must be trenched and laid before the barrier is installed to avoid digging through or undermining the completed barrier.
The biosecurity barrier must be fully installed before a pest-proofing inspection can verify its integrity and compliance with biosecurity standards.

Interior finishing such as flooring, wall linings, and sealed surfaces must occur after the biosecurity barrier is in place to maintain the biosecure zone and prevent contamination from construction activities beyond the barrier.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and prepared before any construction of the animal enclosure can begin to ensure a stable foundation.
The concrete or structural foundation for the enclosure must be completed before the walls, fencing, and superstructure of the animal enclosure can be built upon it.
All necessary construction materials (e.g., fencing, panels, roofing, fasteners) must be procured and delivered to the site before construction work can commence.
Features such as shelters, enrichment structures, water features, and substrate flooring for the animals can only be installed after the main enclosure structure is built and enclosed.
A full inspection of the enclosure's perimeter fencing, gates, and locking mechanisms must be performed after construction to ensure it is secure and escape-proof before animals are introduced.
The enclosure must be fully constructed, checked, and approved before any animals can be moved in, as the structure is essential for their containment and safety.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and excavated to provide a stable foundation and proper space for installing waste management systems such as pipes, tanks, and sorting facilities.
Concrete foundations and substructures must be completed to support heavy waste management equipment, bins, compactors, and containment areas before they can be installed.
Underground conduits for waste chutes, drainage, and utility connections must be laid before above-ground waste infrastructure can be positioned and connected.

Waste management systems such as waste chutes, compactors, and storage areas must be installed prior to closing the building envelope to allow for equipment access and proper integration into the structure.

Final wall, floor, and ceiling finishes in waste storage and handling rooms must follow the installation of waste infrastructure to avoid damage and allow for seamless integration of fixtures and connections.

successor: Ventilation System Installation for Animal Spaces
rationale: The structural framing must be complete to provide mounting points and support structures for ventilation ducts, fans, and equipment within the animal spaces.

successor: Ventilation System Installation for Animal Spaces
rationale: Electrical wiring, conduits, and power outlets must be roughed in before ventilation system installation to provide power connections for fans, controls, and automated ventilation equipment.

successor: Ventilation System Installation for Animal Spaces
rationale: Main HVAC ductwork and plenums must be prepared and routed to the animal spaces before the ventilation system can be connected and installed.

predecessor: Ventilation System Installation for Animal Spaces
successor: Ceiling and Wall Finishing in Animal Spaces
rationale: Ventilation system components such as ducts, vents, and diffusers are typically installed within ceiling and wall cavities that must be closed up afterwards; finishing work cannot proceed until the ventilation system is in place.

predecessor: Ventilation System Installation for Animal Spaces
rationale: The ventilation system must be fully installed before the environmental control systems (thermostats, humidity sensors, air quality monitors) can be calibrated and commissioned to regulate the animal space environment.
Structural framing must be complete to provide the physical enclosure and support surfaces for biosecurity installations such as sealing, cladding, and ventilation systems.
A weathertight roof is required before interior biosecurity fit-out can commence, as moisture and weather exposure would compromise biosecurity seals and materials.
The floor slab must be cured and finished to provide a clean, sealed base for biosecurity barriers, drainage, and wash-down areas.

Biosecurity fit-out must be complete (including sealed walls, floors, and penetrations) before the HVAC and HEPA filtration systems are commissioned, to ensure the airtight environment required for biosecurity containment.
All biosecurity fitting and sealing work must be finished before regulatory inspection and certification can take place, as inspectors need to verify the completed containment systems.

Child safety gates (especially at top/bottom of stairs) need to be attached to secure posts, walls, or balustrades. The staircase or balustrade structure must be in place as the mounting surface before gates can be installed.

Gates that mount to walls require the wall surface to be finished so the gate can be firmly and safely attached. Installing a gate before wall finishing would require removal or risk damage to the finish.

Pressure-mounted gates rely on friction against the finished floor and walls. Even hardware-mounted gates should be installed after flooring to ensure proper clearance, level fit, and that the bottom seal contacts the floor correctly.

It is convenient but not physically required to install the gate before arranging furniture or decorations near the doorway or stair opening, as the gate defines the safe boundary and prevents access during later work.

The child safety gate must be fully installed and operational before the final safety inspection or handover of the building to occupants, as it is a critical safety component for households with young children.
Walls must be framed and sheathed to provide the structural enclosure and backing surface for built-in wardrobes and storage units.
Electrical wiring for lighting or outlets within or behind the wardrobe must be installed before the built-in unit is constructed, or it will be inaccessible.
If the wardrobe is near plumbing walls, rough plumbing must be completed before enclosing the area with built-in storage.

successor: Interior Painting and Wall Finishing (behind unit)
rationale: While it is preferred to paint or finish the wall area behind the wardrobe before installation for a cleaner look, it is not physically required as the unit covers the wall.
Typically flooring is installed before built-in wardrobes to allow the wardrobe to sit on top of the finished floor, but it can be done after with careful trimming; thus it is a soft preference.
The building site must be prepared and foundations laid before any residential space planning can begin, as the structural base defines the physical boundaries and dimensions of the living spaces.
The overall structural design and load-bearing elements must be finalized to establish the framework within which residential spaces can be planned and allocated.
Core utility connections (water, sewage, electricity, gas) must be routed and planned to ensure residential spaces are positioned with access to these essential services.
Interior finishing work (flooring, wall finishes, ceiling installation) cannot commence until the spatial layout and room divisions have been finalized through space planning.
The routing of plumbing pipes and electrical wiring within walls and floors depends on the finalized room layouts and spatial divisions established during space planning.

Landscaping and outdoor works should only begin after the building structure is completed to avoid damage from construction debris, heavy machinery, and material storage. Also, grading and drainage need to be coordinated with the finished building's footprint and roof drainage.
Underground utility lines such as water, sewer, gas, and electrical conduits must be installed before landscaping to avoid digging up finished landscape features like lawns, patios, or trees.

Proper site grading and installation of drainage systems must be completed prior to landscaping to ensure water flows away from the building correctly and to prevent soil erosion or water damage to new plantings and hardscaping.

Landscaping and outdoor works are typically among the final construction activities. Once completed, a final site clean-up and inspection can be conducted to ensure all work is finished and the site is presentable for handover.

While sometimes paving is done before planting, it is generally preferred to complete major landscaping (including planting and softscaping) before applying final paving or hardscaping finishes to avoid damage to new plants from heavy equipment or material spills. However, this can be a soft preference depending on site logistics.

Non-load-bearing partition walls are infill elements that require the primary structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) to be in place so they have defined floor-to-floor boundaries and support structure to attach to.

While it's not physically impossible to install electrical or plumbing after the walls are up, it is standard practice to complete rough-in work within the open wall cavities before enclosing them with partition walls to avoid costly rework and accessibility issues.
The partition walls rest on the finished floor slab below and extend to the underside of the slab above; both slabs must be in place to define the vertical extents and provide bearing surfaces.
The partition wall framing and substrate must be fully erected before any surface finishing, plastering, or drywall joint treatment can be applied.
Door and window frames are typically set into the partition wall openings; the wall framing must exist to provide the rough opening and structural support for the frames.

Substantial completion means the building is fully constructed and ready for occupancy. Handover and inspection must follow substantial completion as it verifies that all work meets specifications before transfer to the owner.
The building must be cleaned and site prepared before handover so that inspectors and the owner can assess the property in its final, deliverable condition.
All building systems (HVAC, electrical, plumbing, fire safety) must be tested and commissioned to ensure they function correctly before the formal handover and inspection.
Outstanding punch list items (defects, incomplete work) must be resolved before handover so the building is delivered in a fully complete state.
The owner or tenants can only take possession and begin moving in after the building has been formally handed over and inspected, as this transfer of responsibility is a prerequisite for occupancy.
Warranty coverage typically commences upon formal handover and inspection sign-off, as this marks the official delivery of the completed building to the owner.
Final closeout activities such as as-built drawing submission, O&M manual delivery, and financial closeout depend on the handover and inspection being completed.
Structural framing (roof trusses, rafters, or decking) must be completed to provide a solid substrate for the roof covering material.
Roof decking or sheathing (e.g., plywood or OSB) must be installed to create the base surface upon which the roof covering is applied.
Roof underlayment (felt paper or synthetic membrane) must be laid down as a moisture barrier before the final roof covering material is installed.
Gutters and downspouts are installed after the roof covering is complete to ensure proper integration with the roof edge and to avoid damaging the finished roofing.
Final roof flashing details around penetrations (chimneys, vents) must be completed and inspected after the roof covering is installed to ensure watertightness.
Steel reinforcement (rebar or welded wire mesh) must be placed and tied before concrete is poured for the slab to provide structural integrity.
Formwork or shuttering must be erected to contain and shape the wet concrete until it cures; the slab cannot be poured without formwork in place.
All embedded conduits, pipes, and sleeves must be laid and inspected within the subgrade or formwork before concrete placement, as they cannot be installed afterward.
After the slab is placed (poured), it must undergo curing and surface finishing (troweling, etc.) before any subsequent loads or trades can work on it.

successor: Vertical Structural Elements (Columns/Walls on Next Floor)
rationale: The floor slab/deck provides the working platform and structural base for erecting vertical elements on the next level; columns and walls depend on the completed slab for support and alignment.
The structural frame (beams, roof trusses, or slab above) must be in place to provide support and attachment points for the ceiling system.
Electrical conduits, HVAC ducts, plumbing pipes, and other mechanical services that run above the ceiling must be installed and inspected before the ceiling is closed up.
The ceiling boards or panels must be fully installed before any finishing work like taping, jointing, painting, or texturing can be applied.
Recessed or surface-mounted lighting fixtures are typically installed after the ceiling is in place to ensure proper alignment and secure attachment.
Although often done after ceiling work to avoid dust and debris falling on finished floors, this is a soft preference for cleanliness rather than a physical necessity.
The structural frame must be complete to provide the load-bearing support for the facade and cladding systems to be attached.
Roof completion provides weather protection and a stable top anchor point before vertical cladding installation begins.
