External cladding must be in place to define the openings and provide the structural support frame for window and glazing units.
While not a hard physical constraint, completing the building envelope before internal partitions simplifies logistics and protects interior works from weather exposure.
The cladding panels and facade system must be fully installed before final external finishes, sealants, and paint coatings can be applied to the exterior surface.
The foundation must be completed to provide a stable load-bearing base for the chimney structure.
The floor slab or deck must be in place to support the chimney's vertical load and provide a base for construction.
The chimney and flue must be built before the roof structure is completed so that the roof can be flashed and sealed around the chimney penetration.
The chimney must be in place to allow proper flashing installation where the chimney penetrates the roof covering, preventing water leaks.
The chimney flue and masonry must be completed before interior finishes so that walls can be built around and finished against the chimney structure.
Site survey and geotechnical investigation must be completed first to understand soil conditions, underground utilities, and site topography before excavation can safely begin.
All necessary permits (e.g., grading permits, excavation permits, environmental clearances) must be obtained before any site preparation or excavation work can legally commence.
Existing structures, vegetation, and debris must be removed from the site before excavation equipment can access and work on the area.
Excavation must be completed to reach the required bearing depth and create the proper foundation footprint before any concrete can be poured for footings or foundations.
Trenches and excavations must be opened before underground utilities such as drainage pipes, water lines, and electrical conduits can be laid in the ground.
The structural frame requires a stable base; foundation and substructure must be completed to support the loads transferred by columns and load-bearing walls.
The site must be cleared, graded, and compacted before any foundation or structural work begins to ensure a stable working platform.
Underground utilities such as drainage, water, and electrical conduits must be installed before structural elements to avoid conflicts and the need to core through or undermine foundations.
Roof structure and weatherproofing depend on the erected frame to provide support; roofing cannot begin until the structural skeleton is in place.
Exterior cladding and curtain walls are attached to the structural frame; the frame must be erected to provide the support and attachment points for enclosure.
The structural frame (steel or concrete) must be in place to support the roof deck and roofing materials; without a completed frame, roof construction cannot proceed.
Load-bearing walls must be built to the full height before the roof structure can be placed on top of them.

predecessor: Pouring of Concrete Slabs (if used as roof deck)
rationale: If the roof deck is a concrete slab, the slab must be poured and cured before weatherproofing membranes can be applied.
The roof must be watertight before interior finishes are installed to prevent water damage to finished surfaces.
Roof-mounted HVAC units and supports are typically installed after the roof deck is complete and waterproofed to avoid compromising the roofing membrane.
The structural frame must be complete to provide the load-bearing support and attachment points for external walls and cladding systems.

The roof structure is typically erected before or concurrently with external walls to provide weather protection and structural stability; however, in many sequences, roof completion precedes wall cladding to allow overhead crane access and sealing of the building envelope from top down.
Windows and doors are installed into the prepared wall openings after the external wall structure and cladding are in place.
Weatherproofing membranes, sealants, and air/vapor barriers are applied to the completed wall and cladding assembly to achieve a watertight and airtight building envelope.

While internal finishes can technically begin before external walls are fully complete, it is standard practice to complete the external envelope first to protect interior work from weather damage and to avoid rework.

Rough framing creates the structural openings (rough openings) that windows and doors are installed into. Without framed rough openings, windows and doors have no structural support or defined space to be placed.

Weatherproofing membrane or house wrap is typically applied to the sheathing before window installation to ensure proper integration of flashing and water-resistive barrier around window and door openings, preventing water intrusion.
While not absolutely required for window installation, completing the roof first protects the interior from rain and weather damage once windows are installed and the building envelope is opened.

Windows and doors must be installed and sealed before interior wall finishes are applied, as the wall finish material (drywall, plaster) is fitted around the window/door frames and requires the rough opening to be fully enclosed.
Exterior siding or cladding is installed after windows and doors to allow proper flashing integration and to create a watertight seal where siding meets window and door frames.
Structural framing (walls, ceilings, floors) must be in place to provide the cavities, chases, and support structures through which MEP rough-in components (conduit, piping, ductwork) are installed.
The building envelope must be weathertight (roof, windows, exterior walls) before MEP rough-in begins to protect electrical components, insulation, and unfinished materials from water damage.
Underslab plumbing, conduit, and ground works require the foundation/slab to be poured, with embedded sleeves and conduits placed, before above-slab MEP rough-in can proceed.
MEP rough-in (wiring, piping, ductwork) must be completely installed and inspected before being enclosed within walls, ceilings, or floors by insulation and drywall.
Rough-in work establishes the backbone infrastructure (conduit, pipes, ducts) that must be in place before final connections, fixtures, outlets, switches, and device terminations can be installed.
The structural frame (walls, columns, roof) must be fully erected and stable to provide the supporting substrate for internal linings and plasterboard installation.
The building envelope must be weathertight (roof cladding, external walls, windows/doors installed) to protect internal lining materials from rain and moisture damage.
All first-fix electrical cables, plumbing pipes, and HVAC ductwork must be installed within the wall and ceiling cavities before they are enclosed by plasterboard and lining.
Plasterboard joints must be taped, stopped, and sanded smooth before any paint, wallpaper, or decorative coatings can be applied to the walls and ceilings.

While floor finishes can logically follow lining to avoid dust and debris damaging the new floors, it is not a hard physical constraint; sequencing may vary depending on project phasing and protection measures.

Plumbing and electrical rough-ins (pipes, wires, outlets) must be installed behind walls before kitchen cabinets, countertops, and bathroom fixtures are fitted, as they are concealed within the structure.
Waterproof membranes must be applied to bathroom and kitchen wet areas and tested before tiles, fixtures, and cabinetry are installed to prevent water damage and mould.
Floor substrates must be screeded and levelled to the correct falls before tiling or installing kitchen cabinets and bathroom vanities to ensure proper drainage and level surfaces.
After cabinets, vanities, and fixtures are installed, the final connection of plumbing traps, taps, and electrical outlets/appliances can be completed, as they need to align with the fitted units.
Wall and floor tiling (especially splashbacks and shower walls) is typically done after fitout of cabinets and fixtures to achieve clean finished edges and proper overlaps between tiles and fixtures.

The building must be substantially complete and all major construction work finished before commissioning activities can begin, as commissioning requires systems to be installed and ready for testing.
All MEP systems (HVAC, electrical, plumbing, fire protection) must be fully installed before they can be commissioned, tested, and balanced.
Building management and control systems must be installed and connected to equipment before functional testing and commissioning can be performed.
The building must be fully commissioned, tested, and officially handed over to the owner/operator before occupants can move in and begin using the facility.

Commissioning and handover typically mark the formal transfer of the building, after which final closeout activities such as warranty documentation, as-built drawings, and O&M manual delivery can be completed.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated before any structural framing can begin, as the frame requires a stable, prepared foundation bed.
Structural frame elements (columns, beams, slabs) are anchored into and supported by the foundation system; the foundation must be cured and ready to bear loads before frame erection.
Underground plumbing, electrical conduits, and drainage lines must be placed and inspected before pouring slabs or erecting frames to avoid costly rework after the structural system is in place.
The roof structure depends on the completed frame (columns, beams, roof trusses) for support; roofing cannot be installed until the load-bearing frame is erected.
Exterior walls (curtain walls, masonry, or panel systems) are attached to or supported by the structural frame; the frame must be in place to provide the structural backing and attachment points.
The structural framing (walls, columns, beams) must be erected to provide the load-bearing support system onto which the roof structure is attached.
Exterior wall sheathing is typically installed before the roof to provide lateral bracing and a complete building envelope, and to allow roof trusses/rafters to bear directly on the sheathed walls.
Once the roof deck is assembled, underlayment and flashing must be installed as the next step to protect the underlying structure from water infiltration before roofing materials are applied.

Although not a strict physical necessity, it is standard practice to complete overhead rough-in work (e.g., wiring, ductwork in attics) after the roof is in place to provide weather protection for workers and materials during these interior installations.

Siding is typically installed after the roof to allow roof overhangs and flashing to be integrated properly, though in some sequences siding can be done simultaneously or before; this is a soft preference for quality and weatherproofing continuity.
External walls require a stable load-bearing base; foundation must be completed to support wall loads and provide a level starting point.
The ground floor slab provides the base platform upon which external walls are erected and anchored.
If the building uses a structural frame, the frame must be in place to provide attachment points and lateral support for external wall panels or infill.
External walls must be completed to support the roof structure and provide perimeter enclosure before roof trusses or decking are installed.
Rough openings in external walls must be framed and in place before windows and doors can be fitted into those openings.

The structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) must be in place before partition walls can be erected, as partitions bear on or are attached to the structural frame and require a stable supporting structure.

Rough-in services (conduit, piping, wiring) within walls must be installed before walls are closed up; however, in many sequences these services are run after partition framing is erected but before final wall cladding. For load-bearing or core partitions, sleeve/blockout placement must precede concrete placement.
Partition walls are erected on top of finished floor slabs or subfloors; the slab must be cured and ready to accept wall layout and installation.
The partition wall framing and boarding must be fully installed and secure before surface finishing (taping, plastering, painting) can commence, as finishes are applied directly to the wall surface.
Typically floor finishes follow wall construction to avoid damaging finished floors. This is a soft preference for work sequence efficiency and protection, not a physical necessity.
Rough openings (window bucks/frames) must be installed and structurally complete before windows can be placed and secured into them.
Exterior sheathing and weather-resistant barrier (WRB) must be installed to provide a continuous drainage plane and moisture protection before window installation; windows integrate with this layer.
Roof must be watertight and roof flashing completed to prevent water intrusion from above before installing windows below.
Windows must be installed and sealed before interior drywall or wallboard is hung and finished to create proper window openings and avoid damage to glass from construction dust/debris.
Windows must be in place to allow proper integration of window flashing and trim with the exterior cladding system, ensuring water-tightness at the window-to-wall interface.
The structural frame and building shell must be complete to provide the rough openings and structural support that external doors are installed into.
The rough openings for doors must be framed and prepared to the correct dimensions before any door units can be fitted.
Exterior wall sheathing and weather-resistive barriers must be in place so that doors can be properly flashed and integrated into the building envelope to prevent water intrusion.

While interior finishes can technically begin before doors are installed, it is preferred to install doors first to allow for proper gaps, trim installation, and to protect interior work from weather exposure during construction.
External doors must be installed before final weather sealing (cauking, gaskets, thresholds) and exterior trim can be applied around the door perimeter.
The subfloor must be properly prepared (cleaned, leveled, and dried) before any flooring material can be installed to ensure adhesion and a flat finished surface.
Underlayment (e.g., vapor barrier, soundproofing, or cushion) must be laid down prior to the final flooring system to provide moisture protection, acoustic insulation, and a smooth base.
All roughed-in MEP work below the floor (conduit, piping, ductwork) must be completed before flooring is installed to avoid tearing up finished floors for access.
Baseboards and trim are installed after flooring to cover the expansion gap around the perimeter and provide a clean finished edge against the wall.
Though painting is often done before flooring to avoid drips, touch-up painting and final wall finishing are typically completed after flooring to repair any scuffs or marks made during installation.
Interior doors are often hung after flooring is installed so that the bottom of the door can be trimmed to the correct finished floor height, ensuring proper clearance.
Cabinets and heavy appliances are typically placed on top of the finished flooring to ensure a consistent floor height and to allow for future replacement without needing to cut around the flooring.
Ceiling assemblies are typically supported by or tied into the wall framing. Walls must be framed to provide the structural support and bearing for the ceiling joists or trusses.

Electrical wiring for overhead lights, fans, and other ceiling-mounted fixtures must be run through the ceiling cavity before the ceiling finish is installed. Running wire after ceiling assembly would require destructive access.
HVAC ducts are often routed through the ceiling plenum space. Ductwork installation must occur before the ceiling is enclosed to allow access for connections and sealing.
Any overhead plumbing lines, sprinkler systems, or drain pipes that run above the ceiling must be installed prior to enclosing the ceiling assembly.

The structural ceiling assembly (joists, subfloor if any, or furring strips) provides the substrate onto which the ceiling finish material is attached. The finish cannot be installed before its supporting framework is in place.
The ceiling surface must be fully assembled and taped/mudded before painting or applying any decorative finish can occur.
Light fixtures are mounted to or recessed into the completed ceiling assembly. The ceiling structure and finish must be in place before fixtures can be installed.
Mobilization of survey crew, equipment, and site access must be established before any on-site survey or investigation can commence.
Vegetation, debris, and existing structures must be cleared/removed to allow unobstructed access for survey equipment and boring/drilling rigs to the exact survey points and borehole locations.

A preliminary topographical survey is typically conducted first to identify ground features and establish control points, which aids in planning borehole locations, though it is a soft preference as geotechnical work could proceed with less accurate reference data.

Soil, rock, and groundwater samples collected during the field investigation must be retrieved before they can be transported to the lab for testing (e.g., grain size, Atterberg limits, triaxial shear strength).

The bearing capacity, soil stratification, and groundwater data obtained from the survey and investigation are essential input parameters for designing foundations; structural design cannot proceed without knowing subsurface conditions.
You must own or have legal control over a site before you can apply for planning permission, as the application requires site details and ownership evidence.
Pre-application advice, feasibility studies, and concept design are typically undertaken before submitting a formal planning application to ensure the proposal is viable and likely to be approved.
While high-level designs may precede planning, the full detailed structural and architectural design work often follows planning approval to ensure compliance with approved drawings and conditions.
Construction contracts and tenders are typically not finalized until planning and building regulations approvals are secured, as the scope and legal requirements are uncertain without them.
Physical construction cannot legally commence without both planning permission and building regulations approval in place, as this would be a breach of planning control and building safety law.
The structural frame and load-bearing walls must be completed to provide the vertical support necessary for the roof structure to be erected upon.
Walls must be built to the full height before the roof can be installed, as the roof typically bears on and ties into the wall top plates or wall structure.
Interior finishes such as drywall, plaster, and ceiling tiles must be installed after the roof is complete and waterproofed to protect them from weather damage.
While some rough-in work can proceed earlier, completing the roof first ensures attic and upper-level spaces are weathertight for safe and efficient MEP rough-in work.
Installing exterior cladding and finishes after the roof is completed ensures that the building envelope is sealed from the top down, preventing water infiltration behind cladding.
The structural frame must be complete to provide the physical space and mounting points for M&E first fix runs (conduits, ducts, cables) within walls, ceilings, and floors.
The building must be weathertight (roof and cladding) before installing electrical cables, conduits, and mechanical ductwork to prevent water damage to M&E components.
First fix M&E (cables, conduits, pipes, ducts) must be installed within wall/ceiling voids before these voids are closed up with insulation and plasterboard/drylining.
Underfloor M&E services (pipes, conduits, cabling trays) must be laid before the floor screed is poured to embed or cover them.
First fix M&E running within walls must be complete before plastering covers and embeds these services permanently.

First fix electrical and mechanical work (cabling, conduits, back boxes, pipework in walls/ceilings) must be completed before second fix can install fittings, sockets, switches, and fixtures onto the prepared infrastructure.
Walls and ceilings must be plastered and finished before second fix M&E components (socket fronts, switch plates, light fittings) can be installed flush to the finished surface.
Ceiling grids or substrates must be in place before installing ceiling-mounted M&E items such as light fittings, smoke detectors, and speakers into the ceiling.
All second fix components (switches, sockets, light fittings, thermostats) must be fully installed before electrical testing, continuity checks, and commissioning of M&E systems can be carried out.

While second fix is often completed before final decoration to avoid damage to painted surfaces, some projects may install second fix items after decoration for aesthetic precision; typically a soft preference to avoid rework.

The structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) must be complete to provide a stable, enclosed space for internal finishing works. Fit-out cannot commence in an area until the structural works are finished and load-bearing elements are in place.

The building must be watertight (roof and external envelope complete) before internal finishes such as plastering, drywall, painting, and flooring are installed, otherwise water damage will ruin the finishes.
External walls and cladding enclose the building, protecting interior spaces from weather. Internal fit-out requires a fully enclosed and weatherproofed shell.

Mechanical, Electrical, and Plumbing (MEP) final connections (e.g., installation of light fixtures, power outlets, sanitary fittings, HVAC grilles) can only be installed after finished ceilings, walls, and floors are in place, as these fixtures are mounted onto or through finished surfaces.

All finishing works (painting, tiling, flooring, carpentry) must be completed before the final clean and handover to the client, as any unfinished work would be damaged during cleaning or would make the building unfit for occupancy.
The exterior walls must bear on a stable foundation. Without completed foundations, there is no structural base to support wall loads.

predecessor: Slab on Grade / Ground Floor Slab
rationale: The floor slab provides a working platform and lateral support for walls at the base; walls are typically erected after the slab is poured.
Exterior wall panels (curtain walls or infill walls) are attached to or supported by the primary structural frame; the frame must be erected first.
The roof structure typically bears on or ties into the exterior walls; walls must be in place to support roof framing and to transfer loads down.
Window and door rough openings are framed as part of the wall assembly; windows and doors are installed after the wall structure is complete.

Although cladding can sometimes proceed in parallel, it is preferred to complete the structural wall assembly first so that the cladding has a continuous backing and weather-tight detailing can be properly executed.
The floor slab or deck must be poured and cured to provide a level bearing surface for the interior partition wall to be built upon.
The main structural frame must be in place to define the building's overall geometry and to which partition walls may tie or be braced against.
Electrical conduits, plumbing pipes, and mechanical ducts that run under the slab must be installed before walls are built, as walls would otherwise block access to the floor area.

Electrical wiring, outlets, switches, plumbing pipes, and mechanical ducts that run inside or through the partition walls must be installed after the wall framing is complete and before the wall is enclosed with drywall.
Gypsum board or other wall cladding cannot be attached until the partition wall framing (studs, tracks, and any insulation) is fully erected and secured.
Interior doors require completed wall framing to have rough openings and support structures for door frames.
Rough electrical and plumbing work within walls must be completed before doors are installed to avoid rework and access issues.
Door casings and trim are installed around the door frame after the door is hung to ensure proper fit and alignment.
While doors can be painted beforehand, final touch-up painting around door frames is typically done after installation for a seamless finish.
Flooring is typically installed after interior doors are hung to allow the door to clear the finished floor height properly.
Structural framing (walls, trusses, or rafters) must be fully erected to provide the support structure that the roofing system is installed onto.
Roof sheathing or decking (e.g., plywood or OSB) must be installed over the framing to create a solid substrate for roofing materials.
Underlayment (felt paper or synthetic membrane) must be laid down over the sheathing to provide a moisture barrier before the final roofing material is applied.
Gutters and downspouts are installed after the roofing is complete so they can be properly aligned with the roof edge and integrated with the drip edge flashing.
While siding can technically be done before roofing, it is standard practice to complete roofing first to avoid damaging finished siding with falling debris or heavy roof loads during installation.

The structural shell, including columns, beams, slabs, and load-bearing walls, must be fully completed and cured before any interior finishing work can begin. Interior finishes applied to an incomplete structure would be damaged by ongoing structural work and settlement.

The building must be watertight with completed roofing, membrane, and flashings before interior finishes are installed. Finishes such as drywall, paint, flooring, and millwork would be ruined by water ingress from an unsealed roof.
External wall cladding, windows, and curtain wall systems must be installed and sealed to protect interior spaces from weather and dust before finish work commences.

All concealed MEP services including conduit, piping, ductwork, and wiring within walls, ceilings, and floors must be roughed-in, inspected, and pressure-tested before they are enclosed by finishes such as drywall, ceiling tiles, or flooring.
After finishes are complete, final trim-out of electrical outlets, switches, light fixtures, plumbing fixtures, HVAC grilles, and thermostats can be installed without damaging finished surfaces.

Final touch-up painting and decorative coatings must be performed after all other finish work is complete to ensure a seamless, unblemished appearance and to cover any scuffs or damage from the fit-out process.

Comprehensive final cleaning and systems commissioning must follow the completion of all interior finishes to protect finished surfaces and ensure building systems operate correctly in a clean environment.
Load-bearing walls require a stable foundation to distribute vertical loads to the ground. Without completed foundations, the walls would have no structural support and would settle or collapse.
The ground must be excavated and graded to proper elevations before any foundation or wall construction can begin, ensuring the site is level and stable for structural elements.
Floor joists, beams, and roof trusses rely on load-bearing walls as their primary support points. These elements cannot be installed until the walls that carry their loads are in place and cured.

If the load-bearing walls are constructed from poured concrete or masonry, sufficient curing time must elapse before applying additional loads from floors, roofs, or upper walls to prevent structural failure.

While it is technically possible to run some utilities before walls are built, standard construction sequencing places rough-in work after walls are erected to allow for proper routing through stud cavities. This is a soft preference as prefabricated or panelized systems could reverse the order.
Rough framing (walls and roof structure) must be complete to provide the structural openings where windows will be installed.
Weather-resistant barrier (house wrap) must be installed before windows to prevent moisture intrusion behind the window frames.
Windows must be installed before siding is applied so that window flanges can be properly integrated with the weather barrier and siding.
Windows need to be in place before interior wall finishing so that drywall can be cut and finished neatly around window openings.
Window trim and casing cannot be installed until the windows themselves are set and secured in the rough openings.
Internal doors require finished wall openings (stud framing and linings) to be installed into. Door frames cannot be fitted without the surrounding wall structure in place.
Doors must have a finished floor level to set the correct threshold height and bottom clearance. Without a completed subfloor, door frames cannot be properly aligned and installed.
Internal doors require the ceiling to be in place to define the top-of-door clearance and ensure the door frame is correctly positioned vertically within the finished room height.

Floor finishes should be installed after doors to avoid damage to finished flooring and to allow the door to swing over the finished floor surface with correct clearance. Installing doors first prevents scratching or indentation of the floor finish.

While it is common to paint door frames and architraves before hanging doors, the final touch-up painting and decoration is typically done after doors are hung to blend joints and fill any gaps. This is a soft preference for quality finish rather than a hard physical constraint.
The structural frame and building envelope must be complete to provide a weathertight environment and structural support for MEP installations.
MEP first fix (drainage, conduits, pipework) is typically embedded within or run beneath floor slabs before they are finished.
MEP services (wiring, pipework, ductwork) must be installed in walls and ceilings before they are enclosed by joinery and carpentry.
All MEP first fix services must be run, tested, and in place before walls are boarded and plastered to avoid rework and access issues.
Electrical rough-in (cables, back boxes, conduit) is part of MEP first fix and must be completed before second fix stages such as fitting sockets and switches.

Second Fix (MEP) involves installing fixtures, fittings, and terminations (e.g., sockets, switches, sanitary ware, boiler connections) which require the first fix (pipework, conduits, cables) to already be embedded within walls, floors, and ceilings before terminations can be made.

Structural elements including concrete slabs, walls, and ceilings must be in place before MEP second fix activities can commence, as pipes and conduits are chased into or fixed to these structural surfaces.

While not always a hard physical requirement, it is strongly preferred to have the building weathertight (windows and roof installed) before second fix MEP work begins to protect electrical and mechanical components from weather damage.
Joinery and kitchen units must be installed after second fix MEP so that pipework and electrical connections can be properly run to the correct locations before they are boxed in by cabinets.

Plastering and drylining follows second fix MEP because sockets, switches, and pipe outlets need to be fitted and positioned before plasterboard and plaster are applied to create a flush finish around the fixtures.
Structural framing must be complete to provide the surfaces (walls, ceilings) that will be decorated and finished.
Roofing must be installed to protect interior spaces from weather before applying interior finishes.
All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work must be completed inside walls/ceilings before they are enclosed by finishes.
Drywall must be installed, taped, and mudded before painting, wallpapering, or applying other decorative finishes.
Flooring is often installed before final wall decoration to allow for easier installation and to protect finished walls from damage during flooring work.
Structural framing must be fully complete and stable before inspections can verify structural integrity and safety compliance.
All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work must be installed and ready before inspections can verify that systems meet code requirements.
Drywall must be installed and finished so that inspectors can verify fire ratings, insulation placement, and overall interior completeness.
Roofing must be completed to ensure the building is weathertight before final inspection and handover can proceed.
Final inspections and official handover must be completed before tenants or owners can occupy the building and begin interior fit-out or move-in processes.
The wall opening must be framed, rough opening sized correctly, and structural blocking installed before the roller shutter door can be mounted and fastened to the structure.

predecessor: Overhead Track Support Steel / Lintel Installation
rationale: Heavy-duty steel lintels or support beams above the opening must be in place to carry the weight of the roller shutter barrel, guides, and tracks.
Power supply and control wiring conduits must be roughed in to the motor location before the door assembly is installed, as retrofitting wiring after installation is difficult and costly.

successor: Motor & Control Wiring Connection / Electrical Trim-Out
rationale: The door unit must be physically installed and the motor mounted before electricians can make final connections to the motor, limit switches, and control panel.
Comprehensive testing of opening/closing cycles, safety edge sensors, and emergency stop functions can only be performed after the door is fully installed and wired.
The mezzanine structure requires a stable foundation to bear its load. Without completed foundation works, the mezzanine cannot be safely erected.
The mezzanine is typically supported off the main structural columns and beams; the main frame must be in place to provide attachment points and load paths for the mezzanine.
Mezzanine decking (floor plates) is laid directly onto the mezzanine structural beams; the structure must be complete to serve as the supporting substrate.

Electrical, plumbing, and HVAC rough-in below the mezzanine is more efficiently performed after the mezzanine structure is in place to allow clear access and spatial coordination, though it could theoretically be done concurrently with careful sequencing.
Handrails and guardrails are mounted to the mezzanine's edge structural members; the mezzanine must exist as a platform before fall-protection rails can be attached.
The structural wall must be framed to provide the opening and support for the clerestory window.
The roof structure above the clerestory must be in place before the window is installed to ensure proper integration and weather sealing.
The window frame must be installed before glazing and sealing can be applied.
Interior drywall and finishes around the clerestory are typically done after window installation to ensure proper integration and detailing.
Exterior weatherproofing, flashing, and cladding around the window must be completed after installation to seal the assembly and prevent water intrusion.
The crane rail or gantry system requires a solid, level foundation and substructure to bear the heavy loads and stresses. Without completed foundations, the crane cannot be safely installed.

successor: Main Steel Structure Erection (if crane is used for lifting)
rationale: An overhead crane is often used to lift and place heavy steel members during main structural steel erection. The crane and its rails must be installed beforehand to serve as lifting equipment for the steel frame.

While it is physically possible to install cladding after the crane is in place, it is generally preferred to have the crane operational first so it can assist in lifting cladding panels or roofing materials, improving efficiency and safety.

It is often preferred to complete the overhead crane installation before interior finishes and MEP rough-in so that the crane can be used to move heavy mechanical equipment (e.g., HVAC units, piping) into the building, though it is not a strict physical requirement.

The crane rail supports and columns are typically anchored into the floor slab or foundation. Final flooring cannot be completed until the crane rail system is fully installed and any grouting or anchoring work is finished.
The ground must be excavated and prepared to the correct level and compaction before any slab can be poured, as the slab requires a stable subgrade.
A compacted granular sub-base (e.g., crushed stone or lean concrete) is required to provide a uniform, load-bearing foundation for the heavy-duty slab to prevent differential settlement.
A vapour barrier must be laid over the sub-base to prevent moisture ingress from the ground into the heavy-duty slab, which could cause durability issues.
All buried services, drainage pipes, electrical conduits, and earthing grids that pass under the slab must be installed and inspected before concreting, as they cannot be accessed afterward.
After pouring and finishing the slab, a minimum curing period (typically 7–14 days) is required to achieve design strength before any loads or subsequent construction can be applied.
The heavy-duty floor slab must be fully cured and capable of supporting the concentrated loads from steel columns, cranes, and erection equipment before steel frame installation can commence.
Perimeter walls and partitions are built on top of or anchored to the finished floor slab, so the slab must be complete and cured before wall construction begins.

A dry-shake hardener or epoxy coating is typically applied after the slab has initially set. While this is part of the slab finishing process, scheduling preference allows the topping to follow immediately.

The workbench or fixed counter must be placed on a finished, level floor surface to ensure stability and proper alignment. Installing the floor prevents damage to both the floor and the workbench during installation.
Wall finishing should be completed before installing fixed counters to avoid damaging finished walls during heavy workbench placement and to ensure the workbench fits flush against finished walls.
Electrical wiring for power outlets and lighting above the workbench must be roughed in before the counter is installed, as access behind or under the counter is needed for running cables.
Power outlets and switches on or above the workbench can only be installed after the counter is in place, so that outlet heights and positions align precisely with the work surface.

Any surface treatment, sealing, or protective coating applied to the workbench top must be done after the counter is installed and secured in its final position to ensure even application and avoid damage during installation.

predecessor: Overhead Electrical and Data Cabling Installation
rationale: Electrical and data cabling must be run in the ceiling plenum before partition walls are installed, as the partitions will enclose and obstruct access to overhead pathways.
Floor coverings should be laid before partitions are placed to allow seamless flooring under the partition bases and avoid difficult cutting and fitting around partitions.
HVAC rough-in must be completed in the ceiling space before partitions are installed, as partitions define room boundaries that affect airflow distribution and access to diffusers.

Partition systems define the spatial layout and cubicle boundaries; desks, chairs, and other furniture cannot be accurately placed until the partition walls are erected and their footprints are finalized.

successor: Final Painting and Wall Finishing of Partition Panels
rationale: Although modular partitions often come pre-finished, any on-site touch-up painting or sealing of joints is best performed after installation to avoid damaging finishes during the erection process.

The structural frame and building shell must be in place to provide the physical substrate and weatherproof enclosure before M&E first fix work can commence, as cables, conduits, pipes and ductwork are installed within walls, ceilings and floor slabs.
The building must be watertight to protect electrical and mechanical components from water damage during first fix installation.
M&E first fix (cables, conduits, pipes, back boxes) must be installed inside walls and ceilings before they can be closed up with plasterboard or plaster finishes.
Underfloor heating pipes, electrical conduits in the slab, and other M&E services must be laid before the floor screed is poured or floor finishes are applied.
Second fix (installing sockets, switches, light fittings, sanitaryware, and appliances) can only occur after first fix rough-in work is complete and wall/ceiling finishes have been applied.
The ground must be excavated, leveled, and prepared to the correct subgrade before any concrete can be placed, as the slab depends on a stable, properly graded base.

A compacted granular sub-base (e.g., hardcore or crushed stone) must be laid and compacted to provide a uniform, load-bearing foundation for the concrete slab. Pouring directly on unprepared ground would lead to settlement and cracking.
A polyethylene vapor barrier or damp-proof membrane must be placed over the sub-base to prevent ground moisture from migrating up through the slab. This must be installed before concrete is poured.
Steel reinforcement bars or welded wire mesh must be positioned and tied within the slab area before concrete placement to provide tensile strength and control cracking.
Edge forms must be erected and secured to define the slab perimeter, control the pour shape, and maintain the correct slab thickness. Concrete cannot be placed without containing forms.

Freshly poured concrete must be kept moist and at a suitable temperature during the curing period to achieve design strength and durability. Curing begins immediately after the pour is finished and finished.
Formwork cannot be removed until the concrete has gained sufficient strength to support its own weight and any applied loads. This follows the pour and a minimum curing duration.

Columns, walls, and other vertical structural elements that bear on the ground slab cannot be built until the slab has been poured and cured to provide a stable, level working platform and load-bearing surface.

Walls and ceilings must be plastered or boarded (drylined) after M&E First Fix to enclose the services. M&E Second Fix requires the finished wall and ceiling surfaces to be in place so that sockets, switches, light fittings, and other fixtures can be surface-mounted and trimmed out flush.

M&E Second Fix installs visible socket fronts, switch plates, light switches, and other fittings. Final painting and decoration must follow so that paintwork can be completed around these fixtures without damaging them, and so that any minor patching around socket cutouts can be blended in.

While floor finishes can technically be laid before M&E Second Fix, it is a soft preference to complete them after to avoid damaging finished floors with ladders, tools, and dropped components during the installation of high-level fittings and socket fronts.

successor: Testing and Commissioning of M&E Systems
rationale: Second Fix completes the physical installation of outlets, switches, sensors, and terminals. All systems must be fully terminated and connected before meaningful testing and commissioning of electrical circuits, lighting controls, and mechanical controls can be performed.

successor: Metal Roof and Wall Cladding Installation
rationale: Metal roof and wall cladding panels are attached to the structural steel frame; the frame must be fully erected and stable to provide the supporting substructure for cladding attachment.

successor: Metal Roof and Wall Cladding Installation
rationale: Roof decking provides the underlying surface and structural diaphragm upon which metal roof panels are fastened; it must be in place before metal roofing can be installed.

successor: Metal Roof and Wall Cladding Installation
rationale: Weather barriers (house wrap, building paper, or air/vapor barriers) must be applied to the exterior sheathing before metal wall cladding is installed to protect the building envelope from moisture intrusion.

predecessor: Metal Roof and Wall Cladding Installation
rationale: Flashing, ridge caps, fascia, and trim pieces are installed over and around the metal panels to seal edges, transitions, and penetrations; the panels must be in place first before these finishing pieces can be properly fitted.

predecessor: Metal Roof and Wall Cladding Installation
rationale: While not a strict physical dependency, final touch-up painting and coating repairs on adjacent surfaces (e.g., exposed steel, trim) are typically performed after cladding installation to blend finishes and repair any scratches or damage that occurred during panel installation.
Structural steel framework must be in place to provide support points and attachment locations for dust extraction ductwork hangers and supports.
The building must be enclosed to protect ductwork and equipment from weather during installation and to allow for proper sealing of roof/wall penetrations.

successor: Dust Collection Equipment Installation (Filters, Fans, Cyclones)
rationale: Ductwork must be installed first to establish the collection network, then the main dust collection equipment can be connected to the duct runs.
Ductwork must be fully installed, pressure-tested, and supported before insulation can be applied to the exterior surfaces.

Ductwork installation should precede sprinkler installation in the same areas to avoid conflicts and rework, though in some sequences sprinkler rough-in can occur concurrently with careful coordination.
The structural steel frame must be in place to provide the primary support structure onto which the mezzanine floor is attached and supported.
The ground floor slab or foundation must be completed to provide a stable working surface and base for erecting the mezzanine supports and columns.
Electrical conduit and wiring installation for the mezzanine area typically occurs after the mezzanine deck is in place, as the floor provides access and support for routing electrical systems.
HVAC ductwork serving the mezzanine level is installed after the mezzanine floor structure is complete, as the ductwork is supported by or routed through the floor structure.
Fire sprinkler piping and heads for the mezzanine area must be installed after the mezzanine deck is in place to properly locate and secure the system to the structure.
Wall and ceiling framing must be complete to provide a substrate for acoustic panels, bass traps, and diffusers.
Wiring, outlets, and junction boxes must be installed behind or within walls before acoustic treatments cover and conceal access to these elements.
Ductwork, vents, and HVAC equipment must be in place before acoustic panels are installed, as the panels may block or interfere with duct runs if installed earlier.
Acoustic panels and treatments are typically the final wall surface layer; painting or applying wall coverings before would be covered or damaged by the acoustic materials.
While it is preferable to install flooring after acoustic treatments to avoid damaging finished floors, acoustic panels can be installed after flooring if protective measures are taken.
The counter frame and base must be structurally installed to provide the physical foundation for the service desk.
Electrical wiring must be roughed in behind or beneath the counter area before the desk is fully enclosed and operational.
Data and communication cabling must be installed before the counter is closed up to support point-of-sale or service systems.
The service desk structure must be open and accessible to allow installation of the final countertop surface or finish material.
Point-of-sale terminals, computers, and other equipment can only be mounted and connected once the service desk is in its open, accessible state.

predecessor: Mounting bracket installation for display board
rationale: The mounting bracket must be securely fixed to the wall or support structure before the display board can be attached to it.

predecessor: Rough-in electrical wiring to display location
rationale: Electrical power and data cables must be run and terminated at the installation point before the display board can be connected and powered on.
The display board must be physically installed and mounted before electrical connections can be made and the unit can be tested for proper operation.

successor: Content management system configuration and programming
rationale: The display hardware must be in place before the software and content settings can be configured and uploaded to the specific unit.

successor: Final calibration and adjustment of display settings
rationale: Physical installation must be complete so that brightness, orientation, and other display parameters can be calibrated on-site for optimal viewing.
The document drop-off box must be placed on a stable, level foundation or slab to ensure structural integrity and proper operation.
Proper drainage and site grading must be completed to prevent water accumulation around the drop-off box, which could damage documents and the unit.
The drop-off box location and access point must be finalized before paving to ensure proper alignment, curb cuts, and vehicle access positioning.
Directional and instructional signage must be placed after the box is installed to accurately indicate its location and provide usage instructions.

It is preferable to install security cameras and lighting after the drop-off box is positioned to ensure optimal coverage of the drop-off area, though this could technically be done beforehand with adjustments.
A stable, level foundation (e.g., concrete slab, footings, or ground anchors) must be completed before any privacy screening panels can be erected to ensure structural stability and alignment.
The vertical support posts or columns that hold the privacy screening panels must be set and secured in place before panels can be attached to them.

predecessor: Utility Line Locating and Rerouting (if underground)
rationale: Underground utilities (gas, electric, water, data) must be located and, if necessary, rerouted before digging post holes or pouring footings to avoid damage and ensure safety.

Once panels are installed, applying protective finish, sealant, or stain is recommended to prolong life and improve appearance, but is a soft preference as it could be done later or skipped altogether.

Final landscaping, decorative planting, or ground cover around the base of the panels is typically done after installation but is a preference (aesthetic/convenience) rather than a physical requirement.
The structural framing (walls, floor slab, and support columns) must be in place to provide a stable load-bearing structure for the accessible service counter to be attached and supported.
Plumbing supply and drain lines for the service counter (e.g., sink or handwashing station) must be roughed-in within the walls and floor before the counter can be mounted and final connections made.
Electrical wiring and outlet boxes for the service counter area must be installed in the walls before the counter is placed to allow proper routing and avoid rework.
The accessible service counter must be fully installed before applying countertop surfaces, laminate, or solid-surface materials to ensure proper fit and alignment.
After the counter is installed, plumbing fixtures such as faucets, drains, and traps can be connected to the rough-in stubs and completed.
The site must be prepared and graded before any signage can be installed to ensure stable footing and proper placement of sign foundations.
Concrete foundations or slabs for signage posts/monuments must be poured and cured before the signage can be mounted onto them.
Walkways, paths, and paved areas must be completed so that wayfinding signs can be accurately positioned along the routes they are meant to direct.
The main buildings and structures must be substantially complete so that directional signage can reference actual building locations and entrances.

It is preferable to complete signage installation before final landscaping so that planting beds, sod, and decorative elements can be placed around the signs without damaging them, though some coordination is possible.
Wayfinding signage must be fully installed and visible before the site can be opened to visitors or occupants to ensure proper navigation.
The lightweight moveable partition typically attaches to or runs along ceiling tracks; the ceiling grid must be in place to support the track system and provide overhead alignment.
The partitions are installed on the finished floor or subfloor; a level, stable floor surface is required for the bottom track or guide rail to ensure proper operation and alignment.

predecessor: Rough Electrical and Data Cabling (in walls/ceiling)
rationale: Any wiring, conduit, or data cables that need to run above the ceiling or within partition cavities must be roughed in before the movable partition frames and panels are installed, to avoid rework or inaccessible areas.

If the partition's bottom track is surface-mounted, the final floor finish is typically installed up to or around the track. If the track is embedded or installed before final floor, the finishing work must account for the installed partition.

successor: Final Painting / Wall Finishing of Adjacent Walls
rationale: Painting and wall finishing can be completed before or after partition installation, but doing so after avoids damaging finishes during partition handling and allows for seamless touch-ups around the partition edges.
The service counter must be installed on a stable, finished floor slab to ensure proper leveling and structural support.

Electrical outlets, data ports, and plumbing connections required for the service counter must be roughed-in within the walls and floor before the counter is installed to allow access for connections.
The walls against which the service counter will be mounted must be framed, enclosed, and finished before the counter can be securely attached and sealed.
The base service counter structure must be in place before the final countertop surface and finishing elements can be installed on top of it.
Final hookups for outlets, sinks, or equipment mounted in/on the service counter can only be completed after the counter is permanently installed in its final position.
The ground must be properly graded and cleared before any foundation work can begin to ensure a stable, level base for the kiosk foundation.
Underground conduit and utility stub-ups for power and data must be installed before pouring the foundation to properly embed and route services through the slab.
Excavation, formwork, and rebar placement must be completed before concrete pouring and mounting of the kiosk base can occur.
The kiosk foundation and base mounting must be fully cured and secure before the main kiosk structure can be assembled and erected on top of it.
Power and data wiring from the utility stub-ups can only be terminated and connected after the kiosk is mounted and its internal electrical panels are accessible.
Framing and studs create the wall cavities through which data and power cables are routed; electrical and low-voltage rough-in cannot happen before the walls are framed.
Overhead mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in must be completed before wall rough-in to avoid interference and to allow vertical drops to be coordinated.
Insulation must follow rough-in because cables and boxes must be in place before insulation is blown or placed; otherwise the insulation would cover access points.
Drywall cannot be hung until all rough-in wiring, outlet boxes, and data jacks are installed inside the wall cavities, as they would be inaccessible after the walls are closed.
Trim-out (switches, receptacles, faceplates) and finish work must occur after rough-in since the cables and boxes are installed during rough-in to allow final connections.

predecessor: Interior Finishing Works (e.g., painting, wall coverings)
rationale: Interior finishes must be completed to provide clean, permanent surfaces for signage installation; applying signage before finishing would result in damage or need for reinstallation.
Flooring must be installed before floor-mounted signs or wayfinding markers can be accurately placed and secured.
Ceiling-mounted signage requires completed ceiling grids for proper attachment and alignment.
Signage installation generates dust and debris; final cleaning must occur after all signage is in place to ensure a pristine finish.
Wayfinding signage is essential for safe and efficient building navigation; occupancy cannot begin until all directional and informational signs are installed and verified.

Electrical outlets, lighting fixtures, and mechanical ductwork must be roughed in before acoustic treatment installation to avoid cutting or damaging acoustic panels and to ensure proper placement around these services.
Structural walls and their sheathing (e.g., drywall or plywood) must be in place to provide a substrate for mounting acoustic panels, bass traps, or other treatments.
If acoustic treatments include ceiling clouds or overhead panels, the ceiling grid or structural ceiling must be installed first to support them.

While painting can be done before installation in some cases, it is preferable to install acoustic treatments after painting to avoid overspray or damage to acoustic surfaces, and to ensure a clean finish.
Acoustic treatment is part of the final room finishing; furniture, equipment, and occupancy should occur after installation to protect the treatments and allow for proper acoustic tuning.
Subfloor must be level, clean, dry, and structurally sound before any flooring finish can be installed to ensure proper adhesion, prevent future damage, and meet manufacturer specifications.
Underlayment (such as vapor barrier, soundproofing, or cushioning layer) must be placed before the finished flooring to provide moisture protection, acoustic insulation, and a smooth base.
All rough-in electrical, plumbing, and HVAC work must be inspected and approved before flooring is installed to avoid the need to tear up finished flooring for rework.
Baseboards and trim are typically installed after flooring is complete so they sit on top of the finished floor, covering the expansion gap and providing a clean finished appearance.
It is generally preferred to perform final painting and wall touch-ups after flooring is installed to prevent paint and drywall dust from damaging or dirtying the new floor surface.

predecessor: Electrical rough-in wiring to point-of-service location
rationale: Power and data cabling must be run to the POS location before the terminal can be physically connected and powered on.

predecessor: Countertop / fixture installation at POS location
rationale: The terminal is typically mounted on or placed atop a counter or fixture; that surface must be in place first.

successor: Network configuration / system commissioning for POS
rationale: The device must be physically installed and connected before network settings, payment software, and system testing can be performed on it.
Software cannot be configured or tested without the physical terminal being in place and connected.
Training is more efficient once the device is installed and operational, though some pre-training could occur without the device.
Structural framing and slabs must be completed to provide the load-bearing support and floor area onto which the glazed partition system will be installed.
Overhead MEP rough-ins (ductwork, piping, conduit) and ceiling grid installation should be completed before partition walls are installed to avoid rework and to allow access for overhead work.
Glazed partition frames and glass must be installed before applying adjacent wall finishes so that finishing materials can be properly trimmed against the partition frame.
It is preferable to install floor coverings after the glazed partition to avoid damage to floors during partition installation, though floor covering can sometimes be installed first if protected.
Final installation of electrical outlets, switches, and other MEP fixtures adjacent to or within the glazed partition must occur after the partition is fully installed and stable.
The floor must be screeded and levelled to provide a smooth, level substrate before underfloor cable trunking can be laid out and fixed in place.
The main structural floor slab or deck must be in place to provide the physical support base for the underfloor cable trunking system.

successor: Floor Covering Installation (e.g. tiles, raised flooring, carpet)
rationale: Cables must be laid and trunking must be closed and secured before the final floor covering is installed over it to allow access and avoid damage.

successor: Electrical Cable Pulling / Cabling in Trunking
rationale: The trunking itself must be physically installed (fixed and joined) before electrical cables can be pulled through or laid inside it.
Trunking and cabling work must be completed and inspected before any final grouting or permanent floor finish is applied, to allow access for adjustments.
Electrical rough-in (conduits, boxes, and pathways) must be in place before structured cabling can be run, as cabling is pulled through the same conduit and pathway infrastructure.
The ceiling grid provides support for overhead cable trays and pathways; cabling is typically installed after the grid is in place to allow proper cable routing.
Structural walls, floors, and ceilings must be framed to define the building envelope and support cable pathways before any cabling can be physically installed.
Cables must be pulled and laid before they can be terminated on patch panels, tested for continuity, and certified in the telecommunications rooms.
Cabling installed within walls must be completed before drywall is closed up, as access to wall cavities is required for cable pulling and is permanently sealed once drywall is installed.
Site mobilization provides access, utilities, and safety perimeters required before any demolition or reconfiguration work can commence.

predecessor: Asbestos / Hazardous Materials Survey and Abatement
rationale: Hazardous materials must be identified and removed before disturbing existing partitions to ensure worker safety and regulatory compliance.
Understanding load-bearing vs. non-load-bearing status of existing walls is required to plan safe demounting and avoid structural collapse.

successor: Rough-In for Mechanical, Electrical, and Plumbing (MEP)
rationale: MEP rough-in work (wiring, conduit, ductwork, piping) within newly configured spaces can only be done after partitions are removed or repositioned to provide open access.

successor: New Partition Framing and Drywall Installation
rationale: New partition construction logically follows demounting and reconfiguration of existing partitions to define the new spatial layout before finishes are applied.
The physical site boundaries, dimensions, and conditions established during site preparation are fundamental inputs needed for accurate space planning and layout design.
The structural grid, column locations, and load-bearing walls define the physical spaces available, so the structural framework must be complete to properly design interior space layouts.
Architectural programming defines the space requirements, functional relationships, and area allocations that directly inform the space planning and layout design.
MEP systems must be designed around the finalized room layouts, partition locations, and space allocations to properly route ducts, pipes, and conduits.
Interior finishing work, including wall placements, flooring, and ceiling installations, directly depends on the approved space plan and layout design to proceed.
The rough opening must be framed and prepared before any door assembly can be installed, as the door unit requires a properly sized and structured opening to fit into.
Wall framing must be complete to define the doorway rough openings into which interior doors are installed.
The door frame (jamb) must be installed and secured before the door slab or assembly can be hung within it.
Door handles, locks, hinges, and other hardware can only be installed after the door slab is hung and properly aligned within its frame.
Painting or staining of the door and trim is typically performed after the door assembly is installed to ensure a continuous finish around the entire unit.
The rough opening must be framed to define the space where the sidelight/borrowed light panel will be installed.
The primary window or door frame adjacent to the sidelight must be installed first to establish alignment and proper fit.
Weatherproofing and flashing must be applied to the rough opening before the sidelight panel is placed to prevent moisture intrusion.
Interior trim and casing around the sidelight panel can only be installed after the panel is securely in place.
Exterior finishes and cladding around the sidelight must be completed after the panel is installed to ensure proper sealing and aesthetics.
The master workstation requires a stable, level foundation and proper site preparation before it can be installed or positioned.

successor: Electrical Connection and Power Supply Setup
rationale: Master workstation must be physically in place before electrical connections can be made to it.
The workstation must be installed and secured before it can be calibrated and commissioned for operation.
Network cabling and control system integration can only be completed after the master workstation is in its final position.
Functional testing and quality checks require the workstation to be fully installed and connected.
A stable foundation and floor surface must be prepared before installing the workstation to ensure structural stability and proper alignment.
The workshop building envelope (walls and roof) must be completed to provide weather protection and enclosed space before setting up internal workstations.
The workstation itself serves as the primary anchor point; tool storage and organization fixtures are mounted adjacent to or integrated with the completed workstation.
Electrical outlets and wiring for power tools must be placed after the workstation is positioned to ensure correct placement relative to the work surface.
Task lighting should be installed after the workstation is in place to ensure proper positioning and illumination of the work surface.
The demonstration bench must be built on top of or integrated with the main frame structure, so frame assembly must be completed first.
Electrical components and wiring for the demonstration bench can only be installed after the bench itself is constructed and positioned.
Components such as actuators, sensors, or displays can only be mounted onto the demonstration bench after the bench structure is complete.
Functional testing of the demonstration bench and its mounted components can only occur after the bench is fully assembled and integrated.
While inspection typically follows completion, it is a quality assurance step that could be performed concurrently in some workflows, making it a soft preference.
The tool storage wall must be mounted on a stable, level floor surface; the floor slab provides the necessary foundation and support.
The structural wall framing defines the location and provides the vertical surface onto which the tool storage wall system is attached or integrated.
It is convenient but not physically required to stock tools onto the wall after it is installed; tools could theoretically be placed elsewhere temporarily.
Electrical outlets should be positioned and wired after the wall structure is in place to ensure proper alignment and to avoid interference with the storage system.
The tool storage wall must be fully installed before the final inspection can verify its correct placement, anchorage, and compliance with specifications.
Lockers need to be mounted on or against framed walls, so wall framing must be complete before lockers can be installed.
Electrical wiring and outlets behind or near the locker area must be completed before lockers are installed, as access to walls would be blocked.
Walls must be painted and finished before lockers are installed, otherwise lockers would need to be removed or masked for painting, causing rework.
Flooring should be laid down before heavy lockers are placed on top, to avoid damaging the floor or requiring lockers to be moved during flooring work.
Occupants can only be assigned to lockers after the lockers are fully installed, secured, and ready for use.
The foundation or slab must be in place before mechanical rough-in can begin, as ductwork and piping are installed within or below the slab.
Mechanical rough-in (ductwork, piping) is installed within wall cavities and ceiling spaces, which require the rough framing to be complete.
While often done concurrently, if coordination is tight, electrical rough-in may follow mechanical to avoid conflicts with ductwork and piping pathways.
Mechanical and plumbing rough-in can often occur simultaneously, but if sequencing is needed, mechanical ductwork is typically installed first as it occupies the largest spaces.
Insulation must be installed after mechanical rough-in is complete so that it can wrap around ductwork and piping without obstruction.
The structural steel framework must be in place to provide support brackets and hanging points for the fume extraction ductwork before ducts can be installed overhead.

The concrete slab and foundations must be completed to provide a stable base for equipment supports, and to allow ductwork penetrations through the slab to be cast-in or core-drilled before duct installation.
The ductwork must be fully installed, sealed and leak-tested before the fume extraction system can be commissioned and fans operated.
Ductwork must be in place to connect to fume hoods or capture points; the hoods cannot be fully connected until the ductwork is run to their locations.

Although ceilings can be partially installed, it is preferable to complete exposed ductwork installation before enclosing ceilings to avoid rework and access issues, but it is not a hard physical constraint if access panels are provided.
The site must be cleared and levelled before safety signage can be installed, as debris and uneven ground would obstruct proper placement and visibility of signs and demarcation lines.
Temporary utilities (power, water, lighting) must be in place to power warning lights, illuminated signs, and allow use of tools for installing demarcation markings.
Safety signage and demarcation must be in place before excavation begins to clearly mark danger zones, exclusion areas, and safe walkways to protect workers from excavation hazards.
Demarcated safety zones, access routes, and warning signs must be established before foundation work commences to ensure safe movement of personnel and equipment around the active work area.

Designated storage areas, delivery routes, and warning signs must be marked before materials arrive on site to prevent unsafe stacking, blocked access, and to clearly communicate hazards to delivery personnel.

The subfloor (typically concrete or timber) must be clean, dry, level, and structurally sound before any sprung timber floor can be installed. The flooring system requires a stable base to be laid upon.
A damp proof membrane (DPM) must be placed over the subfloor to prevent moisture ingress from below, which would otherwise damage the timber floor system.
The resilient underlay or acoustic foam pads must be laid prior to the sprung timber floor to provide the necessary spring action and sound insulation properties.
Once the sprung timber floor is laid, it must be sanded, sealed, and finished to protect the timber surface and achieve the final appearance.
Skirting boards and trims are installed after the floor is complete to cover the expansion gap around the perimeter and provide a finished look.
Acoustic wall panelling requires a stable supporting structure. The wall framing (studwork) must be complete to provide the substrate for fixing the panelling.

Electrical cables and back boxes must be routed and installed within the wall cavity before the acoustic panels are fixed, as access to the cavity is permanently closed off once panelling is installed.
Any plumbing pipework that runs within the wall must be completed and pressure-tested before the wall is closed with acoustic panelling.
Acoustic or thermal insulation inside the wall cavity must be placed before the acoustic panels are mounted, as it would be impossible to install after the panels are fixed.

While painting can be done before panelling with masking, it is often preferred to complete final decoration of adjacent walls or trims after panelling to ensure clean edges and avoid damaging the panels during painting works.

Electrical faceplates (sockets and switches) must be installed after the acoustic panelling is in place so that the panels can be cut accurately to accommodate them and the faceplates sit flush against the finished panel surface.
Structural elements must be fully completed and cured before any interior finishing can begin, as fit-out works are applied onto the finished structural shell.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in (conduits, pipes, ductwork within walls/ceilings) must be installed before walls are enclosed and interior finishes are applied, to avoid destructive rework.
Waterproofing of wet areas (toilets, kitchens, roof slabs) and damp-proofing of external walls must be completed prior to interior finishes to prevent moisture damage to finished surfaces.

Final installation of MEP fixtures (lighting fittings, power outlets, sanitary ware) is performed after or concurrently with interior finishes, but typically after painting and flooring to avoid soiling or damaging fixtures.
All interior finishes (painting, flooring, ceiling, joinery) must be completed before the formal snagging inspection and handover process begins.
Electrical power cabling and conduit must be run in walls and ceilings before AV/IT equipment can be installed and connected to power sources.
Suspended ceiling grids provide the structural support for overhead projectors, speakers, and wiring pathways; these must be in place before mounting AV equipment.
Walls must be framed and enclosed to provide cavities for data cabling, outlet boxes, and mounting surfaces for wall-mounted displays and speakers.
AV/IT cabling in plenum spaces above ceilings must be run and terminated before ceiling tiles are permanently installed, to avoid rework and access issues.

While wall finishing is typically completed before final AV installation to avoid dust damage, some touch-up painting may occur after AV mounting; this is a soft preference to protect sensitive electronics from paint and drywall dust.
Workers must complete safety induction before compliance inspection can verify understanding and adherence to safety protocols.
Formal site access permits must be issued before inspection can verify that only authorized personnel are on site.
Physical safety barriers (e.g., guardrails, edge protection) must be installed so the inspection can verify they meet regulatory standards.
High-risk construction activities may only begin after the safeguarding compliance inspection has confirmed all protective measures are in place and compliant.
The clearance certificate documenting compliance is issued as a direct output following a successful inspection.
Site preparation and earthworks must be completed to provide a stable, graded, and properly drained base before any landscaping, planting, or outdoor recreational features can be installed.

The main building structure must be enclosed to protect interior work, and heavy construction equipment and material staging for the building must be completed before surrounding landscape and outdoor recreation areas are developed.

predecessor: Underground Utility Installation (Water, Sewer, Electrical, Storm Drainage)
rationale: All underground utilities, drainage pipes, and conduits must be installed and backfilled before grading, planting, paving, or constructing outdoor recreational features to avoid re-excavation and damage to finished landscaping.

Landscaping and outdoor recreation construction are among the final finishing activities; once completed, the site can undergo final cleanup, commissioning, and handover without risk of damage from subsequent heavy construction work.

While not a hard physical constraint, it is standard practice to complete all landscape and outdoor recreation work before conducting final punch list walks and inspection sign-offs to ensure the entire project is complete and aesthetically finished.
The structural frame and building shell must be complete to provide the supporting framework and rough opening into which the display window/glazed frontage will be installed.

predecessor: Rough Opening Preparation / Framing for Glazing
rationale: The rough opening must be framed, leveled, and prepared to receive the glazed frontage system before installation can begin.
Waterproofing and air barrier systems must be installed around the opening to prevent moisture intrusion after the glazed frontage is in place.
Interior finishes such as drywall, trim, and painting around the glazed frontage must occur after the window/frontage is installed to allow for proper sealing and aesthetic integration.
Final exterior sealants and caulking around the perimeter of the glazed frontage must be applied after installation to ensure a weathertight seal.
The structural frame must be in place to provide the supporting structure and opening into which the shopfront door/folding facade can be installed.
The rough opening must be prepared, framed, and weatherproofed (flashing, sill pan) before installing the door/facade unit to ensure proper fit and prevent water intrusion.
The floor slab or finished subfloor at the doorway threshold must be completed to provide a level base and proper elevation for the door/facade installation.
Interior finishes around the door frame should follow after door installation to allow for proper trimming, sealing, and finishing of the interface between the door and walls.
The operable door/facade must be fully installed and tested before the building can be commissioned and handed over to the client, as it is a critical functional component of the building envelope.
The existing retail interior fitout must be removed (demolished) to expose the bare structure, allowing new educational fitout works to start on a clean substrate.
The building structure must be assessed and any deficiencies remediated before installing new partitions, ceilings, MEP systems, and finishes for the educational space.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in (e.g., conduit, ductwork, piping) must be run within the ceiling and wall cavities prior to enclosing them with ceiling grids and wall linings during the fitout.
