The core fitout (walls, ceilings, flooring, finishes) must be completed before installing educational specialty items such as whiteboards, smart boards, laboratory casework, and furniture, fixtures & equipment (FF&E).
The fitout must be substantially complete for commissioning and testing of all MEP systems, life safety systems, and specialty educational systems to occur in the finished environment.

The mezzanine/loft learning deck requires a structural floor or slab system below it to support its framing and loads. The concrete slab or floor deck must be in place before the mezzanine deck can be built upon.

The mezzanine/loft deck is typically supported by structural steel columns or framing. These vertical structural members must be erected first to provide the support framework for the mezzanine level.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work that will be located beneath the mezzanine deck must be completed before the deck is closed in, to avoid costly rework or demolition of the deck later.
Guardrails, handrails, and edge protection around the mezzanine perimeter must be installed after the deck structure is complete to ensure worker safety and code-compliant fall protection.

successor: Deck Finishing & Flooring (e.g., Carpet, Tile, Wood)
rationale: Any finish flooring materials applied to the mezzanine deck surface must be installed after the structural deck is fully complete and cured/ready to accept finishes.

successor: Electrical & Data Outlet Installation on Deck
rationale: While outlets can be roughed-in beforehand, final installation of receptacles, data ports, and trim-out on the mezzanine deck is typically performed after the deck is in place to ensure proper positioning.
A site assessment and feasibility study must be completed first to determine whether a change of use is viable and compliant with local zoning laws before applying for planning approval.
Ownership or legal control of the property must be established before applying for a change-of-use planning approval, as the applicant must have a legal interest in the land.
Conceptual design drawings showing the proposed new use and any modifications are typically required as part of the planning application submission.
Detailed construction-ready drawings should only be developed after planning approval is secured, to ensure the design complies with approved conditions and avoid wasted design costs.
A building permit for construction or alteration works can only be applied for after change-of-use planning approval is granted, as the permit must be based on the approved use and design.
The building's facade or curtain wall must be installed first to provide a structural surface for mounting branding elements and signage.
Scaffolding or elevated access systems must be erected before workers can safely reach the facade to install branding and signage.
Electrical conduits, wiring, and power connections for illuminated signage must be roughed-in before the signage units are physically mounted and connected.
It is preferred but not strictly required to clean the facade after signage installation to remove any debris or marks from the installation process.
Branding and signage installation must be complete before the building can be officially handed over, as signage is part of the finished and operational building.

Structural framing and rough-in work (e.g., stud walls, electrical, plumbing, HVAC rough-in) must be completed before acoustic treatment installation because acoustic materials (such as insulation, soundproofing boards, and acoustic sealants) are installed within wall cavities and ceiling plenums that require the structure and MEP rough-ins to be in place first.

At least the inner layer of drywall is typically installed before specialized acoustic treatments (e.g., acoustic membranes, mass-loaded vinyl, resilient channels) because these treatments are sandwiched between drywall layers or applied over the initial boarding to achieve proper sound isolation.

Acoustic treatments (e.g., acoustic panels, sound-absorbing wall coverings, acoustic tiles) must be fully installed and sealed before final finishes and painting are applied, as these treatments are often behind or integral to the finished surface, and painting over or applying wall coverings after acoustic installation ensures a clean, professional appearance without damaging acoustic materials.

While flooring can technically be installed before or after acoustic wall treatments, it is generally preferred to install flooring after acoustic wall treatments to avoid damaging acoustic panels or sealants during floor installation work and to ensure a proper acoustic seal at the wall-floor junction.

Acoustic wall treatments and ceiling treatments often integrate; if suspended acoustic ceiling tiles or acoustic ceiling panels are used, the wall acoustic treatments should be installed before the ceiling finish to ensure proper fit, sealing, and continuity of the acoustic envelope at the wall-ceiling interface.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and graded before fence posts can be set and fencing can be installed along the perimeter.
Underground utilities must be located and marked to avoid damaging them during fence post excavation and installation.
Perimeter fencing must be in place before gates and access control systems can be mounted and integrated with the fence structure.
Cameras, sensors, and alarm systems are typically mounted on or integrated with perimeter fencing, requiring the fence to be complete first.
Landscaping around the perimeter is often done after fencing to avoid damaging finished plants and to allow clean access for fence installation equipment.
Walls and ceilings must be prepared (plastered, finished, and painted) before anti-ligature fixtures can be securely mounted and fixed to the structural surfaces.

Electrical conduit, wiring, and back boxes must be installed in walls/ceilings before anti-ligature fixtures are fitted, as these fixtures often conceal or integrate with electrical services and access would be blocked afterward.
Any concealed pipework for anti-ligature sink or sanitary fixtures must be roughed-in before the fixtures are permanently installed.

While touch-up painting around fixtures is common, as a soft preference it is better to complete final finishes after fixtures to avoid damage; however fixtures can be installed before final paint if necessary.
All anti-ligature fixtures must be fully installed and tested before the room can be declared safe for occupancy or patient use, as these are critical safety elements.
A site must be selected and acquired before planning and regulatory approval can be sought, as the application requires a defined location, property boundaries, and land ownership details.
Feasibility assessments including environmental impact, geotechnical, and zoning analyses must be completed to inform the planning application and demonstrate compliance with regulations.
Preliminary design concepts and pre-application discussions with regulatory authorities are necessary to prepare a formal planning submission that meets requirements.

Full detailed design and engineering work (e.g., structural, MEP) typically cannot proceed until planning permission and regulatory approvals are granted, as the approved scheme sets the parameters for detailed design.

Formal tendering and procurement of construction contracts generally cannot commence until planning approval is secured, as the project scope and conditions of approval affect contract documentation and pricing.

A project brief or initiation document must exist before a safeguarding risk assessment can be conducted, as the assessment needs to understand the nature, scope, and context of the project to identify relevant safeguarding risks.
Understanding who the project will interact with (including vulnerable groups) is essential input for identifying safeguarding risks and determining appropriate mitigation measures.

successor: Development of Safeguarding Policies and Procedures
rationale: The findings and identified risks from the assessment directly inform the development of tailored safeguarding policies, reporting mechanisms, and prevention procedures.
Training content must be based on the specific risks identified in the safeguarding risk assessment to ensure staff and volunteers are equipped to prevent and respond to those particular risks.

successor: Implementation of Safeguarding Measures / Project Activity Commencement
rationale: Safeguarding measures must be in place before project activities begin to ensure the safety of participants; the risk assessment is the prerequisite for designing and implementing these measures.
The building's structural frame and core must be completed to provide the physical enclosure and load-bearing support before any interior fit-out works can commence.
The building envelope must be weathertight (roof, windows, cladding) to protect interior finishes and materials from weather damage during fit-out.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in works (conduits, pipes, ductwork within walls/ceilings) must be installed before being enclosed by interior finishes.
After interior fit-out (ceilings, wall linings, fixtures) is complete, final electrical/plumbing connections, sockets, switches, and trims can be installed without damaging finishes.
Specialist fit-out (partitioning, joinery, built-in furniture) must be installed first so that final flooring, painting, and decorative finishes can be applied seamlessly without rework.
Fire alarm systems must be installed and operational before inspection to verify compliance with fire safety codes.
Fire sprinkler systems must be in place to be tested and inspected for proper coverage and functionality.
Emergency exit lighting and signage must be installed to allow inspection of proper placement and illumination levels.
Fire extinguishers must be mounted at designated locations and have current inspection tags before the compliance inspection.
A passed fire safety inspection is typically a prerequisite for obtaining a certificate of occupancy before the building can be legally occupied.

Building Commissioning & Care Registration requires the construction to be substantially complete and handed over from the construction team, as commissioning involves testing and activating building systems which must be physically installed first.

The building must be commissioned and registered with relevant care authorities before it can be operationally activated and handed over for full facility operation, as commissioning validates that all systems are functioning correctly for safe occupancy.
Building commissioning must be completed and care registration obtained before occupants can move in and use the facility, as these ensure the building is safe, compliant, and ready for habitation.

All building systems (MEP, fire safety, HVAC, etc.) must be installed and individually tested before the overall building commissioning process can begin, as commissioning integrates and verifies all systems together.

Commissioning results and care registration documentation are prerequisites for the final regulatory inspection and certification process, as inspectors need evidence of proper commissioning and registration.
Proper site grading and drainage must be completed before landscaping to ensure water flows away from play areas and to prevent soil erosion or water pooling around equipment foundations.
All underground utilities (water, electrical, data lines) must be installed before landscaping to avoid digging up finished lawns, beds, or play surfaces for utility access.
Any concrete footings, slabs, or hardscape foundations near play areas must be poured and cured before play equipment installation to provide stable anchoring surfaces.

Landscaping and play equipment must be fully installed before the final inspection can occur, as the inspector needs to verify all elements including safety surfacing, equipment anchoring, and site amenities are complete and compliant.

While final clean-up and demobilization typically follow installation, this is a soft preference as some clean-up can occur concurrently; however, heavy equipment removal is best done after all landscaping is complete to avoid damaging finished work.
The shop front assembly requires a stable and level foundation to be installed upon; without the foundation being prepared, the assembly cannot be securely anchored.
The shop front assembly is typically attached to or integrated with the structural wall framing; the wall framing must be in place to provide support and attachment points for the shop front.
Glass panels or windows for the shop front can only be installed after the shop front frame assembly is complete, as the frame provides the structure to hold the glazing.

While finishing work such as painting or cladding is typically done after assembly to protect the finish from damage during assembly, some finishing could theoretically be done pre-assembly; this is a soft preference for quality and workflow efficiency.

successor: Interior Fit-Out Adjacent to Shop Front
rationale: Interior finishing work adjacent to the shop front (e.g., flooring, wall finishes, display areas) cannot begin until the shop front is assembled, as the assembly seals the building envelope and provides access for interior work coordination.
The ground must be prepared, cleared, and excavated to the required levels before any foundation work or wall construction can begin.
The strip footing or foundation for the boundary wall must be poured and cured before the wall itself can be built upon it.
Any below-ground drainage, waterproofing membranes, or damp-proof courses that extend under or through the wall line must be installed before the wall is erected.
Once the boundary wall is complete and cured, the earth on either side can be backfilled and compacted against it to provide lateral support and finish the grade.
The wall structure must be fully erected and cured before any plaster, render, paint, or other surface finishes can be applied.
Structural walls must be in place before internal partitions can be aligned and attached to the building's permanent structure.
The floor surface must be level and finished to provide a stable base for partition footings and tracks.
Overhead support structure and ceiling grid must be in place so that partitions can be fixed and aligned to the ceiling tracks.
Partitions must be erected before electrical cables can be routed through the partition cavities and outlet boxes installed.
Pipes and drain lines for sinks or fixtures mounted on or within the partition require the partition framework to be in place first.
The partition framing must be complete before any cladding, drywall sheets, or finishing panels can be applied to the frame.
Finishing work such as painting is typically done after partitions are fully installed and clad, though it is a logical sequence rather than a strict physical impossibility to do otherwise.
A stable foundation and floor slab must be in place to provide a level substrate and structural support for the door frame and threshold.
The wall framing around the entrance opening must be complete to define the rough opening dimensions and provide structural attachment points for the door frame.
A lintel or header beam above the door opening must be installed to support the load above and create the correct clear opening height.

It is a soft preference to complete door installation before final floor finishes so that the threshold height can be set accurately against the finished floor level, but floors can also be finished first with temporary protection.
The door must be installed so that weatherproofing membranes, flashing, and exterior cladding can be properly lapped and sealed against the door frame to prevent water ingress.
Display window glazing is installed within wall openings; wall framing must be complete to provide the structural opening and support for the window frame.
The window frame must be installed and secured in the wall opening before the glazing (glass panels) can be inserted and sealed into the frame.

Glazing installation must be complete to seal the building envelope before interior finishes are applied; this prevents damage to finishes from moisture and allows for proper sealing around the window.
The glazed display window must be in place before final exterior weatherproofing and cladding can be completed around the window to ensure a watertight seal and proper integration with the facade.
Rough openings for windows must be inspected and approved to confirm correct dimensions and structural readiness before glazing is installed.
The main electrical switchboard supplies power to the tenant distribution boards; it must be installed and energized first to provide upstream power.
Conduits and cables must be run from the main switchboard to the tenant distribution board location before the board can be mounted and connected.
The distribution board must be installed and energized before downstream tenant circuits (lighting, power outlets, equipment) can be connected.
Final testing and commissioning of tenant electrical systems require the distribution board to be in place and operational.
The walls and structural supports must be in place to mount the distribution board enclosure securely.
Ductwork must be installed and accessible before fan coil units can be connected to the duct system.
Chilled water supply and return piping must be in place to connect to the fan coil unit's water coils.
Power supply wiring must be run to the unit location to provide electrical service for fan operation and controls.
Condensate drain lines must be installed to remove moisture collected from the cooling coil.
Final duct connections to the fan coil unit can only be completed after the unit is physically mounted and positioned.

successor: Refrigerant piping connection and testing (if applicable)
rationale: Refrigerant line connections require the unit to be securely installed before final brazing and evacuation.
Final connection of power and low-voltage control wiring to the unit terminals must occur after the unit is mounted.
Commissioning and testing of the HVAC system can only proceed after all fan coil units are installed and connected.
Ceilings are typically installed after fan coil units to allow access for connections and testing, though in some sequences ceiling grid can go first if access panels are provided.
Ceiling supports, hangers, or floor stands must be in place to securely mount the fan coil unit.
The structural framing and building shell must be complete to provide the opening and support structure into which the shop front is installed.
The glass panels and glazing materials for the shop front must be procured and on-site before installation can commence.
The floor slab at the shop entrance area must be prepared and leveled to provide a stable base for the shop front framing and threshold.
It is preferable but not strictly required to install the shop front before internal wall finishes so that the interface between the front and internal walls can be neatly sealed.
Electrical conduit and wiring for entrance/signage lighting must be roughed in after the shop front framing is in place to correctly position fixtures within the shop front structure.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and excavated before any structural shell work can begin, as shell construction requires a stable and prepared foundation base.
Foundations (including pile caps, ground beams, and slab-on-grade) must be completed to provide structural support before the superstructure (columns, slabs, walls of the shell) can be erected.
All below-ground drainage, water mains, electrical ducts, and other buried services must be diverted/installed prior to shell construction to avoid later excavation under the structure.
The structural frame and core must be completed to provide support for roof installation and to enable weathertight enclosure of the building.
Internal walls, MEP rough-ins, and finishing works require the completed structural shell (floors, columns, cores) to be in place before interior subdivision and fit-out can commence.

Conduits and rough-in electrical work must be installed before the first and second fix can begin, as the fix work involves pulling wires, installing outlets, switches, and fixtures into the already-roughed-in conduits and back boxes.

All electrical connections, outlets, switches, and fixtures must be fully installed (first & second fix) before testing and commissioning can occur to ensure the system is complete and ready for energization and verification.

Electrical fixtures such as lights, smoke detectors, and other ceiling-mounted devices must be installed as part of the electrical fix before the ceiling grid and tiles are closed up, to avoid rework.

Ideally electrical second fix (switches, sockets, faceplates) should be completed before final wall finishing and painting to allow neat flush fitting, though some touch-ups can be done after; this is a soft preference for quality and efficiency.

Coordination between MEP services is preferred to avoid clashes; however, electrical first & second fix can sometimes proceed in parallel with or after MEP rough-in. It is a soft preference to sequence MEP rough-in first for spatial coordination.
The main electrical supply must be installed to provide power infrastructure before service charge metering can be connected and installed.
The meter cabinet or enclosure must be in place to house the service charge metering equipment before the meters can be installed.
The main distribution board must be installed as the central point from which service charge metering circuits are derived.

predecessor: Cabling and Conduit Work for Metering
rationale: Cables, conduits, and trunking for metering circuits must be routed and pulled before the meters themselves can be connected and terminated.
After installation, the meters must be commissioned, programmed, and tested to verify accurate reading and communication with the billing system.
Strata title registration requires the physical building to be completed so that individual units can be surveyed, defined, and legally registered as separate lots.
A cadastral survey of the building and individual units is legally required to define the boundaries of each strata lot before registration can proceed.
The development must have received final planning approval and comply with all conditions before strata titles can be registered.
A building approval or construction certificate confirming compliance with building regulations is typically required prior to strata title lodgement.
Individual units can only be settled and handed over to buyers after the strata plan has been registered, as legal ownership transfers depend on the existence of registered titles.
Occupants can only legally move into and take possession of individual units after strata titles are registered and ownership is formally transferred.
The body corporate or owners corporation is formally established upon registration of the strata plan, and ongoing management activities commence only after registration.
Service counter must be installed on a finished floor slab to provide a stable, level base.
Plumbing rough-in (water supply and drain lines) must be in place before the counter can be installed, as the counter will cover or integrate with these connections.
Electrical wiring and outlet boxes must be roughed in before the counter is placed, since the counter may house outlets or require access to wall wiring.
The walls behind and adjacent to the service counter must be framed and finished with drywall before the counter can be securely attached or positioned against them.
The counter base or carcass must be fully installed and secured before the top surface (such as laminate, stone, or solid surface) can be fitted.
The service counter must be in place before sinks or faucets can be mounted to or through the countertop.
Receptacles, switches, and other electrical trim items integrated with the counter can only be finished after the counter is installed.
While backsplash can be completed before the counter, it is often preferred to install backsplash after the counter for a tight fit and clean joint.

The coffee machine is typically a countertop or built-in appliance that must be placed on or into the kitchen countertop. The countertop must be installed first to provide a stable, level surface and the proper cutout (if built-in) for the coffee machine.

If the coffee machine is a built-in unit, the backsplash is installed after the appliance to allow for proper sealing and finishing around the edges of the appliance cutout, ensuring a watertight and finished appearance.

The coffee machine requires a dedicated electrical outlet (typically 120V) near its location. The electrical wiring, outlet box, and circuit must be roughed in and completed before the coffee machine can be plugged in or hardwired.

Many built-in coffee machines require a water supply line for brewing and a drain line for waste water. These plumbing rough-ins must be completed before the coffee machine can be connected and installed.

While often cabinets are installed first and appliances fitted after, in some sequences it is preferable to install the coffee machine after adjacent cabinets to ensure proper alignment and fit. However, this is a soft preference as the order can vary depending on whether the machine is freestanding or built-in.
The canopy/awning requires a structural frame or support system to be in place to be anchored and secured.
The roof deck provides the attachment surface and weatherproofing base for the canopy/awning above.
Installing the awning first prevents interference with siding installation, though siding can be worked around if needed.
The canopy/awning flashing and integration must be completed before the final waterproofing layer to ensure a watertight seal.
The canopy/awning should be in place so that paint and finishes can be applied continuously around and integrated with the awning structure.
The structural steel frame must be erected to provide the supporting structure onto which the glass facade and storefront glazing system is attached.
Floor slabs must be poured and cured to establish the floor elevations and bearing points for the storefront glazing and curtain wall anchorage.
Rough openings, blocking, and sub-framing around windows and storefront areas must be installed to provide the mounting surface and reveals for the glazing system.
Weather-resistive barriers must be applied to the substrate before glazing to ensure a continuous moisture and air seal behind the façade system.

Although interior finishes can technically proceed with glazing open, installing them after glazing is preferred to avoid weather damage and to allow for sealed, conditioned interior conditions. This is a soft preference for schedule optimization.
A stable and compacted sub-base is required to support the pavement/terrace/decking structure and prevent uneven settlement or failure.
Sub-surface drainage must be installed before the pavement/decking to ensure proper water management and prevent water accumulation beneath the finished surface.
Any underground utilities (cables, pipes) must be laid before paving to avoid disturbing the finished pavement surface.
Balustrades and handrails are typically fixed onto or adjacent to the finished decking/pavement surface; the surface must be in place to properly anchor and align safety barriers.

successor: Final landscaping / planting adjacent to terrace
rationale: While soft landscaping can begin before decking, the finishing touches and planting against the pavement edge are best done after the decking is complete to achieve a neat interface.
Signage must be mounted on finished wall surfaces. Installing signage before wall finishes are complete would require removal and reinstallation or cause damage to the signage.
Suspended or overhead signage often attaches to ceiling structures. Ceilings must be in place to provide mounting points and to establish the vertical clearance for signage placement.
Floor-mounted signage and wayfinding elements require finished flooring for proper installation and alignment. Flooring must be complete to establish final floor levels.
Illuminated or electronic signage requires electrical power supply and data cabling to be roughed-in before signage units can be connected and commissioned.
Signage must be fully installed and operational before the building can be formally inspected and commissioned, as signage is part of life-safety and egress requirements.
The ground must be properly graded and prepared to ensure a stable and level base for constructing planters and boundary planters.
Any underground drainage, irrigation, or electrical lines must be laid before planters are built to avoid digging up or damaging the finished planters.
If the planters require a concrete base or footer, the foundation work must be completed first to provide structural support.
The planter structure must be fully constructed and cured (if concrete/masonry) before soil and plants can be added.

Finishing touches such as mulching, edging, and decorative elements typically occur after planters are in place, though this is a logical soft sequencing preference rather than a strict physical necessity.
The building structure, external walls, roof, and base building envelope must be completed to provide a weathertight, structurally sound shell before any interior fit-out can commence.

Electrical conduits, plumbing pipes, ductwork, and other mechanical/electrical rough-in installations within the café area must be installed before walls are closed up, ceilings are finished, and interior finishes are applied.

Final installation of light fixtures, switches, outlets, plumbing fixtures, and HVAC grilles must occur after ceiling grids, wall finishes, and flooring are installed to allow proper alignment and finishing.

Commercial kitchen equipment, counters, and café appliances can only be brought in and installed after the interior finishes (flooring, wall tiles, ceiling) are complete to avoid damage and allow proper layout.
A clean, finished interior is a prerequisite for the final deep cleaning and subsequent handover inspection of the café space.
The ground must be cleared, excavated, and compacted before any foundation concrete can be placed. Foundations require a stable, level, and prepared subgrade to bear loads.
Soil bearing capacity and ground conditions must be assessed before designing and pouring foundations to ensure structural adequacy and avoid settlement failures.
Underground water, sewer, electrical, and other utility lines must be laid in the ground before the slab is poured, as they will be embedded in or run beneath the concrete.

Load-bearing walls, columns, and structural framing require a completed foundation and slab to transfer loads into the ground. The superstructure cannot be erected without a cured foundation in place.
Waterproofing membranes and coatings are applied directly to foundation walls and slabs after they have cured, to protect the structure from groundwater ingress before backfilling.
The structural frame (steel or concrete) must be completed to provide the load-bearing support and attachment points for the facade system and curtain wall.
Floor slabs must be in place to provide working platforms and structural bearing for facade panel installation at each level.
Completing roof waterproofing before facade installation prevents water ingress behind the finished cladding system, though some overlap may be possible.
The building envelope must be watertight before sensitive interior finishes can be applied to avoid moisture damage.
MEP rough-in can begin after the facade is sealed, but some work can proceed in parallel if coordination is tight; it is a soft preference to avoid rework.
The canopy or awning requires the main building structure (framing and roof deck) to be in place to provide a mounting surface and structural support.
Exterior wall finish must be completed so that the awning or canopy can be properly anchored and sealed against the finished facade.
The roof waterproofing must be complete to prevent water intrusion where the canopy/awning attaches to the building; otherwise leaks could develop.

While painting can be done before in some cases, it is preferable to install the canopy/awning first so that trim and paint can be seamlessly applied around the mounted hardware for a clean appearance.
Exterior lighting fixtures that are integrated into or mounted beneath the canopy/awning cannot be installed until the canopy structure is in place to support them.
The ground must be properly leveled, cleared, and graded before any terrace construction can begin to ensure a stable and properly draining foundation.
A concrete slab or structural foundation for the terrace must be poured and fully cured before terrace construction can proceed, as it serves as the base for the terrace surface.
Any underground electrical conduits, drainage pipes, or irrigation lines that will run beneath the terrace must be installed before the terrace is built to avoid costly excavation later.
The main terrace structure must be completed before final flooring materials (tiles, stone, wood decking) are laid down, as the flooring sits on top of the structural base.
Safety railings and balustrades are installed after the terrace structure is built, as they attach to the perimeter of the completed terrace.
Interior finishes such as drywall, painting, and wall treatments must be completed before signage can be installed, as signage is mounted onto finished wall surfaces.
Ceilings must be installed before suspended or ceiling-mounted signage can be affixed.
Flooring must be completed to ensure safe access for installation crews and to avoid damage to finished floors from ladders and equipment.
Electrical rough-in and wiring must be completed prior to installing illuminated signage to allow for power connections.
Signage and branding installation must be completed before final cleaning and commissioning to avoid damage to newly installed signs from cleaning activities.

predecessor: Building Construction - Main Structure / Envelope Completion
successor: Health & Safety / Food Hygiene Compliance Inspection
rationale: The building's main structure and envelope must be complete before food hygiene inspections can occur, as the inspection assesses the finished physical environment where food handling will take place.

successor: Health & Safety / Food Hygiene Compliance Inspection
rationale: Plumbing systems (hand wash stations, sinks, drainage) are critical food hygiene infrastructure and must be installed and operational before the compliance inspection can verify them.

successor: Health & Safety / Food Hygiene Compliance Inspection
rationale: Electrical systems including lighting, power for refrigeration and food equipment must be installed for the inspector to verify compliance with food safety standards.

successor: Health & Safety / Food Hygiene Compliance Inspection
rationale: Proper ventilation, temperature control and extraction systems are essential for food hygiene compliance and must be fully installed before inspection.

predecessor: Interior Finishes - Wall, Floor & Ceiling Cladding
successor: Health & Safety / Food Hygiene Compliance Inspection
rationale: Smooth, cleanable wall/floor/celling finishes in food preparation areas are a key hygiene requirement and must be completed before the inspection can assess them.

predecessor: Health & Safety / Food Hygiene Compliance Inspection
successor: Kitchen / Food Preparation Area Equipment Installation
rationale: Professional food equipment (cookers, refrigeration, dishwashers) should only be installed after the hygiene inspection has verified that all building services and finishes meet food safety standards, ensuring equipment installation does not mask or interfere with unresolved compliance issues.

predecessor: Health & Safety / Food Hygiene Compliance Inspection
rationale: Successful completion of the food hygiene compliance inspection is typically a prerequisite for building handover and commencement of food operations.

predecessor: Health & Safety / Food Hygiene Compliance Inspection
successor: Certificate of Occupancy / Final Compliance Sign-off
rationale: Regulatory food hygiene approval must be obtained before the building can be formally occupied and used for food-related activities.
The door frame must be installed and secured in the rough opening before the door leaf can be hung, as the door hinges attach to the frame.
The rough opening in the wall must be framed, sized, and finished to the correct dimensions before the door unit can be fitted.
The load-bearing wall structure must be built before the door opening can be created within it.
Locks, handles, hinges, and other hardware are typically installed on the door after the door is hung in its frame.
Weatherstripping, sealants, and flashing around the door perimeter can only be applied after the door unit is fully installed in the opening.
Interior trim and casing around the door are installed after the door unit is in place to cover the gap between frame and wall.
The installed door must be checked for proper operation, fit, and security after installation is complete.
The rough opening for the storefront must be framed, weatherproofed, and prepared before the glazing system can be installed.
The primary structural support (steel or load-bearing framing) that the storefront glazing system attaches to must be in place before glazing installation can begin.
Storefront glazing encloses the building envelope; interior finishes must be protected from weather and are typically sequenced after the glazing is installed to ensure a dry interior environment.
Functional testing (water infiltration, air leakage, thermal performance) and commissioning of the storefront glazing can only occur after the glazing is fully installed and sealed.
Exterior perimeter sealants, backer rods, and aesthetic trim pieces are applied after the glazing panels are in place to complete the weather seal and finish.
Gondola shelving must be installed on a finished floor surface to ensure stability and level positioning.
Wall finishes (painting, drywall, etc.) should be completed before installing gondola shelving to avoid damage to finished walls and to allow proper anchoring.
Electrical rough-in for any outlet or lighting that may be behind or integrated with the shelving must be completed before shelving is placed.
Shelves must be fully installed, anchored, and stable before any merchandise or products can be placed on them for safety and load-bearing reasons.
Overhead or aisle signage is typically installed after shelving is in place to ensure proper alignment with the shelving layout, though some signage can be done in parallel.

The refrigerated case must sit on a level, finished floor. Floor preparation (screeding, tiling, waterproofing) must be completed before the case can be placed to ensure stability and proper drainage.
Refrigerant supply and return lines must be run to the case location prior to installation so that the case can be connected to the refrigeration system immediately upon placement.
Power supply conduits, junction boxes, and dedicated outlets must be pre-wired and terminated at the case location before the case is moved into position to allow final electrical connection.
The case must be in its final position before refrigerant lines can be connected and pressure/leak tested.
Final electrical connections, thermostat calibration, and control system commissioning can only proceed once the case is physically installed and anchored.
While shelving can technically be installed earlier, the refrigerated case area is typically stocked with product after the case is operational to maintain cold chain integrity.
The refrigerator must be placed on a level, load-bearing floor surface to ensure stability, proper door operation, and structural integrity.

predecessor: Rough electrical rough-in and conduit installation
rationale: Electrical power supply wiring and conduit must be run to the refrigerator location before the unit can be connected and commissioned.

successor: Refrigerant line charging and leak testing
rationale: The refrigeration system must be fully installed before refrigerant can be charged and tested for leaks, as charging occurs after the unit is in place.
The refrigerator must be physically set in its final position before making final electrical connections and performing startup tests.
While shelves can be installed before the unit is placed, it is more practical to arrange interior components after the refrigerator is in its final location for accessibility and adjustment.
The checkout/POS counter must be installed on a finished, level floor surface to ensure stability and proper alignment.
Power outlets, data cabling, and conduit for POS terminals, scanners, and payment devices must be run in walls and floors before the counter is installed to avoid surface-mounted wiring.

predecessor: Wall framing and drywall (behind counter area)
rationale: The back wall against which the counter is placed must be framed, insulated, and drywalled so the counter can be anchored and sealed properly.

successor: POS terminal installation and checkout system setup
rationale: POS registers, scanners, printers, and payment terminals are mounted on or integrated into the counter after it is installed.

successor: Checkout area signage and customer queue rail installation
rationale: Signage and queue rails are typically installed after the counter is in place to align correctly with the counter layout and customer flow, though minor adjustments can be made if done beforehand.

The building's structural shell (slab, columns, roof, exterior walls) must be complete before any interior fit-out can commence, as the tenant improvement work depends on an enclosed, weather-tight space.
Main mechanical, electrical, and plumbing risers and main distribution lines serving the tenant space must be roughed-in to the point of connection before tenant-level MEP work can begin.
Final interior finishes such as painting, floor coverings, and ceiling tiles must be installed after the main fit-out work (walls, MEP trim-out, fixtures) is complete to avoid damage and rework.
Custom retail fixtures, shelving, and display units are installed after the space is fully built out, including walls, flooring, and power/data outlets, to ensure proper alignment and fit.
Building and fire marshal inspections for tenant improvements can only occur after all fit-out work is substantially complete, to verify compliance with codes and approved plans.
Structural steel framing must be in place to support the weight and mounting points of refrigeration equipment before it can be installed.
A finished, level concrete floor slab is required to provide a stable base for heavy refrigeration units and condensers.
The roof and walls must be enclosed to protect sensitive refrigeration equipment and controls from weather damage during installation.
Power supply conduits, panels, and disconnects must be roughed in to provide the electrical connections needed to operate and commission refrigeration equipment.
Refrigerant piping work and subsequent leak testing can only begin after the refrigeration equipment (compressors, condensers, evaporators) is physically installed and anchored in place.
Commissioning, control wiring, and system startup must follow equipment installation because the installed equipment must be present and connected before it can be tested and programmed.
Pipe insulation can only be applied after the refrigeration equipment is installed and the piping is connected, as insulation must conform to the final routed pipe configuration.

Health department inspections typically occur after rough-in inspections of plumbing, electrical, and mechanical systems are completed, ensuring basic building systems are in place before health-related review.
The physical build-out of kitchens, bathrooms, and other health-sensitive spaces must be substantially complete before health department officials can inspect them for compliance with health codes.
Plumbing systems, including sinks, drains, and backflow prevention devices, must be installed to meet health code requirements before the health department can sign off on the facility.
Health department approval is typically a prerequisite to obtaining a final Certificate of Occupancy, as it confirms the building is safe and sanitary for public use.
While health inspection often occurs before final fixture trim-out, some jurisdictions require inspection after trim-out; this is generally a soft preference with local variance.
Rough openings must be framed and prepared to provide the structural support and correct dimensions for the storefront framing system to be installed.
Structural supports such as steel lintels above openings must be in place to carry the load of the storefront glazing and prevent deflection or collapse.
Waterproofing and air barriers must be applied to the rough opening to prevent moisture intrusion and air leakage behind the storefront system before it is sealed in place.
After the storefront frame and glass are installed, sealants and weatherstripping must be applied to seal joints, prevent air/water infiltration, and complete the enclosure.
Interior finishes around storefront openings are typically completed after the glazing is in place to allow for proper detailing and to avoid damaging finishes during glazing installation.
The bar counter requires structural support and wall framing to be in place before it can be securely mounted or attached.
If the bar counter includes a sink, drains, or water lines, plumbing rough-in must be completed before the bar counter is installed to allow access to pipes behind and beneath the counter.
Any electrical outlets, lighting, or wiring that will serve the bar area must be roughed in before the bar counter is built in place, as access to wall cavities will be blocked afterward.
The bar counter base and cabinetry must be fully installed and leveled before the countertop (e.g., granite, quartz, wood) can be fabricated and placed on top.
The backsplash tiles or panels behind the bar counter are installed after the counter and countertop are in place to create a seamless finish against the wall and counter surface.
The keg storage rack must be placed on a solid, level foundation slab to ensure stability and proper load distribution.
Floor drains must be installed before the keg rack is placed to ensure proper drainage and cleaning access beneath the rack.
Keg lines and couplers are physically connected to the kegs stored on the rack, so the rack must be in place first.
Kegs cannot be loaded onto the rack until the rack structure is fully assembled and anchored.
Lighting is often finalized after rack installation so that fixtures can be positioned to properly illuminate the rack area without obstruction.
The structural frame (walls, columns) must be in place to support the timber roof structure.
The roof deck or sheathing is typically installed first to provide a base and structural diaphragm, after which the exposed timber elements (beams, rafters) can be applied or exposed.
Insulation is placed above or between the exposed timber elements after the structure is complete.
Waterproofing layers are applied over the completed timber roof structure to protect it from weather.
Interior finishes (paint, stain, or cladding) on the exposed timber ceiling can only be applied after the timber structure is fully erected.
Electrical wiring must be installed and routed to pendant and lantern locations before the fixtures can be connected and mounted.
Ceiling structure must be complete to provide mounting support and finished surfaces for pendant lights.
Exterior wall surfaces must be finished to provide proper mounting for lantern fixtures and to seal against weather penetration.
While painting can be done before fixtures are installed, it is typically preferred to have lighting in place to identify any shadowing or blemishes; this is a soft sequencing preference.
All lighting fixtures must be installed before the system can be fully tested, energized, and commissioned for operation.
Structural framing, floor slabs, and load-bearing walls must be completed before any bar joinery can be installed, as the joinery relies on stable structural support and accurate floor levels.
Electrical conduits, power points, plumbing rough-ins and drainage lines for the bar sink and ice wells must be installed within the walls and floors before the bar joinery encloses them.
Waterproofing of the bar area and surrounding wet zones must be completed and tested before joinery installation to prevent water damage behind and beneath the bar.
The joinery carcasses, cabinetry and under-bar structure must be fully installed before the final bar top, benchtop or surface cladding is fitted on top.
Bar joinery must be in place to provide the supporting framework for mounting sinks, taps, and glass washers, and to allow final connection of supply and waste lines.
Beer lines require dedicated plumbing rough-ins (supply and drainage) to be in place before beer taps and lines can be installed and connected.
Floor surfaces must be completed before bar and tap equipment is placed to avoid damage to flooring and to provide a stable, clean base for installation.
Wall surfaces and backsplashes behind the bar area must be finished before taps and lines are mounted to avoid rework and damage to finished surfaces.
Taps and beer lines must be installed and connected before the final bar countertop is placed, as the countertop will cover access to the tap mounting hardware and line routing.

successor: Pressure Testing & Sanitization of Beer Lines
rationale: After beer lines and taps are physically installed, they must be pressure-tested and sanitized to ensure functionality and hygiene before the system is put into service.
The building structure must be complete to provide an enclosed space for kitchen installation, including load-bearing walls and roof.
Electrical wiring, conduit, and junction boxes must be installed in walls and ceilings before kitchen equipment can be connected and final fixtures mounted.
Water supply lines, drainage pipes, and grease trap plumbing must be roughed in behind walls and under floors before kitchen fixtures and equipment can be installed.
Kitchen ventilation hood ducts, makeup air ducts, and HVAC trunk lines must be installed in the ceiling/roof before kitchen hoods and equipment are placed.
The concrete floor must be poured, cured, and waterproofed (with proper slope to drains) before heavy kitchen equipment can be set in place.
After kitchen equipment is physically positioned, gas lines, electrical connections, water lines, and drainage can be connected to each appliance.
Fire suppression systems (Ansul systems) above cooking equipment must be installed after the kitchen hoods and cookline equipment are in place to ensure proper coverage.
While it is common to finish walls after equipment is set for a seamless look, it can be done beforehand in some cases; typically a soft preference for better fit and finish.
All kitchen equipment must be fully installed and in place before health department, fire marshal, and building code inspections can be conducted for final approval.

A clean, cured, and level concrete slab or prepared subfloor is required as the substrate for flooring installation. Any moisture issues, unevenness, or debris would compromise the flooring adhesion, finish, and longevity.

All in-floor conduits, piping, and underfloor services must be installed and inspected before flooring is laid. Once flooring is placed, access to these services would be extremely difficult or destructive.

In wet areas (bathrooms, kitchens, basements), waterproof membranes must be applied and tested prior to floor finishes to prevent moisture damage to the structure and to ensure the flooring system has a proper moisture barrier.

Flooring should be installed before final wall painting in most sequences so that painters can work from the finished floor level and avoid damaging freshly painted walls with floor installation equipment. However, sometimes skirting/trim installation may occur after painting.

Baseboards and skirting are installed over the finished flooring to cover the expansion gap and provide a clean transition between the floor and the wall. The flooring must be completed first to set the final floor height.

Structural foundations and slab work must be completed before outdoor landscaping can begin, as the ground needs to be stabilized and any underground utilities routed before surface-level landscaping.
The main building shell and envelope must be finished so that the biergarten area can be properly integrated, graded, and landscaped adjacent to the completed structure.
All underground utilities serving the outdoor area (irrigation lines, drainage, outdoor lighting conduits) must be roughed in before landscaping, grading, and planting can proceed.
Landscaping and soil preparation should be completed before final hardscape elements like patios and walkways are installed, to avoid disturbing finished paving.

successor: Exterior Amenities Installation (Furniture, Lighting Fixtures, Planters)
rationale: While it is preferable to install amenities after landscaping is complete to avoid damage, some amenities may be installed concurrently; however, final landscaping is best done before permanent fixtures to allow clean access for planting and grading.

The building must be structurally complete and enclosed before any interior fit-out work for a liquor-licensed venue can begin, as the liquor license typically requires defined premises boundaries and a weathertight structure.

The liquor license application must be submitted and approved before fit-out commences, as the fit-out must comply with all conditions stipulated in the license (e.g., sight lines, bar layout, CCTV placement, signage).

Fire authority and emergency services requirements (egress paths, fire suppression, occupancy limits) must be reviewed and integrated into the design before fit-out; liquor licensing authorities often require fire safety sign-off.
The fit-out work must be fully complete before the final regulatory inspection can be conducted by the liquor licensing authority to verify compliance with all conditions.
Liquor stock cannot be delivered or stored on premises until the fit-out is complete and all compliance requirements (e.g., secure storage, temperature-controlled areas, POS system) are operational.

predecessor: Rough-in electrical wiring for front desk area
rationale: Electrical wiring must be roughed in behind walls and floors before the counter structure is built, as the counter will cover the walls.

predecessor: Rough-in data/IT cabling for reception area
rationale: Data and network cabling for computers, phones, and point-of-sale systems must be run before the counter is installed so connections are accessible within or behind the counter.
Flooring should be laid before the counter is placed so the counter sits on top of finished flooring, avoiding uneven gaps or the need to cut flooring around the counter base.

successor: Electrical outlet and device installation at front desk
rationale: Once the counter is built, electrical outlets, computer terminals, phones, and other devices can be installed in or on the counter.
Final surface treatment, sealing, or polishing of the countertop must occur after the counter structure is fully assembled and in place.
The structural frame must be erected and stable to provide a support platform for the facade and exterior cladding systems to be attached.
Roof structure completion is often required before full facade installation to ensure weather-tight enclosure from above and to allow for proper sequencing of cladding attachments.
Exterior cladding must be in place to provide a weather-tight envelope before interior finishes like drywall are installed to prevent moisture damage.

Although often done concurrently, it is preferable to complete main cladding before installing windows to align openings precisely and seal against water infiltration; however, some systems are integrated.
Scaffolding used for cladding installation cannot be removed until the cladding work is fully complete, as scaffolding provides access and safety for the cladding crew.
Flooring must be installed before furniture placement to prevent damage to flooring from heavy furniture and to allow seamless installation without obstructions.
Wall painting and finishing must be completed before furniture is brought in to avoid paint splatters on furniture and to allow unobstructed access to walls.
Electrical outlets, switches, and wiring must be fully installed behind walls and accessible before furniture blocks access to walls.
Bed frame and box spring must be assembled and in place before mattress and bedding can be placed on top.

While curtains and blinds can be installed before furniture, it is often easier to access windows after furniture is placed to ensure proper length and clearance; this is a soft preference for convenience.
Window frames and rough openings must be constructed and properly sized before windows can be installed.
Weather-resistant barriers and flashing around openings must be in place to prevent moisture infiltration once windows are installed.
Structural lintels or headers above window openings must be installed to support loads before window units can be placed.
Windows must be installed before interior finishes can be completed around window openings and to ensure weathertight enclosure.
Window units must be in place so that exterior cladding materials can be properly flashed and sealed around the windows.
Window installation must precede interior trim work as architraves and sills are fitted directly around installed windows.
Window installation must be complete before air leakage and water penetration tests can be performed on the building envelope.
Windows are typically installed before final cleaning but protective films may remain until finishing work is complete.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated to the required depth before any structural framing can be erected, as the foundation system must be in place to support the frame.
Structural framing elements (steel columns, beams, or wood studs) require a stable, cured foundation to anchor to; without it there is no bearing surface or connection point.
Underground plumbing, electrical conduits, and drainage must be installed below the slab before the slab is poured and framing begins, as they cannot be easily accessed afterward.
The roof structure (trusses or rafters) must be framed and erected before roof decking, underlayment, and final covering can be installed, as the roof system relies directly on the frame for support.
Framing creates the wall cavities, ceiling plenums, and chase spaces through which MEP runs are routed; rough-in work cannot commence until the frame defines these spaces.
The structural frame must be complete to provide a stable load-bearing support for attaching facade elements such as curtain walls or cladding panels.
Floor slabs need to be in place to provide working platforms and anchorage points for facade installation crews and equipment.
Basic waterproofing must be applied to prevent water ingress that could damage interior finishes and affect facade anchoring systems.
Exterior envelope must be sealed before interior climate-controlled work begins to protect materials from weather exposure.
Facade structural support system must be in place before installing window units or glazing panels into the facade openings.
Facade installation must be completed before removing scaffolding that provides access to the building exterior.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in must be completed before FF&E installation to allow utility connections and avoid damage to finishes.
Ceiling grids and overhead work must be finished before installing furniture and equipment to prevent dust/debris falling on installed items.
Flooring must be laid and finished before furniture, fixtures, and equipment can be placed on top of it.
Wall finishing must be completed before FF&E is brought into the space to avoid damage to finished walls and allow access for painting and touch-ups.
While not a strict physical dependency, thorough cleaning before FF&E installation is strongly preferred to ensure clean surfaces and avoid moving furniture for later cleaning.
The building structure must be complete to provide the physical framework for installing accessibility features such as ramps, accessible routes, and door widening.
Electrical, plumbing and mechanical rough-ins must be in place before installing accessible fixtures, grab bars, height-adjusted outlets, and accessible restroom fittings.
Wall surfaces need to be finished before mounting accessible signage, handrails, visual alarms, and tactile indicators to ensure proper installation and code compliance.
Flooring must be installed after accessibility features such as ramps, level-thresholds, and tactile warning strips are in place to ensure seamless transitions and proper integration.
Accessibility compliance must be fully completed before the final building inspection and commissioning to verify that all accessibility requirements are met for occupancy permit.
The shelter/canopy structure requires a stable foundation or slab to be installed first to provide load-bearing support and a secure mounting surface.
Vertical support elements such as walls or columns must be erected before the shelter/canopy can be attached or mounted on top of them.
The shelter/canopy structure serves as the primary roof or overhead covering, so it must be in place before final roofing membranes or weatherproofing layers can be applied.
Overhead electrical wiring, conduit, or light fixtures installed beneath the canopy require the shelter structure to be in place first to provide attachment points and routing pathways.
Ceiling or soffit finishes below the canopy cannot be installed until the shelter/canopy framework is complete and structurally sound.
The ground area where the bench will be placed must be excavated and leveled before installing any fixed seating or waiting bench.
If the bench is anchored or bolted down, a concrete slab or foundation must be poured and cured before the bench can be installed.

If the waiting area includes charging ports or electronic displays integrated into the seating, underground electrical or data conduits should be roughed in before bench placement. However, this is a soft preference if the bench is standalone.
After the bench is installed, final wall painting, floor finishing, and touch-up work can be completed around the seating to avoid damaging the bench or requiring rework.
The waiting bench/seating must be fully installed and secured before the space can be considered ready for occupancy and handed over to the client.
The back panel or rear wall must be attached to a stable frame or structure; the frame must be erected first to provide a mounting surface and structural support.
Internal components (e.g., shelves, wiring, insulation) are typically installed after the rear wall is in place, as the back panel defines the enclosure and provides attachment points.
The rear wall closure is typically completed before the front-facing panels or doors are installed, ensuring the enclosure is sealed from the back before finishing the front.
The base or foundation must be level and ready to support the wall panel; installation of the rear wall requires a prepared base to anchor to.

While often done after the back panel is in place so wiring and pipes can be run within the wall cavity, some rough-in may precede wall installation; however, typically the panel provides the cavity access, making it a soft preference to install the back panel first.
The main structural frame must be erected before side panels or screens can be attached, as they require a stable supporting framework.
A solid foundation or base must be completed to provide a level and stable mounting surface for the side panels/screens.
Weatherproofing seals and gaskets are applied after side panels are installed to ensure the panels are properly sealed against the elements.
Interior finishes typically follow exterior panel installation to protect interior materials and allow for proper alignment with the exterior skin.

While not a strict physical requirement, it is generally preferable to complete side panels before running utilities within the wall cavities to avoid damaging exposed wiring or pipes during panel installation.
The ground must be excavated and leveled before support posts/columns can be installed, as they require a stable and prepared foundation.
Concrete footings or foundations must be poured and cured first to provide a solid base for anchoring the support posts or columns.
Primary beams or girders rest directly on top of support posts/columns, so the vertical supports must be in place before horizontal structural members can be installed.
Secondary beams and joists typically span between or are supported by primary beams and columns, requiring the columns to be erected first.
The roof structure rests upon the vertical support system (columns and beams), so columns must be completed before any roof framing can begin.
The ground must be excavated and prepared to the required levels and compaction before ramp sub-base can be laid.
A compacted sub-base layer is required to provide a stable foundation for the ramp structure before concrete or paving can be placed.
Any subsurface drainage pipes or trench drains that pass beneath or adjacent to the ramp must be installed before the ramp is built to avoid later excavation and disruption.
The ramp concrete or paving must be placed and initially set before any final surface texturing or anti-slip treatment can be applied.
Handrail posts or fixings are typically anchored into the ramp structure after the ramp is cast or constructed, as the ramp provides the structural base.

Tactile ground surface indicators and accessibility signage are applied after the ramp surface is finished, but some markings could theoretically be pre-planned; however, typically they follow ramp construction.

successor: Static Route Map / Timetable Board Installation
rationale: The static route map shows the track layout and station positions; tracks must be laid and aligned first to define the actual route geometry and station locations that will appear on the map.

successor: Static Route Map / Timetable Board Installation
rationale: The timetable board displays station names and service information; station platforms must be constructed to know the exact station locations and names to be shown on the board.

successor: Static Route Map / Timetable Board Installation
rationale: The static route map and timetable board require electrical power for illumination/backlighting; power supply must be installed and operational before the board can function.

predecessor: Static Route Map / Timetable Board Installation
successor: Passenger Information System Integration and Testing
rationale: The route map and timetable board is a component of the overall passenger information system; it must be physically installed before the system can be integrated, tested, and calibrated as a whole.

predecessor: Static Route Map / Timetable Board Installation
rationale: While the board can be installed earlier, it is preferred to complete surrounding finishes (wall cladding, signage frames) after the board is mounted to ensure proper alignment and aesthetic integration.
Electrical wiring and conduit must be installed to provide power and communication lines before the emergency call point/intercom device can be connected and mounted.
A mounting box or backbox must be securely installed in the wall or surface to house the wiring and provide a fixing point before the intercom/emergency call unit can be attached.
Wall surfaces must be finished (drywall, taping, painting) before mounting the device to ensure a proper fit, flush mounting, and a clean aesthetic finish.
The emergency call point/intercom must be installed and connected before the overall emergency communication system can be tested and commissioned for functionality.
All emergency call points and intercoms must be fully installed before the final inspection and regulatory sign-off can occur to verify compliance with safety codes.
The ground area must be cleared, leveled, and prepared before a litter bin can be placed to ensure stability and proper positioning.
If the litter bin requires a concrete base or pad for anchorage, the concrete must be poured and cured before the bin can be installed on top of it.
Utility lines (gas, water, electricity) must be located and marked to avoid damage when digging or anchoring the litter bin.

It is preferable to install the bin before final landscaping and paving finishes so that the area can be graded and finished around the bin for a neat appearance, though bins can be added after landscaping if needed.
Litter bins must be in place before the final site clean-up and inspection so that they are available for use and can be checked for proper installation and compliance.
The advertising panel or poster case needs a structural frame or wall surface to be mounted onto; without the underlying structure, there is no support for the panel.

If the advertising panel requires backlighting or electrical connection, the electrical rough-in (wiring, conduits) must be completed before the panel is installed, as access behind the panel will be restricted afterwards.
After installing the advertising panel, final finishing work such as sealing edges, caulking, or painting around the panel should be done to achieve a clean finished look.
The poster case or advertising panel must be installed and secured before any graphic film, poster, or advertisement is applied to it.
The installation of the advertising panel must be completed and verified before final inspection and sign-off can occur, as the panel is part of the completed works.
Ground must be excavated to proper depth and dimensions before any foundation work can begin, as the foundation rests on prepared subgrade.
The soil/base must be properly compacted and leveled to provide adequate bearing capacity for the foundation, preventing uneven settlement.
Accurate positioning and alignment must be marked on site to ensure the foundation is placed in the correct location and orientation.
After the foundation concrete is placed, it requires sufficient curing time to achieve required strength before any load-bearing activities can proceed.

Reinforcement bars are placed within the foundation formwork before concrete is poured; however, if referring to additional structural steel columns, they can only be erected after the foundation has cured.
The bus stop sign or flag pole requires a stable base or foundation to be installed first in order to be securely mounted and remain upright.
The pole structure must be erected before any signage or flag can be physically attached to it.
While often coordinated, the sign/pole typically marks the stop location and can be installed before the shelter structure is built around or near it.
The Stop ID / QR Code Plate must be mounted on a physical pole, so the pole must be installed first to provide a stable mounting surface.
The exact stop location must be surveyed and marked to determine where the pole and ID plate should be placed.

predecessor: Stop ID / QR Code Plate Installation
rationale: The unique identifier from the installed plate must be registered in the system before the stop can be activated in digital databases.

predecessor: Stop ID / QR Code Plate Installation
rationale: The installed plate must be physically in place before it can be visually inspected and verified for correctness and legibility.

predecessor: Stop ID / QR Code Plate Fabrication
successor: Stop ID / QR Code Plate Installation
rationale: The plate must be manufactured/fabricated before it can be transported to the site and installed on the pole.
The sub-grade must be prepared and compacted to provide a stable foundation for the kerb installation; otherwise the kerb will settle or shift.
A concrete bed or haunch is required to set and support the kerb stones in position before they can be aligned and finished.

predecessor: Drainage installation (if kerb includes drainage channels)
rationale: Any drainage pipes or channels beneath or adjacent to the kerb must be laid before the kerb is placed to avoid later excavation and disturbance.
The kerb defines the edge of the pavement; adjacent asphalt or concrete paving is laid up to the kerb to ensure a neat interface and proper runoff.
Mortar joints between kerb units must be pointed after the kerbs are aligned and set; this seals the joints against water ingress and frost damage.
Road markings must be applied on a finished, cured pavement surface to ensure proper adhesion and longevity.
Proper sub-base is required before any pavement layer can be placed to provide structural support.
Traffic signals can be operational before or after markings, but final calibration and testing should align with visible stop bars and bus stop boxes.
Lighting installation can proceed independently, but markings are typically done after pavement and before final street furniture adjustments.
All traffic markings including bus stop boxes must be complete before final inspection and project handover.
The ground must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and uneven terrain before any shelter installation or foundation work can begin to ensure a stable and level base.
Underground utilities such as water, electricity, and sewer lines must be trenched and laid before foundations are poured to avoid digging under or disturbing completed foundations.
Soil must be tested and compacted to the required load-bearing capacity before pouring foundations to prevent settlement or structural failure.
The shelter foundation and base installation must be complete and cured before any superstructure framing can be erected on top of it.
Rough-in work for electrical and plumbing systems within the shelter cannot begin until the shelter structure and its foundation are installed.
A stable, compacted sub-base is required to support the platform surface and kerbs; without proper sub-base preparation, the surfacing would lack structural integrity and would settle or crack.
Drainage systems (pipes, gullies, drains) must be installed beneath or adjacent to the platform before surfacing, otherwise the finished surface would need to be broken up to install drainage later.
Underground utility ducts and service trenches must be laid prior to surfacing to avoid excavating through the finished platform surface.
Line marking, pedestrian symbols, and signage posts are applied to or mounted on the finished platform surface; they cannot be installed before the surfacing and kerbs are in place.

Benches, shelters, and bins are typically installed after surfacing to avoid damage to the new surface, though this is a soft preference as they could theoretically be installed concurrently with careful sequencing.
Tactile surfaces (warning strips, directional indicators) must be installed on a stable, cured concrete substrate to ensure proper adhesion and levelness.
The concrete surface must be smoothed, cleaned, and prepared to receive tactile pavers or coatings for proper bonding and compliance with slip-resistance standards.
Inspection must follow tactile surface installation to verify compliance with accessibility codes (ADA/AS 1428) regarding placement, contrast, and dimensions before project closeout.
It is preferable to clean the site after tactile surfaces are installed to avoid damaging them, but not a hard physical constraint if cleaning is done carefully around them.
The maintenance and cleaning programme can only begin once the building construction is fully complete, as maintenance activities are performed on the finished building structure.
All defects and snags must be rectified before the formal maintenance programme starts, otherwise cleaning and maintenance would be performed on incomplete or defective work.
The building must be formally handed over and all systems commissioned before a maintenance and cleaning regime can be established and implemented.
After the maintenance programme is in place, periodic inspections and reporting can follow as ongoing quality assurance activities, though this is a logical sequence rather than a physical necessity.
Waste disposal and recycling operations are a direct outcome of the cleaning activities within the programme, so they must succeed the maintenance and cleaning programme.
Menu display boards are typically mounted on or recessed into walls, requiring the wall structure (framing, drywall) to be in place before the board can be securely installed.
Most digital or illuminated menu display boards require electrical power, so the electrical wiring and outlet/box must be roughed in before the board can be connected and mounted.
The physical board must be installed, powered, and connected before software content can be loaded, tested, and validated for display.

successor: Final interior finishing and trim work
rationale: While trim and finishing can be done after board installation, it is a soft preference since touch-up paint or trim around the board is aesthetically better done after the board is mounted to ensure a clean fit.

If the menu display board is suspended or mounted from the ceiling, the ceiling structure must be complete to provide the anchor points. Even for wall-mounted boards, overhead work should finish first to avoid dust and debris damaging the board.
Structural framing must be complete to provide the load-bearing support and mounting surface for the cooking equipment platform.
Utility lines such as gas, electrical, and plumbing must be roughed in before the platform is installed to allow access for connections and avoid rework.
The platform must be completed and stable before cooking equipment can be placed and secured on it.
Final hookups of gas, electrical, and plumbing to the cooking appliances can only proceed after the platform and equipment are in position.
While it is preferable to apply final finishes after platform installation, this could be done beforehand if logistics dictate; thus it is a soft preference.
Ventilation hoods must be connected to ductwork to exhaust air; ducts must be in place before the hood can be mounted and connected.
Ventilation hoods require electrical power for fan and lights; wiring and outlet boxes must be installed before the hood can be wired.
The hood is typically mounted under or through the ceiling; ceiling structure and finish must be completed to provide a mounting surface.
The ventilation hood is installed above the cooking surface; the range or cooktop is placed beneath the hood after the hood is in place.
After the hood is physically mounted, final duct connections, sealing, and testing can be completed to ensure proper exhaust function.
The condenser unit must be installed first as it provides the necessary cooling capacity and refrigerant flow required for the refrigeration unit to function.
