Refrigerant piping must be run between the condenser and the refrigeration unit before the unit can be connected and installed.
Power supply wiring and electrical connections must be roughed in to provide electricity for the refrigeration unit's operation.
The refrigeration unit must be fully installed and connected before refrigerant can be charged into the system.
Commissioning and testing can only occur after the refrigeration unit is installed and all connections are made.

The utility connection panel is typically installed in a designated location (e.g., exterior wall or utility room) that requires the ground or foundation to be prepared and excavated for incoming utility lines.
The utility connection panel is often mounted on or near the foundation wall, so the foundation and slab must be in place to provide a stable mounting surface and proper anchorage.

The utility connection panel serves as the point of entry for incoming utility power; the main electrical panel cannot be connected to the grid until the utility connection panel is installed and approved.

The internal electrical rough-in (running branch circuits throughout the building) depends on the main panel being fed from the utility connection panel; power distribution cannot begin without the utility service entry.
The utility meter is typically installed adjacent to or directly downstream of the utility connection panel, and the meter cannot be set until the connection panel is in place and wired.

predecessor: Plumbing Rough-In (Hot & Cold Water Supply Lines)
rationale: Water supply lines must be roughed in and stubbed out at the sink location before the sink can be physically connected to the water source.
Waste drain and vent piping must be installed behind the wall before the sink's P-trap can be connected to the drainage system.
The wall structure must be built to provide mounting support for the sink (whether wall-mounted or supported by brackets).
Wall surfaces should be finished and waterproofed behind the sink area before the sink is mounted to prevent moisture damage and allow proper sealing.

successor: Sink Trim & Fixture Connection (Faucet, Trap, Supply Stops)
rationale: The sink bowl must be set in place before faucets, supply lines, and the P-trap can be physically connected to it.
The sink and its connected fixtures must be fully installed to be included in the water supply system pressure test and flushing procedure.
The sink must be completely installed and functional for the plumbing inspector to verify compliance with code.

Structural steel framing must be in place to support the building envelope and provide the structural grid before storage shelving can be installed, as shelving depends on the building's structural framework for alignment and support.
A finished, level floor slab is required as the base for storage shelving to ensure stability, load distribution, and proper anchoring of the shelving units.

Overhead utilities such as electrical conduits, HVAC ducts, and plumbing pipes must be installed before storage shelving, as shelving may obstruct access to overhead work and it is inefficient to install shelving before overhead rough-in is complete.

While floor finishing can be done before shelving, if the shelving is installed first then final sealing or coating around the shelving feet is a soft preference to avoid damaging the finish during shelving installation.
Storage shelving must be fully installed, anchored, and inspected before any inventory or materials are placed on the racks to ensure structural safety and stability.
The waste bin enclosure requires a stable, level concrete base or slab to be poured and cured before the enclosure structure can be built upon it.
Waste bins can only be placed inside the enclosure after the enclosure walls, foundation, and gate/door are fully constructed and the space is prepared.
Proper grading and drainage around the enclosure area must be completed to prevent water pooling and ensure the enclosure is positioned at the correct elevation.

predecessor: Utility Rough-Ins (if any lighting or drainage nearby)
rationale: If underground utilities or drainage pipes are planned near the enclosure area, they are typically roughed-in prior to pouring the slab or building the enclosure to avoid rework.
Landscaping, paving, or hardscaping adjacent to the enclosure is usually completed after the enclosure structure is in place to ensure tidy edges and proper alignment.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated to the required depth before any foundation work can begin, as the foundation requires a stable, prepared bearing surface.
Soil bearing capacity and ground conditions must be assessed to determine the foundation design and depth requirements; without this data, the slab cannot be safely designed or poured.
Underground utility pipes (drainage, water, electrical conduit) must be laid and inspected before the slab is poured, as these are embedded in or run beneath the concrete slab.
The structural framing of walls and roof requires a cured, load-bearing concrete slab or foundation to anchor and support the vertical and lateral loads.

Waterproofing membranes and damp-proof coatings are applied directly onto the foundation walls and slab edges; once the slab is cured, these protective layers can be installed to prevent moisture ingress.
Site must be excavated and prepared before any underground utilities can be installed, as rough-in work typically occurs in open trenches before foundation/pour.
Underground conduits and piping for electrical, plumbing, and HVAC must be laid in the gravel bed beneath the slab or within the foundation walls before concrete is poured.
All underground rough-in work (plumbing drains, electrical conduits, etc.) must be completed and inspected before concrete is poured, as access is permanently blocked afterward.
Trenches for utility lines must be backfilled and graded only after rough-in pipes and conduits are installed and inspected.
Interior rough-in of plumbing, electrical, and HVAC in walls and floors must follow the underground/slab rough-in, as the below-grade utility stubs must be in place to connect to.
The structural framing provides the load-bearing support system that the canopy or awning attaches to, making it a physical prerequisite.
Roof sheathing creates the underlying deck surface that anchors the canopy or awning and ensures proper water shedding.
Exterior wall finishes must be completed before installing canopies or awnings to ensure proper flashing, sealing, and aesthetic integration against the finished wall surface.

Final trim and decorative elements around the canopy or awning are typically installed after the main unit is in place, but this is a logical sequencing preference rather than a physical impossibility to do otherwise.

Exterior lighting under or near a canopy or awning is typically installed after the canopy is in place to ensure correct positioning and wiring routing, though it could theoretically be done before with careful planning.
The site must be set up with basic safety measures (e.g., welfare facilities, signage, access routes) before a formal health and safety inspection can meaningfully assess compliance.
Excavation and groundworks create significant hazards (trenches, unstable ground) that must be inspected for safety compliance before other work proceeds.
Scaffolding must be fully erected and inspected for safety before it can be deemed safe for workers; a health and safety inspection verifies scaffold integrity and guardrails.
Major construction activities should only commence after the initial health and safety inspection has confirmed that the site setup and protective measures meet regulatory standards.
While routine follow-up inspections typically happen after the initial one, this is a procedural preference for continuous monitoring rather than a strict physical dependency.

Equipment requires stable, cured foundations and concrete slabs to be properly anchored and aligned. Installing equipment before foundations are complete would result in misalignment and structural failure.
Overhead cranes, support beams, and building framework must be in place to lift and position heavy equipment. Without structural steel, there is no means to hoist or support large machinery.
Electrical conduits, panels, and power supply infrastructure must be roughed in before equipment can be connected to power sources and commissioned.
Plumbing connections, piping, and HVAC duct routes must be installed before equipment that requires water, gas, or ventilation connections is placed and commissioned.

Major equipment must be installed and operational before enclosing walls, applying final finishes, or completing ceilings, as equipment may need to be moved into position through unfinished spaces and to avoid damage to finished surfaces.
The Nap Pod requires a stable, level surface to rest on; the floor slab provides the structural support needed before any component can be placed.

predecessor: Rough-in electrical wiring to pod location
rationale: Electrical connections for lighting, ventilation, or charging ports within the Nap Pod must be roughed-in before the pod is positioned, as access behind or under the pod will be restricted after placement.
After the Nap Pod is set in its final position, the electrical connections can be made and finished trim installed around the pod for a clean appearance and safe operation.

successor: Interior finishing and sealing around pod
rationale: Once the pod is in place, the perimeter seals, caulking, and any adjacent wall finishes can be completed to integrate the pod seamlessly into the built environment.

Acoustic performance testing of the soundproofing and ventilation system should follow pod installation to verify occupancy comfort, though it could theoretically be deferred, it is best done immediately after installation.
The recliner chair's frame must be fully assembled before the recliner mechanism and upholstery can be added, as the frame provides the structural foundation.
The reclining mechanical components (springs, levers, gears) must be manufactured or sourced prior to integration into the chair assembly.
The bare frame and mechanism must be assembled first so that foam padding, fabric, and cushion covers can be applied over the structure.
The fully assembled recliner chair must be completed before it can undergo functional testing (e.g., recline motion checks, weight capacity tests) and final adjustments.
The chair must be fully assembled and tested before it can be packaged, wrapped, and prepared for shipment to retailers or customers.
The acoustic privacy screen requires a structural frame or support system to be installed first, as the screen panels or components are mounted onto it.
Overhead structures (such as ceiling grids or overhead supports) must be in place before ceiling-mounted acoustic screens can be installed.

successor: Finish wall and ceiling finishing (paint, texture)
rationale: While it is preferable to complete finishing work after screen installation to avoid damage, it is a soft preference as touch-ups can be performed later.
Acoustic performance testing can only occur after the privacy screen is fully installed to verify that it meets the specified sound transmission requirements.
Electrical and data cabling in the wall or ceiling cavity must be completed before the acoustic screen is installed, as the screen may block access to these services.
Blackout curtains or blinds are typically mounted to or within window frames, so the window frame must be installed first to provide a structural attachment point.
Wall finishing around the window area must be completed before installing curtains or blinds to avoid damaging finished surfaces during mounting and to ensure proper alignment with the finished wall.

predecessor: Electrical Wiring for Window Covering Controls
rationale: If the blackout curtain or blind is motorized or automated, electrical wiring and outlets near the window should be roughed in before installation to allow for power connection.
Final interior decorating and furniture placement is typically done after window coverings are installed so that furniture layout can account for the curtain/blind position and light control.
Blackout curtains or blinds are near-final finishing items; their completion allows the space to be presented as finished for inspection or occupant handover.

successor: Booking and Access Control Kiosk Installation
rationale: The kiosk requires a stable, level foundation and slab to be placed upon; cannot be installed on unprepared ground.

successor: Booking and Access Control Kiosk Installation
rationale: The kiosk needs electrical power and network/ data connectivity; underground conduits and wiring must be in place before the kiosk can be connected and commissioned.

predecessor: Booking and Access Control Kiosk Installation
successor: Kiosk System Configuration and Software Setup
rationale: Physical installation of the hardware must be complete before software, firmware, and access control system configuration can be performed on-site.

predecessor: Booking and Access Control Kiosk Installation
successor: Final Finishes and Landscaping Around Kiosk
rationale: Surrounding paving, curbing, or landscaping can be completed after the kiosk is in place to ensure proper alignment and access, though it is a soft preference as it could be done concurrently with careful planning.

predecessor: Booking and Access Control Kiosk Installation
rationale: End-to-end testing of booking functions and access control mechanisms requires the kiosk to be physically installed, powered, and networked before tests can be executed.
Wall framing and drywall must be completed before lockers can be mounted or placed against walls, as lockers are typically anchored to finished walls.
Flooring must be finished before lockers are installed, as lockers are heavy and would damage unfinished flooring, and they need a level finished surface for proper placement.
Electrical wiring for lighting or power near locker areas must be roughed in before lockers obstruct wall access.
After locker installation, any touch-up painting or finishing around the lockers can be performed to cover scratches or marks from installation.
Lockers and personal storage must be fully installed and functional before occupants can move in and use the storage spaces.
The structural framework must be complete to provide the mounting surfaces and load-bearing support required for sleeping pod installation.
Electrical wiring, plumbing lines, and HVAC ductwork must be roughed in behind walls and ceilings before pods are installed, as pods would obstruct access to these systems.
The floor must be leveled and waterproofed to provide a stable, moisture-protected base for the sleeping pods.
Once pods are in their final position, electrical and plumbing connections can be made from the building's systems into each individual pod.
After pods are installed and secured, interior finishes such as trim, sealing joints, and final aesthetic treatments can be applied around and between pods.

The building structure must be fully enclosed and weathertight before acoustic treatment can be installed, as acoustic materials (e.g., insulation, panels) are sensitive to moisture and require a stable substrate to adhere to or be mounted on.

Ductwork, piping, conduits, and electrical boxes must be roughed in before acoustic treatments are applied, since these services run within walls and ceilings that will be covered by acoustic panels or insulation, and accessing them afterward would damage the acoustic finishes.

Acoustic treatments (e.g., acoustic panels, spray-on coatings, or sound-absorbing insulation behind wall linings) are typically installed as part of or just prior to final interior finishes, and applying paint or wallcoverings over or after acoustic surfaces would damage or reduce the acoustic performance.

While not a physical constraint, it is a technical preference to calibrate and test the acoustic environment (e.g., reverberation time, sound isolation) only after all acoustic treatments are fully installed, to ensure accurate measurement and optimization of the space.
Space planning and interior design must be completed to determine the exact layout, furniture specifications, and equipment requirements before procurement can begin.
Flooring, wall finishes, and other interior finishes must be installed before FF&E can be placed to avoid damaging finishes or requiring rework.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work and ceiling installation must be completed before FF&E is brought in to prevent interference with MEP systems and allow access for installation.
After all furniture, fixtures, and equipment are installed, a final cleaning and punch list walk-through is needed to address any damage, debris, or issues caused during installation.
FF&E must be fully installed and in place before occupants can move in and begin using the space, as the building would be uninhabitable without essential furniture and equipment.

The construction site must be established with basic facilities (site offices, worker amenities, fencing) before hygiene protocols can be implemented, as there needs to be a defined physical area and infrastructure to apply cleaning standards to.
Plumbing rough-ins for washrooms, handwashing stations, and drainage systems must be installed to enable running water, which is essential for effective hygiene and cleaning protocols.
Temporary water supply and electrical connections must be in place to power cleaning equipment and provide water for sanitation activities.

Before beginning interior finishing such as painting, flooring, and cabinetry installation, the work area must be cleaned and hygiene protocols established to ensure dust and debris are minimized and a clean environment is maintained for sensitive finishes.
The final inspection and handover phase requires the site to be clean and hygiene protocols actively maintained to meet health and safety standards before building occupancy.
The ground must be properly leveled and prepared before any structure, including the security gatehouse, can be erected.
A structural foundation must be poured and cured before the gatehouse structure can be built or installed on top of it.

Electrical power and data/communication lines for gatehouse operations (barrier controls, cameras, intercom) must be laid in underground conduits before the gatehouse slab is poured or the structure placed.
The gatehouse serves as the control point for vehicular and pedestrian access; gates, barriers, and bollards are positioned relative to the gatehouse and rely on its electrical and control systems.
The gatehouse defines the controlled entry point; adjacent fencing and gates must align with the gatehouse layout and tie into its security infrastructure.

successor: Final Paving & Road Markings at Entrance
rationale: Road surfaces and lane markings around the entry point should be completed after the gatehouse and barriers are installed to ensure proper alignment with approach lanes, queuing areas, and island positions.
Once the gatehouse structure, power, and barriers are in place, access control, CCTV, intercom, and alarm systems can be installed, connected, and tested as an integrated security solution.
The structural frame requires a stable and level base provided by the completed foundation to transfer loads properly.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated before any structural frame elements can be erected.
Floor slabs are typically poured after the structural frame is in place to integrate with the frame's support system.
The building envelope or cladding system must be attached to the completed structural frame for support.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work follows the structural frame because the frame defines the spaces and supports for MEP systems.
The substrate (concrete, deck, or wall) must be properly prepared, cleaned, and cured to provide a sound base for expansion joint installation.
Formwork defines the joint location and alignment; the expansion joint assembly must be placed within or against the formed opening before concrete placement.
Reinforcing steel must be in place and properly positioned around the joint area before the expansion joint assembly is installed, as the joint may interrupt reinforcement continuity.
Expansion joint assemblies are typically embedded or set in place before concrete is poured so they become integral to the structure; pouring after joint installation seals the joint in place.

After the expansion joint assembly is fully installed and any surrounding concrete has cured, the joint sealant or filler material is applied to complete the water-tight or movement-accommodating system.
A stable, graded subgrade is physically required to provide a level and compacted foundation for the utility tunnel/culvert structure, preventing differential settlement and structural failure.
Groundwater must be lowered or diverted before excavation and placement of the tunnel/culvert to maintain a dry working environment and prevent soil instability or flotation of the structure.
Existing underground utilities in the tunnel/culvert alignment must be relocated or protected prior to excavation to avoid damage, service outages, and safety hazards.

Backfill over and around the completed tunnel/culvert can only be placed after the structure is fully installed, cured (if cast-in-place), and approved, as the backfill provides lateral support and protects the structure.

Pipes, cables, and other utilities can only be placed inside the tunnel/culvert after the structural shell is complete and accessible, providing a safe enclosed space for subsequent installation work.
The site must be acquired and selected before any master planning or layout design can commence, as the planning is inherently tied to the specific site's characteristics, boundaries, and conditions.

Subsurface soil conditions, bearing capacities, and site geology data are essential inputs for deciding building placements, foundation types, and overall site layout, so investigations must precede planning.
Environmental constraints, protected areas, and mitigation requirements must be identified before layout design to ensure compliance and avoid rework of site plans.
The master plan defines building footprints, access roads, utility corridors, and spatial relationships that provide the framework for detailed design of individual structures and systems.
The site layout plan identifies which areas require clearing, which structures to demolish, and the sequence of earthworks, so clearing operations cannot begin until the layout is approved.
Site conditions, geotechnical data, and environmental constraints must be understood before planning construction phases to ensure feasibility and safety.
Regulatory approvals and overall development plans establish the legal and spatial framework within which phased construction can be sequenced.
Design concepts and initial drawings define the scope and interfaces between phases, which are necessary to develop an effective sequencing strategy.
The sequencing plan dictates the order of mobilization, staging areas, and preparation work across phases; physical site work cannot begin without an approved sequence.
Construction execution follows the defined sequence; Phase 1 construction can only start after the overall phased sequencing plan has been established.

Site investigation must be completed first to identify soil conditions, groundwater levels, and potential contamination, which informs the design and methodology of bulk earthworks and site preparation.
Engineering design, including grading plans, drainage design, and earthwork specifications, must be finalized before bulk earthworks can proceed to ensure correct cut/fill volumes and site levels.
Regulatory approvals such as earthworks permits, environmental clearance, and development consents are legally required before commencing bulk earthmoving activities.
Bulk earthworks provide the final graded and compacted platform required to support foundation construction; foundations cannot be placed on ungraded or uncompacted ground.

Underground services such as stormwater drainage, sewer lines, and utility conduits are typically installed after bulk earthworks are complete to ensure correct depths, bedding, and protection within the prepared subgrade.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated before any shared infrastructure (like utility trenches, foundations for shared equipment rooms, etc.) can be installed.
Primary underground ducts for power, data, and water must be laid before shared infrastructure hubs or distribution points are placed on top or connected.

Shared infrastructure (e.g., main power distribution, central water supply, sewage lines, shared data backbone) must be in place before individual buildings can connect to and draw from these central systems.
Roads and pavements should be laid after shared underground utilities are installed to avoid digging up finished roads for utility access.

Final landscaping is typically done after shared infrastructure is in place to avoid rework, but in some cases landscaping can be phased in parallel; thus it is a soft preference rather than a hard physical constraint.
The structural frame must be complete to provide the load-bearing support and attachment points for the facade system across buildings.
The facade design, materials, and performance specifications must be approved before coordination can proceed to ensure alignment with architectural and engineering requirements.
Accurate site survey data and as-built dimensions are needed to coordinate the facade across multiple buildings and account for any deviations.
The cross-building coordination plan must be finalized before installation can begin on any individual building to ensure consistent alignment, joint detailing, and material scheduling.
Installation at Building B depends on the coordinated facade plan to match interfaces, expansion joints, and aesthetic continuity between buildings.
While not physically mandatory, coordinating facade layout early allows MEP rough-in (e.g., duct penetrations, lighting raceways) to align with facade module locations, reducing rework.

predecessor: Substantial Completion / All Construction Works Complete
rationale: All construction works must be physically complete before commissioning and integrated systems testing can begin, as testing requires the installed systems to be in place and operational.
MEP systems must be fully installed before they can be commissioned and tested as an integrated whole.

predecessor: Pre-Commissioning Checks and Individual System Testing
rationale: Individual systems and components must be verified and tested in isolation before integrated systems testing can commence, to ensure each subsystem is functioning correctly before integration.

Commissioning and integrated systems testing must be successfully completed before the building can be handed over to the owner or occupants, to certify that all systems perform as designed and are safe for use.

Although often part of an overall process, formal performance verification and acceptance testing typically follows integrated systems testing to validate the entire building's performance against design specifications.

Estate management and facilities management setup can only begin once the construction works are completed and the building is handed over, as FM operations require a finished physical asset to manage.

Before occupants can move in and daily building operations can commence, the estate management and FM setup (including maintenance contracts, systems commissioning, security protocols, and service providers) must be established and operational.

While post-occupancy evaluation can technically begin during early occupancy, it is more effective and systematic after FM setup is complete so that all building systems and management processes are in place to be evaluated.
The foundation must be completed to provide a stable base before any floor-to-floor height can be established.
Vertical structural elements such as columns and the core define the vertical spacing and must be in place to establish the floor-to-floor height.
The floor-to-floor height must be determined before floor slabs or decks can be installed at that elevation.
MEP systems are routed within the vertical space between floors; the floor-to-floor height must be set to plan vertical chases, risers, and ductwork.

Although partitions often follow after slabs, the floor height influences wall height design; this is a soft preference as partitions could theoretically be planned concurrently but are typically finalized after the floor height is set.
The structural frame (beams, slabs, and columns) defines the basic vertical space; clear height cannot be determined or verified until the primary structure is in place.
The finished floor elevation must be established before any measurement or realization of clear height can occur.
MEP trades (ductwork, piping, conduit) need the confirmed clear height to coordinate routing and avoid conflicts with the finished ceiling plane.
The suspended ceiling system is hung from the overhead structure, and its elevation depends directly on the target clear height.
While some wall layout can be done from the floor plan alone, precise top-of-wall heights are often aligned with the clear height to ensure partitions meet the ceiling uniformly.
The foundation must be constructed before the building height can be established, as the building's vertical structure relies on a stable base.
The site must be prepared and excavated before any vertical construction can begin, which determines the building's total height.
The structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) must be erected to achieve the building's total height.
The roof can only be installed once the building has reached its full height.
Facade and cladding work can only begin after the building's total height is achieved, as cladding follows the vertical structure.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and geotechnically investigated before any multi-story construction can begin to ensure stable foundation conditions.
The foundation design must be finalized and approved before multi-story construction starts, as the superstructure depends on the completed foundation system.
Excavation, piling, and foundation pouring must be fully completed before any vertical multi-story construction can commence, as the building loads transfer through the foundation.
The structural frame and all floor slabs must be completed before roofing can begin to provide weather protection and structural support for the roof.

While some rough-in work for mechanical, electrical, and plumbing can start earlier, full MEP installation typically follows multi-story construction completion to avoid rework and coordinate with finished structure.
The structural frame must be complete to provide a stable load-bearing support for the façade system; façade panels cannot be anchored to an incomplete frame.

predecessor: Floor Slab Pour and Cure per Story
rationale: Floor slabs must be poured and cured to establish the working platform and anchoring points for façade installation at each story level.

The façade must be installed to enclose the building envelope before interior rough-in work begins, protecting interior spaces and materials from weather exposure during mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-ins.
Façade panels must be in place so that all joints, seams, and perimeter seals can be applied to achieve a continuous weather-tight barrier.

It is strongly preferred to complete façade installation before interior finishes to prevent weather damage to finished surfaces, though interior work could theoretically proceed in conditioned temporary enclosures at additional cost.
Reinforcement steel must be placed and tied in columns and walls before concrete can be poured, as the rebar provides structural reinforcement that is encased by the concrete.
Formwork molds must be erected to contain and shape the wet concrete during pouring and curing for columns and walls on that floor.
The slab formwork deck must be in place to support the freshly poured concrete floor slab until it gains sufficient strength to be self-supporting.
Reinforcing steel mesh or rebar for the slab must be positioned and tied on the formwork before concrete is poured over it to create a reinforced concrete slab.
Any embedded items such as electrical conduits, plumbing sleeves, anchor bolts, or embeds must be placed and secured in the formwork prior to concrete pour, as they cannot be installed afterward.
After pouring, the concrete must undergo a curing period to develop design strength before any loads are applied or subsequent construction proceeds on that slab.
Forms and shoring can only be removed after the poured concrete has sufficiently cured and reached adequate strength to support itself and imposed loads.

successor: Vertical Structure Pour (Columns/Walls on Next Floor)
rationale: The floor slab must be poured and cured before constructing the vertical elements (columns/walls) on the next story, as they bear on or are tied into that completed floor.
Interior partition walls are typically built after the floor slab is poured and cured to provide a level working surface and to allow layout from the finished slab.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work on a floor often begins after the slab is poured so that piping and ductwork can be hung from the finished structure.

Vertical MEP risers run through structural shafts, floor penetrations, and core walls. The structural frame, slabs, and core walls must be in place to provide the physical support and openings through which risers are installed.
Sleeves, inserts, and embedded conduits must be cast into floor slabs and walls before riser pipes, ducts, and cables can be routed vertically through those penetrations.
Horizontal branch runs (e.g., on each floor) take off from the vertical risers. The riser mains must be installed and terminated at each floor level before horizontal distribution can be connected.

Firestopping materials are applied around MEP risers where they pass through fire-rated floors and walls. This sealing cannot be completed until the riser pipes, ducts, and cables are in place within the openings.

successor: MEP System Pressure Testing and Commissioning
rationale: Risers must be fully installed and connected before the overall MEP systems (plumbing, HVAC, electrical) can be pressure-tested, flushed, and commissioned as complete systems.

The ground or foundation area must be cleared, leveled, and compacted to provide a stable base for crane outriggers, tracks, or the tower crane foundation, preventing tipping or instability during setup and operation.
A tower crane requires a reinforced concrete foundation (or anchor bolts embedded in a foundation) to be cured and structurally ready before the crane mast sections can be erected and anchored.
The crane or hoist must be fully assembled, tested, and operational before any materials or equipment can be lifted vertically to elevated work areas.
Heavy steel beams, columns, and trusses typically require a crane for placement; therefore crane setup must precede steel erection activities.

successor: Formwork and Concrete Placement for Elevated Slabs
rationale: Elevated concrete slabs (e.g., decks, floors) require hoisted formwork materials, rebar, and concrete via crane or hoist, so the lifting equipment must be operational first.
The structural steel framework must be erected to provide support for the parking roof slab.
The parking roof slab must be fully cured and complete before waterproofing can be applied to ensure a proper waterproof seal.
Roof insulation is installed on top of the completed parking roof slab.
The final wearing surface or topping is placed after the parking roof slab is complete to protect the structural slab.
The poured concrete for the parking roof slab must reach sufficient curing strength before any subsequent loads or activities can begin on the slab.
Parking bay markings must be applied onto a finished paved surface. The paving provides the stable, smooth base required for paint or thermoplastic markings to adhere properly and remain durable.
Freshly laid asphalt or concrete must fully cure before markings are applied, otherwise the marking materials will not bond correctly and may be damaged by residual moisture or surface instability.

After parking bay markings are applied, the overall striping layout (including directional arrows, stop lines, and pedestrian crossings) is completed as a final finishing step before the area can be opened for vehicle use.
The structural opening (wall/frame) must be constructed and finished before a roller door can be installed, as the door frame requires a structurally sound opening to be fixed to.

predecessor: Door Frame Preparation / Head and Jamb Installation
rationale: The roller door curtain and tracks mount to the head, jambs, and lintel; these must be in place before the shutter assembly can be fitted.
If the shutter is motorised, the electrical supply conduit and wiring to the motor location must be roughed in before the door mechanism is installed to avoid later rework.

Roller door tracks often sit on or near the finished floor level; final floor screed or paving should be completed after door installation so the door can be aligned to the correct finished floor height.
Final wiring connection, motor commissioning, and safety sensor testing can only occur once the shutter door is physically installed in its opening.
The slab or foundation must be in place before any mechanical or electrical rough-in work can begin, as these systems are installed within or above the foundation.
Framing must be complete to provide the structural enclosure and support for running mechanical ducts, electrical wiring, and plumbing lines through walls, floors, and ceilings.
Insulation must be installed after rough-in work is complete because insulation encloses and covers the mechanical and electrical systems within the wall cavities.
Rough-in work must be finished before drywall is installed, as the drywall will permanently conceal the mechanical, electrical, and plumbing lines within the walls and ceilings.
The rough-in inspection typically occurs after rough-in is completed and before insulation is applied, ensuring all systems are properly installed and code-compliant before being covered.
Safety systems must be physically installed before they can be commissioned and tested for functionality.
Safety systems require electrical power and connections to function; thus electrical installation must be complete before commissioning.

predecessor: Fire Alarm and Detection System Installation
rationale: Fire detection and alarm components need to be in place for safety system commissioning that involves testing fire suppression and alarm integration.
Safety system commissioning must be successfully completed and verified before the building can be considered safe for occupancy and formally handed over.
Safety system commissioning results are required evidence for regulatory and final inspections before the building can receive approval for use.
The surface must be prepared, leveled, and compacted before any line marking can be applied to ensure a smooth, stable substrate that will hold the paint/marking material properly.
The final pavement layer (asphalt or concrete) must be laid and fully cured before line markings are applied; otherwise, markings will not adhere or will deform as the pavement settles.

Line markings define parking bays, traffic lanes, and pedestrian zones; signage (e.g., stop signs, parking signs, directional signs) must be installed after markings are complete to ensure signs align correctly with marked areas.

Line marking is one of the final finishing activities on a construction project; the final inspection and handover to the client should occur after all surface markings are in place to verify the completed layout.

It is a soft preference to protect fresh line markings with temporary barriers or traffic management measures to allow paint to dry fully and prevent vehicle/traffic damage before the area is opened for use.
The elevator shaft and hoistway must be structurally complete to provide the physical enclosure and support for elevator guide rails, machinery, and cab installation.
The elevator pit and shaft must be waterproofed to prevent water ingress that could damage elevator components and electrical systems during and after installation.

predecessor: Concrete Core / Slab Pouring (at elevator shaft)
rationale: Floor slabs at each landing and the pit floor must be poured and cured to provide the structural bearing surfaces for guide rail brackets and door sills.
The elevator car and guide rails must be in place before landing door frames and doors can be aligned and installed at each floor level.
Elevator controller wiring, cabling, and power connections must follow the mechanical installation of the elevator machinery and car.
The structural frame must be in place to support the escalator components and provide the primary load-bearing structure before the escalator unit can be installed.
The escalator pit and its foundation must be excavated and poured to provide the correct lower landing support and clearance for the escalator truss.
The main escalator truss and drive mechanism must be in place before balustrades and handrails can be mounted onto the structure.
Power and control connections can only be run once the escalator unit is physically positioned and secured, as cable routing depends on the exact location of the drive unit and junction boxes.
Steps and comb plates are installed after the truss is fixed in place and the drive system is operational, as they ride on the continuous step chain within the installed truss.
The door frame requires a prepared rough opening in the wall structure to be installed into.
Wall framing must be complete to provide the structural support and the rough opening dimensions for the door assembly.
Door hardware such as hinges, locks, handles, and closers must be mounted onto the assembled door frame and door leaf.
Typically easier to finish walls after door is installed to achieve clean transitions, but can be done before with careful masking.
The door must be physically assembled and hung before it can be inspected for proper operation, alignment, and clearance.
Handrails and balustrades require a stable structural substrate (slabs, beams, floors) to be in place for anchorage and support before they can be installed.
Handrails on staircases must be mounted onto the completed stair structure; the stairs must exist before the handrail can be fixed to them.

predecessor: Rough-in MEP (Mechanical, Electrical, Plumbing) in Adjacent Walls
rationale: MEP rough-in work behind walls near handrail anchor points must be completed before final finishes and handrail installation to avoid rework or damage.

successor: Finishing & Painting of Adjacent Walls & Ceilings
rationale: It is preferable to complete painting and finishing after handrail installation to avoid paint splatter on the handrail and to achieve neat interface detailing, though it is not physically impossible to paint beforehand.
Handrails and balustrades must be fully installed and secure before the building can be inspected for safety compliance and handed over for use.
Door frames and rough openings must be prepared and framed before any hardware can be mounted.
The door frame must be installed to provide the structural support for mounting emergency exit hardware.
The door leaf (door slab) must be hung in place before exit hardware devices can be attached to it.
While preferred for coordination, electrical connections to alarmed exit devices can sometimes be roughed in beforehand if locations are predetermined.
Final trim, latch alignment, and adjustment of the exit device must occur after the hardware is installed to ensure proper operation.
Functional testing of emergency exit hardware (push/pull operation, latching, and alarm function if applicable) can only be performed after the hardware is fully installed.

The structural framework (columns, beams, slabs) must be in place before circulation spaces can be planned, as these spaces are defined by and contained within the structural grid and load-bearing elements.
The building core (including stairwells, elevator shafts, and main structural walls) must exist to define the vertical circulation pathways around which horizontal circulation is organized.
All below-grade construction including footings, slab-on-grade, and basement walls must be completed to establish the base reference plane from which all circulation levels and paths are planned.
Circulation corridors, aisles, and paths must be defined first to establish the access routes around which all interior partition walls and room divisions are organized and framed.
The spatial layout and routing of elevator banks, escalator zones, and stair locations must be finalized before the mechanical installation of vertical transportation equipment can proceed.
The design must be developed to a stage where it can be evaluated against accessibility standards and building codes before an audit can be conducted.
Complete construction documents are needed for the audit to verify that all accessibility and compliance requirements are incorporated into the detailed plans and specifications.
While audits often inform permit submissions, a preliminary audit can be done before submission; however, ideally the design and documentation should be ready for review prior to the audit.
The audit findings and compliance verification are typically required by authorities before a building permit can be granted.
Construction should not begin until accessibility and compliance issues identified in the audit are resolved and the design is approved, to avoid costly rework and legal violations.

The building layout, floor plans, and spatial configuration must be designed before egress and life-safety analysis can be performed, as the analysis depends on specific room dimensions, corridor widths, exit locations, and occupancy loads defined in the architectural design.

Structural elements such as load-bearing walls, stairwell enclosures, and fire-rated assemblies must be designed first to provide the framework for egress paths, fire compartments, and means of escape that the life-safety analysis evaluates.

The design of fire suppression systems, fire alarms, smoke control systems, and fire-rated construction must be established before the life-safety analysis can assess whether these systems adequately support safe egress under fire scenarios.

Building permits and regulatory approvals require a completed egress and life-safety analysis to demonstrate compliance with building codes (e.g., IBC, NFPA 101) before authorities will review and issue permits for construction.

Detailed egress pathway plans, exit signage layouts, emergency lighting designs, and occupant evacuation plans can only be finalized after the life-safety analysis determines required exit capacities, travel distances, and number of exits.
The wayfinding strategy must align with the approved architectural layout, floor plans, and spatial configuration of the building to accurately place signage and directional cues.
Understanding the overall site layout, entry/exit points, and surrounding context is essential before developing an internal wayfinding system.
Knowing the primary user groups (visitors, staff, patients, etc.) and their navigation needs is critical to designing an effective wayfinding system.
The signage design process depends on the wayfinding strategy's decisions about sign types, locations, messaging hierarchy, and naming conventions.

successor: Floor Numbering / Room Numbering Scheme Finalization
rationale: The numbering scheme must be developed within the framework defined by the wayfinding strategy to ensure logical and intuitive navigation.
The structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) must be in place to provide support and anchorage for the staircase.
Staircase installation creates dust and debris; finishing work should follow to avoid damage to finished surfaces.
Handrails are typically attached directly to the staircase structure after the stairs are cast or assembled.
The staircase must bear on a solid foundation; the ground floor slab must be cast before stair construction can begin.
Staircase structure must be complete before routing conduits, pipes, or services through or under the stairwell.
The elevator shaft and machine room must be structurally complete to provide the physical enclosure and support for elevator installation.
Elevator pit must be concreted and hoistway walls/slabs must be cast to allow rail brackets and guide rail installation.
The elevator machine room needs to be fitted with traction machines and control panels before permanent power and control wiring can be completed and connected.
Final commissioning of the elevator must be done before opening hoistway doors and finishing adjacent lobby areas to avoid damage and allow for adjustments.
Elevator commissioning must be complete before the building can be handed over for occupancy, as the elevator is a critical life-safety and accessibility system.
MEP rough-ins (electrical, plumbing, and mechanical services within corridor ceilings/walls) must be installed before partitions are framed and finished to avoid costly rework and access issues.
Corridor walls and finishes must be completed before ceiling grids and tiles are installed to allow access for finishing work and to prevent damage to ceilings.
While finishing walls before floors is preferred to avoid staining/damaging finished floors, it can sometimes be reversed with proper protection; thus it is a soft preference.
Partition walls must be fully installed and finished before final painting and touch-up work can commence on those surfaces.
Door frames are typically installed as part of partition framing, and doors/hardware are hung after wall finishing to ensure proper fit and avoid damage.
Subfloor must be level, clean, and dry before flooring can be installed; otherwise the flooring will be uneven, fail to adhere, or be damaged.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-ins that run beneath the floor must be completed before flooring is laid to avoid cutting into or damaging the finished floor.

Concrete must be fully cured to its design strength and moisture levels must be acceptable before flooring materials (e.g., tile, vinyl, carpet) are installed to prevent moisture damage and adhesion failure.
Baseboards and wall trim are installed after flooring to overlap and cover the edge of the flooring material, providing a clean finished appearance.

While painting can be done before flooring, final touch-ups on lower walls are often done after flooring to fix any scuffs or marks caused during installation; however this is a preference for finish quality rather than a physical necessity.
The architectural layout and spatial design must be completed to define the geometry, pathways, and zones that will be analyzed for crowd movement and evacuation.
Structural elements (columns, beams, walls) define the physical obstacles and barriers that affect pedestrian routing, so the structural design must be in place before simulation.
A coordinated BIM model containing all building systems and spatial data is needed as the digital environment for running accurate crowd simulations.
Crowd simulation results inform the sizing and placement of exits, stairways, and corridors; egress design must incorporate simulation outputs to ensure safe evacuation.
While not physically required, interior space planning benefits from understanding predicted pedestrian circulation patterns and congestion points identified by the simulation.
Wayfinding and signage design can be optimized using crowd simulation results to place signs where they are most needed for efficient navigation, though it is a soft preference.
Understanding crowd flow patterns can inform logistics planning for phased construction or temporary pedestrian routes around a site, but it is not a physical dependency.
Operational planning for building management (e.g., staffing at entries/exits, event management) can be improved using crowd simulation data, though this is a soft optimization.
Structural framing provides the load-bearing support to which the exterior facade is attached, so it must be completed first.
The roof structure must be in place to provide a stable top connection and weather protection before facade installation proceeds.
Facade openings and framing must be in place before windows and doors can be installed into those openings.
While interior finishes can begin in parallel in some areas, completing the facade helps seal the building envelope, preventing weather damage to interior work.
Scaffolding and exterior access equipment cannot be fully removed until facade work is complete, as it is needed to support facade installation.
The suspended ceiling is typically attached to or hung from the structural slab above. The structural slab must be in place to provide the anchorage points for hanger wires.

Major mechanical, electrical, and plumbing runs (ductwork, piping, conduits) are installed in the plenum space above the ceiling. These must be completed before the ceiling grid is closed in, to avoid costly rework.
The suspension grid (main tees, cross tees, hanger wires) must be fully installed and leveled before individual tiles or panels can be placed into the grid.

successor: MEP Final Connections & Trim (Lighting Fixtures, Diffusers, Sprinklers)
rationale: Lighting fixtures, air diffusers, sprinkler heads, and other ceiling-mounted devices are typically installed into or through the suspended ceiling grid after the grid is complete, allowing precise alignment and fit.

It is common practice to complete wall painting and final finishes before installing ceiling tiles to avoid soiling tiles with paint splatter, but this is a soft preference rather than a hard physical constraint.
The site must be legally owned or leased before any physical preparation work can begin.
Subsurface conditions, soil bearing capacity, and site topography must be assessed to determine appropriate site preparation methods (e.g., cut/fill, excavation depth, dewatering needs).
Environmental permits, grading permits, and construction approvals must be secured before any clearing, grubbing, or earthwork can commence.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and grubbed before excavation for foundations can begin, as debris and vegetation would interfere with excavation equipment and spoil foundation integrity.
Temporary roads, construction laydown areas, and utility connections (water, electricity for construction) require a cleared and graded site surface to be properly installed.
The ground must be prepared, leveled, and foundations laid before bench or seating installations can be anchored securely.
Benches are often placed on concrete pads, paved surfaces, or at-grade finishes; these surfaces must be fully cured before bench installation.
Final grading, drainage systems, and soil preparation must be completed to ensure proper site drainage and stable ground for seating areas.
Once benches are installed, surrounding planting, mulch, and decorative landscaping can be placed around them without risk of damage from installation equipment.
Final site clean-up and finishing touches are typically performed after all furniture including benches are in place to avoid re-cleaning.
The ground must be excavated to create a stable foundation base before the lighting column can be erected.
A concrete foundation must be poured and fully cured to provide a load-bearing base for the column to be bolted onto.
Electrical conduits must be laid underground to the column location before the column is placed, so that cables can be routed into the column base.
Power cables can only be pulled through the column and connected to the luminaire after the column is erected and secured.
The light fixture must be mounted on top of or attached to the column, which requires the column to be in place first.
Plumbing rough-in must be completed before installing a linear drain channel, as the drain pipe connections need to be in place to receive the drain body.
The concrete slab or subfloor must be prepared and poured to the correct slope before a linear drain can be embedded or set into it.
The underlying waterproofing membrane must be installed before the drain channel, especially in wet areas, to ensure a continuous waterproof barrier beneath the drain.
Tile or floor finishing must follow drain installation so that tiles can be cut and set flush to the drain channel edges for proper drainage and aesthetic finish.
The linear drain channel must be fully set and secured before the decorative or functional grate cover can be installed on top to complete the assembly.
Sub-base preparation provides the stable, compacted foundation that the kerb/edge restraint is laid upon, ensuring the kerb remains level and properly supported.
Drainage pipes and systems must be installed before kerbs are placed, as kerbs often guide water flow and drainage inlets must be correctly aligned with the kerb line.
The road base or pavement base course is typically laid and compacted first so that the kerb can be set to the correct finished road level and acts as a restraint to the pavement layers.
The kerb/edge restraint defines the edge of the paved surface; asphalt or concrete paving is then placed up against the kerb, using it as a formwork and edge confinement.
Footpaths are constructed after kerbs are set to ensure the correct height transition between the road and footpath, and to allow the footpath to abut neatly against the kerb face.
The ground must be excavated and leveled to the proper grade before the ramp foundation can be poured, ensuring structural stability and correct slope.
The ramp requires a concrete footing or foundation to support its weight and comply with building codes; the footing must cure before ramp construction begins.
Handrails and guardrails are mounted onto the ramp structure itself, so the ramp must be fully constructed before railings can be attached.
Anti-slip surface treatments, coatings, or textured concrete finishes are applied after the ramp is fully formed and cured to ensure proper adhesion and a slip-resistant surface.

While signage can technically be installed before the ramp is complete, it is more logical and efficient to place ADA-compliant signage after the ramp is finished to ensure correct positioning and visibility at the ramp's entrance.
Site must be cleared, graded, and prepared before any art installation can begin, as the sculpture needs a stable and safe foundation area.
A concrete footing, base, or anchor system must be completed to provide structural support and stability for the sculpture before it can be installed.
Surrounding paving, planting, or hardscape should ideally be completed first to avoid damage to the sculpture during landscape work, though this is a soft preference.
After sculpture installation, final grading, planting, mulch, and site cleanup can be completed around the sculpture, though this is a soft preference as some finishing work can be done in parallel.
Any accent or security lighting intended to illuminate the sculpture must be installed after the sculpture is in place to ensure proper positioning and aiming of lights.
The canopy/arcade structure is typically supported by the main structural frame or columns. The supporting structure must be in place before the canopy can be installed.
If the canopy is roof-integrated or attached below a roof slab, the roof deck must be completed first to provide attachment points and waterproofing continuity.

successor: Exterior Cladding / Finishes to Columns & Soffits
rationale: The canopy/arcade structure must be in place before its underside (soffit) and supporting columns can receive their final cladding and finishes.
Lighting fixtures mounted on or within the canopy/arcade cannot be installed until the structural canopy/arcade is complete.

successor: Rainwater Downpipes / Drainage at Canopy Level
rationale: Drainage components serving the canopy (such as downpipes or gutters) require the canopy structure to be in place for attachment and proper routing.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and prepared before any utility work can commence, as utility trenches and installations require unobstructed access to the designated areas.

Accurate staking and identification of existing utility locations and proposed routes must be completed before diversion or new utility installation begins to avoid conflicts and ensure correct alignment.
Trenches need to be excavated to the required depth and width before utility pipes, conduits, or cables can be laid in them.
After utilities are placed and connected, trenches must be backfilled and compacted to restore the surface and provide support to the installed utilities.

Foundations and concrete slabs should not be poured until all underground utilities are installed and inspected, to avoid risking damage to utilities or having to break concrete for later utility access.
The rough opening framing provides the structural support and defined space into which the door assembly is installed. Without the framed opening, there is no structure to attach the door.
The door frame (jamb and header) must be in place to provide the mounting surface and alignment for the door slab and hardware.

Interior wall finishing (drywall installation and mudding) should be completed after door installation because the door frame provides a reference edge for finishing work, and drywall is typically fitted around the door frame.
The door slab must be hung in the frame before locks, handles, and final hinge adjustments can be made, as these components physically attach to or align with the installed door.

While interior trim/casing typically goes around the door after the door is hung, this is a soft preference because the casing could theoretically be installed before the door slab, though it is standard practice and more efficient to install after.
Conduit and wiring must be installed to provide the electrical infrastructure needed to power the emergency lighting unit.
Emergency lighting units are often ceiling-mounted; the ceiling grid must be in place to support and house the unit.
After the emergency lighting unit is physically installed, final electrical connections, testing, and trim-out can be completed.
Fire alarm testing often includes verifying that emergency lighting activates properly upon alarm signal, which requires the lighting unit to already be installed.
While finishing can technically be done around installed fixtures, it is preferable to install emergency lighting after painting to avoid damage to the unit from paint or overspray.
Ductwork must be installed first to provide the connection point and air pathway for the diffuser.
The ceiling grid (or suspended ceiling structure) must be in place to support and secure the diffuser in the correct position.
Diffusers must be installed and sealed before pressure testing the duct system to ensure accurate measurement of system airtightness.
Diffusers are typically mounted in or through the ceiling tiles; tiles around the diffuser should be installed after the diffuser is positioned and secured.
System balancing and airflow testing require all terminal devices (diffusers) to be installed to measure and adjust air distribution accurately.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and graded to provide an accurate topographical baseline before thoroughfare routes can be planned and staked out.
Soil bearing capacity and subsurface conditions must be known to determine road alignment feasibility, pavement design, and drainage requirements for thoroughfares.
Environmental constraints such as wetlands, protected habitats, or flood zones must be identified prior to laying out road corridors to avoid or mitigate impacts.
The precise alignment, width, and elevation of roads must be finalized and marked before subgrade compaction and earthwork can commence.
Thoroughfare layout defines the road corridor within which utility trenches (water, sewer, power, communications) are placed, and utility routing follows road alignment.
The building must be constructed before its accessibility compliance can be assessed against standards and codes.
Any accessibility issues identified during the assessment must be remediated after the assessment is complete to achieve compliance.
The accessibility assessment must be completed and passed before the building can be granted a certificate of occupancy, as it is a regulatory prerequisite.
All interior and exterior finishing works should be completed so the assessment reflects the final as-built condition of the building.
The building can only be handed over to the client after accessibility compliance has been verified and documented.
Rough framing (studs, joists, rafters) must be completed to provide the structural substrate for attaching wall and ceiling finishes such as drywall, plaster, or paneling.
All wiring, pipes, ducts, and junction boxes must be installed within the wall and ceiling cavities before they are enclosed by finishes; otherwise costly rework would be required.
Insulation must be placed in wall and ceiling cavities before drywall or other finishes are applied to seal the building envelope and meet thermal/acoustic requirements.
Paint, wallpaper, texture, or other decorative coatings are applied over the finished wall and ceiling surfaces (e.g., drywall, plaster) after they are fully installed, taped, and sanded.

While flooring can technically be installed before ceiling finishing, it is standard practice to finish walls and ceilings first to avoid damaging finished floors with dropped tools, dust, or paint drips.

Electrical rough-in work, including running conduit, pulling wires, and installing junction boxes, must be completed before lighting fixtures can be installed, as the fixtures need to connect to the electrical infrastructure.
In suspended ceiling systems, the ceiling grid must be in place to support the mounting of recessed or surface-mounted lighting fixtures.
Structural elements such as steel beams, roof decks, and overhead slabs must be fully installed before lighting fixtures can be mounted or suspended from them.
Ceiling tiles are installed after lighting fixtures are placed within the grid, as the tiles fit around or are cut to accommodate the fixtures.

While not a strict physical constraint, it is preferred to complete lighting installation before final interior finishes to avoid damaging finished surfaces during fixture installation and to allow for proper lighting for inspection of finish work.

Lighting must be fully installed and commissioned (including controls programming, sensor calibration, and dimming tests) before overall building systems commissioning, as lighting is a subsystem that feeds into the larger building management system.
The entrance canopy requires a stable and level base provided by the foundation and slab to ensure proper load distribution and structural support.
The entrance canopy often attaches to or integrates with the main building's structural steel frame, which must be erected first to provide connection points and structural support.
The canopy structure must be in place before its roofing and waterproofing membrane can be applied to ensure a continuous weather-tight seal.
Electrical conduit and wiring for canopy lighting fixtures are routed within or attached to the canopy frame, requiring the structure to be erected first.
The structural frame of the canopy must be completed before architectural cladding, soffit panels, and decorative finishes can be installed to achieve the final appearance.
The rough opening must be framed and prepared (including header, jambs, and sill) before the entrance door can be installed into the opening.
Load-bearing walls must be framed to create the rough opening that will receive the entrance door.
Water-resistant barrier and pan flashing must be installed at the door threshold area before the door is set to prevent water infiltration.
The door slab must be hung and positioned in the frame before locksets, handles, hinges, and other hardware can be fitted and secured.
Casing and interior trim around the door are installed after the door frame is set and the door is hung to achieve proper alignment and gaps.

While siding can often be installed up to the door frame, completing the siding around the installed door allows for proper flashing integration and a finished appearance; however, some sequencing flexibility exists.
The subfloor must be in place to establish the finished floor level and threshold height reference for the entrance door installation.

Door hardware (hinges, locks, latches) is mounted onto the door frame and door leaf; the frame must be installed and secured first to provide the structural support and alignment needed for hardware attachment.
The door leaf must be hung on its hinges before final hardware such as locksets, handles, and closers can be installed, as these components are integrated into the assembled door.

For electrified hardware (e.g., maglocks, electric strikes, access control), electrical rough-in wiring and conduit must be in place before the hardware is physically installed; this is a soft preference if hardware is non-electrified.

Hardware is typically removed or protected during painting; final finish coating should be completed before installing delicate hardware to avoid paint damage, but if hardware is pre-finished this may be a soft preference.
All hardware must be installed before the final adjustments, latching tests, and commissioning of doors can be performed to ensure proper operation and security compliance.
The ground must be properly prepared, leveled, and graded before constructing the entrance ramp to ensure a stable foundation and proper drainage.
A compacted subbase or foundation layer is required to support the structural load of the entrance ramp.
Any underground utilities (water, gas, electric, communications) crossing the ramp area must be relocated or installed before ramp construction to avoid excavation damage later.
The ramp structure/subgrade must be formed and compacted before the final wearing surface (asphalt or concrete) can be applied.
Guardrails or safety barriers along the ramp can only be installed after the ramp structure is built and in place.
The threshold sits on the finished floor or subfloor; the floor must be prepared, leveled, and set before the threshold can be installed.
The threshold is typically positioned at the base of the door frame opening; the door frame must be in place to correctly align and secure the threshold.
The door leaf closes onto or over the threshold; the threshold must be installed first so that the door can be hung and adjusted to the correct clearance above it.

successor: Weatherstripping or sealant application at door bottom
rationale: Weather seals at the bottom of the door interact with the threshold surface; the threshold must be in place before applying seals to ensure proper fit and airtightness.
The rough opening defines the space for the door assembly; it must be framed, and the header and jambs positioned, before the threshold can be set at the base.
The rough opening in the wall must be framed and prepared before any glazing can be installed, as the glass units require a structurally sound and dimensionally accurate opening to sit within.
The surrounding walls must be complete and load-bearing elements in place to support the entrance frame before glazing installation begins.
Waterproofing and air barrier membranes around the opening must be installed prior to glazing to ensure the envelope is sealed behind the glazed unit.
Interior finishes around the entrance should be completed after glazing installation to avoid damage and to allow for proper sealing and trim integration around the installed glazed unit.
After the glazing unit is installed, the perimeter sealant and weatherproofing can be applied and allowed to cure to complete the weather-tight seal.

The entry mat/grating system is typically installed within or set into the finished floor slab or foundation. The concrete slab must be poured, cured, and finished to the proper elevation and location to receive the mat/grating frame.

If the entry mat/grating system includes a drainage channel or connects to any below-slab drainage or electrical systems, those utilities must be roughed in and stubbed up before the slab is poured and the mat system is set in place.

The entry mat/grating system is set at the finished floor elevation, and adjacent finish flooring (tile, stone, hardwood, etc.) is installed up to or butting against the mat/grating frame. This ensures a clean transition and proper alignment.

successor: Wall Framing / Partition Installation (at entry vestibule)
rationale: If the entry mat/grating system extends into a vestibule or recessed entry area, the surrounding walls and partitions must be built after the mat is set to ensure the frame aligns correctly with the wall openings and floor transitions.

The entry mat/grating system should be protected during construction and only final cleaned and commissioned once all adjacent finishes, painting, and overhead work are complete to prevent dirt and debris accumulation in the grating and to avoid damage.

The foundation or slab provides a level, stable base upon which the entrance structure (including door frames, thresholds, and entry steps) must be anchored. Without a completed foundation, the entrance cannot be properly aligned or structurally supported.

Exterior walls define the rough opening for the entrance door. The entrance frame must be installed within the wall opening; without the walls framed, there is no opening to receive the entrance assembly.

Utilities such as underground conduit, drainage, and electrical stub-ups that pass beneath or near the entrance area must be roughed in before the entrance slab and threshold are finalized, to avoid the need for costly re-excavation and slab cutting.

Door frames and entrance assemblies must be installed and squared before interior wall finishes are applied, so that the finish material can be trimmed neatly around the door frame and the reveal is consistent.

The entrance door assembly must be in place and fully installed before final weatherstripping, caulking, and air-sealing can be applied around the perimeter to ensure a continuous building envelope and prevent air/water infiltration.

Structural framing, lintels, and slab edges at the entrance must be completed and cured before any fit-out (cladding, ceilings, flooring) can commence, as fit-out finishes attach to or cover the structure.
Below-slab and exposed slab waterproofing must be installed and tested prior to laying entrance floor tiles or stone to prevent moisture ingress that would damage finished finishes.

Electrical conduits, data cables, fire alarm loops, and any concealed plumbing serving the entrance lobby must be roughed-in and inspected before ceiling grids, wall linings, and floor screeds are installed.

Entrance doors, shopfront glazing, and automatic door operators are installed after the surrounding fit-out (frame grounds, architraves, ceiling bulkheads) is complete to ensure proper alignment and sealing against finished surfaces.

Decorative cladding, feature lighting, signage, and any art installations in the entrance lobby are installed as the final layer after all base fit-out (ceilings, walls, floors) is finished to avoid damage and allow for precise positioning.

The building enclosure must be complete before access compliance inspection can occur, as the inspection assesses entry/exit points, doors, windows, and overall accessible pathways within the finished structure.

Rough-in work must be completed so that access compliance inspectors can verify that accessible routes, clearances, and pathways are not obstructed by exposed mechanical, electrical, or plumbing components.
Interior framing and drywall must be in place to evaluate door widths, hallway clearances, turning radii, and overall accessible path of travel through the completed interior spaces.
Floor coverings must be installed to verify that walking surfaces are stable, slip-resistant, and meet accessibility requirements for level changes, carpet pile height, and surface firmness.
The access compliance inspection must pass before final finishes and occupancy can proceed, as compliance with accessibility codes is a prerequisite for issuing a certificate of occupancy.
The entrance area must be excavated and rough-graded before any entrance maintenance or servicing work can begin, as the entrance structure needs a stable prepared base.
The building's foundation and substructure must be complete to provide structural support for the entrance area before maintenance and servicing can be performed.
The main structural frame enclosing the entrance must be erected before entrance components (doors, frames, thresholds) can be installed and serviced.
Electrical wiring for door operators, lighting, and access control systems must be roughed in before entrance servicing can connect and finish these systems.
Entrance doors, frames, and hardware must be installed and serviced before interior finishes are applied, to avoid damage to finished surfaces and to allow proper alignment and sealing.
Entrance systems (automatic doors, access control, weather seals) must be serviced and operational before final commissioning tests of building systems can be performed.
Entrance installation and servicing must be complete to allow final weatherproofing and cladding integration around the entrance opening.

predecessor: Installation of Entrance Doors and Frames
rationale: Entrance doors and frames must be physically installed before their security features can be assessed.

predecessor: Installation of Locking Mechanisms and Hardware
rationale: Locks, handles, and access control hardware must be in place for the security assessment to evaluate their effectiveness.

predecessor: Installation of Access Control Systems (card readers, keypads, biometrics)
rationale: Electronic access control components must be installed and wired before they can be tested for security.

predecessor: Installation of Surveillance Cameras covering entrances
rationale: Cameras must be mounted and operational to assess their coverage and positioning as part of entrance security.

successor: Final Approval and Handover of Building
rationale: The security assessment must be completed and any issues resolved before the building can be formally approved and handed over.
The site must be graded and prepared before any parking lot construction can begin, including the entrance/exit points.
Underground utilities (water, sewer, electrical, communications) must be installed before paving the entrance/exit to avoid cutting into new pavement.
Stormwater drainage infrastructure including catch basins and piping must be installed beneath the entrance/exit area prior to paving.
