The entrance and exit curbs, aprons, and base layers must be constructed first to provide access for paving equipment and to establish the boundary for the rest of the parking lot surfacing.

The entrance/exit must be physically constructed to tie into the adjacent public roadway, and final roadway connection work (e.g., curb cut, sidewalk ramp) can only be completed after the entrance/exit is in place.
The pavement surface must be properly graded and compacted before any markings can be applied to ensure a smooth, stable base.
The pavement surface (asphalt or concrete) must be laid and fully cured before markings can be applied; marking on uncured pavement would fail to adhere.
Curbs and gutters define the roadway edges, which are necessary reference points for correctly positioning lane stripes and edge lines.
While signals can be installed before markings, the final signal timing and operation verification is best done after markings are in place to ensure proper visibility and coordination.
Roadways must have clear markings before being opened to public traffic to provide safe lane guidance, pedestrian crossings, and regulatory information to drivers.
A solid, leveled foundation base must be prepared before wheel stops can be installed to ensure proper alignment and structural support.
Wheel stops are typically anchored into cured concrete; the concrete must be fully cured to provide adequate holding strength for the anchors.
Parking space dimensions and positions must be marked out to determine exact wheel stop placement locations.
Seal coating must be applied after wheel stops are installed to avoid sealant covering anchor points or wheel stop bases.
Parking space line striping should be applied after wheel stops are in place so that lines align correctly with the installed stops.
The site must be rough-graded and earthwork completed to establish proper subgrade elevation and drainage slopes before curb forms can be set and concrete poured.
The soil subgrade beneath the curb must be compacted to the required density to provide a stable foundation and prevent settlement or cracking of the curb.
Storm drains, water lines, and other utilities that cross under or behind the curb line must be installed before the curb is placed to avoid cutting or damaging the new curb.
Curb and gutter forms the edge restraint for pavement; asphalt or base material is placed and compacted against the finished curb to achieve proper grade and confinement.
Sidewalk slabs typically tie into or are placed adjacent to the curb and gutter; the curb provides the alignment and elevation reference for the sidewalk forming and pouring.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and obstructions before fence installation can proceed, as the fence layout requires a clean and level work area.
The property boundaries, fence lines, and gates must be surveyed and staked before fence construction to ensure accurate placement and alignment.
Access roads are needed to deliver fence materials (posts, panels, concrete, etc.) and equipment to the perimeter areas before installation can begin.

The perimeter fence must be in place before security systems (e.g., cameras, gates, access control) can be installed, as the fence provides the physical boundary for mounting and securing these components.

Erecting the perimeter fence first provides a secure, enclosed site that prevents unauthorized access and protects excavation and foundation work, though it is a soft preference as work can proceed without the fence if other security measures are in place.
Site clearing removes vegetation, debris, and existing structures, providing an unobstructed area needed for subgrade grading and compaction.
Surveying establishes the precise grades, elevations, and boundaries required to perform subgrade excavation and compaction to design specifications.
The subgrade must be properly prepared and compacted to provide a stable foundation before placing the base course material on top.

While utilities often run below the subgrade, some shallow utilities may be installed after subgrade preparation; however, deep utilities should be completed first. This is listed as a soft preference as sequencing can vary depending on utility depth and design.
The subgrade (soil foundation) must be properly graded, compacted, and stabilized before pavement can be laid to ensure a stable base and prevent future settlement or failure.

A base or sub-base layer (e.g., crushed stone, aggregate) must be placed and compacted over the subgrade to provide load distribution and drainage support before the final pavement surface is installed.
Underground utilities (water, sewer, gas, electrical, storm drains) must be installed and backfilled beneath the pavement area before paving, to avoid cutting or patching the finished pavement later.
Pavement must be placed and finished first so that curbs and gutters can be formed flush against the pavement edge at the correct elevation and alignment.
Traffic markings, lane lines, and striping can only be applied after the pavement surface is fully installed, cured, and clean to ensure proper adhesion and durability.
Pavement markings must be applied on a stable, finished asphalt surface. Asphalt paving must be completed first to provide the substrate for markings.
The pavement base and binder courses must be laid and compacted before the surface course and markings can be applied.
The final asphalt surface layer must be placed and cooled/cured before markings can be painted or applied onto it.
Traffic should not be allowed on newly marked pavement until the markings have been applied and cured to ensure visibility and durability.
While signs can be installed before markings, coordinating placement after markings allows for proper alignment and visibility of both traffic control devices.
Electrical conduits, cables, and junction boxes must be run through walls and ceilings before light fixtures can be attached and connected to power sources.
Light fixtures are typically mounted to finished ceilings or drywall surfaces; rough openings and mounting support must be in place before fixtures can be installed.
Ceiling joists and wall framing must be erected to provide structural support for mounting light fixtures and routing electrical cables.
After the main fixtures are mounted, final trim pieces, bulbs, and electrical connections at the switch/breaker must be completed to make the lighting operational.
While lighting is often installed before final painting to avoid damaging finishes, it is a soft preference because painting can be done carefully around installed fixtures if needed.
The surface must be properly prepared (cleaned, leveled, and primed) before any sealing or coating can be applied to ensure proper adhesion and performance of the sealant.
If the surface is concrete-based, the concrete must be fully cured before sealants are applied to prevent moisture trapping and ensure the chemical bond is effective.
All structural framing and building enclosure must be in place so that the surfaces to be sealed are stable and complete prior to sealing work.

Sealing is typically one of the last steps before occupancy, as it protects finished surfaces from damage during subsequent lighter finishing trades and must be complete for the space to be considered finished.
After sealing is applied, a waterproofing or quality inspection must follow to verify the integrity and continuity of the seal before any coverings or occupancy proceed.
The ground must be properly graded and prepared to provide a stable, level base for the cart corral/storage area foundation.
A concrete slab or foundation is needed to anchor the cart corral structure and provide a durable, level surface for cart storage and movement.
The cart corral is typically located within or adjacent to the parking lot; the parking lot asphalt must be paved first so the corral can be installed in its correct position.
Parking lot striping and signage must be applied after the cart corral is installed so that the corral's location is accurately reflected in the lane markings and any no-parking zones around it.
Final landscaping around the cart corral area is typically done after installation to blend the structure into the site, though this is a soft preference as landscaping could be done simultaneously.
Excavation must be completed to create the trench or space where the surface drainage channel will be installed.
A compacted and level sub-base is required to provide a stable foundation for the drainage channel before it is placed.
The drainage channel must be installed and positioned correctly before backfilling material can be placed and compacted around it.
The drainage channel must be in place before the final surface (e.g., asphalt, concrete, paving stones) is laid, to ensure proper integration and continuous drainage.
The channel must be fully installed before connecting it to downstream drainage pipes or outfall structures to ensure a watertight and properly aligned connection.
The ground must be excavated and leveled to provide a stable foundation for gabion baskets, ensuring they sit properly without shifting.
A compacted base or granular foundation is required beneath gabion baskets to prevent differential settlement and ensure structural stability.
The wire mesh baskets must be unfolded, connected, and assembled into their empty form before they can be placed in position and filled with stone.
The empty basket must be placed in its final position before stone fill can be added; filling occurs in situ to ensure proper containment and shape.

successor: Lid Securing / Closing of Gabion Baskets
rationale: After the basket is filled to the required level with stone, the lid or top panel must be closed and tied/stitched shut to contain the fill material.

predecessor: Gabion Basket Installation (including fill and closure)
successor: Backfilling Behind Gabion Wall (if retaining wall)
rationale: If gabions are used as retaining walls, backfill is placed behind them once they are complete; this is a logical sequence but not always strictly required depending on design.
Topsoil must first be stripped (removed) from the area before it can be reinstated. Reinstatement involves replacing topsoil, which requires the original stripping to have occurred.
Bulk excavation and any cut/fill earthworks must be completed before topsoil is placed back, as the final ground levels and subgrade preparation need to be established first.
The subgrade must be properly prepared, graded, and compacted to the required levels before topsoil is spread, otherwise the topsoil would be placed on an unstable or incorrectly graded surface.
Any underground drainage, water supply, electrical, or communication services must be installed and backfilled before topsoil is reinstated, to avoid excavating through newly placed topsoil.
Reinstated topsoil provides the growing medium for grass seeding, turf laying, or planting, so the topsoil must be in place before any landscaping or vegetation establishment can commence.

It is preferable to complete final grading adjustments and surface trimming after topsoil is placed to achieve a neat finish, though this is a soft sequencing preference rather than a strict physical necessity.
A stable and properly graded subgrade is physically required to support the pavement layers; without earthworks and compaction, the pavement would lack a sound foundation.
Subsurface drainage (e.g., drains, pipes) must be placed before pavement construction to prevent water accumulation beneath the pavement, which would cause premature failure.
The granular base or sub-base layer must be compacted and in place to provide the load-bearing platform upon which the pavement reinstatement (e.g., asphalt or concrete) is laid.
Line marking, signage, and surface finishing can only be applied after the pavement surface is fully reinstated and cured to provide a clean, stable substrate.
Traffic cannot be safely reopened until the pavement reinstatement is complete and has achieved sufficient strength to withstand vehicle loads.
Site preparation (clearing, grading, and earthworks) must be completed to provide a stable, properly graded surface and topsoil placement for landscaping and planting.

All underground utilities (drainage, irrigation pipes, electrical conduits) must be installed before landscaping to avoid digging up or damaging planted areas and to ensure proper irrigation infrastructure is in place.

Major building construction (structure, exterior cladding) should be complete to prevent heavy equipment, material storage, and construction traffic from damaging newly landscaped and revegetated areas.
Landscaping and revegetation are finishing works that must be completed before final project inspection and handover, as they represent the final aesthetic and environmental restoration of the site.
Once revegetation is established and the soil is stabilized, temporary erosion and sediment control measures can be removed, though some controls may be left until vegetation is fully established.
The site boundaries, access points, and locations for hoarding must be surveyed and marked out so the fencing can be installed along the correct alignment.
Mobilisation delivers materials, plant, and personnel needed to erect the temporary fencing; the fence cannot be built without these resources being on site.
Hoarding must be in place first to secure the site perimeter, control public access, and comply with safety regulations before any demolition or clearance work begins.
Temporary fencing encloses the construction site, which is necessary before installing security gates, guard huts, and welfare facilities within the secure perimeter.
The site must be securely fenced to prevent unauthorised access and ensure public safety before any excavation or earthmoving operations commence.
Settlement monitoring points must be installed after excavation is complete to measure settlement from the constructed structure, not from excavation disturbances.
Monitoring points need to be in place before backfilling to establish baseline readings and ensure they are protected and accessible for future monitoring.
Settlement monitoring points must be installed and baseline readings taken before any structural loads are applied to measure settlement during loading.
Ground improvement must be completed before installing settlement monitoring points so that baseline readings reflect the stabilized ground conditions.
A reference survey control network must be established first to provide accurate datum points for monitoring point installation and subsequent readings.
The foundation or base area where the pergola will be installed must be properly prepared (e.g., leveled, cleared, and compacted) before any vertical structure can be erected.
Concrete footings or post anchors must be set and cured to provide a stable structural base for the pergola posts.
If the pergola is to be mounted on a deck, the deck substructure and surface must be completed and load-rated to support the pergola.
The pergola frame (posts, beams, rafters) must be fully assembled and secured before laths, louvers, shade cloth, or roofing panels are attached.
Installing lights, fans, or electrical outlets on the pergola structure is safer and cleaner after the frame is complete, though wiring conduits could be roughed-in earlier as a soft preference.
The structural steel frame must be erected to provide the primary support structure onto which the louvred canopy is attached.
The roof structure above the canopy area must be completed to define the upper boundary and provide anchorage points for the canopy.
The canopy provides weather protection and defines the interface edge; cladding must align with and butt against the canopy frame.
Windows and glazing below or beside the canopy must be installed after the canopy to ensure proper weather sealing and integration with the louvre system.

While the canopy itself can be installed earlier, commissioning of automated shading controls is preferably done after canopy installation to calibrate sensors and actuators against the actual installed louvre geometry.

The structural frame (including roof and wall supports) must be fully erected and stabilized before any solar shading devices can be mounted, as shading devices are typically fixed to the building's structural elements.
Exterior wall cladding or finishing must be completed to provide a proper mounting surface and to ensure weather sealing behind the shading device attachments.

For external shading devices (e.g., overhangs, louvers, brise-soleil), the shading system should be installed before or concurrently with window installation to ensure proper alignment, clearances, and integration with the window system.

Touch-up painting and finishing around shading device anchor points is often easier after installation, but this is a soft preference as painting could also be completed before installation with protective measures.
For roof-mounted or roof-integrated shading devices, the waterproofing membrane must be in place to prevent water ingress at mounting points.
The structural framing and deck (floor slab or balcony slab) must be in place to provide a substrate and anchorage points for the balustrade/railing system.

predecessor: Rough-in for drainage / waterproofing at balcony edges
rationale: Waterproofing membranes and drainage provisions at slab edges must be installed before railing posts or base plates are fixed, to ensure continuous waterproofing integrity.

successor: Finishing / Cladding of balustrade infill panels
rationale: The primary balustrade/railing frame structure must be erected before any infill panels (glass, metal, cable) can be fitted and finished.
The main balustrade structure supports the handrail; the handrail is one of the last components to be installed and adjusted for alignment and height compliance.

While coating can sometimes be applied to pre-finished sections, final touch-up painting or coating is typically done after installation to cover welds, cuts, and scratches — a practical sequencing preference rather than a strict physical constraint.

The building structure and shell must be complete before external landscape and hard landscaping works can commence, as landscape works around the building require a finished structure to avoid rework and damage.
External cladding and roofing must be finished to prevent scaffolding, material drops, and debris from damaging newly completed landscaping and hardscape elements.

All underground drainage, sewer, water, and electrical utility connections must be installed and backfilled before hard landscaping and paving are laid, to avoid excavation and disturbance of finished surfaces.
Bulk earthworks, grading, and final site levels must be completed to provide a stable, properly sloped base for landscaping, paving, and hardscape installation.
Landscaping and hard landscaping are among the final finishing trades; once complete, the site can be cleaned and handed over to the client, as no further heavy construction work is required.

Waterproofing must be applied onto a stable, cured concrete substrate. The concrete blinding or foundation slab provides the rigid base required for waterproofing membranes or tanking systems to bond and perform effectively.

Waterproofing and tanking must be completed and tested before placing reinforcement over it, to avoid damaging the waterproof membrane and to ensure watertight integrity before encasing it in concrete.

Backfilling can only commence after basement waterproofing/tanking is fully cured and inspected, because the waterproof layer must be protected and the backfill material would otherwise damage or displace the uncured membrane.

The substrate must be clean, dry, smooth, and free of debris, laitance, or protrusions before any waterproofing membrane or tanking system can be applied, otherwise adhesion and watertight performance will be compromised.

A protective screed or protection board must be installed over the completed waterproofing to shield it from mechanical damage during subsequent construction activities such as rebar fixing and concrete pouring.
Solar panels are typically mounted on the roof structure, so the structural framing and roof decking must be completed to provide a stable mounting surface.
Roof waterproofing protects the building envelope; solar panels should not be installed until the roof is watertight to avoid damage to the structure and interior.
Conduits and wiring pathways from the solar array to the inverter and electrical panel must be in place before panels are mounted and connected.
The solar panels must be physically installed and their wiring run to the inverter location before the inverter can be connected and the electrical system energized.
Commissioning (testing voltage, current, and overall system performance) can only occur after the solar panels are installed and fully connected.

The ground must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and topsoil, and initial excavation must be completed to expose the formation level and provide a clean working area for drainage trenching and pipe laying.
Trenches must be dug to the required depth and gradient before drainage pipes and gulleys can be placed, bedded, and connected.
Once pipes and gulleys are positioned, joints must be made and pressure/water-tightness tests conducted to verify integrity before backfilling.
Backfilling of drainage trenches can only proceed after the drainage system (pipes, gulleys, chambers) is fully installed, inspected, and approved to avoid damage to the system.
Underground drainage must be completed before pouring concrete foundations or slabs, as drainage runs beneath these elements and must be fully functional and tested before being covered.
Shading structures require stable foundations to be built upon before erection can commence.
If the shading structure is attached to or supported by the main building frame, the primary structural frame must be in place first.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and prepared before any erection activities can begin.
If the shading system includes motorized components or lighting, electrical rough-in work must follow the erection of the structure.
Final finishes and cladding around the shading structure area typically occur after erection to avoid damage during installation.
Site survey provides the geographical location, topography, and surrounding context needed to perform an accurate solar analysis.
The building program defines space requirements and functional needs which inform optimal solar orientation strategies.
While not always a strict prerequisite, understanding soil conditions and subsurface characteristics can influence optimal building placement and orientation decisions.
Solar analysis results directly inform the conceptual design phase by dictating building orientation, massing, and glazing placement for passive solar performance.
Solar orientation data is a critical input for building energy models to accurately simulate heating, cooling, and lighting loads.
The colonnade requires a stable load-bearing base; foundation must be completed to support the weight and vertical load of columns.
Columns of a colonnade rest on a stylobate or floor slab; this level surface must be finished to provide proper alignment and load distribution.
The entablature or horizontal beams spanning the columns rest directly on top of the colonnade; columns must be erected first to support them.
The roof structure is supported by the entablature which sits on the colonnade; the colonnade must be complete before any roof framing can be placed above it.

While decorative elements like fluting, painting, or stone cladding can be applied after columns are erected, some finishing can be done pre-installation, making this a soft preference for sequencing.
A stable foundation is required to support the pergola structure; without proper footing or base preparation, the pergola cannot be securely anchored.
The pergola frame must be fully erected before any roofing material, shade cloth, or louvered roof system can be attached to it.
Proper grading and drainage must be completed before pergola installation to ensure water flows away from the structure and prevents future settlement or water damage.
Any electrical, gas, or water lines that will be run beneath the pergola area must be installed before the structure is built to avoid digging under or around the completed pergola.

It is generally easier to install lighting and electrical fixtures after the pergola frame is in place, though some pre-wiring can be done beforehand; this is a strong preference for efficiency rather than a strict physical requirement.
The trellis structure requires a stable, level foundation or base to be properly anchored and erected; foundation work must be completed first.
Trellises are often mounted on or supported by posts or columns; these vertical supports must be installed before the trellis framework can be attached.
While climbing plants can be planted before the trellis, attaching them or training them onto the trellis structure occurs after the trellis is erected for optimal growth support.
The trellis must be fully assembled and installed before any final inspection, painting, staining, or finishing touches can be applied to the completed structure.
A stable, level base or foundation must exist before constructing the raised planter to ensure structural integrity and prevent uneven settling or cracking.
The planter walls/container must be fully constructed before adding soil or growing medium, otherwise the soil would spill out and the structure would not be contained.
The planter structure must be complete and filled with soil before any planting can occur, as plants require the contained soil environment provided by the planter.
While irrigation can be planned alongside, it is most efficiently installed after the planter is built and filled to properly position watering lines within the soil bed.
Proper site grading and drainage must be established before building the planter to ensure water does not pool around or underneath the structure, preventing water damage and rot.
The foundation must be prepared and cured before any boundary enclosure (walls/fences) can be erected on top of it, as the enclosure requires a stable load-bearing base.
Site grading and drainage systems must be completed before boundary enclosure to ensure proper water flow away from the structure and to establish accurate ground levels for wall footing placement.
The boundary enclosure (walls) must be completed to provide structural support for the roof system, as the roof bears directly onto the wall plates.
Interior finishing work (drywall, painting, flooring) requires the building envelope to be closed to protect materials and work from weather exposure and to define the interior spaces.
Door and window frames are installed within the boundary enclosure openings after the wall structure is complete, as the enclosure defines the rough openings for these elements.
The shade structure requires a stable foundation to be anchored to; without it the structure would have no support.
The ground must be leveled and prepared before installing the shade structure to ensure proper alignment and stability.
Any underground utilities (electrical, plumbing, etc.) must be completed before the shade structure is installed to avoid digging and disruption around the completed structure.
The shade structure must be fully installed and erected before it can be inspected for compliance with building codes and safety standards.
Landscaping around the shade structure is easier and cleaner to perform after the structure is in place, but could theoretically be done simultaneously with careful coordination.
The ground must be properly graded and prepared before placing outdoor furniture to ensure stable, level placement and to prevent furniture from sinking or tipping.
Patios, decks, or other hardscape surfaces must be fully constructed and cured before outdoor furniture can be placed on them.

Outdoor furniture is typically placed before final planting around it so that plants can be arranged around the furniture layout, though this is a preference for aesthetic alignment rather than a physical necessity.
Final decorative touches like cushions, umbrellas, and accessories are ideally placed after the main furniture pieces are in position to ensure proper fit and arrangement.

While outdoor lighting can be installed before furniture, it is often preferred to place furniture first to determine optimal lighting placement for seating areas; however this is a soft preference, not a hard constraint.

The site must be cleared, graded, and rough contours established before landscape design can be finalized, as the topography and available space directly influence planting plans, hardscape locations, and drainage patterns.

All underground utilities (water, sewer, gas, electrical, irrigation lines) must be installed before landscape design to avoid conflicts with buried infrastructure and to ensure proper routing of landscape lighting and irrigation systems.

Building foundations, slabs, and major structural elements must be completed so that landscape design can integrate properly with building footprints, drainage around structures, and hardscape transitions.
The landscape design must be finalized to specify plant species, locations, and planting schemes before any trees, shrubs, or ground cover can be installed.

Hardscape elements such as patios, walkways, retaining walls, and decorative paving must follow the approved landscape design to ensure correct placement, dimensions, and aesthetic integration with the overall landscape plan.
The ground must be graded, leveled, and prepared before any planting, turfing, or topsoil spreading can occur. Soft landscaping requires a stable, properly formed base.
Subsurface drainage systems (e.g., French drains, soakaways) must be installed before topsoil and planting to avoid damaging the landscaping later and to ensure proper water management.
Underground utilities (water, gas, electric, data cables) must be laid and backfilled before final grading and planting to prevent excavation damage to newly installed landscaping.

Hardscape elements such as paving, retaining walls, and kerbs must be completed first so that soft landscaping can be installed flush against them and to avoid soil compaction or damage from heavy construction equipment.
Soft landscaping (planting, turf, mulching) is typically one of the final finishing works. The site must be fully landscaped before the final snagging, inspection, and handover to the client.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and surveyed before any boundary walls or fences can be erected to ensure proper alignment and foundation.
Boundary structures such as walls or fences often require footings or foundations to be laid first to provide structural stability and prevent settling.

Landscaping work (e.g., planting, grading) is typically done after boundaries are defined to work within the established property lines, though this is a preference for logical sequencing rather than a strict physical requirement.
Boundary walls or fences are usually erected before the main building construction begins to secure the site perimeter, control access, and clearly demarcate the construction zone.

While utilities can technically be installed before boundaries, it is preferred to have boundaries defined first to ensure utility lines do not cross property lines and to coordinate trenching with site layout.
The ground must be excavated and graded to the proper elevations and slopes before any water feature can be installed to ensure proper drainage, a stable base, and correct alignment.

Underground electrical conduits, water supply lines, and drainage pipes must be roughed in before installing the water feature, as these utilities need to be buried beneath or within the feature's footprint.
A concrete base or structural slab must be poured and cured to provide a stable, level foundation for the water feature's basin, pump housing, and structural components.
The water feature structure (basin, shell, or framework) must be fully installed before waterproofing membranes or liners can be applied to ensure continuous sealing of the completed assembly.

Soft preference: planting around the water feature is easier and cleaner after the feature is in place, but could theoretically be done concurrently. Typically scheduled after to avoid soil and debris contamination of the water system.
The specific site location must be known before microclimate analysis can be performed, as microclimate factors (solar radiation, wind patterns, temperature, humidity) are site-specific.
Local topography (hills, valleys, slopes) directly influences wind patterns, solar exposure, and temperature variations, so a topographic survey is needed as input for microclimate modeling.
Historical weather data, including temperature, precipitation, wind speed/direction, and solar radiation records, must be gathered to serve as baseline inputs for microclimate analysis.

The results of microclimate analysis (prevailing wind direction, solar path, shading patterns) directly inform optimal building orientation to maximize passive solar gain, natural ventilation, and thermal comfort.
Microclimate data determines the placement of vegetation, water features, and shading structures to mitigate wind, provide cooling, and enhance outdoor comfort.
The structural steel frame must be erected to provide the support structure and mounting points for the skylight array components.
The roof deck must be installed to define the roof opening and provide a working surface for skylight installation.
Waterproofing and flashing around the skylight can only be completed after the skylight array is installed to ensure proper sealing and weather-tight integration.
While interior ceiling finishes can be sequenced after skylight installation to avoid damage from overhead work, it is a soft preference as temporary protections could allow some parallel work.

Electrical wiring for daylight harvesting sensors and lighting controls integrated with the skylight must be connected after the skylight array is physically installed and its control system is in place.
The structural frame (columns, beams, roof structure) must be in place to provide support and attachment points for the clerestory window band assembly.
The roof deck above the clerestory must be installed to define the upper boundary and provide weatherproofing before the window band can be fitted beneath it.
Completing the window band before interior finishing is a soft preference to allow for clean sealing, insulation, and drywall work around the window openings without later rework.
The clerestory window band must be fully installed and flashed before exterior cladding is applied around it to ensure proper weather sealing and a clean interface between window and cladding.
The window frame or band structure must be in place before glass panels can be fitted and glazed into the clerestory openings.
Light shelves are typically mounted on walls or integrated with the building structure, so the structural frame, walls, and roof must be in place to provide a mounting surface.
Exterior walls must be sheathed and waterproofed before installing light shelves that penetrate or attach to the exterior wall envelope, to ensure weather-tightness.
Light shelves are often positioned above or adjacent to windows to reflect daylight deeper into the space; windows must be installed first to establish the correct alignment and clearance.
Light shelves should be installed before finishing interior ceilings and drywall to allow for proper integration, mounting, and sealing around the shelf penetration or bracket.
It is preferred but not strictly required to install light shelves before interior painting, as painting after can be more efficient and avoids needing to mask or touch up around the installed shelf.
The foundation must be constructed and cured before any structural framing, including the wing canopy, can be erected to provide a stable load-bearing base.
Reinforcing steel for the supporting structure must be placed before the canopy's concrete or steel framing can be installed.
Support columns or vertical supports that will carry the canopy must be erected before the canopy structure can be placed on top of them.
The structural canopy frame must be complete before roofing membranes, waterproofing, or cladding can be applied to it.
Electrical conduit, lighting fixtures, and other overhead mechanical/electrical/plumbing services within or below the canopy require the structural canopy to be in place for attachment and routing.
The structural roof framing (e.g., purlins, rafters, or trusses) must be fully installed to provide the load-bearing support and substrate onto which translucent roof panels are fastened.
A continuous roof deck or sheathing is typically required as a base layer before translucent panel systems can be laid and secured, ensuring a level and stable installation surface.
Waterproof underlayment and base flashings around roof penetrations must be in place before translucent panels are installed to maintain the building envelope's weathertightness.

While insulation can often be installed from below concurrently or after, it is common practice to complete the translucent panel installation first so that insulation can be fitted tightly against the panels without weather exposure concerns.

successor: Roof Trim and Ridge Cap Installation
rationale: Trim, ridge caps, and edge closures are installed after the translucent panels are in place to seal the panel edges and complete the weatherproofing of the roof assembly.
The structural steel frame provides the primary load-bearing support onto which the solar shading louvres are mounted; without the frame, there is no structure to attach the louvres to.

predecessor: External Wall Cladding / Curtain Wall Installation
rationale: The solar shading louvres are typically integrated with or mounted onto the curtain wall or external wall cladding system; the cladding must be in place to provide the attachment points and alignment references for the louvres.

Louvres are often installed before glazing to allow access for fixing brackets and to avoid damaging finished glass panels; also, the louvre system serves as external shading that must be positioned relative to the windows behind it.

Finishing works such as painting and sealing are typically done after louvre installation to ensure a uniform appearance and to seal any penetrations made during louvre fixing, though some touch-ups can be done concurrently.
Scaffolding is used to access the facade for louvre installation; once the louvres are installed, the scaffolding can be removed as it is no longer needed for this work package.

The tensile membrane sail requires the structural steel frame to be erected first, as the membrane is tensioned and attached to the steel support structure. Without the frame in place, the membrane cannot be anchored or tensioned properly.

The anchor points and foundations that secure the tensile membrane sail's support cables and masts must be fully cured and in place before the membrane can be installed and tensioned, as the structural integrity of the entire assembly depends on these anchor points.

Weatherproofing seals and edge details can only be properly applied after the membrane is fully installed and tensioned on its frame, as the sealing must conform to the membrane's final tensioned shape and connections.

Load testing and final tension adjustments must occur after the membrane is installed, as the testing verifies the performance of the installed system and fine-tunes the tensioning that was set during installation.

While not physically required, it is strongly preferred to complete any overhead electrical conduit, lighting fixture rough-ins, or other utilities that will be mounted beneath or integrated with the sail structure before the membrane is installed, as access becomes much more difficult afterward.
Membrane panels must be installed and laid out before they can be tensioned and commissioned.
The supporting cable net structure must be in place to provide the framework for tensioning the membrane.
Individual membrane panels must be welded and seamed together into a continuous membrane surface before tensioning can be applied.
Perimeter edges must be clamped and detailed to secure the membrane boundaries before tensioning forces are applied.
The completed tensioned membrane must be commissioned before final inspection and testing of the roof system can be carried out.
Cleaning and applying protective coatings is typically done after tensioning is complete, though it could be done partially before if sequencing allows.
Temporary scaffolding and works under the membrane can only be safely dismantled after the membrane is tensioned and structurally self-supporting.
The solar shading system must be physically installed and connected before it can be commissioned and tested for proper operation.
Power supply and control wiring must be in place to energize and test the shading system during commissioning.
The BMS or central control system must be installed and operational to integrate, control, and monitor the solar shading devices during commissioning.
Commissioning must verify proper functionality of the shading system before it can be handed over to the building owner and operators, and before training can be conducted.
Commissioning results and any necessary adjustments must be completed and accepted before the project can proceed to final close-out activities.

Post-occupancy evaluation by definition occurs after the building is completed, fully commissioned, and occupied by users. The evaluation assesses real-world daylighting performance under actual occupancy conditions.

All daylighting components (windows, skylights, light shelves, shading devices, automated blinds, daylight-responsive lighting controls) must be fully installed, calibrated, and commissioned before their in-use performance can be evaluated.
Interior furnishings, partitions, and workstations affect light distribution and glare patterns. The evaluation must reflect actual occupied conditions including furniture layout.

While not a hard physical requirement, post-occupancy evaluation data often informs retrofit or redesign decisions to improve daylighting performance. This is a soft preference as retrofits may be undertaken for other reasons or not at all.

Results from the daylighting evaluation can trigger adjustments to shading controls, blind positions, or lighting setpoints to address occupant comfort issues. This is a soft preference as adjustments may be done proactively without waiting for evaluation results.
The specific site location and its geographic coordinates must be known before solar radiation analysis can be performed, as solar exposure depends on latitude, longitude, and local topography.
The building's orientation relative to the sun's path is a fundamental input for solar radiation analysis; the orientation must be established first.
A geometric massing or BIM model of the proposed building and surrounding context is required to perform solar radiation simulations and shadow studies.
Solar radiation data (solar heat gain, daylight availability) is a critical input for whole-building energy modeling to calculate heating/cooling loads and energy consumption.
Solar radiation results inform daylight autonomy, Useful Daylight Illuminance (UDI), and glare probability assessments, which depend on direct and diffuse solar exposure patterns.
The tunnel connector requires a prepared excavation area to be constructed within; excavation must precede any underground structure installation.
Soil conditions must be assessed and stabilized before tunneling to prevent collapse or structural failure.
Any existing underground utilities in the tunnel path must be relocated or protected before excavation and tunnel construction can begin.
The tunnel structure must be in place before lining and waterproofing can be applied to seal and stabilize the tunnel.

successor: MEP (Mechanical, Electrical, Plumbing) Rough-In within Tunnel
rationale: After the tunnel connector structure is complete, internal mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems can be installed within the tunnel space.
The tunnel must be fully constructed and sealed before backfilling around it and restoring the surface grade above.
Final finishes, lighting, signage, and system commissioning can only occur after the tunnel structure and MEP rough-in are complete.
The transfer deck requires a stable foundation to bear and distribute its loads.
Core walls or supporting columns below the transfer deck must be completed to provide vertical support for the transfer structure.
Upper floor slabs rely on the transfer deck as their structural base for load distribution.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems above the deck require the structural platform to be in place for routing and support.
The façade system above the transfer level depends on the completed structural deck for anchoring and alignment.
The ground must be excavated and leveled before any foundation or podium base can be poured or installed.
Structural piles or deep foundations must be installed to bear the load of the podium base before the podium slab or base can be constructed.
Underground utilities that will pass beneath the podium must be laid and inspected before the podium base is poured, to avoid breaking the slab later.
Waterproofing must be applied directly onto the cured podium base to protect the structure from moisture ingress before any subsequent layers are added.
Columns and core walls rising from the podium require the podium base to be fully cured and load-bearing before vertical construction can commence.
The architectural design must be completed to provide the spatial layout and building geometry that forms the basis for IFC-BIM coordination.
Structural design must be finalized so that its elements (columns, beams, slabs) can be integrated into the IFC-BIM model for clash detection and interface coordination.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing design must be completed to coordinate routing and spatial interfaces with other building systems in the BIM environment.

successor: BIM Model Export & IFC File Generation
rationale: After coordination is complete, the final BIM model can be exported to IFC format for downstream use by contractors and fabricators.
Interface coordination identifies clashes and conflicts; these must be resolved and documented after coordination is finished.
Foundation excavation is the primary trigger for potential differential settlement; monitoring must begin as soon as excavation starts to track any movement.
Monitoring points (e.g., survey markers, tiltmeters) must be installed on the structure and ground before any readings can be taken.
A baseline survey must be completed prior to monitoring to record initial elevations and reference conditions against which all subsequent settlement is measured.

successor: Structural Load Application (e.g., backfilling, superstructure construction)
rationale: Monitoring must be ongoing before and during load application to detect settlement trends; if settlement exceeds thresholds, load application may need to be halted or adjusted.

If monitoring reveals unacceptable differential settlement, remedial measures such as grouting or underpinning can only be designed and executed after the settlement data has been collected and analyzed.
Bolts must be tensioned to their required preload before the joint can be inspected, as inspection verifies the tensioned state and integrity of the connection.
Joint surfaces must be cleaned of debris, grease, and contaminants prior to inspection to allow for accurate visual and mechanical assessment.
All connection components (plates, bolts, gaskets, etc.) must be fully assembled before the completed joint can be inspected and maintained.
Inspection and maintenance must be completed before pressure testing to ensure the joint is properly assembled and any deficiencies are corrected, avoiding test failures or safety hazards.

Inspection and maintenance should be performed before applying protective coatings, as coating over an uninspected joint could hide defects; however, in some sequences coating can be partially applied beforehand if access is preserved.
The site must be cleared, graded, and prepared before any building construction can begin to provide a stable and accessible foundation for all subsequent structures.

predecessor: Utility Infrastructure Installation (Water, Sewer, Electrical, Gas)
rationale: Main utility lines and infrastructure must be installed across the site before individual buildings are constructed, otherwise buildings would need to be excavated or retrofitted later, causing major disruption and cost.

Final landscaping, paving, and site amenities are typically completed after all building construction phases are finished to avoid damage from ongoing construction activities, though some preliminary landscaping may be done earlier.
All buildings within the phased construction must be substantially complete before the entire site can be commissioned, tested as an integrated complex, and handed over to the owner or occupants.
The fire alarm system must be installed and operational before a fire evacuation drill can be conducted, as the alarm is the primary signal to initiate the evacuation.
Emergency lighting must be in place to ensure safe egress paths are illuminated during the drill, simulating real emergency conditions.
Exit signs must be installed to clearly mark evacuation routes, which participants will follow during the drill.

predecessor: Fire Extinguisher and Safety Equipment Installation
rationale: Fire extinguishers and safety equipment must be in place per code requirements before any emergency drill can be conducted.
The building must be officially permitted and deemed safe for occupancy before occupants can participate in an evacuation drill.
After the drill, it is recommended (but not physically required) to inspect fire safety systems and verify they performed correctly during the simulated event.
The evacuation drill is often a prerequisite for final building commissioning or handover, as authorities require proof of a successful drill before signing off on the project.
The structural frame requires a stable and level foundation to bear its load; without completed foundations, the frame cannot be erected.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and compacted before any structural frame components can be placed, to ensure proper alignment and stability.
Underground utilities (drainage, water, electrical conduits) must be laid before the frame is erected, as accessing them afterward would be difficult or impossible.
The structural frame provides the primary support for roof panels and exterior cladding; these envelope elements cannot be attached until the frame is fully erected and stabilized.
Interior walls, MEP (mechanical, electrical, plumbing) rough-ins, and finishes rely on the structural frame for support and spatial definition; they commence only after the frame is complete.
End-gable walls require a stable foundation to bear their load; without a completed foundation the wall cannot be safely erected.
The end-gable wall typically sits on top of the floor platform or wall plate; the floor structure must be in place to provide a level bearing surface.
End-gable walls support the gable-end trusses or rafters; the roof structure cannot be fully framed without the end-gable walls in position to receive roof loads.
Siding and cladding are applied over the completed wall sheathing; the end-gable wall must be fully erected and sheathed before exterior finishes can be installed.
Gable-end trim, fascia, and soffits are attached directly to the end-gable wall framing; the wall must be complete to serve as the attachment substrate.
The roof structure must be in place to provide a mounting surface and opening for the skylight.
The roof deck must be installed to define the opening and provide a base for flashing and skylight installation.
The underlayment provides a water-resistant barrier that must be in place before cutting the roof opening and installing the skylight to prevent water intrusion.
Flashing is installed around the skylight curb to seal the joint between the skylight and the roof, so the skylight must be in place first.
The final roofing material is installed up to and overlapping the skylight flashing; therefore, the skylight and its flashing must be completed before the surrounding roofing material is laid.
The longitudinal roof structure relies on the primary steel frame for support and attachment, so the main structural frame must be erected first.
Roof trusses provide the primary roof support system; longitudinal roof members are installed across or between trusses and thus require trusses to be in place first.
Roof cladding (sheets, tiles, or panels) is fastened to the longitudinal roof structure, so the longitudinal supports must be completed before cladding can be applied.
Insulation is typically laid over or between the longitudinal roof members before the final roofing finish, requiring the structure to be in place first.

Gutters are attached to the edges of the roof structure; while it is strongly preferred to install them after the longitudinal structure is complete, minor adjustments can be made if the structure is partially complete, making this a soft preference.
Legal and administrative approval must be obtained before any physical site work can commence, including surveys.
Surveyors and equipment need to be mobilized and site access established before setting out can begin.
Accurate setting out of grid lines and benchmarks is physically required before any excavation or earthmoving can start.
Foundations must be positioned according to survey marks; setting out defines the exact locations for foundation work.
While often site clearing precedes setting out, in some sequences setting out may be done first to mark areas for selective clearing.
Only the property owner(s) can legally enter into a party wall agreement, so ownership must be verified before negotiation can commence.

The scope of proposed works (including excavation, foundation depths, and wall alterations) must be defined in detailed architectural drawings before adjacent property owners can review and negotiate the party wall agreement.
A condition survey of the existing party wall structure is needed to document its current state and identify potential risks before negotiating terms for shared responsibility and protection.

successor: Issuance of Party Wall Award (Formal Notice)
rationale: The formal party wall award document can only be drafted and served after negotiation between adjoining owners has concluded and terms have been agreed upon.

successor: Commencement of Excavation/Construction Adjacent to Wall
rationale: Physical construction work that affects the party wall cannot legally begin until the party wall agreement (or award) has been finalized and served, as required by the Party Wall etc. Act 1996.

Site setup including securing the area, disconnecting utilities, and implementing safety measures must be completed before any demolition work begins to ensure safe working conditions and legal compliance.
Hazardous materials such as asbestos must be identified and removed prior to demolition to prevent health risks and regulatory violations during the demolition process.
A structural survey is required to assess the condition of the existing extension and identify any load-bearing elements or connections to the main building that must be protected during demolition.

successor: Removal of Demolition Debris and Waste
rationale: Demolition debris and waste materials can only be removed from the site after the demolition is complete to clear the area for subsequent construction activities.

successor: Ground Preparation and Excavation for New Foundation
rationale: New foundation work for the replacement extension can only commence after the existing structure has been fully demolished and the site has been cleared.

The site must be cleared, leveled, and surveyed to establish accurate boundaries and reference points before any foundation work can begin on a narrow plot, as uneven or unprepared ground would compromise structural integrity.

Soil bearing capacity and ground conditions must be assessed to determine the appropriate foundation type and depth for the narrow plot, ensuring the foundation is designed to support the structural loads safely.
Trenches or pits must be excavated to the required depth and width before concrete or foundation materials can be placed, as the foundation is constructed within these excavations.

Waterproofing membranes and damp-proof courses are applied directly onto the cured foundation to protect the structure from rising damp and moisture ingress, and therefore must follow foundation completion.

Load-bearing walls and the vertical structure cannot be erected until the foundation is fully cured and capable of supporting the superimposed loads, as the foundation serves as the base for all subsequent construction.
The roof structure must be completed to provide a stable base and opening for installing the roof light.
Waterproofing is typically installed before cutting into the roof for the roof light to maintain weathertightness, or the roof light flashing integrates with the waterproofing layer.
After the roof light unit is placed, flashing must be installed around it to seal against water ingress.
The ceiling around the roof light cannot be finished until the roof light frame is in place, as the roof light creates the opening and trim that the ceiling finish must work around.
It is preferable to install the roof light before painting so that any patching or sealing around the unit is done prior to final decoration, though not physically mandatory.
A structural survey must be completed first to determine if the wall is load-bearing and to identify any services running through it, ensuring safe removal planning.
If the building is old, asbestos-containing materials may be present in wall construction; abatement must be completed before any demolition work to avoid health hazards.
Legal permits for structural alterations must be secured prior to commencing wall removal to comply with building regulations.
Any electrical wiring, plumbing pipes, or HVAC ducts running within the wall must be disconnected and rerouted before demolition to prevent damage and safety risks.
After wall removal, the floor area where the wall was located will need patching, levelling, and finishing to match surrounding surfaces.
Removing a wall typically damages adjoining ceiling areas, so ceiling repairs and redecoration must follow wall removal.
If the removed wall was load-bearing, a new structural beam or column must be installed to support the load above; this can only be done after the wall is taken down.
If the spatial rationalisation includes building new walls to reconfigure the space, those new partitions are typically built after the old wall is removed for efficient workflow.
Demolition debris from the removed wall must be cleared out of the workspace before subsequent finishing trades can commence.
The parcel must be legally owned and zoned appropriately for residential infill before any development can commence on the narrow lot.
Soil bearing capacity, contamination, and groundwater conditions must be assessed to inform foundation design and avoid structural failure on a constrained site.
Existing utility locations and connection points (water, sewer, stormwater, electricity) must be verified to coordinate trenching and avoid service conflicts during excavation.

successor: Final Inspection and Certificate of Occupancy
rationale: All construction work must be completed before municipal inspectors can certify that the building meets building codes and is safe for occupancy.

While landscaping is typically finished after the main structure is built, it is a soft preference because minor planting or hardscaping could theoretically be done concurrently with final construction stages on a narrow lot.

predecessor: Rough-in electrical conduit and wiring to door location
rationale: Electrical power supply and control wiring must be in place before the automatic door operator can be connected and powered.

predecessor: Install door frame and door leaf
rationale: The automatic door operator is mounted onto the door frame and/or door leaf; the door assembly must be installed first as the structural substrate.

predecessor: Complete overhead support structure / header reinforcement
rationale: Automatic door operators often require a reinforced header or framing to bear the weight and torque; this structural work must precede operator mounting.

successor: Connect power and control wiring to operator unit
rationale: The operator unit must be physically mounted before final electrical connections can be made to its terminals.

successor: Install activation sensors (motion detectors, push plates, safety beams)
rationale: Sensors must be positioned relative to the installed door and operator; the operator location defines sensor placement and wiring.
The operator must be physically installed before it can be programmed, tested, and calibrated for opening speed, force, and safety settings.
The foundation must be completed to provide a stable load-bearing base for the entrance steps.
The ground floor slab must be poured to establish the finished floor level from which the entrance steps will descend or ascend.
Handrails must be installed after steps are complete so they can be properly anchored to the step structure and aligned to the finished stair geometry.
Final grading and landscaping around the entrance can be completed after steps are in place to ensure proper drainage and aesthetic transition, though some rough grading could be done earlier.
The entry door frame and door are typically installed after the steps are complete to ensure correct threshold alignment and step-to-door height relationship.
A stable, level foundation must exist to support and anchor the threshold plate properly.
The door opening frame must be constructed to provide the correct dimensions and structural support for the threshold plate.
The subfloor or underlayment beneath the doorway must be in place to provide a continuous substrate for the threshold plate to rest upon.
The threshold plate serves as the bottom anchor point and reference for the door frame, so it must be installed first to ensure proper alignment and fit.
The threshold plate provides the base surface and sealing point for the door bottom; the door cannot be properly hung or aligned without the threshold in place.
The structural frame must be in place to provide the load-bearing support and attachment points for the curtain wall system.
Floor slabs provide the horizontal structural support and anchorage points required at each floor level for curtain wall installation.
Rough openings and blocking must be framed to create the precise openings and backing for curtain wall mullions and panels.
The curtain wall must be installed and sealed before interior finishes are applied to prevent damage to finishes and to allow proper flashing, waterproofing, and air sealing at the perimeter.

While some MEP rough-in can occur concurrently, final connections and trim at the curtain wall perimeter, such as perimeter heating, electrical outlets, or sprinkler heads, are best completed after the curtain wall is installed to ensure proper fit and coordination.
The door frame must be structurally supported by wall framing before the fire exit/egress door can be installed.
The rough opening in the wall must be framed and sized correctly to accommodate the fire-rated door assembly before installation can begin.
Panic hardware, locks, hinges, and closing mechanisms can only be mounted once the door is hung in its frame.
Fire-rated sealant and perimeter sealing must be applied after the door is installed to ensure the fire-resistance rating of the assembly.
Egress doors must be fully installed before building officials can inspect for compliance with fire and life safety codes (e.g., NFPA 101, IBC).
The door frame must be installed to provide the structural support and mounting surface for the panic hardware/push bar.
The door leaf must be hung and in place because the panic hardware/push bar is mounted directly onto the door surface.
The latch mechanism and cutouts on the door must be prepared to receive the panic hardware's latching components.
The panic hardware must be installed before the door hardware can be fully adjusted and tested for proper operation and compliance with fire safety codes.
Panic hardware installation must be complete for the fire and safety inspection to verify that egress requirements are met.
The directory board must be mounted on finished interior walls to ensure proper attachment and alignment.
Electrical wiring for potential backlighting or power to the directory board must be installed before the board is mounted.
Flooring should be completed to establish final floor levels and avoid damage to new flooring during directory board installation.
The directory board should be installed before final painting touch-ups so that any wall damage from mounting can be repaired and painted over.
The directory board must be in place and functional before the building can be inspected and commissioned for occupancy.
Electrical conduits and low-voltage wiring must be run through walls and ceilings to the door entry points before the intercom units can be physically connected and mounted.

After the intercom/video door phone hardware is installed and wired, the system must be programmed for access codes, video settings, and integration with building security; then tested for audio, video, and door release functions.

predecessor: Door frame and entry door installation
rationale: The exterior door frame and door must be installed so that the intercom/video door phone unit can be properly mounted adjacent to or integrated with the door entry assembly.
It is preferred to complete wall finishing and painting before mounting the intercom unit to avoid dust, paint splatter, or damage to the electronic device during finishing work.

The intercom must be installed and operational before the final electrical trim-out and building commissioning, as it is part of the security and communications systems that need to be verified during final acceptance testing.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and graded before any landscaping can be installed to ensure proper drainage and a stable base for planting.
Utilities such as water lines, irrigation pipes, electrical conduits, and drainage systems must be laid underground before landscaping is done to avoid digging up and damaging finished plantings.

Major construction equipment and heavy machinery needed for foundation work would damage landscaping, so the building envelope must be substantially complete before final entrance landscaping is installed.

Landscaping is typically completed before final project walkthroughs and punch-list completion to present a finished appearance, though this is a sequencing preference rather than a physical necessity.

Hardscape surfaces like paved driveways, walkways, and the entrance plaza must be installed before adjacent landscaping, as heavy equipment for paving and concrete work would crush plants and ruin soft landscape areas.
Security system components (sensors, panels, wiring) require electrical power and conduit paths that must be roughed-in before commissioning can proceed.
All low voltage cabling for security devices (cameras, door contacts, motion detectors) must be installed and terminated prior to system commissioning and testing.

The security system depends on network connectivity for communication between controllers, monitoring stations, and user interfaces; network switches and cabling must be in place before commissioning.
After individual security components are commissioned (tested and configured), the integrated system test with other building systems (access control, fire alarm, BMS) must follow.
The security system must be fully commissioned and verified operational before the final building inspection and handover to the owner/occupant can occur.
The site must be cleared of existing structures, debris, and vegetation before new boundary planting can be installed to ensure unobstructed access and proper soil preparation.
Bulk earthworks and topsoil stripping must be completed so that the ground is at the correct level and properly prepared for planting.
Any underground drainage systems along the boundary must be installed before planting to avoid disturbing the hedge roots later.
It is often preferred to install planting screens before solid fencing so the hedge can establish and provide a softer boundary, though fencing can proceed first depending on the design.

Final landscaping, including mulching, seeding, and topsoiling adjacent areas, should be done after the hedge is planted to integrate it into the finished landscape and avoid disturbing newly planted material.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and compacted before constructing the ramp to ensure a stable foundation.
The ramp requires a proper base/foundation to be laid first to support its structure and prevent settling or cracking.
The ramp structure must be fully constructed before final surface finishing (e.g., concrete pouring, paving, or tiling) can be applied.
It is preferable to complete the ramp before planting or landscaping around the entry area to avoid damaging new plants with construction equipment.
Handrails must be installed after the ramp structure is in place to ensure proper alignment and secure attachment to the ramp.
The staircase structure requires a stable foundation. Excavation and concrete pouring for the staircase base/footing must be completed before any staircase construction can begin.
Proper site grading and drainage systems must be in place around the garden entry area to prevent water accumulation and soil erosion that could undermine the staircase foundation.
Any underground utilities (water, gas, electric) in the path of the staircase must be relocated beforehand to avoid conflicts and safety hazards during excavation.
Railings and balusters attach directly to the staircase structure itself, so the staircase steps and stringers must be fully constructed before railings can be installed.

successor: Landscape Planting & Hardscaping Adjacent to Stairs
rationale: While planting can begin after stairs are built to avoid damage to new plants from construction traffic, it is a soft preference as planting could theoretically be done concurrently with careful staging.
The staircase must be fully constructed, cured (if concrete), and set before any final sealants, waterproofing membranes, or surface treatments are applied to protect the finish.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and graded before any fence or wall foundation can be laid, ensuring a stable and uniform base.
Underground utility lines must be identified and marked before digging post holes or trench footings to avoid service strikes and ensure safety.
The perimeter boundary must be established before interior garden planting to define the area, protect plants, and sequence construction activities.
Gates and entrance hardware are mounted onto or integrated with the fence or wall structure, so the main structure must be complete beforehand.
While not physically required, it is a soft preference to complete fencing before final finishing to avoid damaging finished landscaping during fence installation.
Proper grading and drainage must be established before planting beds to prevent water pooling and ensure plant survival.
Utilities such as irrigation lines, drainage pipes, and electrical conduits must be placed before soil and plants are installed to avoid excavation damage.
The subgrade must be properly compacted and rough-graded to design elevations before topsoil and planting bed preparation can begin.
The planting bed must be fully prepared (soil, edging, amendments) before any plants are placed into the bed.
Mulch is applied after planting bed preparation and planting are complete to retain moisture and suppress weeds without interfering with planting activities.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated before any foundation work for the pergola can begin, ensuring a stable base.
Concrete footings or foundations for the pergola posts must be poured and cured before the structure can be erected on top of them.
Any underground electrical, water, or drainage lines that will serve the pergola area must be installed before the structure is built to avoid digging under or around completed work.
If the pergola has a solid or partially solid roof, roofing materials can be installed after the frame is complete, but this is dependent on design rather than a strict physical necessity.
Lighting fixtures, fans, or outlets mounted on or within the pergola structure can only be installed after the frame is erected, though this is an elective add-on.

Planting, mulching, and decorative landscaping around the pergola should be done after the structure is built to avoid damage to plants during construction and to ensure proper alignment with the finished structure.
The ground must be properly excavated, graded, and compacted to provide a stable and level base for the water feature's structural shell or liner.
Water supply lines, recirculation piping, and drainage systems must be installed in the ground before the pool shell or basin is constructed to avoid digging up completed work.

predecessor: Concrete Foundation / Slab Work (for pool basin)
rationale: The reinforced concrete basin or structural slab must be poured and cured before waterproofing and finishing can begin.
After the pool basin structure is complete, waterproof membranes, sealants, and coatings must be applied to prevent leaks.

successor: Mechanical Equipment Installation (Pumps, Filters, UV Treatment)
rationale: Pumps, filtration units, and treatment systems can only be installed and connected once the basin and plumbing are in place.
The interior decorative finish (tile, stone, plaster) must be applied after the structural basin is complete and waterproofed.

successor: Electrical Connections for Lighting and Control Systems
rationale: Submersible lights, control panels, and automation wiring are installed after the pool structure is finished to avoid damage during construction.
The pool can only be filled with water and tested for leaks, pump operation, and recirculation after all construction, waterproofing, and equipment installation is complete.
Final planting, paving, and decorative stonework around the pool edge is typically done after the pool is built, though some adjacent work could overlap with careful coordination.
A stable foundation or slab must be in place to support the vertical loads of a privacy screen or trellis structure.
If the privacy screen or trellis is attached to a building, the adjacent wall framing must be complete to provide a structural attachment point.
Underground or slab-embedded utilities must be roughed in before digging post holes or pouring footings for the trellis to avoid conflicts.
It is preferable to apply paint or stain after assembly to protect the wood, but this is a soft preference as pre-finished materials could also be used.
Climbing plants or adjacent landscaping are typically installed after the trellis is in place so they can grow up the structure, but this is a sequential preference rather than a physical necessity.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and topsoil to expose the ground where the retaining wall will be built, ensuring a stable foundation.
Excavation for the wall footing or base is required before the wall can be constructed, as the wall needs a prepared trench or excavated area for its foundation.
The subgrade and base material must be compacted and graded to provide a stable, level surface that can support the retaining wall without settling.
Backfilling behind the wall and installing drainage systems (e.g., weep holes, gravel drains) can only occur after the wall structure is built to retain the soil and allow proper water management.
Waterproofing coatings, sealants, or surface finishes must be applied after the wall is fully constructed and cured to protect it from moisture and enhance durability.
The ground must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and topsoil, and excavated to the required depth before any paving base layers can be laid, otherwise the paving will be unstable.
Any underground drainage pipes, cables, or conduits must be installed and covered before paving, because ripping up finished paving to access underground services would waste material and labor.
A compacted sub-base layer (e.g., 100–150 mm of MOT Type 1 aggregate) is required to provide a stable, load-bearing foundation for the paving slabs; without it the slabs would crack or sink.

After paving slabs are laid and bedded, the joints must be filled with kiln-dried sand (or a sealant) and compacted to lock the slabs in place and prevent weed growth; this cannot be done before the slabs are installed.

It is generally preferable to complete paving first and then do final planting, edging, and turfing so that heavy machinery and foot traffic do not damage newly planted beds; however, planting could technically be done concurrently if care is taken.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated to the required depth before any foundation or wall structure can be erected.
A stable foundation (e.g., concrete footing) must be in place to support the masonry or structure of the Ha-Ha wall; building the wall directly on unprepared soil would lead to instability.

successor: Backfilling and Landscaping (on the sunken side)
rationale: The Ha-Ha wall creates a sunken barrier; the earth on the lower (outer) side can only be graded and landscaped after the wall is built to define the retaining level.

successor: Installation of Drainage Systems (behind the wall)
rationale: Proper drainage (e.g., gravel backfill, drainage pipes) must be installed after the wall structure is complete to prevent water pressure buildup behind the retaining face.

successor: Railing or Fence Installation (if on top)
rationale: A decorative or safety railing atop the Ha-Ha wall is typically added after the wall is finished, though this is a design preference rather than a physical necessity.
The rough opening in the wall must be prepared (framed and sized) before a swing door can be installed into it.
The door frame must be installed and secured in the rough opening before the swing door leaf can be hung on the frame.
Wall framing must be completed to define the rough opening dimensions for the door frame.
Hardware such as hinges, locks, handles, and closer mechanisms are installed on the door after the door leaf is hung in the frame.
Painting or finishing is typically done after the door is hung to ensure proper alignment and fit, though pre-finished doors could be installed after painting.
