The rough opening (framed and sized correctly) must be prepared before the bi-folding door can be installed, as it provides the structural support and precise dimensions needed for the door frame.
The floor must be level and finished (or at least prepared) so the bi-folding door's bottom track and threshold have a stable, flat surface to rest on, ensuring proper operation and sealing.
After the door is installed, gaps around the frame must be sealed and weather-stripping applied to prevent air and water infiltration.
Interior trim and casing around the door opening cannot be properly installed until the bi-folding door frame is in place and secured.
Final adjustments to the door's folding mechanism, track alignment, and handle/lock operation must be performed after installation to ensure smooth functionality and security.
Weather stripping is applied around windows and doors to seal gaps. The windows and doors must be installed first so the weather stripping can be properly fitted and adhered to the existing frames.
The rough openings for windows and doors must be framed and prepared before any weather stripping can be applied, as weather stripping attaches to the finished frame surfaces.
While not always strictly required, exterior siding is typically completed before weather stripping to ensure a clean appearance and to avoid damaging the stripping during siding installation.

Weather stripping seals the gap between the window/door and the frame. Interior trim (casing, baseboards) is installed after weather stripping so that the trim can cover any exposed edges and provide a finished look without interfering with the seal.

Weather stripping is part of the building envelope's air sealing. Once installed, the overall air sealing effectiveness can be tested and verified, and final insulation layers can be placed without having to access behind the stripping.
The panic bar must be mounted onto the door leaf, which is attached to the door frame. The door frame must be installed first to provide structural support for the door and the panic bar hardware.
The panic bar is physically attached to the door leaf. The door must be hung on its hinges before the panic bar can be installed onto it.

successor: Door Hardware Final Adjustment and Testing
rationale: After the panic bar is installed, the door closing mechanism, latch alignment, and overall push-to-exit function must be tested and adjusted to ensure code-compliant operation.
Fire and life safety inspections require that panic hardware is installed and functioning before the building can be signed off for occupancy.

predecessor: Rough-in for Electrical (if electric trim or alarm)
rationale: If the panic bar includes electric latch retraction, request-to-exit (REX) switches, or alarm integration, the electrical rough-in (conduit and wiring to the door frame) must be completed before the panic bar hardware is installed.
Power and low-voltage cabling must be run to the access control reader location before the reader can be physically installed and connected.
Conduit for access control wiring must be in place before pulling cables and installing the reader.
The wall or mounting surface must be framed and ready to receive the reader before it can be mounted.
Drywall must be installed and finished so that the reader can be properly mounted flush to the finished wall surface.

successor: Access control system configuration and testing
rationale: The reader must be physically installed before the system can be configured, credentials assigned, and end-to-end testing performed.
The reader is typically integrated with the door strike or magnetic lock, and both must be installed before the full door access system is operational.
Reader installation should be complete before final commissioning walkthroughs, though some adjustments could theoretically occur in parallel.
The entryway mat or grating must be placed on or within a finished, cured concrete slab or solid floor base to provide proper support and anchoring.
If the entryway mat or grating is installed over a drainage system or requires an underlayment for leveling and water management, that underlayment must be placed first.
It is preferable to complete sealing or finishing of adjacent flooring surfaces after the mat/grating is in place so that edges are neatly transitioned.
The entryway mat or grating must be installed so that the door can swing or close over it without obstruction; door clearance is checked after mat placement.
The entryway opening must be framed and defined before the mat/grating dimensions can be finalized and installed.
The rough opening must be framed and prepared before any glazing units can be installed, as the glazing is set into the prepared opening.
Flashing and waterproofing around the opening must be installed prior to glazing to ensure the assembly is weathertight and to prevent moisture intrusion behind the glazing.
Interior trim and casing are installed after the glazing unit is in place, as the trim covers the gap between the glazing frame and the wall finish.
Final exterior sealant application around the perimeter of the sidelight/transom is completed after the glazing is set to seal the unit against the weather barrier.
Air and water infiltration testing of the sidelight/transom assembly must occur after the glazing is fully installed and sealed to verify proper performance.
The structural slab must be in place to provide the base support and anchoring surface for the curtain wall entry section.
The rough opening in the building facade must be prepared and framed to receive the curtain wall entry section.
Waterproofing at the slab edge and opening perimeter must be applied before the curtain wall is installed to prevent moisture intrusion behind the system.
After the entry section is installed, all perimeter joints and seams must be sealed to complete the building envelope airtightness.
Interior drywall, flooring, and trim work adjacent to the entry section should follow after installation to avoid damage and ensure proper alignment with the curtain wall frame.
Electrical wiring must be roughed-in to provide power to the sensor/motion detector before it can be installed and connected.
The overhead sensor is typically mounted to or within the ceiling grid, so the ceiling support structure must be in place first.
Ceiling tiles are installed after the sensor to allow access for mounting, wiring connections, and adjustments to the sensor within the ceiling grid.
The sensor must be physically installed before the lighting control system can be programmed and commissioned to receive input from the sensor.
Sensor installation must be complete before final electrical trim-out and testing, as the sensor is part of the electrical finishing work.
The door frame must be in place to provide the structural support and reveal for the threshold to be properly seated and anchored.
The subfloor or finished flooring underlayment must be completed to establish the correct elevation and a smooth surface for the threshold to sit on.
The rough opening for the door must be framed and squared to provide the correct dimensions for the door unit and threshold placement.
The threshold and weatherseal must be installed first so that the door slab can be hung and adjusted to close properly against the weatherstripping and sit correctly on the threshold.

successor: Final Door Adjustment and Hardware Installation
rationale: The threshold and weatherseal provide the sealing surface against which the door is aligned; final adjustments to latch, strike plate, and hinges depend on the threshold position.

Structural openings (doors, windows, etc.) can only be formed after the foundation and structural frame are in place, as the openings are part of the vertical wall and slab systems that rest on the foundation.
The structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) must be erected first to define the overall building geometry, within which structural openings are then formed.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work (routing pipes, ducts, conduits) typically occurs after openings are formed, as openings define wall cavities and penetration paths.
Doors and windows cannot be installed until the structural openings (rough openings) have been formed and framed to the correct dimensions.
Interior wall finishing (drywall, plaster) must follow opening formation, as the openings define where wall surfaces are interrupted and require trim and framing.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and properly graded before any paving or landscaping can begin to ensure a stable base and proper drainage for the entry paving and planted areas.
All underground utilities such as water lines, electrical conduits, and drainage pipes must be installed and covered before paving and landscaping to avoid disrupting finished surfaces.

While not strictly required, completing the main building's foundation and rough structure first prevents heavy construction equipment and material deliveries from damaging newly paved surfaces and landscaping.
Completing entry paving and landscaping before final exterior finishes allows for clean access and staging areas, though it is a soft preference to avoid soiling or damaging the new finishes.

successor: Final Site Clean-Up and Punch List
rationale: Entry paving and landscaping are among the final site elements; after these are complete, only final cleanup, touch-ups, and inspections remain, as no further heavy construction should occur that could damage the finished entry.
The facade panels must be installed first to provide the substrate onto which waterproofing is applied.
The door frame must be in place so that waterproofing can be properly integrated and sealed around the frame to prevent water ingress at the entry.
Overhead roof waterproofing should be completed before applying facade waterproofing at the entry to ensure water runs off correctly and does not interfere with the facade waterproofing work below.
The entry door should be installed after waterproofing is complete so that the waterproofing membrane can wrap behind or under the door threshold for a continuous water barrier.
Final cladding or finishing layers (e.g., stone veneer, stucco) must be applied over the waterproofing to protect it from UV exposure and mechanical damage.
The parking barrier/boom gate requires a stable and level concrete foundation or base slab to be mounted on. Without this base, the barrier cannot be securely anchored.

The boom gate mechanism requires electrical power for operation and data cabling for control systems (e.g., ticketing, access control). These conduits must be laid in the ground before the barrier is installed to avoid digging up finished work.
Once the barrier is physically installed, it must be wired to the power supply and control system, then tested for proper operation (opening, closing, safety sensors).
The boom gate is often installed before the final paving layer so that the asphalt can be laid flush around the base, ensuring a smooth surface and proper drainage without gaps.
While not a physical necessity, lane markings and directional signage are typically completed after the barrier is in place to ensure correct alignment with the gate's position and traffic flow.
A stable, level foundation is physically required to support the turntable platform before it can be installed.
Electrical and control cabling for the turntable drive mechanism must be laid beneath the platform area prior to platform placement.
Approach tracks must be aligned and connected to the turntable platform after it is fixed in position to ensure correct geometry.
The drive mechanism (motor, gearing, controls) can only be tested and commissioned after the platform is securely installed.
Deck finishing or surfacing is a soft preference to follow installation for access efficiency, though in some cases could be done concurrently or pre-installed.
The wheel stop must be anchored to a stable, level foundation to ensure it remains securely in place and can withstand vehicle impact without shifting.

Proper drainage and grading must be completed before installing wheel stops to prevent water pooling around the stop and to ensure the stop sits at the correct elevation relative to the pavement surface.
While not physically required, it is standard practice to complete wheel stop installation before final striping to ensure parking space markings align correctly with the wheel stop position.

successor: Final Inspection and Parking Lot Opening
rationale: Wheel stops must be installed before the parking lot can be opened for use, as they are critical safety components that prevent vehicles from overrunning parking spaces.
If the wheel stop is to be installed on fresh concrete pavement, the concrete must be fully cured to achieve sufficient strength to anchor the wheel stop bolts without cracking.
The foundation/footings must be completed before the structural slab (parking deck) can be poured, as the slab rests on and is supported by the foundation system.
Any underground plumbing, electrical conduits, or drainage lines that pass beneath the parking deck slab must be installed and inspected before the concrete slab is placed.
The ground or base material must be properly graded, compacted, and leveled to provide uniform support for the structural slab.
Vertical structural elements that rise above the parking deck typically require the deck slab to be cured and in place as a working platform and to transfer loads.
Waterproofing membranes or protective coatings are applied after the concrete slab has cured to prevent moisture damage and provide a durable driving surface.
Geotechnical surveys must be completed before excavation begins to understand soil conditions, groundwater levels, and bearing capacity to ensure safe excavation design and shoring requirements.
Buildings, vegetation, and surface obstructions must be removed prior to excavation to provide unobstructed access for earthmoving equipment and to prevent collapse or debris hazards during digging.
Excavation permits, environmental clearances, and utility relocation approvals must be obtained before breaking ground to comply with legal and safety regulations.

All underground utilities (gas, water, electricity, telecom) must be precisely located, marked, and selectively disconnected or rerouted before excavation to prevent service strikes, gas leaks, or electrocution.
Excavation to required depths and formation levels must be completed before foundation concrete can be poured, as the bearing stratum must be exposed and prepared for load transfer.

Excavation must first be opened to expose the water table; dewatering systems can then be installed and operated within the excavated area to maintain dry working conditions for subsequent construction.
Excavation provides access to the soil strata that require improvement (e.g., compaction grouting, stone columns), and the excavation sequence itself may integrate with ground treatment operations.
The horizontal and vertical track systems must be in place to guide and support the garage door panels.
Torsion or extension springs must be mounted and secured before installing the door panels to provide counterbalance.
The foundation must be completed to provide a stable load-bearing base upon which boundary enclosure elements (e.g., walls, fencing) can be erected.
For buildings, the main structural frame must be in place to support and anchor boundary enclosure elements such as exterior wall panels or curtain walls.
Boundary enclosure elements (walls/façade) must be completed to provide vertical support and perimeter enclosure before roof structure can be placed.

While interior work can start partially before full enclosure, completing the boundary enclosure first protects interior finishes from weather damage and ensures environmental separation, making it a strong preference.

successor: Window and Door Installation in Enclosure
rationale: The boundary enclosure openings (rough openings in walls) must be framed and completed before windows and doors can be physically fitted and sealed into those openings.

Waterproofing requires a clean, smooth, and properly cured substrate surface to ensure adhesion and continuity of the waterproofing membrane. Any debris, dust, or unevenness will compromise the waterproofing system's integrity.

The structural concrete elements (foundations, slabs, retaining walls) must be fully cast, cured, and structurally sound before waterproofing can be applied. Waterproofing cannot be installed on green or uncured concrete as it will not bond properly and may trap moisture.

In below-grade applications, a drainage board or layer is typically placed after waterproofing to protect the membrane and channel water away. However, some systems require preparatory drainage works. This sequence depends on the specific waterproofing system design.

A protection board must be installed directly over the cured waterproofing membrane to shield it from physical damage during backfilling, reinforcement placement, or subsequent construction trades. This is a critical hard constraint for membrane integrity.

Backfilling against below-grade walls can only commence after the waterproofing system and its protective layer are fully installed and cured to prevent damage to the membrane from soil, rocks, and compaction equipment.

The site must be cleared, leveled, and graded before any landscape design can be implemented, as the topography and soil conditions directly influence planting plans, drainage, and hardscape placement.
Underground utilities such as irrigation lines, drainage pipes, and electrical conduits must be installed before landscape layout to avoid disturbing newly planted areas or hardscape elements.
The building structure should be substantially complete before final landscape design and layout, as the building footprint, entry points, and elevations define the surrounding landscape zones.
Landscape layout (marking beds, paths, and features) must precede actual planting and sod installation to ensure accurate placement of all vegetation.
Hardscape elements such as pathways, patios, and retaining walls are installed after the landscape is laid out to ensure proper alignment with the design plan.
Site analysis provides the topographic, environmental, and contextual data needed to inform the layout, programming, and design of open spaces.
The legal boundaries, ownership, and easements of the site must be finalized before planning open spaces to ensure designs are within the permissible area.
Municipal zoning codes, setback requirements, and open space ratios must be understood to design compliant open space layouts.
Environmental constraints such as wetlands, protected habitats, and flood zones must be identified before siting open spaces to avoid ecological damage.
The masterplan defines the locations and grades of open spaces, which directly dictate the cut/fill volumes and grading plans needed for construction.
Detailed planting, hardscape, and amenity designs can only proceed once the overarching open space layout and functional zones are established in the masterplan.
Underground utilities (stormwater, irrigation, lighting) must be routed according to the approved open space plan to avoid conflicts with plazas, planters, and pathways.
The masterplan is often submitted for municipal site plan approval; while some early work may proceed under phased permits, full approval is typically obtained before construction begins.
All debris, waste, and existing structures must be removed from the site before any landscaping can begin to provide a clean and safe working area.
The site must be graded and leveled to the correct contours and drainage slopes before topsoil placement and planting can commence.
All buried drainage pipes, irrigation lines, and utility conduits must be installed and backfilled before soft landscaping to avoid disturbance of planted areas and root systems.
Hardscape elements such as paving, walls, patios, and edging must be completed before soft landscaping to define boundaries and prevent damage to planted areas during hardscape construction.
The main building structure must be complete to prevent damage from construction debris and heavy machinery to newly planted soft landscaping areas.
Soft landscaping should be one of the final site activities; once planting, turfing, and mulching are complete, only final cleanup and client handover remain.
The site must be cleared of debris, vegetation, and existing structures before any hard landscaping can be laid, as the ground needs to be prepared and accessible.
Final ground levels and contours must be established before installing hard landscape elements like paving, retaining walls, or driveways to ensure proper base preparation and drainage.

All below-ground drainage pipes, drainage channels, water supply lines, conduit for lighting, and other utilities must be installed before laying hard surfaces to avoid future excavation and damage to finished hard landscaping.

A compacted sub-base (e.g., MOT Type 1 or similar) must be laid and compacted prior to installing the final hard landscaping finish (paving, block paving, slabs) to provide a stable, load-bearing foundation.

Hard landscape elements such as patios, paths, walls, and driveways must be completed before adjacent planting areas are prepared and planted, to avoid damage to plants from construction traffic and to allow accurate soil levels around hard edges.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and prepared before any boundary treatments such as fences, walls, or hedges can be installed.
Soil conditions must be assessed to determine appropriate foundation and installation methods for boundary structures.
Boundary lines and positions must be accurately surveyed and marked out before installation of fences, walls, or other boundary treatments.
Boundary treatments define the perimeter; landscaping and topsoil work around the edges should follow to avoid damaging newly installed boundaries.
While final inspection typically occurs after boundary installation, some minor adjustments could be made concurrently — this is a practical preference rather than a strict physical requirement.
The ground/site must be properly graded and prepared before placing outdoor furniture and fixtures to ensure a level, stable, and well-drained surface.

Outdoor furniture and fixtures (e.g., benches, tables, permanent seating, bike racks) are typically anchored to or placed on finished hardscape surfaces like patios, plazas, and walkways; these surfaces must be fully installed and cured first.
Any underground electrical conduits for lighting, plumbing for water fountains/drinking fountains, or data lines must be roughed in and covered before installing furniture above grade.

successor: Landscaping and Planting (Final Planting, Sod, Mulch)
rationale: Large equipment and material delivery for furniture installation could damage newly planted landscaping; furniture should be set first, then final planting and mulch applied around it.
Once furniture and fixtures are installed, the site is ready for a final cleanup and punch-list walk-through before handover; this is a logical sequence preference rather than a physical necessity.
The ground must be excavated, leveled, and compacted to provide a stable foundation bed before any load-bearing wall can be constructed.
A continuous strip footing or reinforced concrete foundation must be placed and cured to distribute the wall's vertical loads to the soil; the wall cannot be started without a finished footing.
Underground services that will pass through or under the wall footprint must be installed before the wall is built to avoid costly retrofitting or structural compromises.
The perimeter wall provides lateral support and a bearing edge for the floor slab; the slab cannot be poured or installed until the wall is complete and has achieved sufficient strength.
The load-bearing perimeter walls are the primary vertical supports for the roof trusses or beams; the roof structure cannot be erected until the walls are built and cured.
The foundation provides the structural base that supports the column's load; without a completed foundation, the column cannot be placed.
The column base or footing must be prepared and cured to provide a level, stable platform for erecting the column.
The entablature (horizontal beam) rests directly on top of the colonnade columns and requires the columns to be in place as vertical supports.
Structural beams or arches spanning between columns cannot be installed until the columns are erected to provide the necessary support points.
The capital (decorative top element) must be placed after the column shaft is erected, as it sits atop the column as a crowning element.
A compacted sub-base or hardcore layer must be laid and leveled before paving can begin to provide a stable, load-bearing foundation that prevents settlement or cracking.
Underground drainage pipes and land drains must be installed before paving to ensure water can be carried away from the paved surface and prevent waterlogging or freeze-thaw damage.
Any underground electrical, water, or data service ducts must be laid in trenches before paving to avoid having to cut or dig up the finished surface later.
Planting beds, turf, and decorative topsoil are placed after paving is complete to prevent soil or mud from staining the new paving and to allow clean access for paving machinery.

successor: Installation of Site Furniture (Benches / Bollards / Lighting)
rationale: Fixed site furniture and bollards should be installed after paving is finished to ensure they sit flush on the finished surface and to avoid damaging paving slabs during installation.
Excavation must be completed to create the space and subgrade for the permeable drainage layer.
The subgrade must be graded and compacted to provide a stable, properly sloped base for the drainage layer.
Geotextile fabric is typically placed over the drainage layer to prevent fines migration while allowing water passage.
Drainage pipes or underdrains are embedded within or laid on top of the permeable drainage layer to collect and convey water.
The aggregate base course is placed over the drainage layer to provide a load-bearing foundation for the final pavement or surface.
The structural steel frame provides the primary load-bearing support onto which the courtyard roof/glazed atrium cover is mounted and fastened.
The atrium enclosure walls define the perimeter support and sealing interface for the glazed roof structure to bear upon and weather-seal against.

The roof must be fully enclosed and weathertight before installing electrical, HVAC, and other mechanical services within the atrium to avoid water damage to equipment and to provide a protected working environment.

successor: Interior Finishes (Ceiling Cladding / Soffit Works) Below Atrium Roof
rationale: The glazed roof must be completed and sealed to provide a dry, enclosed environment before installing interior finishes such as ceiling panels, soffits, and decorative elements beneath it.

While cleaning systems can technically be installed concurrently, it is preferential to complete the roof assembly first so that cleaning tracks and lines can be accurately fitted to the as-built geometry and surfaces without risk of damage to finished glass.
The skylight or lantern must be installed on top of or within the structural roof framing and deck. The roof structure must be in place to provide support and an opening for the unit.
Roof sheathing and waterproof underlayment must be installed before the skylight to ensure proper flashing integration and weatherproofing at the skylight penetration.
A framed curb or rough opening sized to the skylight/lantern dimension must be built into the roof structure before the unit can be set in place and fastened.
After the skylight is set in position, flashing must be installed around its perimeter to seal the gap between the skylight frame and the roof, preventing water intrusion.
Final roofing materials (shingles, membrane, etc.) are installed up to and overlapping the skylight flashing after the skylight and its flashing are in place to complete the weatherproof envelope.

Interior finishes around the skylight shaft are typically completed after the skylight is installed to allow for proper trim, sealing, and alignment, though this is a logical preference more than a physical necessity.
Site grading must be completed to establish proper drainage slopes and soil base before planting beds and tree pits can be excavated and formed.
Underground utilities (water, drainage, electrical conduits) must be installed before planting beds to avoid disturbing root zones and to coordinate trenching with tree pit locations.
The subgrade and rough grade must be established and compacted to the correct elevations so that planting beds and tree pits are excavated to the proper depth and alignment.
Tree pits must be excavated and prepared before trees can be placed and backfilled with soil.
Adjacent hardscape elements such as pavers, sidewalks, and curbs should be installed after tree pits are formed to ensure proper alignment and to avoid damaging newly planted areas.
Drip irrigation or sprinkler lines for planting beds are laid after the beds are excavated and formed, so that piping can be routed within the prepared bed areas.
After tree pits and planting beds are excavated and prepared, topsoil and mulch can be placed to finish the planting surface.
Ground must be excavated, leveled, and prepared before any underground pipework for irrigation and water features can be laid, as the pipe trenches and bedding require stable, prepared ground.

Main underground drainage systems should be in place first to avoid conflicts and cross-connections with irrigation and water-feature water supply and return pipes, and to establish the overall below-ground utility routing.

Irrigation and water-feature supply and return pipes must be fully laid, connected, and pressure-tested before hard surfaces (paths, patios, paving) are installed, to avoid costly break-up of finished hardscape for pipe repairs or additions.

Underground pipework for irrigation and water features must be completed before topsoil is spread and planting/ turfing begins, so that pipes are protected and not disturbed by subsequent heavy planting or soil works.

successor: Water Feature Structure Construction (e.g., pond, fountain base)
rationale: Supply and return pipework must be run to the water feature location before the feature structure (pond liner, fountain basin, etc.) is built, to allow proper connection and embedding of pipe terminations within the structure.
The foundation must be completed to provide a stable base for the boundary screen wall or mashrabiya structure.
Load-bearing columns or structural supports must be in place before the screen wall can be attached or framed onto them.
The screen wall must be fully installed before plastering and finishing works can be applied to it and adjacent surfaces.
It is preferable but not strictly required to complete the mashrabiya before running services in adjacent zones, as services may be integrated behind or alongside the screen.
Final paint and decorative finishes must be applied after the screen wall is erected to ensure a uniform and undisturbed finish.

successor: Staircase Linking Court to Upper Galleries
rationale: The staircase must be built on a solid foundation and structural core to ensure load-bearing capacity and structural integrity.

successor: Staircase Linking Court to Upper Galleries
rationale: The staircase links the court to the upper galleries, so the court floor must be in place to provide the lower landing point and anchoring surface.

predecessor: Staircase Linking Court to Upper Galleries
rationale: The staircase provides access to the upper galleries, so the upper gallery floors must be completed after to allow proper alignment and connection.

predecessor: Staircase Linking Court to Upper Galleries
rationale: While it is preferable to finish the staircase before detailed interior works to allow material and equipment transport, it is not a strict physical necessity as alternative access could be arranged.

predecessor: Staircase Linking Court to Upper Galleries
rationale: Handrails and balustrades must be installed after the staircase structure is complete as they attach to the staircase itself for safety compliance.

The site must be cleared, graded, and leveled before any courtyard layout can be defined, as the topography and soil conditions directly influence the courtyard's drainage, foundations, and spatial configuration.

Building foundations and substructures (including retaining walls, basement walls, and under-slab utilities) must be in place before courtyard areas can be precisely planned and surfaced, as the courtyard design integrates with structural elements and utility connections.

All underground pipes, conduits, and drainage systems serving the courtyard (e.g., irrigation, stormwater, lighting conduits) must be installed before courtyard hardscaping and planting commence, to avoid costly rework and ensure proper service connections.

The courtyard layout and design must be finalized to define the exact locations, dimensions, and materials for paved areas, pathways, retaining walls, and other hardscape elements before construction can begin.

Planting beds, trees, shrubs, and turf areas must be designed and located within the courtyard plan before any soil preparation and planting work can proceed, ensuring proper spacing, irrigation access, and compatibility with hardscape.
Site investigation (soil tests, utility location) must be completed before excavation to identify soil conditions, groundwater levels, and buried utilities, ensuring safe and informed excavation.
Existing structures, debris, and vegetation must be removed prior to excavation to provide unobstructed access and avoid interference with excavation work.
Required permits (e.g., excavation permits, environmental clearances) must be obtained before ground disturbance begins to comply with legal and regulatory requirements.
Excavation and ground preparation (e.g., grading, compaction, trenching) must be completed before foundation construction can begin, as foundations are placed directly on the prepared subgrade.

Open trenches and prepared ground are required for laying underground drainage, water, sewer, or electrical conduits; these utilities are typically installed after excavation but before final slab or foundation pouring.
The structural frame requires a stable foundation to bear the loads; the foundation must be cured and strong enough before frame erection can begin.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and excavated to the proper elevations before any structural elements can be placed.
Underground utilities (drainage, water, electrical conduits) must be installed before the structural frame to avoid excavation under or around completed columns and beams.
The roof deck and waterproofing system require the perimeter frame to be in place to support the roof structure and provide a weathertight enclosure.
Exterior cladding panels and curtain walls are attached to the perimeter structural frame; the frame must be erected to provide the supporting structure for the façade.
The ground must be excavated, leveled, and graded to the correct formation level before any paving or hard landscaping can be laid to ensure a stable, well-drained sub-base.
A compacted sub-base layer (e.g., Type 1 aggregate or hardcore) must be placed and compacted to provide a load-bearing foundation and drainage layer directly beneath the paving.

All below-ground drainage pipes, water mains, electrical conduits, and other buried services must be installed and tested before paving is laid to avoid digging up finished paving for service connections.

Although edge restraints are often installed before paving to contain it, in some sequences they can follow the paving if the paving is robust; typically edge restraints should be installed prior to paving for proper confinement.

successor: Final Site Clean and Soft Landscaping (Turfing/Planting)
rationale: Paving and hard landscaping must be completed before final soft landscaping such as turfing, seeding, or planting adjacent beds, to avoid damage to soft landscaping during paving works and to ensure clean edges.
The ground must be properly shaped, leveled, and graded before planting to ensure proper drainage and a stable growing medium for vegetation.
Subsurface drainage systems must be in place before planting to prevent waterlogging and ensure healthy root development.
All underground utilities (water, electrical, gas) must be laid and backfilled before planting to avoid digging up or disturbing newly planted vegetation.
Hardscape elements such as paths, patios, walls, and kerbs should be completed first to avoid damaging soft landscape areas with heavy machinery and material deliveries.
The steel frame provides the structural support onto which the glazed roof panels and atrium cover are mounted. Without the frame, there is no substructure to attach the glazing system.
A solid roof deck or substrate must be in place to provide a base for weatherproofing and to support the glazed roof system's perimeter framing and flashings.
Large glass panels and aluminum framing sections require mechanical lifting equipment for safe placement at height. The hoisting system must be operational before glazing installation begins.
The glazed roof must be installed and watertight before interior finishes below the atrium can be completed, to protect finished surfaces from weather damage and water ingress.

The atrium floor finishing (e.g., tile, stone, polished concrete) should be installed after the glazed roof is in place to prevent weather exposure, debris falling from above, and to ensure a clean, protected environment for the finished floor.
The site must be cleared of existing structures, vegetation, and debris before drainage and stormwater pipes can be laid and earthworks can begin.
The site must be graded to the required levels and contours before drainage trenches can be excavated and pipes installed to ensure proper fall and flow.

Drainage and stormwater infrastructure must be installed beneath the road pavement before the road pavement and kerbing can be constructed, as the pipes are buried and would be inaccessible afterward.
Stormwater drainage around and from building footprints must be completed before concrete foundations and slabs are poured, to allow connection of downpipes and to prevent water ingress.
All buried drainage and stormwater pipes and pits must be installed and backfilled before final landscaping, topsoiling, and planting can be undertaken to avoid re-excavation.

The facade and screen wall finishing systems are installed onto the completed structural frame. The structural frame must be fully erected and stable to provide the supporting substrate for the facade.
Roof must be completed and waterproofed before facade finishing to protect the building interior and upper wall interfaces from water ingress during facade installation.
Interior finishing work (drywall, plaster) should follow facade completion to ensure the building envelope is sealed against weather, preventing moisture damage to interior finishes.
Windows and glazing are integrated into or installed alongside the facade and screen wall system. The facade structure must be in place to receive and seal the window units.
Scaffolding erected for facade access must remain in place until facade finishing is complete. Only after the facade is finished can scaffolding be safely dismantled.

predecessor: Installation of Passive Ventilation System Components
rationale: All physical components of the passive ventilation system (ducts, vents, dampers, controllers) must be installed before commissioning can test and verify their functionality.

predecessor: Completion of Building Envelope (Air Barrier & Insulation)
rationale: The building envelope must be sealed and insulated to ensure the passive ventilation system operates under design conditions; commissioning would be invalid if air leakage paths are incomplete.
The passive ventilation system must be verified and balanced before the building is handed over to occupants to ensure indoor air quality and thermal comfort.
Soft preference: fine-tuning of automated damper or vent controls can occur after commissioning, but ideally adjustments are completed during the commissioning process itself.
Certification of energy performance relies on verified commissioning data, so commissioning must be complete before formal certification can be issued.
The roof framing (rafters, trusses, or decking) must be installed to provide the structural support and substrate onto which the Roof Step Junction is attached.
The roof deck or sheathing provides the continuous surface required for proper seating and waterproofing of the step junction component.
A base layer of underlayment is typically applied before step flashings or junction components to provide initial water protection and a slip sheet.
Subsequent flashing courses (step flashing, counter-flashing) must overlap and integrate with the Roof Step Junction to ensure continuous water shedding down-roof.
Wall cladding or siding that abuts the roof line is installed after the step junction is in place so that it can properly overlap and seal against the junction component.

A stable, level substrate (often the top of the main roof deck or structural slab) must be prepared and cured before stepped parapet masonry or forming can begin, otherwise the wall will lack proper support.
The roof structure must be in place to provide the bearing surface for the parapet wall; building the parapet before the roof deck is unsafe and structurally unsound.
Waterproofing membranes and metal coping caps are installed over the completed parapet wall to protect it from moisture intrusion; they cannot be fitted until the wall itself is built.
Scaffolding erected for parapet construction must remain until the wall is complete and safe; dismantling can only happen after the wall is finished to ensure worker safety.
Base flashing and counter-flashing at the parapet-to-roof intersection must be installed after the parapet wall is built to properly integrate with the wall surface and prevent leaks.
The roof structure must be in place before downpipes can be attached to it, as downpipes are fixed to the roof perimeter or fascia.
Roof covering (e.g., tiles, metal sheeting) must be completed so that gutters can be installed along the roof edge, and downpipes connect to the gutter outlets.
Downpipes connect directly to gutter outlets; gutters must be in place to allow downpipe connection and proper water drainage from the roof.
Downpipes must be installed and connected before they can be linked to underground stormwater drains or drainage piping at ground level.
It is often easier to complete wall cladding or rendering before downpipes are fixed, but downpipes can be installed after; if installed before, finishing work around the pipe may require extra care.
Bearing walls transfer vertical loads to the foundation; the foundation must be in place to support the wall's weight and prevent settlement.

predecessor: Slab on Grade or Basement Slab Placement
rationale: Bearing walls often bear on a concrete slab; the slab must be poured and cured to provide a level, stable base for wall construction.
The building site must be excavated and prepared before any structural elements, including bearing walls, can be built.
Floor joists or slabs typically bear on or are supported by bearing walls; the walls must be in place to transfer floor loads to the foundation.
Roof loads are transferred through bearing walls; the walls must be completed before roof framing can be placed on top of them.
Exterior finishes can be applied after the bearing wall is erected, but this is a soft preference as temporary bracing and weatherproofing could allow some cladding work to proceed concurrently.
While MEP rough-in typically occurs after structural walls are in place, some chases and conduits can be pre-installed, making this a soft preference rather than a hard physical constraint.
Snow guards must be mounted onto the finished roof deck surface to provide a secure attachment base.
Underlayment provides a protective layer beneath the roof covering and snow guards must be installed over it to maintain weatherproofing integrity.
Snow guards are typically installed concurrently with or after the final roof covering is in place, as they need to integrate with the finished roofing material for proper sealing and load transfer.
Snow guard attachment points may require flashing details to be completed or coordinated around the guards to maintain watertightness.
Snow guard installation must be complete before the final roof inspection to verify proper placement and secure attachment.
Roof sheathing provides the structural base onto which drainage components (gutters, downspouts) are attached; without a completed roof deck, drainage systems cannot be securely mounted.
Underlayment (felt or synthetic) protects the roof deck from moisture and must be in place before gutters and flashing are installed to prevent water ingress behind drainage components.
The roof structure must be fully framed to support the load of drainage systems and to establish correct roof slopes for proper water flow to gutters.

Gutters and downspouts are typically installed before exterior wall finishes to allow behind-gutter flashing to integrate with wall waterproofing and to avoid damaging finished siding during drainage installation.

Drainage components such as drip edge and gutter apron flashing are installed as part of or just after the roofing finish to ensure proper water shedding from the finished roof surface into the gutters.
The structural steel frame must be erected and stable to provide the supporting structure onto which roof cladding is attached.
Roof trusses form the primary roof framework; cladding cannot be installed until trusses are in place and secured.
A solid roof deck (e.g., plywood or OSB) must be installed over the trusses to provide a substrate for the cladding material.
Waterproof or vapor-permeable underlayment must be laid over the roof deck before the final cladding to protect against moisture ingress.
Gutters and downspouts are mounted onto or below the roof edge after cladding is in place to ensure proper water drainage alignment.
Flashing details at valleys, ridges, vents, and chimneys are typically installed concurrently with or after the cladding to seal joints and prevent leaks.
Once the roof is weathertight, electrical work inside the attic/roof cavity can proceed without risk of water damage to wiring and components.
Ceilings are installed after the roof is closed and weathertight to protect interior finishes from weather exposure.
Roof sheathing must be applied over the roof truss framework to provide a solid decking surface. The trusses provide the structural support needed to hold the sheathing panels.
Roof framing must be inspected and approved before covering it with sheathing, as per building code requirements.
Roof underlayment (felt paper or synthetic) is installed directly on top of the roof sheathing to provide a water-resistant barrier.
Flashing around roof penetrations, valleys, and edges is installed after sheathing is in place to seal joints and prevent water intrusion.
Roofing shingles or other final roofing materials are applied over the sheathing and underlayment to provide the finished weatherproof surface.
Roof framing requires load-bearing walls to be fully framed and in place to support the roof structure, including rafters, trusses, and roof decking.
The top plates of the walls must be installed to provide a horizontal bearing surface and connection point for roof trusses or rafters.
Roof sheathing (plywood or OSB decking) is installed directly onto the roof framing members and cannot be applied before the roof frame is erected.
Permanent and temporary bracing of roof trusses and joists must follow the erection of the roof framing to ensure structural stability and alignment.
Roof underlayment (felt or synthetic) is applied over the roof sheathing, which itself is installed on top of the roof framing, so the framing must be complete first.
The roof deck or substrate must be clean, dry, smooth, and structurally sound before any waterproofing membrane can be applied; otherwise the membrane will not bond properly and will fail.
Proper drainage slopes and screeds must be in place to prevent ponding water, which would compromise the waterproofing system's performance and longevity.
All plumbing, vent, electrical conduit, and drain penetrations through the roof deck must be roughed in and sealed at deck level before the continuous waterproofing membrane is applied.
Rigid insulation boards are typically installed over the waterproofing membrane to protect it from UV, thermal cycling, and mechanical damage, so the membrane must be fully applied and cured first.

successor: Roof Cover / Wearing Surface (e.g., ballast, pavers, green roof layer)
rationale: The final protective or traffic-bearing roof covering system (gravel ballast, concrete pavers, planting medium, etc.) must be placed over the cured waterproofing membrane to shield it from UV degradation, hail, foot traffic, and physical abuse.
The roof structure or framing provides the structural support onto which roof tiles and cladding are installed; without the frame, there is no substrate to attach the tiling or cladding.

Sarking or underlayment (such as a waterproof membrane) must be laid over the roof frame before tiling to provide waterproofing and a secondary weather barrier; tiling directly onto the frame without underlayment would cause water ingress.

Gutters and fascias are ideally installed before tiling to allow proper integration with the roof edge detailing, but this is a soft preference because in some sequences they can be retrofitted after tiling, though with more difficulty.
Roof-mounted electrical or solar panel installations typically require the completed roof cladding as a base; however, this is a soft preference as some solar systems can be integrated during tiling.
The roof must be watertight (tiling and cladding completed) before installing interior ceilings and finishes to prevent weather damage to finished interior surfaces.
Structural framing must be complete to provide the load-bearing support for the roof structure before any roof inspection or maintenance can safely take place.
The roof deck (sheathing or substrate) must be installed before the roof can be inspected, as there is no roof surface to inspect or maintain without the deck in place.
Underlayment provides the primary waterproofing layer; inspection and maintenance of the roof system cannot begin until this moisture barrier is installed.
Roof must be inspected and confirmed watertight before interior ceiling finishes are installed, to avoid damage from potential leaks that would require costly rework.
The roof inspection and sign-off is part of completing the building envelope; other enclosure elements like exterior wall cladding near roofline depend on a watertight roof being verified first.
The structural roof framing must be in place to provide a stable support and opening for the skylight or rooflight unit to be installed.
Roof decking or sheathing must be installed to create the roof plane and define the rough opening into which the skylight is placed.
The weather barrier or underlayment should be applied to the roof before the skylight is installed to ensure proper integration of the skylight flashing with the roof waterproofing system.
After the skylight unit is placed, flashing must be installed around its perimeter to seal and waterproof the transition between the skylight and the roof assembly.
The final roofing finish material is typically installed up to and overlapping the skylight flashing, completing the weatherproof envelope, which requires the skylight to be in place first.
Structural reinforcement (e.g., steel rebar, columns, beams) must be installed on top of or within the foundation; the foundation provides the load-bearing base for all vertical structural elements.
The ground must be excavated and leveled before any structural reinforcement can be placed to ensure proper alignment, stability, and compliance with engineering specifications.
Concrete footings must be poured and cured to provide a solid anchor base for vertical reinforcement bars and columns.
Reinforcement bars and cages must be fully tied, positioned, and inspected before concrete is poured around them to ensure structural integrity.

Although formwork can sometimes be partially erected before reinforcement, the final formwork assembly must accommodate the placed reinforcement; typically reinforcement is placed before or concurrently, but concrete cannot be poured until both formwork and rebar are in place.

Column reinforcement and vertical structural reinforcement must be completed before upper floor slabs, beams, and additional framing are constructed above, as the reinforced elements provide load transfer paths.

Safety railings are typically anchored to or supported by the concrete slab or structural deck. The slab must be poured and sufficiently cured to provide a stable base and anchoring points for railing posts.
In steel-framed buildings, safety railings often attach to steel columns or beams. The steel frame must be erected to provide attachment points for guardrail systems at elevated floors.
While not physically required, installing safety railings before final edge finishing is a best practice to provide fall protection for workers finishing floor edges and applying surface treatments.

Guardrails provide edge protection that allows workers to safely install exterior cladding or curtain wall systems at building perimeters, though cladding could theoretically be done with other fall protection.

successor: Interior MEP Rough-In Work Near Building Perimeter
rationale: Installing safety railings early provides fall protection for workers performing mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in near open edges, improving safety during these subsequent activities.
Access stairways require stable foundation support to bear structural loads and ensure safety.
The stairway must be anchored to or supported by the finished floor slab at its base.

predecessor: Structural Steel / Concrete Frame (Main Building Structure)
rationale: The stairway often connects to intermediate floor levels or structural landings that must already exist.
Handrails and guardrails are safety components that are installed directly onto the completed stairway structure.
Inspection and load testing of the stairway can only occur after the stairway is fully erected and bolted/welded in place.
The roof hatch must be installed over a completed structural roof deck to provide proper support and anchorage.
The roof structure must be framed with the necessary rough opening before the roof hatch or access door can be set in place.
The roof hatch must be installed and secured before the roofing membrane is applied to ensure proper flashing and watertight integration around the hatch.

Although insulation can be placed around the hatch, it is easier and cleaner to install the hatch first and then fit insulation around the curbs, but this is a soft preference as insulation could be installed prior with careful cutting.
The access door frame and hardware must be in place before interior ceiling finishes are completed to allow proper alignment and trim work around the opening.
The subgrade (soil or base layer) must be properly prepared, graded, and compacted before growing medium is placed to ensure proper drainage and stability.
Drainage layers and systems (e.g., perforated pipes, gravel blankets) must be installed before growing medium to prevent water accumulation and root rot.
Underground utility work must be completed and backfilled before growing medium is placed to avoid disturbing the medium later.
Irrigation pipes and emitters are typically laid directly within or on top of the growing medium, so the medium must be in place first.
Plants, seeds, or sod require the growing medium as their rooting substrate and cannot be installed until the medium is placed and leveled.

The foundation must be fully constructed and cured before structural loads can be assessed, as the load assessment measures how the building's structural elements (including the foundation) will bear and distribute loads.
The structural frame (beams, columns, slabs) must be erected to provide the physical structure whose load-bearing capacity is being assessed.

Material test results (concrete cylinder tests, steel tensile tests, etc.) must be available before load assessment to verify that materials meet design specifications and can safely carry the expected loads.
Load assessment results inform structural sign-off; the building cannot receive final structural approval until load analysis confirms design adequacy.

successor: Construction of Non-Structural Elements (cladding, MEP rough-in)
rationale: Non-structural elements should only be installed after load assessment to ensure that the structural system is verified before adding dead loads from cladding, mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems.
The foundation must be excavated and poured before any structural components like arcade arches can be installed, as the arch requires a stable load-bearing base.
Columns or piers that carry the arcade arch must be erected first, as the arch spans between and rests upon these vertical supports.
The structural arch must be in place before any decorative masonry, cladding, or finishing can be applied to its surface.
The arcade arch supports upper-level structures such as vaulting or upper floors; thus, the arch must be completed before any load from above can be placed upon it.

It is preferred to install mechanical, electrical, and plumbing runs above the arch after the arch is in place to avoid rework, but if necessary some MEP work could be done concurrently with careful coordination.
The ground must be excavated and prepared to the required depth and bearing capacity before pier foundations can be constructed.
Piers provide the vertical support for the deck or superstructure; the deck cannot be placed until piers are complete and cured.
Pier caps sit atop the pier columns to distribute loads from the superstructure; they require the pier to be complete first.
Deep foundations (piles) must be installed and tested beneath the pier location to provide adequate load-bearing support before pier footings are poured.
Formwork and falsework used to cast the pier can only be stripped after the pier concrete has achieved sufficient strength.
Impost blocks are typically placed on top of masonry walls or pillars to provide a bearing surface for arches or vaults; the wall must be built first.
The impost block serves as the springing point (support) for an arch or vault; the arch cannot be built without the impost block in place.
The foundation and supporting structure must be completed and stable before the impost block can be accurately positioned and installed.
Voussoirs (wedge-shaped stones/bricks of an arch) rest on the impost block at the springing point; they cannot be placed before the impost is set.

While load testing typically occurs after the full arch assembly, it is a soft preference relative to the impost block itself since temporary shoring could theoretically allow some preliminary testing without the impost.

The string course is a horizontal band or course of masonry that projects from the face of a wall. Therefore, the underlying masonry wall must be constructed first to provide the structural backing and surface onto which the string course is applied or integrated.

String courses often serve as a decorative or water-shedding element on the exterior wall below the roofline. The string course must be completed before the roof is installed to ensure proper alignment, flashing integration, and weatherproofing sequencing from bottom up.

String courses frequently run horizontally across window heads or sills. If the string course passes through or abuts window openings, it must be built first to establish the correct opening dimensions and bearing surfaces for window frames.

The string course is located in the upper portion of a masonry wall, typically at floor levels or at the eaves. The foundation must be complete to support the entire wall system, including the string course.

While it is conventional to install the string course before applying exterior finishes so that finishes can be worked up to the string course neatly, this is a soft preference; in some cases, finishes could be applied first and the string course installed afterward with careful detailing.
The keystone must be placed on top of the arch, which requires the arch's supporting structure (foundations and abutments) to be completed first to bear the load.

predecessor: Arch ring assembly (left and right sides)
rationale: The keystone is the central wedge-shaped stone at the apex of an arch; the arch's haunches and sides must be built first so the keystone can lock the structure in place.
The keystone is what makes the arch self-supporting by converting vertical loads into compressive forces; only after the keystone is set can temporary supports be safely removed.
The completed arch (with keystone in place) provides the structural base needed to build any walls, roadways, or loads above the arch opening.
The arcade soffit must be installed onto the structural framing; the framing provides the supporting substrate for the soffit.
Finishing work such as painting or stucco application must occur after the soffit is fully installed to achieve a uniform and durable surface.
Soffit-mounted or recessed lighting fixtures require the soffit to be in place for mounting and electrical rough-in.
Overhead waterproofing and roofing work above the arcade must be completed before the soffit is installed to prevent water damage to the soffit material and to allow proper drainage integration.
While column cladding can often proceed independently, coordinating soffit installation first allows for cleaner transitions and trim alignment at the column-to-soffit interface.
The foundation trench or excavation must be completed before the backing wall can be constructed, as the wall requires a prepared base.
Concrete footings or strip foundations must be poured and cured to provide a stable load-bearing base for the backing wall.
The damp-proof course or membrane is typically applied to the completed backing wall to prevent moisture ingress before backfilling.
Soil or aggregate backfill against the backing wall can only be placed after the wall is fully constructed and cured to avoid displacement or damage.
Any decorative or protective cladding (e.g., brick slip, stone facing) must be applied after the structural backing wall is complete and stable.
Column shafts require a stable foundation base to transfer loads; foundation must be completed before column erection can begin.
Column shafts are typically anchored into or supported by footings/pad foundations which must be cast and cured first.
The reinforcing steel cage must be placed and tied within the formwork before concrete is poured for the column shaft.
Formwork (shuttering) must be erected and braced to shape and contain the concrete for the column shaft before pouring.
Beams and slabs bear on or are supported by columns; column shafts must achieve sufficient strength before transferring loads from upper floor systems.
The ground must be excavated to the required depth before the column base can be placed, as the column base sits within or on the excavated foundation area.
A concrete footing or foundation pad must be poured and cured to provide a stable, level bearing surface for the column base to be installed upon.
The column base must be in place and secured (e.g., with anchor bolts set) before the column itself can be erected and attached to the base.
After the column base is positioned and the column is erected, grout is typically poured under the base plate to ensure full contact and load transfer; thus grouting follows base installation.
The column base serves as the anchorage point; the rest of the steel frame above cannot be accurately aligned and bolted until the column base is fixed in its final position.
The stylobate/plinth rests directly on the foundation/footing; it cannot be placed without a stable base to support it.
The ground must be excavated and leveled before the foundation and stylobate can be laid to ensure proper alignment and load distribution.
Columns sit directly on the stylobate/plinth; they require a leveled, stable platform for correct placement and alignment.
Column bases are typically set onto the stylobate/plinth surface, making it a prerequisite for any column base work.
The stylobate/plinth forms the bottom step of the crepidoma that supports the entire superstructure; all upper elements depend on this leveling course being complete.
The fascia and entablature are horizontal elements that sit atop or span between vertical structural supports; columns or bearing walls must be erected first to provide load-bearing support.
In many buildings the entablature is part of the roof edge or cornice system; the roof deck provides the structural substrate to which the fascia is attached.
The entablature's top element (cornice) or the soffit below it is detailed after the main fascia board or entablature body is installed, as they attach to or cap the fascia.

Gutters are typically mounted onto or just behind the fascia board; while it is strongly preferred to install gutters after fascia is in place for proper anchoring, it is not an absolute physical impossibility to do it in reverse order.

The fascia and entablature often serve as a termination or transition detail for exterior wall cladding; cladding must be completed up to the fascia line, and the fascia caps or finishes the wall system.
Reinforcement bars for the arch must be placed and tied before formwork is erected, as the formwork is built around the reinforcement cage.
Concrete cannot be poured for the arch until the formwork and centering system is fully erected, aligned, and secured to support the wet concrete.
The centering and formwork must be in place during concrete curing; only after sufficient strength is achieved can the centering be removed.
The formwork panels and centering frames must be fabricated or assembled before they can be erected and positioned at the arch location.
Support falsework or scaffolding must be erected first to provide a working platform and support for the arch centering assembly.
The foundation must be prepared, leveled, and cured to provide a stable base for column placement. Columns cannot be installed on unprepared ground.

Reinforcement steel (rebar) must be fabricated, assembled, and placed in the foundation or column footings before the column formwork or precast column is positioned, as the rebar provides structural integrity.
Accurate survey marks, grid lines, and reference points must be established to ensure columns are placed at the correct location, alignment, and elevation.
Beams are supported by columns; therefore columns must be erected, aligned, plumbed, and secured before beams can be placed on top of or between them.
Columns provide vertical load-bearing support for slabs and walls. Slab formwork and wall panels require columns to be in place to establish the structural frame and connection points.
The steel frame provides the primary structural support and attachment points for the glazed roof system; without the frame in place, there is no structure to mount the glazing onto.
The perimeter trim or border frames the area where the glazed panels will be seated and provides the sealing edge; it must be installed first to define the boundaries.
For roofs that require a secondary waterproof layer beneath the glazing, the membrane must be laid down prior to installing the glass panels to ensure proper drainage and leak protection.

successor: Interior Finishes Below Roof (Ceiling, Lighting, HVAC)
rationale: The glazed roof must be installed and sealed first to make the building envelope watertight before any interior finishes are applied; otherwise, weather exposure could damage interior materials.
After the glazed panels are installed, sealant and weatherproofing must be applied around the edges and then inspected for leaks before the roof is considered complete.
Fire exit door requires a framed opening in the wall to be installed into; the wall frame must be in place to provide structural support and proper dimensions for the door frame.
The rough opening must be framed, sized, and prepared to the exact specifications required for the fire-rated door assembly to ensure proper fit and fire rating compliance.
After the fire exit door is positioned and hung, the gaps between the door frame and the wall opening must be grouted or wedged to secure the frame and maintain fire integrity.
Fire-rated sealant must be applied around the door frame perimeter after installation to maintain the fire-resistance rating of the assembly and seal any gaps.
Door hardware such as panic bars, door closers, and exit devices must be installed after the door is hung in its frame, as they attach directly to the door leaf and frame.
The ground must be properly graded and compacted before any flooring can be laid to ensure a stable, level base and prevent future settling or cracking.
A structural subfloor (concrete slab, wooden joists, etc.) must be in place and fully cured to provide the load-bearing surface on which the finished floor material is installed.
An underlayment or vapor barrier must be installed over the subfloor to protect the finished flooring from moisture, provide sound insulation, and create a smooth surface for installation.
All below-floor utilities (piping, wiring, ductwork) must be roughed-in and inspected before flooring is laid, as accessing these after floor installation would require costly demolition.

successor: Interior Wall Framing and Wall Finishing
rationale: While walls are typically framed before floor laying in platform framing, in some sequences flooring can be laid first to serve as a working platform; however, it is generally preferred to install wall framing beforehand to avoid damaging the finished floor.
Finished flooring must be fully installed before cabinets and built-in millwork are placed, because cabinets sit on top of the finished floor and need to be leveled on the completed surface.
Typically painting is done before floor laying to avoid drips on the new floor; but if painting is done after, the floor must be protected. This is a soft preference based on finish protection.
Baseboards and trim are installed after the finished flooring is laid because the flooring must extend underneath the baseboards for a clean, finished appearance and to cover the expansion gap.
The rough opening must be framed and prepared (including header, jambs, and sill) before the door unit can be installed.
Door hinges, locks, handleset, and other hardware must be installed after the door is hung in its frame.
Priming and painting are typically done after the door is installed, though some prefer pre-finishing; this is a soft preference as site conditions vary.
Floor underlayment or subfloor must be in place to establish correct door bottom elevation and clearance.
Load-bearing walls and shear panels must be framed before the rough opening can be cut and reinforced for the door.

The structural framework (columns, beams, slabs) must be in place before circulation zones such as corridors and stairwells can be planned and laid out, as they depend on the defined structural grid and floor levels.
Vertical circulation cores (elevator shafts, stairwells) must be built first to establish the primary vertical movement pathways around which horizontal circulation zones are organized.
Floor finishes in corridors and circulation paths must be installed after the circulation layout is finalized to ensure correct alignment, widths, and transitions between zones.
Doors and partitions along circulation routes must be positioned according to the approved circulation layout to ensure proper access, egress, and pathway widths.
Signage and wayfinding systems should be designed and installed after circulation zones are defined to accurately reflect the actual pathways, though some preparatory work can occur in parallel.
The building's layout, floor plans, and spatial configuration must be designed first to provide the geometry and compartmentation needed for egress modelling.
The number of occupants and their distribution across the building must be known to define the population that will be simulated during evacuation.

predecessor: Fire Safety Strategy / Fire Engineering Design
rationale: The fire scenarios, smoke management approach, and fire protection systems must be established to define the environmental conditions and hazards that drive evacuation behaviour in the simulation.
The simulation results (e.g., total evacuation time, bottleneck locations) are used as evidence to demonstrate compliance with building codes and life safety regulations.

successor: Final Egress System Design (Doors, Stairs, Corridors)
rationale: Simulation outputs identify required widths, capacities, and locations of egress components, informing the detailed design of exit doors, stairways, and corridors.
The structural framing (stairs, floors, landings) must be in place to provide a mounting surface and structural support for handrails.
Subfloor or deck sheathing must be installed to create a stable walking surface and secure base for handrail posts or brackets.
Wall framing and sheathing must be complete to provide anchorage for wall-mounted handrails.
While trim and finish work often proceeds after handrails are installed for a clean look, it is a soft preference as touch-ups can be done later.
Handrails must be installed before safety inspections can verify compliance with building codes for guardrails and handrails.
Stairs require a stable structural base; the foundation must be completed to provide load-bearing support for the staircase.

The structural frame (floors, walls, and supporting beams) must be in place before stairs can be installed, as stairs typically connect between floor levels and require the framed openings and landings.
Utilities that will run within or adjacent to stairwells (e.g., lighting conduits, pipes) should be roughed in before stair installation to avoid having to cut into or work around finished stairs.
Stairs must be installed before final wall finishes and painting in the stairwell area, as the stairs define the geometry and access needed for finishing work.
Handrails and guardrails are mounted onto or adjacent to the completed stair structure; stairs must be in place to provide the correct alignment and attachment points for railings.

The path base and sub-base must be prepared and compacted before edge treatment can be applied, as edge treatments (such as edging stones, curbs, or restraints) are installed along the finished path edges to contain the paving material.
The main path paving or surfacing layer must be laid before edge treatment can be completed, as edge treatments often serve to contain and finish the edges of the paved surface.

After edge treatments are installed, final compaction and finishing works (e.g., sweeping, sealing joints, final rolling) are performed to ensure the edge is properly integrated and the path surface is complete.

Soft preference: Landscaping and topsoiling adjacent to the path are typically done after edge treatment to avoid disturbing the edging, but in some sequences they can overlap or be done before if care is taken.
The path layout must be marked and defined before any width variations can be applied to ensure the correct spatial boundaries are established.
The width variation must be fully implemented before the surface finishing is applied, as the finishing treatment depends on the final dimensional profile of the path.
Edge restraints (kerbs, edging) must be placed after the width variation is set to conform to the changing path boundaries.
Trail must be planned and surveyed to determine the exact locations where waypoint markers need to be placed.
The trail surface and path must be prepared before installing markers to ensure proper positioning and stability.
If the waypoint marker is mounted on a post or base, that foundation structure must be in place first before attaching the marker itself.

successor: Trail Signage and Information Board Installation
rationale: Waypoint markers often serve as reference points for informational signage, so markers should be in place first to align with signage placement.
Waypoint marker locations must be installed and marked before official GPS coordinates and trail documentation can be finalized for navigation purposes.
The site must be cleared and prepared before any path gradient or slope work can begin to ensure a stable and unobstructed work area.
Soil conditions must be assessed to determine the appropriate slope design and ensure stability before path gradient construction starts.
The path gradient and slope must be established first to provide the correct profile and drainage grade for the base course layer to be placed on top.
The final slope gradient must be set before drainage systems are installed to ensure proper water flow direction and effective drainage integration.
The path gradient and slope must be fully formed and compacted before the final paving or surface finish can be applied to achieve the correct design profile.
The site must be cleared and graded to establish the base topography and remove obstacles before paths can be planned and laid out.
Underground utilities (drainage, water, electrical conduits) must be installed first to avoid later excavation that would disrupt finished paths.
The path layout plan defines the alignment, width, and geometry; base construction must follow the approved plan to ensure correct positioning.
Surface finishing (concrete, asphalt, paving stones) can only proceed after the path layout is finalized and base layers are in place.
Soft landscaping (turf, shrubs, trees) is often done after paths are laid out to avoid damage to new plants, though it is a soft preference if paths can be installed around existing vegetation.
The ground must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and obstructions before any path construction can begin to provide a clean working surface.
The subgrade must be excavated and shaped to the correct profile and depth to accommodate the base layers and pavement structure of the path.

Any underground drainage pipes, culverts, or utility conduits that run beneath or across the path alignment must be installed and tested before paving to avoid cutting or damaging the finished surface.
The compacted aggregate sub-base and base course layers must be placed and compacted to provide a stable, load-bearing foundation for the paving material.
Edge restraints such as curbs or borders are typically installed after the paving is complete to neatly confine the paving material and provide a finished edge.
