The site must be cleared of obstructions, debris, and vegetation before a path accessibility audit can be conducted, as hidden hazards or overgrown areas would prevent accurate assessment of the path's condition and accessibility features.
Rough grading establishes the basic ground contours and slopes; without it, the path's final alignment and gradient cannot be assessed for compliance with accessibility standards.
The base layer of the path must be installed (compacted aggregate or similar) to provide a stable surface that can be evaluated for firmness, stability, and cross-slope prior to final surfacing.

The accessibility audit must identify any deficiencies in base alignment, slope, or width before the final surface material (e.g., asphalt, concrete, pavers) is laid, as correcting these issues after surfacing would be costly and potentially require demolition.
Accessibility audit findings dictate the exact location, slope, and configuration of curb ramps to ensure they meet accessibility standards and seamlessly connect to the audited path.
Accurate pedestrian desire line analysis requires understanding of existing site conditions, terrain, and physical layout which is captured through site surveys and topographic mapping.
Documenting existing pedestrian paths and worn trails provides baseline data on current movement patterns that must be analyzed to identify desire lines.
The identified desire lines directly inform the layout and alignment of formal pedestrian pathways to match natural movement patterns.
Desire line analysis outputs are essential inputs for developing the overall site circulation plan that integrates pedestrian flows.
Desire line findings help optimize landscape layout to accommodate natural movement routes, though landscaping can proceed with preliminary data.
Cornice is installed at the top of walls, so the wall framing must be in place to provide a substrate for attachment.
Cornice often integrates with the roof edge; roof sheathing must be completed so that the cornice can be properly aligned and fastened to both wall and roof structure.

The cornice is part of the building envelope trim; exterior wall finishes typically abut or wrap around the cornice, so the cornice must be installed first to provide a clean edge and weatherproofing transition.
Gutters are typically mounted to the fascia board which is part of the cornice assembly, so the cornice must be complete before gutters are attached; this is a physical requirement for support.
Soffit vents are installed within the cornice's soffit panel; the cornice must be in place to provide the mounting surface for these vents.
Window openings require the structural wall framing to be in place to define the rough openings and provide support for window frames.
The rough openings must be created in the wall framing before window frames can be physically set into place.
Window openings must be cut and prepared before exterior sheathing can be wrapped and sealed around the window openings for weather protection.
While cladding typically follows window installation, the rough openings should be ready; however, cladding can sometimes be done around windows, making this a soft preference.

Although drywall is finished after windows are installed, drywall must be boarded before the final window trim is fitted. However, window openings (rough openings in framing) must precede drywall for access.
Electrical conduits, junction boxes, and wiring must be in place before fixtures can be mounted and connected.

predecessor: Exterior Wall Sheathing and Weather Barrier
rationale: The exterior walls must be enclosed and weather-tight before mounting exterior fixtures to ensure proper sealing and waterproofing.
Fixtures must be installed before they can be powered on and tested for functionality, photometry, and control verification.
Final grading, paving, and landscaping often follow fixture installation to avoid damage to finishes; a soft preference to coordinate access.
All exterior lighting must be fully installed before final project inspection and close-out can be completed.

Spandrel panels are typically non-structural cladding components that attach to the building's structural frame. The structural steel frame must be erected first to provide the support framework for the spandrel panels to be mounted.
Spandrel panels are installed at each floor level to cover the gap between floors. The floor slab must be placed so that the spandrel panel has a mounting surface and the correct elevation reference.

Spandrel panels often form part of the exterior wall assembly, filling the opaque zones between vision glass. The spandrel panels must be in place before the curtain wall or glazing system is fully installed to ensure a continuous weathertight envelope.

Spandrel panels serve as part of the exterior facade; the air barrier and weatherproofing membrane must be applied over or behind the panels after they are fixed to maintain building envelope integrity.

While interior finishes can technically begin in other areas concurrently, finishing work adjacent to spandrel panels (e.g., drywall, insulation, trim) is typically sequenced after panel installation to avoid damage and to properly seal the interface between the panel and interior walls.
Scaffolding or elevated access systems must be in place to allow workers to safely reach and inspect all areas of the facade, and to perform cleaning operations at height.
The building's structural frame must be complete and stable before facade work can commence, as the facade is attached to or supported by the structure.
Roof must be watertight and drainage systems operational to prevent water ingress behind the facade during cleaning and to ensure the facade's top edge is fully installed and sealed.

Inspection and cleaning of the substrate or existing facade must be completed before new cladding or curtain wall panels are installed, to ensure a clean, sound surface for attachment and to identify any needed repairs.
Once the facade is inspected and cleaned, window and door openings can be precisely fitted and sealed against the clean facade surface, ensuring proper weatherproofing and alignment.
Scaffolding provides safe access to the facade for workers to perform repairs and restoration work at height.
The building structure must be stable before any facade repairs begin to ensure worker safety and prevent further damage during restoration.
Any hazardous materials (e.g., asbestos, lead paint) must be removed from the facade area before repair work commences to ensure health and safety.
Facade repairs must be completed before new windows and doors are installed to ensure proper sealing, alignment, and integration with the restored facade.
Final exterior finishes and paint are applied after facade repairs are completed to provide a uniform, clean appearance and protect the repaired surfaces.
The mounting bracket must be securely installed to provide a stable base for attaching the People Counter Sensor.
Power and data cables must be in place before the sensor can be physically connected and mounted.

successor: Configure and calibrate People Counter Sensor
rationale: The sensor must be physically installed and connected before it can be powered on, configured, and calibrated for accurate counting.
Testing (verifying detection accuracy and connectivity) can only occur after the sensor is installed, configured, and fully operational.
If the sensor is ceiling-mounted, the ceiling structure/finishing must be completed to provide a proper mounting surface and clear line of sight for the sensor.
Electrical wiring and conduit for the occupancy sensor must be installed in walls/ceilings before the sensor itself can be mounted and connected.
Occupancy sensors are often mounted on ceilings or walls; the ceiling surface must be in place to provide a mounting substrate.
Occupancy sensors control lighting circuits, so final trim-out, calibration, and testing of lighting control systems must occur after the sensor is installed and wired.
While commissioning can start in parallel with some sensor installation, full integrated systems testing of occupancy-based lighting control is best performed after all sensors are operational.
Drywall must be complete and finished (taped, mudded, painted) before sensor installation to avoid damage from dust and debris and to allow proper flush mounting.

A pedestrian traffic impact study requires baseline data on existing pedestrian patterns, sidewalk conditions, crosswalk locations, and surrounding land uses, which are gathered through a site assessment.
The study relies on empirical traffic volume data, pedestrian counts, and turning movement counts to model and analyze impacts, so data collection must precede analysis.

Findings from the pedestrian traffic impact study (e.g., identified high-risk crossings, necessary signal changes, sidewalk widening needs) directly inform the design of pedestrian safety improvements and accessibility features.
Any modifications to signal timings, crosswalk placements, or pedestrian phasing must be based on the study's analysis of pedestrian-vehicle interactions and level of service.
Municipal transportation departments typically require a completed pedestrian traffic impact study as part of the permit application package for projects affecting pedestrian facilities.

Crowd simulation modelling requires finalized architectural layouts, floor plans, and space programming data (e.g., room sizes, corridor widths, egress paths) to define the physical environment in which pedestrian movement will be simulated.
A detailed Building Information Model (BIM) or structural design must exist to provide geometry, column locations, and spatial constraints that influence crowd flow patterns and simulation accuracy.
Crowd simulation requires defined occupant loads, usage scenarios, and peak occupancy assumptions per zone to model realistic pedestrian densities and evacuation times.
The simulation must incorporate planned exit locations, stair widths, and fire/safety egress strategies to validate whether the design meets code compliance for safe evacuation.

Results from crowd simulation (e.g., evacuation times, bottleneck identification, level-of-service analysis) are inputs for validating that the design meets building code, accessibility, and life safety requirements.
The architectural design must be finalized to determine the building's layout, room sizes, and intended uses, which are essential inputs for calculating occupancy loads based on building codes.
Applicable building codes and occupancy classifications must be reviewed to determine the correct methodology and factors for calculating maximum occupancy loads.

predecessor: Space Planning and Room Layout Design
rationale: Detailed space plans with room dimensions, floor areas, and functional uses are required to compute occupancy loads per space using code-specified occupant density factors.
Design of fire alarm systems, emergency lighting, and egress pathways depends on the calculated occupancy loads to ensure adequate capacity and compliance with life safety codes.
The number and sizing of plumbing fixtures (toilets, sinks, etc.) are determined based on the calculated occupant load to meet minimum code requirements.
Heating, ventilation, and air conditioning systems must be sized based on the number of occupants as a key heat load and ventilation air requirement input.

While structural live loads are often code-prescribed per occupancy type, refined occupancy load calculations can validate or adjust structural design assumptions, though this is typically a verification step rather than a strict dependency.
Sensors must be physically installed before they can be calibrated and commissioned.
Sensors require power to operate, so electrical power supply must be installed and ready before calibration can begin.
Communication networks are required to transmit calibration data and verify sensor connectivity during commissioning.
Calibrated and commissioned sensors are needed as inputs for overall system integration testing.
Sensors must be calibrated and commissioned before the BMS can be handed over with functioning sensor data.
The building must be constructed and occupied before a post-occupancy audit can be conducted, as the audit evaluates pedestrian behavior and circulation in the completed, occupied building.
The building must be legally occupied (certificate of occupancy issued) before a post-occupancy evaluation can take place.
Actual pedestrian traffic and usage patterns can only be observed once occupants have moved in and are using the building.
The audit must be completed before findings and recommendations can be documented and reported.
Based on audit findings, adjustments to signage, wayfinding, or circulation paths may be implemented, but this is a soft recommendation rather than a physical necessity.
The egress pathways (corridors, stairwells, doors, and exit routes) must be fully installed and in place before they can be inspected for compliance with building codes and safety regulations.

Fire alarm systems are integral to egress compliance as they provide early warning; they must be installed so inspectors can verify proper integration with exit signage, emergency lighting, and overall egress strategy.
Emergency lighting along egress paths must be installed to ensure the inspection can verify that illuminated exit paths meet code requirements for safe evacuation.
Exit signs must be installed so the inspection can confirm that all required signage is properly placed, visible, and meets code-mandated illumination and placement standards.

A successful egress compliance inspection is typically a prerequisite for obtaining a certificate of occupancy, as it verifies that the building meets life-safety egress requirements before occupants can legally use the building.

While some interior finishes can be completed before inspection, final close-out and touch-ups of finishes near egress paths are typically done after the inspection to avoid damage during the inspection process.
The structural frame (columns, beams, primary supports) must be erected first to provide the load-bearing support system onto which the canopy or overhead element is attached.
Roof decking provides the base surface that defines the overhead enclosure; the canopy element is installed atop or integrated with this decking.

Overhead electrical, HVAC ducts, and plumbing rough-ins are typically run before enclosing the canopy to avoid rework, though this is a sequencing preference rather than a physical impossibility to reverse.
The canopy or overhead element must be complete to serve as a substrate or attachment point for exterior cladding, soffits, or finished ceiling materials applied to its underside.
Waterproofing membranes and flashings are applied over the completed canopy assembly to seal joints and transitions, ensuring weather integrity before final finishes.
The partition wall must be built on top of a finished floor slab or concrete deck to provide a stable, level base.

Any mechanical, electrical, or plumbing rough-in work that runs beneath the slab must be completed before the partition wall is installed, as the wall will cover or occupy that area and later access would be costly or impossible.

Overhead structural elements (e.g., beams, floor above) must be in place before partition walls are framed, as the walls may need to align with or tie into the structure above, and to avoid sequencing conflicts.
Electrical boxes and wiring are installed within the partition wall cavity after the wall framing is erected but before final cladding; the wall structure provides the support for these components.

successor: Wall Cladding / Finish (drywall, paneling, or tile)
rationale: The partition wall frame must be fully erected before any cladding or finish materials are applied to its surface.
The wall frame must be built first to create the cavity and support structure into which the recessed shelving unit will be installed.
Any wiring or outlets that need to pass behind or through the recessed shelving area must be roughed in before the shelving unit is installed, as access will be blocked afterward.
If the recessed shelving unit is in a kitchen or bathroom area, any plumbing lines must be roughed in before enclosing the wall cavity with shelving.
Drywall must be installed after the recessed shelving unit is in place so that the drywall can be cut and finished around the shelving unit, creating a flush, seamless appearance.
Painting and finishing work should be done after the shelving unit is installed so that the wall surfaces and the shelving unit itself can be painted or finished together for a uniform look.
Power supply wiring must be installed in ceilings/walls before task lighting fixtures can be connected and mounted.
Ceiling surfaces (drywall, suspended ceiling grid) must be completed to provide a mounting surface and finished appearance before task lighting fixtures are installed.

successor: Task Lighting Fixture Trim and Lens Installation
rationale: The main fixture housing must be mounted and wired before decorative trims, diffusers, or lenses can be snapped or screwed into place.
Final paint touch-ups and ceiling finishing around the fixture cannot be completed until the fixture body is installed to ensure seamless integration.
While commissioning can begin in parallel, full testing of dimming and switching controls is more efficient after all task lighting fixtures are physically installed and connected.
Acoustic lining panels are typically installed into or onto a ceiling grid or suspension system. The grid must be in place to provide the structural support for the panels.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) services such as ductwork, conduit, and piping are normally run above the ceiling before the acoustic panels are installed. Installing panels first would block access and require rework.

Lighting fixtures are often integrated into or mounted through the acoustic ceiling; however, panels must be in place first to mark the finished ceiling plane and provide the backing for integrated fixtures.
Sensors, smoke detectors, and sprinkler heads are typically installed after ceiling panels are in place to ensure proper alignment and penetration through the finished ceiling surface.

successor: Finish painting / final touch-up of ceiling area
rationale: Final painting and touch-ups are usually performed after acoustic panels are installed to blend panel edges and fix any marks from installation. This is a soft preference as some painting could be done beforehand if panels are pre-finished.

successor: Integrated Power and Data Outlet Installation
rationale: Electrical rough-in (cabling, conduits, back boxes) must be completed before outlet installation so that the outlet can be connected to the power and data infrastructure.

successor: Integrated Power and Data Outlet Installation
rationale: The outlet mounting box and bracket require a framed wall cavity to be installed into; the sheathing provides the finished surface for the outlet plate.

predecessor: Integrated Power and Data Outlet Installation
rationale: The outlet must be mounted and its face plate adjusted flush before final wall finishes are applied so that the outlet is properly aligned with the finished surface.

predecessor: Integrated Power and Data Outlet Installation
rationale: Testing and commissioning of power and data circuits can only occur after the outlet is fully installed and connected to verify correct wiring and signal integrity.

predecessor: Integrated Power and Data Outlet Installation
rationale: While furniture can often be placed before outlets are installed (soft preference), it is preferable to install outlets first to ensure access for plugging in equipment without moving heavy furniture.

Soft flooring requires a smooth, clean, and level subfloor surface for proper adhesion and finish. Any debris, moisture, or unevenness in the subfloor would cause defects in the soft flooring installation.
Underlayment provides cushioning, moisture barrier, and sound insulation that must be in place before soft flooring is laid on top.

All electrical wiring, conduit, and plumbing pipes that run beneath or within the floor structure must be completed before installing finished flooring, as accessing them afterward would require removing or damaging the soft flooring.

predecessor: Interior Wall Framing and Drywall Completion
rationale: While not strictly physically required, completing wall construction before flooring prevents dust, debris, and paint drips from damaging the new soft flooring, and allows wall finishes to overlap flooring edges for a clean transition.
Baseboards and trim are installed after soft flooring to cover the expansion gap around the perimeter and to sit on top of the finished floor surface for a clean appearance.

successor: Final Interior Painting and Wall Finishing
rationale: It is preferred to paint walls before flooring to avoid paint drips on the new floor, but if painting occurs after, the flooring must be protected. Typically flooring is installed after painting to avoid damage.
The rough opening in the frame or wall structure must be built and prepared (sized, squared, and finished) before the sliding or folding screen can be installed, as the screen fits into the opening.

Floor finishes (e.g., tile, wood, or concrete) should be completed before installing the bottom track or floor guide of the sliding/folding screen, as the track is mounted on top of the finished floor surface.
The structural support for the overhead track (e.g., header beam or blocking) must be in place before the screen system is installed, as the top track carries the weight of the panels.

The screen's side jambs and frames must be installed before adjacent drywall, trim, or wall finishes are completed, so that the finishes can be run flush against the screen frame for a seamless appearance.

If the sliding/folding screen includes integrated electrical components (e.g., powered operation, sensors, or data cabling), electrical rough-in is typically coordinated to occur after the screen frame is set, but this is a sequencing preference rather than a strict physical necessity.
The upholstered cushion system requires a completed frame structure to provide the underlying support and attachment surface for cushions and upholstery.
The suspension system (springs or webbing) must be installed before cushions are placed, as the cushions rest on and are supported by the suspension system.
Decorative trim elements such as welting, buttons, or nailhead trim are applied to the completed cushion surfaces and cannot be installed before the cushion system is in place.
Final quality inspection of seating comfort, cushion fit, and upholstery finish must occur after the cushion system is fully installed.
The structural frame (studs, joists, etc.) must be in place to define the cavity or area where a niche or recess will be formed; you cannot form a recess into an empty space.
Niches and recesses must be formed before any electrical outlets, plumbing fixtures, or conduit can be roughed in within or passing through that recessed area.
The niche/recess cavity must be formed and enclosed before sheathing or backing is applied over it to close the wall assembly.
Insulation can only be placed after the recess cavity is fully framed; otherwise the insulation would have no cavity to fill.
Finish surfaces like drywall are applied after niches/recesses are formed; the recess shape must exist before it can be covered with finish material.

successor: Pocket Layout Design and Space Planning
rationale: Structural load-bearing walls, columns, and beams define the spatial boundaries and pocket locations in a building; pocket layout cannot be designed without knowing the structural grid and load paths.

successor: Pocket Layout Design and Space Planning
rationale: The overall floor plan determines room sizes, circulation paths, and functional zones; pocket spaces must align with these architectural layouts.

successor: Pocket Layout Design and Space Planning
rationale: MEP risers, ducts, and pipe chases occupy space within walls and ceilings; pocket layout must accommodate these services and avoid conflicts.

predecessor: Pocket Layout Design and Space Planning
rationale: The defined pocket dimensions, locations, and clearances are required before any physical framing can proceed on site.

predecessor: Pocket Layout Design and Space Planning
rationale: Pocket spaces dictate where partitions, cabinetry, and built-in furnishings will be placed; finish works depend on the finalized pocket layout.

Electrical rough-in work including wiring, conduit, and junction boxes must be completed before specialist lighting fixtures can be installed, as the lighting units connect to and depend on this pre-wired infrastructure.
The ceiling grid or support structure must be in place to provide a mounting surface and support for recessed or suspended specialist lighting fixtures.
HVAC ductwork must be installed before lighting to avoid conflicts in ceiling plenum space, and to ensure lighting fixtures are positioned around duct runs without obstruction.
After specialist lighting fixtures are physically installed, final trim-out (lenses, diffusers, decorative covers) and aiming/adjustment of directional fixtures must follow.
Specialist lighting must be fully installed before circuits can be energized and final testing, commissioning, and verification of lighting control systems can be performed.

The building must be enclosed (roof, walls, windows, doors) to protect millwork materials and finished joinery from weather damage, moisture, and dust, and to provide a conditioned environment for precise fabrication.

All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-ins within walls and ceilings must be completed before installing millwork, as millwork often covers or integrates with these services and would otherwise need to be removed or cut for access.

predecessor: Floor, Wall, and Ceiling Finishes (Drywall, Painting)
rationale: Surface finishes such as drywall, plaster, and paint should be completed before millwork installation to avoid damaging the finished joinery with construction dust, paint splatter, or drywall compound.

successor: Final Finish Carpentry and Trim Installation
rationale: Custom millwork and joinery elements (cabinetry, paneling, built-ins) are fabricated and installed first as the base framework, after which finishing trim, moldings, and decorative elements are applied to complete the aesthetic.

While flooring can be installed before millwork in some cases (soft preference), it is generally preferred to install millwork after flooring to allow precise scribing to the finished floor level and to avoid damaging finished floors during heavy millwork installation. However, this can vary by trade sequence.
Wall framing must be complete to provide the structural cavities and backing for running data and power cabling within walls.
Plumbing rough-in should be completed before electrical and data rough-in to avoid conflicts and allow electrical to work around plumbing lines.
Insulation must be installed after rough-in wiring is complete so that wiring is not buried behind insulation, and inspection of rough-in can occur.
Drywall cannot be hung until all rough-in electrical, data, and low-voltage wiring is complete, inspected, and approved.
Trim-out and installation of switches, outlets, and cover plates must follow after rough-in wiring and after drywall is complete.

The soft furnishing and cushion fit-out (including curtains, upholstery, and cushions) must be installed after wall and ceiling finishes are complete to ensure that mounting points, backing boards, and surrounding surfaces are finished and ready, and to avoid damage to soft materials from ongoing finishing work.

Floor finishes (e.g., carpet, tiles, or wood flooring) should be completed before soft furnishings and cushions are placed to prevent soiling, staining, or damaging floor surfaces during the furnishing installation process.

All electrical outlets, lighting points, and mechanical services that will be concealed by or interact with soft furnishings must be roughed-in and inspected before the soft furnishing fit-out to avoid the need for rework or access issues.

Soft furnishing and cushion fit-out must be completed before final cleaning and project handover, as these items are finishing touches that complete the interior and must be in place for the final presentation and inspection.

Soft furnishings (curtains, cushions, upholstered elements) should be installed before loose furniture and decorative fixtures are brought in, to prevent damage to the soft items and to allow proper arrangement of the complete interior fit-out.
The building must be fully constructed and occupied before a post-occupancy performance review can take place, as the review assesses performance after occupancy.
The review is 'post-occupancy', meaning occupants must be in place and using the building for a period of time before performance data can be collected and reviewed.
After identifying performance gaps in the review, remediation or retrofit planning typically follows, though it is a soft preference because not all reviews lead to immediate retrofits.

Findings from the performance review often inform adjustments to building operations (e.g., HVAC schedules, lighting controls), but this is a soft preference as some issues may not require operational changes.
The tread support structure (e.g., stringers, risers, or brackets) must be in place before seating treads can be attached or laid.
The tread must be fully seated and secured before any surface finishing, sealing, or coating is applied.
Handrails and guardrails are typically installed after treads are in place to ensure proper alignment and safe access during installation.
The complete stair assembly including treads must be installed before a final quality and safety inspection can be performed.
Riser panels are typically placed on top of or embedded into concrete slabs; the slab must be poured and cured to provide a stable base and structural support for the riser panel.
Riser panels house electrical distribution components; conduits must be run into and connected to the panel after it is mounted in place.

successor: Cable Tray Installation Adjacent to Riser
rationale: Cable trays often feed into or out of riser panels; they must be positioned and aligned after the panel is installed to ensure proper connection and support.
Riser panels are mounted to structural walls or frames; the framing must be in place to provide attachment points and load-bearing support.

successor: Circuit Breaker and Panel Trim Installation
rationale: Internal components and trim of the riser panel are installed after the enclosure is mounted to avoid damage and ensure proper alignment within the panel.
Handrails and guardrails are typically anchored to structural elements like concrete slabs, steel beams, or floor decks. The supporting structure must be in place before railings can be installed.
Handrails on stairs require the stair structure (treads, risers, and stringers) to be complete so that the railing system can be securely fastened along the stair slope.

Typically, handrails are installed before final painting or powder coating of the railing itself to avoid damage during installation and to allow touch-ups, but this order may be swapped if prefabricated coated rails are used.
Drywall finishing near railings is often completed after railing installation to allow for seamless transitions and caulking at wall-railing interfaces, but this can vary by schedule preference.
Guardrails and handrails are life-safety systems that must be installed and checked before final building inspection and occupancy, as they are required for fall protection compliance.
The structural frame (columns, beams, and floor slabs) provides the load-bearing support to which the aisle stair is anchored; the stair cannot be installed without the primary structure in place.
The physical stair assembly must be manufactured and delivered to site before installation can commence.
Final surface treatments, anti-slip coatings, and safety nosings must be applied after the stair structure is fully installed and secured.
Handrails and guardrails adjacent to the aisle stair are typically installed after the stair stringers and treads are in place to ensure proper alignment and attachment points.
Regulatory and safety inspections of the aisle stair can only be performed after the stair is fully installed, finished, and fitted with all safety components.

Seat nosing is the front edge trim or profile applied to the seating surface (typically on concrete or metal stairs/bleachers). The underlying structural substrate (e.g., concrete stair tread or metal seat pan) must be installed and cured/set before the nosing can be affixed to it.

While often seat nosing is installed as part of or after the main seat assembly, in many construction sequences the nosing is attached to the structural tread first, then the seat cushion or seat board is placed. However this ordering can vary and is often a soft preference based on the specific product system.

If the nosing is cast-in or adhered to a concrete stair tread, the concrete must first be poured and sufficiently cured, or the substrate must be clean and prepared, before the nosing can be installed.
Rake beams transfer inclined loads from roof/upper structure to foundations; therefore foundations must be in place to support the beam.
Tie or ground beams often provide lateral stability and a base for raker beams; they need to be cast before raker beams are installed.
Rake beams typically support inclined roof slabs or decks; the roof/deck construction follows after the raker beams are in place to bear the loads.
Masonry or brickwork laid on the slope supported by the rake beam requires the structural support of the beam to be completed first.

Waterproofing is typically applied after the structural deck/roof is cast, which itself follows the rake beam; however waterproofing could be considered a soft preference if done at a later finishing stage.
Excavation must be completed to create the void or foundation space that the sub-structure infill will occupy.
The foundation concrete must be poured and cured to provide a stable base before any sub-structure infill work (e.g., backfill, lean concrete, or blockwork) can commence.
Waterproofing membranes or coatings must be applied to the substructure walls and base before infill to prevent moisture ingress that would be trapped after backfilling.
The sub-structure infill (e.g., granular fill, lean concrete, or blinding) must be in place and compacted to provide a uniform bearing surface for the ground floor slab.

While some utility rough-ins can occur concurrently, the major under-slab drainage and piping is typically laid after the infill is placed and leveled, though this is more of a practical sequence than a hard structural constraint.
Electrical wiring and junction boxes must be installed before step lights can be connected to the power supply.
Step lights are typically recessed into walls or stairs; walls must be finished and painted before cutting openings and installing fixtures to avoid damage to finished surfaces.
The structural framing of stairs or floors must be complete to provide a mounting surface and correct positioning for step lights.
After step lights are installed, minor touch-ups to paint or caulking around fixtures may be needed, but this is a cosmetic preference rather than a hard constraint.
Step lights must be physically installed before the final electrical trim-out phase where all fixtures are tested and verified for correct operation.
The ground must be properly graded and excavated to establish the correct slope and elevation for the drainage channel to function properly and direct water flow.
Existing underground utilities must be located and marked before excavation for the drainage channel to avoid damaging them during construction.
Backfilling around the drainage channel can only occur after the channel is fully installed, inspected, and approved to ensure structural integrity.
Final paving or surface finishing (e.g., asphalt, concrete slabs) must be done after drainage channels are in place to ensure proper water capture and runoff.
Landscaping and topsoil placement typically follow drainage installation to avoid soil erosion and ensure drainage paths are established, though in some cases partial landscaping could precede it.

Electrical wiring, conduit, outlets, and mechanical ductwork must be installed within the wall or ceiling cavity before acoustic panels are installed, as the panels would block access to these services.
The wall framing, studs, or ceiling grid must be complete and structurally sound to provide a mounting surface and substrate for the acoustic finish panels.
Any acoustic or thermal insulation within the cavity must be placed before the finish panels are installed, as the panels will permanently enclose the cavity.
Acoustic panels are typically installed as a finished surface; final painting, caulking, and touch-up work around the panel edges and joints must occur after the panels are fixed in place.

While often flooring is installed before wall finishes to avoid damage, in many sequences acoustic wall panels are installed before finished flooring to allow the panels to overlap or sit behind baseboards with a clean edge.
A stable foundation is required to support the weight and loads of precast concrete units; without it, installation cannot proceed.
A crane or lifting equipment must be positioned and operational on site before precast units can be lifted and placed into position.
The ground area must be cleared, leveled, and compacted to provide a safe working platform for crane access and material staging.
Precast units must be fabricated, delivered to site, and staged in designated areas before installation can commence.
After precast units are placed and aligned, the connections between units must be grouted and finished to achieve structural continuity and stability.
Steel frame and rake beams require stable, cured foundations and footings to transfer structural loads into the ground; erecting steel without completed foundations is structurally impossible.
Rake beams are typically connected to columns or vertical steel members; columns must be erected and braced first to provide support and alignment for rake beam installation.
Metal decking is laid on top of and supported by the steel frame and rake beams; the structural steel framework must be in place before decking can be installed.

successor: Welding / Bolt Tightening and Connection Completion
rationale: After rake beams are placed into position, final welded connections and bolted connections must be completed to ensure structural continuity and load path.
Roof trusses and rafters bear on or connect to the rake beams and steel frame; the primary steel frame must be erected before roof structural elements can be installed.
The concrete (or other substrate) must be cast and sufficiently cured to provide a stable, hard surface before nosing and finishing can be applied.
The underlying stair tread or slab must be in place and leveled before nosing profiles and surface finishing can be executed.
The substrate must be cleaned, roughened, or prepared to ensure proper adhesion of nosing strips and finishing materials.
After nosing and surface finishing are applied, a final curing or sealing step is needed to protect the finish and ensure durability.
Once nosing and surface finishing are complete, the work should be inspected for dimensional accuracy, slip resistance, and visual quality before handover.

Waterproofing membranes and drainage layers are typically applied over a cured concrete slab or structural deck. The concrete must be poured, set, and prepared (cleaned, dried, smoothed) before any waterproofing can be installed.
For above-grade waterproofing (e.g., on roof decks or exterior walls), the structural framing and sheathing must be complete to provide a substrate for the waterproofing membrane.
Below-grade waterproofing systems (e.g., on foundation walls) must be fully installed, cured, and protected before backfill soil is placed against the wall; otherwise, the membrane could be damaged.
Waterproofing (especially on slabs/roofs) must be tested and accepted before interior finishes are laid, as water intrusion after finishing would cause severe damage and rework.

Above-grade drainage systems connected to landscaping should be installed before final grading and planting to ensure proper water flow, but this is a logical sequence rather than a strict physical dependency.
Seating fixtures require a stable, level, and finished floor surface for proper anchoring and alignment; installing them before the subfloor is complete would result in instability or rework.

Electrical outlets, data ports, or raceways for powered seating (e.g., electric recliners, auditorium seats with charging) must be roughed-in before seats are placed, as the fixtures obstruct wall and floor access after installation.

Painting, wallcovering, and finishing should be completed before seating installation to avoid damaging finished walls when moving large seating fixtures into position and to prevent the need for touch-ups around installed seats.

successor: Final Floor Finishing / Carpet Lay (around fixtures)
rationale: In many installations, seating is placed before the final floor covering (e.g., carpet tiles cut around seat pedestals) to achieve a seamless appearance and to avoid damage to expensive flooring from heavy seat movement.

For powered seats, the seating must be in place and connected before the final electrical trim-out and testing can verify that power connections, switches, and lighting at each seat function correctly.
Columns must be erected to provide vertical support and load transfer for the intermediate floor slab.
Formwork (molds) must be in place to shape and support the wet concrete of the intermediate floor slab until it cures.
Steel reinforcement (rebar) must be laid within the formwork to provide tensile strength and structural integrity to the concrete slab.
After pouring the slab, the concrete must undergo a curing period to reach sufficient strength before any subsequent loads are applied.
Upper-level walls (next story) depend on the completed intermediate floor slab as a working platform and as a structural diaphragm to transfer lateral loads.
The split-level floor plate requires a stable, level foundation or slab to be constructed first, as it bears directly on the structural support below.
Load-bearing walls or columns that support the split-level floor must be erected before the floor plate is installed to provide vertical support.
Interior partition walls built on the split-level floor cannot be framed until the floor deck is in place to serve as their base and working platform.

successor: Rough-in MEP (Mechanical, Electrical, Plumbing) on split level
rationale: MEP rough-in work within the split-level floor zone requires the floor structure to be installed so that chases, conduits, and piping can be run through or under the floor.
Final floor finishes cannot be applied until the structural floor plate is complete and has cured, providing a sound substrate.

Transfer beams transfer heavy loads from upper structural elements to supporting columns and foundations. Without completed foundations capable of supporting the concentrated loads, constructing a transfer beam would lack proper load-bearing support and could lead to structural failure.

Transfer beams are typically supported by columns beneath them. These supporting columns must be constructed to their full design height before the transfer beam can be placed, as the beam transfers loads downward into these columns.

Transfer beams are massive structural elements that require extensive formwork, shoring, and falsework systems to support the wet concrete and reinforcement during construction. The formwork system must be fully installed and inspected before beam construction can begin.

The primary function of a transfer beam is to support upper floors by redistributing loads to columns. Upper structure construction can only proceed after the transfer beam has gained sufficient strength to carry the imposed loads.

The slab at the transfer level often bears on or is monolithically connected to the transfer beam. Pouring and finishing the slab requires the transfer beam to be in place and sufficiently cured to act as a support and load-bearing element.

Secondary beams are typically supported by or framed into primary beams. The primary structural grid must be in place before secondary beams can be installed, as they rely on primary beams for support and connection.

Steel columns must be erected to provide vertical support for the primary beams, which in turn support the secondary beams. The full vertical load path from secondary beams through primary beams to columns must be established.
Metal decking is placed on top of and spans across secondary beams. The secondary beams provide the supporting framework for the metal deck, so they must be installed first.
The concrete slab is poured over the metal decking which rests on the secondary beams. The secondary beams must be in place to support the deck and wet concrete during construction.

Fireproofing is typically applied to steel members including secondary beams after they are installed. However, in some cases fireproofing can be applied off-site or out of strict sequence, so this is a soft preference for on-site application.
The column must be anchored to a finished foundation that can support its load and provide proper structural connection.
The base plate or column base must be installed and leveled before erecting the column to ensure proper alignment and load transfer.
Ground floor slab must be cast to provide a stable working platform and proper embedment for column starter bars or base plates.
Beams span between columns and rely on columns for vertical support; columns must be in place before beams can be erected.
Upper floor slabs are typically supported by beams and columns; columns must be erected to provide vertical support for the slab formwork and concrete.
Bracing connects to columns to provide lateral stability; columns must be erected before bracing can be installed between them.

Non-structural partitions are often built after columns (soft preference) because it is easier to frame around columns after they are in place, but partitions could theoretically be built concurrently or before if detailed around column locations.

predecessor: Structural Frame / Slab Installation at Mid-Level
rationale: The structural frame and slab must be in place to provide a stable attachment surface and support for the guardrail/balustrade system at the mid-level.
Guardrails/balustrades must be installed before decking or floor finishing is completed to provide fall protection for workers during the finishing operations.
While not physically required, installing guardrails early provides safe access for MEP workers performing rough-in work at the mid-level edge areas.

Guardrails/balustrades often serve as part of the edge protection system and may need to be installed before exterior cladding or glazing is applied to ensure safe working conditions at the perimeter.

successor: Final Inspection / Safety Sign-Off at Mid-Level
rationale: Guardrails must be fully installed and secure before the area can be signed off for safety compliance and final inspection.
The staircase must be anchored to a stable, level base. Foundation work must be completed to support the structural loads of the staircase.
The mid-level landing and support beams must be in place before the staircase can be installed to provide the connection points and structural support at the intermediate level.
The raw staircase structure must be erected before finishing elements like handrails, balustrades, and non-slip treads can be applied.
The staircase provides access to the mid-level; the mid-level floor slab/deck can only be fully completed after the staircase is in place to allow material and worker access to that level.

It is preferable to install major mechanical, electrical, and plumbing lines at the mid-level after the staircase is in place to avoid coordination conflicts, though some rough-in could be done earlier with careful planning.
The structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) must be in place to provide load-bearing support and attachment points for fire compartment barriers, which are typically non-structural elements.

Vertical shafts (e.g., elevator shafts, utility risers) must be enclosed first to define the fire compartments and prevent fire/smoke spread between floors, as intermediate barriers seal off these shafts at each floor level.

Penetrations for mechanical, electrical, and plumbing services through the fire barrier must be made and properly fire-stopped before finalizing the compartment, but the barrier itself must be installed first to define where penetrations are needed.
Fire stopping around all penetrations (pipes, ducts, cables) through the barrier must occur after the barrier is in place to ensure the compartment's fire-resistance rating is maintained.

Surface finishes like plastering and painting are typically applied after fire barrier installation, but this is a logical sequence preference rather than a physical necessity — some finishes could be applied beforehand if protected.

Intermediate floors (slabs) require completed vertical supports (columns or load-bearing walls) to transfer loads down to the foundation. The floor slab cannot be placed without the columns/walls to support it.
Finish flooring materials such as screed, tiles, or raised flooring require the intermediate floor slab to be fully cured and structurally complete before application.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work (e.g., conduit, piping, ductwork) for the floor zone can only commence once the floor slab is poured and accessible.
Staircases land on and connect intermediate floor levels; the floor slab must be in place to provide the landing support for the staircase installation.
The foundation and ground floor slab (or basement structure) must be completed to provide a stable base before constructing intermediate floors above ground.
The ground or slab where falsework will be erected must be prepared, compacted, and leveled to provide a stable base for loads.
For structures requiring foundations, the foundations must be completed and cured to support the falsework loads.
Engineered falsework drawings and load calculations must be approved before erection begins to ensure safety and structural adequacy.
Formwork panels are placed on top of the completed falsework/propping system, so falsework must first be erected to support the formwork.
Once falsework is installed and formwork is in place, reinforcement steel can be placed within the forms; falsework provides the support structure needed before rebar placement.
Concrete can only be poured after falsework, formwork, and reinforcement are all in place, as the falsework must support the wet concrete and formwork during curing.
Framing must be complete to provide structural support and mounting points for MEP rough-in work such as conduit, ductwork, and piping.
The slab/concrete deck must be poured and cured to provide a working surface and to embed any necessary slab-embedded conduits or sleeves before overhead rough-in.
Rough-in work must be completed before inspections can take place to verify code compliance of MEP installations.
Insulation must be installed after MEP rough-in is complete to avoid covering un-inspected or unfinished services.
Drywall cannot be installed until all rough-in MEP work is finished and inspected, as the walls would need to be opened up again otherwise.

predecessor: Structural Steel Installation / Main Frame Erection
rationale: The mezzanine structure relies on the main structural steel frame being in place as its supporting substrate; fit-out cannot commence until the primary load-bearing frame is erected and stable.

The mezzanine floor slab or metal decking must be installed to provide the working platform and base on which all subsequent fit-out activities (partition walls, MEP rough-ins, finishes) are carried out.
Ceiling installation follows fit-out because services (electrical, HVAC, data) are roughed-in and walls are framed before overhead ceilings are closed up to avoid rework and allow access.
Painting and final wall finishes are performed after fit-out (partitioning, MEP rough-ins) is complete to prevent damage to finished surfaces and to allow uninterrupted application.
Final floor coverings are laid after all fit-out activities that could scratch, stain, or otherwise damage the flooring (e.g., drywall, painting, MEP work) are finished.
The intermediate slab must be fully cast, cured, and finished to provide a sound substrate before waterproofing can be applied.
The concrete slab must achieve sufficient curing time and strength before waterproofing membranes or coatings are installed to prevent cracking or debonding.
The slab surface must be cleaned, repaired, and primed as needed to ensure proper adhesion of the waterproofing system.
After waterproofing is installed, a water retention or flood test must be performed to verify the integrity of the waterproofing layer before proceeding with subsequent works.
A protective screed or mortar layer must be placed over the waterproofing membrane to shield it from physical damage during further construction activities.
The threshold element (e.g., door threshold or window sill) requires a stable, level foundation or structural opening to be prepared and cured before it can be installed.
Threshold elements are typically set into or against walls and door openings; the walls must be constructed to define the opening where the threshold will be placed.
The rough opening for the door or window must be framed to the correct dimensions before the threshold element can be fitted into place.
The threshold serves as the base component; the door or window frame is installed on top of or into the threshold element, so the threshold must be in place first.
Floor finishes such as tile, hardwood, or concrete adjacent to the threshold are installed after the threshold is set, as the threshold defines the transition and level between surfaces.
The rough opening must be framed and prepared to the correct dimensions before any door or gate assembly can be installed, as the component requires a structurally sound and correctly sized aperture.
The wall or support structure must be fully framed and in place to provide the necessary anchoring points for the door or gate frame, ensuring structural integrity.
Hinges, handles, locks, and other hardware can only be mounted on the door/gate after the door/gate itself is positioned and secured within its opening.
Weatherstripping, seals, and threshold installation must follow door/gate placement to ensure proper fit and create an effective barrier against air and moisture infiltration.
While finish flooring can be installed before the door, it is often preferred to hang the door first to establish the undercut clearance and avoid damaging the flooring material during installation.
A stable and level foundation is required to support the visual screening device, ensuring structural integrity and proper alignment.
The structural framework must be in place to provide attachment points and support for the visual screening device.
If the visual screening device requires power (e.g., for motorized operation or integrated lighting), electrical connections must be made after the device is physically installed.
Finishing work such as painting or wall covering should be completed after the device is installed to ensure clean edges, proper fit, and seamless integration with surrounding surfaces.
A final inspection of the installed device, including its operation and safety compliance, must occur after installation is complete to verify proper functioning.
The rough opening must be framed and prepared to receive the operable partition hardware and track system.
Operable partitions are typically top-hung; the overhead support structure must be in place to bear the weight of the partition system.

predecessor: MEP rough-in above ceiling (electrical, fire alarm, sprinklers)
rationale: Overhead MEP rough-in must be completed before the partition track is installed to avoid interference, as the track occupies header space.
Installing floor finish after the partition allows the partition's bottom seal to sit on the finished floor; however, some sequences allow floor finish first with careful protection.
The partition must be fully installed and adjusted before fire-rating and acoustic performance testing can be conducted.
Before spatial programming can begin, the functional requirements, space types, square footage targets, and user needs must be defined to inform the space allocation and adjacency planning.
Site constraints, dimensions, orientation, and geotechnical conditions influence the feasible building footprint and spatial organization, so site analysis must precede spatial programming.
While spatial programming can begin with preliminary cost assumptions, final space allocations are often refined based on available budget, making this a soft preference.
Spatial programming produces the room data sheets, adjacency matrices, and space program that directly drive the conceptual layout and massing in schematic design.
Once space program is defined, the design team can assess compliance with zoning codes, floor area ratios, and building code limits on occupancy and egress.
Survey data and site boundaries are needed to determine property lines, setbacks, and existing conditions before privacy zones can be designed.
Understanding local zoning ordinances, building codes, and privacy regulations is essential to ensure the layout design complies with legal requirements.
The overall site plan including building footprints, access roads, and lot lines must be established to define where privacy zones will be placed.
The privacy zone layout must be finalized to guide the placement of hedges, fences, walls, or other screening elements for visual and acoustic privacy.
Privacy zone boundaries define the building envelope and orientation, ensuring structures are positioned with adequate setbacks and privacy buffers from neighboring properties.

Access control systems require power for control panels, readers, and locking mechanisms. Electrical rough-in must be completed to provide conduits, wiring, and power sources before access control devices can be installed and connected.
Conduits and backboxes for access control cabling and devices must be installed in walls and ceilings before the access control components can be mounted and wired.
Doors and door frames must be in place to accommodate electric strikes, magnetic locks, and door position switches that are part of the access control system.
All access control hardware (readers, controllers, locks, panels) must be physically installed and wired before the system can be programmed, configured, and tested for proper operation.

It is preferable to complete access control installation before final interior finishes to avoid damage to finished surfaces during device mounting and cabling work, though this ordering can be adjusted if necessary.
A stable foundation is required to provide a level base for installing the threshold, ensuring proper alignment and structural support.
The door/window rough opening must be framed to define the dimensions and location where the threshold will be installed.
The subfloor must be in place to provide the underlying surface that the threshold will sit upon and be anchored to.
The threshold must be installed first to provide a base and anchoring point for the door or window frame to sit upon.
The threshold defines the transition point between flooring surfaces; finished flooring is typically installed up to the threshold after it is in place.
The sun tunnel requires the roof structure to be in place as it penetrates the roof assembly and needs structural support to be installed.
The roof deck or sheathing must be installed before cutting the opening for the sun tunnel, as the unit mounts to and through the roof deck.
Proper roof flashing must be in place to ensure a weather-tight seal around the sun tunnel penetration, preventing leaks.
The sun tunnel's interior diffuser and trim must be installed before the ceiling finish is completed, as the diffuser integrates with the ceiling plane.
It is preferable to install roof insulation after the sun tunnel to properly seal around the penetration, though it can be retrofitted.
The structural frame must be complete to provide a stable mounting surface and support for the solar shading / brise-soleil elements.
External walls and cladding must be installed to define the building envelope and provide the fixing points onto which the brise-soleil brackets or rails are anchored.
Brise-soleil is typically installed before windows/glazing to allow access for bracket fixing and alignment, and to protect glazing from damage during shading installation.
It is a soft preference to complete brise-soleil installation before dismantling façade scaffolding to avoid the cost and complexity of re-erecting scaffolding for the shading work.
It is practical (but not physically required) to complete shading installation before applying final façade finishes so that the finish can be applied continuously around brackets and supports.

successor: Interior Roller Blind / Solar Blind Installation
rationale: Roller blinds and solar blinds are mounted on or within the window frame; the frame must be installed and structurally complete to provide a secure fixing surface for the blind brackets.

successor: Interior Roller Blind / Solar Blind Installation
rationale: Glass panels must be in place before blinds are fitted, as blinds are typically mounted adjacent to or over the glass; installing blinds before glazing risks damage to the blind and obstructs glass installation.

successor: Interior Roller Blind / Solar Blind Installation
rationale: Overhead painting and finishing work (especially near the window head) should be completed before blinds are installed to avoid paint splatter, dust, and scaffolding movement that could damage the delicate blind fabric and mechanism.

predecessor: Interior Roller Blind / Solar Blind Installation
rationale: It is preferable to install blinds after major finishing work is done, but any final touch-up painting or trim work around the window can be completed after blinds are installed if care is taken to protect them (soft preference).

predecessor: Interior Roller Blind / Solar Blind Installation
rationale: Blind installation generates dust and debris from drilling and packaging; final cleaning must occur after installation to ensure the space is clean and blinds are free of construction dust before occupancy.

A detailed architectural design (including building geometry, orientation, fenestration layout, and key dimensions) must be established before daylighting simulation can be performed, as the simulation requires these spatial inputs to model daylight penetration accurately.

Specifications for glazing types, window-to-wall ratios, shading devices, and facade materials must be defined to provide the simulation with accurate optical and thermal properties of the envelope components.
Site context, solar path data, surrounding obstructions, and local climate information are required inputs for daylighting simulations to model solar access and sky conditions correctly.
Daylighting simulation results inform the placement, zoning, and control strategies for electric lighting systems, so the analysis must be completed before interior lighting design can be finalized.
Daylighting analysis affects solar heat gain calculations and thermal comfort predictions, which are necessary inputs for accurate HVAC load calculations and zone planning.
A solar path study requires knowing the geographic location, latitude, and site context (obstructions, topography) to accurately model sun angles and shadow patterns.
Regional climatic data (e.g., typical meteorological year data, cloud cover patterns) is needed to interpret solar exposure and its impact on heating/cooling loads.
Results from the sun path analysis directly inform optimal building orientation and massing to maximize passive solar gain or minimize overheating, depending on climate.
Sun path data (altitude and azimuth angles at critical times of year) is essential to size and position overhangs, louvers, or other shading elements.
The study determines optimal panel tilt, orientation, and placement to avoid shading and maximize annual energy yield.

Solar and daylight analysis provides the necessary solar geometry and daylight intensity inputs that inform the glare assessment; without understanding the sun's path and daylight levels, glare conditions cannot be accurately evaluated.

The facade and envelope design defines window placement, glazing specifications, shading devices, and material finishes — all of which are critical inputs for calculating potential glare; glare assessment cannot be performed without knowing the physical properties of the building envelope.

The overall building orientation and massing establish the geometric context for how sunlight interacts with the building surfaces; glare assessment depends on this spatial configuration to determine incident angles and reflective paths.

While glare assessment results can inform and optimize interior lighting design (e.g., adjusting luminaire placement or dimming controls to compensate for glare), interior lighting can be designed in parallel; however, ideally glare findings refine the final lighting design.

successor: Occupant Comfort Analysis / Thermal Comfort Study
rationale: Glare assessment outputs, especially visual discomfort metrics, feed into broader occupant comfort analyses; however, thermal comfort can be studied concurrently, making this a soft preference rather than a hard constraint.
Structural framing (walls, roof) must be complete to provide the rough openings and structural support needed for window and door installation.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-ins within wall cavities should be completed before windows/doors are installed to avoid rework or damage to fenestration.
Sheathing provides the backing surface and structural diaphragm around window/door openings, which is necessary before installing fenestration units.
Windows and doors must be installed, flashed, and sealed before exterior cladding or siding is applied so that cladding can overlap and integrate with fenestration flashing systems.
Windows and doors must be in place before interior finishes such as drywall, trim, and casing are installed to allow proper fit and finishing around openings.

The building must be fully enclosed (walls, roof, windows installed) before daylight factor measurements can be taken, as the measurement assesses natural light levels within a completed interior space.

Interior finishes including paint colors, surface reflectances, and material properties directly affect daylight factor readings, so they must be completed before accurate measurements can be obtained.
Windows and glazing must be fully installed as they are the primary apertures through which daylight enters the space; without them, daylight factor measurements would be invalid.
Daylight factor measurements inform the design and placement of artificial lighting systems to supplement natural light, so measurements must be completed before final lighting design is finalized.

Daylight factor data is typically submitted as part of sustainability certification submissions; while it is strongly preferred to have the data before certification deadlines, it is a soft dependency as documentation can sometimes be updated later.

predecessor: Slab / Concrete Deck Placement and Curing
successor: Raised Access Floor / Floor Box System
rationale: The raised access floor system requires a stable, level structural slab (concrete deck) as its supporting base. The slab must be fully placed, cured, and achieve sufficient strength to bear the access floor pedestals and live loads before installation can begin.

successor: Raised Access Floor / Floor Box System
rationale: The building structural frame must be erected and stabilized to define the floor levels and provide the vertical support for the slabs that the raised floor sits on.

successor: Raised Access Floor / Floor Box System
rationale: Any below-slab waterproofing or vapor retarder must be installed before the slab is poured; the raised floor system then relies on the completed, protected slab surface.

predecessor: Raised Access Floor / Floor Box System
successor: Floor Covering Installation (e.g., Carpet Tiles, Vinyl)
rationale: Finished floor coverings such as carpet tiles, vinyl, or other walkable surfaces are installed on top of the raised access floor panels after the access floor structure is leveled, secured, and tested.

predecessor: Raised Access Floor / Floor Box System
successor: Electrical Rough-In / Final Trim (Floor Box Connections)
rationale: Floor box cutouts, power/data outlet fittings, and wiring terminations within the raised floor are performed after the access floor panels are in place and the underfloor cable pathways are accessible.

predecessor: Raised Access Floor / Floor Box System
rationale: Where the raised floor plenum is used for air distribution, the access floor must be fully installed and sealed before the HVAC system can be balanced and diffusers placed in floor panels.

predecessor: Raised Access Floor / Floor Box System
rationale: Cable trays and data/electrical cabling run in the underfloor plenum are typically installed after the pedestals are set but before the floor panels are fully closed; however, the access floor system must be at least partially installed (pedestals and some panels) to define the routing space. For final panel closure, all underfloor MEP rough-in must be complete.

predecessor: Raised Access Floor / Floor Box System
successor: Final Testing and Commissioning (Data/Power Floor Boxes)
rationale: Commissioning and testing of electrical and data outlets integrated into the floor boxes occurs after the floor system and floor boxes are fully installed, trimmed, and connected to building systems.
The structural framing or roof structure must be completed to provide a support system for suspending the ceiling grid and tiles.

All mechanical ducts, electrical conduits, and plumbing pipes that run above the ceiling must be installed before the ceiling is closed in, as access would be severely limited or impossible afterward.
Sprinkler heads and fire suppression piping above the ceiling must be roughed in prior to ceiling installation to avoid cutting or dismantling the ceiling later.

While painting of ceiling tiles is typically done before installation, any field touch-ups or integrated finish work should occur after the ceiling grid is in place. This is a soft preference as painting can be done in sequence flexibly.
Recessed light fixtures, troffers, and other ceiling-mounted lighting are installed within or onto the suspended ceiling grid after the ceiling framework is in place.

successor: Interior Partition / Wall completion (top track closure)
rationale: Ceiling installation must precede the final closure of wall top tracks and full-height partition finishing to ensure proper integration and continuous fire/smoke seals.
The reception/concierge desk requires a solid, level floor foundation to be built upon; the slab must be poured and cured before any desk structure can be erected.
Electrical wiring, floor boxes, and power outlets serving the reception desk must be roughed in below the slab or within the floor before the desk is built over or around them.
Data, telephone, and other low-voltage cabling for the concierge workstation must be run before the desk cabinetry is installed, as access will be blocked afterwards.
The reception desk structure must be installed and secured before the surrounding walls and desk surfaces receive their final paint and finish coats, to ensure a clean finish line.
The base desk cabinetry and frame must be fully assembled and in place before the solid-surface or laminate countertop is fitted on top.

While it is preferable to install pendant or task lighting after the desk is in place to align with the final position, lighting could theoretically be installed beforehand if accurately roughed-in. This is a soft sequencing preference for alignment accuracy.
The reception desk acts as a key reference point; adjacent millwork panels, trims, and cabinetry should be installed after the desk is fixed to ensure proper fit and alignment.
The structural frame and floor slabs must be in place to provide the load-bearing support and attachment points for the curtain wall system.
Rough openings must be framed and blocked out to receive the glazed partition and curtain wall frames.
The building envelope waterproofing and air barrier system must be installed before the curtain wall to ensure proper integration and continuity of the moisture protection layer.

While interior finishes can technically begin before the curtain wall is fully glazed, it is preferable to complete the glazed partitions and curtain wall first to avoid damage to interior finishes from dust, vibration, or water infiltration during installation.
It is preferable to complete the curtain wall installation before final MEP connections to partitions and exterior walls to allow proper sealing and integration of services without rework.

MEP services (electrical outlets, lighting, HVAC grilles, data points) must be installed and finished before soft furnishings are placed, as furniture would obstruct access to walls, floors, and ceilings required for MEP installation.

Painting and wall finishes must be completed before soft furnishings are brought in, to avoid dust, splatter, or damage to new furniture, and to ensure final decorations are not obstructed by furniture placement.

Flooring installation (including carpet, tiles, or timber flooring) must be completed before furniture is placed, as heavy furniture would block access for flooring installation and could damage newly laid floors.
Windows and doors must be installed and sealed before bringing in soft furnishings, to provide a weathertight and secure environment for valuable furniture items.

After all soft furnishings and loose furniture are placed, a final clean and snagging inspection is conducted before handover to the client, as furniture placement is one of the last finishing activities.
Planter boxes and biophilic elements require a structurally sound base slab with proper waterproofing to contain soil, water, and drainage systems without leaking into the structure below.

A functional drainage layer (e.g., gravel, drainage mats, or drainage cells) must be placed beneath the planting medium to prevent waterlogging and root rot, ensuring the viability of plants within the planter.

Irrigation supply lines, drainage pipes, and any electrical conduits for lighting or water features must be roughed-in before soil and plant materials are placed, as retrofitting would require destructive demolition.

The planter structure, soil medium, and hardscape biophilic elements (e.g., green walls, trellises) must be fully installed before final planting, mulch, and decorative topsoil can be placed to avoid rework and plant disturbance.

While not a physical necessity, it is preferable to complete planter and biophilic element installation before finishing adjacent interior finishes (e.g., flooring, wall cladding) to avoid soiling or damaging delicate finishes during soil and material handling.

The structural shell and core of the building must be complete before interior fit-out can begin, as fit-out activities require enclosed spaces, structural stability, and prepared substrates for walls, ceilings, and floors.

Major MEP rough-in work such as ductwork, piping, and electrical conduit must be installed within walls and ceiling voids before these spaces are enclosed by interior finishes like drywall, ceiling tiles, and wall cladding.
Interior fit-out establishes the base surfaces and substrates; painting and decorative finishes are applied as the final layer on top of completed walls, ceilings, and millwork.

Flooring materials such as tiles, carpet, or hardwood are typically installed after the main fit-out is complete to avoid damage from subsequent construction work and to ensure a clean, finished surface.

Final installation of light fixtures, switches, and outlets (trim-out stage) occurs after ceiling grids, wall finishes, and cabinetry are in place, allowing precise placement and finishing around completed interior elements.
The structural core and slabs require a stable foundation and substructure to bear and transfer loads. Without completed foundations, the core cannot be safely erected.
Site clearing, grading, and excavation must be completed before any structural core work can begin to ensure a safe and level working platform.
The facade system attaches to the structural core and slabs. The structure must be in place to provide support and anchoring points for the building envelope.
Interior walls are built off the structural slabs and within the core layout. Slabs must be cast and cured before partition layout and framing can commence.

While some MEP rough-in can begin in completed areas before the entire structure is finished, vertical risers and slab penetrations rely on the core and slabs being in place; thus a strong preference exists for core/slab completion before full MEP rough-in.
Structural framing must be complete to provide the support systems and open pathways for MEP rough-in installations such as conduits, ducts, and piping within walls and ceilings.

The concrete slab or deck must be cured and in place before MEP rough-in can begin, as underground or in-slab conduits and piping need to be embedded prior to or just after the pour, and above-slab work requires a finished structural floor.

predecessor: Vertical Enclosure / Exterior Walls – Common Areas
rationale: Exterior walls and the building envelope must be substantially complete to protect MEP rough-in work from weather exposure and to provide the wall cavities where electrical, plumbing, and HVAC rough-ins are installed.

successor: Wall and Ceiling Insulation – Common Areas
rationale: Insulation must follow MEP rough-in so that it can be placed around and behind the installed conduits, pipes, and ducts, and so that rough-in inspections can occur before insulation covers the work.

Drywall cannot be hung until all MEP rough-in (electrical boxes, conduit, ductwork, piping) is complete and inspected, as enclosing these items would prevent access for corrections and would violate code requirements for rough-in inspection prior to cover.
The structural steel or framework that supports the atrium or skylight must be in place before glazing can be installed, as the glazing panels are mounted onto this structure.
