The roof deck and waterproofing around the skylight opening must be completed to provide a weathertight substrate and prevent water intrusion during glazing installation.
Mechanical lifting equipment must be in place and operational to hoist heavy glass panels into position for the skylight or atrium glazing.
Interior finishing work below the atrium/skylight should be done after glazing is complete to avoid damage to finishes from falling debris, tools, or sealants during glass installation.
Water and air infiltration testing of the skylight assembly can only be performed after the glazing and all seals are fully installed to verify the system's weathertightness.
The sidelight panel must be installed within the framed opening; the frame provides the structural support and attachment points for the panel.
The sidelight panel structure must be in place before the glass or glazing unit can be inserted and secured into the panel frame.
Weather sealing and caulking around the sidelight must be applied after the panel is fully installed to ensure a continuous waterproof barrier.
The rough opening must be prepared (measured, cleared, and squared) before the sidelight panel can be placed into position.
Interior trim and finishing work around the sidelight can be done after panel installation for a clean aesthetic, but this is a soft preference as it could theoretically be done concurrently.
The rough opening (framed with header, sill, and cripple studs) must be built before the transom window unit can be physically placed and secured.
The window unit must be set in the opening before exterior flashing, caulking, and weatherproofing can be applied around its perimeter.

successor: Install interior trim and casing around transom
rationale: Exterior weather sealing must be completed before interior finish trim is installed, to prevent moisture damage behind the trim.

successor: Install adjacent wall or door framing (if transom is above a door)
rationale: When a transom sits directly above a door, the transom frame/window is typically installed first so the door frame can align and integrate with the transom assembly.

predecessor: Rough electrical (if transom has integrated lighting)
rationale: Any wiring for transom lights must be roughed in the framing before the window unit is placed, as access to the cavity is blocked afterward.

The recessed entry mat frame or recess must be formed or set into the concrete slab before the concrete cures, or the recess must be cut into the slab afterward. In either case, the slab/foundation must exist before the mat can be installed.
The floor substrate must be level and prepared to receive the recessed mat frame, ensuring proper fit and drainage.
The recessed mat frame is typically installed flush with the finished floor surface; surrounding floor finishes are laid after the mat frame is set so that the finish abuts neatly against the mat.

successor: Entry Door Installation / Door Swing Clearance Check
rationale: The door must swing over or past the mat; installing the mat first allows verification of clearance so the door does not drag on the mat.

successor: Waterproofing / Sealant Application at Entry Threshold
rationale: Sealant around the mat perimeter and at the threshold should be applied after the mat is in place to ensure a watertight seal between the mat frame and adjacent surfaces.
Coat hooks and rails must be mounted on finished wall surfaces; installing them before wall finishes would require removal or cause damage.
Flooring is typically completed before installing wall-mounted fixtures to avoid damaging new floors, but if the coat rail is mounted high, this could be done after.
Coat hooks and rails are generally one of the final fit-out items; after installation, only light cleaning and occupancy remain.
Coat hooks and rails need a solid backing (studs or framing) to be securely anchored; they cannot be installed without underlying structural support in place.
Electrical work within walls must be completed and enclosed before any wall-mounted fixtures are installed, to avoid interference and meet safety codes.
Shoe storage units must be placed on a stable, level floor surface. The floor framing provides the necessary structural support.
The subfloor creates the finished walking surface and base upon which the shoe storage unit will be placed or attached.
If the shoe storage unit is wall-mounted or built into a wall recess, the wall framing must be in place to provide attachment points.
The shoe storage unit should be in place before finishing flooring around or up to it to ensure proper fit and clean edges.
Baseboards, quarter rounds, or other trim should be installed after the shoe storage unit to create clean transitions and conceal gaps.
The umbrella stand sits on the floor; the floor surface must be finished before placing the stand to ensure stability and proper placement.
If the umbrella stand is placed near a wall, wall finishing (painting, plastering) should be completed to avoid damaging the stand or interfering with the work.
An umbrella can only be placed into the stand after the stand itself is installed and secured in its designated location.
It is preferred to install the umbrella stand before final cleaning so that dust and debris from installation can be cleaned up afterward, though not physically required.
Stylists prefer the umbrella stand to be in place when arranging decorative elements so the overall look can be coordinated, though it is a soft preference.
The entry bench/seat requires a stable, level concrete slab foundation to be poured and cured before installation can begin.
The surrounding wall and structural framing of the entry area must be completed to define the space and provide attachment points for the bench/seat.
Any plumbing or electrical rough-ins that would run beneath or behind the bench location must be completed before the bench is installed to avoid future demolition.
Flooring installation must come after the bench is in place so that flooring can be cut and fitted precisely around the bench's base for a clean finish.
Trim work and caulking around the bench edges should be completed after the bench is fully installed to seal gaps and provide a finished appearance.

The console/hall table must be placed on finished flooring; flooring installation must be completed first to provide a level, finished surface and to avoid damaging the table or requiring it to be moved during flooring work.

Wall finishing should be completed before placing the console/table against the wall to avoid paint splatters, dust, or damage to the table, and to ensure the wall is fully finished behind the furniture.
If the console/table is intended to accommodate lamps or electronic devices, electrical outlets behind or near the table must be installed and wired beforehand to provide power access.
Once the console table is in place, decorative items such as vases, trays, lamps, or artwork can be arranged on or above it as a soft preference for final styling and not a structural requirement.
The console table must be fully installed and placed before the final walkthrough or inspection to confirm the space is complete and ready for occupancy.
The rough opening (door or window frame opening) must be prepared and framed before a threshold or sill can be installed, as the threshold/sill sits at the bottom of the opening.
The subfloor or concrete slab must be completed and cured to provide a stable, level base for the threshold/sill to rest upon.
Under-sill waterproofing, flashing, or pan flashing must be installed before the threshold/sill to prevent moisture intrusion at the base of the opening.
The threshold/sill provides the bottom bearing surface and alignment reference for the door or window frame, which sits on top of and is anchored to the sill.
Final sealing, caulking, and trim installation around the threshold/sill must occur after the sill is placed and secured to ensure weathertight closure and a finished appearance.
The building must be weathertight (roof, walls, windows, doors) before installing mailboxes and parcel lockers to protect them from weather damage during construction.
Mailboxes and parcel lockers are typically mounted on or recessed into finished walls; wall framing and drywall must be complete to provide a mounting surface.
Flooring must be installed before placing heavy parcel locker units to avoid damaging finished floors or having to work around freshly placed units.

It is generally preferred to install mailboxes/lockers after painting and trim are complete to avoid painting around them and to minimize risk of paint splatter on the units, though units can be masked off if needed.

successor: Final Electrical and Access Control Wiring
rationale: If the parcel lockers are electronic (keypad, card reader, networked), the lockers must be in place to terminate wiring to the individual compartments, connect power supplies, and test access control systems.
The rough opening must be framed and prepared to the correct dimensions before the door assembly can be installed.
The wall framing must be in place to provide the structural support and opening for the door assembly.
Locks, handles, and other door hardware can only be installed after the door assembly is mounted in the opening.
Weatherstripping and exterior sealing around the door frame must be applied after the door is installed to ensure a proper seal.
Interior door trim and casing cannot be installed until the door frame is permanently set in place.
The subfloor must be properly leveled, cleaned, and prepared before any flooring material can be installed to ensure a smooth, stable, and durable surface.
If an underlayment (moisture barrier, soundproofing, or padding) is specified, it must be laid down before the finished flooring to provide proper insulation and protection.
Baseboards and trim are installed after flooring to cover the expansion gap along the walls and to sit cleanly on top of the finished floor surface.
Doors must be hung and adjusted after flooring is installed so that the bottom of the door clears the finished floor height correctly.
Applying a final sealant or deep cleaning is best performed after installation to protect the new floor, though this is a soft preference if the flooring is pre-finished.
Access control systems require power supply wiring and conduit to be in place before the control panels, readers, and locking devices can be installed and connected.

Access control systems rely on network/data cabling for communication between controllers, readers, and the central management system; this cabling must be run before the access control devices are installed.

Wiring and conduit for door sensors, readers, and magnetic locks often run above ceilings; this work must be completed before ceiling tiles are permanently installed or before the access control devices are mounted.

Electronic strikes, magnetic locks, and electric trim must be installed concurrently with or after the access control wiring and control devices are in place to ensure proper integration and alignment.
After physical installation of controllers, readers, and locking devices, the system must be programmed, configured, and tested before it can be put into operation.

Plastering and drylining must be completed before painting can begin, as paint requires a smooth, finished surface to adhere properly. Painting over unfinished plaster would result in poor adhesion and finish quality.
Primer or undercoat must be applied before the main decorative painting to ensure proper paint adhesion, seal the surface, and provide a uniform base for the topcoat.

Painting and decorating must be completed before final cleaning and handover, as painting can generate dust and debris that needs to be cleaned, and the decoration must be finished for the space to be considered complete for handover.

Painting should be completed before final floor finishes are installed, as paint drips, splatters, and dust from painting work could damage finished floors. Flooring is installed after painting to avoid staining or damaging the floor covering.

First-fix painting and decorating (walls and ceilings) should be completed before final joinery elements like skirting boards and architraves are installed, so that the wall painting is complete and joinery can be fitted neatly against finished surfaces.
Doorways require a framed opening within the wall structure to define the rough opening dimensions
The doorway frame/shell must be installed before the door leaf, hinges, and hardware can be mounted
The doorway frame must be in place so that wall finishing materials can be trimmed around the opening and finished flush to the frame
Rough electrical and plumbing must be completed before the doorway is framed, as these services run through the wall cavity and must avoid the door opening

Soft preference: installing flooring before the doorway frame allows the frame to sit on top of finished flooring for a cleaner appearance, though it can be done after if the flooring is cut around the frame
The subfloor must be clean, level, and fully prepared before a transition strip can be securely installed.
Transition strips bridge the gap between two finished flooring surfaces; both flooring materials must be installed first so the strip can properly cover the expansion gap and transition.

Baseboard or trim can be installed before or after transition strips, but it is often easier to cut and fit baseboard first; however, if the transition strip abuts baseboard, installing it first may allow for cleaner fit — this is a soft preference depending on the sequence.

If the transition strip itself requires sealing or if adjacent flooring needs final finishing coats, it may be done after installation; however, in many cases finishing is done before. This is a soft preference.

Electrical rough-in (wiring, outlets, switches) must be completed before installing the folding partition because once the partition is in place, access to the wall cavity for electrical work is blocked or severely restricted.
Mechanical ductwork and HVAC components within the partition zone must be roughed-in prior to partition installation, as the folding partition enclosure will obstruct access to these systems.
Any plumbing rough-ins within the wall or ceiling cavities where the folding partition is mounted must be completed first, since the partition will cover access points.

Finish flooring is typically installed after the folding partition is in place because the partition's bottom track or guide rail may need to be set relative to the finished floor level; however, in some sequences flooring can precede partition installation if the track is surface-mounted, making this a soft preference rather than a hard constraint.

successor: Final Painting and Wall Finishes in Partition Area
rationale: Wall finishes and painting adjacent to the folding partition must be completed after installation because the partition's mounting brackets and tracks are attached to the structure, and completing finishes first would risk damage or require rework when attaching the partition hardware.
The architectural design provides the overall building geometry, dimensions, and structural grid that define the spatial boundaries within which layout planning occurs.
Site conditions, topography, orientation, and access points must be known to plan spatial layouts that respond to the site context.
Column grids, load-bearing walls, and slab layouts must be established as they determine room dimensions, corridor widths, and spatial module constraints.
The spatial layout defines room functions, partition locations, and ceiling zones, which are prerequisites for routing mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems.
Interior design detailing (finishes, fixtures, furniture layouts) depends on finalized room configurations, sizes, and adjacency relationships.
Partition walls require a completed floor slab to provide a stable, level base for wall construction and to ensure proper load distribution.

The main structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) must be in place to define the building's structural grid and provide support for partition walls, as partition walls are typically non-load-bearing and infill between structural elements.

While not always strictly required, it is strongly preferable to complete rough-in MEP (mechanical, electrical, plumbing) work in the floor slab before partition walls are built, as walls can obstruct access to floor-level services.
Wall finishing such as plastering, drywall installation, or tiling must occur after the partition wall structure (studs or blocks) is fully erected and secured.
Electrical conduits, plumbing pipes, and data cables that run inside partition walls must be installed after the wall framing is complete but before the wall is closed up with finishing layers.
A preliminary design must be established to have a basis for evaluating accessibility compliance before the review can be conducted.
Detailed design development is necessary to produce the drawings, specifications, and layouts that will be assessed for accessibility compliance.
Final construction documents must incorporate any accessibility corrections or revisions identified during the compliance review before they can be finalized.
Building permit applications require evidence of accessibility compliance review and approval before submission to authorities having jurisdiction.
While procurement can begin in parallel, it is preferable to have accessibility compliance confirmed to avoid costly change orders during construction.
Passage doors require framed openings within walls; wall framing must be completed before doors can be installed.
The rough opening (sized to door dimensions) must be framed and prepared before the door unit can be placed.
Trim and casing are installed around the door frame after the door is hung and secured in place.
While painting can be done before or after, it is typically preferred to finish walls before door installation to avoid damage, but final touch-ups often occur after.
Door hardware such as locks, handles, and hinges must be installed on the door after the door is hung in its frame.
The ceiling soffit is typically installed after the structural frame (beams, slabs, and roof deck) is complete because the soffit attaches to or is supported by the structural elements above.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work in the ceiling plenum (ductwork, piping, conduit) must be completed before the soffit is closed up, as the soffit will conceal and block access to these services.
The soffit substrate must be installed first before any surface finishes such as painting, plastering, or application of ceiling boards can be applied to it.
Recessed lighting fixtures and other ceiling-mounted devices are typically installed after the soffit is in place, as the soffit provides the mounting surface and the finished enclosure.

While partition walls can be framed before the soffit, it is often preferred to install the soffit first so that partition top tracks can be securely attached to the soffit where walls run up to it, ensuring better alignment and continuity.
Skirting boards are fixed to finished walls; plastering and painting must be completed first to ensure proper adhesion and a clean finish.
Skirting boards typically sit on top of the finished floor or cover the expansion gap; the floor must be laid before the skirting can be installed correctly.
Skirting boards are often primed and installed, then final paint or touch-up is applied to the skirting itself after installation to avoid damaging the finish during handling and fixing.
Skirting boards often conceal or abut electrical outlets; installing skirting first allows precise cutting for sockets, though sometimes sockets are fitted before skirting as a soft preference.
Skirting boards protect walls from furniture and should be installed before placing furniture to avoid obstruction and ensure a neat edge, but it's a soft preference rather than physical necessity.
Electrical conduits and wiring must be installed before lighting fixtures can be connected to the power source.
Ceiling or wall surfaces must be framed and prepared (rough-in) to provide mounting support and access for the fixture housing.
Testing and commissioning can only begin once the fixture is physically installed and connected.
It is preferable to complete finishing work after fixture installation to achieve a clean trim, though fixtures can be installed after finishing if care is taken.
Lighting is needed for safe and adequate illumination during final floor finishing work such as polishing or sealing.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and excavated before any passage layout can be designed, as the design depends on the actual ground conditions, topography, and boundaries.
Soil and rock conditions must be known through geotechnical surveys to inform the passage design, particularly for foundation requirements, drainage, and structural support.
The overall building structure must be erected first so that passage routes, corridors, and walkways can be designed around the actual column grid and beam locations.
Passage layouts define where walls, ceilings, and pathways will be, which determines the routing for MEP services; rough-in work must follow the finalized passage design.
Floor plans and passage boundaries must be finalized before finishing work such as tiling, flooring installation, and wall cladding can commence in corridors and passageways.
Partition walls require a finished floor slab to provide a level, stable base for construction and anchoring.
Electrical conduits embedded in the slab must be placed before walls are erected to avoid cutting or coring through the finished slab.
Underground/under-slab plumbing lines must be installed and pressure-tested before walls are built to avoid later slab penetration.
Drywall or plaster application requires the wall framing/layout to be fully erected and fixed in place first.
Vertical electrical conduits and outlet boxes are placed within the wall cavity after the wall frame is up but before the wall is closed with board.
The structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) must be in place to provide support and mounting surfaces for MEP rough-in components like conduits, ducts, and piping.
The building envelope should be watertight to protect MEP rough-in materials (e.g., insulation, wiring, ducts) from weather damage before installation.
MEP rough-in (conduits, ducts, pipes) must be in place before insulation is applied, as insulation wraps around or fits between these MEP elements within walls and ceilings.
All MEP rough-in must be completed and inspected before enclosing walls and ceilings with drywall or cladding, as access is needed for connections and testing.
Rough-in works (conduits, wiring, ductwork, piping) must be fully installed before final connections (fixtures, outlets, terminals) can be made, as trim-out attaches directly to rough-in components.
The ground or structural slab must be properly prepared, leveled, and compacted to support the load of the tiered seating platforms before they can be installed.

predecessor: Structural Steel or Concrete Frame (if applicable)
rationale: If the tiered seating platforms are supported by or integrated into a primary structural frame, that frame must be erected first to provide the necessary support structure.
Any utilities that will run beneath or through the seating platform area must be roughed in before the platform structure is built over them, to avoid costly rework.

successor: Seating Surface / Finish Installation (seats, treads, upholstery)
rationale: The structural platforms for the tiers must be complete before the finished seating surfaces, tread covers, or upholstered seats can be installed on top of them.
Handrails and guardrails along the tiers are mounted to or anchored in the platform structure, requiring the platforms to be in place first for proper alignment and secure attachment.
The structural frame (ceiling grid or support framework) must be installed to provide a mounting surface and load-bearing structure for acoustic reflector panels.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work must be completed above the ceiling before enclosing the space with acoustic panels, as these services would otherwise be inaccessible.
Acoustic panels must be fully installed before acoustic testing can be performed to verify the space meets design specifications for sound reflection and reverberation.

While not always a hard physical constraint, it is a best practice to install ceiling/overhead acoustic panels before floor finishing and final painting to avoid damaging finished surfaces and to allow for easier access during panel installation.
Seating installation is typically done after ceiling acoustic treatments are complete to prevent dust and debris from settling on seats and to avoid obstruction of access for panel installers.
Stringers span between columns or vertical supports and require stable vertical support points before they can be placed.
The foundation must be in place to support the columns or bearing points that the stringer will rest upon.
Deck panels or floor plates are typically laid on top of and supported by the stringer/spine framework.
Cross-bracing often connects between stringers or between stringers and other members to stabilize the spine framework, requiring the stringers to be in place first.
Final connection welding or bolting of stringer-to-column joints and stringer-to-stringer splices must occur after stringers are positioned and aligned.
Structural supports and rough openings must be in place before retractable seating can be mounted or installed.
The floor slab must be finished and cured to provide a stable, level base for retractable seating tracks and anchoring.
Seating must be installed first so that permanent floor finishes can be laid up to the seating footprint accurately.
Installation must be complete before the retractable mechanism can be tested for operation, safety, and egress compliance.
While not a hard physical constraint, completing overhead work first minimizes dust and debris falling onto the seating mechanism and reduces the risk of damage.
The structural frame of the staircase (stringers, treads, and risers) must be installed first to provide the supporting structure onto which the soffit (underside cladding) is attached.
Handrails are typically installed after the soffit is finished, as the soffit forms the ceiling/underside of the staircase and handrails must be fixed to the completed structure.
While soffit-mounted lighting can be installed after the soffit is in place, it's often a soft preference; lighting may be roughed-in beforehand but final fit-out occurs after soffit completion.
Painting and decoration of the staircase soffit area must be completed after the soffit is installed, as the soffit provides the final surface for paint and finishes.
Any mechanical, electrical, or plumbing rough-in work that runs through or above the staircase soffit area must be completed before the soffit is enclosed, to avoid rework.
The structural frame (including floor slabs and supporting beams) must be in place before stairs can be installed, as stairs connect different floor levels within the structural framework.
The floor slabs where the staircase lands must be poured, set, and cured to provide a stable base and support for the staircase structure.

While MEP rough-in can begin before stairs in some areas, routing of pipes, ducts, and conduits near or under the staircase must wait until the staircase structure is in place to avoid conflicts and ensure proper fit.
Interior wall finishes, particularly around stairwells and stair openings, cannot be completed until the staircase structure is installed, as the stairs define the final geometry of these spaces.
Handrails, guardrails, and balustrades are physically attached to the staircase structure and cannot be installed until the stairs themselves are in place.
Structural platform works must be completed to provide a stable and level base before any fit-out finishes (e.g., flooring, wall cladding, or ceiling installation) can commence.
Fit-out works must be finished to allow installation of stage lighting and rigging equipment on the completed surfaces and structure without interference or damage to finishes.
Audio-visual system installation requires completed fit-out surfaces (walls, ceilings, floor finishes) for mounting speakers, screens, and running cable containment systems.
Seating layout and auditorium finishing depend on final stage platform dimensions and positions established during fit-out to ensure correct sightlines and clearances.
Final cleaning of the stage area can only be performed after all fit-out works are complete to avoid soiling newly finished surfaces.
The foundation must be completed before any superstructure formwork and concrete work can begin, as the structural loads need a stable base to transfer to the ground.
Steel reinforcement (rebar) must be placed and tied within the formwork before concrete is poured, as the rebar provides tensile strength and must be embedded within the concrete element.
Concrete must be poured and allowed to cure to sufficient strength before formwork can be safely stripped without damaging the structural element.
Immediately after pouring, concrete must undergo a controlled curing process to achieve design strength and durability.

Structural concrete elements (columns, beams, slabs) must be in place and cured before masonry infill walls and blockwork can be constructed, as the masonry relies on the structural frame for support.
Bleacher seating requires a stable, level concrete slab or foundation to be fully cured and ready before seating can be anchored and assembled on top.
Any overhead structural steel supports or superstructure that the bleachers attach to must be erected first; bleachers are often installed after the main structural frame is in place.
Under-slab or in-ground conduit runs for power/data to bleacher areas must be roughed in and inspected before slab pour or bleacher installation to avoid costly rework.
Handrails and guardrails are typically installed after the bleacher framework is in place so they can be properly aligned with the seating tiers and meet safety code requirements.

Painters prefer to have bleacher assemblies complete before final touch-up and striping to ensure a uniform finish, though some pre-painting can occur off-site; this is a logical sequence preference but not a strict physical necessity if components are prefinished.
The structural wall or rough framing must be in place before a framed opening can be created within it, as the opening is cut or formed into the existing structural frame.
If the framed opening is part of a wall that rests on a foundation or slab, the foundation must be completed before the wall and its openings can be framed.
The rough opening frame must be complete before windows or doors can be physically installed into the opening.
Electrical wiring is typically routed through framed walls after openings are created, but this is a sequencing preference rather than a strict physical necessity.
Insulation and drywall cannot be applied over a wall until the framed opening is fully constructed and ready to receive finishes around the opening.
The structural frame and openings for shoji screens must be built and finished before shoji screens can be fitted into place.
The shoji screen itself (wooden lattice frame) must be constructed before it can be installed into the building opening.
The wooden lattice frame must be installed in place before the washi paper is applied to ensure proper tension and alignment of the paper on the screen.

Typically, after shoji screens are installed, surrounding trim and casing can be completed for a clean finish, though some trim may be done beforehand as a soft preference rather than a physical necessity.
The building's rough framing and exterior sheathing must be complete to define the openings where shoji screens will be placed.
The rough opening must be framed to provide the structural support and defined aperture into which the low sill window is installed.
The weather-resistant barrier must be in place around the rough opening to prevent moisture ingress before the window is set.
Flashing and sealing materials are applied around the installed window to create a watertight seal; this cannot be done until the window is positioned and fastened.

Interior trim around the window is typically finished after the window is installed to cover gaps and provide a clean appearance, though this is a logical sequence preference rather than a physical necessity.
Exterior siding is installed up to the window frame after the window is in place to ensure a proper fit and accommodate the window's position.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and graded before placing stone or gravel to ensure a stable base and proper drainage.
Any required excavation for depth or shaping of the stone/gravel feature must be completed before material placement.

predecessor: Installation of Weed Barrier / Geotextile Fabric
rationale: A weed barrier membrane is typically laid down before gravel or stone to prevent weed growth and maintain stability.
Edging is often installed after the stone/gravel is placed to contain the material, though in some designs edging is placed first; this is a soft preference based on design sequence.
Plants bordering the stone/gravel feature are typically planted after the aggregate is in place to avoid soil disturbance and to set the final grade.
The ground must be excavated and prepared to the correct depth and levels before any water feature element can be installed, as the water feature requires a stable, properly graded base.
A concrete slab or structural foundation is required to support the weight of the water feature element and prevent settlement or cracking over time.
Waterproofing is necessary beneath the water feature to prevent water infiltration into the substructure and surrounding areas, which could cause damage or moisture issues.
Drainage pipes, water supply lines, and any recirculation plumbing must be laid and connected before the water feature element is placed, as these are concealed below.
Conduit and wiring for pumps, filters, and lighting fixtures need to be run and terminated before the water feature element is installed, as access becomes restricted afterward.
The structural shell or base of the water feature must first be in place before any decorative finishes such as tile, stone cladding, or coping can be applied.
The water feature structure must be erected before its interior surfaces can be waterproofed or sealed to contain water.
The water feature shell must be set in its final position before pumps, pipes, and fittings can be connected to the pre-installed rough-in plumbing.
Final connection of pumps and lighting fixtures to the electrical system can only occur after the water feature element is in place.
All components must be fully installed and connected before the system can be filled with water and tested for leaks, flow rates, and proper operation.
A feasibility study must be completed before site survey to determine if the project is viable and to identify the general site area for survey.
Preliminary permits or access approvals are often required to legally enter and survey the site.
The site survey establishes the topography and boundaries; geotechnical investigation relies on this layout to determine precise boring locations and understand site constraints.
Foundation design requires accurate site survey data including elevations, boundaries, and sightlines to properly position and design the foundation system.
Site preparation and clearing activities rely on the survey to mark boundaries, identify existing features, and establish the areas to be cleared.
Structural steel must be in place to provide the supporting framework for openings such as doors, windows, and louvers.
Rough framing defines the rough openings and structural support needed before openings can be fabricated and installed.
Opening frames must be installed before glass or window units can be placed into those openings.
Door frames and rough openings must be fabricated and installed before the door units themselves can be hung.
While not physically required, it is preferable to complete opening fabrication before MEP rough-in to avoid conflicts with ductwork, piping, or conduit passing through openings.
The site must be cleared of existing structures, debris, and vegetation before any landscape grading can occur, as grading requires a clean work surface to achieve proper drainage and contours.

Underground utilities such as water, sewer, gas, electrical, and irrigation lines must be installed before landscape grading to avoid disturbing finished grading and to ensure proper depth and coverage of utilities beneath the final grade.

Building foundations and slabs must be completed before final landscape grading to ensure that grading is sloped away from structures for proper drainage and to avoid damaging freshly placed foundations.
Hardscape elements such as patios, walkways, and retaining walls are typically installed after final grading is complete to ensure they are placed on properly compacted and graded subgrade.

Plants, trees, and turf must be installed after final grading and the placement of landscape features (e.g., boulders, berms) to ensure proper soil preparation and that the finished landscape design is realized on the correct grade.
Interior materiality depends on the structural system being in place, as interior finishes are applied to or within the structural frame.
The building must be enclosed and weathertight before interior materials are specified and installed to prevent weather damage to finishes.

MEP rough-in work within walls, ceilings, and floors must be completed before interior materials (e.g., drywall, flooring, ceiling tiles) can be specified and installed, as these services are concealed behind finishes.
The specification of interior materials must be finalized before the actual installation of those finishes can commence.
Custom millwork and cabinetry require the specified materials and finishes to be determined before fabrication and installation can proceed.
Site preparation (clearing, grading, soil stabilization) must be completed before any planting or maintenance activities can occur, as the site needs to be ready for vegetation establishment.

Soil testing and any necessary amendments (pH adjustment, fertilization, organic matter addition) must be completed before seasonal maintenance of planting to ensure the soil conditions are suitable for plant health.
Plants must be installed before they can be maintained; seasonal maintenance activities such as pruning, watering, mulching, and weeding presuppose that vegetation is already in place.

While seasonal maintenance typically precedes final cleanup for the season, some maintenance activities may overlap with or continue into cleanup; however, complete seasonal maintenance is generally preferred before winterization to ensure plants are healthy going into dormancy.

successor: Inspection and Evaluation of Planting Health
rationale: A final inspection or evaluation after maintenance is a soft preference to verify that maintenance activities were effective, but inspection can also occur concurrently or before maintenance is fully complete.
The structural frame (columns, beams, roof structure) must be in place to provide the supporting framework into which clerestory windows are installed.

Clerestory windows are typically located in the upper portion of walls or roof structures; the roof deck must be installed to define the opening and provide weather protection during window installation.
Rough openings with proper headers, sills, and supports must be framed to receive the clerestory window units.
Exterior cladding around clerestory windows must be installed after the windows are in place to ensure proper flashing, sealing, and integration with the window frame.

Interior wall finishes around the clerestory windows should be completed after window installation to allow for proper trim, sealing, and a clean transition between the window frame and interior surfaces.
The shadow projection wall requires a stable and level foundation. Site preparation (grading, compaction) and foundation pouring must be completed first to support the structural load of the wall.

The shadow projection wall serves as a structural or partition element that must be in place before the building's structural frame can be erected, as the wall may provide lateral support or define alignment.

Exterior finishes (e.g., paneling, plaster, or weatherproofing) cannot be applied until the shadow projection wall is fully constructed and secured, as the wall forms the substrate or backing for these finishes.
It is preferable to complete MEP (mechanical, electrical, plumbing) rough-in routing alongside or after the wall is built, though not strictly required if services are surface-mounted.
Painting, coating, or decorative treatments of the shadow projection wall must occur after the wall structure is complete and all associated rough-in work is finished to avoid damage to finishes.
The perforated screen panel requires a structural frame to be fabricated first, as the screen material is attached to or supported by this frame.
The supporting structure or foundation must be in place to bear the load and provide mounting points before the perforated screen panel can be installed.
Once the perforated screen panel is installed, a final inspection and any necessary touch-ups (e.g., painting, sealing) should be performed to ensure quality and aesthetics.

If the perforated screen panel is part of a layered facade system, adjacent cladding or glazing elements that abut or seal against the panel must be installed after the screen panel is in place to ensure proper fit and continuity.

predecessor: Structural Ceiling Work / Concrete Deck Pour
rationale: The structural ceiling (e.g., concrete slab or deck) must be completed to provide a substrate for supporting the reflective ceiling panel grid or suspension system.

predecessor: MEP Rough-In (Mechanical, Electrical, Plumbing) Above Ceiling
rationale: All ductwork, piping, conduits, and wiring that run within the ceiling plenum must be installed and inspected before enclosing them with ceiling panels, otherwise costly rework would be required.

Fireproofing of structural steel and firestopping of penetrations in the ceiling plenum must be completed before installing ceiling panels to meet fire code and to avoid later removal of panels for access.

Ceiling panels are often installed before final wall finishing to allow for touch-up painting and to avoid damaging freshly painted walls with the panel installation process; this is a preference to streamline workflow.
Reflective ceiling panels must be in place to serve as the mounting surface for recessed or surface-mounted lighting fixtures and to ensure proper alignment and light distribution.
The building's structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) must be in place to provide the supporting substrate and anchor points for the brise-soleil system.
The main building envelope must be sealed and waterproofed before attaching exterior shading devices to prevent moisture ingress behind the brise-soleil.
It is common to install brise-soleil before placing exterior glazing units to allow easier access for mounting hardware; however, glazing can be installed first if access is managed carefully.
The brise-soleil elements cover portions of the facade; finishing work around them must proceed after their installation to ensure proper alignment and integration.
Scaffolding or access equipment used for installation must remain in place until the brise-soleil is fully secured; dismantling can only begin after installation is complete and inspected.
Site analysis determines solar paths, building orientation, and surrounding obstructions which are essential inputs for designing effective daylighting systems.
The overall building form, floor plate dimensions, and section profiles must be established before daylighting strategies can be integrated and specified.
Column and beam locations affect window placement, light shelf positioning, and potential light wells, so the structural grid must be defined first.
The daylighting design specifies the required glass types, coatings, and window configurations that must be ordered and fabricated before installation.
Daylighting design determines the zones, sensors, and control integration points that the electric lighting control system must respond to and coordinate with.
While interior finishes can be selected after daylighting design to optimize light distribution, changes to finishes may also be made later without affecting the daylighting design itself.
Structural framing provides the primary support and substrate onto which surface finishes are applied; without the structural frame, finishes cannot be attached or installed.
MEP rough-in work (conduit, piping, ductwork within walls/ceilings) must be completed before enclosing them with surface finishes to avoid costly rework and ensure accessibility for inspections.

Insulation must be placed within wall/ceiling cavities before surface finishes (e.g., drywall, paneling) are installed to ensure thermal and acoustic performance and to meet building code requirements.
A clean, level, and appropriate substrate (e.g., cement board, gypsum sheathing) must be in place before applying finishes such as tile, stucco, or siding to ensure adhesion and durability.
Surface finishes such as drywall or paneling provide the smooth, stable base required for painting and coating; paint cannot be applied directly to unfinished structural materials.
Baseboards, casing, and other trim are installed after wall and ceiling finishes are complete so that trim covers edges and joints cleanly.

While not a strict physical requirement, it is standard practice to complete wall finishes before final flooring to prevent damage to finished floors from dust, debris, and scaffolding during wall finishing work.

successor: Fixture & Hardware Installation (e.g., light switches, outlets, cabinet installation)
rationale: Surface finishes provide the mounting surface and finished appearance for fixtures; electrical boxes are roughed-in earlier, but final installation of covers, switches, and outlets occurs after finishes are complete.

predecessor: Structural Framing and Rough Opening Preparation
rationale: The structural framing (walls, roof) must be complete to provide the rough openings (window/door holes) that receive glazing and fenestration units.
A weather-resistive barrier (building wrap, felt paper) is typically installed before windows and doors to protect the structure from moisture intrusion behind the fenestration.
Windows and exterior doors must be in place to seal the building envelope before interior finishing work begins, preventing damage to interior finishes from weather.
Fenestration units are typically installed before the final exterior cladding so that cladding can be detailed and flashed properly around windows/doors for water-tightness.
While interior trim can technically be installed later, it is typical and efficient to case windows and install sills after glazing is in place, though not a strict physical constraint.
Plumbing rough-in (water supply and drain lines) must be completed before the vanity can be installed, as the vanity covers or accesses these plumbing connections.
Drywall, taping, mudding, and painting must be finished before installing the vanity so that the wall surface behind and around the vanity is complete and ready for mounting.
Flooring (tile, vinyl, or hardwood) should be installed before the vanity so that the vanity sits on top of the finished floor, preventing gaps or the need to cut flooring around the vanity base.
The vanity cabinet base must be set in place and leveled before the countertop can be templated and installed on top of it.
Sinks and faucets are typically installed after the vanity countertop is mounted, which itself depends on the vanity base being in place.
The freestanding soaking tub must be placed on a finished, level floor surface to ensure proper support, stability, and alignment of the tub.

predecessor: Install Rough-in Plumbing (Drain and Water Supply)
rationale: The drain pipe and water supply lines must be stubbed out through the finished floor at the correct location before the tub can be positioned and connected.

predecessor: Complete Wall Finishes (Drywall, Paint, Tile Backsplash)
rationale: Wall finishes should be completed before bringing in the tub to avoid damage to finished walls from moving the heavy tub and to allow for precise positioning against finished walls.

successor: Connect Tub Drain and Water Supply
rationale: After the tub is set in its final position, the drain assembly and water supply lines must be physically connected to the tub's fittings.
Once the tub is permanently positioned, the gap between the tub base and the floor must be sealed to prevent water intrusion and ensure a finished appearance.

predecessor: Plumbing rough-in for shower supply lines
rationale: The water supply pipes (hot and cold) must be run and terminated at the shower valve location before the shower unit can be physically connected.
The shower pan or waterproofing membrane must be in place and tested to prevent leaks before installing any shower fixtures, including the rain shower head.

successor: Shower tile and wall finish installation
rationale: The shower arm and flange must be installed before the final tile or wall finish is applied around the shower head opening to ensure proper fit and waterproof sealing.

successor: Testing shower water flow and leak check
rationale: The rain shower heads and trim must be fully installed before water pressure can be tested and leak checks performed on the completed system.
The king-size bed platform serves as the base that supports the mattress and box spring; the bed frame must be fully assembled and structurally sound before the platform can be placed on top of it.
The platform is typically installed on top of the foundation or box spring to provide a level and sturdy surface for the mattress; therefore the foundation must be in place first.
The mattress is placed directly onto the completed king-size bed platform; the platform must be fully installed to support the mattress.
While a bed skirt is often installed after the platform for aesthetic coverage, it is a soft preference; the order could be swapped if needed.
The headboard is typically bolted or mounted to the bed frame or platform structure after the platform is in place to ensure proper alignment and stability.
The fireplace requires a solid foundation to support its weight and ensure structural stability.
The building frame must be erected to provide structural support and enclosure for the fireplace structure.
The chimney flue must be in place before the fireplace is built to ensure proper venting alignment.
The fireplace body must be completed before the decorative mantel can be attached to it.
Typically wall finishing is done after fireplace installation to allow proper sealing and finishing around the fireplace, though in some sequences it can be done before with careful planning.
Electrical wiring for wardrobe lighting must be roughed in before the wardrobe system is installed, as accessing walls behind the unit after installation is difficult and costly.
The wardrobe system is mounted to finished walls; framing and drywall must be completed to provide a stable surface and finished appearance.
Flooring is typically installed before built-in wardrobes to ensure a seamless finish, though it can sometimes be installed around the unit.
Touch-up painting and final trim work around the wardrobe can be done after installation to cover any gaps or nail holes.
The wardrobe system must be fully installed and functional before the project is considered complete and handed over to the client.

successor: Install Vanity Mirror with Integrated Lighting
rationale: Wall framing and backing must be in place to provide structural support for mounting the mirror securely.

predecessor: Run electrical wiring to mirror location
successor: Install Vanity Mirror with Integrated Lighting
rationale: Electrical wiring for the integrated lighting must be roughed in and terminated at the junction box behind the mirror location before the mirror can be mounted and connected.

successor: Install Vanity Mirror with Integrated Lighting
rationale: Drywall must be installed, taped, and finished so that the mirror can be mounted flush against a finished wall surface.

predecessor: Install Vanity Mirror with Integrated Lighting
successor: Connect electrical supply to integrated lighting
rationale: The mirror must be physically mounted before its lighting components can be hardwired to the electrical supply.

predecessor: Install Vanity Mirror with Integrated Lighting
rationale: While not physically required, it is common practice to install the mirror after the countertop to avoid damage to the mirror during countertop installation and to ensure proper vertical alignment.

The building must be enclosed (roof, walls, windows, structural framing) before interior space planning can accurately measure and design interior layouts, as dimensions and structural elements define the available space.
Columns, beams, and load-bearing walls are physically fixed first; interior design must work around these existing structural elements when planning partitions and spatial divisions.
The exterior shell must be watertight to protect interior finishes and materials; interior design cannot commence without a dry, weather-protected environment.

Design decisions (layouts, material selections, color schemes, lighting plans) must be finalized before actual installation of ceilings, wall finishes, flooring, millwork, and decorative elements can proceed.

Space plans determine the final locations of partitions, rooms, and zones, which dictate where electrical outlets, lighting fixtures, HVAC diffusers, and plumbing points must be placed; rough-in adjustments follow the finalized layout.

Structural framing (walls, ceilings, floors) must be in place to provide pathways and support for running electrical cables and conduits; wiring cannot be installed before the building's structural framework is erected.
Rough-in inspections of the structural and mechanical systems are typically completed before wiring begins to ensure that all hidden systems are approved before closing them up with wiring.
Electrical and data wiring must be fully installed and secured before insulation is placed, as insulation will cover and enclose the wiring within walls and ceilings.

All electrical and data cabling must be run, terminated, and tested before drywall is installed, since once the walls are closed up, access to modify or add wiring becomes extremely difficult and costly.
Trim work such as installing outlets, switches, cover plates, and data jacks can only occur after the wiring has been pulled to the correct locations and terminated in junction boxes.
Structural framing and rough carpentry must be complete to provide the supporting walls, floors, and structural openings into which joinery and cabinetry can be installed.
Electrical wiring, plumbing pipes, and HVAC ducts must be run within walls and floors before cabinetry is installed, as cabinets would block access to these services.
Wall surfaces must be finished (taped, mudded, sanded, and primed) so that cabinets and joinery have a clean, plumb surface to mount against and to avoid damaging finished walls.
Subfloors must be level and prepared before base cabinets are set, as cabinets are installed on top of the finished subfloor and require a stable, level base.
Countertops are templated and installed directly onto the base cabinets after the cabinets are securely placed and leveled.
Sinks, faucets, cooktops, and other fixtures are installed into the cabinetry and countertops after the joinery is in place.

In many sequences, finish flooring (e.g., hardwood, tile) can be installed before cabinets, but it is often preferred to install cabinets first and then flooring around them to save material costs; however, this is a soft preference, not a physical requirement.

Final paint coats are often applied after joinery to touch up any damage, but the bulk of painting is typically done before installation to avoid getting paint on cabinets; this is a sequencing preference rather than a hard constraint.
Paint cannot be applied until drywall is installed, taped, mudded, and sanded smooth because paint requires a smooth, sealed substrate for proper adhesion and finish.
Primer must be applied before decorative paint to seal the surface, ensure uniform paint absorption, and improve adhesion of the finish coats.

Ceilings are typically finished (painted) before wall painting to avoid drips and overspray damaging completed wall paint, though often ceiling painting is done first; at minimum ceiling substrate must be ready.
Painting must be completed before final flooring installation to prevent paint drips, dust, and debris from damaging finished floors, and to allow baseboards/trim to be painted or caulked properly.

While some trim can be pre-painted, final installation of switch plates, outlet covers, door hardware, and cabinet pulls is typically done after wall painting to avoid damaging paint and to ensure clean finish edges.
A stable, level foundation (e.g., concrete slab or flooring) must be in place before any furniture like a Craft & Activity Table can be placed or assembled, to ensure stability and alignment.
The building's walls, roof, and enclosures must be completed to protect interior furnishings such as the Craft & Activity Table from weather exposure and to define the room where it will be located.
Electrical outlets, lighting, and any required plumbing rough-ins must be completed before installing fixed furniture to avoid rework or damage to the table.
Flooring, wall finishes, and painting should be completed before placing the Craft & Activity Table to prevent dust, debris, or damage from finishing work settling on or harming the table.

After the Craft & Activity Table is installed, other decorative elements, seating, and accessory furniture can be arranged around it to complete the room layout, though this is a soft preference for logical staging.
Soft play equipment requires a stable, level substrate with proper drainage to ensure safety and structural integrity of the play structure.

Safety surfacing (e.g., rubber mats, poured-in-place rubber) must be installed before the soft play equipment is placed to ensure proper fall protection and to avoid the need to move the equipment later.
Overhead lighting, electrical outlets near play zones, and any powered interactive elements require rough electrical work to be completed before the equipment obstructs access to walls and ceilings.
HVAC ductwork and diffusers should be in place so that the soft play structure does not block access for final connections and to ensure proper air circulation around the play area.

successor: Final Electrical Connections and Interactive Element Commissioning
rationale: Any powered interactive components within or attached to the soft play equipment (e.g., LED panels, sound modules) require the equipment to be fully assembled before electricians can make final connections and test functionality.
A post-installation safety inspection must be conducted only after the equipment is fully assembled to verify structural stability, proper anchoring, and compliance with safety standards.

While painting, wall decor, and signage can be done before installation, they are more efficiently completed after the equipment is in place to ensure color coordination and proper spacing around the structure.
Electrical wiring behind walls must be completed before installing cubbies to avoid covering unfinished electrical work and to ensure safe installation.
Any plumbing lines behind walls must be roughed-in before cubbies are installed to prevent needing to move cubbies later.
Cubbies are typically attached to or placed against walls; the wall framing must be complete to provide structural support for the cubbies.
Drywall must be installed and finished behind and around cubbies to provide a finished surface; installing cubbies before drywall would require removal or cause damage.
Typically, cubbies are installed before finished flooring to allow flooring to be run up to the cubbies or to avoid damaging flooring, though some sequences may vary.
Mounting brackets must be securely fixed to the wall structure before the display wall can be installed, as the display wall requires a stable support frame.

predecessor: Run power and data cabling to wall location
rationale: Electrical and data cables must be routed and terminated behind the wall location before the display is mounted, otherwise access to terminate connections would be blocked.
Wall surface must be fully finished and painted before mounting the display to avoid damage to the display from dust, paint splatter, or construction debris.
The display wall must be physically installed and secured before power and signal cables can be connected and functional testing can be performed.
Software configuration and calibration must occur after the display is physically installed so that the software can detect and map to the actual hardware.

The structural frame of the building must be erected before any interior or site-specific component like Child-Scale Seating can be installed, as seating typically attaches to or sits within the frame.
The floor area where child-scale seating will be placed must be leveled and prepared to ensure stable and safe placement of the seating.

Although final floor finishing could be done before seating installation, it is often a soft preference to install seating first to avoid damaging finished floors during placement, or to install after to allow seamless flooring.
Walls around the seating area can be finished before or after; a soft preference may be to finish walls first to avoid dust and paint splatter on the new seating.
After child-scale seating is installed, a safety inspection must verify that the seating meets child safety standards before the space is opened for use.
The subfloor must be smooth, clean, dry, and level before safety flooring can be installed to ensure proper adhesion and a uniform surface.
Concrete slabs must be fully cured (typically 28 days) to prevent moisture issues and ensure the flooring adhesive bonds correctly.
A moisture barrier must be laid down prior to safety flooring to prevent moisture migration from the subfloor which could cause adhesive failure or mold.
Wall bases and transition trims are installed after the safety flooring is laid to cover the expansion gap at the perimeter and provide a finished look.
After flooring is installed and any curing time for adhesives has passed, the area can be fully cleaned and sanitized without damaging the new floor surface.
The wall or surface must be cleaned, primed, and smoothed before mural painting can begin, otherwise the paint will not adhere properly and the mural will deteriorate.
The underlying wall or substrate must be fully constructed and cured before any mural painting can be applied to it.
If the mural is on a high or elevated surface, scaffolding or lifts must be erected before painters can safely access the working area.
A protective clear coat or sealant must be applied after the mural paint is fully dry to protect the artwork from UV, moisture, and physical damage.
A final quality inspection and any minor touch-ups typically occur after mural painting is complete to ensure the artwork meets design specifications.
The soft play structure requires a finished, level floor slab to be installed upon, ensuring stability and safety.

Electrical rough-ins (e.g., wiring for lighting, power outlets near play area) must be completed before the soft play structure is assembled overhead or anchored, as access to walls/floors will be obstructed.
Wall finishes should be completed before installing the soft play structure to avoid damage to finished surfaces and ensure unobstructed access.
Safety matting or final floor covering around the soft play structure must be installed after the structure is in place to ensure proper fit and integration.
The completed assembly must be inspected and certified for safety compliance before the play area is opened for use.
The structural framing defines the basic layout and openings of the building; child-proofing measures (e.g., window guards, stair gates) cannot be properly installed until the structure is in place.
Child-proofing such as outlet covers, tamper-resistant receptacles, and electrical safety devices require the electrical wiring and outlets to be fully installed first.
Plumbing fixtures and pipes must be in place before installing anti-scald devices, faucet covers, or other child-safety plumbing accessories.
Interior walls and finishes must be completed so that child-proofing items (corner guards, cabinet locks, wall anchors) can be securely mounted and inspected.
The safety inspection must be passed before the building is deemed safe for children to occupy, ensuring all hazards are mitigated prior to move-in.
The building's structural frame must be erected first to provide the load-bearing support and opening into which the Morning Light Window is installed.
The roof structure must be completed to define the upper boundary and weather envelope before installing a window that interfaces with the roof line.
After the window is installed, its perimeter must be sealed and weatherproofed to prevent air and water infiltration.
Interior drywall, trim, and paint work around the window frame should follow installation to achieve a finished look, though some finishing could theoretically be done concurrently with care.
The window frame must be in place before the glass panes or glazing units can be inserted and secured into the frame.

Electrical rough-in work (wiring, outlets, switches) must be completed before installing children's furnishings to avoid damaging or interfering with the finished furnishings and to ensure power is available for any furniture requiring electricity.
HVAC ductwork and mechanical rough-ins must be finished before furnishings are installed to prevent dust, debris, and access issues that could damage or soil children's furniture.
Plumbing rough-in for any sinks, drinking fountains, or bathroom fixtures in children's areas must be completed before furnishings to avoid water damage or rework.

Overhead structural work such as ceiling installation or overhead MEP rough-ins must be complete before bringing in children's furnishings to prevent dust, debris, and potential damage to finished furniture.

Finish flooring (carpet, vinyl, or tile) must be installed before placing children's furnishings on top of it, as furniture would block flooring installation and heavy furniture could damage unfinished flooring.
After installing children's furnishings, a final cleaning and punch list walk-through is needed to clean up packaging debris, adjust furniture placement, and address any last-minute touch-ups.
Directional or identification signage for children's areas can be installed after furnishings are in place to ensure proper alignment and positioning relative to the installed furniture.
The building cannot be occupied or turned over to the client until all FF&E, including children's furnishings, are fully installed and verified.
The thermal mass wall requires a solid, level foundation base to bear its weight and ensure structural stability. Without the foundation poured and cured, the wall cannot be safely erected.
Steel reinforcement must be placed within the foundation to integrate with the wall's reinforcing bars, providing structural continuity and load transfer.
The thermal mass wall is a load-bearing element that supports the roof structure; the roof cannot be framed until the wall is erected and cured to full strength.
Interior and exterior plaster or finish coatings must be applied after the wall is fully constructed and cured to avoid cracking and ensure proper adhesion.

Rough openings in the thermal mass wall should be formed during construction; however, installing the actual window/door frames is preferably done after the wall is complete to avoid damage during wall construction.
Site analysis provides the geographical location, site orientation, and surrounding context needed to conduct an accurate sun path study.
Local climate data including latitude, longitude, and solar radiation patterns are prerequisite inputs for modeling the sun's path.
Having an initial massing model allows the sun path study to analyze solar exposure and shading on the proposed building form, though a basic sun path study could be done without it.
The sun path study provides the solar position data needed as input for detailed shading and shadow analysis of the building.
Solar gain calculations from the sun path study are essential inputs for building energy performance modeling and HVAC load calculations.
The sun path study determines window placement, shading device design, and interior daylight distribution strategies.
Sun path data informs passive solar heating and cooling strategies, including building orientation and thermal mass placement.
The sun path study results directly determine the optimal building orientation on the site for solar performance.
The external shading device must be anchored to the building's structural frame or load-bearing walls; therefore the structural support must be in place before the shading device can be mounted.

External shading devices are typically attached to or integrated with the building envelope. The wall cladding or exterior finish must be completed to provide a proper surface and weatherproofing for the shading device brackets and connections.

In many systems, external shading devices are installed before or concurrently with the windows they shade, as the devices are fixed to the structure. However, if shading devices are mounted over windows, they must be in place before glazing to allow access for mounting hardware and to avoid damaging installed glass.

It is preferable to complete painting or final exterior coatings before installing shading devices to avoid overspray and to ensure a clean finish, but this is a sequencing preference rather than a strict physical requirement.

Scaffolding or access equipment used to install the external shading device must remain in place until the installation is complete. Once the shading device is installed and secured, scaffolding can be dismantled and removed.
The bedroom's structural elements (walls, floors, ceiling) must be in place before interior layout planning can be spatially verified and implemented.
Electrical wiring, outlet boxes, switch boxes, and any plumbing rough-ins must be completed before interior layout planning can finalize wall finishes and fixture placements.
Layout planning determines wall positions, partitions, and finish scopes; walls cannot be finished until the layout is finalized.
Flooring layout, material selection, and installation sequence depend on the finalized room layout and furniture/zone plan.
Placement and sizing of windows and doors must be confirmed during layout planning before they are ordered and installed.
The thermal envelope (walls, roof, windows, insulation) must be fully installed to create a controlled indoor environment before thermal comfort can be meaningfully assessed.
Heating, ventilation, and air conditioning systems must be operational to regulate temperature, humidity, and airflow, which are key factors in thermal comfort evaluation.
Building systems must be commissioned and verified to be functioning as designed before thermal comfort conditions can be properly measured and assessed.

Interior finishes such as flooring, ceiling tiles, and wall coverings can influence thermal mass and radiant temperature, but a preliminary assessment could be done without them; however, a final accurate assessment requires all finishes in place.
Occupancy should not begin until thermal comfort has been verified to ensure acceptable indoor environmental conditions for occupants.
The rough framing must be complete to provide the structural opening and support for the window frame to be installed.
Weather barrier (house wrap or building paper) must be applied to the wall sheathing before window installation to ensure proper flashing integration and water management.
After the window is placed in the opening, flashing tape and sealant must be applied around the window perimeter to prevent water intrusion.
Siding is installed after windows to allow proper overlapping and integration with window trim and flashing details.
Interior wall finishes such as drywall or plaster are applied after windows are installed to ensure a proper seal and finish around the window frames.
The foundation and structural slab must be completed before any wall construction can begin, as walls require a stable base and anchorage to the foundation.
The primary structural frame must be in place to provide the supporting structure to which the insulated wall panels or framing systems are attached.

Underground utilities (drainage, electrical conduits, water lines) must be routed before wall construction to avoid interference with wall footings and to ensure proper service entry points are established.
The insulated wall assembly must be completed to provide the rough openings and structural support required for installing windows and doors on the east façade.
The insulated wall structure must be fully built before exterior cladding, vapor barriers, and weatherproofing membranes can be applied over the insulation layer.
The foundation or ground preparation must be completed before installing the noise barrier to ensure a stable base.
Surveying and marking the alignment is required to define the exact location where the noise barrier will be installed.
Any underground or overhead utilities in the barrier alignment must be relocated first to avoid interference during installation.
The barrier must be fully installed before final inspection and acoustic performance testing can be conducted.
Landscaping around the barrier (e.g., planting, grading) is typically done after installation, though it could overlap in some cases.
The sink base cabinet provides structural support and a mounting surface for the heavy apron-front farmhouse sink. The sink cannot be installed until its supporting cabinet is in place.

predecessor: Complete rough-in plumbing (drain and supply lines)
rationale: The sink must be connected to drain and water supply lines, which need to be roughed in before the sink is physically installed and connected.

For an apron-front farmhouse sink, the countertop is often fabricated and installed around the sink or the sink is installed before the countertop depending on under-mount vs. apron-front design. Typically, the countertop must be cut and installed to accommodate the apron-front sink,
The physical sink body must be in place before the drain assembly and P-trap can be attached underneath.

successor: Connect water supply lines to faucet
rationale: The faucet must be mounted to the sink (or countertop with sink in place) before water supply lines can be connected.

While it is easier to install backsplash after the sink is in place to align with the sink edges, it is possible to install backsplash before the sink with careful planning, making this a soft preference rather than a hard constraint.
The seam between the apron-front sink and the countertop must be caulked and sealed after both are installed to prevent water damage.
The kitchen island sits on top of the finished flooring, so flooring must be installed before the island is built or placed to ensure proper fit and finish.
If the kitchen island includes electrical outlets or wiring, the rough electrical work must be completed before the island is enclosed or finished.
If the island includes a sink, dishwasher, or other plumbing fixtures, rough-in plumbing must be completed before the island cabinet frames are installed.
The island base cabinet or frame must be in place and secured before the countertop can be measured, fabricated, and installed on top of it.
Sinks, dishwashers, and other drop-in appliances can only be installed after the island frame and countertop are in place to support them.
Open shelving must be mounted on or attached to framed walls, so wall framing must be completed first to provide structural support.
Drywall must be installed, taped, mudded, and sanded before open shelving can be mounted, to ensure a finished wall surface and avoid damaging the drywall during shelving installation.
Walls should be painted before open shelving is installed, as painting around already-mounted shelves is difficult and results in an inferior finish.
Electrical wiring must be run inside the walls before shelving brackets are installed to avoid interference and the need to move shelves to access wiring.

While open shelving must be physically installed before items can be placed on it, the styling is a finishing touch that could theoretically be done incrementally; however, functionally the shelves need to be in place first.
Installing open shelving creates dust and debris from drilling/mounting, so final cleaning must occur after installation to remove construction residue.
The structural framing and roof must be in place before exposed wood ceiling beams can be installed, as the beams are attached to or supported by the primary structure.

Any wiring, conduit, or plumbing that runs above or through the ceiling area must be roughed in before the exposed beams are installed, since access to the overhead space would be blocked or severely restricted afterward.

It is generally easier to install ceiling beams before finishing walls so that beam ends can be properly integrated and any gaps sealed; however, drywall could be done first with careful detailing, making this a soft preference.
Light fixtures that attach directly to or hang from the exposed beams cannot be installed until the beams themselves are in place and secure.

The final finish coating (stain, sealant, or clear coat) must be applied after the beams are fully installed to protect the wood from damage during subsequent adjacent work and to ensure a uniform appearance.
The wall surface must be clean, smooth, and properly primed before tile can adhere correctly; any imperfections or debris would compromise tile adhesion and alignment.
Drywall must be installed, taped, and mudded (finished) behind the backsplash area to provide a solid substrate for tile installation.

It is strongly preferred to install countertops before backsplash so that the tile can sit on top of the counter and a uniform gap can be established; however some sequences allow countertop after tile with precise alignment.
Electrical outlet boxes must be positioned and wired before tile is applied, as the tile must be cut around the boxes; accessing wiring after tiling would require removing tiles.
