Grout can only be applied after the tile has been set and the adhesive has cured; grouting fills the joints between installed tiles.
Electrical cover plates must be installed after tiling is complete because the tile is cut around the boxes and the plates mount over the finished tile surface.
Trim pieces that abut the top edge of the backsplash are typically installed after tiling to create a clean finished transition between tile and cabinetry or wall.
The range needs a level, stable surface to sit on; uneven floors can cause safety hazards and improper operation.
The range requires a dedicated electrical circuit and outlet (typically 240V for electric ranges) to be installed and terminated before the unit can be connected and placed.
If the vintage-style range is gas-powered, the gas supply line must be run and terminated at the appliance location before the range can be connected and positioned.

While the range can be installed before or after adjacent countertops, it is often preferred to install the range first to ensure proper fit and alignment between the range and surrounding countertops.

The backsplash typically runs behind the range; the range must be in final position so that backsplash can be cut to fit precisely around it, or the range must be removed after backsplash and reinstalled, making it more efficient to install range first in some approaches. However, strictly speaking, backsplash can be done before range if the range is pulled out later.
Framing must be completed to establish the structural support for countertops, including base cabinets and support structures.
Plumbing rough-in for sinks and fixtures must be completed before countertops are fabricated and installed to ensure proper alignment and fit.
Electrical wiring for outlets, switches, and appliances must be roughed in before countertop installation to avoid interference.
Sinks and faucets are mounted onto or through the countertop, so the countertop must be in place first.
Backsplash is typically installed after countertops to create a seamless joint between the countertop surface and the backsplash material.
Electrical rough-in (wiring and boxes) must be completed before cabinets are installed, as cabinets would block access to walls for electrical work.
Plumbing rough-in (water supply lines and drain pipes) must be completed before cabinets are installed, as cabinets would obstruct access to plumbing in walls.
Drywall must be installed, taped, and finished before cabinets are mounted, as cabinets attach to finished walls and would need to be removed to access unfinished drywall.

Flooring (especially tile or hardwood) should be installed before cabinets so that cabinets sit on top of finished flooring, or at minimum the subfloor must be fully prepared; in many cases flooring is preferred before cabinets to avoid cutting around them.
Countertops are measured, fabricated, and installed directly on top of the base cabinets; cabinets must be in place and leveled before countertops can be installed.
Sinks (drop-in/undermount) and certain appliances (dishwasher, cooktop, range) are installed into or adjacent to cabinets, requiring cabinets to be fully installed first.
Final cabinet hardware (knobs, pulls) and trim (crown molding, toe kick) can be installed after cabinets are in place; this is a logical sequence but minor adjustments could be made later.
Backsplash tile is installed against the wall above countertops and between cabinets; cabinets must be in place to define the backsplash area and provide edges for tile termination.
Tile must be set on a clean, level, and cured substrate; a prepared concrete slab or subfloor provides the necessary flat, stable base for tile adhesion and prevents cracking.
Cement backer board or similar underlayment provides a rigid, moisture-resistant surface required for tile adhesion and prevents tile cracking due to subfloor movement.
In showers, bathrooms, or other wet areas, a waterproof membrane must be installed beneath tile to prevent moisture damage to the substrate and structure.
Grout fills the joints between tiles and can only be applied after the tile adhesive/thinset has cured sufficiently to hold the tiles firmly in place.
Sealing is typically done after tile and grout have fully cured; while it is a recommended step to protect porous tiles, it is a soft preference based on tile type rather than a physical necessity.
Foundation preparation must be completed to provide a stable, level base capable of supporting the weight of beams and the structural loads they transfer.
Formwork must be erected to provide temporary support and mold for concrete beams during installation and curing.
Beams form the primary horizontal structural framework; slabs or decks are placed on top of or between beams after they are installed.
If beams are cast-in-place, installation of rebar cages and formwork for beams must precede the pouring of concrete into beam forms.
The terrace boundary wall is built on top of the terrace slab/deck, so the slab must be cast and cured first to provide a stable base.
Waterproofing at the junction between slab and wall is typically started before wall construction to ensure a continuous waterproof membrane.
Coping stones or parapet capping are installed on top of the completed boundary wall to protect the wall head from water ingress.
Waterproofing upstand or flashing is applied against the completed wall to seal the junction between the terrace deck and the wall.
Drainage outlets and scuppers are positioned relative to the wall and finished floor level, so the wall must be in place to set outlet elevations correctly.
The terrace railing/balustrade must be anchored to or supported by the finished terrace slab/deck structure, so the slab must be poured and cured before railing installation can begin.

Waterproofing must be completed on the terrace slab before railing installation to ensure a continuous waterproof membrane, as penetrations for railing supports can compromise waterproofing if applied afterward.
Any adjacent structural walls or columns that the railing system attaches to or integrates with must be built first to provide a secure anchoring surface.

successor: Deck / Terrace Floor Finishing (Tiling or Pavers)
rationale: Railing/balustrade installation is often completed before final floor finishes (tiles, pavers) to avoid damaging finished surfaces, and to allow proper detailing around railing posts/base plates.

Railing installation is typically one of the later finishing items that must be in place before the completed terrace area can be handed over or inspected for safety compliance, though some other finishes could theoretically be done concurrently.
The rough opening frame and structural support must be prepared in the wall before the terrace gate or access door can be installed.
Locks, handles, and other hardware are installed after the door/gate is hung in the opening.
Weather seals, caulking, and flashing must be applied around the installed door to ensure water and air tightness.
Interior casing, trim, and paint around the door frame are completed after the door is installed.
Exterior siding or cladding must interface with the installed door frame, requiring the door to be in place first.
The pergola posts require a stable foundation or footing to transfer loads to the ground; the structure cannot be erected without proper footings in place.
The pergola is typically anchored to or supported by the terrace slab or deck; the walking surface must be installed and fully cured before the overhead structure is built upon it.
The overhead structural frame must be fully erected before any roofing panels, louvers, shade cloth, or lattice can be attached to it.
Running wiring for ceiling fans or lights is easier before the overhead structure is fully enclosed, but can be done afterward with surface-mounted conduit; thus a soft preference for early rough-in.
Applying protective stain or paint after the structure is built is typical, but could be done as a soft preference after assembly to protect materials.
Waterproofing and drainage systems must be installed before planter beds can be built to prevent water damage to the structure below and ensure proper drainage for plant health.
The structural slab or deck that supports the terrace planters must be fully cured and load-bearing before planter construction can begin.
Irrigation pipes and emitters must be laid within the planter beds after the planters are constructed, as the irrigation system is integrated into the bed layout.
Soil and plants cannot be placed until the planter bed containers and retaining walls are fully constructed in their final position.
Paving or decking adjacent to planters is typically installed after the planters are built to ensure proper alignment and clean edges, though it can be done concurrently with careful planning.
The foundation and substructure must be completed to provide a stable load-bearing base for the terrace structural slab.
Columns and walls supporting the terrace slab must be erected before the slab can be cast or placed on top of them.
The structural slab provides the substrate for waterproofing; waterproofing cannot be applied until the slab is cured and ready.
Drainage layers and falls are constructed on top of the structural slab; the slab must be complete to support these layers.
Thermal insulation above the slab requires the structural slab to be in place as a base.
The terrace privacy screen must be anchored to or installed on the terrace slab/deck, requiring the structural substrate to be complete before screen installation can begin.
Once the privacy screen is installed, the interface between the screen and the terrace surface must be waterproofed to prevent water ingress.
If the privacy screen has a structural frame or support posts, that frame must be erected before the screen panels or cladding are attached.
It is typical to apply final paint or protective coating after installation to cover any field joints or damage, but pre-finished screens may skip this step.
Screen installation is often sequenced before adjacent railings and accessories to allow alignment and fit, though in some designs the order could be reversed.
The facade interface requires a stable structural base to bear its loads and provide proper alignment.
The facade interface attaches to the building's structural frame; the frame must be in place to provide attachment points and support for the facade system.
The facade interface (including curtain wall mullions, anchorage, and sub-frame) must be installed first to provide the supporting structure onto which glazing panels and cladding are fixed.
The primary facade interface must be in place before weatherproofing membranes, sealants, and flashings can be applied to complete the building envelope.

successor: Interior Finishes Adjacent to Facade (e.g., drywall, flooring)
rationale: While interior finishes can technically proceed after the facade is installed to avoid damage, some adjacent finishing work may be sequenced after the facade interface to ensure proper fit and continuity at perimeter conditions.

Terrace waterproofing membrane and drainage must be fully installed and tested before any furniture or fixtures are placed, to avoid damage to the waterproofing layer and to ensure proper drainage beneath the furniture.

The terrace floor finish (tiles, paving, or decking) must be completed before furniture and fixtures are placed, as the finished surface provides the stable base and final level for positioning furniture.

While landscaping can theoretically be done concurrently, it is preferable to place furniture and fixtures first to establish the spatial layout and avoid damaging newly planted areas during furniture installation.

All furniture and fixtures must be installed and in their final positions before the terrace is cleaned and handed over to the client, as final cleaning is performed after all installation work is complete.
A stable foundation is required to support the terrace structure; terrace construction cannot begin without completed foundations.
The terrace is typically attached to or supported by the main building structure; the building frame must be erected first to provide anchorage and support points.
Waterproofing of adjacent vertical walls or base surfaces must be completed to prevent moisture ingress into the terrace assembly.
The structural terrace slab and substrate must be fully constructed before any floor finishes or tiles can be applied.
Edge protection systems like railings or balustrades must be installed after the terrace structure is complete to ensure safety.
Drainage outlets and downpipes from the terrace can only be connected and tested after the terrace slab and waterproofing are installed.
The roof slab must be cast and cured before waterproofing can be applied, as waterproofing membranes require a stable, clean, and dry structural substrate.
Screeding to provide proper falls for drainage must be completed before waterproofing to ensure water does not pond on the membrane.
Parapet walls must be built before waterproofing so that the membrane can be dressed up the walls to the required upstand height.
Rainwater downpipe outlets and floor drains must be installed and positioned before the waterproofing layer is laid, so that the membrane can be integrated around the drain flanges.
A protective screed or tile bedding layer over the waterproofing membrane can only be placed after the membrane has been fully applied, cured, and tested for water tightness.
The terrace structure depends on the roof being completed, as the terrace is built upon the roof slab.
Waterproofing must be applied and cured before terrace maintenance and inspection can be performed to ensure the terrace is watertight and safe to walk on.
Inspection must be completed before finishing layers are applied, as any issues found during inspection need to be resolved before covering the surface.
It is preferable to have the terrace inspected and maintained before handing over the building to ensure safety and functionality, though not a strict physical dependency.
The structural frame and core of the building must be complete to provide the load-bearing platform and slab onto which terrace landscaping materials (soil, paving, planters) are applied.
A waterproofing layer over the structural slab is essential before any landscaping, soil, or planting is placed, to prevent water ingress and structural damage.
Proper drainage (e.g., drainage boards, pipes, outlets) must be installed over the waterproofing to manage rainwater and irrigation runoff before soil and plants are added.
While paving and hardscape can be laid concurrently with soft landscaping, it is generally preferable to complete major planting and soil placement first to avoid damaging finished paving.

Safety railings around terrace edges may be installed before or after landscaping, but final adjustments and aesthetic integration are typically done after landscaping is complete to ensure proper alignment with finished grades.
The irrigation system must be fully installed, connected, and tested after landscaping is in place to confirm coverage, avoid dry spots, and ensure proper operation over the finished planting beds.
The terrace must be fully landscaped before final cleaning and handover to the client or occupant, as debris from landscaping would soil clean surfaces.
The door frame rough opening must be framed, sized, and prepared before the lockable entry door unit can be installed.
The door frame must be in place before the door slab can be hung and secured within it.
The door must be hung and positioned in the frame before locks, handles, and deadbolts can be properly aligned and installed.
Weatherstripping is applied to the closed door to seal gaps between the door slab and frame, requiring the door to be installed first.
After installation, the door must be checked for proper operation, alignment, and latch engagement before the installation is considered complete.
The rough opening (frame) must be framed and prepared before the operable window unit can be installed into it.
Flashing and weather-sealing must be applied after the window is set in place to ensure proper water tightness.
Interior trim work is typically done after window installation, though it could theoretically be done before in some cases; it's a soft preference for quality and alignment.
The exterior wall sheathing must be complete to provide the structural backing and rough opening needed for window installation.
Exterior siding is installed after the window is in place so that the siding can be cut and flashed to fit around the window frame.
The wall framing and rough openings must be completed to provide the structural enclosure and cavity where the built-in wardrobe will be installed.
Any electrical wiring for lighting or outlets inside or near the wardrobe area must be roughed in before the wardrobe is built, as access behind the wardrobe will be blocked after installation.
If the wardrobe is near plumbing (e.g., in a master suite), any plumbing rough-in work must be completed first, as the wardrobe structure would block access to the walls.

The wardrobe's exterior surfaces and trim must be finished and painted before the final wall painting is completed, or alternatively the wall painting behind the wardrobe must be done prior to installation; typically painting is done after wardrobe installation to ensure seamless finish between wardrobe and walls.

Flooring (hardwood, tile, or carpet) is typically installed after the wardrobe is in place, as the wardrobe sits on top of the finished floor or the flooring is cut around it for a clean finished look.
The writing desk must have its structural frame assembled before it can be completed as a functional desk.
Drawer slides and drawer boxes must be installed after the desk body is fully assembled to ensure proper alignment and fit.
Surfaces must be smoothed and prepared before final assembly of the writing desk to ensure quality finish.
The assembled writing desk must be fully constructed before applying stain, paint, or protective coating to avoid damaging components.
Legs and mounting hardware must be prepared and ready before attaching them to complete the writing desk structure.
The floor must be framed and load-bearing structure completed before any freestanding bookshelf can be placed, as the bookshelf requires a level, stable surface and support.
If the bookshelf is built-in or wall-mounted, the wall framing and finished wall surface must be complete to attach or align the bookshelf properly.
The bookshelf must be fully assembled and installed before books and decorative items can be placed on it.

predecessor: Frame Installation for Privacy Glazing or Curtains
rationale: The frame or support structure for privacy glazing or curtain tracks must be installed first to provide the physical mounting surface and structural support required for the glazing units or curtain tracks.
For ceiling-mounted curtain tracks or overhead glazing, the overhead structure (ceiling, soffit, or beam) must be complete to provide the anchor points and support for the track system.

Any electrical wiring for motorized curtains or powered privacy glazing must be roughed in before the track or glazing is installed, as access behind or above the installation will be restricted afterward.

Interior finishes such as painting and wallcoverings should be completed after privacy glazing or curtain track installation to avoid damage to finishes during installation work and to allow clean, precise edges where glazing meets walls.

Final adjustments, testing of curtain operation or glazing seals, and commissioning of any automated systems must occur after installation to ensure proper function and integration with building systems.
The door slab must be hung on its hinges (or be in place) before door hardware such as locksets, handles, closers, and strike plates can be installed onto the door and frame.

Wall finishing should be completed before installing door hardware to avoid damaging freshly painted or papered walls, and to ensure the hardware is not painted over or obstructed by finish materials.
After all door hardware is installed, final adjustments (e.g., latch alignment, closer speed setting, keying) and functional testing must be performed to ensure proper operation.

Door hardware installation is typically a near-final activity; completing it allows inspectors to verify hardware function, accessibility compliance, and security requirements before project closeout.

All electrical outlets, switches, conduits, ductwork, and plumbing penetrations must be installed before acoustic sealing can be applied, because sealing compound must be applied around these penetrations to prevent flanking paths for sound transmission. Sealing before rough-in would require re-penetrating the seals.

The primary wall structure and at least the first layer of plasterboard/drywall must be in place to provide a substrate for acoustic sealant application at joints, perimeter edges, and service penetrations.
The floor slab and ceiling framing must be complete so that acoustic seals can be applied at the wall-to-floor and wall-to-ceiling junctions, preventing sound flanking through gaps.

Acoustic sealants and tapes must be applied and fully cured before final surface finishes are applied, otherwise paint or decorative coatings would bridge across movement joints or prevent sealant from bonding correctly.

All acoustic sealing and detailing work must be completed before any sound insulation testing can be carried out, as the testing verifies the effectiveness of the installed acoustic treatment and would be invalid if sealing was incomplete.

Rough-in electrical work (running conduits, wires, and installing backboxes) must be completed before fit-off can begin, as fit-off involves installing devices (switches, outlets, fixtures) that connect to the roughed-in wiring.
Drywall must be installed and finished before electrical fit-off because electrical devices are mounted on finished walls/ceilings, and fit-off cannot proceed without enclosed wall cavities.
Suspended ceiling grid installation must be complete to provide mounting points for light fixtures and other ceiling-mounted electrical devices during fit-off.
Electrical fit-off (installing switches, outlets, and fixtures) must be complete before final lighting trim-out and testing can occur, as the devices need to be connected and energized for testing.
All electrical devices must be installed (fit-off complete) before the electrical system can pass final inspection and be commissioned for occupancy.
Structural framing (walls, floors, ceilings) must be complete to provide the physical substrate and support for built-in joinery elements like cabinets, shelves, and wardrobes.

Electrical wiring, outlets, switches, and plumbing rough-ins must be installed within wall cavities before joinery is placed, as accessing these behind finished joinery would require removal and rework.
Plasterboard/drywall lining must be completed and finished before joinery installation so that joinery can be fixed to smooth, level surfaces and trimmed neatly against walls.
Floor finishes or screed must be leveled and prepared to provide a stable, level base for base cabinets, kickboards, and floor-mounted joinery units.

Joinery installation must be complete before final painting and finishing so that paint can be applied neatly around joinery edges and trims, avoiding damage to finished joinery from paint drips or overspray.
Stone, laminate, or solid-surface benchtops must be installed after base cabinets/joinery are in place to allow precise templating, cutting, and secure fixing to the cabinet frames.

While joinery is typically installed before floor coverings to allow joinery to sit on top of the subfloor (with floor finishes butting up to joinery), some sequences prefer floor finishes first. This is generally a soft preference for quality and appearance rather than a physical necessity.
Paint requires a smooth, finished drywall surface to adhere properly; painting over unfinished drywall would result in poor finish and durability.
Primer seals the drywall and provides a uniform base for paint; skipping primer or not allowing it to dry before painting leads to uneven coverage and adhesion failure.
Painting should be completed before flooring to avoid drips, splatters, and dust from painting settling on new floors, which could damage or stain flooring materials.

While often preferred to paint walls before installing trim for cleaner lines, some painters prefer to install trim first and then paint everything together; this is a soft preference based on workflow efficiency.
Painting generates dust, fumes, and potential spills; all painting and decoration work must be fully complete and dry before final cleanup and occupancy to prevent damage to finished surfaces.

The ground area where the bench will be placed must be leveled, cleared, and have a stable foundation (e.g., concrete pad or compacted base) before the bench can be installed to ensure stability and longevity.
The bench itself must be physically fabricated, delivered, and available on site before installation can begin.

predecessor: Utility Trenching and Underground Work (if applicable)
rationale: Any underground utilities or drainage work in the vicinity must be completed before bench placement to avoid digging up or moving the bench later.
Final paving, planting, decorative gravel, or grass around the bench should be completed after the bench is in its final position to ensure proper alignment and clean edges.

It is preferable but not physically required that the bench installation is finished before the final inspection, as inspection can check the bench's stability and finish after installation is complete.
The armchair frame must be fully assembled and structurally sound before any upholstery or cushioning can be applied, as the frame provides the foundational support.
After upholstery is complete, the armchair must undergo quality inspection to ensure fabric is correctly fitted, seams are secure, and there are no defects before it moves to packaging.
Wood must be properly dried and conditioned to the correct moisture content before it can be cut and assembled into the armchair frame, preventing warping or structural issues.
The armchair must pass quality inspection before it can be packaged and dispatched to the customer or retailer.
Foam cushions must be cut and shaped to the correct dimensions before they can be inserted into the upholstery covers during the upholstery process.
The floor must be finished, leveled, and any adhesives or coatings fully cured before placing a heavy sofa to avoid damaging the floor surface or causing uneven settling.

Walls need to be painted or wallpapered completely before moving furniture in, as large furniture like a sofa would obstruct access to walls and could be damaged by paint splatters or wallpaper adhesive.
Electrical outlets and switches behind or near the sofa area must be installed and wired before the sofa is placed, as it would be difficult or impossible to access the walls afterward.

While an area rug can be placed before the sofa, it is often easier to position the sofa first and then align the rug in front of it for optimal visual arrangement and to avoid the rug being shifted out of place.
It is a soft preference to place the sofa first so the coffee table can be positioned at the correct distance and alignment relative to the sofa for comfortable reach and aesthetic symmetry.
The ottoman frame must be assembled first to provide the structural base before adding padding and upholstery.

predecessor: Cutting and Sewing of Cover Fabric
rationale: The fabric cover must be cut and sewn to the correct dimensions before it can be fitted over the ottoman padding and frame.
The completed ottoman must be fully assembled before it can undergo final inspection for quality control.
The ottoman must be fully finished and assembled before it can be packaged for shipment.
The side table must have the main frame or table top structure assembled first so that the side table can be properly attached to it.
The side table component itself must be fabricated or manufactured before it can be installed or attached to the main structure.
After the side table is attached, finishing work such as painting or staining should be done last to ensure a uniform appearance and to avoid damaging the finish during installation.
A quality check is typically performed after installation to ensure the side table is securely attached and aligned properly.
Wood must be cut to appropriate dimensions before the table can be assembled.
Wood surfaces must be sanded smooth before assembly to ensure proper fit and finish.
The table must be fully assembled before applying stain or paint to ensure even coverage and avoid unfinished areas at joints.
The completed table must be inspected for defects, stability, and finish quality before it can be approved for use or delivery.
Finish must be fully applied and dried before attaching hardware components to avoid damaging the finish during installation.
Partitions and screens enclose wall cavities, so all rough-in electrical wiring, plumbing pipes, and HVAC ductwork must be installed before framing/partition walls are closed.
Partitions and screens are typically installed on top of finished or prepared floor surfaces; the floor structure must be in place to support and anchor the partition framing.
Partitions often extend from floor to ceiling/roof deck; the overhead structure must be complete so that top tracks or channels can be secured.
Drywall, plaster, or wall panels are applied directly onto partition framing; the partition frame must be erected first to provide the substrate.
Doors and windows are installed into framed openings within partitions; the partition framing must exist to receive these components.
The planter / green wall requires a structural slab with proper waterproofing to support the weight of soil, plants, and water, and to prevent water damage to the structure below.
A drainage layer must be placed over the waterproofing to allow excess water to drain away, preventing waterlogging and root rot before planting medium and plants are added.
The irrigation piping and drip lines must be installed within the planter area before the soil and plants are placed to avoid disturbing the plants later.
Soil and plants cannot be added until the planter structure, waterproofing, drainage, and irrigation systems are fully installed and tested.
While not physically required, it is good practice to inspect the completed planter/green wall before final project sign-off to ensure all systems function correctly.

Rough-in inspections must be completed to verify that all mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-ins are in place and approved before space layout and furniture planning can begin, as these systems affect the spatial configuration and furniture placement.
Walls and ceilings define the physical boundaries and room dimensions of a space, which are essential prerequisites for accurately planning furniture layouts and spatial arrangements.

MEP rough-in work must be completed before space layout and furniture planning because the routing of ducts, conduits, and pipes determines available wall, floor, and ceiling space for furniture placement and layout design.

Flooring installation is typically completed before furniture placement to protect the finished floor surface and allow furniture to be placed directly on the final flooring, though it could potentially be done after in some cases.

Space layout and furniture planning must be completed before final finishes and furnishing installation because the layout and furniture plan dictates where furniture, fixtures, and equipment (FF&E) will be placed and how final aesthetic finishes will align with the planned arrangement.

The ceiling grid provides the structural support and mounting surface for recessed or surface-mounted ambient/task lighting fixtures; installation of the grid must be complete before fixtures can be attached.
Electrical cables, junction boxes, and conduits must be run and terminated at the lighting locations before the fixtures can be connected and energized.

Wall-mounted task lighting requires finished wall surfaces for proper mounting and to ensure wiring is concealed; similarly, ambient lighting placement references completed partitions to align with room layout.

In ceilings, insulation and vapor barriers must be installed before lighting fixtures to avoid trapping moisture or creating fire hazards, and to comply with building codes for IC-rated (insulation contact) fixture requirements.

successor: Ceiling / Wall Painting and Final Finishes
rationale: Lighting fixtures must be installed before final painting and finishing so that any gaps, caulking, or touch-up work around the fixture trim can be completed seamlessly, and to allow the fixtures to be tested before ceilings are closed.
The fixture must be physically installed before it can be connected to the final power source, tested, dimmers adjusted, and commissioned as part of the building's electrical system.

While not a strict physical constraint, installing lighting fixtures before flooring prevents dust and debris from construction above from contaminating new floor surfaces, and allows workers to see the finished floor for proper lighting alignment.
Furniture must be placed on completed floors to avoid damage to furniture and to ensure floors are fully cured and finished before heavy items are placed on them.
Walls must be painted and finished before furniture is installed to avoid paint splatters on furniture and to allow easy access to walls without obstructions.
Electrical wiring, outlets, switches, and ceiling installations must be completed before furniture is placed, as furniture would block access to walls and ceilings for these installations.

Once furniture is installed, decorative items, artwork, and final staging can be arranged around the furniture for aesthetic completion, though this is a soft preference rather than a hard physical constraint.
Furniture installation generates dust, debris, and packaging waste, so final cleaning and project handover must occur after all furniture is in place to present a clean finished space to the client.
Structural frame and slabs must be complete to provide the physical substrate and floor upon which partitions are built and joinery is installed.

Electrical conduits, plumbing pipes, and HVAC ductwork within walls must be roughed-in before partitions are closed up with drywall or boarding; otherwise walls would need to be demolished to install services.

It is generally preferable to complete overhead ceiling grid before full-height partitions so that ceiling layout can be aligned with partition lines, but in some sequences this order can be swapped; thus a soft preference.
Door frames and window frames are typically installed into the partition openings; the partition structure must exist before doors and windows can be hung or fitted.
Paint and final surface finishes are applied after partitions are fully installed and boarded; painting before partition installation is not physically possible.
Floor finishes such as tiles, vinyl, or carpet are laid after partitions are in place to achieve a clean edge and avoid trapping flooring under walls.
Electrical sockets, switches, and faceplates are fitted into the finished partition surfaces; the partition must exist to host these fixtures.
The structural frame must be in place to provide the rough opening and support for the cluster entry door frame assembly.
The floor slab must be finished to provide a level threshold and proper anchoring surface for the door frame.
The door leaf and frame must be installed before any hardware (locks, handles, hinges beyond temporary hinges, closers) can be mounted on them.
While painting can be done before or after, typically door installation is completed before final painting to allow for proper mudding/tape around the frame and a clean finish line.
Any electrical wiring for maglocks, card readers, or doorbell systems in the vicinity must be roughed in before the door frame is fully set to avoid rework.
Door rough opening must be framed in the wall before the door unit can be installed.
Trim and casing are applied around the installed door; the door must be in place first.
The door must be hung and fitted before final painting or finishing can be applied to avoid damage during installation.
Inspection ensures the rough opening meets specifications before the door is installed.
Door hardware like locks and hinges are attached to the installed door; the door must be hung first.
The structural wall framing (studwork/partition framework) must be complete to provide the supporting substrate onto which acoustic wall lining boards or panels are fixed.
Acoustic insulation (such as mineral wool or acoustic batts) must be placed within the wall cavity before the lining is installed, as it cannot be added after the lining boards are fixed in place.
All electrical cables, conduits, outlet boxes, plumbing pipes, and data cabling that run within the wall must be installed and roughed-in prior to closing the wall with acoustic lining.
Acoustic lining boards must be fixed in place before joint compound, tape, skim coat, or paint can be applied to achieve a finished surface.
Acoustic sealant is applied to joints, edges, and penetrations after the lining boards are installed to ensure airtightness and sound isolation performance.
Trim and architraves are fitted after lining is complete to cover edges and provide a finished appearance, though in some sequences this could overlap.

Structural frame and core (columns, beams, slabs, shear walls) must be completed to define the building's spatial boundaries and provide load-bearing support before any non-structural partitioning or interior fit-out can begin.

MEP rough-in work — including ductwork, piping, conduit, and wiring within walls and ceilings — must be installed before partitions are closed up, otherwise walls would need to be demolished later to access these services.
Floor slabs must be poured, cured, and waterproofed before partition walls are erected on them to avoid moisture damage and ensure a level, stable base for wall framing.

Partition walls must be fully installed and fixed in place before surface finishes such as plastering, painting, tiling, or floor coverings can be applied, as finishes are applied directly to or against the completed partitions.
Partition walls define the openings for doors and windows; frames are installed into the prepared openings in the partitions after the walls are erected.

First-fix (rough-in) installation of all MEP services such as conduits, pipes, cable trays, and ductwork within walls, ceilings, and floors must be completed before second-fix works can commence, as second-fix involves fitting outlets, fixtures, and terminations which require the primary routing to be in place.
Structural elements (columns, slabs, beams, and core walls) must be complete before any MEP second-fix activities, as MEP installations are reliant on the permanent structure for support and access.

Internal partition walls must be erected and first-fix MEP installed within them before second-fix activities such as socket outlet fitting, switch installation, and sanitary ware connection can proceed.

Second-fix MEP works such as fitting sockets, switches, light fittings, grilles, and diffusers must be completed prior to final ceiling and wall finishes to avoid damage to finishes and to allow proper alignment and access for adjustments.

Commissioning (testing and setting-to-work) of all MEP systems can only occur after second-fix installation is complete, as all components must be physically installed and connected before the system can be energised, tested, and balanced for handover.

Access control hardware (controllers, readers, door strikes, etc.) must be physically installed and wired before programming and commissioning can begin, as programming requires the hardware to be in place and connected to configure device addresses, inputs/outputs, and communication settings.

Electrical power and communication cabling (conduit, wire, cable trays) must be run to access control panels, door controllers, and reader locations before these devices can be powered up and programmed.

If the access control system integrates with the fire alarm system for door release on fire alarm, the fire alarm system must be tested and verified first to ensure proper integration and life safety sequencing.

successor: Access Control System Testing and Acceptance
rationale: Full system testing (door lock/unlock cycles, card reader tests, alarm monitoring, integration verification) can only be performed after the system has been programmed and commissioned with all device configurations, credential databases, and access schedules loaded.

User training and credential (card/fob) issuance is logically dependent on having a programmed and functional system, but could technically begin in parallel; however, best practice is to complete commissioning before issuing credentials to avoid security gaps or configuration changes requiring re-issuance.

Snagging and pre-handover inspection can only begin after the building is substantially or practically complete, as the inspection is meant to identify defects and incomplete items in an otherwise finished structure.

predecessor: Final Cleaning & Decommissioning of Temporary Services
rationale: The site must be cleaned of debris and temporary services removed so that inspectors can clearly see all finishes, fixtures, and systems without obstruction.
The snagging inspection identifies defects and incomplete works; these defects must be corrected (rectified) before the final handover can occur.
The formal handover of the building to the client or owner depends on successful completion of snagging inspection and rectification of identified issues.

While it is best practice for the client to walk through after snagging is complete and defects are rectified, the walkthrough could be done concurrently in some arrangements, making this a soft preference rather than a hard constraint.
The bathtub must be placed on a structurally sound floor; floor framing provides the necessary support and level surface for the tub.
A completed subfloor is required to bear the weight of the bathtub and provide a stable, waterproof base before setting the tub.
Drain, waste, vent lines, and water supply pipes must be roughed into the correct position before the bathtub is placed, as access behind/under the tub becomes impossible after installation.
The bathtub must be in place before the surrounding wall finish (tile, surround panels, waterproof membrane) can be installed, as these materials overlap and seal against the tub rim.
Once the bathtub is fixed in position, the final connections for the faucet, spout, showerhead, and drain assembly can be completed with precise alignment.
The shower drain, water supply lines, and valve rough-ins must be installed before the shower enclosure can be set in place, as the enclosure sits over the finished plumbing connections.
A waterproof membrane and shower pan (or pre-slope) must be completed to prevent water damage before the enclosure walls and base are installed.
Cement backer board or other approved wall substrate must be in place behind the enclosure panels to provide a solid mounting surface and moisture barrier.
The shower enclosure frame and panels must be fully installed and secured before the shower door can be hung and aligned for proper operation.
Tile or final wall finishes around the enclosure opening must be installed after the enclosure is in place to ensure clean transitions and proper sealing at the edges.
Plumbing rough-in for the shower drain and supply lines must be installed before the shower tray/base can be placed, as the tray sits over the drain connection.
The subfloor must be level, clean, and properly waterproofed to provide a stable base for the shower tray; an uneven or unprepared subfloor will cause the tray to crack or leak.
Waterproofing membrane on walls should lap over the shower tray flange to create a continuous waterproof seal; the tray must be in place first to define the transition.
Wall tiles or panels are installed after the tray so that they overlap the tray flange, preventing water from seeping behind the tray.
The shower screen or door frame is fixed onto or adjacent to the tray rim; the tray must be fully installed to provide the reference surface for the screen.

predecessor: Install shower valve and rough-in plumbing
rationale: The shower head connects to the shower valve and supply lines; rough-in plumbing must be complete to provide water supply.
Shower head mounts to finished wall; waterproofing and backer board must be installed before final fixture installation.

successor: Final water pressure testing and inspection
rationale: After shower head is installed, the complete shower system can be pressure tested for leaks and inspected.

successor: Install shower trim kit and escutcheon plate
rationale: The escutcheon plate and decorative trim that covers the wall penetration are placed after the shower head arm is installed.

While it is possible to tile after the shower head is installed, finishing tile and grout around the arm usually precedes fixture installation for a cleaner look; this is a soft preference based on common sequencing.
Bidet requires water supply and drainage connections which must be roughed-in before the bidet unit can be installed.
Walls behind and around the bidet need to be fully finished (tiled or painted) before mounting the bidet, as the bidet would block access to the wall surface.
Floor tiles must be laid and set before the bidet is placed on them to ensure proper drainage and a finished look beneath the fixture.
After the bidet is physically mounted, the final water supply connections, shut-off valve, and drain trim pieces must be attached.
Only after the bidet is fully installed and connected can water be turned on to test for leaks, pressure, and proper operation.
The vanity unit must be mounted on finished walls; wall framing and plasterboard provide the structural surface for secure attachment.
Water supply pipes and drainage connections must be roughed in behind the wall before the vanity unit is installed, as the vanity conceals and connects to these services.

predecessor: Electrical Rough-In (Wiring for Lights and Outlets)
rationale: Electrical wiring for vanity lights and power outlets must be run and terminated in the wall before the vanity is fixed in place, as access to the wall cavity is restricted afterward.
Floor finishes and waterproofing should be completed before the vanity is installed to ensure continuous waterproof membrane and to avoid the vanity sitting on unfinished flooring.
The vanity cabinet must be securely installed first to provide support for the countertop and sink that are placed on top of it.
Final plumbing connections (faucets, trap, supply lines) are made after the vanity and sink are in place to connect to the installed sink and supply stubs.

successor: Mirror and Vanity Light Fixture Installation
rationale: While mirrors and lights are often installed after the vanity is in place for alignment and aesthetic coordination, this is a soft preference as they could theoretically be installed independently.

successor: Caulking and Sealing (Joints to Wall and Floor)
rationale: Caulking and sealing around the vanity edges must be done after installation to waterproof joints between the vanity, wall, and floor.
The wall surface must be finished and waterproofed before a mirror or mirror cabinet can be securely mounted; otherwise moisture damage or improper adhesion may occur.
Electrical wiring and junction boxes for any integrated lighting or power must be installed behind the wall before the mirror or cabinet is mounted.
Mirror cabinets often need to be installed first so that the vanity top can be aligned and fitted correctly beneath them.
It is preferable to complete painting touch-ups after mirror installation to avoid paint overspray on the mirror, though not physically mandatory.
Final sealant and caulking around the edges of the mirror/cabinet can only be applied after it is fixed in place to ensure a watertight seal.
The towel rail is mounted on a finished wall surface; wall preparation, plastering, and tiling must be completed to provide a solid, level, and waterproof substrate for fixing the rail.
For electric heated towel rails, electrical cabling, wiring, and junction boxes must be installed in the wall before the rail can be connected and mounted.
For hydronic (central heating) towel rails, hot water pipes must be run to the location and capped off before the rail is connected and fixed in place.
If the towel rail is surface-mounted to tiles, any final sealant or grout around the fixing brackets should be applied after the rail is installed to create a waterproof finish.
The final electrical connection (if not pre-wired) and safety testing of the heated towel rail can only occur once the rail is physically installed and fixed in position.
The door frame must be constructed and installed in the rough opening before the bathroom door can be hung, as the door attaches to the frame.
The bathroom walls must be framed to define the doorway opening before the door can be installed.
The door must be hung in place before locks, handles, and hinges can be mounted onto the door and frame.
The door should be installed before final wall finishes are applied around the door frame to ensure proper fit and seamless integration.
While it is preferable to complete rough-ins before installing the door for easy access, the door can be installed after rough-ins if needed, making this a soft preference.
The drainage piping must be roughed in before the floor drain can be connected and installed.
The waterproofing layer must be prepared and sloped toward the drain before the drain flange can be properly set and integrated with the waterproofing system.
The floor drain must be in place and secured so that the sloped mortar bed can be poured and screeded to direct water to the drain.
Tile and finished flooring are laid after the drain is installed and the mortar bed is set, ensuring that the finished surface slopes correctly to the drain.
The final waterproofing seal around the drain flange must be applied after the drain is positioned to ensure a watertight connection between the drain and the membrane.
Grab bars require solid wall backing (blocking) installed within wall framing to support weight and loads.
If the grab bar is near fixtures (e.g., toilet, shower), plumbing rough-in work must be completed so that grab bar placement does not interfere with or get covered by finished walls.
Any wiring in walls near grab bar locations must be installed before grab bar blocking and final placement to avoid conflicts.
Ideally grab bars are installed after wall finishing for aesthetics, but they can also be retrofit through finished walls; however, blocking must be in place before finishing.
Grab bars must be installed and secured before the building can pass safety inspection and be occupied, particularly in accessible bathrooms and spaces.
Rough-in plumbing must be completed to ensure the wall is prepared and water supply/drainage lines are in place before the soap dish or dispenser can be mounted.
The wall surface must be finished and prepared (tiled or painted) before the soap dish or dispenser can be securely attached to the wall.
While typically done before the faucet for ease of access, this is a soft preference as both can be installed independently if space allows.
The soap dish/dispenser must be in place before final trim and escutcheon plates are installed to ensure a clean finished appearance around the fixture.

The toilet paper holder must be mounted on finished walls (tiled or painted) to ensure proper adhesion and a clean finish. Installing on unfinished walls would require removal and reinstallation after finishing.
Drywall must be in place and taped to provide a solid substrate for mounting the toilet paper holder securely.
While not physically required, it is practical to install the toilet first to properly position the toilet paper holder at the correct distance and height relative to the toilet for user convenience.
After installing the toilet paper holder, final touch-ups such as caulking around mounting brackets or minor paint corrections may be performed to ensure a finished appearance.
Electrical wiring must be run through walls and ceilings to the switch boxes and fixture locations before any fixture can be connected or mounted.
The ceiling surface must be closed and finished so that the fixture has a solid mounting surface and to avoid damaging unfinished drywall around the fixture cutout.
Painting is easier and produces cleaner edges when done before fixtures are mounted, though it is possible to cut in around fixtures afterwards.

successor: Light bulb/trim installation and fixture testing
rationale: The fixture housing must be securely mounted to the ceiling or wall before bulbs, trim pieces, and covers can be installed and power can be safely tested.
All fixtures must be completely installed and operational before the electrical inspector can verify compliance with code.
Sanitary ware (toilets, sinks, showers) must be installed on finished tiled surfaces to ensure proper waterproofing, alignment, and aesthetic finish.
Pipes for water supply and waste drainage must be embedded in walls and floors before sanitary fixtures can be connected to them.
Waterproof membranes must be applied and cured before installing sanitary fixtures to prevent water damage and leaks behind fittings.
Electrical wiring for bathroom lights, exhaust fans, and outlets is typically roughed-in before sanitary ware installation, but minor adjustments can be made after.
Final paint touch-ups and caulking around sanitary fixtures are done after installation to achieve a clean, finished appearance.
The concrete slab or substrate must be fully cured, clean, and smooth before applying waterproofing membrane to ensure proper adhesion and prevent future leaks.
A level blinding layer or screed provides a smooth, even base for waterproofing application, essential for achieving a continuous and defect-free membrane.

A protective layer (e.g., sand blinding, geotextile, or lean concrete) must be placed immediately over the waterproofing to shield it from damage during subsequent construction activities such as rebar fixing and pouring of the structural slab.
Reinforcement steel can only be laid after waterproofing and its protection layer are complete, to prevent steel bars from puncturing or damaging the waterproof membrane.

successor: Concrete Pour for Foundation / Basement Slab
rationale: The main structural concrete pour over the waterproofed area cannot begin until waterproofing and its protection layer are fully installed and inspected, as the waterproofing is meant to be sandwiched beneath the structural slab.
The subfloor must be level, clean, dry, and properly prepared (screeded) before tiles can be laid to ensure proper adhesion and a flat finished surface.

In wet areas such as bathrooms and kitchens, waterproofing membranes must be applied and fully cured before tiling to prevent water damage and ensure the waterproof barrier is intact beneath the tiles.
All plumbing pipes, drains, and fittings must be installed and pressure-tested before tiling, as tiles would cover and permanently conceal these services.
Electrical conduit, switch boxes, and outlet boxes must be positioned within walls before tiling, as tiles are installed over the finished wall surface and cannot be easily disturbed later.
Tiles must first be laid and the adhesive allowed to set before grout can be applied to fill the joints between tiles.

It is preferable to complete tiling before painting walls or installing skirting boards to avoid damaging finished paintwork and to allow tiles to be cut neatly against finished surfaces, though in some sequences painting is done first.
Cabinets and vanities are typically installed after floor and wall tiling is complete so that they sit on top of the finished tiled surface, avoiding the need to cut tiles around fixed cabinetry.
Toilets, basins, and other sanitary fixtures are installed after tiling to ensure the waterproof finish is complete and fixtures sit flush against the tiled surface.
Structural framing must be complete before any electrical cable routing, backbox fitting, and first-fix wiring can be installed within wall and ceiling cavities.
Plumbing pipework and waste runs must be in place before electricians position cables and boxes, to avoid clashes and ensure proper coordination of services within the same voids.
Electrical cables and boxes must be fully routed and terminated before insulation is placed, as insulation goes over or around the services.
All electrical first-fix wiring, backboxes, and second-fix socket/switch plates must be installed before walls can be closed up with plasterboard.

Electrical accessories (sockets, switches, fan isolators) must be fitted and plates installed before tiling can commence, as tiles are cut around access points and the final trim/fit is completed after tiling.

Plumbing pipes and drainage must be installed in walls and floors before fixing bathroom accessories like towel bars, toilet paper holders, and robe hooks, as these accessories are mounted on finished walls where plumbing has already been roughed in.

Electrical wiring for bathroom lighting, exhaust fans, and GFCI outlets must be roughed in before installing bathroom accessories, as some accessories (e.g., lighted mirrors, electric towel warmers) may connect to electrical supply, and all wall work must be complete before final fixtures.

Drywall must be installed and finished (taped, mudded, and sanded) before bathroom accessories can be mounted on walls, as these accessories require solid finished wall surfaces for proper attachment.

Tile installation and waterproofing on bathroom walls must be completed before accessories like soap dishes, grab bars, and towel rings are installed, as tiles provide the finished surface that these accessories mount onto, and waterproofing must be intact behind them.

successor: Final Plumbing Fixture Installation (Sink, Toilet, Shower)
rationale: Plumbing fixtures such as sinks, toilets, and showerheads are installed after bathroom accessories (like towel bars, toilet paper holders) because accessories are mounted on walls and must not block or interfere with fixture placement; also, finishing work proceeds from wall-mounted items to floor-mounted fixtures for clean sequencing.
The rough opening must be framed and prepared with proper dimensions, header, jambs, and sill before the sectional door can be installed.
The track system, brackets, and hardware must be mounted to support the sectional door panels before the door itself can be placed.
The door panels and track must be fully installed before the automatic opener and motor can be attached and calibrated.
Weatherstripping, seals, and finish trim around the door perimeter must be applied after the door is installed to ensure proper fit and sealing.
The torsion or extension springs can only be safely tensioned and balanced after the door panels are fully assembled and installed in the tracks.
The roof structural framing must be in place to provide the supporting framework onto which skylight panels are mounted and fixed.
Roof decking provides the base surface and openings into which skylight curbs and panels are installed; without it there is no substrate.
The skylight curbs and panels must be fully installed and integrated so that the waterproofing membrane can be lapped up and sealed around them to ensure a watertight roof.
Insulation is typically fitted around and up to the installed skylight curbs after the skylight panels are in place to maintain thermal continuity.
Interior ceiling work such as drywall or soffits is typically completed after skylights are installed to allow proper trimming and finishing around the skylight openings for a clean aesthetic.
The column guard or racking protector must be installed after the concrete column or rack structure is erected, as the guard attaches to or surrounds the column/rack.
A stable foundation and prepared site are required before installing protective elements like column guards, as they need a level base to be properly anchored.
Column guards/racking protectors are safety installations that must be in place before the warehouse becomes operational to prevent damage to columns from forklifts or other equipment.
It is preferable but not physically required to have the column protector installed prior to the final inspection so that the inspector can verify its correct placement.
Racking systems require a stable, level foundation (concrete piers or grade beams) to anchor to; without completed foundations the racking lacks structural support.
The site must be graded, compacted, and cleared to proper elevations before racking can be laid out and installed to ensure correct alignment and stability.
Solar panels (modules) are physically attached to the racking structure; the racking must be in place to provide the mounting points for the modules.

While some wire management can begin before racking, final cable routing and attachment to the racking structure is more efficiently done after racking is installed to avoid rework and ensure neat routing.

Module-level wiring and stringing of panels happens after modules are mounted, which depends on racking. However, main conduit and inverter wiring can precede. The direct successor is Module Mounting, which then enables wiring.
Ground beams require stable, excavated ground at the correct levels; excavation must be completed before concrete can be poured.
A blinding layer of lean concrete is typically placed over the excavated soil to provide a clean, level working surface and prevent contamination of the reinforcement and fresh concrete.

predecessor: Reinforcement Steel (Rebar) Installation for Ground Beam
rationale: Steel reinforcement cage must be assembled, positioned, and tied in place within the formwork before concrete is poured to ensure structural integrity.
Formwork (shuttering) must be erected and secured to shape and contain the wet concrete until it cures.
Formwork cannot be removed until the concrete ground beam has achieved sufficient strength to support its own weight and any imposed loads.
Proper curing must begin immediately after concrete placement and finishing to ensure adequate hydration, strength development, and durability.
Backfill material can only be placed and compacted against the ground beam after the concrete has reached sufficient strength to resist lateral pressures.

successor: Ground Floor Slab / Suspended Slab Construction
rationale: Ground beams must be cast and cured to support the edge or internal load-bearing for the ground floor slab; the slab often bears on or ties into the ground beams.
The foundation must be completed to provide a stable and level base for the floor slab to be poured and cured upon.
The ground must be properly graded, compacted, and prepared to support the floor slab and prevent differential settlement.
Underground plumbing, electrical conduits, and other utilities must be laid and inspected before the slab is poured to avoid cutting or damaging the slab later.
A vapor barrier must be placed over the prepared subgrade before pouring the slab to prevent moisture migration from the ground into the slab.
Walls and vertical structural elements are typically built on top of the completed floor slab, which provides the working platform and bearing surface.

While it is common practice to allow the slab to cure sufficiently before applying finishes, some finishing operations could theoretically begin earlier; however, proper curing is strongly recommended to avoid cracking and delamination.
Overhead mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work often begins after the slab is poured as it provides the structural floor and access for vertical risers.
A level, load-bearing foundation must be prepared before the modular workstation can be placed and secured.

Underground or in-wall utility conduits and rough-in connections for electrical, data, and compressed air lines must be completed before the workstation is positioned, as access behind/underneath becomes restricted.
The workstation must be placed in its final location before it can be precisely leveled and anchored to the floor.
Power, data, and compressed air can only be connected to the workstation's built-in ports after the workstation is installed and positioned.

successor: Workstation Component Assembly (Work surfaces, overhead bins, task lighting)
rationale: The main frame of the modular workstation must be in place before bolt-on components such as work surfaces, overhead storage bins, and task lighting can be attached.
The movable partition wall must rest on a finished floor slab to provide a stable base and support.
Movable partition walls require overhead track systems that are suspended from the structural ceiling or roof deck, so the overhead structure must be in place first.
Any electrical cables or conduits that need to pass through or above the partition wall track area must be routed before the track is installed to avoid conflicts and rework.
Installing floor finishes after the partition allows the wall to sit cleanly on top of the finished flooring, but this is a sequencing preference for aesthetics rather than a structural necessity.
Finishing trades benefit from having the partition in place to define room boundaries, but painting can be done before or after depending on access and scheduling preferences.
The building structure must be complete to provide the physical shell and support systems required before interior layout planning can commence.
The building must be enclosed (roof, windows, doors) to protect interior work from weather and allow for environmental control during layout installation.
Initial MEP rough-in work (ductwork, conduit, piping) must be installed before final interior layouts to avoid conflicts and rework.
The ABW layout identifies zones and furniture placement, so final interior finishes must follow the layout plan to ensure aesthetic and functional alignment.
Furniture, workstations, and collaborative zone equipment are placed according to the ABW layout design and cannot be installed until the layout is defined.

The accommodation strategy defines the overall approach to workspace and must be established before a detailed utilisation study can be conducted to assess how space is actually used against the strategy.
The site or building must be selected before a utilisation study can be performed on that specific workspace location.
The utilisation study provides occupancy data and usage patterns that inform how the space should be planned and designed.
Utilisation study findings determine what fit-out and furniture are needed based on actual usage patterns.
While not a physical necessity, understanding how space is currently used helps plan change management activities for any workplace transformation.

The structural shell and core (walls, floors, ceilings, primary MEP rough-ins) must be complete before any interior fit-out work can begin, as fit-out activities depend on stable structures and roughed-in services.
Ductwork, conduit, piping, and wiring within the shell must be installed before ceilings and walls are enclosed by fit-out finishes; otherwise, expensive rework would be required.
In a renovation scenario, existing partitions, finishes, and unwanted elements must be removed before reconfiguring the space and installing new fit-out elements.

Final finishes such as painting, flooring, and decorative elements cannot be installed until reconfiguration (new walls, partitions, ceiling grids) is complete, as those surfaces must be ready for final treatment.

Furniture, fixtures, and equipment are installed only after reconfiguration and fit-out are finished, because the space layout and built-in elements dictate the placement and anchoring of movable and fixed furnishings.
The servery counter must be installed on a finished, level floor slab to ensure stability and proper alignment.
Walls provide structural support and backing for the servery counter; the counter is typically anchored to or abutted against wall framing.
Plumbing for sinks and drainage within the servery counter must be roughed in before the counter can be installed, as the counter will cover or integrate with these connections.
Electrical wiring for outlets, equipment, or lighting integrated into the servery counter must be roughed in prior to installation to avoid retrofitting.
The base servery counter structure must be in place before countertops, sinks, or final surface finishes can be applied or installed.
The pass-through window requires a framed rough opening in the wall to be installed into; without this structural preparation, the window unit has no support or defined cavity.
Exterior wall sheathing must be in place to provide the structural backing and weather-resistive barrier before the window is set into the opening.
The weather-resistive barrier (house wrap) must be applied around the rough opening to ensure proper water management and flashing integration with the window unit.
After the window is placed in the opening, the perimeter must be flashed and sealed to prevent water intrusion and air leakage; this cannot be done prior to window installation.

Interior casing, sill, and trim work around the pass-through window typically occurs after the window is set to achieve a finished appearance, though in some sequences trim could be partially pre-installed.
The communal dining table must be placed on a stable, level floor surface; the floor slab provides the necessary structural base.
The building foundation must be complete to ensure structural integrity before installing any interior components like the dining table.
Chairs and seating must be positioned around the table after the table is installed to ensure proper alignment and spacing.
It is a soft preference to set the table and add decorations after installation to avoid clutter during installation work.
Completing wall finishing (painting, plastering) before table installation reduces the risk of dust and damage to the table, though the table could be installed earlier if needed.
The concrete slab provides a stable, level base for bench seating; benches cannot be installed until the foundation is poured and cured.
Anchor bolts must be set into the concrete foundation before benches can be bolted down securely.
Benches are typically installed before safety rails to avoid obstruction, but this is a preferred sequencing rather than a strict physical necessity.
Any final coating or sealing of surrounding surfaces should be done after bench installation to ensure full coverage and avoid damage to the benches.
Tray rails must be supported by building columns; columns provide the primary vertical support structure required before any horizontal tray rail components can be mounted.
Steel beams and framework must be in place to provide attachment points and support brackets for the tray rail system.
The overhead conveyor track defines the path above which tray rails are aligned; tray rails must follow the same routing and clearances established by the conveyor.
Trays can only be loaded onto and tested on the rail system after the rails are fully installed, aligned, and secured.
Final integration of the tray transport system with conveyor drives and control systems requires the physical tray rail infrastructure to be in place for end-to-end commissioning.
The building shell and structural elements (walls, roof, floor slab) must be complete to provide a weather-tight enclosure before any internal fit-out work can commence.

predecessor: Rough-In of MEP Services (Mechanical, Electrical, Plumbing)
rationale: Ductwork, conduit, and pipework for HVAC, electrical, and plumbing must be installed within walls and ceilings before these surfaces are closed up with finishes.
The spatial fit-out (flooring, wall finishes, ceiling) must be completed to provide a clean, level substrate before heavy kitchen equipment is brought in and installed.

successor: Final Cleaning & Commissioning of Eating Space
rationale: All fit-out dust, debris, and construction activity must be finished before the space can be thoroughly cleaned, commissioned, and handed over for use.

While it is strongly preferred to place furniture after finishes are complete to avoid damage and allow proper installation, some fixtures could theoretically be installed concurrently with careful coordination.
Structural steel framework must be in place before mechanical rough-in can begin, as ductwork, piping, and equipment are supported by or routed through the structural frame.
The floor slab or deck must be poured and cured to provide the base for mechanical equipment and routing of underground or in-slab conduits and drains for the catering area.
Electrical rough-in is typically coordinated alongside mechanical rough-in, but in some sequences electrical is completed first to avoid clashes; this is a soft preference for workflow efficiency.
Mechanical ductwork, piping, and equipment must be installed and inspected before being enclosed within walls, ceilings, and insulation.
Catering kitchen equipment (ovens, hoods, refrigeration) requires mechanical connections (gas, water, ventilation) that must be roughed-in prior to final equipment placement and hookup.
Site must be properly graded, drained, and cleared before hygiene inspection can verify compliance with sanitation and drainage requirements.
Potable water supply must be operational for hygiene facilities; inspection verifies water quality and availability meets health standards.
Proper sewage and wastewater systems must be in place to ensure sanitary conditions before health inspection can be conducted.
Sanitary facilities (toilets, handwashing stations, showers) must be physically complete to be inspected for health code compliance.
Proper ventilation systems must be installed to ensure indoor air quality meets health and hygiene standards before inspection.
Health and hygiene compliance must be verified and approved before applying for an occupancy permit, as it is a prerequisite regulatory requirement.
The building cannot be handed over or commissioned for use until health and hygiene compliance has been formally confirmed.
While not a hard physical constraint, health inspection findings often generate corrective items that should be completed before final close-out for quality assurance.
Inspection of plumbing fixtures, drainage, and ventilation must occur before final finishes are applied (e.g., sealing walls around pipes) to allow access for any required remedial works.
A stable, level foundation and prepared site are physically required to support the modular workstation cluster structure.
Underground or in-slab conduit runs for power, data cabling, and HVAC must be roughed in before the workstation cluster is placed to avoid costly retrofitting.
Once the workstation cluster is installed in its final position, the pre-run utility lines can be terminated and connected to the cluster's internal wiring.
The cluster structure must be fully assembled and in place before installing desktop equipment, monitors, chairs, and other workstation furnishings.
Installation, connections, and fit-out must be complete before the workstation cluster can be inspected, tested, and commissioned for use.
Furniture suite must be placed on a finished, level floor surface to ensure stability and proper alignment.
Room boundaries and wall-mounted components (if any) must be in place before positioning the furniture suite to ensure correct fit and clearance.
Power and data outlets must be roughed-in to the correct locations before the furniture suite is placed, as the suite may cover or integrate with these services.
Audio-visual and computer equipment can only be installed on or within the furniture suite after it is fully assembled and positioned in the room.
Soft preference: decorative items and loose accessories are typically placed after the main furniture to avoid damage and allow proper arrangement, though reordering is possible.
Floor finishing (e.g., tiling, carpet, or screeding) must be completed before furniture is installed to prevent damage to finished floors and to ensure furniture sits level on a completed surface.
Wall painting and finishing must be completed before furniture fit-out to avoid paint splatters and dust settling on new furniture, and to allow unobstructed access to walls for painting.

Ceiling work (including suspended ceilings, lighting fixtures, and MEP services above) must be finished before furniture installation to prevent debris falling onto furniture and to allow access for overhead work.
Electrical, plumbing, and HVAC rough-in work (first fix) must be completed before furniture is placed, as walls and floors need to be open for conduit, piping, and ductwork installation.

Furniture fit-out must be completed before final cleaning and building commissioning, as furniture installation generates dust and debris, and commissioning activities (e.g., system testing) require all furnishings to be in place.

Soft preference: decorative items such as artwork, plants, and accessories are typically installed after furniture to coordinate the overall interior design, though some accessories could theoretically be placed beforehand.
Furniture must be completely installed and secured before occupants can move in and begin using the space, as furniture is essential for functional occupancy.
Structural framing must be in place to provide a substrate for the feature wall installation.
All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work within the wall cavity must be completed before enclosing the wall with the feature finish.
The feature wall is typically a finish layer that requires a smooth, level substrate such as drywall or plaster to be installed and finished first.
Flooring is often installed before wall finish work to avoid damaging the feature wall, but the order can be reversed if careful sequencing is planned.
Feature wall installation creates joints and edges that need to be caulked, sealed, and painted for a finished appearance.
Any applied brand graphics, decals, or signage panels require the feature wall surface to be fully installed and finished before application.
Furniture and millwork can only be placed against or fastened to the feature wall after the wall itself is complete.
The feature wall must be fully installed, finished, and clean before the final quality inspection and punch list walkthrough.
Flooring (carpet, tile, wood) must be fully installed and cured before soft furnishings like chairs, sofas, and rugs are placed, to avoid damage to the floor and to provide a stable, clean base.
Walls must be painted and finished before soft furnishings are brought in to prevent dust, paint splatters, and debris from soiling upholstery and fabrics.
