Ceiling work (painting, texturing, lighting installation) must be completed to avoid dust and debris falling onto finished soft furnishings and seating.
Seating and soft furnishings are a final furnishing step; once in place, the space requires final cleaning and commissioning before occupancy or handover.
All seating and soft furnishings must be installed before occupants or users can move into the space, as these items are essential for the functional use of the building.
The structural shell (walls, roof, floor slab) must be finished before any interior fitout work can commence, as fitout requires a weathertight and structurally stable enclosure.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work (conduits, pipes, ducts within walls/ceilings) must be completed before finishing works like drywall, ceiling installation, and reception desk construction, to avoid rework and damage.

Reception fitout (installation of reception desk, cabinetry, built-in furniture) must be completed before final decorative finishes such as painting, floor covering, and signage installation to ensure a clean, finished appearance and avoid damaging delicate finishes.
The fitout (fixed elements like desk, counters, partitions) must be complete before loose furniture, decorative items, and equipment are brought in, to prevent congestion, damage, and rework.

While commissioning of building systems can partially occur earlier, final integration testing of lighting, AV, and data systems in the reception area is best performed after fitout is complete to ensure all components are properly installed and connected.
The reception desk must be placed on a finished, level floor surface to ensure stability and proper alignment. Installing the floor after the desk would require moving or working around the desk.
Walls behind and adjacent to the reception desk need to be finished (plastered, painted, wallpapered) before the desk is installed, as the desk would obstruct access to the walls.

Electrical wiring, data cabling, and outlet boxes for the reception area must be roughed in and routed to the desk location before the desk is placed, to avoid having to fish wires around or through the installed desk.
After the desk is physically installed, electricians and data technicians can connect the final outlets, switches, and data ports that are integrated into or mounted on the desk.

Soft preference: While some furniture and decorations can be placed before the desk, it is generally more efficient and avoids rearrangement to complete the desk installation first, then arrange the remaining reception area furniture and decorative elements.
Rough electrical wiring must be complete to provide power supply connections and junction boxes for feature lighting fixtures.
Ceiling or mounting surface must be in place to physically support and anchor feature lighting fixtures.
Final electrical connections, switch plates, and trim work can only be completed after feature lighting fixtures are physically installed.
Ceiling painting or finishing is typically done after lighting installation to avoid paint damage to fixtures, though some painters prefer to paint before installation.
Final inspection and system testing require all feature lighting to be fully installed and operational before sign-off.
The building structural frame and shell must be complete to provide the rough opening and structural support for automatic entrance doors to be installed.
The rough opening must be framed, prepared, and measured to the correct dimensions before the door unit can be set in place.
Electrical power supply wiring and conduit must be roughed-in to the door location before the automatic door operator and sensor systems can be connected and powered.

successor: Flooring & Finish Work Adjacent to Entrance
rationale: Final flooring and finish work adjacent to the entrance should be completed after door installation to avoid damaging the door or obstructing installation, and to allow proper alignment with finished floor height.

After the door unit is physically installed, final electrical connections, sensor calibration, and safety testing/commissioning of the automatic operation must be performed to ensure proper and safe functionality.

predecessor: Wall Mounting Bracket / Support Structure Installation
rationale: The display must have a secure mounting structure in place before it can be attached.
Power outlets, conduit, and data cabling must be run to the display location before the display is mounted and connected.

predecessor: Overhead or In-Wall Cable Tray Installation
rationale: Cable pathways for HDMI, power, and control wiring need to be in place before final display connection.
Dust and debris from finishing work can damage the display; the wall/ceiling area should be clean and finished before installing sensitive electronic equipment.
The display must be physically installed before it can be powered on, configured, and calibrated as part of the overall audiovisual system.

successor: Content Management System (CMS) Setup and Testing
rationale: The physical display must be in place and operational before content can be loaded, tested, and scheduled on it.
User training is typically done after installation, though training could theoretically occur before the display is installed using a mock setup.
The frame provides the structural foundation for the waiting chair; without it, the chair cannot support any other components.
The seat cushion must be prepared before it can be attached to the waiting chair frame.
The backrest cushion must be fabricated before it can be installed onto the chair frame.
Armrests must be manufactured before they can be mounted to the sides of the waiting chair frame.
The chair must be fully assembled before quality control checks can be performed to ensure it meets specifications.
Final upholstery and finishing touches can only be applied after the complete chair structure is assembled.
The queue management barrier requires a stable, level foundation or floor slab to be anchored to, so the foundation/slab must be completed first.

successor: Queue Management System Calibration and Testing
rationale: The barrier must be physically installed before the queue management system (e.g., sensors, displays, ticket dispensers) can be calibrated, tested, and integrated with the barrier structure.

While signage can be partially installed beforehand, final placement and alignment of queue-direction signs and wayfinding elements should follow barrier installation to ensure accurate positioning relative to the actual barrier layout.
Row seating systems are typically installed on a finished concrete slab or structural deck, which provides the stable base needed for anchoring the seating support frames.
The row seating structural frame and support rails must be fully erected before individual seats can be mounted onto the system.

successor: Overhead Clearance Verification / MEP Rough-In Above
rationale: Once the row seating system is installed, the final vertical sightline and clearance dimensions are established, allowing overhead ductwork, lighting, and sprinklers to be precisely coordinated above the seating area.
The seating system defines the aisle pathways; floor finishes are laid after the seating frames are in place to ensure precise alignment with the rows and aisles.
Handrails and guardrails at the ends of rows or along stepped aisles must align with the installed seating rows, so they are installed after the seating system is in position.

predecessor: Install electrical conduit and wiring to display location
rationale: Power supply must be available at the mounting location before the display can be installed and connected.

predecessor: Fabricate and install mounting bracket/frame for display
rationale: A structural support bracket or frame must be in place to securely hold the display unit.
The display must be physically mounted before network and data cables can be connected to it.

successor: Power on and test Digital Display / Ticketing Board
rationale: Both power and data connections must be established before the unit can be powered on and its functionality verified.

successor: Configure software and upload content to display
rationale: While software configuration can be done remotely after mounting, it is standard practice to complete physical installation before final content setup and testing on-site.
The site must be prepared and leveled before any ticketing equipment can be installed.
A stable concrete foundation or pad is required to support the ticket dispenser unit.
Power supply conduits and wiring must be run to the dispenser location before the unit can be connected.
The dispenser must be physically mounted and in place before electrical connections and testing can be performed.
The dispenser hardware must be installed before it can be integrated with the central ticketing system and software configured.
End-to-end testing of ticket dispensing is typically done after installation, though could theoretically be simulated earlier.
Coat hooks and luggage storage units are typically mounted on walls; the wall surface must be finished (e.g., painted or clad) before fixtures can be securely attached.
Installing storage elements first allows them to be integrated into the overall interior design, but it is a soft preference as styling can also work around existing installations.
It is generally preferred to install flooring before wall-mounted storage to avoid damage to flooring from ladders/scaffolding, but not a hard physical constraint.
If any electrical work (e.g., wiring for lighting near the storage area) is needed, it must be completed before mounting storage units that could block access to walls.
A stable, level foundation (e.g., concrete pad) must be prepared before the charging station unit can be physically mounted and anchored.
Electrical conduits and trenches from the main power source to the charging station location must be dug and laid before the station can be connected to the grid.

predecessor: Main Electrical Panel and Meter Installation
rationale: The dedicated circuit breaker, panel capacity upgrade, and utility meter must be installed to provide adequate electrical supply to the charging station.

successor: Parking Lot Line Painting and Signage
rationale: Charging station must be fully installed, powered on, and tested to confirm functionality before marking EV-only parking spaces and installing directional/regulatory signage.

successor: Network Connectivity Setup and Software Activation
rationale: Physical hardware commissioning must be complete before network configuration, payment system activation, and over-the-air firmware updates can be applied to the station.

The building structure (columns, beams, slabs) must be complete to provide the physical enclosure and load-bearing support for interior finishes. Applying finishes before structural completion would result in damage or rework.
The building must be watertight before interior finishes are applied to prevent water damage to walls, ceilings, and flooring materials.

predecessor: External Wall and Window Installation (Building Envelope)
rationale: The building envelope (external walls, windows, doors) must be sealed to protect interior finishes from weather exposure and to create a controlled environment for finishing work.

predecessor: MEP Rough-In (Mechanical, Electrical, Plumbing First Fix)
rationale: Concealed services (conduits, pipes, ducts, cables) must be installed within walls, ceilings, and floors before these are closed up with plasterboard, cladding, or finishes.

successor: Final Fixing and Installation of Sanitaryware/FF&E
rationale: Interior finishes (painting, tiling, flooring) must be completed before installing fixtures, fittings, and equipment to avoid damaging finished surfaces during installation.

successor: Commissioning and Testing of MEP Systems
rationale: While commissioning can partly overlap, final commissioning and balancing of HVAC, electrical, and plumbing systems is best performed after finishes are complete to ensure accurate testing under final conditions and to avoid dust or debris affecting sensitive equipment.
All interior finishing works must be substantially complete before the building can be handed over to the client or occupants for use.
A stable, level foundation or slab must be completed before seating can be installed to ensure structural support and proper anchoring.
Utility lines running beneath the slab must be installed and inspected before the slab is poured; seating cannot be placed until this underground work is completed.

While seating is typically installed after the building structure is framed, in some projects temporary seating may be placed earlier; generally the superstructure should be complete to protect seating from weather and debris.

Overhead mechanical, electrical, and plumbing installations must be completed before seating is installed, as accessing ceiling-mounted systems becomes difficult or impossible once permanent seating is in place.
Final floor finishing work adjacent to or beneath seating areas is often performed after installation to avoid damaging finished floors; however, prefinished floors may allow concurrent work.

successor: Final Electrical / AV / Data Connections at Seats
rationale: Power outlets, data ports, or audiovisual connections integrated into or beneath seats must be wired and terminated after the seating units are physically installed.
Final touch-up painting and wall finishing adjacent to seating rows is often completed after installation to address any damage caused during the seating installation process.
The suspended ceiling grid must be attached to the overhead structural framing or roof structure. Without the structural support above, there is nothing to hang the ceiling from.

predecessor: MEP Rough-In (Mechanical, Electrical, Plumbing) Above Ceiling
rationale: Ductwork, piping, conduit, and wiring that will run above the suspended ceiling must be installed before the ceiling grid and tiles are placed, as access to the plenum space is blocked once the ceiling is closed in.
Fire sprinkler piping and heads located in the ceiling plenum must be roughed in and tested prior to ceiling installation to avoid rework and ensure fire safety compliance.

While wall finishing can be done before ceiling installation, it is often more efficient to complete ceiling grid installation first so that the ceiling line provides a clean stopping point for wall painting, reducing edge detailing work.

successor: Final MEP Trim-Out (Lighting, Diffusers, Speakers, Sensors)
rationale: Ceiling-mounted devices such as recessed lights, air diffusers, speakers, and smoke detectors are physically installed into and through the ceiling grid/tiles; the ceiling must be in place to receive and support these fixtures.

Flooring is typically installed after ceiling work to avoid dust and debris from ceiling cutting and handling falling onto freshly finished floors, though this is a constructability preference rather than a physical necessity.

The structural frame (including columns, beams, and floor slabs) must be in place to provide load-bearing support and establish the building's primary grid before non-load-bearing glazed partition walls can be installed.
The floor slab must be finished and leveled to provide a stable, true base for the glazed partition wall's bottom track or channel fixing.

predecessor: Overhead Services Rough-In (MEP rough-in above ceiling)
rationale: Major mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work in the ceiling zone (ductwork, piping, cable trays) must be completed before partition walls are erected; otherwise access for overhead installations would be blocked.

successor: Final Finishing and Decorating (paint, wall coverings)
rationale: Glazed partition walls with their frames must be fully installed before adjacent wall finishes and painting can be completed, as the partitions define room boundaries and finishing works need to abut the partition frames.

It is a soft preference to install floor coverings after glazed partitions to avoid damaging finished flooring during partition installation; however, in some sequencing, flooring can be laid first and partitions installed on top with appropriate protection.
The solid partition wall must be built on a completed floor slab to provide a stable load-bearing base.

The main structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) must be in place before non-load-bearing or load-bearing partition walls are installed, as the partitions often tie into or are supported by the frame.

Ideally, major horizontal ductwork and piping runs above the ceiling or within wall zones should be roughed-in before walls are built to avoid rework, but this can sometimes be done after with core drilling.
The partition wall surface must be fully constructed before plastering, rendering, or drywall finishing can be applied to it.

successor: MEP Final Connections (Electrical Outlets, Switches, Plumbing Fixtures)
rationale: Electrical and plumbing fixtures that are mounted on or through the wall require the wall to be in place before final connections, backboxes, and trim can be installed.
If the solid partition wall contains door or window openings, the wall structure must be completed and the rough opening framed before the door/window frame can be installed.
The rough opening for the sliding or folding door must be framed to the correct dimensions before the door can be installed.
The door frame or jamb must be in place to receive and support the sliding or folding door components.
Weather barriers, flashing, and sealants around the opening must be installed before the door to prevent water intrusion behind the door system.
Interior trim and casing around the door is typically installed after the door is in place for a finished appearance, though it is a soft preference as it could be done concurrently in some cases.
Hardware such as handles, locks, and sliding mechanisms must be installed after the door panels are hung to ensure proper alignment and function.
Final paint or finish touches around the door area are typically done after installation to avoid damaging the finishes during the door installation process.
The acoustic door set requires a properly installed frame to fit into; the door cannot be hung without the frame being in place first.
The rough opening must be framed and sized correctly before the acoustic door set can be installed to ensure proper fit and acoustic sealing.
Acoustic sealants and perimeter gaskets are applied after the door set is in place to ensure airtight and soundproof sealing around the frame.
Hardware such as hinges, handles, locks, and door closers must be fitted after the door set is installed into the frame.
Testing of sound transmission rating (STC) is typically performed after installation to verify acoustic performance, though it could theoretically be deferred.
The mounting bracket must be securely installed on the wall before the AV display screen or smartboard can be attached to it.
Electrical wiring and power outlets must be roughed in behind the wall to supply power to the AV display screen / smartboard.
Conduit for HDMI, data, and control cables must be installed in the wall before the screen is mounted, as access is difficult afterward.
Cables (HDMI, USB, network, power) must be connected to the installed screen after it is mounted and before calibration or use.
The display screen must be physically installed before it can be powered on, calibrated, and tested for proper operation.
The projector must be mounted to a structurally sound ceiling grid or suspension system; the grid must be in place before mounting.
Power and data cabling must be run to the projector location before the projector is physically installed.
Final electrical and data connections (plugging in, terminating cables) can only be done after the projector is physically mounted.
The projection screen position must be aligned with the mounted projector; the projector installation determines screen placement for correct alignment.
System calibration (focus, keystone correction, image alignment) can only occur after the projector is physically installed and connected.
The motorised projection screen must be securely mounted to a ceiling or structural support; the support structure must be in place first to bear the screen's weight.

predecessor: Run electrical conduit and wiring to screen location
rationale: The motorised screen requires electrical power for its motor; wiring and conduit must be installed before the screen can be connected.
Ceiling finishing work (e.g., painting, plastering) should be completed before mounting the screen to avoid damage to finished surfaces and to ensure a clean installation.

successor: Connect and test screen motor and controls
rationale: After the screen is physically mounted, the electrical connections, motor testing, and control system integration can be performed.

While not a strict physical constraint, it is best practice to install the projection screen first so that the projector can be positioned and calibrated relative to the screen's final location and size.
Electrical rough-in wiring must be completed and stubbed out to the floor box locations before the floor boxes can be installed and connected.
Conduit runs for data and power must be laid in the slab or underfloor system before floor boxes can be mounted and terminated.

predecessor: Concrete Slab Pour / Underfloor Deck Completion
rationale: The floor slab or raised access floor must be finished to provide the structural substrate for floor box installation.
Floor boxes are set flush with the finished floor; floor coverings must be cut and fitted around the box lids after installation.
Power and data connections to the floor box receptacles are made during final trim-out after the box is physically mounted and the floor surface is complete.

Wireless Access Points require network (Ethernet) cabling to be run to their location to provide data connectivity; the cable must be installed and terminated before the AP can be mounted and connected.
Wireless Access Points are typically mounted on ceilings or above ceiling tiles; the ceiling grid or mounting structure must be in place to provide a secure attachment point.
Power supply (e.g., PoE switch or dedicated electrical outlet) must be roughed in and available to power the Wireless Access Point.

successor: Wireless Access Point Configuration and Testing
rationale: The physical device must be mounted and connected to the network before it can be configured, assigned an IP address, and tested for coverage and connectivity.

If the AP is recessed or installed above ceiling tiles, the tiles can be placed after the AP is mounted; however, this is a soft preference as some installations allow tiles to be cut and fitted around the AP simultaneously.
Electrical cabling and junction boxes must be installed in the ceiling prior to mounting downlight housings, as the wiring needs to be accessible and routed before fixtures are placed.
The ceiling surface must be complete and finished so that holes for recessed lights can be cut accurately and the trim rings can sit flush against the finished ceiling.
Downlights should be installed before final painting so that any gaps around trim rings can be caulked and painted over for a seamless finish.
The recessed housings must be in place before trims and bulbs can be inserted and connected.

successor: Final Electrical Trim-Out and Switch Connection
rationale: Once the downlight housings are mounted, the final wiring connections at switches and the installation of dimmers or controls can be completed and tested.
Motorised roller blinds must be mounted onto or adjacent to window frames; windows must be installed first to provide the structural mounting surface.
Motorised blinds require electrical power connections; wiring and conduit must be run and accessible before the blinds can be connected.
Blinds are typically installed after walls and ceilings are finished and painted to avoid damage from construction dust and debris.
It is preferable to complete final painting and trim work after blinds to avoid paint splatter or damage, though physically possible in reverse order.
After motorised blinds are physically installed and connected, they must be programmed, calibrated, and tested as part of the building automation system.

predecessor: Rough-in for VAV boxes and diffusers
rationale: Electrical and control wiring rough-in must be completed before the diffuser/grille can be physically installed and connected.
The duct system must be in place to receive and supply air to the VAV diffuser/grille; the diffuser connects directly to the ductwork.
The diffuser/grille is typically mounted into or supported by the ceiling grid; the grid must go in after to integrate around the diffuser.

successor: Final duct pressure testing and balancing
rationale: System balancing and air-flow testing can be performed more accurately once all diffusers/grilles are installed and sealed, though partial testing could be done earlier.
Finished ceiling surfaces are installed after diffusers/grilles to ensure a clean interface and avoid damage to the ceiling finish.
The CO2 / Air Quality Sensor requires electrical power and data connectivity. Wiring and conduit must be in place before the sensor can be physically installed and connected.

predecessor: Mount electrical backbox or junction box
rationale: The sensor is typically mounted onto or into a backbox or junction box that provides structural support and houses connections. The box must be installed first.
If the sensor is ceiling-mounted, the ceiling grid must be in place to provide a mounting surface and proper positioning.

successor: Test and commission CO2 / Air Quality Sensor
rationale: The sensor must be physically installed and connected before it can be powered on, calibrated, and tested for correct operation.
The sensor must be installed and communicating before its data can be integrated into the BMS for monitoring and control.
Power supply and data cabling must be run to the panel location before the panel can be physically mounted and connected.
The panel is typically surface-mounted or recessed into a wall; the wall structure must be ready and finished to support the panel.
The panel requires network connectivity to communicate with the booking system; network drops and switches must be in place.
The physical panel must be mounted and powered before its software and booking interface can be configured and tested.
End-to-end testing of room booking functionality requires the panel hardware to be installed and operational.

The conference table must be placed on a finished floor surface to ensure stability and proper alignment. Installing the table before floor finishing would damage the floor or require the table to be moved.
The conference room walls and ceiling must be completed before the table is brought in, as the table is large and needs to be maneuvered into the room through finished doorways.
Power outlets, data ports, and conduit for conference table connectivity (power, AV, network) must be roughed in before the table is placed, as the table may cover floor boxes or wall outlets.

Audio-visual equipment such as monitors, projectors, and integrated conferencing systems are often mounted in relation to the table position. The table must be in place to determine exact sight lines and cable routing.
While chairs can be placed after the table is in position for optimal spacing, it is a soft preference as chairs could theoretically be placed beforehand and moved aside.
The flooring must be fully installed and cured before placing chairs to avoid damaging the floor surface and to ensure chairs can be safely moved into the room.
Painting and wall finishing should be completed before bringing in chairs to prevent dust, paint splatters, or chemical fumes from contaminating the upholstery.
Any in-floor or in-wall electrical/data wiring work must be finished before chairs are placed, as the work areas need to be clear and accessible.

Chairs are typically positioned around the meeting table; the table must be installed after or concurrently with chairs to ensure proper spacing and alignment, but chairs are usually placed first around the perimeter to then fit the table in.
The room cannot be used for meetings until all seating (chairs) are in place and arranged, as seating is essential for occupancy.
The room must be enclosed with finished drywall before installing fixed millwork like a credenza, as the unit needs to be placed against finished walls.
Flooring must be complete before placing heavy furniture like a credenza to avoid damaging new floors and to ensure the unit sits level on the finished surface.
Electrical outlets and wiring behind the credenza must be roughed in and inspected before the unit is installed, as the credenza will block access to walls.

The credenza/side storage unit serves as a supporting piece of furniture; the main desk or workstation is typically positioned in relation to it, so the credenza should be placed first to establish the layout.

Once the credenza is placed, final connections to built-in power/data modules integrated into the unit can be made; this is a soft preference because workstations could be wired before if access is designed differently.
Whiteboards require a finished wall surface for mounting. Without wall framing and drywall, there is no structural backing to attach the whiteboard.
Wall must be painted or finished before whiteboard installation to avoid damaging the whiteboard surface or requiring removal later.
While not physically required, it is practical to install whiteboards before the room is occupied to avoid disruption and dust affecting other furnishings.

successor: Electrical rough-in and lighting above whiteboard area
rationale: If whiteboard is to be used for presentation, lighting must be positioned to avoid glare. However, electrical rough-in typically happens earlier; the final lighting adjustment can occur after whiteboard is mounted to ensure proper illumination without shadows or glare.
Installing whiteboards is typically one of the finishing touches before a space is inspected and approved for use.
The floor slab/deck provides the structural base upon which demountable partitions are mounted and aligned.
Electrical rough-in within the wall zones must be completed before enclosing the space with partitions to avoid rework.
Partitions must be installed before their surfaces can be painted or finished.
Doors and related hardware are fitted into the partition frames after the partitions are erected.
The building's structural frame and shell must be completed to provide an enclosed, stable environment before any interior fit-out and furniture work can commence.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work (e.g., ductwork, piping, wiring in walls and ceilings) must be installed before enclosing walls and installing furniture, as accessing these services afterward would require destructive rework.
The building must be waterproofed and roofed to protect interior finishes and furniture from water damage before fit-out activities proceed.

After furniture is installed and spaces are defined, final trim-out of electrical outlets, switches, and commissioning of systems can be completed to ensure proper integration with the occupied layout.
All furniture and fit-out must be in place before final cleaning and subsequent handover of the building to the client, as cleaning is the last step before occupancy.

The building structure must be complete and watertight before M&E (Mechanical & Electrical) fit-out can commence, as M&E services are installed within the structural framework (walls, floors, ceilings) and require the structural shell to be in place.
The building envelope must be closed to protect M&E equipment and materials from weather damage during installation. Sensitive electrical components, ductwork, and insulation must be kept dry.
Conduits, sleeves, and embedded conduits for electrical and mechanical services must be cast into slabs and walls during structural works before the main M&E fit-out can proceed.
M&E services such as wiring, piping, ducting, and conduits must be installed within walls and above ceilings before these areas can be enclosed with drywall or plasterboard and finished.
All M&E components must be physically installed and connected before they can be tested, commissioned, and balanced for proper operation.

Final internal finishes such as painting, flooring installation, and decorative elements must be done after M&E fit-out to avoid damage to finishes during M&E installation work and to allow proper integration of fixtures like switches, outlets, and diffusers.

Snagging and post-occupancy commissioning can only begin after the building is substantially complete, as these activities involve identifying and rectifying remaining defects, testing systems, and fine-tuning performance in a largely finished building.
Final inspection and testing of building systems (MEP, fire safety, etc.) must be completed before post-occupancy commissioning can verify performance under actual occupancy conditions.
All snagging items must be resolved and commissioning verified before the building can be formally handed over to the owner/occupant and a certificate of occupancy issued.
The project closeout and final account process typically requires that all snagging and commissioning activities are complete to confirm contractual obligations have been met.
Post-occupancy commissioning provides baseline performance data and defect resolution that must be completed before transitioning to long-term facilities management and warranty periods.
The glazed screen requires a structural frame to be in place to support and secure the glass panels.
Glass panels and associated materials must be procured and delivered before installation can take place.
Waterproofing of the surrounding structure must be completed to prevent moisture ingress behind the glazed screen.
After the glazed screen is installed, joints and edges must be sealed to ensure weather tightness.
Interior finishes such as drywall or trim around the screen are typically done after the screen is in place to ensure clean transitions, though in some sequences work could proceed in parallel.
Low partition walls are typically non-structural and are installed after the main structural or full-height partition walls are in place, as they often attach to or abut these primary walls.
Low partition walls require a finished or prepared floor surface to be built upon, ensuring proper alignment and stability.
While low walls can be built before final flooring, it is often preferred to install flooring after walls to allow for clean edges and avoid damaging finished floor surfaces during wall construction.
Finishing and painting must occur after the wall is fully installed to ensure a seamless and completed appearance.
Any rough-in work for services within or behind the low partition wall must be completed before the wall is built, as access would be obstructed after installation.
The storage wall unit requires a level and stable floor surface to be installed upon. The floor slab must be completed first to provide proper support and alignment.
The storage wall unit typically attaches to or sits against the wall structure. Wall framing must be in place to provide structural support and anchoring points for the unit.
If the storage wall unit includes built-in lighting or electrical outlets, rough electrical wiring must be completed behind the walls before the unit is installed to avoid rework or access issues.

While painting can be done before or after, it is often preferred to paint the wall behind the unit first, then install the unit, and do touch-up painting afterward to avoid getting paint on the unit.
Baseboards and floor trim should be installed after the storage wall unit so that the trim can be cut and fitted neatly around the unit's base for a clean finish.

predecessor: Install wall framing and backing plates
successor: Install Data and Power Outlet Cluster
rationale: The outlet cluster must be mounted to wall framing or backing plates for structural support.

predecessor: Run electrical conduit and wiring to outlet location
successor: Install Data and Power Outlet Cluster
rationale: Electrical and data cables must be pulled to the location before the outlet box/cluster can be installed and connected.

successor: Install Data and Power Outlet Cluster
rationale: Typically outlets are installed after drywall is hung and cut out, but in some construction sequences they can be roughed in before sheathing.

predecessor: Install Data and Power Outlet Cluster
successor: Connect and terminate wiring at outlet cluster
rationale: The physical outlet unit must be in place before electricians can terminate wires and attach receptacles.

predecessor: Install Data and Power Outlet Cluster
rationale: Faceplates are screwed onto the installed outlet cluster as the final trim step.

predecessor: Install Data and Power Outlet Cluster
successor: Commissioning and testing of power/data circuits
rationale: Circuits must be fully terminated at the outlet before they can be energized and tested for continuity and functionality.

predecessor: Overhead Mechanical, Electrical, and Plumbing (MEP) Rough-In
rationale: All ductwork, piping, conduit, and wiring must be installed in the plenum space above the ceiling before the ceiling grid and tiles are placed, as they would be inaccessible afterward without removing the ceiling.
The overhead structural slab or roof deck must be complete to provide the supporting substrate from which the ceiling grid will be suspended via hanger wires.

Spray-applied fireproofing on the structure above must be finished before enclosing the plenum with a suspended ceiling, as the ceiling would obstruct access for fireproofing application and inspection.

Although painting can be done before or after ceiling installation, it is often preferred to complete wall finishes first to avoid damaging freshly painted walls during ceiling work and to allow the ceiling to cover any imperfect cut lines at the wall-to-ceiling interface.

Flooring is typically installed after the ceiling to prevent dust and debris from ceiling work (cutting tiles, drilling anchors) from soiling newly laid floor finishes; this is a soft preference for quality and cleanliness rather than a physical necessity.
The floor plan must be designed first to determine the number and placement of ergonomic chairs needed in the office layout.
The floor must be prepared (cleaned, leveled, carpeted) before placing ergonomic chairs to ensure stability and protect the flooring material.
The ergonomic chair must be fully assembled and available before the workstation setup can be declared complete, as the chair is a core component of the workstation.
The chair must be procured and delivered to the site before it can be unpacked and assembled.
While not physically required, it is preferable to complete electrical wiring first to avoid moving the chair later and to ensure cables are routed properly without interfering with chair placement.
The height-adjustable desk must be placed on a finished floor surface to ensure stability and proper leveling. Installing the desk before floor finishing would require moving the desk later.
Electrical outlets and cabling for the desk's motorized height adjustment mechanism must be roughed in before the desk is installed and connected.
After the desk is physically installed, cables for power and data can be routed and managed through the desk's cable tray system.
Computers, monitors, and peripherals can only be placed on the desk after it is fully assembled and installed in its final position.
The height-adjustable functionality must be tested and calibrated after the desk is installed to ensure proper operation before user occupancy.
The structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) and core elements (staircases, lift shafts) must be complete to provide the substrate and enclosed spaces for fit-out and joinery installation.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in (conduits, pipes, ductwork within walls/ceilings) must be installed before joinery and finishes to avoid rework and to allow services to be concealed behind finished surfaces.
The building envelope (roof, exterior walls, windows/glazing) must be watertight to protect sensitive joinery materials (timber, MDF, veneers) from moisture damage during installation.

Joinery installation (cabinets, wardrobes, wall panels, skirting, architraves) must be in place so that painting and finishing trades can complete cut-ins, touch-ups, and uniform coating around the installed joinery.

Floor joinery such as skirting, stair nosing, and base cabinets must be installed before finished floor coverings to allow proper detailing, expansion gaps, and a clean interface between floor finishes and joinery.
Structural framing and the building shell must be complete to provide enclosed spaces where MEP rough-in work can be performed, and to support the mounting of conduits, ducts, and pipes.
Concrete slabs or decks must be poured and cured before MEP rough-in can begin, as floor penetrations and embedded conduits rely on the finished slab surface.
Structural overhead inspections must be passed to ensure that the ceiling grid and supports are safe and ready for MEP trades to install overhead conduit, ductwork, and piping.
MEP rough-in must be completed and inspected before drywall and ceiling grids are installed, as these finishes would permanently conceal the MEP work and make rework extremely costly.
Rough-in of conduit, piping, and ductwork must precede the trim-out phase where outlets, switches, fixtures, diffusers, and terminal devices are installed.
Interior finishes such as painting, flooring, and wall coverings must be fully completed before furniture is brought in to avoid damage to finished surfaces and to ensure proper layout.
The space must be thoroughly cleaned and free of construction dust and debris before furniture installation to protect furnishings and maintain quality.
All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-ins and trim-outs must be finished so that furniture placement does not interfere with access to utilities and so that final connections can be made.
Ceiling grids, tiles, and lighting fixtures must be fully installed before furniture layout to ensure proper clearance, alignment, and that lighting positions are coordinated with workstations.
Furniture commissioning and layout must be completed before the space can be occupied, as furniture placement defines the functional workspace and is necessary for move-in readiness.
The door frame must be installed to provide a structural support and mounting surface for the locking door set.
The door leaf must be hung on its hinges before the locking mechanism can be installed, as the lock interfaces with both the door and frame.
The locking mechanism must be fully installed before testing the door's operation and lock function to verify correct alignment and security.
Final adjustments to the door hardware (e.g., strike plate alignment, latch adjustment) must occur after the locking set is installed to ensure proper fit and function.
The main electrical switchboard supplies power to downstream distribution boards, so it must be installed and energized first to feed the landlord circuit distribution board.

predecessor: Install Conduit and Cable Trays for Landlord Circuits
rationale: Cabling infrastructure must be in place before the distribution board can be connected and terminated.

successor: Test and Commission Landlord Electrical Systems
rationale: Commissioning activities require the distribution board to be physically installed and connected to perform insulation resistance and load tests.

predecessor: Mount Enclosure and Busbars for Distribution Board
rationale: The physical enclosure and internal busbars must be mounted and secured before the distribution board assembly is complete and ready for cable connections.
The furniture package is installed after rough carpentry/framing because walls and structural frameworks must be in place before built-in or room-specific furniture can be positioned and secured.
Painting and wall finishing must be completed before furniture is brought in to avoid dust, paint splatter, and damage to finished furniture surfaces.
Flooring (tile, hardwood, carpet) must be installed before furniture placement to ensure proper coverage under and around furniture items and to prevent scratching or damaging finished floors.
Electrical rough-in and outlet/switch placement must be completed before furniture is installed so that furniture layout can accommodate electrical access points.
After furniture is placed, a final clean and punch list walkthrough is performed to address any damage, adjustments, or touch-ups caused during furniture installation.
Structural works (walls, slabs, columns) must be completed before any internal fit-out can begin, as finishing works require stable structural surfaces to build upon.

predecessor: MEP Rough-In (Mechanical, Electrical, Plumbing - First Fix)
rationale: First-fix MEP installations (conduits, pipes, wiring in walls/ceilings) must be in place before walls are closed up with plasterboard, painting, and final finishes.
Waterproofing of bathrooms, kitchens, and wet areas must be completed and tested before tiling, flooring, and wall finishes are applied.

After painting, flooring, and wall finishes are complete, second-fix electrical (sockets, switches, light fixtures) and plumbing (tapware, sanitaryware) can be installed without damaging finished surfaces.
Built-in wardrobes, kitchen cabinets, and joinery are installed after wall finishes and flooring are complete to ensure accurate fit and to avoid damaging finishes during joinery installation.
Fire safety upgrades such as fire doors, dampers, and sealants require wall and floor openings to be cut and prepared first before installation can proceed.
Electrical cabling for fire alarms and detection systems must be routed within walls and ceilings before firestopping and sealing works are completed.
Fire-rated sealants, intumescent coatings, and firestopping materials must be applied to penetrations before they are covered by final finishes such as plasterboard or ceiling tiles.

Fire detection and alarm devices can only be tested and commissioned after all fire safety upgrade installations (e.g., fire doors, dampers, sealants) are in place to ensure proper system integration.
Regulatory inspection and certification of fire safety compliance must occur after all upgrade works are completed to verify that all fire protection measures meet code requirements.
The property must be acquired and identified as a potential HMO before it can be inspected and assessed for licensing compliance.
A baseline condition survey is needed to understand the current state of the property prior to the formal HMO licensing inspection, ensuring all relevant areas are reviewed.
The formal HMO license application must be submitted to the local authority before the official inspection can be scheduled and conducted.
Any issues or non-compliance items identified during the inspection must be rectified through remedial works before the property can be certified as compliant.
The inspection and compliance check must be completed and passed before the local authority can issue the HMO license.
Structural work must be complete to provide the framework and wall/floor openings through which plumbing pipes and fixtures can be installed.
Existing structures and debris must be cleared from the extension area before any new plumbing installation can begin.
Underslab drainage and water pipes must be laid before the concrete slab is poured; foundations must be in place to support plumbing penetrations.
Plumbing first-fix (pipe runs, drainage) should be completed before electricians install cables and backboxes to avoid clashes and ensure proper sequencing of hidden services.
All concealed plumbing pipes and fittings must be installed and pressure-tested before walls are closed up with plasterboard or plaster.
Walls and structural framing must be in place before electrical wiring can be run through the building cavities and conduit paths.
Conduits, junction boxes, and outlet boxes must be installed and positioned before pulling new wire and extending circuits through them.
Electrical wiring must be completely run and inspected before insulation can be placed over or around it, to avoid fire hazards and ensure code compliance.
All new wiring and circuit extensions must be finalized, secured, and inspected before walls are closed up with drywall.
New or extended circuits must be fully wired to the panel before switches, outlets, and lighting fixtures can be connected and trimmed out.
The physical building or room must be constructed and fitted out before a tenancy agreement or room licence can be issued, as the agreement/licence pertains to a specific existing space.
Design and planning approvals must be in place before the building is constructed, and only after construction can the tenancy agreement be signed for the completed space.
The tenant must have a signed agreement or licence in place before they can legally take possession and move into the premises.

While utilities are often connected before tenancy begins, the formal agreement/licence establishes who will be billed and responsible for utilities, so it typically precedes or coincides with finalising utility arrangements for the specific tenant.
A formal handover and inspection of the property to the tenant normally occurs after the tenancy agreement is signed, to document the condition of the premises at the start of the tenancy.
The timber frame structure requires a stable and level foundation to bear its load. Without completed foundation footings and slab, the timber frame cannot be erected safely or properly anchored.
Site grading, drainage installation, and ground compaction must be completed before any structural framing begins to ensure a stable base and avoid soil movement issues.
The roof structure relies on the timber frame walls and posts for support. The roof cannot be installed until the vertical and horizontal framing members are in place to carry the roof loads.
Exterior sheathing, weather resistive barrier, and cladding require the timber frame to be erected to provide the structural substrate and nailing surface.

Interior partitions and mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work must follow the main timber frame erection because the timber frame defines the primary structural grid and load paths that interior systems must fit within.
A level, structurally sound foundation is required to support and anchor wall panels; panels cannot be erected without a completed substrate.
Where panels are infill between structural bays, the primary steel frame must be erected first to provide the supporting grid.
Services that run through or beneath wall positions must be installed before panels are placed to avoid costly rework.
Wall panels typically need to be in place to support or receive roof elements and to provide lateral stability during roof installation.
Wall enclosures must be completed to allow enclosed interior work; interior trades require the weathertight shell before proceeding.
The loft floor joists or framing must be installed and securely fastened before decking can be laid on top to create the walking surface.
The decking material (e.g. plywood or OSB) must be fully installed to serve as the structural base before any underlayment or subfloor layers are applied over it.
Finish flooring materials such as carpet, laminate, or tile require a complete structural deck as a stable substrate before they can be installed.
Safety railings around the loft opening depend on the finished floor deck as a mounting surface, and workers need a safe walking surface to install rails.

successor: Loft Ceiling Below – Drywall / Finish Work
rationale: The deck provides structural support and a working platform for finishing the ceiling of the space below the loft; any ceiling work below requires the deck to be complete.
Load-bearing walls and vertical structural elements must be completed to provide support for roof trusses and rafters.
Top plates on wall assemblies provide the bearing surface and anchoring point for roof trusses and rafters.
Roof sheathing is installed directly onto the trusses/rafters to form the structural roof deck.
Soffit and fascia trim components are attached to the edges of the roof framing and cannot be installed until the trusses/rafters are in place.
Roof underlayment is laid over the sheathing which sits on the trusses/rafters, so trusses must be installed first to support the entire roof system.
The roof structure must be in place to provide the structural support and opening for skylight installation.
Roof decking provides the continuous surface onto which the skylight curb and flashing are mounted.
The rough opening for the skylight must be framed within the roof structure before the skylight unit can be installed.
Skylight must be in place so that roof flashing can be installed around its perimeter to seal against water intrusion.
Roofing materials (shingles, membrane, etc.) are installed up to and around the skylight flashing after the skylight is set, to ensure a watertight seal.
The rough opening must be framed to provide the structural support and correct dimensions for the barn door or sliding door to be installed.
Wall sheathing provides the backing surface and structural integrity required for mounting the sliding/barn door track and hardware.
Electrical wiring must be completed before the door is installed to avoid interference and to allow access for wiring within the wall cavity.
Trim and casing around the door are installed after the door is hung to properly fit and finish the opening.
Flooring is typically installed after doors are hung to ensure proper clearance and to avoid damaging flooring during door installation.
The loft opening and structural framing must be completed before the access ladder or stair can be installed to provide the necessary support and opening.
The loft floor or ceiling structure must be in place to provide a landing point and structural support for the top of the ladder or stair.
It is preferable to install the access ladder first to allow safe access for installing insulation, but insulation can also be installed partially beforehand.
The access ladder or stair must be in place to allow workers and materials to safely access the loft space for finishing work.
The access ladder or stair must be fully installed and functional before the final safety inspection and handover of the loft conversion.
A stable structural foundation is required to support the deck or outdoor platform, preventing settling or collapse.
Rough framing establishes the primary structural support (joists, beams, ledger board attachment) that the deck platform is built upon.
Railings are attached to the completed deck platform for safety and structural attachment.
Surface finishing, staining, or sealing is applied after the deck structure is fully built to protect the material.
While exterior lighting can be roughed-in earlier, final fixture installation is typically done after the deck is complete for proper placement and wiring routing.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and topsoil to expose the native soil or engineered fill where foundations will be placed.
Excavation to the required depth and grade is necessary to create a stable, level base at the proper elevation for footing construction.
The subgrade must be compacted to the specified density and verified through soil tests to ensure adequate bearing capacity before placing footings.
Accurate surveying and staking of building corners and footing locations is required to ensure the foundation is positioned correctly according to design drawings.
After footing concrete is placed, it must be allowed to cure to achieve design strength, and waterproofing or damp-proofing coatings can be applied before backfilling.
Footings provide the load-bearing base upon which foundation walls (stem walls or continuous walls) are constructed; walls cannot be built without completed footings.
Plumbing rough-ins and underground utility conduits are laid after footings are in place but before slab-on-grade placement, as they run beneath the slab.

Backfilling around foundations typically occurs after footings and foundation walls are complete and waterproofed, but it is a soft preference as some backfill may be staged earlier if needed for access.
Structural framing and building enclosure must be complete to provide the physical substrate (walls, ceilings, floors) for running conduit, boxes, and wiring.
Mechanical ducts and large plumbing lines are typically installed before electrical to avoid conflicts and to allow electrical raceways to be routed around or after these bulkier services.

successor: Wall / Ceiling Insulation and Drywall Installation
rationale: Electrical rough-in (boxes, cables, conduits) must be installed and inspected before enclosing them behind insulation and drywall.

successor: Trim-out and Finish Electrical (switches, devices, fixtures)
rationale: Rough-in wiring and boxes must be in place before finish devices (switches, receptacles, lighting fixtures) can be connected and installed.

successor: Inspection and Testing of Electrical Systems
rationale: After rough-in is complete, electrical inspections (continuity, grounding, code compliance) are performed before walls are closed and final connections made.
Plumbing rough-in requires access to the ground/floor slab for underground drainage, water supply lines, and floor waste piping, which must be placed before walls and vertical runs are started.
Underground plumbing (sewer, water mains) must be laid in trenches below the building footprint before any above-ground rough-in begins.
In slab-on-grade construction, underground plumbing pipes and stub-ups must be placed and inspected prior to pouring the concrete slab.
Plumbing pipes, vents, and waste lines are installed inside wall cavities; walls cannot be closed in (drywalled) until rough-in plumbing is complete and inspected.
A formal inspection of the installed rough-in plumbing must occur before any covering (walls, insulation, slab) is placed to verify code compliance.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated before any deck structure can be built; deck footings and foundations require a prepared subgrade.
Concrete footings or piers must be poured and cured to provide a stable load-bearing base for deck posts and framing; cannot build deck without foundation support.
Underground gas, electric, or water lines must be identified and moved if they conflict with deck footing locations to ensure safety and code compliance before digging or pouring.
Stain, sealant, or protective coating must be applied after the deck structure (framing and decking boards) is fully assembled to protect the wood from moisture and UV damage.
Railings are attached to the completed deck frame and decking surface; they cannot be installed until the deck floor structure is in place to provide a mounting surface.
Structural framing (walls, columns, beams) must be erected before internal linings can be installed, as linings are fixed onto the structural frame.
The roof and waterproofing must be completed to protect interior spaces from weather before internal lining and painting work can commence.
External cladding or enclosure must be in place to create a weather-tight envelope before internal finishing works like lining and painting begin.
All electrical conduits, plumbing pipes, and HVAC ductwork must be roughed-in within the wall cavities before they are enclosed by internal linings.
Internal lining and painting should be completed before flooring is installed to avoid damaging finished floors with paint drips, dust, or scaffold movement.
Permanent fixtures such as cabinets, light switches, power outlets, and trim are installed after painting is complete to avoid paint marks on fixtures and allow clean finish work.
Joinery items like kitchen cabinets, wardrobes, and shelving are installed after painting to ensure clean lines and prevent damage to painted surfaces.
The property must be identified and secured before applying for a planning permit or zoning approval, as the permit application requires specific property details and boundaries.

An environmental assessment and site analysis must be completed to provide required information for the planning permit application, demonstrating that the proposed development complies with environmental regulations and zoning requirements.
Preliminary architectural designs and schematics are necessary to submit with the planning permit application to show compliance with zoning bylaws, building codes, and land use regulations.

Detailed engineering and construction drawings cannot be finalized until planning permit and zoning approvals are obtained, as these approvals may impose conditions or design modifications that must be incorporated.

The planning permit/zoning approval is typically a prerequisite for the building permit application, as the building permit authority requires evidence of zoning compliance before issuing a building permit.
The ramp requires a stable, level foundation or slab to bear on; without the slab/foundation in place, the ramp structure cannot be properly supported.
The ground must be excavated and rough-graded to the proper elevations before the ramp base or slab can be poured and the ramp formed.
The ramp structural surface must be fully cured and complete before any anti-slip coatings, sealants, or surface finishes can be applied.
Handrails and guardrails are attached to the ramp structure; the ramp must be built and stable before railings can be anchored to it.

successor: Final Inspection and Accessibility Compliance Check
rationale: The ramp must be fully constructed (including surface finish and handrails) before it can be inspected for compliance with accessibility codes (e.g., ADA).
A stable foundation must be prepared before installing a step-free threshold to ensure proper load bearing and alignment.
The subfloor must be in place to provide a continuous, level surface that the threshold will integrate with.
Any services running beneath the floor area must be completed before installing the threshold to avoid rework or damage.
The threshold must be installed before the final floor finish is applied so that the finish can be brought flush to the threshold level, creating a seamless step-free transition.
The threshold provides the baseline for door frame positioning and clearance; doors are installed after to ensure correct bottom clearance and weather sealing.
Grab rails and handrails require solid wall framing and sheathing to be in place as backing support for secure attachment and load-bearing capacity.

Rough-in electrical and plumbing work must be completed behind walls before grab rails and handrails are installed, to avoid interference with concealed utilities and to prevent damaging finished railings.

Grab rails and handrails are typically installed over finished wall surfaces (e.g., drywall, tile, or fiberglass reinforced panels) to ensure proper sealing, waterproofing, and a clean finished appearance.

Installing grab rails and handrails after final painting allows for touch-up painting around the mounting flanges; however, this is a soft preference because painting can also be done first if careful masking and touch-ups are planned.

Grab rails and handrails must be installed before final inspection and occupancy because building codes require these safety grab rails and handrails to be in place for code compliance and occupant safety.
Before widening any doorway, a structural assessment must be completed to determine which walls are load-bearing and to plan the necessary reinforcements.
Building permits for structural modifications must be approved before any widening work can legally begin.
If the doorway is in a load-bearing wall, temporary shoring and rough framing must be in place to support the structure before cutting into the wall.
After the doorway is widened to the correct dimensions, new drywall, trim, and finishing work can be installed around the newly sized opening.
The new, wider door frame and door can only be installed after the doorway opening has been cut to the proper width.
The external walls must be built on top of the completed foundation and substructure to provide structural support and load distribution.
The ground floor slab provides the base upon which external walls are erected, ensuring a level and stable working surface.
Where a structural frame (steel or concrete) supports the building, the frame must be erected before infill external walls are installed to provide the structural skeleton.
External walls enclose the building perimeter and provide the bearing surface for roof structure connections; the roof cannot be installed until the walls are in place to support it.
Windows and doors are fitted into prepared openings within the external wall assembly; the wall structure must be erected and stable before these openings can be formed and fenestrations installed.
The foundation or concrete slab must be fully poured, cured, and leveled to provide a stable, level base for low-threshold windows, which sit at or near floor level.
Rough wall framing must be complete to define the window openings and provide structural support for the window frames.
Waterproof membrane, flashing, and weather-resistive barriers must be installed around the rough openings before window installation to prevent moisture ingress and ensure proper sealing.
Windows must be installed and sealed before interior finishes are applied so that the wall assembly is weathertight and the window reveals can be properly finished.
Windows must be installed and flashed before exterior cladding is placed to allow proper integration of window flashings with the building wrap and cladding system.
The staircase must be structurally evaluated to ensure it can support the stairlift system, including the rail, carriage, and user weight.
The stairlift must be physically mounted and the rail secured before electricians can safely connect power, install the charging dock, and test the lift mechanism.
The stairlift must be completely installed, tested, and operational before end-users can be trained on safe usage, controls, and emergency procedures.
The staircase area must be cleared of obstructions, furniture, and debris to provide safe and unobstructed access for installers to work on the stairlift.
A formal inspection and safety certification can only be conducted once the stairlift is fully installed and operational to verify compliance with regulations.
The main building structure must be complete before accessibility adaptations can be installed, as ramps, widened doorways, and accessible routes depend on the underlying structural framework.

predecessor: Rough Flooring and Base Surface Preparation
rationale: Floor levels need to be established and prepared to allow for slope adjustments, threshold ramps, and level access installations required for accessibility.
Accessibility features such as tactile paving, grab rail bases, and recessed floor indicators must be installed before final floor finishes are applied to integrate them seamlessly.

While painting can be done after accessibility fittings, it is preferred to complete accessibility adaptations first to avoid rework around grab rails, wheelchair turning spaces, and accessible fixtures.
All accessibility features must be fully installed and operational before the final compliance inspection and handover to verify adherence to accessibility standards and regulations.
A referral from social services or occupational therapy is required before a Disabled Facilities Grant (DFG) assessment can be initiated, as the assessment is triggered by an identified need.
An occupational therapy assessment must be completed to identify the specific needs of the disabled person, which forms the basis for the DFG assessment to determine eligible works.
The DFG assessment findings and recommendations must be documented before a formal grant application can be submitted to the local authority.
A detailed specification of the required adaptation works can only be prepared after the DFG assessment has determined the scope and nature of the necessary modifications.
Contractors can only provide quotations and schedules of works once the DFG assessment has defined what adaptations are needed, as the assessment determines the specific work items.
The site must be prepared and leveled before any fixed workstation can be installed, as the workstation requires a stable and ready foundation.
Foundations must be in place to provide structural support for fixed workstations, which are typically anchored to the floor.

Electrical and data cabling must be run in walls/floors before fixed workstations are placed, as these workstations typically require power and network connections that are integrated into the structure.
After the fixed workstation is installed, it must be tested for power connectivity, data connectivity, and ergonomic functionality before being put into use.

While flooring and painting are typically completed before fixed workstation installation, minor touch-ups may occur after; however, it is a soft preference to avoid rework or damage to the workstation.
Desk partitions/screens are typically installed on top of finished flooring. Installing them before flooring would damage the flooring or require rework.
Electrical floor boxes and underfloor wiring need to be in place before desk partitions are installed, as partitions may cover or obstruct access to these elements.

While not a strict physical constraint, completing overhead work (ceiling, lighting, overhead ducts) before installing partitions avoids dust/debris falling on finished partitions and reduces the need for rework.

Desk partitions/screens are structural components that define individual workstations. Desks and other workstation furniture are placed relative to the partitions and require them to be in place first.

successor: IT / Data Cabling Termination at Workstations
rationale: IT and data cabling needs to be routed through or along desk partitions/screens. The partitions must be installed first to provide the pathway and termination points for the cabling.
The cable management tray is mounted underneath the desk surface. The desk must be assembled and installed first to provide the structural surface for the tray to attach to.

The cable management tray must be installed before placing computers, monitors, and peripherals on or under the desk, as the tray is used to route and store cables; installing it afterward would require moving equipment out of the way.

Cables should be routed through the cable management tray after it is installed, so they can be organized and secured within the tray channels; routing cables first would require re-routing them once the tray is in place.
While not physically required, completing flooring and baseboards first avoids having to work around the desk and tray during final floor finishing, reducing the risk of damage to the installed tray.

Final inspection should be done after the cable management tray is installed to verify that all cables are properly organized and that the tray is securely fastened, though this is a quality assurance preference rather than a physical necessity.
Flooring must be completed before workstations are installed, as workstations are placed on top of the finished floor surface. Installing flooring after would require moving or damaging workstations.
Ceiling work must be finished before workstation installation to avoid dust/debris falling on workstations and to allow access for overhead work without obstruction.
All mechanical, electrical, and data cabling rough-in work in the ceiling and walls must be completed before workstations are installed, as workstations will block access to walls and ceiling spaces.
Wall painting and finishing must be completed before workstation installation to avoid paint splatter on workstations and to allow unobstructed access to walls.
Workstations must be in place before IT/data cabling can be terminated at each workstation location, as the exact position of data ports depends on workstation layout.
Workstations serve as the base furniture; additional furniture items (chairs, filing cabinets, accessories) can only be placed after workstations are fully installed and positioned.
Final cleaning and commissioning activities must occur after all workstation installation is complete to avoid re-cleaning due to installation debris and to ensure the space is ready for occupancy.

Power and data cabling rough-in is typically installed above the ceiling or within walls, but in slab-on-grade or deck situations, the slab must be poured and cured before overhead or in-wall rough-in work can commence. Additionally, any under-slab conduits must be placed before the pour, so the slab completion is a prerequisite.

Wall framing must be complete to provide the structural cavities and support for running power and data cables through walls. Cabling cannot be routed until studs, headers, and wall plates are in place.
If cables are routed above a suspended ceiling, the overhead structure or ceiling grid must be roughed in to provide pathways and support for cable trays, conduit, or J-hooks.

Insulation must be installed after electrical and low-voltage cabling rough-in to avoid covering or interfering with cables. Installing insulation first would block access for cable routing and inspection.

successor: Rough Electrical / Data Trim-Out (Devices and Plates)
rationale: Rough-in cabling must be terminated, pulled into boxes, and inspected before trim-out (installation of outlets, switches, jacks, and faceplates) can occur. The rough-in phase provides the installed cable that will later be connected to devices.
Electrical rough-in (conduit, wiring, junction boxes) must be installed before lighting fixtures can be laid out and commissioned.
The ceiling grid or structure that supports lighting fixtures must be in place before lighting layout and fixture mounting can begin.
Lighting layout and commissioning (including fixture installation, wiring checks, and basic testing) must be completed before final electrical trim-out and comprehensive system testing.
All lighting systems must be fully installed, commissioned, and verified functional before the building can be occupied or the project closed out.
While lighting installation typically precedes final finishes for access reasons, it is a soft preference rather than a strict physical necessity, as finishes can be worked around lighting.

The workbench must be placed on a stable, level surface. Foundation preparation ensures the ground or floor is properly compacted, leveled, and cured before installing the workbench to prevent instability or shifting.

Vises, clamps, power tools, or other benchtop equipment must be securely mounted onto the workbench after it is installed and stable, as the workbench provides the structural platform for these attachments.

While it is practical to organize tool storage (shelves, pegboards, drawers) after the workbench is in place to optimize layout and accessibility, it could partially be done beforehand if the workbench location is predetermined.

Electrical outlets and lighting should ideally be positioned after the workbench is placed to ensure proper alignment and accessibility, but electrical rough-in can be done earlier with flexible positioning.
All materials and components (lumber, fasteners, hardware, work surface) must be procured and available before assembly of the workbench can begin.
The cabinet must be installed and secured before tools can be placed inside it.
Floor finishing (e.g., concrete curing, tile setting) should be completed to avoid dust, debris, or damage to the cabinet and to ensure a level final surface for cabinet placement.
Wall finishing should be done before installing cabinets to avoid painting over or damaging the cabinet and to ensure clean edges.
While not physically required, installing the cabinet before running electrical lines to it is preferred so that conduit and outlets can be positioned correctly relative to the cabinet location.
Wall framing must be complete to provide a structural surface to anchor the tool storage cabinet.
The wall frame (studs) must be in place to provide a structural backing for attaching the pegboard panel.
Electrical wiring within the wall must be completed and secured before covering the wall with pegboard, as access behind the panel would be restricted afterward.
Insulation must be placed inside the wall cavity before the pegboard panel is installed to seal the wall assembly.
Once the pegboard is in place, trim pieces (e.g., edge molding, baseboard) can be installed to provide a finished edge; this is a logical sequence but could be done concurrently if needed.
Pegboard hooks, shelves, and other accessories can only be mounted after the pegboard panel itself is securely attached to the wall.
Wall framing provides the structural support needed to securely anchor overhead storage shelving.
Finished wall surfaces are required to mount shelving brackets or supports flush and securely against the wall.
Overhead storage shelving is often suspended from or braced against the ceiling structure, which must be fully framed and stable.
Any overhead wiring, conduit, or junction boxes must be installed before shelves are placed to avoid access and safety conflicts.
Overhead storage shelving must be installed and secured before the space can be deemed complete and ready for occupancy or storage use.
Site preparation, including clearing, levelling, and basic earthworks, must be completed before any construction can begin to provide a stable and safe building platform.
Foundations and concrete slab must be poured and cured before the workshop structure can be erected on top of them.
Underground plumbing, electrical conduits, and drainage lines must be installed and inspected before the floor slab is poured and the building structure is erected.
The workshop building must be fully constructed, enclosed, and fitted out before heavy equipment and machinery can be brought in and installed.
The completed workshop fit-out must be finished and ready before the final quality inspection and handover to operations can take place.

Electrical circuits are typically run through walls, ceilings, and floors. The structural framing must be in place to provide the cavities and pathways for running electrical cables and mounting boxes before installation can begin.
For services entering the building from below, underground conduits and utility connections must be laid and stubbed up before interior electrical circuit installation can commence.
Electrical cables, boxes, and conduits must be installed within the wall and ceiling cavities before they can be enclosed by drywall; otherwise the wiring would be inaccessible.
The rough-in wiring (circuit installation) must be complete before final connections can be made to switches, receptacles, light fixtures, and other trim-out devices.
