While insulation can sometimes be installed after wiring, it is typically more efficient to place insulation after electrical rough-in to ensure full coverage around cables and boxes; this is a soft preference based on workflow efficiency rather than a physical necessity.
Structural steel framing must be in place to provide support and hanging points for heavy dust collection ducts and to define the building envelope through which ducts will run.
The concrete slab or foundation must be completed to provide a stable base for duct supports and to ensure proper alignment of duct runs from equipment to collection points.
The ductwork must be installed first so that it can be connected to the main dust collection equipment (baghouse, cyclone, or filter system) at the proper tie-in points.

While electrical rough-in can partially proceed in parallel, final connections for damper actuators, sensors, and fan controls on the duct system require the ductwork to be in place for accurate positioning.
Insulation and weatherproof cladding can only be applied after the bare duct sections are fully installed, connected, and leak-tested to avoid covering unsealed joints.
The workspace area must be cleared, leveled, and prepared before any workbench can be fabricated or installed to ensure proper alignment and stability.
Raw materials such as lumber, metal framing, bolts, and work surface materials must be procured and available on-site before fabrication can commence.
Any electrical outlets, conduits, or plumbing lines that will run beneath or behind the workbench must be roughed in before the workbench is installed to avoid rework and accessibility issues.
The workbench must be fully assembled and installed in its permanent location before the work surface can be finished, sealed, or coated to protect against spills and wear.
Tools such as vises, clamps, power strips, and shelving units should be mounted only after the workbench is securely installed to ensure correct positioning and load distribution.
The structural framework (walls, roof structure) must be in place to provide a surface and cavity for insulation installation.
The roof must be completed to protect the insulation materials from weather damage and to provide the overhead enclosure for wall and ceiling insulation work.
Insulation must be installed before interior cladding (e.g., drywall, panels) is applied, as the cladding covers and encloses the insulation.

While electrical rough-in can partially proceed before insulation, running cables within insulated cavities is more efficient after insulation is placed; however, this is a soft preference for sequencing coordination.
The vapor barrier (if required) is typically installed over the insulation on the warm side to prevent moisture ingress, so insulation must be in place first.
Site must be cleared and leveled before tools can be organized and laid out in the workspace.
Concrete foundations and slabs must be poured and cured before work areas for tool storage and layout are established on site.
Materials should be delivered and stored first so that tool layout can account for material handling and access requirements.
Temporary power, water, and lighting must be in place to support powered tools and workstations before organizing tool layouts.
Contractor mobilization and establishing site access/security is necessary before bringing tools onto the site and planning their layout.
While excavation can begin before full tool organization, having tools organized improves efficiency for earthmoving equipment coordination.
Tools and workstations must be organized and laid out before structural framing begins to ensure efficient access to tools during construction.
Organized tool layout improves workflow efficiency when electrical rough-in work commences, though not a strict physical dependency.
The foundation must be fully constructed and cured before safety inspections can verify load-bearing capacity, structural integrity, and compliance with building codes.
Structural framing must be completed so that inspectors can assess the structural stability, connections, and adherence to engineering specifications.
Electrical rough-in work (wiring, conduit, boxes) must be installed before inspection to verify compliance with electrical safety codes before walls are closed.
Plumbing rough-in must be completed so that inspectors can check pipe routing, pressure testing, and drainage compliance before concealment.
Walls cannot be closed with drywall until all rough-in inspections (structural, electrical, plumbing) have passed, as inspectors need access to verify work before concealment.
Insulation should only be installed after inspection approval ensures that all systems behind the insulation are safe and compliant.

While finishing work (painting, flooring, trim) typically follows inspection approval, in some cases minor finishing can proceed concurrently; however, it is standard practice and a soft preference to complete inspections first to avoid costly rework.
Guardrails are typically mounted onto the concrete deck or slab; the deck must be poured and sufficiently cured to provide a solid anchorage surface.
In some sequences, guardrails are installed before waterproofing to avoid damage to the membrane; however it can be a soft preference depending on design.
The guardrail provides the core structure; subsequent finishing work (e.g., painting, caps, anchor bolt covering) must occur after installation.
Safety testing and inspection of guardrail systems can only be performed once the guardrails are fully installed.
Guardrails are part of the superstructure; the substructure (piers, abutments, foundation) must be complete to support the deck on which guardrails are mounted.
The central spine beam must be supported by the building's vertical structural elements (columns and foundation) which must be completed first to bear the load.
Secondary beams and joists typically connect to or are supported by the central spine beam, so the spine beam must be in place first to provide the main structural ridge or support line.
The central spine beam is a primary structural element that supports the roof deck or slab above, so it must be fully installed and cured before the decking or slab can be placed on top.
The scaffolding, formwork, or steel erection system that positions and holds the spine beam must be set up before the beam itself can be lifted, aligned, and secured into place.

While not a strict structural requirement, it is preferable to run overhead conduits, ducts, and piping after the spine beam is installed since the beam defines the ceiling plane and support points for hangers.
The tread fixing bracket must be attached to a stable structural support; the stair stringer provides the primary structural framework onto which brackets are mounted.
Tread fixing brackets are designed to support and secure stair treads; treads cannot be properly installed until their supporting brackets are in place.
Once the bracket is positioned, it must be securely fastened (e.g., bolted or screwed) to the stringer before any load-bearing tread is placed onto it.
After brackets are installed, treads are placed and alignment is checked; this is a logical sequence as alignment depends on bracket position, though minor adjustments could be made concurrently.
Accurate layout marks on the stringer are needed to position brackets at the correct rise/run intervals before installation can begin.
The structural slab must be prepared and cured to provide a stable base for the glass balustrade panel installation.
Waterproofing must be completed before installing balustrade panels to ensure the waterproof layer is continuous beneath the balustrade fixings.
The embedded base channels or slots for the glass panels must be cast into or fixed to the slab before the glass panels can be inserted and secured.
The glass panels must be in place and secured before the top handrail can be mounted onto them.
Capping or cover trim installation over the glass panel fixings can only proceed after the glass panels themselves are installed.
Stairs require a stable structural base; foundations must be completed to support the load of the stair structure and provide anchorage points.
Stairs must be attached to the building's structural framework (floor slabs, beams, or walls); framing provides the supporting structure for stair stringers and landings.
Rough-in services behind walls and below floors adjacent to stair areas must be completed before stairs are installed to avoid rework or damage to finished stairs.
Stairwell walls and adjacent walls are typically finished after stairs are in place to achieve proper alignment and coverage around the stair structure.
While painting is typically done after stairs to avoid paint drips on new stairs, it is a soft preference because stairs could be protected with coverings if needed.
The stair structural design must be based on the architectural floor plan to ensure proper alignment with floor levels, headroom clearances, and spatial layout.
Staircases bear on floor slabs/landings; the structural framing of adjacent floors must be designed first to determine support conditions and load transfer paths.
Foundation design for stair support elements (if any) requires soil bearing capacity data from geotechnical investigation.
Reinforcement placement and bar bending schedules can only be prepared after the structural design (size, span, loads) of the stair is finalized.
Formwork layout and shoring design depend on the stair geometry, dimensions, and structural configuration determined during structural design.
Tread surface finishing is applied to concrete stair treads, which must first be poured and placed before any finishing work can begin.
The formwork for stair construction must be installed and set before concrete is poured and the tread surfaces can be finished.
Concrete must undergo initial curing and reach sufficient green strength to support finishing operations like floating, troweling, or brooming of the tread surface.
After finishing the tread surface, the concrete must be allowed to cure properly and be protected from damage, foot traffic, or weather before further construction proceeds.
Handrails and guardrails are typically installed after the tread surface is finished and cured, to avoid damaging the finished surface during railing installation.
Structural walls and framing must be in place to provide the rough openings and support structure necessary for window installation.
While not strictly physically required, it is preferred to complete rough-in utilities before window placement to avoid interference and ensure proper routing around window areas.
After windows are placed (framed/positioned in openings), the glazing, weatherproofing, and sealing operations must follow immediately to ensure the building envelope is watertight.
Interior finishing around windows requires the windows to be in place so that drywall and trim can be properly installed and finished against the window frames.
Exterior cladding (e.g., brick veneer, siding) is installed after windows are placed to ensure proper flashing, integration, and a weather-tight seal around window openings.
The structural frame must be in place to provide support and load-bearing capacity before exterior wall openings can be cut or formed.
The opening must be created before any window or door frames can be installed into it.
Weatherproofing materials like flashing and sealants are applied around the opening after it is formed to protect against water infiltration.
Glass and glazing units can only be placed into the opening after the wall opening has been formed and prepared.

successor: Interior Finishing around Openings (e.g., drywall, trim)
rationale: While interior finishes often follow after openings are formed, in some cases they can be done concurrently; however, it is generally preferred to complete the opening before finishing to avoid rework.
Excavation involves removing overburden and soil covering archaeological remains; Reveal cannot begin until the area is excavated to expose the top of the deposit or feature.
Loose dirt and debris must be cleaned from the surface to clearly see and define the boundaries of the archaeological context before it can be properly revealed and documented.
Recording (photography, drawing, description) must occur immediately after Reveal while the context is fully exposed and undisturbed.
Sampling for artifacts, ecofacts, or dating materials should follow Reveal, as the archaeologist needs a fully revealed context to identify and collect representative samples.
The physical removal of a context or deposit can only proceed after it has been fully Revealed, recorded, and sampled, as removal is destructive and irreversible.
Accurate 3D building geometry is required to set up the daylight simulation model.
Surface reflectances and glazing transmittances must be defined for realistic daylight simulation.
Surrounding buildings and obstructions affect daylight availability and must be modeled before analysis.
While daylight factor uses CIE overcast sky, having location-specific weather data improves accuracy of sky model selection.
Daylight factor results help identify areas with excessive daylight that may require glare evaluation.
Daylight availability informs lighting energy savings and cooling load calculations in energy models.
Daylight factor results directly inform window size, placement, and shading design decisions.
Steel coils must be received and inspected for quality and dimensions before cutting and forming can begin, as the material must be available and verified.
Coils must be stored in designated areas before being moved to the cutting line for processing.
Production job orders must be issued to authorize the cutting and forming operation for specific product specifications.
The flat sheet metal must be cut to length and pre-formed before it can be fed into the roll forming machine to create the final profile shape.
Cutting produces rough edges that must be smoothed via deburring before further processing or assembly.
After cutting and forming, the parts must be inspected to ensure dimensional accuracy before proceeding to downstream operations.
The glazing system must be fully installed before any performance testing can commence, as testing evaluates the installed assembly's performance characteristics.
Window frames must be installed and properly sealed to provide the structural support and enclosure necessary for meaningful glazing performance testing.
Final close-out and commissioning of the curtain wall system cannot proceed until glazing performance testing confirms the system meets specified performance criteria.

Interior finishes such as drywall, trim, and painting adjacent to glazed areas should only proceed after performance testing is complete to avoid damage to finishes during testing or need for rework if testing reveals issues requiring access.

The building enclosure cannot receive final approval and sign-off until glazing performance testing verifies that the installed glazing meets design specifications for thermal performance, air infiltration, water penetration, and structural integrity.
The drip edge must be installed on top of the roof deck (sheathing) to provide a solid nailing surface and direct water away from the fascia.

Drip edge is typically installed over the roof deck but under the underlayment on the rakes, and over the underlayment on the eaves; some underlayment may need to be in place before drip edge installation on rake edges.
After the drip edge is installed (especially at the eaves), the remainder of the underlayment is laid over it to ensure proper water shedding.
Roof shingles or the final roof covering are installed after the drip edge is in place, as the drip edge forms the finished edge that directs water into the gutters.

While gutters typically go after the roof is finished, and the drip edge is installed before fascia in many sequences, this ordering can vary by design; drip edge must be installed before gutters are attached to ensure water flows properly into the gutter system.
Edge flashing is installed along the edges of the roof deck; the roof deck must be in place to provide the substrate for the flashing.
The waterproof underlayment is typically laid before edge flashing, as flashing is placed over the underlayment to provide a weather-tight seal at the roof edges.
Edge flashing is installed prior to the final roof covering so that the roofing material can overlap and integrate with the flashing for water shedding.
Edge flashing often interfaces with fascia boards or gutters; the flashing must be in place before these trim and drainage components are fitted.
While not a strict physical constraint, soffit installation is often sequenced after edge flashing to allow proper integration and alignment at the roof edge.
The expansion joint must be installed after the perimeter wall or foundation structure is in place, as the joint accommodates movement between the building structure and adjacent elements.

Waterproofing is applied over or adjacent to the expansion joint to ensure a continuous water barrier; the joint must be installed first so that the waterproofing can properly seal the transition area.
Exterior cladding is installed after the expansion joint to allow for proper detailing and movement accommodation at the perimeter transition.
Subgrade and drainage work must be completed before installing perimeter expansion joints to ensure a stable base and proper drainage around the joint location.
The structural frame or slab edge must be completed to define the perimeter geometry where the expansion joint will be placed, ensuring accurate alignment and anchorage.
The edge beam is typically cast on top of or against a concrete slab, so the slab must be in place first to support or form the edge beam.
Formwork must be erected and secured before concrete can be poured into it to shape the edge beam.
Steel reinforcement must be positioned and tied within the formwork before concrete is placed to ensure structural integrity.
Concrete must be poured before the curing process can begin to achieve design strength.
Curing must reach sufficient strength before forms can be safely removed without damaging the beam.
Edge beams provide the perimeter support and attachment points for exterior cladding panels.
Waterproofing is optimally applied after edge beams are in place to seal joints at slab edges, though some waterproofing can be done beforehand with later detailing.
The edge beam often connects to or is supported by the main structural frame, so the frame must be erected first.
The edge beam defines the perimeter edge, and decking or soffit panels are typically installed up to the edge beam.
The structural frame (columns, beams, or load-bearing walls) must be in place to support the canopy, as the canopy is typically attached to or rests upon the primary building structure.
If the canopy is roof-mounted or adjacent to the roof, the roof deck must be completed to provide a secure base and waterproofing before canopy work begins.
Although not a strict physical dependency, completing the canopy before installing adjacent cladding simplifies detailing and ensures weather sealing at the interface.

successor: Final Electrical and Lighting Rough-In Below Canopy
rationale: Electrical fixtures mounted to or routed through the canopy require the canopy structure to be in place before conduit, wiring, and fixture installation can proceed beneath it.
If the canopy includes glass panels or translucent infill, the supporting canopy frame must be erected first before glazing panels can be installed and sealed.
The verge is installed along the edge of the roof, so the roof structure and decking must be in place first to provide a mounting surface.
The fascia board is typically installed before the verge as it provides the backing or trim along the roof edge that the verge components (such as bargeboards or verge trim) attach to or overlap.
Gutters are often installed after the verge because the verge defines the roof edge profile and the gutter hangers or brackets are attached to or beneath the verge/roof edge.

Verge installation typically completes the roof edge, so the main roof tiling or cladding must be finished up to the edges before the verge can be finalized, but the verge finishing work may also cap off the tiles.

While scaffolding is often removed after verge work is done for safety and access, this is a soft preference rather than a strict physical necessity as partial dismantling could be sequenced differently.
Fascia boards are typically installed first to provide a nailing surface and support for the barge board at the gable end of the roof.
The roof decking must be in place to provide structural support and a mounting surface for the barge board along the gable.
Trusses or rafters must be erected first as they form the primary roof structure that supports the decking and subsequent barge board installation.
Barge board is installed at the gable end to close off the roof edge, and underlayment is then applied over the decking and up to the barge board to ensure waterproofing continuity.
Roof tiles or shingles are laid after the barge board is in place, as the barge board provides the finished edge and flashing point at the gable end.
The structural frame (steel or concrete) must be erected first to provide a stable support structure onto which edge protection barriers can be fixed or anchored.
Edge protection barriers must be installed before concrete pouring on elevated slabs to ensure worker safety and prevent falls from height during construction.
Edge protection is required along roof perimeters before roofing activities commence to protect workers from falling off the edge of the building.
Edge protection barriers must be in place before cladding is installed to provide fall protection for workers operating at the building perimeter.
While not physically mandatory, installing edge protection first creates a safer working environment for glaziers working near open edges; it is a strong safety preference.
Edge sealing is applied to the perimeter of concrete slabs to protect the edges; the slab must be in place before its edges can be sealed.
Concrete must be fully cured before edge sealing can be applied to ensure proper adhesion and prevent moisture entrapment.
The slab edges must be clean, dry, and free of debris for the sealant to bond effectively.
Edge sealing prevents moisture and contaminants from migrating under floor coverings, so it must be completed before installing final floor finishes.

Edge sealing is part of the concrete finishing scope; while inspections often occur after all finishing work is done, it is a soft preference as the inspection could theoretically be done concurrently.
Excavation must be completed to expose the foundation walls and perimeter area where waterproofing is applied.
The concrete foundation walls must be fully poured and cured before waterproofing membranes or coatings can be applied to them.
Sufficient curing time is required for the concrete foundation to develop adequate strength and surface integrity before waterproofing materials are applied.
Drainage boards and geotextile fabrics are installed over the waterproofing membrane to protect it and facilitate water drainage to the drainage system.
Backfilling around the foundation can only proceed after waterproofing is fully applied and cured; otherwise, the waterproofing membrane would be damaged or inaccessible for inspection.
The roof edge components (fascia, drip edge, gutters) must be installed onto the completed roof deck structure, which provides the structural base and nailing surface for edge attachments.

Underlayment is typically installed before roof edge flashing and drip edge to ensure proper water drainage from the underlayment over the edge flashing, preventing moisture infiltration behind the membrane.

Roof edge metal (drip edge) is installed before the final roof covering (shingles, tiles, or metal panels) so that the covering overlaps the edge metal, ensuring water runoff from the finish material over the edge flashing.
Gutters are attached to or mounted below the roof edge/fascia; the roof edge trim and drip edge must be in place to define the water runoff path before gutters are installed.

While soffit can sometimes be installed before roof edge, it is a soft preference to complete roof edge first to avoid damaging soffit panels when working on the edge trim and to ensure proper alignment of fascia over soffit.
The site must be cleared and prepared before any survey can be conducted, as debris or uneven terrain would obstruct accurate measurements.
Existing property boundaries or reference markers need to be established before surveying the edge to ensure alignment with legal property lines.
The edge survey defines the exact footprint and alignment of the structure, which is needed before excavation can begin to ensure the foundation is placed correctly.
The edge survey provides precise boundary and elevation data that is essential for planning the routing of underground utilities.
Survey data is often required as part of permit submissions, though preliminary permits may sometimes be filed before the survey is complete.
The wall frame must be constructed to provide the structural opening and support for installing the window.
A rough opening with proper dimensions, headers, and cripple studs must be framed in the wall before the window unit can be placed.
House wrap or building paper should be installed around the rough opening to provide moisture protection before window insertion.
The window must be set in place before flashing and sealant can be applied around its perimeter to ensure watertight installation.
Window casing and interior trim work typically follows window installation, though this is a logical sequence rather than a strict physical necessity.
The structural frame (concrete/steel skeleton) must be fully erected and stabilized to provide a secure mounting surface and load-bearing support for facade panels.
Floor slabs at each level must be cast and cured to provide the horizontal anchoring points and edge supports that glazed facade panels attach to.
A weather-resistant barrier or air/water membrane must be applied to the building exterior before enclosing with glazed panels to prevent moisture ingress and air leakage.
Interior drywalling, plastering, and painting cannot commence until the glazed facade is installed to protect interior spaces from weather, dust, and temperature fluctuations.
External scaffolding and access equipment cannot be fully removed until the glazed facade panel installation is completed, as scaffolding provides the working platform for installation.
A geometric model of the building is required to define the spaces, openings, and surfaces for daylight calculations.
Surrounding obstructions (adjacent buildings, trees, topography) must be modeled to accurately simulate sky view and shading effects on daylight factor.
Surface reflectances for walls, floors, ceilings, and glazing materials are needed to compute how light is inter-reflected within spaces.
Window sizes, locations, and glass optical properties (visible transmittance) directly affect the amount of daylight entering the spaces and must be defined before simulation.
The daylight factor results inform design decisions such as adjusting window sizes, adding shading devices, or modifying interior layouts to meet daylight performance targets.
Structural framing (joists, trusses, or ceiling grid supports) must be in place before any ceiling surface can be attached or installed.
Electrical wiring, ductwork, and plumbing runs within the ceiling plenum must be completed and inspected before enclosing them with a reflective ceiling surface.
Fireproofing spray-applied to structure and any required insulation above the ceiling must be installed prior to the ceiling surface to avoid rework and access issues.

Reflective ceiling panels or drywall must be in place to serve as the mounting substrate and to properly align recessed lighting fixtures, which are typically installed after the ceiling surface is complete.

successor: Painting and Finish Work (Walls and Trim)
rationale: While not a hard physical constraint, it is standard practice to complete ceiling surfaces before wall painting and trim to avoid overspray and damage to finished ceiling materials.
The structural framing must be in place to provide support and attachment points for solar shading devices such as louvers, fins, or overhangs.
Exterior wall surfaces must be finished so that solar shading elements can be properly anchored and sealed against the building envelope.
Roof structure and waterproofing must be complete where solar shading is integrated with or attached to the roof edge or parapet.
Windows and glazing must be installed so that external shading devices can be positioned relative to the window openings for proper solar control and clearance.

successor: Building Enclosure Air and Water Barrier Testing
rationale: Solar shading installation punctures the building envelope; final air and water barrier testing must occur after all penetrations (including shading attachments) are sealed and complete.
The foundation provides the load-bearing base upon which the wall is constructed; the wall cannot be built without a stable foundation in place.
The ground must be leveled and prepared so the foundation and wall layout can be accurately established.
Utilities such as drainage, water, and electrical conduits that pass under or through the wall footprint must be installed before the wall is built to avoid later excavation or core drilling.
The exterior wall provides vertical support for roof trusses or framing; the roof cannot be installed until the bearing walls are complete and properly anchored.
Sheathing and weather-resistant barrier are applied directly onto the wall frame; the frame must be fully erected before these layers can be installed.
The structural steel frame must be in place to provide the load-bearing support structure onto which the north face glazing panels are installed.
Sequencing glazing work from north to south can avoid material handling conflicts, but is a soft preference rather than a physical necessity.
Glazing must be completed and weather-tight before interior finishes can be installed to prevent water damage to finished surfaces.
The north face glazing system must be fully installed before air and water infiltration testing can be performed on that elevation.
Glazing installation must be complete before staging and scaffolding can be removed from the north face of the building.
The parapet sits atop and is supported by the north face wall; the wall structure must be complete before parapet construction can begin.
The parapet forms the edge of the roof system; the roof deck is typically installed prior to the parapet to provide a base and waterproofing integration.
Coping caps the top of the parapet wall to provide weatherproofing and finish; it must be installed after the parapet structure is complete.
Gutters and downspouts are often mounted to or integrated with the parapet; the parapet must be in place to provide the mounting surface.

successor: Exterior Cladding or Finish Above Parapet Level
rationale: Any finishes or cladding that extend above the parapet line (e.g., cornices, decorative elements) should follow parapet construction, though this is a logical sequence preference rather than a strict physical necessity.
The lintel rests directly on top of the columns and cannot be installed until the supporting columns for the north face are erected and stable.
Columns must have a properly prepared foundation to bear the load before they can be erected.

successor: North Face Upper Wall or Roof Structure Placement
rationale: The lintel serves as a horizontal structural beam spanning the columns, and any wall or roof elements above it require the lintel to be in place for support and load distribution.

successor: North Face Finishing Work (e.g., cladding, sealing)
rationale: Finishing work such as cladding, sealing, or aesthetic treatments typically follow lintel installation as the structure must be in place first, though some finishing could theoretically proceed in parallel if access allows.

predecessor: Material Procurement and Delivery (North Face Lintel)
rationale: The lintel material (stone, steel, concrete, etc.) must be procured, fabricated, and delivered to the site before installation can commence.
The north face cannot be revealed until the structural north wall is fully constructed and load-bearing elements are in place.
The reveal process requires all exterior finishes (cladding, waterproofing, insulation) to be completed on the north face before it can be formally revealed or unveiled.
Scaffolding must be erected to enable workers to access the north face for finishing work before the reveal can take place.
Inspection of the north façade can only occur after the north face has been fully revealed and is accessible for visual and structural review.
Interior fit-out of the north zone can proceed more efficiently after the north face reveal since the exterior envelope is sealed, though it may partially overlap as a soft preference.
The shading device is typically mounted on or adjacent to the glazing system; the glazing must be in place to provide structural support and alignment for the shading device.

predecessor: Complete Structural Frame / Façade Support System
rationale: The structural frame or façade support system must be erected to provide the load-bearing substrate for attaching the shading device.
Functional testing (e.g., sun tracking, motorized operation, or manual adjustment) can only occur after the shading device is fully installed and connected.

successor: Install Interior Finishes on North Face
rationale: Interior finishes work can proceed during or after shading installation, but completing the shading first avoids potential damage to interior surfaces during exterior device mounting.
The shading device is often the outermost layer of the façade assembly and should be installed after primary cladding but before final weather seals are closed, ensuring proper integration.
The structural frame must be erected to provide the supporting structure within which the ventilation opening will be installed.
Wall panels must be in place to define the location and boundaries for the ventilation opening cutout or frame.
The ventilation opening must be fully installed before ductwork can be connected to it.

successor: North Face Air Sealing and Insulation
rationale: Air sealing and insulation around the ventilation opening can only be completed after the opening assembly is in place.
Interior finishing work such as drywall and trim around the ventilation area is typically performed after the vent opening is installed, though it could be staged differently with temporary covers.

predecessor: Excavation for North Face Drainage Channel
rationale: The ground must be excavated to the required depth and profile before the drainage channel structure can be installed.

successor: Backfilling and Compaction around North Face Drainage Channel
rationale: The drainage channel must be fully installed and secured before backfill material can be placed and compacted around it.

successor: Connection of Drainage Pipes to North Face Drainage Channel
rationale: The channel must be in place to serve as the connection point for drainage pipes that outlet water from the channel.

successor: Paving or Surface Finish over North Face Area
rationale: The drainage channel must be installed and covered (e.g., with grates or lids) before final paving or surface finishing can proceed over the area.

successor: Excavation for North Face Drainage Channel
rationale: Overall site grading must establish the drainage slope and alignments before precise excavation for the drainage channel can begin.
The building site must be cleared and excavated to the required depth before any foundation work can begin.
Soil conditions must be assessed and the ground prepared (compacted/levelled) to support the foundation interface.

predecessor: Utility trenching and underground services installation
rationale: Underground utilities (drainage, water, electrical conduits) must be laid in trenches before the foundation interface is constructed, to avoid later excavation through the foundation.

successor: Vertical wall formwork and reinforcement for north face
rationale: The foundation interface provides the structural base and anchor points for the north face wall construction; walls cannot be safely erected without a completed foundation interface.

successor: Waterproofing and damp-proof membrane application on north face
rationale: Foundation interface must be fully cured and set before applying waterproofing membranes to ensure proper adhesion and protection against moisture ingress.
Scaffolding must be in place to provide safe access to the north face facade for surveyors to inspect and measure the facade.
Survey data (dimensions, conditions, defects) of the north face facade must be collected before the facade design can be finalized to ensure accurate specifications.
Quantities and types of materials required for the north face facade can only be determined after the survey is complete.
Any necessary repairs or surface preparation work on the north face facade must be informed by the survey findings.
The roof junction sits atop the north face wall assembly; the wall structure must be built first to provide the load-bearing support for the roof junction connection.

The roof sheathing panels must be installed before the junction element can be connected, as the junction ties the roof plane to the wall and requires the sheathed deck for proper fastening and weatherproofing integration.
Roof flashing at the junction between the wall and roof must be installed after the junction component is in place, as the flashing wraps over and seals the transition point.

successor: North Face Insulation and Interior Finish
rationale: While interior finishing can technically begin before the junction is fully complete, it is strongly preferable to finish all structural connections at the roof-wall junction first to avoid rework and ensure a continuous thermal envelope.
The roof framing members (rafters/trusses) must be erected and aligned before the junction component can be installed, as the junction connects the roof framing to the wall framing.
The structural framing of the north face must be complete to provide a surface onto which insulation can be attached and supported.

predecessor: North Face Weather Barrier / Sheathing Installation
rationale: Sheathing or weather barrier must be installed over the framing before insulation can be placed, to protect the insulation from moisture and provide a continuous substrate.
The vapor barrier is installed over the insulation to control moisture diffusion, so insulation must be in place first.
Interior finishes such as drywall or paneling are installed after insulation to enclose the building envelope and provide a finished interior surface.

successor: North Face Electrical / MEP Rough-In Inspection
rationale: While insulation is typically installed after MEP rough-ins are inspected, in some sequences the final inspection is deferred until after insulation; this is a soft preference based on inspection access requirements.
Structural steel frame must be in place to provide support and attachment points for the glazing system on the north face.
The curtain wall mullions and transoms must be installed first to create the framework into which the glazing panels are placed and sealed.
Waterproofing must be completed behind and around the glazing zone to prevent moisture intrusion once the glazing is in place.

successor: North Face Glazing Sealant and Gasket Installation
rationale: Glazing panels must be installed first before sealants and gaskets can be applied to weatherproof and seal the joints between panels.

Interior finishes near the north face glazing are typically completed after glazing to avoid damage to finishes during glass installation, though some overlapping work may be possible with careful sequencing.
The thermal bridging assessment must be performed on the completed exterior wall assembly to evaluate actual thermal performance.
Insulation must be in place before thermal bridging can be assessed, as the assessment evaluates heat flow through insulated and uninsulated components.
The assessment findings must be complete to inform the design of thermal bridging remediation measures.

successor: North Face Window and Door Installation
rationale: Thermal bridging assessment results may impact window and door placement and detailing to minimize thermal breaks.
Scaffolding must be erected to provide safe access to the north face of the building for cleaning and maintenance work.
Scaffolding can only be dismantled after the north face cleaning and maintenance work is completed, as the scaffolding is needed for access during the work.
The north face must be cleaned and maintained before a final inspection can be conducted to verify the quality and completeness of the work.
Scaffolding removal can only begin after all north face cleaning and maintenance tasks are finished, as the scaffolding provides the working platform.
A preliminary surface assessment must be performed first to identify required cleaning methods, repairs, and safety concerns before commencing the actual cleaning and maintenance work.
The U-value calculation requires knowing the type and thickness of insulation material to compute thermal resistance.
The U-value calculation needs the full wall assembly layers (cladding, sheathing, air gap, etc.) defined to compute overall thermal transmittance.

predecessor: North Face Stud Size and Spacing Determination
rationale: Framing dimensions affect the thermal bridging component in the U-value calculation.
The calculated U-value must be reviewed and approved against energy code requirements before construction can proceed.
The construction team needs the approved U-value and corresponding assembly specifications to build the wall correctly.
Shade sails require a stable structural deck or slab to anchor their support posts; without the slab, the posts have no secure foundation.
Shade sails are often tensioned between steel columns or existing structures; the steel frame must be in place to provide attachment points for the sail hardware.

While landscaping can proceed before shade sails, it is preferable to complete sail installation first to avoid damage to finished planting and paving from access equipment needed for tensioning hardware.

If lighting is integrated into or near the shade sail structure, the sail should be installed before final electrical connections to ensure correct positioning of light fixtures relative to the sail membrane.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated to form a stable foundation base before any masonry or wall construction can begin.
A concrete footing or foundation strip is required beneath the wall to provide load-bearing support and prevent settlement or overturning.
Any drainage pipes, electrical conduits, or water lines that will run beneath or near the wall must be installed before the wall is built to avoid later excavation and damage.
Soil must be backfilled and compacted against the completed wall to provide lateral support and proper drainage, which can only be done once the wall structure is in place.

successor: Wall Cladding / Finishing (e.g., render, stone veneer, paint)
rationale: Surface finishes and decorative cladding are applied after the structural wall is complete to avoid damaging the finish during construction and to ensure a uniform final appearance.
The retractable awning must be mounted onto a structurally sound frame or roof structure. Without the framing and roof structure in place, there is no support system to attach the awning to.

The exterior wall surface (e.g., siding, stucco, brick) to which the awning mounting brackets are anchored must be completed first, as installing the awning before wall finishing would interfere with access and require removal or damage to the awning.

For motorized retractable awnings, electrical wiring to the switch and motor location should be roughed in before the awning is installed to avoid difficult retrofitting; however, this is a soft preference if a surface-mounted conduit solution is acceptable.

successor: Interior Ceiling and Wall Finishing (near awning area)
rationale: Once the awning mounting brackets penetrate the exterior wall, finishing work such as drywall patching, painting, and trim around interior mounting points must be completed after the awning is installed to properly seal and finish the penetration.

Heavy machinery and material staging for landscaping could damage the installed awning; therefore, finishing major landscaping work and final cleanup should be done after awning installation to avoid damage and soiling.
Site must be properly graded and drainage installed to ensure water flows away from paved surfaces, preventing pooling, erosion, or sub-base failure.
A compacted aggregate base is required to provide a stable, load-bearing foundation for paving stones or poured slabs.
Excavation to proper depth must be completed to accommodate the base layers and paving thickness.
Paving must be installed first so that adjacent planting beds are at the correct finished grade relative to the hardscape.
It is preferred to complete paving before final clean-up to avoid soiling or damaging the new paved surfaces.
A stable and level foundation (e.g., concrete footings or gravel base) must be completed before the decking platform can be installed to ensure structural integrity and prevent sinking or shifting.
The underlying support frame (joists, beams, posts) must be built and secured before deck boards or platform panels can be laid on top.
Railings, balustrades, or guardrails are typically attached to the deck surface or frame after the decking platform is installed to ensure proper alignment and safety.

Applying sealant, stain, or weatherproof coating is recommended after the deck boards are laid, but could theoretically be done on pre-finished materials; considered a soft preference for optimal curing and even coverage.
A final quality and safety inspection must occur after the decking platform is fully installed to verify compliance with building codes and load-bearing requirements before the deck is put into use.
The outdoor kitchen requires a stable, level concrete slab or foundation base to support the weight of the BBQ station, countertops, appliances, and cabinetry.
Gas lines for the BBQ grill and water supply lines for the sink must be roughed in underground and stubbed up through the slab before the kitchen structure is built over them.
Electrical conduits for outlets, lighting, and appliance connections must be run in the slab or walls before the outdoor kitchen framing and finishes are installed.
The base cabinets, BBQ unit, and supporting structure must be fully assembled and in place before the stone or concrete countertops can be templated, fabricated, and installed on top.
The BBQ unit, sink, and other appliances must be set into their final positions before the gas fitter and plumber can make the final hookups to the stub-outs.
The ground must be properly graded and prepared to provide a stable, level base for the heavy masonry or stone structure of the fireplace/fire pit.
A concrete foundation or slab is required to support the weight of the fireplace/fire pit and prevent settling or cracking.
Gas lines for gas fire pits/fireplaces or electrical lines for ignition systems and lighting must be run underground before the structure is built on top.
The fireplace/fire pit is a focal point; patios, pavers, or stone surrounds should be laid around it after it is in place to ensure proper fit and integration.
It is a soft preference to place furniture and decor after the fireplace is complete so the layout can be finalized around the finished feature.
A rated electrical box must be securely attached to the ceiling structure to support the fan's weight and provide wiring access before the fan unit can be mounted.
Properly rated outdoor electrical cable must be pulled from the switch to the fan location before connecting the fan's wiring.
The wall switch or remote controller wiring must be completed and tested so that the fan can be connected to its power source during installation.
Any ceiling or soffit finishing (e.g., drywall, wood, or vinyl) must be finished before the fan is mounted so that the mounting bracket sits flush against the finished surface.

successor: Install Fan Blades and Light Kit
rationale: The fan motor housing must be securely mounted to the ceiling before attaching blades and any light kit, as these components add weight and require the motor assembly to be in place.
The fan must be fully assembled and connected to power before it can be turned on and tested for balance, speed settings, and proper operation.
Proper site grading and drainage systems must be installed before planting to ensure water flows away from plant roots and prevents soil erosion or water pooling.
The soil must be prepared, cleared of debris, and graded before any planting can occur to provide a suitable growing medium.
All underground utilities (water, gas, electric, telecom) must be laid and buried before planting to avoid damaging new plants during trenching or excavation.
It is preferable to complete hardscape elements such as walls, pathways, and patios before planting to avoid soil compaction and damage to plants from heavy equipment.
The track, rails, or support brackets for outdoor curtains/blinds must be securely mounted to the structure before the curtain fabric or blind slats can be attached.
For motorized outdoor curtains/blinds, electrical rough-in (conduit, wiring, switch boxes) must be completed before installing the finished motorized curtain system.
Exterior wall surfaces (stucco, siding, brick, paint) should be finished before mounting curtain/blind brackets to avoid damaging finished surfaces or requiring rework.

successor: Install Outdoor Lighting / Fixtures Near Curtains
rationale: Outdoor lighting fixtures near the curtain area can be installed before or after curtains, but doing so after risks damaging the curtains during fixture installation.
Structural framing requires a stable, level base provided by completed foundations to transfer loads safely to the ground.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and excavated before any structural framing can be erected to ensure proper working conditions and access.
Underground pipes, conduits, and drainage systems must be in place before framing to avoid conflicts and to ensure that foundations are not disturbed later.
The roof structure and covering depend on the completed frame to provide support and structural integrity.
Exterior wall panels, sheathing, or cladding are typically fastened directly to the structural frame and cannot proceed until the frame is in place.
The site must be graded and prepared before any underground electrical conduits, cables, or outdoor electrical equipment can be installed.
Underground water, gas, and sewer lines must be in place before outdoor electrical trenching and conduit work to avoid conflicts and rework.
Foundations and slabs must be poured and cured before outdoor electrical rough-in can begin, as conduits may embed in or attach to foundation elements.
Outdoor rough-in (conduits, boxes, wiring) must be complete before final outdoor lighting fixtures, receptacles, and equipment can be installed and connected.
All outdoor electrical conduits and rough-in work must be completed and inspected before final concrete pours or paving to avoid cutting into hardened surfaces.

The glazing bars/muntins are installed into the window or door frame to create divided-light panels. The main frame must be in place first as it provides the structural perimeter and support for the muntin grid.
The rough opening for the window or door assembly must be framed before any window components like glazing bars can be installed, as the frame supports the entire window unit.
Glazing bars and muntins create the grid framework that holds individual glass panes; the glass panes are set into the spaces created by the muntin grid, so the grid must be installed first.

Weatherstripping and sealants are applied around the completed glazing assembly (including muntins) after glass is installed to ensure the assembly is watertight and airtight. Sealing cannot occur before the muntin grid is in place.
Interior trim work around windows (such as casing and stops) typically follows glazing installation, but this is more of a construction sequence preference rather than a physical necessity.
The ground must be excavated and prepared before any underground or slab plumbing lines can be installed for the outdoor kitchen.

The plumbing rough-in for an outdoor kitchen/BBQ must be placed in or under the concrete slab before the slab is poured, or the slab must be in place to serve as the base for above-slab plumbing runs.
Main water supply and drain lines to the outdoor kitchen area must be run underground before the plumbing rough-in connections can be made at the kitchen location.
Plumbing lines are typically installed before gas lines to avoid cross-contamination and to allow proper separation between water and gas piping.
While not a strict physical dependency, plumbing is often roughed-in before electrical to allow unobstructed access to plumbing chases and to coordinate layout.

successor: Slab/Concrete Pour (if plumbing is under slab)
rationale: If plumbing rough-in pipes are placed in the slab formwork, the concrete must be poured after the plumbing is inspected and in place to encase the pipes.
The plumbing stubs must be roughed-in and pressure tested before framing and cabinetry are built around them, ensuring access for connections and inspection.
Window reveals are formed within wall openings; the wall structure must be built first to create the opening where the reveal will be installed.
The window frame defines the boundaries of the reveal; the reveal is typically finished around the installed window frame.
The window reveal must be completed and set before final wall plastering or finishing can be applied up to the reveal edges.
The reveal provides the finished opening and seating for the window sash or glazing unit; the sash is installed after the reveal is complete.
Soft preference: painting and trim work around the window are typically done after the reveal is finished to achieve a clean aesthetic, but could theoretically be done before in some sequences.

The window lintel is typically installed as part of or after the masonry wall is built up to the window sill level, providing the vertical support on each side (window jambs) for the lintel to rest upon.
The rough opening for the window must be framed or formed so that the lintel can be placed across the top of the opening to support the structure above.
Precast concrete lintels or steel lintels must be manufactured and cured or fabricated before they can be lifted and installed into position above the window opening.
The window frame is installed within the opening after the lintel is in place because the lintel provides the necessary structural support and load-bearing header above the opening.

The masonry work above the lintel (brickwork, blockwork, or stone) can only proceed after the lintel is installed, as the lintel itself supports this upper masonry and transfers loads to the sides of the opening.
Window frames must be installed first to provide the structural mounting surface for hinges, handles, locks, and other hardware.
Glass panels must be installed and seated in the frame before window hardware (e.g., locking mechanisms, stays, hinges) can be fitted to secure the glass.
All hardware must be installed before windows can be adjusted, balanced, and tested for proper operation and security.
Weatherstripping and final perimeter seals are applied after hardware installation to ensure proper fit around operating mechanisms and to avoid interfering with hardware adjustment.

While interior trim can be installed after hardware, it is a soft preference because trim work is often sequenced later for aesthetic reasons and to avoid damage, though hardware installation could theoretically be done after trim in some cases.
The louvred window must be inserted into the prepared window frame, which provides structural support and proper alignment for the window assembly.
Load-bearing walls must be erected and cured before any window openings can be fitted, as the wall provides the structural opening and support for the window.
Installing weatherproofing around the opening before the window is placed is a best practice to ensure a proper seal, though it could technically be added afterwards in some cases.
Sealants and caulking around the louvred window edges must be applied after the window is securely in place to fill gaps and ensure weather-tightness.
Interior trim and architraves around the window opening must be installed after the louvred window is fixed in position to cover the joint between window frame and wall.
Window openings are formed within framed walls, so the wall framing must be in place to define the rough opening dimensions and provide structural support.
Structural sheathing (e.g., plywood or OSB) is typically installed on framed walls before cutting openings for windows to maintain structural integrity during construction.
Window flashing must be applied directly against the rough opening surfaces to waterproof the opening; this cannot be done until the opening is formed.
The rough opening must be formed and verified for correct dimensions and plumbness before the window unit can be ordered or installed.
The window unit physically requires an existing rough opening formed in the wall to be placed and secured into.
The building's structural frame and shell must be complete to provide the supporting openings and rough openings into which windows are installed.
Rough openings must be properly sized, squared, and inspected to ensure windows will fit correctly and be structurally supported.

predecessor: Exterior Wall Sheathing / Weather Barrier Installation
rationale: Weather-resistant barriers and sheathing behind the window area should be in place to prevent moisture intrusion before window units are set.
Once windows are installed, they must be immediately flashed and sealed to ensure the building envelope is watertight and airtight.
Interior finishing such as drywall around window openings should only proceed after windows are in place to allow for proper trim, shimming, and sealing from the interior side.
Window frames must be fully installed to provide a structural surface for sealing and weatherproofing materials to adhere to.
The glass panes must be set in the frames before perimeter sealing and weatherproofing can be applied around the window assembly.
Exterior wall sheathing provides the surrounding substrate against which window sealing and flashing are integrated to ensure a continuous weather-resistant barrier.
Sealing must be complete to protect the building envelope from moisture before cladding or siding is installed, which would otherwise obscure access to the window seals.
Weatherproofing ensures the window assembly is watertight before interior finishes are applied, preventing moisture damage behind finished walls.
The structural frame must be in place to provide support and load-bearing capacity for the solar shading or window canopy installation.
Exterior wall cladding typically needs to be installed before mountable components like shading devices can be attached to the building envelope.

While shading canopies are often installed before or alongside glazing, it is preferred to have shading in place prior to glass installation to protect glazing from debris and provide immediate solar control.
Final exterior finishes and sealant application around shading devices must occur after installation to ensure proper weatherproofing and integration.
Roof waterproofing at canopy attachment points must be completed before installing shading structures that penetrate the roof or mounting points to prevent water ingress.
The rough opening (door/window opening) must be framed and prepared before the roll-up shutter can be installed, as the shutter mounts to the surrounding structure.
A structural lintel or overhead support must be in place to bear the weight of the rolled-up shutter and its housing.
For motorized shutters, electrical conduit and wiring should be run to the shutter location before installing the shutter mechanism, though it can sometimes be done after.
Any finishing trim, cladding, or sealant around the shutter frame must be applied after the shutter unit is securely mounted.
Final electrical connections to the motor and control switches can only be completed after the shutter unit is physically installed.
The rough opening must be framed and prepared to the correct dimensions before the sliding glass door unit can be installed.
Weather-resistant barrier, flashing, and sealants must be applied around the rough opening to prevent water intrusion before the door is set in place.
The subfloor at the door threshold must be level, clean, and properly prepared to support the door frame and track system.
Interior casing, trim, and drywall finishing around the door opening can only be completed after the sliding glass door frame is permanently installed.
Exterior siding, brick molding, or cladding that abuts the door frame must be installed after the door is set to ensure proper sealing and a weathertight finish.
The rough opening (framed and sized) must be complete to provide the structural space and support for the bi-fold door system.
Floor covering (tile, hardwood, carpet) under the door path must be installed first so the door can be set to the correct finished floor height and operate smoothly.
Walls must be framed and sheathed to define and create the rough opening for the bi-fold door.
Trim and casing are applied around the installed door frame to cover gaps and provide a finished appearance.
While painting can be done before installation, it is often preferred to paint after installation to achieve a seamless finish and touch up any scratches from installation.
The transom frame must be installed and secured in the opening before any glazing material can be placed into it, as the frame provides the structural support and containment for the glass.
The rough opening must be properly framed, leveled, and weatherproofed to receive the transom assembly before glazing can proceed.
The glass or glazing panels must be cut to size and delivered to the jobsite before installation can begin.
Weatherproof sealants and gaskets must be applied after the glazing is placed to secure the glass and prevent water infiltration.

Interior trim around the transom is typically installed after glazing is complete to cover the edges and provide a finished appearance, though this is a sequencing preference rather than a strict physical necessity.

The sill or threshold plate must be installed on a level, cured foundation or slab. Any foundation work, including pouring and curing of concrete, must be completed to provide a stable base for the sill plate.

A sealant, gasket, or foam weatherstrip is typically placed on the foundation before the sill plate is set, to create a moisture and air barrier. Thus the sealant application must precede the plate installation.

predecessor: Anchor Bolt Placement (in wet concrete or after curing)
rationale: Anchor bolts must be embedded in the foundation or slab (either set into wet concrete or installed in drilled holes after curing) before the sill plate can be positioned and bolted down.

The sill plate serves as the base for the wall framing; stud walls are erected on top of and fastened to the sill plate. Therefore wall framing can only begin after the sill plate is installed and secured.

In some construction sequences, floor joists or subfloor may be installed after the sill plate is in place, though this depends on the structural system. It is a logical progression rather than a strict physical necessity.
The rough opening (door/window frame) must be prepared and sized correctly before security grille can be installed.
The grille must be positioned in the opening before it can be anchored and secured in place.
Trim and finish work around the grille is typically done after installation for aesthetic purposes, but not physically required.
The structural glazing frame must be anchored to the primary building structure; without the steel framework in place there is no structural support to attach the mullions to.
Mullions are typically installed from floor slabs or working platforms; the slab at each level must be cured and load-bearing before mullion installation can commence on that level.
Glass panels are directly fixed into or onto the mullion frame; the frame must be erected and aligned before glass infill can be inserted and secured.
Weather seals and gaskets are applied around the interface between the glass panels and the mullion frame; the frame must be in place to serve as the substrate for sealing.

successor: Curtain Wall Air & Water Barrier Testing
rationale: Water penetration and air leakage tests on a curtain wall or glazing system can only be performed after the frame and infill are installed, as the frame is the primary structural element of the assembly.
The rough opening in the building facade must be framed and prepared to the correct dimensions before the revolving door assembly can be set in place.
The floor slab at the door location must be poured, leveled, and finished to support the weight and anchoring of the revolving door base.
Any structural steel supports or lintels above the opening must be in place to bear loads before the door frame is installed.
Power and control wiring for sensors, motors, and safety devices must be connected after the door assembly is positioned so that conduits can be run directly to the door components.
The revolving door must be installed before interior floor finishes are applied around the threshold, as the door base and tracks are integrated with the floor system.
The ramp must be built on a stable, level foundation and slab to ensure proper structural support and correct elevation alignment with the building threshold.
Proper grading and drainage around the building entrance must be completed to ensure water flows away from the ramp area and to establish the correct ground levels before ramp construction.
The building threshold or door sill must be installed so that the ramp can tie into it at the correct height and transition smoothly without a gap or trip hazard.
While not always required, it is practical to complete the ramp before final paving near the entry so that the ramp surface can be blended or matched with the surrounding finish.
Handrails and guardrails must be installed after the ramp is in place so that they can be anchored to the ramp structure and aligned precisely with the ramp slope and edges.

The structural steel frame provides the primary load-bearing structure onto which the street-level signage band must be mounted or attached. The signage band cannot be installed without the underlying frame in place.

The street-level signage band is typically integrated into the building's exterior envelope or curtain wall system. The envelope must be completed to define the mounting surface and weatherproofing for the signage band.

The signage band establishes the landmark street-level identity of the building; interior fit-out and final finishes for ground-floor retail or lobby spaces depend on the signage band's position and supporting infrastructure being complete.

successor: Scaffolding / Hoarding Removal at Street Level
rationale: Permanent street-level scaffolding and construction hoarding cannot be fully removed until the signage band is installed, as the band's installation may require access equipment and the band itself completes the facade appearance.

predecessor: Electrical Rough-In and Conduit to Signage Locations
rationale: Power supply conduits, junction boxes, and electrical rough-ins for illuminated signage must be installed within the wall/frame cavities before the signage band can be physically mounted and connected.
The building's structural frame and shell must be completed to provide a stable mounting surface and opening for the shopfront/storefront system.
Rough openings in the building envelope must be framed and prepared to the correct dimensions before the storefront system can be installed.
The building envelope must be properly waterproofed and weather-sealed around openings before storefront installation to prevent moisture ingress behind the installed system.
Glass panels and glazing are typically installed after the supporting storefront frame is in place to provide the finished transparent enclosure.

Interior finishes are typically sequenced after storefront installation so that interior materials can be fitted flush against the installed storefront system and to avoid damage to interior finishes during storefront installation.
The threshold surface must be clean, dry, and free of debris, dust, or grease for the waterproofing membrane to adhere properly.
The structural subfloor or deck beneath the threshold must be in place to provide a stable substrate for waterproofing application.
The door frame must be installed so that the threshold waterproofing can be properly integrated and sealed against the frame, preventing water ingress at the joint.
The waterproofing membrane or sealant must be allowed to fully cure and dry according to manufacturer specifications before any subsequent work proceeds.
The waterproofing must be complete and cured to provide a watertight base before the physical threshold piece (e.g., metal or stone saddle) is installed and bedded in sealant.

successor: Floor Finishing (e.g., Tiling, Flooring) up to Threshold
rationale: Waterproofing protects the substrate from moisture damage; finished flooring adjoining the threshold should be installed after waterproofing is complete to maintain the water barrier continuity.
Security shutters are typically mounted to the frame or structure around doors/windows, so the frames must be in place first to provide the attachment surface.
Walls with openings must be completed and cured before shutter brackets can be securely anchored to the structure.
If shutters are motorized, electrical conduit and wiring for shutter motors and controls must be roughed in before the shutters are installed.
It is preferable to install shutters before final finishes to avoid damage to completed paint or cladding during shutter installation, though not a strict physical necessity.
Motorized shutters must be physically installed before their electrical connections can be finalized, tested, and commissioned.
The window or door frame must be structurally installed and the rough opening prepared before glazing (glass) can be fitted into it; otherwise there is no supporting structure for the glass.
Old or damaged glass must be removed from the frame before new glazing can be installed or maintenance performed on the glazing system.
After the glazing unit is placed in the frame, sealants and weatherproofing must be applied around the perimeter to ensure water-tightness and thermal performance.

Interior trim work and finishing around the window or door is more conveniently completed after the glazing is installed, though it could theoretically be done beforehand (soft preference for work sequencing).
After glazing installation or maintenance, the glass surfaces must be cleaned and the installation inspected to verify proper fit, sealing, and operation before the area can be considered complete.
The ground must be cleared and excavated to expose the foundation footprint before any wall construction can begin.
Perimeter walls require a continuous foundation or footing to bear the structural load and provide a level base.
Underground drainage, conduit, and water pipes beneath the wall line must be installed before the footing and wall are placed, as retrofitting is extremely difficult.
Backfill material can only be placed against the wall after the wall structure is complete and has achieved sufficient strength to resist lateral earth pressure.
The interior floor slab is typically poured after the perimeter walls are in place, as the walls act as a form and containment boundary for the concrete slab.
Picture rails are attached to wall framing; framing must be in place to provide structural support for mounting.
The wall sheathing or substrate (e.g., drywall or plaster backing) must be in place to provide a surface for securing the picture rail.
Picture rail must be installed before final wall finishing so that paint and trim can be applied seamlessly around or up to the rail.
While artwork can be hung any time after the rail is installed, it is a soft preference to complete hanging after the picture rail is fully secured and finished.
If wiring or outlets need to be positioned relative to the picture rail height, it is preferable but not strictly required to install the rail first to avoid interference.
Cornice moulding is installed where the wall meets the ceiling; wall framing provides the structural substrate and nailing surface for attaching the moulding.
The cornice moulding covers the joint between the wall and ceiling; the ceiling must be in place so the moulding can be fitted flush against it.
Exterior wall sheathing or cladding provides the finished surface against which exterior cornice moulding is sealed and fastened.
Cornice moulding is typically painted or finished after installation; performing painting after installation allows the moulding and wall/ceiling to be painted continuously without gaps.
Inspection of trim work including cornice moulding must occur after installation to verify quality, alignment, and adherence to specifications before sign-off.
Dado rails are mounted onto wall surfaces, so the wall framing (studs) must be completed and sheathed to provide a structural substrate for attachment.
Dado rails are typically installed over finished drywall; the drywall must be hung, taped, mudded, and sanded smooth before the dado rail can be affixed.

It is often more efficient to paint the wall area above the dado rail before installation to avoid masking and paint bleed, though the rail can be painted separately; this is a soft preference for finish quality.

Dado rails are installed at a height above the floor; however, flooring should be completed before dado rail installation if the rail extends to the floor (e.g., as a skirting/baseboard). For dado rails placed mid-wall, flooring can occur after, but in typical sequences flooring is done first to avoid damaging the rail. Assuming dado rail as a mid-wall decorative element, flooring after is acceptable but generally flooring is completed before trim work for a clean finish.
The dado rail installation is part of the trim carpentry scope, so it must be completed before a final inspection or punch list walk-through for interior millwork.
Wainscoting panels are typically attached to wall framing or studs, so the wall structure must be in place to provide a mounting surface.

predecessor: Drywall Installation or Plastering (on lower wall portion)
rationale: While wainscoting can be installed over drywall, in many cases the wall behind the wainscoting may be finished differently; however, if the wainscoting covers the lower wall, the upper wall finishing above the wainscoting is typically completed first for a clean look.
Electrical boxes and wiring must be installed behind the wainscoting before the panels are placed, as they would be inaccessible afterward.

successor: Trim and Molding Installation (chair rail, baseboard, corner trim)
rationale: Chair rail, baseboard, and other trim pieces are typically installed after the wainscoting panels are in place to cover edges and create finished transitions.
Final painting or staining of the wainscoting and any caulking/sealing at joints is done after panels and trim are installed for a uniform finish.
Accent spotlights are typically mounted on or recessed into ceilings, so the ceiling structure must be in place before the spotlight can be installed.
Electrical wiring and junction boxes must be run and in place before the accent spotlight fixture can be connected and installed.
After the accent spotlight is installed, final adjustments to the fixture's aim, focus, and trim (e.g., bezel or baffle) are typically performed to achieve the desired lighting effect.

Once the accent spotlight is installed, lighting can reveal imperfections in the wall or feature finish; touch-up painting or finishing is often done after installation to ensure a flawless appearance under the actual lighting conditions.
The accent spotlight must be installed and connected before the full electrical system can be tested and commissioned to verify all fixtures function correctly.
Electrical power and control wiring must be in place to supply the daylight control blind motor and control system.
The daylight control blind must be mounted to or within the window frame; without the frame in place there is no structural support for the blind.
Glass panels must be installed in the window frames before blinds are attached, as the blind is typically mounted to the glazed frame and glass protects the interior.
While not strictly required, installing blinds after wall finishing prevents damage to finished surfaces and allows for proper alignment with interior finishes.
The blind must be fully installed and operational before the space is occupied or commissioned, as it is required for occupant comfort and daylight control.
The foundation or base surface must be prepared, leveled, and cured before the display plinth can be installed to ensure structural stability and proper alignment.

predecessor: Route electrical and data cabling to plinth location
rationale: Electrical power and data/AV cables must be run to the plinth location prior to installation so that connections can be made without requiring later disruption or exposed wiring.
The plinth must be securely installed and level before any display screens, monitors, or exhibits can be mounted onto it.

successor: Connect electrical and AV services to plinth
rationale: Final connection of power and audiovisual cables to the integrated display plinth can only be completed once the plinth is in its final position.

successor: Apply final finishing and sealing around plinth
rationale: Any adjacent floor, wall, or decorative finishes that abut the plinth should be completed after the plinth is installed to achieve a clean, integrated appearance.
The conduit is typically embedded in or placed on top of the structural slab, so the structural slab must be in place before conduit installation can begin.
Electrical boxes and backboxes must be positioned and mounted before conduit runs can be connected to them.
If conduit is embedded in a slab, the concrete pour must occur after the conduit is laid and secured to avoid burying incomplete work.
