Conduit must be fully installed, joined, and inspected before wires or cables can be pulled through it to avoid damage and ensure code compliance.
It is preferential to complete conduit runs before enclosing walls to avoid rework, but conduit can be retrofitted if necessary.
Wall framing requires a stable load-bearing base; the foundation or slab must be cured and ready to support vertical loads before any wall framing can begin.

Any underground or in-slab rough-in electrical conduits, plumbing lines, or underfloor services must be placed and inspected before framing starts, as they would be inaccessible after the walls are built.
Load-bearing walls and partitions must be erected and braced to provide the structural support for roof trusses or rafters; the roof structure rests directly on the wall top plates.
Exterior sheathing and cladding materials are attached directly to the framed wall studs; the framing must be in place to provide the substrate and nailing surface for sheathing.
After walls are framed, electricians and plumbers can run cables, conduits, pipes, and boxes through the open stud cavities before the walls are closed with drywall or insulation.
Plastering requires a finished masonry substrate to adhere to; brick/block walls must be complete before plaster can be applied.
Electrical conduits, back boxes and wiring must be embedded in walls and ceilings before plastering covers them up.
Plumbing pipes and rough-in fittings for bathrooms/kitchens must be installed within walls/ceilings before plastering encloses them.
Paint and decorative finishes require a smooth, cured plaster surface as their substrate; plastering must be complete and dry before painting begins.

While flooring can technically be done before or after plastering, it is standard practice to plaster first to avoid dust/debris damaging new floors and to achieve clean edge finishes at wall-floor junctions.
Paint cannot be applied to unprepared surfaces; the substrate must be clean, dry, smooth, and free of defects (e.g., holes, cracks, dirt, grease) to ensure proper adhesion and finish quality.

Plaster or drywall joint compound must be fully set, dried, and sanded smooth before any paint or decorative coating can be applied; painting over wet or unsanded plaster will cause cracking, peeling, and poor finish.

predecessor: Primer Application (if separate from paint system)
rationale: When using a separate primer coat, the primer must be fully dry before the topcoat or decorative paint is applied to ensure proper bonding and uniform appearance.

Painting and decorating should be completed before floor finishes are installed to prevent paint drips, overspray, and dust from damaging the finished flooring and to avoid the need for masking or protection of expensive floor coverings.

While final cleaning and touch-up painting can overlap, it is generally preferred to complete the main paint application before the dedicated final clean stage to allow paint to cure and to clean up any overspray or splatter without damaging fresh paint.

Artwork must be mounted on finished wall surfaces. Installing artwork before wall finishes are complete would damage both the artwork and the wall finish, and artwork cannot be properly positioned until the final wall surface is in place.
Ceiling work (painting, installing ceiling tiles, or other finishes) must be completed before artwork installation to avoid dust, debris, and overhead work damaging the installed artwork.

Lighting fixtures that will illuminate artwork must be installed and operational before artwork is hung, so that positioning and aiming of lights can be coordinated with the artwork placement, and to avoid moving artwork after it is installed.

While it is preferable to complete floor finishes before artwork to avoid dust and traffic, artwork is often installed after floors are finished. However, in some sequences floor finishing could still occur after artwork if careful protection is provided, making this a soft preference rather than a hard constraint.

Artwork installation is one of the final finishing activities. Once artwork is hung, the space can undergo final cleaning and punch list completion, as no further construction dust or debris-generating work should occur above or around the artwork.
Fire suppression systems (sprinklers, standpipes, fire pumps) must be physically installed before they can be tested and commissioned.
Fire alarm devices (detectors, pull stations, notification appliances, panels) must be installed before testing their operation and verifying proper communication.
The fire system must be fully tested and commissioned by the contractor before the local fire marshal or authority having jurisdiction conducts their final inspection and grants occupancy approval.

Testing often requires access to above-ceiling components, devices, and piping; permanent ceiling and wall finishes should be installed after testing is complete to avoid cutting, patching, or damage from access panels being opened repeatedly.

While it is strongly preferred and often legally required to complete commissioning before occupancy, some jurisdictions may allow temporary certificates of occupancy before full commissioning is finished under certain conditions.
The balcony guardrail requires the structural balcony slab or deck to be cast and cured first to provide a solid base and anchoring point for the guardrail posts and brackets.
The main structural frame supporting the balcony must be erected and stable before guardrails can be installed, as the rails often tie into columns or edge beams.

Waterproofing is typically applied to the balcony deck surface before guardrails are installed, so that the membrane can run continuously under the rail base plates without being interrupted by posts.

successor: Balcony Railing Glass / Infill Panel Installation
rationale: The guardrail frame (posts and handrails) must be erected and anchored first to provide the support structure into which infill panels, glass panels, or balusters are fitted.

Installing guardrails may scratch or damage the balcony surface finishes; touch-up painting or coating is best performed after guardrails are in place to cover these blemishes and achieve a uniform appearance.
The balcony slab or deck provides the structural base on which the parapet wall is built; the wall cannot be constructed without a supporting floor.
The main building structural frame at the balcony level must be in place to integrate and support the parapet wall.
Waterproofing should be applied to the slab before parapet construction to ensure continuous sealing underneath the wall.
Coping or capping is installed on top of the completed parapet wall to protect it from water ingress and provide a finished edge.
Flashing details (e.g., metal flashings at wall-to-slab junctions) are installed after the parapet wall is built to seal joints.
If a separate railing or balustrade is mounted onto or adjacent to the parapet, the parapet must first be constructed to provide the anchoring surface.
Final exterior finishes like plaster, render, or cladding on the parapet face are applied after the wall is fully constructed and cured.

While drains and gutters can be roughed in earlier, final positioning and connection of drainage elements relative to the parapet is typically done after the parapet wall is built to ensure proper alignment and falls.

successor: Balcony Door / Sliding Glass Door Installation
rationale: The rough opening in the wall must be framed before any door unit can be installed.

successor: Balcony Door / Sliding Glass Door Installation
rationale: The exterior wall sheathing and weather-resistant barrier must be in place to protect against moisture before installing the door unit.

successor: Balcony Door / Sliding Glass Door Installation
rationale: The floor deck or subfloor adjacent to the balcony door must be complete to provide a stable platform and proper threshold support.

predecessor: Balcony Door / Sliding Glass Door Installation
rationale: Exterior trim, drip cap, and flashing must be installed after the door to seal the gap between the door frame and the rough opening.

predecessor: Balcony Door / Sliding Glass Door Installation
rationale: While interior finishes can technically proceed before the door, it is standard practice (soft preference) to install the door first to allow drywall to be fitted neatly against the door frame.
The foundation provides the base support for the entire structure; the balcony brackets must be anchored to a stable foundation or load-bearing wall that has already been built.
Balcony structural brackets are typically bolted or welded to load-bearing walls or columns. These structural elements must be erected and cured before brackets can be attached.
If the primary structure is concrete, it must reach sufficient strength before bearing bracket loads. If steel frame, the frame must be erected and aligned before bracket attachment.
The brackets or cantilever connections serve as the support framework onto which the balcony deck or slab is placed. The deck cannot be installed without the underlying bracket support in place.
Once brackets are secured, the balcony deck, waterproofing membrane, and safety railings are installed sequentially. The structural connection must be verified before these finish activities.

The balcony soffit/ceiling is typically installed below or as part of the balcony structure. The structural slab or deck must be in place to provide the supporting framework and surface onto or beneath which the soffit is attached.
The balcony framing (including joists, beams, and supports) must be completed to create the structural cavity and attachment points for the soffit/ceiling finish.

Waterproofing on the balcony deck above is typically installed before the soffit below to prevent water ingress and allow for proper drainage detailing, as the soffit can conceal or limit access to these membranes once in place.

Electrical conduit, junction boxes, and lighting fixtures are often installed in or through the soffit/ceiling, but the rough-in must be completed after the soffit structure is in place or concurrently. However, soffit finish work (e.g., drywall, cladding) must follow electrical rough-in. This ordering ensures wiring and boxes are embedded before final cladding.

The finished surface material (e.g., drywall, stucco, wood, metal panels) is applied after the soffit substrate and framing are complete. This is a hard constraint because the finish cannot be installed without the underlying soffit structure.

Painting or coating is typically the final step after the soffit finish is installed. It is a soft preference because it could be done later or at a different stage, but logically it follows the finish application.
The electrical outlet must be mounted on or within the balcony structure, so the structural framing and decking must be in place first to provide the substrate for mounting.
The conduit or wiring pathway must be run to the outlet location before the outlet box and device can be installed.

Waterproofing must be applied to protect the electrical components from moisture; penetrating the waterproofing later would compromise its integrity, so outlet installation should occur after waterproofing or with proper sealing.
The outlet must be installed and functional before final trim, fascia, or finishing work is completed to avoid rework and ensure the outlet is properly integrated.
Testing of the electrical outlet (e.g., GFCI testing, voltage check) can only occur after the outlet device is physically installed and wired.

The thermal break must be installed on a stable, clean, and level substrate. Foundation or subfloor surfaces must be fully prepared (cured, cleaned, and leveled) before any thermal break material can be applied or placed.

Thermal breaks are typically installed within or between structural framing members (e.g., stud walls, floor joists, or slab edges). The framing must be in place to define the cavity or interface where the thermal break will be inserted.

An air or weather barrier is often applied over or continuous with the thermal break to ensure a complete envelope seal. The thermal break must be in place first so that the barrier can properly overlap and seal at the transition.

Exterior cladding (e.g., siding, brick veneer, curtain wall) is attached over the thermal break layer. The thermal break must be fully installed to provide the required thermal separation before the cladding system is applied.

While interior finishes typically follow thermal break installation, this is a soft preference because in some systems the thermal break is embedded within the wall assembly and interior finishes could theoretically be installed simultaneously or in a different order, though standard sequencing places thermal break first to avoid thermal bridging issues.

predecessor: Balcony Slab / Deck Concrete Pouring & Curing
rationale: The metal railing posts must be anchored into or bolted onto a structurally complete and cured concrete balcony slab. The slab must be hard and load-bearing before posts are installed.

predecessor: Layout & Marking of Post Positions on Balcony Slab
rationale: Accurate marking based on structural/architectural drawings is needed to position each post correctly before drilling anchor holes and setting the posts.

successor: Balcony Metal Railing Top Rail & Handrail Installation
rationale: Top rails and handrails span between and attach to the posts; the posts must be securely fixed in place first to provide structural support for the rails.

successor: Balcony Metal Railing Infill / Baluster Installation
rationale: Infill panels, balusters, cables, or glass panels are installed between posts; the posts define the frame and must be erected first.

successor: Grouting / Sealing of Post Base Anchors
rationale: After posts are aligned, plumbed, and temporarily bolted, the anchor bolts or base plates must be grouted or sealed against moisture to finalize the connection.

The glass balustrade system is mounted onto the finished balcony slab. The structural slab must be cast and cured to provide a stable base and anchor points for the balustrade post base plates or channel shoes.

Waterproofing must be applied to the balcony slab before balustrade installation to ensure a continuous watertight seal around post fixings and to prevent water ingress that would be difficult to reseal after the glass panels are in place.

Floor tiles or pavers are typically laid up to the base shoe or bottom clamp of the glass balustrade, creating a neat finish. Installing tiles first would obstruct the balustrade base fixing and risk damaging finished tiles during balustrade installation.

If a separate top handrail (e.g., stainless steel or timber) is specified to clamp onto or sit above the glass panels, the glass panels must be in place to set the handrail alignment and fixings accurately.
After the glass panels are installed and fixed, perimeter sealant is applied to weatherproof the interface between glass, frame, and balcony slab. This cannot be done before the glass is in position.
The concrete slab must be fully cured and structurally complete to provide a stable substrate for waterproofing membrane application.

It is preferred that railing posts are installed before waterproofing so that post bases can be properly flashed and sealed into the waterproofing system, though it can be done after with additional detailing.
The balcony surface must be clean, dry, and free of debris, dust, oil, or loose particles to ensure proper adhesion of the waterproofing membrane.
Tile or pavers must be installed on top of the cured waterproofing layer to protect the membrane from UV exposure and mechanical damage, and to provide the finished walking surface.
Drainage components and flashing details (scuppers, drains, weep holes) must be integrated into or completed after the waterproofing membrane to ensure proper water flow and prevent ponding or leaks.
After installation, the waterproofing system must be allowed to cure fully and then be tested (e.g., flood testing) to verify integrity before any overlying materials are placed.
Scaffolding must be erected to provide safe access for inspectors to examine all parts of the balcony structure.
Formwork must be removed to expose the cured concrete/structural elements so they can be visually inspected and tested.
Concrete must reach sufficient strength before structural loading and inspection can safely take place.
Structural inspection must be completed and approved before waterproofing is applied, as waterproofing would conceal structural defects and prevent access for required checks.
Typically railing installation follows structural inspection to ensure the supporting structure is sound, though in some cases railing can be installed earlier if not attached to inspected elements.
The substrate must be clean, dry, and free of debris, dust, or old sealant for the new sealant to properly adhere.
Any cracks, holes, or uneven surfaces must be repaired and leveled before caulking to ensure a uniform seal and prevent future leaks.
Primer must be applied and fully cured to promote adhesion of the sealant to the substrate materials.
Sealant and caulking at joints and penetrations must be completed before the waterproofing membrane is installed to ensure continuity of the waterproofing layer.
After application, the sealant needs adequate time to cure and form a proper seal before any subsequent work or traffic is allowed on the balcony surface.
The ground must be excavated to the required depth and shape before a caisson can be placed or constructed.
The site must be surveyed, cleared, and leveled before caisson installation can commence.
The caisson component must be fabricated or prefabricated off-site before it can be installed or placed on site.
After the caisson is placed, any infill concrete must be poured and allowed to cure.
The caisson foundation must be completed before above-ground structural elements can be built upon it.

The ground must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and topsoil, and excavated to the required depth before a raft foundation can be laid, as the raft slab needs to rest on undisturbed, prepared subgrade.
A geotechnical investigation must be completed to determine soil bearing capacity and confirm that a raft foundation is suitable, before designing and pouring the raft.
The excavated subgrade must be compacted and leveled to provide a uniform, stable base for the raft foundation to avoid differential settlement.

A thin layer of lean concrete (blinding) is typically poured over the prepared subgrade before reinforcement placement to provide a clean, level working surface and prevent soil contamination of the steel.

After the raft foundation is poured, sufficient curing time must be allowed for the concrete to gain adequate strength before any subsequent construction loads (e.g., walls, columns) are placed on it.
Once the raft foundation concrete has cured, waterproofing membranes or coatings are applied to the raft slab to protect the structure from groundwater ingress before backfilling or building above.
The raft foundation must be complete and cured before load-bearing walls, columns, or any vertical structural elements of the superstructure can be erected, as they depend on the raft for support.

While some drainage can be laid before the raft, any underfloor services that penetrate or sit above the raft slab typically must wait until the raft is poured; this is a logical sequence preference to avoid rework.
The ground must be excavated and prepared to the proper depth and location before earth anchors can be placed.
Soil conditions and bearing capacity must be assessed to determine anchor type, depth, and placement requirements before installation can begin.
After the earth anchor is installed, it must be tensioned and proof-tested to verify it meets design load requirements before being put into service.
Once the earth anchor is placed and secured, the excavation can be backfilled and compacted around it to restore the ground conditions.

successor: Attaching structural elements (e.g., retaining wall, foundation)
rationale: The earth anchor must be fully installed and tested before it can be connected to the structural element it is designed to stabilize or support.
Site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and existing structures before ground improvement can commence to provide unobstructed access and a workable surface.
Geotechnical investigations (soil borings, tests) must be completed to determine soil conditions and design appropriate ground improvement methods.
Temporary access roads, water supply, and power must be established to support heavy machinery required for ground improvement (e.g., vibroflotation, stone columns, dynamic compaction).
Ground improvement must be completed to achieve the required soil bearing capacity and settlement characteristics before foundation elements (footings, piles, raft slabs) can be installed.
After ground improvement, the prepared subgrade must be tested and verified for compliance with specifications before laying base courses or slabs-on-grade.
The toe protection must be placed on a properly excavated and prepared foundation to ensure stability and proper load transfer.
A bedding layer or filter fabric is typically required beneath riprap to prevent soil erosion and migration of fine particles through the stone.
The toe protection must be placed at the base of a finished slope or embankment; the embankment itself must be constructed and graded prior to placing toe protection.
Backfill operations adjacent to the toe protection can only proceed after the riprap is in place to prevent displacement of the stone.
Surface finishing and revegetation work above the toe area should follow after the toe protection is installed to avoid disturbing the placed stone.

The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and existing structures before any earthmoving can begin, as obstructions would prevent access for cut and fill equipment and may contaminate the fill material.
Accurate site survey and setting out of reference points, levels, and boundaries is required to guide excavation depths and fill placement to achieve the designed grades and contours.
Temporary access roads and haul routes must be established to allow dump trucks, excavators, bulldozers and compactors to enter and operate across the site during earthworks.

After cut and fill operations achieve the required subgrade levels, the compacted earth must be tested for density and bearing capacity to verify it meets specification before subsequent works proceed.
The building foundation cannot be constructed until the earthworks are complete and the subgrade is properly prepared, leveled, and compacted to the design formation level.

Vegetation, topsoil, and organic matter must be cleared from the slope area before compaction can begin; otherwise, compressible materials would cause settlement and prevent achieving required density.
The slope must be cut or filled to its rough grade before compaction can be applied; compaction works on placed or exposed earth materials at the target elevation.
Compaction must be completed first to densify the soil; final grading and trimming to precise design contours can only be performed on a stable, compacted surface.
Erosion control measures (e.g., matting, revegetation, or blankets) are applied after the slope is compacted and at final grade; installing them before compaction would damage them.
Drainage channels, berms, or subdrains are constructed on the compacted slope; installing drainage before compaction would result in misalignment or damage to drainage structures.
The tread (horizontal walking surface) must be installed first as the riser face vertically abuts and is supported by the tread below it in a stepped terrace configuration.
The underlying ground or sub-base must be properly graded and compacted before any terrace components, including riser faces, are placed to ensure stable support and drainage.
The riser face forms the vertical support for the next tread above; the upper tread cannot be installed until its supporting riser is in place.
Backfill material behind the riser face can only be placed after the riser is erected to avoid disturbing the alignment and structural integrity of the riser.
Sealant or waterproofing treatment at the interface between riser and adjacent components must be applied after the riser is fully positioned to ensure continuous protection against moisture ingress.
Vegetation, topsoil, and organic materials must be removed from the foundation area before placing embankment fill to ensure proper compaction and prevent settlement.
The native ground surface must be graded, scarified, and compacted to a specified density before embankment material can be placed, providing a stable foundation.
Soil borings and laboratory testing must be completed to determine borrow source suitability, moisture-density relationships, and design specifications for the embankment fill material.
Subsurface drainage systems and culverts must be installed prior to embankment placement to control groundwater and prevent hydrostatic pressure buildup that could compromise embankment stability.
The embankment must be completed and compacted to design grade before any pavement structure layers (base or subbase) can be placed on top of it.
Embankment must be shaped to final grade and cross-section before permanent erosion control measures (riprap, turf, gabions) can be installed on the slopes.

While utilities can sometimes be trench-installed after embankment completion, it is far more efficient and avoids rework to place utility conduits and ducts after the embankment is at approximate grade but before final grading.
The embankment fill provides the final subgrade support for the road or platform; paving cannot commence until the embankment is fully placed, shaped, and compacted to design elevation.
The ground must be properly graded and compacted to provide a stable, level foundation for the access ramp structure.
The ramp's supporting footings or foundation walls must be in place before the ramp structure can be built upon them.
Any underground utilities crossing the ramp area must be relocated or protected before excavation and ramp construction begin.
The structural ramp (formwork/rebar) must be fully erected before the final surface material can be placed and finished.
Handrails and guardrails are safety elements that must be installed after the ramp structure is complete so they can be properly anchored.
The ground must be excavated and prepared to the required level and condition before anchor or ground nail installation can begin, as nails require a stable, prepared subgrade.
Precise surveying and layout marking are needed to determine the exact locations for anchor or ground nail placement.
After the anchor or ground nail is placed/driven into the ground, grouting must follow to bond the nail to the surrounding soil or rock.
Once anchors or ground nails are installed, shotcrete or surface stabilization can be applied to hold the excavated face and integrate with the nail heads.
Load testing is typically performed after anchor installation to verify capacity, but in some sequences testing may occur in parallel or at a later stage; generally it follows installation.

The tree must first be planted in the ground before a guard or stake can be placed around/supported against it. The guard surrounds the trunk and the stake supports the tree, both requiring the tree to already be in position.
The tree pit must be excavated to receive the tree before the tree and subsequently the guard/stake can be installed.

It is preferable to apply final grading, topsoil, and mulch after the guard and stake are in place so that the finished landscape level accommodates the guard base and the mulch sits cleanly around the tree, though this is a soft preference since it can be done in reverse order with touch-up work.

Once the guard is installed, access to the tree for irrigation connections and watering may be partially obstructed; irrigation lines and drip emitters should be positioned around the guard/stake after it is in place to ensure proper coverage.
Any adjacent paving, curb, or hardscape must be completed before installing the tree guard to avoid damaging the guard and to ensure the guard sits flush with finished hardscape surfaces.

The bird netting structure is typically suspended from or attached to the main structural steel frame, so the steel frame must be erected first to provide support and anchorage points for the netting.
Bird netting is often installed beneath the roof deck or within the roof structure; the roof deck must be in place to define the area where netting is needed and to provide attachment points.
It is generally easier to install ceiling or soffit finishes after bird netting is in place, as the netting may need to be accessed or adjusted before enclosing it with finished surfaces.

successor: Final Cleaning and Pest Control Inspection
rationale: Bird netting must be fully installed and secured before final cleaning and pest control inspections can verify that the building is bird-proofed and ready for occupancy.
Trees must be planted and established before any pruning or training can be performed on them.
Pruning and training shapes the tree structure and promotes fruit or wood production, which should be done before the first harvest to ensure optimal yield.
Pruning and training is typically performed early in tree development; health inspections may follow to assess the tree's response.
The ground must be properly graded, cleared of debris, and prepared before planting trees to ensure proper root establishment and soil conditions.
All underground utilities (water, gas, electric, sewer lines) must be installed before tree planting to avoid excavating near established trees and damaging root systems.
Soil must be tested and any necessary amendments (pH adjustment, nutrients, drainage improvements) added before planting to ensure trees have optimal growing conditions.
Hardscape elements like paths, patios, and retaining walls should be installed before tree planting to avoid construction equipment damaging newly planted trees and to ensure proper siting.

While irrigation can be installed before or after planting, it is often more practical to install drip irrigation or soaker hoses after trees are placed so emitters can be positioned at each tree's root ball.
Mulch should be applied after trees are planted to retain moisture, regulate soil temperature, and suppress weeds around the newly planted trees.
Final fine grading and topsoil placement is often done after tree planting to ensure proper grade levels around the tree root balls and avoid soil compaction over roots.
Soil testing must be completed first to determine the specific nutrient deficiencies, pH levels, and soil composition, which inform the type and quantity of fertilisers and amendments required.
Vegetation, debris, and obstructions must be removed from the site before fertiliser and soil amendments can be evenly applied across the prepared ground surface.
Rough grading establishes the general topography and drainage patterns, providing a stable and uniform base upon which soil amendments can be incorporated.

Fertilisation and soil amendment must be completed prior to seeding or laying turf to ensure that nutrients and conditioners are already incorporated into the soil, creating an optimal growing medium for the new vegetation.

While irrigation can theoretically be installed before or in parallel, it is common practice to complete soil amendment first to avoid compacting amended soil with heavy trenching equipment, and to allow the irrigation system to be designed around the final soil levels.
The site must be cleared of debris, weeds, and vegetation that can harbor pests and diseases before any pest management program can be effectively implemented.
Soil analysis identifies existing pathogens, nematodes, and pest populations in the soil, which is essential information for designing an appropriate pest and disease management strategy.

Pest and disease management activities (such as applying pesticides, monitoring, and control measures) are reactive to the presence of plants/crops that can be affected; planting must occur first to establish the host plants that require protection.
After implementing initial pest and disease control measures, ongoing monitoring of plant health and pest populations is needed to assess treatment effectiveness and adjust management strategies.

Pest and disease control must be completed before harvesting to ensure that harvested produce is free from pest damage and chemical residues within safe limits, and to allow required pre-harvest intervals for any pesticide applications.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and prepared before any harvesting can take place, as harvesting requires access to mature crops or timber on a prepared site.
Crops or trees must be planted and grown to maturity before they can be harvested.
Irrigation systems must be in place during the growth period to ensure crops reach harvestable maturity.
Fertilizers and pest control measures must be applied during the growth cycle to ensure healthy, harvestable yield.
After harvesting, the collected crops or timber must undergo processing (e.g., threshing, cleaning, drying) before storage or use.
The hole must be dug before the tree pit structure or tree can be placed into it.
Once the tree pit is installed (including tree and root ball), the surrounding area must be backfilled to secure the tree.
Proper drainage (e.g., gravel or drainage matting) must be in place at the bottom of the pit before installing the tree pit to prevent waterlogging.
The overall site must be cleared and graded to the proper level before digging specific tree pits.

successor: Installation of Tree Guards or Grates
rationale: Tree guards or grates are installed around the tree after it is placed in the pit to protect it without interfering with planting.
The ground must be excavated and prepared before installing any fixed structure like a tree guard or bollard frame to ensure proper foundation and alignment.
The concrete base or foundation must be poured and cured to provide a stable anchor for the bollard frame or tree guard.
Any underground pipes, cables, or drainage must be laid before installing fixed ground-penetrating elements to avoid damaging utilities.
The bollard or guard frame must be in place before final paving or hardscaping around it to achieve a clean finish and proper integration.

successor: Tree Planting (if guard is around a tree)
rationale: The protective guard must be installed before planting the tree so the tree can be placed within the guard without disturbing the frame.
The planting area must be cleared of debris, vegetation, and graded to proper drainage slopes before trees can be planted to ensure soil contact and prevent water pooling.
Underground utilities must be located and marked before digging planting holes to avoid damaging gas lines, water pipes, or electrical conduits.
Soil must be tested, loosened, and amended with compost or other conditioners to provide adequate nutrients and drainage for tree root establishment.

While irrigation is ideally installed before planting to avoid root disturbance, in practice it can follow planting; however, planting must be substantially complete to finalize irrigation layout around placed trees.
Trees must be planted and staked before applying mulch around their bases and completing final landscape grading to avoid covering or damaging newly planted trees.
The area must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and obstructions before excavating tree pits to ensure safe and unobstructed access to the excavation locations.
All underground utilities must be located and marked to avoid damaging existing services (gas, water, electric, telecom) during excavation of tree pits, which is a critical safety requirement.
Rough grading and bulk earthwork operations should be completed first so that the final ground levels and site topography are established before individual tree pits are excavated to correct depths.
The pit must be excavated before any preparation work such as placing drainage gravel, installing drainage pipes, or soil conditioning can be carried out within the pit.
The excavated pit provides the physical space required for placing the tree root ball; tree planting cannot begin until the pit has been dug to the correct dimensions.

Subgrade must be prepared and proof-rolled to ensure a stable, uniform base before backfilling the root zone. Any instability in the subgrade would compromise the compaction and performance of the root zone layer.

predecessor: Installation of Drainage System (e.g., perforated pipes, gravel blanket)
rationale: Drainage infrastructure must be installed beneath the root zone before backfilling, as the root zone mix is placed on top of the drainage layer. Backfilling over an incomplete drainage system would make installation impossible or require re-excavation.

successor: Installation of Irrigation System (pop-up sprinklers, drip lines)
rationale: Irrigation pipes and sprinklers are typically laid within or immediately on top of the compacted root zone mix. Backfilling and compaction must be complete to provide a stable base for irrigation installation without risk of pipe damage or uneven settling.

successor: Final Grading & Fine Leveling of Root Zone Surface
rationale: After the root zone material is backfilled and compacted in lifts, final grading is performed to achieve the precise surface contours required for turf or planting. This fine grading cannot be done before compaction, as the surface would shift during compaction.

The root zone must be fully placed, compacted, and finely graded to the correct specification before any turf (sod, seed, or hydroseed) is installed. Installing turf on uncompacted or incomplete root zone would result in poor root establishment and surface failure.
Tree grates and guards are installed within or adjacent to sidewalks and curbs. The sidewalk and curb must be in place first to provide the proper base and alignment for the tree grate and guard.
The tree must be planted before the grate and guard can be installed around it, as the grate is designed to fit around the tree trunk and provide soil protection.
Underground utility lines must be completed before tree grates are installed to avoid the need to excavate or disturb the grate and guard later for utility access.
Once tree grates and guards are installed, final landscaping and grading can be completed around them to provide a finished appearance, though this is a soft preference for aesthetic sequencing.
Soil type, drainage, pH, and site conditions must be known to select tree species that are compatible with the local environment.
Knowledge of local climate, frost dates, and USDA hardiness zone is required to choose species that will survive and thrive.
The spatial layout, functional zones, and aesthetic goals of the landscape must be defined before selecting specific tree species.
Specific tree species must be selected before nursery stock can be ordered and delivered.

successor: Site Preparation and Planting Bed Layout
rationale: Planting locations, spacing, and bed preparation depend on the species selected and their mature size requirements.
The ground must be leveled, cleared of debris, and properly graded before constructing any planter structure to ensure stable foundation and proper drainage.
If the planter box is built on a slab or requires a concrete base, the foundation must be cured and set before the planter walls or box structure can be erected.
Any drainage pipes, irrigation lines, or utility conduits that run beneath the planter must be installed before the planter box is built to avoid excavation damage later.
The planter box structure must be fully constructed and cured (if masonry) to contain the soil before soil can be placed inside.
Irrigation lines and drip emitters within the planter are typically installed after the box is built and before final planting, as the box defines the planting area.
Trees and plants can only be placed into the planter after the planter box structure is complete and filled with soil.
While finishing touches like mulch and decorative stone are typically applied after planting, they could in theory be done earlier if staging materials, though this would be impractical.
The site must be cleared of vegetation and prepared before deadwood piles can be placed, as the piles need a designated area free of obstructions.
The raw materials (logs, branches, brush) must be delivered to the site before they can be assembled into a deadwood habitat pile.

Revegetation around the deadwood pile is typically done after the pile is in place to avoid disturbing the structure during planting; however, some planting could theoretically occur first, making this a soft preference.
The deadwood habitat pile must be completed before the final inspection of the habitat features can be conducted.
The ground must be cleared, levelled, and prepared before any structure like a compost bay can be built to ensure stability and proper drainage.
A solid concrete base or paving slab foundation is required before constructing the bay walls to provide a level, stable surface and prevent ground moisture rising into the compost.
The bay structure must be fully constructed before any composting material can be placed inside it.
Covers or lids are typically added after the bay is built, though they could be installed concurrently if prefabricated; this is a logical preference for ease of construction.

successor: Landscaping and Final Grading Around Bay
rationale: Final landscaping such as adding gravel, bark mulch, or turf around the bay is typically done after the structure is in place for a neat finish, but this is a soft preference rather than a hard physical constraint.
The ground must be properly prepared, cleared, and leveled before installing timber edging to ensure a stable and even base for the timber elements.
The soil subgrade must be compacted to provide adequate support and prevent settling or shifting of the timber edging after installation.
Any required sub-surface drainage or gravel base must be installed before timber edging to prevent water pooling and rot in the timber.
After the timber edging is positioned and secured, the area behind it must be backfilled and compacted to lock the edging in place and provide lateral support.
The timber edging defines the boundary for the finished surface material (paving, gravel, mulch, etc.), so the edging must be complete before the adjacent surface layer is applied.
The climbing plant support structure needs a stable base; site preparation including excavation, leveling, and foundation pouring must be completed before any vertical support members can be erected.
Underground utilities and drainage lines must be placed before support posts or footings are installed to avoid digging up or interfering with the completed support structure.
The support structure must be fully installed and stable before climbing plants or vines are planted and trained onto it, as the structure provides the necessary framework for vertical growth.

successor: Installation of Irrigation/Drip Lines for Green Wall
rationale: While irrigation can be designed and laid out earlier, final attachment of drip lines to the support structure is best done after the structure is in place to ensure proper alignment and coverage for the plants.

Landscaping finishing work such as spreading mulch or decorative ground cover around the base of the support structure should be done after the structure is erected to create a neat, finished appearance and avoid re-work.
The ground must be cleared, graded, and prepared before any planting or installation of native hedgerows can begin to ensure proper soil conditions and layout.
Soil must be tested and any necessary amendments (compost, pH adjustment) applied before planting to ensure the native hedgerow species can establish and thrive.
Any required sub-surface drainage or swales must be installed prior to hedgerow planting to prevent waterlogging and ensure proper root development.

While irrigation can be rough-installed before planting, final connection, adjustment, and drip-line placement around the hedgerow plants typically occurs after planting to avoid damage and ensure correct positioning.
After the native hedgerow is planted, an erosion control blanket or mulch layer must be applied to protect the soil, retain moisture, and suppress weeds around the new plants.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and graded before laying any path material to ensure proper drainage and a stable base.

predecessor: Sub-base Preparation (Compacted Soil or Geotextile Fabric)
rationale: A compacted sub-base or weed barrier fabric must be installed before gravel or bark mulch is placed to prevent weed growth and provide structural support.
Edging (e.g., metal, plastic, or stone borders) must be installed before pouring/spreading gravel or mulch to contain the material and maintain a clean edge.
While not a hard physical constraint, it is practical to complete the path before planting adjacent beds to avoid disturbing the path material during planting work.
Gravel paths typically require compaction or tamping after spreading to lock the stones in place and create a stable walking surface.
Site survey and soil testing must be completed before clearance to identify contaminated soils, underground utilities, and site boundaries to ensure safe and compliant clearance operations.
Required environmental permits and approvals must be obtained before any vegetation removal or ground disturbance begins to comply with regulations and avoid legal penalties.

predecessor: Site Security and Access Control Setup
rationale: Site perimeter fencing, access gates, and security measures must be installed prior to clearance to control entry, prevent theft, and ensure safety during active work.
Vegetation removal and scarification of the topsoil layer must be completed before bulk earthworks can commence to expose the ground surface for accurate grading and compaction.

Clearance and scarification expose bare soil, making it vulnerable to erosion; therefore, erosion control measures such as silt fences and sediment basins must be installed immediately after clearance to prevent environmental runoff.
The site must be cleared and prepared before installing habitat features to ensure safe access and proper placement of deadwood and structures.
Erosion control measures must be in place before habitat installation to prevent soil disturbance and sedimentation during the installation process.
Deadwood material is often sourced from harvested trees, and the harvesting area must be cleared before deadwood can be arranged as habitat features.
Habitat features must be in place before final restoration and planting so that vegetation can be integrated around the structures and deadwood piles.
Monitoring typically begins after installation is complete, though this is a procedural preference rather than a physical constraint.
The site must be cleared of debris, vegetation, and obstructions before seed broadcasting to ensure good seed-to-soil contact and uniform distribution.
Soil testing must be completed to determine pH, nutrient levels, and any required amendments before seeding to ensure optimal growing conditions for the new seed.
Any required soil amendments (lime, fertilizer, compost) must be applied and incorporated into the soil before seeding to provide a suitable seedbed and nutrients for germination.
The soil must be tilled or cultivated to a fine, loose consistency to create a proper seedbed that allows seeds to make good contact with the soil for germination.
A light mulch layer or erosion control blanket must be applied immediately after seeding to protect seeds from birds, wind, and water runoff, and to retain moisture for germination.
Soil testing must be completed first to determine existing nutrient levels, pH, contaminants, and soil composition before any amendments can be designed and applied.
Site must be cleared of existing structures, debris, and demolition waste before soil can be accessed and amended.
Rough grading and earthmoving must be completed so the soil surface is at the proper elevation and contours before amendments are incorporated.

While some erosion control measures (e.g., perimeter controls) may be installed before, detailed surface stabilization and revegetation-based erosion control typically follow soil amendment to protect the newly conditioned soil.
Soil must be properly amended, impoverished (if required for specific plant communities), and conditioned before any planting, seeding, sodding, or landscaping work can begin.

Subsurface drainage (e.g., french drains, perforated pipe) is often installed before or concurrently with soil amendment, but final surface drainage adjustments and fine grading to work with the amended soil profile follow amendment.
After amendments are tilled or mixed into the soil, fine grading to achieve final surface tolerances and smoothness must be performed before paving or hardscape installation.
Soil conditioning and settlement must be completed before rigid hardscape elements are placed to avoid differential settlement and cracking.
Site assessment must identify which invasive species are present, their extent, and density before any management actions can be planned and executed.
Regulatory permits and landowner/stakeholder approvals are legally required before initiating invasive species removal, herbicide application, or biological control measures.
Invasive plants must be removed or controlled first to clear the area and reduce competition before native species can be successfully established.
Removing invasives can disturb soil; erosion control measures (e.g., silt fencing, mulching) must follow to prevent soil loss until native vegetation re-establishes.
Post-removal monitoring is needed to detect regrowth or re-infestation, but this is a soft preference as some monitoring can overlap with replanting phases.
Legal and contractual site access must be established before any ecological survey work can commence on the site.

predecessor: Desk Study and Existing Data Review
rationale: A preliminary desk study reviewing existing ecological records, designated sites, and habitat maps is required to inform and scope the field survey methodology.
The field survey data (species, habitats, protected areas) is the primary input needed to assess ecological impacts.
Survey results identify constraints and opportunities that must be known before designing mitigation measures (e.g., translocation, buffer zones, habitat creation).
Regulatory submissions (e.g., protected species licenses, biodiversity net gain statements) require current survey data as supporting evidence.

The ground must be excavated and prepared before any boundary permeability modifications (such as installing cutoff walls, slurry trenches, or grouting) can be performed, as these modifications require access to the subsurface.
Soil and groundwater conditions must be understood through geotechnical investigation to design the appropriate permeability modification method (e.g., grouting, diaphragm walls, jet grouting).

Permeability modifications (e.g., cutoff walls or grout curtains) must be completed before foundations are constructed to ensure the foundation is protected from groundwater ingress or soil instability.

While backfilling often occurs after permeability treatments, in some sequences backfilling may proceed concurrently in zones not being treated; however, typically the modification must be complete to avoid disturbing the treatment.
Permanent waterproofing and drainage systems are installed after the boundary permeability has been modified to provide a complete water management system for the structure.
The ground must be cleared and excavated to the required depth and dimensions before footings can be placed, as the footings need a prepared, stable subgrade.
The soil subgrade must be compacted and graded to the correct bearing capacity and level before pouring or placing the footing/foundation base to prevent settlement and ensure structural stability.
The exact location, orientation, and elevation of the footings must be surveyed and staked out before excavation and forming of the footings can proceed, ensuring alignment with structural drawings.

Footings or the foundation base must be fully cured and have achieved sufficient strength before masonry or concrete foundation walls (stem walls) can be constructed on top of them, as the walls depend on the footing for load transfer.

While under-slab utilities are often laid after footings are poured and before the slab is placed, it is a workflow preference to coordinate utility rough-in after footing completion to avoid damaging fresh footings.
Coping stones are installed on top of finished walls or parapets to provide a finished edge and weather protection. The wall structure must be complete to support the coping.
Coping stones cap the top of parapet walls, so the parapet must be built first to provide the substrate for the coping.
The roof deck or substrate adjacent to parapets must be prepared before coping installation to ensure proper flashing integration and waterproofing continuity.
Counterflashing or cap flashing is often installed over or integrated with coping stones to create a waterproof seal; the coping provides the anchor point for the flashing.
Sealants and waterproofing at joints between coping stones and between coping and wall must be applied after coping stones are set in place to ensure weathertight seals.
Weep holes are built into masonry walls during construction to allow water drainage; the wall must exist before weep holes can be installed.

Weep holes are placed above flashing to allow water to escape; flashing must be installed after or concurrently with weep hole placement but typically weep holes are positioned above the flashing layer.
While weep holes should be kept clear, exterior finishes like stucco or siding are typically applied after weep holes are in place, though care must be taken not to block them.
Weep holes are typically located at the base of walls above the foundation; the foundation and subfloor must be complete before the lowest course of masonry and weep holes are installed.

Weep holes should be verified as clear and functional before final inspection and water testing of the building envelope, though this is a quality assurance preference rather than a physical necessity.
The wall foundation must be built first to provide structural support for the gate opening within the wall.
The surrounding wall structure must be partially erected to define the opening location and provide anchoring points for the gate frame.
The gate opening must be prepared before the gate door and frame can be installed into the opening.
The opening must be created and reinforced before the wall finishing work around the opening can be completed, as the opening defines the boundary for finishes.
The gate opening must be complete and the frame installed before hardware such as hinges and locks can be mounted.
The pilaster/pier requires a solid foundation/footing to bear its vertical load and transfer it to the ground; the foundation must be in place before any vertical structural element is erected.
The ground must be excavated, leveled, and compacted before the foundation/footing for the pilaster/pier can be placed; soil preparation is a prerequisite.
Steel reinforcement cage must be positioned and tied within the pier formwork before concrete is poured to ensure structural integrity.
The formwork mold must be assembled and braced to contain the wet concrete and shape the pilaster/pier before the concrete pour can occur.
After the pilaster/pier is poured, it must undergo a curing period to achieve design strength before any loads can be applied or subsequent construction can proceed.
Beams and girders typically bear onto pilasters/piers; the vertical support must be fully constructed and cured before horizontal structural members are placed on top.
If the pilaster/pier is an integral part of a wall system (e.g., engaged pilaster), the vertical support must be built before the adjacent masonry infill or wall panels are constructed.
Pilasters often serve as abutments or springing points for arches; the pier must be complete to support the arch thrust and weight.
While damp-proofing can be sequenced later, it is good practice to apply waterproofing to below-grade portions of the pier soon after curing to protect against moisture ingress before backfilling.
Gate posts require a stable foundation or concrete footing to be set in, so foundation preparation (excavation, forming, pouring footings) must be completed before gate posts are installed.
Gate hinges and hardware must be attached to the gate posts after the posts are firmly set and cured in place.
The gate posts must be in place and secure before the gate leaf or panel can be hung on them.
Adjacent fencing or wall sections connect to the gate posts, so the posts must be erected first to provide the attachment point.
While not a strict physical necessity, finishing work such as capping, painting, or sealing the gate posts is typically done after installation to protect and dress the completed posts.
Electrical wiring must be installed within the wall cavity before the fixture housing can be mounted, as the housing covers and connects to the wiring.
Wall framing must be complete to provide the structural support and cavity for mounting the light fixture housing.
Sheathing or backing material must be in place to provide a secure mounting surface for the fixture housing.
The fixture housing must be installed in the wall cavity before wall finishes are applied, so that the housing is recessed and the finish can be cut around it.

successor: Light Fixture Trim and Bulb Installation
rationale: The housing must be securely mounted and connected to power before the decorative trim, lenses, and bulbs can be attached to complete the fixture.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, structures, and debris before excavation can begin to ensure unobstructed access for excavators and to define the excavation boundaries.

Soil bearing capacity, groundwater levels, and underground utility locations must be known before excavation to determine safe excavation methods, shoring requirements, and to avoid damaging buried services.
Excavation must be completed to design depth and the setting out (staking of column positions) finished before foundation elements such as footings, piles, or blinding concrete can be placed.
Trenches for stormwater, sewer, and water supply lines are typically excavated and laid within the open excavation area before backfilling, requiring the main excavation to be complete first.
Formwork must be in place to contain the wet concrete and shape the footings before pouring can occur.
Reinforcing steel must be positioned and tied within the formwork to provide structural reinforcement before concrete is poured.
Excavation must be completed to create the space and reach the required bearing strata for footings before concrete can be placed.
After pouring, the concrete must undergo a curing period to gain sufficient structural strength before any loads are applied.
Formwork cannot be removed until the poured concrete has achieved enough strength to support its own weight and any imposed loads.
Masonry walls require a solid, level foundation to bear the load of the bricks/blocks. Without completed foundations, bricklaying cannot structurally commence.
The ground floor slab or base must be poured and cured before load-bearing masonry walls can be erected on top of it.
The building site must be cleared, leveled and excavated for foundations before any masonry work can begin.
Load-bearing masonry walls must be completed to support the roof structure above them.
Concealed plumbing pipes within masonry walls must be installed after the walls are built but before final finishing.
Electrical wiring conduits and boxes embedded in or running through masonry walls can only be placed after the walls are erected.
Masonry surfaces must be complete and cured before they can be plastered, rendered or finished.
Mortar materials (cement, sand, lime, water, admixtures) must be procured and delivered to the site before any mixing can begin.
Bricks, blocks, or stones must be stored, sorted, and prepared (e.g., wetting if necessary) prior to laying with mortar.
Working platforms and scaffolding must be in place to safely support masons applying mortar at height.
Fresh mortar must be mixed and applied to bed joints and perpends immediately before placing masonry units to ensure proper bond and workability.

Tooling and finishing of mortar joints (striking, pointing) must occur after mortar is applied and while it is still plastic but has begun to stiffen, to achieve proper compaction and weather-resistant finish.
The foundation must be prepared and leveled before the damp proof course (DPC) can be installed, as DPC is typically laid on top of the foundation walls to prevent rising damp.
Excavation must be completed to expose the foundation area where the DPC will be installed at the base of the walls.
The concrete foundation must be poured and cured to provide a solid base for the DPC membrane or course to be installed.
The DPC must be in place before any masonry work above the DPC level can commence, as the DPC acts as a waterproof barrier that must be continuous within the wall construction.
The DPC at wall level must be installed prior to pouring the floor slab to ensure proper integration and continuity of the damp proofing system between walls and floor.
Rendering requires a stable substrate; the wall must be built and cured before any plaster or render can be applied to its surface.
Internal wall framing must be erected to provide a backing surface for lath and plaster or drywall finishing.

predecessor: Plumbing & Electrical Rough-In (First Fix) within Walls
rationale: All pipes, conduits, cables, and outlet boxes must be installed inside the wall cavity before the wall is closed up with render or plaster to avoid costly retrofitting.
Paint, wallpaper, and decorative finishes require a smooth, cured render or plaster surface to adhere properly.
Wall tiles must be fixed onto a rendered/plastered surface (or onto a waterproof render/backer board) that has been properly prepared and cured.
A stable foundation must be prepared before the Trellis Framework can be installed, as the framework requires a solid base for structural support.
Ground anchors or footings must be in place to secure the trellis framework to prevent tipping or collapse under load.
The trellis framework must be complete and stable before climbing plants can be installed, as the plants require the structure for support.
Cross-bracing can be installed after the main framework is erected for added stability, though it could also be done concurrently as a soft preference.
Final alignment and leveling adjustments must occur after the trellis framework is assembled to ensure the structure is plumb and square.
A stable foundation or base must be prepared before an upright post can be installed to ensure structural support and vertical alignment.
The exact location and alignment must be marked and surveyed before setting the post to ensure proper positioning.
Horizontal beams or cross-members can only be attached once the upright post is securely in place to provide vertical support.
Final anchoring, grouting, or concrete curing around the post base must occur after the post is positioned to secure it permanently.
Plumbness and vertical alignment verification can only be performed once the post is erected and temporarily braced.
The cross beam must be anchored to a solid foundation; foundation must be poured and cured before beam placement.
Cross beams typically span between columns; columns must be erected to provide vertical support and connection points for the beam.
Cross beams serve as primary horizontal supports for decking or floor slabs; the deck cannot be placed until the supporting beams are in position.
After the beam is positioned, it must be permanently bolted or welded to its connections before structural loads can be applied.
Lateral or temporary bracing is often installed after the cross beam is in place to stabilize the frame before additional loads are added.
Diagonal bracing is typically installed within wall frames to provide lateral stability; the wall studs must be erected first to provide the structural frame onto which bracing elements are attached.
The bottom plate of the wall must be secured to the floor or foundation before diagonal bracing can be anchored at its lower end.
The top plate must be in place to provide the upper connection point for diagonal bracing elements.

Sheathing (e.g., plywood or OSB) is typically installed over the frame after diagonal bracing is in place, as the bracing provides necessary temporary lateral stability and must not be covered prematurely.

Exterior cladding or siding is applied after bracing is complete because the bracing contributes to the structural rigidity of the wall assembly and must be inspected and fully installed before covering.
The lattice panel requires a stable and level base support structure, typically a concrete foundation or slab, to be installed and cured before the panel can be mounted securely.

Lattice panels are often attached to or supported by the building's structural frame (columns, beams, walls); therefore the frame must be erected first to provide the attachment points and load-bearing support.
Lattice panels serve as a substrate or infill for exterior cladding, insulation, and finishing layers; the panels must be in place before final finishes can be applied over them.

successor: Electrical and MEP Rough-In Behind Panels
rationale: Any electrical wiring, plumbing, or mechanical services that run behind or through lattice panels must be installed after the panels are fixed, as the panels create the enclosure space for these services.
The climbing plant support wire needs to be attached to a solid structural wall or column. The wall or column must be constructed first to provide a substrate for mounting the wire system.
The support wire must be installed before planting climbing plants so that the plants can immediately be trained onto the wire system as they grow.

The support wire may be mounted onto or through exterior finishes; typically the wire is installed before final finishing or the finishing is done around the wire. In many sequences, rough mounting happens before finish work.

While not directly attached to foundations, the overall structural stability (including foundations) must be complete before any above-ground wall attachments are made, but this is an indirect dependency.
A scaffold or working platform may be needed to safely access the height at which the support wire will be installed along a wall or facade.
The post base anchor requires a stable foundation base; excavation must be completed to expose the footing area where the anchor will be placed.
Post base anchors are typically embedded or bolted into cured concrete footings; the concrete must be poured and sufficiently cured before anchor installation.
The post base anchor must be in place (embedded or bolted) before the vertical post can be mounted and secured onto it.
After the post base anchor is positioned and the post is set, the anchor bolts must be tightened to secure the connection.
It is good practice to align and plumb the post after it is placed on the anchor, though in some cases alignment can be adjusted simultaneously; this is a soft preference for quality control.

Pergola rafters must be supported by the pergola posts, which provide the vertical structure and attachment points for the rafters. Posts must be installed and secured first to bear the load of the rafters.

Pergola beams (or ledger board) are typically installed on top of the posts before rafters are placed, as rafters sit on or attach to the beams. Beams provide the horizontal support framework for the rafters.
If the pergola is being covered with a solid roof, roof sheathing or roofing material is installed on top of the rafters. The rafters form the structural framework that supports the roof covering.
Blocking or cross-bracing between rafters is installed after the rafters are in place to provide lateral stability and prevent rotation or movement of the rafters.

While finishing can theoretically be done before installation, it is often preferred to apply paint, stain, or sealant after all rafters are installed to ensure a uniform finish and to cover any cuts or attachment points made during installation.
A stable, compacted subgrade is physically required to support the walkway pavement and prevent uneven settling or cracking.
A properly graded and compacted aggregate base layer provides drainage and a load-bearing platform, which is structurally required before any paved surface can be laid.
Edge restraints or formwork define the perimeter and thickness of the paved surface and must be in place before pouring concrete or laying pavers.
Control joints must be cut into the concrete after it has been placed and finished, while it is still green, to control cracking.
Fresh concrete must cure for a specified period to gain strength before any loads or further construction can occur on the surface.
The road base or sub-base must be compacted and prepared before edging kerbs are installed to provide a stable foundation and proper alignment.
Underground drainage pipes and services must be laid before kerb installation to avoid excavating around finished kerbs and to ensure proper drainage alignment.
Edging kerbs define the boundary and formwork for paving; pavement material is placed and finished against the installed kerbs to create a clean edge and proper confinement.
Final landscaping, topsoiling, and grass seeding adjacent to the kerb are typically done after kerb installation to avoid damaging the new kerbs during earthworks.
Road or pavement line marking is applied after edging kerbs are in place to ensure markings align correctly with the defined kerb lines.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and existing structures before any excavation and foundation work can begin, as these activities require a clear and accessible work area.

Accurate site surveying and staking out of building footprints and excavation limits must be completed before excavation and foundation work can commence, as they provide the necessary layout and grade references.

predecessor: Temporary Utilities and Site Access Setup
rationale: Temporary power, water, and site access roads must be established before heavy excavation equipment and foundation construction can be mobilized and operated.
The foundation must be fully completed, cured, and inspected before any structural framing (columns, beams, slabs) can be erected on top of it.

Underground utilities that pass through or beneath the foundation must be installed after excavation and foundation work, as the foundation provides the base and penetrations are coordinated during foundation construction.
A stable foundation and base are physically required before erecting the trellis framework, as the framework must be anchored to a prepared base to ensure structural stability and alignment.
All trellis components (steel beams, connectors, fasteners) must be procured, delivered, and inspected for quality and completeness before erection can commence.
The site must be cleared of debris, vegetation, and obstacles, and properly graded to provide a level working area for safe erection of the trellis framework.
Cladding and panels are typically mounted onto or supported by the trellis framework, so the framework must be fully erected and stable before any cladding installation can begin.

While not always a hard physical constraint, it is a standard construction sequencing preference to run electrical conduit and plumbing lines after the framework is in place, as the framework provides support routes and avoids rework.
Site must be graded, cleared, and leveled to provide suitable soil conditions and space for planting.
Soil must be analyzed and properly conditioned (e.g., pH adjustment, nutrient addition) to support healthy plant growth before planting can begin.
Underground drainage and irrigation systems must be installed prior to planting to avoid damaging new plants during excavation.
Mulch and top-dressing are applied after planting to retain moisture, suppress weeds, and protect newly planted vegetation.
Post-planting care such as watering, fertilization, and staking must occur after plants are in the ground to ensure their survival and proper growth.
Plants must be in the ground and established before any maintenance or pruning can occur.
Plants need to be established with sufficient root growth before pruning, to avoid stress and ensure plant health.
Pruning often precedes fertilization to avoid stimulating new growth that would then be cut off; however, this is a preference for optimal growth cycles rather than a strict physical necessity.
Pruning opens up the canopy and exposes inner branches, making it easier to inspect for pests and diseases, and pruning cuts must be checked for signs of infection.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and graded before building a raised bed to ensure a stable, even foundation and proper drainage.
Any drainage pipes or irrigation lines that will run under or near the raised bed must be installed first to avoid excavating under the finished bed structure.
A compacted gravel base, concrete footing, or other foundation layer must be placed before assembling the raised bed frame to provide structural support and prevent settling.
The raised bed structure must be fully assembled and in place before it can be filled with growing medium or soil.
Plants or seeds can only be placed into the raised bed after the bed structure is built and filled with growing medium.
The building's foundation must be fully cured and load-bearing before any frame erection can begin, as the frame transfers all structural loads to the foundation.
The site must be cleared, leveled, and prepared to provide a stable working platform and access for cranes and frame erection equipment.
Underground plumbing, electrical conduits, and drainage must be installed before the frame is erected, as these would be impossible or extremely costly to install under the completed structure.
The structural frame provides the supporting structure for the roof; the roof system cannot be installed until the frame is complete and stable.
Exterior wall panels and cladding are attached directly to the structural frame, which must be erected first to provide the supporting substrate.
Structural framing provides the substrate and support for sealing and weatherproofing membranes; without the frame in place, there is nothing to apply weatherproofing to.
The roof deck must be installed to provide a surface for waterproofing membranes and sealants to protect the building interior from moisture ingress.
Exterior sheathing (e.g., plywood or OSB) provides the continuous surface onto which weather-resistive barriers and sealants are applied.
Weatherproofing must be complete before cladding is installed because the weather-resistive barrier acts as the primary defense against moisture; cladding is installed over it.
Weatherproofing around rough openings must be applied before windows and doors are installed to ensure proper flashing and sealing against water infiltration.

The structural frame and core (columns, slabs, shear walls) must be complete to provide the physical support and enclosed spaces where mechanical and plumbing systems are installed. MEP rough-in cannot proceed without the building's primary structure in place.

The roof and exterior enclosure (walls, windows) must be weathertight before installing mechanical and plumbing systems to protect equipment and materials from water damage and environmental exposure.
Underslab plumbing (drainage, water supply lines) and mechanical ductwork in slabs require the ground slab/foundation to be poured and cured before MEP rough-in can commence.

MEP rough-in (piping, ductwork, conduits) must be installed, inspected, and pressure-tested within walls and ceiling spaces before they are enclosed by drywall/plasterboard and ceiling linings. This prevents destructive rework.

Mechanical ductwork and plumbing risers often run in ceiling spaces and service shafts. Electrical and data cabling should generally follow mechanical rough-in to avoid conflicts in routing and to ensure proper separation between wet and electrical services.

Seating surfaces (like benches, bleachers, or stadium seats) require a structural frame or support structure to be installed first, as the seating surface must be anchored to or mounted on the structural framework.
For seating surfaces in arenas or theaters, the underlying subfloor, deck, or terrace structure must be completed to provide a level and stable base for installing seating.
The seating surface (seat pan or bench) must be in place before seat backs can be attached, as the backrest typically mounts to the seat structure.
Armrests are typically attached to the sides of the seating surface or to the frame that holds the seat, so the seating surface must be installed first.

While seat numbering is typically done after seating surfaces are installed for accurate mapping, it is a soft preference as labels could theoretically be applied to seats before installation in some cases.
The backrest must be attached to the frame, so the frame must be assembled first to provide a stable structure for mounting the backrest.
The structural metal or wood frame of the backrest must be fully welded/constructed before any cushioning or upholstery can be applied to it.
The backrest must be in place before the seat cushion is installed to ensure proper alignment and fit within the chair frame.
The foam padding must be molded and cured before the fabric or leather cover can be stretched and fastened over it.
While armrests can sometimes be installed before the backrest, installing the backrest first provides better access and alignment for attaching armrests to the backrest sides.
The seat frame provides the structural foundation and attachment points for the legs or supports, so the frame must be assembled first to secure the legs properly.
The raw materials for the legs must be cut, shaped, and machined to the correct dimensions before they can be attached as supports to the seat.
The legs/supports must be installed on the seat first so that the base or mounting brackets can be properly aligned and fastened to the completed leg assembly.
Legs and supports must be fully installed before stability and load tests can be performed to verify the seat's structural integrity.
While not strictly required by physics, it is preferred to install legs early in final integration to allow positioning and balancing of other components on the seat.
The armrests must be attached to a completed chair frame that provides the structural mounting points and support for the armrest components.
