All armrest parts (padding, brackets, covers) must be fabricated and prepared before assembly onto the chair frame.
Armrest installation must be completed before final upholstery and trim work so that the covering materials can be smoothly integrated over and around the installed armrests.
The armrests must be fully installed before the final quality inspection can check for proper alignment, stability, and finish of all chair components including the armrests.
The positions for brackets and anchor bolts must be marked out first to ensure accurate placement.
Anchor bolts need to be set into or fixed onto a cured concrete foundation; the foundation must exist before brackets can be fixed.
Steel columns are typically bolted or fixed onto the anchor bolts/brackets, so the brackets/bolts must be in place first to receive the columns.
Steel beams often connect to columns which sit on anchor bolts/brackets; the brackets/bolts must be fixed before the structural steel frame erection.
The entire steel frame relies on anchor bolts for base connection; brackets and bolts must be fixed before any steel frame erection commences.
The ground must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and topsoil, and excavated to the required depth and footprint before any foundation concrete can be placed.
Soil bearing capacity and ground conditions must be assessed to determine foundation design depth, type, and reinforcement requirements before pouring the base pad.
The exact location, alignment, and levels for the foundation must be marked out on site before excavation and formwork can begin.

After the base pad is poured, sufficient curing time must be allowed for the concrete to gain strength, and waterproofing membranes must be applied before backfilling or erecting superstructure elements.

Steel reinforcement cage must be placed and tied within the foundation excavation before the concrete pour; this is actually concurrent or immediately prior to the pour, but the full foundation / base pad must be understood as the completed reinforced concrete element.

The ground must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and topsoil, and excavated to the required depth and dimensions before any concrete can be placed, as the foundation must rest on undisturbed or properly compacted soil.
Formwork (shuttering) must be assembled and braced in place to define the shape and dimensions of the foundation, providing a mold into which the wet concrete is poured.

Steel reinforcement bars (rebar) must be cut, bent, tied, and positioned within the formwork before concrete is poured, as the rebar provides tensile strength and must be fully encased in the concrete.

After pouring, the concrete must undergo a controlled curing process (keeping it moist and at appropriate temperature) to achieve the required strength and durability; curing cannot begin until the concrete is placed.

While curing should ideally finish first, waterproofing membranes or coatings are typically applied after the concrete has sufficiently cured and dried. This is a strong preference but can sometimes be done with partial curing depending on the product used.

Backfilling around the foundation walls can only occur after the foundation concrete has been poured and has achieved sufficient strength, as the soil pressure from backfill would otherwise displace or damage uncured concrete.
Seats must be anchored to a completed floor structure to ensure proper alignment, stability, and load distribution.
Wall finishing (painting, paneling, etc.) must be completed before seating is installed to avoid damaging finished walls or obstructing access for finishing work.
Electrical wiring and conduit installation must be completed before seating is installed, as seats may cover floor outlets or require power connections for motorized or heated seats.
Seat installation must be completed before final floor finishing around/under the seats (e.g., carpet cutting and tucking, tile edging) to achieve a clean, finished look.
Seat installation is one of the last major interior finishes; the space cannot be deemed complete or ready for occupancy until seating is fully installed and secured.
Structural elements like walls, columns, and slabs must be completed before surface treatments (plastering, painting, tiling) can begin, as the surfaces need a stable substrate.
Concealed MEP installations (conduits, pipes, wiring) behind walls and ceilings must be completed prior to closing up surfaces with finishes to avoid costly rework.
The building envelope must be watertight before interior finishes are applied to prevent water damage to finished surfaces.
All finishing work including painting, tiling, and flooring must be completed before final cleaning and commissioning to avoid soiling or damaging finished surfaces.

While many fixtures can be installed after finishes, it is generally preferred to complete painting and wall finishes before installing light fixtures, switches, and sockets to avoid damaging them during finishing work.
Materials must be procured and delivered to the site before they can be inspected for quality and compliance with specifications.
Site preparation (clearing, grading, excavation) must be completed so that inspectors can verify that the site conditions meet the required standards before proceeding.
Foundations must be laid and cured before an inspection can verify their structural integrity, dimensions, and compliance with engineering drawings.
Inspection must confirm that formwork, reinforcement, and preparations are correct before concrete can be poured, as any defect would be impossible to correct after pouring.
Quality checks of rough-in work and structural components must be completed before MEP systems are installed, as they conceal the inspected elements behind walls and ceilings.
The building must first be constructed and finished before any periodic maintenance or re-finishing can be performed, as there is nothing to maintain or refinish beforehand.
After re-finishing or maintenance work is completed, the space must be allowed for finishing (e.g., drying, curing) before it can be re-occupied and used normally.
A quality check or inspection typically follows maintenance and re-finishing work to ensure standards are met, though this is a procedural preference rather than a hard physical constraint.
A condition survey or assessment of wear and tear must be completed before maintenance and re-finishing can begin, to identify what areas need attention and what work is required.

successor: Periodic Maintenance & Re-finishing (Application of New Finish)
rationale: Surfaces must be properly prepared by cleaning, stripping old finishes, and sanding before new finishes or coatings can be applied during re-finishing.
General site access, security fencing, and staging areas must be established before any repair work can commence.
A security assessment is needed to understand the extent of vandalism damage and ensure the site is safe for workers to enter before repairs begin.
It is logical to perform final cleaning and demobilization after repairs are completed, though some cleaning may overlap; thus it is a soft preference.
Inspection and quality control must follow repair and replacement work to verify that all vandalism damage has been properly corrected and materials meet standards.
The ground must be leveled and cleared of debris before building a raised bed to ensure a stable base and proper drainage.
A gravel base or foundation layer is often needed for drainage and to prevent the raised bed from sinking or shifting.
The raised bed structure must be fully assembled and in place before it can be filled with soil or growing medium.
Drip irrigation or soaker hoses are typically laid out within the raised bed after it is built but before planting.
Plants or seeds cannot be placed into a raised bed until the bed structure and soil are in place.
The rainwater downpipes from the roof gutters must be installed first so they can be directed into the water butt or harvesting tank.
A level, stable base (e.g., concrete slab or compacted hardcore) must be prepared before placing the water butt or tank to ensure it is stable and level.

successor: Overflow Pipe Connection to Drainage System
rationale: The tank must be in position before its overflow pipe can be connected to the drainage system.

successor: Connection to Garden Irrigation System or Hose
rationale: While technically the connection can be made after the tank is placed, it is typically done afterward to avoid damage to the hose/pipe during tank positioning.
The tank must be installed before any inline filter or leaf separator fitted between the downpipe and tank can be fully connected.
The potting bench needs a level, stable concrete slab or foundation to sit on; installing the bench before the foundation is poured would not provide structural support.
Shelving and storage units that attach to or sit above the potting bench must be installed after the bench is in place to ensure proper alignment and spacing.
If the potting bench includes an integrated sink, the bench must be in its final position before connecting water supply and drainage lines to ensure correct fit and access.

successor: Electrical Outlet Installation at Bench Location
rationale: Electrical outlets intended for the potting bench area should be wired after the bench is positioned to guarantee proper placement relative to the bench surface.
The potting bench is typically placed against a wall; framing and wall sheathing must be complete to provide a finished surface for the bench to rest against or attach to.
The site must be cleared of debris, vegetation, and existing structures to allow proper layout, surveying, and installation of perimeter fencing without obstruction.

predecessor: Site Surveying / Layout / Earthworks Cut & Fill
rationale: The site must be graded and surveyed to establish proper boundary lines, elevations, and fence alignments before installing the perimeter enclosure.

Perimeter fencing must be installed first to secure the construction site, control access, and establish the boundary before mobilizing equipment, materials, and setting up temporary facilities onsite.

A secured perimeter is required to prevent unauthorized access, protect valuable equipment and materials, and ensure safe working conditions before commencing foundation excavation and substructure work.
Site security and access control via fencing must be established before underground utility trenching and installation begins, to protect both workers and equipment and prevent theft or vandalism.
Edging must be installed after the subfloor or deck surface is prepared, as it defines the perimeter and finishing edge of the flooring surface.
Edging is typically the final trim or border piece that covers the expansion gap and provides a finished look around the perimeter after the main flooring material has been laid.
Baseboard or quarter round trim is often installed after edging to cover the transition between the floor edge and the wall, though in some cases it can be done concurrently.
Edging completes the visual perimeter of the flooring, so final inspection and finishing touches like caulking or touch-up paint typically follow its installation.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and graded before any pathway construction can begin to ensure a stable and properly sloped base.
A compacted gravel or crushed stone base layer must be laid and compacted to provide a stable subgrade that prevents settling and shifting of the walkway.
Any underground pipes, conduits, or drainage lines that will run beneath the path must be installed before the walkway is built to avoid trenching through the finished surface.
Plants, sod, or decorative mulch should be installed after the walkway is completed to avoid soil displacement onto the finished path and to allow precise planting up to the edges.
While fences can be built before or after, installing the walkway first allows alignment of gates with the path and avoids damaging new path surfaces during fence post installation.
The ground or surface where grow bags or containers will be placed must be leveled and cleared of debris to ensure stability and proper drainage.

predecessor: Hardscape Base Preparation (if on hard surface)
rationale: If placing grow bags on a patio or hardscape, the base must be prepared to allow for drainage and prevent water pooling.
It is preferable to plan and install irrigation supply lines before positioning containers to avoid having to move them later, though drip lines can be added after.
Grow bags and containers must be in their final position before filling with growing media, as filled containers are heavy and difficult to move.
Plants cannot be placed into grow bags or containers until the container itself is positioned and ready.
The ground must be prepared and leveled before any structural elements like trellis supports can be installed to ensure stability and proper alignment.
Concrete footings or foundations for trellis posts must be poured and cured before the trellis structure can be erected to provide a stable base.
Any underground electrical, irrigation, or drainage lines in the area must be installed before placing trellis posts to avoid conflicts and excavation damage.
The trellis or support structure must be fully erected before plants can be trained onto it, as the structure provides the framework for plant growth.
Soft preference: final grading and mulching can be completed after trellis installation to give a clean finished appearance around the bases, though it could also be done prior in some sequences.
The cloche structure requires a stable foundation or base to be prepared before it can be erected or installed.
The structural frame of the cloche must be assembled first to provide support before glass or glazing panels can be installed.
Once the cloche structure is complete, interior finishing work such as flooring, lighting, and planting can begin.
The irrigation controller needs a water supply line to control; the main supply line must be in place before the controller can be connected and programmed.

predecessor: Run electrical conduit and wiring to controller location
rationale: The irrigation controller requires electrical power to operate; conduit and wiring must be roughed in before mounting and connecting the controller.
The controller must be installed before it can be wired to and control the irrigation zone valves; otherwise the valve connections have no control signal.

successor: Program irrigation schedule and system commissioning
rationale: Programming the timing and zones requires the controller to be physically installed and powered; commissioning can only occur after the controller is operational.

successor: Complete landscape finish grading and planting
rationale: While not physically required, it is best practice to have the controller installed and operational before final planting so that the irrigation system can be tested and adjusted to protect new plantings.
The site must be cleared of existing structures, debris, and vegetation before soil preparation can begin, as soil amendment requires access to bare ground.
Boundaries and grading limits must be staked out before soil work commences to ensure preparation occurs within the correct areas.
Amended soil must be prepared and in place before final grading and topsoil placement can be performed, as these activities depend on the underlying soil being conditioned.
All soil amendments (e.g., pH adjustment, compost incorporation, tillage) must be completed before planting to ensure a proper growing medium for vegetation.
Soil must be properly prepared and amended to support seed germination and root establishment before any turf installation can occur.
Underground utilities must be identified and marked before any excavation or construction to avoid damage and ensure safety.
All construction materials including framing lumber, corner brackets, screws, and soil must be on-site before bed assembly can proceed.
The raised bed frame must be fully assembled and in place before it can be filled with soil mix.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and graded before any fencing can be erected, as the fence line needs to be accessible and the ground must be prepared for post installation.
Boundaries, property lines, and fence alignments must be surveyed and marked out prior to fence installation to ensure the fencing is placed on the correct boundaries and within legal limits.

Perimeter fencing is required to secure the construction site, control access, and prevent theft or vandalism before the main building construction begins. Site security is a prerequisite for starting superstructure work.
Temporary site utilities (water, power, sanitation) are typically installed within the secured perimeter after fencing is in place, ensuring services are protected and access is controlled.
Construction materials and equipment can only be safely delivered and stored on site once the perimeter is secured with fencing to prevent unauthorized access and material theft.
Drainage and substructure works must be completed before laying paths and hard landscaping to ensure a stable base and proper water management, preventing future settlement or water damage.
Ground levels must be finished and compacted before hard landscaping to provide a proper foundation for paths, patios, and other hard surfaces.
External wall finishes should be complete before laying adjacent paths to avoid damage to new walls from construction traffic and to allow correct alignment of paths against finished wall faces.
Roof completion and rainwater downpipe installation must precede hard landscaping to ensure water is properly channeled away from path areas and to avoid rework of paths for drainage connections.
Hard landscaping must be completed before soft landscaping to avoid soil compaction and damage to planted areas from construction traffic during path and paving installation.

While fencing can be installed before paths, it is preferable to complete hard landscaping first to ensure accurate alignment and to avoid damaging newly installed fences with heavy materials and equipment.

A level, stable, and well-drained base is required before any structure can be erected; the ground must be cleared, graded, and compacted to support the foundation or base frame of the greenhouse or cold frame.
The foundation, base frame, or ground anchor system must be in place to provide a structural anchor and load-bearing surface onto which the greenhouse frame components are erected.

Underground or buried utility lines (irrigation water supply, electrical conduit, gas lines for heating) must be laid before the structure is erected; otherwise, trenching and pipe installation would be blocked or extremely difficult once the greenhouse is in place.

The structural frame (aluminum, wood, or steel) must be fully erected and braced before glazing materials (glass, polycarbonate, or polyethylene) can be installed; the frame provides the support and attachment surfaces for the panels.

While benching and shelving can technically be placed after the frame is up, it is a soft preference because some benching systems are modular and freestanding; however, it is most logical and efficient to install them after the structure is enclosed to protect materials from weather.
Compostable organic waste materials must first be collected and separated from non-compostable waste before they can be processed in a composting operation.

A dedicated composting pad or area must be prepared with proper drainage, impermeable surface, and leachate collection systems before composting activities can commence to prevent environmental contamination.
Large organic materials must be shredded or ground into smaller particles to increase surface area for microbial activity before the active composting process begins.
Feedstock moisture must be adjusted to the optimal range (typically 50-60%) before active composting to ensure proper microbial activity and aerobic decomposition.
Feedstock must be properly mixed to achieve an optimal C:N ratio (typically 25:1 to 30:1) before active composting to support effective microbial decomposition and prevent odor issues.
Soil test results are required to determine which crops are suitable for the field and to plan nutrient management in the rotation sequence.
The field must be cleared and prepared before planning the rotation, as the current state of the land (e.g., residue, weeds, compaction) influences crop selection and sequencing.
The crop rotation plan determines which crops will be grown in which fields and seasons, which is needed before ordering the appropriate seeds.
Nutrient requirements depend on the crop sequence defined in the rotation plan; fertilizer plans must be tailored to the specific crops and their rotation order.
The rotation plan defines the sequence of crops across seasons, which is the foundation for creating the detailed planting schedule.
The ground must be prepared and leveled before a compost bin can be placed to ensure stability and proper drainage.
The bin structure must be fully assembled and in place before any organic waste materials can be added to it.
The composting bin must be installed first so that aeration pipes, turning mechanisms, or tumbling features can be integrated into or attached to the bin.
While not strictly required, installing a moisture management system (e.g., a cover or irrigation line) after the bin is in place allows for proper alignment with the bin's design.
If a concrete pad or gravel base is specified for the compost bin, that foundation must be cured and set before the bin is placed on top to prevent sinking or uneven settling.
The frame or support structure must be assembled and in place before the tumbler drum can be mounted onto it.
The tumbler must be installed and secured before it can be filled with organic waste materials for composting.
A level, stable base or foundation must be prepared to support the tumbler assembly before installation can begin.
The ground must be prepared, leveled, and foundation laid before installing the organic waste input point to ensure structural stability.
Drainage and plumbing lines for organic waste collection must be in place before the input point can be connected and installed.
The organic waste input point must be fully installed before it can be connected to the waste processing or composting system.
Functional testing of the organic waste handling system requires the input point to be installed, though some testing could theoretically be done without it.

successor: Surface Finishing and Landscaping Around Input Point
rationale: Final finishes, paving, and landscaping around the organic waste input area must be completed after the unit is installed to ensure proper alignment and access.
A level, stable and properly prepared ground surface is physically required before any heavy equipment or structural component like a screening unit can be installed.
The screening unit requires a load-bearing concrete foundation or pad to be cast and fully cured before the equipment can be placed on it, preventing settlement or structural failure.
Feed and discharge conveyors must be aligned and connected to the screening unit's input/output chutes, which requires the screen to be in its final position first.

Power supply and control cables need to be run to the screening unit's motor and control panel; this can only be completed once the unit is set in place and its electrical connection points are fixed.
Full system testing, including running material through the screen, can only commence after the screening unit is mechanically installed, aligned, and electrically connected.
Compost materials (e.g., organic waste, bulking agents) must be collected and piled before turning can begin, as turning mixes and aerates an existing pile.
A compost pile or windrow must be formed (layered and built) before it can be turned; turning is performed on an established pile to aerate and homogenize it.

After turning, moisture levels are often checked and adjusted (adding water or dry amendments) because turning exposes the inner material, allowing better moisture assessment and distribution; this is a soft preference as moisture can be adjusted at other times too.

Turning aerates and homogenizes the active composting pile; once the active phase is complete, the compost enters a curing/maturing phase where it is left undisturbed to stabilize. Turning must finish before curing begins.

predecessor: Site Selection and Permitting for Compost Area
rationale: The location for the compost area must be selected and relevant permits obtained before any physical site preparation work can begin, as the boundaries and legal compliance requirements dictate the scope of preparation activities.

successor: Installation of Compost Bins or Windrow Systems
rationale: The ground must be cleared, leveled, and prepared before compost bins, windrow systems, or any composting infrastructure can be installed on the site.

successor: Layout and Marking of Compost Pads and Aisles
rationale: Once the site is prepared (cleared and graded), the specific locations for compost pads, working aisles, and equipment access routes can be marked out and laid out.

successor: Installation of Drainage and Runoff Control Systems
rationale: Site preparation must be completed first to provide a clean, graded surface upon which drainage systems, swales, and runoff collection features can be installed to manage leachate and stormwater.

successor: Delivery and Stockpiling of Compost Feedstock Materials
rationale: While feedstock delivery can technically begin before site preparation is fully complete, it is more practical and organized to prepare the site first so that materials can be placed directly in their designated storage areas without obstruction.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and graded before any wall construction can begin to ensure a stable foundation.
Concrete footings or foundations must be poured and cured to provide structural support for the compost bay walls.
Underground utilities must be identified and marked before excavation or construction to prevent damage and ensure safety.
Materials such as concrete blocks, rebar, or treated timber should be delivered to site prior to wall construction to avoid work stoppages.
Backfilling around the completed walls can only proceed after the walls are fully constructed and cured to prevent structural damage.
Drainage pipes or weep holes around the compost bay walls must be installed after walls are built to ensure proper water management.
The concrete floor slab inside the compost bay should be poured after the walls are in place to ensure a seamless connection and containment.
Surface finishing, waterproofing, and curing processes can only begin after the wall structure is fully erected.
The wall must be framed to create the cavity or alcove where the recessed shelf will be installed.
Any electrical wiring that will run behind or near the shelf must be roughed in before the shelf is installed, as access will be blocked afterwards.
Drywall must be installed around the recessed shelf to finish the wall surface; the shelf must be in place first so the drywall can be cut and fitted around it.
Trim and molding around the recessed shelf must be installed after the shelf is fixed in place to cover gaps and provide a finished appearance.
Painting is typically done after the shelf is installed to ensure a uniform finish, though it could be done in stages if the shelf is painted separately and installed later.
Wall framing must be complete to define the alcove recess where seating will be installed.
Electrical wiring for outlets or lighting in the alcove area must be run before seating is built in, as access behind the seating would be blocked.
The floor surface beneath the seating area must be prepared and leveled before installing the alcove seating base.

Typically painting is done before seating is installed, but if the alcove seating is built-in, painting and wall finishing behind and around it should ideally be completed first to avoid difficult touch-ups.
Trim and baseboards are fitted after the seating is in place to ensure clean transitions and proper fit against the seating structure.
Accurate measurements of the alcove width, height, and depth are required before the wardrobe can be designed, manufactured, or installed; otherwise the wardrobe will not fit.
The wardrobe must be built to the specific alcove dimensions before it can be physically installed on site.

predecessor: Prepare alcove (clear debris, ensure level walls/floor)
rationale: The alcove must be clean, level, and free of obstructions so the wardrobe can be properly positioned and secured.
Wardrobe doors (sliding or hinged) can only be fitted after the main carcass is installed and secured in the alcove.

successor: Interior shelving and hanging rail installation
rationale: Internal fittings like shelves and rails are installed after the wardrobe frame is in place to ensure correct alignment.
The alcove bookcase is built into a recessed wall space, so the wall framing must be completed first to define the alcove opening and provide structural support.
The wall surfaces surrounding the alcove must be finished before installing a built-in bookcase to ensure a clean, finished look and proper fit against the walls.

Trim and molding around the bookcase (such as crown molding or baseboard returns) must be installed after the bookcase is in place to cover gaps and create a seamless transition between the bookcase and the wall.
While the bookcase could be painted before installation, final touch-up painting is typically done after installation to cover any nail holes, patched seams, or scuffs from installation.

If the bookcase design includes integrated lighting or covers existing outlets, rough-in electrical work must be done before, but final outlet covers or light fixtures should be installed after the bookcase is in place to ensure proper alignment.
The alcove cabinet must be installed against or within a framed wall; without wall framing, there is no structural support or defined alcove space.
Drywall provides a finished surface behind and around the alcove cabinet; installing the cabinet before drywall would require removal or cutting around the cabinet, compromising finish quality.
If an alcove cabinet supports a countertop, the cabinet base must be secured and level first to provide proper support for the countertop.

Trim and molding around the alcove cabinet are typically installed after the cabinet is in place to cover gaps and provide a finished appearance, but this is a best practice rather than a physical necessity.
Any electrical wiring that needs to run behind or through the alcove cabinet area must be roughed in before the cabinet is installed, as access would be extremely difficult or impossible afterward.
The framework (typically a rectangular open frame) must be assembled first to provide the structural support for the desk surface.
Wall cleats or brackets must be installed before the desk can be mounted to the wall within the alcove.
Cable trays or grommets are installed after the desk is in place to route cords properly through or beneath the desk.
Items like monitor arms, keyboard trays, or task lighting are typically mounted after the desk is secured, though some could be pre-installed if desired.
Final caulking, trim, and paint touch-ups around the desk edges should be done after the desk is fully installed to achieve a clean, finished look.
The wall framing must be in place before electrical outlets can be installed, as the outlets are mounted to the studs and the wiring runs through the framed cavities.
The electrical wiring (cables, boxes) must be roughed-in to the wall cavities before the outlet receptacles can be wired and installed into their boxes.

Electrical outlets must be mounted and boxes set to the correct depth before drywall can be installed, as the drywall needs to be cut around the outlet boxes and the boxes must be flush with the finished wall surface.

Electrical outlets must be in place before trim work (e.g., outlet covers, baseboards, decorative trim) can be installed, as the covers attach directly to the outlets and the surrounding finish work completes the alcove appearance.
The outlet installation must be complete before an electrical inspection can verify correct wiring, grounding, and code compliance.
The curtain or blind must be mounted on or within the window frame; the frame provides the structural support and attachment points.
Glass must be in place before installing coverings to protect the interior and provide a surface to gauge fitment.
Installing trim after the blind allows the trim to cover any mounting brackets or edge gaps for a finished appearance.
Final painting or touch-ups are preferably done after the blind is fitted to blend mounting points seamlessly.
Trim and moulding must be attached to finished walls; the wall surface (framing + drywall) must be complete before any trim work can begin.
Any base or substrate that the moulding will be applied to must be level, square, and properly prepared to ensure proper adhesion/fastening and alignment.
Trim and moulding are typically installed before final painting, so that the moulding can be caulked, primed, and painted along with the walls, ensuring a seamless finish.

It is a common soft preference to install trim and moulding before adding light fixtures, sconces, or outlets in the alcove so that wiring and mounting can be coordinated, but in some cases fixtures can be installed first and trim worked around them.
Base moulding and shoe moulding must be installed after flooring is laid so that the trim covers the expansion gap and sits flush on top of the finished floor surface.
The wall frame (studs, plates) must be erected first to define the structural cavity into which a recess can be formed or framed out.
It is preferable to route any conduits or pipes within the wall cavity before enclosing it with recess trim, but if access panels are provided this can be done later.
The recess framing or form must be complete so that drywall can be cut and fitted around the recess opening and finished flush.

successor: Recessed Fixture Installation (e.g., shelf, niche, outlet box)
rationale: The structural recess must exist before any fixture, shelf, or device can be physically placed or mounted inside it.
Final surface finishes (paint, texture, wallpaper) are applied after the recess is fully formed, drywalled, and taped/mudded to achieve a continuous surface.
Alcove fit-out and joinery require the structural walls and ceilings to be in place so that joinery elements have a stable, defined surface to attach to and fit within.
Electrical and data cabling must be run within wall cavities and ceilings behind the joinery before the fit-out encloses these areas, otherwise costly rework would be required.
Plumbing rough-in for any sinks, drains or services within the alcove must be completed before joinery installation, as the joinery will cover and restrict access to pipework.
Painting and finishing touch-ups must occur after joinery installation because the joinery elements define the final surfaces and edges that need to be painted or sealed.
Light fixtures, switches, and power outlets installed within or adjacent to the alcove joinery must be fitted after the joinery is in place to ensure proper alignment and finish.
The alcove surface must be cleaned, repaired, and smoothed before waterproofing can be applied; waterproofing membranes will not adhere properly to dirty or uneven surfaces.
Cement backer board or equivalent substrate must be fully installed and secured as the structural base before waterproofing coating or membrane can be applied over it.

Waterproofing must be fully cured and tested before tiling begins, as the waterproof membrane serves as the moisture barrier behind the tile, and tiling over uncured waterproofing will compromise the seal.

While corner beads can be installed before waterproofing in some methods, best practice often places them after waterproofing to avoid penetrating the membrane; this is a soft preference depending on the waterproofing system used.
The alcove surfaces must be properly prepared, cleaned, filled, sanded, and primed before painting can begin to ensure proper paint adhesion and a smooth finish.
If the alcove requires new plaster or rendering, this must be completed and fully dried/cured before painting can be applied to prevent moisture damage and paint failure.

Architectural features such as coving, cornices, or architraves must be installed before painting to allow for seamless painting over these elements and to avoid damaging newly painted surfaces during installation.
Any built-in shelving, cabinets, or storage units should be installed after painting to avoid paint marks on the fixtures and to allow for a clean finish behind and around the installed units.
Flooring (tiles, hardwood, carpet) should be installed after painting to prevent paint drips, splatters, and dust from damaging the finished floor surface.
The foundation excavation must be completed to provide a stable base and access for structural reinforcement of the alcove area.
Formwork must be in place to shape and contain the concrete or reinforcement materials during the structural reinforcement process.
Structural reinforcement (rebar and steel placement) must be installed before concrete can be poured to ensure the reinforcement is embedded within the concrete for structural integrity.
Inspection and testing typically follow reinforcement installation to verify compliance with specifications, though in some cases partial inspection may occur concurrently.
Backfilling must only commence after the structural reinforcement and any associated concrete work has cured to avoid disturbing the reinforcement.
Window seat structure needs to be attached to the wall framing for support and stability.
The window must be installed first so the window seat can be properly aligned and fitted beneath the window opening.
Wall finishing around the window seat should be done after the seat frame is in place to ensure seamless integration and proper trim work.
Flooring is typically installed before or around fixed seating, but it is a soft preference for seat to come first to allow precise cutting and fitting of flooring around the seat base.
If the window seat includes built-in lighting or outlets, rough electrical should be completed first; otherwise this is a soft preference for general sequencing.
The rough opening must be framed, sized, and prepared before any window jamb lining can be installed, as the jamb lining fits into the rough opening.
The window frame (or window unit) must be installed and secured in the rough opening before jamb lining can be fitted around the frame.
Window casing and interior trim are installed over and around the jamb lining, so the jamb lining must be in place first.
The jamb lining provides the finished interior surface and tracks/guides for window sashes; sashes are installed after the jamb lining is complete.
While jamb lining is typically installed before final wall finishing for a clean edge, it is a soft preference as some sequences allow drywall to be installed first and then trimmed.
The window must be installed in the rough opening before the head soffit can be built around it, as the soffit encloses the top of the window frame and provides a finished transition.
The rough opening framing for the window must be complete and properly sized before the head soffit can be framed, as the soffit attaches to the surrounding structure above the window.
The roof overhang or eave structure above the window must be framed and sheathed to provide a mounting surface for the soffit and to define the depth and slope of the soffit enclosure.
The exterior wall sheathing must be installed to provide a substrate and proper alignment for the soffit, ensuring a flush and weathertight interface between the soffit and the wall plane.

The window head soffit must be fully installed before final exterior trim, fascia, and soffit finish materials (such as aluminum, vinyl, or wood soffit panels) can be applied, as the soffit serves as the structural base for the finished cladding.
The seat cushion requires a completed frame to be mounted upon; the structural support must exist before the cushion can be attached.
Once the seat cushion is installed, final upholstery and trim work can be applied over and around the cushion for a finished appearance.
The foam core of the cushion must be molded and cured before it can be installed as a finished component.
The fabric or leather cover must be sewn and prepared before it can be placed over the foam and installed onto the frame.
After the seat cushion is installed, a final quality check of the seating system can be performed to verify fit, comfort, and fastening.
Electrical wiring must be roughed in behind the wall before the drawer unit is installed, as access to the wall cavity is required for wiring.
The drawer unit carcass must be installed first so that drawer fronts, pulls, and soft-close hardware can be properly aligned and attached.
Walls must be finished and painted behind and around the drawer unit area before installation, as it would be difficult or impossible to paint after the unit is in place.

successor: Flooring installation (if unit sits on finished floor)
rationale: Typically flooring is installed before cabinets, but if the drawer unit is installed first as a temporary measure, flooring can be trimmed around it later; this is a preference rather than a physical necessity.

predecessor: Delivery and staging of Storage Drawer Unit
rationale: The unit must be delivered and staged on site before it can be physically installed.
Wall framing must be completed before attaching any shelving units to the wall, as the shelf needs a stable structural support.
Drywall must be installed and finished before mounting a bookshelf to ensure a smooth finished wall surface and proper anchoring.
Floor finishing should ideally be completed before installing a floor-standing bookshelf to avoid damaging finished flooring or having to work around the shelf.
If the bookshelf is built-in, final painting is often done after installation to blend the shelf with the wall; however, a pre-finished shelf may be installed after painting.
Baseboards or trim should be installed after a built-in bookshelf to allow proper fit and seamless transition between the shelf and adjacent trim work.
The rough opening must be framed and prepared to the correct dimensions before any window sash or casement unit can be installed.
The main window frame or buck must be in place to receive the operable sash or casement, as the sash hinges or slides within that fixed frame.
Flashing and weatherproofing at the rough opening must be completed before installing the sash to ensure water intrusion protection behind and around the unit.
The sash frame must be in place before glass panes or insulated glass units can be installed into the sash (for field-glazed windows).
The sash must be installed in its frame before operating hardware (hinges, locks, crank operators) can be attached and adjusted for proper function.
Interior trim casing is typically installed after the window unit is set, but this can sometimes be done concurrently; it is a soft preference for fit and finish quality.
Final exterior sealant bead around the sash/frame joint must be applied after the sash is fully installed to close the weather seal.
The structural frame (including support brackets and mullions) must be in place to provide a mounting surface and load-bearing support for glazing units.
Rough openings must be framed, measured, and prepared to the correct dimensions before glazing units can be fitted.
Weather barriers, flashings, and sealants around openings must be installed first to prevent water ingress behind the glazing units.
Interior trim, drywall finishing, and paint near windows can only be completed after glazing units are installed to avoid damage and ensure proper alignment.
Final exterior sealant beads and weatherproofing around the perimeter of installed glazing units must be applied after units are in place to achieve an airtight and watertight seal.
The structural framing must be complete to provide a substrate for installing joinery and millwork elements such as cabinets, trim, and paneling.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-ins behind walls and in ceilings must be finished before enclosing them with millwork to avoid rework and ensure code compliance.
Drywall must be hung, taped, and finished to provide a smooth, finished wall surface for attaching trim, crown molding, and built-in cabinets.
Flooring is typically installed before baseboards and toe-kicks to allow clean intersections and proper fitting of millwork against the finished floor surface.
Joinery and millwork must be installed before final painting and touch-ups so that paint can be applied to the installed trim and any gaps or nail holes can be caulked and painted over.
Base cabinets and millwork must be installed and leveled before countertops can be templated, fabricated, and placed on top of them.
Final installation of outlets, switches, and fixtures on or adjacent to millwork (e.g., under-cabinet lighting, sinks) is conveniently done after millwork is in place for precise positioning.
The building structure must be complete and enclosed before insulation can be installed; insulation is applied to completed structural elements like roof, walls, and floors.
Roof insulation is typically installed as part of or after the roof structure is completed; without a finished roof, insulation would be exposed to weather and cannot be properly fitted.
Windows and doors must be installed to create the building envelope before draught-proofing strips and seals can be applied around openings.
External wall construction must be finished so that cavity insulation or external wall insulation can be installed against the completed masonry.
Internal plastering and wall finishes are applied after insulation is in place to cover and protect the insulation layer; plastering onto bare walls before insulation would be incorrect sequencing.

While often first-fix services are roughed in before insulation (in walls), some services may be installed after insulation. Typically first fix is done before or alongside insulation, but internal service runs are completed after insulation is placed so as not to disturb it.
External insulation systems require the insulation boards to be fixed before the final render or cladding finish is applied on top.
Underfloor heating units must be installed onto a prepared, level concrete floor slab or base before any floor coverings are applied.
Supply and return pipework must be roughed-in and pressure tested before connecting to the radiator or underfloor heating manifold.

successor: Floor Screed / Floor Covering (tiles, wood, laminate)
rationale: Underfloor heating pipes or radiator bases must be installed before the final floor screed or floor covering is poured/laid over them.
Radiators and underfloor heating manifolds must be installed and connected before the overall heating system can be filled, bled, and pressure-tested.

While radiators are typically installed after plastering and painting are complete to avoid damage, underfloor heating units are installed before floor finishes. For radiators, painting should be done before installation to allow clean finish behind the unit.
Electrical rough-in work (conduit, wiring, and backbox mounting) must be completed before the fire alarm panel can be installed as the panel requires incoming power and pre-run cables.

successor: Fire Alarm Device Installation (detectors, pull stations, horn/strobes)
rationale: The fire alarm panel is the central control unit; all field devices (smoke detectors, pull stations, notification devices) connect back to the panel, so the panel must be in place and powered before those devices can be wired and commissioned.

successor: Fire Alarm System Programming and Configuration
rationale: Programming, addressing, and configuration of the fire alarm system cannot be performed until the panel hardware is physically installed and energized.

successor: Fire Alarm System Testing and Commissioning
rationale: End-to-end testing, verification of alarm signals, and commissioning of the fire alarm system must follow panel installation and device connection to ensure the system functions as designed.

successor: Final Inspection and Fire Marshall Approval
rationale: Authorities having jurisdiction (AHJ), such as the fire marshal, require the fire alarm panel and all connected components to be fully installed and operational before conducting the final life safety inspection.
Hose reel cabinets require a water supply connection from the fire main piping system. The fire main piping must be installed first to provide the necessary water feed.
Hose reel cabinets are typically recessed into or mounted onto walls. The wall framing must be completed to provide structural support and proper rough opening for cabinet installation.
The hose reel cabinet must be securely mounted and in place before the fire hose can be connected inside the cabinet.
The cabinet body must be installed before trim work and doors can be fitted to complete the assembly.
The hose reel cabinet and its connections must be fully installed before the fire protection system can be inspected and pressure tested.
The structural frame (roof or wall) must be in place to provide a mounting surface and structural support for smoke vent components.
The roof deck must be completed to create the opening and base onto which the smoke vent will be installed.
Smoke vents must be installed and flashed before the waterproofing membrane is applied to ensure a watertight seal around the vent opening.
Smoke vents are typically integrated with fire alarm systems; the vent must be physically installed before the combined system can be functionally tested.

Installing the smoke vent before ceiling finishes allows for any necessary adjustments and avoids damage to finished surfaces, though it is a practical preference rather than a strict physical requirement.
Fire safety signage must be mounted on finished walls and structures; installation cannot begin before the building shell is complete.
Fire exit signs and emergency lighting signage require electrical power connections, so the electrical rough-in and wiring must be completed first.
Signage must indicate fire alarm pull stations and fire equipment locations, which need to be installed and finalized before directional signage can be placed.

It is preferable to install signage after painting and ceiling installation to avoid damage to signage or rework, but this is a soft preference—signage can be installed before final finishes if necessary.
Fire safety signage must be in place and clearly visible before the building can pass final fire safety inspection and receive an occupancy permit.
Fire Risk Assessment requires finalized building design to evaluate fire safety measures, escape routes, and material compliance.
The structural framework must be in place to assess fire compartmentation, load-bearing fire resistance, and spread paths.

successor: Installation of Fire Detection and Alarm Systems
rationale: Fire Risk Assessment determines the required type, placement, and sensitivity of detection and alarm systems based on identified hazards.
The assessment specifies sprinkler zoning, water flow requirements, and suppression coverage areas needed to mitigate identified fire risks.

successor: Fire Stopping and Passive Fire Protection Installation
rationale: Fire Risk Assessment identifies compartments, penetration seals, and fire-resistance ratings required before passive protection can be installed.
Fire alarm system must be operational to simulate emergency alert during drill.
Building must be legally occupied and approved for occupancy before conducting safety drills.

predecessor: Install Emergency Exit Signs and Lighting
rationale: Emergency egress routes and illumination must be functional to safely guide occupants during drill.
Automatic fire suppression must be in place as a safety measure before simulating fire emergency.
Successful fire drill is a prerequisite or soft requirement often checked before final commissioning to verify life safety systems.
Fire alarm systems must be installed and operational before an inspection can verify their functionality and compliance with fire codes.
Sprinkler systems must be fully installed and pressurized before inspection to verify coverage, flow rates, and code compliance.
Fire extinguishers must be mounted and accessible at required locations before the inspector can verify correct type, placement, and inspection tags.
Emergency exit signs and lighting must be installed and functional to be tested during fire safety inspection.
A passed fire safety inspection is typically a prerequisite for the building authority to issue a certificate of occupancy, confirming the building meets life safety requirements.
The project cannot be formally completed or handed over to the owner until fire safety compliance has been verified and signed off by the inspecting authority.
Structural framing (steel or concrete) must be in place to provide surfaces and supports for fireproofing materials, sprinkler piping, and fire alarm devices.
MEP rough-in work (ductwork, conduit, piping) must be completed so fire protection systems can be routed around or through these services without interference.
Fire sprinkler heads and smoke detectors must be installed and tested before ceilings are enclosed, as they are concealed above the ceiling grid.
Although not a strict physical dependency, it is preferable to complete fire protection work before finishes to avoid damage to finished surfaces during installation and testing.

successor: Fire Alarm System Testing and Commissioning
rationale: All fire protection components (sprinklers, detectors, panels) must be installed before the integrated system can be tested and commissioned for functionality.
The evacuation plan must be based on the building's physical layout, including floor plans, exits, stairwells, and room configurations, which are determined during the design phase.
The locations of fire alarms, sprinklers, smoke detectors, and fire extinguishers must be known to design effective evacuation routes and assembly points.
The number of building occupants directly affects evacuation route capacity, stairway width requirements, and assembly area sizing, so occupancy must be known before planning evacuation.
The evacuation plan must be finalized and documented before occupants can be trained on it and before drills can be conducted to test its effectiveness.
Evacuation route maps, exit signs, and directional signage must reflect the approved evacuation plan, so signs cannot be installed until the plan is complete.
Structural framing must be in place to provide the support and attachment points for ceiling features.
MEP rough-ins such as ductwork, piping, and electrical conduits must be installed above the ceiling before the ceiling design can be finalized and closed in.
The ceiling design and installation must be complete before applying any final finishes like paint or texture to the ceiling surface.
Ceiling design must be in place to provide mounting points and reveal channels for recessed or surface-mounted lighting fixtures.

It is generally easier to build partitions after the ceiling is installed so that partitions can be aligned to ceiling grids or feature lines, though it is possible to do in reverse order with careful planning.
The structural frame (including roof deck) must be erected to provide the supporting framework and openings into which glazing systems (skylights, curtain walls, windows) are installed.
Basic weather barrier, flashing, and rough openings must be prepared so that glazing units can be properly seated, sealed, and integrated into the envelope.
Once glazing is in place and sealed, interior finishes can be installed without risk of water damage and with natural daylight available for better work conditions.
After glazing is complete, the building envelope is effectively sealed, allowing accurate HVAC load testing, air balancing, and commissioning under final conditions.

Daylight-responsive lighting controls and dimming systems can only be calibrated and commissioned once the actual glazing and fenestration are installed and their light transmission characteristics are known.

The building's structural frame and enclosure (walls, roof, etc.) must be completed before any greenery or biophilic elements can be installed, as these elements need a supporting structure to attach to or be placed within.
For rooftop gardens, green roofs, or any planted areas, waterproofing and drainage systems must be installed first to protect the building structure from water damage and root penetration.
The irrigation system and water supply connections must be in place before planting, as plants require a water delivery system for survival and maintenance.
The growing medium (soil, substrate, or engineered growing material) must be placed and prepared before any plants, trees, or vegetation can be installed.

Specialized lighting for living walls, green facades, or biophilic features should be installed after the greenery is in place to ensure proper positioning and coverage for plant health and visual effect.
The greenery and biophilic elements should be installed and established before final project handover to ensure the living systems are healthy and operational for the building occupants.
Flooring must be installed before setting tables to avoid dust, debris, and potential damage to tableware from ongoing flooring work.
Wall painting must be completed before table setting to prevent paint splatters, dust, and fumes from contaminating clean tableware and linens.
Ceiling work and lighting installation must be finished to avoid dust/debris falling onto clean table settings and to ensure proper lighting conditions are in place.
Tables must be set with appropriate tableware before food can be served, as serving requires plates, cutlery, glassware, and napkins to be in place.
Tables must be fully set and ready before guests can be seated and the event can commence, to provide a complete dining experience.

Structural works (columns, slabs, beams, load-bearing walls) must be completed to provide a stable, enclosed shell before any interior finishing can commence. Starting fit-out without structural completion risks damage to finishes and safety hazards.
The building must be weathertight (roof, external walls, windows, doors installed) to protect interior materials from rain, moisture, and dust, which could ruin finishes and cause mould.

Concealed mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-ins (conduits, pipes, ducts, cables in walls/ceilings) must be installed before wall boarding and finishing, as they would be inaccessible and require destructive rework afterwards.

The primary fit-out (partition walls, ceiling grids, flooring underlayment, MEP second fix) provides the substrate for final decorative finishes like paint, wallpaper, ceramic tiles, and trim installation.
After interior fit-out is substantially complete, the project undergoes snagging (defect identification) and commissioning of MEP systems to verify everything functions correctly before handover.

Architectural layouts and space planning define room dimensions, ceiling heights, and space functions which are fundamental inputs for determining lighting layout, fixture placement, and illumination requirements.

Structural elements such as ceiling grids, beam locations, and slab penetrations dictate where lighting fixtures can be mounted and how conduits can be routed, so structural design must be established before detailed lighting design.

Power circuits, switch legs, and conduit pathways for lighting must be roughed in before fixtures can be installed and commissioned; however, lighting design must precede rough-in, so this is an iterative relationship — lighting design before rough-in, rough-in before commissioning.

Lighting fixtures must be installed, wired, and tested before ceiling tiles, drywall, and other finishes are completed, as finishing work encloses ceilings and makes fixture access and wiring difficult.

Commissioning of lighting systems (including testing, calibration, and dimming/control verification) must be fully completed and signed off before the building can be turned over for occupancy, ensuring all life safety and functional lighting requirements are met.
Flooring, wall coverings, and painting must be completed before furniture installation to avoid damage to finishes and to provide a clean, finished surface for furniture placement.
Electrical rough-in work (wiring, outlet boxes) must be completed before furniture is brought in to ensure power outlets are accessible and to avoid interference with furniture layout.
HVAC ductwork and diffusers must be installed before furniture to ensure proper airflow clearance and to avoid having to move furniture during HVAC work.

Final cleaning and punch list items should be performed after furniture installation to clean up any debris from furniture assembly and to touch up any damage that may have occurred during installation.
The building cannot be occupied or moved into until all furniture is procured and installed, as furniture is essential for the functional use of the space.

The structural frame and shell must be complete before M&E services installation can begin, as M&E systems are typically installed within the building's structural envelope and require the structure to be enclosed and load-bearing elements in place.
Roofing and waterproofing must be completed to protect the interior from weather, allowing M&E equipment and materials to be stored and installed in a dry, weathertight environment.
Floor slabs and concrete works need to be completed and cured before M&E services can be routed through floors, embedded in slabs, or mounted on finished floor surfaces.
M&E services such as ductwork, piping, conduits and cabling must be installed before ceilings are closed and walls are finished, to allow access for routing, connections and testing.
All M&E installations must be physically complete before testing and commissioning can commence, as commissioning involves verifying that installed systems operate correctly.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) rough-in work must be completed before the ceiling grid is installed, as the grid would block access to overhead systems.
The structural framing (roof or floor above) must be in place to provide support for the suspended ceiling grid hanger wires.
The grid framework must be fully installed before ceiling tiles can be placed or laid into the grid.
Final connections of lighting fixtures, sprinklers, and HVAC diffusers that mount into or through the ceiling grid must occur after the grid is installed.

successor: Interior Painting and Finishing of Upper Walls
rationale: It is preferable to complete painting of walls and upper finishes before installing the grid to avoid damaging the grid, but it is not a hard physical constraint if careful masking is used.
Electrical and data cabling must be roughed-in and terminated before workstations can be installed, as workstations are placed over floor boxes and require live power/data connections.
Ceiling grids, tiles, and lighting must be installed before workstations to avoid damaging furniture with overhead work and to ensure proper alignment of lighting with workstations.
Flooring must be fully installed and cured before workstation assembly to prevent damage to the floor covering and to allow accurate layout and anchoring of workstation panels.
Workstations must be fully assembled and installed before occupants can move in furniture, equipment, and personal items; the workstations form the primary layout of the workspace.

Final cleaning and paint touch-ups are typically performed after all furniture is in place to clean construction dust and repair any scuffs or damage caused during furniture installation, though this can sometimes be done concurrently.
The storage locker unit must be placed on a level, cured concrete slab foundation to provide stable structural support and prevent settling or misalignment.
Electrical conduit and wiring for lighting and power outlets within the storage locker area must be roughed in before locker units are installed to avoid rework or inaccessible wiring.
If the storage locker area includes utility sinks or floor drains, rough plumbing must be completed before locker installation to ensure pipes are in place and accessible.
Interior wall finishing in the storage locker area should be completed after locker installation to avoid damage to finished surfaces and to ensure seamless integration of lockers against walls.

Final flooring (e.g., vinyl, tile, or epoxy coating) should be installed after locker units are in place to create a continuous, finished floor surface around the lockers and avoid trapping debris beneath them.
The vision panel or sidelight must be installed within or onto a frame structure; the frame provides the structural support and mounting surface for the panel.
The rough opening in the wall must be framed and prepared to the correct dimensions before the vision panel/sidelight unit can be fitted and secured.
The vision panel/sidelight frame and unit must be in place before the glass panes or glazing material can be installed into the panel.
Weatherproofing sealants and gaskets around the vision panel/sidelight can only be applied after the panel unit is fully installed in its opening.
Interior trim and finishing around the vision panel/sidelight is typically done after installation, but could theoretically be done simultaneously in some cases.
Door frames require rough openings with proper dimensions, headers, and studs to be in place before the door frame can be installed.
The finished floor height must be established before setting the door frame to ensure proper clearance and swing clearance.
Walls must be framed and sheathed to provide the structural support and rough opening into which the door frame is installed.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-ins behind walls must be completed before door frame installation to avoid rework and damage to the new frame.
Door frames must be installed before drywall can be finished around the opening, as the frame provides the trim reveal and jamb depth reference.
The door and frame must be in place before hinges, locks, latches, and other hardware can be fitted and aligned.
Architraves and casing trim are installed around the door frame after the frame is fixed in position and plumbed.
Doors and frames are typically installed before final painting so that paint can cover the frame and door surfaces uniformly, including edges.

While doors can be installed before finished flooring, it is a soft preference to install floor coverings after the door frame to allow undercutting the door for floor clearance and avoiding damage to new flooring.
The raised floor pedestals require a stable, level, and cured concrete slab as the base substrate for mounting. Installation cannot begin until the concrete has reached sufficient strength.

Cabling infrastructure (trays, conduits, and data/electrical cables) must be laid out in the plenum space below the raised floor before the floor panels are installed, otherwise access would be blocked.
Although not physically dependent, completing overhead work first avoids dust and debris falling onto the finished raised floor surface and reduces risk of damage to the panels.
Final floor finishes (carpet tiles, vinyl, or other coverings) are laid on top of the raised floor panels, so the panel system must be fully installed and leveled first.

successor: IT Equipment / Server Rack Installation & Cabling Termination
rationale: Servers, racks, and network equipment are placed on the raised floor; the stable, level floor system must be complete before heavy equipment can be rolled in and positioned.

Floor finishes must be completed before skirting installation because skirting boards are typically installed on top of or against finished floor surfaces to cover the expansion gap and provide a neat finish.

Wall surfaces must be fully finished (plastered, painted, or wallpapered) before skirting and trunking are fixed, as these are mounted directly onto the wall surface and would be damaged or obstructed if installed before wall finishing.

Primary electrical and data cabling within walls/ceilings must be roughed-in before cable trunking is installed, as the trunking will house and conceal final cable terminations and must be accessible for pulling cables through.

Skirting trunking provides the mounting base and cable pathway for power sockets, data outlets, and other electrical fixtures installed at skirting level; these can only be fitted after trunking is securely in place.

While skirting is typically installed after floor finishes, if carpet is used, the carpet is often trimmed and fitted up to or tucked under the skirting; installing skirting first provides a clean edge for carpet fitting, but this is a preference rather than a physical necessity.
Flooring and ceiling finishes must be completed before furniture installation to prevent damage to finished surfaces and to provide a clean, stable base for furniture placement.
Painting and wall finishes must be completed prior to furniture installation to avoid dust, paint splatter, and damage to furniture, and to allow unobstructed wall access for finishing work.

MEP rough-in work (electrical, plumbing, and HVAC) must be finished before furniture installation to ensure that all utility infrastructure is in place and to avoid needing to move furniture to access walls, ceilings, or floors for utility work.

Furniture installation must be completed before final cleaning and commissioning to allow for cleanup of debris and dust generated during furniture assembly, and to enable final system checks and punch-list items in a fully furnished space.
All furniture must be installed and in place before occupants can move in, as the space is not functional or habitable without desks, chairs, workstations, and other furnishings.

A workplace condition survey assesses the state of the building after construction or renovation is complete, as the survey evaluates the finished physical space for safety, functionality, and compliance.
The workplace condition survey must be completed before occupants can move in, to ensure the space meets safety and operational requirements for workers.
If the survey identifies deficiencies, remediation work may be scheduled. While often required, this is a soft preference if no issues are found.
The survey results may feed into or be a prerequisite for obtaining formal certification or passing the final regulatory inspection.
Base cabinets require a level, finished floor surface to sit on and be properly anchored.
Plumbing rough-ins for sinks and dishwashers must be run within walls and floor before cabinets are installed to avoid needing to cut through or remove cabinets later.
Electrical wiring for outlets, switches, and under-cabinet lighting must be in place before cabinets are mounted, as they will cover wall access.
Countertops are installed directly on top of base cabinets; cabinets must be leveled and secured first to support the countertop.
Sinks, dishwashers, and other drop-in appliances are installed into or adjacent to base cabinets only after the cabinets are in place.
Electrical wiring must be run within walls before cabinets are installed, as cabinets would block access to wall cavities and make post-installation wiring impossible or destructive.
Wall cabinets require a completed wall structure (studs and sheathing) to be securely mounted; no cabinet can be attached before the wall is framed.
Drywall must be fully installed, taped, and finished behind wall cabinets; installing cabinets first would leave unfinished drywall and require cutting around cabinets, compromising the finish.
Wall cabinets define the vertical envelope for countertops in kitchen/bath layouts; countertops are typically installed after wall cabinets to ensure proper alignment and fit.

While cabinet doors and hardware (handles/knobs) are typically installed after cabinets are mounted to avoid damage during installation, it is a soft preference for convenience rather than a physical necessity.
Cabinets must sit on a finished, level floor surface to ensure proper alignment and stability.
Cabinets need to be anchored to structurally complete walls for support and attachment.
Electrical wiring behind cabinet locations must be completed before cabinets are installed, as access to walls is blocked after installation.
Countertops are installed on top of base cabinets; tall/pantry cabinets are part of the cabinet set that supports or aligns with countertops.
Final hardware (handles, pulls, hinges) and trim (crown molding, fillers) are applied after cabinets are securely mounted in their final position.
Countertops must be installed on top of base cabinets, which provide the structural support and mounting surface for the countertop material.
Plumbing for sinks and electrical for outlets/disposals must be roughed in behind walls before countertops are installed, since countertops cover and block access to these areas.
The wall surface behind the countertop should be complete and finished so that the countertop can be properly fitted and sealed against the wall.
Sinks are mounted into or under the countertop cutout, so the countertop must be in place before the sink and faucet can be installed.
The backsplash tiles are installed above and abutting the countertop surface; the countertop provides the bottom edge reference line and support for the first row of tiles.
The wall surface must be smooth, clean, and primed before tiles or backsplash material can be properly adhered to ensure a durable bond.
Countertops must be installed first so that the backsplash can sit flush against or overlap the countertop surface for a seamless finish and proper waterproofing.

Electrical boxes and wiring for outlets must be in place before backsplash installation, as the backsplash tile will be cut around the boxes; retrofitting electrical work after tiling would require destructive removal.
After tiles/backsplash material are installed, grout must be applied to fill joints and a sealer applied to protect against moisture and stains.
A bead of caulk must be applied at the seam between the backsplash and countertop after the backsplash is fully installed to prevent water intrusion and provide a finished look.
The cooktop/hob is typically installed into a cutout in the countertop, so the countertop must be in place first to provide the structural support and the precise cutout for the cooktop.
Electrical wiring and junction boxes must be roughed in and the circuit breaker properly sized before the cooktop can be connected to the power supply.
For gas cooktops, the gas supply line must be run and terminated at the appliance location before the cooktop can be connected.
The cooktop must be seated and secured into the countertop cutout before the final sealant or finishing trim around the edges can be applied to create a watertight and finished appearance.

While the cooktop can function without the hood immediately installed, it is a strong safety and code preference to have ventilation operational before cooking, and hood alignment above the cooktop is easier to coordinate before countertop finishes are complete.
Electrical power supply wiring must be run and terminated at the junction box before the range/oven can be connected and installed.
Gas supply piping must be installed and pressure-tested before connecting a gas range/oven.
Flooring must be completed before installing the range/oven so the appliance sits on the finished surface and to avoid damaging the flooring during heavy appliance placement.
The range/oven must be in place so that countertop sections can be cut and fitted around it for a precise seam.
Backsplash and wall finishes behind the range should be completed after the range is installed to ensure proper fit and sealing at the edges.

predecessor: Rough-in plumbing for kitchen water supply and drain lines
rationale: The sink drain, P-trap, and water supply lines must be roughed into the wall and floor before the sink cabinet and sink can be physically connected.

predecessor: Kitchen countertop installation and cutout for sink
rationale: The sink is mounted into or under the countertop; the countertop must be installed and the sink cutout prepared before the sink can be set in place.

successor: Plumbing fixture trim-out (connect supply lines, drain, faucet)
rationale: After the sink is physically set, the water supply lines, faucet, and drain assembly can be connected and sealed.
Backsplash tiling and cabinet trim work should be done after the sink is in place to ensure proper fit and sealing around the sink rim.
It is standard practice to seal the countertop after all fixtures are installed to avoid sealant being disrupted, but this can be done before sink installation if desired.
The subfloor must be prepared (e.g., leveled and underlayment installed) before plumbing pipes can be laid and routed beneath the kitchen floor.
Interior wall framing must be completed so that plumbing supply lines and drain lines can be run through the stud cavities and properly secured.

Plumbing pipes must be installed first to avoid conflicts; electrical wiring can then be routed around the plumbing, and code typically requires plumbing to be roughed in before electrical in shared wall spaces.

Once the plumbing rough-in is complete, insulation can be installed around pipes (but not directly covering them in a way that would impede inspection), ensuring that the plumbing is in place before enclosing the walls.
Drywall cannot be hung until the plumbing rough-in is finished and inspected, because the pipes and fittings need to be accessible and visible for inspection before being concealed behind drywall.
Electrical wiring and boxes need to run through wall cavities and be attached to studs, which requires the framing and sheathing to be in place first.
Framing must be inspected and approved before closing up walls with electrical work to ensure structural integrity.
Insulation is installed after electrical wiring is run, as the wiring must be in place within the wall cavities before insulation is added.
Drywall covers the wall cavities; electrical boxes and rough wiring must be completed and inspected before drywall is hung so that wiring is accessible and properly placed.
The rough electrical work must be finished before the inspection can take place to verify code compliance of wiring and boxes before they are covered by insulation and drywall.
Structural framing (steel beams, columns, and decking) must be erected before any ventilation ducts can be routed, as the ducts are typically suspended from or attached to the structural frame.
The roof must be in place to provide a weathertight enclosure before routing ventilation ducts, preventing water damage to ductwork and insulation.
