The site must be cleared, leveled, and prepared before any structural layout can be marked, as column positions depend on a stable and correctly graded surface.
Column grid lines are typically established after the foundation is poured and cured, because the grid layout defines where columns will be placed on top of or within the foundation system.
Columns cannot be installed until their exact positions are laid out on site; the grid layout provides the reference marks for placing and aligning columns.
Formwork for slabs and decks depends on the column grid to correctly position supports, shoring, and form panels relative to the column locations.
Rebar cages and reinforcing steel for columns must be placed in accordance with the established grid lines to ensure proper alignment within the structural frame.
The spatial zoning plan (defining land-use areas, building envelopes, and functional zones) must be finalized and approved before any spatial zoning activity can be physically implemented on site.
Accurate topographic and geotechnical data is required to determine buildable zones, setbacks, and no-build areas before spatial zoning can be established.
Legal ownership or rights to the land must be secured before permanent spatial zoning boundaries can be demarcated and enforced on the property.
The spatial zones (e.g., building footprints, buffer areas, access corridors) must be defined before excavation can commence, as excavation follows the approved zone boundaries.
Zoning defines where utility corridors, roads, and service lines may be placed; infrastructure routing must align with the designated spatial zones.
Structural elements like columns, beams, and slabs must be in place before measuring spaces, as the survey captures the actual built dimensions and spatial boundaries defined by the structure.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-ins (conduits, ducts, pipes) are typically installed before final space measurements to ensure that all penetrations and service routes are accounted for in the survey.
Accurate space measurements are required to order and install finishes such as drywall, flooring, ceiling tiles, and wall cladding to the correct dimensions.
Custom-built cabinets, countertops, and millwork must be fabricated based on precise as-built field measurements to ensure proper fit within the surveyed spaces.

successor: Final MEP Trim-Out and Fixture Installation
rationale: While some fixture installation can start from rough dimensions, final placement of outlets, switches, lighting, and plumbing fixtures ideally uses verified as-built measurements for accurate positioning, though this is a strong preference rather than a physical impossibility.

As-built scanning captures the actual constructed state; scanning can only occur after construction of the building or element is complete, otherwise the scan would not represent the final as-built condition.

The physical structure must exist in its finished form for as-built scanning to capture accurate dimensional data; site preparation and foundation work are prerequisite to any superstructure that needs scanning.
Temporary structures like scaffolding can obstruct the scanner's line of sight and must be removed to capture an unobstructed 3D point cloud of the permanent works.

successor: BIM Model Update / Digital Twin Creation
rationale: The raw point cloud data from the 3D scan is the primary input for updating the BIM model or creating a digital twin; this modeling work cannot proceed without the scan data.
Quality control checks comparing as-built conditions to design specifications rely on the scan data as the reference for actual built geometry; verification therefore follows scanning.
The as-built 3D model derived from scanning forms a core part of the project's handover documentation package; final deliverables and close-out activities depend on the scanning being complete.

successor: Interior Fit-Out / MEP Installation (if scanning before finishes)
rationale: In some workflows, scanning of exposed structure and MEP is done before permanent finishes are applied so that hidden elements are captured; however, this is a sequencing preference rather than a strict physical necessity if scanning can be done post-fit-out.

A structural assessment must be completed to confirm that the internal walls are non-load-bearing and that their removal will not compromise the building's structural integrity. Approval from a structural engineer is required before any demolition work can proceed.
Demolition work typically requires permits from the local building authority to ensure compliance with safety regulations and building codes. Work cannot legally commence without these permits.

All electrical wiring, plumbing pipes, and gas lines running through or attached to the internal walls must be safely disconnected and capped by qualified tradespeople before demolition to prevent electrocution, flooding, or gas leaks.
The debris and rubble generated from demolishing the walls must be removed from the worksite before any subsequent finishing or construction work can begin in the area.

successor: Rough Framing and New Wall Construction
rationale: New walls, partitions, or framing for altered room layouts can only be constructed after the existing internal walls have been demolished and the area is cleared and prepared.
Structural framing (roof trusses, joists) must be fully installed to provide the support structure onto which ceiling systems are attached.

All ductwork, wiring, conduit, and piping that run above the ceiling must be roughed-in before ceiling grids and panels are installed, as accessing these after ceiling completion would require costly removal.
Insulation above the ceiling must be placed before ceiling boards or tiles are fitted to ensure thermal and acoustic performance is achieved.
Ceiling work (including potential dust, debris, and overhead access) should be completed before floor finishes are applied to avoid damage and contamination of flooring materials.

Ceiling installation is typically completed before wall painting and final decorative finishes to allow a clean, top-down sequence and avoid rework, though some touch-up painting can occur afterward if needed.
The subgrade (earth/gravel base) must be compacted and leveled to receive the floor levelling material; without a stable subgrade, the floor level will be uneven and may crack.
Any underground drainage, plumbing or conduit pipes must be laid and backfilled before floor levelling to avoid digging up the finished level floor.
Floor levelling creates a smooth, even surface necessary for installing tiles, vinyl, carpet, or other finished floor coverings.

While walls can be framed before floor levelling in some sequences, achieving a true level floor before erecting partitions ensures precise vertical alignment and door thresholds; however, it is a soft preference as walls are often framed first.
It is preferable to complete floor levelling before final painting and finishing to avoid dust and debris settling on freshly painted surfaces, though it is not a physical necessity.
The glazing panel must be installed into a prepared frame; the frame provides the structural support and enclosure for the glass or panel unit.
The rough opening must be measured, cleaned, and verified for squareness and dimensions before the glazing panel can be placed.
Weatherproofing sealants or gaskets are applied around the glazing panel after it is positioned to ensure watertightness and air sealing.

Interior trim or bezels are typically installed after the glazing panel is in place to cover edges and provide a finished appearance, though this is a sequencing preference rather than a physical necessity.
Quality control checks such as air leakage tests, water penetration tests, and visual inspection must be performed after the glazing panel is fully installed and sealed.
The rough opening frame structure must be built and prepared before the transom bar can be installed, as the transom bar sits within or spans the framed opening.

The transom bar serves as a horizontal structural member that supports or separates the transom window/panel above from the door or glazing below, so it must be in place before the transom unit can be installed.

successor: Glazing or Panel Infill Above Bar
rationale: The transom bar provides the bottom support and framing for the glazing or panel infill above it; glass or panels cannot be installed without the supporting bar in position.

successor: Trim and Finish Work Around Transom
rationale: While not physically mandatory, finishing trim, molding, and sealants around the transom area are typically applied after the transom bar is in place for a clean finished appearance.
If a structural lintel or header is required above the opening to carry loads, it must be installed before the transom bar so the bar is properly supported and the load path is correctly established.
The operable sash must be installed into a prepared frame; the frame provides the structural support and guiding channels for the sash to operate properly.
The wall opening must be framed and ready to receive the window unit before the operable sash can be placed.
Weather seals and caulking around the operable sash can only be applied after the sash is fully installed and aligned in its frame.
Hardware such as hinges, locks, and balancing mechanisms must be fitted and adjusted after the sash is in place to ensure correct operation and alignment.

Although trim can be installed after the sash is in place, it is a soft preference as trim could theoretically be pre-fitted; however, standard practice positions trim after sash installation to achieve a clean finish.
The window or curtain wall frame must be installed first to provide the structural support and enclosure into which the double-glazed IGU is seated and secured.
The rough opening in the wall must be framed, weatherproofed, and prepared to the correct dimensions before the IGU assembly can be installed.
Once the IGU is placed, the perimeter must be sealed with weatherstripping and air barriers to ensure thermal performance and prevent air and water infiltration.
Interior window trim, sill, and finish work can only be completed after the IGU is fully installed and secured in the frame.
The structural sealant and glazing gaskets applied around the IGU require a curing period after installation before any subsequent handling or loads can be applied.
The rough opening (framed and sized window opening) must be prepared and squared before the triple-glazed unit can be installed into it.
Structural framing must be completed to create the opening that will receive the triple-glazed window unit.
Weather-resistant barrier and window flashing must be installed around the rough opening prior to setting the unit to ensure proper water management and sealing.
After the triple-glazed unit is placed, the gaps around it must be sealed and insulated to achieve thermal and air-tightness performance.
Interior window trim and drywall finishing around the window typically occur after the unit is installed, though this is a logical sequence preference rather than a strict physical impossibility.

The window opening (rough opening) must be framed, weatherproofed, and sized correctly before a single-glazed window unit can be installed; otherwise the window cannot be physically placed or secured.
After the single-glazed window is set in place, gaps around the frame must be sealed and insulated to prevent air and water infiltration; this cannot be done before the window is installed.
Interior wall finishes (drywall, trim, paint) around the window area are applied after the window is installed to ensure proper integration and a clean finished appearance.
Exterior cladding or siding around the window is installed after the window is fitted to create a weathertight seal and proper flashing integration.

For a single-glazed window assembly, the glass pane is installed into the frame after the frame is mounted in the opening; this is a logical and physical ordering within the window installation process itself.
The picture window requires a framed rough opening in the wall to be set into, so wall framing must be completed first.
The rough opening must be measured, cut, and prepared with proper headers and supports before the window unit can be placed.
Weather-resistive barrier and flashing must be applied to the rough opening before the window is installed to ensure proper water management.
After the window is set in the opening, the gaps must be insulated and sealed to prevent air and water infiltration.
Interior trim and casing around the window cannot be installed until the window unit is securely in place.
The exterior siding is finished around the installed window frame; the window must be in place for proper integration and flashing.

predecessor: Structural Wall Construction / Concrete Pouring & Curing
rationale: Windows require structurally sound and fully cured wall openings to be properly installed without risk of structural damage or misalignment.
The rough openings for windows must be framed, measured, and prepared to the correct dimensions before windows can be set into place.
Flashing and waterproofing membranes must be installed around rough openings prior to window placement to ensure a proper weather-tight seal and prevent water intrusion.

Windows must be installed and sealed before interior wall finishes are applied so that the finishes can be worked neatly around the window frames and to avoid damaging newly finished walls during window installation.
Windows must be properly fixed and sealed before exterior cladding or siding is installed around them to ensure continuous weatherproofing and a clean appearance.
Window frames must be installed and fixed in place before air-tightness testing can be performed, as the test measures the seal around installed frames.
Glass panes must be installed and sealed within the frames before air-tightness testing can verify the overall window assembly integrity.
Sealants and gaskets around window frames must be applied and cured to ensure a proper seal before conducting air-tightness tests.
If the air-tightness test identifies leaks, remedial sealing works may be needed, but this is a conditional soft preference based on test results rather than a strict physical requirement.

Air-tightness testing must be completed before internal finishes such as plastering are applied, because testing may require access to window junctions and any leaks found would need remediation that would damage finished walls.
The building envelope design, including wall assemblies, roof details, and fenestration, must be fully developed to provide the geometric and material inputs needed for thermal bridging analysis.
The structural framework defines the actual thermal bridge paths (e.g., slab edges, balcony penetrations, roof parapets) that must be assessed in the thermal bridging analysis.
Preliminary energy modeling can inform which thermal bridges are most critical, but a full thermal bridging assessment typically feeds into the refined energy model rather than being dependent on it.
The quantified thermal bridging heat loss values (psi-values and chi-values) are required inputs for accurate whole-building energy modeling and code compliance calculations.

The thermal bridging assessment identifies required thermal break details, insulation continuity strategies, and mitigation measures that must be incorporated into construction drawings and field installation.
The site survey provides baseline topography, existing vegetation, and spatial context data necessary to evaluate views and visual connections from and within the site.
The conceptual massing defines building orientation, height, and placement, which are prerequisites for analyzing how views and visual corridors will be affected or enhanced.
Findings from the view/visual study inform design refinements such as adjusting window placements, building rotation, or landscape screening to optimize desired visual connections.
The visual study identifies key view corridors and sightlines, which guide where planting, tree placement, or screening elements should be located to preserve or enhance views.
Visual impact analysis results are typically presented to stakeholders and community members as part of the review process to address concerns about viewsheds and aesthetics.

The window frame provides the structural support and mounting surface for the external shading device (e.g., louvers, blinds, or awnings). The shading device cannot be attached until the frame is securely in place.

The glass panes must be installed in the window frame before external shading devices are mounted, as the shading device is positioned over or around the glazing. Installing the glass afterward would be impossible or could damage the shading device.

The exterior wall surface (cladding, masonry, or finish) must be completed to provide a proper sealing and anchoring surface for the shading device brackets and supports. Installing shading before cladding would require rework.

Any painting, coating, or sealant application adjacent to the shading device must be done after installation to ensure continuous coverage and to avoid masking or damaging the installed shading device.

Scaffolding or temporary access equipment used for installing the shading device must remain in place until the device is fully installed and secured. Dismantling too early would prevent safe installation and adjustment of the shading device.
Pony walls are typically built on top of floor framing; the floor structure must be in place to provide a base and support.
A subfloor provides the flat surface upon which the pony wall is framed and anchored.
Sheathing and bracing are applied to the pony wall frame after it is erected and secured.
The top plate is installed on top of the pony wall studs after the wall is framed and in place.
Rough-in work within the pony wall cavity typically occurs after the wall frame is erected, though could theoretically be done before in panelized construction.
Screen walls require a stable foundation to bear their load and prevent settlement or cracking.
The ground must be properly graded and leveled before constructing the screen wall to ensure proper drainage and a level base.
Underground utilities (drainage, electrical conduits, etc.) should be installed before the screen wall is built to avoid disturbing the wall's foundation later.
Final grading and backfilling against the wall can only be completed after the screen wall structure is in place to avoid rework.
Surface finishes, cladding, or decorative treatments on the screen wall can only be applied after the structural wall is erected.
Excavation must be completed to expose the foundation area and provide a proper working surface for constructing the retaining wall.
The base soil must be compacted and prepared to support the structural load of the retaining wall before construction begins.
Backfilling can only commence after the wall (or partial section) has been built and cured sufficiently to withstand lateral earth pressures.
Drainage components behind the wall must be installed after the wall structure is in place to ensure proper integration and water management.
Waterproofing is typically applied after the wall is complete but is a preference to protect against moisture; in some sequences it could be partially concurrent.
The ground must be excavated to the proper depth and width before the stem wall can be formed and poured, as the stem wall sits within the excavated trench.
The concrete footing (or spread footing) must be poured and cured to provide a stable load-bearing base upon which the stem wall is constructed.
Vertical and horizontal reinforcing steel (rebar) must be placed and tied within the formwork before concrete is poured for the stem wall.
Formwork (e.g., plywood or metal forms) must be assembled and braced to define the shape and dimensions of the stem wall before concrete placement.
After the stem wall concrete has cured, dampproofing or waterproofing coatings/membranes are applied to the exterior surface to prevent moisture intrusion.
Soil must be backfilled and compacted against the exterior of the stem wall only after the concrete has fully cured and waterproofing has been applied.

successor: Slab on Grade or Floor Slab
rationale: The interior floor slab is typically poured after the stem wall is complete, as the stem wall acts as a containment form and support for the slab edge.
The wood or metal stud walls of the structure are erected on top of the stem wall, which provides the level bearing surface and anchor bolt embedment.

Anchor bolts are set into the top of the wet concrete of the stem wall (or into grouted cells) to secure the sill plate and superstructure framing; this must occur before or as part of stem wall completion.
Plumbing, electrical, and other underground utilities that pass through the stem wall or slab area must be roughed in before the slab is poured, which itself follows stem wall completion.
The half-height partition must be anchored to and rest upon a completed floor slab; the floor provides the structural base for the partition.

Any electrical floor boxes or conduits that will be located under or within the partition footprint must be installed before the partition is built to avoid cutting or damaging the finished partition later.

The half-height partition defines the boundary for finish flooring; flooring materials (tiles, carpet, etc.) are typically installed up to the partition base, so the partition must be in place first to establish the edge condition.

While not always physically required, it is preferential to complete half-height partitions before adjacent full-height walls to allow easier access for alignment, bracing, and installation of shared studs or connections.
The partition must be fully installed, including its framing and boarding/surface, before any paint, wallcovering, or finish coating can be applied to it.
Masonry walls require a stable, level foundation to bear the load of the wall and prevent settlement cracks. The foundation must be fully cured and structurally ready before any masonry work begins.
The ground floor slab or structural floor must be in place to provide a base for the masonry wall to rise from, especially for load-bearing walls.
The building site must be excavated, graded, and cleared before any structural work including masonry walls can commence.
Roof structures typically bear on top of masonry walls; the walls must be completed and sufficiently cured to support roof loads.

Rough openings for doors and windows are formed within the masonry. However, final door/window installation can sometimes begin after walls are partially complete, but full installation typically follows complete wall construction to ensure proper fit and sealing.
The foundation provides the structural base and load-bearing support for walls; wall reinforcement cannot be installed until the foundation is fully cured and ready to receive wall elements.

Formwork defines the geometry and containment for concrete walls; reinforcement bars (rebar) must be placed and tied inside the formwork before concrete is poured, but formwork must first be erected to provide the mold.
Reinforcement steel must be fully installed, tied, and inspected before concrete is poured into the forms; pouring concrete over rebar embeds the reinforcement within the structural element.

While some MEP embedments can be placed before/alongside rebar, any conduits, sleeves, or pipes that pass through reinforced walls must be positioned and secured before concrete is cast; this typically follows or is coordinated with rebar installation.
Reinforcement bars must be cut, bent, and fabricated to the required specifications before they can be transported to the wall location and installed/tied in place.
Wall capping and waterproofing can only be applied after the wall structure (blockwork or masonry) has been fully constructed and cured, as the capping sits on top of the wall.
The mortar used in wall construction must be sufficiently cured before capping is installed to ensure structural stability and avoid cracking.
Wall capping and waterproofing must be completed before plastering or rendering to prevent moisture ingress behind the finished surface.
Final wall finishes such as painting can only be applied after waterproofing is complete to protect the finish from moisture damage.
Backfilling against walls should only occur after waterproofing is fully applied and cured to avoid compromising the waterproof membrane.
The DPC must be installed on top of the foundation walls; excavation and trenching must be completed first to expose the footing level where the DPC is applied.
The foundation walls must be fully poured, set, and cured to provide a stable solid base for DPC application; DPC cannot be applied to wet or uncured concrete.
The DPC must be in place before backfilling to ensure the continuous damp-proof barrier is not damaged and to prevent moisture bridging across the DPC level.
The DPC provides the horizontal moisture barrier that must be integrated with the floor slab construction to prevent rising damp from penetrating the finished floor.

All subsequent wall construction above the DPC level relies on the DPC being in place to prevent rising damp from travelling up into the walls; walls built above must be laid on top of the DPC membrane.
The rough opening must be framed to provide the structural support and cavity into which the interior window frame is installed.
The exterior window unit is typically installed first from the outside, providing the primary weather seal and glazing before interior framing and trim work begins.
Flashing and weatherproofing must be completed around the exterior window to prevent water intrusion before enclosing the interior side with window framing.
Interior trim and casing are installed around the completed window frame to finish the transition between the frame and the wall surface.
Drywall is cut and fitted around the interior window frame after the frame is in place, and the finishing work (mudding, taping) completes the wall assembly.
The window frame must be installed in the rough opening before the interior window sill can be fitted, as the sill is typically attached to or sits against the interior side of the window frame.
The wall structure including framing and exterior sheathing must be complete to provide the rough opening and support for the window sill.
Weatherproofing must be applied to seal the window opening from moisture intrusion before interior finish components like the sill are installed.

The window sill is typically installed before the surrounding interior wall finish work so that drywall can be butted against the sill and finished neatly, and so that the sill is not damaged by subsequent mudding and sanding work.
The interior window sill must be in place before the vertical and horizontal window casings (trim boards) are installed, as the casing pieces typically rest on or abut the sill.
The window unit must be installed and secured in the rough opening before trim casing can be applied around it; the casing attaches directly to the window frame and the surrounding wall framing.
The wall framing and sheathing must be complete to provide a surface for the casing to attach to and to establish the correct opening dimensions.
Drywall must be installed, taped, and mudded around the window opening so that the casing can be nailed over the finished drywall surface, covering the gap between drywall and window frame.

While painting can be done before trim (backpainting behind), typically trim is installed first and then the final paint coat is applied to both walls and trim together for a clean, uniform finish; this is a common sequencing preference rather than a hard physical constraint.

Caulking between the casing and the wall is typically done after the casing is nailed in place to seal gaps; however, this could technically be done concurrently, so it is a soft sequencing preference.
The window opening must be framed, weatherproofed, and structurally ready before the interior window sash can be installed.
The exterior window frame and casing must be in place to provide a weather-tight seal and structural support before the interior sash can be mounted.
Insulation around the window opening must be installed before the interior sash to ensure thermal efficiency and prevent air leakage.
The interior window sash must be in place before interior trim and architraves can be fitted around it to achieve proper finish alignment.
While painting can be done before sash installation, it is generally preferred to install the sash first to achieve clean edges and proper alignment, then paint or touch up around it.

The window opening must be framed and the rough opening prepared before any interior window hardware (such as locks, handles, or cranks) can be installed, as there is no structure to mount the hardware onto.
The window unit itself must be installed in the rough opening before interior hardware (e.g., sash locks, tilt latches, or crank handles) can be attached to the window frame or sash.
Interior trim and window casings are installed after the window hardware is in place, as the casings often cover the window frame edges and must fit around or accommodate the hardware components.

While painting can occur before hardware installation, final touch-up painting around the hardware is typically done after installation to ensure a clean finish; this is a soft preference for aesthetic quality rather than a physical necessity.
The hardware must be installed before the window can be fully tested for proper operation, locking, and adjustment to ensure functionality and security.
The window frame must be installed first to provide the structural support and attachment surface for the interior window head components.
The rough opening must be prepared, framed, and squared before any window components including the interior head can be installed.
Exterior sheathing around the window opening must be in place before interior window head work can proceed to ensure weather tightness and structural integrity.
The interior window head must be installed and secured before any casing or trim can be applied around the top of the window opening.
The interior window head installation must be complete before wall finishes can be applied to ensure proper integration and a seamless appearance at the window head.
The window frame must be installed and secured in the rough opening before the interior window jamb can be fitted around it, as the jamb attaches to or surrounds the frame.
The rough opening framing (studs, header, sill) must be complete to provide the structural support and boundaries into which the window assembly, including the interior jamb, is installed.
Exterior sheathing and weather-resistant barrier must be installed to protect the wall cavity from moisture before interior finishes like the window jamb are placed.
The interior window jamb provides the surface against which the window casing (trim) is fastened; casing cannot be installed until the jamb is in place.
The window jamb establishes the finished opening; drywall mudding and taping around the window is done after the jamb is installed to achieve a seamless transition between wall and jamb.
Interior window mullions are attached to or supported by the interior wall framing, which must be in place to provide structural support and backing.
The window units or rough openings must be installed first so that interior mullions can align with and be secured between or adjacent to the window frames.
Interior mullions must be fully installed and secured before drywall or finish cladding is applied, as the mullion is a structural/trim component that gets covered or butted by finished surfaces.
Trim and casing around windows and mullions are installed after the mullion is in place to achieve proper fit, alignment, and aesthetic finish.

While painting can technically proceed in stages, it is standard practice to complete mullion installation before final painting to avoid damage to finished paint and to ensure uniform coating over all surfaces.
The window frame must be installed first to provide the structural opening and support for the interior window transom element.
Interior wall framing must be completed to define the rough opening and provide attachment points for the transom.
Running electrical wires near the window area is easier before the transom is installed, avoiding obstacles and allowing clear access.
Trim and casing around the transom cannot be installed until the transom itself is in place.
Painting and finishing the wall surface is typically done after transom installation to avoid damaging the transom, though some prefer to paint before to achieve cleaner edges.
Final sealing and glazing of the transom unit must occur after the transom is installed to ensure proper weathertightness and fit.
The rough opening (stud-framed window opening) must be framed and in place to provide the structural support and cavity for the sidelight unit to be installed.
The main window or door frame that the sidelight adjoins must be installed first, as the sidelight typically fits into or abuts the primary frame.
The weather-resistant barrier (house wrap) should be applied around the rough opening before sidelight installation to ensure proper waterproofing and moisture management.
Interior trim and casing around the sidelight can only be installed after the sidelight unit is fully set and secured in the opening.
Drywall finishing around the sidelight opening is completed after the sidelight is installed to allow for proper gap sealing and a clean finished edge.
The rough opening in the wall must be framed, sized, and prepared before the fixed window unit can be installed into it.
Flashing and weather-resistant barriers must be applied around the opening to prevent water intrusion before the window is set in place.
Trim casing, drywall finishing, and paint around the window frame can only be completed after the window unit is fully installed and secured.
Final sealant and caulking around the interior perimeter of the window must be applied after the window is properly positioned and fastened.
While painting can be done before or after installation, it is often preferred to paint after the window is installed to achieve a seamless finish between the frame and the wall.
The rough opening (framed and sheathed) must be created before the window can be physically installed into the wall.
The window must be set and secured in the opening before interior wall finishes can be applied around it to create a clean, finished appearance.

successor: Install window hardware and operator mechanism
rationale: The window frame must be installed in the opening before cranks, handles, locks, and other operating hardware can be attached to it.
The window must be fully installed before it can be tested for smooth operation, sealing, and proper adjustment.
The window must be procured and delivered to the site before installation can occur.

The rough opening (stud framing, header, and sill) must be built and sized correctly before any window can be installed, as the window requires a structurally sound and dimensionally accurate frame to be placed into.

If the sliding interior window is installed in an exterior wall, exterior sheathing and weatherproofing should precede interior window installation to protect the assembly. However, for purely interior partitions this is not applicable.

Electrical wiring, outlet boxes, plumbing lines, or other MEP rough-ins within the wall cavity must be completed before installing the window frame, as access to the stud cavity would be blocked once the window is set.

The window frame and its nailing flanges or mounting brackets must be in place before drywall can be hung and finished around the opening, as the drywall butts against the window frame and is trimmed with casing.

Casing and decorative trim around the window cannot be installed until the window unit itself is securely mounted and fastened, as the trim covers the gap between the window frame and the finished wall surface.
The rough opening must be framed and prepared to the correct dimensions before the casement window unit can be installed into it.
Wall framing must be complete to provide the structural support and rough opening for the casement window.
Weather-resistant barrier or building wrap must be applied to the exterior walls before window installation to prevent moisture intrusion behind the window flange.
Interior trim and casing around the window cannot be installed until the casement window unit is securely in place.
The window unit must be installed before the surrounding drywall can be finished and taped to the window frame for a seamless interior finish.
The interior wall rough openings must be framed before the window unit can be installed into the opening.
Any electrical, plumbing, or mechanical rough-ins that pass through or near the window opening must be completed before the window is set, as access to the wall cavity will be blocked.
The window unit must be installed before the surrounding wall finish can be applied, as the finish needs to be trimmed tight to the window frame.
Paint and trim work around the window must be performed after the window is in place to achieve a clean, finished appearance at the junction of frame and wall.
While not physically required, it is preferred to complete all window installations before final cleaning so that glass is not smudged or damaged during subsequent work.
The window frame or rough opening must be prepared and structurally complete before the acoustic interior window unit can be fitted into place.
After the acoustic window unit is installed, gaps around the frame must be sealed with acoustic caulk to maintain soundproofing performance.
Trim, casing, and moldings around the acoustic window can only be installed after the window unit is securely in place.
Optional acoustic testing to verify STC ratings is typically performed after installation and sealing are complete to validate performance.
Walls and structural framing must be complete to provide the support and proper opening dimensions required for acoustic window installation.
The rough opening (framed and sized) must be prepared before the steel-frame window can be installed, as the window unit needs a properly framed, level, and square opening.
The window must be set and fastened into the opening before any sealing, caulking, or weatherproofing can be applied around its perimeter.
Trim work (casing, architraves) around the window can only be installed after the window frame is securely in place.

While painting is often done after installation for finish quality, it could theoretically be done partially before installation; however, standard practice is to paint after installation to avoid damage during handling.
The building's main structural steel framework must be erected before interior non-load-bearing window frames can be installed, as the window fits within the completed structural bays.
The rough opening must be framed and prepared before the window can be installed, as the window requires a structurally sound and properly sized opening.
Weather barrier or membrane must be installed to protect the opening from moisture before placing the window unit.
The window must be securely installed before trim and casing can be applied around it.
Drywall work around the window requires the window to be in place to establish the finished opening edges.
While painting can be done before window installation, it is preferable to paint after installation to ensure seamless finish and avoid drips on the new window.
The wall frame must be constructed and the rough opening created before an interior window can be installed, as the window frame is fitted into the wall opening.
The rough opening must be measured, leveled, and framed to the correct dimensions before the aluminium window unit can be placed and secured.
Drywall, plaster, or other interior wall finishes must be applied after window installation to allow for proper sealing, trimming, and a flush finish around the window frame.
Sealing gaps and applying insulation around the installed window frame must occur after the window is placed to ensure thermal and moisture protection.
Decorative trim or architraves around the window are installed after the window unit is fixed in place to cover the gap between the frame and the wall surface.
The wall framing must be complete to define the structural opening dimensions and location for the window rough opening.
Exterior sheathing around the window opening must be in place to provide a backing surface and weather barrier before interior preparation work begins.
The header beam above the window opening must be installed to support loads above the opening before interior rough opening work can proceed.
The rough opening must be prepared (measured, shimmed, leveled, and flashed) before the window unit can be set into the opening.
While not physically required, it is common practice to complete window rough openings before running electrical wiring near windows to avoid interference and ensure proper clearance.
The window frame must be installed and structurally sound to provide a surface and support for the glazing (glass) to be set into.

predecessor: Exterior Wall Sheathing & Weather Barrier Installation
rationale: Exterior walls and weather barriers must be in place before interior glazing to protect the glazing material from weather damage and to ensure proper integration with the building envelope.
The rough opening must be prepared, measured, and inspected to ensure correct dimensions and structural readiness before the window glazing is installed.
Interior trim and casing around windows are installed after the glazing is in place to cover gaps and provide a finished appearance.
Interior painting and wall finishing should generally be done after glazing installation to avoid damaging the glass and to achieve clean paint lines around the window edges.
Drywall must be installed and finished (taped, mudded, sanded) before window trim can be applied, as trim is installed against finished drywall surfaces.
The window unit itself must be installed, flashed, and sealed in the rough opening before interior trim and casing can be fitted around it.
Insulation in wall cavities around windows must be in place before interior trim is installed, as the trim would otherwise need to be removed or would block access to the insulation.

Trim and casing are typically installed before finished flooring to allow the casing to sit above the finished floor height or to allow flooring to be fitted up to the trim; however, some installers prefer flooring first. This is a soft sequencing preference rather than a hard physical constraint.
Windows must be physically installed before they can be painted and finished.
Wall framing must be completed to provide the structural opening and support for windows before they are painted.
Drywall around window openings must be installed and taped before the window trim and surrounding surfaces can be painted.
Paint and finish the window frame first so that trim (casing and stools) can be installed on top of the finished surface without getting paint on them.
Painting should be completed before final flooring is installed to avoid paint drips, spills, or damage to finished flooring surfaces.
Window frames must be installed and secured in the rough opening before any interior hardware (such as locks, handles, hinges, or sash supports) can be attached to them.
Glass panes must be set into the window frame before interior hardware like sash locks, lifts, or balance covers can be installed, as the hardware often secures or interfaces with the glazed sash.
The interior wall surfaces surrounding the window must be framed and sheathed to provide a stable mounting surface and reveal for interior window trim and hardware installation.

Interior window hardware such as sash locks, handles, and operator cranks must be installed before the interior trim and casing can be fitted, as the trim often conceals hardware components or must be aligned with the hardware's position.
After all hardware components are installed, the window must be operated to verify smooth function, proper alignment, and secure latching before final finishing or occupancy.
The window frame must be installed and structurally secured before acoustic sealing can be applied to the interior gap between the frame and the wall opening.
Exterior weatherproof sealing must be completed first to protect against moisture ingress, ensuring the interior acoustic sealant adheres properly and is not compromised by water damage.
Any insulation placed around the window rough opening must be installed before the interior seal is applied, otherwise the seal would need to be broken to access the cavity for insulation.
Acoustic sealing must be completed prior to interior wall finishing so that the sealant around the window perimeter can be covered and concealed by the finished wall surface.
Acoustic sealant around the window opening must be in place before trim or casing is installed, as the trim covers the sealed joint and would need to be removed if sealing were done later.
The window frame must be installed before the fire-rating inspection can be performed, as the inspection evaluates the installed assembly's fire-resistance rating.
Fire-rated glazing or glass must be installed in the window frame before the inspection can verify the fire-rating compliance of the complete window assembly.
Fire-resistant sealants and gaskets around the window perimeter must be applied prior to inspection to confirm the integrity of the fire-rated barrier.
The fire-rating inspection must be completed and approved before enclosing the window assembly with wall finishes, to allow access for verification and any necessary corrections.

It is a soft preference to have the fire-rating inspection completed before final project closeout to ensure all fire-safety requirements are met, though closeout could theoretically proceed with corrective work pending.
Balusters/spindles are mounted onto the staircase stringers or treads, so the main staircase structural frame (stringers) must be in place to provide the support surface.
Balusters are typically secured into the stair treads (or the stringer alongside them); treads must be installed to provide the anchoring point.
Although balusters often support the handrail, in many sequences handrails are installed after balusters; this ordering is a soft preference since some methods pre-assemble handrails.
Handrails are typically mounted on top of or between the balusters, so balusters must be in place first to support the handrail.
Painting or staining should occur after baluster installation to ensure all surfaces, including joints and connections, are properly finished and to avoid damaging the finish during installation.
Stair nosing requires a solid, cured concrete substrate to be properly anchored and aligned; installing nosing before concrete is poured or cured would lack structural support.
The stair structure (formwork or rough framing) must exist to define the geometry and provide a surface for nosing attachment.
Stair nosing is typically installed as part of the edge protection before applying final floor finishes (tiles, carpet, or paint) to achieve a clean transition and proper overlap.

It is common practice to install stair nosing before handrails so that the nosing edge reference is established for railing height measurements, though technically railing can be retrofitted after nosing.
Any embedded conduits or services within the stair structure must be roughed in before the final nosing is applied to avoid cutting or damaging the nosing material.
Stair stringers are typically fastened to the floor framing or floor structure; the rough floor framing must be in place to provide a landing and support for the top of the stringers.
The stair layout (rise and run calculations) must be completed before stringers can be cut and installed, as the stringers are marked and cut according to the layout dimensions.
Stringers serve as the structural support for treads; treads are fastened directly onto the stringers, so the stringers must be in place first.
Risers are attached to the vertical faces of the stringers; the stringers must be erected before risers can be installed.

While it is physically possible to install handrails before stringers in some configurations, standard practice and safety favor installing handrails after the stringers are in place so the stair structure is stable for measuring and attaching rails.
Stair enclosure walls must be built on a stable load-bearing surface; the foundation or slab provides the base and anchors the walls.
The floor and roof framing define the vertical alignment and bearing points for the stair enclosure walls, ensuring proper fit and structural support.
The enclosure walls form the structural shaft and support for the stair stringers; stairs cannot be installed until the surrounding walls are built.

successor: Rough-In MEP (Mechanical, Electrical, Plumbing) within Stairwell
rationale: Rough-in work for lighting, conduit, and fire suppression within the stairwell must follow the wall erection to access interior cavities and surfaces.

successor: Fireproofing / Spray-Applied Fire Resistive Materials on Stair Enclosure
rationale: Fireproofing is applied to the completed wall assemblies to meet fire-resistance ratings for the stair enclosure.
The rough opening must be framed to provide the structural support and dimensions for the door to be installed.

successor: Door Hardware Installation (Hinges, Closers, Panic Bars)
rationale: Hardware such as hinges, closers, and panic bars must be attached to the door after it is hung in place.

successor: Fire Caulking / Firestopping of Door Frame Gaps
rationale: Fire-rated sealant must be applied around the installed door frame to maintain fire compartmentation integrity.

successor: Final Adjustments and Latching Mechanism Testing
rationale: The door must be installed and hung before latching mechanisms can be aligned and tested for proper operation.

predecessor: Wall Framing and Drywall Installation (around stair enclosure)
rationale: The walls forming the stair enclosure must be framed and finished to provide the proper substrate and opening for the fire door assembly.
The stair structural frame or carriage must be supported on a stable foundation or substructure; without proper foundation work, the stair structure cannot be safely installed.
The stair frame typically connects between floor levels, so the supporting floor slab or deck at the base of the stairs must be in place to provide a bearing surface and anchor point.
The structural frame/carriage forms the primary load-bearing skeleton of the stairs; treads and risers are installed onto this frame.
Handrails and balustrades are typically attached to the stair structural frame or its supporting structure, so the main frame must be in place first.
Finishing work such as painting, cladding, or covering of the stair structure can only proceed after the structural frame is erected and stable.
The foundation must be completed to provide structural support for the precast concrete stair installation.
The main structural frame (beams, columns, slabs) must be in place to define the floor levels and openings where the precast stair will be installed.
Finishing works such as plastering, painting, tiling, or applying non-slip surfaces to the stair can only proceed after the precast stair is installed and secured.
Handrails and balustrades are attached to the precast stair structure and therefore require the stair to be in place first.
While some MEP work can be done concurrently, final routing of conduits, pipes, and lighting near the stairwell is best done after stair installation to ensure proper fit and clearance.
The spiral/helical stair must be supported by a structural floor slab. The floor provides the base and load-bearing surface for the stair.
Foundations must be completed to provide structural support for the entire building, including the area where the spiral stair will be anchored.
The main structural frame or core walls must be in place to provide lateral support and connection points for the spiral stair.
The stair structure must be fully installed before safety railings and balustrades can be attached to it.
MEP rough-in work adjacent to or passing near the stair area can only be finalized after the stair structure is in place to avoid rework and ensure correct routing.
The alternating tread stair must be anchored to or supported by the structural frame (beams, floors, or walls). Without the structural frame in place, there is no support structure for the stair.
The stair's base and landing areas require a level, prepared subfloor or deck surface to bear on. The subfloor must be installed before the stair can be placed.

Guardrails and handrails for the alternating tread stair are typically attached to the stair stringers or adjacent structure after the stair is fixed in position; they cannot be properly fitted before the stair is in place.

While finish flooring can sometimes be installed incrementally, it is more efficient to complete the stair installation first so that finish flooring can be butted tightly against the stair base and landings for a clean appearance.
The stair must be fully installed and secured before a building inspector can verify compliance with code requirements for alternating tread stairs (e.g., tread depth, rise, headroom).

The structural framing must be complete to provide support and attachment points for the stair stringers, risers, and treads. Stairs cannot be installed without the underlying floor and wall framing in place.
Concrete foundation or slab must be cured and in place to serve as the base landing or support for the stair system, especially for stairs terminating at ground level.

Rough electrical wiring should be completed before stair installation to avoid the need to run wiring under or through completed stairs, which would be difficult and require removing stair components.
Stairs must be installed before drywall and painting on adjacent walls can be finished, as the stairs define the final wall heights and access for finishing work around the stairwell.
The stair structure must be fully installed and secured before railings and balusters can be attached, as railings mount directly onto the stair stringers or treads.
Rebar must be installed and fixed in place before concrete can be poured, as rebar provides the structural reinforcement within the concrete stair.
Formwork must be erected and secured to create the mold and support structure for the wet concrete before pouring can begin.
Concrete must be poured and allowed to achieve initial set before formwork can be stripped and curing can commence.
Surface finishing and waterproofing can only be applied after the concrete has been poured and the surface is ready for treatment.
The floor or base area where the stair formwork will sit must be screeded and leveled to ensure a stable, level foundation for the formwork and subsequent concrete pour.
The stair balustrade is mounted on or anchored to the structural stair frame, so the staircase must be fully framed to provide a stable base for balustrade installation.
Balustrade posts and rails often align with or are fastened to the treads/risers; the walking surface must be in place to correctly position and secure the balustrade.
Running wiring for stair lighting behind or alongside balustrade components is easier before the balustrade is installed; however, it can sometimes be done afterward with fishing techniques.
The balustrade must be installed first so that painting, staining, or sealing the handrails and balusters can be applied as final finish work without obstruction.
The balustrade is a critical safety component of the staircase; inspection must occur after installation to verify compliance with building codes for guardrail height, strength, and spacing.
The stair structure must be framed and structurally supported before any finish treads or decorative coverings can be applied, as the treads attach to the rough framing.
Stringers provide the angled support structure for treads; treads cannot be installed until stringers are in place and secured.
Landings and adjacent floor areas must be level and prepared to ensure proper alignment and fit of stair treads and finish materials.
Handrails and balusters are typically mounted onto or adjacent to the finished treads; the treads must be in place to establish final heights and attachment points for railings.

While painting can begin before stairs are finished, final trim touch-ups and stair skirt board painting are often done after tread installation to ensure a seamless finish without overspray or damage to new treads.

The structural framing of the stairs must be fully installed and stable before any safety inspection can be conducted, as the inspection assesses the integrity and stability of the installed structure.
All stair treads and risers must be in place so the inspection can verify proper dimensions, slip resistance, and compliance with building codes for step geometry.
Handrails and guardrails must be installed prior to the safety inspection so that the inspector can verify their height, strength, and compliance with safety codes.

While it is preferable to apply final finishes after inspection to avoid covering potential defects, it is a soft preference because finishes could be applied earlier if the inspection is done in stages.
The stairs must pass safety inspection and be certified as compliant before they can be opened for regular use or occupancy to ensure user safety and legal compliance.
A design must exist before it can be assessed for compliance with accessibility and DDA (Disability Discrimination Act) requirements.
Accessibility assessment reviews the architectural plans and spatial layouts to ensure they meet DDA standards for paths of travel, door widths, ramps, and accessible facilities.
If the assessment identifies non-compliance issues, the design must be revised before proceeding further to ensure legal accessibility requirements are met.
A certified accessibility compliance assessment or report is typically required as part of the documentation submitted to the building authority for permit approval.
The results of the compliance assessment often inform the detailed construction drawings to incorporate required accessibility features such as accessible toilets, ramps, and signage.

The door frame rough opening must be prepared (sized, shimmed, and leveled) before the pivot hinge corner door can be installed, as the door requires a properly dimensioned and structurally sound opening to mount to.

Flooring at the threshold area should be completed before door installation to establish the correct undercut clearance and ensure the door swings properly without obstruction or later damage to finished flooring.
The pivot hinge door must be hung and aligned in its frame before the handle, lock, and door closer can be installed onto the door leaf and jamb.
Final trim and casing around the door frame are installed after the door is hung to ensure proper alignment, clearance, and a finished appearance.

successor: Final painting/finishing of door and frame
rationale: While painting can be done before hanging in some cases, final touch-up painting is typically performed after installation to cover any scratches or damage that occurred during the hanging process; this is a soft preference for quality rather than a physical necessity.
The sliding corner door track must be mounted onto the wall framing or structure; the framing provides the necessary support and attachment surface for the track.
The door panels cannot be hung or installed until the track is in place, as the track guides and supports the sliding panels.
Hardware such as rollers and guides are attached to or aligned with the track; the track must be installed first to ensure proper fit and operation.
The corner door frame must be assembled within the wall opening, so the wall framing that creates the rough opening must be completed first.
The rough opening must be measured, cut, and prepared in the wall framing before the door frame assembly can be installed.
The door frame must be fully assembled and secured in place before the door can be hung on its hinges.
Drywall must be installed around the door frame after the frame is in place to ensure proper fit and finishing around the door opening.
The door frame must be fully assembled before trim and casing can be applied around the door opening for a finished look.
The rough opening frame for the door must be constructed to provide the structural support and defined space into which the corner door jamb will be installed.
The door jamb must be in place to provide the hinge mounting surface and strike plate area before the door leaf can be hung.
The jamb is the interior framework; casing trim is applied around the jamb on the wall surface, so the jamb must be installed first.
Weatherstripping can be applied after the jamb is installed to seal gaps, though it may also be done after the door is hung for precise fit.
The wall assembly must be framed, sheathed, and have the rough opening created before the door jamb can be set into place.
The door frame provides the structural support and reveals into which the threshold is fitted; the threshold sits beneath and against the frame.
The rough opening must be framed, leveled, and squared to receive the door assembly including the threshold.
The door slab or panel hinges off the frame and swings over the threshold; the door cannot be hung before the threshold is in place as it provides the bottom seal and clearance reference.
Weatherproofing (caulking, flashing, or gasketing) at the threshold perimeter must be applied after the threshold is mechanically fastened in position.
The subfloor or sill plate must be clean, level, and structurally sound to provide a stable bearing surface for the threshold.
The glass panel requires the door frame to be in place to be mounted or set into.
The glass panel must be installed before it can be sealed around the edges to ensure weather tightness.

successor: Corner Door Hardware Installation (handle, lock, hinges)
rationale: Hardware components are attached to or interact with the glass panel assembly after it is in place.

predecessor: Structural Opening Preparation and Rough Framing
rationale: The rough opening must be framed and prepared to receive the glass panel assembly.

predecessor: Corner Door Glass Panel Delivery and On-site Inspection
rationale: The glass panel must be delivered and inspected for damage before installation can proceed.
The door frame must be installed to provide the structural mounting surface for the corner door hardware set.
Walls must be framed and sheathed to define the door opening and provide support for the door frame and hardware.
The rough opening must be properly sized and prepared before any door hardware can be installed.
The corner hardware set must be installed first to serve as the attachment points before the door can be hung and aligned.
Corner hardware must be in place before final adjustments and operational testing of the door can be performed.
The corner door closer mechanism mounts onto or within the door frame; the frame must be installed first to provide the structural support and mounting surface.
The door closer mechanism interacts with the door leaf (panel) to control closing; the door must be hung before the closer can be attached and adjusted.
The closer mechanism must be physically installed before its internal hydraulic or spring tension can be calibrated to achieve the correct closing speed and force.
Full operational testing of the door (open/close cycling, latch engagement) can only occur after the closer mechanism is installed and adjusted.
Final cosmetic trim, cover plates, and finishing touches around the closer are completed after the mechanism itself is in place to avoid damage and ensure proper fit.
The corner studs must be nailed to the bottom plate, which must be in place to provide a base for the corner framing.
The floor platform (subfloor) must be completed to provide a stable work surface and anchoring surface for wall framing including corners.
The top plate is installed on top of the wall studs, including corner studs; corner framing must be complete before the top plate can be attached.
Wall sheathing (e.g., plywood or OSB) is applied over the framed wall assembly after studs and corner posts are in place.
Drywall is attached to the completed wall framing; corner studs must be framed and in position to serve as backing for drywall corners.
The rough opening framing must be completed to provide the structural support and designated space for the corner door to be installed.
Wall sheathing provides the necessary backing and surface for the corner door frame to be properly mounted and sealed against.
Flashing and weatherproofing must be applied after the door is installed to ensure proper sealing around the door frame and prevent water infiltration.
Drywall finishing around the door opening can only be completed after the corner door is installed to ensure seamless integration and proper gap coverage.
Exterior siding must be installed after the corner door to properly flash and trim around the door frame, ensuring a weather-tight seal.
The foundation must be poured and cured to provide a stable, level surface for the door frame fabrication and installation.
The rough opening for the corner door must be framed to define the dimensions and location before the door frame can be fabricated to fit.
The door frame must be fabricated before the door slab can be hung and installed within it.
Weatherproofing and sealing around the frame can only be applied after the frame is fabricated and installed in its final position.
Interior trim, casing, and finish work around the door require the frame to be fully fabricated and in place to ensure proper alignment and fit.
The wall structure must be framed before any openings can be formed in it, as the opening is cut or created within the framed wall assembly.
Typically sheathing is applied before cutting openings, though it can also be done after; but standard sequence installs sheathing first for structural integrity before forming openings.
The opening must be fully formed and prepared before windows or doors can be placed into it.
The opening formation creates the space; the header or lintel is then installed across the top of that opening to support the load above.
The opening must be completely formed before it can be inspected for compliance with dimensions and structural requirements.
The corner door must be installed in place before waterproofing can be applied around its frame and sealing surfaces.
The door frame must be properly aligned, leveled, and secured before waterproofing can be applied to ensure an even and effective seal.
Wall surfaces around the door must be cleaned, smoothed, and primed (if required) to ensure proper adhesion of waterproofing materials.
Waterproofing must be fully cured before any cladding, siding, or decorative finish is applied over or around the door area to avoid trapping moisture.
It is preferable but not strictly required to perform water leakage testing after waterproofing is complete and cured to verify the seal effectiveness before enclosing the area.
A stable foundation or base is physically required before constructing any stone rubble wall, as the wall's weight and structural integrity depend on a prepared load-bearing surface.
A protective cap or coping layer is placed on top of the completed wall to prevent water infiltration and weathering; this cannot be installed until the wall is fully built.
Backfilling behind a rubble retaining wall must occur after the wall is constructed to provide lateral support and proper drainage; backfilling before would undermine construction.
The area must be cleared and excavated to the required depth and alignment before rubble wall construction can begin.
While mortar pointing typically follows wall construction, dry-stone walls may not require it, so this is a common sequencing preference rather than a hard physical requirement.

The door frame must be installed and structurally in place before finishing and painting can be applied to the corner door, as painting over an uninstalled or unfinished frame would be impossible and the paint/finish would be damaged during subsequent installation.

Corner walls surrounding the door should be finished and painted first to establish clean edges and trim lines, and to avoid painting over door hardware or damaging the door finish during wall painting.

predecessor: Corner Door Hardware Pre-Installation (Hinges, Lockset Prep)
rationale: Hardware prep work such as mortising hinges and drilling for locksets must be completed before painting so that these cutouts are properly primed and painted, preventing exposed raw wood and ensuring a uniform finish.
The door surface must be sanded smooth and a primer coat applied before the final finish and paint coats can be applied, as paint will not adhere properly to an unprepared or unprimed surface.

successor: Corner Door Hardware Final Installation (Knobs, Locks, Plates)
rationale: Final hardware such as knobs, locks, and strike plates are installed after painting to avoid getting paint on the hardware and to ensure clean, professional installation without obstruction.

The door is typically painted in a horizontal or shop position before being hung in the frame to achieve a cleaner finish; hanging the door after painting avoids drips, runs, and damage to the wet paint during handling.
A reinforced masonry wall requires a stable foundation to bear its load and provide a base for construction.

predecessor: Footing and Slab on Grade Preparation
rationale: The wall must be built on top of prepared footings or slab to ensure proper load transfer and structural integrity.
Vertical and horizontal steel reinforcement must be placed and tied within the wall formwork or masonry units before concrete or grout is placed.
The wall must be fully cured and structurally complete to support roof framing and connections.
Masonry walls must be erected before conduits, pipes, and boxes can be installed within the wall cavities.
Surface finishing and coatings can only be applied after the masonry wall is complete and cured.
Structural concrete walls require a solid load-bearing foundation to distribute their weight and resist lateral loads. The foundation must be cured and strong enough before wall construction begins.
Steel reinforcement (rebar) must be placed and tied within the formwork before concrete is poured to provide tensile strength to the wall.
Formwork (molds) must be erected and secured to shape and contain the wet concrete until it cures. Without formwork, the concrete cannot be placed in the correct geometry.
After concrete placement, the wall must be allowed to cure to achieve design strength before formwork can be safely removed and before subsequent loads are applied.
Floor or roof slabs typically bear on or are supported by structural walls; the walls must be complete and sufficiently cured to carry the load of slabs poured above.
The rough opening for the window must be framed before the splayed reveal can be installed, as the reveal is built into and finishes the edges of the opening.
The surrounding wall structure or masonry must be in place to provide the substrate and structural context for the splayed reveal to be constructed against.
The splayed reveal forms the finished jambs and head of the opening, and the window frame is typically set against or within the reveal to achieve proper alignment and sealing.
The splayed reveal must be completed and stable before plasterers can finish the internal wall surfaces up to the reveal edges, ensuring a clean junction.
While the sill can be installed after the reveal, they may be integrated; typically the reveal is formed first to define the opening profile before adding the sill.
The structural frame or load-bearing walls must be in place to provide the supporting substrate onto which internal wall lining (e.g., plasterboard or drywall) is fixed.
The building must be enclosed and weathertight (roof complete) before installing internal linings to prevent moisture damage to plasterboard and insulation.
Stud walls or internal partitions must be erected to provide the framework for attaching wall linings.
Thermal or acoustic insulation must be placed inside wall cavities before they are closed off by the lining.

predecessor: MEP Rough-In (Electrical, Plumbing, Data) within walls
rationale: All wiring, conduits, pipes, and boxes must be run through the wall cavities before covering them with lining, otherwise costly rework is required.
After fixing plasterboard or wallboards, the joints must be taped, filled, and sanded to create a smooth finish.
Wall lining provides the surface that must be in place before applying primer, paint, or wallpaper.
Although preferable to complete wall lining before floor finishes to avoid damage, a soft preference is noted as sequencing can vary; some trades may install floors before skirting boards.
Door and window architraves and skirting boards are fixed onto the lined wall surface after lining is complete.
The foundation or footing must be completed and cured to provide a stable and level base for the formwork and the concrete wall to be constructed upon.
Rebar cages and reinforcement mats for the wall must be placed and tied before formwork is erected, as the formwork encloses the reinforcement and prevents access after installation.
Accurate survey and layout marking of wall lines, corners, and elevations is required before formwork placement to ensure correct positioning and alignment.
Formwork creates the mold into which concrete is poured; therefore formwork must be fully erected, aligned, braced, and inspected before any concrete placement can occur.

Waterproofing is typically applied after formwork stripping, not before pouring, but this is a soft constraint since scheduling can vary; however the formwork erection itself must precede the wall construction that makes waterproofing possible.
Waterproofing membranes and coatings must be applied to cured concrete surfaces. The concrete must be fully set and cured to provide a stable, clean substrate for waterproofing adhesion.

Concrete must complete its initial curing period (typically 7-28 days) to reach sufficient strength and dryness before waterproofing can be applied, as applying to uncured concrete can trap moisture and cause delamination.
Surfaces must be clean, free of debris, dust, oil, and laitance, and properly primed to ensure proper bonding of waterproofing materials.

Backfilling against foundation walls cannot begin until exterior waterproofing membranes are fully applied, cured, and protected, as the waterproofing layer must be in place to prevent moisture ingress from the surrounding soil.

successor: Installation of Drainage Board or Protection Board
rationale: Protection boards and drainage mats are installed directly over the completed waterproofing membrane to shield it from damage during backfilling and to facilitate groundwater drainage.

The shared wall between closets is a load-bearing or partition wall that requires a stable foundation and floor slab to be built upon. Without the foundation and slab, the wall cannot be safely erected.
The shared wall between closets connects to and is framed as part of the overall structural framing. Adjacent room framing defines the boundaries and support points for this wall.
Electrical wiring for outlets and switches in the closets is typically run through the wall cavities after the wall framing is complete but before drywall is applied.

If the shared wall contains any plumbing (e.g., for a nearby bathroom), it must be installed after the wall is framed but before the wall is closed up. This is a soft constraint as plumbing may not be present in this particular wall.
Drywall cannot be installed until the wall framing is complete, as drywall is attached directly to the wall studs. The shared wall must be fully framed before it can be covered.
Electrical and plumbing rough-ins must be completed before closet rod installation to avoid interference and ensure clear access to walls.
Closet rod requires finished wall surfaces (framed and drywalled) to support mounting brackets or flanges securely.
Walls must be painted or finished before installing closet rods to avoid paint splatter and ensure clean edges around hardware.
Closet rod installation provides the primary hanging bar, and shelves or organizers often integrate with or rely on the rod's position for spacing and alignment.

While flooring can be done before or after rod installation, it is often preferred to install closet rod first to avoid scratching new flooring during hardware installation, though this is a soft preference.
The rough opening must be framed to provide the structural opening into which the bi-fold closet door is installed.
Drywall must be installed and finished around the closet opening before the door is mounted, as the door frame and tracks attach to finished walls.
Wall and trim painting should be completed before installing the bi-fold door to avoid paint drips on the door and to achieve clean edges around the frame.
Flooring (e.g., carpet, hardwood, tile) must be installed before the door so the door clears the finished floor height and the bottom pivot bracket can be properly set.
After the bi-fold door is hung, final adjustments to the track, pivot brackets, and door alignment must be performed to ensure smooth operation.
The closet opening must be framed and drywall finished before a sliding door system can be fitted, as the door tracks and frame attach to the finished wall and rough opening.

predecessor: Closet interior shelving and rod installation
rationale: It is much easier to install interior closet shelving, rods, and storage systems while there is full access without the door in place. This is a soft preference for construction efficiency, not a physical necessity.

Flooring is typically installed up to or slightly under the door track; however, it is often preferred to install the door after flooring to ensure proper clearance and finished appearance. This can vary in sequencing.
After mounting the sliding door and hardware, any nail holes, gaps, or caulking around the door frame can be touched up, and final paint can be applied for a seamless finish.
The rough opening dimensions must be verified and squared before ordering or installing the sliding closet door to ensure the door system fits properly.
Rough framing provides the structural opening and support needed for the closet door frame to be installed.
Wall sheathing creates the wall surfaces that the closet door frame fits into and attaches to.
The door frame must be in place before drywall can be cut and finished around it to create a clean transition.
The door frame (jambs and header) must be fully installed before the door slab can be hung on hinges.
