Trim casing around the door frame is applied after the frame is secured and the wall finish is complete.
Electrical wiring and junction boxes must be installed in the closet ceiling before the lighting fixture can be physically mounted and connected.
The closet walls and ceiling structure must be framed to provide the mounting surface and support for the lighting fixture.
The ceiling drywall must be installed and finished to provide a finished surface for mounting the closet light fixture.

While the light fixture can be installed before painting, it is often preferred to paint the closet ceiling first to avoid paint splatter on the fixture; this is a soft preference for quality of finish.
Lighting must be installed first to provide adequate illumination for the closet shelving installation work, and to ensure the fixture does not interfere with shelf placement.
The electrical outlet must be mounted on the framed wall; framing provides the structural cavity and support for the outlet box.
Electrical cables must be run to the outlet location before the outlet box and receptacle can be installed and connected.
The outlet box must be installed and secured to the stud before drywall can be hung, as the drywall is cut around the box.

successor: Outlet Trim and Cover Plate Installation
rationale: The receptacle must be wired and mounted in the box before the trim/cover plate can be attached.
While not physically required, it is standard practice to install and wire the outlet before painting so that any touch-ups around the outlet are done together, and to avoid paint on the receptacle.
The closet rod bracket needs to be attached to the wall framing; the wall must be framed before any brackets can be mounted.
Drywall is typically installed over wall framing before closet rod brackets are mounted, as brackets are screwed into the wall surface.
The brackets must be mounted first to support the closet rod, which rests in or attaches to the brackets.
While brackets can be installed before or after painting, it is often preferable to paint the walls first to avoid getting paint on the hardware.
The closet ventilation louver is typically mounted into or through the closet wall or door. The wall or door framing must be in place to provide a structural surface for the louver installation.
The louver provides ventilation pathways. Any plumbing work that might run through the same wall cavity should be completed before the louver is installed to avoid conflict and allow access.
The louver must be in place before final wall finishing so that the finishes can be applied neatly around the louver frame and any gaps can be sealed.
The louver installation must be complete so that painters and trim carpenters can work around it, ensuring a clean finished appearance and proper integration with the surrounding surfaces.

successor: Final Inspection / Commissioning of Passive Ventilation
rationale: The louver must be installed and fully functional before the ventilation system can be inspected and commissioned to verify airflow performance.
Electrical rough-in work needs to be completed before framing can enclose the walls, as running wires after framing would require cutting through studs.
Plumbing rough-in must be done before wall framing is complete so pipes can be installed within the wall cavity before it is enclosed.
HVAC ductwork must be installed before framing is finished, as ducts need to be routed through wall and ceiling spaces before they are closed up.
Insulation is installed within the framed wall cavities; the stud walls must first be constructed to provide the cavities for insulation.
Drywall is attached to the stud framing; the stud walls must be in place and secured before drywall can be hung on them.
The closet framing and rough-in work requires a completed concrete slab or foundation to build upon, providing a stable base for wall framing.
Electrical wiring must be installed after the closet walls are framed so that wires can be run through stud cavities and outlet/switch boxes can be mounted to the framing.
Wall insulation must be placed after the closet is framed so it can fill the cavities between studs before drywall is installed.
Drywall sheets are hung on the completed closet wall framing; the framing must be fully erected and secured before drywall can be attached.

Permanent closet shelving and organizer systems are typically installed after drywall and paint are complete, but the rough-in framing defines the closet cavity dimensions and provides the structure for mounting components.
The closet door frame must be constructed and secured in place before any door can be installed, as the door components attach directly to the rough framing.
For closets on exterior walls, the wall sheathing and weather barrier must be completed before doors are hung to protect interior from weather.
Electrical rough-in for closet lighting or switches should be completed before door installation to avoid interference and allow easy access.
It is preferable to paint the closet interior before installing doors to achieve clean edges, but doors can be installed first and painted later.
Typically flooring is installed before closet doors to allow continuous flooring under the door, but this order can be reversed if needed.
Interior walls must be fully painted or wallpapered before installing shelving and rods, as these would obstruct access to walls and could be damaged during wall finishing work.
Flooring should be installed first to avoid having to work around installed shelving and rods, and to ensure shelving sits on top of finished flooring for proper height alignment.
The closet must be framed and drywalled to provide the structural surfaces (wall studs, drywall) into which shelves and rods are anchored.
Any minor touch-up painting around newly installed shelving and rods is easier to perform after installation, though it is a soft preference since major painting should already be done.
The closet area should be completely fitted with shelving and rods before final cleaning and occupancy to avoid re-cleaning or having to move items around later.
Closet framing must be complete to create the cavities and spaces where insulation will be placed.
Electrical wiring, outlets, and switch boxes must be installed before insulation to avoid burying wires behind insulation and to allow proper inspection.
Any plumbing lines running through closet walls must be roughed in before insulation to ensure access and code compliance.
Insulation must be installed before drywall or wall boards are hung, as the insulation needs to be enclosed within the wall cavities.
A vapor barrier (if required by code) is typically placed over the insulation before drywall, so insulation must be in place first.
Electrical wiring must be installed within the closet walls and stud cavities, so the framing must be completed to provide access and support for the electrical boxes and cables.
Insulation is installed after electrical rough-in to cover the wiring and maintain thermal and fire barrier integrity; installing insulation first would block access for electrical work.
Drywall must be installed after electrical rough-in to enclose the wiring and outlets; electrical boxes need to be flush with the finished drywall surface.
The main feeder conduit or service rough-in to the electrical panel must be in place before branch circuit wiring (like closet circuits) can be pulled and terminated.
All electrical rough-in work, including closet circuits, must be completed and ready before the inspection can be scheduled and performed to verify code compliance.
Drywall installation requires the wall framing to be in place as the structural support for attaching drywall sheets.
Electrical wiring must be run inside the walls before drywall is installed, as it would be impossible or destructive to add wiring after the walls are enclosed.
Paint and primer must be applied over finished drywall; drywall finishing (taping, mudding, sanding) must be complete before painting can begin.
Baseboards and trim are typically installed against finished, painted walls; drywall must be finished and smooth for proper trim attachment.
Shelving is mounted on or against finished walls; drywall must be complete to provide a finished surface and to allow proper anchoring.
The rough framing must be in place to provide the structural surfaces (walls, door opening) onto which trim and casing can be installed.
Drywall must be installed, taped, and finished before trim is applied, as trim typically covers the drywall edges and is nailed into the framing through or alongside the drywall.
Trim and casing must be installed before they can be painted or primed; painting raw trim before installation would result in an incomplete finish on nailed/joined areas.

While shelving can technically be installed before or after trim, it is standard practice to complete trim work first to avoid damaging shelving materials and to ensure a clean finished look at the junction of shelving and trim.

Trim and casing are typically installed before finished flooring (or at least before the final floor covering), as casing sits over the flooring and base trim may need to be cut to fit around flooring transitions.
Base cabinets provide the structural support and foundation required for countertop installation; countertops cannot be placed without finished cabinets underneath.
The countertop must be installed before the sink can be mounted into the cutout; the sink sits within the countertop opening.
Backsplash tiles or panels are installed above the countertop and must align with its surface; countertop provides the base edge reference.
Flooring must be completed before countertop installation to ensure proper height alignment and to avoid damaging finished floors with heavy stone or material slabs.
Walls must be completed and finished to provide the perimeter support and accurate measurements for countertop templating and installation.
The roof or exterior wall structure must be framed to create the opening where the skylight will be installed.
Roof sheathing must be in place to cut the opening and provide a mounting surface for the skylight curb and flashing.
The skylight unit must be set in place before flashing and counterflashing can be installed around its perimeter to seal against water intrusion.
Final roofing material is laid up to and over the skylight flashing after the skylight is installed, ensuring a continuous waterproof layer.
The drywall and trim work around the interior skylight shaft (light well) can only be completed after the skylight is physically installed and sealed.
Base cabinets must be installed on a finished, level floor surface to ensure stability and proper alignment.
Base cabinets are typically anchored to wall studs; wall framing must be complete to provide structural support.
Plumbing rough-in must be completed before cabinets are installed, as cabinets often enclose or cover pipes and access must be available for connections.
Electrical rough-in for outlets, switches, or appliance connections behind or within base cabinets must be complete before cabinets are placed.
The sink is typically mounted into or under the countertop, which rests on base cabinets; cabinets must be in place before the countertop and sink are installed.
Door hinges, drawer slides, and trim pieces are typically installed after cabinets are set in place, but this is a soft preference as some hardware can be pre-installed.
Base cabinets are often installed before wall cabinets to establish alignment and reference height, but wall cabinets can technically be installed first with proper planning.
The wall surface must be smooth, level, and prepared before tiles, glass, or other splashback materials can be adhered or fixed to it.
Base cabinets are typically installed first to establish the countertop height and layout; the splashback then sits above the countertop and behind the benchtop.
The benchtop must be in place because the splashback typically sits on top of or abuts the benchtop surface, forming the joint between counter and wall.

successor: Electrical fitting (power points / switches on splashback)
rationale: If electrical outlets or switches are to be mounted through the splashback, the splashback material must first be installed so that cutouts can be accurately made and the fittings can be flush-mounted.

While rangehood ducting may be roughed in earlier, the splashback is ideally installed before the final mounting of the cooktop/rangehood so that the appliance can overlap or seal against the finished wall surface.
Plumbing rough-in for sinks must be completed before countertops are installed, as the counter will cover and block access to plumbing connections.
Base cabinets must be permanently installed and leveled to provide the structural support and substrate for countertops.
Accurate field measurements and template fabrication must be completed before the actual counter material can be fabricated and installed.
Backsplash tiles are installed after the countertop is in place so that the backsplash material overlaps and seals against the counter surface for a watertight finish.
Sinks and countertop-mounted fixtures (faucets, soap dispensers) are installed after the countertop is set, as they are mounted into or through the countertop material.
Plumbing pipes and drainage lines must be embedded in or run beneath the foundation slab before the concrete is poured; plumbing rough-in occurs during foundation stage.
The ground must be excavated and graded to the proper levels before underground sewer and water lines can be laid.
While some plumbing can begin after foundation, the bulk of above-ground rough-in plumbing for walls and ceilings requires wall and roof framing to be in place to run pipes through studs and joists.
All rough plumbing work must be completed and visually accessible before the municipal or third-party inspection can take place to verify code compliance.
Electrical wiring often runs alongside plumbing; however, plumbing should be installed first to avoid conflicts and ensure clear access for electrical runs.
Plumbing pipes must be installed and inspected before insulation is placed, as insulation will cover and block access to pipes and joints.
All plumbing rough-in must be complete, tested, and inspected before walls are closed up with drywall, otherwise future repairs would require demolition.
The wall lining or sheeting must be installed before splashback tiling or panels can be fixed, as the splashback is applied onto the finished wall surface.

Kitchen cabinets (including benchtops) must be installed first so that the splashback tiles or panels can be set to the correct height above the benchtop and fit precisely between cabinets and benchtop.

Plumbing rough-in for sinks and tapware must be completed before splashback installation so that pipes can be concealed behind the finished wall and the splashback can be cut and fitted around any exposed pipework.

Electrical rough-in wiring for power points, switches, and rangehoods must be completed before splashback tiling so that cables are in place behind the wall and the splashback can be cut around electrical boxes.
Final installation of power points, switches, and rangehood trim must occur after splashback tiling, as these fittings are mounted onto/through the finished splashback surface.
The sealing of the benchtop-to-splashback joint and any grout sealing must be performed after the splashback tiling/panel fixing is complete to ensure watertightness.
Any final paint touch-ups around the splashback area should be done after the splashback is installed to cover any damage or marks from the tiling process.
The site must be selected before its solar orientation can be assessed, as the assessment depends on the physical location and context of the building site.
The solar orientation assessment determines optimal building placement, window positioning, and shading strategies, which must be established before the detailed building layout design begins.
While not physically required, understanding solar orientation early can influence foundation placement and thermal mass considerations for passive solar heating.
Solar orientation results inform heating and cooling load calculations, allowing HVAC system sizing and zoning to be optimized for solar gain patterns.

A topographical survey provides the site contours, existing vegetation, and neighboring structures that affect solar access and shading, which are essential inputs for an accurate solar orientation assessment.
The shelf board must be cut to the correct dimensions before it can be installed in the shelving unit.
Sanding must be completed before installation to ensure smooth surfaces and edges, as sanding after installation would be difficult.
Finishing (staining or sealing) must be done before installation to allow proper drying and to avoid damage to surrounding structures.
Support brackets must be securely mounted to the wall or frame before the shelf board can be placed on them.
The desired height and level position of the shelf must be measured and marked before installing supports to ensure correct placement.
The shelf bracket must be anchored to wall studs or framing; without wall framing in place, the bracket has no structural support.
While drywall can be installed after the bracket, it is preferable to have drywall finished to mark exact bracket placement and avoid cutting around the bracket later.
The shelf board rests on or is fastened to the bracket; the bracket must be secured first to provide support for the shelf.
It is a soft preference to wait until all brackets are installed before testing, but testing can be done per bracket as a quality check.
Bracket positions must be measured and marked on the wall before drilling holes and installing the bracket to ensure proper alignment and spacing.
The foundation or base frame must be assembled first to provide a stable mounting surface and reference for the upright/side panel installation.
The upright/side panels form the vertical structural supports; the top frame or crossbeams must be attached after the uprights are in place to create the overall frame enclosure.
Bracing and stiffeners are installed after the upright/side panels are positioned to add lateral stability and rigidity to the structure.
Exterior cladding or covering panels are attached after the upright/side structural panels are in place and secured.
Internal components (shelves, brackets, wiring, etc.) are typically mounted after the side panels are erected, though this could be done concurrently in some designs.
The shelf slab must be installed first to provide the base surface onto which the shelf edge or lip can be attached.
The shelf edge/lip defines the front boundary of the shelf, so surface finishing (painting, laminating, or sealing) should occur after the edge/lip is in place to ensure a clean, contiguous finish.
The edge/lip must be fully secured before any loads are placed on the shelf to prevent damage or displacement of the lip element.
Adjustable shelf pins are inserted into pre-drilled holes in the cabinet side panels. Without drilling the holes first, there is no place to insert the pins.
The side panels must be constructed and in place before shelf pins can be installed, as the pins are mounted into the side panels.
The adjustable shelf pins must be inserted into the holes first to create the support ledges before a shelf can be placed onto them.
While shelf height adjustment can technically begin after pins are installed, it's a soft preference as the adjustment involves repositioning the pins themselves to different holes.
Wall anchors must be fixed into the wall framing or structure; without the frame or substrate in place, there is nothing to anchor into.
The mounting surface must be clean and level so that the anchor can be properly seated and achieve full load capacity.

successor: Hanging / Mounting of Object (e.g., shelf, cabinet, equipment)
rationale: The anchor must be securely installed into the wall before any load-bearing object can be hung or mounted onto it.

successor: Plumbing / Electrical Rough-In (if passing through same wall cavity)
rationale: It is often easier to run pipes or cables before anchors are placed to avoid obstructions, but anchors can be installed first if careful coordination is maintained.
Finishing paint or sealant should ideally be applied after anchor installation to cover any exposed hardware, but this is a cosmetic preference rather than a structural requirement.
Shelving rails need to be attached to wall studs; wall framing provides the structural support for mounting the rails.

While shelving rails can be mounted directly to studs before drywall, typically drywall is completed and then rails are installed; however if mounting through drywall into studs, drywall should be finished first for a clean appearance.
Electrical wiring must be run in walls before shelving rails are mounted, to avoid interference and ensure wiring is properly routed behind the wall surface.
Shelving brackets attach directly to the rail/track system; the rail must be securely mounted first to support the brackets.
Shelves rest on brackets that are inserted into the rail/track; the track and brackets must be in place before shelves can be laid on top.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and tested for bearing capacity before any base or plinth can be constructed, as the plinth requires a stable, load-bearing surface.
Excavation to the required depth and formation level must be completed to provide the space and subgrade for the base or plinth foundation.
The subgrade must be properly compacted and a granular sub-base (if specified) laid to prevent differential settlement before the plinth concrete or masonry is placed.

Columns, load-bearing walls, or superstructure elements require a finished base or plinth to support and transfer loads; the plinth provides the starting bearing surface for vertical structural members.
The damp proof course is typically laid at plinth level to prevent moisture rising from the ground into the walls; the plinth must be finished to receive the DPC.
The top cap/crown sits atop the pile and transfers loads from the superstructure to the pile. The pile must be installed first to provide the foundation support for the crown.
The pile top must be cut and leveled to the design elevation before the crown can be placed to ensure proper load transfer and alignment.
Reinforcement extending from the pile into the crown must be placed before the crown concrete is poured to ensure structural continuity.
The crown/cap provides the load-bearing platform and connection point for the superstructure; columns or steelwork cannot be erected until the crown is finished and cured.
Once the crown concrete is placed, sufficient curing time is required before any subsequent loads (e.g., formwork removal, superstructure loads) can be applied.

Shelving requires a structurally complete wall framework to be mounted onto. Wall framing provides the vertical studs and structural support necessary for securely attaching shelving brackets or supports.

Drywall provides the finished surface on which shelving is mounted. Shelving must be installed after drywall is complete to avoid damaging unfinished walls and to ensure proper mounting onto the final wall surface.

Electrical wiring must be run within walls before shelving is installed, as shelves can obstruct access to wall cavities needed for wire routing. Completing electrical rough-in first prevents the need to remove shelves later for electrical work.

While painting can be done before shelving, the final coat is often completed after shelving installation for a seamless finish. However, this is a soft preference as painting can be completed before installation with careful touch-ups later.

Flooring is typically installed before shelving to avoid damaging shelves, but if shelving is wall-mounted and floor-installation uses heavy equipment, shelving may be done first. This is a soft preference as the order can vary based on shelving type and flooring method.
Structural walls (e.g., stud framing, masonry, or concrete walls) must be fully erected and stabilized before any preparation work like cleaning, patching, or fixing can begin.
Electrical wiring, conduits, outlet boxes, and plumbing pipes must be installed within the wall cavities before the walls are closed up or prepared for finishing.
Insulation must be placed inside wall cavities before the wall surface is prepared and fixed (e.g., before drywall is hung or plaster is applied).
Wall surfaces must be properly prepared (cleaned, patched, sanded, and fixed) before primer and paint or other wall finishes can be applied for a smooth, durable result.
Wall surfaces must be sound, flat, and properly prepared before tile adhesive can be applied and tiles installed, ensuring proper adhesion and a level surface.
Raw lumber must be selected and inspected for defects before any cutting and sizing can begin, as the quality and dimensions of the source material determine the cutting plan.
Cutting dimensions and the layout plan must be established before boards are cut, otherwise there would be no specification for length, width, or quantity.
Edges must be cut to final size before banding or finishing can be applied; applying banding to uncut boards would result in waste and misaligned edges.
Shelf boards must be cut to the correct size before they can be assembled into the shelf unit or installed in position.
Rough cut edges and surfaces must be sanded smooth after cutting to achieve the required finish quality; sanding cannot be done before cutting as material would be removed from areas later cut away.

Structural framing (walls, ceilings) and rough-in work (MEP rough-ins, electrical boxes, plumbing lines) must be completed before surface finishing, as these elements are enclosed behind finishes and cannot be accessed once surfaces are painted or finished.
Drywall must be installed, taped, and mudded, then sanded smooth before any painting or surface finishing can occur, as paint requires a smooth, prepared substrate.
Plaster or stucco application and curing must be complete prior to painting or finishing to ensure proper adhesion and avoid damage to uncured surfaces.

Painting and wall finishing should be completed before flooring installation to prevent paint drips, overspray, and debris from damaging finished floors, and to allow for easier edge work along baseboards.

Final trim (baseboards, door casings, crown molding) and hardware (door handles, light switch covers) should be installed after painting to avoid getting paint on these items and to ensure clean paint lines behind them.
The foundation must be fully constructed and cured before load capacity can be assessed, as the load assessment tests the bearing capacity of the foundation elements.
The structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) must be in place to perform load testing and assess the capacity of the structural system.
Concrete elements must reach sufficient design strength through proper curing before load testing can be safely conducted.
Load capacity assessment results must be reviewed and approved before the final structural inspection can certify the building's safety.
While interior fit-out can theoretically begin in parallel, it is preferred to complete load assessment first to ensure structural safety before adding finishes and non-structural elements.
The structural shell must be completed before shelving can be reconfigured, as the shelving systems need a stable, enclosed building structure for proper anchoring and layout.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-ins must be completed before installing or reconfiguring shelving to avoid interference with systems and to allow access for rough-in work without obstruction.

Flooring is typically installed before shelving to ensure a level surface and to avoid having to work around shelving, though this is a soft preference as shelving can be placed after flooring is finished.
Shelving must be fully installed, adjusted, and stable before merchandise can be stocked on shelves to ensure safety and proper product presentation.

Signage is typically placed after shelving is configured so that signs align with the final shelf layout, though this is a soft preference as signage could be installed concurrently or adjusted later.
The wall mounting plate requires a solid, level concrete slab to anchor to; the slab must be fully cured and prepared before the plate can be mounted.
Drainage around the foundation must be in place before mounting the wall plate to prevent water intrusion and ensure long-term stability of the connection.
Wall studs are typically anchored to or seated on the wall mounting plate; the plate must be in position to provide the base attachment point for the studs.
The wall mounting plate often serves as the bottom plate or sill plate; subsequent bottom plate components or the wall framing itself depends on it being installed first.
Wall sheathing is applied after the wall frame, including the mounting plate, is erected and secured; the plate provides the bottom support for the entire wall assembly.
The frame must be assembled first to provide the structural support into which the Shelf Upright / Side Panel is attached.
The Shelf Upright / Side Panel must be in place to serve as the mounting surface for shelf brackets.
Shelf boards rest on brackets attached to the uprights/side panels, so the uprights must be installed first.
Back panels are typically fastened to the side panels/uprights, requiring the uprights to be in position first.
The base panel provides a level foundation and reference surface for positioning the vertical uprights/side panels.
The shelf must be installed in place before its edge or lip can be applied, as the edging is attached to the front edge of the installed shelf.
The shelf must be cut to its final dimensions before the edge banding or lip can be applied, to ensure the edging fits precisely to the cut edge.

While surface finishing can technically be done before or after edging, it is often preferable to apply edging first so that any finishing coats cover both the shelf surface and the edge material for a uniform appearance.
Brackets can be installed before or after edging, but it is often easier to apply edging without brackets in the way, making edging first a soft preference.
The edging/lip must be applied and fully set before the final inspection can verify the edge condition and perform any touch-up work.
A hole must be pre-drilled to accommodate the fastener; the fastener cannot be inserted into solid material without a prepared hole.
Components to be joined must be correctly positioned and aligned before fasteners are installed to ensure proper fit and structural alignment.
Surfaces must be clean and free of debris to allow full engagement of the fastener threads or anchor expansion.
After the fastener is initially placed, it must be tightened to the required torque specification to achieve the designed clamping force.
Once the fastener is fixed, a structural or load check may be performed to verify that the connection meets design requirements.
Shelf installation requires a completed wall structure to attach shelves securely; shelves cannot be installed before the wall framing is in place.

Shelf installation typically requires finished wall surfaces (like drywall or plywood sheathing) to provide a proper mounting surface; raw framing is not a suitable surface for most shelf installations.
Electrical wiring and boxes must be installed before shelves are mounted, as shelves may obstruct access to walls where electrical work needs to be completed.
Once shelves are installed, they can be used for storage and organization of items; this is a logical sequence but not a strict physical constraint as items could be stored elsewhere temporarily.
Shelving must be fully installed to be included in the final inspection of the constructed space; inspection cannot be completed before shelf installation.

Wall framing must be installed and structurally complete before any surface preparation (such as drywall or plastering) can begin, as the framing provides the substrate to which wall surfaces are attached.
Electrical wiring, outlets, and switch boxes must be installed within the wall cavities before the wall surface is closed up, otherwise access would be lost requiring costly demolition.
Plumbing pipes and drain lines inside walls must be installed and pressure-tested before walls are enclosed, as they cannot be accessed after surface preparation is complete.
Ductwork and HVAC components within wall cavities must be installed before the wall surface is applied, as they become inaccessible once walls are closed.
Wall surfaces must be properly prepared (sanded, patched, and smoothed) before primer and paint can be applied, as paint will not adhere correctly to unprepared or uneven surfaces.
Wall surfaces must be clean, smooth, and properly prepared before wallpaper can be applied; any imperfections will show through or cause adhesion failure.
Wall surfaces must be prepared (e.g., cement backer board installed or drywall taped and floated) before tile can be set, ensuring a flat and stable substrate for tile adhesion.
Panels must be cut to their final dimensions before edge banding can be applied, as edge banding covers the exposed edges of the cut panels.
Panel surfaces and edges must be smoothed and prepared to ensure proper adhesion of the edge banding material.
Edge banding must be completed before assembly so that components have finished edges before being joined together, avoiding damage to the banding during assembly.
Typically edge banding is completed before drilling to avoid chipping or damaging the banding, though in some cases drilling can occur first if holes are hidden.
Edge banding must be applied and finished before any final coating or sealant is applied to the entire panel assembly.
The structural design must be approved to define the load-bearing capacity and parameters before calculating shelf loads.
The shelf layout and configuration must be determined to know the dimensions, spacing, and arrangement needed for accurate load calculations.
Material types (e.g., steel, wood, concrete) and their properties must be specified as they directly affect weight and load distribution calculations.
The calculated shelf loads are essential inputs for designing foundations that can support the weight and forces transmitted through the shelves.
Load calculations determine the required material grades, thicknesses, and reinforcements needed before shelves can be fabricated or ordered.
Countertops are installed on top of base cabinets; cabinets must be in place to support and properly align the countertop.
Plumbing rough-ins for sink supply and drain must be completed before the countertop is installed, as access to the wall and floor behind/under the countertop is needed.
Electrical wiring for under-cabinet lighting and outlets must be roughed in before countertop installation, as the countertop covers portions of the wall and access would be blocked.
The sink is mounted into or under the countertop opening; the countertop must be in place before the sink can be installed and sealed.
Backsplash tiles or panels are installed above and abutting the countertop; the countertop provides the bottom edge reference and must be complete first.
The seat back panel must be mounted onto a completed frame structure, so the frame assembly must be finished first.
Upholstery material (fabric or leather) is applied over the rigid seat back panel, so the panel must be in place before upholstery can be attached.
The back shell (plastic or composite cover) is fitted onto the rear of the seat back panel after the panel itself is installed.
Functional testing of the recline mechanism can be performed after the seat back panel is mounted, though it could partially be tested earlier; this is a logical sequencing preference.
The final quality inspection of the seat assembly must occur after all components including the seat back panel are installed.
The deck support structure (joists, beams, or framing) must be in place to provide a load-bearing surface for the decking material to be fastened to.
Seats must be mounted on top of or anchored through the completed decking platform; the platform provides the base surface for seat installation.
Railings are typically anchored to the deck platform or its framing; the decking must be in place to define the walking surface elevation and provide attachment points.
Waterproofing or sealant application is a soft preference; it can be done before or after, but typically applied after decking is laid to protect the surface.
The foundation or ground preparation must be completed to ensure a stable, level base that supports the seat platform structure without settling or shifting.
The back frame must be assembled and structurally complete to provide a mounting surface and support structure for attaching back cushions and bolsters.
The foam padding material for the back cushion must be cut, shaped, and prepared before it can be installed as part of the back cushion/bolster assembly.
The fabric or upholstery cover for the back cushion must be sewn and finished before it can be fitted over the foam and attached to the back structure.
The back cushion/bolster must be installed before final upholstery detailing, trim attachment, and finishing work on the back section can be completed.

Although quality checks can begin on other parts earlier, a comprehensive inspection of the back assembly is preferably done after the back cushion/bolster is installed to verify fit, comfort, alignment, and upholstery quality in one pass.
The seat frame provides the structural support and mounting points for the under-seat storage compartment, so the frame must be assembled first.
The under-seat storage compartment attaches to or sits within the floor mounting brackets, which must be installed beforehand to provide a secure base.
The seat cushion is installed on top of the under-seat storage compartment; the storage compartment must be in place to support the cushion above it.

While wiring can sometimes be routed before or during compartment installation, it is generally preferred to install the compartment first and then route wires around it to ensure proper fit and avoid pinching.
The storage compartment is a structural/substrate component that must be fully installed before finishing trim and upholstery pieces are added over or around it.
The hinged lid or access hatch requires a supporting frame or structure to be mounted onto. Without the frame installed, there is no structural interface to attach the hatch.
After the hatch is installed, the perimeter must be sealed to prevent water ingress and air leakage. Sealing cannot be completed before the hatch is in place.

Insulation around the hatch area is typically installed after the hatch is fitted to ensure proper fit and continuity of the thermal envelope, though in some cases insulation can be pre-installed if designed for it.

successor: Hinged Lid / Access Hatch Trim and Finish
rationale: Final trim, painting, or finishing of the hatch interior/exterior surfaces can only be performed after the hatch is fully installed and operational.
The rough opening must be framed and prepared to the correct dimensions before the hatch assembly can be placed and secured.
The nosing profile must be installed on top of the completed stair tread to form the finished edge; therefore the tread and riser structure must be in place first.
The nosing/seat edge detail is typically anchored into or adhered onto the prepared substrate, so the underlying surface must be ready.
Once the nosing is installed, sealants, caulking, and final finish coatings are applied over the nosing joint to ensure waterproofing and a clean appearance.
Handrails and guardrails often bear on or align with the nosing edge; the nosing must be in place to establish the finished edge location before railing posts are set.
The nosing detail is a visible safety edge; final quality checks and approvals are performed after the nosing and all adjacent finishes are completed.
Structural brackets/corbels are typically mounted on or anchored to structural columns to provide lateral support or load transfer points; the column must be in place to receive the bracket.
Corbels often project from concrete beams or slabs to support precast elements or other loads; the main structural element must be cast and cured before the corbel can be formed or attached.
Corbels and brackets frequently serve as bearing seats for precast beams or girders; the bracket must be in place to provide the support ledge before the beam can be set.
Brackets may support cladding attachment; while often sequenced after bracket installation, there may be workarounds such as alternative support systems, making this a soft preference.
Brackets/corbels often support mechanical units, piping, or cable trays; the support bracket must be in place before the equipment can be mounted on it.
The door and frame must be prepared (cut, sized, and positioned) before hinges can be attached, as hinges physically mount onto both the door and frame.
Mortises (recesses) must be cut into the door edge and frame to receive the hinge leaves; hinge installation cannot begin until the recesses are prepared.
The hinge must be fully installed (screwed into door and frame) before the door can be hung and aligned for proper swing and clearance.

While it is standard practice to install hinges before door knobs and locks for workflow efficiency, it is not a strict physical requirement; hardware could theoretically be pre-installed if carefully handled.
Final adjustments (e.g., hinge screw tightening, shimming) and swing testing can only occur after the hinge is fully installed and the door is mounted.
The cabinet box structure must be fully assembled to provide a stable mounting surface and attachment points for the lid stay and soft-close mechanism.
Hinges must be installed first to properly align the lid before the soft-close mechanism and lid stay can be attached and adjusted for correct operation.
After installing the lid stay and soft-close mechanism, the lid must be adjusted to ensure smooth opening and closing action with proper damping.
The soft-close and lid stay mechanism must be installed before functional testing can verify that the lid closes softly and stays open as intended.
Concrete foundations and slabs must be fully cured and complete before carpentry framing can begin, as carpentry is erected on the concrete substructure.
Load-bearing masonry walls must be constructed before roof carpentry and structural timber framing can be installed, as the masonry provides support for timber elements.
Steel columns, beams, and roof trusses must be erected before any timber infill, roof purlins, or joinery can be fixed to or fitted within the steel framework.
Roof carpentry (rafters, trusses, roof decking) must be completed before roof waterproofing membranes and roofing sheets can be installed.
Electrical conduits and back boxes are installed within timber stud walls and ceiling voids after carpentry framing is in place but before wall/ceiling finishes are applied.
The structural frame must be fully assembled to provide a stable base for attaching upholstery materials.
Support springs must be installed on the frame before padding and upholstery fabric can be applied over them.
Padding or foam layers must be placed over the springs/frame to create cushioning before the final upholstery fabric is installed.
Upholstery must be completed before a final quality check can assess the finished appearance, fit, and workmanship.

While some trim can be installed concurrently, final detailed trim work (e.g., nail heads, piping, decorative touches) is typically done after upholstery to avoid damage, though it is a soft preference as it can be done concurrently in some workflows.
Paint cannot be applied to unfinished drywall surfaces. Drywall must be installed, taped, mudded, and sanded smooth before any paint or wall finish can be applied.
Primer must be applied to bare drywall or substrate surfaces before the final paint coats to ensure proper adhesion, uniform absorption, and coverage.
Ceiling surfaces must be fully installed, finished, and often painted before wall painting is completed to avoid splatter and drips damaging finished walls.

Painting and finishing must be completed before flooring installation to prevent paint drips, spills, and overspray from damaging finished floors, and to allow for proper baseboard and trim installation over finished flooring.
Paint work must be complete before installing final trim, switch plates, outlet covers, door hardware, and other fixtures to avoid damaging paint and to allow for clean, professional finish lines.
The structural foundation must be fully constructed and cured before an engineer can assess and sign off on its integrity and load-bearing capacity.
The main structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) must be erected and cured to allow the engineer to inspect and verify structural stability before proceeding.
Steel structural elements must be fully erected, bolted/welded, and inspected prior to the engineer's sign-off on the overall structural system.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in cannot commence until the structure is signed off, ensuring that MEP installations proceed within a structurally approved and safe environment.
Interior partitions and finishes depend on the structural frame being certified, as changes or rectifications to the structure after finishing would be extremely costly and unsafe.

Skirting boards are installed on top of the finished floor level. If the floor is not leveled and screeded first, the skirting boards would not have a consistent base to align to, leading to gaps and improper fit.

Skirting boards are mounted against finished wall surfaces. Wall plastering and finishing must be completed beforehand to ensure the skirting boards have a smooth, stable surface to attach to and to achieve proper sealing.

Any electrical cables, conduits, or plumbing pipes that run beneath the floor or within the lower part of walls must be installed before skirting boards are fitted. Once skirting is installed, access to these services is restricted or requires removal of the skirting.

successor: Final Floor Covering Installation (e.g., tiles, hardwood, laminate)
rationale: In standard construction sequencing, skirting boards are installed after the subfloor preparation but before the final floor covering (if the skirting is to sit atop or against the finished flooring). However, depending on the method, some installations place skirting after final flooring; this ordering reflects the common approach where skirting goes up before the final floor finish to allow a clean edge.

Skirting boards are typically painted or finished as part of the overall decoration. Final painting can be done after installation, but it is a soft preference because painting can be performed before installation (pre-primed/pre-painted skirting) or after. Sequencing is often driven by workflow efficiency rather than a physical necessity.

The structural frame must be complete to provide the supporting framework for mounting electrical conduits, junction boxes, and light fixtures. Electrical fit-out cannot proceed without a finished structure to work within.

The building must be weatherproof (roof and external walls enclosed) before electrical fit-out begins, as electrical components, wiring, and fixtures are sensitive to moisture and must be installed in a dry interior environment.

HVAC ductwork and large mechanical services must be roughed-in first to avoid conflicts with electrical conduit runs and to establish spatial coordination, ensuring adequate clearance for both systems before electrical rough-in begins.

Electrical wiring, junction boxes, and light fixture supports must be installed and roughed-in within ceiling spaces before ceiling tiles or boards are installed, as access to above-ceiling services is required and would be blocked by finished ceilings.

Electrical cables, switch boxes, socket outlets, and back boxes must be installed within wall cavities before plasterboard/drywall is fixed, as the wall finish would conceal and permanently enclose these electrical elements.
Structural framing must be complete to provide mounting surfaces and support for lighting fixtures and integrated lighting systems.
Electrical rough-in including wiring, conduits, and junction boxes must be installed before integrated lighting fixtures can be connected and mounted.
Ceiling grid or finished ceiling must be in place as integrated lighting is typically mounted into or suspended from the ceiling system.
While lighting is often installed before final wall finishes for access, it's a soft preference as finishing can be done around lighting with careful protection.
Integrated lighting systems must be fully installed before system-level commissioning, dimming tests, sensor calibration, and integration testing with building management systems can occur.
The USB / Power Outlet must be mounted on or within wall structures; framing provides the structural support for electrical boxes and wiring.
Electrical cables and wiring must be run to the outlet location before the outlet device can be connected and installed.
The electrical junction box (receptacle box) must be mounted in the wall before the USB / Power Outlet device can be inserted and secured.

Typically, the outlet is wired and temporarily installed, then drywall is cut around it; however, in many sequences the box is installed before drywall and the outlet trim/faceplate is installed after drywall and painting are complete.
The outlet device must be fully connected and screwed into the electrical box before the decorative faceplate or cover can be attached.
The outlet must be installed and wired before it can be tested for correct voltage, polarity, and ground continuity to ensure safe operation.
The tunnel must be excavated before the crawl tunnel entry component can be installed, as the entry structure requires an existing tunnel opening to connect to.
The ground around the tunnel entrance must be stabilized to provide a secure foundation before installing the crawl tunnel entry structure.
Electrical conduits leading into the crawl tunnel must be installed after the entry point is established to ensure proper alignment and entry into the tunnel.
Lighting fixtures within the crawl tunnel should be installed after the entry is complete to allow safe access for electricians and to run wiring through the entry point.
Safety rails and fall protection around the crawl tunnel entry opening must be installed after the entry structure is in place, as they attach to the entry frame.
The ground must be excavated and prepared to create the necessary space and foundation for constructing the structural cave shell.
Foundations must be in place to support the structural cave shell's weight and load distribution.
The cave shell must be structurally complete before interior waterproofing and lining can be applied to protect against moisture and ground water.
Electrical, plumbing, and HVAC rough-in work requires the structural shell to be in place so that conduits, pipes, and ducts can be run through and embedded within the structure.
Interior finishes are applied after the structural shell is complete to ensure a stable substrate for wall and floor materials.
Child-safe latches need to be mounted onto cabinet doors and drawers, so the doors and drawers must be installed first.
Both child safety installations can be done independently, but it is convenient to complete latch installation before outlet covers to avoid interference.
Painting should be completed before installing hardware to avoid paint splatter on the latches and doors.
Flooring installation is typically done before cabinet hardware installation to avoid damage to new flooring from dropped tools or hardware.
All child-safety devices must be installed before the final safety inspection can verify they are properly placed and functional.
Wall framing provides the structural support and mounting surface required for attaching the Interactive Wall Panel.
Electrical wiring for power and data connections must be routed within the wall cavity before the panel is installed, as the panel will cover access to these rough-in connections.
A solid backer board or sheathing surface is needed behind the finished wall to provide a stable substrate for mounting the Interactive Wall Panel.
It is a soft preference to complete surface finishing before panel installation to avoid damaging the panel; however, if the panel is installed first, finishing work can be done carefully around it.
The Interactive Wall Panel must be physically installed before its touch sensors, displays, or interactive features can be calibrated, tested, and commissioned.
The bench or ledge must be built on top of a stable, level floor or foundation; the subfloor provides the necessary structural base.
If the bench or ledge is attached to or abuts a wall, the wall framing must be in place to provide structural support and mounting surface.

Any plumbing lines that will run within or beneath the bench (e.g., for a utility ledge or built-in seating with storage) must be roughed in before the bench is constructed, to avoid demolition later.
Any electrical wiring for outlets, lighting, or charging ports integrated into the bench/ledge must be roughed in before enclosing it with the bench structure.
Finish flooring or tile must be installed after the bench/ledge is built so that the flooring material can be cut and fitted tightly against the bench/ledge base for a clean, finished appearance.
Drywall and wall finishing should be completed after the bench is in place so that joints between the bench and wall can be properly taped, mudded, and finished.
Baseboard, crown molding, or decorative trim around the bench/ledge must be installed after the bench is built to create seamless transition details.
Final paint or stain on the bench and adjacent wall surfaces occurs after the bench and trim are fully installed to achieve a uniform finish without overspray or drips on unfinished surfaces.
The roof structure must be framed to provide the structural opening and support for installing the skylight or light well assembly.
Roof decking creates the continuous surface into which the skylight opening is cut and provides the substrate for flashing and curbing.
Underlayment must be installed around the skylight opening to ensure a continuous water barrier, as skylight flashing ties into this layer.
The skylight unit must be placed in the opening before the flashing and curb can be installed to seal and secure it to the roof.
The skylight shaft and interior trim around the light well must be completed before ceiling finishes are applied to integrate the light well opening with the finished ceiling.

A thorough geological and structural survey of the cave site is required to identify hazards, assess rock stability, and determine the optimal construction approach before any installation work begins.
Engineering drawings, structural calculations, and installation plans must be finalized to specify dimensions, reinforcement needs, and material placements before physical construction can commence.
All construction materials such as steel supports, concrete, lighting, flooring, and ventilation components must be procured and delivered to the site before installation can proceed.
Safety protocols, access scaffolding, fall protection systems, and emergency evacuation routes must be established before workers can safely enter and operate within the cave construction zone.

After the cave structure is constructed and installed, interior finishes such as wall cladding, flooring, electrical wiring, and aesthetic treatments can be applied without risk of damage from ongoing structural work.

Systems like lighting, ventilation, drainage, and climate control can only be commissioned and tested after the cave construction is complete to ensure they are installed within the finished structure.
The completed cave installation must undergo final structural and safety inspection and receive certification before it can be deemed ready for occupancy or use.
The building must be structurally complete and enclosed (roof, walls, floors) before any internal fitout works can commence, including soft play installation.

Electrical wiring, lighting, HVAC ducting, and plumbing rough-ins must be installed in the ceiling and walls before soft play structures are built, as they would otherwise be blocked or require costly retrofitting.
The subfloor must be leveled, cleaned, and prepared to receive safety matting and soft play equipment foundations.
Soft play equipment must be fully installed and secured before the final safety inspection and certification can be carried out to verify compliance with playground safety standards.
It is preferable but not strictly required to complete soft play installation before final painting and wall finishes, as the equipment could be protected and walls painted around it if needed.
The structural frame and core must be in place before fire safety assessments can be conducted, as egress paths and fire compartmentation depend on the building's permanent structural layout.
Fire dampers, smoke control systems, and fire alarm rough-ins must be installed prior to assessment to verify their functionality and compliance with fire safety codes.
Fire-rated walls, corridors, and partition layouts define egress paths and compartment boundaries, and must be built before a meaningful egress assessment can be performed.

successor: Fire Stopping & Passive Fire Protection Installation
rationale: The assessment identifies gaps and deficiencies that require fire stopping; corrective fire stopping work follows the assessment results.
The fire safety and egress assessment is a prerequisite for final regulatory inspection and issuance of a certificate of occupancy, confirming the building meets life safety requirements.
Sprinkler heads are typically mounted into or through ceiling grids. The ceiling grid provides the structural support and alignment reference for positioning the sprinkler head.

predecessor: Overhead Piping and Supply Line Rough-In
rationale: The sprinkler head must be connected to the fire suppression water supply pipes. The overhead branch lines and drops need to be installed first so the sprinkler head can be attached to the piping system.

Sprinkler heads project through the finished ceiling plane. Installing ceiling tiles or finish panels after the sprinkler head allows proper cutting, fitting, and alignment of the head relative to the finished surface.

successor: Fire Suppression System Pressure Testing and Inspection
rationale: The sprinkler head is the terminal device of the fire suppression system. The full system, including all connected heads, must be pressure tested and inspected to verify functionality and code compliance before the system is placed into service.

It is preferable to install sprinkler heads before final painting and finishing so that any minor touch-up around the escutcheon plate can be done seamlessly, though this is a soft preference to avoid rework rather than a hard constraint.
The wall framing must be completed to create the rough opening and structure that will house the concealed door.
Any electrical wiring, switches, or plumbing that will pass through or near the door cavity must be roughed in before the concealed door is installed to avoid interference.
The concealed door must be installed before the surrounding drywall is hung and finished so that the door can be properly integrated and taped/mudded to achieve a seamless hidden finish.
Any trim or casing around the concealed door must be installed after the door is in place to ensure proper alignment and seamless blending with the wall surface.
Painting and final wall finishing must occur after the concealed door is installed so the door and surrounding wall can be painted uniformly for a concealed appearance.
The secret compartment is built within the wall cavity, so the wall framing must be constructed first to provide the structural enclosure and space for the compartment.
The outer layer of drywall must be installed before the secret compartment framing so the compartment can be recessed into the wall properly.
The concealment features (e.g., hidden hinges, magnetic catches, false panels) can only be installed after the compartment structure is complete to ensure proper fit and alignment.
Interior painting, shelving, or lining of the secret compartment must happen after the compartment box/frame is built, as the finishing materials are applied to the final structure.
The final concealing layer of drywall or trim that hides the compartment entrance can only be applied after the compartment and its door mechanism are fully installed and operational.
The false wall structure requires a supporting frame (typically metal studs) to be installed first, as the false wall is built onto this framework.
Electrical wiring, outlets, and switches that will be inside or pass through the false wall must be roughed in before the wall is enclosed and finished.
Any plumbing pipes running within or behind the false wall must be installed before the wall is closed up to avoid costly rework.
HVAC ducts that pass through the false wall cavity must be installed before the wall is built to ensure proper routing and accessibility.
The false wall frame must be fully constructed and secured before drywall sheets can be attached to its surface.
The trap door frame or surrounding structure must be installed first to provide the mounting surface and structural support for the trap door assembly.
The floor area around the trap door must be fully decked to establish the correct elevation and opening dimensions before the trap door can be fitted.
The trap door must be installed before surrounding floor finishes (tile, carpet, etc.) are applied so that finishes can be properly terminated at the door edge.
Safety guardrails around the trap door opening must be installed after the trap door is in place to ensure proper alignment and fall protection.
Functional testing of the trap door's hinges, latch, and opening mechanism can only be performed after the door is physically installed.
The bookcase door must be attached to a fully assembled frame that provides the structural support and hinge mounting points.
The door component must be fully constructed, trimmed, and prepared before it can be installed onto the frame.
Hinges, handles, and latch mechanisms must be mounted after the door is positioned on the frame to ensure proper alignment and function.
Final painting, staining, or sealing should be done after installation to ensure uniform coverage and to address any touch-ups needed from handling during installation.

While shelves can typically be installed before or after the door, installing shelves after the door is in place allows for easier adjustment and ensures that the door clears the shelves properly without obstruction.
The hidden staircase must be installed within the structural frame of the house; the frame provides the load-bearing support and enclosure needed for the staircase.

successor: Finish flooring and interior wall coverings
rationale: The staircase must be in place before finishing work such as flooring and drywall, so that the finishes can be fitted around and up to the staircase properly.
The staircase needs a stable, level base; the foundation slab provides the structural floor from which the staircase can be built or anchored.
Handrails and safety elements must be installed after the staircase structure is in place to ensure proper alignment and secure attachment.

predecessor: Design and procure hidden staircase components
rationale: All custom staircase components (treads, risers, hinges, mechanism) must be designed, manufactured, and delivered before installation can begin.
The electromagnetic lock is typically mounted on the door frame and strike plate; the frame must be installed first to provide a mounting surface.
Electromagnetic locks require power and control wiring to the door frame; electrical rough-in (conduit, wiring, junction boxes) must be completed before the lock can be connected and energized.
For sliding or overhead doors with electromagnetic locks, the track or header system must be in place so the lock components can be aligned properly.
The electromagnetic lock must be physically installed and wired before the access control system can be programmed, tested, and calibrated for that specific lock.
Safety testing (e.g., confirming the lock releases on fire alarm, panic exit, or power loss) can only be performed after the lock is fully installed and powered.

Plumbing pipes, electrical conduits, and wiring must be installed within walls, floors, and ceilings before these spaces can be enclosed or concealed. Once concealed spaces are built, accessing these rough-ins would require demolition.
Structural framing (stud walls, floor joists, roof trusses) defines the concealed spaces (wall cavities, ceiling plenums, etc.) and must be erected before any enclosure or concealment can occur.

Heating, ventilation, and air conditioning ducts are typically routed through ceilings, attics, and mechanical chases that become concealed spaces. Ducts must be installed and tested before concealment to allow for leak checks and repairs.

Thermal and acoustic insulation is placed within wall cavities and ceiling spaces before they are closed up. Installing insulation after concealment is impossible without removal of finished surfaces.

Fire-resistive seals, fire blocking, and applied fireproofing materials must be completed in concealed plenums and vertical shafts before these spaces are permanently enclosed, as required by building code and fire safety regulations.
False walls are typically built on top of finished floor slabs. The floor slab provides the structural base and load-bearing surface needed to support the false wall framework.

Primary structural elements (load-bearing walls and columns) must be in place before false walls can be installed, as false walls are non-structural partitions that fit between or around structural elements.

Electrical wiring that needs to run within or behind the false wall cavity must be installed before the false wall framing is closed up, otherwise retrofitting would require demolition or surface-mounted conduits.
The false wall must be fully installed (framing and board fixed in place) before plastering, skim coating, or other surface finishes can be applied to the wall.
Electrical outlets and switches mounted in the false wall require the wall structure to be in place so that back boxes can be fixed and devices installed into the finished wall surface.
The door frame must be installed and set in place before the concealed door can be fitted into it, as the door hangs on the frame.

predecessor: Wall Framing and Drywall Rough Opening
rationale: The wall structure and rough opening must be complete to provide the cavity and support for a concealed (flush or hidden) door installation.
The concealed door must be fitted and adjusted before final wall finishing so that the door can be made perfectly flush with the finished wall surface, allowing seamless blending.

successor: Floor Finishing (if door is floor-mounted or bottom track required)
rationale: In some concealed door systems with bottom tracks or floor guides, the door fitting should precede floor finishing to allow proper alignment, though this can be sequenced differently depending on the system.
The concealed door must be hung and operational before hardware such as handles or locks can be installed on the door leaf.

Soundproofing materials (e.g., insulation batts, acoustic membranes) are installed within wall, floor, or ceiling cavities. The structural framing must be complete to provide the cavities and support surface for the soundproofing.

Any wiring, conduit, pipes, or boxes that will run inside walls must be in place before soundproofing is installed, since the soundproofing will cover or be placed around these services. Retrofitting after soundproofing would require removal and reinstallation, compromising acoustic performance.
Ductwork and ventilation runs within walls or ceilings must be completed prior to soundproofing to ensure acoustic sealing around penetrations and to avoid disturbing the soundproofing later.

Soundproofing materials (acoustic batts, mass-loaded vinyl, resilient channels) must be fully installed before being enclosed by drywall or other finishes. Drywall directly covers and protects the soundproofing, and the assembly's acoustic performance depends on the correct layering order.

After soundproofing is in place, all edges, joints, and penetrations must be sealed with acoustic caulk or tape to achieve the required sound transmission class (STC) rating. This sealing is part of the finishing process that follows installation of the base soundproofing materials.
Electrical power and cabling infrastructure must be in place before security system components can be installed and connected.
Security systems rely on network connectivity for communication with control panels and monitoring stations; network cabling and switches must be installed first.
Conduits and backboxes for security sensors, cameras, and control panels must be embedded in walls/ceilings prior to pulling cables and mounting devices.
All security components must be integrated and wired before the full system can be powered on, configured, programmed, and tested for functionality.

Although security devices can be installed before final finishes, it is preferable to complete integration first to avoid damaging finishes during cable runs and mounting; however, this is a soft preference, not a physical necessity.
Transfer trusses are typically supported on columns, so columns must be installed first to provide vertical support.
Foundations must be completed to support the columns that in turn support the transfer truss.
Transfer trusses often support roof or floor structures above; the truss must be in place before decking can be installed on top.
Permanent bracing between trusses can only be installed after the transfer truss is erected to ensure stability of the structural frame.

While transfer trusses are often part of the steel erection sequence, some general steel framing may need to be in place to provide stability; however this is a soft preference as the truss may be erected early depending on the erection plan.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated before pilotis (elevated columns/pillars) can be installed, as the pilotis require a stable and prepared foundation bed.

Concrete footings or foundation pads must be cast and cured beneath each piloti location to transfer the structural loads to the ground; pilotis cannot be erected without these load-bearing foundations in place.

The pilotis columns must be completed and have achieved sufficient strength before the ground floor slab or deck can be poured or placed on top of them, as the slab rests on or is supported by the pilotis.
The raised pilotis serve as the vertical structural support for all upper floors; the upper columns, beams, and slabs cannot start until the pilotis are erected and stabilized.

While it is possible to run some utilities concurrently or after, it is more efficient and standard practice to rough-in underground and under-slab utilities once the pilotis are in place and the area beneath is accessible, but this is a sequencing preference rather than a strict physical necessity.
The steel beams and columns that will be joined by the moment-resisting connection must be fabricated, cut, and prepared to the specified dimensions before the connection can be assembled on site.
Vertical columns and support members must be erected and securely positioned before moment connections can be made between beams and columns.
All steel sections, bolts, plates, and welding equipment must be delivered to the site and the work area prepared before connection work can commence.

After the moment-resisting connection is assembled (beams positioned and bolted/tacked), the welded joints and high-strength bolt tightening must be inspected and tested to verify structural integrity.
Once moment connections are complete, the frame gains its lateral stability; permanent bracing, diaphragm connections, or concrete deck placement can then proceed, relying on the rigid frame action.

The architectural design must be completed and approved to define the physical boundaries, structural elements, and spatial layout that will house the social spaces. Social Space Programming requires this baseline to allocate functions appropriately.

The building's structural frame and envelope must be in place to create the physical volume where social spaces will be located. Programming these spaces before structure is built risks mismatches with actual dimensions and load-bearing constraints.

Basic MEP rough-in must be completed before programming social spaces because utility routing (HVAC ducts, power conduits, plumbing lines) dictates ceiling heights, wall placements, and service zones that directly impact social space design.

Interior finishes (flooring, wall cladding, ceiling systems) must follow social space programming because the programming defines the functional zones, furniture layouts, and circulation patterns that dictate where specific finishes are applied.

FF&E installation depends on the completed social space programming to determine what furniture types, quantities, and configurations are needed for each programmed area such as lounges, breakout zones, or collaborative hubs.
A preliminary design or concept must exist before its structural feasibility can be assessed; there is no structure to evaluate otherwise.
Soil conditions, bearing capacities, and site constraints are essential inputs to determine whether a proposed structural design is feasible.
The feasibility assessment must confirm that the proposed structure can be built before investing effort in detailed engineering and design.
Foundation design depends on the feasibility assessment conclusions regarding load paths, soil-structure interaction, and whether the structure is viable.
Material procurement should only proceed after the feasibility assessment confirms the structural concept is viable and specific material requirements are known.

A clear project brief outlining client requirements, budget, and scope must be developed before integrated design workshops can commence, as the workshops require this foundational information to guide multidisciplinary collaboration.
Site conditions, constraints, and opportunities must be documented and analyzed prior to integrated design workshops so that all design team members can work from the same site context information.

Key design consultants (architect, structural engineer, MEP engineer, etc.) must be formally appointed before integrated design workshops can be held, as these workshops require the full multidisciplinary team to collaborate effectively.
The collaborative decisions, design concepts, and integrated strategies developed during the workshops form the basis for schematic design documentation and further detailed development.

The outcomes and agreed-upon design directions from integrated design workshops establish the framework for subsequent design coordination meetings where specific system interfaces and details are resolved.

The structural design must be established to define the load-bearing elements, connections, and structural system before any load path analysis can be performed. Without a structural design, there are no elements to analyze for load transfer.
The architectural design defines the building geometry, massing, and spatial layout which determines how loads are distributed and collected before they enter the structural system.
Material properties (strength, stiffness, density) directly influence load transfer mechanisms and must be known to accurately model load paths through the structure.
The results of load path analysis determine the magnitude and direction of forces in each structural member, which is essential for correctly sizing beams, columns, slabs, and foundations.
Load path analysis traces forces from their point of application down to the ground; the resulting reaction forces and moments at the base are required inputs for designing foundations.
A stable and level foundation must be prepared before the transfer structure can be installed, as it provides the necessary base and load-bearing support.
Excavation must be completed to create the proper space and subgrade for the transfer structure's foundation and installation.
Reinforcement steel must be placed and tied within the foundation prior to installing the transfer structure to ensure structural integrity and load transfer.
The transfer structure must be installed first as it serves as the load-distributing element that supports the superstructure above.

successor: Column/Shear Wall Construction Above Transfer Level
rationale: Vertical structural elements above the transfer level cannot be constructed until the transfer structure is in place to distribute loads from above to the foundation below.
Complex formwork often requires the structural steel frame to be in place to provide support and attachment points for formwork systems, especially for geometry that integrates with steel elements.
Reinforcement bars must be placed before formwork is erected around them, as the formwork encloses the rebar cage and defines the concrete shape.
The formwork must be fully assembled, aligned, and secured before concrete can be poured into it to achieve the intended complex shape.
A quality and dimensional check is typically performed after formwork erection and before pouring, but is a procedural preference rather than a physical necessity.
Scaffolding and safe access platforms must be erected first to allow workers to safely assemble complex formwork at height or in difficult positions.

The building must be completed, handed over to the owner/occupant, and officially closed out before any post-occupancy evaluation can take place, as the evaluation assesses the building's performance during actual use.
Building systems (HVAC, lighting, security, etc.) must be fully commissioned and operational to allow meaningful evaluation of occupant comfort, energy performance, and functional space usage.
The space must be occupied by its intended users for a sufficient period to gather data on how the space actually performs, user satisfaction, and functional effectiveness.

Although not a strict physical dependency, findings from the evaluation often inform adjustments to building systems (retro-commissioning) to improve comfort and efficiency, making this a recommended subsequent activity.

successor: Lessons Learned Documentation / Feedback for Future Projects
rationale: The evaluation results provide valuable insights that should be documented and fed back into the design and construction process for future projects, but this is a knowledge-management preference rather than a physical construction constraint.
