The floor plate requires a stable and level base; the foundation or slab on grade must be completed to provide structural support and a working surface for floor plate construction.

Vertical columns or core walls that penetrate the floor plate must be erected first so that the floor slab can be cast or placed around and connected to these structural elements for load transfer and lateral stability.
Underground or in-slab plumbing, electrical conduits, and other utilities must be laid and inspected before the floor slab is poured to avoid costly cutting and rework of the finished floor.
Interior walls are built on top of the finished floor slab; the floor plate must be complete to provide the base surface for wall layout, anchoring, and vertical framing.

While mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in can begin once the floor is in place to support equipment and lay out overhead runs, some prefabrication can occur earlier; however, final installation of ceiling-mounted services is typically sequenced after the floor plate is structurally complete.
Structural design depends on soil bearing capacity, foundation type, and site-specific geotechnical data; without geotechnical survey results, structural loads cannot be accurately calculated.
The structural engineer needs the architectural layout, column grids, floor plans, and spatial program to develop the structural framing system that supports the architecture.
Steel fabrication requires approved structural drawings, member sizes, connection details, and shop drawings derived from the completed structural design.
Foundation dimensions, reinforcement, and depth are determined by structural design calculations; foundation work cannot proceed without finalized structural engineering drawings.
The erection of columns, beams, slabs, and lateral load-resisting systems requires complete structural design drawings, member schedules, and connection specifications.
Structural analysis requires data on the completed foundation system (dimensions, material properties, load paths) to verify that the foundation can safely support the superstructure loads.

Site preparation and excavation must be completed to establish the ground conditions and subgrade that inform the structural analysis model, including soil bearing capacity and foundation depth assumptions.
Actual material properties (concrete compressive strength, steel yield strength) obtained from testing are needed as input parameters for accurate structural analysis calculations.
The architectural design must be finalized to define the building geometry, loading conditions, and spatial constraints that the structural analysis will evaluate.
The results of structural analysis (forces, moments, shear, deflections) are required inputs to perform detailed member sizing, reinforcement design, and connection detailing.
Reinforcement bar sizes, spacing, and placement configurations determined through structural analysis must be finalized before rebar fabrication and installation can proceed.
Formwork design depends on member dimensions and loading requirements that are confirmed only after structural analysis is complete.
Concrete pouring can only commence after structural analysis has verified that the structural elements will perform safely under expected loads.
The overall structural design and load analysis must be completed first to identify the load paths that need optimisation.
Material properties influence load distribution; material selection must be known before optimising load paths.
Foundation design determines load transfer to the ground; load path optimisation depends on how loads are transmitted through the foundation system.
After load paths are optimised, individual structural members can be precisely sized based on the optimised load distribution.
Connection details depend on the optimised load paths to ensure joints can handle the redistributed forces.
Accurate material quantities are required to calculate embodied carbon emissions from construction materials.
BIM models provide the geometric and material data needed for embodied carbon calculations.
Structural design determines the type and amount of structural materials (concrete, steel, etc.), which significantly impact embodied carbon.
Embodied carbon assessment informs low-carbon material selection and procurement decisions.
Embodied carbon results are typically required inputs for sustainability certifications like LEED or BREEAM, though timing can sometimes overlap.
Material specifications depend on finalized design details to determine exact material types, quantities, and performance requirements.
The overall project schedule and milestones must be established before material scheduling can align procurement with construction phases.
Materials must be specified and scheduled before purchase orders can be issued to suppliers.
Delivery schedules and logistics coordination can only be planned once material specifications and procurement timelines are finalized.
Materials must be identified and procured before their lifecycle can be analyzed, as the LCA requires specific data on material types, sources, and supply chains.
The materials to be used in the project must be selected during preliminary design before a lifecycle assessment can be performed on them.

LCA results can inform material choices in detailed design, but detailed design can sometimes proceed in parallel if material decisions are already locked; this is a soft preference to allow sustainability optimization.
LCA data is a fundamental input for sustainability certifications (e.g., LEED, BREEAM) and environmental reporting, which cannot be completed without the lifecycle analysis results.
LCA insights on material end-of-life can inform waste management strategies, but basic waste planning can start earlier; using LCA results improves waste reduction targets.
The project must be initiated and planned before procurement can begin, as procurement activities are based on project requirements, budgets, and schedules established during planning.

An organizational sustainability policy with procurement criteria must be established before sustainable procurement can be implemented, as it defines the environmental and social standards to be applied.
Potential suppliers must be evaluated for their sustainability credentials, certifications, and compliance before procurement orders can be placed, ensuring only qualified vendors are engaged.
Sustainable procurement must be completed to arrange for the purchase and contracting of materials before those materials can be delivered to the construction site.
Procurement of sustainable materials and products must be completed so that the required resources are available on-site before construction activities can commence.
Materials must be procured and delivered to the site before they can be sampled and tested for certification.
Raw materials must first be extracted or manufactured before representative samples can be taken for quality testing and certification.
Materials can only be formally accepted and stored for use after they have been tested and certified as meeting specifications.
Concrete mix designs and reinforcement materials must be tested and certified before placement in structural elements to ensure strength and durability.
Structural steel must be certified (mill certificates, weld testing) before it can be erected to guarantee load-bearing capacity and compliance with design specifications.

A feasibility study and project initiation must be completed first to determine if deconstruction is viable and to establish project goals, budget, and scope before detailed deconstruction planning can begin.
A thorough structural survey and condition assessment of the existing building is required to understand what can be safely disassembled and how, informing the deconstruction plan.

Identification and preliminary planning for removal of hazardous materials (asbestos, lead, etc.) must be done before detailed deconstruction planning, as these materials require special handling and sequencing.
The deconstruction plan must be fully developed and approved before any physical deconstruction work can commence to ensure safe, efficient, and orderly disassembly.
Material salvage and sorting workflows are defined within the deconstruction plan; therefore, the planning phase must be complete to direct how materials are to be recovered, sorted, and routed.
Material Passport Creation requires detailed design specifications, including material types, quantities, and sources, which are defined during the design phase.
The actual materials to be used must be identified, sourced, and their specifications confirmed before a Material Passport can document them accurately.
A Building Information Model provides the structured data about building components and materials needed to populate a Material Passport.
The Material Passport must be finalized to guide material selection, tracking, and circularity targets during actual construction activities.
A completed Material Passport informs end-of-life material recovery, recyclability, and waste management strategies for the building.
Overall project planning and design must be completed first to define the scope, materials, and construction methods, which are necessary inputs for effective waste minimisation planning.
Understanding what materials will be procured and their quantities is essential to plan for waste reduction, reuse, and recycling strategies.
The waste minimisation plan must be developed first to guide the actual on-site implementation of waste sorting, reduction, and disposal activities.
Construction activities should not begin until waste minimisation strategies are planned to ensure proper segregation, material handling, and waste reduction measures are in place from the start.
The waste minimisation plan establishes targets and procedures; waste auditing and monitoring are performed afterwards to measure compliance and effectiveness against the plan.

The materials and products to be verified must first be selected and sourced before their environmental product declarations or green labels can be verified, as EPD verification requires specific product data and material composition information.

An Environmental Product Declaration (EPD) is based on a Life Cycle Assessment study; the LCA must be completed to provide the data that will be verified and certified in the EPD verification process.
The actual production process must occur to collect real manufacturing data, energy consumption, and emissions data that will be verified in the EPD or green label certification.

Buyers and contractors can only procure materials with certified green labels or verified EPDs after the verification process is complete, ensuring that purchased products meet the sustainability claims.

Green building certification submissions (e.g., LEED, BREEAM, Green Mark) require verified EPDs and green labels as supporting evidence; verification must be completed before these documents can be submitted for project-level certification.

The building's foundation must be in place before structural analysis can be performed, as the foundation supports the entire structure and its stiffness characteristics directly affect the overall structural behavior.
Material properties (e.g., Young's modulus of concrete/steel) must be known from testing before accurate structural analysis and stiffness tuning can be conducted.
The main structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) must be erected so that the actual as-built structural system exists to be analyzed and tuned for stiffness.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) routing must follow the finalized structural layout and stiffness-tuned elements to avoid conflicts with structural members and ensure load paths are respected.

The building envelope (cladding/facade) is attached to the primary structure; thus, the structure must be analyzed and stiffness-tuned first to ensure it can support facade loads without excessive deflection.
Lateral load testing is performed on piles to determine their lateral capacity. The piles must first be installed before they can be tested.
The reinforcement cage is part of the pile structural element; it must be placed before testing the lateral response of the completed pile.
The concrete for the pile must be poured and cured to sufficient strength before any load testing can be safely and meaningfully performed.
Load testing results may influence pile cap design or certify pile capacity; pile cap construction typically proceeds after test verification and acceptance.
Formal acceptance of pile lateral capacity is based on test results, so testing must be completed before the pile can be signed off as acceptable.
Formwork provides the mold into which concrete is poured; without proper formwork installation, the concrete cannot be contained and shaped.
Reinforcement steel must be in place within the formwork before concrete is poured to ensure structural integrity.
All embedded items (electrical conduits, plumbing sleeves, anchor bolts) must be positioned and secured before concrete is poured, as they cannot be placed afterward.
A formal inspection by the engineer or quality control team is required to verify formwork, rebar, and embeds are correct before any concrete is placed.
After pouring, concrete must undergo a controlled curing period to achieve required strength and durability before any further construction loads are applied.
Formwork cannot be removed until the poured concrete has gained sufficient strength to support its own weight and any imposed loads.

Surface finishing (troweling, brooming) typically follows immediately after pouring while concrete is still plastic, but it is a soft preference as some finishing can be delayed or omitted depending on spec.
Soil properties, site class, and seismic hazard parameters must be known to determine design ground motions and foundation response for performance-based seismic design.
A preliminary structural system (lateral force-resisting system, framing type) must be established before detailed performance-based design can evaluate its seismic response.

successor: Detailed Structural Analysis (Nonlinear Response History Analysis)
rationale: Performance objectives and target drift/strain limits defined in design must be verified through detailed nonlinear analysis.
The design outcomes (member sizes, reinforcement, connections, ductility detailing) from performance-based design must be fully documented before construction can proceed.
Although often mandatory for PBD, a peer review can technically begin after design is substantially complete; however, it is a soft constraint as minor redesign iterations may occur during review.
The structural frame must be erected to create the building floors and columns whose relative lateral displacements (drift) are to be measured.
The foundation must be completed to provide a stable base for the structure; drift measurements relative to the ground require a fixed reference point.

predecessor: Installation of Lateral Load-Resisting System (Shear Walls/Bracing)
rationale: The lateral force-resisting system must be in place to generate meaningful inter-story drift under load; drift monitoring assesses the performance of these elements.

successor: Structural Load Testing and Performance Verification
rationale: Drift monitoring data must be collected first to verify that the structure meets design drift limits before formal load testing and sign-off can proceed.

It is preferable to complete drift monitoring before installing cladding, as the cladding can mask structural movements and make sensor access difficult; however, cladding can be partially installed if access for sensors is maintained.

A soft story is typically a story (floor level) in a building that has significantly less stiffness or strength than the stories above or below it. In construction, the foundation and lower structural elements must be built first before any upper floor structure, including a soft story, can be erected.

The structural frame of the building must be in place to define the vertical load path and lateral force-resisting system before a soft story condition can be recognized or constructed as a specific floor level.

Interior finishes (drywall, flooring, ceilings) cannot be installed until the soft story structural elements, including any required seismic retrofitting or lateral bracing, are complete to avoid rework and ensure structural integrity.
The building enclosure and exterior cladding for that level must wait until the soft story structural elements are fully erected and stabilized to provide a sound substrate for attachment.

Viscous fluid dampers are typically installed between structural steel members (such as beams and columns) to provide seismic energy dissipation. The steel frame must be in place to provide the anchorage points and structural support for the dampers.
Viscous dampers require bolted or pinned connections to structural steel. Anchor bolts and base plates must be set and grouted to ensure that connection brackets have a solid load-bearing surface.

The damper unit itself must be positioned first so that its end brackets can be accurately aligned, welded, or bolted to the steel structure to achieve the precise geometry required for proper damper operation.

After dampers are installed, load testing and commissioning verify that damper stroke, force output, and seal integrity meet specifications. This is a quality-assurance preference rather than a physical necessity.

Once dampers are installed and tested, architectural elements such as fireproofing, drywall, or cladding can close in the structure. This sequencing avoids damaging finished surfaces during damper placement and is a preference for workflow efficiency.
A ridge is a raised elongated landform or structural component that requires a stable foundation or base before it can be constructed.
In construction, a ridge (ridge beam or ridge board) is the peak of a roof structure, so roofing installation depends on the ridge being in place first.
Roofing tiles or slates are laid from the ridge down, so the ridge must be completed first to establish the top edge and allow proper overlapping and weatherproofing.
The ridge beam or ridge board in a roof structure typically rests on and is supported by the top plates of the wall framing, so wall framing must be completed before the ridge can be installed.

Ridge vents are typically installed after the ridge is formed, but this could be considered part of the same phase and may be done concurrently in some designs, hence a soft preference rather than a hard constraint.
The gable is part of the roof structure and sits atop the wall framing. Walls and roof framing must be erected first to provide the structural support base for the gable.
The gable defines the shape and edge of the roof slope; roof sheathing boards are installed after the gable is in place to attach to the rafters and gable end.
Soffit and fascia trim are installed along the eaves and gable ends after the gable structure is complete to provide finishing and weatherproofing.
The exterior siding on the gable end wall cannot be applied until the gable frame is fully constructed and sheathed.
Wall framing must be completed to provide the vertical support structure onto which the roof pitch is built.
Trusses or rafters define the roof pitch angle and must be installed before the roof pitch can be established.
The roof pitch must be framed and set before sheathing panels can be applied over the rafters/trusses.
Roof underlayment (felt or synthetic) is applied directly over the sheathed roof deck, which requires the roof pitch structure to be complete.
Final roofing materials (shingles, tiles, metal panels) can only be installed after the roof pitch framing and sheathing are in place.
Walls must be completed to provide vertical support for the roof structure.
Roof sheathing is laid on top of the roof span/trusses, so the spanning structure must be in place first.
Ceiling finishes are attached to or hung from the roof structure, requiring the roof span to be complete.
Gutters and drainage systems are mounted to the roof edge/fascia, which requires the roof span to be in place.
The foundation and supporting walls must be fully cured and load-bearing before the roof can be installed.
Wall framing must be complete to provide structural support and a mounting surface for the roof overhang.
Roof sheathing provides the underlying structural deck that the overhang framing attaches to and extends from.
The roof overhang structure must be in place before waterproof underlayment can be applied over it to ensure continuity of the weather barrier.
Soffit materials are attached directly to the underside of the roof overhang, so the overhang frame must be complete first.
Fascia boards and gutters are mounted to the edge of the roof overhang, requiring the overhang to be fully constructed first.
The rooflight kerb requires a prepared structural opening in the roof to be mounted onto; the opening must be cut and reinforced before the kerb can be installed.
The kerb forms the raised upstand and supporting frame; the glazing or dome unit is then fitted onto or into the completed kerb.
The kerb must be in place so that the roof waterproofing membrane can be dressed up the sides of the kerb and flashings installed to seal the penetration.

While the kerb does not strictly require ceiling finishes to be completed, it is preferable to complete the kerb installation before finishing the ceiling lining around the rooflight opening to allow proper detailing and trimming.
The roof structure and decking must be substantially complete to provide the base and support for the rooflight kerb installation.

predecessor: Roof Deck Slab Casting / Concrete Works
rationale: The roof deck slab must be cast and cured to provide a structurally sound and stable substrate before waterproofing can be applied.
Proper screeding ensures correct drainage slopes and a smooth surface, which is essential for effective adhesion and performance of waterproofing membranes.
Parapet walls must be built to allow waterproofing to be turned up and sealed at the wall-roof junction, preventing water ingress at edges.
Waterproofing membrane must be fully installed and tested before placing thermal insulation or protective screed on top to avoid damage and ensure watertight integrity.

successor: Roof Tiling / Floor Finishing (if accessible roof)
rationale: Final roof finishes (tiles, pavers, or wearing surface) must be laid over the waterproofing system only after it is fully cured and leak-tested.
The roof structure (trusses, rafters, decking) must be in place and structurally complete to provide a substrate for roof tiling and slating to be installed upon.
A waterproof underlayment (roofing felt or synthetic membrane) must be laid over the roof deck before tiles or slates are installed to provide a secondary weatherproof barrier.
Gutters and downpipes are typically installed after the roof covering is completed so they can be properly aligned with the roof edge and integrate with the finished roof system.

Running electrical cables and installing fixtures in the attic is safer and more convenient after the roof is weathertight to protect workers and materials from weather exposure, though it is not a strict physical dependency.
Interior ceiling work (plasterboard, plastering) must occur after the roof is fully tiled and watertight to prevent water damage to interior finishes from potential leaks during roof installation.
The structural frame (columns, shear walls, and core) must be completed to provide vertical support for roof framing.
A concrete roof deck or metal deck must be in place to serve as the working platform and base for roof framing components.
Roof sheathing, panels, or cladding materials are applied directly onto the roof framing structure and cannot be installed before the framing is erected.
Insulation and waterproofing membranes are installed over the completed roof deck/framing system to protect the building envelope.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work on the uppermost floors often depends on the roof structure being in place to support overhead distribution and vertical risers.
Safe access to the roof requires scaffolding or other access equipment to be erected before any roof inspection can take place.
The roof structure must be fully erected and stable before a comprehensive roof inspection can be performed to assess its condition and integrity.
The roof deck (sheathing/boarding) must be in place as the surface to be inspected and surveyed for compliance and condition.
Inspection and survey results determine the condition of the roof deck and inform the type and method of waterproofing or covering to be applied.
Any defects, damages, or structural issues identified during inspection must be addressed and repaired before subsequent layers are installed; the inspection triggers necessary repairs.

The floor slab must be supported on stable foundation elements (footings or foundation walls). Without a completed foundation system, the slab has no structural support and will crack or settle unevenly.
The ground or sub-base beneath the slab must be properly graded, compacted, and prepared to provide uniform support and prevent differential settlement or slab failure.
A vapor barrier (polyethylene sheeting) must be laid over the prepared sub-base before pouring the slab to prevent moisture migration from the ground into the slab.
Load-bearing walls and vertical structural elements require a completed floor slab to build upon, as the slab provides the working platform and anchorage point for walls.

Although curing is not a separate construction activity per se, sufficient curing time (typically 7 days) before applying floor finishes or placing heavy loads is a soft constraint to avoid slab damage. However, many schedules build this into the slab activity itself rather than as a separate successor.

Structural framing must be completed to provide support for ceiling grid systems, and MEP (Mechanical, Electrical, Plumbing) rough-in work such as ductwork, piping, and conduit must be installed above the ceiling before ceiling tiles are placed, as they would be inaccessible afterward.
Ceiling tiles are placed into a suspended ceiling grid or T-bar system; the grid must be fully installed and leveled before tiles can be laid in.
It is generally preferred to paint walls before ceiling tiles are installed to avoid overspray on tiles, but ceiling tiles can be installed first and walls touched up afterward.
Flooring is typically installed after ceiling work to prevent debris from damaging finished floors, but this is a preference for cleanliness rather than a physical requirement.

successor: Final Electrical and Light Fixture Trim-Out
rationale: Light fixtures and other ceiling-mounted devices are often installed concurrently with or after ceiling tiles, but the tiles must be in place to complete the finished ceiling appearance and support for trim pieces.

Main ceiling runners form the primary support structure of the suspended ceiling grid. Ceiling grid runners (cross tees) cannot be installed until the main runners are in place to provide the anchor points and grid framework.
The exact positions for ceiling grid runners must be marked on the main runners or walls before installation to ensure proper alignment, spacing, and fit within the overall ceiling grid layout.
Ceiling tiles are laid into or clipped onto the completed grid runners. The grid runners must be fully installed to provide the supporting framework before any ceiling panels can be placed.

Many lighting fixtures are integrated into or suspended from the ceiling grid. The grid runner framework must be completed to support the fixtures and allow proper placement within the ceiling system.

While MEP rough-in work (electrical, plumbing, HVAC) above the ceiling should ideally be completed before enclosing with grid and tiles, some adjustments can be made after grid installation. However, it is a strong preference to complete overhead MEP work first to avoid rework.
Hanger rods are typically attached to the ceiling structure or overhead support system, so the ceiling must be in place first.
The hanger rod must be securely installed before any items can be suspended or hung from it.
Hanger rods for suspended ceilings or mechanical supports must be installed before ceiling finishes are applied, as they are part of the overhead support framework.
Floor joists require a stable, level foundation (such as foundation walls or beams) to bear the load; the substructure must be complete to provide bearing support.
Sill plates are anchored to the foundation and provide the direct bearing surface and anchoring point for floor joists.
Subfloor sheathing is fastened directly to the top of the floor joists to create a working platform and structural diaphragm.
Load-bearing and partition walls must be erected on top of the completed floor joist and subfloor assembly to transfer loads properly.
Running utilities through or below floor joists is often easier once joists are in place but could theoretically be done partially in advance; typically a practical sequencing preference.
The ceiling cornice is installed where walls meet the ceiling; wall framing must be complete to provide the structural support and nailing surface for the cornice.
Ceiling cornice is typically applied over finished ceiling surfaces; the drywall or ceiling board must be in place before cornice can be attached.
Wall surfaces must be finished with drywall prior to installing cornice, as the cornice covers the joint between wall and ceiling.

While painting can be done before cornice installation, it is standard practice to install cornice first so that the painter can paint over the cornice and trim uniformly, avoiding cut-in lines; this is a soft preference for finish quality.
Cornice work creates dust and debris; finishing flooring after cornice avoids contamination and damage, though not physically required.
The ceiling surface must be installed first to provide the physical substrate into which the downlight recess can be cut or mounted.
Electrical cables and junction boxes must be run to the downlight locations before the recess housing is installed, as the wiring needs to be accessible and terminate inside the recess housing.
The recess housing must be fixed in place before the trim ring, reflector, and light bulb/LED module can be inserted and connected.
The recess housing flanges or edges are typically painted over or finished seamlessly with the ceiling surface, so painting must occur after the recess is installed.

If insulation is being placed above the ceiling, it is often installed after the recess housing to ensure proper clearance from heat sources and avoid covering the housing. However, this can sometimes be done before if the housing is IC-rated.

The concrete slab or floor base must be fully cured, finished, and stable before surveying and setting out can be performed, as any movement or fresh concrete would distort the reference points and compromise accuracy.

Survey marks and setting out lines (gridlines, levels, start points) must be established before any tile or paver installation can begin, as these provide the positional and level reference for the laying pattern.
Setting out defines the exact locations for chases, trenches, and service penetrations in the floor, so the trenching or chasing must follow the set-out lines.
The screed must follow the established levels and thickness marks from the survey; setting out provides the height and slope reference for the screeding operation.
All floor coverings require the set-out lines (centerlines, starting edges, expansion joint locations) to be marked on the prepared substrate before installation can proceed.
The ceiling grid is typically suspended from the structural framing above; the structural frame must be complete to provide support for the ceiling grid.

MEP rough-in work (ductwork, piping, conduits) must be installed above the ceiling before the ceiling grid is put in place, as accessing these systems afterward would require removing or cutting through the grid.
Ceiling tiles or panels are placed into the grid after the grid framework is fully installed and leveled; the grid provides the support structure for the tiles.

successor: Final MEP Trim-Out and Fixture Installation
rationale: Lighting fixtures, diffusers, sprinkler heads, and other ceiling-mounted devices are typically installed after the grid is in place, as the grid provides the mounting framework.

While walls can be painted before the ceiling grid, it is often preferred to complete wall finishing after ceiling grid installation to avoid damage to finished walls from grid installation activities and to ensure a clean interface at the wall-ceiling junction.
The concrete slab must be poured, finished, and fully cured before its flatness and level can be surveyed, as the survey measures the final hardened surface.
Any applied screed or topping base layer must be complete and set so that the survey reflects the finished level.
Optional surface preparation may be done before survey to remove high spots, but survey is typically done after initial finishing.
The flatness and level survey must be completed to verify tolerances before applying final floor finishes, as non-compliance would require corrective work before finishing.
Equipment installation requires a verified level surface to ensure proper alignment and operation; survey results confirm the floor meets specifications.

The structural soffit is the underside of a structural slab or deck system. Therefore, the slab or deck must be placed and cured first to provide the structural element whose underside forms the soffit surface.
Formwork must be erected and aligned to define the shape, level, and position of the soffit before concrete placement can occur.
Reinforcing steel must be placed within the soffit formwork before concrete is poured, as the reinforcement provides tensile capacity and must be embedded within the concrete section.
The concrete soffit must be cast and reach sufficient strength before the supporting formwork can be safely removed without causing structural damage or collapse.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) services that are suspended from or attached to the soffit (e.g., conduits, ductwork, piping) can only be installed once the soffit is fully cured and formwork is removed, providing the finished structural surface for anchoring and support.
Interior wall lining (e.g., plasterboard/drywall) must be attached to a structural framework; framing provides the necessary substrate for fixing the lining.
Electrical wiring, outlets, and switch boxes must be installed within the wall cavity before the wall lining is closed up, otherwise access is lost.
Plumbing pipes, drains, and supply lines running inside walls must be placed and inspected before enclosing them with wall lining.
Insulation (batts or spray foam) must be placed in wall cavities before the lining is installed, as it cannot be added after the wall is closed.
Once wall lining boards are fixed, the joints between boards must be taped and plastered to create a smooth finished surface before painting or decoration.
The structural frame (steel or concrete) must be complete to provide the load-bearing support for the cladding attachment system.
The roof structure must be in place to provide lateral support and weather protection during cladding installation.
The weather-resistant barrier (WRB) and building wrap must be installed directly onto the sheathing before the cladding goes on to protect against moisture infiltration.

Windows and doors are typically installed after the cladding opening is prepared, but sometimes windows are installed first; more commonly, rough openings are framed, cladding is applied, then windows are fitted and flashed.
While painting or staining can be done after cladding, it is often done before or simultaneously; this is a soft preference since some finishes need the cladding substrate complete.
Exterior cladding must be completed to seal the building envelope before interior finishes (drywall, insulation, painting) begin to prevent weather damage to interior materials.
Stud frame infill walls require a stable floor slab to bear upon and to provide a level base for installation.
The main structural frame (columns, beams, girders) must be in place to define the bays where stud frame infill walls will be installed.
Exterior sheathing or cladding panels are attached directly to the stud frame, so the stud frame must be built first.
Electrical, plumbing, and mechanical rough-in work inside the stud wall cavities cannot occur until the stud frame is erected.
Batt or spray insulation is placed within the stud cavities after the framing is complete and before the interior finish is applied.
Cavity closures are installed within the wall cavity at openings; the wall framing must be erected first to define the cavity and opening where the closer will be placed.
Cavity closers are fitted into the cavity around openings before the window or door frames are installed, as they seal the cavity and provide a backing for the frame.
Cavity closers must be in place before external insulation is applied, as they close off the cavity at openings and prevent thermal bridging and air leakage.
The damp proof course at openings must be installed as part of the cavity closer system to prevent moisture penetration; the DPC is integrated with or installed prior to the cavity closer.

While cavity closers are typically finished before internal lining, some minor adjustments can be made after; it is a soft preference to complete closer installation before plastering for a clean finish.
Window reveal extensions are fitted around the window frame to extend the depth of the reveal, so the window must already be installed in the opening before the reveal extension can be added.

The window reveal extension must be in place before internal plastering and finishing can be applied, as the reveal provides the substrate and edge for plasterboard and plaster to be finished against.
The structural wall opening must be constructed and cured before the window and its reveal extension can be installed, as the reveal extension attaches to the wall structure.
The window reveal extension must be fully installed and finished before painting and decoration can commence, as the reveal surface needs to be prepared and painted as part of the interior finish.

The structural framing (walls, roof, floor) must be in place before thermal bridge mitigation details can be applied, as the mitigation measures (e.g., continuous insulation, thermal breaks) are installed directly onto or within the structural frame.
Exterior sheathing (e.g., plywood, OSB) provides the substrate onto which many thermal bridge mitigation materials (such as continuous exterior insulation) are attached or applied.

While often done in conjunction, it is preferable to complete the air barrier before thermal bridge detailing to ensure continuity and avoid compromising either system, though in some sequences they can be done simultaneously.

Thermal bridge mitigation details (such as thermally broken clips, spacers, or剥离 strips) must be installed first to provide the attachment points and separation that allow continuous exterior insulation to be applied without creating new thermal bridges through fasteners.

The thermal break components and insulation layer must be fully installed before the final exterior cladding or siding can be attached, as the cladding is mounted over or through the thermal insulation system.
The hole must be drilled to the correct depth and diameter before the mechanical fixing anchor can be inserted.
The exact location for the anchor must be marked and inspected to ensure alignment with structural requirements before installation.
Drilled holes must be cleared of dust and debris to ensure proper anchor seating and load capacity.
After the anchor is placed in the hole, it must be torque-tightened to expand and lock it into the substrate.
A pull-out test may be performed after installation to verify anchor holding capacity, depending on specification requirements.
Structural load analysis must be completed first to determine the required wall thickness based on lateral earth pressures, surcharge loads, and other structural forces acting on the wall.
Geotechnical data including soil bearing capacity, groundwater conditions, and soil classification is essential to design the appropriate wall thickness for the specific site conditions.
The final wall locations, lengths, and functional requirements must be established through architectural layout before thickness specifications can be finalized for each wall segment.
Once wall thickness is specified, the reinforcement design (bar size, spacing, cover, and detailing) can be developed to match the structural requirements within the defined thickness.
Formwork dimensions and configuration depend directly on the specified wall thickness; formwork cannot be designed or ordered until the exact thickness is known.
Demolition and site clearance must be completed before substrate preparation can begin, as the area needs to be free of debris, old structures, and obstructions to provide a clean work surface.
A structural assessment or survey must be completed first to identify the condition of the substrate and determine what repairs are needed before preparation work can start.
The substrate must be properly prepared and repaired before any primers or base coats can be applied, as coatings will not adhere properly to unprepared or damaged surfaces.
Substrate must be smooth, clean, and structurally sound before a waterproofing membrane can be installed; defects in the substrate would compromise the membrane's integrity.
All substrate repairs and leveling must be complete before final flooring or finishing layers are installed, as they require a stable and even base.
The structural frame must be in place to provide a stable substrate and support for cladding or render materials.
The roof should be completed to provide weather protection before applying external cladding or render, preventing water damage to newly applied finishes.
Rough-in services within walls must be completed before enclosing them with cladding or render to avoid costly rework.

Cladding or render is typically applied around window and door openings; however, in many sequences, windows are installed before final cladding/render to ensure proper flashing and sealing. This represents a common sequencing dependency.
External cladding or render must be completed to seal the building envelope before interior finishes are applied, protecting them from weather exposure.
The building must be structurally complete and enclosed to create a stable, sealed environment for airtightness testing.
The roof must be installed to ensure the building envelope is fully enclosed before testing air leakage.
External walls must be clad and sealed to form part of the continuous air barrier required for valid testing.
Windows and doors must be installed and sealed to prevent uncontrolled air leakage that would affect test results.
Airtightness testing should be conducted before internal finishes are applied to allow access to seal any identified air leakage points.

The building envelope components (walls, roof, floor) must be constructed first because their material properties, insulation levels, and assembly details directly determine the thermal transmittance (U-value) that will be calculated in the modelling process.

Accurate U-value calculation requires knowing the specific thermal conductivity and thickness of each selected building material, which must be decided and procured before the modelling can be performed.

The final architectural design including wall, roof and floor build-ups, dimensions and orientations must be completed before thermal modelling can proceed, as U-value calculation depends on the precise design specifications.

The calculated U-values from thermal modelling serve as essential input data for the overall energy performance assessment and certification process, as EPC calculations require the thermal transmittance values of building elements.

U-values of building envelope components are fundamental inputs for calculating heating and cooling loads, as these loads depend on the rate of heat transfer through walls, roofs, floors, and glazing.
Fire-stopping seals gaps around penetrations through fire-rated walls and floors; the structural framing creates the compartments and openings that need to be sealed.
Fire-stopping is applied around pipes, ducts, cables, and conduits after they are installed; the MEP services must be in place so that fire-stop sealants and collars can be fitted around them.
Fire-stopping is often installed within wall cavities and at service penetrations before the second layer of board is applied, requiring the first layer and studs to be in place.

While fire-stopping should ideally be completed before final door installation to avoid rework, doors can sometimes be hung earlier with sealing done later; this is a soft preference for quality and sequencing efficiency.
All fire-stopping and cavity barriers must be fully installed and cured before the building's passive fire protection system can be inspected and certified for compliance.
Legal ownership or rights to the property must be established before party wall assessments can be commissioned, as the assessment involves agreements between neighboring property owners.
Accurate boundary lines and existing site conditions must be surveyed first to inform the party wall assessment regarding shared walls and boundary features.
The assessment of existing boundary and party wall conditions must be completed before formal party wall agreements or awards can be drafted and served to adjoining owners.
Findings from the party wall assessment regarding shared foundations and structural interfaces are needed to inform foundation and structural design near boundaries.
Assessment of boundary conditions and party walls must be completed before any excavation near boundaries to ensure compliance with party wall legislation and to protect adjoining structures.
The site must be acquired before any site-specific assessments like heritage constraints can be commissioned or conducted.
Heritage constraints must be identified before design work begins to ensure the design respects protected elements, listed structures, or conservation areas.
Heritage findings often inform planning applications; the assessment must be complete to submit accurate heritage impact statements or conservation area appraisals with the planning submission.
Detailed design must incorporate heritage constraints (e.g., material specifications, retention of historic fabric) derived from the assessment.
While not strictly required, geotechnical findings (e.g., buried archaeology) can inform the heritage assessment; this is a soft preference for comprehensive understanding.
Corner beams require a stable foundation to bear loads; the foundation must be poured and cured before erecting structural beams.
Corner beams typically connect to or rest upon steel columns; columns must be in place to support and anchor the corner beam.
Corner beams provide edge support and formwork containment for adjacent floor slabs; the slab pour must wait until beams are in place.
While cladding can technically proceed in other areas, attaching cladding to the corner beam area is easier and more structurally sound after the beam is installed, though not a physical necessity.
Corner beams often serve as bearing points for roof trusses at building edges; trusses cannot be placed until the supporting beam is secured.
The corner tie beam requires a stable foundation to support its load and ensure proper alignment.
Corner tie beams are typically installed atop wall frames to tie corners together, requiring walls to be erected first.
Corner tie beams provide lateral support and connection at the top of walls, which is necessary before roof framing can be safely installed.
In multi-story construction, corner tie beams support the floor joists or structure above, requiring them to be in place before upper floor framing begins.
The column reinforcement cage must be placed on a prepared foundation or footing that provides a stable base and proper anchorage for the vertical reinforcement.

predecessor: Column Reinforcement Cage fabrication (off-site or on-site assembly)
rationale: The reinforcement cage must be fully assembled (ties, stirrups, and longitudinal bars tied together) before it can be lifted and placed into position.
Formwork must be placed around the completed reinforcement cage to mold the concrete; the cage defines the internal reinforcement that the formwork encloses.
Concrete cannot be poured until the reinforcement cage is in position because the steel is intended to be embedded within the concrete to provide tensile strength.

predecessor: Column reinforcement cage positioning and alignment check
rationale: Prior to finalizing the installation, the cage must be aligned and positioned correctly (cover, plumbness) to ensure structural integrity and compliance with drawings.
The foundation must be completed and cured to provide a stable base and anchorage for the corner column before any column splice work can begin.
The lower column section must be erected and plumbed to its base before the splice connection to the upper column section can be made.
The corner column must be fully spliced and continuous to provide structural support for beams that frame into the column at that location.
The splice creates the connection between lower and upper column sections, so the upper column segment can only be placed after the splice is completed.
It is preferable to complete the column splice before pouring the surrounding floor slab to avoid rework, but the slab could be placed first if construction joints are carefully detailed.
The site must be cleared of debris, vegetation, and existing structures before surveyors can safely access and establish accurate grid lines and reference points.
Survey equipment storage, site office, and welfare facilities must be in place to support survey teams before marking out begins.
Excavation cannot commence until the exact column positions have been surveyed and marked on the ground to ensure accuracy.
Steel fixers need the surveyed column center points and grid lines to position reinforcement cages correctly.
Formwork panels must be aligned to the surveyed column positions to ensure structural geometry and verticality.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and obstructions before any excavation can begin to ensure unobstructed access and accurate layout for column pit locations.
Survey and layout must be completed to mark the exact positions of column centers and pit boundaries before excavation can proceed.
Underground utilities must be located and marked prior to excavation to prevent damage to services and ensure worker safety.
The excavation pit must be fully prepared and cleaned before reinforcement steel cages can be placed into the column pits.
Excavation and pit preparation (including dewatering and base preparation) must be complete before concrete can be poured into column foundations.
Excavation must be completed to create the space and proper elevation for the column footing before concrete can be placed.
A blinding layer of lean concrete is typically poured over the excavated soil to provide a clean, level working surface and prevent reinforcement from being contaminated with soil.
Formwork must be erected and secured to contain the wet concrete and shape the footing properly during pouring.

predecessor: Reinforcement Steel Placement for Column Footing
rationale: Reinforcement bars must be cut, bent, tied, and positioned within the formwork before concrete is poured so that the steel is encased within the concrete.
Freshly poured concrete must undergo a curing period to gain strength and durability before any further construction loads are applied.
Formwork cannot be removed until the concrete has reached sufficient strength to support its own weight and maintain its shape.

Backfilling is typically done after concrete has cured sufficiently, but in some sequences backfilling may begin earlier if the concrete has adequate strength; this is a soft preference for safety and quality.
Column starter bars or dowels are embedded into the wet concrete during pouring; the main column reinforcement can only be placed after the footing concrete has been poured and set.
Column formwork must be erected first to provide the mold and support structure into which the rebar cage is placed and fixed.
Rebar must be fully fabricated, placed, and fixed in position within the formwork before concrete can be poured to ensure reinforcement is correctly embedded.

Inspection of rebar placement and formwork alignment typically follows rebar fixing to verify compliance before concrete pour, though it is a quality control preference rather than a physical impossibility to do otherwise.
Rebar bars must be cut and bent to the required shapes and sizes before they can be transported to the column location and fixed into position.
Concrete curing can only begin after concrete has been poured, which itself requires rebar to be already fixed in place.
Formwork must be installed and secured before concrete can be poured into it to shape the column.
Steel reinforcement cage must be placed and tied inside the formwork before concrete is poured to provide structural strength.
Any embedded conduits, sleeves, or anchor bolts must be positioned in the formwork before concrete is poured; they cannot be added after.
Concrete must be poured and cured (gain sufficient strength) before formwork can be safely removed without damaging the column.
Surface finishing, patching, or grouting of tie holes can only proceed after the column concrete has been poured and sufficiently cured.
Steel columns require a solid foundation and base plates to be installed first to provide a stable supporting surface and proper load distribution before column erection can commence.
Accurate survey marks and layout lines are required to position each column precisely according to design coordinates, ensuring alignment and structural integrity.
Steel columns must be delivered, inspected for defects, and verified against specifications before they can be lifted and installed.
Primary columns must be erected and bolted in place to provide the vertical structural frame before beams and girders spanning between columns can be installed.
After columns are erected and temporarily bolted, they must be braced and adjusted to plumb and vertical alignment before accepting permanent connections and further steelwork.
The column must be fully cast and cured to sufficient strength before any inspection or load testing can be performed; otherwise the concrete would not support the test loads or inspection personnel.
Formwork and rebar must be placed and tied before concrete can be poured into the column.
Inspection and load testing must be completed and passed before any finishing work such as plastering, painting, or waterproofing can commence on the column.

successor: Vertical Structural Load Transfer to Columns
rationale: The columns must be inspected and load-tested to verify their load-bearing capacity before upper-floor beams, slabs, or structural loads are transferred onto them.
Inspection and load testing of ground-floor columns must be completed before constructing upper-floor framing to ensure the supporting structure is sound.

Fire protection material (e.g., spray-applied fire-resistive material or intumescent coating) must be applied to the steel column only after the column is erected and in its final position, otherwise the coating would be damaged during handling and erection.
The column surface must be cleaned of dirt, grease, rust, and mill scale to ensure proper adhesion of the fire protection material; application over contaminated surfaces would lead to delamination.

If a primer or anti-corrosion coating is required before fireproofing, it must be applied and fully cured first, as fire protection materials are designed to bond to primed steel, not to raw steel over primer.
Inspection of fireproofing thickness, adhesion, and coverage can only be performed after the fire protection material has been applied and cured to verify compliance with fire-resistance ratings.

It is preferable to complete fire protection before enclosing the column with ceiling or cladding to avoid costly rework and ensure full coverage, though in some sequences cladding could be installed and fireproofing applied through access panels.
Column reinforcement bars must be installed and tied before the column-to-slab connection detail can be executed, as the connection detail involves integrating slab reinforcement with the column.
Column formwork must be erected and aligned to define the column geometry before the connection detail can be formed at the column-slab interface.
The column must be cast and cured to sufficient strength before the slab connection detail can be constructed, as the column provides the vertical support and anchorage for the slab connection.
The column-to-slab connection detail must be completed to provide the bearing surface and connection interface before slab formwork can be installed around the column.
The connection detail must be finished to integrate slab reinforcement bars with the column connections before slab reinforcement can be fully placed and tied.
The column must be cast and cured before it can be lifted or transferred to its final position.
Formwork must be removed so the column is free and accessible for handling and transfer operations.
Concrete must achieve sufficient strength before the column can be safely lifted and moved without cracking or failing.
The column must be transported to its installation location before it can be erected/placed into position.
Once the column is transferred to its location, it must then be aligned, plumbed, and secured in place.
Columns must be placed on a stable foundation; the foundation layout determines where columns are positioned.
Beams span between columns, so the column positions (spacing) must be established before beams can be installed.
The slab layout and reinforcement depend on the column grid and spacing for structural continuity.
Column spacing defines the layout positions; actual vertical column erection follows the marked spacing.
The column drop panel is a component that attaches to or is supported by the column structure, so the column must be installed first to provide the necessary vertical support and connection point.
Column drop panels are typically integrated with or placed on top of slab formwork at column locations; the formwork must be in place to support the drop panel during concrete placement.

The drop panel reinforces the slab-column connection; slab reinforcement (particularly bottom steel) is often placed over or integrated with the drop panel, so the drop panel must be installed first before the slab reinforcing bars are laid out.

successor: Concrete Pour for Slab and Drop Panel
rationale: After the column drop panel is positioned and tied into the slab formwork and reinforcement, the concrete slab and drop panel are typically poured monolithically; the panel must be fully placed before concrete is poured.

Column vertical reinforcement extends through the drop panel zone; the rebar cage must be in place before the drop panel is installed to ensure proper integration and continuity of reinforcement through the slab-column joint.
The column splice connection physically joins two column segments; the lower column section must be erected and in place to provide a base for the splice connection to be made.

predecessor: Alignment and Plumbing of Lower Column
rationale: The lower column must be properly aligned and plumbed before splicing the upper column to ensure overall verticality and structural integrity.
The upper column section is erected onto and connected via the splice; therefore the splice connection must be completed first to receive and secure the upper column.
Continuity plates are part of the complete splice connection detail; they are installed after or during the splice connection to transfer forces across the joint.

After completing the splice connection (bolting or welding), inspection and torque checking are required to verify the connection meets specifications before proceeding with subsequent steel erection.

The column setout survey marks the exact positions and alignments of columns on the slab or footing. This can only be done after the concrete column has been poured and cured, as the survey establishes the reference points for subsequent work on or around the column.

The column setout survey provides the precise location and alignment data required to correctly position and fix cladding or other finishing elements around the column. Without the survey, cladding installation cannot be accurately placed.
The setout survey establishes the exact positions where reinforcement cages must be placed, ensuring correct cover and alignment before concrete is poured.
Formwork must be set up based on the surveyed column positions to ensure columns are cast in the correct location and with proper plumbness.
The site must be cleared and excavated to expose the foundation level where column positions are to be surveyed, ensuring unobstructed access for survey equipment and marking.
Column reinforcement (rebar) must be installed and tied before formwork can be placed around it, as the formwork encloses the reinforcement cage and cannot be installed afterwards.
The exact column position and alignment must be marked on the slab/deck before formwork can be positioned to ensure correct placement.
The underlying concrete surface or slab where the column sits must be cleaned, roughened, and prepared to receive the column formwork and ensure a proper connection.
Concrete can only be poured into the column after the formwork is completely installed, aligned, braced, and secured to contain the wet concrete and maintain the column shape.
Before concrete placement, the installed formwork must be inspected for alignment, plumbness, bracing stability, and tightness to ensure safety and quality of the final column.
Column formwork provides the mold within which the reinforcement cage is placed and fixed; formwork must be aligned and braced before rebar is installed to ensure proper cover and positioning.
Reinforcement bars must be cut, bent, and prepared to the required dimensions before they can be placed and tied within the column formwork.
Concrete cannot be poured until the reinforcement cage is fully assembled, tied, and inspected, as the rebar is embedded within the concrete element.
Before concrete is placed, the fixed reinforcement must be inspected for compliance with drawings, spacing, cover, and tying; this inspection is a mandatory quality hold point.
Cover blocks or spacers to maintain the concrete cover around reinforcement are typically placed after or concurrently with the final fixing of the rebar, and must be in position before concreting.
Rebar (reinforcement steel) must be installed and tied in place before concrete is poured, as the rebar provides the structural reinforcement that must be embedded within the concrete column.
Formwork cannot be stripped (removed) until the poured concrete has gained sufficient strength to be self-supporting, typically after initial curing.
Curing (moisture and temperature control) must begin immediately after concrete is poured and finished, to ensure proper hydration and strength development of the concrete.

Columns must be poured and cured to their full strength before the supported slab or beam formwork and reinforcement can be placed, as the columns are the load-bearing supports for the upper structure.
Column formwork must be installed and set before stripping can occur, as stripping is the removal of this formwork after concrete has cured.
Concrete must be poured into the column forms and achieve sufficient strength before the forms can be safely stripped.
Concrete must undergo initial curing to reach adequate strength (typically 12-48 hours depending on mix and conditions) before formwork can be removed without damaging the column.
After stripping forms, the exposed concrete column surface must be inspected for defects such as honeycombing, surface voids, or cracking.
While curing begins before stripping, final wet curing or curing compound application is often performed after stripping to ensure proper moisture retention for strength development.
The column schedule defines the placement, sizing, and reinforcement of columns, which must be based on approved structural design calculations and drawings.
Column positions are referenced to the building grid, so the grid layout must be established before column locations can be scheduled.
Columns transfer loads to foundations; the column schedule must align with the foundation design to ensure load paths are coordinated.
The column schedule specifies the reinforcement details (bar sizes, spacing, lengths), which are required before rebar can be cut and bent for column cages.
Column dimensions from the schedule determine formwork dimensions and configurations needed for pouring concrete.
Column formwork must be erected to define the shape and position of the column before its eccentricity (offset from the intended alignment) can be measured or checked.
Reinforcement steel must be placed and tied within the column formwork prior to verifying the column's eccentricity, as the rebar position influences eccentricity.

The eccentricity of the column (its alignment deviation) must be checked and approved before concrete is poured, because once concrete sets, correction of misalignment is extremely difficult and costly.

Eccentricity measurement is part of the alignment/position check; verticality (plumbness) is typically assessed after the eccentricity/position has been confirmed as part of quality control prior to concreting.
The surveyor must establish the reference grid and set out the column centerline position before eccentricity (the deviation from that planned position) can be measured.

The slenderness ratio (effective length / radius of gyration) is a computed design parameter based on the structural element's geometry and support conditions. It must be determined during structural analysis before fabrication or construction.
The radius of gyration depends on the cross-sectional properties of the selected material (e.g., steel section, timber dimensions). Material must be chosen to compute the slenderness ratio.
The slenderness ratio is calculated from the member's effective length and its cross-sectional radius of gyration, which requires the member dimensions to be defined first.

The slenderness ratio directly determines whether a compression member will fail by buckling (Euler buckling) or by material yielding. It must be known before performing buckling capacity checks per design codes.

The slenderness ratio must be verified against code limits (e.g., AISC, Eurocode) to ensure the member is not too slender before proceeding with fabrication and construction, as excessive slenderness would require redesign.

Column Inspection and Testing cannot be performed until the column has been concreted and the concrete has gained sufficient strength to allow testing (e.g., slump test, cube test, or non-destructive testing).
Formwork must be installed and secured before concrete can be poured; once concrete is poured and cured, inspection and testing takes place.
Reinforcement steel must be placed and tied before concreting; after concreting and curing, the column can be inspected and tested for compliance.
Any defects identified during inspection must be addressed before finishing; also, finishing work (e.g., plastering, painting) should only commence after the column passes inspection and testing.
The column must be inspected and tested to verify its structural integrity and strength before it can safely support design loads from floors or beams above.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and topsoil before any foundation work can begin to provide a clean working area.
The exact positions and levels of the pad foundations must be marked out on site before excavation and concrete pouring can commence.
The ground must be excavated to the required depth and dimensions before the pad foundation concrete can be placed.
Ground beams connect pad foundations and require the pads to be in place and cured before beam construction can proceed.
Structural columns are typically founded on pad foundations, requiring the pads to be fully cured before column installation.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and obstructions removed before pile driving or boring can commence.
Soil borings and geotechnical analysis must be completed to determine pile type, length, and load capacity requirements before piling begins.
Pile positions must be accurately marked on site according to engineering drawings before piling can start.

successor: Pile Cap and Ground Beam Construction
rationale: Pile caps and ground beams are cast on top of the piles to distribute loads; piles must be completed first.
Pile testing (e.g., PDA or static load test) is performed after pile installation to verify capacity and integrity before proceeding.
The ground must be cleared and excavated to the required depth before caissons can be installed, as caissons are deep foundation elements placed into the excavated ground.
Soil properties and bearing capacity must be determined through geotechnical investigation to design the caisson depth, diameter, and reinforcement before installation can proceed.
Accurate survey and layout marking of caisson positions is required before drilling or excavation for individual caissons can begin.
The caisson hole must be excavated and cleaned out first before the steel reinforcement cage can be lowered into the shaft.

Concrete placement (typically via tremie method) for the caisson can only commence after the excavation and reinforcement cage are in place, making it a direct successor to the caisson foundation excavation activity.
The ground must be cleared and prepared before any micro-pile drilling or installation can begin.
Understanding soil conditions and load-bearing capacity is essential to design micro-pile depth, diameter, and reinforcing requirements.
Underground utilities must be identified and marked to avoid striking them during micro-pile drilling.
Micro-piles must be installed and cured before compressive or tensile load tests can be performed to verify design capacity.
The pile cap or grade beam that transfers structural loads to the micro-piles can only be constructed after the micro-piles are in place and have achieved sufficient strength.
Site mobilization (including site access, temporary facilities, and utility connections) must be completed before any investigation work can begin on site.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and existing structures to provide unobstructed access for soil investigation equipment and personnel.
Soil samples collected during the investigation must be obtained before they can be tested in the laboratory for physical and mechanical properties.
The soil bearing capacity, stratification, and subsurface conditions revealed by the investigation are essential inputs for designing appropriate foundations.
Assessment of soil conditions from the investigation determines whether ground improvement (e.g., compaction, grouting, or replacement) is needed and informs the design of such treatments.
Excavation must be completed to create the space and formwork for the foundation before concrete can be poured.
Formwork must be in place to shape and contain the wet concrete during pouring and curing.
Reinforcement steel must be positioned and tied within the formwork before concrete is poured to ensure structural integrity.
After pouring, concrete must be allowed to cure and gain strength before any subsequent construction loads are applied.
Formwork cannot be removed until the poured concrete has set and achieved sufficient strength.

The site must be cleared of vegetation, structures, and debris before excavation can begin to provide unobstructed access for excavating equipment and to ensure the excavation area is properly defined.
Accurate survey and staking of foundation corners and excavation limits must be completed to guide the excavation equipment and ensure the foundation is placed in the correct location and alignment.
Geotechnical investigation must be completed to determine soil bearing capacity, groundwater conditions, and excavation safety requirements before excavation proceeds.
All necessary regulatory permits for excavation and construction must be obtained before ground disturbance begins to comply with legal and safety requirements.
Existing underground utilities (gas, water, electric, telecom) must be located and marked to avoid damaging them during excavation and to plan for any necessary utility relocations.
The excavated foundation pit must be complete before drainage systems and waterproofing membranes can be installed around the foundation walls.
Excavation to the required depth must be completed before pile caps or deep foundation elements can be installed at the correct elevation.

A level layer of lean concrete (blinding) is poured over the excavated base to provide a clean, level working surface for reinforcement and formwork placement; this cannot occur until excavation is complete.
Steel reinforcement bars cannot be positioned until the excavation is finished and the base is prepared, as the rebar cage must be placed within the excavated foundation pit.
Formwork for the foundation walls and footings can only be erected after excavation is completed and the foundation footprint is fully exposed.
The foundation must be excavated before waterproofing can be applied to expose the foundation walls and provide work access.
The foundation concrete must be poured and fully cured to provide a solid, dry surface for waterproofing membranes or coatings to bond properly.
The foundation surface must be cleaned of dirt, debris, form oil, and protrusions to ensure proper adhesion of waterproofing materials.
Drainage boards and protection boards are installed directly over the cured waterproofing membrane to protect it from backfill damage and facilitate water drainage.
Backfilling can only commence after waterproofing is fully applied and cured to avoid damaging the waterproofing layer or contaminating the fresh membrane.
The foundation must be excavated to expose the bearing surface before load testing can be performed on the foundation material.
The foundation surface must be prepared and leveled to provide a uniform bearing area for proper load testing setup and accurate results.
If the foundation involves cast-in-place concrete, the concrete must reach sufficient curing strength before load testing to avoid damaging the uncured material and to obtain valid test results.
Load testing must be completed and results analyzed before the foundation can be formally approved or signed off for subsequent construction activities.
Load testing verifies that the foundation can support the design loads; superstructure construction must not commence until the foundation's load-bearing capacity is confirmed.

The perimeter edge formwork supports and shapes the concrete at the slab edges; the slab edge formwork must be installed first to define the boundary and provide the structural support for the perimeter edge formwork to be attached or aligned.

Reinforcement steel must be placed within the slab area before the perimeter edge formwork is fully closed and secured, as the rebar needs to extend into or be tied at the perimeter zone and access is restricted once formwork is in place.

The perimeter edge formwork acts as the containment barrier for wet concrete; concrete cannot be poured until the formwork is completely installed, braced, and checked to prevent leakage and maintain the slab edge profile.
Formwork stripping is the removal of the formwork after the concrete has cured; logically, the perimeter edge formwork must be in place during the pour and curing period before it can be stripped.

Waterproofing is often applied after the formwork is stripped and the concrete edge is exposed; however, in some sequences waterproofing can be done prior to formwork installation if the formwork is external, making this a soft preference rather than a strict physical necessity.
Formwork must be installed and securely positioned to create the mold for casting the slab thickening or downstand beam concrete.
Steel reinforcement bars must be placed and tied within the formwork before concrete is poured to provide structural strength.
The slab thickening / downstand beam component itself is formed by pouring concrete; after the concrete is poured, finishing works like screeding and curing can proceed.
Formwork can only be removed after the poured concrete in the slab thickening or downstand beam has achieved sufficient strength to be self-supporting.
The overall slab reinforcement layout must be completed to ensure proper alignment and continuity of reinforcement into the thickening or downstand beam area.
Construction joints are typically placed in concrete structures; the concrete foundation must be poured and partially set before construction joints can be formed or cut to control cracking.
Reinforcing steel must be in place and properly positioned before construction joints are formed, as the joint location and details often depend on the reinforcement layout.
Formwork must be erected to define the shape of the concrete element before construction joints can be established within or between poured sections.
After construction joints are formed and the surrounding concrete is poured, proper curing must begin to ensure the joint and adjacent concrete achieve design strength and durability.
Waterstop installation or joint sealant application at construction joints can only proceed after the joint has been formed and the concrete has attained sufficient strength.
The structural frame must be in place to define the segments between which expansion joints are installed, allowing for thermal and structural movement.
Foundations must be complete to provide a stable base and define the structural grid where expansion joints are placed to accommodate differential settlement and movement.
Expansion joints in the structural frame must be installed before continuous floor slabs are poured, so the joints can be incorporated to control cracking from thermal movement.
Expansion joints must be in place before walls and partitions are built, so the joints align properly through the entire building envelope to allow uniform movement.
Expansion joint locations must be established before cladding is installed to ensure the façade system accommodates building movement without cracking or buckling.
Saw-cut joints must be made after the concrete has been placed, finished, and has gained sufficient initial set to prevent raveling, but before uncontrolled cracking occurs.
