The concrete must reach an initial set (typically within 4-12 hours after placement) so that saw-cutting does not cause raveling or damage to the surface; yet cutting must occur while the concrete is still green enough to allow the saw blade to cut aggregate without excessive wear.
After saw-cutting, the concrete must continue or resume curing to ensure proper hydration and strength development; joints may need sealing or curing compound application afterward.

If joint sealant is required, it is typically installed after the saw-cut joints have been cleaned and dried, and the concrete has sufficiently cured; however, this is a design specification rather than a physical necessity for structural integrity.
Submarine cables and anchoring systems must be installed on the seabed before the floating surface power platform can be positioned and connected.
The floating platform hull and deck structure must be fully assembled and launched before it can be floated into its operational position.
All power generation units (turbines, generators, transformers) must be installed and secured on the platform before the floating operation can commence.
Mooring lines and anchors must be pre-installed at the deployment site to allow immediate securement when the floating platform arrives.
Onshore substation and grid interconnection point must be prepared before the floating power unit begins transmitting electricity to shore.
The surface hardener/sealer must be applied to a finished, cured concrete slab. Freshly placed concrete must be finished to the proper surface profile before any sealer or hardener can be applied.

Concrete must be properly cured (typically 7–28 days depending on specifications) to reach adequate strength and dryness before applying a surface hardener or sealer, as applying to uncured concrete can trap moisture and cause adhesion failure.

The concrete surface must be thoroughly cleaned of dirt, grease, curing compounds, and laitance, and may need mechanical roughening (e.g., grinding or etching) to ensure proper penetration and bonding of the hardener/sealer.

After application of the surface hardener/sealer, sufficient drying or curing time must be allowed as per manufacturer specifications before the surface can be subjected to foot traffic, equipment loads, or subsequent coatings.

successor: Final Inspection and Acceptance of Concrete Floor
rationale: The surface hardener/sealer is typically one of the final finishing steps for a concrete floor; final inspection and acceptance of the completed floor surface should occur after the sealer/hardener has been applied and cured.
A stable, graded subgrade surface is required before placing the radon barrier to prevent punctures and ensure proper sealing.
A smooth, compacted base layer is needed to provide a uniform bedding surface for the membrane, preventing damage from sharp stones or uneven ground.
The membrane must be fully installed and sealed before concrete is poured to create a continuous gas barrier within the foundation system.
Plumbing and conduit runs should be installed after the membrane to avoid penetrating the barrier unnecessarily, but careful sealing around penetrations is critical.

successor: Radon Vent Pipe / Passive Depressurization System
rationale: The vent pipe collection tee is typically laid on top of the membrane before concrete pour, so the membrane must be placed first.
Excavation must be completed to create space for drainage infrastructure and establish proper grading for water flow.
The subgrade must be properly graded and compacted to provide a stable base for drainage channel installation and ensure proper slope for water drainage.
Any underground utilities such as plumbing connections must be roughed in before the drainage channel is placed to avoid conflicts and rework.
The floor drain must be positioned and secured in place before concrete is poured so that it is embedded and integrated into the finished slab.
Drainage channels and floor drains are typically installed before waterproofing membranes are applied around them to ensure a watertight seal and proper drainage integration.
The rebar cage for the foundation must be in place before holding-down bolts are cast into the concrete, so the bolts can be positioned and tied to the rebar to ensure proper anchorage and alignment.
The bolts must be accurately laid out, positioned, leveled, and secured to a template before concrete is poured; the cast-in step embeds the positioned bolts.
Holding-down bolts are cast-in (placed and secured) prior to or during the concrete pour, but the concrete pour itself embeds and fixes them in the foundation.
After the holding-down bolts are cast into the wet concrete, the concrete must cure to develop sufficient strength to hold the bolts in place before any steel column erection loads are applied.
Holding-down bolts must be cast and cured in the foundation before steel columns can be erected and bolted down to the foundation via these bolts.
Pile caps are structural elements that transfer loads from columns to piles. Piles must be installed and set before the pile cap can be constructed on top of them.
The area must be excavated to the required depth and dimensions before formwork, reinforcement, and concrete placement for the pile cap or ground beam can begin.
A blinding layer of lean concrete is typically poured over the excavated soil to provide a clean, level working surface and prevent reinforcement from contacting soil before the pile cap is cast.
After the pile cap concrete has cured and achieved sufficient strength, the excavated area around the pile cap can be backfilled with soil or compacted fill material.
Columns and walls transfer loads into the pile cap or ground beam; they cannot be started until the pile cap/ground beam is complete and has cured sufficiently to support the load.

The steel tube must be fabricated, delivered, and erected in position before it can be filled with concrete, as the tube serves as both the structural formwork and the reinforcing cage for the concrete core.
A prepared foundation or baseplate connection is required to support and anchor the CFST column before the steel tube is erected and subsequently filled with concrete.
The steel tube must be erected, plumbed, aligned, and temporarily braced in its final position before concrete placement can commence to ensure proper geometry and structural integrity.

After the concrete is placed inside the steel tube, it must be allowed to cure and gain sufficient strength before any further structural loads (e.g., beams, slabs, subsequent columns) can be applied.

Beams, girders, or floor slabs that bear on or connect to the CFST column can only be installed after the column is fully concreted and the concrete has reached the required strength, as the completed composite section is needed to transfer loads.
The reinforced concrete box column requires a stable foundation/footing to bear and transfer its loads to the ground. The column cannot be erected without an existing supporting foundation.
Formwork must be assembled and positioned prior to placing concrete for the box column, as it defines the shape, dimensions, and alignment of the hollow box section.
The steel rebar cage must be placed and tied within the formwork before concrete is poured to provide the required tensile strength and structural reinforcement for the box column.

After the concrete for the box column is poured, a proper curing period must follow to allow the concrete to achieve its design strength before any subsequent loads or construction activities are applied.
The column formwork can only be removed after the concrete has sufficiently hardened and gained enough strength to be self-supporting without deformation.

Beams, slabs, or other superstructure elements that bear onto or are supported by the column can only be constructed after the box column is completed and has achieved adequate strength to support these subsequent structural elements.

predecessor: Steel Reinforcement Installation for Box Column
rationale: Steel reinforcement must be placed and tied before concrete is poured to form the composite box column structure.
Formwork must be erected and braced to define the shape and contain the concrete for the composite box column.
The foundation or base plate must be ready to receive and anchor the composite box column before erection can commence.
After the composite box column is installed and poured, sufficient curing time is required for the concrete to gain strength before any loads are applied.

successor: Steel Beam Connection to Box Column
rationale: Steel beams or structural members can only be connected to the composite box column after it is fully installed and its concrete has achieved adequate strength to support the connections.
The column cap plate sits on top of the steel column, so the column must first be erected to provide a support surface for the cap plate.

successor: Welding of Cap Plate to Column
rationale: The cap plate must be positioned and set in place before any welding operations can fuse it permanently to the column top.
Column cap plates often serve as bearing surfaces for beams or girders; beams must be connected after the cap plate is installed to ensure proper load transfer.
While alignment verification can begin after cap plate placement, minor adjustments may still be possible; this is a quality assurance soft preference rather than a strict physical necessity.
The column (which supports the cap plate) is anchored to a foundation; the concrete must be sufficiently cured to bear the load before the column and subsequently the cap plate can be installed.
Web stiffeners are steel plates welded to beam webs; the beam must be fabricated before stiffeners can be attached.
Stiffeners must be welded onto the beam web before the beam is hoisted and positioned to ensure structural integrity and safe handling.
All welds connecting the stiffener to the web must be inspected for strength and compliance after installation.
Diaphragm plates are typically installed to connect and stabilize steel beams; therefore, the steel beams must be in place first.
Columns provide the vertical support structure; diaphragm plates often tie into the column/beam connections and require the columns to be erected first.
The primary steel frame must be fully assembled and connected before diaphragm plates can be installed to ensure structural alignment and load transfer.
In composite steel decks, diaphragm plates are part of the steel framing that must be in place before concrete is poured over the deck.
While not physically required, it is best practice to inspect diaphragm plate welds/bolts shortly after installation before subsequent work covers them.
Shear connector studs are welded onto steel beams. The steel beams must be erected and in place first to provide the substrate for stud attachment.
Metal decking is typically placed over steel beams before shear studs are welded through the deck. The deck must be installed to mark stud locations and to provide access/work surface.
Shear connectors are designed to be embedded in concrete to create composite action. The concrete slab must be poured after the studs are installed so the studs become embedded in the concrete.
Often rebar is placed after stud installation or concurrently, but some designs require rebar to be positioned first. This is typically a soft preference depending on design and access requirements.

Shear stud welds must be inspected and tested (e.g., bend test) before concrete is poured to ensure the studs meet quality and strength requirements, as defective studs cannot be repaired after concrete is placed.
The column must be erected, plumbed, and secured in place before beams can be connected to it because the beam-to-column moment connection relies on the column as the vertical support element.
Column position and alignment must be checked and accepted before moment connections are made; otherwise, misalignment would cause connection fit-up issues and structural geometry errors.
The steel beams must be delivered to site, inspected, and approved before they can be lifted and connected to columns.
The beam must be positioned and temporarily connected to the column before final bolting (tensioning/torque) and/or welding of the moment connection can be executed.

successor: Inspection and NDT of Moment Connection
rationale: After the moment connection is bolted and/or welded, nondestructive testing (NDT) and inspection must be performed to verify the quality and integrity of the completed connection before it can be considered load-bearing.

successor: Decking and Slab Pour for This Bay
rationale: The structural steel frame (including moment connections) must be completed and stable before metal decking and concrete slab can be placed on that level/bay, as the slab relies on the steel frame for support.
Anchor bolts must be embedded in or placed on top of the foundation concrete before it fully cures, so the foundation concrete pour must precede anchor bolt installation.
Steel columns are bolted to the anchor bolts embedded in the foundation; the anchor bolts must be in place and set before columns can be erected.
Anchor bolt locations must be precisely marked on the foundation based on survey and layout to ensure accurate positioning.
Columns require a stable foundation to bear loads; without completed foundations, columns cannot be properly anchored or supported.
Reinforcement steel must be placed and tied within the column formwork before concrete is poured during column erection.
Column molds or formwork must be assembled and positioned to shape the concrete during the column erection process.
Floor slabs are supported by beams and columns; columns must be erected before the slab can be poured above them.
Rebar cage provides the structural reinforcement that is placed inside the column formwork before concrete pouring.
Formwork molds must be assembled and ready to receive rebar and concrete for column construction.
Columns must be built on top of completed foundations or footings to provide proper load transfer and structural support.
After column concrete is poured (part of fabrication), it must undergo curing to achieve design strength before any loads are applied.
Beams and slabs are typically supported by columns; column fabrication must be complete to provide vertical support for subsequent superstructure elements.
Steel columns must be erected and positioned before welding can be performed on them.
Welding must be completed before inspection can verify the quality and integrity of the welds.
Inspection identifies defects that must be repaired before the column can be accepted.
After inspection passes, surface finishing may proceed, though it could be done before inspection in some cases.
Welds must be inspected and approved before structural load testing or final sign-off can proceed.
The column base area must be cleaned and prepared before grouting to ensure proper adhesion and fill of the grout material.
The column must be set in place and properly aligned/plumbed before grouting the base to secure its final position.
The base plate must be positioned and leveled before grout can be poured underneath and around it to fill voids.
Grout requires adequate curing time to achieve design strength before any further loads can be applied or subsequent work proceeds.
Final bolt tightening to the specified torque must be performed after the grout has cured to avoid disturbing the grout bed and losing alignment.
Fireproofing is applied to structural steel members; steel must be erected and in place before fireproofing can be applied.
All steel connections, bolting, and welding must be finished before fireproofing is applied, as fireproofing would obstruct access to connections.
Metal decking is often installed on steel beams before fireproofing is applied to the underside of the deck and beams.
Fireproofing must be cured and in place before MEP rough-in work begins, as running conduits, pipes, or ducts through or around fireproofed steel can damage the fireproofing if done prematurely.

While it is common to frame walls after fireproofing to avoid damaging the fireproofing, some projects may sequence differently; however, best practice is to apply fireproofing first to ensure full coverage of steel without obstruction from walls.
Column reinforcement (rebar) must be in place before surveying and plumb checking, as the survey is performed on the installed reinforcement cage to verify its alignment and position.
Formwork must be assembled around the reinforcement before the plumb check can be conducted, as the survey verifies the vertical alignment of the formwork assembly.
The survey and plumb check must be completed and accepted before concrete can be poured; pouring without verification risks out-of-plumb columns that cannot be corrected after concrete sets.
If the survey reveals misalignment, formwork adjustment may be needed before concrete pouring; this is a conditional activity rather than a mandatory successor.
The column surface must be cleaned, smoothed, and primed before painting to ensure proper adhesion and a quality finish.
Primer must be applied and dried before the final paint and coating layers to ensure proper adhesion, corrosion resistance, and uniform finish.
Columns must be erected, aligned, and fixed in their final position before painting to avoid damage to the painted surface during installation and alignment adjustments.
After painting and coating, the column requires a curing or drying period for the coating to harden and achieve its intended durability and performance.
The painted and coated column must be fully finished before the final quality inspection can assess the coating quality, thickness, and uniformity.
Formwork must be erected to provide the mold and temporary support for the wet concrete of the downstand beam before the beam can be cast.
Steel reinforcement bars must be placed and tied within the formwork before concrete is poured to ensure the structural strength of the downstand beam.
The downstand beam must be cast and have gained sufficient strength before its supporting formwork can be safely removed.
The downstand beam is typically a primary structural element that must be completed to provide support and a stop-end for the adjacent slab concrete pour.
Waterproofing is generally applied after the beam and slab structure are fully cured, though this is a logical sequence preference rather than a strict physical impossibility if done out of order.
The formwork must be installed first to provide the mold and support structure for placing and tying the reinforcement cage within the perimeter beam.

The reinforcement cage must be fully assembled, tied, and positioned inside the formwork before concrete can be poured, as the rebar provides tensile strength and must be embedded within the concrete.
Individual rebar pieces must be cut and bent to the required shapes and dimensions before they can be assembled into the reinforcement cage.
Rebar materials must be delivered to site and inspected for quality and compliance before any cutting, bending, or assembly work can commence.
Cover blocks (spacers) are typically placed on the completed reinforcement cage to maintain the correct concrete cover between the rebar and the formwork, and this is done before concrete pouring.
Shear connectors are welded or bolted onto steel perimeter beams after they are erected. The beam must be in place to receive the connectors.
Shear connectors embedded in the perimeter beams provide composite action between steel and concrete. The concrete is poured over the connectors, so connectors must be installed first.
Formwork for the composite concrete deck is placed after shear connectors are installed, as the connectors protrude from the beam top flange and formwork must be detailed around them.
Shear studs are a common type of shear connector. The welding process of studs onto the beam top flange must be completed to have the shear connector installed.
The perimeter beam must be set in its final position, leveled, and aligned before shear connectors are attached, to ensure proper connector placement and composite action.
Perimeter beam-to-column connections require the steel columns to be erected and stabilized first, as the beams connect into the columns.
In many sequences, the floor deck must be in place to provide a working platform for crews to safely access and make perimeter beam-to-column connections.
Perimeter beams and their connections to columns form the structural frame that supports exterior cladding; cladding cannot be installed until the perimeter structural connections are complete.
Fireproofing is applied to steel connections after they are completed; applying fireproofing before the connection is made would be impossible as the connection joint would be inaccessible.
Quality inspections, including bolt torque checks and weld inspections, must follow the completion of the connection to verify it meets specifications before subsequent work proceeds.
The bearing pad is placed on top of the perimeter beam formwork; the formwork must be in place before the pad can be installed.
Bearing pads are typically set on the cured or partially cured beam surface; reinforcement must be in place before the final bearing pad location is established.
Bearing pads are placed on the finished top of a perimeter beam; the beam must be cast and sufficiently cured to support the pad and subsequent loads.
The bearing pad provides a level, load-distributing surface for the steel superstructure; girders or trusses cannot be placed until the bearing pads are in position.
While deck formwork could theoretically be installed alongside, best practice is to have bearing pads in place first to ensure correct alignment and load paths for the deck system.
Perimeter beams rest on and are supported by columns, so columns must be installed first to provide structural support.
The foundation must be completed to support the columns and structure before perimeter beams can be installed.
Formwork must be set up to cast or place the perimeter beams in the correct position.
Reinforcement steel must be placed and tied before concrete is poured or beams are erected to ensure structural integrity.
Perimeter beams provide the edge support for floor slabs or decks; slabs can only be placed after the perimeter beams are in place.
Exterior walls or cladding systems typically attach to or are supported by perimeter beams, so beams must be installed first.
Formwork must be installed before reinforcement can be placed, as the reinforcement bars need to be positioned and tied within the formwork mould.
Bottom reinforcement bars must be laid in the beam formwork before the perimeter beam reinforcement (typically stirrups and side/top bars) can be fixed and tied.
Perimeter beam reinforcement must be fully fixed and tied before the side formwork panels are closed, as access is needed for tying and inspection.
All reinforcement must be fixed in position before concrete can be poured to encase the steel.

successor: Electrical Conduit / MEP Embedment in Beam
rationale: MEP conduits and embedments are often placed after reinforcement is fixed but before side formwork is closed and concrete is poured.
Steel beams must be erected and in place before welding can commence, as welding joins the erected beams.
Beams must be properly aligned and fit up before welding to ensure correct geometry and joint preparation.
Tack welding is typically performed to hold beams in position before the final continuous welding of perimeter beams.
Welding must be completed before non-destructive testing (NDT) and visual inspection can be performed to verify weld quality.
Post-weld grinding and finishing of weld surfaces can only begin after the welding process is complete.
Perimeter beam survey and setting out requires stable foundation elements (pile caps or footings) to be completed first, as the beam alignment is referenced from these structural points.
The site must be cleared and roughly graded to allow unobstructed access for surveying equipment and to establish accurate baseline levels for the perimeter beam layout.
Any required shoring or excavation support must be in place before surveying the perimeter beam to ensure a safe and stable working area for survey crews.
The survey and setting out establishes the exact alignment, width, and depth reference points for the perimeter beam trench, which must be marked before excavation can begin.
Once the beam layout is set out on the ground, reinforcement bars can be positioned according to the surveyed alignment and cover requirements.
Concrete must reach sufficient strength (typically 28-day cure or specified percentage) before load testing can be performed without damaging the beam.
Formwork and temporary shoring must be removed so the beam is self-supporting and can freely deflect under test loads.
Load testing is typically completed before steel framing bears on the beam, though in some sequences steel erection can begin on other areas concurrently.

successor: Deck and Slab Placement on Perimeter Beam
rationale: The load test verifies beam capacity; subsequent dead loads from deck/slab should only be applied after the test confirms structural adequacy.
Inspection and approval of reinforcement placement and formwork must occur before concrete is placed and cured, which is a prerequisite to load testing.

The cavity tray is typically installed at the base of the cavity wall above ground level; the foundation and substructure must be complete to provide a stable base and to establish the floor level datum from which the cavity tray location is determined.

The DPC is laid at the base of the wall to prevent rising damp; the cavity tray is installed above the DPC to direct water that enters the cavity back to the outside, so the DPC must be in place first.

successor: Brickwork / Blockwork (Inner & Outer Leaf) Above Tray Level
rationale: The cavity tray is built into the cavity wall at a specific level (e.g., above openings or at the base); the wall leaves above it cannot be constructed until the tray is positioned, as the tray must be lapped and integrated continuously with the wall build-up to ensure water is shed outward.

Insulation is placed after the tray is installed because the tray must be correctly lapped over the inner leaf and any insulation must not bridge the cavity or block the weep holes; installing the tray first ensures proper water-tight detailing.

Weep holes are installed immediately above or at the level of the cavity tray to allow moisture collected by the tray to drain out; the tray must be in place first so that weep holes align correctly with the tray's weephole outlets.
Flashing membrane is applied over the sheathing or decking to provide a weather-resistant barrier; the structural substrate must be in place first.
Flashing membrane is installed on framed walls; framing must be complete to provide a surface for membrane application.
Flashing around windows and doors requires rough openings to be framed so that membrane can be integrated with the opening.
Flashing membrane must be applied around rough openings before windows and doors are installed to ensure proper water drainage and sealing behind the units.
Flashing membrane serves as the weather-resistive barrier and must be fully installed before cladding or siding is applied to protect the building envelope.

The membrane protection board is installed directly over the waterproofing membrane to shield it from damage during subsequent construction activities. Therefore, the waterproofing membrane must be fully installed and cured before the protection board can be applied.

The concrete slab or structural deck must be properly prepared, cleaned, and leveled before any waterproofing or protection board can be installed, as the protection board system relies on a stable and even substrate.

In below-grade or retaining wall applications, the membrane protection board must be in place to protect the waterproofing layer before backfilling can commence, as backfill material would otherwise directly contact and damage the waterproofing membrane.

In vertical or horizontal applications where a reinforced cast-in-place concrete wall or topping slab is placed against the protection board (blind-side waterproofing or sandwich system), the protection board must be installed first to act as a separation and protection layer before concrete is poured.

While inspections can theoretically occur before protection board installation, best practice is to inspect the membrane first, then install the protection board. Once the board is installed, the membrane is no longer visible, so any required visual inspection of the waterproofing membrane must be completed before the protection board goes on.
The termination bar is used to secure and seal the edges of the waterproofing membrane; the membrane must be installed first so the bar can clamp it in place.
Termination bars provide a clean edge for flashing to overlap, ensuring watertightness at terminations; flashing is installed after to cover the bar.
The substrate must be clean, dry, and properly prepared for membrane adhesion; termination bar installation follows membrane placement on the prepared surface.

It is standard practice to inspect and test the waterproofing system after termination bars are secured to verify no leaks at edges; this is a quality assurance preference rather than a physical necessity.
The structural surface must be fully constructed and cured before any waterproofing membrane and its termination bar can be installed.
Panels must be prepared, cut, and aligned into position before seam welding can begin, as welding joins the prepared panels along their edges.
Edges of panels must be cleaned, deburred, and free of contaminants to ensure proper weld penetration and quality during seam welding.
Panels should be temporarily tack-welded or fixed in position to maintain alignment and prevent movement during continuous seam welding.
After seam welding is completed, the welded joints must be inspected (e.g., visual inspection, non-destructive testing) to verify weld quality and integrity.
Post-weld grinding and surface finishing are typically performed after seam welding to smooth out weld beads, though in some sequences this may be optional or deferred.
The membrane must be fully installed before it can be tested or inspected for defects, continuity, and proper adhesion.
Testing and inspection must identify any defects before repairs can be performed on those specific areas.
Formal acceptance or sign-off can only occur after the membrane has passed all required tests and inspections.

successor: Covering/Protective Layer Installation (e.g., ballast, insulation, topping slab)
rationale: Overlying protective layers or coverings must not be placed until membrane integrity is confirmed through testing and inspection.

successor: Follow-on Work (e.g., roofing completion, waterproofing system handover)
rationale: It is standard practice to complete membrane testing before proceeding with subsequent finishing work, though not a physical necessity if testing is done in stages.
The membrane surface must be clean and free of debris, loose materials, and contaminants to ensure proper adhesion and effectiveness of the repair or remediation materials.
The exact location, extent, and nature of the membrane damage must be identified through leak detection and assessment before targeted repair or remediation can be performed.

After applying repair materials (patches, sealants, coatings), sufficient time must be allowed for curing or drying before the membrane can be subjected to any loads, water testing, or subsequent construction activities.
The repaired membrane must be water-tested to verify that the remediation was successful and no further leaks exist before proceeding with covering or enclosing works.

A protective layer or cover over the repaired membrane is recommended to shield it from damage during subsequent construction activities, though in some cases the membrane may be left exposed temporarily.
Formwork must be erected to provide the structural support and mold for the vault rib before it can be placed.
Steel reinforcement must be placed within the formwork before the vault rib concrete or structural elements can be installed.
The vault rib must be fully installed and secured before concrete can be poured over it to form the vault structure.
The vault rib must be complete and have gained sufficient strength before formwork can be safely removed.
Waterproofing is typically applied after the vault rib is complete, though it is a soft preference as some waterproofing could precede rib installation in certain sequences.
The vault keystone requires a stable foundation and supporting walls to be in place before it can be installed, as it is the final locking piece of a vaulted structure.
The supporting walls and side arches must be fully constructed to provide the lateral support needed before the keystone can be placed at the apex of the vault.
A temporary supporting frame (centering) must be built to hold the vault's voussoirs (wedge-shaped stones) in place during construction until the keystone is inserted to lock the structure.

The keystone is the final locking piece; only once it is securely in place can the temporary centering be safely removed, as the keystone provides the compressive closure that makes the vault self-supporting.
The vault structure must be completed (including the keystone) before waterproofing and roofing layers can be applied to protect the structure from weather.
Voussoirs are wedge-shaped stones that must first be quarried and extracted from the source before they can be shaped and placed.
Raw stone blocks must be cut into the precise wedge/tapered shape of a voussoir before they can be installed in an arch.
A temporary supporting frame (centering) must be built to support the voussoirs during arch construction, though typically the centering is erected before voussoir placement begins.
The keystone is the final, central voussoir placed at the crown of the arch; all other voussoirs must be positioned before the keystone can be inserted to lock the arch.
All voussoirs including the keystone must be fully placed and set before the arch can bear load and the centering/formwork can be removed.
The foundation must be prepared and stable before the vault web can be constructed, as the vault web rests on the foundation structure.
The centering (temporary formwork or falsework) must be erected first to support the vault web during its construction.
After the vault web is constructed (poured/laid), it must undergo curing to gain strength before any further loads are applied.
The vault web structure must be complete before finishing work such as pointing, sealing, or decorative treatment can begin.
The vault web must be fully constructed and sufficiently cured before the centering/falsework can be safely removed.
The vault haunch concrete cannot be poured until the vault formwork is installed and properly aligned to support the haunch geometry.
Reinforcing steel for the vault and haunch area must be placed and tied before concrete can be poured for the vault haunch.
The vault haunch serves as a transition/connection element; the main vault concrete pour cannot proceed until the haunch is completed and cured to ensure structural continuity.
Post-tensioning operations require the vault haunch to be in place and sufficiently cured to transfer prestressing forces through the haunch connection.
The vault haunch bears on or connects to supporting columns or piers, which must be built and cured first to provide structural support for the haunch.

predecessor: Erect vertical formwork and reinforcement for vault
rationale: The vault crown is typically cast in place; the formwork and rebar cage must be fully assembled and positioned before concrete placement begins.
Fresh concrete must be allowed to cure and gain sufficient strength before any further loads or finishing work is applied.
Formwork cannot be removed until the concrete has reached the required compressive strength to be self-supporting.

successor: Apply waterproofing membrane to vault crown
rationale: Waterproofing is typically applied to the exposed exterior surface after formwork removal to protect the concrete from moisture ingress.

successor: Install roof finishes and architectural cladding above vault
rationale: The structural vault crown must be fully finished (cured, waterproofed) before adjacent roof systems and cladding can be installed to avoid rework and ensure proper interface detailing.
The vault impost serves as the supporting ledge or springing point for a vault. The vault must be constructed first to provide the structural base onto which the impost is placed.
Vault ribs rest directly on or spring from the impost. The impost must be in place to provide the bearing surface for the ribs.
The vault impost is typically built into or supported by the wall. The wall must be constructed first to provide structural support for the impost.
The vault webbing fills the space between ribs and rests on the impost at the springing level. The impost must be in place to support the edges of the webbing.
Temporary centering or formwork is often required to support the vault construction up to the impost level. The centering must be erected before the impost can be built upon it.
Excavation must be completed to create the space and proper subgrade for placing formwork and subsequent concrete.
The foundation or footing must be cast and cured before centering formwork for columns or walls can be erected on top.

predecessor: Rebar / Reinforcement Installation (for mat or footing)
rationale: Reinforcement steel for the base element must be in place before centering formwork can be aligned and secured, as the formwork encloses the rebar.
Formwork provides the mold into which fresh concrete is poured; pouring cannot occur until formwork is fully erected, braced, and aligned.
For elements such as columns or shear walls, the centering formwork is often placed first and then reinforcement cages are positioned or tied inside the formwork before concrete placement.
Vault spandrels are the panels or surfaces between vault ribs; the ribs must be installed first to provide the structural framework and support for the spandrel panels.
Formwork or centering must be in place to shape and support the vault spandrel during construction before it gains its own structural integrity.
The spandrel surface defines the lateral boundary of the vault; the web infill between ribs is placed after the spandrel boundary is established.
Finishing work such as pointing, tooling, or surface dressing typically follows spandrel installation, though this is a practical progression rather than a structural necessity.
Waterproofing is applied to the completed vault structure including the spandrel surface to protect against moisture ingress; the spandrel must be in place first.
The buttress must be built on a stable foundation to distribute its lateral load-bearing forces properly into the ground.
Buttresses are typically attached to or built integrally with walls to provide lateral support; the wall or a portion of it must exist to anchor the buttress.
Buttresses must be in place to provide the necessary lateral stability for the walls that support roof or floor loads before those structural elements are installed.
In masonry or gothic construction, buttresses are required to counteract the lateral thrust from arches or vaults; the arch/vault construction cannot proceed safely without the buttress in place.
While finishing work can technically occur later, it is preferred to complete the buttress structural work before applying finishes to avoid rework and ensure a continuous surface.
Vault abutments need stable support; foundation must be built first to bear the loads transferred by the arch/vault.
The vault abutment provides the lateral support to resist thrust from the arch or vault; the arch cannot be erected without the abutment in place.
Backfilling and waterproofing against the abutment is typically performed after the abutment is complete, though some backfill could be done earlier in staged construction.
Excavation must precede the placement of abutment foundations and concrete pours to expose bearing strata and provide working space.
The vault abutment must be complete to support the ends of the vault/arch onto which the deck or slab is later cast or placed.

Flying buttresses are structural supports that transfer the lateral thrust of a vaulted ceiling or roof outward and downward to a pier or foundation. The foundation and supporting piers must be completed first to bear the load.

The flying buttress is an external arch that braces the main nave wall at its upper section (typically where the vault thrust occurs). The wall must be in place for the buttress to connect to and stabilize.

Rib vaults generate the outward lateral thrust that flying buttresses are designed to counteract. The vaults must be erected (or at least their springing points set) so that the buttress can be positioned to resist the thrust.

successor: Roof installation over the side aisles
rationale: The flying buttress arches over the side aisle roof; therefore the buttress structure must be complete before the side aisle roof can be installed beneath it.

successor: Upper gallery or clerestory window installation
rationale: While clerestory windows can be installed concurrently, finishing the buttress first allows the wall to be fully stabilized, making it safer to install large windows in the weakened wall area below the vault thrust.
Pendentives require a stable structural base; the entire building substructure and load-bearing walls must be complete to support the weight transferred through pendentives.
Pendentives typically spring from the tops of columns or piers at the corners of a square space; these vertical supports must be in place to receive the pendentive.
Pendentives are structural elements that transition the weight of a dome from a square bay to a circular base; the dome must rest on the completed pendentives.
Pendentives complete the structural transition zone; only after they are fully cured and load-bearing can the temporary falsework supporting the dome above be safely struck.

Decorative finishes such as mosaics or frescoes on the pendentive are typically applied after the structural concrete or masonry has cured, but this is a soft preference as some decorative work could theoretically be done concurrently if scaffolded.
Squinches are structural elements that transition the load from a dome or drum to the supporting walls below; therefore, the walls must be built first to provide the bearing surface.
A squinch is specifically designed to support a dome or superstructure above a square or polygonal space; the dome cannot be placed until the squinch is in place to provide the transitional support.
The entire weight of the wall, squinch, and any superstructure rests on the foundation; without a sound foundation, the squinch cannot be safely installed.

The squinch supports the dome or upper structure, and the roof or weatherproofing layer must be installed after the structural support (including the squinch) is complete to ensure structural integrity and proper load transfer.
A squinch may be built using corbelled stone or brickwork, requiring temporary formwork or careful corbelling preparation before the squinch arch or half-cone structure is erected.
The ground must be cleared and excavated to the general level before vault layout can be marked out on site, as the vault footprint needs a prepared subgrade.
Final vault dimensions, alignment, structural details, and reinforcement schedules must be approved before setting out can commence to ensure accuracy.
A primary survey control network with permanent benchmarks must be in place to provide reference points for accurate vault positioning.
Vault excavation to final depth can only proceed after the vault outline and levels have been precisely set out to guide the excavator operator.
Formwork panels and reinforcement bars cannot be positioned until the vault geometry and alignment have been clearly marked on site.
Centering (formwork support) must be erected on a stable, level base provided by completed foundations; otherwise the centering would lack structural support.
Reinforcement bars for the concrete element are typically placed before centering is fully assembled, or in some sequences the bottom reinforcement is laid prior to centering erection.
Centering serves as the supporting structure onto which formwork panels are placed; formwork cannot be installed without the centering frame in place.
Concrete can only be poured after both centering and formwork are erected to contain and support the wet concrete.
The striking (removal) of centering and formwork must occur after concrete has cured and gained sufficient strength; this cannot begin before centering is complete.
The vault masonry requires a stable and level foundation to support the significant weight and thrust of the masonry vault structure.
Workers need scaffolding or centering/falsework to access the height of the vault and support the masonry units during construction.
A temporary supporting structure (centering or formwork) must be built to support the arch/vault stones or bricks until the keystone is placed and the mortar sets.
The centering or falsework can only be removed after the vault masonry is fully completed, the keystone is placed, and the mortar has cured sufficiently to bear loads.
The vault structure must be completed before constructing the roof or upper floors above it, as the vault serves as the structural support and base for subsequent levels.

The formwork for the vault must be fully installed and secured to provide the mold and structural support necessary for concrete casting; concrete cannot be poured without a formwork structure in place.

Steel reinforcement bars (rebar) must be placed and tied within the formwork before concrete casting to provide tensile strength to the vault structure; concrete cannot be cast without reinforcement in place.
After concrete is cast, it must undergo a controlled curing period to achieve the required strength and durability before any subsequent loads or finishes can be applied.
Formwork can only be removed after the vault concrete has been cast and sufficiently cured to be self-supporting; premature removal would cause structural failure.

It is standard practice to apply waterproofing after the concrete has cured, but this is a soft preference in terms of the casting sequence itself — waterproofing could theoretically be delayed further, though it should not precede casting.
The concrete must be cast and reach sufficient strength before the formwork/centering can be removed (struck). Striking too early would cause the concrete to collapse or deform.
The centering/formwork must first be erected to support the wet concrete; striking is the removal of this same centering, which can only occur after its purpose is fulfilled.
Adequate curing time must be allowed for the concrete to gain sufficient strength to be self-supporting before the centering is struck. Standards specify minimum curing durations before decentering.

Once the centering is removed, the exposed concrete soffit surfaces become accessible for finishing works such as plastering, painting, or other surface treatments. This is a soft preference as some finishing could theoretically be done before striking in limited areas, but normal sequence is after.
The concrete surfaces beneath the centering can only be inspected for defects, honeycombing, or surface quality after the centering has been removed.
The vault base slab or mudmat must be prepared and cured before backfilling and haunching can commence, as the backfill and haunching rely on a stable base support structure.

The vault walls must be fully constructed, cured, and stripped of formwork before backfill and haunching can begin; otherwise, the lateral earth pressure from backfill would damage uncured or unsupported walls.
Waterproofing must be applied and inspected before backfill is placed, as the backfill would permanently cover and make the waterproofing inaccessible for application or repair.
Protection and drainage boards over the waterproofing membrane must be installed prior to backfill to shield the membrane from damage during backfilling operations.

successor: Final Slab / Top Slab Construction of Vault
rationale: Backfilling and haunching around the vault walls must be completed before constructing the top slab or final cover, as the backfill provides lateral support and the haunching forms part of the structural base for the top slab placement.
The vault structure must be fully constructed and concrete cured before waterproofing can be applied, as waterproofing membranes require a stable, cured substrate.
Formwork must be removed to expose the vault surfaces for waterproofing application.
The vault surface must be clean, dry, and free of defects to ensure proper adhesion of the waterproofing membrane.
Backfilling must occur after waterproofing is complete to protect the waterproofing membrane from damage and to seal the structure against moisture ingress.
Drainage systems (e.g., drainage board, perforated pipes) are typically installed over or adjacent to the waterproofing layer to manage groundwater and relieve hydrostatic pressure.
The vault must be physically built (masonry laid, mortar cured) before any structural analysis can measure its actual load paths, deflections, and stress distribution.
Formwork supports mask the vault's self-supporting structural behavior; analysis is only meaningful after the centering is struck and the vault is under its own weight.
Analysis results (crack patterns, stress concentrations, stability margins) are required as input to design any necessary strengthening or repairs.
The analysis must be completed and reviewed before a formal sign-off on structural safety can be issued.

Although finishing often follows analysis, it is a soft preference because minor finishing could theoretically proceed in parallel if deemed safe; however, standard practice completes analysis first to avoid covering defects.
Scaffolding must be erected to provide safe access to the vault for repair and repointing work.
A thorough inspection and assessment must be completed first to identify damaged areas, determine required repairs, and plan the repointing work.
After repair and repointing, debris, loose mortar, and dust must be cleaned up from the vault area.
Waterproofing or sealing should be applied after the repointing is complete and mortar has cured to protect the newly repaired joints.
Scaffolding can only be dismantled after vault repair and repointing work is finished to maintain safe access until completion.
Formwork provides the temporary support structure necessary to shape and cast the vault intrados surface, so it must be installed first.
Steel reinforcement must be positioned within the formwork before concrete is poured to form the intrados.
Formwork cannot be removed until the vault intrados concrete has gained sufficient strength to be self-supporting.
Waterproofing membranes or coatings are applied to the cured intrados surface to protect against moisture ingress.
Aesthetic finishing of the underside of the vault is typically done after the intrados is cast and cured, though some finishing could theoretically be integrated.
The formwork provides the necessary support and shape for casting the vault's extrados surface.
Reinforcement steel must be placed within the formwork before concrete is poured to form the vault extrados.

The extrados is the outer/upper surface of the vault, which is typically cast after the inner (intrados) concrete or as part of the same pour from bottom up; structurally the lower portion must be placed first.
Waterproofing is applied directly onto the cured extrados surface to protect the vault from moisture ingress.
Backfill material is placed over the vault only after the extrados is complete and waterproofed to avoid damage to the vault structure.
The ground must be excavated to the required depth and dimensions before any concrete pier can be constructed, as the pier footing needs to be placed on stable, prepared substrate.
Steel reinforcement cage must be assembled and positioned within the excavation before concrete is poured for the vault pier, as the rebar provides structural integrity within the concrete.
Formwork molds must be erected and braced to define the shape and dimensions of the vault pier before concrete can be placed.
The vault pier must be fully cured and achieve sufficient strength before vault walls can be built upon or tied into it, as the pier serves as a vertical load-bearing support for the walls.
While waterproofing can often be done after the pier is complete, it is a soft preference because partial waterproofing could be applied earlier in the sequence if needed for scheduling flexibility.
The structural steel frame must be in place to provide the supporting framework to which spandrel panels or fill materials are attached between floors.
Floor slabs define the vertical separation between floors, and spandrel fill connects the edge of the slab to the exterior curtain wall, requiring the slab to be cast first.

Spandrel fill provides the opaque backing and thermal barrier behind spandrel glass or panels; the glazing or curtain wall system must be installed after or concurrently with the spandrel fill to seal the building envelope.

successor: Exterior Insulation and Finish System (EIFS) or Cladding
rationale: While cladding often follows spandrel fill to complete the exterior finish, in some systems they are installed simultaneously; this is typically a logical sequence preference rather than a strict physical necessity.

successor: Interior Wall Finishing Adjacent to Spandrel Area
rationale: Interior finishes at the spandrel zone (e.g., drywall, insulation) can be completed after the spandrel fill is in place, but in some sequences they may proceed in parallel; this is a soft preference for quality control and access.
The pier or vault support column requires a stable foundation to bear its load; the footing must be constructed and cured before the column can be erected.
Reinforcing steel must be placed and tied within the column formwork before concrete is poured for the Pier / Vault Support Column.
Formwork molds must be assembled and braced in position before the concrete placement for the column can begin.
The vault or arch supported by the column cannot be constructed until the column is complete and has gained sufficient strength to carry the load.
Beams and girders that frame into the column require the column to be fully erected and cured to provide bearing support and connectivity.
Centering (falsework) must be erected on a stable, level foundation that can support the loads. Therefore, the foundations or footings must be completed first.
In some cases, the formwork panels are assembled on the falsework, but the falsework centering system itself requires the underlying support structure to be prepared and materials staged beforehand.
The falsework provides the temporary support platform on which reinforcement steel for beams, slabs, or arches is placed. Reinforcement cannot be positioned without the falsework in place.

Concrete for elevated structural elements such as beams, slabs, or arches is poured onto formwork that is supported by the centering/falsework system. The falsework must be fully erected and stable before concrete placement.
Formwork panels are placed directly onto the centering/falsework structure to create the mold for wet concrete. The falsework must be complete before formwork can be installed on top of it.
Formwork provides the temporary support structure and mold needed to shape and cast the vault soffit; without formwork in place, the intrados cannot be formed.
Reinforcement bars must be installed within the formwork before concrete is placed to ensure structural integrity of the vault soffit.
The intrados (inner surface/soffit) must be completed first as it forms the structural base and interior profile upon which the extrados (outer/back surface) of the vault is built.
The vault soffit concrete must be cast and sufficiently cured before the supporting formwork can be safely removed to avoid collapse or deformation.

While waterproofing typically follows the complete vault structure, it is a soft preference to allow for curing time and sequential finishing; the intrados must exist before waterproofing can be applied to the vault top.
The abutment must be built on a stable foundation; excavation and preparation of the foundation area must be completed before abutment construction can begin.
If deep foundations are required, piles must be driven and tested before the abutment is constructed on top of them.
Backfill material behind the abutment can only be placed after the abutment structure is complete and has gained sufficient strength to withstand lateral earth pressures.
The bridge deck or superstructure must be supported by the abutments; therefore abutments must be completed and cured before deck installation begins.
Approach slabs connect the roadway to the bridge deck and rest on the abutment; they cannot be placed until the abutment is complete.
Tie rods are tension-only bracing elements that connect between structural steel members. The supporting columns and beams must be in place to provide the bearing points for the tie rod connections.
Tie rods often brace roof structures; once installed they provide the necessary stability for the roof decking and cladding to be placed on top of the framing.

Tie rods that are connected at the base to foundation anchors (e.g., in tension-only braced frames or cable/rod bracing) require the foundation anchor bolts to be set and cured before the rod can be tensioned and secured.

After the rod is mechanically installed (placed through sleeves, end connections made), the final step is to tension or torque the rod to the specified preload. This cannot occur before the rod is physically in position.

Although tie rods themselves are typically not welded, adjacent welded connections (e.g., gusset plates or brackets welded to beams) should be inspected before the rod is installed to avoid rework; however this is a soft preference because the rod can sometimes be installed and later adjusted.
Concrete must reach sufficient strength before formwork can be safely removed to prevent structural damage or collapse.
Reinforcement must be placed and tied before concrete is poured, and formwork striking occurs only after concrete has cured over the reinforcement.
Concrete must be poured and allowed to cure within the formwork before the formwork can be struck (removed).
Once formwork is removed, the exposed concrete surface can be finished, patched, or treated; this is a soft preference as finishing could theoretically be delayed.
Waterproofing cannot be applied to the vault exterior until the formwork is removed and the concrete surface is accessible.
The vault must be fully excavated and exposed before waterproofing can be applied to the exterior surfaces.
Concrete surfaces must be fully cured (typically 7–28 days) to ensure proper adhesion of waterproofing membrane and to prevent trapped moisture from causing blistering or delamination.
Surface must be cleaned, patched, and primed to remove dust, debris, and laitance, ensuring a sound substrate for waterproofing adhesion.
After application, the waterproofing membrane must be allowed to cure and be tested for integrity (e.g., flood test or electronic leak detection) before backfilling proceeds.
Backfilling against the vault walls can only commence after the waterproofing system has been fully applied, cured, and approved, to avoid damaging the membrane.
Site mobilization establishes access, safety protocols, and staging areas necessary before any vault inspection can commence.

predecessor: Structural Shoring and Temporary Support Installation
rationale: Temporary shoring may be required to stabilize the vault structure before inspection to ensure inspector safety and prevent collapse during survey.
Inspection must identify conditions requiring cleaning; debris removal follows after survey to address identified issues without obscuring defects.
Survey results inform the specific repairs needed; planning and design cannot proceed without knowing the existing conditions and defects.

Inspection identifies moisture intrusion points, which guides where waterproofing is needed; however, some waterproofing could be done independently, making this a soft preference rather than a hard constraint.
The rough opening (framed hole in the wall) must be built before the fixed picture window can be installed, as the window fits into the framed opening.
House wrap or weather-resistive barrier must be applied around the rough opening before window installation to provide a water-tight seal and prevent moisture intrusion.
Interior trim or casing around the window can only be installed after the window is set in place and secured.
Exterior flashing and siding that abuts or covers the window frame must be installed after the window is in place to ensure proper water management and a finished appearance.

While interior painting and wall finishing can technically proceed before the window is installed, it is a soft preference to do it after to avoid damage to the window and ensure a clean finish around the edges.
The structural frame (roof structure) must be in place to provide support and mounting points for the roof light component.
Roof decking provides the substrate and opening into which the roof light is installed; the opening must be framed and cut before the roof light can be placed.
Flashing must be installed after the roof light is in place to seal the gap between the roof light and the roof deck, preventing water ingress.
Interior ceiling finishes and paint around the roof light opening can only be completed after the roof light unit is installed and the rough opening is closed.

successor: Electrical Wiring (if skylight with integrated light/fan)
rationale: If the roof light includes electrical components (e.g., an integrated light or exhaust fan), electrical connections are typically made after the unit is physically mounted, though this could be done concurrently with some planning.
The rough opening (frame opening in the wall) must be framed, sized, and prepared before any window can be installed, as the window fits into this structural opening.

Weatherproof membranes, flashing, and sill pans must be installed around the rough opening prior to window placement to ensure a watertight seal and prevent moisture intrusion behind the window frame.
Interior and exterior trim and casing are installed after the window is set and secured in the rough opening, as they cover the gap between the window frame and the wall finish.

While interior finishes can proceed after window installation, it is a soft preference because drywall and painting could technically be done before window installation but would risk damage and require later touch-ups around the opening.

Exterior cladding or siding is installed after the window is in place so that the window flanges can be properly integrated with the weather barrier and the siding can be cut and flashed around the window frame.
The rough opening must be framed, checked for square/level, and prepared with appropriate weatherproofing and flashing before the pivot window unit can be installed.
The pivot window must be physically placed and fastened in the opening before the perimeter can be sealed with caulk, foam insulation, or weatherstripping.
Interior trim, casing, and drywall finishing around the window must occur after the window unit is installed to properly overlap and cover mounting flanges.
Exterior siding or cladding that abuts the window frame must be completed after the pivot window is installed to ensure proper flashing integration and weathertight fit.
The load-bearing wall structure must be erected before the rough opening for the pivot window can be framed within it.
Wall framing must be complete to provide the structural opening and support for the door frame and hinges.
The rough opening must be framed, sized, and prepared to the correct dimensions before the solid timber door can be installed.
The door must be hung in place before hardware such as hinges, locks, and handles can be fitted and aligned.
Architraves and trim are installed around the door frame after the door is hung to ensure proper fit and finish.
While painting can be done before or after installation, typically final touch-up painting and staining of the door unit is done after hanging to achieve a seamless finish.
The wall frame must be constructed to provide the structural opening and support for the glazed door frame.
The rough opening must be properly sized, squared, and prepared with headers and cripple studs before the door unit can be installed.
Sealing, caulking, and weatherstripping around the door frame must be applied after the door is installed to ensure a proper airtight and watertight seal.
Interior wall finishes should be applied up to the door frame after installation to create a clean transition between wall and door.
Exterior cladding or siding must be installed after the door to properly flash and integrate the door assembly with the building envelope.
The rough opening must be framed to provide the structural support and dimensions necessary for French door installation.
Weatherproofing around the rough opening prevents moisture intrusion before the door is set in place.
Trim and casing are installed after the door is fitted to cover the gap between the door frame and the surrounding wall.
Interior finish work such as painting or drywall finishing around the door area is typically done after installation to achieve a clean appearance, though can be done before with careful masking.
Door hardware such as handles, locks, and hinges must be installed after the door itself is mounted and aligned.
The rough opening for the pocket door must be framed within the wall before the door track and frame can be installed.

successor: Drywall hanging on the pocket door side
rationale: The pocket door frame and track must be fully installed before drywall can be applied over the cavity to create the pocket.

successor: Door slab hanging and hardware installation
rationale: The track and frame must be in place before the door slab can be hung and sliding hardware attached.
The pocket door must be fully installed and operational before trim work can be completed around the opening.
Rough-in services must avoid the pocket cavity and be completed before the pocket door is installed to prevent interference with the track and door operation.
The door frame must be in place before a screen door can be mounted, as the screen door attaches to the frame.
The rough opening must be prepared (sized, squared, and framed) before the door frame can be installed.
Weather stripping around the screen door should be applied after the door is hung to ensure proper sealing and fit.
Hardware such as handles, hinges, and door closers are attached directly to the installed screen door and cannot be properly aligned before the door is mounted.
After installation, the door must be adjusted for proper swing, closure, and latch fit, and then tested for functionality.
The door frame and jamb must be installed within the rough opening of the wall framing. The wall structure (studs, headers, cripples) creates the opening that receives the door frame.
The rough opening dimensions must be verified for correct width, height, and plumbness before installing the door frame and jamb to ensure proper fit and function.
The subfloor provides the finished walking surface and the base plane from which door frame heights are measured. Door jambs sit on or above the finished subfloor.
The door slab is hung onto the installed frame and jamb assembly. The frame must be securely in place, plumb, and square before the door can be mounted on hinges.
Door trim and casing are fastened to the jamb and wall surface. The jamb must be installed and shimmed before decorative trim can be applied around the door opening.
Structural framing (walls, floors, roof) must be in place to define the location and dimensions of rough openings for windows and doors.
Exterior wall sheathing is typically installed over the framing before rough openings are cut or framed out for windows and doors.
Rough openings must be prepared (framed, sized, and reinforced) before windows and doors can be installed into those openings.
While not a strict physical dependency, it is standard practice to complete rough openings before running electrical and plumbing lines through wall cavities to avoid rework and interference.
Rough openings must be fully prepared so that insulation can be properly installed around window and door frames without obstruction.
Structural framing provides the base substrate and support for flashing and weatherproofing materials.
Sheathing creates a continuous surface for weather-resistive barriers and flashing to be applied and properly sealed.
Flashing around roof penetrations and edges requires the roof deck to be in place for proper integration and sealing.
Flashing must be installed around rough openings before windows and doors are set to ensure proper water drainage and sealing integration.
Weather-resistive barriers and flashings are installed beneath exterior cladding to provide the primary moisture management layer.
Rough openings for windows and doors must be framed and prepared before any window or door units can be installed and finished.
The building's structural frame (walls, floors, roof) must be complete to provide the load-bearing support and enclosure needed for window and door installation.
Exterior sheathing and weather-resistive barriers (house wrap) must be installed before windows and doors to ensure proper flashing integration and water tightness.
Windows and doors must be fully installed and trimmed before interior wall finishes can be applied to ensure clean edges, proper gaps, and to avoid damage to finished surfaces.

While flooring can be installed after windows and doors to avoid dust and debris accumulation on the new floor, it is a soft preference as flooring is sometimes done beforehand with protective coverings.
Windows and doors must be set, flashed, and finished prior to final siding/cladding to allow for proper integration of trim, flashing, and weather sealing around openings.
Exterior paint and caulking around window and door frames must be applied after the units are fully installed and trimmed to seal gaps and provide weather protection.
The window or door frame must be installed first to provide a structural opening and reveal into which the sill board can be fitted and secured.
The rough opening must be framed, leveled, and squared before the sill board can be placed to ensure proper fit and alignment.

predecessor: Weather Barrier / Flashing Installation (at rough opening)
rationale: Weather-resistive barrier and sill flashing must be applied to the rough opening before installing the sill board to prevent water intrusion behind the sill.
The sill board is typically installed first to provide a level bearing surface and integral pan, onto which the window or door unit is then placed and fastened.
Interior trim, casing, and stool must be installed after the sill board is in place to cover the gap between the sill and the finished wall surface.

Sill plates must be anchored to a cured foundation to provide a level, stable base; installing a sill plate before the foundation is fully cured would result in instability and failure to meet structural anchorage requirements.
Sill plates serve as the direct bearing surface for floor joists or the bottom plate of wall framing; floor framing cannot begin until sill plates are in place and properly anchored.
In platform framing, the sill plate forms the base upon which exterior walls are erected; wall framing depends on the sill plate being installed and bolted down.
Termite pretreatment of soil and foundation must be completed before installing wooden sill plates to prevent future termite infestation through the sill-to-foundation interface.
Anchor bolts must be embedded in the foundation concrete during or immediately after the pour; sill plates are then placed over these bolts and secured with nuts and washers.
Sill nosing attaches to the bottom of window or door frames; framing must be complete to provide the structural support and reveal for nosing installation.
The rough sill (the structural base under the window opening) must be in place to provide a substrate for the finish sill nosing material.
Weatherproofing and flashing must be installed at the sill before adding finish nosing to ensure the water control layer is continuous behind the trim.
Sill nosing provides the finished ledge and support surface; the window or door unit sits on top of and seals against the nosed sill.
Casing and trim around the window or door abut and overlap the sill nosing; trim work must follow to achieve proper fit and finished appearance.
The sub-sill must be placed on a prepared, level foundation surface to ensure proper load distribution and structural stability.
The rough opening for the window or door must be framed before the sub-sill can be installed within it.
The sub-sill serves as the base support for the window or door frame and must be in place before the frame is set.
Sub-sill must be installed first so that flashing and waterproofing membranes can properly overlap and seal around it to prevent water intrusion.
The sub-sill provides the structural base onto which a sill pan (if used) is placed before the window or door is installed.
The rough framing and window opening must be fully constructed before sill flashing can be installed, as the flashing is applied directly onto the rough opening's sill area.
The weather-resistive barrier (house wrap) must be installed before sill flashing so that the flashing can be integrated and lapped over the WRB for proper water drainage.
The sill flashing must be in place before the window unit is set into the opening, as the flashing directs water outward and the window sits on top of it.
Sill flashing is installed first so that jamb and head flashings can be lapped over it in a shingle fashion, ensuring water sheds from top to bottom over each layer.
It is a practical preference to complete all window flashing work before interior finishing begins, to avoid damage to finished surfaces from potential water intrusion during construction.
The sill weatherbar must be installed onto the window or door frame, so the frame must first be in place.
The window or door unit is typically installed after the sill weatherbar is attached to the frame, as the weatherbar sits beneath the unit to provide drainage and sealing.
The air and water barrier (weather-resistant barrier) is often detailed over the weatherbar flanges to ensure continuous water shedding and airtightness.
The rough opening must be properly framed, shimmed, and prepared before the sill weatherbar can be installed onto the sill pan or frame.
A sill pan or base flashing is often required beneath the weatherbar to direct water outward; the weatherbar sits on top of or integrates with the sill pan system.
The sill drip edge is installed onto or after the window sill to direct water away; the sill must be in place first.
The drip edge over the sill is typically integrated with or covered by the exterior cladding or siding, so it must be installed before the cladding goes over it.
Flashing and weatherproofing layers are often applied after the drip edge to ensure proper water shedding and seal continuity.
The rough opening for the window must be framed and prepared before any window components including the sill drip edge can be installed.
Interior window trim and sill can be installed after the exterior drip edge is in place, though this is a logical sequencing preference rather than a strict physical constraint.

The acoustic sill seal is applied to the top of the foundation or subfloor before the bottom plate of the stud wall is set, or alternatively the sill seal is placed under the bottom plate. Rough framing must be prepared (or at minimum the bottom plate laid) to receive the sill seal.

The acoustic sill seal is typically installed between the subfloor and the bottom plate of walls to reduce sound transmission. The subfloor or foundation must be in place to provide a surface for the seal to adhere to.
The sill seal must be in place beneath the bottom plate before wall sheathing is applied, as the sheathing covers the wall assembly including the sealed bottom plate connection.

While not physically required, it is best practice to complete the acoustic seal at the sill before enclosing the wall with drywall to ensure the continuous air-tight and sound-dampening seal is achieved and inspectable.

Flooring materials (e.g., carpet, hardwood, tile) are installed after the wall framing and sill seal are in place, as the sill seal is part of the wall-to-floor interface that gets covered by finished flooring.
The low sill threshold is installed at the bottom of a wall opening; the wall sheathing provides the backing and structural surface onto which the threshold is mounted.
The rough opening (including the sill plate and jambs) must be framed in place to provide the structural support and defined opening for the low sill threshold to be installed.
The low sill threshold forms the base of the opening; windows or doors are set onto or against the threshold, so the threshold must be in place first.
Weatherproofing and flashing details (e.g., sill flashing) are installed over and around the threshold to shed water; the threshold must be in place to integrate these waterproofing layers correctly.

While the threshold is typically installed before interior finishes to allow for proper transition, floor finishing can technically proceed after threshold installation with careful coordination, but it is a soft preference to finish the threshold first for a cleaner interface.
The sill bracket/cleat component must be fabricated or procured before it can be installed on site.

predecessor: Structural Steel or Masonry Wall Erection
rationale: The supporting structure (steel frame or masonry wall) must be in place to provide a mounting surface for the sill bracket/cleat.
The sill bracket/cleat serves as the support and anchor point for the actual sill component; therefore it must be installed first.
The bracket/cleat provides the substrate for flashing and waterproofing layers that protect the sill area from moisture intrusion.

successor: Final Cladding or Finish Work Around Opening
rationale: Once the sill bracket/cleat and sill are in place, surrounding cladding and finishing can proceed, though this is often a logical sequence rather than a strict physical requirement.
The perimeter sill trim is installed after the wall sheathing is in place because the sill trim typically sits against or is fastened to the sheathed wall assembly.
