Perimeter sill trim often abuts window and door frames; those frames must be installed first so the sill trim can be cut and fitted to the openings.
The perimeter sill trim serves as a finished edge detail; exterior cladding or siding is installed after it so that the cladding can overlap or butt against the trim piece for a weathertight seal.
After the sill trim is fastened in place, sealant and caulking are applied along joints to provide weatherproofing, though this is a standard best practice rather than a strict physical necessity.

predecessor: Building Weather Barrier / House Wrap Installation
rationale: The weather barrier (house wrap) must be installed over the sheathing before the sill trim is attached, so that the trim can be integrated into the drainage plane and proper flashing details can be achieved.
The foundation or substrate must be prepared, leveled, and cured before sill installation can begin, as the sill plate rests directly on the foundation.
Rough framing inspections typically occur before sill installation to ensure the structure is ready for the next phase, though this may vary depending on local practices.
Sill plates must be installed and anchored to the foundation before wall studs and framing can be erected on top of them.
Sill plates must be positioned and bolted down with anchor bolts embedded in the foundation before the framing can proceed.
Sill plates form the bottom plate of the wall assembly; subflooring and floor decking typically follow after walls are framed on the sill.

The rough opening must be framed and prepared (including checking for proper size, level, and square) before sill flashing can be installed, as the flashing is applied directly to the building's rough opening structure.
Sill flashing must be installed before the window or door unit is placed, because the flashing sits beneath the unit to direct water outward and protect the sill from moisture intrusion.
Sill flashing is installed first at the bottom of the opening, followed by jamb flashing and head flashing, to ensure proper water-shedding layering (bottom-up sequence).
The exterior sheathing and WRB (e.g., building wrap) must be in place so that sill flashing integrates with theWRB, typically with the WRB cut and lapped over the flashing's back dam.

While air sealing can often be done concurrently or after installation, best practice is to complete air sealing after sill flashing to ensure continuity of the air barrier without puncturing the flashing membrane.
The windows and doors must be installed first to expose the sill area that requires sealing and pointing. Sealing cannot be done before the sill surface is accessible.
Surrounding masonry and brickwork must be completed so that sills are fully set and gaps between sill and wall are exposed for sealing and pointing work.
The rough opening must be prepared and cleaned so that the sill area is free of debris and ready for sealant application and pointing.
Sill sealing and pointing must be done prior to final waterproofing and DPC application to ensure continuous moisture protection across sill junctions.
Sill sealing and pointing must be completed before interior finishes to prevent moisture ingress behind finished walls and to allow proper sealing integration with the building envelope.
Sill thermal testing requires the sill to be physically installed in place before any thermal performance testing can be conducted.
If thermal testing reveals deficiencies, remediation or repair work may be needed, but this is contingent on test results rather than a strict physical requirement.
Thermal testing must be completed before final sealing and weatherproofing to allow access for testing equipment and to verify thermal performance before enclosing the assembly.
Balustrades and guard rails require a structural base (concrete slab, deck, or stair landing) to be installed and cured before they can be securely anchored or fixed in place.
The structural slab or landing must achieve sufficient strength to support the loads imposed by the balustrade and to allow safe drilling/fixing for anchors.

Where balustrades penetrate a waterproof membrane, waterproofing should generally be completed first to maintain a continuous water barrier, though in some sequences the balustrade base can be detailed later.
Where handrails are mounted onto or integrated with the balustrade structure, the balustrade framework must be in place to support the handrail.

successor: Final Finishing and Painting of Balustrade
rationale: Installation should precede final finishing coats to avoid damaging completed paintwork during installation, though pre-finished components are sometimes used.
The window or door frame provides the structural opening and support that the sill sits within, so the frame must be in place before the sill can be properly fitted or replaced.

Any structural repairs to the surrounding wall or masonry opening must be completed before sill installation, as the sill bears on this substrate and cannot be installed if the supporting structure is not sound.
Weatherproofing sealants are applied around the installed sill to seal joints between the sill and the frame/wall; this sealing work requires the sill to already be fixed in place.

Interior finishes around the window or door opening, such as drywall, plaster, and paint, should be completed after the sill is installed to ensure a clean, continuous finish without damaging the sill.

While glazing is often installed after the sill, it is a soft preference because some sill designs can be replaced with glazing already in place; however, for ease of access and to avoid damage to the glass, it is generally preferred to install the sill first.
Reveal lining is installed around window and door frames to cover the gap between the frame and the wall. The frame must be in place first to provide a surface for the reveal to attach to.
The wall structure must be framed to provide the rough opening and structural support before the reveal lining can be fitted around the opening.
Flashing and weatherproofing around openings must be installed before reveal lining to ensure water tightness behind the lining.
Reveal lining creates a finished edge around openings; internal wall linings or plasterboard are installed up to the reveal, so the reveal must be in place as the termination point.
Architraves are trim pieces fixed around the reveal lining to cover the joint between the lining and the wall, so the reveal must be installed first.
The rough opening must be framed and sized before reveal jambs can be installed, as the reveal jamb attaches to the rough framing to define the finished opening.
Reveal jambs are typically installed around windows or doors after the unit itself is in place, to provide a finished interior trim around the opening.
Reveal jambs must be installed before drywall finishing so that the drywall can be taped and mudded flush to the jamb, creating a seamless transition.
While painting can be done before installation in some cases, typically reveal jambs are installed before final painting and trim finishing for a clean appearance.
Sealant around the reveal jamb edges is applied after installation to ensure weatherproofing and a finished seal between materials.
The soffit framing provides the structural support and substrate onto which the soffit reveal is formed; without framing, there is no surface to receive the soffit finish.

The soffit sheathing or panel installation must be complete before the reveal (the visible finished edge or gap detail) can be created, as the reveal is formed at the intersection or edge of these panels.
All MEP rough-in work within the soffit cavity must be completed prior to finishing the soffit, including the reveal, to avoid cutting or damaging the finished reveal for late installations.

Recessed lighting or other fixtures mounted into the soffit require the soffit and its reveal (the finished edge detail) to be complete so that fixtures can be properly fitted and aligned to the finished surface.

While finishing (painting or coating) can sometimes be done after the reveal, it is a soft preference to complete the reveal first so that paint/finish can be applied continuously across the reveal and adjacent surfaces without lap marks or masking issues.
The rough opening must be prepared (framed and sized correctly) before the window frame setback can be installed, as the setback is measured and set relative to the rough opening.
Waterproofing and flashing must be applied to the rough opening before setting the window frame to ensure proper weather sealing behind the frame.
The window frame must be positioned at the correct setback depth before it can be permanently fastened or anchored to the wall structure.
Once the frame is set at the correct setback, insulation and air sealing around the frame can be applied to fill gaps and prevent thermal bridging.
The frame must be positioned at the correct setback depth before the operable sash or glazing unit can be installed into the frame.
Shadow gap detail is typically installed against finished wall surfaces; wall framing must be complete to provide the substrate and structural support for the shadow gap trim.
Shadow gap details are fixed onto finished plasterboard/drywall surfaces to create the recessed shadow line effect; drywall must be installed and finished before the shadow gap detail can be applied.
The wall surface must be smooth and finished before installing shadow gap details to ensure a clean, precise edge and proper adhesion/fixing.

Shadow gap details are often painted along with the wall; however, they must be installed first so that the paint finish can seamlessly cover both the wall and the shadow gap trim for a uniform appearance.

Flooring is typically installed after shadow gap details to allow the flooring material to tuck neatly under or abut the shadow gap trim; however, this may be a soft constraint depending on whether the shadow gap is at floor level or wall-ceiling junction.
The damp proof course at the reveal is installed within or onto the masonry walls; the wall structure must be built first to provide the substrate for the DPC installation.
The DPC at reveal is placed around window or door openings; the frame must be installed first so that the DPC can be properly integrated and lapped with the frame.
The DPC must be in place before plastering or rendering the reveal surface to ensure the damp-proof barrier is continuous behind the finish.
The DPC at reveal must be completed before final installation of windows/doors to ensure proper sealing and weatherproofing around the opening.
Internal finishes (plaster, paint) should only be applied after the DPC is installed to prevent moisture ingress behind the finished surface.
Formwork or shuttering must first be installed in place to define the shape and boundaries of the concrete element before any reveal (indentation or groove) formwork can be added.
Steel reinforcement must be positioned within the formwork before revealing formwork is set, as the reveal detail is typically integrated into the formwork system after rebar is in place.

The reveal formwork/shuttering creates grooves, indentations, or decorative patterns in the concrete surface; concrete must be poured after the reveal formwork is in position so the impression is cast into the concrete.
Once concrete is poured against the reveal formwork, it must cure to gain strength before the formwork (including reveal elements) can be stripped.
The reveal formwork/shuttering must be removed (stripped) after the concrete has cured, so that the revealed pattern or groove is exposed on the finished concrete surface.

successor: Window/Door Frame Installation in Deep Reveal
rationale: The structural wall and masonry opening must be built and cured before the window/door frame can be installed into the deep reveal opening.

successor: Window/Door Frame Installation in Deep Reveal
rationale: The rough opening (including lintel, jambs, and sill) must be framed and prepared to the correct dimensions before the frame can be placed into the deep reveal.

predecessor: Window/Door Frame Installation in Deep Reveal
successor: Window/Door Installation (Fitting the sash/casement into the frame)
rationale: The frame must be installed, leveled, and secured in the deep reveal before the actual window sash or door leaf can be fitted into that frame.

predecessor: Window/Door Frame Installation in Deep Reveal
rationale: The frame must be in place before flashing and waterproofing membranes can be applied around its perimeter to seal the interface between frame and wall.

predecessor: Window/Door Frame Installation in Deep Reveal
rationale: While plastering can technically be done before the frame, in a deep reveal the frame is typically installed first to define the reveal depth, and plastering then finishes up to the frame edge.
The reveal lining must be fixed onto the structural frame or window/door frame. Without the frame in place, there is no substrate to attach the reveal lining to.

Reveal linings are typically installed after or concurrently with wall linings to ensure proper alignment and a seamless finish around openings. The wall lining provides the reference surface for the reveal.
Windows and doors must be installed first so that the reveal lining can be fixed around the installed openings, creating the finished internal surround.
Architraves are fixed over the junction between the reveal lining and the wall lining to cover the gap, so the reveal lining must be in place first.
The reveal lining must be fixed before it can be painted or have any final finish applied to it.
The building's substructure must be complete to provide a stable base and the wall assembly where cavity closers are installed.
Cavity closers are installed within the wall cavity; therefore the wall structure (including inner and outer leaves) must be erected first.
Cavity closers seal the cavity at openings and junctions; insulation can then be installed continuously without interruption at openings.
Cavity closers must be in place to provide a proper thermal break and seal before internal finishes are applied over the inner leaf.

The thermal bridge assessment at the reveal area assesses the thermal performance around the window installation. Windows must be installed first so that the reveal assembly (including frame, insulation, and connections) is complete and can be evaluated for thermal bridging.

Air sealing around the window perimeter should be completed before the thermal bridge assessment because the assessment evaluates continuity of insulation and potential thermal breaks; air sealing affects the thermal envelope continuity.

The thermal bridge assessment identifies areas where additional insulation or thermal break materials are needed. Insulation installation at the reveal should follow the assessment to address any identified thermal bridging issues.

Cladding installation can only begin after the thermal bridge assessment is complete because the assessment may identify the need for corrective measures (e.g., additional insulation or break materials) that must be finished before the cladding covers the reveal area permanently.
Weatherproofing and sealing of reveals can only be applied after the exterior wall assembly and sheathing are installed, as the reveals are gaps or joints in that assembly that need to be sealed.
After weatherproofing and sealing the reveals, the exterior cladding or final finish layer is installed to cover and protect the weatherproofed joints.

successor: Water/Air Barrier Testing (e.g., Blower Door Test)
rationale: Verifying the effectiveness of weatherproofing should follow sealing to confirm air and water tightness prior to full enclosure.
The substrate around reveals must be structurally sound, clean, and prepared before any weatherproofing sealant or membrane can be applied.
Completing weather sealing before interior finishing prevents moisture infiltration that could damage interior surfaces, but it is a logical dependency rather than a physical impossibility.

Door headers are structural components that sit within framed wall openings; the rough framing (studs, cripples, king studs) must be in place to create the opening and provide bearing surfaces for the header.

The door header provides the structural support above the door opening; the door frame and door slab cannot be installed until the header is in place to transfer loads and define the rough opening height.

Wall sheathing (plywood/OSB) is applied over the framed wall including the header; the header must be installed so sheathing can be fastened to it and so the wall assembly is complete before exterior covering.
Drywall is installed over the framed wall; the door header must be in place to provide a nailing surface and to define the door opening before drywall can be cut and hung.
The foundation or slab must be completed before any wall framing (including door headers) can be erected, as the walls bear on the foundation.
The head clearance warning indicator must be mounted on or within the parking structure's structural frame, so the frame must be in place first.
The warning indicator requires electrical power for operation (typically lighting or sensor systems), so electrical rough-in must be completed to provide power at the installation location.
The warning indicator is typically mounted at or near the ceiling/soffit level; finishes around the indicator must be installed after the device is in place to ensure proper fit and alignment.
The warning indicator must be physically installed before final connections and testing of its electrical/electronic components can be performed.

successor: Parking Stall Striping and Signage Installation
rationale: While striping and signage can be done before or after indicator installation, it is practical to install the indicator first so that height warning signage can be positioned to align with the indicator location.
Door frames require the rough framing (wall studs and headers) to be in place to provide the structural opening and support for hanging the door.
External wall sheathing must be installed to define the final door opening dimensions and provide structural stability before the door unit can be installed.
The rough opening must be measured, framed, and properly sized/shimmed to accommodate the specific door dimensions before hanging the door.
Door casing and trim are installed around the door frame after the door is hung to cover the gap between frame and wall and provide a finished appearance.
Locks, handles, and additional hinges are typically installed after the door is hung in the frame, as precise alignment requires the door to be in its final position.

successor: Detailed Design or Verification of Vertical Alignment
rationale: The head-height survey establishes the actual vertical clearances at critical locations (bridges, tunnels, overhead utilities), which are essential inputs for detailed design to ensure vehicles can pass safely.

The route must be preliminarily defined so that survey teams know which specific overpasses, tunnels, and overhead obstructions along the alignment need to be measured for headroom/vertical clearance.

successor: Procurement / Fabrication of Vertical Clearance Signage
rationale: Although signage can be designed in parallel, the exact clearance values from the survey are preferred to finalize sign text and placement, making this a soft dependency.
A traffic management plan is helpful to safely conduct on-road surveys, but alternative traffic control methods could be implemented if the plan is not fully developed first.

successor: Construction of Overhead Obstruction Adjustments (e.g., raising bridges, lowering road)
rationale: Survey data determines which obstructions violate minimum clearance and by how much, so physical adjustment work cannot be designed or executed until the as-built head heights are known.

Design Development establishes the layout, spatial configurations, and design details of the building, which are necessary before an accessibility assessment can evaluate compliance with accessibility standards.
Detailed construction documents and drawings are needed for the accessibility assessment to review and verify that all design elements meet accessibility code requirements.

The accessibility assessment must be completed and its findings incorporated before applying for building permits, as many jurisdictions require proof of accessibility compliance as part of permit submission.
The accessibility assessment must be finalized to ensure all accessibility requirements are integrated into the design before construction begins, preventing costly rework.
The accessibility assessment establishes the baseline requirements that will be verified during final inspection and commissioning to confirm the completed building meets accessibility standards.
Structural frame members (columns, beams, etc.) require a stable foundation base to transfer loads; the foundation must be completed and cured before any vertical structural elements can be erected.
The site must be cleared, graded, and excavated to proper elevations before any structural framing can begin to ensure proper alignment and load-bearing capacity.

Underground utilities such as drainage, plumbing, and electrical conduits must be placed before structural columns and footings are poured to avoid conflicts and the need for core drilling through structural members.
The roof structure (trusses, beams, decking) relies on the vertical columns and horizontal beams of the structural frame for support; the frame must be in place to carry roof loads.
Exterior wall cladding (curtain wall, brick veneer, metal panels) is attached to or supported by the structural frame; the frame must be erected to provide the backing structure.

The thickened edge beam is typically poured monolithically with or on top of the foundation slab; the ground surface must be prepared and the slab/footing base must be in place to support the edge beam formwork and reinforcement.
Formwork defines the shape and dimensions of the thickened edge beam and must be erected and secured before concrete can be placed.
Steel reinforcing bars must be tied and positioned within the formwork before concrete is poured to ensure structural integrity of the beam.

successor: Wall Framing / Masonry Above Edge Beam
rationale: The thickened edge beam provides the bearing surface and structural support for walls erected above it; walls cannot be started until the beam has cured and gained sufficient strength.
The concrete must be placed and allowed to cure to design strength before formwork can be safely removed and subsequent construction loads applied.
The frame connection node is installed at the junction of steel frame members; the steel frame must be erected first to provide the structural points where connection nodes are placed.

successor: Structural Welding and Bolting of Connections
rationale: The connection node must be positioned and installed before permanent welding and bolting can secure the frame connections.
Load testing verifies the integrity of installed connection nodes and can only be performed after the nodes are fully in place.
The foundation with anchor bolts provides the base anchorage; connection nodes at column bases require anchor bolts to be set before node placement.
Gusset plates must be fabricated and cut to the required dimensions and hole patterns before they can be installed at the connection points.
The main structural members (columns, beams, trusses) must be erected and positioned so that the gusset plate can be bolted or welded to connect them at the joint.
Once the gusset plate is positioned at the joint, it must be permanently fastened via bolting or welding to secure the structural connection.

successor: Inspection and quality control of connections
rationale: After the gusset plate is installed and fastened, inspection of the connection (e.g., bolt torque, weld integrity) must be performed to verify compliance with structural specifications.

Fireproofing spray or coating is typically applied after connections, including gusset plates, are fully installed and inspected, though it is a safety requirement rather than a physical interference constraint.
Haunches are typically supported on foundation elements such as footings or pile caps, which must first be constructed to provide a stable base.
Haunches often connect to or are cast monolithically with columns; the column reinforcement must be in place before the haunch can be formed and poured.
Haunches provide bearing support or moment connection for beams and girders; the haunch must be completed before beams can be seated on it.
Haunches often act as transitions between columns and the deck or superstructure; the deck slabs and formwork are placed after the haunch is in position.
If the haunch is part of a post-tensioned concrete system, the haunch must be sufficiently cured before post-tensioning forces are applied to avoid cracking or failure.
A corbel is a structural bracket that projects from a wall, so the wall must be built first to provide a supporting surface for the corbel to be attached or built upon.
The wall that supports the corbel requires a proper foundation, so foundation work must precede both wall construction and ultimately corbel installation.
Corbels are often used to support roof overhangs, beams, or upper deck structures, so the corbel must be in place before the supported structural element is installed.
If corbelled masonry continues upward (corbelling as a technique), the lower corbel course must be completed before subsequent courses are laid above it.
While not physically required, decorative finishes and trim around the corbel are typically applied after the corbel is installed for ease of access and proper alignment.

successor: Welding and Bolting of Steel Connections
rationale: Steel columns and beams must be erected and positioned before their connections can be welded or bolted.

successor: Welding and Bolting of Steel Connections
rationale: Connection points must be aligned, fitted, and temporarily secured before permanent welding or bolting can be performed.

successor: Welding and Bolting of Steel Connections
rationale: Steel members must be prefabricated and delivered to site before field connections can be made.

predecessor: Welding and Bolting of Steel Connections
rationale: Welds must be completed before they can be inspected and tested for quality and integrity.

predecessor: Welding and Bolting of Steel Connections
rationale: Fireproofing spray or coating must be applied after all welding and bolting is complete to avoid damaging the fireproofing during connection work.
Formwork for walls and columns must be installed on a stable, cured base. Foundation or slab provides the bearing surface and reference elevation for formwork alignment.

predecessor: Rebar / Reinforcement Placement (for the structural element being formed)
rationale: For many structural elements like columns and walls, rebar cages must be placed and tied before the formwork is closed around them, as the formwork encloses the reinforcement.
Formwork provides the mold into which fresh concrete is placed. Concrete cannot be poured until the formwork is fully assembled, aligned, and secured.
Concrete must be poured into the formwork before it can begin curing. The formwork retains the concrete in its desired shape during initial curing.

Striking (removing) the formwork is the direct successor activity to installation. Concrete must achieve sufficient strength before formwork can be struck, but the formwork must first be installed and the concrete poured before striking can occur.

The structural frame design must be based on accurate site conditions and foundation requirements, which are determined during site preparation and excavation. The foundation system must be designed to support the structural frame loads.

Soil bearing capacity, settlement characteristics, and subsurface conditions from geotechnical investigation are critical inputs for designing the structural frame's foundation system and load distribution.
The structural frame must be designed to support the architectural layout, including column locations, floor-to-floor heights, and building geometry defined in architectural design.

The foundation system must be designed and detailed in the structural frame design before concrete can be placed, as the foundation must accommodate column bases, reinforcement details, and load transfer elements specified in the frame design.

Steel member sizes, connection details, and material specifications for beams and columns are determined during structural frame design, which must be completed before steel can be ordered and fabricated.
The frame must be fully assembled before inspection can occur, as inspection verifies the completeness and quality of the assembled frame.
All welding work on the frame must be completed so that the quality of welds, joints, and structural integrity can be inspected.
The frame must be properly aligned and leveled before inspection to ensure it meets dimensional tolerances and specifications.
Any surface treatment or painting can only begin after the frame passes inspection, as defects found after painting would be costly to rectify.
Secondary components, cladding, or panels should only be installed after the frame is inspected and approved to avoid rework from hidden defects.
Column sections must be fabricated before they can be spliced together at the joint.
The lower column section must be erected and in place before the splice joint connecting it to the upper section can be executed.
The splice joint must be completed (bolted/welded) to connect the upper column section to the lower section before the upper section can be considered fully erected and stable.
If grouting is specified for the splice, the mechanical connection (bolting/welding) must be completed first before grouting can be applied.

successor: Inspection and Testing of Column Splice
rationale: While inspection typically follows completion of the splice, it is a quality control step that could theoretically be performed concurrently; however, standard practice requires inspection after work is done for quality assurance.
The steel reinforcement cage must be in place before column casing can be installed, as the casing encloses the rebar and cannot be placed after the cage is complete.
Formwork provides the mold and support for the column; casing/enclosure is typically placed around or after formwork to contain concrete or encase the structural element.
If the column casing is a permanent enclosure (e.g., architectural cladding), concrete must be poured and set first so the casing can be applied over the finished structural column.
Surface finishing and painting can only commence after the column casing/enclosure is fully installed to ensure a smooth, continuous surface for finishes.
While not physically required, it is preferred to complete casing before rough-in inspections to allow unobstructed access to verify all embedded elements are properly enclosed.
Formwork must be installed and secured before concrete can be poured into it to shape the rectangular column.
Reinforcement steel must be placed inside the formwork before concrete is poured to provide structural reinforcement.
The column must be built on a prepared foundation or base slab to transfer loads properly to the ground.
Concrete must be poured and cured to sufficient strength before formwork can be safely removed.
Columns support beams and slabs above; beams and slabs cannot be constructed until columns are in place to carry the load.
The site must be cleared and excavated to expose the foundation area before column positions can be marked out on the ground.
The ground must be tested and compacted to provide a stable working platform before accurate grid lines and column positions are set out.
Initial site survey and leveling must be completed to establish reference benchmarks and datums from which column grids are set out.
Column positions must be accurately marked on the ground/ slab before reinforcement cages can be fabricated and placed in those exact locations.
The column locations must be clearly set out before formwork can be erected around those positions.
The ground must be prepared, excavated, and foundation footings/pile caps poured and cured to provide a stable load-bearing base for the steel column.

predecessor: Steel Column Base Plate Fabrication & Delivery
rationale: Base plates with anchor bolt holes must be fabricated, delivered, and set in the foundation before the column can be erected and bolted down.
Anchor bolts must be embedded in the foundation concrete and the concrete must reach sufficient strength to resist pull-out forces before the column can be erected and tightened.
Beams and girders frame into columns; the column must be erected, plumbed, and temporarily braced before connecting beams to it.
Permanent bracing (rods, cables, or cross-bracing) or temporary guy wires must be installed after the column is in place to prevent buckling and ensure stability under load.
Steel roof decking, purlins, and roofing systems are supported by the column-and-beam frame, so the column must be erected before these topping-out activities.
Fireproofing is applied to the exposed steel column surface after erection and connection work is complete to avoid damage during subsequent steel assembly.
Exterior wall panels, curtain walls, or masonry veneer attach to or align with the steel frame; the column must be erected and stabilized before cladding can begin.
The site must be cleared of debris, vegetation, and existing structures before any excavation work can begin to provide unobstructed access and a safe working area for digging.
Accurate surveying and marking of column positions is physically required to ensure excavations are dug at the correct locations as per the structural drawings.
The excavated pit and constructed footing formwork must be complete before steel reinforcement bars can be placed and tied inside the footing.
Excavation, footing formwork, and reinforcement placement must be finished before concrete can be poured into the footing to form the structural base.
The footing concrete must be cured and the formwork removed before excavated earth can be backfilled and compacted around the completed footing.
Rebar materials (steel bars, ties, etc.) must be procured and delivered to the site before any fabrication or assembly can begin.
The fabricated rebar cage must be fully assembled before it can be placed and positioned in the formwork or excavation.

While formwork can sometimes be installed before cage placement, typically the cage is fabricated and placed before or concurrently with formwork; however, final formwork adjustment may depend on cage position.
Concrete cannot be poured until the rebar cage is fully fabricated, assembled, and in its final position within the formwork, as the rebar provides structural reinforcement.
Individual rebar must be cut and bent to specified dimensions before they can be tied or welded together into a cage assembly.
Column reinforcement must be placed and tied before column formwork can be erected, as the formwork encloses the reinforcement cage and prevents access for tying once closed.
Setting out and marking column positions and slab soffit levels on the deck is necessary before formwork can be erected to ensure correct alignment and elevation.
Column formwork typically bears on or is braced against the slab formwork; therefore the lower-level slab formwork must be in place to provide support and a working platform.
Column formwork must be fully erected, aligned, and secured before concrete can be poured into the form to shape the column.
Concrete must be poured and gain sufficient strength before the formwork can be stripped (removed) from the column.
Formwork must be installed and secured to create the mold that shapes and contains the concrete for the column before concrete can be poured.
Steel reinforcement bars must be placed and tied inside the formwork to provide structural strength before concrete is poured.
The column position, alignment, and verticality must be surveyed and marked before formwork and concrete work can proceed to ensure correct placement.
After concrete is poured and vibrated, it must undergo a controlled curing period to achieve design strength and prevent cracking before any loading or further work.
Formwork cannot be removed until the poured concrete has gained sufficient strength to support itself and any applied loads.
Reinforcement (rebar) must be fully installed and inspected before concrete is poured and curing begins, as the steel provides structural integrity.
Formwork must be erected and secured to contain the wet concrete before pouring and subsequent curing can take place.
Concrete must be poured into the formwork first; curing is the process that follows immediately after concrete placement to maintain moisture and temperature for proper hydration.
Curing must be completed (typically 7–14 days or until specified strength is achieved) before formwork can be safely removed without damaging the column.
While testing can be done on cured concrete samples, it is a soft preference because some initial checks may occur earlier; however, final acceptance tests typically require completed curing.
Steel plates, beams, or raw materials must be procured and delivered to the fabrication yard before any cutting, welding, or assembly can begin.
Fabrication cannot start until the detailed shop drawings for the steel columns have been reviewed and approved by the engineer, as they specify dimensions, connection details, and material grades.
Fabricated columns must be completed and ready before they can be loaded and transported to the construction site.
Surface preparation, primer coating, and final painting (if done in the shop) must follow fabrication to protect against corrosion before installation.
Columns must be fully fabricated, inspected, and approved before they can be lifted and installed at the building frame.
Steel columns require a stable, level foundation (concrete footings or slab) to transfer loads to the ground; erecting steel on unprepared ground would cause instability.
Beams and girders are supported by columns; columns must be in place to provide vertical support before horizontal structural members can be installed.
The roof structure relies on the column grid to transfer loads; columns must be erected and braced before roof trusses are placed.
Vertical plumbing risers and stacks are often integrated within or alongside steel columns; the structural column frame must be in place to support and route plumbing lines.
While not physically required, sequencing façade work after column erection avoids interference and allows the structural skeleton to be completed first for dimensional verification.

Column splicing (connecting reinforcement bars between column segments) can only be performed after the lower column section has been cast and cured, providing a physical base for the splice connection.
The reinforcement bars (rebar) must be assembled and placed within the column formwork before splicing can join them to the next column section's reinforcement.
Formwork for the lower column segment must be in place to support concrete placement and provide the geometry needed for the splice connection.
After splicing reinforcement bars between lower and upper column segments, the upper segment formwork can be completed and concrete can be poured, encasing the splice connection.

Once splicing is complete, inspection and testing (e.g., mechanical splice tension tests, visual inspection of welded or grouted couplers) must verify the integrity of the connection before the next construction activities proceed.
The column must first be poured and allowed to cure before any inspection and plumb survey can be performed to verify its vertical alignment and quality.
Formwork must be installed and the column cast before the plumb survey can check the column's verticality against design specifications.
Reinforcement steel must be in place and the column poured before a meaningful inspection of the finished column can occur.
The inspection and plumb survey must be completed and the column verified as acceptable before formwork can be safely stripped and removed.
Any defects, misalignment, or out-of-plumb conditions identified during the survey must be documented and rectified before proceeding with surface finishing work.
The cap plate sits on top of a column or post to distribute loads and provide a bearing surface; therefore, the column/post must be installed first.
The cap plate provides a flat bearing surface and connection point for beams or girders; beams/girders are placed on top of or connected to the cap plate.
The cap plate must be manufactured, cut, and prepared to its final dimensions before it can be transported and installed on site.
Once the cap plate is positioned on top of the column, it must be welded or bolted to secure the connection before further loads are applied.
The column or post supporting the cap plate requires a stable foundation or base to be in place; without the foundation, the column cannot be erected.
Columns must be erected and stable before beams can be connected to them; the beam-to-column connection physically depends on the column being in place.
Columns must be verified as plumb and properly aligned to ensure accurate beam-to-column fit-up and connection integrity.
Columns cannot be erected without completed foundations and base plates installed to support and anchor them.
The beam must first be connected to the column (typically bolted or welded) before the opposite end of the beam can be secured to another support or before the connection is fully tightened.
The initial fit-up and connection of the beam to the column must be performed before final welding or full tension bolting of the moment connection can be completed.
Lateral bracing systems often attach to beam-to-column joints; the connections must be established before bracing can be installed.

While metal decking can sometimes be placed before all connections are fully tightened, it is standard practice to complete beam-to-column connections first to ensure a stable structural frame for deck installation.
Steel columns must be erected first to provide the structural framework onto which connections are fabricated.
Bolts and fasteners must be prepared and staged before connection fabrication can commence to ensure smooth assembly.
Connection fabrication must be completed to create the attachment points before steel beams can be erected.
Connection fabrication produces the joints that must be inspected for quality and compliance before acceptance.
Steel members must be laid out and marked in their correct positions to guide accurate connection fabrication.
Bolt tightening and tensioning is performed on structural steel connections after the steel members (columns, beams) have been erected and aligned.

predecessor: Alignment and Plumbing of Steel Structure
rationale: The steel frame must be properly aligned and plumbed before final bolt tightening to ensure correct geometry and load distribution.
In typical steel erection sequences, bolted connections are tightened (snug-tight or pre-tensioned) prior to welding to maintain alignment and prevent distortion.

successor: Inspection and Testing of Bolted Connections
rationale: Final inspection (visual or torque testing) must follow bolt tightening to verify compliance with specified tension and quality standards.
Fireproofing spray or board application is applied after bolted connections are fully tightened and inspected, as covering bolts before final tightening would block access.
The vault structure (such as the arch or dome framework) must be erected first to provide the supporting surface onto which the soffit is applied or attached.

predecessor: Masonry or Concrete Work for Vault
rationale: The structural masonry, concrete, or load-bearing vault elements must be completed before the soffit (the underside finish) can be installed.

Electrical, plumbing, or mechanical rough-in work that is concealed within or above the soffit must occur after the soffit is installed, as the soffit provides the finished ceiling surface and access for embedding services.
The final plastering, painting, or decorative finish applied to the soffit surface can only begin after the soffit substrate is fully installed and secured.
Recessed lighting or fixtures mounted into the vault soffit require the soffit to be in place to provide the mounting surface and housing.
Stringers provide the structural support framework for the stairs; treads must be placed on top of stringers.
Tread material must be cut to proper length and shape before it can be installed onto the stringers.
Risers (vertical boards) are typically installed after treads (horizontal boards) to create a finished stair face; the riser sits behind or below the tread.

Handrails are generally installed after treads are in place so they can be properly aligned with the stair step locations, though this is a practical sequencing preference rather than a physical impossibility.
Paint, stain, or sealant application should occur after tread installation to avoid damaging the finish during handling and installation.
Risers are typically mounted on or anchored to the foundation slab; the foundation must be poured and cured before riser installation can begin.
Any underground piping, conduits, or sleeves that penetrate the slab or grade beam must be placed prior to riser installation to allow correct alignment and embedment.
Risers provide the vertical transition from underground to above-grade piping; horizontal branches or mains can only be connected after the riser is in place and secured.

successor: Wall / Slab Pour (if riser is embedded)
rationale: If the riser is cast into a concrete wall or slab, the riser must be positioned and braced before the concrete is placed.
Above-grade piping, valves, and equipment that connect to the riser can only be roughed-in after the riser is installed and its top elevation is fixed.
The vault arch rib requires temporary support (centering/formwork) to hold it in place during construction; the centering must be erected first to provide the necessary structural support.
The arch ribs form the primary structural framework of the vault; the infill or webbing between ribs can only be placed after the ribs are in position to define the vault geometry.
Finishing materials such as plaster or render are applied to the completed rib and infill assembly; the rib must be fully installed and stable before surface finishes can be applied.

The vault arch ribs bear on supporting walls or abutments; these supporting elements must be fully completed and have gained sufficient strength to carry the vault loads before rib installation begins.

The centering/formwork can only be removed after the vault arch rib and any associated masonry or concrete have achieved adequate strength to be self-supporting; premature removal could cause collapse.
Columns must be cast and cured to provide vertical support and bearing surface for centering formwork to rest upon.
A stable base slab or foundation must be in place to support the centering system (props/falsework) and to transfer loads safely.
The centering formwork provides the mold and support platform onto which steel reinforcement bars are placed and tied for the slab/beam above.
The formwork must be fully erected, aligned, and secured before concrete can be poured into it to form the structural element.
Striking (removing the centering formwork) can only occur after the concrete has been poured and cured; the centering erection is the prerequisite setup that must happen first.

Masonry vaults require temporary formwork or centering to support the stones or bricks during construction until the keystone is placed and the mortar sets. The centering must be built and in place before any masonry can be laid on it.
Workers need elevated platforms to reach the vault surface, transport materials, and safely lay masonry units; scaffolding must be erected before vaulting work commences.

The vault's lateral thrust is typically resisted by massive abutments, buttresses, or supporting walls. These supporting structures must be completed and sufficiently cured to bear the loads imposed by the vault during and after construction.
The centering or formwork can only be removed (struck) after the vault masonry is fully laid, the keystone is in place, and the mortar has cured sufficiently for the vault to become self-supporting.
Weatherproofing layers (e.g., lead sheeting, tiles, or mortar capping) on the extrados of the vault can only be applied after the masonry vault structure itself is complete and stable.
Concrete must be poured and allowed to achieve sufficient strength before formwork can be safely removed. Striking formwork too early can cause collapse or deformation of the concrete element.
Concrete must undergo adequate curing to reach the required compressive strength (typically 70% of design strength) before formwork is struck. Premature striking risks structural failure.

After formwork is struck, temporary backprops must often be installed to support the freshly stripped concrete element until it reaches full design strength, preventing excessive deflection or collapse.
Inspection of the concrete element for defects, alignment, and quality can only be performed after the formwork has been removed to expose the concrete surface.
The structural frame (including beams, columns, and floor slabs) must be completed to provide the supporting structure onto which stair flights are installed.
Stair flights rest on or are anchored to concrete floor slabs, which must be poured, cured, and reach sufficient strength before load-bearing stair installation can commence.
Handrails and balustrades are physically attached to the stair flight structure itself; the stair flight must be in place before these safety components can be mounted.
Finishing materials such as treads, risers, and flooring coverings are applied to the installed stair flight structure and cannot be completed before the stair flight is in position.

While some MEP (mechanical, electrical, plumbing) rough-in work can proceed concurrently, final routing of conduits, pipes, and cables through or adjacent to the stairwell is easier and more accurately aligned after stair flights are installed, though this is a soft preference rather than a strict physical necessity.
Scaffolding provides safe access to the ceiling/soffit area for plastering work.
All mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work must be completed before soffit plastering because once plastered, access to the ceiling void for installing conduits and pipes is blocked.
Any structural defects, leaks, or substrate issues in the ceiling must be resolved before plastering to ensure a sound base.
Freshly applied plaster must be allowed to dry and cure before any subsequent finishes can be applied.
Plastering provides the smooth substrate required for paint or decorative finishes; painting cannot commence until plastering is complete and cured.

A comprehensive site assessment and documentation of existing conditions must be completed before the heritage conservation survey can begin, as the survey relies on understanding the current state, historical context, and any prior alterations to the site.

Approvals from heritage authorities and relevant permits must be secured before commencing the conservation survey, as legal and regulatory compliance is required to proceed with any investigative or conservation work on heritage-listed or culturally significant sites.

Engaging with local communities, Indigenous groups, or heritage stakeholders should ideally be conducted prior to the survey to define scope, gain cultural insights, and address sensitivities, though in some cases simultaneous consultation may be possible.

The data, findings, and condition assessments from the heritage conservation survey are essential inputs for developing the conservation treatment plan, which cannot be formulated without understanding the specific heritage values, deterioration patterns, and required interventions.
The survey identifies areas of concern, material types, and structural elements that require further detailed analysis and testing, so the survey must precede any invasive structural investigation.
Structural framing (walls, ceiling supports) must be in place to provide support and attachment points for supply duct hangers and supports.
The overall HVAC ductwork layout and main trunk lines must be planned and roughed in before individual supply ducts can be connected to the system.
Supply ducts must be fully installed before insulation can be applied to prevent condensation and improve thermal efficiency.
Supply ducts enclosed in walls or ceilings must be installed and inspected before drywall is closed up, as ducts are inaccessible after drywall is in place.
Supply duct terminations must be in place before diffusers and registers (air outlets) can be attached to the duct openings.
Return ducts are part of the ductwork system and must be roughed in as part of the overall ductwork installation before individual return duct components can be placed.
Duct insulation is typically applied after the return duct is installed to ensure complete coverage and thermal efficiency.
System balancing and airflow testing should occur after all ductwork, including return ducts, is installed to verify proper performance.
Framing must be inspected and approved before enclosing ductwork within walls and ceilings to ensure structural and fire safety compliance.
Return ducts must be fully installed before drywall is placed, as the ducts run within wall and ceiling cavities that will be enclosed by drywall.
Exhaust ducts require structural support and hangers attached to steel beams/framing, which must be in place before ductwork can be suspended or mounted.
The floor slab must be cured and load-bearing to support duct runs, support stands, and provide a stable working surface for duct installation.
Thermal/acoustic insulation and fireproofing lagging are applied to the exterior of installed ductwork after ducts are in place and sealed.
Pressure testing, smoke testing, and airflow balancing of the exhaust duct system must be performed after duct sections are fully assembled and sealed.
Fire dampers, volume control dampers, and motorized exhaust dampers installed within the duct system must be tested for operation after the ducts are in place.
The fresh air intake duct must be supported by the building's structural steel frame, which provides the primary support structure before any ductwork can be installed.
The roof deck provides the upper enclosure and mounting surface for the fresh air intake hood and duct penetration, required before ductwork can be run through the roof.

The outdoor air louver forms the weatherproof opening through which the fresh air intake duct connects to the outside; the louver must be in place first to establish the intake point and weather barrier.

successor: Fresh Air Intake Duct Pre-Commissioning Inspection
rationale: The fresh air intake duct must be fully installed and sealed before the air handling unit can be connected to it, to ensure the duct system is complete and airtight for proper airflow.
The fresh air intake duct must be in place to serve as the substrate for insulation; insulation cannot be applied until the duct is fully installed and supported.
The flexible duct connector must be attached to rigid ductwork, so the rigid duct sections must be installed first to provide a connection point.
Flexible duct connectors link air handling units or terminal boxes to ductwork; the HVAC equipment must be in place first so the connector can bridge the equipment to the duct system.
Insulation is applied over the installed flexible duct connector to prevent condensation and thermal loss; the connector must be in place before insulation can be wrapped around it.
The flexible duct connector must be fully installed and sealed to ensure an airtight connection before the HVAC system can be tested for air balance and proper airflow.

While typically the connector should be installed and tested before enclosing the ceiling for access and future maintenance, it is a soft preference because in some cases access panels can be provided after drywall.
The VCD is installed within the ductwork system; the ductwork must be in place to provide a mounting location and connection points for the damper.
Leak testing must be performed after the damper is installed to verify the complete duct system including all dampers is airtight.
System balancing requires all dampers to be in place and operational so airflow can be properly adjusted throughout the duct network.
While insulation can be installed up to the damper location, it is preferable to insulate after damper installation to avoid interfering with damper operation and access for adjustments.
Structural supports and hangers for the ductwork and damper must be in place before the damper can be safely mounted overhead.
Diffusers are the terminal units of an HVAC air distribution system; ductwork must be in place to supply conditioned air to the diffuser location.
Diffusers are typically mounted into or suspended from the ceiling grid; the ceiling support structure must be installed first to provide a mounting surface.
Air balancing requires all diffusers to be installed and connected so airflow measurements and adjustments can be performed at each terminal.

While diffusers can be installed after ceiling tiles are placed (by cutting openings), it is generally preferred to install diffusers first or concurrently to avoid tile damage and ensure proper alignment.

If the diffuser includes an electrically operated damper or sensor, rough-in wiring should be completed prior to diffuser installation for easier connection; however, this is a soft preference as wiring can be added later.
Physical ductwork must be installed before clash detection can verify that the installation matches the BIM model and identifies clashes with other building systems.
A digital BIM model containing all building systems (HVAC, plumbing, electrical, structural) must be created and federated before clash detection can be performed to check for inter-system conflicts.
Any clashes or coordination issues identified during the BIM clash detection process must be resolved, requiring rework or adjustment of the installed ductwork before the system can be finalized.
Clash detection must confirm that ductwork does not conflict with other building systems before the layout can be formally approved for continuation of construction.
Duct coordination and clash resolution must be completed before insulation is applied, as insulation would cover conflicts and make rework more difficult and costly.
Ductwork must be installed first to provide the housing and connection points for the air filter bank. The air filter bank is typically installed within or attached to the ductwork system.
The AHU must be in place because the air filter bank is often integrated as part of the AHU assembly or mounted directly to it. The filter bank serves as an intake component for the AHU.
The filter bank must be installed and in place before the system can be balanced and commissioned, as filters affect airflow, static pressure, and overall system performance.
All filters must be installed before the HVAC system is started and tested to prevent debris from entering and damaging system components such as coils and fans.

While not a strict physical requirement, it is preferable to install the filter bank before ceiling installation and final finishing to allow easier access for installation and to avoid having to cut or modify finished surfaces later.
Structural framing must be in place to provide support and attachment points for ductwork.
Roof must be installed to protect ductwork from weather damage before installation.
Ductwork occupies overhead space; electrical conduits and wiring are often routed around ducts, so ducts should be in place first to avoid conflicts.
Similar to electrical, plumbing pipes need to be routed around ductwork; installing ducts first helps coordinate space in ceilings and walls.
Ducts are often insulated after installation; thermal and acoustic insulation wraps around ductwork, so ducts must be in place first.
Shop drawings and detailing must be completed before fabrication begins to provide the precise dimensions, layouts, and material specifications needed for manufacturing duct sections.
Raw materials such as galvanized steel, aluminum, or stainless steel sheets, as well as insulation and sealants, must be procured and on-site or in the workshop before fabrication can commence.
The building's structural frame (steel or concrete) should be sufficiently complete to allow measurement verification and to enable the fabrication of ductwork to actual field dimensions.
Fabricated duct sections must be completed before they can be transported and installed in their final positions within the building.
Fabricated duct sections must be complete before insulation can be applied to them, either in the shop or on site.

successor: Duct Pressure Testing / Air Leakage Testing
rationale: Ductwork must be fully installed before pressure testing can be performed to check for air leaks.

predecessor: Duct Pressure Testing / Air Leakage Testing
rationale: Testing identifies leaks that must be sealed before the system can be considered complete.

predecessor: Duct Pressure Testing / Air Leakage Testing
rationale: Duct leakage testing must be completed before ducts are insulated, as insulation would conceal leaks and make repairs difficult.

predecessor: Duct Pressure Testing / Air Leakage Testing
rationale: Duct integrity must be verified before connecting HVAC equipment and commissioning the system to ensure proper airflow and performance.

predecessor: Duct Pressure Testing / Air Leakage Testing
rationale: Ducts must be tested and sealed before ceilings are enclosed to allow access for inspection and repairs.
Ducts must be fully installed and in place before they can be cleaned.

successor: Final HVAC System Balancing and Testing
rationale: Ducts must be clean before balancing airflows and testing system performance to avoid debris interfering with measurements.

All HVAC equipment (air handlers, chillers, boilers, pumps, ducts, diffusers, VAV boxes, etc.) must be physically installed before testing, adjusting, and balancing (TAB) can be performed on the system.
The complete ductwork system must be installed and sealed before air balancing can measure and adjust airflow rates at terminals.
All hydronic piping (chilled water, hot water, condenser water) must be installed before water balancing can take place.
Power must be run and connected to all HVAC equipment (fans, pumps, compressors, controls) before they can be started and balanced.
Building automation system (BAS) controllers, sensors, actuators, and DDC controls must be installed and operational to monitor and adjust setpoints during TAB procedures.

successor: Final System Startup and Integrated Testing
rationale: TAB must be completed before full-system integrated commissioning and startup, as balanced flows are prerequisites for verifying overall system performance.
Air and water flows must be balanced before temperature control loops can be properly calibrated and verified against design conditions.

successor: Final Filter Installation and Cleanliness Verification
rationale: While preferable to balance with final filters in place for accurate pressure drops, some projects install final filters after balancing to keep them clean; this is a soft preference for accuracy.
TAB must be completed and documented before the building can be handed over for occupancy, as it ensures HVAC systems meet design specifications for comfort and code compliance.

Radiant ceiling panels are typically installed after the main overhead mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work is completed, as these services run above the ceiling plane and must be in place before panels can be mounted.

predecessor: Ceiling Grid or Suspension System Installation
rationale: Radiant ceiling panels are either laid into or hung from a ceiling suspension grid; the grid must be installed first to provide the structural support for the panels.

If insulation is placed above the radiant panels, it may be easier to install after panels are in place to avoid disturbing them; however, insulation could alternatively be installed before panels depending on access.
The radiant panels must be physically mounted in their final position before the hydronic supply/return piping can be connected to each panel and the system pressure-tested.
Any finishing work, painting, or touch-up around the perimeter of the radiant panels should occur after the panels are installed to achieve a clean, integrated appearance.
The radiant manifold must be mounted on or after the slab is poured and cured, as the manifold connects to tubing embedded in the slab.
Insulation beneath the slab must be in place before any radiant tubing or manifold work begins to ensure proper thermal performance.
The radiant tubing must be laid in the slab before the manifold can be connected to it at the distribution point.
After the manifold is installed and all tubing connections are made, the entire radiant system must be pressure-tested before the slab is finished or covered.
The manifold must be in place and connected before the system can be flushed of debris and filled with water or glycol solution.
Radiant wall panels require a framed wall structure to be mounted onto. The framing provides the structural support and cavity for routing electrical connections and plumbing for the radiant system.
Electrical wiring and junction boxes must be installed within the wall cavity before radiant panels are placed, as the panels cover the wall surface and access would be blocked after installation.

If the radiant wall panel is hydronic (water-based), the supply and return piping must be run inside the wall before the panel is installed, as the panel connects to these lines and the wall would be closed off afterwards.
Radiant wall panels are typically finished with drywall compound, tape, and paint to create a seamless surface. The panel must be in place before these finishing layers are applied.

It is a soft preference to complete radiant wall panels before flooring to avoid damaging finished floors from scaffolding or work activity, but flooring could technically proceed beforehand if protective measures are taken.
Heat transfer plates must be placed on a stable, flat subfloor or underlayment surface to ensure proper contact and heat distribution.

predecessor: Layout and Secure Radiant Tubing Pathways
rationale: Tubing pathways must be marked and the tubing loosely placed so that heat transfer plates can be positioned over or alongside the tubing runs before final fastening.
The aluminum plates must be in place to receive and securely hold the radiant tubing, ensuring good thermal contact.

successor: Pour or Install Finished Floor Surface
rationale: Heat transfer plates must be fully installed before the finished floor (e.g., concrete, tile, hardwood) is placed over them to avoid accessibility issues and damage.
Plates must be installed with tubing secured to allow for a complete system pressure test before covering with finished flooring.
Radiant piping must be installed before thermostats can be placed since the thermostat controls and monitors the radiant zone system which requires the piping to be in place.
Electrical wiring and power supply rough-in must be completed to provide power and connectivity for the thermostat/zone controller installation.
Wall surfaces must be finished before mounting the thermostat/controller to ensure proper anchoring and finished appearance.
The thermostat and zone controller must be installed and connected before the radiant system can be commissioned, balanced, and tested for proper operation.
While final electrical trim can proceed in parallel, it is preferred to have the thermostat installed first so that final connections and terminations can be verified and tested together.
Zone valves are installed onto piping systems; piping must be in place before zone valves can be mounted and connected.
Zone valves must be installed and in place before the overall HVAC system can be tested for proper operation and balancing.
The actuator must be physically mounted on the zone valve before control wiring can be connected to it.
The zone valve must be physically installed before it can be commissioned and calibrated for operation.
Insulation is typically installed prior to valve installation for accessibility, but it is a soft preference as insulation can be worked around if needed.

predecessor: Rough-in Plumbing for Hot and Cold Water Lines
rationale: Hot and cold water supply lines must be roughed in and stubbed out to the valve location before the thermostatic mixing valve can be physically connected to the water supply.

successor: Connect Supply Piping to Mixing Valve Outlet
rationale: The mixing valve must be mounted and secured before downstream piping can be attached to its outlet port to deliver tempered water.

successor: Pressure Test Hot Water Distribution System
rationale: The mixing valve must be in place and connected before the entire hot water distribution system can be pressure-tested, because the valve is a component of that system.

successor: Commission / Balance Hot Water Recirculation System
rationale: Temperature balancing and flow adjustment of the recirculation loop can only be performed after the thermostatic mixing valve is installed and operational.

predecessor: Mount Mixing Valve Bracket or Support
rationale: The valve's mounting bracket or support structure must be securely fastened to the wall or framing before the valve itself can be attached.
Electrical rough-in must be completed before infloor tubing is installed to avoid conflicts and ensure access for wiring without damaging the tubing.
Plumbing rough-in must be completed before infloor tubing to avoid interference and allow proper routing of pipes before tubing is laid.
The subfloor or base surface must be clean, level, and prepared before tubing can be laid to ensure proper installation and coverage.
Concrete or lightweight gypcrete must be poured over the infloor tubing to embed it, protecting it and providing thermal mass for the radiant heating system.
Immediately after installation and before covering with concrete, the tubing must be pressure tested to ensure there are no leaks, as leaks would be catastrophic once slab is poured.
Radiant loop tubing must be installed and connected before pressure testing can be performed to verify system integrity.

successor: Pour/Place Concrete Slab Over Radiant Loops
rationale: Pressure testing must be completed and pass before concrete is poured over the radiant loops, as any leaks would be inaccessible for repair after slab placement.

While the manifold connection can be done before testing, typically the loops are tested individually or prior to permanent manifold connections to isolate leaks; final connection to the system is often completed after successful testing.

predecessor: Install Piping for Radiant System (Supply/Return Lines)
rationale: The supply and return piping must be installed to allow the system to be filled and pressurized for testing.
Edge insulation is typically installed before slab pour and can be done before or after pressure testing, but final insulation checks or adjustments may occur after testing passes.
The radiant tubing must be fully installed, laid out, and secured in position before concrete can be poured over it, as the tubing is embedded within the concrete slab.
The radiant tubing system must be pressure-tested and verified leak-free before concrete is poured, because after the pour the tubing becomes inaccessible for repairs.
The subgrade must be properly graded, compacted, and leveled to provide a stable base before the concrete slab (with embedded tubing) is poured.
A vapor barrier and/or rigid insulation layer is typically placed beneath the slab to control moisture and thermal loss, and must be installed before the concrete pour.
After the concrete is poured over the radiant tubing, it must undergo a specified curing period to gain adequate strength and prevent cracking before any subsequent loads or finishes are applied.
Immediately after pouring, the concrete surface must be screeded, floated, and troweled to achieve the required finish and flatness before it sets.

While supply/return lines may be connected beforehand, final connections from the embedded tubing to the distribution manifold and circulation system occur after the pour is complete and concrete has cured.

predecessor: Install mounting brackets and structural support
rationale: Mounting brackets and structural supports must be in place before the heater can be physically attached and secured.

predecessor: Complete rough electrical wiring to heater location
rationale: Electrical supply wiring must be run to the heater location before the heater unit can be connected to power.

successor: Connect electrical supply and test heater
rationale: The heater must be physically installed before final electrical connections and functional testing can be performed.

successor: Install ceiling or wall finish around heater
rationale: Finishing work around the heater (e.g., drywall, trim) should occur after the heater is mounted to allow proper fit and clearance.
System commissioning typically follows installation to verify performance, but could be done concurrently if needed.
The building structure and enclosure must be defined before radiant system layout can be designed, as radiant tubing placement depends on slab geometry, floor plan, and structural zones.
Overall mechanical system zoning and load calculations must be completed to determine the heating/cooling zones that the radiant system will serve.
The radiant system design and layout must be finalized before hydronic piping and manifolds can be installed, as it defines tubing routes, manifold locations, and circuit lengths.
Radiant tubing layout must be completed and secured in place before any slab or gypcrete can be poured over the tubing.
Control zones and sensor locations are determined by the radiant layout design, so rough-in of thermostat wiring and controls must follow the completed design.
The dormer roof structure (rafters, ridge board, etc.) must be erected first to establish the dormer's frame, against which the cheek walls can be built and supported.
The dormer floor or base platform must be framed to provide a structural base and support for the cheek wall construction.
The main roof must be cut and framed to create the dormer opening before the cheek walls can be installed, as they sit within or against this opening.
The cheek wall framing must be complete before exterior sheathing (e.g., plywood or OSB) can be applied to the wall.
The cheek wall framing must be built and the rough opening formed before the dormer window can be installed into that opening.
The dormer roof is an extension of the main roof structure and must be built after the main roof framing is in place to ensure proper integration, structural support, and waterproofing continuity.
The dormer roof rests on the dormer walls; therefore, the wall framing for the dormer must be completed before the roof can be installed to provide the necessary structural base.
The dormer roof structure must be in place before sheathing can be applied to it, as the sheathing is fastened directly to the roof framing.
Flashing and waterproofing at the intersection of the dormer roof and main roof must be installed after the dormer roof is complete to seal the joint and prevent water intrusion.
Exterior siding or finish on the dormer walls is typically installed after the dormer roof is in place to allow proper lapping and flashing integration at the roof-to-wall intersection.
The dormer framing provides the structural support onto which the fascia board is attached. Fascia boards cannot be installed without the underlying frame being complete.
The roof sheathing covers the dormer frame and provides the surface edge against which the fascia board is fitted. Fascia boards are installed along the edges of the roof sheathing.

The fascia board forms the outer edge that the soffit (underside of the eave) attaches to. Soffit installation typically occurs after fascia is in place, as the soffit fits beneath and against the fascia.
Gutters are mounted directly onto the fascia board. The fascia must be securely installed first to provide the mounting surface for gutter brackets and the gutter system.

While it is physically possible to paint fascia at a later stage, it is standard practice and more efficient to paint or finish the fascia board before gutters and soffits are installed, to avoid overspray or needing to work around those elements.
The dormer soffit is installed onto the framed dormer structure; the framing provides the structural support and attachment surface for the soffit.
Sheathing covers the dormer framing and provides a solid substrate; soffit installation requires sheathing to be in place for proper attachment and finish.
The roof deck must be installed to define the roofline and provide the underlying surface adjacent to the dormer soffit area.
Soffit must be installed before the surrounding siding and trim work so that the siding can overlap or butt against the soffit for weatherproofing and a finished appearance.

While windows are often installed before soffit in some sequences, typically soffit finishing is done after windows are set to allow proper flashing integration; this is a soft preference depending on design.
The roof structure must be framed to provide the supporting structure into which the dormer window frame is integrated.
Roof sheathing provides the substrate and opening for dormer installation; the dormer frame cannot be placed until the roof deck is prepared.
The window frame must be in place before the glass or glazing units can be installed into it.
Flashing is applied around the dormer frame after it is installed to seal against water intrusion.
Exterior siding and trim are installed after the dormer frame is in place to finish the exterior wall integration.
The dormer structure must be framed and built before the lintel can be installed, as the lintel spans the opening within the dormer.
The lintel provides structural support above the dormer opening; roof sheathing and covering can only be applied after the lintel is in place.
The lintel forms the top of the dormer window opening; the window frame cannot be installed until the lintel is fixed in position above the opening.
The main wall framing must be complete to provide the structural support into which the dormer and its lintel are integrated.
Exterior cladding and finishing around the dormer opening can only be installed after the lintel is in place to ensure proper weatherproofing and structural continuity.
