The dormer sill sits on top of and is supported by the dormer frame structure; the frame must be in place to provide a mounting surface for the sill.
The roof decking provides the underlying structural surface and waterproofing layer that the dormer sill integrates with; decking must be complete before cutting and fitting the sill.
The dormer window frame sits directly on the dormer sill; the sill must be installed to provide a level base and structural support for the window unit.
Flashing is installed around the sill to create a watertight seal; it wraps over and integrates with the sill, so the sill must be in place first.

While siding and trim can be installed after the sill, it is a soft preference because trim can be fitted around the sill later; however, best practice is to complete sill first to ensure proper drainage and aesthetics.
The main roof framing must be in place to provide structural support and attachment points for the dormer header beam.
The exact location and dimensions of the dormer opening must be marked on the roof before the header beam can be positioned and installed.
The roof sheathing and framing must be cut to create the dormer opening before the header beam can be placed across the top of the opening.
Jack rafters that frame the dormer opening bear on or connect to the header beam, so the header must be in place first.
The header beam forms the top support for the dormer side walls; side wall framing cannot proceed without the header beam installed.
Dormers are structural projections that are built into and onto the roof; the main roof framing must be in place to provide the structural support and opening for the dormer.
The roof deck provides the base surface onto which the dormer is integrated; sheathing must be complete to establish the roof plane for dormer layout and cutting.
Underlayment is applied continuously over the entire roof surface including dormers; dormer construction must be finished so that the underlayment can wrap seamlessly over the dormer structure.
Flashing details around dormers (step flashing, counter-flashing) must be installed after the dormer structure is complete to seal the junction between the dormer and the main roof.
The dormer's exterior walls must be framed and constructed before they can be sheathed with OSB or plywood and before siding is applied.
The dormer roof structure and framing must be built first to provide the substrate and support for the roof covering (tiles or slates).
Sarking, felt or underlay must be installed over the dormer roof structure before tiles or slates are laid to provide waterproofing and a weather-resistant barrier.
Roof battens must be fixed to the sarking/underlay to create a fixing base onto which tiles or slates are securely attached.
Ridge and hip tiles cap the junction at the top of the roof slopes, and can only be installed after the main field tiles/slates are laid on the dormer roof.

Flashing work (lead or metal flashings around dormer cheeks and junctions) is typically completed after or concurrently with tiling to weatherproof the transitions, but critical flashings sealing the sides rely on the tiling being in place.
The glazing (windows) cannot be installed until the dormer frame is built and structurally complete, as the frame provides the rough opening and structural support for the windows.
Sheathing must be installed on the dormer frame to create the proper wall enclosure and weather-resistant barrier before windows can be set into the dormer openings.
Flashing and waterproofing details around the dormer openings need to be in place before glazing installation to ensure proper drainage and prevent water intrusion behind the windows.
Exterior and interior trim work around the dormer windows must be performed after the glazing is installed because the trim is fitted directly against the installed window frames.

Air sealing and insulation around the dormer windows can only be completed after the windows are installed and secured in place, as the insulation fills gaps between the window frame and the rough opening.
The dormer frame (studs, rafters, headers) must be fully constructed to create the cavities into which insulation is installed. Without framing, there is no structure in which to place insulation.

The exterior sheathing (plywood/OSB) must be applied to the dormer frame to enclose the exterior side before insulation is placed, preventing insulation from falling out and providing a backing surface.
The roof deck (sheathing over dormer rafters) must be installed to enclose the top of the dormer before insulation is placed in the roof/ceiling assembly.
A vapor retarder/barrier is installed over the insulation (on the warm-in-winter side) to control moisture diffusion. This must occur after the insulation is in place.
Interior finish (drywall/plasterboard) covers the insulation and vapor barrier. Drywall cannot be installed until the insulation and vapor barrier are in place within the framed cavities.
The roof deck provides the structural base and opening location for the dormer; without the roof deck in place, there is no surface to cut or form the dormer opening through.
The main roof's structural framing (rafters, trusses) must be complete so that the dormer opening can be properly integrated and structurally supported within the existing roof system.

After the opening is formed, headers and trimming members must be installed around the opening to provide structural support and proper load transfer before any dormer walls or roof components are added.
The dormer walls must be framed directly off the structural opening; the opening defines the footprint and structural connection point for the dormer walls to attach to the main roof.

Once the opening is cut through the roof deck, the exposed edges must be flashed and weatherproofed promptly to prevent water intrusion into the building envelope before proceeding with dormer construction.
A thorough site survey and assessment is required to understand existing conditions, structural loads, and constraints before designing a dormer and submitting for planning approval.
Architectural drawings and design proposals for the dormer must be prepared as they form the core submission documents for planning approval.
A structural feasibility study is required to confirm that the proposed dormer design is structurally viable; this information supports the planning application.
Detailed structural engineering design for the dormer can only commence after planning approval is granted, as the approved design sets the parameters for load calculations and structural detailing.

While some preliminary material sourcing may occur, full procurement and ordering of dormer-specific materials such as roof windows and structural timber should wait until planning approval is secured to avoid wasted expenditure if the design is rejected or modified.
The rake cap sits on top of the rake (fascia) board along the gable edge of a roof, so the rake board must be installed first to provide a mounting surface for the cap.
While soffit is typically installed before rake cap in most sequences, if rake cap is installed first, soffit can follow; however, this is often a preference rather than a hard constraint.
Rake caps are installed along the gable trim and must be in place before gutters are installed along the eaves to ensure proper flashing integration and water diversion.
The roof deck (sheathing) must be installed before rake caps because the rake cap attaches to the edge of the roof structure and requires the deck to be in place for proper alignment and fastening.
Rake cap installation must be completed before rake edge flashing is installed, as the cap forms part of the edge detail that flashing integrates with to prevent water intrusion at the gable ends.
The eave cap is installed at the top of wall framing, so the wall frame must be in place to provide structural support and attachment points for the eave cap.
Eave caps interface with roof sheathing at the eaves, so roof sheathing must be completed to provide the proper surface and alignment for eave cap installation.
Fascia boards are typically installed after eave caps because the eave cap provides the underlying support and nailing surface for the fascia at the roof edge.
Gutters are mounted to the fascia or directly below the eave cap; the eave cap must be in place to define the roof edge profile before gutters can be attached.
The eave cap covers the top edge of the soffit assembly, so soffit panels must be installed after the eave cap is in place to ensure proper overlapping and weather sealing.
The parapet wall must be built before the cap/coping can be installed, as the coping sits on top of the wall as a protective covering.
The roof membrane is typically installed before the coping, as the coping often secures the membrane edge and flashing at the parapet top.
Counterflashing is installed over the coping to cover the gap between wall and membrane, and must be completed after the coping is in place.
Water testing of the roof edge and parapet details should occur after coping installation to verify weatherproofing, though this is a quality control step rather than a physical requirement.
Scaffolding or access equipment around the parapet can be removed after the coping is installed, but this is a sequencing preference for safety and efficiency rather than a hard physical constraint.
The roof deck provides the structural base upon which the edge cap is mounted; the cap cannot be installed without a completed deck.
The waterproof membrane must be in place before the edge cap is installed to ensure a continuous waterproof barrier and proper flashing integration.
Insulation is typically placed beneath the membrane and edge cap; the cap secures the edge of the insulation and membrane system.
While gutters can sometimes be installed concurrently, it is preferred to install the edge cap first so that the gutter hangers can be properly aligned and secured under the cap's drip edge.
The edge cap is the final piece of the roof perimeter flashing system; inspection of the completed flashing assembly must occur after the cap is in place.
The roof decking provides the structural base upon which the ventilated ridge cap is installed; without a completed deck surface, the ridge cap has no substrate to attach to.
Underlayment must be in place over the roof deck to provide a weather-resistant barrier before the ridge cap is installed, preventing moisture intrusion at the ridge.

The ventilated ridge cap is applied at the peak of the roof, and the adjacent field shingles must be installed first so that the ridge cap overlaps and integrates with the shingle courses for proper weatherproofing.

successor: Install Ridge Vent / Ridge Cap Shingles (Finishing)
rationale: The ventilated ridge cap itself serves as the final ridge closure component; once it is in place, any finishing ridge shingles or cap pieces are applied over or along it to complete the ridge detail.
The ridge cap is typically the last major roofing component installed, so completing it is a prerequisite before the final roof inspection can be performed.
The snow guard cap strip is installed on top of the snow guards, so the snow guards must be in place first.
The cap strip is a finishing component; final roofing inspections and system sign-off typically occur after all components including cap strips are installed.
It is a soft preference to test the snow management system only after all components including cap strips are installed to validate the full assembly.
The roof cap sits on top of the roof deck and cannot be installed until the deck surface is in place to provide structural support.
Roof underlayment (e.g., felt paper or synthetic membrane) must be laid over the deck before the cap can be installed to provide waterproofing and a proper substrate.
Base flashing and step flashing around penetrations and edges must be installed prior to the roof cap to ensure proper water shedding and integration.

In many assemblies, the roof cap (often a rigid cap sheet or metal cap) is the outermost layer; insulation above the deck may be installed before the cap, but if any insulation sits on top of the cap, it cannot be placed until the cap is secure.
The roof cap is a finishing element; a final inspection must occur after all cap components are in place to verify complete installation and water tightness.
The roof deck must be fully installed to provide the structural base onto which cap sealing and caulking is applied.
The waterproof membrane or underlayment must be in place before cap sealing and caulking can be applied as a final weatherproofing layer over the membrane.
Cap flashing must be installed so that the sealing and caulking can seal the joints and edges between the flashing and roof components.
The sealing and caulking must be fully cured and complete before a final roof inspection and water testing can be performed to verify weathertightness.
It is standard practice to complete all sealing and caulking work before final cleanup and handover of the roof area to prevent contamination or damage to finished seals.
The roof must be fully installed before any inspection or maintenance of the roof cap can take place, as the cap is part of the roof assembly.
Inspection and maintenance of the roof cap must be completed before final certification can be issued, as certification requires verification that all roof components are in acceptable condition.
Safe access to the roof cap area must be established before any inspection or maintenance work can be performed at height.
Any necessary repairs or adjustments identified during inspection must be made before applying final weatherproofing seals around the roof cap.
Safety barriers and fall protection systems must be in place before workers access the roof cap area for inspection and maintenance work.
The roof deck provides the structural base onto which flashing is integrated; flashing cannot be installed without the roof deck being in place.
Flashing is typically installed over or integrated with the underlayment to ensure water tightness; underlayment must be in place first.
Flashing at wall-roof intersections requires wall sheathing to be installed to provide a surface for flashing attachment and integration.

Flashing must be integrated before the final roofing material (shingles, tiles, etc.) is applied, as flashing is installed as part of the waterproofing layer beneath or integrated with the roofing material.
Flashing integration around penetrations and intersections must be completed before exterior cladding is installed to ensure proper drainage and waterproofing behind the cladding.
The subfloor requires a stable, level foundation (slab or crawlspace) to be installed and cured before any subflooring can be placed.
Concrete or masonry foundations need sufficient curing time to achieve strength before bearing the load of the subfloor system.
Underlayment (e.g., plywood or OSB sheeting) is laid directly on top of and fastened to the subfloor structure, so the subfloor must be in place first.
Wall framing is erected on top of the completed subfloor deck, which provides the working platform and load-bearing base for walls.

While floor coverings (tile, hardwood, carpet) typically follow subfloor and underlayment, in some cases they could be done later; however, standard sequencing places them after subfloor completion to protect the finish.
The subfloor must be clean, level, and fully prepared before any floor covering or transition strip can be installed, as the transition strip sits atop the finished flooring and subfloor system.
Transition strips bridge the gap between two different finished flooring surfaces; therefore, both adjacent floor coverings must be fully installed first.
While baseboards can be installed before transition strips, it is common practice to install transition strips first to ensure proper overlap and clean visual lines at the floor interface.
Transition strips are often installed before final sealing or finishing coats so that the sealant can lap onto the strip edges for a continuous moisture barrier.

Floor transition strips must be installed before heavy furniture is placed or the space is occupied, as moving furniture across an unfinished floor joint can damage both the flooring edges and the strip material.
The concrete or deck surface must be prepared, cleaned, and cured before applying anti-slip coating to ensure proper adhesion.
A primer must be applied and dried before the anti-slip coating to achieve proper bond strength with the substrate.
The anti-slip coating must be applied and then allowed to cure/dry fully before any foot traffic or subsequent finishes are placed over it.
The anti-slip coating/nosing must be fully installed and cured before the final inspection can verify compliance with safety and quality standards.
Once anti-slip coating is applied, adjacent finishing works (e.g., painting, tiling) should be completed or protected to avoid contamination of the fresh coating.
A level, cured, and clean subfloor (concrete slab or plywood underlayment) is physically required as the base for any flooring material; installing flooring on an unprepared surface leads to failure.
All conduit, piping, and wiring that run beneath the floor must be installed and inspected before the finished floor goes in, as accessing them afterward would require tearing out the flooring.
In typical construction sequences (e.g., platform framing), floor decking is completed first to provide a stable work platform for erecting walls on top of it.

Finished floors should be installed before baseboards, trim, and cabinetry to allow those elements to sit flush on top of the flooring and to avoid damaging the finished floor surface with heavy cabinet installation.
Floor installation must be fully completed and cured (if applicable) before the building can be used or occupied to prevent damage to the flooring and ensure safety.
The concrete slab must be poured and fully cured before grinding can begin, as grinding on uncured concrete would damage the surface and result in poor finish.
The subfloor must be leveled and smoothed to ensure uniform grinding depth and prevent damage to the grinding equipment.
Sealers and coatings require a clean, polished surface for proper adhesion; grinding and polishing must be completed first to achieve the required surface profile.
After grinding and polishing, the floor should be cleaned to remove dust and debris, but this is a soft preference as cleaning can sometimes be done in parallel with other finishing trades.

successor: Installation of Floor Coverings (e.g., tiles, carpet)
rationale: Typically polished concrete is the final floor finish, so floor coverings are not installed over it. However, in some cases polished concrete serves as a base; but this is a soft preference rather than a hard constraint.
The floor must be smooth, level, and free of debris before waterproofing can be applied to ensure proper adhesion and uniform coverage of the waterproofing membrane.
The concrete slab must be fully cured (typically minimum 28 days) to prevent moisture entrapment and ensure the waterproofing membrane bonds correctly without cracking or blistering.
All underground and in-slab plumbing pipes, drains, and floor wastes must be installed and pressure-tested before waterproofing, as any subsequent modifications would breach the waterproof membrane.

The waterproofing membrane must be fully cured and tested (e.g., flood testing) before tiles or finished flooring can be installed on top, to protect the membrane from damage and ensure a watertight seal.

In wet areas, it is good practice to complete floor waterproofing before wall framing to allow the membrane to extend up walls; however, this can be reversed if careful detailing is used, making it a soft preference.
A structural assessment must be completed before floor demolition to identify load-bearing elements, hidden utilities, and potential hazards, ensuring safe demolition planning.
Any hazardous materials such as asbestos or lead paint must be abated prior to floor demolition to prevent exposure to toxic dust and debris during the demolition process.
All utilities (electrical, plumbing, gas) serving the floor area must be disconnected and isolated before demolition to prevent electrocution, flooding, gas leaks, or fire.
Demolished floor materials must be removed and disposed of immediately after demolition to clear the workspace, maintain safety, and prepare for subsequent construction activities.
After the existing floor is demolished and removed, the exposed subfloor or slab must be prepared (cleaned, repaired, leveled) before new flooring or structural work can be installed.
The floor slab must be fully installed, cured, and structurally sound before any inspection and testing can be performed to verify its integrity.
Concrete must achieve sufficient curing time to reach design strength before conducting strength tests (e.g., compressive strength tests) and surface inspections.
Reinforcement must be placed and tied before concrete is poured; post-pour inspection verifies proper cover, spacing, and structural compliance.
All floor tests (e.g., flatness, levelness, moisture, strength) must pass before applying final floor finishes, coatings, or toppings to avoid trapping defects or moisture issues.
Floor structural integrity must be verified before vertical elements are erected on top of it, ensuring the supporting floor can safely carry the loads.
The timber stud frame must be erected on a solid, level base, which is typically the concrete ground slab. The slab provides the foundation and anchoring point for the bottom plate of the stud wall.
The floor structure must be in place to provide a platform and base for the timber stud walls to be erected upon.
Any below-slab or in-slab waterproofing and services must be completed before walls are erected, as access to the slab area becomes restricted after framing.
The roof or ceiling framing bears onto the top plate of the stud wall; the vertical stud frame must be complete to support the roof structure.
External cladding, lining, or sheathing is fixed directly onto the timber stud frame; the frame must be fully erected and braced before sheathing can be applied.

Vertical battens (counter battens) are installed over and perpendicular to horizontal battens to create a drainage cavity and provide a nailing surface for the final cladding. The horizontal battens must be fixed to the structure first.
The water-resistive barrier must be installed over the sheathing before any battens are placed, to protect the building envelope from moisture intrusion.

successor: Install Final Cladding (e.g., siding, weatherboards, metal panels)
rationale: Vertical counter battens provide the structural nailing surface and the drainage cavity for the final cladding material; cladding cannot be attached directly to the structure without this furring layer.

While some flashings may be installed prior, final trim and flashings that interface with the cladding surface are best installed after the counter battens are in place to ensure proper alignment and integration with the drainage plane.
The starter strip and J-channel are typically installed over the wall sheathing to provide a mounting base and edge trim for siding. Sheathing must be in place first to give a solid backing.
House wrap (weather-resistant barrier) is installed over sheathing and before trim/j-channel to provide moisture protection behind the siding and trim.

The starter strip serves as the bottom attachment point and support for the first course of siding panels. J-channel around windows/doors receives and secures siding edges, so siding cannot be installed before these trims are in place.
Corner posts typically interlock with or cover the ends of J-channel and starter strips at building corners, so the starter/J-channel must be installed first to allow proper overlapping and sealing.

While soffit can be sequenced before or after J-channel in some cases, it is preferable to install J-channel first at the soffit-to-wall transition to ensure proper alignment and a finished look, though not a strict physical necessity.
Wall surface must be prepared (clean, smooth, and free of debris) before corner trim or stop bead can be properly installed and adhered.
Corner trim and stop beads serve as guide edges for plaster/stucco application; the first coat cannot be applied until the beads are secured in place to define corners and termination points.
The structural substrate (framing and sheathing) must be in place to provide a mounting surface for nailing or adhering corner trim and stop beads.
Corner beads and stop beads must be fully installed before the final finish coat is applied, as they define the corner profile and control the thickness and edge of the finish layer.

successor: Taping and Joint Compound Application (for drywall corners)
rationale: For drywall systems, corner beads must be installed before taping and joint compound work begins, as the bead provides the metal or vinyl corner reinforcement that gets embedded in the compound.
Flashings must be installed around windows and doors after they are in place to seal the gaps between the frame and the surrounding wall.
The rough openings must be framed and the exterior sheathing installed to provide a substrate for flashing installation around windows and doors.

The weather resistive barrier (house wrap or building paper) is typically installed over the sheathing but integrated with flashings; window and door flashings are often installed after the WRB is in place or integrated with it to ensure proper water drainage and continuity.
Exterior cladding or siding is installed over the flashed openings to cover and protect the flashings, ensuring water is directed outward and does not penetrate behind the cladding.

Interior drywall, trim, and finishes around windows and doors are typically completed after exterior flashings are in place to prevent moisture damage to interior materials, though this is a practical preference rather than a strict physical requirement.
Wall ties are used to connect masonry walls to other structural elements; the masonry walls must be in place before wall ties can be installed to connect them.
Wall ties fix the masonry wall to the structural frame; the frame must be erected first to provide the substrate for tie attachment.
Wall ties are installed within the cavity wall; insulation is typically placed around or after the ties are fixed in position.

successor: Inner Leaf Blockwork / Inner Wall Construction
rationale: Wall ties connect the outer masonry leaf to the inner leaf or structure; ties must be placed as the inner leaf is built up, but the outer leaf and tie positioning precedes completion of inner leaf courses.
It is good practice to complete all wall tie fixing before finishing surfaces, but not a strict physical necessity in all cases.
The structural frame must be complete to provide a stable load-bearing surface for cladding attachment.
The roof structure must be in place to provide overhead protection and a top anchor point for cladding panels.
The waterproofing membrane must be applied to the structural substrate before cladding to ensure the building envelope is watertight.
Window and door frames are typically set into the cladding openings, so cladding must be installed first to define the rough openings.
Interior finishes such as drywall and plaster must be protected from weather; cladding provides the weather-tight enclosure needed before interior work proceeds.
Boards must be cut to their final dimensions before priming, as cutting after priming would damage the primer coating and create uncoated edges.
The board surface must be sanded smooth and cleaned of dust/debris to ensure proper adhesion of the primer to the substrate.
Boards may need to be acclimated to the job site moisture content to prevent warping or adhesion failure after priming.
Primer must be fully applied and dried before any topcoat or paint can be applied, as the primer provides the necessary base for paint adhesion and sealing.

Priming must be completed before boards are installed in their final positions, as it is impractical to properly prime edges and backsides after installation, and primer needs to cure in a controlled environment.
The cladding panels must be installed and fixed in place before any painting or finishing can be applied to their surfaces.
The cladding surfaces must be cleaned, sanded, primed, and treated to ensure proper adhesion of paint and finish materials.
Safe working access (scaffolding, platforms, or lifts) must be erected to allow workers to reach all cladding surfaces for painting and finishing.

successor: Inspection and Quality Control of Cladding Finish
rationale: Quality control inspection of the paint and finish work can only be performed after the painting and finishing process is fully complete.

successor: Protection and Curing of Finished Surfaces
rationale: Protective measures and curing time for the painted/finished surfaces must begin only after painting and finishing application is complete.

The exact layer composition, material types, and thicknesses of the wall assembly must be fully detailed before the U-value (thermal transmittance) can be calculated, as the U-value depends on the thermal resistance of each layer.
The thermal conductivity (k-value) and thickness of each material in the wall assembly must be known to compute the overall thermal resistance and U-value.
The calculated U-value serves as the input for checking whether the wall assembly meets building code or energy standard thermal performance requirements.
The U-value is a required input parameter for whole-building energy modeling; however, placeholder values could be used initially, making this a soft preference rather than a hard constraint.

The U-value and the temperature gradient across the wall assembly are needed to assess the risk of interstitial condensation, which requires knowing the thermal performance of the completed wall build-up.
The thermal insulation properties (type, thickness, placement) are critical inputs for calculating surface temperatures and condensation risk (glazing/thermal bridging).
The heating, ventilation, and air conditioning design determines internal temperature and humidity conditions needed for condensation risk assessment.
The building envelope design (walls, roof, windows, air barrier) defines the thermal and moisture performance characteristics that condensation analysis depends on.

Regulatory compliance (e.g., Building Regulations Approved Document F and L in the UK) typically requires a condensation risk analysis report to be submitted before the building warrant or final approval can be granted.

successor: Final Insulation and VCL (Vapour Control Layer) Installation
rationale: The condensation risk analysis may recommend changes to insulation placement or VCL type/position; therefore the as-built installation of these layers must follow the analysis.
Scaffolding must be erected to provide safe access to external walls before any maintenance or re-coating work can begin.
A thorough inspection is required to identify cracks, damp issues, or surface damage that must be repaired before re-coating can be applied.
The wall surface must be cleaned of dirt, mold, and loose material to ensure proper adhesion of the new coating.
Scaffolding can only be dismantled after all wall maintenance and re-coating work is complete, as it is still needed for access.

successor: Final Quality Inspection of External Walls
rationale: A final inspection of the coating finish, coverage, and quality must be performed after the re-coating work is completed to ensure it meets specifications.
Fabric wall panels require a structural wall framework to be in place to attach to, as they are non-structural finishes mounted onto the framing.

Electrical wiring and outlets must be installed within the wall cavity before fabric panels are placed, as accessing wiring after panel installation would require damaging or removing the finished panels.
Any plumbing lines inside the wall must be completed before enclosing the wall with fabric panels, to avoid costly rework and damage to the finished surface.
Insulation must be placed within wall cavities before fabric panels are installed, as the panels permanently enclose the wall space and prevent later access for adding insulation.
Baseboards and trim are typically installed after wall paneling/finish is complete, as they abut the finished wall surface and cover the gap between the wall and floor.
Padded wall tiles require a stable wall framing structure to be installed first, as they are mounted or adhered to framed walls.
A smooth, solid substrate (e.g., plywood or drywall) must be in place before padded wall tiles can be attached, ensuring proper adhesion and a flat surface.
All rough-in work (conduit, wiring, pipes) within the wall cavities must be completed before wall tiles are installed, as accessing these after tiling would require removal.
Trim and baseboards are installed after padded wall tiles to cover edges and provide a finished appearance, ensuring clean transitions and protecting tile edges.

Any painting or touch-up work adjacent to the padded wall tiles is typically done after tile installation to avoid damaging the tile surface, though this is a soft preference as paint can be applied before with careful masking.
The structural wall must be completed to provide a stable mounting surface for the green/living wall modules.
Waterproofing must be in place behind the living wall to protect the building structure from moisture damage.
Irrigation supply lines and drainage connections must be roughed in within the wall cavity before modules are mounted.
Living wall modules must be mounted and secured before plants can be inserted into the module pockets or trays.
Modules must be in place so that drip lines and irrigation emitters can be connected to the module-integrated watering system.
Gypsum board substrate requires a completed metal stud framework to be mounted onto, as the gypsum boards are screwed directly into the studs for support.

All electrical wiring, outlet boxes, plumbing pipes, and other rough-in services must be installed within the wall cavities before the gypsum boards are installed, as they become inaccessible once the substrate is closed up.
Insulation must be placed inside the wall cavities before gypsum board is applied, as the boards permanently enclose the insulation within the wall assembly.

The taping and joint compound finishing process can only begin after the gypsum boards are fully installed and secured, as the joints between boards must be prepared and filled to create a smooth surface.
Paint and other wall finishes require a complete, taped, and mudded gypsum board surface as the base substrate for proper adhesion and aesthetic appearance.

Wall framing sub-structure requires a completed foundation or slab to provide a stable, level base for framing. The load-bearing walls must be anchored to the foundation, which must be fully cured and structurally ready.

Sill plates must be installed and anchored to the foundation before wall framing can begin, as the bottom plate of the wall frame sits directly on the sill plate to transfer loads and provide a connection point.

Termite treatment and moisture barriers must be applied to the foundation area before enclosing the sub-structure with wall framing, as it is physically difficult or impossible to properly treat these areas once the walls are erected.

Rough-in of electrical wiring, plumbing pipes, and other MEP services within sub-structure walls can only begin after the wall framing is complete, as the stud cavities, top plates, and blocking provide the chase and support for these installations.

Wall sheathing (such as plywood or OSB) is applied directly to the exterior face of the framed walls. The structural frame must be fully assembled and plumb before sheathing can be attached to provide lateral stability and enclosure.
The substrate must be clean, dry, and free of dust, oil, or debris to ensure proper adhesion of the adhesive and mechanical fixing.
Any cracks, voids, or uneven surfaces must be repaired and leveled before applying adhesive or mechanical fixings to ensure a sound and durable bond.
Where specified, a primer must be applied and fully cured to promote adhesion between the substrate and the adhesive system.
After installation, the adhesive must be allowed to cure undisturbed for the manufacturer's specified duration before any loads are applied.
Mechanical fixings may penetrate the substrate; sealing around fixings must follow installation to maintain weathertightness.
Scaffolding and access equipment must be in place to allow workers to safely reach all surfaces that need preparation and priming.
The work area must be free of debris, dust, and obstructions to ensure a clean surface for effective preparation and primer adhesion.
A thorough inspection of the substrate must be completed to identify defects, moisture issues, or structural problems before preparation work begins.
After priming, sufficient drying and curing time is physically required before any subsequent coating or finishing can be applied.
The primer must be fully applied and cured before the final decorative or protective coating can be applied to ensure proper adhesion and finish quality.
Wall framing provides the structural support and substrate onto which soft wall panels are attached; panels cannot be installed without a framed wall surface.

Electrical wiring and outlet boxes must be placed within the wall cavity before panels are installed, as the panels will cover the wall surface and access would be impossible or require destructive removal afterwards.
Any plumbing pipes running inside the wall must be installed and inspected prior to panel installation since the panels conceal the wall cavity.
Wall-mounted electrical fixtures, switches, and outlets are installed after panels are in place so that they can be properly mounted flush against the finished panel surface.
Although not strictly required, trim and molding are typically installed after wall panels to cover panel edges and provide a clean finished look; it is a preferred sequence for aesthetic quality.
Wall framing provides the structural support and substrate that wall coverings are applied to; without framing, there is no surface to cover.
Electrical wiring, outlets, and switch boxes must be installed within the wall cavities before wall coverings are applied, as covering the walls would block access to the interior framing.
Plumbing pipes and fixtures within walls must be installed prior to covering, as access to the wall cavities is needed for proper installation and inspection.
Insulation must be placed within wall cavities before wall covering is applied, as the covering will permanently enclose the insulation.
Wall coverings (drywall, paneling, etc.) must be fully installed and finished before painting or final wall finishes can be applied to the surface.
The rough opening must be framed, sized, and prepared to the correct dimensions before a bi-fold window panel can be fitted into the wall opening.
Window flashing and weatherproofing membrane must be applied around the rough opening to prevent water intrusion before installing the bi-fold window panel.
Interior and exterior trim or casing around the bi-fold window panel cannot be installed until the window panel itself is securely in place.

successor: Insulation and Air Sealing Around Window
rationale: Spray foam or other insulation and air sealing around the window frame must be applied after the bi-fold window panel is installed to fill gaps between the frame and rough opening.
Drywall finishing, taping, and mudding around the window area cannot be completed until the bi-fold window panel is installed and the opening is enclosed.
The friction stay or hinge stay must be attached to the door frame; therefore the frame must be installed first to provide the structural mounting surface.
The hinge stay connects the door leaf to the frame; the door must be hung before the stay can be properly aligned and fixed.
After installing the stay, the door's opening and closing friction may need fine-tuning; this is a preferred sequence for optimal functionality but not an absolute physical necessity.
The stay must be fully installed before the door assembly can be inspected for proper operation and compliance.
The window frame must be installed first to provide a structural mounting surface for the hardware and locking mechanism.
The glass must be set and secured in the frame before the locking hardware can be attached, as the locking mechanism engages with the sash and frame around the glazing.
Hardware and locks must be fully installed before functional testing of window opening, closing, and locking can be performed.
While some weatherstripping can be applied before, final perimeter sealing is preferably done after hardware installation to ensure proper alignment and compression around the locking points.

Interior trim work and paint touch-ups around the window are typically done after hardware installation to avoid damaging fresh paint with hardware installation tools and to achieve a clean finished appearance.
The window frame must be installed first to provide the structural opening and support that the reveal and sill will interface with and finish around.
The rough opening in the wall (framed and sheathed) must be prepared before the reveal and sill can be formed or installed to create the finished window opening.
The reveal and sill provide the finished edge and surfaces around the window; subsequent plastering or drywall work abuts these finished elements.
The reveal and sill form the frame and support surface into which the window sash (operable part) and glazing units are installed.
The reveal and sill must be fully installed to provide the substrate for weatherproofing seals and flashings around the window opening.
The rough openings in the wall frame must be built and sized correctly before windows can be physically installed and set into position.
Window flashing and waterproof membranes must be applied around the rough opening prior to window installation to prevent water ingress and ensure a weathertight seal.
The window frames and sashes must be set and secured in the opening before glass panes (glazing) can be installed into the frames.
Windows must be installed and flashed before exterior cladding is applied, as cladding typically butts up against the window frames and integrates with the flashing system.
Windows must be in place so that interior finishes can be trimmed around the window openings and the reveals can be properly finished.

predecessor: Wall Masonry Construction (up to window sill level)
rationale: The window opening can only be formed after the masonry wall has been built up to the sill level, as the opening is created within the wall structure.
The sill provides the base support and drainage surface for the window opening, and must be in place before the opening is fully formed above it.

The lintel or beam must be installed above the window opening to support the masonry above it; this is typically done concurrently with or immediately after forming the opening, but structurally the lintel must be in place before continuing masonry above the opening.
The window frame can only be installed after the rough opening has been formed and finished in the masonry, as the frame fits within the prepared opening.

successor: Masonry Work Above Window (Lintel zone completion)
rationale: The masonry work above the window opening, including completing the lintel zone and continuing the wall upward, can only proceed after the opening and its supporting lintel are in place.

Window and door frames must be installed and secured in the structural openings before glazing and sash components can be fitted, as the frames provide the supporting structure and reveal for the glazing units and sash frames to be placed into.

The structural framing and creation of rough openings (for windows and doors) must be completed to provide the necessary apertures into which window and door assemblies, including glazing and sashes, are installed.

Weatherproof membranes and flashings around window and door openings should be installed prior to glazing and sash fitting to ensure a continuous water barrier behind and around the installed units, preventing moisture ingress.

While it is common practice to complete glazing and sash fitting before interior wall finishes to allow for sealing and trimming around the window frames, this is a soft preference as temporary sealing can allow wall finishing to proceed first in some sequences.

The glazing and sash units must be fitted in the openings before the exterior cladding or façade system is finished around those openings, so that the cladding can properly overlap, trim, and seal against the installed window frames.
Windows must be installed first so that flashings can be integrated around the window frames to seal against water ingress.
The structural rough opening must be framed and ready before windows and their flashings can be installed.
Sheathing provides the substrate to which window flashings are applied and integrated with the weather-resistant barrier.
The WRB (house wrap or felt paper) must be installed before flashings so that flashings can be properly lapped and integrated with the WRB to create a continuous water-shedding surface.
Exterior cladding is installed after flashings are complete so that flashings are covered and the cladding does not trap water behind it without proper flashing drainage.
Interior finishing can begin after windows are flashed and weatherproofed to avoid water damage to interior finishes if flashings are incomplete.
The window joinery (frames, sashes, etc.) must be physically installed and fixed in place before any painting or finishing can be applied to them.
Surfaces must be sanded, cleaned, and primed as needed before paint or finish can be applied to ensure proper adhesion and a quality finish.

Glass panes and glazing beads should be installed before final painting so that paint can be applied up to and around the glazing, and to avoid damaging freshly painted surfaces during glass installation.

It is standard practice to complete painting before final cleaning and touch-ups to avoid re-soiling finished surfaces, though this is a logical workflow preference rather than a strict physical necessity.
Window handles, locks, hinges and other hardware should be installed after painting to avoid getting paint on the hardware and to ensure a clean, professional finish.
Window hardware (hinges, handles, locks, stays) must be attached to already-installed window frames; the frame must be in place and secure before hardware can be mounted.
Glass panes or sashes must be installed in the frame before hardware such as locking mechanisms, stays, and handles can be fitted and adjusted for proper operation.
Weather seals and final sealants are applied after hardware is installed and adjusted, as the hardware must be in its final position for seals to close properly and prevent air/water infiltration.
Testing of window operation (opening, closing, locking) must occur after hardware is fully installed and adjusted to verify correct function and alignment.

While interior trim and painting can technically be done before hardware adjustment, it is standard practice to install and adjust hardware first to ensure the window operates correctly before covering with trim and finishing work, avoiding rework.
The rough opening (door frame) must be framed and structurally complete before a solid door panel can be installed, as the door requires an existing framed opening to be mounted into.
The door frame/jamb must be installed and secured within the rough opening before hanging the solid door panel, as the door hinges attach to the frame.
Door hardware such as handles, locks, and hinges (if not pre-installed) must be mounted after the solid door panel is in place to ensure proper alignment and function.

While trim is typically installed after the door panel is hung for aesthetic fit, it is a soft preference as casing can be fitted around a door at any stage, though doing so after ensures proper gaps and alignment.

The solid door panel must be installed before final painting or finishing can be applied to the door surface, as painting a door off its hinges or before installation can lead to damage and fit issues.
The frame must be installed first to provide a structural opening and support into which the glazed lite or glass insert can be placed and secured.
The rough opening must be prepared (sized, framed, and weatherproofed) before any glazing unit can be installed to ensure proper fit and sealing.
Glazing gaskets or bedding sealant must be applied to the frame recess before inserting the glass to cushion the lite and create a weather-tight seal.
The glass insert must be in place before glazing beads or stops can be installed to retain and secure the glass within the frame.
After the glass is positioned, perimeter sealant or caulking is applied around the edges to complete the weather seal and prevent air/water infiltration.
The rough opening must be framed to provide the structural support and cavity for the door assembly, including the sill or threshold.
The subfloor must be in place to provide a level and stable base for the threshold to sit upon and to establish the finished floor height reference.

Flashing and weatherproofing must be installed at the rough opening base before the threshold is placed to ensure water is directed away from the structure and to prevent moisture intrusion beneath the sill.
The threshold provides the bottom support and seal for the door jambs and slab; the door assembly must be installed on top of and anchored to the threshold.

successor: Interior Floor Finishing (e.g., tile, hardwood, carpet)
rationale: Finished flooring is typically installed up to the threshold (or butted against it), so the threshold must be in place to define the transition point and to allow flooring to terminate neatly against it.

The glazing bead/stop bead is a component that holds the glass or infill panel in place within the frame; the frame must be installed first to provide the structural support and mounting surface for the bead.

The glazing bead/stop bead functions as a retainer that secures the glass panel within the frame; the glass or infill panel must be placed in the frame opening before the bead can be installed to hold it in place.

While the bead itself is often considered a final trim piece, subsequent interior finishing work such as painting or caulking around the bead typically occurs after the bead is installed to achieve a clean finished appearance.
Weatherproofing sealants are typically applied over or around the installed glazing bead to create a watertight seal between the bead, the frame, and the glass.
The rough opening must be framed and prepared to receive the window/door unit before any of its components, including the glazing bead, can be installed.
The door lockset requires a fully installed and secured door frame to mount onto; the lockset cannot be fitted without the frame in place.
The door leaf must be hung on its hinges and properly aligned within the frame before the lockset can be installed, as the lockset bore holes and latch must align with the frame strike plate.
The striker plate (or strike plate) is mounted on the door frame to receive the lockset's latch or deadbolt; it must be positioned precisely based on the installed lockset's latch location.

After the lockset is installed, the door must be tested for latch engagement, alignment, and smooth operation; any adjustments to hinges or strike plate can only be finalized once the lockset is in place.
It is a soft preference to complete lockset installation after painting to avoid getting paint on the hardware, though touch-up painting can be done later if needed.
The door handle/lever set must be installed onto a door that is already hung and in place. The handle cannot be attached before the door itself is installed.
The door frame must be installed and properly aligned before the door (and subsequently the handle) can be positioned.
The door must have the necessary holes (bore holes for the handle, latch, and deadbolt) pre-drilled or routed before the handle/lever set can be installed.

While the handle itself is installed after painting, minor touch-up painting or finishing around the hardware may be done after installation to cover any scratches or adjustments, but this is a soft preference rather than a hard physical constraint.
Trim and baseboards around the door area are typically installed before hardware, but some finishing work may follow handle installation as a soft sequencing preference.
The intumescent strip is typically fitted into grooves or channels on the door frame, so the door frame must be installed first to provide the surface and recess for the strip.
The intumescent strip is installed in the door frame before the door leaf is hung, as the strip seals the gap between frame and leaf; installing the leaf first would block access.
Fire door testing for smoke and fire integrity can only occur after all components including the intumescent strip are installed, as the strip is critical to the door's fire-rated performance.
The frame groove must be clean, dry and free of debris to ensure proper adhesion (if adhesive-backed) or fit of the intumescent strip.
Soft preference: Painting is often done before strip installation to avoid masking; however, if the strip is painted over it could reduce its effectiveness, so finishing is typically completed first.
The rough opening frame must be constructed to provide the structural support and defined opening dimensions for the single glazed lite door to be installed into.
The door frame (jambs, head, sill) must be installed and secured in the rough opening before the door slab/hinges can be mounted.
Weatherstripping, caulking, and flashing around the door must be applied after the door is installed to ensure a watertight and airtight seal.
Final door hardware such as locks, handles, hinges, and door closers are typically fitted to the installed door after it is hung in the frame.
Interior trim and casing around the door is typically installed after the door is hung for a finished appearance, though this is a logical sequence preference rather than a physical necessity.
The rough opening (door frame) must be prepared, framed, and sized correctly before any door can be installed. The opening provides the structural support and dimensional reference for the door.
The door must be set and secured in place before casing and trim can be applied around it to conceal gaps and provide a finished appearance.
Weatherstripping seals the perimeter of the installed door; the door must be in place for the weatherstripping to be properly fitted against its edges.
Hardware components such as locks, handles, and hinges are mounted directly onto the installed door; the door must be hung to correctly align and attach these items.
While painting can be done before installation, final touch-ups around the door frame and edges are typically performed after the door is installed to ensure a seamless finish.

successor: Timber Solid Door with Glass Installation
rationale: The door frame must be installed and properly aligned before the timber solid door with glass can be hung, as the door hinges and hardware need a secure frame to attach to.

predecessor: Wall Framing and Rough Opening Preparation
successor: Timber Solid Door with Glass Installation
rationale: The wall framing and rough opening must be completed to the correct dimensions to accommodate the door unit before installation can proceed.

predecessor: Timber Solid Door with Glass Installation
rationale: The door must be hung in its frame before door hardware such as locks, handles, and latch plates can be fitted and aligned correctly.

predecessor: Timber Solid Door with Glass Installation
successor: Glass Panel Protection and Final Finishing
rationale: Protective coverings and final sealant/finishing around the glass panel must be applied after the door is installed to avoid damage during installation.

predecessor: Timber Solid Door with Glass Installation
successor: Interior Painting and Wall Finishing (adjacent areas)
rationale: While painting can technically be done before door installation, it is preferable to install doors after painting to avoid paint drips on the door and to achieve cleaner finish lines around the door frame.

successor: Steel Solid Door with Glass Installation
rationale: The rough opening (frame) must be prepared and installed before the steel door with glass can be fitted into it.

successor: Steel Solid Door with Glass Installation
rationale: The surrounding masonry walls must be built to define the opening and provide structural support for the door frame.

predecessor: Steel Solid Door with Glass Installation
rationale: Door installation must be completed before finishing work such as painting, caulking, and sealing around the door and frame can be done.

predecessor: Steel Solid Door with Glass Installation
rationale: Doors must be hung and properly aligned before door hardware such as locks, handles, hinges, and door closers can be installed.

predecessor: Steel Solid Door with Glass Installation
rationale: After the door is installed, the glass panels can be glazed and sealant applied to ensure weather-tightness and security.

predecessor: Frame Installation and Rough Opening Preparation
successor: Aluminium Solid Door with Glass Installation
rationale: The rough opening must be framed, prepared, and measured correctly to receive the door. The door cannot be installed without a properly prepared opening.

successor: Aluminium Solid Door with Glass Installation
rationale: Load-bearing walls and structural supports must be completed before any door installation to provide the necessary structural integrity and anchoring points.

predecessor: Aluminium Solid Door with Glass Installation
rationale: The door must be hung and positioned in the frame before hardware such as locks, handles, and hinges can be fitted and aligned properly.

predecessor: Aluminium Solid Door with Glass Installation
rationale: Weatherproofing seals and caulk are applied after the door frame is set to ensure a tight seal and prevent water/air infiltration around the door perimeter.

predecessor: Aluminium Solid Door with Glass Installation
rationale: Wall finishes and paint around the door frame are best completed after installation to cover any gaps or damage caused during installation, though this can be done beforehand if carefully masked.
The door frame must be installed and securely fixed in place before the door leaf can be hung, as the door hinges attach to the frame.
The surrounding wall structure must be completed and the rough opening formed before the door frame and door can be installed.
The door leaf must be hung in place before hardware such as handles, locks, and hinges can be fitted onto it.

While finishing can sometimes be done off-site or before installation, typically the door is installed first and then final touch-up painting and sealing of edges is completed on-site for a seamless finish.
Flooring is usually installed after doors to allow for proper clearance and to avoid damaging the flooring during door installation, though this is a soft preference rather than a physical necessity.
Doors must be physically manufactured before they can undergo fire testing, as there is no sample to test otherwise.
Doors must be tested and certified for fire resistance before they can be installed on-site, as building codes require certified products for installation.
Raw materials and components must be procured to manufacture the door samples used in fire testing and certification.
The door frame must be installed to provide the structural opening and support for the door leaf, which holds the glass panel.
The door leaf (whether pre-assembled or built on site) must be in place to receive the glazing panel; glass is installed into the prepared door frame or panel opening.
The glass panes, seals, gaskets, and setting blocks must be on-site and inspected for defects before installation can commence.

successor: Door Hardware Installation (e.g., handles, locks, hinges)
rationale: Hardware should be installed after glazing to avoid damaging glass during hardware fitting and to ensure proper alignment with the complete door assembly.
After glass is installed, the door assembly can be fine-tuned for fit, and weather seals around the door and glass can be completed to ensure airtight and watertight performance.
Doors must be manufactured, delivered, and installed before any maintenance or re-glazing work can be performed on them.
The door must be physically installed in its frame before re-glazing or maintenance activities can take place.
New glass or glazing materials must be procured and available on-site before the re-glazing activity can proceed.
Re-glazing and maintenance should be completed before installing hardware that might obstruct access to glass panels or require a finished door surface.
Maintenance and re-glazing must be finished to allow for a complete quality inspection of the door assembly including glass panels.
The frame provides the structural support and housing into which louvre blades are mounted. Without a completed frame, blades cannot be physically attached or aligned.
After the louvre blades are assembled into the frame, they must be adjusted and aligned to ensure proper operation, spacing, and angle for airflow or shading.
Weather seals are applied around the assembled louvre blades to prevent water infiltration and air leakage. Sealing cannot be completed until the blades are fully installed in the frame.
The roof deck provides the structural base and opening through which the skylight diffuser is installed; without the roof deck in place, there is no frame or aperture to mount the diffuser.
The waterproof membrane prevents water ingress around the skylight opening; the diffuser should be installed after the membrane is in place and properly flashed to ensure a watertight seal.
The rough opening with structural curbs or framing must be completed to define the skylight aperture and support the diffuser assembly.

The diffuser is typically integrated into the ceiling plane; ceiling finishes (drywall, acoustic tiles) are installed after the diffuser is in place to achieve a clean, finished edge around the skylight.

While not physically required, coordinating electrical work after diffuser installation avoids rework if diffuser placement shifts, ensuring light fixtures align properly with the diffused natural light source.
Shading fins are attached to the building's structural frame or façade support system, which must be in place to provide a mounting surface and load-bearing capacity.
Shading fins are typically anchored to or integrated with the exterior wall or cladding system, which must be finished to define the precise alignment and attachment points for the fins.

While shading fins are often installed before windows for access reasons, in some sequences windows may be installed first; however, installing fins first protects the window area and provides shading reference, making this a soft preference for workflow efficiency.
The attachment points and penetrations created during shading fin installation must be sealed and waterproofed to prevent moisture ingress and ensure building envelope integrity.

Scaffolding or access equipment used to install the shading fins at height must remain in place until all fin installation and adjustments are complete; dismantling can only begin after fin installation is finished.

Site analysis provides the geographical context, solar path data, and surrounding building locations necessary to understand how shadows will be cast on and around the site throughout the day and year.
Solar path analysis determines the sun's trajectory across the sky at different times and seasons, which is the foundational data required to calculate and model shadow patterns.
A conceptual massing model of the proposed building is needed as the physical geometry that will cast shadows; without it there is no building form to analyze for shadow impact.

Shadow pattern results inform design iterations such as adjusting building orientation, height, or setbacks to mitigate negative shadow impacts on adjacent properties or public spaces, but this is an iterative design preference rather than a physical necessity.

Daylight analysis for interior spaces builds upon shadow pattern data to understand which building surfaces receive direct vs. indirect sunlight, directly affecting window placement and daylight factor calculations.
The shading devices must be physically installed and in place before they can be commissioned, tested, and verified for proper operation.
Power supply and control wiring must be run to shading device locations prior to commissioning to enable functional testing of motors and controls.
The BAS or shading control system must be installed and operational to integrate with and commission the automated shading devices.
While not a strict physical requirement, it is good practice to complete shading device commissioning before final finishes and punch list to avoid access issues and rework if adjustments are needed.
Commissioning must verify that shading devices operate correctly before occupants are trained on their use and the system is formally handed over to the building owner.

The architectural design (including building geometry, layout, and envelope details) must be established before light simulation can be performed, as the simulation requires defined spaces, openings, and material properties as input.
A digital BIM model containing the building's geometry, surfaces, and glazing is necessary as the foundational data source for running accurate lighting simulations and daylight analysis.

Structural elements such as columns, beams, and floor slabs define the building's internal volumes and shading patterns; these must be designed to ensure the light simulation reflects realistic conditions.

Results from light simulation and modelling inform the selection, placement, and specification of artificial lighting fixtures (e.g., luminaire types, layouts, and controls) to meet required illuminance levels and energy targets.
Lighting simulation outputs (daylight factors, solar heat gains, and artificial lighting loads) are key inputs for whole-building energy modelling and thermal load calculations.
The leaded light panels must be fabricated in a workshop before they can be installed on site.
The structural frame or rough opening must be built and ready to receive the panel before installation can begin.
The panel must be placed in the opening before glazing beads or stops can secure it in place.
Weather seals and caulking around the panel can only be applied after the panel is installed in its frame.
Finishing trim around the leaded light panel is typically installed after the panel is in place, though in some cases trim can be partially pre-installed.
The glazing bar is attached to or supported by the frame; the frame must be in place first to provide structural support.
Glazing bars hold glass panels in place; glass installation cannot proceed until the supporting glazing bars are installed.
Weather seals are applied around and between glazing bars and glass; the glazing bars must be in place for the sealing to be effective.
The rough opening must be prepared and dimensionally accurate before any glazing bars can be installed within it.
Functionality testing typically occurs after glazing is complete, but this is a quality assurance preference rather than a physical impossibility to start earlier.
The rough opening must be framed to provide the structural support and defined space into which the casement window can be installed.
The weather-resistant barrier around the rough opening must be in place to protect the wall assembly from moisture intrusion before the window is set.
After the window is placed, flashing and sealant must be applied around its perimeter to ensure a watertight and airtight installation.
Interior trim work typically follows window installation to cover gaps and provide a finished appearance, though in some sequences it could be done later, so it is a soft preference.
Exterior siding must be installed after the window is in place so that siding can be properly lapped and sealed against the window frame for weatherproofing.
The window frame must be assembled and installed in the wall opening before the sash window can be fitted into it.

predecessor: Glazing and small pane division installation
rationale: The glass panes and dividing mullions/muntins that create the 'small panes' appearance must be installed before the sash unit can be considered complete.

successor: Installation of window hardware (locks, handles, pulleys)
rationale: The sash window must be fully assembled and in place before hardware such as locks, handles, and pulley systems can be attached to it.
Weather seals and stripping must be applied after the sash window is installed to ensure a proper fit and airtight closure.
Architectural trim, architraves, and finish moldings around the window are installed after the sash window unit is in place to cover gaps and provide a finished appearance.
The rough opening in the wall frame must be built and sized correctly to accommodate the fanlight unit before installation.
After the fanlight is installed, the gaps around it must be sealed with caulking or glazing compound to ensure weather-tightness.
Interior trim and casing around the fanlight can only be applied after the fanlight unit is fixed in place.
Exterior weatherproofing elements such as flashing must be installed after the fanlight is set to properly overlap and seal the joints.
The dormer window structure must be installed on top of the roof framing; the roof must be framed and sheathed to provide the structural opening and support for the dormer.
Roof underlayment (weather barrier) must be in place before cutting into the roof for the dormer to prevent water ingress during and after installation.
After the dormer window unit is set into place, flashing and weatherproofing around the dormer must be applied to seal the joint between the window and the roof structure.

successor: Interior Drywall and Finishing of Dormer Interior
rationale: The interior walls and ceiling of the dormer alcove cannot be drywalled and finished until the window unit is fully installed and sealed from the exterior.

successor: Exterior Siding or Roofing Completion Around Dormer
rationale: Final siding, shingles, and trim around the exterior of the dormer must be completed after the window is installed to integrate it seamlessly into the roof assembly.
The glazing bars are attached to the structural frame of the window or curtain wall; without the frame in place, there is no supporting structure to mount the glazing bars onto.
The rough opening must be properly sized, leveled, and prepared before any glazing components (including glazing bars) can be installed.
Glazing bars form the subframe or mullion/transom grid that holds the glass panels; glass panels cannot be placed until the supporting glazing bar grid is in position.
Sealants and gaskets are applied after the glazing bar framework is installed to create weather-tight seals between the bars and the glass panels.

While it is typical to install finishes and trims after the glazing bars are in place to achieve a clean aesthetic, this is a logical sequencing preference rather than a strict structural necessity, as trims could be installed concurrently in some cases.
Glass pieces must be cut to size and shape before they can be fitted into the lead came framework.
A clean, level work surface and layout of the design cartoon are needed before assembling the lead came and glass pieces.
The full-scale design pattern must be drawn out to guide the layout and assembly of lead came and glass.
All lead came joints must be assembled and in place before they can be soldered together to create a rigid panel.
The assembled leaded glass panel must be fully soldered and stable before waterproofing cement is applied to the came channels.
Glass panels must first be fabricated and prepared before they can be cut into smaller panes.
Raw glass material must be delivered and stored on-site before any cutting operations can commence.
A dedicated cutting table, tools, and safety equipment must be prepared before glass cutting can begin.
Cut glass panes must first be cut to size before their edges can be smoothed or seamed for safety and fitting.
Glass panes must be cut before they can be assembled or installed into window frames or glazing systems.
Scaffolding must be erected to provide safe working access to the roof or leaded areas before re-leading work can commence.
The existing defective lead covering must be stripped away before new lead can be dressed and installed.
Any damaged roof decking, battens or structural elements must be repaired or replaced to provide a sound substrate for the new leadwork.
New lead flashings, soakers and weatherings are dressed after the main re-leading to integrate with adjoining elements and ensure watertight detailing.
Scaffolding can only be removed once the re-leading work is complete and all lead sheets are securely fixed, to maintain safe access until finishing.
Putty repointing seals the edges of window glazing; the glazing must be installed first so that the putty can be applied around the glass to create a weathertight seal.
The surface around windows or masonry joints must be clean, dry, and free of old putty, debris, or dust to ensure proper adhesion of the new putty.
After putty is applied and shaped, it needs to cure/harden before paint or primer can be applied over it to protect the putty and achieve a uniform finish.
Once putty repointing is complete, a quality check should be performed to verify uniform application, adhesion, and proper sealing before declaring the work finished.
The building structure must be assessed to ensure it can support the window restoration work and that there are no structural risks to the heritage windows.
Scaffolding must be erected to provide safe access to the heritage windows for restoration work.
Temporary weather protection must be in place to shield the open window openings and interior spaces from rain, wind, and dust during restoration.
Interior wall finishes around the window openings can only be applied after the restored windows are installed and sealed to prevent moisture damage.
Scaffolding cannot be removed until the window restoration work is complete, as the scaffolding is required for safe access to the windows.
Final exterior painting and weatherproofing is best performed after the restored windows are in place to ensure a seamless finish and proper sealing around frames.
Drip moulds are installed at the base of walls or above windows/doors to direct water away; the wall structure must exist first.
Drip moulds must be in place to effectively channel water before weatherproofing or cladding finishes are applied over or around them.
Drip moulds need to be installed before final exterior finishes to ensure proper water drainage and seal integration.
Drip moulds are often integrated with window and door openings to shed water away; frames are typically set first and the drip mould is then fixed to the underside or head.
While not physically required, coordinating drip moulds with roof drainage elements improves water management and prevents staining; typically a recommended sequencing preference.
The ferrous metal stock must be procured, received, and quality-inspected before fabrication of the saddle bar can begin.
The raw ferrous material must be cut to specified dimensions and prepared (e.g., cleaned, deburred) before the saddle bar forming or machining operations can start.
After fabrication (forming, welding, or machining), the saddle bar typically requires heat treatment to relieve internal stresses and achieve desired mechanical properties.
The fabricated saddle bar must first be complete and inspected before surface protection (e.g., galvanizing, painting, or other coating) can be applied.
The ferrous saddle bar component must be fully fabricated and finished before it can be assembled into the larger system or structure.
Tie wire is used to secure rebar intersections; rebar must be fabricated and placed first before tie wire can be applied.
Tie wire is used to tie intersecting rebar together at specified spacing; rebar must first be positioned in place.
Inspection of rebar placement must occur after tie wire has been applied to ensure all intersections are properly secured.
Concrete cannot be poured until rebar is fully tied and secured in place to prevent displacement during the pour.
Rebar must be cut to the required lengths before it can be positioned and tied with tie wire.
Structural framing must be complete to provide the rough openings and support structure for window installation.
Rough openings must be verified for correct dimensions, plumbness, and levelness before windows can be ordered and scheduled for installation.
Exterior wall sheathing provides the backing and weather-resistant barrier around window openings before windows are installed.
The window schedule defines what windows are needed, their sizes, types, and locations, which is the prerequisite information for physically installing the windows.
Once the window schedule is finalized and windows are installed, glazing and sealant work can proceed to weatherproof the window assemblies.
The subfloor must be installed and finished before base molding can be applied, as base molding is installed at the junction of the wall and floor, requiring a stable finished floor surface.
Walls must be framed and finished (including drywall or wallboard installation) before base molding can be attached, since base molding is mounted onto the finished wall surface.

While base molding is typically installed after subflooring but before finished floor covering in many cases, some installers prefer to install base molding before the final floor covering to avoid damaging walls; however, this ordering can vary by technique and is not a strict physical requirement.

Base molding must be installed before final painting or finishing of the trim can occur, as the molding needs to be in place to receive paint, stain, or sealant and to allow for caulking and touch-up of adjacent wall surfaces.
Casing trim is installed around door and window frames, so the frames must be in place first to provide the surface and reference for the trim.
Casing trim is applied against finished walls; drywall and painting should be completed so the trim can be installed flush against a finished surface and painted over or caulked properly.
While flooring can be installed before trim, it is generally preferred to install casing trim first so the flooring can be run up to the trim for a cleaner finished edge, avoiding gaps.
