Baseboards and quarter rounds typically meet or are mitered into casing trim at doorways; casing must be in place to establish the corner joint and ensure a seamless transition.
After casing trim is installed, nail holes and seams need to be filled and painted for a finished appearance; this is a logical soft preference for quality and aesthetics.
Chair rail requires a finished wall surface to be mounted on; wall framing provides the structural support for the wall.
Chair rail is installed on finished drywall; the drywall must be hung, taped, mudded, and sanded before trim can be applied.
While chair rail can be painted after installation, it is common practice to have the wall surface primed and at least base-painted before installing trim to avoid painting behind the rail.
Chair rail should be installed before final coat painting so that paint can be applied cleanly up to the edge of the rail and any caulking at the seam can be painted over.

Chair rail is typically installed before baseboards when both are present, as baseboard installation can be done after chair rail without interfering; however, this is a conventional sequencing preference rather than a strict physical requirement.
Crown molding is installed against finished walls; walls must be drywalled, taped, mudded, and painted before molding can be attached.
Crown molding meets the ceiling, so the ceiling must be finished (drywall, texture, paint) prior to installation to allow proper fit and sealing.
Corner beads on wall corners must be in place and finished before crown molding is cut and installed for clean miters and transitions.
After crown molding is nailed in place, gaps at the top and bottom edges must be caulked and paint touch-ups applied to blend the molding with the wall and ceiling.

While flooring can be installed before or after crown molding, installing crown molding first is a soft preference to avoid damaging new floors from ladders and dropped tools, and allows baseboard installation after flooring for a cleaner look.
Quarter round molding is installed at the base of walls where they meet the floor, so it requires a finished floor surface and stable subfloor to be in place before it can be securely attached.

predecessor: Flooring installation (hardwood, laminate, tile, or vinyl)
rationale: Quarter round covers the expansion gap between the flooring and the baseboard, so the flooring must be fully installed first.
Quarter round is typically nailed or glued to the baseboard at the floor junction, so baseboards must be in place for the quarter round to attach to.

successor: Final wall painting or touch-up painting
rationale: While painting can be done before quarter round, doing final touch-up painting after installation allows for covering nail holes and caulk seams for a clean finish.

successor: Base shoe or shoe molding installation (if separate)
rationale: If quarter round is used as the primary transition molding, other shoe moldings that sit in front of it must come after, but typically quarter round IS the final trim piece at the floor.
Shoe molding is installed at the base of walls where they meet the floor; a finished subfloor surface must be in place to provide a nailing/support surface.
Shoe molding is a trim element that butts against finished wall surfaces; walls must be completed (drywalled, taped, mudded, and painted) before trim can be applied.

Shoe molding is typically installed after the floor covering is laid, as it covers the expansion gap between the flooring and the wall. However, in some sequences it can be installed after the baseboard and before carpet. But the most common sequencing: shoe molding is the very final trim step after flooring.
Shoe molding requires caulking and painting (or staining) after installation; any final paint touch-ups on the molding and adjacent surfaces must occur after it is fastened in place.

Shoe molding is typically applied along the bottom of baseboards (or in place of baseboard in some cases); baseboards must be installed first to provide the upper reference for shoe molding placement.

Trim (baseboards, casings, crown molding) must be installed against finished walls. If drywall, taping, mudding, and painting are not complete, the trim would either be damaged during wall finishing or would not sit flush against the finished surface.

Baseboard trim typically sits on top of finished flooring. Installing flooring after baseboards can damage the trim and leaves gaps underneath. Most construction sequences require flooring to be finished or at least rough-installed before baseboards are cut and fitted.
Trim is applied to the framed door/window openings and wall edges. The rough framing (studs, headers, cripples) must be in place and sheathed before any finish trim can be attached.
Window and door units must be installed and secured in their rough openings before casing trim can be applied around them. Trim covers the gap between the frame and the rough opening.

After trim is installed, nail holes need to be filled, caulked, and touched up with paint. Additionally, paint edges where trim meets walls require final touch-up to achieve a clean finished appearance.
Materials must be measured and marked at the cut locations before any cutting can take place, as miter cutting requires precise marking to ensure accurate angles.
The correct material must be selected and inspected for defects before cutting, as miter cutting a flawed or incorrect piece wastes material and time.
After miter cutting the pieces, they must be dry-assembled or test-fitted to verify the accuracy of the miters before final assembly or joining.
Miter-cut ends often have rough edges or splinters from cutting; sanding and finishing the cut edges must follow cutting to smooth the miter faces prior to assembly.
The mitered pieces must be cut to the correct angle and length before they can be glued and joined together in final assembly.
Coping (the top finishing element on a wall) requires the concrete or masonry wall to be fully cured and stable to provide a solid base for installation.
The wall structure must be fully built and set before coping can be installed, as coping serves as the cap or top covering of the wall.
Waterproofing is often applied to the top of the wall before coping is placed, to prevent moisture ingress beneath the coping.
After coping is installed, joints and edges typically require sealant or final waterproofing treatment to ensure watertightness.
Coping is the topmost element; any adjacent finishes or capping details on parapets can only be completed once the coping itself is in place.
Lumber, drywall, or other materials must be cut to size and prepared before they can be nailed or fastened into place.
The positions for studs, joists, or other framing members must be marked and laid out on the structure before nails or fasteners can be driven.
For hardwoods or brittle materials, pilot holes may be pre-drilled to prevent splitting before nailing; this is a soft preference as not all nailing requires pre-drilling.
Fasteners secure the structural frame or substrate in place, which must be complete before sheathing, siding, or cladding can be applied over it.
After nailing and fastening is finished, a quality and structural inspection must occur to verify that all connections meet code and load requirements before proceeding to subsequent work.
Caulking and sealing materials require a clean, dry, and dust-free surface to properly adhere; contaminants or moisture prevent bonding and cause sealant failure.
Some substrates require a primer to ensure proper adhesion of the sealant; the primer must be applied and fully dried before caulking can be installed.

predecessor: Installation of Backer Rod (if joint is deep)
rationale: Backer rod must be placed in deep joints before sealant application to control sealant depth, provide support, and prevent three-sided adhesion.
Freshly applied sealant requires adequate curing time before any subsequent work can be performed over or adjacent to it to avoid disturbing the sealant.

Paint or coatings must be applied after caulking is fully cured; painting over uncured sealant can cause cracking, poor adhesion, and finish defects. Many sealants are not paintable until fully cured.
Rough framing must be complete before sanding and surface preparation begins, as sanding is applied to framed surfaces and the structure must be stable and enclosed.
Drywall must be installed, taped, and the joint compound applied before sanding can smooth out the seams and surfaces.

In some sequences, a primer coat is applied before sanding to seal the surface, but typically sanding precedes priming. However, if a pre-sanding primer is used, it must be applied first. More commonly, sanding precedes priming and painting.
Sanding creates a smooth surface for primer adhesion; priming must follow sanding to seal the prepared surface before painting.
Sanding ensures a smooth, clean substrate for paint or stain to adhere properly; painting cannot occur before surface preparation is complete.
After sanding, dust must be cleaned from the area before finishing coats are applied; this is a soft preference in some sequences but strongly recommended for quality.
The wall surface must be properly prepared (clean, smooth, and possibly primed) before scribing can be applied; scribing on an unprepared surface would not adhere properly or produce accurate lines.
The wall must be fully constructed and structurally complete before any scribing work can be performed on its surface.
Design plans and layout markings must be established beforehand to guide the scribing process accurately.
Scribing creates the decorative or functional lines on the wall; painting or final finishing must follow after scribing to preserve the integrity of the scribed design.
Although not a strict physical necessity, it is standard practice to inspect scribed work immediately upon completion to verify alignment and accuracy before subsequent trades proceed.
The area must be cleared of debris and prepared before new trim work can begin to ensure a clean surface for installation.
Trim is a finishing element that requires the structural framing to be complete so that it can be measured, cut, and installed against stable walls and openings.
Drywall must be hung, taped, mudded, and sanded before trim installation so that trim pieces (baseboards, casing, crown molding) have a finished surface to abut against.

While painting can be done before trim in some sequences, typically trim is installed first so that walls can be painted/trimmed caulked and touched up; however, it is a common preference to paint walls before trim to avoid taping, making this a soft ordering preference.
Baseboard trim (which is part of trim work) must be installed after flooring or at least after subfloor preparation so that the trim sits properly over the finished flooring material.
Bleacher assembly requires a stable, level foundation to ensure safety and structural integrity. The foundation must be prepared and cured before any bleacher components can be installed.
The ground must be properly graded and leveled to provide a uniform surface for bleacher installation and to ensure proper drainage away from the structure.
If bleachers are mounted on a concrete slab, the concrete must be poured and fully cured to achieve the required load-bearing capacity before assembly begins.
Individual seats (if separate from the frame) must be installed after the main bleacher frame structure is assembled to provide proper attachment points.
The auditorium seat must be anchored to or placed on the finished floor slab; the floor provides the structural base and level surface required for seat installation.
Electrical conduits for seat-mounted lighting or power outlets must be roughed in below the floor before seats are installed, as access is blocked once seats are fixed in place.
It is preferable to complete final floor finishes before installing seats to avoid damage, but if necessary, finishes can be completed around installed seats with careful work.
Seat numbering and signage are physically applied to or mounted on the installed seats, so the seats must be in place first.
The bench seating unit requires a stable, level foundation or base support to be installed first, as the bench cannot be structurally supported without it.
If the bench seating unit is to be mounted on a concrete base or pad, the concrete must be fully cured and set before the bench can be secured in place.
Site grading and drainage must be completed to ensure water does not pool around the bench foundation, preventing future settlement or deterioration.
If the backrest is a separate component that attaches to the seating unit, the seating unit must be in place first to serve as the anchor point.
Final finishes or sealants (if applied on-site) should be done after the bench is fully installed to ensure even coverage and protection of all surfaces.
The seat riser/step structure requires a stable, level foundation or base slab to bear its load and ensure proper alignment.
Seats or benches are mounted onto the riser/step structure, so the structural support must be complete first.
Handrails and guardrails are typically anchored to the riser/step structure and provide safety, so the structure must exist first.
Surface finishes (e.g., concrete topping, non-slip coating, tile) are applied on top of the completed riser/step structural substrate.
Any buried conduits, drainage pipes, or electrical lines that pass beneath the riser area must be installed and inspected before the structure is cast or built over them.
The seat mounting bracket must be attached to a stable frame; frame welding provides the structural base for bracket placement.
The seat cushion must be mounted onto the bracket; the bracket must be in place before the cushion can be attached.
Seat belt anchor points are typically integrated with the seat mounting bracket structure; bracket installation must precede seat belt anchoring.
Mounting holes must be prepared (drilled/tapped) in the frame before the bracket can be bolted or welded into position.
Seat rails must be mounted onto the fuselage structure; the fuselage must be structurally complete to provide the mounting surface and structural integrity for rail attachment.
Seat rails are typically attached to the floor grid of the aircraft cabin; the floor grid must be in place to anchor and align the seat rails.
Insulation and sealing under the floor must be completed before seat rails are installed to avoid having to remove or work around the rails later.
Seats are mounted directly onto the seat rails; the rail system must be fully installed and secured before any seats can be attached.

While some wiring can be routed overhead or through other paths, seat rails may need to be in place to secure cable management clips or raceways attached to the rails; this is a soft preference for orderly routing.
Seat numbering and signage must be installed on a solid, finished floor surface, so concrete floor pouring must be completed first.
Seat numbers and signs are affixed to the installed seating units; therefore, the seating or bleacher structure must be in place before numbering and signage can be applied.
Seat numbering and signage must be fully installed and verified before the final inspection can validate that all seating areas are properly labeled for occupancy and safety compliance.
Seat numbering and wayfinding signage must be completed before the venue can open to the public or host events, as attendees require clear seat identification and directional cues.
A stable, cured concrete foundation is physically necessary to support the seating area structure and prevent settlement or collapse.
The ground must be properly graded and leveled before any seating installation to ensure proper drainage, stability, and alignment.
Underground conduits and junction boxes for power or data to the seating area must be installed before the seating structure is placed over them.
The seating units are installed first; surrounding finishes like paving or tiles are laid up to the installed bases to create a clean, integrated appearance.
Handrails and guardrails are installed after seating is in place so they can be positioned correctly relative to the seating layout for safe egress and compliance with code.

The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated before any substructure elements (foundations, footings, riser supports) can be installed, as the substructure directly bears on the prepared ground.
Deep foundation elements such as piles must be driven/cast and cured before the substructure (pile caps, ground beams, riser base slabs) can be constructed on top of them to transfer loads safely.
Below-ground pipework, ducts, and utility connections need to be laid and backfilled before substructure concrete is poured, to avoid later excavation that could undermine the substructure.

The substructure (foundations, ground slab, riser base) provides the load-bearing platform and anchorage for the vertical superstructure frame; erection cannot commence until the substructure has cured and achieved design strength.

Waterproof membranes and tanking systems are applied to the external faces of the completed substructure (retaining walls, base slabs) before backfilling, to protect below-grade spaces from water ingress.

The seat frame provides the structural support needed for upholstery. Upholstery materials (foam, fabric, leather) cannot be applied until the frame is fully fabricated and ready for padding and covering.
Foam and padding layers must be installed onto the seat frame before the final upholstery fabric or leather can be stretched and fastened over them.
The finished upholstered seat must be completed before it can be assembled into the vehicle or furniture piece and installed in its final position.
Upholstery and finishing work must be complete before the final trim inspection can verify seam quality, material alignment, and overall appearance.
It is preferred to finish upholstery first so that final cleaning and detailing can remove any dust or debris generated during the upholstery process without re-soiling the seat.
The retractable seating system must be delivered and unpacked on-site before it can be commissioned, as no equipment is available to test or calibrate without its physical presence.
The seating system must be fully installed and assembled in its operational location before commissioning can begin, as commissioning checks operation of the assembled system.
Electrical power supply and control wiring must be roughed-in and terminated at the seating system to allow functional testing and commissioning of motors, controls, and safety systems.
Commissioning must verify that the system operates correctly before end-user training can be conducted on a fully functional system.
Successful commissioning of the retractable seating system is required as a prerequisite for final inspection and occupancy sign-off, ensuring all moving parts and safety features are verified.
Seating must be physically installed before an inspection can verify its accessibility compliance, including proper spacing, location, and configuration.
Floor surfaces and finishes around seating areas must be completed to allow inspection of accessible pathways, slopes, and clearances required for wheelchair seating areas.
Accessible signage (e.g., identifying accessible seating locations, directional signs) must be in place for the inspector to verify compliance with visibility and placement requirements.
While not a hard physical dependency, typically the accessibility inspection is completed before final closeout to ensure any non-compliance issues can be addressed before project handover.
A certificate of occupancy or use permit often requires proof of accessibility compliance, so the inspection must be passed before the space can be legally occupied or used.
The seating capacity cannot be surveyed until all seats/bleachers are physically installed and in place.
The official seating capacity count from the survey is required documentation for applying for the occupancy permit.
The seating capacity survey results must be finalized before the final building inspection can verify occupant load compliance.
Floor finishing must be complete to ensure accurate measurement and safe access for surveying the seating area.
The backrest must be attached to a completed bench frame structure for stability and proper alignment.
Cushions or padding can only be added after the backrest frame is securely installed to avoid damage or misalignment.
Surface finishing must be done after the backrest is installed to ensure uniform appearance and coverage across the entire bench.
A stable, level foundation or base must be prepared before the bench seat can be installed to ensure structural stability and proper alignment.
The bench seat components must be fabricated, delivered, and available on site before installation can commence.
The bench seat must be fully installed and anchored before any surface finishing treatments (e.g., staining, sealing, painting) are applied to protect the material and achieve a clean finish.

While the bench seat can be installed before final landscaping, it is often preferred to complete adjacent paving or planting first to avoid damaging the bench during landscape work; however, this is a soft preference rather than a physical necessity.
Final inspection and approval of the completed bench seat installation must occur after the bench is fully in place and finished.
The bench frame must be fully assembled to provide structural support and mounting points for the armrests.
The armrest component must be fabricated or manufactured before it can be installed onto the bench frame.
Armrests are typically installed before cushions to allow clear access to mounting hardware and to ensure proper alignment.
Final finishing touches like sanding and painting should be done after armrest installation to ensure a uniform and seamless appearance across all components.
Raw materials must be cut and prepared before they can be shaped and assembled into the armrest component.
Raw timber must be cut, planed, and prepared before it can be shaped into bench legs.
Bench legs must be fully fabricated before they can be attached to the bench frame or seat structure.

While some finishing can be done before assembly, the final surface treatment of the legs is typically done after they are attached to avoid handling damage; this is a soft preference for workflow efficiency.
Bench legs must be completed to allow final inspection of the assembled bench, including leg stability and alignment.
A stable, level foundation must be prepared before the bench base frame can be installed to ensure proper alignment and structural integrity.
The concrete foundation or pad must be fully cured to support the weight of the bench base frame without shifting or cracking.
All frame materials (timber/steel) must be cut and prepared to the required dimensions before assembly of the bench base frame can begin.
The base frame provides the structural support onto which the bench seat panels or slats are mounted; the seat cannot be installed without the frame in place.
The backrest frame typically attaches to or is supported by the base frame, so the base frame must be completed first to provide a stable anchor point.
The shoe storage cubby must be placed on a finished floor surface to ensure stability and proper alignment. Installing flooring first provides a level base.
The cubby is typically mounted to or placed against a wall; the wall structure must be complete to attach or position the cubby securely.
Baseboards should be installed after the cubby is in place so they can fit flush against the cubby's sides, creating a finished appearance.

Touch-up painting is typically done after all millwork and built-ins are installed to cover any nail holes, gaps, or scuffs; this is a soft preference as painting could be done before in some sequences.

successor: Mudding and Taping (if drywall needed behind)
rationale: Any wall finishing behind the cubby must be completed before the cubby is installed, as it would be inaccessible afterward.

The coat hook rail must be mounted on a finished wall surface. If the wall is not plastered and painted, the rail cannot be properly attached or aligned, and the finishing work would be damaged if done after rail installation.

Typically, trim work like baseboards or crown molding is installed after wall-mounted fixtures to allow for clean transitions and cutting around fixtures, but this is a soft preference for aesthetic finish order.
Once the coat hook rail is installed, any final touch-up painting around the mounted fixture should be completed to cover any screw holes or wall damage from installation.
Storage drawers are typically installed within or below base cabinets, so the base cabinets must be in place to provide the structural support and enclosure for the drawer.
Drawer slides must be mounted to the cabinet frame before the drawer box can be inserted and attached to the slides.
The drawer box must be fully constructed before it can be installed into the cabinet opening.
The drawer front or face panel is attached to the front of the installed drawer box, so the drawer must be in place first.
Drawer pulls or knobs are mounted onto the drawer front after the front is attached, requiring the drawer to be fully installed first.

While it's common to install flooring before cabinets for a cleaner look, if cabinets are installed first, flooring can still be installed up to the base of the drawers. This is a soft preference for sequencing.
The cushion or seat pad needs a supporting frame (like a chair frame or sofa frame) to be in place before it can be attached or placed.

predecessor: Cushion / Seat Pad Fabrication (cutting & sewing cover)
rationale: The cushion pad and its cover must be fabricated and assembled before the completed cushion/seat pad unit can be installed onto the frame.
After the cushion/seat pad is installed, final upholstery details like piping, trim, or decorative nails can be added.
The cushion/seat pad must be in place for final quality checks including fit, comfort, and appearance, though inspection could theoretically be done earlier in a less complete way.
The spring or webbing base that provides support under the cushion must be installed before the cushion/seat pad is placed on top.
The bench mounting bracket must be anchored to the column base plate, which provides the structural foundation for the bracket.
Columns must be verified for plumbness and alignment before brackets are mounted to ensure proper bracket positioning and alignment.
Accurate survey marking is required to identify the exact locations for bracket installation relative to column positions.
Bench beams are supported by or connected to the mounting brackets, so brackets must be in place before beams can be installed.
Loads from the bench system are transferred through the mounting brackets; thus brackets must be installed before any loading can be applied.
The ground must be leveled, cleared of debris, and properly graded before any bench can be installed to ensure a stable, level foundation.
If the bench requires a concrete base or footings (e.g., for permanent or heavy-duty benches), the concrete must be poured and fully cured before the bench can be anchored or mounted.
It is operationally more efficient to install the bench first, then landscape and plant around it to ensure proper alignment and access, though this is a soft preference.
Final cleanup and inspection are typically performed after all major installations, including benches, are complete to ensure a tidy finished site.
The site must be properly graded and excavated to establish stable foundations and working surfaces before any wall preparation work can begin.
Foundations must be poured and fully cured to provide a solid base for wall construction. Wall preparation cannot start without completed foundations.
The concrete slab on grade must be prepared and cured to serve as the floor substrate before walls are laid out and prepared.
All underground plumbing and electrical conduits must be installed beneath the slab before walls are erected to avoid costly rework and access issues.

Wall blocking and preparation (including installing backing, fire blocking, and nailers) must be completed before vertical framing members and stud walls can be erected, as blocking provides critical support structure.
Rough openings for windows and doors must be prepared and blocked before the actual window and door units can be installed.
Wall blocking must be in place to provide mounting points and fire-blocking before electricians can run wiring and install boxes within wall cavities.
Wall blocking and backing must be installed to support plumbing fixtures and pipes before rough-in plumbing work can proceed inside walls.
All wall blocking and preparation must be complete before insulation can be placed in wall cavities, as blocking defines cavity boundaries and fire safety compartments.
Flooring must be installed on a stable, cured concrete slab to provide a proper substrate and prevent cracking or moisture issues.
Underfloor MEP rough-ins (drainage, conduits, piping) must be completed before flooring is laid to avoid cutting or damaging finished flooring later.
While typically flooring is installed after painting to avoid damage, some sequences prefer flooring first; this is often a soft preference based on protecting finished floors.
Baseboards and trim are installed after flooring to cover the expansion gap and provide a clean transition between floor and wall.
Cabinets and heavy appliances are typically set on top of finished flooring to ensure proper height and avoid having to cut flooring around them.
The retaining core requires stable foundation conditions; excavation and foundation preparation must be completed first to provide a proper base and ensure structural integrity.
Backfilling around the retaining core can only commence once the core structure is fully in place and cured, as the core provides the necessary containment and support.
Drainage systems (e.g., weep holes, drainage pipes) are typically installed against or through the retaining core after it is built, to manage hydrostatic pressure.
Waterproofing membranes or coatings are applied to the completed retaining core surface to protect it from moisture ingress.
Reinforcement steel (rebar) must be placed and tied within the formwork prior to concrete placement for the retaining core, as the steel provides tensile strength embedded within the core.
Excavation must be completed to expose the ground and create a trench or area where the footing can be placed.
The soil or subgrade must be compacted and leveled to provide a stable, load-bearing base for the footing.
The exact location, alignment, and dimensions of the footing must be surveyed and marked before pouring or placing the footing material.
Formwork must be erected to contain and shape the concrete for the footing before pouring.
The wall base footing must be fully cured and provide a solid foundation before any wall elements (blocks, poured walls, etc.) can be built on top.
While waterproofing is often applied after footing cure, some waterproofing can be done concurrently; however, it is standard practice to complete the footing first.
Backfilling cannot commence until the footing is in place and has achieved sufficient strength to resist lateral earth pressures.
A stable foundation or footing must be in place to support the precast concrete plank; otherwise, the plank cannot be safely installed.
The structural frame (columns, beams) must be erected to provide bearing surfaces for precast concrete planks.
The precast concrete plank forms the structural roof deck; waterproofing must be applied over the completed deck to seal the building envelope.
Workers can run MEP services beneath the deck after the planks are in place; however, some prefabrication may happen earlier, so this is a soft preference for safety and access.
Ceiling finishes (e.g., drywall, suspended ceiling) cannot be installed until the structural roof deck (precast concrete plank) is complete and secure.
The site must be cleared of vegetation, debris, and existing structures before any earthmoving or excavation can begin, as obstructions would prevent access and grading operations.
Accurate survey stakes, benchmarks, and grade markings are required to guide excavation depths, cut/fill lines, and slope angles before earthwork commences.
Soil bearing capacity, compaction characteristics, and groundwater conditions must be known to determine excavation methods, slope stability, and compaction requirements.
Existing underground utilities (gas, water, electric, telecom) must be located and marked to avoid damage during excavation and grading operations.
Properly excavated and graded subgrade at design elevations and compaction is required before concrete footings, foundations, or slab-on-grade can be placed.

successor: Installation of Underground Utilities and Drainage
rationale: Trench excavation for underground pipes, conduits, and drainage systems must be completed during the earthwork phase before backfilling and final grading.
Fill placement and compaction during grading must be tested and verified before subsequent construction can proceed on the prepared subgrade.
Excavation must be completed to create the space and proper ground conditions for placing formwork and pouring concrete for footings.
The soil/base must be properly compacted and leveled to provide a stable foundation for footing formwork and concrete.
Surveying and setting out of exact footing locations and levels is required before formwork can be positioned and concrete poured.
After pouring, the concrete footings must undergo a curing period to gain sufficient strength before any subsequent loads are applied.
Waterproofing application can only commence after the footing concrete has been poured and set sufficiently.
Masonry walls require a stable, level bearing surface; the foundation or slab must be fully cured to support the weight of masonry units without settling or cracking.
Fresh mortar must be available to bond masonry units; mortar preparation (batching, mixing) must be completed before or concurrent with laying walls.
Safe access at the required working height is physically necessary for masons to place and align units above ground level.
Mortar joints must be tooled and allowed to cure after the units are laid; this finishing step cannot proceed until the units are positioned and initially set.
Vertical or horizontal reinforcement and grout placement occur after the masonry units are laid to specified courses, filling the cores or bond beam channels.
Lintels or structural beams spanning door/window openings are placed on top of the completed masonry courses that form the opening's sides.
Cleaning excess mortar and applying sealers or treatments is typically done after the wall is complete, though some initial cleaning is done as work progresses.
The surface must be properly prepared (cleaned, smoothed, and primed) before sealing and finishing can be applied, as sealants and finishes will not adhere properly to unprepared surfaces.
The underlying substrate (e.g., concrete, drywall, wood) must be fully installed and cured before any surface sealing or finishing can be applied.
Structural framing and support systems must be completed to provide the base onto which surface materials and finishes are applied.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-ins (wiring, piping, ductwork) behind walls/ceilings must be completed before sealing and finishing, as access behind finished surfaces would be permanently restricted.
After sealing and finishing are complete, the area undergoes final cleaning and any necessary touch-up work to prepare for occupancy or subsequent non-structural installations.
Although fixtures and trims are often installed after surface finishing to avoid damage, some may be installed before depending on sequence; generally, finishing first prevents soiling of fixtures.
If sealing and finishing is a preparatory or base coat step, any final decorative coatings or paints must be applied after sealing is complete to ensure proper layering and adhesion.
Electrical wiring and junction boxes must be installed and roughed in before lighting fixtures can be mounted and connected to the power supply.
The ceiling grid or structure must be in place to provide the physical support and mounting surface for recessed or surface-mounted lighting fixtures.
Ceiling insulation must be installed before lighting fixtures to ensure proper thermal envelope and to prevent fixtures from being blocked by insulation material.

While some fixtures are installed after drywall, integrated fixtures (e.g., recessed lighting) typically require the ceiling finish to be completed around or after the fixture housing is set; however this is often a soft preference depending on the fixture type.

successor: Lighting Control System / Dimmer Switch Installation
rationale: The physical lighting fixtures must be installed before control devices (dimmers, switches, smart controls) can be fully wired, tested, and commissioned to operate the specific fixtures.
The ridge cable is installed along the ridge of the roof, so the roof deck must be in place to provide the structural surface and support for the ridge cable system.
The ridge cable must be fully installed and secured before the final roof covering (such as shingles or metal panels) is applied over the ridge, as the cable is concealed beneath the covering.

Snow guards are often installed after the ridge cable to ensure proper alignment and integration with the ridge snow retention system, though this is a preferred sequence rather than a strict physical necessity.
The structural framing, including ridge beams and rafters, must be completed to provide the anchorage points and support structure for the ridge cable system.

Once the ridge cable (which may be part of a lightning protection system) is installed, the electrical grounding path can be tested and inspected; this is a preferred sequence for system verification.
Valley cables are structural components that are installed on top of roof sheathing; the sheathing must be in place to provide the base surface and structural support for valley cable installation.
Roof underlayment (felt or synthetic) is typically laid over sheathing and before any exposed metal components to provide waterproofing; valley cables are installed over the underlayment.

Valley cables form the metal flashing channels at roof valleys; roof tiles or shingles are installed after and overlap the valley cable to create a watertight seal, with tiles cut and fitted around the cable.
Valley cables serve as primary valley flashing; additional step flashing or counter-flashing integration at the valley edges occurs after the valley cable is secured in place.

The roof framing structure, including rafters and valley rafters, must be fully erected to define the valley geometry and provide the structural support onto which sheathing and subsequently valley cables are installed.

The perimeter cable is typically installed around the foundation or building footprint, which requires the foundation excavation to be completed first to expose the area where the cable will be placed.
Concrete foundation must be poured and cured before perimeter cable (e.g., grounding cable or perimeter security cable) can be installed around or embedded near the foundation.
Perimeter cable must be laid in trenches around the foundation before backfilling can occur, as the cable would be buried and inaccessible after backfill.
If the perimeter cable runs under the slab, it must be installed before the concrete slab is poured to avoid needing to core or break the slab later.
Perimeter cable is often pulled through underground conduits; the conduits must be installed first to provide a protected pathway for the cable.
The mast requires a stable foundation or base to be installed first to provide structural support and load distribution.
The ground must be prepared and excavated before the mast can be positioned and secured in place.
For tension masts, anchor points and guy wire foundations must be installed prior to mast erection to provide lateral stability.
Cables or conductors are strung between masts after they are erected, as the masts serve as the support structures.
Guy wires are attached and tensioned after the mast is erected to stabilize it against wind and load forces.
The site must be cleared of obstacles and debris before any ground anchor installation can begin to provide clear access and a safe working area.
The ground surface must be graded and leveled to the proper elevation before anchor installation to ensure accurate placement and load distribution.
Soil conditions and bearing capacity must be assessed to determine anchor type, depth, and design specifications before installation begins.
Mass excavation to the required subgrade elevation must be completed before ground anchors can be installed at the proper depth.
Ground anchors must be installed and secured before foundation reinforcement can be placed, as the anchors may need to integrate with or pass through the rebar cage.
Anchors must be fully installed and tensioned (if applicable) before concrete is poured so that the anchor heads or tie-ins are properly embedded and aligned in the foundation.
Clamp / Lacing System is used to secure and route electrical harnesses; therefore, the harness must first be installed before clamps and lacing can be applied.
Cables must be routed along the designated paths before clamps and lacing can secure them in place.
After clamps and lacing are applied, the cable installation can be inspected to verify proper securing and routing compliance.
Applying additional cable ties after lacing is a soft preference for extra bundling security, not a physical necessity.
Continuity testing must be done after all harnesses are fully clamped and laced to ensure no damage occurred during the securing process.
Gutters are attached to the roof edges; the roof structure must be in place to provide support and alignment for gutter installation.
External wall cladding or rendering must be completed before gutters are installed to ensure proper flashing integration and weatherproofing at the wall-roof junction.
Downpipes connect directly to gutters/drainage channels to carry water down; gutters must be in place first to define the collection points and connection locations.

While not physically mandatory, it is preferable to complete gutter and drainage channel installation before final landscape grading and soffit works to avoid rework and ensure drainage outlets are correctly positioned.
For ground-level drainage channels, the concrete slab or foundation must be poured and cured to provide a stable base and correct fall for channel installation.
The turnbuckle must be physically installed in place before tensioning can be applied to it; tensioning is the act of tightening the turnbuckle after installation.
Cables, rods, or other structural elements must be connected to the turnbuckle ends before tensioning, as tensioning adjusts the effective length of these connected elements.
After tensioning the turnbuckle, the achieved tension or tightness must be verified/measured to ensure it meets design specifications.

successor: Lock Turnbuckle (Jam Nut or Cotter Pin)
rationale: Once the turnbuckle is tensioned to the correct amount, the jam nuts or locking mechanism must be secured to prevent the turnbuckle from loosening over time.
While not strictly physically required before inspection, tensioning should be completed prior to final inspection to allow the inspector to confirm that all tensioning is properly done.
The specific fabric material must be selected and procured before any fabric panels can be manufactured or installed on-site.
The wall structure and backing surface (e.g., plywood or drywall) must be in place to provide a mounting surface for fabric panels.
Electrical wiring, outlets, and data cabling behind the wall must be completed before covering the wall with fabric panels, as later access would require panel removal.
Trim and molding pieces that abut or frame the fabric panel edges must be installed after the panels are in place to create clean finished edges.
While not strictly required, final painting is typically done after fabric panel installation to avoid paint splatter on the fabric and to touch up any areas around the newly installed panels.
The fabric roof membrane requires a supporting steel frame structure to be in place before it can be tensioned and attached.
Anchor points and foundation systems must be fully cured and load-bearing to secure the tensioned fabric membrane.
Edge seals, flashings, and weatherproofing work must follow the fabric placement to ensure watertight connections at perimeter and penetration points.
Interior trades typically wait until the roof is installed to protect against weather damage, but sequencing can sometimes overlap with protective measures.
Final tensioning of the fabric membrane and structural adjustments must be performed after the fabric is placed and clamped to achieve the proper stress distribution and architectural shape.
Cables must be installed and properly positioned in the ducts or sheathing before tensioning can be applied.
The dead-end anchorages must be installed and secured before tensioning forces can be applied to the cables.
In pre-tensioned precast applications, formwork installation typically precedes cable tensioning to provide the casting bed and alignment for the strands.
In pre-tensioning, concrete is cast around the already-tensioned cables; tension is transferred to the concrete after it cures. The cables must be tensioned before concrete placement.
Concrete must be placed and cured while the cables remain under tension so that the bond develops and the prestressing force transfers to the concrete upon release.
The membrane material must be manufactured and stored before any patterning or cutting operations can be applied to it.
The membrane must be physically delivered to the work location before it can be patterned or cut on-site.
The membrane must first be cut to its required shape and size before it can be placed and positioned at its final location.
Individual membrane panels must be cut and patterned before they can be joined together through seaming or welding.
The edges of the membrane must be cut to shape before edge detailing and termination details can be executed.
Fabric must be cut to the required shapes and sizes before pieces can be welded or seamed together.
Fabric material must be inspected and approved for quality and defects before welding or seaming begins, to avoid joining defective material.
Welded seams must be completed before air tightness or leak testing can be performed to verify seam integrity.
The completed welded and seamed fabric assembly must be finished before a quality control inspection of the fabrication work can occur.
The fabric membrane must be fully welded and seamed into its final configuration before it can be transported to the site and installed in its permanent location.
A conceptual design or initial geometry must be established before form-finding analysis can begin, as form-finding requires a starting shape or design intent to analyze and optimize.
Site conditions, boundary conditions, and foundation constraints must be known to inform the form-finding process, as they affect the feasible structural forms.
Material properties such as stiffness, strength, and weight directly influence the outcome of form-finding analysis; the analysis requires knowledge of the material to be used.
The optimized geometry derived from form-finding analysis must be finalized before detailed structural members can be sized and connections detailed.
The final form found shape is a prerequisite for producing construction drawings and specifications that reflect the actual geometry to be built.
Fabric must be installed before it can be cleaned or maintained, as cleaning is performed on already-installed fabric surfaces.
Cleaning and maintenance of fabric elements must be completed before the final inspection and handover to ensure the fabric is in pristine condition for the client.
It is preferable to clean and maintain fabric elements before installing furniture and equipment to avoid soiling or damaging the fabric during subsequent installation works.
The structural frame (walls, roof structure) must be in place to provide a mounting surface and support for the membrane installation.
The roof deck or substrate must be clean, dry, smooth, and properly prepared to ensure adhesion and proper installation of the membrane.
Flashing details (edge metal, pipe boots, wall flashings) are installed over or integrated with the membrane to seal penetrations and edges, so the membrane must be in place first.
In some roof assemblies, insulation is placed above the membrane; in that case, membrane must be down first to serve as the waterproofing layer beneath the insulation.
Water testing of the roof membrane is typically performed after installation to verify watertight integrity, though in some sequences flood testing occurs incrementally.
The structural framing or wall assembly must be in place to provide a cavity or surface for the acoustic liner/insulation to be installed onto or within.
MEP services within walls/ceilings must be roughed-in before insulation/liner is installed, as the liner would obstruct access to these services.
The acoustic liner/insulation must be fully installed before enclosing finishes (e.g., drywall, ceiling tiles, wall panels) are applied, as the liner is placed behind the finish surface.

Post-installation acoustic testing is typically performed after the liner is in place to verify acoustic performance, though this is a quality assurance preference rather than a physical impossibility to do otherwise.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and prepared before building the planter bed frame to ensure stability and proper alignment.
All required materials such as lumber, screws, brackets, and tools must be acquired before construction can begin.
Lumber must be cut to the specified lengths for the frame sides and corners before assembly can take place.
The weed barrier fabric is typically laid inside the completed frame to prevent weeds from growing up through the bed.
The planter bed must be fully constructed before filling it with soil; otherwise, the soil would spill out.

While irrigation can theoretically be installed after filling, it is easier and more convenient to lay irrigation lines within or along the frame before or after filling, but this is a soft preference rather than a physical necessity.
The ground must be excavated, leveled, and compacted before any floor structure can be poured or installed.
A properly prepared subbase (e.g., gravel base, vapor barrier) is required to support the planter base or floor slab.
Any drainage pipes or utility lines that will run beneath the planter base must be placed before the concrete or structural floor is poured.
Once the concrete planter base/floor is cured, waterproofing membranes or coatings must be applied to protect the structure from moisture.
The base floor must be complete to provide a foundation and anchor point for the vertical planter walls or edge forms to be built upon.
The ground must be properly graded, cleared of debris, and leveled before landscape fabric can be laid; otherwise the fabric will not lie flat and may be punctured by rocks or roots.
Any drainage pipes, French drains, or gravel drainage layers must be placed before the root barrier/fabric, as the barrier is laid on top of the prepared sub-base and drainage system.
Underground utilities (water, gas, electric, data) must be located and buried before installing root barrier to avoid future conflicts and the need to cut through the barrier.

The landscape fabric / root barrier is designed to separate the sub-base from the decorative surface layer (gravel, mulch, or soil), so the cover material must go on top of the fabric to hold it in place and provide the final landscape finish.

Plants are typically installed by cutting X-shaped slits in the fabric; therefore the fabric must be fully laid before planting, and this order ensures the root barrier function is intact around each plant.
Edging and coping are typically installed after concrete slabs are poured and finished because they form the perimeter or top edge of concrete structures like pools, walkways, or walls.
Coping stones or edging materials are often placed on top of masonry or block walls to cap and protect them, requiring the wall structure to be complete first.
Proper ground preparation and grading must be completed to provide a stable, level base for installing edging and coping elements.
Waterproofing or sealant application is often done after edging and coping installation to seal joints and prevent water infiltration between coping stones and the structure.
Final landscaping and surface finishes are typically completed after edging and coping to avoid damaging the finished edges and to achieve a clean aesthetic transition.
Topsoil must be stripped and stockpiled to expose the soil surface that will receive fertilisation and conditioning treatments.
Vegetation, debris and roots must be cleared from the site before soil conditioning can take place to ensure access to bare soil.
The site must be graded to final contours before fertilisation and soil conditioning to prevent washout and ensure even distribution of amendments.
Seeding must follow soil conditioning because fertilised and conditioned soil provides the nutrient-rich seedbed necessary for germination and plant establishment.
Sod or turf must be laid after soil conditioning so that the root zone has adequate nutrients and soil structure for establishment.
The site must be cleared and prepared before any pruning or deadheading can begin to ensure safe access and visibility of the plants.
Plants must be planted and established before any pruning or deadheading can take place, as this work is performed on established vegetation.
The debris and cuttings generated from pruning and deadheading must be collected and disposed of after the activity is complete.
Mulching and soil amendment can follow pruning and deadheading to improve soil conditions and aesthetics, but this is a soft preference based on logical sequencing rather than a physical necessity.
Irrigation installation is often done after pruning to avoid damaging new systems, but the order can be flexible depending on scheduling constraints.
The ground must be properly graded and prepared with appropriate soil conditions before any planting can occur to ensure proper drainage, soil stability, and root growth conditions.

Underground utilities such as irrigation lines, drainage pipes, and electrical conduits must be installed before planting to avoid disturbing root systems and to ensure utilities are placed at correct depths without damaging newly planted vegetation.
Soil must be tested for pH, nutrients, and contaminants, and any necessary amendments (fertilizers, lime, compost) must be incorporated prior to planting to establish optimal growing conditions.
Mulch and soil erosion control measures are applied immediately after planting to retain moisture, regulate soil temperature, and prevent weed growth around newly planted specimens.

While irrigation lines are installed underground before planting, the final connection, above-ground components, and system testing occur after planting to ensure water delivery is properly positioned and calibrated for the newly installed plants.
Trenching and excavation must be completed to expose and access underground irrigation pipes and components before any maintenance can be performed.
The water supply to the irrigation system must be shut off to ensure safe working conditions and prevent water damage or injury during maintenance.
Safety barricades, signage, and confined space permits must be in place before workers can enter irrigation trenches or valve boxes.
Trenches and excavations can only be backfilled and compacted after all irrigation repairs, replacements, or adjustments are complete to avoid re-excavation.
After maintenance is performed, the system must be tested under pressure to verify repairs, check for leaks, and ensure proper operation before restoring normal service.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and excavated before any structural elements can be placed. Foundations cannot be installed on unprepared ground.
Load-bearing foundations (footings, pads, piles) must be completed and cured before structural framing, columns, beams, or walls can be erected on top of them.
The main structural frame and load-bearing elements must be in place before roof trusses, decking, or building envelope systems can be installed.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work typically begins after the structural skeleton is complete, as pipes, ducts, and conduits are routed through the structural framework.
External cladding, curtain walls, and façade systems are applied onto or attached to the completed structural frame, requiring the structure to be stable and fully erected first.
A stable foundation and anchor points must be established before installing the wire rope guide system to ensure proper alignment and load-bearing capacity.
The primary structural framework must be in place to provide attachment points and support for the wire rope guide system components.
The wire rope guide system must be fully installed before tensioning and fine-tuning the cables to achieve the designed alignment and tension specifications.
The wire rope guide system must be completed before any operational or load testing can be performed to verify system performance and safety.
The previous season's crops must be fully harvested and removed from the field before new planting can occur, as leftover plant material would obstruct seeding or transplanting operations.
Soil conditions (nutrient levels, pH, salinity) must be assessed before replanting to determine if any soil amendments or treatments are needed for the new crop cycle.
The soil must be tilled, leveled, and prepared (e.g., plowing, disking, bed formation) to create a suitable seedbed or planting medium before any replanting can occur.
Any necessary fertilizers, lime, compost, or other soil amendments must be applied and incorporated into the soil before planting to ensure proper nutrient availability for the new crop.
The irrigation system must be inspected, repaired if needed, and configured for the new planting layout before seeds or seedlings are placed, as post-planting water delivery is critical.
Newly planted seeds or transplants require immediate watering to settle the soil around roots/seed and initiate germination; irrigation cannot start before planting is complete.
Pre-emergent herbicides are often applied after planting to prevent weed germination, though some formulations are applied before planting; this is a common practice but timing can vary by product.
Plastic mulch, straw mulch, or row covers must be applied after seeds/transplants are in place (unless pre-planted mulch with punched holes is used, which would be a different process).

Additional fertilizer applications during the growing season occur after plants are established, but the exact timing depends on crop growth stage rather than being an immediate post-planting requirement.
Post-planting monitoring for germination/establishment, pest pressure, and weed competition can only commence after the replanting is complete and plants are in the ground.
The ground must be leveled, excavated, and any concrete footings or foundation pads must be cured before the pergola frame can be installed in order to provide a stable and level base.
Post holes must be dug and concrete footings poured and fully cured to support the vertical posts of the pergola frame; otherwise the structure would lack proper anchorage.

The pergola frame (beams, rafters, and columns) must be fully erected and secured before any roofing material, lattice, or shade slats are attached, as the roof structure relies on the frame for support.
Any decorative cladding or trim that wraps around the pergola posts or beams must be applied after the frame is fully assembled to ensure a proper fit and alignment.

While lighting can theoretically be added later, routing conduit and mounting fixtures is significantly easier and safer when the frame is exposed and accessible, making it a strong preference to do before roof installation.
The ground must be prepared and excavated before any plant training infrastructure can be installed.
Concrete foundations must be set and cured to provide stable support for plant training ties and clips.
Steel reinforcement must be in place within the concrete to ensure structural integrity before attaching training ties and clips.
Training ties and clips are needed to secure and guide climbing plants onto vertical support posts.
Ties and clips must be installed first to then train and guide plant growth along desired paths.
After installation, a soft preference exists to inspect and adjust ties/clips for optimal plant training, though it is not physically mandatory.
The ground must be excavated and prepared to the required formation level before the root barrier membrane can be laid, as it must be placed on a stable, prepared subgrade.
The subgrade must be compacted and levelled to provide a smooth, uniform surface for the root barrier membrane to be installed without punctures or uneven loading.
A protective geotextile or sand blinding layer is often placed immediately over the root barrier membrane to shield it from damage during subsequent construction activities.
The root barrier membrane must be fully installed before backfill material or overlying layers (e.g., soil, gravel, or slab sub-base) are placed above it.

successor: Concrete Slab / Pavement Construction (if directly above)
rationale: If a concrete slab or pavement is to be constructed directly above the root barrier, the membrane must be in place first to prevent root ingress from below.
Soil must be prepared, enriched with compost, and brought to the correct grade before any planting can occur to ensure proper root establishment and plant health.
The base planting soil layer and any aggregate drainage materials must be in place before climbers are planted to provide the correct growing medium and drainage conditions.

predecessor: Installation of Drainage Matting & Protection Board
rationale: Drainage matting and protection boards behind planting areas must be installed first to prevent water damage to structures and ensure proper water management before soil and plants go in.

Irrigation pipes, driplines, or emitters must be placed after climbers are planted to avoid damaging the root balls during trenching and to allow precise positioning around the newly installed plants.
Mulch and final surface finishes are applied after planting to protect the soil surface, retain moisture around the new climbers, and provide a clean aesthetic finish without disturbing the plants.
The ground must be cleared, leveled, and graded before any planter bed can be installed to ensure proper drainage and a stable base.
Any underground drainage pipes, irrigation supply lines, or electrical conduits serving the planter must be laid and inspected before the planter structure is built or soil is placed.

predecessor: Foundation / Base Slab (if planter is on a built structure)
rationale: If the raised planter is located on a concrete slab or structural deck, the slab must be poured and cured before the planter walls are constructed on top.
The planter structure (walls, base drainage layer) must be fully constructed before clean fill, planting mix, and amendments are added.
Drip lines, emitters, and surface irrigation components are installed after the planter is built and before plants are placed.
Plants cannot be installed until the planter structure, soil, and irrigation are in place and ready to receive vegetation.
After plants are installed and watered in, mulch and decorative top dressing are applied to complete the planting bed.

Columns and beams provide the main structural framework and support points for the trellis system; the trellis and wires must be anchored to or suspended from the structural frame, requiring it to be built first.
Foundations and footings support the columns and the overall trellis structure; they must be completed before any above-ground trellis installation.
The trellis and wire system must be in place before planting vines or vegetation, as the plants will need the support structure for training and growth from the outset.

While irrigation can technically be installed before or after the trellis, installing it after avoids interference and allows the trellis layout to guide precise irrigation placement; this is a soft preference for construction efficiency.

Drip lines and mulch are typically laid after the trellis and wires are installed to align with the trellis rows and avoid disturbing the wire system; however, it is a sequencing preference rather than a physical necessity.
Pruning and training can only begin after the plant has been established in the ground. There is no plant structure to prune or train before planting and initial establishment.

Pruning stimulates new growth, and applying fertilizer immediately after pruning ensures nutrients are available to support that new growth. While not physically impossible to do before, it is best practice to prune first.
After pruning, the plant's canopy is reduced, so its water demand changes. Adjusting irrigation scheduling post-pruning is optimal but not physically mandatory.
Pruning opens up the canopy, making pest and disease detection easier. Monitoring should follow pruning for effective scouting, but this is a soft preference rather than a physical necessity.
For deciduous plants, major structural pruning is done during dormancy to minimize stress and sap loss. Pruning during active growth can damage the plant, making this a hard physical constraint.
Scaffolding must be erected to provide physical access to the building facade for inspection.
Inspection should precede cleaning to identify areas needing special attention, though cleaning could theoretically begin without inspection in some cases.
The inspection results are required to identify defects and plan the necessary repair and restoration work.
Repair work cannot be specified or executed without first knowing the condition of the facade through inspection.
The building envelope must be substantially complete before a meaningful condition inspection of the facade can be performed.
Underground water supply lines and electrical conduits must be installed before the irrigation system can be commissioned and tested.
The site must be roughly graded and cleared before irrigation piping and sprinkler heads can be placed and the system commissioned.
All irrigation pipes, valves, and sprinkler heads must be physically installed before the system can be pressurized, tested, and commissioned.
Commissioning ensures the system operates correctly without leaks or coverage gaps before final landscaping, topsoil, and sod are placed over the irrigation lines.
While commissioning can occur before fine grading, it is preferred to complete final grading after the irrigation system is tested to avoid rework if adjustments to sprinkler heads are needed.
The site must be cleared of existing structures, debris, and vegetation before new plants can be installed to provide a clean, accessible planting area.
Final grading and soil preparation must be completed to establish proper drainage and soil conditions before planting begins.
All buried utilities (irrigation lines, drainage pipes, electrical conduits) must be installed before planting to avoid disturbing or damaging newly planted vegetation.
Mulch and topsoil are typically applied around newly planted specimens after they are in the ground to retain moisture and suppress weeds without burying the plant crowns.

While irrigation can be partially tested before planting, full system activation and fine-tuning around the specific placement of plants should occur after replanting to ensure each plant receives adequate water.
A thorough structural assessment must be completed before any maintenance or repair work begins to identify all damaged or deteriorated areas requiring attention.
Safe access scaffolding or elevated work platforms must be erected to allow workers to reach the support structure for maintenance and repair activities.
Temporary shoring or propping must be installed to safely support the structure while repairs are carried out, preventing collapse or further damage.
Any hazardous materials such as asbestos or lead paint must be removed prior to repair work to ensure worker safety and regulatory compliance.
After repairs are completed, load testing and structural verification must be performed to confirm that the support structure meets required strength and safety standards.
Scaffolding and access systems can only be dismantled once the maintenance and repair work on the support structure is fully completed.
A final quality control inspection must be conducted after all repair work is finished to verify that the work meets specifications and standards.
Stones must be positioned before the joints or gaps between them can be formed or filled.
Mortar must be prepared and available before it can be applied into the joints between stones.
The joints or gaps must exist (formed by placed stones) before mortar can be applied into them.
Joints must be formed or filled before they can be finished or tooled for appearance and weatherproofing.
A stable foundation or base course must be laid before stones are placed and joints are formed above it.
The ground must be excavated and leveled before any bedding layer can be placed, as the bedding layer requires a stable, prepared subgrade surface.
The subgrade soil must be compacted and proof-rolled to achieve adequate bearing capacity before placing the bedding layer, otherwise the bedding material may settle unevenly.
Any separation or reinforcement geotextile must be laid directly on the prepared subgrade before the bedding layer is placed above it.
The bedding layer provides a uniform support surface and protective cushion for buried pipes or conduits, so pipe laying cannot begin until the bedding is in place.
After pipes are laid on the bedding, haunching material is placed and compacted around the sides of the pipe, which requires the bedding layer to already be present.
The subgrade must be properly graded, compacted, and approved before placing sub-base material, as the sub-base relies on a stable and uniform subgrade for support and thickness control.

Subsurface drainage pipes and related drainage layers must be installed before placing the sub-base, otherwise the sub-base would block access and prevent proper installation and backfill of drainage elements.

The granular base course acts as a load-bearing platform for the overlying pavement layers; the base course or pavement slab cannot be placed until the sub-base is compacted and finished to the required profile.

Kerbs or edge restraints are typically installed after the sub-base is placed and shaped but before the final surface course, though in some sequences kerbs may be placed earlier if used as a guide; this is a soft preference for smooth workflow.

Utility trenches and conduits are often laid after sub-base to avoid disturbing the compacted layer, but shallow utilities can sometimes be placed before; typically a preference to avoid rework and maintain compaction integrity.
All vegetation, debris, and existing structures must be removed from the site before any earthworks or formation preparation can begin.
The fertile topsoil layer must be removed to expose the underlying subgrade material before formation level can be prepared.
Bulk excavation to achieve the required formation level must be completed before the subgrade layer can be shaped, compacted, and finished.
The subgrade/formation layer provides the foundational load-bearing surface; the sub-base layer cannot be placed until the subgrade is fully prepared, compacted, and approved.
Geotextile membranes are often placed directly on the prepared subgrade surface before subsequent layers; the subgrade must be complete to provide a stable base for the membrane.
Subsurface drainage pipes and gravel blankets are typically laid on or within the subgrade formation; the formation level must be prepared first to achieve correct drainage gradients and support.

All pavement layers (base, binder, wearing course) or concrete slabs rely on the subgrade for structural support; the subgrade must be complete and compacted to specification before any pavement works commence.
The sub-base must be prepared and compacted to provide a stable foundation before edge restraints or kerbs can be installed.
Any underground drainage pipes or services must be laid before kerbs are installed to avoid excavation damage to the newly placed kerbs.
Typically the lower pavement layers are placed before kerbs, though in some sequences kerbs can be installed first depending on design.
Kerbs and edge restraints define the boundary and level for paving; the paved surface must be laid up to the finished kerb line.
After kerbs are set and cured, the area behind them must be backfilled and compacted to provide lateral support.

The subgrade must be properly prepared, graded, and compacted to provide a stable, uniform base for stone paving. Installing stone on an unprepared subgrade would lead to uneven settlement and pavement failure.
A load-bearing aggregate base course must be placed and compacted over the subgrade to distribute loads and provide drainage before stone pavers can be laid.
Edge restraints or curbs must be installed prior to paving to contain the stone pavers laterally and prevent spreading or shifting of the paving units.
After stone pavers are laid, joint sand must be swept into the gaps or sealant applied to lock the pavers in place and prevent weed growth and water infiltration.
Once stone paving is installed, a plate compactor must be used to tamp the pavers into the bedding layer, ensuring uniform leveling and seating of the stones before final joint treatment.
Sub-base material must be spread and leveled to a uniform layer before compaction can begin, as compaction requires a consistent layer thickness to achieve proper density.
The sub-base material must be conditioned to the optimal moisture content before compaction, as proper moisture is essential for achieving maximum dry density and compaction efficiency.
Quality control tests (such as field density tests) must be performed after compaction to verify that the specified compaction requirements have been met.
While surface finishing can follow compaction, it is a soft preference as minor grading adjustments can sometimes be done during the final compaction passes rather than strictly after.
Formal inspection and approval of the compacted sub-base layer must occur after compaction is complete to ensure it meets specifications before subsequent layers are placed.
Joint filling/pointing is the finishing step that seals the gaps between bricks, blocks, or stones after they have been laid and the mortar has initially set.
The mortar joints between masonry units must first be formed and allowed to partially set before pointing/filling can be applied.
After pointing is completed, the applied pointing mortar must be cured (kept moist) to achieve proper strength and prevent cracking.
Excess mortar and stains from pointing must be cleaned off the masonry surface after pointing is complete to achieve the final appearance.
Waterproofing or sealants are typically applied after pointing is fully cured to protect the joints; this is a hard constraint if waterproofing is specified, otherwise a best practice sequence.
Stone must be fully installed and set before any cleaning or maintenance can be performed.
Grouting and sealing must be completed first to avoid damaging fresh joints during cleaning and to ensure the stone surface is ready for final treatment.
Cleaning and maintenance must be completed before final inspection to present a clean, finished surface for quality assessment.
Cleaning must precede sealing or coating application to ensure the stone surface is free of dirt, debris, and residues for proper adhesion.
Cleaning and maintenance must be finished before the building or area is handed over to the client or occupants.
Skirting tiles are installed at the base of walls, so the wall surface must be finished (plastered, painted, or otherwise prepared) before skirting can be fixed to it.
The floor must be screeded and leveled before skirting tiles are installed, as skirting sits on top of the finished floor level and requires a flat, stable substrate.
Main floor tiles are typically laid first, and skirting tiles are installed afterwards to cover the expansion gap between the floor and wall, providing a neat finish.

While skirting is usually installed after main wall painting, final touch-up painting along the top edge of the skirting is often done after installation to cover any gaps or sealant marks. This is a soft preference for aesthetic finish rather than a physical necessity.

Skirting tiles should be installed before architraves or door casings are fitted, so that the skirting butts neatly into the architrave. However, this can be done in the reverse order with careful cutting, so it is a soft preference for best appearance.
Tile requires a clean, level, and structurally sound subfloor to prevent cracking and ensure proper adhesion.
A moisture barrier (e.g., waterproof membrane) must be installed beneath tiles in wet areas to prevent water damage and mold growth.
Fresh concrete or leveling compound must fully cure before tiling to avoid moisture-related adhesion failure and cracking.
Plumbing pipes and electrical conduits that run beneath or through the floor must be roughed in before tiling to avoid cutting or damaging finished tile.
Grout can only be applied after tiles are set and the thin-set mortar has cured; sealing occurs after grout dries.
Baseboards and trim are installed after tiling to cover the expansion gap and provide a clean finished edge.

successor: Cabinet and Vanity Placement (if floor tile)
rationale: Typically cabinets are set before floor tile to avoid tiling under cabinets (saves material), but if tile is installed first, cabinets go on top afterward.
The frieze rests on top of the columns in classical architecture, so columns must be in place to support the frieze.
In some configurations, the frieze is part of the entablature and sits above the architrave but below the cornice; the supporting beam/architrave must be in place first.
The frieze is typically mounted on or against a wall or structural backing, so the wall must be completed to provide attachment surface.
In classical entablature, the cornice sits directly above the frieze, so the frieze must be in place before the cornice can be installed above it.
