If a pediment is present, it rests above the entablature (which includes the frieze), so frieze must be complete before pediment is placed.
The foundation or support structure must be in place before the rosette component can be installed, as it provides the base for attachment.
The rosette must be physically installed before any finishing work such as painting, gilding, or surface detailing can be applied.
The rosette is typically mounted before the surrounding ceiling or wall surface is fully finished, as the rosette may overlap or abut the finished surface.
If the rosette serves as a mounting base for a chandelier or light fixture, the rosette must be securely installed before the lighting fixture can be attached to it.
The structural framing of the ceiling or wall must be completed to provide the substrate to which the rosette is fastened.
Egg-and-dart molding is typically applied as a decorative trim; it requires a flat, stable substrate or sheathing surface to be installed first so the molding can be properly fastened and aligned.
The structural framing of the building must be complete to provide the support and nailing surface for the molding installation.

Priming and painting the molding must occur after it is installed; painting cannot be done on loose or uninstalled pieces, and applying finish before installation would damage the coating during handling.
Typically the final trim inspection happens after all decorative moldings are in place to verify proper installation and alignment before sign-off.

Egg-and-dart molding is often installed at the junction of walls and ceilings; interior wall finishing such as drywall taping, mudding, and texturing should be completed before the molding is applied to ensure clean edges and proper fit.
Pilasters are vertical structural elements that must be supported by a stable foundation; without proper foundation work, the pilaster would lack adequate load-bearing support.
Pilasters are often engaged with or attached to walls; the wall structure must be in place or at least started to provide the backing or integration surface for the pilaster.
Pilasters frequently serve as supports for arches, entablatures, or cornices; these elements cannot be placed until the pilaster is erected to bear their load.
While finishing typically follows structural installation, it is a soft preference because some decorative work could theoretically be done in parallel or with temporary support in certain cases.
It is generally easier to finish the wall after the pilaster is in place to ensure seamless joints, but this is a workflow preference rather than a physical necessity.
The capital (column top/crown) sits atop a column or pillar and requires a stable foundation and erected structural support to bear its load.
The capital is the topmost element of a column, so the column shaft must be fully erected and stable before the capital can be placed on top.
The entablature rests directly on top of the capitals of columns; capitals must be in place to support the entablature beams.
In arcades or vaulted structures, arches spring from the capitals (imposts); capitals must be completed to provide the bearing point for arch construction.
The stone carving, sculpting, or ornamental detailing of the capital must be completed as part of the capital fabrication before the capital element is considered finished and ready for installation.
The finial sits at the apex of the roof, so the roof sheathing must be in place to provide the structural base for the finial mounting.
Waterproofing underlayment must be applied before adding any roof-mounted decorative elements like finials to ensure weather sealing beneath the finial.
Ridge flashing must be installed before the finial to create a watertight seal at the roof peak where the finial attaches.
It is standard practice to complete all roof-mounted elements including finials before the final inspection to verify completeness.
Scaffolding should remain in place until all roof work including finial installation is complete to ensure worker safety and access.
The stone must first be roughly shaped into a block or slab before the detailed acanthus leaf carving can begin, as carving requires a stable, pre-formed base material.
The stone surface must be smoothed and prepared to provide a proper canvas for the intricate acanthus leaf design, ensuring the carving tool can glide and cut accurately.
The acanthus leaf pattern must be drawn or transferred onto the stone surface as a guide before carving can commence, otherwise the carver would have no layout to follow.
After the primary acanthus leaf carving is completed, fine detail finishing (such as undercutting, veining, and polishing of the leaf edges) can be performed to refine the sculpture.
The carved acanthus leaf must be fully shaped before any final polishing or sealing (e.g., applying wax or protective coating) can be applied to the completed decorative element.
The bas-relief panel must be attached to a finished wall surface; the wall needs to be prepared (cleaned, leveled, or structured) before the panel can be installed.
The artistic design, mould creation, or carving of the panel must be completed before the panel itself can be manufactured or placed.
Once the panel is installed, final detailing, painting, sealing, or protective coating can be applied to complete the bas-relief.
After the panel is in position, any surrounding architectural trim, frame, or adjacent decorative elements can be installed flush against it.
The stone block must first be quarried and roughly shaped before any carving, including cartouche carving, can begin.
The surface of the stone must be smoothed and prepared to provide a suitable canvas for the detailed cartouche carving.
The design of the cartouche (oval outline and hieroglyphic text) must be planned and marked on the stone before carving begins.
The carved cartouche must be completed before any paint or color can be applied to the incised hieroglyphs and border.
The cartouche carving must be finished as part of the overall monument detailing before the final polishing and inspection of the complete structure can occur.
A fixing plate or backing must be securely attached to the ceiling substrate to provide a stable mounting surface for the plaster ceiling rose.
Any electrical cables for a light fitting that will pass through the ceiling rose must be routed and terminated before the rose is plastered in place, as access will be blocked.
The ceiling rose must be installed before the final plastering and painting of the ceiling, so that the joint between the rose and the ceiling can be finished seamlessly.
The ceiling rose provides the mounting and decorative base for a light fitting; the light fixture cannot be attached until the rose is securely in place.
Any final caulking, touch-up paint, or decorative detailing around the rose is best done after installation, though this is a soft preference for appearance rather than a structural requirement.
Quoins are structural cornerstones that reinforce and decorate the corners of masonry walls. The wall structure must be built up to the point where quoins are placed at the corners.
The foundation must be completed to support the weight of the wall and the quoins at the corners.
Quoins are typically set in mortar; the mortar mix must be prepared and ready before placing the quoins.
After quoins are set in place, the mortar joints around them need to be finished, pointed, and tooled for weatherproofing and aesthetics.

While quoins are often installed before final cladding or plastering to define the corners, in some cases cladding can be done before quoins if quoins are applied as decorative overlays. Typically, quoins are installed first to serve as a guide for the finished wall surface.
Pediment is a horizontal architectural element that sits atop columns or a wall structure, so the supporting vertical structure must be completed first to provide a bearing surface.
In classical architecture, the pediment typically rests on columns (most commonly the entablature above the columns). Columns must be erected to support the pediment.
The pediment is formed by the horizontal cornice of the entablature and the raking cornices above it; the entablature must be in place to define the base of the pediment.
The pediment fills the triangular gable at the end of a roof; roof sheathing is laid over the pediment's backing structure, so the pediment must be installed first to close and finish the gable end.
Classical pediments often support decorative acroteria or statues at their apex and corners; these elements are installed on top of the finished pediment structure.
Festoon and swag lighting require electrical power supply; MEP rough-in for electrical conduits and wiring must be completed before festoon/swag installation to provide connections and avoid rework.
Festoon and swag elements are typically suspended from or mounted to the ceiling; the ceiling structure must be in place to provide anchorage and support.

Electrical trim-out and fixture installation (e.g., connecting light fixtures, switches, and covers) logically follows the placement of festoon/swag wiring and supports to complete the electrical system.
It is preferred to complete painting after festoon/swag installation to avoid damaging newly painted surfaces during the installation work, though it is not a strict physical requirement.
Festoon and swag lighting must be fully installed so that electrical inspectors can verify proper installation, grounding, and compliance with codes before the system is energized and signed off.

Tracery is a decorative stone framework typically set into window openings. The surrounding wall structure must be completed first to provide the structural support and defined openings for the tracery to be installed into.
In Gothic architecture, tracery often fills arched window openings. The arches must be completed first to define the shape and provide the load-bearing frame that the tracery will occupy.
The individual tracery elements (mullions, ribs, foils) must be precisely cut and shaped off-site or on-site before they can be assembled and installed into the window opening.
The stone tracery framework must be fully installed and set before glass panels can be fitted into the compartments (lights) created by the tracery pattern.

Fine carved details on the tracery (such as cusps, crockets, and finials) are typically refined or completed after the main tracery elements are installed in situ to ensure proper alignment and integration with the surrounding stonework.
Cresting is installed at the top or ridge of a wall/roof structure; the wall framing must be in place to provide the structural support and attachment point for the cresting component.
Cresting is typically mounted along the ridge of a roof; the roof decking must be completed to provide a stable base and proper alignment for cresting installation.
Cresting pieces are often integrated with or installed under the final roofing material at the ridge; the roofing finish must follow to ensure weatherproofing and proper overlap.

Cresting is a decorative architectural feature; exterior trim and finishing work (such as fascia, soffit, or decorative molding) is completed after cresting to ensure clean transitions and a cohesive finished appearance.

While not a strict physical requirement, it is practical to keep scaffolding in place until cresting installation is complete since cresting is a high-level exterior component; removing scaffolding early would require re-erection for access.
Structural framing and exterior sheathing must be complete to provide a stable substrate for ornamental plasterwork; plaster cannot be applied to an open or unfinished frame.

All concealed MEP (mechanical, electrical, plumbing) rough-ins within walls and ceilings must be completed before plaster is applied, as accessing these systems after plaster would require destructive demolition of the finished ornamental work.
Interior framing defines the surfaces to which ornamental plaster is applied; plaster cannot be installed until the underlying framing, lath, or substrate is fully in place.

Ornamental plasterwork (moldings, cornices, medallions) is typically applied over a base plaster or scratch coat that provides the keying surface; the base coat must be set and ready before detailed ornamentation begins.

Painting and decorative finishes are the final surface treatments that must follow ornamental plasterwork, as paint is applied over the cured plaster surface and would be damaged if applied beforehand.

Flooring is typically installed after overhead and wall plasterwork to avoid damaging finished floors with falling plaster debris, though in some sequences flooring may precede plaster if adequately protected; this is a strong preference rather than an absolute physical necessity.

predecessor: Quarrying and Transport of Stone Blocks
rationale: Raw stone blocks must be extracted and delivered to the construction site before they can be carved, shaped, and dressed into final building elements.
Stones must be carved, dressed, and finished to their precise dimensions and profiles before they can be laid in walls, arches, or other structural assemblies.
Decorative features such as carved reliefs, moldings, and ornamental details must be completed in the stone workshop before final installation at their permanent positions.
Rough carving and dressing must precede any fine surface finishing, polishing, or texturing work on the stone faces.

Although site layout and foundations are typically established first, some carving can proceed in parallel with foundation work; however, precise carving dimensions depend on finalized foundation levels and layout.
The surface must be properly prepared (cleaned, smoothed, and primed) before gilding can be applied to ensure adhesion and a smooth finish.
The underlying structure or object must be fully fabricated before decorative surface treatments like gilding can be applied.
Gilding must be completed before applying any protective sealants or clear coats to preserve the gilded surface and prevent tarnishing.

While gilding is typically completed before final installation to avoid damage, in some cases touch-ups may be performed after installation, making this a soft preference rather than a hard constraint.
Inspection of the gilded and patinated surfaces must occur after these processes are complete to evaluate the quality and appearance of the decorative finish.
The building structure must be stable and secure before delicate ornament restoration can begin; otherwise, vibrations or structural movement could damage restored ornaments or pose safety risks.

Ornament surfaces must be cleaned of dirt, grime, and biological growth before restoration work commences to ensure proper adhesion of repair materials and to accurately assess the condition of ornaments.
Safe and stable access platforms must be erected to reach elevated ornaments before restoration work can be performed at height.
A thorough photographic and measured survey of the existing ornament condition must be completed prior to restoration to establish a baseline and guide conservation decisions.
Protective coatings (such as sacrificial lime washes or consolidants) must be applied only after restoration is complete to seal and protect the restored ornament surfaces.

Decorative painting and graining requires a smooth, prepared surface to adhere properly and achieve a quality finish. Plastering and surface preparation must be completed first to provide a suitable substrate.

Primer and undercoat layers must be applied and fully dried before decorative painting and graining can commence, as they provide the necessary base for the decorative finish and ensure proper adhesion.
Decorative paint and graining effects must be completed and fully cured before a protective clear coat or varnish can be applied over them to seal and protect the decorative finish.
The decorative painting and graining work must be finished before the final inspection and any necessary touch-ups can be performed, as the decorative finish is the final aesthetic layer.

Ceilings are typically painted before walls and decorative finishes to avoid drips and overspray damaging completed decorative work, though this is a practical sequencing preference rather than a strict physical constraint.
The surface must be properly prepared (cleaned, smoothed, primed) before color rendering specifications can be applied, as the finish will not adhere or appear correctly on an unprepared surface.
The color rendering must be fully applied and cured before final inspection and any touch-up work can be performed, as inspection must evaluate the completed finish.

Protective coatings are typically applied after color rendering to seal and protect the finished surface, though some coatings may be mixed with the color render; this is a soft preference based on standard sequencing.
The underlying substrate (e.g., drywall, concrete, or plaster) must be installed before any color rendering specification can be applied to it.

Lighting fixtures and other wall-mounted elements are typically installed after color rendering is complete to avoid damaging the finished surface, though this is a soft preference in some construction sequences.
The accent wall requires a smooth, finished drywall surface as the substrate for paint or wall covering.
Primer must be applied to the wall before the final warm color paint to ensure proper adhesion and color uniformity.

successor: Installation of Wall-Mounted Fixtures (shelves, artwork, lighting)
rationale: Wall-mounted fixtures should be installed after the accent wall is complete to avoid damaging the finished paint or wall covering.
Completing the wall before flooring work prevents paint drips or debris from damaging the floor surface.
Furniture and decor should be brought in after the accent wall is finished to avoid scuffs or dust accumulation on the wall.
Interior wall finishing (plastering, priming) must be completed before color scheme design can be finalized, as the color selection depends on the final wall texture and surface conditions.
Flooring materials and colors need to be selected and installed before finalizing the interior color scheme to ensure harmonious coordination between floor and wall colors.
The type, placement, and color temperature of lighting fixtures affect how paint and finish colors appear, so lighting layout must be determined before final color selection.
The color scheme design must be completed and approved before any paint can be ordered, mixed, and applied to walls, ceilings, and trim.
While trim installation can technically proceed with temporary finishes, final color selection for trim and millwork is best completed before installation to ensure consistent staining or painting.
Structural framing must be complete to provide a stable substrate for surface preparation work.
Rough carpentry (sheathing, framing) must be finished before surfaces can be prepared for painting or staining.
Drywall must be installed, taped, and mudded before any surface preparation (sanding, priming) for paint can occur.
Masonry or concrete work must be cured and complete before applying surface treatments like sealers or paint.
Surface preparation (cleaning, sanding, filling) must precede primer application to ensure adhesion and a smooth finish.
All surface preparation steps must be completed before the final color coat is applied to achieve proper adhesion and appearance.

Tile and stone require a flat, smooth, and structurally sound subfloor. Any unevenness or debris can cause tiles to crack, lift, or be installed at improper heights. Subfloor prep (including cleaning, patching, and self-leveling compound) must be fully cured before tiling begins.

predecessor: Waterproofing and Crack Isolation Membrane Application
rationale: In wet areas (bathrooms, showers, kitchens) waterproofing membranes must be applied and cured before tile installation to prevent moisture damage. Crack isolation membranes also protect tile from substrate movement and must be in place first.

All plumbing pipes, drain lines, and electrical conduits that will be behind or beneath the tile must be roughed-in, inspected, and closed up before tiling. Tiling over unfinished rough-ins would require destructive removal of tile later.

Grout is applied into the joints between tiles after the tile adhesive (thinset) has cured. Sealing (impregnating or top-sealing tile/stone) typically follows grouting once grout has cured, to protect both tile and grout from stains and moisture.

While trim can be installed before tile in some sequences (e.g., tile butted to baseboard), the typical best-practice sequence installs tile first, then baseboard/quarter-round on top to cover expansion gaps and provide a clean finished edge. This is a soft preference because it can be reversed with careful planning.
Surfaces must be prepared (cleaned, primed, or base-coated) before color samples can be accurately evaluated and selected, as the final color appearance depends on the underlying surface condition.

The type of material (e.g., drywall, wood, metal, fabric) must be known before selecting colors, as different materials absorb and reflect paint/stain differently and may require specific product types.
Paint and coating materials cannot be ordered or purchased until color specifications have been finalized during the consultation.
The actual painting or coating application cannot begin until the colors have been selected and approved through the consultation process.
While not strictly mandatory, understanding the ambient and artificial lighting conditions significantly impacts color selection, as lighting dramatically affects how colors appear in the space.
Raw lumber must be harvested and milled into usable timber before any chair components can be created.
Wood must be dried to the proper moisture content to prevent warping, cracking, or instability in the finished chair.

predecessor: Wood Cutting and Shaping (Legs, Seat, Backrest)
rationale: Individual chair components (legs, seat panel, backrest spindles, stretchers) must be cut, shaped, and sanded before the chair can be assembled.
The assembled chair must be fully sanded smooth and have finishes (stain, paint, varnish) applied after assembly to ensure even coverage and a polished appearance.
The finished chair must be inspected for defects and then packaged for shipping or storage only after all finishing work is complete to avoid damaging the finish.
The office chair needs a stable, finished floor surface to roll on and be positioned correctly; flooring must be completed before chair assembly.
Chairs are typically needed after or alongside desk placement to ensure proper ergonomic alignment and spacing within the workstation.
Power outlets and floor boxes must be installed before heavy furniture like chairs and desks are placed to avoid obstruction and rework.
Chairs must be assembled and placed before employees can occupy their workstations.
Carpet or finished flooring must be fully installed and cured before heavy rolling chair casters are placed on it to avoid damaging the floor.
The lounge chair frame (metal or wood structure) must be fully assembled before any upholstery or cushion attachment can begin, as the frame provides the structural support.
Plastic armrests or shell components must be manufactured and cooled before they can be integrated into the lounge chair assembly.
Seat and back cushions can only be attached after the chair frame and support structure are fully assembled, as cushions are mounted onto the completed frame.
The fully assembled lounge chair must undergo quality control inspection after all assembly steps are completed to verify structural integrity, stability, and finish.
The completed lounge chair must be fully assembled and inspected before it can be packaged for shipping to prevent damage and ensure it meets customer specifications.
Raw lumber must be milled, planed, and cut to the correct dimensions before any chair components can be fabricated or assembled.
All individual parts (legs, rockers, seat, back slats, armrests) must be cut, shaped, and sanded before assembly can begin.
The chair must be fully assembled, glued, and clamped before any stain, paint, varnish, or sealant is applied to avoid finishing interior joints that need adhesive bonding.
The assembled rocking chair must be inspected for structural integrity, joint tightness, and rocking motion smoothness before it can be approved for use or shipping.
Finishing (staining, sealing, polishing) must be fully cured before the final quality inspection to ensure the finish is evaluated in its final state and not damaged during handling.
Materials must be procured before they can be used in assembly of the folding chair.
The frame components must be cut and shaped before they can be assembled into the folding chair structure.
The fabric seat and back panels must be prepared before they can be installed onto the chair frame.
The completed folding chair must be assembled before it can be inspected and load-tested for safety and durability.
The folding chair must be fully assembled and tested before it can be packaged and shipped to customers.
Chair components (seat, backrest, legs) must be fabricated before they can be assembled into a stacking chair.
After assembly/stacking, the chair must be inspected to ensure it meets safety and quality standards.
The work area and tools must be set up before the stacking assembly process can begin.
The finished stacking chair must be fully assembled before it can be packaged for storage or shipment.
Raw materials such as plastic/metal and fasteners must be on-site before chair fabrication and assembly can commence.
The bar stool frame provides the structural foundation; the stool components cannot be assembled without a completed frame.
All wooden parts must be cut to their specified dimensions before assembly can begin.
Wood components must be sanded and finished prior to assembly to ensure smooth surfaces and proper coating adhesion.
The completed bar stool must be inspected for structural integrity, stability, and finish quality after assembly.
Seat cushion and upholstery are added after the stool frame is fully assembled to access attachment points.
The walls and structural framing must be complete before installing a counter stool, as the stool requires a defined physical space and support structure.
While not strictly required, electrical wiring is typically roughed in before final finishes and furniture placement to avoid rework.
Flooring must be laid before placing counter stools, as stools sit on the finished floor and the floor must be complete for proper stool placement and stability.
Counter stools are among the final items placed before occupancy, as they are finish furnishings that complete the space for use.
Stools are typically placed before final decorative touches (e.g., table settings, cushions) since they establish the seating layout for the space.
The frame must be fully assembled to provide structure before applying upholstery material.
Upholstery must be applied to the chair frame before final finishing and detailing can occur.
Finishing work must be complete before the chair can be inspected for defects and quality standards.
The chair must pass inspection before being packaged and shipped to customers.
All materials including wood, foam, and fabric must be procured before frame assembly can begin.
The wheelchair frame must be manufactured first to provide the structural base onto which all other components are attached.
Wheels must be produced before they can be mounted onto the wheelchair frame during assembly.
The seat cushion must be fabricated prior to being installed onto the wheelchair frame.
Brake components must be pre-assembled before they can be integrated into the wheelchair during final assembly.
The wheelchair must be fully assembled before it can undergo quality and safety testing to ensure it meets specifications.
The chair's structural frame must be fully assembled to provide a stable base before any other components like the seat, backrest, or armrests can be attached.
The height-adjustable gas lift mechanism must be installed into the chair base to enable the seat height adjustment function before the chair can be fully assembled.
The five-star base with caster wheels must be assembled first to provide mobility and stability before attaching the upper chair components.
The structural frame and moving parts of the chair must be in place before upholstery, foam padding, and fabric covers are fitted over them.
Armrests are mounted onto the assembled chair frame and seat structure, so the main chair assembly must be completed first to provide the correct attachment points.
Raw materials (wood, leather, foam, etc.) must be procured and prepared before any chair assembly can begin.
The chair's structural frame (metal or wood) must be fully fabricated and ready before the saddle seat can be attached.
Leather or fabric upholstery is applied to the saddle seat only after the chair frame and seat base are fully assembled.
The completed saddle chair component must be finished before it can be integrated into the final product assembly line.
Inspection and testing of the saddle chair occurs after the chair is fully assembled to ensure structural integrity and finish quality.
The kneeling chair frame must be fully assembled before the kneeling chair can be considered complete, as the frame provides the structural foundation.
Knee pads must be securely attached to the chair frame before the kneeling chair is finished, as they are essential components for user comfort and function.
The base support (tilting mechanism or fixed base) must be installed prior to completion to ensure stability and proper ergonomic function.
Quality inspection can only begin after the kneeling chair is fully assembled to verify all components meet safety and performance standards.
The kneeling chair must be completed before it can be packaged and prepared for shipment to customers.

The throne or ceremonial chair must be placed on a stable, finished floor surface. The foundation and flooring must be complete to support the weight and provide a level base for the ceremonial chair.

Any decorative canopy, baldachin, or surrounding architectural framing for the throne must be built around it after the chair is positioned, as the chair defines the spatial center and alignment of the ceremonial setting.

successor: Ceremonial Space Furnishing and Final Decoration
rationale: The throne serves as the focal point of the ceremonial space; other furnishings, tapestries, lighting fixtures, and decorative elements are arranged in relation to the throne's position and orientation, so they must be installed after the throne is in place.
The frame must be fully assembled before casters and glides can be attached, as the casters and glides are mounted onto the bottom of the frame structure.
Casters and glides must be installed before the final inspection can be performed, as the mobility and stability features need to be checked during final testing.
The cantilever chair's frame (typically metal or bentwood) must be assembled first as it provides the structural support and the characteristic cantilever spring action for the entire chair.
Raw materials such as steel tubes or laminated wood strips must be cut, bent, and formed into the desired shape before they can be welded or joined into the frame assembly.
The seat pan and backrest (which may be upholstered, webbed, or molded) can only be mounted onto the completed cantilever frame after the frame is fully assembled and stable.

Upholstery padding, fabric or leather coverings, and any final surface finishing (painting, powder coating, polishing) must be applied after the seat and backrest are attached to avoid damaging finishes during the attachment process.
The completed cantilever chair must undergo final inspection for structural integrity, finish quality, and safety before being packaged and shipped to the customer.
The lumbar support must be inserted into the chair frame; therefore, the frame must be assembled first to provide a structure to attach the lumbar support to.
The seat cushion typically covers or is positioned over the lumbar support area; installing the cushion after the lumbar support ensures proper alignment and coverage.
The backrest cover (upholstery) is installed after the lumbar support is in place so that the support is concealed and secured within the backrest assembly.
The lumbar support mechanism (e.g., lever, cable, or pneumatic component) must be prepared or pre-assembled before the lumbar support is inserted into the chair to ensure functional readiness.
Raw materials such as wood, metal, and fabric must be procured before chair manufacturing can begin, as these are the physical inputs required for production.
The chair design and engineering specifications must be finalized and approved before manufacturing can commence to ensure correct dimensions, materials, and assembly methods.
Chairs must be fully manufactured before they can undergo quality inspection and testing to verify they meet safety and performance standards.
Manufactured chairs must be completed before they can be packaged and labeled for storage or shipment.
Chairs must be manufactured and procured before they can be delivered to the construction site and installed in their final locations.
Chairs must be placed on finished flooring to avoid damaging unfinished surfaces and to ensure stable placement. Floor finishing must be completed before chair installation.
Painting and wall finishing should be completed before bringing in chairs to avoid paint splatters, dust, or damage to the chairs and to prevent chairs from obstructing wall access.
Electrical and data outlet installation must be completed before furniture placement to ensure outlets are accessible and not blocked by chairs, and to avoid moving chairs once installed.

Chairs are typically positioned relative to desks and workstations. However, in many sequences chairs are placed first to define seating positions, then desks are positioned around them, or vice versa. In standard office fit-out, chairs are placed after or concurrently with desks, but logically chair placement precedes final desk alignment.
Chair installation and placement is a final furnishing step that must be completed before the space can be occupied and used by personnel.
The upholstery cannot be applied until the chair's structural frame is built and assembled, as the frame provides the physical substrate for attaching padding, springs, and fabric.

Upholstery must be completed before the final quality inspection and finishing touches (e.g., applying protective coatings or attaching final trim) can be performed, as the upholstered surface is part of the final product that needs to be checked.

If the chair is part of a larger furniture set or requires integration with other components (e.g., attaching to a base or frame), upholstery must be done first so the final assembly does not damage the fabric or padding.
The fabrics, foams, and padding materials must be cut and prepared to the correct dimensions before they can be applied to the chair frame during upholstery work.
Upholstery is one of the final finishing steps; the chair must be fully upholstered before it can be packaged and shipped to the customer to avoid damage to the upholstery materials.
The workstation must be physically set up (desk, chair, computer, monitor, peripherals in place) before an ergonomic assessment can evaluate their positioning and make adjustments.
Employees need to be present and assigned to their workspace before their posture and work habits can be assessed ergonomically.
Adjustable chairs, sit-stand desks, monitor arms, and other ergonomic furniture must be installed and available before an assessment can recommend or verify their proper use.
The assessment identifies specific ergonomic aids (e.g., wrist rests, footrests, specialized chairs) needed; procurement must follow the assessment's recommendations.
Adjustments to monitor height, chair settings, keyboard placement, and overall layout are based directly on the findings of the ergonomic assessment.
The diffuser panel is typically mounted into or onto the ceiling grid system. The grid must be in place to provide structural support for the panel.
The HVAC ductwork supplying air to the diffuser must be installed and terminated at the diffuser location before the diffuser panel can be connected and secured.
Any electrical wiring for lighting integrated into the diffuser or controls for airflow must be roughed in before the panel is installed.
Diffuser panels are often installed as part of the ceiling system; surrounding ceiling tiles are placed after the diffuser panel is secured in position.
Air balancing and system commissioning require all diffusers to be installed and properly connected before airflow measurements and adjustments can be performed.

A complete and accurate architectural model (including geometry, materials, and glazing properties) is required before daylight simulations can be performed, as the simulation software relies on the building model as input.
Surrounding buildings, obstructions, and site context must be modelled to accurately simulate daylight availability and overshadowing effects.
Location-specific weather files and sky models (e.g., CIE standard skies) must be obtained to provide realistic daylight conditions for the simulation.
Daylight simulation outputs (e.g., illuminance levels, daylight factors) serve as inputs for glare analysis and visual comfort evaluation.

Daylight simulation results inform thermal and lighting energy models, but some energy analysis can be run with assumptions if daylight data is not yet available, making this a soft preference rather than a hard constraint.
The simulation results must be analysed to iterate and optimise facade design, window placement, shading devices, and internal layout for improved daylight performance.
The site location must be known before solar path analysis can be performed, as the solar path varies significantly based on geographic location and latitude.
The topographic survey provides the terrain contours and site obstructions needed to model accurate solar access and shadow patterns.
Historical solar radiation, cloud cover, and weather data for the site must be gathered before meaningful solar path modeling can be conducted.
The results of the solar path analysis directly inform how the building should be oriented and massed to optimize passive solar gain and daylighting.
Solar path data is essential for designing effective shading devices (overhangs, louvers, fins) that block summer sun while allowing winter solar gain.
The structural frame (columns, beams, slabs) must be in place to provide the physical support and openings within which apertures (windows, doors) are positioned and sized.
Walls must be built first to define the locations where apertures will be cut or formed for windows, doors, and other openings.
The apertures must be precisely positioned and sized before windows and doors can be physically installed into those openings.
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing rough-in work within or adjacent to wall openings depends on knowing the exact aperture locations and dimensions.
Final finishing work around apertures (such as plastering, cladding, or trim) can only proceed after the apertures are positioned and sized correctly.
The roof structure must be framed to provide a structural opening and support for the skylight unit before installation can proceed.
Roof decking or sheathing must be installed to create the finished roof surface through which the skylight opening is cut.
Proper waterproof membrane must be laid around the rough opening before the skylight is installed to ensure a watertight seal.
The ceiling shaft and framing for the skylight well should be prepared to align with the roof opening, though some adjustments can be made after.
Flashing must be installed immediately after the skylight is placed to seal the joint between the skylight frame and the roof surface against water ingress.
Final roofing material (shingles, tiles, or metal panels) must be installed after the skylight and flashing to overlap the flashing edges and complete the waterproofing.
The skylight well and ceiling area can be drywalled and finished after the skylight is in place to ensure proper alignment and trim details.
If the skylight is motorized or solar-powered, electrical wiring connections are typically completed after the unit is physically installed.
Light shelves are often attached to or integrated with the exterior wall assembly; the exterior sheathing and cladding must be completed to provide the proper substrate and alignment for mounting.

While it is physically possible to finish interiors after light shelf installation, it is preferred to complete the light shelf first to avoid damaging finished surfaces and to allow proper integration with the window and wall assembly.

It is a soft preference to install light shelves before lighting rough-in because the light shelf affects daylight distribution, which can inform sensor placement and dimming zone layout, but electrical work can be done concurrently or before if needed.
The building must be enclosed (windows, walls, roof in place) to accurately measure natural light ingress and glare conditions.
Windows and glazing must be installed to assess actual glare from daylight through the glass panels.
Electrical rough-in for lighting should be completed before glare assessment so that integrated daylighting and electric lighting interactions can be evaluated.
Glare assessment results may dictate changes to interior surface finishes (e.g., matte vs. reflective paints, blinds, shades) to mitigate glare.

successor: Final Lighting Fixture Installation and Commissioning
rationale: Glare assessment informs the final placement, type, and dimming settings of lighting fixtures to ensure glare is controlled before commissioning.
Wall framing provides the structural support and attachment surface needed to securely mount the display shelving unit.
Drywall must be finished and painted before shelving is installed to avoid damage to finished surfaces and to ensure proper alignment of the shelving unit against the wall.
Electrical wiring for any integrated lighting or power outlets within the shelving unit must be roughed in before the unit is placed to avoid rework or access difficulties.
Products cannot be placed on the shelving unit until the unit itself is securely installed and stable.

While the final inspection can be conducted after shelving is installed, it is a soft preference to allow the inspection team to verify all display fixtures are properly secured before the area is stocked.
The Memory Wall requires a stable, level base to be constructed upon; foundations and slabs provide the necessary structural support.
The Memory Wall may need to be integrated with or attached to the building's structural frame, which must be erected first.
Any embedded wiring for lighting, interactive displays, or data connectivity within or near the Memory Wall must be roughed in before the wall assembly is completed.
Final surface finishes, protective coatings, and decorative cladding around the Memory Wall must be applied after the wall structure is in place.
Painting around the Memory Wall area is typically done after installation to avoid damage, though it could be done before with careful masking.

successor: Commissioning and Testing of Interactive Elements
rationale: Any digital or interactive components integrated into the Memory Wall must be tested and commissioned after the wall is fully constructed and connected to power and data.
The trophy and award cabinet is typically mounted on or recessed into finished interior walls; walls must be finished (painted, drywall complete) before cabinet installation.
Flooring must be installed and leveled before placing a heavy cabinet to ensure proper support, alignment, and to avoid damaging the floor.

Ceiling work (including any crown molding or overhead lighting) should be completed before cabinet installation to prevent dust and debris falling onto the finished cabinet and to allow unhindered overhead access.
Trophies, awards, and decorative items can only be placed into the cabinet after the cabinet is fully installed, secured, and ready for use.

If the cabinet includes integrated lighting, electrical connections should ideally be roughed-in before cabinet installation, but final trim-out (connecting switches, outlets) can occur after the cabinet is in place; this is a soft preference for sequencing convenience.
The media storage unit requires a stable, level foundation and a prepared base area before it can be installed or placed.
Media must be physically placed into the storage unit before it can be loaded, configured, or indexed for use.
The building or room enclosure must be complete (walls, roof, weatherproofing) to protect the media storage unit from environmental damage before installation.
Power outlets and electrical infrastructure must be in place to provide necessary power for the media storage unit's operation (e.g., drives, cooling, control systems).
The storage unit must be installed and operational before it can be integrated into the larger media system and undergo testing.
The keepsake storage box system must be installed on a stable, level foundation slab to ensure structural integrity and proper alignment.
Wall framing and sheathing provide the structural cavity and mounting surface required to install the recessed or wall-mounted keepsake storage box system.

The keepsake storage box must be fully installed and secured before drywall and paint are applied so that the box is flush with the finished wall surface and the surrounding finish can be neatly trimmed.
It is preferred that trim and molding are installed after the keepsake box to allow clean edges and a professional finish, though the box could be retrofitted if needed.

successor: Final Electrical and Low-Voltage Wiring (if lighting included)
rationale: Any integrated lighting or low-voltage components within the keepsake storage box must be wired after the box is physically installed to ensure proper connection and code compliance.

The storage systems require a level, cured concrete foundation or slab to bear the load and provide a stable mounting surface. Without adequate foundation, the storage racks or systems cannot be safely installed.
The building structure must be in place to provide vertical clearance, lateral support, and overhead connections for storage systems, especially tall racking that may be tied to the building frame.
If overhead cranes are used to assist in lifting and placing heavy storage racks or components, the crane system should be operational before storage system installation begins.
Storage systems must be fully installed, anchored, and inspected before any inventory or materials can be placed onto the racks or shelves for storage.

While floor finishing can sometimes be done in phases, typically final floor sealing or coating is completed before storage rack installation to avoid damaging the finish under rack bases. However, in some sequences it may follow.
The foundation must be fully poured and cured to provide a stable load-bearing base for wall construction; mounting walls on an incomplete foundation would cause structural instability.
The floor slab provides the substrate upon which walls are mounted; walls cannot be properly positioned and secured without a completed floor slab.
Prior to wall preparation, the structural framing must be inspected and approved to ensure the building's skeleton can safely support the wall loads.
Wiring, conduits, and pipes must be installed within or through the wall cavities after walls are mounted but before they are closed up with drywall or cladding.
Insulation is placed into wall cavities after the walls are erected and secured, as the wall structure defines the spaces to be insulated.

The building envelope (walls, roof, windows, doors) must be enclosed and weathertight before climate control systems (HVAC) are installed to protect equipment from weather damage and ensure proper sealing.
Structural framing including roof and floor decks must be in place to support ductwork, air handlers, and other HVAC components.
Electrical wiring, conduits, and power supply must be roughed in to provide power for HVAC equipment, thermostats, and control systems.
While some insulation may precede ductwork, final insulation installation around ductwork and in walls should follow HVAC rough-in to ensure proper coverage and avoid interference with duct runs.
HVAC ducts, diffusers, and registers must be installed before ceiling grids and drywall are closed in, to allow access for connections and avoid rework.
The display case requires a level, stable floor foundation to be installed upon; the slab must be poured and cured before any case installation.
Electrical conduit and wiring for display case lighting and power must be roughed in behind walls/floor before the case is placed, as access becomes impossible afterwards.
Final connection of lighting fixtures and power outlets within the display case can only be completed after the case is fully installed and secured in position.
While not physically required, it is preferred to complete painting and wall finishing after the case is installed to ensure seamless caulking and trim integration, avoiding damage to finished walls.
The physical artifacts and heirlooms can only be placed into the display case after it is fully assembled, anchored, and cleaned; placing objects earlier would risk damage or require re-handling.
Pegboard requires a finished wall surface to be mounted onto; wall framing provides the structural support needed for attaching the pegboard securely.
Pegboard should be mounted on finished drywall to provide a smooth, clean surface. Installing pegboard before drywall would result in an uneven finish and the pegboard would not be properly seated.
Walls should be painted before installing pegboard to avoid painting around the pegboard and to achieve a clean finish behind the storage system.
Once the pegboard is installed, tools can be hung and organized on it. This is a logical sequence but not a hard physical constraint, as some tools could be stored elsewhere temporarily.

The workbench should be positioned relative to the tool storage wall for efficient workflow; installing the pegboard first ensures proper alignment and spacing between the work surface and the tool wall.
